author: Alamichel, Marie-Françoise
title: Sumer is icumen in: chants et saisons dans la Grande-Bretagne médiévale
publication: La Ronde des saisons: Les saisons dans la littérature et la société anglaises au Moyen Age
abstract: The celebration of the return of the pleasant season in Sumer is icumen in (c. 1225) is a common ME motif. Poems welcoming spring are traditionally linked up with song, particularly that of birds. OE literature, by contrast, focusses on winter; accordingly, its poetry is melancholy. OE poetry, however, is more interesting than the late lyrics that do not allow for any variation. In Chaucer’s romance poetry, summer and winter are the only seasons contrasted. OE literature tends closer to reality, at least in Maxims II, where the four seasons are described (51). In the laws, the four seasons are defined for agricultural purposes (Liebermann 444-55). Byrhtferð in his Enchiridion likewise distinguishes four seasons, which he associates with the ages of man from youth to old age, as well as the four humours. The Phoenix also distinguishes between four seasons and awards the symbolic values of death (winter) and rebirth (spring). The bird’s mythical kingdom knows no winter, and breaks with the sombre landscapes typical of OE literature (52-3). The song of the phoenix is all bright and sunny, while OE literature centres around winter and the sad world of man (52-4). Bede’s account of the conversion of Edwin comes to mind, as do the wintry connotations of Grendel’s landscape. The cold of winter is typically contrasted with the society of the hall. The Wanderer calls himself wintercearig “ravagé comme l’hiver” and remarks that human structures are winter-beaten (54). The Seafarer similarly decries the hardships of winter endured at sea. To him, the cuckoo’s song, which revives the world of nature and men, is a call to return to sea. The revival of the natural world allows the approach of the end of the world; such apocalyptical connotations of spring are common in e.g. Ælfric’s homilies and the Blickling Homilies. It signals renewal but also acceleration towards the end. This theme may also be found in numerous biblical passages, such as Job 14.1-2; James 1.9-11; and, citing Isaiah, 1 Peter 1.24. Thus the cuckoo becomes a messenger of melancholy, announcer of Judgement Day (54-5). Other works, however, use the cuckoo and its season as positive elements: thus Guthlac 743-6. The prose Life of Guthlac shows the saint’s holiness by displaying his lack of interest in the songs of birds, which normally draws young men. Thus spring, birdsong, and human love are linked indirectly. ME literature focusses almost exclusively on this relationship, to the exclusion of other seasons; but there is a transitional period in which both occur. The cuckoo has the role of announcing spring, later fulfilled by the nightingale (55). The ME Mirie it is while sumer ilast echoes the OE motif of melancholy expressed by winter images. This and other poems express that spring makes up for winter’s hardships (55-6). The Owl and the Nightingale has the nightingale accuse the owl that he only sings in complaint in winter and at night, when all humankind suffers; the nightingale, by contrast, sings in spring, when both mankind and nature rejoice (56-7). Some poems bring spring, music, and religion together in praising Christ and Mary mother of God, and in describing heaven, which enjoys eternal spring (57). Mary has been honoured for her fertility, but above all the resurrection connotes the renewal of nature; it is for this reason that Easter is celebrated in spring. Most of all, however, spring connotes the renewal of human love, in turn reflected also in the Modern Devotion with its mystical love of Christ. ME poetry as a whole brings flowers, birdsong, and love together (58). The nightingale takes over from the cuckoo announcing spring in the late thirteenth century. The most seasonal details are given in the Romance Arthour and Merlin, which has the seasons follow Arthur’s fortunes (59-60). Sir Orfeo has its king lost in the snow with just its harp to comfort him; he does not play in good weather. All medieval literature suggests that music can only be good in spring, not in winter. Music, love, joy, and happiness are directly connected with the renewal of nature (60).

author: Anderson, Earl R.
title: The Seasons of the Year in Old English
abstract:
[See also Enkvist and Fischer, who wrote earlier, regarding the relative stability of seasonal terms]

Since a number of Anglo-Saxon authors make explicit the fact that the year has four seasons, it seems that this was not common knowledge but reflects Latin learning. This article proposes that although the four-seasons system was in use, it was instead the traditional Germanic bipartite division that was linguistically and culturally central in AS England; the poetic corpus sometimes reflects the one, sometimes the other tradition. This reading differs from that of Fischer, who argues that the four-season system was traditional (231-2). Formalist theory conceives of language as forming a contrast between centre and periphery on all levels: phonology, syntax, vocabulary, etc. Peripherality is defined by criteria such as assymmetry, low frequency, and limited distribution (233-4). OE and IE word sets with four seasons typically contain horizontal parallelism between words for summer and winter, but not for spring and autumn (which are thus found to be assymmetrical). Germanic began with winter and jer, both used synecdochically to mean “year,” after which sumer came about from Celtic sam “half” + paradigm suffix -er; OE missere, too, reminds of the bipartite division. The Latin four-way division then spread directly into the various languages (234-5). The uniquely Germanic winter most likely developed from IE wed-, “water,” thus referring to the wet season (235-6). Bede explains the name of October (winterfyllð) by its demarcation of the end of summer and the beginning of winter. “Winter is the most prominent of the Old English seasonal terms, by reason of its antiquity, stability, and its role as a synecdoche for ‘year’, as a metaphor for adversity, or as a combination of these” (236). The synecdochic usage of plural wintras is well-established. Klaeber considered winterstund a diminutive intensifier, antonymic to sumerlong, but Anderson believes it a synecdoche for “one season” or “one winter’s (or year’s) space” (236-7; from Bosworth-Toller). Winter has long signified adversity in Germanic tradition; OE and MnE examples are enumerated (Wdr, And, Deor, Bwf). For its uses as metaphor, synecdoche, and most stable seasonal signifier, winter has proved to possess great centrality in OE (237-8). OE gear “year” derives from Gmc *gera-, denoting the warm season or, synecdochically, a year. In Bwf, gear refers to spring, but the Runic Poem has ger refer to autumn, and other contexts have it denote “summer” in the inclusive sense: all except winter (238-9). The MED does better than Bosworth in defining sumer, but still misses the point in allocating to it only half the year rather than three quarters. OE sumer is a metaphor for pleasure (Daniel; 239-40). Lencten, from *langa- because its days grow longer, connotes creation. It had the additional meaning of “Lent, the forty-day fast before Easter,” which meaning replaced it in the late medieval period when spring came to refer to the season (240-2). Hærfest has little to legitimise it as an OE season: Tacitus claims that the Germani were unaware of both name and season, and OE occurrences mostly refer to harvest specifically. It seems most peripheral as a season name (242-3). The above discussion shows that winter and sumer were central in OE, whereas lencten and hærfest were not; additional evidence comes from the fact that they have since been replaced. Significantly, learned and popular seasonal traditions have gone side by side even into the early modern period (244). Such practice is current even today. Other semantic fields exhibiting Roman influences alongside Germanic traditions include weekdays, colours, geometric names, and gems. Interpretatio romana was a technique preferred by Anglo-Saxon scholars: Roman words were analysed through an equation with supposed Germanic parallels (Jupiter=Thor, Mercurius=Odin, etc.). Examples of this method are given, and the mentioned semantic fields are treated to show that the seasonal assymmetry is one of several (244-9). The four-season system in OE is often a learned tradition contrasted with its popular counterpart; and usually four-season treatments are found to have Latin sources (249). Ælfric refers to the four seasons but notes that such things are strange and difficult to the unlearned; the Consolation mentions them but translates its Latin source. Maxims II uses the four seasons for superlatives, giving a popular etymology for lencten by reference to lengest. The Menologium collapses months, the liturgical calendar, and seasons for its temporal reference, as does Elene. The system of The Menologium has obvious Latin sources [PS: and so does Elene] (250-1). The twelve months are used mostly for liturgical reference, and are thus learned (251-2). AS calendars show Mediterranian influence in depicting men sowing the field in January (252-3). The Menologium makes clear that chronology is a matter for the learned; it draws a distinction between generally-known days and seasons and learned knowledge (253-4). The Phoenix also shows Latin influence on OE chronology. An innovation in this OE translation (242b-59a) compares the regeneration of the phoenix to the annual cycle of the seasons, including the image of the seed for regeneration, a commonplace metaphor for man’s regeneration on judgement day (254-5). Bwf has been interpreted as a metaphor for the four seasons, to which Enkvist replied that it knows no regular seasons at all, “only violent changes in nature.” Anderson proposes that Bwf reflects the bipartite system (255-6). The Finnsburh episode especially shows a dependence on this system: as in the Icelandic sagas and the OE elegies, winter represents a time of anxiety when man is caught up between conflicting loyalties (256). Vickrey even proposes that the seasons in this episode do not describe the actual time passed but “the full course of Hengest’s revenge.” Anderson believes that both are true; Klaeber is cited to consider the passing of time in the episode “a trivial statement of matter-of-course fact” (256-7). Winter imagery in Grendel’s mere has also been read as metaphor; its hrinde bearwas are also found in the Visio Pauli and the hell described in Blickling Homily 17 (257-8). Anderson’s reply: “[t]he role of winter as symbolic of adversity is significant, but there is no reason to deny these [Bwf] passages their literal meaning.” The symbolic role appears in Sfr where, as in the OE and ON Runic Poems, seasons are also contrasted by the comparison of hail to grain (258-61). Some attention is paid to the interpretation of Sfr 49b woruld onetteð and to the reading that the poem moves through four seasons. The cuckoo mentioned in the poem, however, resides in England for five months, so that a bipartite division of the year seems more applicable (259-61). The same long concept of summer is expressed in the thirteenth-century Sumer is icumen in and similar lyrics (261-2). It is concluded that the Germanic two-season system and the Latin four-season system coexisted in the OE period, the latter of which was introduced by interpretatio romana and the former of which is reflected only in Bwf and Sfr (262-3).

[discussion:] What evidence does Anderson have that OE/Germanic sumer referred to three-quarters of the year rather than half? Surely he cannot refute the ON computistical and ritual evidence to the contrary, or the term missere? And Anderson’s adoption of Strutyinski’s four-day week seems somewhat uncritical (and unnecessary).

author: Anderson, Earl R.
title: The Seasons of the Year
abstract:
[This chapter is essentially a repetition of the article in ASE. I will note only such points as seem of particular interest.]

“Winter is the most prominent of the Old English seasonal terms, by reason of its antiquity, lexical stability, and its role as a synecdoche for ‘year,’ as a metaphor for adversity, or as a combination of these” (226). Winter as a metaphor for adversity is “very ancient” in Germanic tradition. Deor’s refrain refers to the cycle of the seasons as well as specific changes. Wdr combines synecdoche and metaphor in 64-5a: “[f]orðon ne mæg wearþan wis wer, ær he age / wintra dæl in woruldrice” (227). OE sumer symbolises “plaisance,” but this symbolic opposition of winter and summer is cultural, not universal: Chinese tradition opposes spring and autumn in this respect (230). Liturgy connects spring to the time of Creation. Half of Bosworth’s citations of lencten refer to Lent. This suggests peripherality of lencten (231-2). An extended Hebrew analogue to OE season terms is brought in (239-46). The lencten hrimigost maxim is treated and explained by reference to Ælfric, who points out that the earth needs time to warm up after winter (248). OE month names disappeared about Ælfric’s day (250).

author: Andersson, Theodore M.
title: The Discovery of Darkness in Northern Literature
publication: Old English Studies in Honour of John C. Pope
eds: Robert B. Burlin and Edward B. Irving
abstract:
Argues that Germanic literature, but North Germanic literature in particular, uses nighttime as a context for military action, mystery, horror, and visual deception whereas classical and non-Germanic medieval literature employs it only as a time of inactivity and a structural divider. Explains this differentiation by the suggestion that Germanic peoples were always accustomed to nighttime combat, something the Romans feared.

Vernacular romance uses nighttime only as a time for lovers (2). Various sagas and a few eddic poems are cited for their interest in nighttime action (4-7). The prominence of darkness in the Beowulf account of Grendel is admitted (7); German participation in this motif is downplayed (8-9; no mention of the Old Saxon Genesis). A range of classical sources is cited to demonstrate that the central classical peoples thought nighttime combat was a source of confusion and a bad idea, although some of their enemies were known to attack at night (9-11).

author: Árni Björnsson
title: Góa
abstract:
Gói/Góa (the latter is a late seventeenth-century spelling) began on a Sunday in the course of our February (18-24 Gregorian, 8-24 late Julian). The name occurs in many early mss, and, together with Gormánuðr and Þorri, is one of the few months that is never called anything else (5). Góimánuðr occurs only in the Hauksbók redaction of Landnámabók, where it is said to have been named after Gó, daughter of Þorri (5-7). The name gói is found across the Nordic languages, including Sami, and is even more widespread than Þorri. While the meaning and origin of the word are uncertain, it is most commonly thought to derive from a word for snow. This reading also accords with the explanation in the episodes on the settlement of Norway [Hversu Noregr byggðisk and Fundinn Noregr/Orkneyinga saga], which place Gói in a genealogy full of snow, winter, and element names. Clearly, then, Þorri and Gói were originally lunar month-names that were later made into saga characters or month-spirits (7). The compiler of the Landnámabók redaction in Hauksbók was familiar with these stories, which are slightly different one from another (7-8).

It has often been suggested that the medieval market and spring assembly at Uppsala may have been a successor or parallel to the góiblót. This event was called distingen, possibly from dísaþing. The connection with the sacrificial feast is made in Óláfs saga helga ch. 77, which speaks of a “höfuðblót. . . að gói.” Dísablót is mentioned in a number of sagas (8). Although no clear descriptions or exact dates of the event exist, it is clear that it takes place near the vetrnætr. This time of year was natural for feasting, since it took place shortly after the annual slaughter; but the deity honoured was subject to regional variation. There is no evidence to support the notion that the same dísir were worshipped across Scandinavia, and the word denoted a variety of female spirits (8-9). However, the Uppland-Swedes may well have worshipped the dísir at a different time than the Norwegians, i.e. after midwinter. There is thus little reason to assume a chief dís named Gói, even if the Swedes had their main sacrifice in a month of this name.

The existence of the word góiblót and its explanation in the texts on the settlement of Norway suggests that a memory or oral tradition regarding a feast at this time existed in early Iceland. It is not improbable that in pre-Christian Iceland, and perhaps thereafter, something was set up to mark the completion of each lunar cycle in the winter months. A 1728 letter by síra Jón Halldórsson to Árni Magnússon is the only proof that a welcoming of the spirit Gói existed, in much the same way as was done for Þorri. Wives were accustomed to go out and welcome Þorri in like an honourable guest, asking her to be mild rather than harmful; husbands then did much the same thing for Gói (9). If such a custom existed about 1700, it was probably much older. An 1864 letter by Jón Árnason tells the opposite story: the women received Gói, the men Þorri. Young men were to welcome home Einmánuðr, and girls harpa. Jón Árnason believed that these rituals were the successors of þorrablót, góiblót, einmánuðarblót, and sumarmálablót. [#Icelandic_unclear:]Early twentieth-century Icelanders no longer honoured these traditions (10). In the western quarter, in most cases by far, it was the husbands’ task to welcome Gói. In the north and east, it was very common for men to serve their wives in one way or another on the same day (10-11). Welcoming Gói thus seems to have been the men’s task. In the southern quarter, however, it was the women’s, and here the welcoming song was little known. Similarly, Þorri was welcomed by women in Vesturland but by men in Suðurland. This may be explained by the fact that at the start of Gói, the winter fishing-season had begun in the south and most men were out at sea. #[?]This may also explain why góiblót was not as strong a tradition as þorrablót. But it should also be borne in mind that the beginning of Þorri was more significant in that it represented the mid-point of winter. Moreover, Gói began on a Sunday, so that [#? smávegis tilbreytni í mat skar sig síður úr]. However, several respondents remembered more food and snacks on this day than on a regular Sunday (11). After the Conversion, the first day of Gói usually fell in Lent, problematising any feasting and significant changes in diet. Weddings were not allowed at this time. In the ninteteenth-century revival, the coming of Þorri will thus have received greater attention than that of Góa (12). The term góublót was little used at this time, although it is attested; rather was the term konudagur popular, and bóndadagur as its counterpart. These terms were probably around by the mid-nineteenth century, but not in writing until 1911 (13). Some early modern poets refer to Góa as a person. One poet makes her as old as the settlement of Iceland (16). Other poets date her father Þorri’s birth to the first century CE, and one poet in 1812 makes Góa 1700 years old (16-18). Other poems are cited that mention a góuprís or associate Góa with volcanic activity (18-19).

While most sources understand Gói as a daughter of Þorri, some early nineteenth-century poems speak of them as a couple (20-2), and one speaks of them as siblings (22).

Weather rhymes call Þorri dry, Góa stormy (sometimes warm/thawy), and einmánuður wet, and proverbs say that in mid-Góa the ice had gone so soft that horses no longer needed to be shod for the snow; that there is little use (?evidence) for Góa-ice; and that the heating-stone had entered into the earth in mid-Góa (22-3). It was considered good luck (esp. for the rest of the month’s weather) if the first day of Góa was harsh, but bad luck if it was dry and mild (23); but some turn it around. One tradition has two old women quarrel on the beach all night whether the month’s start was a good one (23-4). If all Góa is good, then Harpa will be cold (24). Such suspicions with regard to good Góa led to the word góugróður for things fleeting and rootless, first found in print in the early twentieth century. Yet some plants and berries found in this month were deemed fit for eating (25). Góustraumurinn referred to the peak river-flow about this time of year. In some regions, this flood brought the year’s greatest fish-catch (25-6). In other parts, the flood was the time for farmers to check their livestock carefully; any imperfections led to slaughter of the sheep in question, to ensure a healthy livestock during the birthgiving-period. Each successive flood was thought to worsen disease, but especially the Góustraumurinn. Góuvæll is the sound foxes make in the last months of winter to attract mates. The word could be used figuratively to refer to complaints and whining. The slushy weather typical of this time of year led to special footwear for children called góuvefjur (26). Weather grumbling in verse was common only in the western half of the country (26-7). Góa was thought capricious and irritable at times (27).

In one tradition, Góa is mild of character and may be won by kindness, while Þorri cannot; this reflects their respective gender. When the month was over, however, she was assessed negatively in addressing Einmánuður (27-8). Góa is variously thought of as tall and fat or tall and pretty, goodly or a hag. One folk tradition has an evil woman try to starve her mother-in-law in a shed where she is without food in the New Year; each of the late winter months then feeds her in turn. Þorri gives her a cow, Góa a bigger shed[?] (28-9).

Another tradition consisted in giving Góa a red string of wool, which was hung in a conspicuous place throughout the month in order to humour Góa. If the string moved in a certain direction, that predicted the month’s main wind direction (29-30).

Góuþræll referred to the worst day of the month (esp. in Suðurland); fishermen preferred not to row out on this day. It was particularly ominous if it coincided with the Annunciation (25 March) (31-2). German summary (32-3).

author: Árni Björnsson
title: Icelandic Feasts and Holidays
abstract:
Briefly discusses medieval calendar systems and Icelandic almanac traditions (7-9). The weather at the Conversion of St Paul (25 January) was thought to be indicative of that of weeks to follow (13; cf. ME lyric 110).

The welcoming of Þorri is described, and the complications on whether husband or wife was to receive him; on this, see “Góa” (14-15).The term Þorrablót occurs in only one medieval text, [Fundinn Noregr] in Flateyarbók. That text suggests that Þorri was a winter deity, but this narrative is clearly an allegory and the original meaning of Þorrablót must have been forgotten by the time it was composed (15). Nevertheless, Þorri seems to have been privately worshipped until present times (14-15). A revival began in the 1870s (15-16).

“Solar Coffee” celebrates the return of the sun over the mountaintops in late winter (17). Candlemas received its connotations of light after Pope Sergius I in 690 ordered all the year’s candles to be consecrated on 6 January, and its procession came to involve candles. Folklore in Iceland has it that sun on Candlemas heralds a spell of snowy weather. Winter fishing season in the south began the day after Candlemas (18).

Regarding Lent, it is pointed out that the slaughtering of pregnant livestock is uneconomical, hence the institution of springtime fasts among pastoral people such as the Hebrews. Easter was originally the feast of the newborn lambs and hence the return of meat on the menu (19). Fasting in Iceland is discussed (19-21). Shrove Tuesday was the only carnivalesque feast in Iceland, associated with eating, revels, and sexual excess (22-3). The weather on Ash Wednesday is considered prophetic for the time to follow (24).

The Ember Days may have been preperatory fasts before Easter, Whitsun, and Christmas. In Iceland, the poor benefitted from these fasts by legal obligations on the part of the independent (36). Gói/Góa is discussed along the same lines as in the article by that name (27-9). Einmánuður has traditions similar to those of Þorri and Gói/Góa. In Norway and Iceland, it was used to discuss fence-making and the like (30-1).

Summer begins with Harpa, whose name is no longer transparent and appears from the seventeenth century onwards; Snorri calls it gaukmánuðr and sáðtíð. Summer begins on a Thursday April 19-25 (o.s. 9-15) (39). Migratory birds and their behaviour have been used as omens forecasting the season’s weather (39-40). On the first day of summer, much work was halted (40-1). Much like the first days of the previous three months, this day was dedicated to either young men or young women. By the mid-eighteenth century, sumardagurinn fyrsti was “in most places considered second only to Christmas and New Year in terms of celebration,” even though stocks would have largely run out at this time of year (41). Summer presents “seem to antedate even Christmas presents as a custom among the common people” and are documented from 1545 onwards (42).

The Anglo-Saxon St Walpurgis became revered in Germany as a protector against sorcery and shapeshifting; hence fires were lit in her name on hilltops and mounds. Iceland does not have a Walpurgis tradition, though mainland Scandinavia does have tales concerning Walpurgis Night. Though spring festivals were held at various times in different parts of Europe, May was widely held to be the first month of summer: thus even the Roman goddess Maya was associated with youth and flowers. Frankish and Carolingian kings held their annual review of the troops on 1 March and later 1 May, a custom that left traces in popular culture outliving the actual military practice (44-5).

10 May was “Last Feed Day,” when tenant farmers returned livestock to its owners.

The winter fishing season in southern Iceland ended 11 May, both in Julian and Gregorian dating (46-7).

“Midsummernight is one of the four nights of the year that are thought to be the most portentous and in which there is most widespread belief; the others are Christmas Eve, New Year’s Eve, and Twelfth Night, all of which are in the darkest winter.” Continental belief in peak activity of evil spirits in this night led to bonfires, but not in Iceland, where the brightness of the night would prevent trolls from coming out (52). Stones, herbs, and dew found in this night were thought to be imbued with medical and magical properties (52-3).

Þorláksmessa á sumri commemorates the translation of Þorlákr’s remains; it was a great feast especially before the Reformation. Its origins and development are described at length (55-8).

On Decollation Day (29 August), weather has been thought to change (59-60).

Gifts and feasting were common after all the season’s hay had been collected, often mid- to late September (60-1).

Sheep roundup is in mid-September, often the Thursday or Friday in the 21st week of summer (63).

Michaelmas has been widely associated with harvest feasts and the like, perhaps also because of its proximity to the autumnal equinox. In Iceland, the slaughtering season began on Michaelmas; and the post-haymaking bonus was often given on this day. The autumn fishing season began on Michaelmas in southern Iceland (64).

6 October was “Feed Day,” when tenant farmers received the livestock they were to feed over the winter (64).

Gormánuðr “chyme month, gore month” appears related to the slaughtering season. Árni claims it had no other name [PS: but vetur is surely attested, see Hastrup]. The banquet at the start of winter is, with jól, the most-mentioned seasonal feast. This is because livestock was slaughtered at this time of year, and not all of it could be preserved. This point of the year also followed on the grain harvest and/or grain imports (65). The contemporary sagas do not mention the winter nights. Any pagan sacrifices at this time were not intended to welcome winter, who was unwelcome, but rather to pacify him. In Christian times, alterations to the feast were desirable, but Michaelmas preceded the slaughtering season. Instead, All Saints’ Day was used. The Milky Way, sheeps’ intestines, and spleens of cattle or horses were used for winter weather auguries (65-7).

All Saints’ Day is often mentioned in Icelandic works, suggesting great liturgical and popular importance. It was one of three holidays for the ferryman at Kaldadarnes. A feast is also mentioned at this time of year in modern times, and by most accounts it was held on All Saints’ Day (67-8).

Ýlir is related to Gothic jiuleis and English Yule. The variant forms of the next month, mörgsugr etc. are listed (69).

Advent begins the ecclesiastical year. The time between slaughter and Christmas was immensely busy, particularly in woolwork: products had to be made that could be traded for Christmas groceries, and debts had to be settled before the end of the year (70-1).

44 Icelandic churches were dedicated to St Nicholas, and Sturlunga saga says a banquet was dedicated to him annually. Two sagas, a poem, and fragments of another survive. (72-3).

The Yuletide Lads are mentioned from the seventeenth century onwards (73-4).

St Lucy (13 December) was little venerated in the north before the Reformation, but what cult there was was in Iceland. After the Reformation, she became an evil spirit, in part because her name resembles that of Lucifer (75).

Þórláksmessa in winter was initially of limited importance because it was overshadowed by Christmas. In modern times, it has been Þórláksmessa in summer that has been all but forgotten while the winter feast has gained importance. Christmas preparation peaked around this time (75-6).

Cultures around the world have celebrated around Christmas time. This timing is probably linked to the solstice or the shortness of the day. Rome knew the Saturnalia, celebrated about mid-december, and the Compitaliae, in early January. The co-occurrence of these feasts suggests that feasts at this time of year served both to encourage the lengthening of the days and to celebrate that process. New Year took over both functions after it came to be celebrated on 1 January in 153 BC (76-7). The inversion of class relations was characteristic of these feasts (77-8). The word jól has not been explained to satisfaction, but scholars tend to explain it as “sacrifice.” Its original time is often thought to be either mid-January or mid-December by Gregorian reckoning; mentioned most often are 13 January and 13 December, which however is dating events by a dating system not then in use (78-9). The month name Ýlir suggests the earlier date, while Snorri asserts that miðr vetr was the time of the celebration, which in his time meant 12-13 January. Árni Björnsson takes the stance that there were two feasts, like in Rome, at a lunar event prior to the solstice in order to help the sun renew its cycle and again after the solstice to celebrate that renewal [there seems to be little further evidence for this stance; it was probably made up just to suit Árni’s fancy]. For the December feast it is pointed out that evil spirits were considered to be active at that time of year, and Snorri’s tale of the swallowing of the sun is brought in (79). It is speculated that jól may originally have been celebrated in the family until chieftains began to organise great feasts to which their subjects contributed provisions [cf. Hutton]; Snorri says each should contribute ale or else money (79-80). Árni suggests jól may have had fertility rites associated with it: in any case a very old reference is to “the game of Freyr.” Solid food is never mentioned (80).

The speculation that Jesus was born in winter first followed on the supposition that a population enrolment would have taken place at the start of the year; 6 January was thus widely celebrated. 25 December is first found in 354 and was officially adopted by the Church about 440. 25 December was at that time the exact day of the solstice, but also the birthday of the invincible sun (81). When the interests of Church and empire began to converge, the Church adopted a popular existing feast and gave it Christian meaning (82-3).

Sagas of Icelanders suggest that pre-Christian jól involved specially-brewed ale and lavish feasts. Eyrbyggja saga and Fóstbræðra saga [Greenlandic part] are cited for descriptions (83-5).

Grágás forbids all but the most basic labours during Christmas: feeding livestock, milking, brewing, slaughtering, and cleaning the stables, emphasising the feast’s association with food and drink (86). Sturlunga saga and the bishops’ sagas makes frequent reference to ale and banquets, gift-giving, and entertaining at Christmas (88-9). Christmas presents were exchanged only between chieftains, though a type of bonus in the form of e.g. socks did exist (94).

In the Roman area, New Year’s Day was 1 January from 153 BC to Charlemagne’s time, when it was moved to 25 March [previous to 153 BC it had been 1 March]; but in some places, 25 December was celebrated. In England, 25 December was New Year’s Day until the twelfth century, when it moved to 25 March (97). In Iceland, 25 December was the rule until the sixteenth century (97-8). Because of such shifts, the original associations of folklore traditions are unclear; supernatural events such as the elf ride are in modern times connected with New Year’s Eve, but sometimes Christmas Eve (98). “Sitting out” to learn about the future is also done during New Year’s Eve (98-9). Elves were also welcomed/allowed into the home on either Christmas Eve or New Year’s Eve (99). The “pantry drift” was the arrival of (sweet, edible) hoarfrost into the pantry when left open during New Year’s Eve (99-100). New Year’s bonfires are first documented in 1791. Elsewhere, bonfires are customary at different times of year, but New Year’s bonfires are largely exclusive to Iceland (100).

author: Árni Björnsson
title: Þorrablót
abstract: The first thirty or so pages of this work tell little that is not also in “Góa,” recapitulating medieval evidence but focussing especially on traditions recorded from the seventeenth to the nineteenth centuries. It then turns to the revival in even more recent times. The second half of the book consists of music scores and texts of Þorri celebrations.

author: Axford, Yarrow, et al.
title: Climate of the Little Ice Age and the Past 2000 Years in Northeast Iceland Inferred from Chironomids and Other Lake Sediment Proxies
abstract: A particularly relevant study for Icelandic climate variation in the Middle Ages. Finds a low for the LIA in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries; discusses the difficulties of establishing a starting-point for LIA; and discusses the relative insignificance of the MWP, suggesting we might not have awarded it such significance had not Iceland been settled in this period (20).

author: Baker, Peter S., and Michael Lapidge
title: Byrhtferth’s ‘Enchiridion’
abstract:
For his arithmology, Byrhtferth could use not only the Church Fathers but also the long Pythagorean tradition (lxi-lxxiv). Nevertheless, he took a thoroughly independent approach to sources, using Augustine, Gregory, Bede, and Haymo of Auxerre instead of Eucherius, Isidore, Alcuin, Hrabanus Maurus, and the anonymous Liber de numeris available in his day (lxxiv-lxxv). As sources for the Enchiridion are listed the Benedictine offices (lxxv-lxxix); pedagogical works such as Bede’s De arte metrica and De schematibus et tropis; Isidore’s Etymologiae; the Disticha Catonis; Caelius Sedulius’s Carmen paschale, etc (lxxix-lxxxiii). He closely followed Aldhelm (lxxxiii-lxxxiv), and used Isidore’s as well as Bede’s De natura rerum. The quadrivium arrived late in England, but Byrhtferth’s tutor Abbo of Fleury will certainly have brought the most important texts with him. Of this group, Boethius’s Consolatio is quoted in the Enchiridion, and so is Macrobius’s commentary on the Somnium Scipionis (lxxxiv-lxxxvi). His computistical sources were Bede, Hrabanus Maurus, Helperic, Ælfric, and a number of smaller sources (lxxxvi-xcii). Of the four Church Fathers, Ambrose is conspicuously absent; of the later Church Fathers, Isidore and Bede are the most obvious influences on the Enchiridion (xcii-xciii). Haymo’s Homiliae de tempore are an obvious Carolingian source (xciv).

Byhrthferth associates seasons, cardinal directions, ages of man, elements, qualities, and humours (10-14). He uses solar/cosmic imagery to describe his mental state (16). He emphasises the primacy of the sun to an almost religious degree (18). Lists the Anglo-Saxon month-names (24) and weekdays (28). Months and seasons are now discussed in great detail, remarking on important feast days, duration of day and night, zodiac sign, number of days, etc. (56-85). The bisextile day [29 Feb] and the saltus lunae receive particular attention (58-69). In his treatment of the seasons, Christian feasts are discussed mostly in January and March (which is also the Creation month), with Pentecost often in June and the fast in December; although the Ember Days occur four times, he only mentions them for December. Other months are dedicated more exclusively to month and day length, zodiac signs, etc (56-79). Solar events are four, like the seasons, ages of man, elements, and letters in ADAM and DEUS (75).The four seasons are discussed; lengtentima begins 7 February; sumor on 9 May; and hærfest on 7 August. The qualities of the months are listed in terms of heat and humidity, and they are associated with the four elements and the classical virtues. The three Christian virtues are also brought into the diagrams (82-7). There is a section on poetry (88-93) and the embolisms (95-103). The division of year and day into points, minutes, etc. is discussed (104-13), as are day and night (112-17) and the planets (116-21). Comets are understood as bad omens (120). The dating of Easter (122-61). Figures of speech (162-9), lunar letters (168-75), notae, weights, alphabets and numerals (174-95). Book four deals with arithmology. Three ages of the world are identified (but cf. six ages, 232-41), the number four referring only to the evangelists, seasons, the names DEUS and ADAM, solar events, winds, elements, cardinal directions/regions of the world (climata cosmi, i.e. partes mundi), and ages of man; the interrelations of these things are set out (198-203). All numbers receive a similar reverential treatment and parallellisation, except for eleven and to some extent thirteen (196-231). The fourth book ends with a discussion of the six ages of the world (cf. three, above) following Bede, who in turn followed Augustine; so also Ælfric and the Napier 62 homilist (see commentary). The work concludes with a lengthy exhortation to live a godly life.

author: Bakhtin, M.M
title: Forms of Time and of the Chronotope in the Novel: Notes Towards a Historical Poetics
abstract: Central to Bakhtin’s analysis of the novel here is that time and space are inseperably interwoven—they form chronotopes [PS: I suppose a skeptic might call them settings] as organising principles of narrative literature (84). The chronotope chosen is so specific to a genre that it may be said to define it, time being the primary organising principle of the literary chronotope; later literary forms fail to describe their contemporary historical time-space, instead depicting chronotopes that have long become obsolete in history (84–5). Bakhtin sets out to demonstrate chronotopicity by tracing chronotopes through the genres of Greek novel, which were so perfectly formed that modern novels have added no new patterns. He begins with Greek romance (86–110). In this genre, time has no duration that can be measured; begin-state and end-state are natural phases in a process, but all the adventure that happens in between is disconnected from time, it is a hiatus (esp. 90). Because Greek romance centres around spatial shifts (abductions, escapes, pursuit), it requires a large geographical matrix; but this matrix is entirely abstract, containing no unnecessary detail (99–100). Since chance plays a crucial narrative role in this chronotope, the narrative detail of the world described has to be kept to a minimum, since realism would restrict the freedom of chance events (100). Even the hero’s homeland is foreign: it does not correspond to the reader’s world, and so to the reader it does not strike a contrast with the foreignness of lands foreign to the hero (101). Society is not described in an interconnected way: objects and events are unconnected (102). Other genres, such as Alexandrine poetry, use a [geographically] very small but concrete chronotope (103). In Greek romance, however, since chance directs events, characters cannot act, change, or develop; things can only happen to them, and they emerge unchanged. The events that befall him, indeed, are a test of the hero’s selfhood, which is confirmed by his retaining his identity and picking up his life where he left off following the adventure (105–6). A subtype of this is the novel of ordeal (106–8). Characters in Greek romance are always individuals—they can act only for themselves; they are not public or political characters (108). Nevertheless, a character often acts superficially as though a public person, e.g. by way of monologues, and legal processes often play key roles in the affirmation of their identities—but these events are inconsistent with their internal identities; society receives meaning in connection with the individual, not vice versa (108–10). "The chronotope of the Greek romance is the most abstract of all novelistic chronotopes", and nothing in its world is built, altered, or destroyed (110). Two Greek novels belong to the adventure novel of everyday life (111–29); these mix adventure-time with everyday time (111). The adventures in these novels are no hiatus from real time; instead, they represent a significant development in the protagonist’s life (111). Metamorphosis is a mythological wrapper for development, but one of punctuated equilibrium, as between eras, seasons, and economic processes (113). Only in the later, Roman, tradition did the word metamorphosis come to connote abrupt magical change (114). In Apuleian adventure, metamorphosis portrays the whole of a character’s life through moments of crisis; we are shown how he became his later self. “There is no evolution” but “crisis and rebirth” (115). Early Christian “crisis hagiographies” similarly depict two identities, that of sinner and that of saint (115–16). But the adventure novel still takes place in “adventure time”, the time separating initial identity from altered identity; chance remains a key player (116). Nevertheless, the protagonist possesses primary initiative, in which guilt, moral weakness, and error rather than creative initiative are the driving forces; he himself has to undertake the solution. The hero emerges “purified and reborn” (116–17). The narrative sequence is guilt > punishment > redemption > blessedness (118). As in romance, he is private and isolated (119). The chronotope of the adventure novel is more concrete and detailed along the protagonist’s spatial “path of life”, although he himself and key turning points in his life remain untouched by everyday life (120–1). There is a tension in the novel between public life and the private individual, a contradiction that was not solved in ancient times; modern novels often employ figurants to depict private life in the background of the action, as ways of eavesdropping on the lives of others (122–7). Everyday time in the adventure novel was not cyclical, although an agricultural cyclical time existed that was bound up with nature and myth. (127–8). Everyday time does not run parallel with the sequence from guilt to blessedness, although there are points of perpendicular intersection (128). Ancient biography and autobiography is type 3 (130–46), and it may be divided into Platonic and rhetorical (130–1). In the latter type, the individual’s life is strongly public (132–3). To Greeks, everything about life could be seen and heard; inner existence not externalised only began with Hellenistic literature, and even among the Romans this process of internalisation was not completed (133–5). Bakhtin spends several pages describing the Roman biography (136–41). In Plutarch, biographical time is specific and revealing of personal character, but not the key to a character’s change. Historical reality [=time] does not cause change, it merely manifests it; character is predetermined (141). Specific features of character, however, may manifest themselves at different times; this is the disclosing of character, not its formation (141–2). The analytic biography divides a life into thematic rubrics and breaks time up accordingly (142). Three modifications of the biography to accommodate internal private life are discussed (143–6). [PS: Space is not discussed for this third category of novel at all.] Attitudes towards time present/past/future in the ancient novel are discussed (146–51). The concept of historical inversion is introduced, which places ideals like perfection and purpose in the past, i.e. a golden age (147). If such ideals exist in the present, they exist in a different spatial context, often out of reach (147–8). Reality becomes divided along a vertical axis of upper and lower [PS: heaven and hell] rather than a temporal axis of present and future. The future is thus “emptied out”. A different form of emptying out the future is eschatology, in which a future beyond a certain point is denied (148–9). Even in these genres, an actual future exists; in narrative description, this is anticipated in the present in tangible dimensions: an individual’s promise may be measured today in his physique and strength (149–50). In folklore, man’s life takes place in a realistic here-and-now, thus being a realistic fantastic; such folkloric realism inspired all written narrative, including the novel (150–1). The chivalric romance (151–5) largely follows Greek romance in its use of adventure-time and in its chronotope, but sometimes (e.g. in Parzival) it comes closer to the Greek adventure novel. Like in Greek romance, the testing of the protagonist fulfils a central organising role (151). New in chivalric romance is that the unexpected chance violation of the laws of the real world is no longer limited to selected important moments but has become the new normal. The protagonist’s very identity thus depends on the miraculous being normal and expected (151–2). Also new is the portrayal of chance, no longer abstract but depicted in fairies, wizards, and enchanted spaces; and misfortunes no longer occur, only adventures interesting to the protagonist as well as the reader (152–3). The heroic deed distinguishes chivalric from Greek romance: this is a deed through which the hero glorifies himself or those in whose name they are carried out (153). Heroes are here more individualised: Greek heroes resemble each other, and no cycles can be written around a single character; in chivalric romance, no two heroes resemble each other, and the cycle, not the novel, is the narrative unit (153). Finally, in chivalric romance the hero and his world are of the same miraculous, heroic kind (153–4). All these things which set off chivalric romance from Greek romance bring it closer to epic; this genre is midway between epic and novel (154). While in Greek romance adventure-time was consistent within itself (one day is like the next), in chivalric romance time is miraculous within itself; “it becomes possible to bewitch time itself” (154–5). Space is correspondingly relative in this genre: its usual relations may be violated, usually not in a folkloric “free” relation between man and space but in subjective distortion. This chronotope disintegrated in later romance and never returned in the same fullness (155). The late medieval vision has a high degree of symbolism of time and space; it may be said that time makes no appearance in the vision at all; to the extent that it does, it is to be read allegorically or symbolically. These works demonstrate a “feeling for the end of an epoch” through attention for its contradictions (155–6). Langland and Dante are good demonstrations of how time does not run in these visions; simultaneity is their only time, the world is exclusively vertical in extent (156–7). The characters encountered in these visions are temporal and historical, but they are brought into a vertical framework; the same can be said for the authors’ historical and political perceptions, which are markedly temporal yet now contained in an extratemporal space (157–8). Rogue, clown, and fool are discussed (158–67). Rabelais is discussed, with particular attention to his use of space, bodies, defecation, sexuality, death, and laughter (167–206). Since the medieval world-view was disintegrating, Rabelais needed to place the passing of time on a new material footing, and to do this he created a new chronotope whose fundaments were available in folklore (205–6, and in detail 206–24). In a pre-class, agricultural society, a differential understanding of time had first formed in which social everyday time was taken apart and reconstituted in language. This time was collective (i.e. measured by the events of collective life); all that exists in this time exists just for the collective. The inner time of an individual had not yet been formed; labour and consumption were both collective (206–7). Labour was the measure of time. Productive growth is the issue of time: with time, the world gives fruit rather than diminish or decay; all perishing is perceived as a sowing leading to more growth. Moreover, growth is not just quantitative but also qualitative, as all things lead to a flowering; all things tend towards the future, both all labour-processes and human generation. Consumption, in itself focussed on stasis and the present, was not perceived in isolation from productive labour; past, present, and future were not yet precisely distinguished (207). This mode of time is “profoundly spatial and concrete”: human and natural events are measured in the same time, and the same imagery of conception, growth, ripening and harvest applies to all things (208). Only later did time become individualised and split up into different parallel plots (that of history and that of personal life), remaining unified only in the abstract (208–9). In folkloric time, no setting can be static; earth, sea, and stars exist not as objects of individual perception and not as background but as actors in the collective process of labour. In the literary stages of plot construction, material for narrative events and settings becomes scarcer, with landscape and sociopolitical matrix reaching an irrelevance to the plot inasmuch as their unchanging nature needs not be perpetual, as long as it exists within the current narrative movement (209). All these aspects of folkloric time are positive, but a negative aspect is its cyclicity, as it “limits the force and ideological productivity” of time and takes away the forward impulse of folklore, so that growth never really comes to full fruition (209–10). Folkloric time explains the coherence of ritual (210). All things in this matrix are equally valid, food and drink as well as the phases of human and astronomical life (210–11). As social classes form, narrative is rapidly reinterpreted: parts of the matrix relevant to man (food, death, sex, etc.) become part of everyday life, i.e. enter into ritual and gain a magic significance. An example is bread, which in ritual becomes a different product than bread as sustenance (211–12). As these aspects of life become differentiated, ritualistic violations emerge as a category (the Saturnalia are a good example of this, and laughter comes to play a central role in conjunction with death, sexuality, food and drink, warding off disgrace through fictive disgrace) (212–13). As class society develops further, the elements of the matrix become further individualised, personal, everyday affairs, though they all are sublimated in literature and religious ritual (213). They no longer occur in the same context: sexuality and defecation are banned from formal discourse, but sexuality does show up in its sublimated form: love (213–14). The greatest divorce between members of the matrix comes about with financial relations, in capitalism and slavery; here, what had been common becomes maximally abstract and loses its significance outside of its private realisation (214–15). Love (the sublimation of sex) came to play a central role thanks to its intersection with life-phases (marriage, childbirth) as well as with multiple lives (215–16). Death becomes an ultimate end, severed from social continuity (death as sowing and its connection with its counterpart of childbirth) and the loftier on that account. Some links from the ancient matrix, however, are strengthened: thus death is associated with the grim reaper, night, etc.; but as metaphor and in religion, it loses its cyclicity (216). The historical time-sequence runs parallel to these individual sequences and incorporates them, but is not fused with them; modern novels have attempted to overcome this duality by finding historical aspects to private life and casting historical events in a private light. Nature now became a mere setting, landscape; but in language and some folklore aspects of the ancient matrix are preserved (217). Even in real literature this tendency sometimes surfaces. The classical epic is based in the unified time of folklore, achieving a limited realisation of historical time by portraying individual lives as surface action to a collective life. Individuals represent the whole and so their everyday life coincides with that of the whole, while larger events affect all indiviual lives in the same way, and petty private matters do not exist; neither does disinterested background. Yet epic time itself is entirely past, unequivocally divorced from the present time of author and audience (218). Comedy (in Aristophanes) is based on elements from the ancient matrix: food, ritual indecency, and laughter form the basis of this genre, in which they lose their private character and their significance is exaggerated (218–19). In Lucian, the everyday sphere of food and sexuality is used in all its low quality to undercut the loftiness of an ideology that had become false (220–1). Petronius brought all the links in the ancient sequence from birth to tomb back together, but on the everyday level (221–4). The idyllic chronotope (224–42) gives time a firm grounding in a small space. In this limited space, generations pass by but the narrative retains a unity of space. This space is not intrinsically connected with space external to it, and the idyllic life cannot be separated from it. The focus on unity of place renders the divisions between lives and generations blurry, yielding a cyclical rhythm (224–5). The idyll is further limited to a small number of realities, excluding the trivial details of reality; the realities that exist occur in their sublimated form (love not sex, etc.) (225–6). Finally, the idyll links human life up with the progression and cycles of nature, even if primarily on a metaphorical level (226). In the eighteenth century, a type of elegy also developed with an idyllic component (graveyards evoking the cycle of life, etc.) (228). The idyll greatly influenced the modern novel, namely in five directions: provincial novel, Bildungsroman, Sentimental novel, family novel, and miscellaneous novels making use of the ancient matrices (228–9). (These are explored, 229–33). “The destruction of the idyll” becomes a common literary theme in the later eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries (233); the various approaches to this theme are discussed (233–5). Only laughter was never submilated (236–7). Influences on Rabelais are discussed (238–42). The concluding remarks discuss a number of specific chronotopical settings: the road, the castle, parlours/salons, and threshold (243–50). The remainder of the essay adds discussions of how the chronotope works and interacts with other chronotopes, the role of the author etc.; all concluding remarks were added on in 1973.

author: Barrar, Kathleen
title: A Spacious, Green and Hospitable Land: Paradise in Old English Poetry
publication: Bulletin of the John Rylands University Library of Manchester
abstract: OE poetry does indeed describe pleasant landscapes, particularly in its depiction of paradise, which it gives a rural, idyllic quality (105). It differs from the rather succinct Vulgate description (106). Early Christian literature looked to apocryphal descriptions of paradise for inspiration, such as The Apocalypse of St Peter, which was influenced by the classical locus amoenus. Traditional paradise descriptions in this tradition involved “temperate weather conditions. . . ; trees in perpetual leaf. . . ; delicious scents. . . ; attractive birdlife; ground watered by (particularly four) natural springs” (106-7). Of all OE poetry, Judgement Day II, based on Bede’s poetry, comes closest to this locus amoenus (107-8). “Paradise motifs” occur in Genesis, The Phoenix, and Guthlac, and include green, wide plains, perpetual leaf, streams, blossom, scent, birdsong, and lists of absence. Genesis A has a lacuna that would likely have described paradise (108). Genesis A is even more anthropocentric than the Vulgate. The emphasis on a green land may reflect the harsher northern-European context of the OE text (109) [PS: is greenness not also an ideal in hot/desert regions?]. Magennis understands greenness as both imported and indigenous (109-10). Hospitality and spaciousness are two elements apparently specific to OE paradise (110-14). Woodland descriptions again suggest greenness, but shelter, esthetics, and traditional religious functions of woods and groves may also play a role (114-19). Descriptions of postlapsarian earthly paradises are discussed, again with emphasis on greenness (119-24). The conclusion of the work echoes Howe rather than the body of the article (125).

author: Baume, Andrew
title: Lancastrian Normandy and the Calendar of Medieval Warfare
publication: La Ronde des saisons: Les saisons dans la littérature et la société anglaises au Moyen Age
abstract:
In the early medieval period, warfare concerned everyone, and autumn was the favoured season, although spring was no uncommon season either. In autumn, there were no more agricultural duties, and provisions were plentiful, both for supply and for plunder. The rise of the paid soldier has recently been emphasised, sometimes replacing the feudal host. However, it was only the very distinguished who could afford to keep a professional army. When paid indentured armies did become the norm during the Hundred Years’ War, autumn remained by far the prime season of warfare, and autumn raiding remained vital. Often, booty rather than fighting appears to have been the objective of the English. The first part of the Hundred Years’ War consisted in the English engaging in repeated seasonal raids and ransoming, certainly not as part of a grander scheme (61). The second phase of the war constituted a capital break, in which the English maintained a professional army permanently in the wider area of Normandy. This new situation was formative in the development of new social relationships between civilians and soldiers, and of a new policy of determination that abandoned instinctive warfare. This paper studies this transformation.

One corrollary of the year-round professional army is the disappearance of seasons without hostilities. Thus Torcy-le-Grand in the boggy flood-plain of the Varenne was recovered from the French in the winter of 1429-30, with the help of paid Norman auxiliaries (62). Likewise in the winter of 1431-2 a year-long siege was carried out at Bonsmoulins, which after its capture was demolished by a civilian contractor (62-3). In the winter of 1443-4, an English unit blocked a French advance, which blockade came to require large-scale food-supply operations. In all these events, plunder as a source of income and supplies gives way to paid services. Until the late thirteenth century, there are records of higher noblemen refusing to take the king’s money in return for military service, apparently because of its implications in terms of discipline and the division of spoils. This attitude is characteristic of the free warrior of earlier times. Soldiers in Lancastrian Normandy were supervised by civilians: a 1429 record has a Norman official ask the people in church whether they have any complaints about the military commander, and this seems to have been the new rule (63). Keeping soldiers in check was both required for efficiency and natural because they were paid forces. Moreover, (obedient) Norman civilians were considered subjects just like the English. Military trespasses against civilians were punished (63-4). The English government’s strict policies were economically motivated: the second phase of the war was to be self-supporting through local taxes, so that a healthy Norman economy was essential for success. Arbitrary plundering or unofficial taxes harmed the economy and thus the English cause (64). Although damage was indeed done, the English government at least tried to avoid it; and the numbers documented are surely exaggerated (64-5). The long-term effects of this new war were less disruptive of the economy. Plundering is economically inefficient; ransoming is better, but is still economically disruptive. [A long-term campaign needs to take control of the economy rather than destroy it.] It has proved difficult to prove long-term beneficial effects of a war on any parties in particular (65). Unlike in other regions in France, the war in Lancastrian Normandy was financed from within: it was entirely surrounded, and any break of its lines would result in economic damage. This situation entailed socio-economic consequences (65-6). The region was taxed enormously, and, despite uprisings, authorities managed to maintain a steady flow of income (66). This success may be explained by rapid monetary velocity (the immediate local spending of revenue) and the influx of bullion from England (soldiers were paid in English money for their first six months, and were made to spend it locally; and more money was sent to try and alter the fortunes of war, effectively impovering England). The balance between this influx and the economic disruption of the war cannot be determined by direct evidence (66-7). Significant is that in 1442, a tax was established on transactions rather than moveable goods or revenue, which may be suggestive of economic development of new types at a time which is held to have been wholly disorganised (67). In conclusion, the rise of professional warfare led to a clearer distinction between civilian and soldier, and brought the seasonal basis of warfare to an end. Professional soldiers were more dependent on civilians. On the other hand, the great modern wars were in a sense all seasonal affairs since all able-bodied men were mobilised (67-8).

author: Becker, Gustav
title: Isidori Hispalensis ’De natura rerum liber’
abstract: This edition dedicates one of its apparatuses to a running quotation of sources. Much of the work appears to be based on Ambrosius’s Hexaemeron. Isidore explains why day is understood to have been primary until the fall, from which point onwards night has preceded day (4-5). Lists Hebrew feast days and explains other special days as well as solstice and equinox (5-8). Night is explained as the absence of the sun, given for the repose of the body [PS: so also Bede, Byrhtferth, Ælfric]. Nox derives from nocere “hinder,” because it hinders the eyes (8). Night has seven parts [PS: so also Byrhtferth, ?Bede] (8-9). The names of the months are explained, and the institution of kalends, nones, and ides (11-13). The year is discussed; the word can also be used to refer to the entirety of human existence on earth (14). Different ways of measuring and beginning the year are discussed, as well as units made up of a few years (14-17). The seasons, according to Ambrose, are alternating turns of changes (17); their nature is explained by way of biblical quotations (17-18) and each receives a full definition (18-19). The seasons begin 22 February, 25 May, 25 August, and 22 November (19). Winter is to be understood allegorically as a time of tribulation, summer as persecution of the faith, spring as peace or renewed faith (20). Solstices and equinoxes are briefly explained (20-1). The world signifies man on a mystical level, and Scripture sometimes uses it to refer to sinners (21). Cites Virgil and Lucanus for their references to the icy north (22). The five climate zones are explained (23-4). The four elements are defined not by heat and humidity but as thin, sharp, and mobile (fire); thick, sharp, and mobile (air); thick, blunt, and mobile (water); and thick, blunt, and immobile (earth). Ambrosius is cited for their respective heat and humidity, and their relationships with one another are explained (24-5). The sky represents the Church, which shines with the light of its saints. Scripture also seems to refer to its prophets as “the heavens” (25-6). Caelum is from caelare “chisel” (Ambrosius; 26). The seven parts of the heaven are described (26-7), as is its spherical nature (27-8). The seven planets (28-9). Skepticism regarding there being waters above the heaven is foolish: if God could create ex nihilo, then he can keep the waters from falling down (30). The sun is fiery (30-2). The sun is larger than the moon, but farther removed (32-3). It has to move by itself rather than remain stationary, since it rises and sets in a different place every day (33-4). Its shift from north to south, moreover, with the accompanying change in the sun’s distance from the earth, was so intended to prevent the sun from scorching the earth; moderation is the point of the four seasons (34-5). Low altitude and consequent heat of the sun are also used for the punishment of humankind (35). The moon reflects the light of the sun (36-8). The moon mystically represents this world, since it falls short of the month just as this world falls short. The moon waxes only to disappear and reappear, teaching humankind that they are to die but live again (38). Also, it receives light from the sun as does the Church from Christ (38-9). The moon has seven phases (39). The lunar year is defined (39-40). Solar (40-2) and lunar eclipses (42-3) are explained cosmologically and symbolically. Stars and planets (44-53). Night is explained as a great shadow (54). Thunder and lightning derive from the breaking of clouds, or represent divine reproach (54-7). Rainbows (57-8). Clouds (58-9). Rain (59-60). Snow, according to Ambrose, is water stiffened into solid form by the blowing of icy winds. It represents the ?beauty of the righteous at Judgement Day, when their clothes will be white as snow (60). In a similar way, rain is “bound” into ice as hailstones, representing the hardness of treason, cold with the stiffness of malice, whereas snow represents unbelievers, cold and slow and pressed down into the lowest stiffness of mind; or instead humans frozen in love, whitened by baptism but not burning with the spirit of love (60-1). The origin of winds (61-2). Septentrio (N), cold and snowy, dry and cold, straight from the pole, drying the clouds. Thrascias, (NNW), brings snow and hail. Aquilo or Boreas (NE/NNE) is cold and dry, binding the clouds together rather than sending them apart, which has earned it the devil’s image, who binds the hearts of men with the frost of iniquity [PS: cf. with this traditions of Satan’s throne being in the north/east]. The eastern Subsolanus is moderate of character. Vulturnus (ESE) dissolves and dries out all in its path. Eurus (SE) brings rain. Auster (S) is the southern wind, warm and humid. Euroauster (SSE) is warm. Austroafricus is warm. Zephyrus (W) compensates for the rigour of winter, bringing forth flowers. Africus creates storms, rains, and thunderstorms. Corus brings clouds to the east (62-3). Storm represents the roar of divine judgement; still weather is the joy of the eternal light (64). Advice is given on the forecasting of weather changes (64-6). Pestilence (67-8). Tides (68-70). Why the sea does not increase with the rain (70-1); why it is bitter (71); on the Nile and other rivers (71-4). How the earth is supported (75). Earthquakes are caused by wind entering the holes in the earth’s sponge-like structure (76-7). Mount Etna (77-8). The world’s three continents are described in T-O fashion (78-9).

author: Beckman, Natanael
title: Isländsk och medeltida skandinavisk tideräkning
abstract: According to Völuspá, Vafþruðnismál, and Alvíssmál, the sun, stars, and moon move so that creatures may tell the time (5). Man faces the problem of having to combine incompatible natural measures (5-7). Usually, this is done by intercalation: thus the lunar cycle of 19 solar years harbours 235 lunations (19 x 12 + 7 embolisms [intercalary lunar months]). Similarly with weeks: every year has a concurrent, a spare weekday, so that a year does not contain a full number of weeks. The cycle to reconcile week and solar year (often called solar cycle, for no good reason) is 28 solar years, since 28 x (1 concurrent day + 0,25 leap day) = 35 days, or five weeks. The solar cycle helps one find the Sunday letter (Table IV), which combines with the lunar cycle to find the weekday (Table VI); Easter is found in Table III (7-8). The solar cycle “begins” nine years BCE. Thus (9 + 1224) / 28 x remainder = the year’s number in the cycle for 1224 (namely, 44 [#and therefore 44 – 28 = 16?]). A year’s position in the lunar cycle (gyllental) is carried out similarly: (1 + yyyy) / 19 x remainder (8). The great Easter cycle is the period in which these two cycles coincide (every 532 years, e.g. in 1064). The most common form in Scandinavia (Table IV) used 1140 as its basis. The formula is (yyyy – 1139) / 28 (keep the remainder for use in the table’s other column). The remainder of (1 + yyyy) / 28 is the golden number, which will yield the year in which the relevant lunar cycle began (8-9). The calendarium perpetuum (Table I) is explained (10-11). Clergymen were expected to announce the correct dates of feast days, and they could be punished if they did not (11-12). Rím I probably dates to shortly before 1195 in our calendar (13-14). Rím II contains some original speculations about questions such as how come the midnight sun occurs in places where there is no afternoon darkness (15). The Icelanders had a year that consisted of full weeks, so 364 days; they used intercalary weeks, not days, so that a leap year consisted of 371 days. The year was divided into a winter of 6 x 30 days, beginning on a Saturday in October, and a summer of 6 x 30 + 4 (+ 7 intercalary) days (16), beginnning on a Thursday in mid-April. The author sets out to distinguish between Nordic and borrowed elements (16ff.). Rune sticks are of no assistance, since they are Julian or even Gregorian calendars. The seven-day week is semitic, but it need not have come with Christianity—if it did, then why did the clergymen bother to translate Roman heathen names into Germanic god names? The existence of the seven-day week among the Sami (borrowed from Scandinavian usage) is also evidence for a prechristian Germanic seven-day week. Moreover, Rím I uses Greek and Arabic names, at that time unusual in Continental Europe (16-17). Oddi has some original theories: thus he does not define the summer solstice as the time when the sun’s position undergoes no apparent change, but the time when its distance from its vernal equinox position is ninety degrees. In the 1120s, he believed this moment to take place on 15 or 17 June, at 9am or 3pm alternately. We do not know how he got to these times (18-19). Oddi’s second theory concerns the sun’s change of noon height throughout the year (sólargang), measured in solar radii from 1 to 13. This theory not quite accurately takes the equinoxes to be in mid-March and mid-September (19-20). Evidence for 14 April and 14 October as the start of summer and winter is discussed. These dates are about three weeks after the calendrical equinoxes (20-1). Bits from Rím I and Ari are translated (21-2). Iceland clearly had two calendar traditions, the Icelandic week-year and the Julian calendar; the former was the foremost in the popular mind, while the latter was used for ecclesiastical purposes; but no people would keep track of both (23). The option of fixing the Icelandic calendar in the Julian calendar will have been considered; a single line in Rím I refers to the linking of the start of summer to the Annunciation (26-7). Grágás decrees that the lawspeaker is to announce the misseristal, the week of the Thing, and the days for fasting at the end of the Althing (27). However, a way was necessary for the people to fit the Church feasts into their own week-calendar. A formula was found in a reform, probably shortly after 1140. The author’s identity is uncertain, but a certain Bjarni Bergþórsson (d. 1173) is named. The formula may be that in Rím II. The alternative, a combination of a multiplication and a division, was a problem before the introduction of Arabic numerals. Another issue with the fixing of the week-year into the Julian calendar was when to insert intercalary years. For a long time, the custom was to wait for a year with Sunday letter D: every Sunday letter occurs five times in a solar cycle, so the necessary five weeks were accommodated. Only in leap years some irregularities remained, for which reason it was possible to take recourse to C or E years (28-9). The rímspillir presented Icelanders with the difficulty that in such years, feast days occurred a week earlier. The years of the intercalary week were so chosen that the following spring, time of the Church feasts, was least affected (29-30). It is explained why the D year was the best option, and how year 9 of the solar cycle is a rímspillir even in the Julian calendar (30-1). The rímspillir could be avoided by situating the intercalary week in a different part of the year, namely in Þorri. Presumably, this was not chosen because the term sumarauki was already fixed in the people’s memory. The rule that gói began on a Sunday was a convenient fact for Easter calculation; but if summer had long begun on a Thursday, then the gói rule was based on it (31). The article now turns to study everyday time-reckoning. Several of the Icelandic month-names occur so seldom, that it is doubtful that they had a real existence. The law text that refers to them has no names for them (Grágás 1852 p. 37). The main sources are Bókarbót and Snorra Edda 1.510f. The first is unlikely to have extended beyond learned circles; the second focuses on literary usage and has little to suggest their actual usage as terms. Gaukmánuðr, sáðtið, eggtíð, stekktíð, sólmánaðr, selmánuðr, kornskurðarmánaðr, haustmánaðr, frermánuðr, hrútmánuðr occur in Snorri only; but gauksmessa for 1 May is attested. Gormánuðr, mörgsúgr occur only in Bókarbót. Miðsumar is mentioned in Rím I, but it is not made explicit that a month is referred to; it might be a shorter period, such as a week. Heyannir seems to refer to the agricultural hay period rather than to a month, especially since in Grágás it is said to extend through the fourth and fifth months of the season (1879 p. 450). The similarity between the names tvimánuðr and einmánuðr is noted, according to Beckman because they mean “last-but-one” and “last month.” Haustmánaðr is unlikely to have been used. Ýlir is Bókarbót’s name for frermánuðr, and this term is cognate with Gothic jiuleis and OE geola; both Gothic and OE have two consecutive months with the same name (ærra, æftera geola for December and January). The third winter month is not only called mörgsúgr and hrútmánuðr but also jólmánuðr (32-3). The popularity of the various names is discussed. Months may have seldom been used to specify a date, but instances exist. It is likely that the thirty-day month existed in learned culture only. The existence of a four-week month is unlikely. Norwegian material on months is so scarce that no full year can be reconstructed (34). Snorri discusses four seasons in the context of the months of the year. Autumn and spring begin at the equinoxes, in the twelfth century about mid-September and mid-March. Winter begins when the sun sets at eyktarstað (3.30pm), which is in October for southern Iceland; summer begins at the moving days (a Thursday 21-27 May). Weeks and week numbers are the primary calendrical units; weeks began on a Saturday for the learned sources, but farmers had them begin on a Friday. Rím I speaks of a summer of 184 days, and a winter of 180; this makes clear that the thirty-day month was decisive in the dividing of the seasons. If weeks had been central, the seasons could have begun on the same day of the week by a division of 183 plus 181 days (35). The Latin system of dating with Kalendae, Nonae, Idus was never used by the people of Iceland (36-7). The modern system of dating (quarta die mensis februarii) was used sporadically. Dating according to the Icelandic (economic) year (búskaparár) was more common (þríðiudagin i fimtu viku vetrar). Easier is to refer to important events directly (at sumarlálum, fyrir vetrnætr) (37). In Norway, the beginning of winter and summer were connected to specific days and could be used in the same way as saints’ days. Dating by the Church calendar was by far the commonest method in all of Scandinavia (38). Icelandic intercalary rules are found in twelfth-century documents, but their methods cannot be much older since they require a thorough and detailed understanding of the Julian calendar. They are likely products of Bjarni from about 1140-73. There is no basis for the common opinion that the week-year was common to all Scandinavian peoples (38-9). The origins of the bipartite division of the year are a matter of speculation; one expects them to be based on some astronomical observation, however local these may be. In summer, day and night were defined by sunrise and sunset; in winter, dawn and dusk were clearly part of the day. Possible methods were the height of the sun and its angle from the south, or regional descriptions of where it stood (39-40). Skafthá refers to the time when the sun is positioned over the tip of an upright spear from the perspective of a standing man (about 3pm in May). An ætt is one-eighth of the horizon, i.e., a 45-degree section of the horizon, which was seen as a three-hour period. In reality it could vary between 2.5 and 3.5 hours (40). This variability is problematic if the tidal cycle was equated with two ættir, since then one could be surprised by the high tide (40-1). Rím I gives the tidal cycle as one-fourth of a dygn. Specific locations had eyktamörk that indicated the time of day when the sun passed over them. It is important to remember that an ætt was not a fixed compass direction but a 45-degree stretch of the horizon.
