The azimut receives definition in law as eykt: eyktarstað is 52,5 degrees, about 3pm or nón (41-2, 44). Of the stars, Arcturus was the most used as the brightest star in spring; it was likely used to tell the time from the winter solstice until midsummer when no stars could be discerned (42-4). The cardinal times of day were dagmál, hádegi, nón or eykt, and miðr aptann. Both hores aequales and hores inaequales were used (44). Dating by the moon is discussed (45-50). Speculations are made concerning the prechristian year. Beckman believes that a natural year with lunar months was used, with which it was attempted to calculate the vernal equinox; these units were complemented with weeks. The Scandinavian year was an economic year (50-1). There is a note about seasons named after proper names (51). Medieval doubts are discussed regarding the year of Christ’s birth (51-3).

author: Beckman, Natanael, and Kristian Kålund
title: Rímtöl
abstract: The first council of Nicaea in 325 led to the rise of the computus ecclesiasticus. The church’s main feasts now required knowledge of the courses of both sun and moon, and a system was required to enable the less learned to determine the date of Easter. Bede’s De natura rerum is a central text on which many of these early medieval systems were based. It was, however, not the only source: Rím also uses the periods of the planets, absent from Bede but present in Isodore, and similar minor divergences from Bede derive from such authors as Honorius Augustodunensis. The odd saga reference suggests that the Church calendar may have penetrated name-giving early on, and Snorri confirms that this was common practice in his day. Vallaljóts saga mentions a row over labour on Michaelmas, suggesting that Sundays until then were the only days of rest. Epiphany is said in Landnámabók to have been introduced in 1056 (I-II). The Julian calendar as a method of dating is first evidenced from inscriptions and annals about 1130. Gulatingslög ch. 15 declares it punishable for a priest to misinform anyone about feast days (II-III). Iceland had its own prechristian calendar consisting of 364 days, corrected by Þorsteinn surtur about 965 to be as precise as the pre-Julian Roman calendar. The old misseristal and the Julian calendar were used side by side in later times (III-IV). Ari’s information about these matters has met with scholarly suspicion. Certain is that the old calendar would not die at the introduction of the new one (IV). The Althing especially required a definite method of calculation. If the week-year was used for this, then a couple of decades would show a great shift, as Ari notes: the shift would amount to 1,25 days per year. A correction must have seemed necessary (V). While Ari was chronologically close to the action of 965, some of his information does not match the other sources. The Easter table introduced in AM 249 l (pp. 69f.) shows week-corrections, but not every seventh year as dictated by Þorsteinn’s reform, but every five or six years, thus amounting to five, not four, per solar cycle (28 years). Þorsteinn’s calendar differed from the Julian by 0,25 day per year, which amounts to 42 weeks in the 168 years between Þorsteinn and Ari; but Ari does not mention this. He seems to have used an amended Þorsteinnian calendar (V-VI). The 35 spare days per solar cycle correspond exactly to the Sunday letters in the Rím: leynistafir are Sunday letters to be used in January and February of the leap years; the remaining difference of a day is avoided by means of the Rímsspillir (VII-VIII; see p. 66). The remaining difficulties suggest that the definitive method of calculation was post-Ari. This definitive method has its terminus a quo in Ari’s Íslendingabók and its terminus ad quem is the date for the original of MS L, which MS is dated to about 1187 (VIII-X). There was a specifically Icelandic type of Easter table called talbyrðingr. All Easter tables follow Bede, who follows Dionysius in turn. The system is based on 19-year moon cycles (X-XI). Ari refers to Easter tables in 1120. The oldest Easter table found in Iceland is in AM 732 a VII, 4to, which covers the lunar cycle of 1121-39, and of which a diagram is here printed and discussed (XII-XIII). While Bede divides his Easter cycle into 28 lunar cycles, the Icelandic table uses 19 solar cycles (XVI). All Easter tables are unnecessarily complex if their purpose is only to show the date of Easter. Such a simple table is called talbyrðingr (XIV-XIX). Gerlandus’s Computus is discussed (#XIX-XXII). The calendar reform seems to have been introduced with few difficulties: while the two methods are essentially different and the change required knowledge of both, we find no mention of a troublesome transition (#XXII). Rím I may be regarded as a textbook on calendar calculation, needed by the goði who was appointed to make such calculations. It stood in a remarkable didactic tradition of the twelfth century (#XXII-XXIII). Its author shows a fondness of calculation, and many of its calculations have no Continental model. Bjarni enn tölvísi Bergþórsson (var. Þorgeirsson) is thought to have been the author (XXII). Sources are discussed, especially Oddi (XXIV-XXVIII). By the Rím’s reckoning, Christ would have been born in the year 8 CE (or right at the beginning of 9 CE) according to our calendar. He had Icelandic followers in this manner of calculation, until the Tabula Gerlandi was followed in adapting our year 1 as the year of Christ’s birth (XXVIII-XXIX). Bede, Isidore, Libellus Helprici, and Honorius Augustodunensis are named as sources (XXIX-XXX). A number of problems are listed which this list of sources fails to explain (XXX-XVI). Ptolemy’s Almagest was unknown to Bede but the Arabs’ primary source. It came to the west in the guise of Al Ferghani’s works especially, translated in 1134. It was via John de Alta Villa that this branch of astronomy reached Iceland. An Icelander was in Palestine in the 1150s (XXXVII-XXXVIII). The actual European renaissance of astronomy was thirteenth-century. Rím II was most certainly a product of this discovery of Arab astronomy. (XXXVIII-XLV). Its place of composition may be determined by its treatment of tidal reckoning to be southern Faxaflói, i.e., the Reykjavík area. Reykjavík itself was of too little significance in the period; but Viðey monastery, founded in 1226 and in bloom under the sovereignty of earl Gizur in the latter half of the thirteenth century, is a likely locale. However, the author’s description of the midnight sun gives one the feeling that this phenomenon does not occur in his place of origin. Also, he discusses Oddi’s observations in such a way that it seems they did not correspond to his own. (XLV-L). Sources are discussed (L-LIV). The question of interpolations and the original length of the work are addressed (LIV-LVI). Rím II uses newer and better sources than Rím I, but it also contains a wealth of original thought (LVI-LVII). Language is discussed (LVII-LVIII). Beckman disagrees with the opinion that Rím III is post-Gregorian reform: its author shows no familiarity with the shortcomings of the Julian moon calendar (LIX-LX). Its difference from Rím II consists in its approach. Rím II follows an older tradition, trying to deduce its computistics from their deeper causes; Rím III is more concerned with calculations and commentary on Latin mnemonic verse. It has a very learned air to it and leaves many Latin words untranslated, but it is less learned than II in knowledge. The work’s language is commented on (LX-LXI). It is a collection of well-known Latin verses, without explanation whenever they seemed clear (LXIII). The extant Icelandic calendars are discussed (LXIV-LXVIII). Textual criticism (LXXV-CVII). On previous editions (CVIII-CXIII). Multidisciplinarity is discussed (CXIV-CXXXIV). Grammar (CXXXV-CXLVII). The Scandinavian elements in Sami computus and astronomy are surveyed (CXLVII-CLVI). Russian Sami begin their year in about September (CXLVIII). Sami chronological loanwords were borrowed in widely different eras. Like the Germanic Scandinavians, they had a preference for week-reckoning; but their word for “week,” vakko, is an obvious Scandinavian loan. Nearly all the weeks of the year have Sami names of their own, mostly formed from an ecclesiastical feast day name in the respective week. The Sami month is a week-month of twenty-eight days, so that the year consists of thirteen months. There has never been a definite set of rules for leap or concurrent periods (CXLVIII-CL). A number of unconnected observations are made concerning Sami time-reckoning (CL-CLI), including the observation that Sami midwinter takes place about a month after Germanic midwinter; it is likely based on climate not solstice, as February in Lapland is harsh (CLI). An Astrophysia Lapponica by an eighteenth-century priest in Lapland is printed (CLII-CLVI). One of his observations is that the Sami begin their year at the winter solstice, and the editors note that North American natives have the same practice (CLIII). The early Scandinavian practice of telling the time by the stars is discussed (CLVI-CLXV). A number of auxiliary tables and calendars are printed (CLXVI-CXCIV). The remainder of the introduction consists in Kålund’s description of the MSS (CXCV-CCXXXIII).

author: Buckland, P.C., et al.
title: Bioarchaeological and Climatological Evidence for the Fate of Norse Farmers in Medieval Greenland
abstract: The Scandinavian settlements in Greenland, begun in 985 according to ON sources, had disappeared by the end of the fifteenth century. While the Little Ice Age has often been blamed for their demise, regional variation within the North Atlantic region precludes the use of such categories (88). Subsistence in Greenland was based primarily on “milk and meat from cattle, sheep and goats,” supplemented in dire periods with “seals and seabirds in the spring, and caribou drives with hunting dogs in the autumn.” While there is evidence of the consumption of wild fruits, domesticated plants did not contribute significantly to the diet (89). By 1300, stone had become an important ingredient of architecture [but the article refers to public buildings only]. European trade was based on walrus hide and ivory (90). A comparison of bones identified in farms in northeast Iceland and western Greenland show the complementary nature of fish and walrus of these areas, as well as the differences in diet (91). Analysis of flies shows that the Scandinavian Greenlanders, unlike both Inuit Greenlanders and Scandinavians in Iceland, used every bit of meat and fat on game animals, suggesting that the climate in Greenland required a more efficient use of protein but that the Scandinavian population had a greater need of this than its Inuit counterpart (902). Despite long contact with Thule-style Inuit hunters, the Scandinavians failed to copy Inuit dress and marine hunting equipment, limiting their variation of prey. Absence of fishery indicates absence of maritime adaptation. A decline in the demand for walrus ivory contributed to economic stagnation (94). Radiocarbon dating suggests abandonment in the early fourteenth century. Evidence of abandoned construction wood in an area with great wood shortage confirms this dating. Hunting dogs were butchered, probably in desperation (94). Calcium and sodium levels indicate an abrupt climate change between 1400 and 1420. In central Greenland, the fourteenth century was colder than the fifteenth. 1308-19 and 1343-62 represent the lowest values in winter and summer respectively (94). In Iceland, the fourteenth century was climatically unstable and colder than the fifteenth. Years of grass failure led to a decrease of livestock, farm abandonment and human deaths [see Ogilvie 1984]. Iceland’s economy was increasingly integrated into fish exports to Europe. Greenland, by contrast, relied on luxury exports, whose demand diminished. All of Europe saw a decline in population in the fourteenth century, but the role of climate is controversial. While the same goes for Greenland, its prolonged colder periods in the fourteenth centuries may have been sufficient cause for abandonment. “[A]ll the bioarchaeological evidence from the Norse sites indicates the precarious nature of their subsistence. This vulnerability was exacerbated by a conservative social system, wider economic changes and activities which degraded the very parts of the ecosystem upon which they depended.” None of the climatic low periods affected the Inuit population (95).

author: Burlin, Robert B
title: Inner Weather and Interlace: A Note on the Semantic Value of Structure in Beowulf
publication: Old English Studies in Honour of John C. Pope
eds: Robert B. Burlin and Edward B. Irving, Jr.
abstract: Identifies interlace in the order in which things are told in Bwf. The winter imagery of the Finn episode is discussed (81-3). By detailing on winter, both the passage of time and the quality of Hengest’s problem are indicated. “Winter” forms an envelope pattern. The description of spring is equally long but empty and general (82). The description of spring is similar to that of Sfr: the bright picture of regeneration contrasts with the hero’s dilemma. The passage is meant to emphasise the pity as well as the reality of such events, denying man’s power over them in a sense approaching that of wyrd (83-4).

author: Burton, Richard
title: Nature in Old English Poetry
abstract: Bwf has very frequent reference to winter but none to summer. OE literature shows that Anglo-Saxons did have an eye for nature, but they only described “the sterner mood of nature.” The explanation is to be sought first in the origins and locale of the poem: the low countries and Scandinavia have a grimmer climate than England. The pars pro toto winter for “year” is presumably a homage to the importance of this season to the Germanic peoples. A second explanation lies in the less joyful character of the pagan religion (476-7). The fact that Wdr refers to nature only twice shows how little in fashion natural reference was in the poetry of the time. The prominence in OE verse of the sea is noted, as is the poverty of the AS colour scheme (478). WfL, too, contains natural description, and The Ruin does so indirectly, by dwelling on the effect of time and nature on man’s creations. Sfr contains a long and graphic description of nature. Brunanburh and Maldon refer to the beasts of battle (478-81). When Bwf describes joy, it is inside the hall. It is in the hall that the swimming-contest is related (481). Genesis is discussed (483), Exodus, Judith, The Phoenix, etc. (484-7).

author: Caciola, Nancy
title: Wraiths, Revenants and Ritual in Medieval Culture
abstract: Studies late medieval (twelfth- to fifteenth-century) conceptions of life after death, suggesting that a popular material outlook on life and death contrasted with a learned spiritual understanding. The most obvious written sources on medieval views of death were either compiled or committed to writing by the educated classes and thus provide little information regarding popular culture, and what they provide is often systematised beyond its authentic nature (4-5). The dichotomy also of populus and elite is a modern construct, often set along the line of doctrine versus ritual and praxis, itself related to orthodoxy versus superstition (5). It is emphasised that the dichotomy is useful but relational and ahistorical (6). Medieval death need not be absolute or permanent; it has been defined as an age class (7). In learned tradition, spiritus had three parts: animal, natural, and life spirit, together forming a physical substance in the body amounting to the essence of life (7-8). In this respect it rivalled the theological concept of the soul, with which it was harmonised by the scholastics (8-9). In the religious domain, spirit lost much of its material substance, turning into an abstract principle where in the life sciences it held more of a middle ground between material and abstract (9). Tales of the dead as they survive are in reality learned Latin interpretations of vernacular hearsay (10-11). There is evidence that people conceived of life and the afterlife as embodied, as examples demonstrate; according to the “official” view, bodies are like articles of dress, and revenants are mere dead matter moved by Satan, an inversion of the true resurrection (11-15). Belief in revenants has been attested for Iceland, England, the Low Countries, northern France, and parts of Germany. Glámr and Kárr inn gamli of Grettis saga are briefly discussed, and Þórgunna and Þórólfr of Eyrbyggja saga; and Víga-Hrappr of Laxdæla. Outside Iceland, the phenomenon has been largely neglected despite obvious similarities (a footnote cites half a dozen studies on Icelandic revenants) (16-17). These tales describe not demonic possession but autonomous resurrection (17-18). Moreover, they often have evil intentions (18-20, though an exception occurs in Walter Map 2.28); in many of these tales, the material presence of the corpse is apparent. William of Newburgh emphasises that revenants are a recent phenomenon and expresses his puzzlement at the concept (20-2). A collection from about 1400 consistently speaks of spiritus, but the appearances are clearly material (22-3). Several of the accounts here listed exclude the possibility of demonic possession (16-24). Iconography knows a dance of death-motif (danse macabre) also found in French literature; this motif was soon adopted by the clergy to send a message of memento mori (24-6). The uniformity of the motif across time and space is emphasised (26-7). But not all the dead were thought to return: bad living and/or bad dying were responsible for this (27-9); in Iceland, death at sea, dying at the hands of a draugr, and dying through loss of self-control were particularly likely to lead one to return from the grave (28-9). Manuals to prevent the newly dead from returning are attested (29-35); it is noted that bodies of water were often considered liminal boundaries between the world of the living and that of the dead (30 and note). The dead never return once the flesh has rotted off their bones; the death of the flesh occurs at a later point in time than the death of the personality (32-3). Feasts of the dead were fairly widespread but appear to have been thought of as less corporeal than the revenant proper; these spirits could only be “met” by leaving one’s body behind (37-8). Walter Map tells of living men seizing brides from among a danse macabre; female revenants seem more inclined to dance than to terrorise (38). Dances of the dead, the living, and mixed groups are discussed at great length (37-44). In conclusion, the various traditions agree that revenants result from bad living or bad dying, they agree on the existence of an afterlife, and some northern European communities seem to have bridged the gap between living and dead through dance (45).

author: Cigman, Gloria
title: The Seasons in Late Medieval Literature: Mutability and Metaphors of Good and Evil
abstract: SGGK, Troilus and Criseyde, Henryson’s Testament of Cresseid and the Towneley Play of the Nativity invert the traditional symbolism of the seasons. In Genesis, there is no indication of changeful climate. Although an Anglo-Latin drawing shows the tree of knowledge empty after Adam’s banishment, God’s pronouncement does not suggest rest from working the land, and therefore it does not suggest seasonal change (132). Ælfric describes an Egypt devoid of seasonal change (132-3). Consolatio 1.5m praises the order imposed on the world through the seasons, and laments the absence of such order in man. This absence, indeed, is an essential element of literature: it is not to the perfect workings of paradise that we devote our words, but to attempts to control one’s life (133-4). Later ME literature tends to link outer and inner weather and seasons. SGGK begins in midwinter, but sheltered by the season-defying walls of Camelot. The seasonal cycle is invoked briefly before the narrative returns to the next winter, now unveiled. The social customs surrounding Gawain’s promise lose their admirable nature (134-5). Despite great imaginative differences between SGGK and other contemporary works, seasons are displayed strikingly similarly—by “sharp contrasts of weather.” The Towneley Nativity describes the unbiblical winter season in comparison with hostile attacks, in which the latter are not the more terrifying of the two; sleet and icicles express the winter weather. This picture is a close match to SGGK. The difference is that the latter tries to distance his winter from that in reality by means of images and poetics, whereas the play intends to take away any distance between biblical teachings and reality (136-7). It expresses mutability by reference back in time to Noah’s flood (Nativity 183-6) and implied reference forward in time to the hot summer day on which the play is staged. The implication is that between Fall and Judgement Day, all is mutable except the city of God, and a choice may still be made. In both works, winter carries unusual connotations: it is when Christ is born and when Gawain’s spiritual worth is tested (137). The cycles of the four seasons and the twenty-four hours are made into analogues: night, too, has evil associations but it moves towards dawn. Gothic cathedrals, too, fit the comparison: from the west, the side of darkness, they enter the church facing its point of rising (138). To Chaucer, spring does not yet exist, and his Tales rarely mention the seasons to begin with. Winter is mostly used synecdochically. Nighttime is used at times as a setting for the bawdy fabliaux. An exception occurs in The Merchant’s Tale when January and May are names signalling a mismatch between an old man and a young girl (138). The central function of the seasons in Troilus and the Testament is in sharp contrast to the Tales. Troilus describes the development of a love in harmony with the development of the year. The functions of day and night are inverted since the lovers act in secrecy. The cycle of the seasons is not mentioned after Criseyde’s betrayal of Troilus, although time elapses emphatically. The romance begun in the month of hope has turned out a delusion and ends in sorrow (139). Henryson transforms Criseyde into a villain, a type: she elects evil. She is abandoned by Diomed, becomes a prostitute and contracts leprosy; here we find the winter not mentioned in Troilus. The Testament’s narrator emphasises that a sad story befits a sad season (Testament 6-7; Cigman 140). The works here treated suggest that winter should be an analogue to old age in terms of wisdom. However, winter is not an end to life but “a necessary prelude to regeneration.” ME literature recognises the inevitability of the cycle but links it up with mutability and human responsibility, often forming a reconciliation between God’s constant will and man’s freedom of will. The constancy of nature exposes the mutability and fallibility of man’s actions (141).

author: Clark, S.L., and Julian N. Wassermann
title: The Passing of the Seasons and the Apocalyptic in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
abstract:
The works of the SGGK poet are unified by their theme of the judgement of men separating the saved from the damned. SGGK’s excursus on the passing of the year [ll. 495-530] follows immediately on a reflection on the unexpected ends of human endeavours in a sublunar world (5).

(I)SGGK is about the Noah-like rescuing of one man from the doomed city of Camelot. The Green Knight with his axe and holly-bob offers both life and death, reward and punishment, introduced by trumpets. Both in Purity and in SGGK, the individuals can save only themselves, not their societies (5-6). SGGK’s structure is based on two feasting courts, directly derived from the apocalyptic feasts representing the separation of saved and doomed in Purity [see also Tolkien and Gordon 1969: xvii], which opens with the parable of the wedding feast and ends with an inversion of the tally: whereas the parable has many blessed feast-participants and one evil man outside, the feast of Belshazzar has the evil inside and the single good man outside. In SGGK, the many sinful feast-participants of Camelot are challenged by a single outsider, who later receives one sinner of their lot into his court. This second court lacks the trappings of decadence, fish being its feast-fare and all activities interspersed with masses (6-7). Rather than just being a contrast, this juxtaposition presents a chronological development: a city grows evil and collapses, a remnant escaping to found a new city subject to the same fate. The implication is that the poet’s society will likewise come down (7-8). The tension thus expressed between past and present, linear and cyclical progress, itself represents a “lack of certainty of value” characteristic of “the apocalyptic mentality”--it is “apocalyptic ambivalence” (8).

(II) The poet understands the passing of time as bringing with it corruption. Fourteenth-century society was unstable to its very core (8-9). Many of its events were understood as signs of the end. Given the obvious corruption of the Church and the general unreliability of the world, salvation became the business of the individual, and more specifically of the few illuminated minds. The old order in which predestination of nobility mattered gave way to the new order in which predestination to be saved was the key. Climatic and ecological fluctuations further suggested the approach of the end (9). The natural world, once a mirror of the divine plan, came to be regarded as corrupted by the fall of man and thus hostile, opposing the spiritual as the flesh opposed the soul (9-10).

(III) The uncertainty and hostility of the natural world are central to SGGK and penetrate even the courts in their green elements. Gawain, called faultless in his five senses, is explicitly led astray by those same five senses, suggesting that one ought not to rely on them. The natural world progresses towards “winter, death, and damnation, while inside the court is foolishly unaware of the nature of the world outside” (10). The description of the passing of the seasons begins and ends in nature, thus offering no comfort. It differs from Chaucer’s Prologue in its silence with regard to spiritual analogues (10-11). Things grow only to be harvested, or else to rot and die [PS: but that is an image with spiritual symbolism]. “Nature here reflects the harshness of divine judgment which favors the few over the many.” Even spring is a chastisement in its coinciding with Lent. The description of the seasonal cycle also echoes the poem’s structure from Camelot to Bercilak’s court and back [PS: rather its structure from Christmas to Christmas!]. As for Nebuchadnezzar in Purity, so also for Gawain in SGGK exile into nature is a means of purging (12). Outside the court, Gawain struggles with nature at large; but winter is his worst affliction. The deliverance he finds in Bercilak’s court is likewise purging. Outside, the hunt with its trumpets is an apocalyptic event, just as the Green Knight’s “assaying” of Arthur’s court evokes the final assaying of souls (12-13). After his stay at Bercilak’s, the natural world again besets Gawain; and after afflictions of the natural world and flesh, it is the devil himself he faces at the Green Chapel. But what Gawain did not realise is that all three represented judgement: judgement is everywhere (13-14). After his enlightening experience, Gawain returns to Arthur’s court in the role of Purity’s Daniel: in both texts, only the messenger understands the message of doom. The SGGK poet clearly viewed the natural world as a divinely-written book, but in more of a threatening sense than Vincent of Beauvais had understood it (14). SGGK bespeaks a theology of the elect rather than merit-based salvation, taking place on an individual level without intervention of the Church, and experienced directly rather than rationally. In hindsight, SGGK theology foreshadows protestantism (14-5).

author: Cushman, Robert E.
title: Greek and Christian Views of Time
abstract:
To the Greeks, time was circular; Christian doctrine gave it a linear dimension. This paper compares Platonic and Aristotelian conceptions of time with Augustine’s. Plato identified time as taking part in all change (i.e. in those things which do change, and are thus subjected to time), and as a measure of all change, both of position and of substance (254). He contrasted the “always becoming and never existent,” i.e. matter, with the “always existent and never becoming,” i.e. the divine (254-5). Everything in the first category is doomed to a finite, and therefore imperfect, existence, and hence to temporality. Plato’s understanding of this contrast between time and eternity was likely formed in his thinking about epistemology: he decided that knowledge cannot depend on the senses but must rely on what truly is, i.e. on Forms, which are eternal. The cosmos is an everlasting but moving image of eternity, whose movement constitutes time. For some purposes, then, time, like matter, comes into being along with the cosmos (255). “Time is the number or measure of motion”; but this motion has to be ordered: time is the indicator that order has been imposed on matter (255-6). In Greek tradition, time was often identified as the seasons coming full circle. In Plato, however, new astronomical thought is visible. Time units came about at the generation of the heaven; but the year was now defined as the sun’s orbit, from winter solstice to winter solstice. Physical time is “a co-implicate of the uniform movement of bodies through space.” However, time does retain a cyclical dimension, since Plato describes it as elliptical, with generation always returning to its starting-point. Whether its progress depends on the solar cycle or on the cycle of generation, then, time is always cyclical (256). The present does not exist for things subject to time, since it passes away too quickly. However, if a present state were actuated, this would entail the end of the difference between becoming and being, and there would be no more time (256-7). Time and becoming cannot exist without the co-existence of eternity and being; thus time is an indicator that the realm of becoming is an imperfect state of being between existence and nonexistence. Since becoming is cyclical and can never reach being, Plato does not anticipate a future moment or divine event at which the ideal Good may be realised (257). He did not conceive of teleological time (257-8).

Aristotle’s conception of time was a systematisation and elaboration of Plato’s sporadic observations. He recognised in physics three types of change: motion, alteration, and growth. Time is required to determine velocity; and such physical context constituted Aristotle’s approach to time. He followed Plato in reading time as both a concomitant and a measure of change. However, he opposed Plato’s implication that time exists only with relation to motion and change, even though he accepted the absence of time in the outermost heaven (258). He held time to be partly independent, because (1) no cosmic cycle could be taken as a universal standard of time lapse; (2) time is ubiquitous, whereas motion is local; (3) velocity among moving bodies is variable, unlike time; since the former is measured against the latter, time must be a constant (258-9). Aristotle accepted the coexistence of time and the cosmos, but he defined it as correlative. He seems everywhere to push for a semi-independent status of time, but his agreement with Plato stops him short of so doing, yielding his conclusion that “time is neither identical with movement nor capable of being separated from it.” He includes reflection and motion of the soul in his reading, thus arriving on the verge of teleological time; but he goes no further (259). Motion depends on position before and after; time depends on motion. “Before-and-afterness” is a temporal analogy to the spatial “behind-and-before” (259-60). It is thus only by analogy that time depends on motion and its dependents. Aristotle’s time is still physical time; he raised the question whether time exists independent of consciousness, and appears to answer in the negative. Therefore, he failed to discover teleological and thereby historical time. Like Plato, he did not distinguish between organic motion (growth) and physical motion (displacement), though he does not use organic motion as a measure of time since it is difficult to number. Limiting himself to physical time, he thus limited himself to cyclical time (260). When discussing organic motion, he focussed on decay rather than growth (260-1). However, his contribution of inward motion was a necessary step toward the Augustinian understanding of time.

Augustine discusses time in Confessiones book 11. Time was created with the rest of creation; before this, there was only the eternity of which God partakes (261). Augustine divides time into past, present, and future, states depending on transience. Time travels irreversibly from future through the present to into the past. Time is thus measured against human experience, hinted at but not explored in Aristotle’s change of the soul (261-2). It cannot, in fact, exist without human experience, as the present does not take up any time, and the past and the future cannot be said to exist at any time of speaking (262). Augustine refuses to rely on the motions of the heavenly bodies for either the definition or the measure of time, neither does he allow time as the measure of motion, since this consists in time being made up of spatial units (263). Time, he says, is a stretching out (distentio); and the object of this stretching appears to be the mind, since past, present, and future are contained in memoria, contuitus, and expectatio (263-4). The duration of time is quantified only in the act of remembering, beholding, or expecting. Thus time is “duration of creaturely existence.” This dependence on a consciousness capable of remembering, beholding, and anticipating explains how Augustine comes to teleological and historical time; these acts form no part of physical time, and only the soul knows history (264). For nature, time is either multidirectional or cyclical. This sets history apart from nature (264-5).

author: Dresbeck, LeRoy
title: Techne, labor et natura: Ideas and Active Life in the Medieval Winter
publication: Studies in Medieval and Renaissance History
abstract: This paper demonstrates in its depiction of medieval ways of surviving the winter that technology-only and society-inclusive approaches of the history of technology need not exclude each other. History of technology is also history of ideas (83-4). The later medieval technological revolution that fundamentally changed society coincided with an effort to improve winter conditions, thus yielding an aspect of society in which its change may be studied. Three approaches are possible: devices and processes; the impact of technology on the imagination; and patterns found in the synthesis of the first two (84). In the high Middle Ages, philosophers began to consider the effects of technology. Thus William of Conches (d. 1154) observed the creation of protection against the elements and claimed that it consisted of an imitation of nature. Hugh of St Victor advised on the construction of roofs in such a way as to prevent their structure collapsing under the weight of rainwater (85). Efforts to keep out the weather led to altered social relationships. Matters such as survival, fashion, and the seasonal organisation of life are therefore as important as a study of the tools (85-6). Early medieval Europe was a time of important technological developments, such as a significant increase in crop returns, though few contemporary writers commented on such changes (this was to change in the twelfth century) (86). For the earlier period, other methods were necessary. The plan (c. 820) for the monastery of St Gall, in present-day, Switzerland, shows how the Mediterranean pattern of monastery layout had to be altered to defend against the cold, including the first European evidence of a chimney (86-7). Prehistoric technological innovations, such as skis, skates, and trousers, convey little information about the societal values pressing for such changes. This changed in the Middle Ages. There are records of monks complaining of the cold in the scriptorium, which solidified the ink and made it difficult to hold one’s pen properly. Thus a quarter of the year’s work could be lost. Fourteenth-century illustrations show scribes with hand-protective gear (87-8). Domestic architecture generally was altered to shut out the cold and reduce draughts, while heating from within, all measures taken to enable the transplantation of the Mediterranean way of life to northern regions (88-9). While some innovations were Classical, the twelfth and thirteenth centuries were a time of great innovation as well as colder climate (89). Economic growth and urbanisation stimulated innovation. The twelfth-century renaissance was multi-faceted and included the harnessing of water- and wind-power. Such cooperation with natural forces showed that the environment need not be hostile, a new sentiment expressed in Roger Bacon’s thirteenth-century letters (89-90). A century later, Henry of Langenstein held that the craftsman’s improvements of the human conditions merited him with eternal life (90). Thus labour itself received a moral and a spiritual value, being both a way of strengthening the body and of improving existence; sin and poverty were grouped as similar evils (90-1). The need for survival was abandoned by theologians in favour of the doctrine of improvement of the human condition. Improved housing enabled wintertime labour instead of survival (91). Unprecedented urbanisation, population numbers, and economic growth enabled unprecedented specialisation. By this time, no-one could take care of all his needs (92). Later theologians compared the virtues and vices of various professions, expressing increased societal complexity but also the need and possibility for every individual to earn his salvation in this world. Occupational surnames became popular between 1150 and 1300 (92-3). By the thirteenth century, society had become highly organised, as illustrated by the introduction of the concordance and alphabetisation. Fireplaces and meal preparation gained an interest in the domestic situation, as seen in taxes (94-5). Between the twelfth and fourteenth centuries, technical manuals and books on technical processes made their appearance. Methodological study enabled a part-by-part analysis of the universe. The rate of innovation was higher during the Middle Ages than in the early Modern period [PS: according to your one source] (95-6). It has been claimed that Europeans became attached to “things and creatures possessed during one’s lifetime” between the twelfth and fifteenth centuries, signalling an increase in the joy of life. The material world was revaluated as essentially good. Empiricism allowed knowledge through the senses (96-7). In response to developing technologies, the default appeal to custom was superseded by a more dynamic legal system. An Aristotelian optimism with regard to the physical world superseded the Platonic distrust of things physical (97-8). Artists came to depict things, and technological developments led to changes in the vocabulary of, for instance, fireplaces (98-9). Clothing fashions gained the attention, and theologians decried this thing-centredness. Rather than a new focus on life in this world as opposed to the next, this world came to be regarded as the place in which to win salvation. The poverty-versus-luxury debate died down as conditions improved on the whole (99-101). Hugh of St Victor refers to marble firesides and panelled halls as places of temptation (101-2). In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, technology, labour, and nature converged in the public mind to affirm the physical world, which could be improved through institutional change (102-3). This is especially visible in the environment, as e.g. Hugh of St Victor identifies heat and humour as the two elements of physical life, the first of which brings life (103). The chimney found in the St Gall plan was first joined to a fireplace by trial and error about 1100. This entailed a multitude of difficulties involving the physics of draughts and non-flammable materials. The technology matured about the time it became crucial to defend against the worsening climate (103-4). As a rule, craftsmen were uneducated and relied on practical knowledge and trial and error, which may have made them more dynamic since they did not rely overly heavily on classical traditions (104-5). What technical manuals survive are more down-to-earth (less concerned with the supernatural) than scienctific works (105-6). Winter technology included distilling liquor and changes in dress such as form-fitting clothes made possible by the button (106). Households grew smaller at a time when smaller living- and working-spaces became the norm. Finding refuge in a back room was a practice known even in Italy, and reflects the innovation of the personal chamber. As a consequence of this chambering, privacy became a desired commodity; single, private land-holdings superseded the disordered life of the Viking Age in Britain (106-7). Among the social difficulties associated with urbanisation, complaints over architectural constructions designed to keep out the weather (and thus flood neighbouring plots) are notable (107-8). Chimneys entailed dangers of falling onto neighbouring properties as well as being fire hazards.The introduction of brick and plaster in the early thirteenth century was well timed to coincide with this problem. The chimney’s dependence on a wall led to the chambered house, which could therefore be more efficiently heated, even though much of the heat escaped through the chimney so that more fuel was required per square unit of floorspace. The introduction of plaster panelling and glass windows contributed to greater efficiency; and yet the growing population quickly deforested its environment (108-9). This process was reinforced by architectural developments. Coniferous trees gained the supremacy, since they produce wood more quickly. An energy crisis ensued in which the cost of transporting wood from far off formed the central problem (109-10). Charcoal and then coal took the place of wood as a fuel. Coal became so widespread that the late thirteenth century saw the regulation of air pollution. As the climate grew colder and more humid, peasant houses came to be raised on boots. At the end of the medieval period, nightclothes came into use for the first time since their abandonment in the late Roman period. Fumigation came into use as a measure against the pest. As newly-gained wealth widened the gap between rich and poor, moralists came to dwell on the poor people’s suffering from cold (110-12). Documentary sources leave gaps in the information about the age (112-13). The winter season made little impact on art. Representations come mainly from the artist’s imagination, e.g. labourers carrying wood. Snow was sometimes personified in the thirteenth century. The early fifteenth century, when the Little Ice Age intensified, saw a sudden rise in the depictions of winter. Snowfights and snowmen occur, in one instance with one of the participants barefoot. Transportation, the feeding of animals, and other scenes expressive of positive feeling towards winter are found [footnote refers to examples]. Architectural developments such as chimneys, fireplaces, and glass windows may be traced through art. This very art could also be more easily produced in winter thanks to improved technology (114). Man’s active influencing of his environment in this way served to blur the distinction between the natural and the artificial, and reduce the enmity between man and nature (115). Technology between the end of Classical era and the beginning of the Industrial Revolution has served to improve the conditions of life through a better interaction between nature and society (115-16). The manipulation of nature became the foundation of the Western eclipsing of Chinese technology, and led to the conception of the present world as a pleasant place. The historian must study not only the technology but also the mindset of the age (116-17).

author: Dresbeck, LeRoy
title: Winter Climate and Society in the Northern Middle Ages: The Technological Impact
publication: On Pre-modern Technology and Science: A Volume of Studies in Honour of Lynn White, Jr.
eds: Bert S. Hall and Delno C. West
abstract: Cold weather represented an incentive for (protective) technology in the Middle Ages, as adjusting ones’s environment to increase comfort allowed for greater activity during the winter months. Conversely, scholars may study protective technology to gauge medieval temperatures, which are otherwise encoded in subjective accounts (177). In the course of the Middle Ages, the Mediterranean garden monastery found its way to northern Europe as a series of closed-off buildings, some of whose rooms were heated (178). “The debilitating effect of the cold was one of the major themes in the literature of Northern Europe in the Middle Ages,” such that Brendan’s Isle of Delights was invented out of longing for a place without winter. Ausonius (fourth century) complained of the cold of southern Gaul, while Bishop Daniel of Winchester in 732 pointed out that Christianity came from warm lands, while pagans held the frozen north. Early ascetics favoured the cold as a way of mortifying the flesh (see esp. endnote 15); in the high medieval period, authors were interested not in the cosmic implications of winter but instead described its effects on their bodies. “Thus, aversion to wintertime was a common theme in medieval literature” (179). Classical motifs expressing the same sentiment were often employed in the Middle Ages, but these later accounts convey the notion that man is not helpless but can improve his situation: Ausonius in the fourth century finds no hearth warm enough but in later times, heating is considered essential to one’s well-being (178–9). A 1255 letter in August orders the covering of masonry against the winter. Thus timely preparation was indispensible to make it through the winter successfully. Winter preparation was hard work, and a Parisian relief suggests “how depressing medieval people found the winter season.” Hell included the extremes of cold (179). Cold weather was considered a bad time for certain medical treatments, while several types of disease had a stronger presence in winter and lack of certain food types lessened resistance (179–80). When safe from all these dangers, winter was the best time to work in the forest, hunt, and win construction sand from beaches. In wetland areas, it was the best time for travel. Social life thrived when labours were less demanding. Many types of work, including that requiring dexterity of the fingers such as writing, were difficult in winter (endnote 34 cites several examples of ink freezing and/or drying more slowly because of the cold). Economic growth was greater in warmer areas [these few sentences seem somewhat confused, PS]. Recent studies have shown that climate worsened in the course of the thirteenth century (180). Praepositinus of Cremona associated spring with wantonness, summer with greed, autumn with pride/arrogance, and winter with unreliability. The increase in rain as the climate worsened required technical solutions around the house. “Contrary to common belief, the late autumn and winter were the seasons when people were best fed during the Middle Ages, and this corresponded to the period when climate made its greatest demand upon the human body.” The introduction of new foods and agricultural techniques, as well as the distilling of liquor, made winter survival easier. Clothes developed in similar ways (181; see endnotes 39–45 for detailed references, particularly note 41 on the consumption of meat at various times of year). House construction developed to insulate, reduce draught, and increase heating sources. The thirteenth century was pivotal in these developments (181–2 and endnotes 47–61). Private rooms made their appearance in the twelfth century, following the advent of chimneys and individually heated rooms. The development of the chimney is traced (182–6). Because of chimney and private rooms, thirteenth-century scribes could work throughout the winter (185). “A study of the medieval winter is more than a chronology of past climates. It involved the entire spectrum of intellectual and social life” (187). This article has extensive endnotes well worth following up.

author: Dubois, Marguerite-Marie
title: Le Rondeau du Coucou
publication: La Ronde des saisons: Les saisons dans la littérature et la société anglaises au Moyen Age
abstract: Introduces the biological oddities and the etymology of cuckoo (16-17), and points out that the bird connoted the joy of natural renewal in ME, but in OE it simply embodies the end of winter (17; this is introduced as quite the contrast). Seafarer and Husband’s Message associate the cuckoo with melancholy: the former because its protagonist contrasts past comforts on land with the coming discomforts and dangers of life at sea. Thus while the bird is recognised as sumeres weard, it conveys the sad message of solitary departure into a dangerous environment, thus contrasting with its ME connotations (17-18). Sumer in fact refers to a 90-day period from 9 May to 6 August (18), while OE knew a bipartite spring, foreweard lencten or middlewærd and æfterweard lencten (18-19). ME sumer, announced by the cuckoo, is not “l’été véritable” but rather late spring (19). After discussing a number of linguistic features of Sumer is icumen in, the hypothesis is launched that the scribe of this poem in its known form was a Germanic speaker, perhaps a Fleming (19-20).

author: Enkvist, Nils Erik
title: The Seasons of the Year: Chapters on a Motif from Beowulf to The Shepherd’s Calendar
abstract:
Chronology has always been based either on natural change or on the movements of heavenly bodies. Many northern tribes have, wholly unconnected, used half-years. Indo-Europeans have been argued to have had the same practice, but evidence is questionable. Early Indian and Greek texts have three seasons, Greek sometimes four. The Greek words were first based on such natural circumstances as the time for warfare, but as science developed came to be fixed by the stars. Hiems and ver seem to be the only Latin seasons derived from PIE. Purely philological evidence is warned against (1-2). Words for summer and winter are the only season words present in all Germanic langages. Scandinavian vár, vår “spring” derive from Sanskrit vasar, Latin ver; but most other Gmc languages have a cognate of lencten. Autumn is hærfest or haust. Icelanders used misseri, half-years, long into the Christian era. Winters were used for counting years; and a northern tradition of debates between summer and winter existed, although these of course were greatly influenced by classical tradition (3). It is pointed out that Tacitus’s three Gmc seasons need not correspond to the Roman frame; and his reference to autumni bona suggests that he was thinking of harvest rather than a season. Bede speaks of two seasons. The Eddas do not, but they may contain much later influence. ON summer and winter are represented by giants; autumn and spring are not. A case can be made for two original seasons, but it is also possible that a third original season was first lost; in any case it was Roman learning that brought the spread of today’s system (4). “Anglo-Saxon heroic poetry was strongly preoccupied with winter; apparently the year was divided into two main seasons, a grim season that furnished poets with much excellent material, and a pleasant season whose delights were not as a rule thought worthy of poetic treatment.” Prose and Christian poetry introduced the other seasons. Lencten became ambiguous when it adopted the second meaning “Lent”; hærfest was similarly polysemous. These two seasons had no unambiguous reference for centuries (5). We cannot know much about the Anglo-Saxon climate (5-6). The rigid nature of OE poetry may have rendered it slow to adopt any new themes. Thus the grim, wintery vocabulary of OE poetry could not easily adjust itself to the Continental tradition of spring and summer poetry (7-8). Emile Pon has argued that in contrast to Eddic poetry, OE verse takes a rationalistic approach, so that “myth and metaphysical conjecture” are absent, while realism abounds. The focus on death and judgement day is illustrated by means of winter imagery. OE poetry was strong in realism but lacked finesse in abstract description; winter was the most concrete of seasons and could therefore best bear description, while the other seasons take abstract adjectives (8-9). Bwf is preoccupied with pagan events, but lacks the metaphysics of Eddic poetry of the same genre; instead, it uses landscape and organic descriptions to set a mood (9). Winter is the season most referred to in Bwf; but synecdoches for “year” are of no relevance. In the Finnsburh episode, the description of the passing of winter makes sense from a chronological and explanatory point of view, so that no passion for spring may be distilled (9-10). The dissolution of the sword is further likened to the melting season; God is mentioned as the agent working this change. Winter is always described in vigorous terms; spring is denoted with “weak generalizations. . . . Pretty passages on a friendly nature were not in fashion. . . . In Beowulf, there are thus no regular seasons in the modern sense of the word: there are only violent changes in nature. Weather, day and night were much more significant than the seasons of the year” (11). Wdr and Sfr primarily describe inner weather not outer weather; they stand between the two traditions of Germanic epic and lyric. Seasons are used to illustrate mood rather than to explain physical action. Wdr brings in winter as an intensifier of the exile’s suffering. Sfr has the first unambiguous contrast between mood and season in English: “the spring only heightens his cares” (lines 48ff.). Other heroic poems contain few references to the seasons (11-14). Saints’ lives contain rather traditional season references. Descriptions of the pleasing seasons are first found in religious writings such as Christ, Andreas, and Daniel. Only The Phoenix has non-winter contribute to the poem’s dominant theme (Enkvist 14-22). These writings show the Anglo-Saxons finally adopting Continental themes (22-4).

[appendix II on lencten and spring:] Lencten in BT mostly refers to spring; but legal and later religious prose use it to mean Lent. Many instances of this latter usage are cited, as are poetic instances where it means “spring.” Enkvist concludes thay “Old English lencten, a West-Germanic word related to German Lenz, acquired a special religious sense and became ambiguous. This explains the reluctance of many Middle English poets to use it in their descriptions of spring” (197). A list is provided of “selected instances of words for ‘Spring’ and ‘Autumn’” from 1480 onwards (198-210).

author: Fischer, Andreas
title: Sumer is icumen in: The Seasons of the Year in Middle English and Early Modern English
abstract: The four OE seasonal terms underwent a number of changes after the OE period. Thus sumer was extended to include spring (79). Words for summer and winter have known hardly any variant forms, contrary to spring and autumn. Polysemy of lenten and harvest made these terms unstable. New words for spring include borrowings; metonymy; and a combination of metonymy and metaphor (79-86). It is proposed that the eventual success of spring and fall is due to their identity as members of the third group. Spring will have come about in a drag-chain due to the narrowing sense of lent, while fall appears to be the result of a push-chain by analogy with spring (86). Digital corpora show that Chaucer used the narrowed-down sense of lent only, while he further uses ver and prime temps; Shakespeare uses Ver in a personified way only (88-9). The division into four seasons has an astronomical basis in the equinoxes and solstices, and a natural basis in mid-latitude, but there the time of transfer does not correspond; southern and central European cultures will have attached most importance to the agricultural cycle, which favours four seasons: “growth/planting, maturation, decay/harvesting and rest.” Accordingly, most European languages know four seasons (89). Polar regions, on the other hand, know a two-way natural distinction primarily based on sunlight. Linguistic evidence and Tacitus suggest that a bipartite division was original, after which spring and autumn were introduced in that order. “By the time of the earliest written records the Germanic languages had acquired four-season systems, but there were, and are, remnants of the older two-season one.” Further evidence of the bipartite system consists in the general Germanic stability of terms for summer and winter as opposed to those for the other seasons (90).

author: Frandon, Véronique
title: Iconographie des saisons dans l’Occident médiéval
abstract: While modern man no longer has a use for the seasonal cycle, medieval representations are rare but diverse. Greek tradition knew the three horai “hours,” young goddesses who served as guardians of crops and fertility, embodying the passing of time. They are typically represented dancing in a circle, and they are told apart by their attributes. In the fifth to fourth centuries BCE, these three hours came to be assimilated into the four seasons, which were based on the two solstices and equinoxes. This rationalised view of the seasons spread gradually through the sciences, but it did not fully take over until the Roman period. The first representations of the four seasons differed little from those of the hours, but they occurred in more varied domains. In Roman times, the seasons occurred in various contexts, and depictions were based on the Hellenistic tradition of female personifications, whether dancing or standing with attributes. They were also found engaged in agricultural activities, under influence of the calendar tradition (2). Christian art developed a tradition of funerary depictions of the seasons, representing phases of earthly life. The medieval world adopted the four seasons in many contexts, such as poetry, courtly literature, agricultural treatises, medical texts, exegetical texts (esp. on Genesis), and encyclopedic literature. The seasons received a place in the framework of microcosm-macrocosm, the four elements and humours, the ages of man, and the cardinal directions. Most representations of the seasons are to be found in this varied scientific domain, often as diagrams rather than redundant illustrations (3). The remainder of the article discusses two pictures. The first (p. 2) is dated to c. 1450 and contains five characters, four of which are engaged in agricultural activities while the fifth sits indoors by the fire. Their activities connect them with September-October, October-November, June-July, January-February, and winter (3-5). Spring is conspicuously absent. This may be explained by positing that man and his labour are central, rather than the agricultural cycle: spring is traditionally depicted by characters holding vegetables, the diversions of the higher classes, or sometimes by farmers working the vine (5). The second image (c. 1490-5) consists of four frames, vertically juxtaposed, ranging from spring to winter. The text it illustrates dwells long on changes in nature and animal behaviour. This image appears to evoke the slow decline of human life as it approaches death, thus abandoning the cyclical basis (6-7). Medieval seasonal depictions illustrate man’s submission to the earth and the seasons, their attempts to govern the space and rhythm of the passing of time, and their progressive mastery of nature, thus allowing for contemplation and emotion (7).

author: Frandon, Véronique
title: Les saisons et leurs représentations dans les encyclopédies du Moyen Age: l'exemple du De universo de Raban Maur (1022-1023)
publication: L’enciclopedismo medievale: Atti del convegno “L’enciclopedismo medievale,” San Gimignano, 8-10 ottobre 1992
abstract: Studies illustrations of the seasons in Rabanus Maurus’s encyclopedia De universo for their meaning beyond the text as well as the relationships between text and image. Schemata are left unconsidered because they are “diagrammised thought,” direct illustrations of the text (55). As in calendars, the seasons in De universo are represented rather by human activities than by personifications and attributes, though they coexist, as when people are depicted holding vegetables or tools characteristic of the season. This represents a transitional phase between the classical personification and the medieval agricultural labours. These images deserve to be studied both for their particular representation and because the pictures occur twice, which is surprising given the rarity of the theme in medieval art [?]. The seasons are represented in book 10, chapter 1 and again in chapter 11 (56). Chapter 1 is entitled De temporibus. The image occurs between two columns, namely the table of contents and the beginning of chapter one, and is bordered below by the end of the page. The encyclopedia is illustrated in the manner of scrolls, with images at the end of the column (57). Chapter 1 discusses the division of time, suggesting it may be mastered. Time is divided according to nature, custom, and authority, human and divine, but especially divine (58). The word for season is everywhere tempus until the twelfth century. Saison is a twelfth-century coinage, from Latin satio < serere “to sow.” The text around this image concerns the division of time as a whole, and cannot justify the depiction of the four seasons alone (63). Genesis 1.14 uses tempora, here understood by Augustine as the four seasons, and so medieval commentators avoided the ambiguity of the word by falling back onto Augustine, who understood the seasons as cosmic movements rather than durations of time (63-4). The four seasons form a contrast with the single, constant season of eternity. By the Middle Ages, agricultural labours had come to symbolise the cycle of changes and the labour required of postlapsarian man (64). Thus the first image is a blend of the time of Genesis with the time representing the four seasons to which man is subjected (64-5). Spring is depicted as a young man in noble dress holding leafy branches, symbolising fertility. He stands in no relation to the other characters [PS: and there is no circularity]: this is where the procession begins. The soul on which he stands both sets him apart and suggests the earth from which spring derives its fruits. Dress and attributes make this, perhaps, a triumphant entry (65). The next character is bearded, signalling maturity, harvesting wheat; he represents summer. He holds a sickle. His short tunic is fastened around the waste so as not to hinder him. Like spring, who was en trois quarts, this figure, in profile, faces right, and his sickle touches the vine of the autumn scene, emphasising continuity. He looks towards the next figure, and wheat and vine appear to stand on the same soil; the plants touch (65-6). Autumn is as young as spring, simply dressed in a red garment. He is perched on a branch of the tree in which there grows a vine, picking grapes, with bare legs and feet. He is spatially lifted above the other characters, in contrast with his humble dress (66). The tree is the pivot of the image, forming a vertical axis, separating spring and summer from winter. However, the linear image is not disrupted. The vine serves to distribute, divide into groups. The grape-picker serves as a bridge, preventing an opposition. His bright dress draws the reader’s eye upward, while the basket along the trunk guides it back down. The ascent coincides with nature’s full maturity (66-7). This scene would have had spiritual connotations to the monastic mind. The tree links heaven and earth as by a ladder, allowing one to ascend to God. It may also symbolise the virtuous life. It may suggest the similarity between crescere and credere [!]. It may furthermore evoke Zacchaeus climbing a tree to see Christ’s entry into Jerusalem. Finally, it may evoke the tree of life, the cross, and Christ (67-8). The grape-picker may be harvesting the fruits of good works that will lead him to eternal life. The true vine is Christ (John 15.1), which makes the harvest his Passion. This tree and vine entangled symbolise the Crucifixion above all, which, like the combination of tree and vine, has regenerative meaning: one dies so that the other may live (68). At the same time, the Eucharist is evoked by the proximity of wheat and grapes. The bunches of grapes and the ears of wheat have roughly the same shape and colour; the grape basket has the elongated shape of a cup. The tree’s touching of the text “de dominice die” and the picker’s stooping position are also suggestive of the Eucharist. Thus Christ, the Passion, and the Eucharist are brought together and associated with summer and autumn (69). These harvesting-and-picking scenes resemble the “Tellus” tradition as found in a Pisa Exultet, a hymn song on Holy Saturday. This illustration accompanies the text of the earth’s rejoicing over the driving away of darkness (69-70). Traditionally, a female personification is used; but in the Pisa manuscript, the labours of wheat and vine are illustrated (70). The two pictures have a lot in common. Are the labours here advertised, in view of the economic developments of the tenth and eleventh centuries? These activities were central both economically and spiritually (70-1). Winter is, again, bearded, pushing a plough. The picture expresses difficulty of labour, as though representing the labour imposed on man after the killing of Abel [PS: ?] (71-2). This scene takes up the greatest space, a whole column, underlining the importance of the earth. This downward focus contrasts with the previous scene, while the sterility of the winter scene connotes death. The activity, however, foreshadows a new beginning. Man labours his field for it to be fertilised by the word of God, thus attaining salvation. But winter is long [it takes up a great deal of horizontal space] (72). This image, both simple in form and rich in its implications, may symbolise Creation (spring), the Passion (summer and autumn), and the awaiting of Judgement Day (winter), thus encompassing time as created and ordered by God, and pertaining to man (72-3). This accords with the spirit of Rabanus’s work, since he dwells long on the division of time according to the divine will. To him, the future is purely eschatological. In chapter 11, however, he associates with each of the seasons a Christian allegory: spring represents life, summer the future blessedness, autumn the final judgement, and winter death. The circular timeframe of the seasons is thus applied to the linear time of Christian history. Frandon’s reading of the image differs little from this perspective [PS:!]. In both image and text, a desire is found to express a Christian, linear, purposeful time through natural, circular time. The second image is situated at the start of chapter 11, entitled “De vicissitudinibus temporum,” and uses the right-hand column and margin of the page (73). The chapter tells of the four seasons and their participation of the four qualities of dry and humid, hot and cold, and follows Isidore’s etymologies. The seasons are also associated with the cardinal directions and are in this characterised by different states of vegetation rather than by human labours. But Rabanus Maurus adds a symbolic reading: spring corresponds to baptism and the resurrection; summer prefigures the future blessedness and the burning of the faith; autumn is Judgement Day (harvest of souls); and winter is the time of death, of mankind’s last tribulations [PS: NB that the seasons here lose their proper sequence] [cf. Jacobus de Voragine, see note 49] (74). The image consists of four characters in close horizontal alignment, engaged in agricultural activities much like those of the previous illustration (74-5). The left-hand character, spring, shown en face, holds vegetables and flowers in his hands. His frontal position is emphasised by his being closer in perspective, i.e. his feet reach lower than those of the others. Unlike the spring figure of the previous image, he is not in motion. The branches he holds do, however represent a beginning, life, and rebirth. Summer is harvesting wheat en profil. Although he is turned to the right and has a bent knee as though moving, his posture is not as dynamic as that in the previous image. He appears to represent the reaper of good works awaiting Judgement Day (75). Autumn, á trois quarts, carries a jug of wine on his shoulder and a basket of grapes in his hand. This is not quite traditional: one would expect him in the process of picking grapes. All the same, the grapes, his bare legs, and his tunic fastened round the waist express activity. His á trois quarts position expresses motion, and serves to display his attributes rather than his activity; it also contrasts with the two en profile characters surrounding him. The jug and his arm, holding it, form a disruption of the image and its narration. With his jug near the ears of wheat and his basket near the winter-character, this part of the image serves as a centre. Does it again suggest the Eucharist? (75-6) Rabanus associates autumn with Judgement Day. This may be expressed by the basket of grapes. The figure’s stretching it towards the winter figure prevents the interruption of the narrative suggested by his posture. Winter is hoeing. He is the only character not standing straight up. This, and his bare legs and fastened tunic, express activity. However, here too his movement is limited (76). His bending-over suggests the decline of death. This succession of seasons has a beginning and an end (76-7). Text and image thus combine well to suggest the real (labours) and symbolic (typological) modes of the seasons. The uniformity of this image and the lack of movement suggests that time is ordered, mastered. However, alternation and succession are also suggested, for instance in the en profile-appearance of the solstitial seasons versus the more static positions of the equinoctal ones. Both linear and circular time are thus expressed. Rather than being redundant, the two depictions of the seasons represent different things: the first a binary understanding of time (youth-old age; high-low), the second circularity (77). The first has more symbolic meaning (77-8). These images show that the early eleventh century was a time in between the classical circular understanding of time and the medieval linear reading (78).

author: Granlund, John
title: Veckoräckning och veckoår
abstract: Southern Sweden used to count in weeks rather than months and days from 25 March to 36 June on the Julian calendar, i.e. during agricultural spring. These weeks were counted backwards. Each week was associated with specific agricultural tasks, while taboos rested on specific tasks in others. Michaelmas to Christmas knew a similar week-system, probably used for weather prognostications in the following agricultural spring weeks. Similar week-systems existed in Iceland, German Silesia, Estonia, and Karelia. Unlike the system in Sweden, Germany, and the Baltic, which began their year on 25 December, Iceland began it in the second week of April. Iceland also differed in its limited agricultural significance, for which reason it based its calendar on political events instead. Quarter-year units were important, at least in Iceland and southern Sweden. The week-year must have been common throughout northern Europe, and formed around the time when “the Roman and German names of the week days were fused to a certain unity.” Differences within Sweden are explained by different agricultural cycles. In Iceland and Norway, trade and animal husbandry were economically dominant, for which reason the start of the year was shifted four weeks ahead, starting the year with the spring quarter [PS: cf. Nordberg]. At the introduction of the Julian calendar, the Swedish year probably started a quarter earlier, namely at the autumnal equinox. The backward counting makes sense when, and must be based on, the rune-stick calendar. Week-counting became irrelevant with the introduction of the Julian calendar.

author: Greenfield, Stanley B.
title: Sylf, Seasons, Structure and Genre in The Seafarer
abstract: Begins with an analysis of sylf (35b; Greenfield 199-206). Then notes that the winter image of 31-3a is a description of land not sea. “At this moment for the speaker there is nothing happy about the way of the world for even the fortunate non-sea-voyager”; worldly life is transient and the speaker is part of that transience: his voyage leads to heavenly permanence. His epiphany or conversion is imitated by the poem’s structure: “the seafaring and homiletic halves” may be seen “as the objective correlative for the speaker’s experience” (206-7). The winter in the poem is literal and triggers the speaker’s “recognition of his own mortality.” The spring that follows is also literal [cf. Enkvist 11-14], and 53-5a provide a summer image because the cuckoo is called “sumores weard” [PS: but it arrives in spring! See Anderson 1997, 2003 et al.]. The homiletic half of the poem provides a symbolic autumn in its image of the world’s decline and the ageing of man (208). The winter imagery also serves to connote the fall of man, which, after all, introduced change of season. Winter commonly signifies mankind’s sinfulness. Spring represents the regeneration of salvation, summer refers to hardship on man’s voyage (since the cuckoo is sad of voice), and autumn illustrates the impotence of worldly ways (208-9). The poem is judged to have affinities with penitence, apocalypse, and wisdom literature (209-10).

author: Gunnell, Terry
title: The Coming of the Christmas Visitors. . . Folk Legends Concerning the Attacks on Icelandic Farmhouses Made by Spirits at Christmas
abstract: Indexes a number of types involving supernatural creatures returning to a farm every Christmas Eve, often posing a danger to its residents. The motif is found to have developed in two different forms in Iceland and Norway, and it was also known in the other North Atlantic islands but not or hardly on the mainland of the British Isles. The tradition’s relationship to the Beowulf/Grendel narrative is also noted.

author: Gunnell, Terry
title: Ritual Space. Ritual Year. Ritual Gender: A View of the Old Norse and New Icelandic Ritual Year
publication: First International Conference of the SIEF Working Group on the Ritual Year: Proceedings. Malta, March 20-24 2005
abstract: Explains the ritual year in Iceland as a movement from the inside, the family, and the feminine (winter) to the outside and the masculine (summer). Summer festivities are longer in duration, further apart from one another, and take place all day, whereas winter events take place in the evening are are usually over by midnight. Early winter and midwinter were associated with prophecy, a “liminal time” at which one could peek into other worlds and the future. Midnight has the same associations (295-6).

author: Gunnell, Terry
title: The Seasons of the Dísir: The Winter Nights, and the Dísablót in Early Scandinavian Belief
abstract: After an introduction into the nature of Old Norse written sources (117-21), Gunnell presents ritual evidence, starting with Procopius’s account of the festival anticipating the sunrise in the northernmost regions of Thule (121-2). The eleventh-century Thietmar of Merseburg and Adam of Bremen refer to festivals occurring in Lejre, Denmark, and Uppsala, respectively, comprising sacrifices and taking place every nine years. Thietmar refers to January, while a scholium to Adam speaks of the vernal equinox. The latter says it was dedicated to Þórr, but Saxo says it concerned Freyr (122). Ágrip claims that Óláfr Tryggvason’s conversion included substituting Christmas, Easter, St John’s Eve, and Michaelmas feasting for pagan sacrifices. This suggests a spread of pre-Christian ritual feasts through the year around these dates, and Ynglinga saga confirms this picture by speaking of a sacrifice at the start of winter, at midwinter, and the start of summer (122-4). Elsewhere in Heimskringla, in Hákonar saga góða, Snorri refers to a sacrificial feast at the vetrnætr and the celebration of jól (124). The three feasts of Ynglinga saga are repeated in Ólafs saga helga (124-5). The Gulaþingslög enforces the brewing of special ale both at Christmas and at the vetrnætr (125). Thus there seem to have been three main seasonal feasts in pre-Christian times, all of which were morphed into Christian feasts without great difficulty (125-6). Winter began on the Saturday between 10-16 October on the Julian calendar; and its typical morph into All Hallows suggests that it originally took place in late October, i.e. about the time of the Gaelic Samhain. Since the Scandinavian year was bipartite, the Winter Nights were both a beginning and an end (126-7). They lasted for three nights, and Gunnell refers to Árni Björnsson for the idea that these belonged to neither season, summer ending on a Wednesday and winter beginning on a Saturday [PS: surely this contradicts the computistical works? Check. cf. also Bocarbót p. 78, which makes clear at least that all days are accounted for in the month-reckoning]. The vetrnætr involved a feast with friends and family, the slaughter of animals, and weddings; but they appear to have been semi-public, invitation-only affairs. While games were played, the core of the feast seems to have been conducted indoors, and concerned sacrifice (128-9). Gísla saga links the vetrnætr with Freyr; but two other Íslendingasögur refer to the dísir, here defined as “minor goddesses” with male characteristics and close affinities with the valkyrjar and fylgjur (129-30). Þiðranda þáttr ok Þorhalls gives the impression that the vetrnætr were invite-only feasts involving sacrifice, in which a distinction is drawn between inside and outside, outside being dangerous territory, and in which the dísir could assist or endanger depending on whether they received due tribute (131-3). Swedish evidence rather links the dísir to spring festivals (133-5). Thus it may be concluded that two festivals existed, both dedicated to horse-riding dísir moving in from the wild, situated at the coming of winter and the coming of spring/summer, involving the entire nation and sacrifice (135). Festivals regularly came to centre around Christmas, when also the Scandinavian jolareia (“Christmas Ride of the Dead”) is believed to take place, sometimes led by a female figure (135-6). Grýla-traditions provide an interesting parallel (see Gunnell 2001) (136-8). In conclusion, the winter period in Scandinavia seems to have been under the power of female spirits governing over life and death.
