Their sex may be explained by winter and the home belonging to women, while summer and the outdoors belonged to men (138-9).

author: Hanscom, Elizabeth Deering
title: The Feeling for Nature in Old English Poetry
publication: Journal of English and Germanic Philology
abstract: A Romantic article cataloguing and assessing OE poetic references to nature, hoping to prove that "feeling for nature" existed before the Conquest. Discusses the respective attention paid to each of the seasons, flowers, plants, grass, trees, storm and foul weather, rain, dew, mist, moors and fens, mountains and hills, sun, moon, stars, specific periods of the day, the sky, and clouds. Notes the emphasis on winter, and states of OE poets that “if they did not write of the calmer months with equal force, it was because of lack of poetic feeling, not of poetic ability. The fact seems to be that they were impressed only by stern and rough manifestations; when the great harp of nature was struck with sufficient strength, when the icy hand of winter smote the clanging strings, then they lifted up their voices and sang with glee of wailing wind and surging ocean.” “Winter” is used synecdochically for “year,” but also in compounds as an intensifier: winterceald, winterbiter, winterrim, winterscur (446). The sun, however, is a popular and praised subject; but only for its light, not its heat (455-8).

author: Hansen, Finn
title: Naturbeskrivende indslag i Gísla saga Súrssonar
abstract: A brief article demonstrating that nature description in Gísla serves two general purposes: an informative purpose (explaining social circumstances, e.g. it is light out so a rider can easily be recognised) and an “antithetical dramatising” purpose (disquiet among men but quiet in nature foreshadows catastrophe).

author: Harding, Wendy
title: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight as a Winter’s Tale
publication: La Ronde des saisons: Les saisons dans la littérature et la société anglaises au Moyen Age
abstract: SGGK’s winter setting is uncommon in Arthurian romance. The seasons in this work have been studied with regard to the ages of man, pathetic fallacy, and Celtic tradition [see footnotes]. In additional to their philosophical functions, the seasons in SGGK portray a contrast between nature and civilisation. Both these readings are part of the composition, but neither of them is final (69). Pearsall and Salter capitalised on the seasons as mirroring human life (69-70). Late medieval courtly literature represents the seasons as dividing the classes of society, with peasants suffering in harsh seasons while the nobility rest in comfort (see, e.g., the Très riches heures of Jean, Duc de Berry, verbally echoed in SGGK) (70). In its miniatures, January shows the aristocratic New Year, which is depicted as though summer is celebrated in the mansions of the rich (70-1). February, by contrast, depicts winter’s scarcity by the portrayal of peasants working out of doors. Whereas the seasons shape and determine the peasant’s rhythm, it is feasts that provide the rhythm of the aristocratic life, seasons being a distant backdrop. In the August miniature, it has been argued, the peasants really inhabit the open space, while the courtiers exist in a frame of their own, passing through (71). The New Year’s Day description of Guenevere rivals the January miniature of the Très riches heures (71-2). The descriptions of Arthur’s court on this day suggest the joys of spring rather than winter (“for all wat3 þis fayre folk in her first age”) (72). Analogues to seasonal description as gathered by Elisabeth Brewer invariably link spring with youth, play, and merriment (72-3). The New Year’s scene in SGGK inverts the memento mori that winter should be, suggesting that Camelot has the power to govern the seasons. The next Christmas, the castle of Hautdesert expresses the same notions; Gawain in his new garment is even said to resemble the spring (73-4). “Courtly life excludes not only the churlish but also all signs of winter, old age, and decay.” However, Gawain’s promise to the Green Knight forces him to leave this paradisical environment and subjects him to the forces of nature. The inescapable coming of winter is expressed in ll. 527-31 (74). This suggests the transitory nature of all things earthly. Gawain’s departure brings sadness into the otherwise untouched sphere of Camelot, and yet the knights continue to speak merrily (75). The Green Knight is considered a representative of the savage, and thus a threat to Camelot. Gawain travels through unfamiliar countries, but his greatest enemy is said to be the winter (ll. 726-32) (76). Gawain thus suffers like the peasants in the February miniature, plus alienation from his surroundings. During his last night in Hautdesert before the meeting with the knight, he is aware of the winter weather outside. At the Green Chapel, Gawain adds to the oppositions inside:outside, summer:winter, civilisation:wild the new opposition of godly:diabolical (77). The Green Knight’s appearance is a blend of noble and wild, but the court at Camelot identify him according to his otherliness (78). In the Green Knight, then, the poet brings together qualities that are supposed to be mutually exclusive, and it is inside the familiar castle that Gawain undergoes his biggest test (78-9). Gawain’s failure to acknowledge his aunt Morgan la Faye in the lady’s chaperone may be explained by the courtly exclusion of death and ugliness in favour of youth and beauty. According to the Secretum secretorum, “[summer] is likenyd to the spouse that is faire and pleasaunt in hir parfite age”; in winter, “the aire and the tyme waxeth blak, and the erthe is like to a womman of grete age, naked, and in decrepitude nygh to deth.” When Gawain sees his failure in courtly behaviour, he seems to anticipate exile from the summer of the court (79). Since the court can only be merry, it has to laugh off Gawain’s fault by joking about the green baldric he wears as a token of his infidelity. To Gawain, his meeting with the Green Knight has ended his springtime; but the court try to dispel his winter mood with laughter, since it is an element alien to Camelot (80). Neither has the final word: the poem ends by reference to Christ’s crown of thorns, showing that suffering and bliss are necessary and complementary elements of salvation. To the court, their Christmas feasting is an assertion of their victory over the winter season rather than a spiritual feast. In the poet’s final words, then, New Year’s Day is both an end and a beginning, nature’s death and the birth of Christ. The court’s binary understanding of the world is limited, but the reader is invited to take the wider, Christian view (81).

author: Harrison, Kenneth
title: The Moon and the Anglo-Saxon Calendar
publication: The Framework of Anglo-Saxon History to A.D. 900
abstract: Describes the pre-Christian calendar as first lunar, then lunar-solar.

author: Hartshorne, Richard
title: Six Standard Seasons of the Year
publication: Annals of the Association of American Geographers
abstract: Astronomical seasonal definitions are of little use to the individual, whose definition of a season is largely temperature-based (166). The four seasons were inherited from Classical usage in the Mediterranean, where the winter lasted for only 2.5 to four months (166-7). The non-frozen part of the year was originally subdivided into the season of growth and the rest, but eventually a third warm season, autumn, was recognised (167). Transposed to northern Europe, this definition results in rather different seasons, in which the summer corresponds in temperature to the Mediterranean spring and autumn, the autumn corresponds to winter, and the winter corresponds to nothing at all; between winter and spring, there is a quarter-year period in which nothing will grow yet, which corresponds to the Mediterranean winter (167-8). This new meaning of the four seasons served well, but if standardisation is sought, more than four seasons are required to recognise the seasons in the various regions. Four kinds of season may be defined on a temperature base, namely cold (below zero), cool (zero to ten), warm (ten to twenty), and hot (above twenty) (168). This scheme may be expanded by adding “dead winter” (below -10) and a season of over 30 Celsius (168-9), but these do not apply to important [!] parts of the world. By the four-way definition, most European nations have three season types (but forming a sequence of four seasons), while other localities have only one or two season types; very few have all four (169). Only the Da regions go through a succession of six seasons (but four seasonal types) per annum (173). For lack of better terms, early and late may be added: thus the Da sequence is “the early warm season, the hot season, the latter warm season, the early cool season, the cold season, and the latter cool season” (173-4). This six-season cycle is particularly useful in comparing differences within a single Köpper-type, where differences may exist in the duration of the respective seasons (174).

author: Hastrup, Kirsten
title: Temporal Categories
publication: Culture and History in Medieval Iceland
abstract: Time is both a universal and a cultural, society-bound dimension. This chapter studies cultural time in Iceland. Time-reckoning was defined in 1920 by Nilsson as “the continuous counting of the time-units,” a use preceded by “time-indications,” which is “a discontinuous way of measuring time on the basis of concrete phenomena of nature” (17). Phenomena by which time is measured are heavenly movements and progressions of nature. These natural phenomena are integrated into social conceptions of time (18). This chapter attempts to reconstruct early Icelandic time categories and demonstrate the social binding of time (19). The solar day (sólarhringr) was central to the temporal understanding. It was divided into two twelve-hour dægr, which could mean day or night depending on context. The 24-hour unit was made up out of eight áttir (eighths). These units were spatio-temporal: they referred to the space the sun traversed on the horizon in a three-hour period, and they were accordingly named after the four cardinal directions and their compounds. Time reference thus consisted of three-hour blocks, since any átt referred to the full range of 45 degrees (19-20). Any of these eight “exact” points was indicated by a dagsmark, often indicated physically (spatially!) by means of eyktarmörk, landscape points (sometimes artificial) that indicated the time of day when the sun would pass them. Boundary points between dagsmörk were indicated by the expression jafn-nærri-báðu (+ gen. ok gen.) (21-2). Eykt may be an equivalent of átt; an exact hour of the day; both; or, more generally, “time.” A more relative time-unit (and less frequent) was skafthá, referring to the time when the sun could be seen over the tip of a spear in upright position. While this unit and the others may seem imprecise, they were of legal standing (22-3). Similarly, in winter it must have been impossible to determine the location of the sun, so that rismál, for instance, could not always be six; instead, it was a pragmatic unit: it had taken place by the time when the related action (here rising) had. Thus no confusion could arise about whether or not the hour had passed [PS: until you start making precise appointments]. Sun-altitude measures such as skafthá were used only sporadically. At night, stars could be used for telling time; Arcturus (dagstjarna) was the most important star to Icelanders (23-4). Weeks were important in the organisation of the year. They were calculated according to the sun, not the moon; some degree of calculation was therefore needed. The names of the weekdays were originally gods’ names, but a Christian revision managed to root out all but sunnudagr and mánadagr [PS: does that perhaps signal something concerning the importance of the heavenly bodies to the Icelanders, or is it rather an indication that the clergy were less determined to eradicate these not necessarily heathen names?]. At the foundation of the Althing, a misseri consisted of 26 weeks, but summer had four more days (the auknætr). The misseri was the primary unit: it connoted the change of seasons, while ár did not even exclusively signify a temporal unit (24-7). Misseri transitions were festive occasions. Summer began with sumarmál on the Thursday between nine and fifteen April, while winter started with the vetr-nætr beginning on the Saturday between the eleventh and the eighteenth of October. The year’s division into weeks was not calibrated with its division into months. Since 52 weeks make 364 days, the calendar shifted around the natural year. This mistake was discovered and amended about 950, when an extra week (sumarauki) began to be included every seventh year. When Christianity came to Iceland, the traditional and the Julian calendars were brought into harmony (26-7). The lawspeaker had as one of his tasks to pronounce the misseristal (calendar) at the Althing, after which the goði were to announce the dates at the next leið (autumn thing); thus the Althing regulated time-reckoning. Numbered weeks made up the form of these communications, counting forward in summer until midsummer, after which they would count the number of weeks left to summer. Once per sun cycle (28 years), feasts would occur a week earlier than normally. This anomaly was known as rímspillir (calendar-spoiler) or varnaðar ár (precaution year). However, such anomaly occurs only when the calendar is viewed in relation to another calendar; internally, all is regular (27-9). The month is an ambiguous unit, since it seems there was a second, nonmathematical month calendar in which the names of the months were derived from a variety of conceptual systems; indeed, they may not denote months in the sense of “thirty-day units.” While a mathematical, “fixed method of time-reckoning” was in use, probably a result of Christian influence, this second system, probably older, seems to have been a “discontinuous series of time indications.” Month names derive from social and economic events as well as from nature. Bócarbót seems to be a text aiming to implement all these names into the calendar, translating traditional names into the thirty-day system, as well as attempting (unsuccessfully, as it would seem) to define the month in relation to the week. Both Grágás and Bócarbót take the misseri as their primary unit (29-31). Summers saw more frequent use of week numbers than winters, while month names are more scarcely found for summer months than for winter months (see also 44). Sólmánuðr may reflect the occurrence of the solstice in that period or, alternatively, the fact that it got most sun-hours. In Rím, the word is used in an indefinite sense to refer to the time the sun takes to travel through one sign of the Zodiac; it thus means “solar month.” It also occurs with the referent “one of the year’s twelve months,” as it seems primarily in an indefinite sense, although a definite usage is found in Snorra Edda (31-5). The respective derivations of the other month-names are discussed, including the referent of the “double month.” “[T]he month names seem to be secondary applications of terms whose primary popular use as time-indicators is otherwise defined” (35-40). “The fact remains that months were part of the conceptual time of the Icelanders, although they never entered popular usage (Björnsson 1915: 275). For most practical purposes the week-reckoning remained all-important, and probably only the learned people of the Freestate would have been able to translate the two systems of time-reckoning into one another.” The great variation in month names demonstrates that these units could not have been months in any precise sense (40-1). While leaders tried to adopt the mathematical system, the original reference of the names of the time-units affected the people’s understanding of them. The month names seem unstable because they shift on the Julian calendar, but internally they are consistent: haustmánuðr had not occurred until the time for harvest was there. The importance of months in winter may be explained by the lack of agricultural or economic events that served as a time-line of their own: an abstract system had to be found, and this was merged with old names (44). The difference between chronicle and history is discussed, and the distinction between absolute, learned, extrinsic chronology versus relative, popular, intrinsic chronology. It is argued that a middle form existed in Iceland, namely the intrinsic, absolute chronology mediating between the learned and popular traditions. This third category is illustrated by dating according to lawspeakers, whose terms differed in length; this resulted in varying precision (45-8).

author: Henel, Heinrich
title: Ælfric’s ‘De temporibus anni’
abstract: Ælfric bases his almanac almost exclusively on Bede and Scripture (liii), but he innovates here and there. Thus he gives a number of examples explaining how it may be known that the sun and stars are big (12). The text opens with the week of creation as the creation of day, night, and the heavenly bodies (2-10). Ælfric follows his sources in figurative readings, such as the sun representing Christ (14-16). The vernal equinox is discussed as the beginning of the world (16-18); night is discussed, instituted for man’s rest (18-26), but most of this chapter is devoted to explaining the interplay between sun and moon (20-4). The year is discussed in terms of the zodiac, customs of placing the beginning of the year, the lunar year, and the seasons (28-40). An innovation is the illustration that someone who walks around his house has a shorter course than one who walks around the town; in the same way, the moon’s course is shorter than the sun’s (32-4). Also unaccounted for is the remark that “the day that grows longer,” i.e. the spring day, is cold because the earth is permeated with winter cold and takes time to heat up [cf. Maxims 2]; the opposite is true for autumn (38). The world (40-2) is defined as heaven, sea, and earth (42). The earth is immobile [following Bede]. The equinoxes (44-52), the bissextus (52-6), and the saltus lunae (58-66). Stars, shooting stars, comets, and planets (66-70). The winds and the four elements (72-6), rain, including the story of Elias who prayed for a drought (76-80); hail and snow (80); thunder (82).

author: Henisch, Bridget Ann
title: The Medieval Calendar Year
abstract: The Labours of the Months tradition was dependent on two images, that of seasonal occupation and that of the zodiac sign (1). The tradition per month was strict, such that the theme was easily recognisable (1-4). The calendar tradition flourished from the ninth to the early sixteenth century; at the end of this period, many Books of Hours were still produced, particularly in Flanders. The tradition was popular in the entire Western world (4-7). Its depictions could be found in many contexts, and their level of earnest and support of their context depended on their usage (7). The labour depicted was based on man’s toil as dictated in Genesis 3 (8). While society was typically regarded as consisting of rulers, clergy, and workers, the last category typically met with disgust in real life; in the pictorial tradition, however, contempt is absent (8-10). The depictions are calm, with appropriate weather, tools and clothes in good condition, and no trace of death or decay except when animals are slaughtered for the winter. Even there, the annual recurrence of the picture and the bloodless image express comfort not horror (10-13). Moreover, there is a sense of enjoyment without wasteful cessation of labour (16). Surprisingly, the tradition is without religious overtones (16), social context (16-18), or rebellion against the organisation of society (18). Principles of selection are puzzling: vines and grapes play a central role in the calendar, and yet the tradition was very popular in northern Europe. Possibly this was related to the significance of wine to worship (18-19). Similar considerations apply to wheat, while the most frequent foods receive no mention (19). Sheep-farming is rare in the tradition (19-20). Women begin to appear with greater frequency in later calendars (20-3). Trade is seldom hinted at. The tradition thus represents an unrealistic, pleasingly peaceful and simplistic view of society (23-5). The image provided may have been a soothing illusion for the duke in his manor (25-7). While agriculture has the tradition’s main focus, food is normally only portrayed in winter. There are two reasons for this: in winter, agriculture came to a near-complete standstill throughout Europe, and there was an aesthetic-emotional need for something less barren than the outside world (29-32). When winter was portrayed allegorically, hunger and misery were central among its features (30-2). The serenity of the calendar tradition called for a change of focus at this time of year (32). Some outdoor activities such as the gathering of firewood is admitted, but preferably the focus is on the resulting fire, food, or feast (32-4). While Easter falls in spring, the calendar tradition did not recognise this event. January was the month for cooking and feasting; December shows some cooking but no extravagance. While bread was needed all year round, it only makes it into the pictorial tradition in wintertime (34). Indoor food processing and preparation, including threshing and grainmaking, was a good winter activity because it could be done indoors (34-5). Thirteenth-century French poet Colin Muset described how the barren weather triggers a longing for fire and wine indoors (37-8). The zodiac signs for January and February express the wetness of the season (38-9). These two months are ambiguous because they represent the new year but also the old, in the Roman tradition that started the year at the vernal equinox; thus January and February are either depicted as a young man or as an old man by the fire (39-42). Any references to cooking or food in medieval calendars are marginal (45) and plain (48). Spring features the theme of the pleasure garden from the late fifteenth century onwards, and labour makes way for recreation; gardens are now maintained that do not serve the food chain (51-2). While Jesus had once been mistaken for a gardener, gardeners enjoyed little respect and were traditionally regarded as selfish; the calendrical change marks a change in attitude (53). Gardens underwent a development from private pleasure to bait for envy (54-5). Bigger windows were developed to provide a view of the gardens (55-6). The courtly tradition of the late fifteenth century was reflected in calendrical spring depictions of garden activities, which emphasised on containment of the picture within a frame, the garden within a strictly-defined area, and the plants within smaller plots (56-81). Sheep and shepherds were a central image in depictions of high summer. Sheepfarming was of great economic and religious significance, and additionally provided vellum for manuscript production; but this importance is not reflected in the calendars. Shepherds only gained a place in the calendar, in April (sending the flocks out) and June-July (shearing), in the late medieval period; their labour was simplified to match the calendar’s simple form (85-88). Both these images were common in classical times, but not in the early or high Middle Ages (88-93). The impopularity of pastoral depictions may have to do with the gulf between its theoretical idealisation but actual revulsive status (93-5). It was the domestic shepherd that was depicted, never the far-travelling merchant shepherd (95). Pastoral life was often viewed as more primitive than agriculture (95-7). Visions of heaven, by contrast, were often made up of meadows rather than a city (97). The idealised character of the shepherd is discussed (97-103). Autumn is depicted mainly in harvest; the range is limited to hay, wheat, grapes, and livestock (107-33). Three more thematic chapters deal with the child, woman, and the development from the depiction of toil to the depiction of leisure.

author: Henisch, Bridget Ann
title: Winter Comforts: Cooking Scenes in Medieval Calendars
abstract: The traditional medieval calendar illustration relied on two systems: twelve labours of the months, and twelve zodiac signs representing the sun’s progress through the sky. The conventional nature of these illustrations made it possible for the illustrator to vary details (25). Food is central in these depictions; cooking is not, though hints may be discerned here and there. Thus the slaughter of a pig typically represents December; but one tradition actually displays the collection of its blood for the preparation of black puddings (25-6). In the winter months following December may be found the rare occasions when actual cooking scenes occur, both because the agricultural lapse provided the space for it and because these cooking scenes filled an aesthetic and emotional need in winter. Winter was “a season passionately detested in the Middle Ages.” The aesthetic beauties of winter “were beauties still waiting to be discovered. . . . Fear was the dominant reaction—fear of famine, fear of sickness, fear of bone-chilling cold. Fear of death.” The representations of winter echo these fears. A representation of winter decorating a wall in the Queen’s Chamber at Westminster Castle bore the official description “the figure of Winter which, by its sad look and other miserable portrayals of the body, may be justly likened to Winter itself.” The Duke of Gloucester had the sotelties of one of his dinner’s represent the seasons; the fourth of these was winter, “with its grey locks, feeble and old, sitting on cold, hard stone, niggard in heat, and heavy of cheer” (26). The calendar tradition accorded poorly with this sentiment, since its interest was in serenity not suffering. “The convention is pierced with no sense of sin, no sense of paradise lost” (26-7). All is harmony, in contrast with literature, which always resounds with memento mori. Calendar art is based around the certainties of a succession of seasons rather than the vicissitudes of postlapsarian life. Accordingly, the sufferings of winter were played down by a focus on the activities offsetting them, such as the blazing fire and later the chopping of wood. Cooking soon followed, aided by the fact that winter was the time for feasts. December shows bread-making at most (27). Bread-events in summer find no reflection in the calendar illustrations, because the illustration of agricultural activities left no space for them (27-8). January typically displays a feast, if mostly an intimate one, displaying a single man at table by a fire (28). February typically shows a man in his working outfit, huddling over a fire. The January fire in these illustrations may even be a direct descendant of the Roman New Year’s fire into which incense was poured for luck in the new year; many medieval January depictions even show Janus himself, looking back towards the old year and ahead towards the new (28-9). In another tradition, however, March brought the new year, and so February illustrates the very verge between the cold of winter and the green spring of the new year (29-30). Winter represents old age, and the old man by the fire reflects this association. As such, the tradition was originally one of the depiction of sadness; but over time, the cheer of the fire took over as the focal point of the tradition. An unusual illustration depicts a woman standing over a cooking pot. Stewing is the preferred cooking method in calendars, but exceptionally a roasting is depicted. A thirteenth-century French carving shows a man toasting a fish over a fire, a reference to the month’s zodiac sign of Pisces (30). Smoking and curing may also be found (30-1). Servants in these scenes may be references to January’s zodiac sign, Aquarius, the water-carrier (31-2). The illustrations are normally of basic cooking activities, not the sophisticated or extravagant. An exception is the occasional depiction of pancake-baking. The calendars show us “everyday life as it ought to be” (32).

author: Hill, Thomas D.
title: The Tropological Context of Heat and Cold Imagery in Anglo-Saxon Poetry
abstract: Whereas languages worldwide seem to make use of the figurative pattern associating temperature with emotions (extreme heat/cold is a negatively-perceived emotion; moderate heat/cold is positive), biblical and patristic usage adds a system of moral symbolism: “the fiery hot love of perfect charity, and the icy cold of unrepentent sinfulness” (522-3, at 523). Hill lists numerous examples from Gregory and Augustine (523-7); the former uses the trope without context, while Augustine takes it in as a system: “for Gregory hot and cold are simply signs of charity or sin, while for Augustine the significance of this whole pattern of imagery is that it expresses the organic relationship of sin and charity as well as their absolute polarity” (527). OE poetry follows the same scheme, especially in Solomon and Saturn and Judgement Day I, though brief uses exist also in Elene, The Seafarer, and Andreas (527-32). In Solomon and Saturn in particular, the figure used is more like Augustine’s system than like Gregory’s incidental usage; moreover, the assertion in the poem that hot and cold, snow and sun cannot coexist is very similar to a passage in Augustine’s writings stating that snow cannot be warm (528-30).

author: Howes, Laura L.
title: Time and Landscape in Middle English Poetry
publication: Inventing Medieval Landscapes: Senses of Place in Western Europe
abstract: Points out that “pedestrian” movement is central to Middle English literature: one has to travel in a line to get from one place to another, and in gardens as in nature and even towns, this is typically a journey of discovery, offering no grand overviews. Works like SGGK and Sir Orfeo rely on this principle but then override it in fairy teleportations and connections between the various courts and places. The pedestrian quality of medieval life, without satellite photography, must have made such transformations the more appealing.

author: Hüe, Denis
title: L’hiver du Moyen Âge
publication: Farai chansoneta novela: Essais sur la liberté créatrice au Moyen Âge, Hommage à Jean Charles Payen
abstract:
Opens by pointing out that external factors, too, impress themselves on man’s understanding of time. It is saint Michael and the saint John of summer and winter who have long been central in the perception of time, including not just flow and duration but also climate and degree of heat and aridity. Just as in today’s world summer primarily connotes sun, medieval man was not deeply accustomed to time-reckoning, as the lexical nature of much computistical literature suggests. But in Romance literature, spring was the pleasant season, associated with rejuvenation (211). There is less evidence for views of the other seasons. What evidence there is derives from the many debates of summer and winter. This tradition starts off with a single text from the Aesopian tradition, and two Carolingian texts are found, one of which attributed to Alcuin; more texts are known from the twelfth to fifteenth centuries (211-12). Vincent de Beauvais defined the etymologies of the seasons, going back on Isidore de Seville (Etymologiae 5.35; Speculum naturale 5.64, Douai 1624, col. 1132). Tempora derives from temperare “moderate; mix in the right proportions.” Each of four seasons is divided into three parts. “Ver a virore, quia viret”; “Aestas dicitur ab aestu, id est a colore, et aestu quasi usta, id est exusta et arida”; “[autumnas] a tempestate vocatur”; and hiems is from hemisphaerium, because the circle of the sun is shorter then. Thus what stands out is the green of spring, the scorching of summer, the tempests of autumn and the short days of winter. The perception of the seasons strikes one as rustic [!] (212). Because of the confusion over the dating of Easter, the start of each season differs markedly between traditions; thus the contrast between a good and a bad season is far clearer than temporal definition. It seems that the cycle of the seasons since classical times has its origin in a rural calendar, marked by the labours of the field; in this tradition, the existence of four seasons is more important than when the respective seasons began. To medieval man, the seasons had agricultural meaning, so that each month was associated with a certain labour of the field; but the four seasons also corresponded to the ages of man, the humours, and the elements (213). Pierre Bersuire [c. 1290-1362] in his Reductorium morale presents a representative picture of the religious significations of the seasons (213-14). Summer is described as sparing in clouds and thus bringing clarity, while making birds sing and yielding the fruits of the earth sowed in other seasons. Winter, cold and humid, engenders phlegm, ice, snow, clouds, and rain, and more mud and refuse than all other seasons. Because the sun is at such great distance, the world grows cold and shrivels up, undoing all the beauty of the preceding summer. This season is associated with Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces. Bersuirse in his first reading reads summer as the time of paradisical glory, in which Christ the Sun of Righteousness draws close to mankind. The heat represents love, the clarity of the sky truth, the softness of the dew devotion; the length of the days represents eternity, the birdsong deeds of grace. A second interpretation of summer has it represent Judgement Day, with the sun (of Righteousness) overhead and voluptuous desire withering away in its sight, and forcing each to reveal the secrets of his heart. The third interpretation reads summer as penitence (contrition, confession, satisfaction): just as in summer the pores open to carry out the humours, contrition opens the way to confession, the sweat of labour, and satisfaction (214-15). Winter is given a negative characterisation: the Sun of Righteousness is far from mankind, and the nights of ignorance and error are long, while the days of true wisdom are short, and man is surrounded by shadows. Vices abound in the nights of winter. The cold represents impiety, ice and its binding power represent obstinacy, snow refers to hypocritical conversation, and the clouds to indiscretion. Capricorn represents pride, while Pisces represents voracity and avarice. Winter is also a time for worldly prosperity, when there is great appetite for food. But the lazy refuse to work: it is an easy time for peasants. Wells, springs, and the sea do not freeze over in winter, because they are always in movement and/or salty; Bersuire affirms that nearly all men are frozen in their impiety, but that the bitterness/saltiness of contrition and the movement of their good deeds can keep them from freezing up. Accordingly, the wells represent the humble. The overall value awarded to winter is thus sin and, by extension, death (215-16).

To Alcuin, summer and winter are classical topoi before they are seasons. He employs a Virgilian theme and rhetorics in the classical dactylic hexametre form introduced by two shepherds with classical names. Spring and summer are synonyms to him, sharing the same values and characteristics (216). His shepherds rest in summer [no, the flocks rest in the pasture: “pascua sit pecori, requies et dulcis in arvis” (“may there be pastures for the cattle, and sweet rest in the pastures”)], which is at odds with the carolingian calendar. Later calendars place their rest in February, and winter was surely the time of rest since Alcuin. In the first French translation of his Conflictus hiemis et aestatis, however, the shepherds only rest when forced by the cold and the ice: winter has thus lost its positive recreational value and won a negative value of inactivity (216-17). Here may be witnessed two different currents, idealised and realistic. If summer remained the season of beauty, it was no longer for the same reasons. Summer remains the season of love, but in the debates, winter contests summer’s monopoly on this market: after all, winter was the season for resting; but this is particularly true of the wealthier classes, and thus the theme becomes lest rustic (217). The Kalendrier des bergiers describes summer as easy, with game animals, fruits, and vegetables; water and tea are drunk in great quantities (217-18). Winter, however, is described as the time of year when nature yields the greatest amount of meat to restore body heat; strong wines are also drunk at this time of year. Naturally, this calendar was not really intended for shepherds. A feudal picture developed in the debates, with the contrast shifting to nature and artifice, vegetables and meat, poverty and riches, serf and master. In an Anglo-Norman debate, winter comes to argue in terms of power, while summer speaks in terms of moral virtues. Summer points out that it feeds the rest of the year. In the course of the debate, it becomes clear that winter is English and summer French. In later versions, the balance between summer as provider and winter as consumer concludes the debate: the alternation is accepted (218-19). The explanation that the fifteenth century had better climate than earlier times seems far-fetched (219-20). Metrics are briefly discussed: the Anglo-Norman debate has summer and winter use different metres. It also brings in explicit moral sides: summer accuses winter of being a servant of Lucifer (220). The religious feasts become a weapon in the battle in Recueil Montaiglon, but summer surprisingly does not counter winter’s claim for superiority with Christmas by pointing out that it has Easter, or the Assumption. Possibly this is done to preserve the balance. The poet does hint at summer’s good hand in the matter when he has summer ask whether winter can revive the dead (220-1). Thus the genre combines classical, courtly, ecclesiastical, political, and religious images, to whose diversity but also cohesion it owes its survival (221).

author: Hultgård, Anders
title: Fimbulvetr ou le Grand Hiver: Étude comparative d’un aspect du mythe eschatologique des anciens Scandinaves
abstract: A remarkably extensive essay on a concept so fragmentarily attested in the sources. For the larger part, however, it summarises early scholarship on eddic eschatology, especially that of Axel Olrik [“Om Ragnarok,” Aarbøger for nordisk Oldkyndighed og Historie 1902, 157–291, esp. 167–75]. References in Gylfaginning, Vsp, and Vm are cited, but additional possible references in Hyndluljóð and again in Vsp are also rehearsed, although the latter of these (Vsp 41 “svört verða sólskin / of sumor eptir”) is rejected (14–25). The author emphasises (beyond its worth) the differences between the Prose Eddic as well as the Poetic Eddic accounts of the fimbulvetr, the latter group of which supposedly reflects variety in oral tradition (12–17). Note 35 on p. 21 lists earlier scholarship on the fimbulvetr. The old argument that Vsp and Vm differ in their representation of fimbulvetr inasmuch as they describe different geographical environments is rejected (22). Note 38 on p. 22 points out that buddhism and Christianity alike speak of fire and ice, see Hultgård’s other article “Hettan och kölden efter döden”, Hett om kalla fakta: Aktuell forskning om temperaturen, människan och naturen. Ed. Leif Åberg. Stockholm: Vetenskapsrådet, 2003. 101–12. Saxo’s king Snio is mentioned: Olrik has thought of this character as referring to a first mythical age, in which the cold and the snow reigned; Hultgård discredits this as rather speculative[, but it may be supposed Olrik had the Fornjótr-narrative in mind, with which Saxo’s episode in 8.11–13 is surely related] (26). A misguided tradition is mentioned (and rejected) in which climatologists have tried to situate the genesis of the fimbulvetr-myth in ancient sudden shifts in climate (26–8) The remainder of the article focuses on analogues, first in Judaic tradition (Jubilees, Job, and less relevant weathers in Deuteronomy and Leviticus among others), which Hultgård believes has not been demonstrated to have influenced the Scandinavian fimbulvetr [contra Hugo Meyer] (28–31), then Persian (properly 31–5). The latter has sufficiently close parallels (a destructive winter, survived by some humans who hide out against it and re-emerge to embark on a new era) for the author to devote the remainder of the article to comparison; his conclusion is that they represent different branches of an ancient Indo-European tradition regarding the end and rebirth of the world (35–9, conclusion at 38–9). Further oddities include the statement that this eschatological winter is unique to Scandinavia and Iran, and discussions of authors who have held them to derive from the collective memory of this or that severe winter, contra others who believe the Persian tradition travelled north to Scandinavia (37–8).

author: Hutton, Ronald
title: The Stations of the Sun: A History of the Ritual Year in Britain

author: Jackson, Kenneth
title: Seasonal Poetry
publication: Studies in Early Celtic Nature Poetry
abstract: Divides its Irish and Welsh nature poetry into three kinds: the annunciation of a season, the description of a season, and weather poetry. Summer is announced by way of blackbirds, cuckoos, and larks; its blossom replaces harsh weather. Winter is announced with ice and cold, and a low solar path. May Day is a common element in the poetry announcing summer, while Winter’s Day fulfils a similar function in the winter poetry. It is characterised by falling leaves, flooding, yellowing, and starving creatures (149-50). These themes are reminiscent of the Continental Natureingang of medieval Latin and the vernaculars, by vagantes, troubadours, and Minnesingers. In these, spring imagery forms the backdrop of young people loving, dancing, and singing, while winter signals the end of joys (150-3). This theme reached England and Ireland by the thirteenth century, though it is not attested in Irish manuscripts before the seventeenth (153-4). The similarities between this school and early Irish poetry are abundant (154-5). The Celts could not have borrowed it from the Continent, though, since the Celtic type exists in the ninth century; they must thus be independent of each other (155). The popular view is that both developed from folk poetry already in existence. This consisted of a begging-song announcing the season as well as a dancing-song tradition welcoming spring (155-7). Recent scholarship has been more sceptical regarding the existence of folk-poetry, but it is still most likely that the Natureingang evolved from dancing-songs (157-8). A third type is the contest of summer and winter, a rhetorical play involving dressing up and acting out. Summer wins out in the end. Alcuin’s Conflictus veris et hiemis may have derived from this tradition, and some Irish poems with similar themes may have similar origins (158-9). All of the elements discussed may date back to European traditions from pagan times (159). It may be asked whether the Irish lyrics derive from this carol tradition; the emphases on May Day and Winter’s Day do suggest so (159-60). 1 May and 1 November marked the beginning of Celtic summer and winter, when the two great festivals were also held (160). Fertility rites surrounding May Day are known from early sources, but there is no mention of song or dance, although a fourteenth-century poem suggests that dancing was regarded as typically Irish. The Old Woman of Beare tells of joyful maidens on May Day. There is some evidence of autumn fertility rites/laments as well (160-2). A gnomic function may underlie some of the nature poetry, although no truly gnomic literature existed in Ireland. Compared with Hesiod’s Works and Days, Irish nature poetry takes the form of objective description of the processes of nature. The Works and Days functioned as a kind of almanac, the first cry of cuckoo or swallow each signalling certain elements of spring (163-4). Birdsong had similar functions in Britain: a calendar by a Pseudo-Bede notes for specific days of the year that birds began and stopped their song, and a second similar source is found in OE. An OI poem focusses specifically on birdsong throughout the year (in The Martyrology of Tallaght 94ff.) (164-6). Similarly, the rising of stars serves an almanac function in Hesiod, while the lengthening or shortening of days is used in OI poetry. There is also an OI poem telling when the different herbs are best harvested (166-7). The form of the almanac poems derives from martyrologies. The poems on birdsong are derivative of this tradition. Even the herb poem derives its use of kalends from the ecclesiastical tradition. The OE Menologium similarly stems from the ecclesiastical calendar tradition, but it differs from it in its descriptions of the passing of the seasons (167-8). Its style is typically OE, resembling the description of nature as found in the elegies in particular. Its author was evidently elaborating his dull calendar with indigenous elements of nature description (168-9). This native interest in the passing of the seasons is probable, but difficult to prove. Calendar poems are more likely to have borrowed from native tradition than vice versa (169-70). OI weather-lore poetry may have been another source of influence. The Prophecy of Néde closely resembles poem XXVII in phrasing (170-1). The prose Ezra almanacs (The Auguries of Esdras), based on medieval Latin sources, foretell the character of the seasons based on a weekday in the first week of January, resembling poem XXXIB (172). Seasonal poems have typically been ascribed to hermits, but this is unlikely, as the hermits seldom mention the seasons and their personal tone is lacking from these poems. Also, the worldly images in the poetry cannot be theirs (172-3). The poems are probably not Fennian, and have been attributed to Finn mac Cumaill only because of a general likeness of theme (173-5). “The ultimate source for seasonal poetry in Ireland and Wales may be no more than a general interest in the phenomena of the seasons rather like but distinct from the interest implied in the nature-gnomic poetry, but the very definite genre of seasonal announcement seems to demand some more specific explanation” (175).

author: Jones, Charles W.
title: Bedae opera de temporibus
abstract:
The 172-page introduction to this edition discusses the development of the ecclesiastical calendar (3-122) and Bede’s computistical works (123-72).

[II: The Early Paschal Computation] Lists traditions on the year and date of the Passion (6-7). Explains the definition of Nisan and the relationship between Easter and Passover (7-9). Antisemitic sentiment separated the two festivals (9). The Romans decided to celebrate not on 14 Nisan but on the Sunday after, which led to many councils and controversies (10-11). The new definition relied on both lunar and solar year. A reconciliation of these two cycles required the use of intercalations, the most common of which was the nineteen-year cyce (11). Early Roman Easter tables are discussed (11-17). The Nicean Council was the most significant conference on the dating of Easter, although it made no formal prescriptions with regard to the calculation to be followed, other than stigmatising the Quartodecimans who celebrated on 14 Nisan (17-18). At least in Constantine’s understanding of the council’s ruling, Easter must never fall on 14 Nisan; but it appears the council gave no positive ruling as to what dates would be acceptable (18-20). The vernal equinox became relevant to prevent the celebration of two Easters in one year (20-22). The council repeated the earlier edict of Arles that the entire Church should observe Easter on the same day, but no such uniformity existed in practice, since different equinoxes and moons were used (22-5). Post-Nicean Easter tables show wide variety of practice (25-6). The Romans restricted the Easter limits from the logically possible 35 days to the 31 of 22 March to 21 April (26-7). A calendar showing up in Rome did not forbid 14 Nisan before the equinox, which resulted in peculiarities continuing through later Roman calendars. Eastern and Western tables differed, but in reality they celebrated Easter on the same day, according to the Alexandrian reckoning, violating the 21-April limit (27-8). Rome held strictly to this limit, probably to avoid conflicts with annual celebrations of the city’s foundation (28). Theophilus, Bishop of Alexandria, drew up the Easter table in the late fourth century that directly inspired Bede’s (29-30). He proposed to postpone Easter by a week when Nisan began on a Sunday, thus violating the 21-April limit (30-1). Theophilus’s 19-year cycle was universally adopted in the centuries that followed, and is here explained (31-3).

[III: The Cyrillan Easter-Table] The Cyrillan table is not a forgery as has been claimed (34-5). Alexandrian reckoning was introduced into Milan either by Ambrose or in his time (35-7). The Cyrillan table is a revision of Theophilus’s which may have been in general use in the Greek world (37-8). The prologue attributed to Cyril is false (38-9). A hitherto unknown redaction of the Prologus is printed (40-3). Its authorship and purpose is discussed (44-7). The authorship of the Cyrillan table is discussed (47-9), and that of the previously-known Prologus (49-54).

[IV: Easter-tables in Rome and the West] Rome seems to have followed Alexandrian Easter dating except when it fell on 22-5 April, since this represented a conflict with the natalis urbis dies. Various tables and authors are discussed (55-77).

[V: Easter in the British Isles] The British tradition began with Columban about 600, who held that Easter could not be celebrated during moons 22 and 24, which rose after midnight and hence at a time of darkness. It becomes clear that he held to a March 25 equinox and moons 14-20 (78-81). Anatolian Canon (82-5). Equally uninteresting (85-172).

[De temporum ratione] Most relevant is chapter 15, on the Anglo-Saxon months:

January giuli (geola) named for the turning of the sun
February solmonath “month of cakes” offered to the gods
March hredmonath named after the goddess Hreda
April eosturmonath (easter-monaþ) named after the goddess Eostre, & feast
May thrimilchi 3 milkings per day at that time of year
June lida blandus “gentle,” navigabilis “navigable”
July lida
August weodmonath month of weeds, because they are plentiful then
September halegmonath month of sacraments/holy rites/holy feasts
October winterfilleth full moon of winter
November blodmonath (blod-monaþ, cf. blot-monaþ!) month of sacrificial offerings
December giuli

The year began on 25 December. What is now Christmas Eve was Modranect “night of mothers,” ut suspicamur for a waking ceremony. In common years, the lunar months were evenly distributed across the (four!) seasons; in embolismic years, summer had an extra month, which was squeezed in between the lidas; hence these years were called thrilidi. Originally, however, there were only the two seasons of summer and winter.

Relevant for their figurative connotations are the chapters on day and night (5–7), equinoxes and solstices (30), the four seasons, elements, and humours (35). The day is air lit up by the sun (5). Sun and moon symbolise Christ and the Church (6). Night is given to mankind for rest; it consists of seven parts (7). The PL edition and Wallis translation have a very long chapter 66 detailing the world ages, but Jones ends at ch. 65.

[De temporibus liber] repeats more briefly the contents of DTR.

The epistles concern the ages of the world and the dating of the spring equinox respectively.

author: Jones, T. Gwynn
title: The Seasons
abstract: Opens with Classical evidence of a lunar Celtic year. A first-century Calendar bears witness to a 365-day year, divided into twelve months of 30 and 29 days. An intercalary month was used every 2.5 years, or twelve days per year; its days bore the names of months. Each of these was prophetic of a month in the year to come (145-6). The year began on the “Winter Kalend” of 1 November; the “Summer Kalend” was the first of May. New Year’s Day in January is probably a Roman borrowing. November, Mis Tachwedd, is probably named for the slaughtering of animals, like OE blotmonað [and ON gormánuðr]. Slaughter-rituals have survived to the present day, although no apparently religious features survive (146). In North Wales, cattle was slaughtered around Calan Gaeaf, after which friends and dependents were invited to a feast (146-7). Bonfires are still lit on Nos Galan Gaeaf (147-50). Games of this night are described (149-51). Winter’s Eve, Summer’s Eve, and St John’s Eve were the three Ghost Nights (y Tair Ysbrydnos), on which the spirits of the dead were particularly active (151-2) [cf. Árni Björnsson; Gunnell1; Gunnell2; Gunnel3]. On Winter’s Eve, people would go to church to hear spirits call out the names of the doomed (152). Mayday and Midsummer were the other two big celebrations besides Winter’s Eve. Surviving games and rituals suggest traditional combats between summer and winter (152-4). Mayday pole-dancing involved the felling of a birch; Welsh poetry consistently associates the birch with love. Midsummer celebrations, though not as well-attested, appear to have been of a similar kind to those of Mayday (154-5). Harvest celebrations are listed (155-7). New Year’s Day gift-begging is discussed as a survival of pre-Christian tradition (157-8). After the introduction of the Gregorian calendar, many customs were still celebrated on 12 January; one of these is detailed (158-9). Shrove Tuesday, Good Friday, Whitsuntide customs (159-60). Christmas customs were not nearly as important as New Year’s celebrations, but a few are described (162-4).

author: Klein, Stacy S.
title: Gender and the Nature of Exile in Old English Elegies
publication: A Place to Believe in: Locating Medieval Landscapes
eds: Clare A. Lee and Gillian R. Overing
abstract:
To Anglo-Saxon authors, geographic detail was not important; rather, what concerned them was the allegorical potential of a given location (114–15). The elegies have a special relationship to place, since they describe its loss. Gender divides the experience of exile: men bewail their consignment to perpetual movement, while women lament being trapped in one place. The male speaker gains a spiritual understanding of transience from his imposed wanderings; the local stasis of the female embodies her spiritual inertia (115–16). When the female speaker considers journeying, external factors stop her from so doing (116–17). She is also locked in the present, unlike the speakers of Wanderer and Seafarer who look back to a time of earthly glory and forward to heaven (117). To the latter speakers, the privations and dangers of travel serve as educational tools on their spiritual journey (118). They are skilled not only at metaphorical travel, but also at temporal travel, looking back at heroic society and forward to heaven; the retrospection is no lapse but a stimulant to continue on their course (120). The female speakers undergo no spiritual change, so her exile cannot be read in analogy with the male travels. The natural world in the female elegies is merely an externalisation of their psychological state (120–1). The pagan landscape of The Wife’s Lament reveals its speaker’s lack of Christian-spiritual progress (121–2). The male speakers show ambivalence towards the heroic world, while female speakers see in it the cause of their suffering (122–3). When women do look back to happier times, it is personal joys, not heroic values, that they mourn (123–4). Although male voices also mourn social bonds, these are more an image for the worldly status that was lost, whereas the female interest is in the relationships for their own sake (124–5). Both Wanderer and Wife’s Lament speak of past joys as seeming to have not existed at all; only the former has a blessed future to place against it. Female voices assert the importance of male–female relations physical and emotional, dismissed as transient by the male voices (125). The female voices do not reject the values that have caused their misery but persist in them; indeed, the sad female voice is a stock ingredient of heroic literature (126–7). Female elegiac voices are nevertheless antiheroic in focussing on individual loss only, not the loss of broader societal constructs as in heroic poetry. The female elegist’s wish for revenge within the social sphere is similarly antiheroic, as women in heroic literature serve male interests (127–8). The Wife curses her lover and in so doing condemns him to sit, an effeminisation (128). Early medieval society limited the movement of its women, which is almost synonymous with sexual licentiousness; but the female elegists refuse to sit and wait for their men, focussing their energy instead on the destruction of those for whom they are supposed to wait, embodying an urge to reconsider the female role (129–31).

[A brilliant article; one arguable weakness is that an artificial distinction is drawn between female elegies and female complaints in the “heroic mode” (the Geatish woman in Beowulf), while The Lament of the Last Survivor is counted with the male elegiac tradition. This distinction allows Klein to argue that elegies in female voices don’t bewail societal collapse (127).]

author: Klinck, Anne L.
title: The Old English Elegies: A Critical Edition and Genre Study
abstract:
Attempts to define Old English elegy with reference to themes of “exile, loss of loved ones, scenes of desolation, the transience of worldly joys” as well as a “lyrical-reflective mode” characterised by “monologue, personal introduction, gnomic or homiletic conclusion, and the ordered repetition of words and sounds” (11-12, at 11). A lengthy textual, contextual, and linguistic discussion of the nine (or ten) poems (Wanderer, Seafarer, Riming Poem, Deor, Wulf and Eadwacer, The Wife’s Lament, Resignation, Ic wæs be sonde/Riddle 60, The Husband’s Message, and The Ruin) and the Exeter Book (12-30) leads up to the poems’ individual discussion. Wdr is read as a single monologue with only a brief insertion of a windowed speech (30-1). Linguistically, it departs from Sfr; the two also differ in contents inasmuch as Wdr concerns a fated exile whereas Sfr tells of chosen exile (32-3). Wdr may have received formative influence from Boethius, but need not have consciously been written to reflect this (33-4). Attempts have been made to find Christian sources for Wdr, but more useful is to distinguish between worldly and transcendental values, as the poem describes a movement from one to the other (34-5). Sfr is mostly read as a monologue, but has also frequently been understood as a dialogue or a blend of two poems (35-7). An allegorical, spiritual reading is often understood for the sea voyage, and the peregrinatio genre has likewise been proposed (37). The motif of the sea as allegory is a universal across cultures (37-8). Resignation shares with Sfr a journeying motif, although in Res it leads more directly to the next world. Similar also is the allegorical voyage of Christ II (38). Wdr and Sfr both contrast hall life with the outdoor winter experience, which is described in terms also found in Christ II (38-9). Differences between Sfr and Wdr are great (39). Sfr essentially operates on two levels: temporal and transcendental (39-40; cf. p. 35 for Wdr). The Riming Poem has been appreciated artistically only recently (40). It contains a clear bipartite structure, contrasting former happiness with present bitterness parallel to the decline of the world (40-1). Its persona seems to be a former ruler (41). Its vocabulary is difficult (41-2). Job has been suggested as a source, and Thomas of Celano’s Dies irae is a thirteenth-century analogue (42). Höfuðlausn shares a context and background with it, and their verse forms are “very similar”; “[a] connection between the two poems is thus very likely” (42-3). Deor is the only OE poem with a fully-formed refrain. ON, Latin, and OE charm influences have been suggested (43-4). It has been associated with Wulf and Eadwacer, which follows it in the manuscript, and its form resembles The Seasons for Fasting in that it also uses stanzas. Unlike most OE elegies, Deor is placed in a (pseudo)historical framework (44). The poem has Boethian sentiments. Its understanding of wyrd and its use of both Weland and Theoderic suggests that the poet knew the Alfredian translation of the Consolatio (45). Wulf and Eadwacer has been read in myriad ways. It may be an erotic woman’s song (47-9). WfL’s many readings are briefly mentioned (49-50). Klinck understands the speaker to be a woman, and there to be only one man (50-1). Structure is less clear in this poem than in the other elegies, but the same movement may be discerned (51-2). The focus on suffering as a consequence of the various episodes described blurs their temporal order (52). Its categorisation within the group of elegies is discussed: it belongs with the love poems rather than with Wdr and Sfr (52-3). The possibility of an oral “saga background” for the narrative cannot be proved, since no names or context are given (53), and various other contexts have been proposed (53-4). Resignation overlaps between exile and penitential prayer (54-5). It has been argued that a folio is missing. The journey/exile has often been read as symbolic (55), but occasionally as a literal peregrinatio (55-6). Klinck has elsewhere pacified these two readings. Like several OE elegies, there is here a bipartite framework (56). Riddle 60 and The Husband’s Message were probably separate compositions (56-7). The latter is a formal love-lyric (58). It is sometimes associated with WfL, though the two differ widely in form and content (58-60). The Ruin is perhaps the most straightforward, but also the most badly damaged. The elegiac character of this poem comes out in its dwelling on past glory and present ruin (61). Bath has been suggested as a referent (61-2). Morally, it has been read as Babylon (62). Wdr, The Ruin, and Maxims II all refer to ruins as enta geweorc, a term applied to the sword-hilt in Bwf. This may also carry pagan connotations. The de excidio tradition may have been an influence (62-3). Rather than move towards eschatology, The Ruin ends in retrospection, the poet losing himself more and more in the glory of the past (63). The genre of OE elegy is explored in the light of theories of genre (223-5), and “the sense of separation” is identified as its core element (225-6). Gnomic conclusions with the aim of consolation occur in several of the poems (226-7); Fictional autobiography is a formal feature in some of the poems, as is verbal repetition (227). The vocabulary is saturated with words for sorrow, longing, and the absence of joy (227-8). Water serves as a separating element in six elegies. Words formed with wræc-, -læs, bi- are frequent (228). Falling is a frequent image (228-9). The verb hreosan in particular is associated with rime and snow; a “bad-weather theme” is suggested by the frequency of words like stanclif, stanhliþ, storm, hrim, hrið, hruse, hægl, nipan, niht, cnyssan, beotan. Also traditional are the longing for a voyage and binding imagery (229). Wisdom poetry is characterised by sceal and bið (229-30). Oral funerary laments are discussed as sources: it is observed that no funeral context is given in any of the poems. First-person laments seem more likely as sources (230-1). Christian sources have often been proposed for the wisdom poetry, and may only apply to the love lyrics in an allegorical sense (231). All the elegies were written down in a monastic environment that must have shaped them (231-2). Worldly insecurity is a consistent characteristic of the “homiletic elegy” (232). This reflects the Christian environment in which these works were composed/compiled, but Germanic literature is also familiar with this function (232-3). Boethius’s Consolatio was an influence on Deor, and likely a spiritual background for all the homiletic elegies (234). Certain literary devices in the elegies were described and applied in Latin literature of the time; these stylistic figures may be seen in all homiletic literature of the age (234-5). While the poetic form of Latin elegy is not used in OE, OE elegies move away from the common Germanic form by a greater reliance on repetition and rhyme, and a correspondence exists in subject matter (236). A direct or indirect influence by the Latin elegiac mode seems to exist (236-7). Specific connections have been proposed but cannot be proved (237-8). A possible connection between The Riming Poem and Höfuðlausn is discussed (238). Deor and Wulf resemble ON verse in form, as do some of the charms in terms of their repetition of lines (238-9). The contemporary existence of OE and Celtic elegiac verse traditions is no coincidence, and the Celtic literature is closer to the OE in atmosphere than any other tradition. The traditions also share their heroic milieu. The Welsh poems, too, have the de excidio theme of the OE elegies. Anglo-Welsh relations must have existed, but Klinck argues against a borrowing from the Old Welsh (239-41). The wish to go on a voyage is also present in the Celtic, and particularly Irish, material, if not in elegies (241-2). It is suggested that the form of the OE elegy developed in Continental times, “as an autobiography with mournful content” typically involving exile. The tradition may have relied on themes and motifs from Welsh, and it probably took inspiration from the classical and Christian Latin elegiac mode. Its form is set apart by repetition, possibly inspired by ON (242-3). The possibility is left open whether some of the poems were written by women (244). OE words that might be used to refer to elegy are discussed (244). OE elegy is defined as “a discourse arising from a powerful sense of absence, of separation from what is desired, expressed through characteristic words and themes, and shaping itself by echo and leitmotiv into a poem that moves from disquiet to some kind of acceptance” (246). A number of Latin, Old Welsh, and ON analogues is appended (254-303). Two are seasonally relevant: Ovid’s Tristia 3.4b speaks of being in the cold land nearest Ursa Major (i.e. the north), bordering on inhospitably cold land. The poem laments the separation from wife and homeland (262-3). The Old Welsh Claf Abercuawg / Sick Man of Abercuawg expresses sadness at hearing the cuckoo, not for the cuckoo’s own sake but because the speaker has a “wound” (apparently emotional) in the cuckoo’s season. It also makes clear that early summer is a time for battle (st. 17) (268-75).

[Textual notes]: In context, Wdr 24b, 57a “waþema gebind” is most likely a large unit of water rather than the binding of ice, a meaning found in Bwf 1133 “isgebind(e)” (110). Hrimceald and hrið “storm” are Scandinavianisms from hrímkaldr and hríð “storm, snowstorm” (117). Wdr 77b “hryðge” is another hapax, often read as “snow-covered” or “snow-swept” alongside “storm-beat” by analogy to ON hríð (121-2). Sfr has the hapax hrimgicelum (l. 17a), which is “constructed on the same lines as isgicel, ‘icicle’” (128). There has been some discussion concerning the identification of the bird stearn (l. 23): Goldsmith found the stern an unlikely candidate since it is not a winter bird (from isigfeþera, l. 24a; 129). The cuckoo’s association with melancholy occurs also in Husb, and has been considered a Celtic element, though also found in German, Slavic, and Baltic folklore (see Sieper; Gerhard Dietrich). The cuckoo has positive connotations in Guthlac 744 and Conflictus, although the latter presents Hiems’s negative view as well (see Pheifer) (137). WfL 37b “sumorlangne dæg” is understood as a drawn-out period of time, contrasting with GenB 370a “winterstunde” (185). Klinck does not refer to anyone for this reading, but so also Klaeber (“Zur jüngeren Genesis.” Anglia 49 [1926]: 361-75); Gordon (Anglo-Saxon Poetry, 1926). In 47b-52a, “the elements of rocky slope, storm, hoar-frost, proximity to water, and a “dreary hall” form a composite of traditional elegiac motifs (cf. Wan 46-48 and 75-77, Sea 29b-33a, Ruin 3-4)” (187).

author: Knowlton, E.C.
title: Nature in Older Irish
publication: Publications of the Modern Language Association of America
abstract: Discusses nature similes in descriptions of personal appearance (92-6) and nature metaphors (96-7). The description of physical nature sometimes serves a metaphorical function as well (97-9). Nature in OI received the central focus, whereas elsewhere it was used as a backdrop. It refers to spring less often than southern or eastern literature (99). The birds were a popular theme, and the blackbird most of all (99-100). The cuckoo was similarly popular, and considered cheerful; modern Irish and OE have given it a role of sadness (100-1). Other birds are referred to in a footnote. References to animals and plants are briefer (101). There is not much literature touching on all the seasons, but it is clear “that the Irish disliked wind, storms, and winter” (101-2). One poem rejoices in the coming of summer; its images evoke mood and are not mere conventional description (102). Another uses birdsong and colour to express summer joy (103-4). It uses greater variation in sensory impression. Man is reduced to the background (104). A winter poem lists sounds typical of the coming of winter (104-5). Another poem tells how the extreme cold precludes the rest of animals, while signalling the comfort of the home by a brief reference to a pot over the fire (105-6). Eve’s lament similarly expresses an Irish dislike of winter (106-7). Poems rejoicing in nature similarly suggest a preference for summer (107-10). Later Continental monastic literature is somewhat similar, but not as strong in its love for nature (110-11). The fierceness of the sea found frequent expression. The sea sometimes connoted fear or melancholy, sometimes joy or courage (111-14). Two longer prose passages describe storm at sea and are cited here in translation (114-17). They are similar to each other in method and both have classical undertones, suggesting that they stand in the same tradition. Compared with OE sea descriptions, the OI has greater emphasis on colour and on “the pleasant, restful hours at sea.” OE has a large body of literature dealing with the sea (117). Wonder-voyages often include nature description echoing the pleasures of nature back home (117-20).

author: Lamb, H.H.
title: Climate: Present, Past, and Future
abstract: [From chapter 17: Climate in Historical Times {423-73}] Justifies the study of past climate by the fact that man’s increasing influence on his environment has rendered the original environmental indicators useless (423-4). Describes climate factors such as temperature and moisture from the Roman period onwards (424ff.). In the past 2500 years, temperatures have fluctuated within a range of about 1-1,5 degrees when measured per century (432). The early Middle Ages witnessed higher sea levels than today’s (433). While indications are all from the North Sea, subject to tectonic warping, a global sea level range of one metre must be concluded (433-4). The Medieval Warm Period is summed up as generally peaking in 1150-1300, but with significant highs also in the later tenth century. New Zealand may have peaked as late as 1200-1400. Stable vineyards could exist 300-500km farther north than today (435). Tillage in England occurred up to 350 metres higher than today, and tree lines were higher (436-7). Oats and barley could be grown in Iceland, though oats were given up and the barley production was halved about 1200. Trøndelag supported wheat and Malangen some hardier grains, but this was given up some time between 1000 and 1500/1600. Northern England and Wales had crops at high altitudes, as did the Scottish Highland fens before 1300 (437). In the Western Settlement of Greenland, Norse settlers buried their dead in what is now permafrost. In the thirteenth century, the majority of Greenlanders had never seen bread, but some wealthy inhabitants tried to grow grain; barley, oats, and rye have again grown there since the twentieth century. Greenland sea water was as much as four degrees warmer than today, though this cannot reflect the global situation (438). The climate worsening of 1200-1400 is described. The English and Hanseatic ports profited from the newly harsher conditions further north (449). The deterioration is seen in the increase in Arctic sea ice; advances of inland ice; lowering of tree lines; increasing wetness; increasing frequency in the freezing of waters; more severe windstorms, floods, and sand shifting disasters; harvest failures; abandonment of crops and settlements; and incidence in disease (451-2). The Little Ice Age is divided into stages (463-73).

author: Pfister, C., G. Schwarz-Zanetti, and M. Wegmann
title: Winter Severity in Europe: The Fourteenth Century
abstract: Measures winter severity across the fourteenth century. 1303-28 were cold, 1329-54 average, and 1354-75 extremely variable. The last quarter of the century had winters slightly colder than the average twentieth-century winter. Based on western European chronicle evidence.

author: Lamb, H.H.
title: Climate, History and the Modern World
abstract:
NB this edition has been superseded by the second, from 1995; page numbering differs substantially between the two (by some 8pp. in relevant sections). One notable difference is the recognition in the second edition that the MWP was not hemispherical in scope, the Pacific (China, Japan) not having participated.

[From chs. 1: Introduction; 2: The Climate Problem; 10: Through Viking Times to the High Middle Ages; 11: Decline Again in the Late Middle Ages] Until recently, men had no access to longitudinal climate observations, so that climate seemed unreliable to them; nonetheless, it was for practical purposes considered a constant factor until about 1960. Even now, many practices are based on this presumed constancy (1-2). Today, interest in climatological development is renewed, both because of concern over man’s effects on it and because some hope to influence it for reasons of sustainability or warfare. The second millennium CE has witnessed significant change: warming until 1050, then cooling, and most recently unpredictable fluctuations. The assumption of constancy is therefore no longer useful, and the climate of the future is object of study (2). The social effects of climate change are most apparent in marginal regions such as the polar and arid regions. Climate is a factor in history, but most views of history consider it a constancy (3-4). As the technology of climate reconstruction advances, catastrophes in climate and history seem to have coincided (4). Many hold that any changes in climate must be man’s doing. While man’s influence is certain, a thorough analysis of climate has to be based on all the observable changes (4-5). Cycles are often supposed in both climate and human affairs; the former must be studied and the latter divided into climate-related and climate-unrelated cycles (5-6). Man has not evolved beyond the determining influence of climate and environment (7). Climate is conventionally defined within a thirty-year range (8). Climate was viewed as a constant on the basis of early measurements: the entire nineteenth century had been measured, and despite fluctuations, the end-of-century climate had largely returned to the initial values of the century. This new scientific view opposed popular belief of unpredictable fluctuations. The new view had practical advantages (10-11). In Europe, North America, and the European Arctic, a clear break [! a cooler period preceding the MWP] occurred after AD 400, while lower latitutes and the Antarctic continued in their warmer period, sometimes until the near-global warming of 1000-1200 (162-3). The Carolingian empire was established in a time of particularly cold winters, while summers alternately brought floods and droughts. The three to four centuries that followed it witnessed a warming. Cultivation limits and treelines came to a high that has not since been reached. Greenland warmed from 600 onwards, and California saw a maximum in temperature between 1100 and 1300 (163). Oak treerings provide a chronology of three millennia, but they are harder to interpret because they are influenced by both temperature and rainfall. The narrow rings of 910-930 and the 990s must, by comparison with documentary records, reflect prolonged and repeated drought (163-4). An increase in seafaring occurred about this time. Irish monks settled the Faroes as early as 700-725 and Iceland possibly about the 790s, while Norse settlement of Iceland began in the 860s. Scandinavian seafaring was likely triggered by the mastery of the sail; but the explorations of the Arctic, Greenland, Newfoundland, and probably the Canadian Arctic was helped by the retreat of sea ice. Ohthere reported a voyage to what seems the White Sea, while Harald Hardråde is reported to have sailed north beyond the reach of land. The 70-72 degrees coast of Greenland was discovered by Icelanders in 1194, and the region was used for hunting sea mammals until the return of sea ice shortly afterwards. In 1342, the 65 degrees route to Greenland was abandoned for a more southerly one (164-5). American seafaring did not last long, but this was probably because of trouble with the natives. Greenlandic waters were at least as warm as today, judging by the cod bones found in Norse middens. If Landnámabók is right about Þorkell Farserkr swimming across Hvalseyjarfjörður, the water temperature of that bay must have exceeded today’s upper limit by four degrees (165-6). Graves found in permafrost suggest a similar change in land temperature (166). Grain was grown in Iceland from the settlement to the late sixteenth century. Woodland has been estimated at one-fifth of the country initially and one percent by the thirteenth century. A pre-1090 midden contains evidence of luxurious, partly imported foods, while birches have not attained their size of that period since. At Kvisker, oats were given up and barley growth was halved about 1200 (166-8). Norway saw a sharp increase in forest clearance between 800 and 1000; this ground was again lost after 1300 (168). British tillage was also extended to greater altitudes about 1100-1300 (170-1). The same period gave birth to lots of churchbuilding and the crusades and is generally recognised as a time of great prosperity, technological and agricultural advances (171-2). The warm period lasted longer in Europe than in Greenland, namely until about 1300 or 1310. It is suggested that problems with architecture in the early fourteenth century were a result of increased soil moisture rather than design flaws. In European mountain regions, the warm period and subsequent decline are reflected by aquaducts, mine resumption because of warmth, later mine abandonment because of flooding, and advancing glaciers (172-3). Norse Greenlanders noted a deterioration of climate 1197-1203 due to Arctic cooling. The Dorset Inuit moved south in the twelfth century, probably as a result of a combination of competition and a harsher climate.
