The northernmost “West” settlement disappeared about 1350 due to conflict or disease; although the East Settlement subsisted, its inhabitants grew to 13cm less tall than at the beginning of the settlement. Regular European-Greenlandic trade ceased after 1369, but imported clothes from about 1500 have been preserved in graves. Sailors accidentally arriving to Greenland in 1540 found no survivors (178-9). The many fifteenth-century explorations were particularly badly timed (179-80). The Icelandic economy declined from 1200 onwards, and average stature declined by 6cm between the tenth and the eighteenth centuries. Cold years with sea ice yielded little hay and sheep died. Grain was given up, glaciers advanced, and volcanic eruptions also contributed to harsher conditions. The use of polar bear skins suggests a great deal of sea ice in the fourteenth century (179-81). The first symptoms of a worsening climate in Europe were storms, floods, and sand storms in the thirteenth century (181-6). Cooling began suddenly in the early fourteenth century, and a particularly cold series of winters occurred in the 1430s (186-8). Diseases such as ergotism were widespread. The bubonic plague seems to have originated in Asia immediately after exceptional rainfall and flooding in 1332 (188-9). Desertion of farms and settlements occurred already before the plague set in, reportedly due to a fall in population numbers since the famine but also due to soil exhaustion and shortage of seeds (189-91). Norwegian abandonment of farms began before 1200. The Norse population moved south and coastwards, while Sami hunters enlarged their territories. By the 1430s, the fish-rich Lofoten region had been abandoned for 95 percent; meanwhile, coastal settlements grew (191). Western Norway also suffered (191-3). The central and southeastern regions expanded until the plague. Parts of Denmark were also subject to desertion (193). The climate was a definite factor in changes in agriculture and husbandry. The growing season shortened by some three weeks, and crop failures increased. Scottish clan warfare may be explained by the social stress resulting from a deteriorating climate (193-4). Cultivation limits throughout Europe fell sharply (194-5). The Hussite uprising in the 1420s and 1430s may have been fueled by poor conditions (196).

author: Pheifer, J.D.
title: The Seafarer 53–55
abstract: The spring passages in both Guthlac 742-4 and The Seafarer 48-52 are joyful, but the cuckoo’s song brings on melancholy in the latter, not the former. Rieger has attempted to explain this by casting the poem as a dialogue between an aged mariner and a novice, in which the old man is given the cuckoo lines. Kluge has a similar reading, but attributes the lines to the young man. Both understand the cuckoo as a joyful messenger of spring. Sieper cites Slavonic and Celtic instances in which the cuckoo brings sorrow and death (282). Anderson follows Sieper, suggesting that sumeres weard is a traditional epithet of no relevance to the mood of the passage (282-3). Whitelock understands the bird as a messenger of joy, but bringing the opposite for this ascetic. The passage feels like a conventional formula, which also seems to be expressed in The Husband’s Message 20-3, which similarly has the sad cuckoo foreshadow a sea-voyage. Thus the convention seems to be that the cuckoo, joyful messenger of spring, calls seafaring men back to their perilous task. The Conflictus hiems et veris states more explicitly and more generally that the cuckoo signals the return of hardship and war on land and sea after the winter comforts. This, however, is the opinion of Hiems, countered by Ver, who regards the cuckoo as the herald of house-construction, peaceful travels, and the rejuvenation of the land (283). The latter is the dominant voice of the poem, which ends with a general incantation of the cuckoo by the assembled shepherds. These passages explain the ambiguity of the cuckoo in The Seafarer; the affinity of the Conflictus with OE poetry has long been recognised (284).

author: Le Goff, Jacques
title: Discorso di chiusura
publication: Popoli e paesi nella cultura altomedievale: 23-29 aprile 1981
series: Settimane di studio del centro Italiano di studi sull’alto medioevo
abstract: Studies the connections between space, geography, and culture between the sixth and eleventh centuries. The first part (806-17) mostly concerns political and geographical space. The second (817-27) discusses the new organisation of space after the collapse of the Roman Empire. Spatial centres were Jerusalem, churches, monasteries, and pilgrim centres; palaces; castles (818-20). Travel centred around pilgrimage, war, and trade (820). One could not be familiar with all regions and had to rely on guides (821); sea and forest were necessary parts of travel, yet they symbolised danger and adventure (821-2). There is mention of Claude Carozzi, who is said to have discussed the geography of the afterlife (no reference); but two afterlives/otherworlds can be distinguished, Christian and non-Christian (825). The present world and the next not only share a resemblance, there is continuity between them (825-7). Cultural geography is discussed (827-35). This section opens with a discussion of antique geography and the subsequent Christian allegorisation of the field (828-9). Cartography (830-2). After the fifth century AD, barbarians shifted in the public opinion from noble savages to the triptych of foreigners, invaders, pagans (832): “[l]’ethnologie du Haut Moyen Age est xénophobe” (833). The exotic is discussed (833-5). The role of the Alexander legends is emphasised in the spread of this motif (833-4).

author: Linderholm, Hans W., and Björn E. Gunnarson
title: Summer Temperature Variability in Central Scandinavia During the Last 3600 Years
abstract: A Scots pine treering from the central Scandinavian mountains provides a proxy for summer temperatures 1632 BC–AD 2002. Striking warm periods were 450–550 and 900–1000; cold periods were 300–400 and 1550–1900. Earlier proxies from Sweden and Finland indicate that this proxy is reliable. Summer temperatures are most easily recognised, since they are influential on pine growth close to the treeline.

author: Manker, Ernst
title: The Underlying Factors of Lappish Nomadism
publication: The Nomadism of the Swedish Mountain Lapps
abstract: Briefly explains the precise, non-roaming type of migration practised by intensive Sami reindeerherders (contrast extensive reindeer breeding, which is mostly non-migratory). The herders’ year is divided into eight seasons, “our” ordinal seasons and four compounds that have compound names. This division is a direct result of the migratory behaviour of reindeer. Summers are spent in coastal or mountaneous areas while forests provide shelter against the elements in winter. The only real nonmigratory periods are spring (calving season) and autumn (rutting season), although generally the cardinal seasons see less migration than the compounds (26).

author: Martin, B.K.
title: Aspects of Winter in Latin and Old English Poetry
publication: Journal of English and Germanic Philology
abstract: Studies non-patristic Latin influence on OE winter formulas and poetic diction. The theme of winter binding things is found in Andreas 1255b-6a, 1257b-9; Sfr 32a; Wdr 24, 57; Bwf 1132b-3a, 1608-11; Maxims I.71-7; Menologium 205 (375-9). Other Germanic poetry shows little such usage; but the theme abounds in Latin works known to the Anglo-Saxons (380-2). A second theme present in both Latin and OE literature is that of icicles forming on the person (385-9). It is suggested that some of the traces of Latin learning in OE poetry indicate a continuation of conventions in education and composition (390).

author: Matonis, Anne T.E.
title: Some Rhetorical Topics in the Early Cywyddwyr
publication: Bulletin of the Board of Celtic Studies
abstract: Places the poetry of Dafydd ap Gwilym in a Continental context by pointing out corresponding motifs. The locus amoenus consisted of “a beautiful, natural site. . , a meadow or clearing, a tree (or several. . .), a brook, bird-song” as well as, particularly in medieval poetry, “a soft breeze, flowers, woodland, and shade”; the topos was inevitably conflated with others, such as the seasons and human love (48). The locus amoenus is traced from the Carmina Burana via the Roman de la Rose and French lyrics, as well as Chaucer, to the Welsh lyrics of Dafydd ap Gwilym (49-56). The topos of the seasons is similarly widespread from Virgil onwards. Correspondences are pointed out between Latin and Welsh poetry in the motifs of spring as progenitor; spring’s fertility; its contrast with winter; and nature clothed (57-61). The remainder of the article studies the topos of courts (61-72).

author: McCormick, Michael
title: Seasonal Rhythms
publication: Origins of the European Economy: Communications and Commerce, A.D. 300–900
abstract:
Questions the conventional assumption that medieval travel was not undertaken in winter. On land, winter and spring problematised the finding of fodder for horses and mules for large groups especially, yet Charlemagne mounted an attack travelling in December, January, and March. Smaller groups, such as messengers, travelled in winter with less difficulty (445). Frozen waterways could be used as roads, though land was safer and easier. The Alps, too, were easier to cross in summer, but winter crossings are well-attested (447). Once land routes became the default way to northern Europe, there was no longer a winter hiatus for papal documents to this region. Examples and travel speeds are given, of envoys as well as larger groups (447-8). October and November were important months for land-travel, despite the risk of delaying into winter. Autumn was nevertheless chosen because northern travellers feared the diseases of southern summer (449-50; a footnote cites evidence).

On sea, the winter was more problematic. In classical times, Mediterranean blue-water travel is believed to have stopped from 10 November to 10 March (mare clausum), with 14 September and 27 May signalling the beginning and end of the risky season (450). The 674-8 naval siege of Byzantium was annually interrupted from October to April despite the short distance involved, and Carolingian evidence confirms this pattern (450-1). But exceptions are attested, though these reflect on the urgency of the errands involved; also, seasonal patterns in wind strengths and directions must have diversified sailing according to [vessel build and] sailing experience (451). Statistical analysis shows that April through October were the most-travelled on the Mediterranean, though all months show some activity; April and August were the most-favoured (452-4). April, May, and October became a time for seafaring only for the African fleet of late Roman times, due to financial and military need; early medieval Mediterranean sailing patterns resemble the Roman African schedule (454-5). Technology (the lateen sail) and climate are suggested as explanations, but the use of small vessels and shoreline sailing would have been more influential factors keeping the influence of the weather at bay (455-8). Winter was at its most absolute in January and February; November, December, and March were times of low activity, but activity still; in all, 20% of sailing movements took place during the winter months [winter having five months!] (458). In classical times, November through March was a time of storms, but also of poor visibility (short days, clouds, precipitation, fog) (459). Winter voyages are listed and discussed, showing that medieval sailors were more prone to winter sailing than their classical forebears (459-62). A detailed account of a voyage from Greece to Italy is discussed (462-4). A surprising number of voyages during bad sailing months were military raids, conducted when the enemy was not patrolling the waters or otherwise expecting attack from sea (462-7). In conclusion, land and sea were travelled around the year, especially local and short coastal seafaring; long-distance sailing in winter was mostly limited to urgent political and military activity. Sailing in these months was slow; economic activity was therefore more common in early spring and late autumn (467-8).

author: McCormick, Michael, Paul Edward Dutton, and Paul A. Mayewski
title: Volcanoes and the Climate Forcing of Carolingian Europe, A.D. 750–950
abstract:
Emphasises the need to study the climate of the first millennium CE, which is often said to have been much like that of the twentieth century but slightly cooler (865-6). Written sources on climate are widely available for the first and last few centuries of the period (866). Volcanic activity presents both objective information and implications for the climate. Consequent harsh winters ensured documentation. The GISP2 data show there was more volcanic activity about 700-1000 (867). Volcanic eruptions are clear causes of climate cooling (867-9). Greenlandic ice sheet data reflect this, although factors such as the proximity of the volcano influence the quantity of SO4 deposit (879). A canonical study describes the first major warming in our era as having taken place 800-900 and again 950-1100, from which point a slow decline started until the real cooling set in about 1400 (871-3). Tree production at the sites of Swiss glaciers represent an independent record regarding ice advance and retreat. The Gorner Glacier was small from the later eighth century to the late thirteenth century, thus defining the MWP [for these parts]; the Grosser Aletch Glacier advanced 600-700 and again from about 900 (874). Proxy evidence also suggests that 800-900 brought increased (mild) westerly winds to Europe, while the fifty years following cooled down (874-6).

Ice core data and documentary evidence agree to an extent about the most important volcanic events 750-950 (876). The subjectivity of written records is warned against; yet nine major multiregion anomalies may be identified for this period (876-8). Eight, all of them harsh winters, are individually described and took place 763-4; 821-2; 823-4; 855-6; 859-60; 873-4; 913; and 939-40 (878-89). The first of these is documented in ASC and by the abbot of Wearmouth-Jarrow, who claims it slowed book production (878-9). The possibility of ice-crossings is a type of documentary evidence used repeatedly, as is the completely snow-covered state of the land. [Since the article studies the Carolingian era internally, it is of little use in the identification of MWP within a longer timeframe. Rather, it demonstrates that the eighth century up to 820 witnessed only one volcano-caused cold winter, but the ninth and early tenth many.]

author: McGovern, Thomas H.
title: Management for Extinction in Norse Greenland
publication: Historical Ecology: Cultural Knowledge and Changing Landscapes
abstract:
Asks what killed the Scandinavian settlements in Greenland, and whether their extinction holds any lessons for present-day climate challenges (127-8). Documentary sources are few and unreliable, but they do provide insight into the world-view of the colonising culture. Archaeology provides a complementary resource (128). Exploration of Greenland followed disputes over land in Iceland (128-9). Settlements are at their most vulnerable in their first years. A successful pioneer would gain lasting authority (129). The naming of areas gave the pioneer lasting legal and magical power (129-30). Skalla-Grímr is referred to as having wisely set up his farm to depend on a variety of resources. Such strategies may have resulted in wide dispersal of farms rather than the creation of villages. Later on, however, smaller, specialised seasonal stations seem to have been created that were later upgraded to year-round farms. An increase of the population may have created a need for communal labour (130). West Greenland has similar plant life to Iceland, but only at lower elevations. Domestic animals depended critically on summer pasture and hay for winter fodder, and the Norse Greenlanders used the pastures at full advantage (131). Soon after the arrival of a bishop, the clerical community of Garðar outgrew Eiríkr’s farm (131-2). One aspect of Garðar’s success was in its suppressing of nearby settlement, giving it a surplus of pasture-lands (132-3). The unusually large stone churches in Greenland are expressive of both status and piety (133-4). Documentary and climatic sources make clear that cereals were never a viable resource in Greenland. While the locations of the settlements suggests a reliance on domestic animals, zooarchaeological evidence suggests instead a strong reliance on wild animals. Seal and caribou bones have been found in the greatest numbers, followed by caprines (sheep and goats) and cattle (134). Nets and boat drives seem to have been used for the seal hunt (134-5). Cattle and some caprines were kept in the byre most of their lives, and dung was not removed [during winter?] (135). The animals barely met the conditions of life, so the community must have depended strongly on the few larger herds as buffers in case of calamity and in keeping the herds viable. If the Icelandic model was copied, 15 to 25 farms would pool seasonal labour. Sizes of settlement suggest this pattern (136). Communal hunting and resource redistribution also seem to have been in place, judging by bone distribution (136-7). A hierarchy may be seen: larger farms were allowed to depend on domestic animals, while poorer farmers relied on the seal hunt (137). The same hierarchy and communal strategy speak from the annual trips to the northern walrus hunting grounds. Little walrus ivory has, however, been found in Greenland, suggesting that it was reserved for export. Fish was not traded for grain as in other North Atlantic communities. Trade appears to have been limited to high-value goods: walrus products were exchanged for stained glass, church bells, fashionable clothes and church vestments, timber for building, wine, and iron. Even these imported goods were hard to get by (138). The dangerous northern hunt that financed the trade thus had few benefits for the majority of Greenlanders (138-9). The voyages in six-oared open boats must have cost many lives, and the boats must have been very valuable for shortage of timber. The northern hunt was thus costly in terms of lives, resources, and labour. When the Icelanders landed in their Eastern Settlement, native presence was archaeological only. The Thule tribe came south about 1100-1150. Documentary sources record contact with skrælings dressed in skin and unfamiliar with metal (139). Hostilities did not prevent a further southward movement of the Inuit. Contact must have increased in the period up to 1500 (139-40). Norse artefacts have been found in Inuit settlements, but very few Inuit finds have been done in Norse settlements (140).

A Medieval Climatic Optimum existed c. 900-1200; starting about 1250, temperatures began to fall by a total of some four degrees. Climate instability must have caused further impact on human settlement. Greenland was probably hit hardest of all the North Atlantic settlements. Increased sea ice problematised trade and travel. Climate determinism is often believed to be valid for just this locality (140-1). This view ignores the survival of the Inuit; the fact that the Norse settlement survived until c. 1475-1500; and the fact that not all resources were depleted at the time of extinction (141). Pasture productivity data combines with zooarchaeological evidence to predict large shortfalls in a worst-case scenario of 30% reduction in fodder production (141-2). The poorer farms in particular had worse pasturage and would be greatly affected. The zooarchaeological evidence for the smallholders’ greater reliance on the hunt makes sense in the light of this prediction (142-3). Only the episcopal farm of Garðar will have far outstripped the requirements of self-sufficiency (143). Elite farms were thus least and last affected; most involved in animal husbandry; and served as buffers in times of need. Garðar must have received a proportionate economic and political primacy (143-4). Whatever the doctrinal or political complications, the partly ecclesiastical elite closely sanctioned their leading role (144-5). Many of these economic strategies did not hold up in times of climatic decline, and formed a direct cause of extinction. West Greenland has a perpetually unstable climate as a consequence of ocean currents. The Inuit responded with flexibility of lifestyle, moving up and down the coast according to climate and season (145). The Norse could not engage in this flexibility because their reliance on domestic cattle tied them to the few coastal pasture zones, and the political elite were precisely the least likely to give up on these locations since it was they who were wealthiest in domestic animals. Hunting parties could extend their hunting ranges but were still tied to these coastal regions (145-6). Drift-ice and changing fashions severely damaged the walrus trade. Evidence of Norse Greenlanders trying to force their wares onto passers-by suggests that no attempt was made to restructure trade. A shift towards a primary dependence on whale, seal, and walrus seems logical, although this would involve the adaptation of Inuit techniques. There is no evidence for such a move (146). The Norse failure to exploit ringed seals further strained survival, since the much-relied on migratory harp seal’s movements are greatly affected by climate change (147-8). Effective trade and exchange with the Inuit could have been greatly beneficial (148). “Cognitive maladies” that may have affected Norse Greenlandic managers include false analogy between ecosystems; too general an emphasis on initial abundance while resilience was more important; short observational series; managerial detachment; reactions out of phase; and failure to consider negative developments their own problems (149). The Norse world-view was strongly dualistic, opposing the safety of the familiar and the homestead with the danger of the natural world. Christian cosmology confirmed this dualism. “In this light, the elaborate magical buffering associated with the trops to the Nordsetur hunting grounds becomes immediately comprehensible” (149-50). This world-view may also explain hesitation to engage with the Inuit who, like trolls, were thought not to bleed when wounded, and whose cosmology was radically different from the Norse: they may simply have refused to accept innovation from the Other (150-1). Even so, cultural conservatism, like climate determinism, cannot be taken as a final explanation of extinction: cultural barriers can be overcome in the course of a single generation. Had the Norse been an egalitarian society, they would likely gradually have adopted Inuit technology by way of natural selection. Instead, they were purposefully rejected (151-2). The gradual adoption of Inuit technology would have resulted in a gradual loss of power on the part of the Norse elite (152-3).

author: McKinnell, John
title: Misalliance and the Summer King
publication: Meeting the Other in Norse Myth and Legend
abstract: Typically, humans and gods confronting the Other are of the opposite sex to that of the character they encounter; and heroic females are near-absent. Such narratives are often morally ambiguous (1-10). A history of mythographical and psychological approaches is evaluated (11-36). The several ON genres are discussed; it is concluded that the mythological “canon” seems to be a recent construct, so that the best approach is to scan the entire corpus for mythological themes and use MS dates as a rough guide to the time of composition (37-49). Possible ritual origins of the Vanir motifs are discussed (50-61). Unfortunate marriages are discussed (62-9), after which narratives with the Summer King/Winter King motif are treated (69-80). In this motif, a king makes an expedition to the north or east and meets a “Winter King,” whose daughter he marries but abandons after they have produced children; he dies in a way reminiscent of barrenness or fertility [PS: cf. Kalevala] (70-1). The Summer King feels ambivalent towards his potential offspring: he wants a son and successor, but conceiving a child with one who is essentially “other” entails the risk that his child may have “her” loyalties, thus being “other” (78-80). The question is put forward whether older men may sometimes have conceived of themselves as antagonists, Winter Kings; in Hrólfs saga kraka, this is undoubtedly the case (80). The motif of a goddess winning an “other” lover is discussed; this lover is nearly always a human ruler, since to have a goddess setting up house in Jötunheimr would constitute a move into a barren land as well as a divine subjection to a giant husband (81-94). The völva and various völva-related motifs are studied (95-108). Æsir versus otherworldly females motifs usually constitute either confrontation (Þórr) or exploitation (Óðinn). Chapters eight and nine deal with the former (109-46), while the latter is treated in chapters ten and eleven (147-80). The helpful giantess is studied (181-96); contact with the dead (197-217), and the return of the dead lover (218-31). The appendix summarises Otherworld material not available in English (235-47).

author: Mehl, Jean-Michel
title: Games in their Seasons
publication: Customs, Culture and Community in the Later Middle Ages: A Symposium
abstract: Documentary evidence suggests that dice-games and soule (a variable, violent type of village football) were mostly played in winter in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries (passim). Ovid and Martial similarly associated December with dice-games (80). Divination may explain this positioning of dice-games at the end of the year (80-1). Soule was likely restricted to this time of year because it “rang[ed]. . . across woods and fields,” which would be in agricultural use at all other times of year (82).

author: Meulengracht Sørensen, Preben
title: The Sea, the Flame, and the Wind: The Legendary Ancestors of the Earls of Orkney
publication: At fortælle Historien: Studier i den gamle nordiske litteratur
eds: Michael Dallapiazza, Olaf Hansen, and Gerd Wolfgang Weber
abstract: Studying the ideology of the genealogy of the Fornjótr-line, Meulengracht Sørensen observes that this line is a personification of “nordic winter and northern nature” (222). The meaning of the name Fornjótr is uncertain, but the Flateyarbók compiler read it as “the old Jute,” in which “Jute” should be taken to mean “man” [or “giant,” since this is how Fornjótr is depicted in Snorra Edda]; based in Jutland, his line sets out to conquer the north (222-3). The age of this genealogy is a matter of debate. There is no reason to assume Fornjótr’s sons fire, wind, and sea to derive from the Greek tradition of the four elements: their kinship was traditional in the north (223-5). The genealogy is a blend of historical, legendary, and mythical, so that the Orcadian earls might benefit from the noblest blood (225-7). The myths were not given a place in history, but rather expressed a myth about origin and fate; it was the Christian authors who then proceeded to root them in history through euhemisation (227). The Orcadian genealogy, however, stands out in its suggestion of a Scandinavian rather than a Trojan origin. Also, it refuses to bring the descendants of Óðinn into the family, while other genealogies begin here (228). The suggestion is that the Fornjótr-line is indigenous to Scandinavia, and was present when the Æsir arrived from Asia. Since the line of Hálfdan, descendant of Fornjótr, produced no daughters for the first three hundred years, and the immigrants are said to have married indigenous women, the lines remained separated for the first three centuries (228-9). This may suggest a sense of nordic pride, in originating from fierce rather than pleasant climes, and descending from giants, the enemies of the gods. These aboriginals are no lesser category than the gods, capable of magic and sea-travel, and the inventors of the ski. After the gói abduction scene, Fornjótr’s line intermarries with the royal line of Heiðmörk, heartland of the Ynglingar. The hieros gamos-myth of the king marrying a foreign woman is traditional in Old Norse literature (229). Ynglingatal is a good example of this; and it has the Ynglingar intermarry with characters corresponding to the winter- and nature-personifications of the Fornjótr-line. Orkneyinga saga tells the story from the point of view of the otherly aboriginals, shedding the strife-motif to describe a marriage between equal partners after making peace with the abductor. Thus the Orcadian earls have a genealogical claim to be more Norwegian than the kings of Norway (230).

author: Meyer, Kuno
title: Four Old Irish Songs of Summer and Winter

author: Mills, William J.
title: Metaphorical Vision: Changes in Western Attitudes to the Environment
publication: Annals of the Association of American Geographers
abstract: Studies diachronically the role of metaphor in the perception of the natural world. Metaphor is here read not as collapsed simile but as a confused perception of identity. “In this process, we extend to the unfamiliar those words and concepts we have found useful in comprehending the familiar.” As such, metaphor creates language (237-8). When nature is approached as though it were a book, a human being, or a machine, this usage is metaphorical only in retrospect; when current, such usage was considered literal. The particular metaphor used by a society to understand its entire world is “highly indicative of the needs and aspirations of that society.” The replacement of such a metaphor by another signals profound societal changes (238). Petrarch and the Middle Ages at large are often misunderstood as having no aesthetic appreciation of nature. Augustine’s and Petrarch’s rejection of nature should rather be understood as following from a different overarching metaphor (238-9). Books and writing have always been natural seats of divine wisdom, of which their metaphorical aptness is a natural application. In Christianity, the Bible is God’s immediate revelation; any further revelation (i.e. the natural world) was thus naturally considered derivative, a second book. Augustine’s and Petrarch’s disdain concerns only the observation of the natural world as physical objects without regarding their symbolic meaning. The corollaries of viewing nature as a book are that it has a divine author; that it conveys a message; this message may contain several layers; and it is written in legible characters. In the seventeenth century, however, nature came to be read for its own sake, and the metaphor ceased to apply (239). St Paul lays the foundation for the book-metaphor that was to reach systematic maturity in the Middle Ages, although the Babylonians already used similar metaphors (239-40). John Chrysostom took an egalitarian approach, pointing out that the illiterate and the poor could afford no other book, while any one language could not be read by people of different languages. The Irish philosopher Eriugena expressed the core of Christian symbolism when he wrote that “[t]here is nothing, in visible and corporeal things, that does not signify something incorporeal and invisible.” Medieval artists rejected realism accordingly (240). A derivative metaphor is that of signatures, suggesting that God has left his imprint upon everything visible, and in the natural world one could read not only spiritual truths but also facts of relevance to the present life. Thus physiognomy, and the doctrine that like plants have like medical uses, etc (241). The Renaissance thought of the world as a macrocosm to man’s microcosm, a doctrine based on the idea that man was created perfect [in God’s image], and on an anthropocentric world-view (241-2). Today’s geographic vocabulary is still expressive of such anthropocentrism. The human body is suitable as a metaphor of the world because it is a unity of many parts; its life cycle is an apt metaphor for change and development; order in the human form and in nature can be treated as the same thing; and the suitability of the idea that to know oneself is to know the world (242). (. . .) Galileo’s generation stopped imitating nature and wished to control it. This development has been identified as the immediate cause of the machine metaphor (245-8). None of the metaphors used in these periods were restricted to that period; but in each of the periods only one of them is used as a vehicle around which to develop the period’s understanding of the world (248).

author: Mora, Maria José
title: Un invierno entre los hielos: Los paisajes de la poesía anglosajona
abstract: Criticises Burton’s 1894 article “Nature in Old English Poetry” and dismisses the Romantic idea that the hibernal emphasis of OE poetry derives from a fatalistic outlook and the reality of everyday life. Burton’s article is summarised (225–30), after which Mora sets out to describe the uses of winter in Bwf, which she says are two or three (namely the Breca episode, the Finn episode, and perhaps the hrinde bearwas; not a word of the melting sword) (230–2). The fixation on winter is thus not as omnipresent as Burton suggests (232–3). Bede and ASC are read for an understanding of the physical climate in Anglo-Saxon times (233–4), and the riddles are briefly discussed (234–5). Andreas uses winter imagery to emphasise Andrew’s sufferings against which his mental/spiritual fortitude forms the greater contrast (235–6), particularly considering the implicit contrast with the ideal of the hall, which is discussed in the context of Edwin’s conversion (236–8). Following a quotation of Adam’s lament in GenB, it is observed that the contemplation of winter landscape need not evoke any particular sentiment in Anglo-Saxons, since the reverse may equally well be the case, a mood evoking the description of winter landscape (238). The Phoenix and JDayII describe the absence of seasonal extremes (238–9). The winter imagery in OE poetry seems a literary device to intensify the expressiveness of a description of affliction like that of Adam, Andrew, or Hengest (239–40). The Romantic approach to OE poetry is once more denounced for its selective reading, and Dale is quoted (240–1). The mid-twentieth century shift towards a more Christian reading of OE poetry is described (241–2).

author: Motz, Lotte
title: The Winter Goddess: Percht, Holda, and Related Figures
abstract: Attempts to establish through folkloristic sources that female deities were worshipped in Old Germanic societies. The divine nature of such figures as Percht and Frau Holle may be deduced from the stern Church responses (151). They were venerated in sacred time, i.e. between Christmas and Epiphany, and were presented with food offerings. The evening or night of veneration, or landscape features, are named after these spirits, and so are customs, e.g. Perchtenjagd. Superhuman powers are attributed to the spirits, such as Frau Holle’s causing of snow by shaking her pillows. These characteristics occur in varying combinations (152), and are discussed in turn (152-7), including the Wild Hunt (153-4), associations with spinning (154), and their dealing of punishments and rewards (154-5). The women often have a connection with young women or babies, and educate through their system of reward and punishment (155). They inhabit the woodlands or mountains, and are sometimes associated with particular landscape features; but they are never associated with settled, or economic, areas [except insofar as forests are economic areas] (155-6). Sometimes she is considered wholly evil. She has certain animal characteristics and is mostly an asexual creature (156). More specific local traditions are noted (157). These spirits may be grouped with others worldwide as the supernatural stewards of nature. A subcategory of these is the Lord of Beasts, a motif originating in hunting societies, in which one spirit controls all animals (157-8). These often came to govern domesticated animals and cattle as well, and as societies developed they would extend their rule to humankind. Germanic societies have given the rule of the wild to various supernatural races, depending on region. In the regions with the most conservative traditions, however, Perchta/Holda has been preserved (158). As noted, late December and early January are the typical time of their veneration. This time corresponds to the pre-Christian jól. Pagan midwinter feasts are often condemned in Christian writings, which decry the custom of dressing up as beasts (159). The julbukk tradition of Norway may be seen in this tradition. Wolf disguises are most common in midwinter. Olaus Magnus tells of a Baltic tradition of dressing up as wolves during the twelve nights of Christmas; and German werewolf traditions centre around this time, December being sometimes called Wolfsmonat (159-60). Similar traditions may be found in non-Germanic regions. A ritual relationship between hunter and prey lies at the root of such customs. Winter is the time for them because winter is the hunting season (a mating season for wolves and stags), when agricultural life comes to a standstill. The development of ski-hunting facilitated the winter hunt, and the existence of Old Norse skishoe-deities may be significant in this respect [PS: see also the Fornjótr-genealogies for skishoe-names] (160). The educative function of the female spirits is in some respects reminiscent of initiation rites, as does their association with spinning, a magic-laden activity (160-1). Clerics tended to identify Hulda with Diana, but this association does not explain the spirit’s origin (161-2). Giants, like Holda and Percht, belong to winter, as the class-name hrímþurs suggests: Skaði travels on snowshoes, and Hversu Noregr byggðisk has several giantess winter-names [in the Fornjótr-line]. Midwinter is the time of their greatest activity, as evidenced in Grettis saga and Bárðar saga Snæfellsáss (162). Also like Percht and Holda, the Old Norse giantesses are nocturnal (162-3). Giantesses also have animal names and characteristics, and all Germanic regions know traditions of the wild hunts. Thus Percht and Holda are very northern in their characteristics (163).

author: Neville, Jennifer
title: Representations of the Natural World in Old English Poetry
abstract: OE had no word for “the natural world,” since it had no concept excluding the supernatural. Their conception of “the Other” comes close, but they had no word for this, either. Hence this book will include discussions of phenomena today considered to form no part of the natural world (1-3). In Anglo-Saxon times, people had less protection against the British weather and indeed the weather seems to have been colder and stormier until the end of the period. Yet it must not be supposed that the weather was the only force influencing political relations. The individual, however, was weak as a result of malnutrition and had a low resistance against disease, which was therefore a major enemy (3-6). Few animals posed a threat: wolves, bears, and boars could be dangerous but mostly when provoked. Their primary danger lay in their meddling with crops; and agriculture existed only in a primitive, unreliable form. A fear of natural phenomena, then, is understandable (6-7). On the other hand, rodents and other crop thieves have not found their way into OE poetry; but natural threats are represented as more dangerous than human threats (7-8). Excepting the beasts of battle, no animal occurs frequently in OE poetry, and the absence of some is hard to explain (9-10). Representation always serves an agenda; thus the natural world may be introduced for the depiction of something inferior to man, e.g., to insult someone [PS: but AS names often contained animal names!], or to draw an analogue, e.g., a beehive representing a state. Some agendas, such as didacticism, may be easily identified (10-12). Early medieval representations of the natural world have often been portrayed as inferior to what went before and what came after, as a Greek remnant or a dormant in-between period. A culture, however, is a product of its history, and so the period must have contributed to the cultural flowering of the high Middle Ages. Romantic critics, on the other hand, sought in OE poetry fresh, original conceptions of nature but their judgements were dominated by contemporary fashions (13-16). The natural world according to OE literature conforms to no pattern from which the Anglo-Saxons may have borrowed their concept; no progress towards a more Christian view is to be found; and there is no consistency, suggesting that the creation of a working cosmological understanding of the natural world was no central concern of the Anglo-Saxons. A typically Anglo-Saxon natural world, therefore, is not to be found. The question why no attempts at unification were made is ultimately unanswerable (16-18). Adam, “the first ‘Anglo-Saxon’ exile,” describes the natural discomforts to which the first couple must be exposed after the fall in Gen A; this description contrasts the power of the natural world with the powerlessness of man, thus defining his condition. OE poets always invoked the natural world with a definite purpose in mind, and the point of interest is the power of the natural world opposing man. The natural world thus typically defines man’s concerns. This is no necessary focus: contemporary Irish and ON poems refer to natural forces opposing other elements of nature not man (19-22). One would expect to learn of human nature in homilies and gnomic literature, and one does; but other literature is equally informative of the human condition, albeit indirectly. Man partakes of both evil and good, and this duality determines his condition; but he also lives in the natural world, which is not subject to Christian mythological forces. Nonetheless, not all of the natural environment has been portrayed: it was used to make observations about man. Bede’s story of the sparrow in the hall reflects on the human condition by making man subject to the forces of nature: man is continuously under siege by the natural world. (22-5). This natural world does not partake of morality, although in patristic writings it does, whether on the side of God or Satan. Although Augustine’s incitement to study the natural world seems to have been taken in by the Anglo-Saxons, this does not show in their representations of the natural world. In the creation account of Genesis A, the world is useless until it surrounds humanity (26-31). Its function in defining humanity is borne out not only by OE poetry but also by OE prose and Anglo-Latin literature. Monsters described are the negation of man’s characteristics (31-5). Sfr contrasts the sounds of nature with his own misery, while a contemporary Irish poem takes delight in nature. OE poets could express joy, but they used hall life, not the natural world, for this purpose; the antithesis has inversed polarity in comparison with the Romantic approach. Virgil presented the natural world as a force to be conquered by human effort; Anglo-Saxon literature considers it beyond man’s influence. While there is a Welsh parallel to Sfr’s cuckoo-inspired misery, the OE poet does not explain the origin of the sorrow derived from the natural world (36-43). Nevertheless, neither Sfr nor Bwf explicitly calls the world evil; and when Guthlac is beset by demons, no description of the natural world appears—in fact, the demons find that he takes pleasure in his dwelling. Andreas, however, is beset by natural hardships; but they are not called the devil’s doing. This poem, however, ascribes to the natural world a different kind of agency: the weather binds not only water but also humanity, so that endurance becomes the nearest equivalent to heroic agency (43-7). Other works have the natural world encroach upon humanity, even unto destruction. Thus The Ruin, Wdr 101-15. Where such passages are read as pathetic fallacy, in the light of the present analysis they are more correctly described as opposing human interests (ON does have pathetic fallacy). Sermo Lupi, by contrast, ascribes the deterioration of the world to human agency. Vercelli Homily 9.122-30, however, compares hell to harsh weather conditions. “Literal accuracy and fidelity to previous authorities do play a role in some of these representations of the natural world, but such issues are subordinated to the purpose of locating the human race in its place amidst external powers, of confining and thus defining humanity” (47-52). The depiction of reverse traits in the natural world is no mere pessimistic reflection on the human condition: it also represents an antagonist force out there, calling for defence. This, however, is a consequence, not the cause, of the Anglo-Saxons’ view on humanity (53). The “defining and confining” view of the natural world offers a new perspective on the aspects of Anglo-Saxon culture already studied. In Maxims I 50b-8a, waves are used to represent political unrest; they beat against walls representing stable government, just as The Ruin and Wdr point out the need for “social structures.” The natural world is only used as a metaphor for humanity as a whole when a negative aspect of humanity is described; thus wælwulfas and hildewulfas, terms lowering the status of the Vikings below humanity but raise their forces to the level of the unconquerable natural forces (53-7). The construction of Heorot has often been compared with that of the world. In both creation accounts, it is the external forces that determine the structure built to withstand them. The world preceding creation is a negation of the cultivated, cultured world, and the Bwf poet recounts the story shortly after the completion of Heorot. Both constructions take place after the defeat of external enemies, both are carried out through their lord’s word, and both lords fill them with gifts at completion. An extensive comparison between God’s and man’s creation can be made, but the latter is ultimately more complex, since man is not omnipotent and is fated to strive after an ideal he cannot achieve. Societies that are able to defend themselves are circles of light surrounded by the natural world, so that Beowulf’s journey from his own kingdom to Denmark is presented as a dangerous journey (57-69). The destructive agent Grendel, monstrous in a modern definition, represented the natural world to Anglo-Saxon minds, as there was no clear dichotomy between the natural and the supernatural. The Danes’ inability to deal with Grendel has been called a flaw in their society; but seeing that the poet does not blame them, it may be better to see Grendel as part of the natural world, inherently ungovernable and unconquerable by men. As a healðegn, Grendel is a parody of human society. The reaction of the Danes must be to maintain the rules and responsibility lacking in the natural world. Once Grendel comes under Beowulf’s power, he begin to take on a more recognizable shape, having hand, fingers, joints, etc.; his defeat consists in an integration into human society, a denaturalization. Although there are hints that Hrothgar’s kingdom will fall prey to internal strife, the poem leaves Denmark in an ideal state: in peace because able to defend itself (70-81). In the Geatish kingdom, too, defeat at human hands is suggested, but the only danger within the bounds of the poem is posed by the natural world. Although subdued, the dragon does manage to disrupt the structure of society by taking out its leader, thus leaving it undefended (81-4). The natural world is also invoked to describe the state of exile: in WfL, the natural descriptions function to show her state external to society. The specifics of the natural world do not have symbolic referents, and they are seldom mentioned: general traits such as darkness and coldness are more common, functioning as negation (84-8). Beowulf stands out because he interacts with his environment; but it is often difficult to distinguish between the individual and the representative of a society. Often such a distinction appears unnecessary, since every human being suffers the same helplessness. This observation prompts the question whether an underlying abstract group notion is supposed at all. Menniscnes “humanity” and geferscipe “society” are absent from OE poetry (89-92). But its formulaic nature favours the concrete, so that this peculiarity may be explained by a poetic convention rather than an inability on the part of the poet to conceive of such a concept (92-5). MS illustrations and laws might shed some light on this point: the illustrations of Junius 11 show a reflection on exegesis but do not include the Platonic abstraction of later times. We do not, however, know why. Law codes concentrate strongly on the rights of the individual, but kindred groups such as the ASC’s Angelcynn also play a role. Evidence, then, is inconclusive. The indefinite nature of this sort of evidence indicates once more the importance of definition through a representation of the natural world (95-9). Imprecision is a characteristic of OE verse: the natural world is often depicted as “an undefined danger,” as in the Journey Charm (99-101). The dangers of the mære are not specified: what seems to matter is that there are dangers to it. A general definition of “alien harmer” seems in order. This definition reminds one of Grendel, who has certain general and specific characteristics in common with the incuba, which is sometimes glossed mære. Vagueness in these contexts emphasizes the confrontation of power with powerlessness (101-10). This is the more the case when neither the individual nor the natural world he is confronted with is specific. In poems like Judgement Day II and Christ II, the power of the natural world is intended to incite readers to seek out a higher power. Self-control and endurance are, however, also striven after, as in Maxims I 50-1 and Wdr 11b-14. In yet other contexts, one is expected to control not only oneself but also one’s environment: thus the Exeter Riddles describe how man uses nature to make parchment or to make a pen out of reed. Such objects are denatured like Grendel’s arm (110-15). The charms are bent on invoking non-human powers and applying them for human purposes. Disease is as such also part of the natural world. The agency of diseases is hard to determine. Understanding the nature and cause of disease is the most important part of the study of medicine; Anglo-Saxons strove to reach it by inferring, for example, that disease is related to divine will. Penance might thus lead to cure. Charms like wið færstice tried to transform the unknown into something one could do battle with (115-22). Unlike the agents in medical texts, saints were nonymous. Saints were often described in military, heroic terms. The demons of Guthlac initially object not to his saintliness but to his presence on their land (122-8). Beowulf too is limited by the natural world and by his actions out there, beyond society. Although he also does battle with men, his status rests mainly on his confrontations with the outside world; and the story of his exploits among men is immediately appended by the tale of his swimming feat, in which he confronts both man and nature. With regard to his feats in the natural world, Beowulf is often contrasted with men who have failed to achieve the same (129-33). Thus when the expedition reaches Grendel’s mere, all men sit down and Beowulf is left to perform the task (135-6). His death may be said to reduce him to human proportions: none can ultimately resist the power of the natural world. In his wish to be buried in a “bright barrow” on the ocean’s promontory, Beowulf wants to remain a beacon on the outskirts of human society (137-8). Nature is sometimes described as a revelation of God’s power (Christ and Satan 1-18); this is, however, a poetic technique rather than a core belief (139-42). God’s superiority makes his relationship with the natural world uncomplicated; this explains the uniformity in creation accounts (142-4). Yet this relationship is subject to conflicting descriptions. Also, natural characteristics such as frost carry entirely different connotations when described in relation to God’s power than when described in relation to man’s powerlessness. OE literature has no cosmological system: no texts provides a more sophisticated picture than that of the “cosmic hall.” Pre-Christian religion seems to have been closely linked to the natural world, but little of this is to be found in OE literature (144-8). This is because influential writers have actively prevented its entrance into writing. Yet one expects a certain amalgamation such as that advised by Pope Gregory. The God of Genesis shows such amalgamation, though not of religions: he is presented as a heroic warrior. His appearance as such in The Dream of the Rood is incomplete and incongruous (148-52). The absence of such amalgamation concerning the universe is surprising. It may be explained by the inclination of OE verse towards a description of factual matter in maxims. The Anglo-Saxons did have many cosmological sources available, but they seem to have little interest in the larger plan: Byrhtferth follows Bede but focusses on symbolic numbers and computus rather than structure. Although the concept of the macrocosm was known, it was not used as a framework in which to place the cosmos (152-7). Alfred is the exception in his translation of the Consolatio; but he emphasizes God’s power in the cosmos rather than its workings (157-60). The Order of the World similarly has God uniting the elements of the cosmos, but it tells man to focus on creator rather than process (160-3). The contradictory of the natural world, threat and representative of God’s power, is therefore not discussed in OE poetry. The difficult questions are avoided, and no concept like Boethius’s concentric circles is formed. Augustine’s understanding of nature as a book of revelation was not taken in. God’s authorship of disease was sometimes taken to be a tool for retribution, or for population control (163-70). Most poets, however, have shrunk from such a connection, so that Grendel, for instance, operates outside God’s will, even though such a reading is heretical (170-1). A tradition came about that took the middle ground between the scourge of God and independent agency: Cuthbert describes the sea as an agent, it being mere implication that this was done by God’s will. Poetry usually leaves more distance between God and the natural world: it is by withdrawing his hand that God punishes man, not by striking with it. In Exodus, he actively protects. In short, the poets left God’s relation to the natural world an unsolved paradox (171-7). While the Anglo-Saxons described the natural world as a force enclosing human constructions, they themselves enclosed the natural world and made it a construction in shaping it into what they wanted it to be in their literature (178). This total power over the natural world existed in man’s postlapsarian state only in writing (179). The Anglo-Saxon attitude towards writing suggests great consciousness, including consciousness of their ideas concerning the natural world; but this question cannot be answered authoratively (181-3). Wisdom literature is thought presents the natural world as governed by a just God, but it offers no consistency in this respect: hostility is also a frequent characteristic. The natural world is not always an important ingredient of wisdom literature. Here and there there seems to be an interest in the natural world for its own sake (183-90). The Physiologus follows Augustine in supposing that religious knowledge is to be found in the natural world; in this way, the horrors of nature become acceptable through their metaphorical interpretation. A reduction of the natural world to human terms is characteristic of all OE wisdom poetry (190-6). Words were considered central to this process. Solomon and Saturn describes knowledge as something with which to struggle until it is fixed in writing, when it becomes something pleasing (196-8). The description of the natural world in wisdom literature seems to be highly conscious (199-201). Representations of the natural world are various, and cannot be caught in a single paradigm; but they are not random, and they always seem to be linked to central themes of OE poetry. Such thematic associations explain to a great extent the lack of unity between the representations. The purposes the Anglo-Saxons had in describing the natural world may have proved incompatible with the twelfth-century tradition, for which reason OE poetry may have failed to anticipate that tradition. Such a systemized picture of the natural world would leave no place for representations emphasizing human survival. Its absence from poetry does not prove that philosophers did not conceive of the natural world in such a way (202-6).

author: Neville, Jennifer
title: The seasons in Old English poetry
publication: La Ronde des saisons: Les saisons dans la littérature et la société anglaises au Moyen Age
abstract: As the Romantics noted, Anglo-Saxon poetry shows a quantitive preference for winter over the other seasons (37). Nevertheless, it is clear that ASE had more seasons. Anderson argues persuasively that the bipartite and four-season systems existed side by side for some time; the latter is treated rather explicitly, suggesting infamiliarity (38-40). No exclusive word for season is found [PS: cf. Latin tempus, as discussed in Frandon, “Les saisons”]. Spring and autumn are ambiguous (40-1). OE poetry tends to describe events in repeated cycles; thus Deor, the rise and fall of kings in Bwf; and pride and fall in Genesis. Though this motif need not be native, it seems to be well-integrated (41-2). However, “cycles” in Bwf are not circular or continuous; they lead to a definite end. This linear theme of the seasons illustrates the progression from creation to doomsday. While many references to the seasons are indeed cyclical and therefore cannot refer directly to doomsday (Maxims I 71-4; Bwf’s Finn episode; WfL; Wdr), not all seasonal references are pathetic fallacy: thus Sfr 48-52 describes the opposite, a mind being influenced by nature (42-5). This passage links the decay of the world to that of the individual, an idea inspired by the larger commonplace of the close bond between microcosm and macrocosm. This connection is also found in Sermo Lupi; Byrhtferth’s Enchiridion; and Blickling Homily X (45). The existence of a premillennial eschatological anticipation has been documented (45-6). It is proposed that “the ageing world” was a connotation of the seasons in OE poetry; while this connotation is dormant in some poetry, it is essential for the structural explanation of such passages as Solomon and Saturn 282-307, 312-26 (46-8).

author: Nilsson, Martin P.
title: Folkfesternas samband med år och arbetsliv
abstract: Feasts and ritual gatherings may be divided into those that represent milestones in human life and those marking milestones in the calendar-year. This publication concerns the second group, determined by the succession of the seasons. These seasons depend on the course of the sun, which determines human behaviour in terms of work and rest, herd movement, fishing and hunting seasons, and winter survival on the gathered provisions. All these occupations can be associated with rites of secular or religious import, although the difference cannot easily be told when it concerns a time in which magic and religion are intertwined, since magic often had practical aims (1). Not every repeated rite constitutes a feast or feast rite. For something to be a feast requires a gathering of people. The precondition of a feast is thus a social gathering at a given time (1-2). For annual feasts, this time is a season or time of year, though no detailed calendar tradition need be required. The importance of the transition to agriculture as a basis for subsistence is often underestimated with regard to annual feasts. The agricultural cycle has given rise to a coincident ritual cycle (2). Agriculture also requires fixed habitation, entailing important social changes. Gathering- and herding-cultures rely on small groups coming together in larger parties at intervals, but agricultural cultures consist in single farming families doing work that for the absence of social gatherings cannot be read as a succession of feasts. Customs are therefore carried out in gatherings with neighbours, a situation entailing certain consequences. If temples are built, these become centres of feast activity. Churches were such centres in Christian times. Christmas, too, was a church feast; and ON legal sources instruct their subjects to celebrate jól in gatherings larger than the immediate family. Only in the nineteenth century were the social pillars removed from such feasts as Christmas in Sweden (2-3). Feasts often represent the conclusion of labour, and have done since as early as Aristotle’s day (3). As Aristotle also remarked, the conclusion of labour typically provides the spare time required for a feast (3-4). Certain sociologists have embraced this understanding, particularly with regard to Arctic countries, in which no [agricultural] labour is possible for part of the year. Here, winters are spent indoors and sustenance comes from provisions; there is a lot of time for feasting. Similar considerations apply to Scandinavia, and the sagas make clear that one did not leave the home in winter. This is the real cause for the superlative importance of jól in Scandinavia into the nineteenth century. Tacitus makes clear that the Germanic peoples once used a lunar calendar, when he says they would meet at new moon or full moon, times they considered to bring good fortune in the beginning of undertakings. There is, however, evidence that the calendar was lunisolar at least towards the end of the pre-Christian period, since Bede refers to intercalations and the dísaþing calculation suggests the same (4). In late pagan times, a solar calendar pushed out this lunisolar calendar, if it existed, because the week-year used in all of Scandinavia depends on Julian elements. This calendar divided the year into two halves, beginning on 14 October and 14 April (4-5). Christianity brought the ecclesiastical Julian calendar and obliged everyone to partake of Christian feasts; neglect was punished. The dating of Easter was complex, thus encouraging the spread of runestaves. The moveable feasts were inconvenient for popular usage, since popular calendars relied closely on the natural year. This explains why Easter and Pentecost never gained great influence. Each big Church feast was preceded by a vigil, which was celebrated by the people. In Sweden, this practice was extended to the secular Mayday by the creation of Valborgsmässaafton (5). The fixed holidays consist mainly of Christmas and saints’ days, the latter group being of various significance. They were often used for dating. Since popular feasts tend to settle on a fixed day of the year, and favour public holidays, they often embraced Church holidays (5-6). Folk customs were themselves bound to particular times of year, and the nearest Church feasts were chosen as the days on which these popular feasts could be celebrated. Jól/Christmas is the most obvious example of such a shift in time; the vetrnætr have never been linked with any one Christian feast because there are no Christian feasts in autumn of greater significance than Michaelmas. Thus both Michaelmas and All Hallows have been used in Norway. Agricultural tasks, too, may be loosely linked up with the calendar, though precise timing depended on latitude. Spring was for ploughing and sowing. No feast was associated with the start of the agricultural year, but the custom of eating sowing-cake is attested, and similar customs existed at the end of the sowing-season. No fixed Church feast exists at this time of year (6). Right in the middle of spring labours, however, we find Mayday, the only feast not linked to a Church holiday. It ultimately originates from France (6-7). Its celebration varies from maypole dancing through carols to bonfires. The carols were not followed by a banquet, which was delayed until the end of agricultural spring labours. This again indicates the condition of spare time placed on feasting; in southeastern Skåne, the May carols were delayed until Midsummer. Bonfires are celebrated at various times of year; this may be explained by regional differences in the coming of spring, since bonfires were supposed to include greens. It probably originated at this time to protect animals that went out into the pastures for the first time (7). Classical feasts intended to protect the crops are also found in Scandinavia, if often in Christian guise. The Moving Days are a direct descendant of the Roman Ambarvalia intended for this purpose (8). Midsummer was Sweden’s largest feast after jól. This may be explained by climate: nature is at its prettiest at Midsummer. A second necessary condition is the leisure of this period: in early June, sowing was done but hay-harvest did not commence until July. The feast of John the Baptist corresponded to this time. There is no evidence for the belief that Midsummer celebrations, like jól, were inherited from pre-Christian times: the earliest reference is to a St John’s Ale. Midsummer was a big celebration throughout Europe and there it can be traced back to the conversion, but it need not have been brought to Scandinavia from there (8-9). The most distinctive Midsummer tradition is the maypole, which, however, originated around Mayday celebrations. It was moved because Swedish climate did not allow it in May. The eldest Midsummer bonfire reference is in Olaus Magnus. It later spread to Walpurgis night because it fits better there in the Swedish climate. Water rites also existed (9). The belief is repeated that Midsummer in Scandinavia seems to be a belated May festival, so forced by climate and agricultural calendar (9-10). The early summer lapse “lilla hoveln” is short, and is followed by hay-harvest and crop-harvest, which finishes at different times depending on autumn weather. General festivities to celebrate the end of the harvest are thus hardly possible throughout Scandinavia. Some customs are known, such as catching a hare or leaving out straw for Óðinn’s horses. Norway and Sweden are very sparing in their harvest festivities, while Denmark and Skåne show some affinity with Continental traditions dependent on a better climate, in which the last wagonload of crops is decorated with flowers and greens (10). Only distinct regions of Sweden have Michaelmas traditions. Here, the harvest has to be in by Michaelmas and people move home from their shielings by the same date. Two days’ holiday belonged to Michaelmas. These were the moving days for servants (10-11). St Martin’s Day was in Britain and the Continent associated with the slaughter and the end of the summer economy; in Scandinavia, this feast was too late in the season; it was celebrated only in Skåne. Threshing followed the harvest; the completion of threshing was celebrated in Sweden and Norway. No natural deadline existed, but the work had to be done by jól, when a long resting-period began. Jól became Scandinavia’s biggest festival because of its high latitude. Certain arctic tribes similarly considered winter a time for feasting. It may be traced back to the birth of the sun-God at the solstice in late classical tradition. There is no evidence to suggest that Nordic jól was associated with the solstice; in fact, it was celebrated some three weeks late (11). In Christian times, Christmas Eve and Christmas Day attracted some of the customs originally associated with the New Year, which had been the greatest feast in late antique and early medieval times (11-12). When studying the origins and significance of a festival, it has to be borne in mind that a distinction between primary and secondary traditions can seldom be drawn, and that despite changes in timing, celebrations are crucially bound to particular seasons. Accordingly, traditions cannot be regarded as having an ancient core surrounded by newer traditions. It is their time within the year that holds the key to their function (12).

author: Nilsson, Martin P.
title: Primitive Time-reckoning: A Study in the Origins and First Developtment of the Art of Counting Time Among the Primitive and Early Culture Peoples
abstract: Refers to O. Schrader, Sprachvergleichung und Urgeschichte II.235 for the explanation of the pars pro toto custom of counting nights rather than days: in primitive societies, the moon has usually been the prime reference for time, and the moon comes out at night (15). In Indo-European times there were three seasons: only hiems, ver, and summer are present in the majority of languages. This confirms Tacitus’s finding (71-2). Spring, however, will not have had the same status as the other two, since the Indo-Europeans must have distinguished between the wet and the dry season. Greek first knew the same three seasons, but a second transitional season, that of fruit harvest, may be seen in Homer (72). Swedish höst still refers to agriculture, and sometimes skyr may be found as a fifth season, that of harvest, occurring between höhöst and efterhöst. In some parts of Scandinavia, the seasons are still referred to as times of specific activities (74-5). Jakob Grimm doubted Tacitus’s statement on the Germanic seasons, but he withdrew his criticism on the grounds that the Germanic peoples of Tacitus’s day knew grain harvest but not fruit harvest (75). Festivals are not to be used as evidence of seasonal transition, since they are not bound to the beginning or end of a season (76). It is important to abandon the idea that a season is made up of a fixed number of days (77). Icelanders still [!] reckon in weeks. While it has been argued that this derives from the Church calendar, it is in fact pre-Christian (78). All of Scandinavia, including the Sami, used to count in weeks. The Sami have borrowed these from the Scandinavians, as they have also borrowed the Summer Night and the Winter Night (14 Apr/Oct; 79-80). A division of the year by these two points in time may be found on many rune staves, which will have been the origin of the week-year (81). The year need not be cut in half precisely: southern Germanic tribes counted five months for the winter. It is the longer winter season in the north that has contributed to the six-month reckoning that is so prevalent among northern peoples (82). Pars pro toto reckoning of “winter” for year is “almost the rule among all peoples who live under a climate that has a winter with snow and ice” (94). Exceptions are noted (94-7).

author: Nordberg, Andreas
title: Jul, disting och förkyrklig tideräkning: Kalendrar och kalendariska riter i det förkristna Norden
publisher: Kungliga Gustav Adolfs Akademien för svensk folkkultur
abstract:
[Introduction (9-14)] points out that computistics has not recently been studied and that both early studies and the rare reiterations of more recent times apply unreasonable premises concerning the early Scandinavians’ calendrical skills and customs (9-10). Sums up some of the literary genres containing computistical information and recognises some of their problems (10-12). Justifies and explains his use of technical terms (12-14).

[1: Ekon av förgången tid] In a dialectal study of central Sweden, a number of monthnames came up that seem to have belonged to a lunar calendar. The names that were preserved all concerned the first quarter of the year, and only two of them had stable names: jultungel, attested throughout Scandinavia, and distungel, distingstungel, found only in central Sweden (15). Medieval attestations of the distungel and its computation according to the Epiphany are discussed. This relationship indicates a connection between jul and disting as holidays or ritual seasons: the Epiphany marks the end of jul, by which the beginning of the next holiday is calculated. The rule was then adjusted to fit the Catholic calendar, which enters its fast after the Epiphany and has it lead up to Easter, a feast roughly coincident with the disting (15-18). This also explains the integration of distungel into Church computistics. While in Iceland (not in Sweden and Norway) a shift of the calendar year relative to the lunar year led to a discrepancy between mathematical and astronomical moon phases (see appendix 3), the name of the lunar month was preserved for its rootedness in the calendar tradition (18-19). However, the jultungel stretched from 6 January to 4 February when Epiphany coincided with a new moon, thus not covering Christmas at all. It is therefore commonly assumed that not only the distungel but also the jultungel is a relic from pre-Christian times that made its way into the Christian calendar (19). Indeed early sources such as Tacitus tell us that the Germani had meetings and celebrations at new moon and full moon (19-20). Icelandic sources likewise suggest blót at new moon; but similar practices have been attested for almost all peoples of the world (20). Circumstantial evidence suggests that the jultungel and distungel go back at least to the migration age, when large-scale sacrifice already took place in Uppsala (20-1). Both these events are identified as lunar months, and months with cognates of jul are many; typically, two successive jul-months are found (21-2 [NB the Gothic and OE forms of fruma jiuleis are incorrectly translated, and the discussion on the precise beginning of the Gothic month is futile since it clearly concerns a relative dating against the Julian calendar]). These indications stretch back to the fourth century CE and may be traced back to the first century CE when the jul-peoples last lived in close proximity, suggesting that the tradition may even have preceded the current era. The beginning of this double month was probably based on a lunisolar calendar; such a system is believed to have been used in pre-Christian Scandinavia (22). The Julian calendar was not introduced instantly in all aspects of Scandinavian life: some elderly people in the early twentieth century still counted the time of year by the heavenly bodies. However, this was found mostly for the first quarter of the year, suggesting that the calculation of Christmas and Easter preserved the tradition (23). It is thought that it took until the mid-twelfth century before the Julian calendar had penetrated the everyday spheres of Scandinavian society (24). Two arguments have been given for this time: the attestation of rune sticks in conjunction with the visit to Norway and Sweden of the papal delegate Nicholas Breakspear, and evidence from the Rím texts (24-5). The period just before the middle of the thirteenth century would be fitting in the light of the general expansion at this time of the Church into various aspects of society (25-6). The nature and shortcomings of the Julian calendar are introduced, as is the Gregorian reform and the formula to calculate between Julian and Gregorian dates. One change in the reform was the dates of solstices and equinoxes from 24-5 to 21-2; but by virtue of the imprecision of the Julian calendar, the calendrical solstice and equinox occurred later than the astronomical. The astronomical timing may be found with a formula (26-7). About 1155, the difference had significantly reached seven days (27).

[2: Årsindelningar och veckoräkning] As in the Gregorian calendar, the pre-Christian year knew two half-years, each made up of two further parts, so that a year was divided into four. These quarter-years were, however, further divided into weeks in accordance with a lunisolar calendar, though it is unclear how, indicating that they may not have been in full unison. Relics of the week-division outside Iceland suggest a relationship between the week-division and the labour (agricultural) season. The lunisolar calendar, on the other hand, may have been of importance with regard to religious, legal, and economic cycles, for instance to determine the time of assemblies. Like the week-division, however, the lunisolar calendar seems to have relied on the year’s division into quarters (29). The week-division as attested in Iceland was probably brought in from Norway at the settlement; but in Norway, unlike in Iceland, it seems to have given way to the Julian calendar in more formal contexts (29-30). Thus Norwegian evidence of the week-year is mainly limited to certain times of year, such as the time for sowing or harvesting, activities that were bound to certain weeks. Outside Iceland, southern Sweden and Dalarna provide the best attestations of the week-division, though Norway, Zealand, and other parts of Sweden also show evidence; none of this precedes the seventeenth century. The earliest evidence outside Iceland is from sixteenth-century Schleswig; later evidence has also been found among the Sami, in Estonia and Karelia. Icelandic sources tell us that the 364-day week-year was brought into unison with the solar year by an intercalation of a week once every few years; but an older practice seems to have been to count one day twice every year. This solution has been found in Finland and Estonia as well as among the Sami, while evidence of the same system has also been found in Sweden (30). The origin of the week-year is difficult to establish. A minority believe that it is an altered form of the Church week-system. It is more likely, though impossible to prove, that the week-system originated among the Continental Germani. The names of the weekdays were taken from the Roman week (31). While this transfer is mostly dated to the third century CE, this hypothesis fails to explain why the Julian system was not borrowed along with the names (31-2). It is unlikely that names of weekdays were borrowed without their calendrical context; and such a context might be the model of the Germanic week-year. The names and the system could then have reached the north in the early Roman iron age or in the Migration Period, or indirectly via the Anglo-Saxons. The northern quarter-system is attested in two parallel forms (32). Both are thirteen-week periods (mál). The first type of week-year began on 25 December, the Julian solstice, retaining the Christmas style that made the birth of Christ the first day of the year. This tradition began in eighth-century Francia and was used in Scandinavia before its conversion; it began to be replaced in Germany in the thirteenth century. The congruence between the Nordic quarters and the Julian calendar indicates that the week-system in the attested shape cannot predate the Scandinavian conversion; i.e., the existing week-system was brought into unison with the Julian calendar after the conversion (33). The preexistence of a week-system is evidenced by the Sami week-year, which seems to have used the astronomical solstices and equinoxes; Bede and Snorri write of similar systems (33-4). The second quarter-system is found in Iceland and based on the vetrnætr, which in their attested form were dated three Saturdays after the Christian-Julian date of 27 September, Cosmas and Damianus.
