The next quarter began at miðvetr, a Friday between 9-16 January. Sumarmál marked the beginning of the third quarter, the third Thursday after the Annunciation (25 March), i.e. 9-15 April. Miðsumar marked the fourth quarter and was celebrated on the Sunday between 13-20 July, but a week later in leap years (34-5). The unusual form of this calendar is explained by its reliance on the Christian-Julian system: the feast days used correspond to equinoxes (35). All the quarters in this system, however, occur some three weeks after both Christian and solar events. This suggests that the pre-Christian terms miðsumar and miðvetr refer to moments after the solar events (35-6). In Norway, the week-system gave way to the Julian calendar and is little attested; Rím II says that the Norwegian summer and winter began 14 April and 14 October rather than on fixed weekdays, so that the Sunday letter was redundant for their calculation (36-7). The Norwegian quarters are less well attested than the days that mark the beginning of summer and winter, which also carried legal significance. Midwinter was known, and mostly marked on 13 January, though sometimes it was 12 or 14; its preservation may be explained in part by its coincidence with Knut’s day. Midsummer is less attested and is timed to 13 or 14 July. Sami tradition is similar (37). Swedish evidence is less clear, but present (37-40). Sami, Estonian, and Finnish evidence is discussed: here too, seasonal markers exist around mid-October, January, April, and July (40-2). The plural form of the winter nights and summer nights is discussed in conjunction with the assumption that the day began at dusk (42). The shift of the three-month unit may have taken place in order to bring the calendar into unison with the economic and climatic cycle of the north. Beckman thought it might have to do with the sun’s entrance into constellations or the season-dependent brightness of stars like Sirius; Nils Lithberg thought the division indicated a lunisolar calendar (42-3). However, since half-years had legal significance, it is unlikely that these units would have shifted later than the early iron age. If this legal status existed before the Julian calendar was introduced in the north, as the evidence suggests, the starting-dates of the quarters cannot have coincided with full moons, since the lunisolar calendar moves across the solar year, twelve lunar months being eleven days short of a solar year. The four seasons would thus have been impractical as judicial terms. Solar events, by contrast, were more useful as judicial markers; and the week-year that was used is a solar construct. The shift in the three-month period is likely to have its origins in the week-system; it is no coincidence that quarters are typically found in societies that use a week-year (43). In Iceland, the events are found to be dated as three weeks after the Christian feasts of Cosmas and Damian or the Annunciation, feasts that coincide with solar events, suggesting that in pre-Christian times the nordic markers were also linked to these solar events (44). The old Scandinavian system has its markers precisely 28 days, or four weeks, after the solar events, as may be seen if they are converted into their Gregorian dates. This demonstrates that the quarterly system had its origins in the Scandinavian week-year (44-5). Only the spring equinox shifted by 30 not 28 days; but the equinox was hard to recognise by observation, so much so that it was best determined by the middle point between two solstices. This method works accurately for the autumn equinox, but in spring the earth’s relative proximity to the sun causes the equinox to be a few days earlier (45-6). At the Nicaean council, the shift of the Julian year relative to solar events had been solved by basing church events on the astronomical equinox that was now 21 April, while the equinox for worldly calculations remained 25 April (46-7). When Christianity came to the north, two sets of equinoxes thus existed, both incorrect from an astronomical perspective. When the Scandinavians fixed the date for sumarmál to the Thursday four weeks after the equinox, they must have used neither of these but instead 15 March, the astronomically correct date. This rule was later adapted to the Christian-Julian calendar. This shows that the quarterly system predates Scandinavian Julianism, and that it originated in a Nordic week-year system (47).

[3: Månmånadsräkning och bundna månår] Before the conversion, the Scandinavians probably used a lunisolar calendar as a framework for their week-year. One can use the sidereal month, measuring the moon’s course across the sky relative to the stars, or the synodic month, observing the moon’s phases; the latter is by far the more common and it is to be expected that this method was used in Scandinavia (51). Since the synodic month is about 29,5 days, a synodic year is roughly 11 days shorter than a solar year. In order to bring the two into harmony, it is customary to add a thirteenth month roughly every third year; consequently, a fixed date may vary across the solar year by about 30 days (51-2). It is hard to determine from what point the lunar phase was counted, namely from the absence of moon [nytändningen], from the youngest moon, or a few days after (52). Observatorial and artificial methods of determining the new moon were available in pre-Christian times (52-4). To judge by these and by matters of practicality, it is most likely that the astronomical moon phase was used rather than the visible appearance of the moon (54). It is, however, likely that the latter method was used in informal practice (54-5). The Icelandic week-year and the month-system incorporated into it are described (55). Month-names are well-attested for winter, but not for summer, probably reflecting the agricultural and economic significance of the seven-day unit (55-6). The variety of winter month-names is discussed, as are their etymologies. The month-names jólmánuðr, þorri, and gói are the eldest, and the first of these has Anglo-Saxon and Gothic counterparts (56-7). Bede details the Angles’ lunisolar calendar in De temporum ratione (57-60). Bede’s month names refer to pre-Christian rites and practices, although his interpretation has been questioned (60-1). However, Bede’s calendar corresponds to the Nordic calendar in many aspects, such as the division into half-years and quarters, the insertion of the intercalation in the summer, and certain month names, such as thrimilci / trimjölkingen (61-2). Bede says that the Angles began their year on 25 December (62). Bede’s modranect has been incorrectly read as “mother of all nights”; it is a plural genitive and should be read as “night of mothers,” suggesting associations of fertility. It occurred in between the two giuli months and was thus associated with the new moon (63). However, Bede’s remark that the winter solstice occurred right between the two giuli months cannot be correct, since lunar months had no stable position within the solar year (63-4). The Icelandic writings indicate that the two months ýlir and jólmánuðr met on 10-17 December, when in the mid-twelfth century the solstice took place (14-15 December). Bede’s words are probably to be understood as implying an astronomical cycle of 8 or 19 years that made the two months surround the solstice more or less precisely (64). If so, all other variables in the lunisolar year, such as the time of the intercalations, will have been calculated according to the winter solstice. Summer also knew two months with the same name; the two solstices thus always occurred right in between two combined months (65). On the basis of these data, an intercalary rule may be deduced in which an intercalary month is added at the summer solstice for every year in which the second jólmánuðr begins fewer than eleven days after the solstice; thus the first jólmánuðr moon never begins after the solstice, while the second never commences before it. This precise positioning is a conjecture that will be motivated in chs. 4-5 (65-6). Eddic poetry and Scandinavian laws hardly speak of lunar months, though a puzzling phrase nú ok neðan occurs, sometimes in contexts where it must mean “month” (66-70). Nordic evidence for a lunisolar system is indexed (70-4).

[4: Tideräkning och rituella cykler] The sagas indicate that there was a cycle of four feasts coinciding with the four quarters. Snorri repeatedly mentions three of these, at the beginning of winter, in midwinter, and at the beginning of summer. The winter nights are the best attested (76-7). While midsummer celebrations are poorly attested, they are not without textual evidence; and the assemblies took place at this time, doubtless with festivities (77-8). An important question in this respect is whether the feasts were dated precisely to the solar events. The written sources are vague, suggesting that the festivities had no precise place in the quarter; it is likely that they were calibrated according to the phases of the moon (78). It is possible that the Nordic peoples made use of the 19-year cycle that would have manifested itself in the variations in the time separating winter solstice and second jólmánuðr (78-9). There is, however, no evidence of this cycle that can be linked with certainty to the Nordic peoples. Instead, late iron age evidence indicates that certain festivities used an eight-year moon cycle (79-80). Many references suggest a nine-year ritual cycle; if read inclusively, this number matches the eight-year lunar cycle (80-3). That inclusive counting was used may be recognised from Skírnismál 21, where eight rings are said to drip from Draupnir every ninth night; this only makes sense if the nine is read inclusively (83-4). Völuspá tells how the gods designed the courses of the heavenly bodies for the purpose of time-keeping (84-5). This mythical-cosmological aspect of time is expressed in sacrifices til árs ok friðar (85-6). Thietmar describes sacrifices of 99 individuals of each species, and he also mentions the nine-year (i.e., eight-year) interval which is made up of almost precisely 99 lunar months. This need not be coincidence (86). Adam of Bremen describes the sacrificial feast at Uppsala as having taken place once every ninth year; nine individuals of nine species were sacrificed, one per day for nine successive day (86-7). Adam clearly uses inclusive counting in one of these numbers, since the total number of sacrifices he mentions, 72, is eight when divided by nine; thus eight individuals of eight species must have been sacrificed per day for nine successive days if the numbers are correct (87-8). Since the number eight is implausible in a religious context, it is likely that the period concerned nine days and the number of sacrifices per day also nine, but that the sacrifices took place during the eight evenings and nights within the nine-day period (90). Snorri speaks of a week, but if the motsting and lyktarting are included between which the disting was supposed to take place according Upplandslagen, the entire event took nine days (90-3). The eight sacrificial evenings are further discussed (93-6).

[5: Julens och distingens plats i der förkyrkliga året] It has been a fashion among early scholars to conceive of jól as a solstitial feast (100-1). Prokopios’s picture of a mountaintop welcoming of the sun may reflect actual practice, but it cannot be known whether it is based on Germanic or Sami practice; as such, it must be dismissed as evidence (101-2). The only precise description of pre-Christian jól is by Snorri and tells of three nights’ celebration, some four weeks after the solstice (102). This leads to the question whether the Scandinavians had their winter celebration at the solstice or four weeks later at midwinter night. The answer is that jól was bound up with both events: this is why there were two lunar months both named after jól, the first of which always shone on the solstice, while the second always shone over midwinter night (102-3). What lunar phase midwinter night was bound to is unknown, but since jól is plural, it may have consisted of multiple feasts (103-4). If a full moon in the second yulemonth marked the festive climax, this full moon could have occurred between 5 January and 2 February (104). Snorri’s account seems to indicate a feast surrounding midwinter night, which in the Gregorian calendar is 19-21 January: this period is precisely in the middle of the possible dates for the second full yulemoon (104-5). Thietmar’s information concerning the sacrificial feast in Lejre accords with this period (in the tenth-century period described, the full moon would have occurred between 31 December and 29 January), suggesting that he is describing the same feast (106-7). Snorri describes the disting as taking place in gói, whose full moon when interpreted according to the time from which our information stems fell between 5 March and 3 April; Snorri’s information thus accords well with that of Adam of Bremen, who has the feast take place at the vernal equinox, i.e. 21/22 March (107-9). However, Snorri elsewhere says it took place at midwinter (here he speaks of allra Svía þing). He seems to have misunderstood the disting for the midwinter celebration (109-10). Snorri notes that the celebration had been moved forwards from gói to Candlemas [2 Feb] after the conversion. The shift probably occurred in fact and was carried out to prevent collision between the pagan feast and Lent; the time must be incorrect, since the disting was timed according to the moon. Snorri did visit Sweden in a year in which the disting was on 1 February. Alternatively, Snorri may have meant that it was timed in the moon around Candlemas, which is true [though not very accurate, PS] (110-11). The natural justification of a feast in this period is that it is the coldest of the year (111-12). The rule that the disting was to take place at the first full moon after the first new moon after Epiphany is spelled out in a sixteenth-century work, but Snorri’s description seems to indicate that it already existed in the thirteenth century (112). He says that the shift took place at the introduction of Christianity, which we may date to the middle of the twelfth century (112-13). The Epiphany was used to date the moveable feasts of the Church, and the julting came to be connected with the same computistical tradition. That it was still dated according to the lunar cycle may be explained by the role of the moon in the dating of the Christian moveable feasts, though there is no reason to see in this the first cause of its connection with the lunar month (113-14). Three appendices: “Jul, hökunótt och vintersolståndets lockelse,” “Vem var Mundilfœri?”, and “Aun, gyllentalscykler och tunglets färd under Auni-traditionen om ynglingakungen Aun hos Snorri och Olof Rudbeck” (119-46). English summary (147-59).

author: Ogilvie, A.E.J.
title: Climate and Society in Iceland From the Medieval Period to the Late Eighteenth Century
abstract: Distinguishes between “first-order impact” and “second-order impact” of climate on society. Among the former are effects on grain cultivation, grass growth, hay yield, sea fishing, thermal effects on domestic animals and man, and the physical impact of climate (221-55); the second category includes livestock mortality, farm desertion, begging and crime, and human health and mortality (256-82). The abstract concludes that “climate has had an important and statistically significant influence on Icelandic society. However, the major impacts on society were invariably the result of a combination of factors related to agriculture (strongly dependent on climate), fishing (less clearly climate dependent), and to the prevailing political context which influenced the ability of the society to adapt or to ameliorate the stresses imposed by climate.” Climatic mentions in medieval writings (sagas, annals, geographical descriptions) are listed (44-77). The climate up to and including the eighteenth century is reconstructed (135-88). In the main, the sagas are rejected as evidence, although references to e.g. grain growth in the family sagas can be used with caution (131-5). The Landnámabók account of Flósi’s naming of Iceland is unreliable: the account was written much later, and Melabók, the most reliable redaction, does not have it. See S. Rafnsson, Studier i Landnámabók, 1974 (136). The Skarðsárbók redaction refers to a “great dearth winter” in which the elderly and the needy were thrown off cliffs (975, 1056-9) (138).

author: Ogilvie, A.E.J.
title: Climatic Changes in Iceland A.D. c. 865 to 1598
abstract: Introduces the geography and present-day climate of Iceland, including such factors as the warm and cold currents and the close proximity to Arctic pack ice, whose presence near Iceland is highly variable. In simplification, it may be stated that periods of high pack-ice incidence occur in times of colder climate (233-4). The large literary output in the Middle Ages makes up for the fact that common palaeoclimatic methods such as tree rings and ice cores do not work in Iceland. At the same time, writings need to be scrutinised for reliability (234). The Sturlunga and Biskupa sögur are identified as the most climatologically reliable sagas (235). The annals were also used for analysis; of these, the post-1394 section of Gottskálksannáll is particularly useful and reliable (236). The Biskupa-Annálar Jóns Egilssonar (1548-1636) are also useful, as are Skarðsárannáll (1400-1640) and Ballarárannáll (1597-1665). More general remarks on climate occur in Landsnámabók, and Konungs skuggjá refers to winter conditions with regard to maritime navigation. Guðmundar saga biskups Arasonar contains an introduction to Iceland, its geography and climate. The Description of Greenland contains navigational information. The first works to give detailed information on pack ice are the Brevis commentarius de Islandia and the Qualiscunque descriptio Islandiæ/Íslandslýsing from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries (236-8). Of Flóki Vilgerðarson it is said that when about 865 he settled in Iceland, he neglected to gather hay for his livestock which subsequently died; and he spotted pack ice (238). There are, however, doubts concerning the reliability of this story (239). Other Landsnámabók and Skarðsárbók passages refer to severe winters, particularly in 975 and 1056-8, whereas 1058-9 was unusually mild. The annals refer to 1078 as particularly snowy; several sagas share an account that may refer to the 1056-8 period (239). Þorgils saga ok Halflíða speaks of agriculture in the twelfth century; Guðmundar saga biskups Arasonar confirms this, but emphasises that it is only barley, and only in a few southern locations. The import of grain against the export of dried cod may have been more profitable; but there is evidence that the climate also effected a decrease in agriculture. 1186-7 and the 1190s were difficult periods according to several sources (240). 1199-1200 was particularly severe and cost a great deal of cattle, while 1203 saw a frosty spring and summer (240-1). 1204 was again harsh. 1211 knew “a ‘good’ winter and a wet summer.” The 1230s were harsh, but 1238 was mild. 1251-2 is the next harsh winter on record. There are no references to sea ice between 1234 and 1260, but in 1261, a severe winter according to Íslendingabók, it is said to have reached around the entire coast. Polar bears occur in the 1270s (241). 1284-6 were harsh and saw famine and farm desertion; so also the early 1290s. 1306 saw relatively much pack ice, as did 1320-1 and 1323. 1330 was good but its summer lacking in grass; 1340 was very mild but 1341 and 1348 were extremely harsh (242-3). The 1350s were variable. The Description of Greenland says that the pack ice in the 1360s made the Greenland route dangerous; but this source and the particular comment must not be given disproportionate weight. More reliable sources, however, also point to harsh winters but some good summers in the 1360s (243). Most, but not all winters in the 1370s were severe. The rest of the century knew epidemics but there are no references to the weather (244). The rest of the article discusses the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries (244-7). A table is drawn up containing all references to weather and climate (247). It is concluded that there is some evidence for a milder early period, among which the settlement itself is significant. At least two saga age farms disappeared in glaciers in the eighteenth century. The scarce references of harsh winters may be evidence that people were simply not used to such conditions. Since the variability that springs from the sources accords with the present-day climate, the faint signs of climate change may also be reliable (247-8).

author: Ogilvie, A.E.J., and Graham Farmer
title: Documenting the Medieval Climate
publication: Climates of the British Isles: Present, Past and Future
abstract: Proxy and historical data may be used to reconstruct medieval climatic fluctuations in England. Secondary compilations of historical climate data are typically unreliable; Lamb’s study also falls subject to this criticism (112-13). Sources should be scrutinised for time, place, and authorship, and general reliability (114-15). Relevant contemporary observations include temperature, precipitation, and, in Iceland, sea-ice. England was richer in written documents on weather events; its first weather diary is by William Merle, of Lincolnshire, and covers the years 1337-43. A number of Church establishments have also kept records in account rolls; this type of evidence derives almost exclusively from southern England. Data are available as early as the twelfth century, but only becomes useful in volume by the thirteenth. Decline sets in in the fifteenth, presumably as a result of the Wars of the Roses. Íslendingasögur are unreliable for climate data since they are literary productions; biskupa sögur and Sturlunga saga are of a more historical nature, and annals and geographical descriptions were also produced (115). Moderately useful data commences in the twelfth century and peaks in the fourteenth (115-16). Dating issues are outlined with regard to the Julian and Icelandic calendar systems (117). Reliable data for England is not available for all years, but it may be assumed that years for which there are no data were unremarkable. Account rolls are biased towards (dry) summer and (wet) autumn descriptions, since these were agriculturally important; but extreme winters may be supplemented from narrative sources. Oft-repeated formulas and data may signal literary commonplace, spoiling the account as a witness (117-19). The best remedy is to find duplicate statements in different accounts (119). For England, results show severe winters scattered throughout the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries; on three occasions is there mention of the Thames being frozen over. Two hot and dry summers are reported, and five successive wet summers, resulting in crop failures (119). Icelandic evidence begins about 1180; severe winters occur now and then, including the range 1233-6 and the time around 1287, when a sequence of harsh winters resulted in starvation. Mild years seem to have occurred c. 1395-1440 (119-20). Sea-ice evidence derives mainly from Konungs skuggsjá (c. 1250) and Grænlandslýsing Ívar Bárdarsonar (after 1364). The former suggests high incidence of sea-ice between Greenland and Iceland at the time of its composition. The annals mention sea-ice in 1261, 1274, and 1275; the latter two of these also saw polar bears. In 1306 there was ice all summer in the north; and more sightings are listed. A description in Guðmundar saga biskups Arasonar suggests that sea-ice was a common phenomenon at the time of its composition (c. 1350) (123). Grænlandslýsing Ívar Bárdarsonar indicates that the customary sailing route to Greenland had become too dangerous for the increase of sea-ice. This may, however, be a later interpolation; other sources are better relied on to reach the same conclusion (123-9). Footnote 43 lists literature on the existence of a see-saw between temperatures in Greenland and northern Europe. Despite dearth of data, some specific years suggest such a see-saw for England and Iceland (e.g. 1254), while at other times temperatures move together (e.g. 1290). Data suggest a more complex picture than the simple Medieval Warm Period-Little Ice Age sequence, notably a colder period 1260-1360. Historical data does not support a Medieval Warm Period. Studies on other parts of Europe confirm a warming trend about 1200, and stable temperature but more precipitation 1200-46. The term “Medieval Warm Period” should not be used as lightly as it often is (130). English and Icelandic evidence presents a somewhat similar picture on a decade-to-decade basis (130-1).

author: Pfister, C., et al.
title: Winter Air Temperature Variations in Western Europe During the Early and High Middle Ages (AD 750-1300)
abstract: Confirms the Medieval Warm Period and Little Ice Age for Western Europe by way of documentary evidence.

author: Ogilvie, A.E.J., L.K. Barlow, and A.E. Jennings
title: North Atlantic Climate c. AD 1000: Millennial Reflections on the Viking Discoveries of Iceland, Greenland and North America
abstract: Introduces area, inhabitants, and settlement (34-6). Notes that climatic variation in the North Atlantic is the result of a complex of factors and is not directly related to global changes (36). Various elements of North Atlantic climate are explained (36-7). Marine sediment analysis suggests a warm period between 730 and 1100 (37). The Greenland settlers’ likely route through the Denmark Strait suggests that this must have been a period of little sea ice, while more ice was present about the time the western settlement was lost; and such is precisely the outcome of the Nansen Fjord sediment-core record (37-8). There is good reason to believe the accounts that tell that the settlers of Iceland found it a fertile island: there had been no men to interfere with vegetation. There is no unambiguous record of sea ice before 1145. Icelandic settlement is evidence enough of a mild climate, as is the fact that certain farms have been engulfed by glaciers in later times (39). Greenlandic ice cores suggest a mild settlement period, while it seems certain that climatic decline played a part in the loss of both settlements (40-1). The name Vinland probably derives from vín “grape, and wine was a costly product in medieval Scandinavia. L’Anse aux Meadows has no grapes, though some parts of North America do (41). Wallace believes that the westward sea route would have been accessible for some two months per year, but that hostilities and logistics rather than climate led to the abandonment of the American settlement(s) (42-3). An interesting point is that Ogilvie believes that the settlement period may have been comparable to warmer years of the twentieth century, such as 1998 (36, 42, 43).

author: Orton, P.R.
title: The Wife’s Lament and Skírnismál: Some Parallels
publication: Úr dölum til dala: Guðbrandur Vigfússon Centenary Essays
abstract: Opening with a concise but fairly thorough review of scholarship on the narrator’s circumstances in WfL (205-6 and passim), proceeds to interpret some of its specific aspects, notably herheard (herh-eard) as ‘grove-dwelling’ rather than ‘heathen temple-dwelling’ but nevertheless with the sense ‘heathen temple/sanctuary-grove’ (209-11) and bitre burgtunas as an ironic reference to the low-lying land surrounding her dwelling-place (211-12). The precise nature of her dwelling-place also receives abundant attention, and it is concluded that she lives in a system of underground caves, whether natural or excavated (212-15). Specific parallels are made with Skírnismál (217-19); these are quite reasonable until Orton insists that the tree-roots below which Gerðr is condemned to sit are Yggdrasill’s and therefore a cosmic reference, and contrasts the human characters of WfL with the mythical characters of Skírnismál (219-22). The natural temple-theory is further explored with a view to harmonising the two accounts, leading to the conclusion that the ON and OE stories represent no textual relations but may nevertheless share “a certain kind of historical link” (223-5, at 224). The hieros gamos-explanation of Skm is mentioned and considered, but no conclusion is reached (225-6); “if the link between our two texts lies in a pagan ritual, the English and Norse traditions deriving from it have certainly diverged considerably” (226). Ing, an Anglo-Saxon Freyr, is considered as the lord of WfL (226-8), and The Husband’s Message provides a parallel of a distant lord contacting the woman by proxy using a message in runes (228). Freyja (228-9) has been compared with Gerðr and resembles the WfL narrator in a husband’s departure, her grief over him, and her search for him (229). Njörðr/Nerthus and Skaði are discussed (229-30). Orton proceeds to reconstruct by acknowledged conjecture: in pre-migrational times, the Baltic region that knew Nerthus (Angli, Ingævones) knew a myth about a fertility goddess weeping over and seeking her departed husband only to be condemned to an isolated and sterile environment (231). Some process of “reverse-euhemerization” [!] de-mythicised the characters to yield the WfL narrative (231-2). The sacred grove as a microcosm of the cosmos provides the link between (initial) cosmic and (later) human readings (232).

author: Pearsall, Derek
title: Rhetorical ‘Descriptio’ in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
abstract: Studies description in SGGK in relation to rhetorical precepts. Matthew of Vendome modified Ciceronian categories of rhetoric, transferring classes of inventio to descriptio where this cannot be done. This treatment resulted in rhetorical justification for descriptio temporis and descriptio loci using the attributes of time and place (129-30). The description of the Green Knight is based on the same principle found in Matthew, namely “description through enumeration of detail” (130). The descriptio feminae appears to have gained great popularity shortly after Matthew’s writing, so that it had become a cliché by Geoffrey of Vinsauf’s time. Chaucer seems to actively avoid it by the adoption of new elements in the Book of the Duchess, and Lydgate leaves it out of his Troy Book. SGGK similarly uses a different type of descriptio feminae. Matthew’s discussion of a descriptio quatuor temporum anni basically confirms a convention long in place. The description of spring, as conventionally adopted in Chaucer’s General Prologue, is the most common. SGGK describes all four seasons according to convention (500-33). The description suggests the unstoppable passing of time as well as contention between summer and winter. Winter receives fuller treatment at a later point (726-32). Sunrise and sunset are briefly described in SGGK (131). Seasons in SGGK are described in conjunction with landscape: spring and summer include the locus amoenus-motif (131-2). All landscape is conventional except for the fox-hunt (132). SGGK nature description has often been read as original, an expression of Naturgefühl. This is false: it concerns literary convention, and each seasonal description constitutes descriptio opportuna in service of the narrative, amplifying Gawain’s state of mind. Geoffrey of Vinsauf prescribes that the parting of lovers should be preceded by a description of spring, presumably to heighten contrast. SGGK uses similar rhetorical motives (132-3). It is likewise a mistake to take the poem’s nature description for realistic: realism was not a criterion. Further scenes that show rhetorical influence are the arming of the hero and the hunt (133). Whether the SGGK poet knew Matthew or derived his knowledge from other manuals or directly from French examples, a relationship with the rhetorical tradition is clear (133-4).

author: Pearsall, Derek, and Elizabeth Salter
title: Landscapes and Seasons of the Medieval World
abstract:
[Ch. 1: Classical Traditions] The depiction of landscape originated in the hellenistic and Roman period. Since Greek literature and art was strongly anthropocentric, it showed no interest in landscape (3-4). The Odyssey, however, has functional uses for landscape (“[t]ypically, we have to look in the Odyssey for the scenery of the Iliad,” 4), and it also introduces the idealised landscape of the locus amoenus (4-5). Virgil takes Homer’s landscape description and elaborates on it in a consciously poetic way (5-7). The possibility of such depiction being influenced by the visual arts is discussed, with special attention to the use of the term scaena with regard to poetry (6-7). However, Virgil’s most exact use of natural detail occurs in similes (7-8). The well-ordered land is portrayed as a necessary condition for a well-governed state, both in Vulcan’s shield and in the Georgics (7-8). After some discussion of other poets, it is concluded that “[t]he blending of landscape reality into a comprehensive poetic vision seems. . . to be Virgil’s peculiar achievement” (8-9). The pastoral depends for its identity on the expression of feeling for nature. Its features are first fully developed in Theocritus’s Idylls (c. 280 BC). His example was to be followed for the next 2000 years, “to dominate poets writing even in far Northern lands where shade and water are by no means difficult to come by [contrary to Theocritus’s homeland]” (9-10). Yet Virgil’s Eclogues, influenced by Theocritus, influenced most directly the European notion of pastoral landscape, although in the Georgics he understands the garden as a model of good husbandry rather than an opportunity for idyllic scenery (10). Ovid is therefore the best example of the fully-developed locus amoenus, becoming a source for all subsequent landscape description (10-12). Hellenistic landscape painting derived from the Alexandrian tradition (12-20). In late classical poetry, landscape begins to serve allegorical purposes and becomes an erotic ideal (20-3). The arrival of the Middle Ages coincides with castle and church becoming the antinatural focus of poetry (23-4).

[Ch. 2: The Early Middle Ages] Carolingian and Byzantine mss passed classical landscape on to the Middle Ages, albeit in a “stylized and denuded form.” The rhetorical figure of the locus amoenus also served as a vessel for preservation. Reality was not heeded; eschatology took centre stage, and landscape was thought a distraction (25). The Carolingian court barely allowed art in churches, and the images that did exist were codified icons, in which it was recognition, not realism, that mattered; visualization served the higher purpose of salvation history. At the same time, the countryside became the central background of life in the Middle Ages; and such circumstances do not trigger a love of landscape. Where its beauties do find expression, it is typically the enclosed garden, reminiscent of paradise, that is described. Garden courts of churches and monasteries sometimes received the label paradisus (25-7). Byzantine miniatures present a picture characteristic of the Middle Ages. These representations were ultimately based on the Alexandrian “mountain-and-tree” landscapes displayed in Greek Septuagint art. Some secular mss still contained impressionistic Hellenistic influences. But the Byzantine miniatures typically contain “no sense of landscape, of space or air, and the backgrounds are no different, as backgrounds, from the draped walls which appear in other miniatures” (27-9). Irish and Hiberno-Saxon illumination does not display landscape; instead, it develops initial decoration, suggestive of the worship of the Word. Initial plants and animals appear “as elements in a geometric design only, distorted and convoluted, not as natural objects.” c9-10 Irish nature poetry, by contrast, does use naturalism and observation (33-6). Carolingian illumination estranged their long-dead models into background that no longer bore reference to nature. Reims was an exception, combining classical landscape with the northern enthusiasm for linear design (36-41). OE poetry knew no “taste for landscape”; instead, it focuses on nature’s “grim realities,” suggesting the hardships of exile. AS poets had a “striking attachment. . . to. . . winter landscapes” that was “due to their effectiveness as images of exile, and of the harsh penitential discipline of the life of the peregrinus”; such images “provide the rhetoric of misery and sorrow.” It is not right to read them as pure allegory; they are better read as types, i.e., valid as realism and experience but serving a larger purpose in their conveyance of spiritual truths. The existence of kennings suggests a greater interest in word-play than in descriptive accuracy (41-3). The description of Bwf’s mere is discussed. Such OE symbolic landscape is very Christian in its colouring, and betrays a familiarity with the homiletic tradition. “There is thus already present in Old English literature the medieval Christian tendency to polarize all landscape into symbols of heaven and hell” (43-4). ON literature, by contrast, is realistic and functional, perhaps with the exception of Gunnar’s epiphany in Njáls saga, which, however, still carries the functionality of a farmer’s crop analysis. The chansons de geste and romances reintroduce the landscape of rhetorics and the locus amoenus (46-53). The plesaunce landscape develops in collocation with the motif of secular love; and the late medieval sense of enclosure forms an important contrast to the classical wide vistas (53-5).

[Ch. 3: Landscapes of Paradise] The earthly paradise entails the double element of an unattainable perfection. Its literary description, however, was not out of reach. The description of paradise came to be a topos of locus amoenus in which to celebrate the natural world. Its earthly location was a reminder that grace had not been entirely revoked from humankind. Accordingly, all the world’s freshwater was supposed to derive from the rivers of paradise, a notion often recalled in poetic descriptions of gardens thus irrigated (56-9). As is recognised in Pearl, the earthly paradise prefigured more than just the heavenly, but also the inward and the Church, alongside its historical existence (59-60). No strict chronology of literary traditions could do justice to the various readings of the earthly paradise possible at any one medieval period (60). While Philo and Ambrose read the Fall narrative as an allegory juxtaposing reason and the senses, others insisted on a historical reading (as well) (60-1). Sensual aspects of paradise were also outlined (61-2). Gregory of Nyssa represented paradise and heaven as once more open to man (62-3). Gardens and hunting parks of the real world recalled paradise (63-4). Accordingly, classical landscapes could easily be adapted for Christian purposes, as was done in the case of The Phoenix, whose poet “compares the harsh landscapes and weathers of the North with the temperate pleasures of the land of the phoenix in a way which moves subtly between the real, the ideal and the spiritual” (64-7). The OE Genesis describes paradise with great attention to weather. The Junius 11 artists reduce the landscape to a symbolic one (67-9). Throughout the medieval period there was a tendency to conceptualise and allegorise paradise (69-71). Realism and the spiritual were fruitfully mingled, thus preventing the domination of any one domain over another (71-4). In the visual arts, realistic landscape came to prevail in depictions of paradise (74-5).

[Ch. 4: The Enclosed Garden] The hortus conclusus was the backdrop for both secular and religious paradisal motifs. The higher classes in particular desired to be walled off from “the wild or roughly practical countryside beyond the castle gates” (76-7). The relationship between literary and historical courtly gardens is unclear (77). Persian models are said to have inspired Western gardens at the time of the Crusades: the sixth-century King Chosroes I of Persia already had an artificial garden to remind him of summer in winter (77-8). Western garden scenes are not much different (78-9). They evoke heaven, striving to improve on nature (79-80). But they are alternately given biblical and profane meaning (80-2). In the Decameron, the garden is the retreat-reality that attempts to exclude external the reality of the plague; but the same stern reality led the painter Traini to portray the courtiers’ garden as spiritually doomed (82-3). Most art and literature, however, made use of parallels between worldly and religious garden images (83-118).

[Ch. 5: The Landscape of the Seasons] Seasonal and metereological alternation strongly signalled mutability to the medieval mind. Classical poetry had provided it with the notion of reading the skies to predict future movements of the heavenly bodies, while seasonal progress had been described in terms of the procession of four personifications of four different ages, as well as the labours of the seasons. Both reappear in medieval poetry (119-20). The visual arts were furthermore inspired by Hellenistic and Roman models including ritual, signs of the zodiac, and personifications of seasonal features (120). To some extent, however, these models were transformed to match the medieval worldview. In classical literature, natural beauty was doomed to perish, and nature also was a means of destruction. These things confused the medieval mind. To the Christian, all nature was a reminder that it was better before the fall: nature was a curse. The Wanderer and The Seafarer express a sense of exile and desolation in the face of winter weather (120-3 and note 18). Even the summer season was cause of unease, since it provided no lasting stability (123-4). However, God had provided man with a means of controlling uncertainty to some extent through the law of labour (124-5). Boethius advocated calm of mind as a force by which to overcome adversity, and pointed out that all apparent chaos is ruled by the stability of the divine mind; this applied to the seasons as well (Consolatio 4.6m ll. 25-33) (125-6). However, chaos could only be so fully controlled within the confines of a philosophical treatise. Theological works would make the point that any chaos in the present world was man’s own fault (126-7). Natural evils could be internalised as one party in man’s inner struggle (127). Hildegard of Bingen compared the seasons to the soul’s dichotomy between good and evil (127-8). Most of all, the cursed earth meant that man’s interaction with nature was a struggle as well as a fundamental reality upon which any understanding of landscape had to be built (128-30). The fattening-and-slaughter season of November and December gained attention in the visual arts, as did winter, portrayed either by man’s indoor entertainments or by depictions of the winter weather laying him under siege (130). Active landscapes, however, provide the “most rewarding” information: May as a park for leisurely entertainment, April for ploughing, sowing, flower-picking, etc. (130-1). Painters used the labours of the months, landscapes being minor backdrops for human activity (131-2). There always remains a preoccupation with allegory, as may be seen from seasonal references in Piers Plowman (132-4). Book 9 of Bartholomaeus de Glanville’s De proprietatibus rerum (c. 1240) discusses years, months, and the liturgy, including depictions of the months, rooting all in theology (134-5). Here and elsewhere, the custom in central and northern Europe was to describe winters indoors; not until the fourteenth century are winter landscapes described (135-6). In the depiction of January, poetry innovated more than did painting (136). Some pictorial innovations and developments are described (137-46). SGGK has at least three winter scenes reminiscent of the calendar tradition. Its outdoor scenes express the same idea negatively: it would be better to be indoors. They also resemble later calendar depictions of winter landscapes (147-50). The Franklin’s Tale contains December verses conservative for their time in terms of their inspiration (150). Its passage from May to December is one from “unthinking confidence into stern reparation” (151). In SGGK, “[w]inter is, by turns, horrifying and beautiful: it repels and engages. . . . by turns, local, identifiable, and more generally symbolic of states of mind, of emotions” (151-2). Calendar art is further discussed (153-60).

[Ch. 6: Late Medieval] The fourteenth and fifteenth centuries saw a gradual move from a symbolic reading of nature to one focussing on the aesthetics of its form as philosophically sufficient (161-2). A late thirteenth-century motif of tree-leaves in the wood of Southwell Minster has been attributed to a decline in the tradition of contemptus mundi and a shift towards the notion of nature as an expression of God’s love, following St Francis and Aquinas. There are, however, limits to what may be deduced from the Southwell leaves, which in their ad hoc and unsystematic form cannot be taken to represent the new movement (162). These and similar carvings of this time were not influenced by a decline of the contemptus mundi, whose vigour was in fact only renewed by St Francis’s efforts (162-3). Early gothic book illumination similarly displays a categorised but not individual representation of nature. What realism exists in the early fourteenth century occurs in marginal miniatures and initials (163-4). Side and bottom margins show the first signs of realism (164). Perspective is seldom used (164-5). Like this persistence of two-dimensional landscape, stereotyped spring introductions, too, persisted, especially in lyric. Their purpose is formal, typically to introduce themes of love-longing (165). Occasionally, as in one Harley poem, the spring opening almost eclipses the love theme (166), but evokes no coherent scene. Religious lyric also began using the spring opening, suggesting congruences and contrasts between the natural cycle and spiritual events such as the crucifixion (166-7). Autumn and winter openings are used to introduce penitential themes; the landscapes are here empty, serving as occasions for poetry (167). In romance, the landscape setting remains polarised between enclosed garden and forest-exile wilderness (167-8). A few late thirteenth-century romances, notably Kyng Alisaunder, use season and landscape as narrative tools of punctuation and transition. Spring and daybreak are the most common themes here. Such passages “function partly as ornament, partly as a stereotyped means of alerting a listening audience to transitions and new matter” (168). The device also occurs in Arthour and Merlin and Richard Coeur de Lion; these three works are generally attributed to the same author. The later Sowdone of Babylone employs the same device here and there (168-9). This motif stems from classical epic (169-70) (endnote 40 refers to Webster, Hellenistic Poetry and Art p. 70 for examples). Such uses of landscape are slow to take hold in England; Chaucer shows no interest in landscape with the exception of symbolic uses of gardens. His wild places lack the descriptive detail of their classical models (171-2). French poetry shows in greater detail the development of the idealised garden motif, representing an allegory of good government (172-7). It is remarked that “just as the first true winter scenes are in the de Berri manuscripts, the first objective winter description in poetry, that is, the first in which the tribulations of winter are simply recorded and not used to echo some theme of love or life or death, is in Deschamps, Balade 793 (175-6). Both Ovid (Tristia 3.4.52) and Virgil (Georgics 3.354-5) see nothing appealing in winter (176). Late fourteenth-century English poetry developed a different kind of landscape realism, consisting in an almost arbitrary enumeration of detail in concrete nouns, some of which detail is purely a result of alliterative demands. Accordingly, the alliterative landscape realism can often be rich and sensory on its surface but lack actual realism (177-9). Middle English poems deriving from Latin sources show little interest in landscape themes, the poet of The Destruction of Troy making an exception for storms at sea (179). The SGGK poet forms a major exception, describing various landscapes in great detail. Here, however, landscape realism is found not so much in the rhetorical effect of landscape transition and the winter journey as in the casual landscape descriptions in such episodes as the boar-hunt and Gawain’s journey to the Green Chapel (179-80). Italy produced a new naturalism in art (180-2). Boccaccio, on the crossroads between two traditions, describes a paradisical garden at great length in his Decameron that is, however, explicitly limited by the bounds of season and climate (morning of the third day) (182). Petrarch brings a fuller realism. Compared to Langland’s Piers Plowman, Petrarch, too, admires the landscape but he takes the next step of rebuking himself for elevating the natural world over himself. Piers delights in the landscape without thinking of its moral symbolism and is rebuked for so doing (182-3). Nonetheless, Petrarch’s ascent is described with great realism, and his use of mountains for panoramic views contrasts with classical and medieval horror at mountain landscape. His approach signals the return of “the cultured enjoyment of Nature” (183-5). This naturalism next showed up in miniature and full-scale painting, beginning in Flanders (185-92). Some echoes of this development are seen in English miniature art (192-3). Lydgate shows the early fifteenth-century state of affairs, modelling nature to fit human practicality and aesthetics. Textures are compared to those of artefacts, the weather is Mediterranean, and the landscape has a strong sense of enclosure. Reality is scarce, but in the absence of allegory, realism is intended (193). Lydgate is little interested in realism, and seems to draw his inspiration from formal painting, as does Dunbar (193-4). Other poets represented nature more immediately (194-7). Encyclopaedic and philosophical seasonal description emphasised nature’s cycle, growth and decay, universal order, and likeness to human life (197). The moralisation of human life shines out in Lydgate’s Secreta secretorum and Henryson’s Morall Fabillis (197-8). Gavin Douglas’s translation of the Aeneid is discussed in detail (200-4).

author: Phelan, Walter S.
title: The Christmas Hero and Yuletide Tradition in ‘Sir Gawain and the Green Knight’
abstract: Proposes that both the Christmas liturgy and SGGK are centred around handsel, the exchange of gifts (1–23).

author: Rat, Jean-Michel
title: Les activités maritimes du Haut Moyen Age en relation avec les saisons
publication: La Ronde des saisons: Les saisons dans la littérature et la société anglaises au Moyen Age
abstract:
The early Middle Ages testify to great maritime activity, but this activity was dictated by the seasons. This paper studies, first, descriptive literature on seasonal seafaring, and second, a more intellectual context (23). Maritime activity is linked up with the passing of the seasons, and takes in some of its varied motifs. All the while, the literature travels between Christian and pagan, real and imaginary; but also between winter and spring, the subject of the present discussion.

(1) Maritime activities in the early Middle Ages may be categorised as either ordinary or exceptional: trade and fishery constitute the normal category, while ad-hoc activities and activities triggered by special circumstances are exceptional: piracy, war, and, most of all, exile (24). A letter of Alcuin’s to King Æthelred in 793 describes the sea as an ally that has borne no warships to English shores since the coming of the Anglo-Saxons until the Viking attacks at the time of his writing. The letter describes the sea as a medium of commerce and communications, and a place where heroes and saints are made (24-5). Ordinary maritime activity follows the dictates of the seasons and responds to the immediate needs of the land. Trade was conducted across the Channel, as well as some piracy. Durable and intense trade across the Channel secured a more or less permanent source of income to the several Anglo-Saxon kingdoms. The importance of this trade to the Anglo-Saxons was great, although they have traditionally been viewed as an agricultural people. The sailor in Ælfric’s Colloquy states his business in a general fashion, not naming his trading-partners. The frequent literary references to storms suggest the dangers presented to these merchants by the elements (25-6). Among their annual journeys are those to Saint-Denis, a twelve-day journey on which they would embark in mid-June, after 634. An Anglo-Saxon citizen named Botta lived in Marseille as a negotiator. Harbours dotted the southeastern coast of England, while hardly any existed west of ?Hamwith, demonstrating that sailors preferred to use the shortest sea-routes. Bristol, similarly, was engaged in a lively trade with Ireland. Fishery was divided over the year according to the type of fish. Autumn was for herring, at the mouth of the ?Yare. The need to fill demands is expressed by Ælfric’s fisherman, who regrets the fact that he fails to do so. The expansion of Christianity rendered sea-voyages necessary both to introduce the new religion, to maintain ties, and to go on pilgrimage. Travelling by sea ceased annually at the coming of autumn. Several different routes to the Continent were used. Many precautions were taken against dangers on such journeys, and particularly the voyage. Any delays for bad weather or disembarkment in hostile territory could be fatal. Monks employed self-chastisement. They prayed for forgiveness of the sailors and salvation for themselves and their fellow-travellers (26). Pilgrimages [author: the sea] were fitting places for contemplation: a letter of St Boniface’s recommends it to an abbess who cannot find tranquillity at home.

The Vikings had a near-monopoly on piracy, but the Anglo-Saxons occasionally partook of it as well, in any season. Pirates are at ease out at sea, and welcome the thunder, since dark skies camouflage their approach and help disperse their victims.

War was associated with the voyaging season. The Vikings in particular ceased their raiding in autumn and winter, when they would set up winter-quarters as of 851. ASC again mentions winter-quarters in 855. These camps were set up on islands, and war resumed in spring (27-8). In 877, a storm causes the shipwrecking of 120 enemy boats at Swanage. Only a summer tempest can explain the loss of such a great number of boats, since only when taken by surprise, i.e. outside the stormy season, can such losses occur. Alfred’s military campaigns suffered from desertion: soldiers did not hesitate to leave the battle-field to return to agricultural duties, particularly the harvest. Accordingly, Alfred decides to divide his force into two groups, one of which always remains behind to attend to agricultural duties (28). In 897, Alfred commands the institution of a large naval fleet against the Vikings. That summer, a naval battle takes place. In the same summer, 20 enemy ships are lost due to thunderstorms. Again at the end of a summer, on 12 September 1066, the Normans attack (28-9).

Exile as a legal punishment could send someone onto a voyage. Such exile came to be regarded as divine punishment, and the penalty was undergone in hopes of a better afterlife. The exile underwent the humble repentance of a destitute sailor. Anglo-Saxon law was designed to protect individuals against the inobservance of the law [by others]. The penalty was thus isolation, a punishment that was awarded at any time of year (29). The sentiments expressed in The Seafarer are suggestive of the experience (29-30).

(2) The seasons are the natural backdrop of the reality of everyday life, temporal markers expressed by descriptions of the natural world and maritime activities. The depiction of the seasons allows the sea to be studied in its various states. The year divides into spring-summer and autumn-winter, i.e. the pleasant and the unpleasant, the warm and the cold, joy and deprivation. This dualism pervades all OE thought and literature. There is a perpetual tension between antagonistic elements. The same holds true for everyday life and poetic depiction. Spring and summer are characterised by the cuckoo, blossom, the renewal of nature, departures on sea-voyages, and joy. Man and nature rejoice after a period of slumber. The joy, however, is tempered by the renewed danger of hostile, i.e. Viking, attacks; and the call of the cuckoo signals time of departure for all sailors (31). Sfr associates the cuckoo’s call with the renewal of marine adventure, as does The Husband’s Message. Autumn and winter are associated with physical and psychological hardship, storm, exile, ice, rime, and frost, again found in Sfr, which describes a winter experience in an open boat (31-2). This sailor is not in the navy. His sailing is without respite even in winter. The worse of marine dangers is shipwreck, whose fear haunts the sailor perpetually. Ælfric’s sailor gives expression to his fears of experiencing shipwreck, thereby losing goods and possibly his life (32). The poem calls on the senses. So does The Phoenix, in which a beautiful world is contrasted with the present. No unfavourable weather exists where the phoenix lives, no cold seasons; but the trees are in perpetual bloom (32-3). Anglo-Saxon life, and that of the sailor in particular, was profoundly influenced by weather and seasons.

The sea is essential and primordeal to the Anglo-Saxons, guaranteeing a secure economy. It is both an obstacle and a link between peoples. The seasons interact with the sea, some favouring voyages while others render them impossible. It is an obstacle that has to be overcome in order to meet the needs of the islanders. Having to undertake a voyage leads to anxiety for the sailor and his dear ones, while carrying out the actual voyage entails a whole new set of uncertainties. Accordingly, The Wife’s Lament expresses worry for the lord (33). Maritime activities follow a cycle, as do the seasons on land. The sea is a medium by which one may reflect on the grander elements of the universe. Symbolically, it represents a passage between earthly and eternal life. In Bede, life on earth is represented by a bird’s flight through a hall while the elements rage outside; this allegory, too, may be read to represent the alternation of the seasons.

Old English has a specific vocabulary to deal with the sea, combining maritime activities, the seasons, and the natural world. Chroniclers and poets make frequent use of the characteristics of sea and seasons. According to Pollington, the lexical field of water contains over 300 words; climate contains over 80; and time contains over 260, demonstrating the richness of the combined field (34). The sea, in conclusion, is a beloved subject of the Anglo-Saxon poet, but a duality lies at its core: it is generous in summer, but hostile in winter; it is seductive but deadly; but to the sailor, it is indispensible (35).

author: Salmon, Vivian
title: Some Connotations of cold in Old and Middle English
abstract: Maldon speaks of cold water despite the sunny August setting. In his edition, Gordon explains that cald here also carries the symbolic meaning “fateful.” Salmon proposes that the collocation of cald and ceallian rests on alliteration only, and that the implication of cald depends instead on its association with certain nouns (314). ON kuldi, related to kaldr, meant “cold” and “malice” by figurative extension. The jaws of the wolf Fenrir are called kaldir (Vafþrúðnismál 61); Bwf 2396 has “cealdum cearsiðum,” where ceald has been translated “bitter, hostile,” “painful, pernicious, evil,” “painful, grievous.” Cold therefore must have nonliteral connotations not deriving from ON (since the passage !cannot derive from ON; 315-16). ON kaldr often connotes hostility when applied to a weapon; English does not know the collocation until about 1665 for iron and 1816 for steel. Yet Bwf 3021-4 speaks of a morgenceald spear, and uhtan, cald, and gar co-occur in Genesis B 315 (316-17). ON and OE know the collocation köld rödd / cald reord “cold voice,” according to critics “hostile,” “deceitful,” or “treacherous” in ON, and, according to Martin, “hostile” in OE without reference to the ON occurrences (317-18). Kaldr / cald also collocate with wæter, sær, etc. In OE, the context often refers to danger or hostility, and the ON occurrences inconclusively suggest the same (318-20). ME cold red, though rare, likewise suggests deceit or hostility; this concept is probably a borrowing from ON (320-1). It is speculated that the deceitful and hostile connotations of cold may have something to do with the northern, and therefore cold, locations of Niflheimr and Satan’s throne (321-2).

author: Senn, Harry
title: Werewolves: Seasons, Ritual, Cycles
abstract:
In the Eastern European countryside, groups of bachelors wearing animal masks haunt the villages between Christmas and Epiphany, singing chants and playing musical instruments. Werewolves show themselves on the eve of religious holidays such as Christmas and Easter. At these times, sexual relations are outlawed in the canons; children conceived at these times are believed to take on animal characteristics, notably wolfs’ characteristics, and suffer from bad luck. According to legend, these children are werewolves and resent their parents’ responsibility for such ill luck. Christmas to the New Year is the prime time for werewolves and vampires, with Easter to Pentecost in second place. They are nocturnal creatures: in the Balkan and Czechoslovakia, they eat sun and moon in their desire for darkness [PS: cf. Eddic mythology]. In Italy, werewolves are people conceived at new moon, or sleeping under a full moon on certain weekdays (206). In certain areas, a play is performed in which an animal is killed and resuscitated (206-7). Many folklorists read in the animal folk plays and masquerades echoes of a belief in the return of of the spirits of the dead. This paper will explore the configuration of masks, animals, and nature in the Romanian countryside, studying the integration of magic into the surrounding community (207).

The periods around Easter and Christmas here mentioned form part of the larger period between winter solstice and spring equinox. Gaignebet has read pre-Lent carnivals as echoing Indo-European beliefs with regard to animals, stars, and religion. The Christian calendar, he proposed, developed from a pre-Christian system of forty-day periods (1.5 moon phases) emphasising new and full moons. The carnival followed natural patterns such as the coming out of hibernation of the bear and associated beliefs on the further duration of winter (cf. groundhog). Thus carnival signals the darkest, last part of winter. In Gaignebet’s system, Christmas and Easter alternate full moons, with new moons at carnival (2 February) and Ascension (1 May) (207-8). February was the time for the remembrance of the dead and the welcoming of animal spirits in Roman and Greek society. In Rome, 15 February was the feast of the Lupercalia, when wolf- or goat-priests whipped girls to make them fertile (208). The festival probably symbolised fertilisation and rejuvenation through marriage. Dionysius was also worshipped in winter, with processions in which people dressed like satyrs, bacchae, and sileni (209). During the twelve nights of Christmas in present-day Greece, people dress up as the beastly callicantzari that take over the world in the dark of the winter solstice. Children born on Christmas Day or between Christmas and Epiphany are believed to turn out to be callicantzari, a word that in some areas simply means werewolf (209-10). A number of horse-related traditions centre around midwinter throughout southern Europe and in England. Mock terrorism is a stock motif of these traditions (210). The molinde New Year’s “carols” of southern Transylvania tell such stories as a lamb warning his shepherd of a death-plot; but the latter accepts his fate. Romanian peasants neglect the Christian theme of good shepherd and emphasise the ritual elements of the tradition (211-12). It is asked what role fate plays in this story; Eliade uses the term “cosmic Christianity” for this attitude (212). Other carols describe hunts. Transylvanian traditions have been regarded as evidence of an “ancient magical-mystical religion among the pre-Roman Dacians in which the animal realm held a divine status” and “the wolf was a quasi-divine symbol of death and leader of souls to the other world” (213).

author: Simek, Rudolf
title: Die Form der Erde und ihre Zonen
publication: Altnordische Kosmographie: Studien und Quellen zu Weltbild und Weltbeschreibung in Norwegen und Island vom 12. bis zum 14. Jahrhundert
series: Ergänzungsbände zum Reallexikon der Germanischen Altertumskunde

author: Sorrell, Paul
title: Like a Duck to Water: Representations of Aquatic Animals in Early Anglo-Saxon Literature and Art
abstract: Irish and Anglo-Latin texts are quoted for their interest in creatures transcending the most common taxonomies (29–30). Leviticus classifies as unclean any animal that transgresses the features or mode of transportation of its wider class, e.g. scaly fish must have fins to be fit for eating (30), and Maori culture knows a taboo on amphibic reptiles for similar reasons (30–1). Recent work has pointed out that taxonomical anomaly has been exaggerated, as the “anomalous” classes sometimes outnumber the “typical” ones and ethnographic generalisation is often at fault (31). Aldhelm’s riddles on animals have parallels of perception in zoological taxonomy in present-day traditional societies (31–2). [I will not now read the rest of the article because its relevance to my current research seems limited.] The article demonstrates that Celtic and Germanic cultures shared similar zoological perceptions.

author: Stobo, Marguerite
title: The Date of the Seasons in Middle English Poetry
abstract: Points out that spring was held to begin in February (about St Valentine’s Day, which corresponds to late February in the modern, Gregorian calendar). This raises the question whether May belonged to spring or summer. The Roman tradition, brought to British learning by Bede, had the seasons begin on 7 February, 9 May, 7 August, and 7 November. Several OE calendars follow this programme, as do the Menologium and Byrhtferth’s Manual; but the system appears to have lost popularity from the thirteenth century onwards. When they are mentioned, it is usually indicated that these were the dates used among the Romans and Greeks; they are mentioned alongside an English set, beginning 22 February, 24 May, 23 August, and 25 November, corresponding to those in Isidore’s De Natura Rerum 7.5. Sometimes they are shifted about slightly in order to match them to saints’ days. Another system related the four seasons to the sun’s position in particular zodiac signs (when entering Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn); the dates attached to these events vary. ME lyrics seem to favour late March as the beginning of spring. April and May are often linked, so that it seems they were considered the same season; The Wife of Bath’s Prologue connects March-April-May with pleasure. The birds’ references to summer in The Parlement of Foules seem to be about looking forward to summer rather than about its immediate presence [PS: cf. Anderson 1998; 2003; etc.]

author: Thonneau, Marie-José
title: Terre, Automne, Mélancolie: Âges de la vie humaine et tempéraments
publication: La Ronde des saisons: Les saisons dans la littérature et la société anglaises au Moyen Age
abstract:
Since ink is associated with black bile, melancholy is the ruling temperament of writers. It is regarded as a sin or a disease inseparable from the activity of writing. Its definition is ambiguous: sometimes it is black bile, seated in the spleen, sometimes it consists of brain vapours (91). The elements, states, temperaments, and humours are introduced:

  • white bile: choleric, warm and dry, liver, fire
  • blood: sanguine, warm and humid
  • phlegm: cold and humid, come from the brain via the nostrils
  • black bile: dry and earthly, the cause of sadness and chagrin, can develop into madness; seated in the soul (91-2).

Two illustrations are studied. The first depicts the ages of man and the temperaments by four female characters and written associations (93-4). The second is a diagram on the ages of man with, again, season, humidity and temperature, and humours written in (95). The canonical system of four is summarised. Some sources also introduce an animal for each humour: a monkey for blood, a lion for yellow bile, a boar for black bile, and a sheep for phlegm. The most dangerous season is not winter but autumn, when atrabile exerts such a great influence on body and brain (96). The medicinal herbs that benefit the melancholy are discussed; it is toxicity that counterbalances black bile, and so toxic plants are beneficial (97-8). Four heavenly bodies are also connected with the system of four: Jupiter for the sanguine, Mars for the choleric, Saturn for melancholy, and Venus or the moon for the phlegmatic (99). Saturn/Kronos is associated with philosophers, old age, and cruelty (99-100).

author: Tille, Alexander
title: Yule and Christmas: Their Place in the Germanic Year
abstract: Opens his book with a defence of Tacitus’s tripartite Germanic year, stating that “[t]he tri-partition of the Germanic year is an unshakable fact” despite Grimm and others claiming that Tacitus misunderstood the Germanic concepts; the three Germanic legal gatherings are cited in support. Grotefend and, to an extent, Weinhold, are referred to for this argument (1–5). An Anglo-Saxon law-code states that handmaidens were to receive gifts three times in the year (3–4). Nevertheless admits the lexicographical evidence for a bipartite year (5–6), “a fact, as well warranted as the tri-partition of the economic year itself” (5). The tripartite year must therefore be “of foreign extraction,” namely Egyptian (6). Cites an impressive array of Indo-European tripartite systems (6–7). Periods of sixty days (two months) seem to have had special significance, and also show up in Germanic systems. The etymological difficulties with the Germanic (bi)month-names suggest they were borrowed from Egyptian, Syriac, or somesuch (7–8). Double months like those in Anglo-Saxon tradition are evidenced in a wide range of Indo-European languages, suggesting that the year may once have been divided into six parts (8–9). Germanic tradition follows the same pattern, as evidenced mainly in legal codes (9–11). The origin of the seasonal names is discussed (11–12), including the probable etymology of lencten from lang-. Since this is not found outside West Germanic, it is probably late (11). Further evidence for two-month units is rehearsed (11–15). The Germanic peoples thus seem to have had both a tripartite and a sexpartite division of the year, which go nicely together (15–16). The tripartite system, borrowed from the Middle East, was confirmed by the economic and climate conditions of the new Germanic homeland; had it not, it would not have been retained: winter lasts four months on average, while the agricultural year divides into rest, cultivation, and harvest (16). Counting by nights and winters is discussed; the start of winter began the year, but this is not exclusively Germanic (17–18). 1 November is initially proposed as the start of the Germanic year [so also the Christian liturgical year!], but see below (18–19). The confused identity of Germanic month-names (associated sometimes with the earlier month, sometimes with the later) is surely a product of their adoption in the place of Roman month-names; the Germanic sixty-day tides would have begun halfway a Roman month, thus leading to overlap (19–20). Hence the Yuletide would have stretched from mid-November to mid-January, and the year would have started in mid-November; a fourteenth-century text from Xanten confirms 11 November and also lists the times of the other tides (20–1). Roman legions in Gaul and Germany seem to have gone into winter-quarters before mid-October, when rain, not cold, prevented warfare; warfare was never practised beyond frost. Caesar once had to retreat in autumn because the rain prevented sleeping in the fields (24). Germanicus once attacked a Germanic tribe at their autumn feast; Tille deduces [by his own estimation of when winter would have set in!] that this “first Germanic festival on historical record” took place in the first half of November (24–5, at 25). Martinmas is adduced as a festival at this time, begun in Gaul, and Bede affirms that there was a festival in November/Blotmonath (26). The popular celebration of Martinmas is described (26–33). Martinmas is the earliest seasonal event mentioned in Anglo-Saxon laws, as this is when ciricsceat [church tax in the form of corn] was due, although the payer’s parish was determined by the Midwinter-point (34). It survived into the twelfth century (34–5) and longer in Spain and Germany (35–6). Geese or birds as gifts for the clergy at Martinmas are attested from the sixth century (37). Medieval accounts run from Martinmas to Martinmas, as did the tax year (38–9). In Frankfurt, the winter was counted from Martinmas till St Peter ad cathedram (22 Feb), judging by laws regarding out-of-gate citizens (39); and further Continental evidence is produced (39–40). Pfannenschmid is quoted for further corroboration (40–1). Farm servants changed their place at Martinmas [contrast the Icelandic Moving Days!] (41). Legal assembly evidence similarly suggests the importance of autumn (42). The Peter’s penny was imported (42–3). Of the three annual assemblies (autumn, spring, summer), the summer one must have been the least significant on account of it interfering with the time for warfare [contrast Icelandic evidence]. A mid-July festival existed among Germanic, Slavic, and Celtic peoples, but this had nothing to do with the summer solstice. A Germanic solstitial reckoning is thus impossible (44–5). The Scandinavian year began between 9 and 14 October (45). Early Dutch evidence for a Midsummer on 25 July is cited (45). OE on sumere is placed in mid-July (46). [summary incomplete]

author: Tolkien, J.R.R., and E.V. Gordon
title: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight

author: Trausti Einarsson
title: Hvernig fann Þorsteinn surtur lengd ársins?
abstract: Refers to Finnur Jónsson (Skírnir 1961, pp. 171-4) for the recognition that Oddi must be using the Roman way of counting when he intercalates every seventh, i.e. sixth, year. Asks how Oddi came to such a close approximation of the solar year (139-40). His methods to find the angle of the sun are clear: he must have used directions of sunset. For the length of the year, a multi-generational observation of the solar course over Breiðafjörður’s clear landmarks will have been combined with the observation, generally noted according to Ari, that the alþingi was shifting backwards (140-2).

author: Trausti Einarsson
title: Nokkur orð um sumaraukagreinina í Íslendingabók

author: Vial, Claire
title: Fêtes et saisons dans Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
publication: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight: Essays and Studies
abstract:
SGGK has a constant emphasis on festivity in the two courts not found in other Arthurian works (notably Malory). On one side, this festive emphasis is rooted in references to the liturgical year at and around Christmastime, while never referring to the months of the year. These liturgical references contribute tone to the narrative (61-2). In the narrative, liturgical time is secondary only to the mythical time of Brutus’s founding of Britain. This prehistory is introduced to suggest the themes of heroism and treason, but foremost to bring in the succession of fortunes. The first liturgical dating, “upon Krystmasse,” sets in the actual narrative time (62-3). The liturgical feasts serve as markers, stages of the narrative (63-5). It is no coincidence that Gawain leaves Arthur‘s court the day after All Saints’ Day, corresponding to the old pagan feast of the death, the Celtic Samain. All the events, moreover, take place in winter, when life and death contrast between castle and the outdoors (65). The fits typically begin with festivity, and the third also ends with it; the poem itself ends with a return to the mythical time of Brutus (65-6). Fit 1 is especially well-structured through the repetition of motifs (66-7). The customs associated with the feasts are indicative of two, even three traditions. The Nativity is a central Christian feast, the New Year a popular feast, and the Arthurian banquet a literary feast (67). Christmas is characterised by a banquet, music, dancing, singing, and the Christmas Game. The Green Knight disrupts the habitual pattern and brings an uncertainty into the narrative, namely whether he is serious. His proposal of a game makes use of the full range of meanings of that word, from sport to contest (68-9). The audience would have been familiar with a New Year tradition in which doors and windows were kept open on New Year’s Day: the first to enter the house on that day was interpreted as an augury for the new year. The Green Knight’s coming must be seen in this context, and must have led to some uncertainty: peace or evil? Demons were often represented in green (69). New Year gift-giving is described; in the poem it takes the form of a lottery, and gifts could not be refused, including that of the ax (69-70). The banquets are briefly discussed (70-1), as is courtly decorum (71-2). The liturgical, popular and Arthurian temporal cycles are the temporal framework and thematic matrix of the poem (72).

As winter celebrations, all pleasures take place indoors (the hunt is a duty rather than a leisure activity). The indoor fire is a theme that comes close to representing social life (73-4). Warmth of human interaction is suggested by the gathering of communities such as Arthur’s knights (74). Joy is central to both courts (74-6). The youth of the members of the Arthurian court is repeatedly emphasised (76-7). Abundance is a further theme (78). Gawain individually suffers the opposites of these themes, suffering and deprivation. The warmth of the court is contrasted with the cold of his journey (79). Solitude is also a motif of his journey, and this solitude allows for the description of his personal feelings (79-80). The journey is governed by a time of seeking and deprivation. The desert landscape and the cold of winter express this. The winter season becomes a character in the narrative, e.g. by the impoverished nature of the fast (81). Unlike in other Arthurian works, the emphasis in this poem is not exclusively on action: time and space are also involved (81-3).

author: Williams, J.E. Caerwyn
title: The Nature Prologue in Welsh Court Poetry
abstract: Studies the purpose and origins of the Welsh nature prologue, cataloguing opinions and with extensive reference to foreign traditions. Since Murphy and Flower, religion and anchorism have been generally held responsible, though Latin influence and pagan origins have also been argued (70-1).
