Davies explained the relative absence of nature poetry in the englynion-period by saying that peasants who depend on nature will not turn to it for its beauty (71). Jackson has rejected Davies’s theory that the nature prologue developed from the nature-tagged maxim, attributing it to foreign influence instead; he also pronounced them unconnected in content with the poems’ bodies (72-3). The Continental nature prologue has sometimes been thought to have developed in Spain under Arabic influence (73). Jackson’s understanding of the gorhoffedd genre disproves Davies’s idea that people who work in nature do not appreciate its beauty (73-4). Williams claims that “[t]he bond between men and nature must have been stronger in early times than it is now, and as shall see [sic], it is vividly expressed in the idea that Spring rather than Winter was the time for love.” Lloyd-Jones has proposed that the nature prologue served to indicate the time of year of the events described in the poem. However, the Court Poets did not otherwise care to place events within any context (74). Some passages are cited, however, which clearly situate the action in a month or period. Whitsun and spring in general also connote the return of life, as well as the renewal of hostilities (74-6). The spring prologue is widely held to have been the original nature prologue (76). It has sometimes been traced to classical authors such as Ovid, Horace, and Catullus; medieval Latin authors such as Ausonius and Venantius Fortunatus have also been proposed as sources, the latter of which associated Christ’s Resurrection with spring (76-7). Irish royal inaugurations carried matrimonial symbolism, and the rebirth of nature could conceivably be linked to this image (77). Liturgical literature was bound to certain times of year, so reference to season would be natural (77-8). The clerici vagantes are discussed as a source for the Minnesang. The nature prologue was first coupled with love interest by Eugenius Vulgarius about 910 (78). The spring-motif in medieval Latin was found by Scheludko to have no unified rules (78-9). The troubadours and Minnesinger used the nature prologue as well. An Arabic influence on the troubadour lyric cannot be conclusively proved or disproved (79). Rhetorical and folk-song models to nature description are discussed (80-1). A Carmina Burana stanza associates spring with lovemaking. Bishop Grosseteste decried clergymen’s participation in the “Bringing in of May or Autumn” (Epistola 107.317; Williams 81). Popular influences are discussed (82). Williams asks whether “there was ever. . . a time when it was customary to refer to one of nature’s phenomena as a way of introducing an expression of feeling in poetry,” a question that must be asked in connection with the common assumption that poetic reference to winter connotes gloom whereas spring produces joy in an audience. “There can be no doubt that under the conditions prevailing in the Middle Ages and later, especially in the northern countries, the community as a whole suffered the rigours of Winter and were overjoyed at the coming of Spring and at the harvesting of successive crops before the advent of another Winter with its hardships, and that it welcomed the festivities which gave it an opportunity to express its feelings. One can imagine that poets would gladly seize the opportunity to use these communal feelings for their own purposes” (83). Kuhn has proposed that nature and the beloved had come to represent to the Minnesinger externalised representations of their own feelings (83-4). The cuckoo’s song brings melancholy in Kintevin keinhaw amsser, a poem in the Black Book of Carmarthen (77, 86).

author: Wyatt, Ian
title: Narrative Functions of Landscape in the Old Icelandic Family Sagas
publication: Land, Sea and Home: Proceedings of a Conference on Viking-period Settlement, at Cardiff, July 2001
eds: John Hines, Alan Lane, and Mark Redknap
abstract: Argues that landscape descriptions in the sagas are unreliable as witnesses to the historical surroundings in which the sagas are set, since they are instead motivated by narrative functions. Brief illustrations from Gísla, Heiðarvíga, and Bárðar saga Snæfellsáss are included, but for further evidence the author refers to his PhD dissertation “The Form and Function of Landscape in the Old Icelandic Family Sagas”, Leeds 2001. Also cited is Paul Schach’s equally unpublished PhD “The Use of Scenery in the Íslendingasögur”, University of Pennsylvania 1949.

author: Þorsteinn Vilhjálmsson
title: Time-Reckoning in Iceland Before Literacy
abstract: The need for a calendar is illustrated by the alþingi: the country was too large to send messengers, so a simple calendar was necessary to determine the start of the assembly. Also, the short agricultural season made it important to be able to tell the time and utilise it. For many agricultural purposes, the observation of nature is more reliable than abstract time-reckoning; but sowing and the rutting season are better deduced from time. Íslendingabók is cited on the sumarauki. It is explained that Ari’s rule of intercalating in the sixth year rather than the seventh if two leap years have passed since the last intercalation makes sense only if the numbers are read in the Latin way (thus every sixth year, but the fifth in case of two leap years—see Ginzel 3.66). Odda tala is explained; its index of solstices is off due to the accumulated error of the Julian calendar, but after correction follows the actual solstices rather than the Church tradition, which had them nearly a week later (21 June, 21 December). Rím II says that these latter dates are true for the middle part of the world, thus rendering explicit its independence of observations. Like Björn Olsen, Þorsteinn remarks that Oddi is wrong in believing the intervals between the solstices to be equal in length; this may betray its Julian nature rather than own observation. It is suggested that Oddi’s information may be a crystallisation of knowledge gathered over time rather than a single man’s own observations. The second and third parts of the tala seem useful for navigation mainly. Influence from the Continent seems to have been restricted to a small degree of (oral) knowledge at most. After Oddi, nature observation in the north becomes less independent.

author: Dilworth, Craig
title: Too Smart for Our Own Good: The Ecological Predicament of Humankind
abstract:
Ch. 1 sets out the physical and evolutionary/biological principles upon which the argument is based. The chapter forms an impressively cumulative unit, reading almost like a Tractatus logico-philosophicus except in full paragraphs and sections. The physical principles include entropy (energy tends to dissipate); the work then gradually moves towards systems within the biosphere and the way the various principles hold therein.

Ch. 2 introduces relatively new movements within anthropology, archaeology, and economics.

  • Anthropology: Since the 1920s, Hobbes's "war of one against all" has been challenged. Hunter-gatherer societies do very well and live far more efficiently than agricultural ones. As in all other species, internal (abortion, abstinence, infanticide) and external checks often make sure they remain in balance with their prey.
  • Archaeology: However, once homo species (sapiens and otherwise) developed superior hunting techniques, they began making hunted species (esp. large mammals, birds) extinct. Normally, this problem occurs only when two conditions are met: (a) a hunting species moves into new territory where the prey are unfamiliar with their hunting techniques, and (b) the prey species is not the hunting species's only source of food. In these situations, overshoot and a gradual balancing-out follow. Equilibrium was never restored where men made species extinct. Many species went extinct just as man moved in/moved away from their habitats. [Some of the species specified as having gone extinct survive today (e.g. kiwi), so some imprecision seems in place.]
  • Economy: unfortunately a much shorter section than archaeology, which in turn is shorter than anthropology. The stated reason for this (though not explicitly presented as a reason) is that the ecological approach to economics has not met with general agreement. It is pointed out that the GNP is unjustly taken to be a measure of social welfare, since it includes sectors that exist precisely because that welfare is in danger. A balanced economy can only be one based exclusively on renewable resources. Already John Stuart Mill believed that unrestricted economic growth should not be an aim.

Ch. 3 A species's tendency to increase its population beyond sustainable levels, first pronounced for humans by Malthus, is a universal biological principle. Darwin and Wallace were influenced by Malthus and understood this population pressure to be a necessary prerequisite to natural selection both intra- and interspecies. Each organism, group, and species fights to counteract entropy. Internal checks on population growth are culture, maintained through traditions; shifts in culture will tend detrimentally to affect population equilibrium. External checks always relate to mortality (positive); internal checks can relate either to mortality or to fertility (preventative).

Ch. 4 Scarcity stimulates technological development, but that development allows a greater use of resources so that internal checks on population growth slacken, in turn leading to new scarcity. Unlike the previous principles set out, this one (the Vicious Circle Principle) applies only to humankind. The population increase following a technological improvement makes humankind genetically dependent on that technology. Taken to its logical extreme, the scarcity resulting from unckeched population growth will lead to diminishing returns from the technology -> decreased population support -> economic decline -> possibly, population reduction. The remainder of ch. 4 describes several of the social implications of the VCP, a number of which seem to follow less necessarily from the principles set out than the material discussed thus far. Marxist thought shines through on rare occasion.

Ch. 5 This the longest chapter of the book describes the biological evolution of hominids and homo sapiens, explaining how the VCP not only is compatible with human evolution but explains human evolution. Technological development makes humans dependent on that technology (e.g. fire enables life far from the equator, where people then need that fire to survive), a process that triggers the rotation of the vicious circle between population size and technology.

[I have not summarised chapters 6 and 7, which extend the reasoning to the present day and the future respectively. They present a strong anticapitalist stance that follows directly from the book's long buildup; the final chapter expresses no optimism for the creation of a sustainable human ecology, precisely because the principle described in this book is in our genes.]

author: Earl, James W.
title: Beowulf’s Rowing-match
abstract: Argues that Beowulf and Breca may have swum rather than rowed.

author: Gelling, Margaret
title: The Landscape of Beowulf
abstract: Recognising that the landscape of Bwf is a fantasy construct, proposes that place-name evidence may shed light on the intended landscape (7). Claims that the field of OE landscape terms is free of synonyms, and a single system across England; Bwf hlið, hop, and gelad may be enlightened by place-name evidence (7-8). In southern England, hlið meant a hill with a concavity; only in the north did the ON sense ‘slope’ exist (8). Such clefts would be natural hiding-places for monsters (8-9). Hop was probably not influenced by ON hóp ‘small land-locked bay’ but rather meant either ‘enclosure in marsh or wasteland’ or ‘remote valley,’ the latter sense being heavily concentrated in Wales and the north. Bwf must use the former general sense, ‘piece of enclosed ground in marsh,’ with the association ‘secret place’ (9). This usage is best attested in Kent and Essex and shows up occasionally in ‘northern counties’ (9-10). ‘Lair’ would be a good translation in Bwf (10). The recent redefinition of gelad ‘difficult water-crossing’ is noted, while lad is ‘artificial water-channel’; although place-names in -gelad are difficult to reconstruct, its sense may be ‘water-crossing liable to be rendered impassable by flooding’ (10-11).

author: Hübener, Gustav
title: Beowulf und nordische Dämonenaustreibung (Grettir, Heracles, Theseus usw.)

author: Hulbert, James R.
title: A Note on the Psychology of the Beowulf Poet
publication: Studies in English Philology: A Miscellany in Honor of Frederick Klaeber
eds: Kemp Malone and Martin B. Ruud
abstract: A brief article proposing that the landscape of the Grendels is not, as Lawrence suggests, a confused representation of a waterfall but rather an attempt to evoke a mood of horror. [My only qualm with the article is that Hulbert reads the author as someone whose “psychological type” is not of the visual kind, where one should really speak of an artistic school not individual psychology (192-3).]

author: Jorgensen, Peter A.
title: Beowulf’s Swimming Contest with Breca: Old Norse Parallels
abstract: Hálfdans saga has a parallel to the Breca episode involving swimming in armour, fighting water-monsters, a contest (water-wrestling), and staying out for a considerable time. There is also a counterpart to Unferð “the evil counsellor” (52). Both texts also contain Sigemund-references (53). Örvar-Odds saga also tells of water-wrestling (53). Vilmundar saga contains water-wrestling and a bear attack in the water (53-4). This episode is related to one in Finnboga saga and Hemings þáttr (54). Þorsteins saga Víkingssonar likewise, and this version has parallels with the Beowulf-Grettis saga conglomerate of underwater fights (55). Grettis saga has further swimming feats, and this text has many parallels with Beowulf (55-6). Ans saga and Egils saga einhenda provide further parallels, the latter the closest, containing also an episode in which a giant’s right arm is cut off (56). It is proposed that the swimming feats are a motif that is preserved in a more primitive form in Beowulf and developed further in Scandinavia (56-7). Celtic tradition has no closer analogue and is therefore less likely as a place of origin (57-8).

author: Lehmann, W.P.
title: Beowulf 33, isig
abstract: Proposes that isig had connotations of death and mourning, the rune is having been supposed by Krause (Runeninschriften, 1937, p. 76) to refer to Hel, the goddess of death, which together with the hail-rune “was used to threaten the dead and to keep them from returning as ghosts” (ibid.). The Blickling homily also has “isgean bearwum” (“icy groves”), and [for some reason] the Metres of Boethius passage similarly connotes mourning and death. In its context, the Bwf word means “dedicated through appropriate rites for its funeral function” (578).

author: Liberman, Anatoly
title: The ‘Icy’ Ship of Scyld Scefing: Beowulf 33
publication: Bright is the Ring of Words: Festschrift für Horst Weinstock zum 65. Geburtstag
eds: Clausdirk Pollner, Helmut Rohlfing, and Frank-Rutger Hausmann
abstract:
Discusses the various readings and interpretations that have been proposed for isig ond utfus, and settles on ‘shining with metal.’

Discards pathetic fallacy and figurative readings (Stanley; Lehmann) on the grounds that words in Beowulf always have a literal meaning as well as a figurative one, and that isig had to have a literal meaning before it could be used figuratively; but it is not so found [it is, in fact: see BlHom 16, where isig forms a parallel to the hrinde bearwas of Grendel’s pool]. Points out that the Germanic languages are forever confusing words for iron and ice, and proposes that this has happened here. In this reading, it continues the train of thought begun with hringedstefna: “There stood in the harbor the ring-adorned ship, / aglitter with metal and ready for its last voyage.” If the form isig was ambiguous between ice and iron, the word hringedstefna would have made the reading clear to a contemporary audience.

author: Nelles, William
title: Beowulf’s sorhfullne sið with Breca
abstract: Focuses on Breca’s role and Unferð’s designation of the swimming/rowing expedition as sorhful. Accepts the rowing-reading but claims it has not been taken to its logical extreme (300). Objects to Frank’s conclusion that Unferð porposefully misrepresents the affair as a swimming-match, which there is no need for doing (300-1). Advances ridiculously weak linguistic evidence for this position (301-2). There is no race, but Unferð is not representing it as such, either; it is rather a test/contest of endurance (302-3). It is suggested that Breca is washed out of his boat and drowns; this is suggested by the passivity of holm up ætbær, the homeland he seeks being in the afterlife (303-5). There is a parallel to such a joint swimming-expedition in Færeyinga saga, making clear that this type of narrative is not atypical (305-6). The Unferð jester theory is rejected, for which is substituted the idea of Unferð as a trusted adviser of his king, probing the challenger (306-7). Beowulf’s response is sober, and he seems to admit some degree of guilt (307-8). The discrepancy between five and seven days is explained by Beowulf staying with Unferð for five, after which Breca survives for another two (308-9). Unferð is not a fratricide but abandoned his family in their need, just as Beowulf abandoned Breca (309).

author: Rauer, Christine
title: Beowulf and the Dragon: Parallels and Analogues
abstract:
Methodologically and bibliographically a very useful book for Bwf and analogue studies.

[Introduction and ch. 1: The Analogues of Beowulf] Describes the recent landscape of source studies (1–4) and points out that Bwf is not normally included in this discourse, as all its analogues fall short of some of the three requirements of thematic/verbal parallels, antecedence, and a plausible historical context for the influence (9–23).

[2: The Dragon Episode] Describes in some detail the dragon episode and its codicological context (24–41). Discusses the various analogues to Bwf, including Norse, Celtic, and classical works, and notes limitations and possible scenarios of influence to all these (41–51).

[3: Dragon-Fights in Hagiography and Other Literature] Analyses the narrative patterns of a large body of hagiographical dragon-fights, many of which were current in northwestern Gaul and the British Isles and would have been available to an Anglo-Saxon poet working 750–950. Although this homogeneous body of texts differs from Bwf in central elements, the dragon’s habits and habitat as well as the hero’s approach to the dragon observed from a distance by the larger populace correspond between Bwf and the vitae. Apt is the observation that Beowulf is not personally harmed by the burning of his hall but has to be notified, suggesting that an itinerant hero, like the itinerant saints of the hagiographical analogues, is underlying (77). Throwing the dragon off a mountain is parallelled in various saints’ lives (79). Like St Magnus, Beowulf is abandoned by people flying into the woods or to a tree; like the saints, Beowulf summons the dragon from his cave (80–1). The hero’s old age is sometimes matched, as is the dragon’s sense of smell (81–2). The secular, Scandinavian analogues lack all this overlap with the hagiographical tradition, as there is no summoning out and no old age, nor do dragons fly or breathe fire (82–6).

[4: Dragon-Fights in Anglo-Saxon England: Samson and Michael] Goes to considerable length to demonstrate the existence of a cult of St Samson in Wessex beginning in the early tenth century (89–112). Samson’s ninth-century Vita II adds many narrative details to the pre-existing Vita I which it shares with Bwf; all of these also existed in accounts of Samson’s first three monster-fights, but are nowhere else told of his fourth, against the dragon. The later version thus seems to have rearranged and expanded traditional material (from earlier passages of Vita I and Vita II) to arrive at its dragon-fight. This text could have influenced the dragon-episode of Bwf (115–16). A hagiographical text on the archangel Michael is contained in the Homiliary of Saint-Père that was so influential in Anglo-Saxon England, and whose earliest surviving copy was written in Bury St Edmunds (116–18). No OE poetic accounts of this dragon-fight survive, but it was a popular subject of Anglo-Saxon iconography (119). The Latin text, however, tells of a destructive fire-breathing dragon occupying a mountain and which is is dragged to or into the sea after its death, the latter element being unique to Bwf and this text (119–23). Blickling homily 16, a famous analogue to Grendel’s mere, is also a text on St Michael, suggesting that the Bwf poet was interested in this material (123–4; see further Orchard, Pride 51). This interest in St Michael thus links the Grendel episode and the dragon episode (124).

author: Sarrazin, G.
title: Altnordisches im Beowulfliede
publication: Beiträge zur Geschichte der deutschen Sprache und Literatur
abstract: Responding to Sievers 1886, tries once more to give Bwf a Danish descent by adding in more supposed Scandinavianisms. [See further Sievers 1887]

author: Sarrazin, G.
title: Der Schauplatz des ersten Beowulfliedes und die Heimat des Dichters
publication: Beiträge zur Geschichte der deutschen Sprache und Literatur
abstract: Claims that the setting of Bwf is Zealand, and Heorot represents Lejre, which precisely matches the landscape of Bwf, unlike Roskilde, which is too close to the sea (159-60). The burial-mounds of Lejre are still believed to house trolls. The nearby Hellige Skov is the required sacrificial grove (161). North of Lejre is marshland with marsh-pools (162) and a river (162-3). A local folktale account of a water-troll is given (164-5), as well as a medieval Latin account (165-6). ON grindill means storm, so Grendel must have been regarded as a Stormerregend. It is only natural that the tale made it to Iceland, where it survives in Grettla (167). An eyewitness account confirms the largely accurate landscape-description of the poet (167-70). The linguistic and stylistic differences between Bwf and OE prose or the “Caedmonian” poetry are large, suggesting that Bwf may have been written by a Dane (171-3). ON vocabulary seems obviously present (173-6), as is syntax (176-8). The poet will have been from Zealand, although southern Sweden is also possible (179-81). An appendix lists further Scandinavianisms in Bwf (181-3). [See further Sievers 1886]

author: Sievers, Eduard
title: Altnordisches im Beowulf?
publication: Beiträge zur Geschichte der deutschen Sprache und Literatur
abstract: Responding to Sarrazin 1886b, essentially points out why Sarrazin’s Scandinavianisms cannot be Scandinavianisms.

author: Sievers, Eduard
title: Die Heimat des Beowulfdichters
publication: Beiträge zur Geschichte der deutschen Sprache und Literatur
abstract: Responding to Sarrazin 1886a, points out factual problems with the latter’s use of diction to provide Bwf with a Danish descent. [See further Sarrazin 1886b]

author: Smithers, G.V.
title: The Making of Beowulf: Inaugural Lecture of the Professor of English Language, delivered in the Appleby Lecture Theatre on 18 May, 1961
abstract: After recalling Bwf’s connection with the Bear’s Son, points out specific parallels with Harðar saga and Norse tradition in general. Proposes that the dragon recalls a draugr (the dragon is thought identical with the last survivor), and suggests that this makes the two parts of Bwf into a unity because Grendel and his mother are likewise akin to troll and draugar in ON tradition, but the Bwf poet seems not to have been aware of this connection (up to & incl. 12). Scandinavian tradition can thus shed light on Bwf despite the chronological gap (13). Smithers goes to some length to argue that the fornaldarsögur can reflect old myth and legend, as demonstrated by Sigurðr and rock-carvings, as well as by the Scandinavian subject-matter of Bwf itself, and perhaps by the type of grave-mound story found in the dragon episode (12-14). Similarities between the Völsunga saga account of Fáfnir and Bwf’s account of the dragon are emphasised, again with the identity of the dragon and the last survivor in mind (14-16); it is suggested that they are variants of the same story (16). The christianisation of Bwf has blurred how the curse on the gold leads to the hero’s death; but the poet describes the treasure as useless to men because once buried, it could only benefit the dead, according to pagan tradition (16-19). Þórr and the Miðgarsormr presents a closer parallel to Bwf than Sigurðr, as Bwf has altered the original ending of the latter narrative (19-20, ref. to Olrik, Ragnarok); some have argued that Bwf conflates the two (20, refs to Neckel and Olrik). This reasoning is unsatisfactory because it rests on only one parallel; instead, it may be proposed that the ending of Bwf is simply a modification of the traditional fight in the grave-mound, with the hero’s sacrifice recalling Christ (21).

author: Wentersdorf, Karl P.
title: Beowulf’s Adventure with Breca
abstract: Emphasises the puzzling nature and status of the swimming contest (140-1). In the light of the assumption that Beowulf and Breca rowed rather than swam, sets out to find whether the exaggerated nature of the expedition is also a result of critical misreading (141-2). No evidence for an ancient or AS interest in swimming contests, although the Greeks wrote about swimming feats, and Latin authors describes the Germanic peoples as great river-swimmers, never mentioning the open sea (142-5). Scandinavian narrative literature speaks of its heroes as great swimmers (145-7). Swimming as a contest is mentioned by scholars, but the main sources of evidence, the sagas, speak of water-wrestling not swimming (148-9). Only Egils saga einhenda shows a swimming contest, and it too has swimmers lose their way and drift for a day and a night; here too, the contenders are boys; but there the correspondences end (149-50; ref. to Brandl for the conclusion that the analogue is superficial). The sagas do provide parallels to the idea of swimming with armour (150-1, citing Panzer). Keeps holding up the concept of “long-distance swimming contests” and denies that there is any evidence for them in Germanic literature (e.g. 153). Points out the linguistic difficulty of sund, claiming that the Proto-Germanic *swemjan and *swumda simply referred to movement in or over water. The former demonstrably survived into OE and ME with all its early senses, including floating (155-7). and Wentersdorf argues that the latter did the same (157-9). The Breca expedition is interpreted as a contest at rowing (159). The opening lines of The Wanderer clearly refer to a rower (160). The other swimming episodes of Beowulf are likewise reconsidered as rowing episodes, including the one at Grendel’s mere (161-2). Rowing was important to Germanic peoples as to the Greeks; there is little evidence of contests, but plentiful reference to rowing (163-4).

author: Evernden, Neil
title: Beyond Ecology: Self, Place, and the Pathetic Fallacy
publication: The Ecocriticism Reader: Landmarks in Literary Ecology
abstract:
Proposes that the scientific approach, with its separation of subject and object, is insufficient for the study of ecology, which is by its very definition an all-inclusive system. Instead, John Dewey's definition of the aesthetic is relevant to ecology, in which aesthetics are defined in the interrelationship between object and observer.

A difficulty in this regard is the definition of the individual, as one can often point out processes on which an organism depends but which form no real part of it (93-5). As an example of ecological interrelations interfering with the sense of self, the fish cichlid is named, which displays a sense of territory bearing no relation to its own small size; instead, the only physical dimension that seems to matter is that of the territory, which it will defend more fiercely the closer to its centre a threat moves (97-8). By contrast, [Western] man tends to retreat within itself as far as possible, insisting with Descartes that even the body is not part of the self, let alone the body's environment (98-9). By contrast, an environmental approach to man must focus on "the relation of self to setting" (99). While a utilitarian approach to landscape sees in it nothing but food and waste, landscape artists invite us to imagine landscape as part of us (99-100). In an inclusive understanding of environment, pathetic fallacy is no fallacy (101). This understanding has interesting implications for the urban environment and its potential to be a real environment at all (100-1).

In the light of the interrelatedness between self and environment, and the deeply personal nature of significance of place, practitioners of the arts and humanities are needed in environmentalist dialogue, as the environment cannot be understood without an understanding of aesthetics.

author: Fromm, Harold
title: From Transcendence to Obsolescence: A Route Map
publication: The Ecocriticism Reader: Landmarks in Literary Ecology
abstract: It has been man's physical inferiority that prompted him to extol the virtues of reason: nature could not be physically overcome, so transcendence was sought in what set man apart (30-1). With the rise of industrialism, religion was backgrounded: the dangers and fragilities of human existence were soon lessened, so life came to be less and less a thing that people felt a need to transcend (31-2). In the past, spiritual fulfilment was experienced as a need among the masses to be able to face the physical challenges of life on earth; with progress, that need has fallen away (32-3). Indeed, human existence has been systematised to such an extent that exposure to nature is often minimal, and an elementary understanding of ecology is not needed for survival (33-4). The mind's new independence is based not on the fact that it has no counterpart in nature, but on its perceived independence from nature, as nature's roles are all mediated by technology (34). Now, however, environmental destruction threatens to undermine this newfound superiority/independence (34-5). People questioning the need to improve environmental quality are in effect asking whether the constructs that we have come to regard as life should be sacrificed for the sake of the physical safeguards of life, such as clean air (36-8). This is a new form of the mind-body problem, but one that fails to recognise man's connections to and dependence on the earth (38-9).

author: Howarth, William
title: Some Principles of Ecocriticism
publication: The Ecocriticism Reader: Landmarks in Literary Ecology
abstract: A broad-based overview of the history and landscape of ecocriticism, with references to some seminal works in its various subfields at the end of the article.

author: Manes, Christopher
title: Nature and Silence
publication: The Ecocriticism Reader: Landmarks in Literary Ecology
abstract: Points out that nature has no voice in Western culture, unlike in animism, where it speaks to men (15-17). However, digging more deeply, animism is universal and exists also in Western culture, as is suggested by animal references in names of cars and sports teams, not to mention the voice of written culture (17-18). In more strongly animistic cultures, however, environmental destruction does not exist, and the wild is not distinguished from the domestic, nature and culture never being strongly distinct, which suggests that Western attitudes towards the outside world is far from universal (18). European animism greatly diminished in the Middle Ages, among other things by the introduction of Christian exegesis (the book of nature) and literacy (18-20). The former of these funnelled all nature into the single signification of divine reference (19-20). In its function of the scala naturae, nature was sometimes seen as valuable for its biodiversity; but the Renaissance transformed the concept into evidence of human superiority (20-1). The anthropocentrism of humanism still haunts the sciences today, and even environmental ethics (21). Empiricism asks questions with reference to nature, but nature's meanings are to be found in us (21-2). Although postmodernism has at least challenged the centrality and coherence of the human subject, only deep ecology has challenged the centrality of man in environmental ethics. Biologists at least admit that humans are not the goal of evolution, contradicting the scala naturae (22). Humanists in the environmental debate have continued to claim a special status for man (22-4). There are several more pages emphasising the need to move away from anthropocentrism and a focus on reason as the supreme goal of evolution, and asking how we are to learn a language that does not place man on a pedestal (24-6).

author: Turner, Frederick
title: Cultivating the American Garden
publication: The Ecocriticism Reader: Landmarks in Literary Ecology
abstract: Asks probing questions about the definition of nature and natural (40-5). Examines current views on the matter in the light of American history, which was shaped by Puritanism, whose rejection of compromise denied any spiritual value in nature (45-6), and the frontier, which confirmed a duality between self and other, but also combined with Puritanism to create a new desire to abandon civilisation and live in nature, as expressed in Thoreau, leading to the quest for "natural" qualities in man such as natural equality and natural selfishness (46). Following Rousseau, indeed, natural man was asocial or antisocial; the US constitution has incorporated this emphasis on the individual above all else (46-7). Natural equality, however, is a myth: indeed, the division of labour could not prosper without differences in natural endowment (47). Moreover, self-interest has been shown to be no solitary and overriding principle in the human psyche (47-8). While European culture and art has better managed to mediate between nature and culture, but ultimately the European world-view is one of limits to both nature and culture, whereas the American ideal is one of creation ex nihilo (48). To establish a new conceptual model, we should rely on human intention, not human instinct, as the former is more evolved than the latter (49). All human activities may be understood as analogous with gardening: technology, too, is nature and must not be distrusted, but we must take responsibility for all nature. The stewardship of nature must not be shunned or denied but embraced responsibly (49-50). The article's conclusion is a bombastic and somewhat grotesque sermon on the metaphorical American garden that must now be designed (50-1).

author: White, Lynn Jr.
title: The Historical Roots of Our Ecological Crisis
publication: The Ecocriticism Reader: Landmarks in Literary Ecology
abstract: As a first step towards understanding how man has altered his environment, White draws attention to the history of science and technology, which, he proposes, were once separate fields (the first aristocratic and theoretical, the second working-class and pragmatic); they were only merged in the mid-nineteenth century (5-6). The modern forms of both, however, are deeply Western: it was the West that began putting wind- and water-power to general use about 1000 CE, and so the Middle Ages were a critical stage in the development of the modern technological model (6-8). It was the West that introduced the deep plough in the seventh century; in the early ninth, calendar illustrators turned from personification to human labour (8). Also in the Middle Ages, Christianity became the dominant religion in Europe; its Western subtype is the most anthropocentric religion in the world, making man master of his surroundings (9-10). Animism was firmly rejected, thereby allowing nature to be freely exploited (10). In the later Middle Ages, natural theology became more scientific in the modern sense, understanding phenomena as self-contained, with God's agency only their ultimate cause (11-12). Since science and technology in their Christian form have led us to the present time of crisis, these fields of thought cannot help us unless we rethink their religious basis (12). Saint Francis of Assisi may provide a clue: this "greatest radical in Christian history since Christ" rejected the anthropocentrism of Western Christianity. The remedy to the present predicament may lie in his view that all creatures are equal (13-14).

author: Benson, Larry D.
title: The Originality of Beowulf
publication: The Interpretation of Narrative: Theory and Practice
abstract:
The current (=1970) impossibility of ascertaining what share the poet or compiler of Beowulf had in the creation of its narrative and plot structure (described on pp. 1-4) is a consequence of our unquestioning acceptance of long-standing assumptions that (a) Beowulf’s central plot must be indebted to extensive preexisting sources and (b) the poet left those source narratives largely intact in transmission (4-5). Beowulf shows evidence of such practice in the Sigemund and Finnsburh narratives, so it is assumed it holds true throughout. This practice is seen in much of medieval literature, from Boccaccio and Chaucer to Saxo. The Junius manuscript is similarly synthetic, but here it concerns scribal editing rather than the merging of disparate oral materials; and Beowulf is earlier than this compilation (5-6). Eighth-century OE poetry seems to use its sources far more creatively than Chaucer did, taking a single kernel or episode and expanding it with poetic devices (7). As an example, Benson first gives not OE poetry but Alcuin’s Latin versification of Edwin’s vision and the Karolus Magnus et Leo Papa, also Latin (7-10). The OE Exodus does the same, as do Genesis, Christ and Satan, and the Cynewulf poems (10-11). The unique feat of Beowulf as a long heroic poem of the eighth century makes it hard to believe that any sources of similar extensiveness were used or ever existed; it should therefore be expected to have resulted from poetic amplification like that in the works just mentioned (11-12). Nevertheless many still hold that the central plot in Beowulf must have been based on something more substantial than just the draugr episodes reflected in Grettis saga but must likewise have borrowed the hero’s associations with the geatas, Hrothgar, and the monsters. Beowulf’s name shows hin to be an intruder in his family context (13). Although he is often assumed to have been a well-known traditional character, his name does not show a spread proportionate to such fame (13-14). Charter place-names are insufficient evidence for the existence of an epic tale like that of Beowulf (14-15). Böðvar Bjarki in Bjarkamál, Saxo, Hrólfs saga kraka, and the Bjarka rímur are the only Scandinavian parallels to a hero with a bear-name. Benson criticises the tendency to take the most recent (i.e. saga and rímur) redactions of the tale as the most authentic (15-16). The several parallels with Beowulf are briefly rehearsed and the widespread conclusion is noted that either Beowulf influenced the Scandinavian narrative or, more likely, that a Bear’s Son tale underlies both (16). These parallels, however, rely on highly selective readings and on later developments in the Scandinavian versions; the strongest links with Beowulf derive from the saga of Siward, who lived in Northumbria and whose story greatly contaminated the one under study but was not itself related to Beowulf either (16-18; Olrik and Olson are credited with the authorship of this argument). The rímur innovations are rationalisations of a confused narrative. The relationship of the Bjarki narrative to that of Grettla is clear, but that does not bring it any closer to Beowulf (19).

The only evidence of a preexisting Beowulf-poem is the Breca-episode in Beowulf itself, which seems to reflect a tale in which a Beowulf is humbled in a swimming-match. For his role-inversion to work, Beowulf must have been an obscure character; and his name links him with the Brondingas said to have been ruled by Breca in Widsith (21-2). The kenning beowulf for “bear” is disputed (22-5).

Benson now discusses the Sandhaugar episode of Grettis saga. A footnote lists scholars who believe Beowulf to have directly influenced Grettla (26-7 n. 48); this position is difficult, though the reverse is even more problematic. The likeliest solution is a parallel development going back to a common source (26-7). A reconstruction is made based on solely those parts in which the two works agree (27). Both swimming and wrestling are required skills for this shared tale, suggesting that the underlying tale may have included the Grendel element as well as other aspects of Beowulf’s central narrative (28); the Kárr inn gamli episode of Grettla and the hero’s boasting verses contains further analogues, though in nonessential details only (28-9). All of the saga’s relevant episodes rely on a well-attested grave-dweller story, in which the hero descends below the earth using a rope; this recognition renders unnecessary the possibility of Grettla deriving from a tale containing both Grendel and the dragon (29-30). The kernel of Beowulf remains a heroic killing of two monsters of opposite sex and environment (hall versus water); Beowulf is that tale newly configured to match the other traditional tales used by the poet (30). The most important addition is a dragon fight without a precise analogue but with the Sigemund tale as his source. Beowulf’s life is one of a gradual lessening of glory following his epic defeat of Grendel, ending in defeat at the hands of the dragon; in this resides the originality of Beowulf, as the work is a complex reflection on the nature of heroism (31-4). All digressions and allusions serve to create a context against which Beowulf’s actions must be viewed (34-9). The hero’s actions are futile, not anti-heroic (39); his childlessness is another expression of this futility (40-1).

author: Fjalldal, Magnús
title: The Long Arm of Coincidence: The Frustrated Connection between ‘Beowulf’ and ‘Grettis saga’
abstract: Argues against a genetic relationship between the two texts. The book discusses in great detail, but with a selective focus, the history of scholarship on the matter, examining Beowulf and Grettir as heroes, the fights, the hæftmece/heptisax, and landscape, as well as the various theories concerning the precise relationship between the texts. As Fjalldal relies largely on a downplaying of general resemblances in order to compare narrative details instead [which, of course, differ inasmuch as the motifs are used in different genres, societies, landscapes, and narrative traditions], as well as on the differences in approach and opinion among those who have recognised a connection between the two texts, the book is unconvincing. In the end, his solution to the analogues lies in the existence of various parallels to specific Glámr/Sandhaugar-motifs in other sagas[, thus implicitly suggesting that the author of Grettis saga accidentally assembles a variety of disparate elements to form a close parallel to Beowulf, while the existence of such elements are nowhere acknowledged to confirm the existence of shared Anglo-Norse narrative traditions but rather the opposite] (ch. 10, =pp. 119-29). In his conclusion, Fjalldal asserts that Beowulf does not appear to have derived from a folktale, but the Sandhaugar episode of Grettis saga has generally been thought by Icelandic scholars to be “a genuinely indigenous folktale” (131-3, at 133).

author: Gering, Hugo
title: Der Beówulf und die Islaendische Grettissaga
abstract: Announces Vigfusson’s discovery of the Beowulf–Grettla parallel and retells Grettla at great length. Then briefly points out the similarities. Gering contends that Vigfusson is right in identifying the Sandhaugar episode as related to Beowulf, but not so with the Glámr episode (86).

author: Jorgensen, Peter A.
title: Grendel, Grettir and Two Skaldic Stanzas
abstract: The second stanza in Grettla’s waterfall-cave episode contains details found in Bwf but not in the Grettla prose; if the compiler can be shown to have misunderstood this verse, a preexisting Icelandic Grendel-poem must be assumed (55). Mellu vinr is open to interpretation: vinr ‘friend’ could mean lover, parent, or husband, although here mellu vinr may simply be a kenning for giant. Lengi for the duration of the fight corresponds to Bwf not Grettla (56). The compiler refers to the heptisax as a fleinn before explaining that it could both thrust and chop; the handle, he says, is wood, again recalling a spear (56-7). The preservation of the word heptisax has to be explained by alliterative necessity, appearing alongside harðeggjat and höggvit while OE hæftmece alliterates with Hrunting (57). Grettla and its verse tell us the monster wields the heptisax, but the second stanza may be reconstructed with harðeggjar and höggva to read (prose order) “ek lét heptisax höggva harðeggjar af skepti” (I caused the heptisax to chop the hard edges from the shaft) (57-8). A tricky argument is made in which the three extant versions of the passage are less likely to be original than a fourth, combined reading: the extant versions try to make sense of what is no longer understood (58-9). This reading, with Grettir wielding the heptisax, supports existing theories that the corresponding Bwf passage with a hæftmece and a sword on a wall is a confusion of two versions (59). Arguments that the stanzas are fourteenth-century are dispelled (59-61).

author: Malone, Kemp
title: Grendel and his Abode
publication: Studia philologica et litteraria in honorem L. Spitzer
abstract: Builds a persuasive argument identifying Grendel’s mere as (an inlet of) seawater, basing himself on the vocabulary used for it in comparison with the application of such terms elsewhere as well as information provided in Blickling homily 17. At the end of his paper (307), Malone argues that Scandinavian reflexes of the tradition in Grettis saga and Orms þáttr came to Iceland from England as a result of Anglo-Norse relations during or following the Viking Age.

author: Smith, Charles Sprague
title: Beówulf Gretti
abstract: Announces Vigfusson’s find and places the parallels side by side in translation (49-64). Acknowledges the connection between the Saundhaugar and Grendelmother narratives (64-5). Samsons saga is also mentioned as a parallel, “though not so striking” (65). The Glámr episode is more problematic (65-). The two hall-fights in Grettla are “identical,” but the fight with Glámr is aesthetically better and therefore the model of the Sandhaugar episode (66). The Glámr episode is very much a parallel to the Grendel story, and what is lacking survives in the Saundhaugar version (66-7).

author: Stedman, Douglas
title: Some Points of Resemblance Between Beowulf and the Grettla (or Grettis saga)
abstract: After some discussion of Grendel’s bearlike appearance, concludes that he is a monster in man-form (6-8). Grendel and Glámr are then compared: both dislike the sound of music (this is a factor in Glámr’s aversion to churchgoing) (8-9), and both have big, monstrous heads (9-10). Grettir’s curse has no counterpart in Beowulf (10). Other parallels listed include the damaging of the hall (11-12). Grettir’s waterfall expedition has several minute parallels in Beowulf’s descent into the mere (second enemy in the cave; hero’s companions abandon him; description of a weapon in the cave, 13). There is an interesting reference to Stopford Brooke [Early English Literature, vol. 1], who reportedly describes the Grendelcave as a tidal cave, its entrance below the low-tide point (14). Both texts speak of a firy light in the cave (14-15), and the monsters use weapons (15). Both heroes also have only one friend in the end (Wiglaf/Illugi) (17-22). Thomas Arnold is quoted as saying that Beowulf preserves the older version of the tale compared to either Grettla or Hrólfs saga kraka/Saxo (22); Chadwick points out that the existence of a historical Grettir Ásmundarson must mean that the older story became attached to his name but contends that there is no evidence that it derived from Anglo-Saxon material; Chadwick implies that both may deriver from a Danish source, as this is where the OE story plays. Chadwick eventually provides two possible explanations: OE > mainland Scandinavia > Iceland or “common property of the Northmen” > two independent versions (22-3). Stedman argues that the similarities are so close that the Grettla author must have known Beowulf as a result of AS missionary activities (23). Parallels with Hrólfs saga kraka has Boðvar Bjarki, a man who can turn into a bear, kill a bear who haunts the Lejre royal house at jól; the episode shares various details with Beowulf (23-5). In the conclusion, the swimming power of Grettir is further brought into comparison with Beowulf’s (25), and loneliness is further added as a property of both (25-8).

author: Stitt, J. Michael
title: ‘Beowulf’ and the Bear’s Son: Epic, Saga, and Fairytale in Northern Germanic Tradition
abstract: Excerpts and summarises the widest number of analogues to Beowulf I have yet seen, most of them Scandinavian though some are as distant as Vedic, Iranian, and Chinese traditions. Distinguishes sharply between written and oral folktale [here called Märchen] traditions (passim). Points out that the known Beowulf text could not have been the only source to transmit the tale to Grettla because the latter contains the fight-by- a-cliff episode known from the Two Troll-tradition but absent from Bwf (96). “[T]he Grendel episode. . . must be understood in terms of Scandinavian traditions” and does not derive from Irish sources, as the great number of analogues now known and their complex interrelations exclude straightforward manuscript transmission (203). The argument that the Irish versions are primary because arms coming through windows and chimneys invite their being cut off, but Bwf and Grettla have misunderstood why the monsters lose their arms, is dismissed on the grounds that the several saga authors using the motif feel no need to explain the incident, suggesting that it is part of their tradition even if it ultimately derived from Irish sources [!] (203-4). Stitt makes the same argument with regard to the hero-sleeping motif, in Irish sources a result of a sleeping spell but sufficiently widespread to render it impossible to show that they derive from Bwf (204). It has been proved that the Irish Hand and Child tale has influenced modern Scandinavian folktales, but its medieval impact is unknown (204). The Grendel episode and the modern folktale AT301 (“The Three Stolen Princesses”) are related but the former is not simply a version of the latter. “The Grendel episode does have folktale origins, but ‘folktale’ is a general term that embraces many quite distinctive genres” (204-5, at 205). The dragonslayer motif is Indo-European, as are other specifics in Bwf (205, see also earlier in this book). Saga evidence consists of members of the Two Trolls-tradition and the Gravemound Battle tradition, both of which are internationally attested but are largely representative in form of their respective genres (205-6). Two stable traditions may be recognised, one mythic-heroic and the other folktale, the second of which (including the House on the Woods) has been imposed over the former, which is a simpler construction; the medieval texts preserve the stable motif of nontreacherous abandonment at the sight of gore, suggesting the transmission of a stable structure (or the stable transmission of a structure, 206). A final conclusion is that because it seems to be a consistent pattern for the folktales to borrow from the mythic-heroic tradition rather than vice versa, “for all the importance of generic considerations, this factor alone cannot explain the two strands of tradition in Scandinavia. Some form of conservation of narrative tradition is also at work.” This means that “the Beowulf poet, and the saga redactors after him, created specific versions of a widely known tradition” rather than repeatedly borrowing [piecemeal] from folktale tradition (207). I don’t think Stitt at any point suggests an order of influence other than ruling out Irish primacy and direct Beowulf–Grettla influence, but he emphasises that Beowulf is part of a Scandinavian configuration of an Indo-European set of motifs (ch. 2 [29-41] on Indo-Iranian dragonslaying traditions; chs. 3-5 [43-169] on the Scandinavian traditions of Two Trolls and the Gravemound Battle; ch. 7 [193-208] draws conclusions).

author: Turville-Petre, Joan
title: Beowulf and Grettis saga: An Excursion
abstract: “Direct influence of the poem on the author of the saga is easily ruled out” (347). Describes Beowulf as differing from Grettla in being a myth in Northrop-Frye’s sense of the word, which is rather vaguely stated (348). The central idea of Beowulf is that of the deliverer, a motif present but not dominant in Grettla, whose hero has strong connections with the outside, a ghostly world that is strange rather than frightening (348-9). The Heorot/Sandhaugar episodes follow the same pattern, rehearsed in point-by-point fashion; the Glámr episode has been “overvalue[d]. . . as an analogue” (349). The more orderly presentation of the material in Grettla does not point to older date, but rather to individual treatment of the material (349-50). Studies the analogous images of fire, sword, and light, concluding that the former is simply a domestic image in both works; the sword in Grettla is furniture, but it fulfuls an important function in Beowulf; and the light is divine in Beowulf (350-1). The heptisax/hæftmece is the most striking analogue (352). The Grettla sword is described in confusing terms as the compiler tries to make sense of the verse description. In terms of its first element, the heptisax is compared to Bwf 1563 fetelhilt and described as a sword with a loop that could be hung around the arm (352-3). It seems Grettir’s weapon is the one given him by the farmer whose draugr he overcame in Norway (353-4). The underwater episode of Beowulf stands closer to a hypothetical source than does that of Grettla, since it is pivotal to Beowulf’s career unlike with Grettir (355). Beowulf’s name, a kenning for bear, links him with Scandinavian tradition in Bjarkamál/Saxo; Chambers has shown the widespread underlying [non-extant] existence of a bear-man who descends into the underworld through a hole (356).

author: Boer, R.C.
title: Beowulf [Review of Chambers’s Beowulf: An Introduction, first ed.]
abstract: Disagrees with Chambers’s analysis; reasserts his points expressed in his edition Grettla and book on Bwf that the unity of the two fights has to be judged before comparison can be made with the Bear’s Son folktale (107); that the Glámr episode in Grettla is primary, the Sandhaugar episode an interpolation differing greatly in setting from the Bwf account but textually related, as the word heptisax shows, and related by narrative inasmuch as the troll-woman loses an arm and disappears into a gorge (107-8 [what Boer means is that Glámr and the turning to stone are Icelandic, but these other elements glued onto the existing tradition using Bwf]). Thus the fights in Bwf do not for a narrative unit (108). The relevant passage of Orms þáttr was clearly copied from Grettla (109). Criticises Chambers’s reasoning regarding the single authorship of Bwf (109-10). Points out points of disconnection within Bwf, such as the introduction of Grendel after he has already been killed; in fact, Bwf combines two variants of one tale, of which the one with the fight in the mere is the original (110). Glámr agrees with the hall-fight, but Sandhaugar contains traces of a development from the mere-fight (111-12). Suggests that Beowulf was originally a Scylding playing a role in the dragon-tale; this would have been Beowulf son of Scyld (113-15). Discusses some connections between characters and historical persons (115-16), the Finn episode (116-18).

author: Carney, James
title: The Irish Elements in Beowulf
publication: Studies in Irish Literature and History
abstract: Although not on the whole persuasive, this chapter contains a number of clever and insightful observations. Argues that Beowulf has borrowed the Breca episode and the fight with Grendel’s mother from the Táin Bó Fraích, which borrowed it from the Vita Columbae, but the Bwf author also had direct access to the latter text (86–9, 114–28); that Irish water-monsters and the Hand and Child tale show Irish tradition to have been formative for Bwf, and Grettla derivative (89–101); that Irish sources based on Isidore’s Etymologiae provide a source for Bwf’s confusion between Cainite and Hamite ancestry as well as the various types of creature evolved from this ancestor (102–14); . Particularly keen are the observations that Glámr and the Sandhaugar troll could not be related because Glámr was once human, suggesting that the Bwf narrative is the original (95); that both Grendel and Glámr have bad religion to thank for their wretched condition, suggesting that the narrative developed in Christian times (94–6); and that the Cainite vagus et profugus in terra seems to shine through in Glámr’s curse over Grettir, again suggesting that the saga compiler was working from a Christian source like Bwf (96). The suggestion is made that since Ireland was known to lack serpents, the monsters must have been restricted to the water; the [assumed] popularity of the vita of St Samson of Dol, which involves fights with serpents, required adaptation (122–4). Among the more striking parallels between Bwf and the Táin Bó Fraích is the exchange with the watchman/coastguard, who in each case remarks on the time he has held his profession and the particular quality of one of the travellers (119–20, 126); the other similarities are far less convincing.

author: Deutschbein, Max
title: Die sagenhistorischen und literarischen Grundlagen des Beowulfepos
abstract: Emphasises the Migration Age as a formative period for Germanic epic and the Germanic elegiac mindset of rise and fall, while also being the primary source of subject matter for Germanic literature (103-4). The same is true for Bwf, the oldest work of Germanic literature (dating from c. 700); but it tells of Scandinavians rather than Angles, Saxons, and Jutes, and Danes especially. The Danes were unknown to Antiquity, but are mentioned after the Migration Age, when their state was formed; the Angles must have observed their doings from up close (104-5). The diverse wars of the Geatas are likewise recorded, and some are confirmed from Frankish sources. It is in poetic form that this knowledge could survive the centuries accurately; hence the poetry should be regarded as based on history. Thus Bwf also can at many points be read as history, especially on fifth- and sixth-century Scandinavia (105-6). The central subject matter, however, is Beowulf’s monster-fights; yet the hero need not be considered a mythical character, or the monster-fights symbolic, if one can reduce them to their archetype (108-9). The dragon-fight resembles Sigurðr’s, but most of all Þórr’s (109). The origin of the treasure recalls the motif in which a greedy man becomes a dragon to guard his possessions; it surely derives from Scandinavian tradition as a transmission that must be considered historical (109-10). No ancient Scandinavian analogue for the first half of Bwf has been found; the late Grettla surely derives directly or indirectly from Beowulf itself. The motif must therefore have accrued to the tradition in England (110). The absence elsewhere of the fantastic in Saxon literature renders an Anglo-Saxon origin problematic; but no such difficulties surround a Celtic origin (110-11). Celtic tradition tends to combine the fantastic with a single hero (111). Some Irish tales with heroes fighting water-monsters are mentioned (111-12). The Fled Brierend or Feast of Bricriu is named specifically a an analogue to Bwf (112); it is summarised (113) and a translated passage is quoted (113-14). Unferth’s name and words recall the strife between the guests at the Irish feast (114). The Irish poet was an honoured and feared character, feared for his potentially devastating mockeries. Hence Hrothgar allows him to challenge his guest rather than invoke his malice against himself (114-15). The monsters in Bwf are also incrementally hard to defeat, as in Fled Brierend. Bwf is furthermore an epic formed on the basis of a lay—not a series of lays, as was once believed—, which is not a Germanic commonplace, but it is an Irish commonplace (115). Bede’s HE shows how much contact there was between Ireland and Northumbria, and Bwf must be reckoned Northumbrian (115-17). Specifically, Hiberno-English contact commenced at Aldfrid’s court (Northumbria, 680-705), which would thus be a reasonable context in which Bwf could have been written (117-18).

author: Puhvel, Martin
title: ‘Beowulf’ and Celtic Tradition
abstract: A book of very short chapters presenting at times unconvincing Irish analogues to aspects of the Grendel narrative in a needlessly unconvincing manner. The final chapter is the only full-length one, because it has to introduce, discuss, and discredit all the Scandinavian parallels, which it does not, however, disavow entirely. The controversy over the Bwf–Grettla relationship is misrepresented as either Icelandic folktales > Bwf or Bwf itself > Grettla; the author discredits Chambers’s opinion, instead favouring the latter sequence (esp. 116, 124 but more widely 111–124). A considerable amount of attention is given to comparing the Hand and Child tale’s claim to formative influence over Bwf with the Bear Son’s, in the former’s favour. The book concludes without any firm commitments, and unfortunately does not provide an index of versions of the Hand and Child tale.

author: Scowcroft, R. Mark
title: The Irish Analogues to Beowulf
abstract:
[A highly intelligent and balanced discussion on the relationships between the various witnesses to narrative and motifs in Beowulf; only its suggestion that Grettis saga derives from Beowulf itself seems unfeasible.]

The Hand and the Child has been found in an eleventh-century Welsh text, while twelfth-century applications in an Irish text and Chrétien de Troyes’s Conte du Graal show it without the kidnapping motif; two eighth-century Irish versions substitute a cooked pig for the infant. All early versions have a single hero rather than the Skilful Companions or Werewolf motifs (23-4). Kittredge was therefore wrong to identify Hand and Child as a motif properly belonging to the Skilful Companions tale (24-5). Scowcroft argues (following Dehmer in 1928) that the Hand and the Child uniquely combines the Defence of the Hall with the Descent to the Monster’s Lair, in which it parallels Bwf (25). Kittredge’s position has proved conclusive for folklorists inasmuch as the Hand and Child narrative is not recognised as a type of the Bear’s Son tale; but the question of the narrative’s relationship to Beowulf remains (25-6). The debate over Irish or Scandinavian folktale connections has resulted in a stalemate situation (26-7). Scowcroft observes that folktale traditions have a status more like genre or convention than literary source, so that a tale can originate in Denmark and yet follow an Irish pattern in England (27). Individual international motifs tell us little, but extensive arrangements of them inform us about an author’s reception of inherited tradition, and come as close as one can get to a historical argument. Many Grendel analogues do not qualify for this principle (27). The Bear’s Son is a motif-archetype so broad that it will accommodate most heroic exploits; the Hand and the Child is a narrative pattern, represented by a series of motifs and helping fit Beowulf and Grettis saga into a specific slot under the heading of the Bear’s Son (28). Chambers’s position is polluted by his motive, namely to give Beowulf a Danish home thereafter mildly revised in England. This approach is too textual for an oral tradition, and the Danish subject matter of Bwf has been regarded by others as an English-born theme. If the present paper shows that Scandinavian analogues are a motif-index rather than a coherent archetype, non-Scandinavian analogues must no longer be excluded from consideration (28-9). It will be proposed that the Hand and Child became part of the Bwf-tradition in England and from there moved to Scandinavia from Bwf itself, directly or indirectly (29).

States that only Sandhaugar is a real Grettla-analogue to Bwf because it combines the same two narratives, though the same combination is also found in Hand and Child tales; if poem and saga were influenced by these, this does not contradict their mutual relationship but rather reinforces it, since it sets them apart from other Scandinavian material (29-30). The two fights in Bwf derive from two variants; the fight with Grendel’s mother possibly recalls the removal of an arm in her claiming back her son’s arm; in Hrothgar’s apostrophe to the arm; in Beowulf’s seizing her be eaxle and his reference to their fight as a hand gemæne (30). Pulling off the arm is particular to Bwf and 15 Irish variants; all others involve a weapon. The bare-hands motif remains unexplained, except in Bwf, which gives three different reasons, signalling an attempt at rationalisation of an otherwise ‘blind’ motif (31-2). The poet has duplicated the monster, showing he understood the structure of the narrative; but several inconsistencies remain in the account (32-3). Bwf follows the Norse paradigm of killing a monster whenever you see one, but nevertheless copies the Irish two-part structure. Grettla copies both episodes, but treats the second as a sequel rather than a resolution; this distances it further from the prototype than Bwf inasmuch as the attacker from episode 1 does not play the defender in episode 2 (33). Carney has pointed out that both Grendel and Glámr stand in a hostile relationship with God, while Grettir is cursed with a Cain-like fate; Glámr thus echoes the prototype without forming a full analogue inasmuch as it lacks an episode 2; these elements could not have been deduced from the Sandhaugar episode (34-5). Chambers’s use of Samsons saga does not qualify for reconstruction, as it is no full analogue and a third Scandinavian witness to the pattern is required to prove a Scandinavian prototype (i.e. any prototype can only be constructed from three or more witnesses, 36). The haft motif is similarly inconclusive, as Hrólfs saga contains no episode 2 with a sword on a wall, and none of this survives in Saxo apart from the name Hialto (36-7). The Bjarki evidence is stronger in later witnesses than in earlier. The hæftmece/heptisax parallel must be either textual or chance; it is proposed that they are chance parallels, each coined in a poetic tradition (37); but later it is suggested that the Norse poet coined a new weapon based on his reading of Bwf (39). The reference of these words is discussed, and it is asked why Bwf transfers it from the sword on the wall (the real motif) to Hrunting (37-9). Grettir’s pseudonym is discussed and proposed spawned by Beowulf’s description as a guest at the mere and Grendel’s as a hall-thegn in Heorot (39). In view of consensus of the texts’ connection, the Cain/antireligious motif must similarly be cognate; the prototype must then be English, as Beowulf predates the conversion of Iceland (40-1). More discussion of literary borrowing; the objection that textual borrowing would yield closer parallels and oral borrowing looser ones is considered but discarded (41-2). The secondary possibility is now also admitted that the Hand and Child motif may have accrued to the narrative in Iceland straight from Ireland (42-3).

Essential to the Hand and Child narrative is a binary, reciprocal structure in which the defender and attacker of episode one change roles in episode two; there are often further points of symmetry associating these characters but also their victims and halls as well as the action (43-4). Individual authors rework accidents, not constituent parts of the narrative (44-5). In Bwf, external states of affairs mirror and prefigure internal situations; the prefiguring of wars also prefigures recurrent attacks on Heorot (45). The monsters’ abode is a reversal of Heorot, and the conflicting landscapes are symbolic, uniting a troll-cave, Cain’s desert, Leviathan’s ocean, and hell itself. The monsters are antetypes of Danish internal strife (47). Unferth is studied as the focus of the similarity between the Danes and their monsters (47-8); so is his sword (48-9). Fratricide is a recurring theme in the poem, but a distinction is drawn between murder (Grendel, Unferth) and vengeance (Grendel’s mother, Beowulf). The emphasis on fratricide supposedly links the story back to its prototype (49-50). Beowulf’s own inner contrast between the monstrous and the virtuous reflects the Hand and Child narrative with its reciprocal episodes (50). The poets fondness for contrastive pairs similarly outlines the antagonism and affinity between monsters and men (51-2). Kaske’s fortitudo and sapientia are discussed with regard to Hrothgar et al. (52-3). The gifstol-passage serves to define Grendel as an anti-thane and a reflex of Cain (53-4). If the same structure is applied to the monsters, Grendel’s mother is an anti-woman, illustrating the moral ambiguity in the distinction between murder and revenge (53ff.). Bwf is unusual in making the monster’s female companion his mother, thereby heightening the bachelor-opposition of Beowulf and Grendel, the maternal status of Grendel’s mother and Wealhtheow, but leaves out a counterpart for Hrothgar (54-6). The difference between “criminal and obligatory homicide” is challenged (56). A theme expressed by the duplication of the prototype is the tendency of violence to beget violence, a notion also expressed in virtually all the digressions (56-7). The resolution of this cycle requires sapientia (57).

A variant of the sapientia et fortitudo-image is now transposed onto the Swedish part of Bwf, which is read as a higher-level episode two [perhaps unnecessarily] (58-64). The final conclusion on the relationship with Grettis saga is that “the author of the saga was familiar with the poem or the tradition to which it belonged” (64).

author: Scowcroft, R. Mark
title: The Hand and the Child: Studies of Celtic Tradition in European Literature

author: Jeay, Madeleine
title: Sanguine Inscriptions: Mythic and Literary Aspects of a Motif in Chrétien de Troyes's Conte du graal
publication: Telling Tales: Medieval Narratives and the Folk Tradition
eds: Francesca Canadé Sautman, Diana Conchado, and Giuseppe Carlo Di Scipio
abstract: A somewhat loosely ordered reflection on the triad of white (snow), red (blood), and black (hair/raven) in medieval French romance, especially the Conte du graal, and folktales. The main emphasis is on the blood-on-snow image, and on psychoanalytical readings. Its endnotes contain a good number of references to studies of the motif in romance and folktale.

author: Baudry, Robert
title: Et l'absence, éloquente, de geste...
publication: Le geste et les gestes au Moyen Âge
abstract: Discusses episodes in French romance in which the absence of action—in the guise of transfixion, ecstasy, the paralysis of fear, and the like—conveys information about the character's intimate processes. Focussing on Lancelot, Perceval, Gawain, Guinevere, and Galad, one of the episodes it briefly mentions is Perceval's fascination with the goose blood on the snow in the Conte du graal. A footnote contains references to more detailed studies of the blood-on-snow motif.

author: Meyer, Matthias
title: Filling a Bath, Dropping Into the Snow, Drunk Through a Glass Straw: Transformations and Transfigurations of Blood in German Arthurian Romances
publication: Bibliographical Bulletin of the International Arthurian Society
abstract: Discusses various functions and occurrences of blood imagery in German romance. Includes a brief discussion of the blood on the snow, comparing the versions by Chrétien and Wolfram (413–14). Stresses the connection between the blood-dripping sword and bleeding goose in Chrétien, a connection that is not brought out in Wolfram. "In the blood drop scene Parzival is confronted with his life, and, as Bumke has argued, in the end has a notion if not yet explicit knowledge of his future tasks" (414).
tags: romance,middle high german,arthur,blood,snow,chretien de troyes,wolfram,conte du graal

author: Gallais, Pierre
title: Le sang sur la neige (le conte et le rêve)
publication: Cahiers de civilisation médiévale Xe–XIIe siècles
abstract:
Before it was used in Chrétien de Troyes's Conte du graal, the motif of blood on snow existed in folklore only. The motif is copied, always in connection with Perceval, in Perzival, Peredur, and the prose Tristan; it is transposed onto Tristan in the Tavola ritonda, and occurs transformed in Perlesvaus. It is very common in folktales (37). Scholars have discussed the passage in Chrétien/Wolfram and its symbolism, but without relating the significance of the episode to folk-tradition (37–8). A study of this kind—which can here only be undertaken in sketch-form—would be able to illuminate the episode in Chrétien's text and the tradition that arose from it. The Irish and Welsh texts that have been proposed as Chrétien's model can be no such thing, since Chrétien did not read these languages, and the Welsh text follows Chrétien rather than vice versa. Instead, it may be expected that he simply collected it from the folk-tradition in France. (One reason among several for supposing that Chrétien was not borrowing from the Welsh Peredur is that the motif occurs centrally in his text, not initially as it does in the folk-tales, and to deprive Chrétien of this deliberative authorial initiative is to make him a mere transmission node, while postulating an anonymous genius writing shortly before him, whom we then might as well call Chrétiende Troyes. [Clearly this argument is flawed!]) Some of the complications surrounding the absence of black are introduced, but the author states he does not have the time to discuss the matter in full, and moreover the black is not systematically central to the motif even in the other accounts; instead, blood on a white surface (usually snow) is the core of the motif (38).

In folktales, the motif always occurs in the beginning. In most cases, the protagonist is a young prince on the hunt who, following a kill, is prompted by the sight of blood on the snow to wish for a girl with skin like snow and cheeks (or lips) like blood, and sometimes hair black as the raven in the narrative). In half the cases, the motif is inverted—the subject is a girl, the object a young man (38–9). The sight in these cases serves to bring out a hidden lack through analogy, thus setting the stage for a quest or adventure. The object is always a "real" person who is eventually married, not an otherworldly creature. "Le sang rouge répandu sur la neige blanche implique sans ambiguïté ce monde-ci et exclut l'Autre Monde." The motif always announced motherhood, because the union always results in a child. Since the protagonist is nearly always a prince or princess, the motif thus concerns the begetting of an heir (39). "Il n'y a aucun doute que le symbolisme du spectacle lui-même soit d'ordre sexuel" (39–40, at 39). The contrast in colours, the number three, and the bleeding are all associated with sexual intercourse, and specifically with defloration. The image announces that the union to come cannot be left unconsummated (39–40). Too often, critics have read the episode as a deep spiritual experience, denying sexual implications. The fact that Chrétien displaces the traditional motif does not take away its original ramifications (40).

Consummation does not take place at Perceval and Blancheflor's first meeting, which is presented as too soon. This delay is due to the way Perceval's mother has raised him, blocking a natural development, and so the blood on the snow is not initially introduced since this is aimed at lifting such a blockage. Later, with Blancheflor and rule beckoning, there is no further need to censor the motif (40‐1). With its function shifted from presentiment to memory, the fulfilment to come is now consummation rather than finding the individual. The metaphor of the chase, in which the protagonist of the folk-motif is usually engaged when the blood-motif occurs, is here irrelevant: Perceval already has Blancheflor, so the chase is transferred to the raven. The action, to which Perceval is merely a spectator, is also represented differently: rather than a mere butchery, the kill is expressed in a vocabulary on the crossroads between warfare and sexuality.

All the transformations carried out on the traditional motif correspond to the Freudian dream (41). The Conte du graal cannot be dissected in rational terms only; it relies heavily on the subconscious. The passage should be read not as ecstasy, hallucination, or contemplation, but as a waking dream which makes the repressed and forgotten reappear in a different form. Chrétien has injected the workings of his own dreams into the text. It would be interesting to explore more of his writings from this perspective, in which he has adapted folk-material with the transformative powers of the dreamer (42).

The article's first footnote has a wealth of references to scholarship on the blood-on-snow motif (37).

author: Ehlert, Trude, and Gerhard Meissburger
title: Perceval et Parzival: Valeur et fonction de l'episode dit 'des trois gouttes de sang sur la neige'
publication: Cahiers de civilisation médiévale Xe–XIIe siècles
abstract: A structural-comparative study between the blood-on-snow episodes in the two texts, emphasising that the two texts stand on different footings and the motif must therefore be judged separately in each case. In Chrétien, the drops of blood free Perceval from his love-connection and enable him to pursue his other goal, the grail. In Wolfram, by contrast, courtly love does not hinder other knightly pursuits; indeed, it favours them. Footnote 3 gives a lengthy list of discussions of the blood-on-snow motif in Chrétien and Wolfram (197).

author: Schmid-Cadalbert, Christian
title: Der wilde Wald: Zur Darstellung und Funktion eines Raumes in der mittelhochdeutschen Literatur
publication: Gotes und der werlde hulde: Literatur in Mittelalter und Neuzeit, Festschrift für Heinz Rupp zum 70. Geburtstag
abstract:
While scholars have traditionally emphasised the symbolic connotations of the wild, the forest also had a real-life economic and geographical presence in the Middle Ages. This article seeks to demonstrate that this dual nature is visible in the literature (24–5).

Wilt and wald are thought to be cognates; wilt has no precise counterpart in Latin or the romance languages (25). In OHG and early MHG, the noun wilt is not used to refer to a landscape category but rather to individual wild animals (25–6); in this, it seems the Latin example is followed (26).
