Hartmann and Gottfried first use wilde as a landscape category contrasting with the court, and carrying its opposite (and therefore negative) values. About 1200, the forest became a central motif in MHG literature. The roman d’Antiquité and the epic had focussed on urban life, the social space, the centre; hence everything outside that central space has negative connotations (27). About 1200, the wild forest is drawn into the centre of the romance world, and wilde becomes the opposite of werlt (28).

As Le Goff has pointed out, the medieval West long remained a juxtaposition of inhabited and wild domains, the European forest playing the role elsewhere fulfilled by the desert. The forests of central and eastern Europe had much more forest than Flanders, Tuscany, and the Paris basin, however (29). Especially the edge of the forest was an economic area: cattle and swine could forage there, it supplied wood for construction and fuel, as well as berries, honey, mushrooms, resin, foliage, and the like (28–9). Forest management and taxation are attested as early as the eighth century (29).

Narrative literature does not mention the forest as an economic space for farmers. It does mention the hunt. By the tenth century, the spatial dominance of civilisation stopped north of the Alps, where topographical names in -wald demonstrate the duality of landscape. By the twelfth century, however, the forests have shrunk considerably due to appropriation of land and the growth of agriculture (29). Wood-rights become more strictly regulated in the twelfth to fourteenth centuries; by 1200, the wild forest in its sense of large continous tracts of unsettled forest is no longer a reality for most. Rather than threaten, the wild forest now beckons (30). Around 1200, many cities were founded with Wild- in their names (30–1). It is interesting that in this time the wild forest gets to be referred to as wild on a regular basis in the narrative literature. This concept is filled with subjective associations such as exile and madness; the wild becomes thoroughly subjectified. Parallel to the individualisation of narrative spaces, this is also the time of the privatisation of space (31).

In the narrative literature, the wild is only described in relation to man, be it as a threat or as a safe haven (32). It should be noted that the wild does not always mean a complete absence of human characters other than the protagonist; sometimes it just refers to travel-space other than the high road. The wild is a place not routinely inhabited, but it can nevertheless harbour a locus amoenus or hortus conclusus (33). Wild animals are a common motif of wild spaces; people inhabiting them are outlaws (33–5).

"Die wichtigste Funktion, die der wilde Wald in der mittelhochdeutschen Literatur hat, ist die einer Raumschwelle zwischen diesseitiger Welt ind jenseitigem Ort" (35). Examples of this threshold function are quoted and discussed (35–40). In Gottfried's Tristan, the wild trades places with the inhabited world because the latter has become a hostile place by virtue of disapproving of the romance (39).

Further motifs discussed are losing one's way in the wilderness (40–3) and becoming wild oneself (43–4). In conclusion, the one-sided view that the forest was a threatening other is found wanting, as are the notions that the forest functions as a locus of exile and a place for the knight errant to be tested: these are instead otherworldly places, and the forest serves instead as a threshold between the social and the supernatural world (45–6).

author: Power, Rosemary
title: Journeys to the Otherworld in the Icelandic fornaldarsögur
abstract: Compares five Old Norse legendary expeditions to the otherworld (Þorsteins þáttr, Helga þáttr, Eiríks saga víðförla, Yngvar saga víðförla, and Vilhjálms saga sjóðs) and argues they represent a single strand of oral tradition (156–63). They are then compared to Þórsdrápa and Snorri's account of the Útgarðaloki episode (163–4); of the latter it is said that it was likely influenced by the tradition found in the legendary sagas rather than vice versa (164). One of Saxo's two versions of the Útgarðaloki-narrative (164–6) is closer to the Þorsteins þáttr-account (165). A series of Irish and Welsh analogues are then studied (167–9). The English The Turke and Gowin is then brought in and said to be far closer to Þorsteins saga than to Þórsdrápa, and it is concluded that the English work must derive from the adventure found in the Norse text, though the beheading game was added later among some other motifs (169–71). Jóns saga Ásmundssonar is an Icelandic folktale with some analogues to the legendary material (171–2).

author: Lid, Nils
title: The Mythical Realm of the Far North: As It Appears in the National Finnish Epic Kalevala and the Scandinavian fornaldar-saga Tradition
abstract:
Points out analogies between the stealing of the Sampo in Finnish tradition and the stealing of Iðunn's apples, Ægir's kettle, and Grotti's handmill in Eddic tradition, but observes that these shared motifs need not suggest a historical connection (58–9). Posits the hypothesis that if the Sampo-legend has any historical basis to it, it must first have existed in "prose legends" later versified (59). "The Norwegian troll-ballads" seem to go back on cycles believed to predate the settlement of Iceland; "[t]hey are later codi[fi]ed there at the time when the ballads were being composed in Norway (59–60, at 60). This codification survives in the legendary sagas, in which a "very old tradition is, however, maintained to a certain degree only." The common feature between Norwegian ballads and Icelandic legendary sagas consists in journeys to a northern otherworld populated by supernatural creatures, usually to free a captive girl and sometimes to obtain a precious object. The countries in question are often geographically defined, but nevertheless at a remove from the actual countries of that name, as in Saxo's Biarmia ulterior. If I understand Lid correctly in the oddly-formulated next paragraph, the Norwegian ballads are subject to fairytale influence, but the legendary sagas are not, as these contain legends, frequently realistic in form (60). Examples are Bósa saga (60–1) and Egils saga ok Ásmundar, both of which contain strong similarities to the Sampo tradition; it seems Kaarle Krohn may have been right to suggest the Kalevala material was composed in southwestern Finland during the Viking Age. Moreover, a Sami tradition knows a witch controlling two birds that sink ships, reminiscent of both the Kalevala and legendary sagas; the birds are called vuogo, from Proto-Norse hugi, also the name of one of Óðinn's ravens, and moreover a word used in Norwegian (as hugr) to refer to a disguise made by sorcery (61).

Pohjola derives from pohja, meaning "bottom" in the same way in which Scandinavian tradition speaks of the northern land as trollebotn or sinus septentrionalis (61–2). Thule seems to have been used with very similar connotations. However, pohja and pohjola also simply mean "north", in opposition with etelä which derives from etu- "front" because houses and tents faced this way; thus pohja refers to the "bottom" (botn) of a house (62). In Sami, the posjo side of the tent has ritual significance. Northern traditions thus associate this direction with the otherworld, and some Native American tribes tell of an access-point to a world of birds and dwarfs, or giants (62–3). More bird-and-dwarf-beliefs among the Inuit and Sami are mentioned (63–4). If the Sampo is interpreted as the world-pillar, as its etymology suggests, Finnish tradition may derive from an older belief in this northern otherworld; such a world-pillar exists also in Scandinavian tradition (no reference) (64). In all these traditions there is also a large female guarding the northern realm, with no male counterpart (63‐4). All these legendary journeys may be imagined to have their basis in actual expeditions to the north (64–5).

author: Power, Rosemary
title: Le lai de Lanval and Helga þáttr Þórissonar
abstract: Referring to some other secondary literature on European romance influences on Old Norse legendary sagas, proposes that Helga þáttr was inspired by the beginning of Lanval.

author: Le Goff, Jacques
title: La vie matérielle
abstract:
If the western world was a world of limited progress in the Middle Ages, there was nevertheless progress, if mostly of a quantitative nature (249). The two greatest technological developments, the watermill and the plough, had long existed but underwent much of their spread and some development in the Middle Ages (249–50). Several inventions, including the windmill, may have been borrowed from the East (250). A variety of reasons explains why innovation was hindered in the West (250–2). The Church culture did stimulate metalworking, computistics, architecture and related crafts and artwork (252–4). Novelty was abhorred as sinful, a position that severely held back progress (254).

Mechanics saw little development in the Middle Ages, not in the last place because the leading philosophy of the time favoured the static virtue of impetus over the vanity of motion (254–6).

Wood was the universal construction-material (258). High-quality wood in large pieces for construction was hard to obtain, even if as a substance wood was plentiful; it was even exported to the Muslim world (258–9). So was iron (259). It too was valuable, as the Benedictine Rule demonstrates by its elaborate instructions on how to care for iron tools (259–60). The value of iron tools and ploughs is demonstrated in narrative sources (260–2). But stone, not iron, was the other central raw material in the Middle Ages. Architecturally, stone was higher-status than wood (262–3).

Agriculture was the sector most affected by the technological underdevelopment of the Middle Ages. It was the economy on which life, riches, and power depended, but the land was infertile inasmuch as it was primitively tilled, in terms of poor tools, poor methods, and the use of swingploughs intended for shallow Mediterranean soils which merely scratched the northern clay soils. The wheeled plough was a great improvement to this, although intensifying labour by ploughing three to four times and breaking the clods by hand in between ploughings had a greater effect (263–4). Fertilisation was an area even more lacking, on account of the relatively small number of animals kept (264–5). The chief consequence of these shortcomings was that farming was largely extensive rather than intensive. Many lots were recent forest clearance, with the consequence that the land was poorly worked as well as poorly fertilised, making fallow widely necessary (265). The tendency to self-sufficiency, considered a matter of honour and prescribed in the Benedictine Rule, further limited output (265–6). St Bernard condemned the Cistercians' initiative to build mills, as these formed social hubs which might endanger their souls. But the consequence of manorial autarky was that each farm grew many different crops, disregarding strengths and weaknesses of geography and local soil. The consequence was low production: one northern French estate yielded between 2 and 2.7 times as much as had been sown; English grain harvests were 3.8 for wheat and barley, 2.4 for oats (266). Some regions yielded much more on account of fertile soils (266–7).

Mills improved the energy supply, but there was no straightforward increase in their use (267). Most energy was still from human and animal power. An improved harness brought improved horse-performance about the year 1000 (267–8). However, the strongest horses were used in war, not for economic purposes (268). Oxen were not universally replaced by horses: although it has been calculated that the ox was less cost-effective, and medieval accounts state the value of a horse at two oxen, many seem to have been discouraged by the high initial cost of a horse, its dependence on oats, and, sometimes, the fact that it could not be eaten (268–9). Where oats were difficult to grow, i.e. in southern Europe, the ox remained the draught animal of choice. In industry, transportation over water, and in the country-side, human power was primary (269). Here too, productivity was limited, as the working-class was precisely that segment of the population that was malnourished (269–70). As human power was valuable, the Church shifted from an emphasis on virginity to one on procreation: its slogan "croissez et multipliez" was primarily a response to limits on medieval technology. This problem was seen also in a decrease in portage services, which seem to have disappeared after the twelfth century; but human portage did remain primary for transportation, along with pack animals (270–1).

Sea transport profited insufficiently from the considerable technological developments. Among other explanations for this is the fact that law required vessels to be below a certain size, so that they could be converted for war purposes when required. The stern-post rudder was not as important an invention as has sometimes been thought, and the compass was not introduced until after 1280; the quadrant and astrolabe were instruments of the Renaissance (271–2).

Le Goff has a fairly lengthy exposition on limits to mining (272–7).

"L'économie de l'Occident médiéval a pour but la subsistance des hommes. Elle ne va pas au-delà." Where the economy appears to have served purposes beyond subsistence, this is because subsistence is a socioeconomic concept, not just a material one. Subsistence only means material subsistence (food, clothes, and shelter) for the lowest classes. Based on this strict reading of subsistence, the medieval economy was based around the land, to such a degree that land was initially measured by units that would support a peasant family, each of which was given a uniform tract of land (mansus or terra unius familiae). To the higher classes, subsistence included whatever it took to maintain rank, including imports (contrast Dyer’s understanding of the concept of subsistence). Economic growth was not the aim of labour; instead, labour was meant for moral purposes such as avoiding idleness and sloth, or subjugating the body. The economic aims of toil consisted in subsistence of self and the poor. Thomas Aquinas wrote that labour has four ends: subsistence, warding off idleness, mortifying the body against carnal desire, and procuring a source for almsgiving (278). Necessity was so central to livelihood that authors deemed it an excuse for theft or breach of the Sunday rest; but wanting more for oneself than dictated by necessity was an economic form of pride and thus a major sin (278–9). This led to a stern condemnation of economic planning beyond subsistence, but landlords and monastic administrators especially did professionalise management practices in the face of some continued distrust; this professionalisation was a result of food crisis rather than an interest in profits (279–84). When economic growth occurred (as in the eleventh and twelfth centuries) this resulted exclusively from population growth; increasing yields was a secondary aim (284). Loans existed almost exclusively for consumption not production; Christians could not exact interest among themselves (284–5). With all forms of credit condemned as usury, economic growth was effectively precluded; the scholastics, including Thomas Aquinas, distinguished between (praiseworthy) subsistence wealth and (condemnable) monetary wealth (285). All classes were structurally hindered from accumulating capital and thus from enjoying economic growth: peasants paid rents, tithes, and alms; the Church divided its money among its higher employees, construction of churches, and the poor. The lay aristocracy was encouraged, though not obliged, to spend its profits on Christian charity and in chivalric generosity; the honour code of lords had it that they should spend without calculating their losses. Thus largesse and poverty together paralysed the economy (285–6). What accumulation existed did so in the form of hoarding precious objects and coins, which could be melted down in case of emergency (286).

The feudal system was itself an obstruction to economic growth, and it furthermore caused the low level of technology. Essentially, feudalism consisted in the appropriation of all profits by the land-owning class (286). Everywhere at least into the fourteenth century, lords spent their revenues on unproductive expenditures (287). Late medieval English lords were able to invest only three to six percent of their revenues (287–8). This was all from feudal sources; a crisis in feudal income occurred from the late thirteenth century, which first prompted lords to seek external income in cash fiefs or in warfare or sometimes sale of agricultural yields or the buying of rents. Thus when economic progress began to be practised, it was viewed as procuring a feudal right, not a path to economic growth; mills and roads were built in order to raise a tax on their use (288). When peasants increased their holdings it was to alleviate the burden of dues under which they were placed. Some allod-holders farmed land independently of the feudal system, but they still depended on the lord governing the region, who still exacted taxes and also monopolised the markets (289–90).

The subsistence of the medieval West was perpetually under threat of falling short. Hunger was much feared, as is suggested from the interest in food and food-miracles in narrative literature (290–3). A common downward spiral was bad weather > bad harvest > shortage > rise in prices > morbidity/mortality (293). Climate changes could have profound effects owing to technological limitations (293–4). Knowledge of food-preservation was very poor (295–6). The worst danger was repeated crop failure, but the main victims were the poor (296–7). The Elucidarium states that hunger is one of the punishments for original sin; but both hunger and servitude were in practice limited to the poor. It was thought remarkable that the plague struck the rich as well as the poor; famines seldom did. On some occasions, the poor were shipped off to more fertile regions in order to alleviate an urban famine (297–300).

Livestock were slaughtered in times of famine because both they and their fodder (if oats) could be eaten by men; the Church occasionally gave dispensation to eat meat during Lent. Famine was often followed by ergotism from eating food unsuitable for consumption (300–1). Owing to malnutrition and poor medical knowledge, life expectancy was low even if infant mortility is accounted for. Even upper-class skeletons display serious caries from malnutrition (301–2). The most prolific diseases are listed (302–3).

The precarious nature of this style of subsistence is once again emphasised. The modest technological developments did not stop agriculture from being extensive in nature, and extensive agriculture destroyed wealth inasmuch as slash-and-burn both wasted timber and put a heavy strain on the soil. At times, technology made matters worse by exterminating woodland. South of the Alps, forest-protection (against felling and foraging) began about 1300 (304–5). Soil exhaustion endangered the largely agricultural economy; but when the monetary economy expanded, mines were soon exhausted (305–6). A third limitation was manpower. Initially, there was plenty of it; beggars were a supported and relatively respected class, so unemployment was socially accepted. However, as the population stopped growing manpower became more valuable, and able-bodied beggars were denounced; labour had become expensive. The plague escalated this situation in 1348 (306–7).

On the whole, however, the Middle Ages were a period of gradual economic expansion largely corresponding to a rise in quality of life. This growth began with the population, which doubled between the late tenth century and the mid-fourteenth (the arrival of the Black Death) in Western Europe. 1200 was a time of particularly large growth. Before this, the population of Europe had fallen by more than half between AD 200 and 700; in the fourteenth century it fell by a third. The population about 1300 was just a little larger than that of Rome at its peak. The same developments may be seen in agricultural production, prices, and wages, although wages were only earned by a small proportion of the population (307–9).

It is asked whether the medieval economy was natural or monetary. A natural economy is mostly closed, as all exchanges are kept to a minimum: one fulfils most of one's needs within the manor. After careful consideration, it is pointed out that money was never absent from the medieval economy, and that the use of barter was limited, but that coin remained in archaic use through its material and representative rather than nominal value (309–13).

The final section of the chapter describes class differentiation and development (314–18).

author: Le Goff, Jacques
title: Material Culture (Tenth to Thirteenth Centuries)
abstract: A translation of this item.

author: Eadie, J.
title: Sir Gawain's Travels in North Wales
abstract: Discusses Gawain's route on his way to find the Green Knight. Comes to the conclusion that þe holy hede of the text is Holyhead, though most scholars have found this unlikely. Gawain travels in three stages: [the mythical] Logres, North Wales, and the Wirral. That Anglesey is on his left means he must be coming from the south, but it may also function metaphorically inasmuch as Gawain is looking for a person he associates with evil.

author: Heyworth, P.L.
title: Sir Gawain's Crossing of the Dee
abstract: Points out that the sands in the river Dee, to the southwest of the Wirral peninsula, have been known to shift considerably between tides, which might explain why SGGK speaks of fordez in the plural even though Gawain has only one river to cross (124–5). To account for the forlondez ("headlands"), however, Gawain would have had to cross the Dee somewhere between Flint and Hawarden, where the northern shore has promontories in early maps (125–6).

author: Dodgson, John McNeal
title: Sir Gawain's Arrival in Wirral
publication: Early English and Norse Studies Presented to Hugh Smith in Honour of his Sixtieth Birthday
abstract: Proposes a two-stage fording of the river Dee, in accordance with the plural fordez, from Point of Air to West Kirby via Hilbre Island (19–20). If part of this crossing seems improbable, at least it has a history in legend (20–3). Þe Holy Hede might refer to West Kirby. It is significant that Holyhead in Anglesey has also been referred to as Kirkby: the reference to þe Holy Hede might be a periphrasis or analogical reference to Kirby (23–4). To a local audience, it would be fitting to send Gawain across the Dee by a legendary rather than a more feasible passage (24–5). This reading suggests some familiarity with the district on the part of the poet (25).

author: Niles, John D.
title: The Economics of Beowulf
abstract: Points out the importance of understanding the economic system portrayed in Bwf for understanding the poem as a whole. The central idea is that all honour is bankable, as made clear by the institution of the wergild but also by the poem's references to treasure.

author: Cady, Diane
title: Symbolic Economies
series: Oxford Twenty-First Centiry Approaches to Literature
abstract: A theoretical discussion whose main thrust is that language and money, among other fields, are "isomorphic. That is, that they are not identical but, as Howard Horwitz suggests, 'have related morphologies and arise out of kindred networks' " (126). A number of medieval Latin instances are cited where authors use metaphors from one of these fields to refer to the other. Gender is then brought into the discussion, primarily with reference to Piers Plowman.

author: Murfin, Ross C., Peter G. Beidler, and Laurie Finke
title: Marxist Criticism and the Wife of Bath
abstract: This chapter really consists of three items, which are best independently cited: Murfin has written the indispensable historical introduction "What is Marxist Criticism?" (155–66), Beidler has provided "Marxist Criticism: A Selected Bibliography" (166–9) as well as the brief "A Marxist Perspective" (169–70), while Finke has contributed the excellent essay "All is for to selle: Breeding Capital in the Wife of Bath's Prologue and Tale" (171–88). The first item does a good job of distinguishing yet relating the history of Marxist literary criticism and that of Marxist political thought, while also relating the former to structuralist criticism and other fashions of the time. Finke draws attention to the Wife's use of marriage as a monetary investment which breeds capital, not children, while also pointing out the role of marriage and sexuality in the switch from feudalism to capitalism.

author: Watts, Michael
title: The Inevitable but Uneasy Relationship between Economics and Literature and Drama
abstract: This introduction to a reader of literary passages dealing with economic subjects explains that while the work of authors of narrative literature differs greatly from that of empirical economists, it has considerable overlaps with the work of economic theorists, as both these groups start with the individual, trying to understand his or her behaviour through motivations, and then coming up with new inputs to see how the subject will respond (xviii). Authors of literature, meanwhile, are bound by many of the laws of economics in their depictions, for the simple reason that a more economically realistic narrative is more credible (xix). Because writers' economic insight differs from that of economists either in quality or otherwise, there is often great distrust between the two groups (xix–xx). Because popular authors reach larger audiences than economists, the consequence may be that the general public take novelists at their word in economic matters while ignoring the expert opinions of economists (xx). The remainder of the introduction considers what economists and literary critics respectively have to gain from the cross-pollination of their fields (xxi–xxiii).

author: Mann, Jill
title: Price and Value in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
abstract: Studies the dynamics between market value and knightly honour in SGGK's understanding of pris.

author: Delany, Sheila
title: Sexual Economics, Chaucer's Wife of Bath and The Book of Margery Kempe
publication: Feminist Readings in Middle English Literature: The Wife of Bath and All Her Sect
abstract: Discusses the economic positions, powers, and strategies of Alice of Bath and Margery Kempe.

author: Müller-Boysen, Carsten
title: Die Rolle der Wikinger im Wirtschaftsleben des mittelalterlichen Europa
abstract:
This excellent article challenges the twin notions that Viking raiding appeared suddenly and that Scandinavian raiders and traders should be regarded as distinct groups. The doctrine of sudden appearance was fuelled by Alcuin's letter concerning the Lindisfarne raid, as well as other Frankish and Anglo-Saxon sources that take hostile views and often the role of victim. Moreover, Alcuin wrote as a clergyman, seeing history as divine punishment. It is not to be expected that Alcuin placed his observations in a historical context (249–50). Francia was attacked by Germanic raiders up until the sixth century, and the creation and inspection of defence works along the Frankish and Kentish coasts about 800 suggest that attacks were already taking place here, although they have not been recorded [PS: or attacks on Lindisfarne and more immediately neighbouring communities led them to take advance measures!] (250–1). The Saxons in particular engaged in a good deal of raiding between the fourth and sixth centuries, from Orkney to the Bay of Biscay, including Normandy and the Loire estuary, leading to defence works on either side of the Channel. The Saxon boats, like those of the Vikings, could easily be portaged. It may thus be assumed that the times for which report is extant represent quantitive, not qualitative, anomalies (251). The time that went before cannot have been one of universal peace, and it is questionable whether the Viking raids changed the history of Europe as much as has sometimes been suggested (251–2). Since trade relations with Scandinavia persisted even during the time of greatest raiding activity, trade was never rendered entirely impossible as a result of Viking activity (252).

The Vikings responded promptly to political turmoil, suggesting that they learned about current affairs, perhaps not just from Scandinavian traders but also from the bragging of foreign traders. Thus long-distance trade may have been a prerequisite for Viking raiding. Among other factors that have been proposed as causes of Viking raiding and expansion, the growth of long-distance trade has recently become more prominent. The Scandinavians' successful eastern and southern trade provided the capital that enabled their western raids (253). Lewis has proposed that the raids of the 840s–860s were a consequence of the shortage of Arabic coin with which the Scandinavians would have bought what they now decided to take by force (253–4).

It is important to note that raiders and traders were not two distinct groups. Raiders relied on trade, which allowed them to loot portable property and exchange it for more useful goods. Indeed, by spending their loot, raiders lessened their negative impact on European economies. Moreover, there is considerable evidence for truces and periods of trade in between raids (255). The sagas too, even in their more reliable passages, suggest that raiding was an occasional pursuit (256–7). Although hidden theft was frowned upon, open raids and warfare were not necessarily condemned in the same way.

author: Mantel, Kurt
title: Wald und Forst in der Geschichte: Ein Lehr- und Handbuch
abstract:
A very thorough account of woodlands in central Europe. Opening with an account of the etymology of Wald in conjunction with Wild, and of Forst, the author then compares and contrasts the two terms in historical and current usage, where Forst has more commonly been used for legal and economic purposes, although the term Wald has been more persistent in southern Germany. Today, Wald refers to two concepts: the wide, general landscape and the economic landscape (36–9). Following a disucssion of early postglacial forest and pollen analysis, the author turns to human influences on the forest landscape. Forest is identified as a highly resilient landscape, rapidly rebounding from fire and storm; accordingly, Heinrich Cotta wrote in 1817 that if man left Germany, it would be entirely covered in woodland after a hundred years (52). Considerable attention is given to the question of woodland cover at the time of settlement. It is argued that the nineteenth-century reliance on classical Latin authors, who claimed all of Germany was covered in forest, does not stand up to scrutiny, among other things because those same authors are referring to specific wooded areas, suggesting that the in-betweens they are silent about were not wooded. All the same, it seems 75% of central Europe was covered with woodlands when it began to be settled (52–5). The common opinion that the forest was man's first enemy in these parts is false: early cultures were small and relied on the forest, living near its edge and only clearing the light desiduous forest, leaving the ancient forests alone. It was only in the Middle Ages, when mountainous forested areas were settled, that forest clearance may be called a "Kulturtat" (55–6).

Small or monadic cultures did not affect the degree of forestation, and they avoided the ancient forests. Only in the late Stone Age (3000–1800 BCE) did clearance become a phenomenon, when agricultural peoples migrated into the area from the east. Clearance was thereafter not a consistent tendency, but after numerous periods of clearance and recovery the tendency towards clearance continued in the Bronze and Iron Ages (56). Sedentary society led to forest clearance for the purpose of settlement. Considerable deforestation may be assumed to have taken place in the prehistoric period, but in a more decentralised way. Also unlike medieval clearance, it took place not in ancient forest, but in less dense oak-, hazel-, and birch-areas. It may be assumed that the cool, moist Iron Age saw some reforestation (57).

In early historic times, growing Germanic populations could not move beyond the Roman limes and were thus forced to engage in increased clearance in their own territories (57–8).

The first period of medieval clearance took place in the sixth and seventh centuries. Beginning with land expansion of existing settlements, these clearances followed the rivers upstream and led to new settlements nearer the denser forests. The advance of the Franks forced their opponents into elevated areas and deeper forests, where they cleared forest to make way for their new settlements. The great period of medieval clearance took place in two acts: the eighth and ninth centuries proceeded in all places but the large, continuous forests, but the peak of deforestation took place in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, the time of the high medieval empire. In this period, it was the higher levels of mid-elevation mountainous areas that were cleared. Population growth caused this wave of deforestation: the population of western Germany is thought to have doubled in the period 900–1100, then quadrupled [NB ambiguity] in the twelfth century (58). Place-name evidence is briefly discussed (59), as is the development from communal clearance to feudal clearance (59–61). It is pointed out that the enmity that has often been assumed between society and forest cover implies that anyone is free to engage in clearance, but regulations were soon put into place that limited clearance [and thus treat forest as a scarce resource] (61). The first prohibition is ninth-century (61–2). The number of prohibitions then rises steadily in the high and later Middle Ages (62–3). Motives varied from securing hunting-grounds to economic interests such as swine-pasturing and woodstocks, although the latter did not provide immediate monetary benefit (63).

In the high Middle Ages, and especially in the fourteenth century, forests stopped shrinking and then regained some lost ground where settlements were abandoned. Typhoid (1309–17) and the Black Death (1348ff.) were responsible for this. Another consequence of these events was a greater urbanisation and thus greater spatial concentration of the population (63). Most of the land that was returned to forest was that of the most recent period of settlement (1100–1300), namely on strict forest soil and in the mountains. Accordingly, reforestation was rare in northwestern Germany (64).

The fourteenth century represented the completion of German settlement and therefore the end of large-scale clearance. The western German landscape, especially in its division between field and forest, is shaped by initial centuries of clearance and fourteenth-century reforestation; today's level of forestation is thus much like that of 1400 (64). The remainder of this section discusses postmedieval developments (64–76). Friedrich List's nineteenth-century model of economic stages is then brought in to shed light on society's interaction with woodlands. List distinguished five groups engaging with forest in different ways, in order of their prevalence in the various stages of macroeconomics: (1) hunters and gatherers, who practise their trade in the forest; (2) shepherds, nomads of the forest; (3) farmers, who pasture their livestock in the forest but also use the forest as a source of wood for construction and consumption; (4) large manufacturing operations, which a lot of wood for fuel and heat; (5) industry and trade, using a great deal of wood for construction. List differs from other economic stages-theorists in focusing on resource use rather than products or economic politics (77). The first stage is strongly nomadic (hunters, gatherers, shepherds) and does not affect the extent of forest cover, since these societies are small by nature. This changes when these groups stop being nomadic. At this point, the same forest is used for pastureland, agricultural land, and hunting, in which the first two affect the forest through immediate effects, whereas the hunt is more prominent in its secondary effects (78). Use of wood has its own stages, beginning with local consumption in the Middle Ages, followed by industrial exploitation of the sixteenth through eighteenth centuries and modern forestry (plantation etc.) since the nineteenth (79–80). The forest has been a source of human nutrition (Nährwald) from the very beginning (Genesis 1 is mentioned). Since the beginning of sedentary societies, indirect nutritional uses such as swine pasturage have been added. From the Middle Ages to the eighteenth century, the forest also delivered wood for domestic and industrial uses (Plünderwald); this usage eventually exhausts the forest. After the eighteenth century, a more sustainable forestry was undertaken (Kulturwald). Since the nineteenth century, forest began to serve environmental protection (Schutzwald. The recreational forest (Erholungswald) came about in the twentieth century [!] as a restorative environment to offset the industrial damage to human health and quality of life (80). The main categories here are Nutzwald, Schutzwald, and Erholungswald (81). Hunt, apiculture (beekeeping) and fishery are the oldest human uses of the forest, and all these survived into sedentary societies, if in different forms. The hunt was aimed in the first place at nutrition and obtaining materials for clothes and tools, with self-protection as an additional aim of the hunt for predators. Beekeeping and fishery had no real effect on the forest itself (81). In the prehistoric period, the same was true for the hunt, except on occasion when burning resulted in forest fires. Even up to the sixteenth century, hunting had no immediate effect on the forest. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the sport evolved into the massacring of game and altered the forests around residences of nobles. After that, the hunt became regulated (81–2). Into the Middle Ages, a large proportion of predators kept the forest populations in check. Intensified hunting led to a reduction in predators and many extinctions (aurochs, bison, elk, bear, wolf, lynx). As a consequence, deer and boar populations grew (82–4). The development and effects of hunting regulations are summarily traced (84–5). Honey was the only sweetener in Europe prior to the discovery of America; its exploitation is discussed (85–9). Fishery is very briefly discussed (89).

The discussion then turns to the forest as a subservient to agriculture, a very close connection up to the end of the eighteenth century (89–90). This connection lost significance in the nineteenth century as a consequence of agricultural reforms (90–1). The forest pasture (Waldweide) is discussed (92–7), and the practice and regulation of swine pasture (97–101), and the procurement of fodder and animal litter (102–7), as well as burning and cultivation of forest fields (107–11).

A substantial section (113–35) discusses the role of tree and forest in mythology and folk-tradition. It is a little too uncritical of early sources. It discusses the world tree, as well as holy groves and forests, and suggests (following Grimm) a connection between pagan holy forests and later royal forests, in which the king's sole right to the forest has taken the place of the religious cult (116–17). The tree is a symbol of life and fertility, and the pine's function at Christmas serves this purpose; pine branches were collected on Christmas Eve by the early sixteenth century, and the development of the Christmas tree is discussed (117–24). The author then turns to the effects of tree cults on forest conservation (124–6), popular religion (including ideas concerning spirits inhabiting trees and the relationship between Christianity, paganism, and trees, 126–9), and trees in folk-narrative, where no narratives are recounted but lists of folktales are provided, as well as a discussion of proverbs and anthems (129–35). The remainder of the chapter deals with art (135–9), the aesthetic role of the forest in history (139–44), and conservation (144–7).

The remaining three chapters of the book deal with the forest as a judicial zone (149–89), wood as an economic resource (191–319), and the development of modern forestry (321–476).

author: Hieatt, Constance B.
title: The Realism of Dream Visions: The Poetic Exploitation of the Dream-Experience in Chaucer and His Contemporaries
abstract:
Rather a bland work, but worth consulting before publishing on this topic.

[Introduction and ch. 1] Repeatedly claims that when modern critics hear of dream-visions, they tend to think of fourteenth-century love-visions. Very odd! Remarks on the pleasant landscapes characteristic of dream-visions (21).

[Ch. 2] Divine origins of dreams and the association between dreamlore and damnable astrology made both spiritual and physiological origins to some degree mandatory (25). Various classical and medieval categorisations are listed (24–9). Then the Roman de la rose's attitude towards dreams is discussed with reference to Macrobius (30–1). Vincent of Beauvais asked whether the referent of a prophetic dream was set in stone (32).

[Ch. 3] Discusses authorial comments on the value of dreams: Chaucer gives various readings, suggesting some degree of scepticism and the opinion that this field was yet unresolved (34–44). Other fourteenth-century references to dreams are discussed very briefly (44–5), leading to the conclusion that virtually all poets were aware of the multiple potential causes of dreams (49).

[Ch. 3] Compares medieval discussions on dreams with those by Freud and Jung (50–60).

[Ch. 4] Discusses Pearl and The Book of the Duchess with primary interest in the psychological basis of the dreams in these works (61–73).

[Ch. 6] Discusses The House of Fame, The Parliament of Fowles, and The Legend of Good Women individually (74–88).

[Ch. 7] Piers Plowman (89–97).

[Ch. 8] The Parliament of the Three Ages and Winnere and Wastoure (98–102).

[Ch. 9] Allegory (103–11).

author: Spearing, A.C.
title: Medieval Dream-Poetry

author: Roll, Susan K.
title: Toward the Origins of Christmas
abstract:
The best work on the late Roman origins of Christmas I have yet found. It opens with an anthropological understanding of the experience of time as the convergence of indigenous and exogenous rhythms (indigenous and exogenous from the perspective of the individual) (15–17). It then discusses Eliade's view of festal time as a cyclical time rising above the level of normal, linear time by virtue of its recurrent ritual (17–20). A lengthy section is devoted to considerations of this nature, discussing the perception of religious and festal time (1–41). The remainder of the chapter discusses Christian liturgical time, also including climatological and political considerations (41–56).

The next two chapters (57–106 and 107–64) investigate the origins of the date of Christmas, first according to patristic calculations and then according to the syncretist hypothesis which brought Christian tradition in line with the feast of the Invincible Sun. The investigation is conducted with great balance, pointing out that the connection between the two religious traditions is one of balance of evidence, not one of causal proof (107–8 and passim).

The book contains two further chapters dealing with the historical spread of Christmas (165–224) and temporal, liturgical, and cultural aspects of Christmas today (225–73).

author: Hooke, Della
title: Trees in Anglo-Saxon England: Literature, Lore and Landscape
abstract:
A thorough study of the role of trees in Anglo-Saxon literature, accompanied by a well-balanced account of historical forest extent and development and an account of specific tree species attested in Anglo-Saxon sources.

The historical section (part II: "The Nature and Distribution of Anglo-Saxon Woodland", pp. 113–64) contains a brief but much-needed overview of current thought on woodland through the centuries, pointing out that the post-Roman regeneration of English woodlands supposed by many earlier scholars is not borne out by the evidence. Indeed, Hooke claims with reference to her own earlier work that temperate climates do not support the regeneration of dense woodland unless herbivores are actively removed from the area (113–18), although she later cites evidence that a forest can exist for centuries without any regeneration, then to take advantage of any temporary reduction in grazing levels to regenerate (131). Human activity seems to have been decisive in the Bronze Age deforestation of Britain, and the extent of prehistoric deforestation may be recognised, among other things, from aerial-photographic evidence of early human activities not possible in woodland. Where woodland remained, its character often changed, as it was now preserved for economic reasons (114–15). "In Anglo-Saxon times, there was more woodland in Britain than there is now, but even then, less than in most European countries today" (116). The remainder of the chapter studies woodland distribution (118–30) and the character of Anglo-Saxon woodland (130–33).

I have not yet consulted parts I ("Tree Symbolism", 1–109) and III ("Individual Tree Species in Anglo-Saxon England", 189–282).

author: Putter, Ad
title: ‘Sir Gawain and the Green Knight’ and French Arthurian Romance
abstract:
[Ch. 1: The Landscape of Courtly Romance] Notes that the Gawain-poet alters the appearance of the narrative's landscape to match narrative circumstance: Gawain travels through a terrible winter, but the weather looks up as he arrives at Hautdesert, only to turn ugly again at his departure. This use of landscape derives not so much from rhetorical tradition as from Arthurian romance: a similar scene is found in the Old French Perlesvaus (10–14). The combination found in SGGK between geographical detail and symbolic landscape is found also in the French Yder; in these instances, the geographical detail serves the reader, but not the hero, who remains a knight errant (14–16). It is precisely when the European wild forests have largely disappeared that they begin to make their appearance in narrative literature (so also Schmid-Cadalbert, pp. 29–31). The twelfth century saw the most dramatic forest-clearing, just as Chrétien de Troyes was writing (16–17). In romance, forests are dreaded by their passers-through; in this respect, the SGGK-poet uses the adjective anious, also used of forests in Old French (17–18). The various causes for this anxiety are set out in the pages that follow, and include the landscape's density and extent, absence of humans, and presence of wild animals (18–22). The forest and its inhabitants are also associated with paganism and atheism, and wilderness has long been a symbol of spiritual error (22–3). The resulting sentiment felt by the knight errant is one of loneliness, which he does not hesitate to express in complaints (23–4); he also commonly meditates on his own follies (24).

The most typical forest-motif in courtly romance is its role as "the reprehensible counterpart of the court, and the joie which the courtly milieu demands.... [T]he knight errant is immersed in a savage environment that is indifferent, even antithetical, to the cultural refinement for which he stands" (24). Accordingly, the forest is often described in negatives (24–6). "As the space in between the centres of civilization where knights usually take their lodging, the representations of the forest in courtly romance succeed in providing the marked contrast needed to differentiate the structural unit of the quest from other units such as the feast or hospitality" (26). A good summary of the typical narrative function of the romance forest is found on pp. 26–7.

The remainder of the chapter describes in greater detail the transition from forest to court in both SGGK and French romances (27–41) and the socioeconomic implications of the court–forest dichotomy (41–50). Castle and forest are subtypes of the juxtaposition between city and countryside (so Le Goff). With the rise of the city as the cultural centre of society, the forest that lay in between such centres was stigmatised (41–2, again Le Goff is cited). Medieval authors refer to people living in or around forests, such as the Irish, as barbarous (42–3), and the word-field of the forest was used to express "ignorance or uncouthness" (43–4, at 43). In thought and writing, the notion of the perilous forest long outlived any real threat the landscape may once have represented (45–6); the figure of the Wild Man likewise prospered in this imaginary landscape (46–7). Although the forest as hunting-grounds receives a positive evaluation as a place of exhilaration and sport, this idea too depends on the contrast between court and forest (48). Moreover, the hunting-forest was typically an artificial construct and therefore less wild, and perceived as less perilous (48–9).

[Other chapters deal with hospitality, Gawain's temptation, courtly honour, and "The Social Function of Courtly Romance".]

author: Stanley, E.G.
title: Wolf, My Wolf!
publication: Old English and New: Studies in Language and Linguistics in Honor of Frederic G. Cassidy
eds: Joan H. Hall, Nick Doane, and Dick Ringler
abstract: Refutes the notion, stemming from Grimm, that wolves were associated with outlaws across Germanic tradition, and that for the common Germanic term warg there is a corresponding common Germanic sense "wolf". In fact, the only evidence of an extension of the term to animals (and apparently not just to wolves) is found in Icelandic; OE wearh means simply "felon, criminal". The term wulfheafedtreo, thought to point to an Anglo-Saxon connection between criminals and wolves, is obscure. The term "wulf" is nowhere associated with criminals, and thus the character by that name in Wulf and Eadwacer should not be understood to be an outlaw.

author: Hiatt, Alfred
title: Beowulf off the Map
abstract: Questions the utility of depicting medieval literary geographies using modern maps, but also points out that Bwf specifically has not even a medieval sense of geography, relying instead on "a shifting sense of regional space" which cannot be studied with reference to geographical systems of any era (17–18, at 18). Suggests that the Ptolemaic term chorography should instead be used to reflect the more local use of cultural space found in the poem, with the understanding that the chorography of Bwf should be read in literary, not cartographical terms. Briefly discusses medieval mappae mundi before discussing in detail the various geographical and topographical references in Bwf. Finally, points out that Nicholas Howe's "migration myth" is problematic in its supposition that Bwf bears a northern emphasis (there is no south to contrast with) or has a concept of a Germanic geographical unit, and proposes that reading Bwf without a map may help wean scholars off the sense that it is an epic centred on a homeland, where instead its fantastic use of geography has more in common with romance.

author: Dance, Richard
title: The Battle of Maldon Line 91 and the Origins of call: A Reconsideration
abstract: A very thorough investigation countering E.G. Stanley's contention that the verb ceallian as it occurs in Maldon is of indigenous derivation. Dance proposes instead to reinstitute the derivation from ON kalla while fully acknowledging that the hapax hildecalla (in Exodus) represents an indigenous weak noun deriving from the same Germanic root as kalla.

author: Liuzza, Roy Michael
title: Anglo-Saxon Prognostics in Context: A Survey and Handlist of Manuscripts
abstract: Bewails the lack of recent interest in prognostics, and the tendency in early (and current) scholarship to treat it as a different thing altogether from other genres which were however written in the same hands in the same manuscripts (181–3). The prognostics texts are then divided into categories (183–90). What unites them is an interest in astrology in its most concrete form, typically without interest in explanations (190). Their survival in monastic manuscripts suggests that they are a product of the monastic reform (195–6; they “appear to emanate from Winchester, one of the centres of the monastic reform,” 210). Even Ambrose, Bede, and Ælfric agree that there is some scientific truth to full moon auguries (200–1). In the context of the monastic interest in prognostics, Liuzza writes that “[h]ours were counted and seasons reckoned not by dawn and dusk, seedtime and harvest, but by liturgical observance; . . . As the farmer feels the alternation of summer and winter, so the monk feels the succession of Advent and Christmas, Lent and Easter, . . .” (207). It is the required knowledge of lunar and solar cycles in monastic settings that created a context in which prognostics could flourish (207–9). A manuscript list is given (212–30).

author: Nørlund, Poul
title: Kirkegaarden paa Herjolfsnæs: Et bidrag til diskussionen om klimateorien
abstract: A response to criticism's of his book Buried Norsemen at Herjolfsnes, this article discusses burial practices that may have been in use in Norse Greenland and connects this with climate change. Since the corpses in the deepest graves at Herjolfsnes (90cm measured from reconstructed medieval levels) were buried on top of plant remains, permafrost must have begun deeper down in the soil than in Nørlund's day. This suggests also that inhumation was practised at least in the warmer months of the year.

author: Nørlund, Poul
title: Buried Norsemen at Herjolfsnes: An Archaeological and Historical Study
abstract:
[ch. 4: Burials and Burial Customs (59-68)]: The Herjolfsnes dig of 1921 found 110-120 burials plus a considerable number of burials in very bad condition, adding up to a total of about 200 burials. These are all from the smaller half of the cemetery that has survived, the rest having washed into the fjord. The burials were closely packed, often three or four layers on top of each other (59).

"The dead were either buried in a wooden coffin or wrapped in their old clothes, only rarely in both. The shroud must be understood as a substitute for a coffin. Not a single coffin built of stone was found, which must be denoted as a highly peculiar circumstance since such stone-lined graves were very common in Europe and would have been much easier to procure than the wooden coffins, not least in a land where the lack of timber was balanced by an abundant supply of natural stones in all shapes and sizes. Not even the medieval custom, so common in Scandinavia, and perhaps also elsewhere in Europe, of placing a couple of stones on end at the head, was observed.

"If we are to take the shroud as a substitute for the coffin, we must conclude that coffin-burial was preferred by those who could afford it. That this was actually so is very clearly evidenced by the distribution of the coffins and shrouds (see map of the finds). For the most part the coffins are closely packed round the walls of the church where the most coveted burial-places were...." (60).

Burial in one's own clothes or in a shroud should not be understood as a sign of poverty; this was the common method in Europe for common people from Antiquity to the seventeenth century, but there remains often haven't survived (61). Lids seem to have been reused (61-2). The next few pages deal with specific graves and the custom of placing crosses in the graves. There is evidence of "a gradual discontinuance of the use of absolution crosses" (67). Practical and ritual functions of leaving charcoal in graves (67-8).

[Ch. 5: The Coffins (69-86)]: Deals with measurements, materials, etc.

[Ch. 6: The Costumes (87-192)]

[Ch. 7: Tombstones (193-6)]

[Ch. 8: The Wooden Crosses (197-219)]: Deals with crosses left on the chests of the dead.

[Ch. 9: Smaller Finds (220-7)]

[Ch. 10: Did a Deterioration of the Climate occur [sic] in Greenland in the Late Middle Ages? (228-44)]: The theory of climate deterioration, following an earlier one based on misconceptions, began about 1880 when G. Holm supposed a milder climate at the time of Greenlandic settlement on the grounds that

  • it would have been impossible to collect enough winter fodder under nineteenth-century conditions; in case of milder climate, the cattle could have been left out grazing for a larger part of the year
  • historical records indicate an increase in drift-ice, and must be assumed to accept the Norse could sail to and from Julianehaab (228-9).

A scientific approach was provided in 1913 by O. Petterson, who posited a shift in hydrographic conditions to explain a climate worsening in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries all the way from Greenland to central Asia; he then goes on to ascribe these hydrocirculatory changes to fluctuations in the pull-forces from sun and moon, one extreme of which was reached in 1433. Petterson's theories remain much disputed and should be regarded as a working theory (229-30).

Nørlund discusses various lines of evidence, beginning with the less authoritative written sources Konungs skuggsjá (description of Greenlandic farming) and Eiríks saga (confusion of name of mountain between Bláserk and Hvítserk) (230-1); the migration of Inuit, which tends to seek out conditions of transient ice (neither ice-free nor permanently-frozen conditions): in the fourteenth century, they migrate south aggressively (231); ice is never mentioned as a hindrance in the exploratory sagas (231-2); direct mention that the sailing-course had to be altered for the drift-ice (232-3); drift-ice descriptions in Konungs skuggsjá (235-6). The 1921 dig supports the theory of climate deterioration by the fact that wood and textiles are so well preserved. Preservation was better as the archaeologists dug deeper; and eventually coffins were found in the ground that was frozen in summer. In these, the shrouds were often well preserved but the bodies were not, often not even a bone. The presence of plant roots piercing the textiles and part of the coffins likewise suggests the soil had not always been frozen (237-9). The gradual rising of the earth, which causes coffins to end up deeper in relative terms, is slow in Greenland, and the difference can be calculated by the church foundations and other stone constructions, while the upper limit of grave finds provides an upper limit of medieval soil level (239). Two coffins are mentioned whose bottoms would have been at 35 and 60cm below the medieval surface; the lids would have been covered by only 20-25cm of soil. One coffin found must have had its bottom 120cm below the medieval surface (239-40). "From the table [on pp. 262-7.] it will appear that the finds that were in such a state that they could be exhumed lay at a depth below the old surface ranging from 30 to fully 130 cm. What lay above a depth of 55 cm. was as a rule not well preserved, a great part of the best things lay at a depth of at least 1 m., while the earth in South Greenland according to the experience of myself and others does not thaw nowadays in more than abt. 70-80 or at most 90 cm.'s depth" (240-1; he must be speaking of 1921 depth throughout this quotation, so the 20-25cm has to be subtracted to reach medieval levels). "We must suppose, then, that the coffins, crosses, or dresses that are best preserved originate from burials that took place at midsummer time when the thaw had reached its deepest level. They lay from the beginning immediately on the frozen bottom and only thawed during the warmest season every year. In this way the putrefaction of the body took place slowly and at long intervals without damaging the surrounding shroud. Later on the summer-temperature fell, and what was still left of these interments became encased in the frozen earth wich also preserved those plant-roots that had had time to penetrate into these deeper layers during the summer" (241). "[L]ocal conditions" play a role, so that depth is not always directly proportionate to preservation, but that qualification cannot explain the general tendency; examples are given of textiles found at various depths (241-2). In some cases of layered graves, "the deepest are the most decomposed": "No. 49 lay at a depth of about 65 cm. below the old surface and was so decomposed that it could not be preserved. Above it, at a depth of only 55 cm., lay gown No. 43 which was perforated by roots, it is true, but the material of which was nevertheless well-preserved, and above this again, at a depth of 45 cm., No. 60, of which about the same may be said. The child's shroud No. 85, found besides No. 60, must, however, have been too near the surface (at a depth of abt. 40 cm.) to keep in good preservation" (242). The remaining few paragraphs of the chapter mention plant-evidence and various European evidence. In the list of finds (262-7), the deepest find is at 135cm; there are a few of 130 as well, and several of 120. In the case of coffins, it is not stated whether the depth is the base or top depth, but maybe let's assume the latter.

author: Kamphausen, Hans Joachim
title: Traum und Vision in der lateinischen Poesie der Karolingerzeit
abstract:
[1: Psychology] Both dream and vision may be understood as either subjective (a product of the mind) or objective (a spectacle presented to the visionary from without) (9–10). Freud read dreams as exclusively heir to psyche, and robbed them of any prognostic power; in Antiquity and the Middle Ages, a dream could be true, false, or nonsensical from a prophetic perspective, but there was no single Classical understanding of dreams, nor did Classical interpretation end with Antiquity (12–13). The interpretation of dreams falls into folk-interpretation, theoretical interpretation (by doctors and philosophers), and literary interpretation, undertaken by poets without scientific ambitions. All three are secular; medieval dreamlore was based on them, but transformed them through a Christian lens (13). Each of them is discussed in turn (14–30). The first of these may be traced back to Assyrian, Egyptian, and Babylonian dreamlore; Antiphon introduced it to Greence, where physicians adopted it as a diagnostic tool (14–15). Artemidor attempted to turn the tradition into a scientific one, but his system was too sophisticated to be widely adopted (15–17). Alphabetical dreambooks, by contrast, found an easy audience (17–18). As concerns literary dreams, their large number suggests that the belief in prognostic dreams was widespread. Homer distinguishes between true and false dreams; Virgil follows him in this, and specifies midnight as the time of occurrence of Penelope's prognostic dream (18–20). As regards theoretical divination, dreamlore from Socrates onwards has been characterised by a dualism between transcendental and rational-biological explanations. Physicians and philosophers tried to systematise dream-divination as a subfield of prognostics, and this tradition led straight to the patristic understanding of dreams, which shaped medieval dreamlore by enriching this preexisting tradition with biblical insights (20–1). While classical dreamlore is multifaceted, the overarching understanding is of dreams as psychological, i.e. it reflects the soul (21–2). The attempts at classification furthermore led to a differentiation between dreams on the one hand and visions on the other (22). Macrobius was of great importance, though his originality should not be overstated. He distinguished between prognostic and agnostic dreams, but also provides a finer categorisation: agnostic dreams are insomnium (when the mind is troubled) and visum (vague appearances in the time before deep sleep sets in); prognostic dreams are oraculum (a parent or figure of authority apperas to the dreamer), visio (seeing that which will come to pass), and somnium (a figurative prophetic dream, requiring interpretation). Here is the Macrobian distinction between dream and vision: the former manifests itself in symbols, the latter is literal (22–3). Agnostic dreams derive from physical and mental stress and thus include nightmares and love-related dreams (23). Macrobius's understanding of prognostic and agnostic dreams is given some Classical context (23–5), and it is observed that the question of prognostic dreams leads to the question of divine intervention (25), a question itself related to the distinction between inductive and intuitive divination, the latter of which concerns knowledge from within (26ff.). Cicero distinguishes three types of dream-prognostic: (1) the soul, being of divine origin, is capable of divination by its own strength; (2) knowledge imparted by immortal souls inhabiting the air; (3) God himself imparts foreknowledge. Tertullian was to come to a Christian understanding of the same division (28–30).

author: Anlezark, Daniel
title: Three notes on the Old English Meters of Boethius
abstract: Discusses the authorship of the Metres.

author: Barrett, Helen M.
title: Boethius: Some Aspects of his Times and Work
abstract: [Highly selective summary] A thinker in Boethius’ day might be expected to be a neoplatonist. Boethius was also and primarily influenced by Plato himself (102, 111); by the stoics, although he was critical of them; by Aristotle; and also by Neoplatonism although he was also critical of this branch (102-104). In Boethius’ time, paganism was no longer a living alternative to Christianity: its practice was punishable by death. Boethius’ family had long been Christians, and the Senate in which Boethius took part was a stronghold of orthodoxy (139-40). Fortescue was wrong in thinking that Boethius did not know he was to die; 1.4p clearly shows he was aware of this. His excuse that Boethius is in exile not prison is countered by the common reference of exile to a foreign prison (155). Boethius’ heart and custom were with pre-Christian philosophy; so it was natural for him to write in philosophical terms. He drew a sharp distinction between fides and ratio (160-1). 4.4p has a reference to punishment of the soul after death, but the discussion of such things are said by Philosophia not to be her purpose now (161). Christianity must in Boethius’ day have had an air of controversy; this provides a good reason not to put his final treatise in Christian terms (162).

author: Bately, Janet
title: Those Books That Are Most Necessary for All Men to Know: The Classics and Late Ninth-Century England. A Reappraisal
publication: The Classics in the Middle Ages
eds: Aldo S. Bernardo and Saul Levin
publisher: State University of New York Press
series: The Classics in the Middle Ages: Medieval & Renaissance Texts & Studies
abstract: Studies the Alfredian knowledge of classical literature. Asser says Alfred used flosculos, passages copied here and there (47); and he is likely to have used Boethian commentaries (49). Alfred has omitted much in his opening passages of his Consolation. Fortune’s speech is performed by Wisdom instead, which explains the omitted reference to Perses (51). Perhaps Alfred knew nothing of Perses and such classical figures; but he has used an external source on Fabricius. He has wilfully omitted Trojan and certain other classical references, and many names are replaced with indefinite references. He considered an explanation of the hydra necessary; his information is of the tradition of Hyginus and Isidore, and possibly Mythographus 1 (51-3). Some of Alfred’s geographical data are listed, as well as his possible sources (53). There are significant innovations in the Circe episode (56-7). Sources of the OE Orosius are discussed, and options are given for similarities between the two (57-63).

author: Gurevich, Aaron J.
title: Medieval Chronotope
abstract:
Medieval literature contains elements that were not consciously crafted by their authors but instead reflect contemporary mental categories (225, 228). Time and space in Bakhtin's understanding of the chronotope are among the foremost of these, but Bakhtin "did not play close attention to" the medieval incarnation of this phenomenon (225).

In the Nibelungenlied, the older, eddic layer is merged with a high medieval chivalric counterpart. Time in the MHG text is much slower than that in the eddic poetry; action takes place at one of two courts, Worms and Vienna (226–7). "Siegfried ... represents an archaic type of a lonely hero", associated with magical elements and invincible until he abandons his own world in favour of that of the chivalrous Burgundians. Similarly, Brunhilt belongs to the world of myth and is incompatible with Burgundy; Gunther is strongest in his own world, but has to accept help from another mythological character in order to win Brunhilt in her home court (227–8). The different chronotopes in the epic are separated by bodies of water. The Nibelungenlied contains not one but several chronotopes, each centred around a hero (228).

The Latin exempla that describe miracles are a relevant class of text because they represent encounters with the supernatural (229–30). Rudolf von Schlettstadt in his Historiae memorabiles describes such events, and "[t]ime here is the historical time and not the time of fairytale" (230). "[T]he most striking aspect of the exempla is the intrusion of the inhabitants of the other world into the earthly one .... [T]he earthly time, for this very [sic] moment, seems to change its direction under the pressure of eternity." The restricted space of the earthly protagonist comes to contain elements of both supernatural realms (230–2). In some exempla, characters are simultaneously on earth and in one of the eternal realms: "for a moment, both worlds are fused" (232–3). An associated peculiarity is that the eternal forces involved lose their absolute qualities: God can be vengeful, demons less than absolutely evil (233).

Visions do not present space as continuous: the afterlife consists of a series of disconnected loci (235). Time should be eternal but is not consistently such: Judas undergoes different punishments on different weekdays, and the Last Judgement tends strongly to be personal, not universal (it takes place immediately upon [temporary] death, not after the second coming) (236–7). This "coexistence of the two eschatologies in the same world picture" follows from the audience's disposition to swift retribution, which led them to an instinctive preference for, and expectation of, this immediate eschatology (237). The visions are indifferent to time (237–8). The peculiar nature of time in the visions and exempla seems connected with the disconnected spatial configuration of the realms beyond; visions and exempla each have a chronotope with its own logic.

The implication of this discussion of medieval chronotopes seems to be that "medieval mind [sic] did not perceive any objective time and space existing independently of the person but rather imagined specific 'chronotopes' which were inalienable attributes of the individuals" (238).

author: Mazzuoli Porru, G.
title: Beowulf, v. 33: īsig ond ūtfūs
publication: Studi linguistici e filologici per Carlo Alberto Mastrelli
eds: Luciano Agostiniani, Vittoria Grazi, and Alberto Nocentini
abstract: Following a brief overview of previous research on the interpretation of the phrase isig ond utfus, proposes that an explanation lies in the fact that Scyld Scefing is a Dane, so that Baltic burial rites may apply. Alfred's Baltic excursus in the Old English Orosius tells how a certain tribe among the Estonians are able to produce cold at any time of year, and (with regard to another tribe?) that the Estonians lay out the dead for up to six months, however long their estate can keep the party going. The remainder of the article is concerned with the identification of the tribe in question.

author: Sandison, Helen Estabrook
title: The ‘chanson d’aventure’ in Middle English
abstract:
In Old French, this twelfth-century genre is characterised by the narrator reporting how he rode or walked by a forest or meadow at a given time of day (usually dawn) looking for distraction when he encountered a girl. This encounter provides the lead-up to the narrative proper (1–9). Actions are of two kinds: in the chanson dramatique, the girl (or nightingale)'s monologue or sometimes a female-dominated dialogue constitutes the action, the narrator being an observer only (9–15); in the pastourelle, the protagonist woos the lady with scant reference to their difference in station and disparaging her own poor lover (15–18). A love lament by the narrator alone is sometimes substituted (18). Mary is often substituted for the girl (18–22).

Though English derivatives existed as early as about 1300, the genre gained prominence there in the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. This book concerns the English type from 1300 to about 1550 (22–3). Here too the day (the other day) and hour (dawn, or morning) are provided alongside the reason for the excursion; exceptions to the morning are found in late examples, including noon, evening, and night, the first of which is on one occasion chosen "to symbolize the hot madness of youth" (26). "Spring is the favourite season of the English wayfarers, and May their chosen month; Summer now and then shares their favour. Yet the English poets do not dwell, as one might expect, on the freshness and beauty of reviving Nature," in contrast with their French models (26–7). This may be explained by the supposition that they are borrowing from contemporary and therefore late French texts whose preludes are "condensed and lifeless"; but post-Chaucer English poets sometimes elaborate on their models (27–8). Other seasons than spring are used occasionally; winter is found twice (28). The English tend to walk where the French ride (29–30).The setting follows from the French and is the side of a forest or less often "meadow, hillside, valley, or river's brim" (31–3, at 31). The wild charm of the deep wood is an English innovation not found in the French. "His marked preference for the 'wylde wode' lends to his narratives a fresh realism that offsets his failure to recount the delights of new-come Spring" (33). The English poets are less interested than the French in their own state of mind (35–6). In only half the English "adventure songs" are the actors people in whose feelings the poet has an interest; in religious songs they become Mary or abstractions, and in other texts they become birds (38–40). The English poets often neglect to keep up the pretense that they themselves overheard or witnessed the action (41–2).

Ch. 3 deals with the poems' themes, which are more often didactic, religious, or occasional than love. This chapter deals with love songs first, after which it turns to religious songs (46–93).

The appendices print previously unedited texts (100–29) and an index of ME chansons d'aventure (130–47), of other poems referenced (148–50), and a subject index. The work is rife with footnotes.

author: Walter, Philippe, Jean-Charles Berthet, Christine Bord, and Nathalie Stalmans
title: Le devin maudit: Merlin, Lailoken, Suibhne, Textes et étude
abstract: An edition and translation of the three 'mad king' texts. The introduction (by Walter, 5–48 and entitled "Sous le masque du sauvage") discusses origins and tradition, asserts that Celtic elements may be identified in the Latin–Christian Vita Merlini, and suggests a connection between madness and the kalends of May (in the Vita Merlini, Merlin's madness begins during spring Rogationtide, and this season also coincides with Carnival) (21–3). It also discusses the motif of wild men being able to talk to animals; in folklore, animals talk to people at certain times of year, especially on Christmas Eve (25–6). It also goes into a lot of detail concerning Merlin' prophecies.

author: Lot, Ferdinand
title: Études sur Merlin, I: Les sources de la Vita Merlini de Gaufrei de Monmouth

author: Harman, Eleanor, Ian Montagnes, Siobhan McMenemy, and Chris Bucci
title: The Thesis and the Book: A Guide for First-Time Academic Authors
abstract:
A useful little collection first published in 1976. I recommend reading the first chapter, the last, and definitely the fifth.

Halpenny's chapter (3–10) provides a good overview of what is involved in turning the dissertation into a book.

The second and third chapters are written by a cranky old man named Robert Plant Armstrong; the first of these ("The Dissertation's Deadly Sins", 11–19) nevertheless contains some useful warnings, while the second ("Revising the Dissertation and Publishing the Book", 20–33) has perhaps some valuable things to say in its shorter first sections, but then devolves into a hopeless second half on publication which is too flowery and ethereal to have made it past a self-respecting editor, while dealing with a part of the editing world which it is not necessary for the author to be familiar with.

Dowling's "Avoiding the Warmed-Over Dissertation" (38–8) is mostly a friendly first-hand experience recounted over a quick cup of coffee, offering little practical advice.

Olive Holmes's contribution ("Thesis to Book [...]", 39–77) is the longest but without a doubt the best in the collection. Opening with a discussion of academic tendencies that should be rooted out when the dissertation is converted to a book, it then moves to general advice on style.

Barbara Reitt's contribution (78–86) is a checklist with binary questions, many of which seem a little broad to answer for the book in general, though they may fruitfully be kept in mind when reading individual paragraphs and sections.

The final chapter is a very helpful essay providing the aspiring author with an insight into the publisher's interests as well as instructions on how to go about contacting a publisher (Allan Pasco, 87–101).

author: Bately, Janet
title: Time and the Passing of Time in The Wanderer and Related OE Texts

author: Bernardine, M., Sr
title: Boethius, A Christian Socrates
abstract: Compares Boethius with Socrates and briefly outlines his importance. Holds that it is “permissible”   that Boethius does not refer to Christianity because of his aim to find “a justification and a        confirmation of the dogmas of faith” through reason alone (29).

author: Bolton, W.F.
title: How Boethian is Alfred’s Boethius?
publication: Studies in Earlier Old English Prose
publisher: State University of New York Press
abstract: Proposes that Alfred’s changes to the Consolatio were entirely in keeping with the tradition of the time, as may be seen from its strong echoes of Alcuin; Alfred gave his people the Consolation as it existed in his time; no sixth-century manuscript was available to him.

author: Bouman, A.C.
title: Egill Skallagrímsson’s Poem Sonatorrek
publication: Patterns in Old English and Old Icelandic Literature
abstract: Proposes that Sonatorrek was influenced by Boethius’s De consolatione Philosophiae, heard by Egill in Old English translation during his insular sojourn.

author: Brinegar, John
title: Some Some sources of the Old English Boethius
