abstract: Proposes that Alfred used “Bede’s De natura rerum; Virgil’s Aeneid and Servius’s commentary on it; a mythographical work like that of the Vatican mythographers; Eutropius’s Breviarium; Gregory the Great’s Homilia XXXIV in Evangelium; Ambrose’s Hexameron; and the Biblical books of Wisdom, Sirach, and Proverbs” (2). His identification of the Evening Star with the Morning Star may have come from Bede (3-5). Ambrose's Hexameron seems to be the source for certain characteristics of fire and water; Alfred seems to have had access to a full text of this work (5-6). Inserted mythology looks as though it came from Servius and the second Vatican mythographer (6-8). Historic Roman characters seem to come from Eutropius (9-10). Biblical sources are listed in the remainder of the article (11-12). “More books may have survived the Danish than is commonly supposed, . .” (13). A “fair familiarity” with the writings of Virgil and Servius is somewhat surprising (13-14). The Bible was the most influential source to Alfred's alterations (14).
comments: Given at the first annual        symposium of The Alfredian Boethius Project, University of Oxford, July 2003.

author: Chadwick, Henry
title: Boethius: The Consolations of Music, Logic, Theology, and Philosophy
abstract:
Fragment summarised: “The religion of Boethius.” 247-53.

Boethius’s De fide catholica presupposes a disjunction between faith and reason; this is no commonly held view in the sixth century (248). His choice not to explicate his Christianity in his Consolatio is sometimes attributed to his disappointment with the passivity of the Roman clergy at his imprisonment (possibly, the pope was his good friend); but the implicit Christian allusions in the work make this view unlikely. The work contains nothing specifically pagan (248-9). With regard to Christianity as for paganism, “[e]verything specific is absent, and probably consciously avoided.” This is because of the author’s purpose with the work: the Consolatio “is a work written by a Platonist who is also a Christian, but it is not a Christian work” (249). Every Platonic view Boethius expresses is also found in the young Augustine, who writes even later, in De civitate Dei, that “no philosophers are so close to us as the Platonists.” Yet Augustine differs from Boethius in his interpretation of the workings of fate (heimarmene; 249-50). Much of Boethius’s vocabulary concerning prayer is said by Mohrmann to apply also to early Latin religions, but we know too little about such religious vocabulary to be able to determine its Christianity or lack of such; it is probably neutral. This insecurity on our part, however, suggests Boethius’s purposeful artistry (250-1).

author: Firestone, Ruth H.
title: Boethian and Anti-Boethian Elements in the Nibelungenlied
abstract: Argues that the Nibelungenlied is Boethian in its conception because the motivating characters in the conflict receive “guidance toward a resolution which would bring order and happiness to all,” but do not obtain it due to a selfish use of free will; and anti-Boethian because evil is seen to exist in a positive sense, with the end of showing “that joy ends in suffering, rather than, as in the courtly romance and the Consolatio, that suffering ends in joy” (5).

author: Fortescue, A.
title: De consolatione philosophiae libri quinque
abstract: [Caput II: De Religione Boethi] A number of medieval thinkers had condemned the Consolatio because it did not speak out for Christianity; in the seventeenth century, Boethius was even considered a pagan by some. Although his theological works were recognised as his, they were deemed “sine ratione” (xxv-xxvi). Nitzsch, in Das System Des Boethius, judged that Boethius had merely an “äusseren Bekenntnis nach Christ, aber sein System wurzelt in der antiken Philosophie und entbehrt nicht nur gänzlich einmal mit dem Christenthum.” Nonetheless, Boethius had his proponents also in Nitzsch’s day and more recently (xxvii-xxviii). There is today little strife concerning Boethius’ outward religiosity; it is his inner faith that is debated (xxviii). It has been suggested that Boethius lost his faith after he wrote his theological works, in order to write which he must have studied theology. The question is, therefore, whether it can be demonstrated that Boethius, who had always professed Christianity, lost his faith in the end. Attempts at such a demonstration have been made on the grounds of his silence on Christ and revelation in the Consolatio, his alleged preference for pantheism in the same, his statement that the world is perpetual and not created by God, his claim that men’s souls precede their bodies ontologically, and his silence regarding resurrection and man’s need of divine grace (xxix). Many of those who embraced Christianity had first been taken with Greek philosophy; hence, it is not surprising that they should want to strengthen Christian doctrine with the tools of reason. Augustine is the best example of such practice (xxxi). Moreover, it is not surprising that one who is fully versed in philosophy and has largely devoted his life to it, desires this same philosophy when his honours and freedom are taken from him. One cannot say that Boethius faced death without a prayer to God, since he was not certain that he would die at the time he wrote the Consolatio. Philosophia tells her Prisoner he will have hope in the future; and he replies he hopes it will hold (2.4p; xxxv). We have no evidence that this lifelong Christian, who wrote at the end of his Consolatio that “Hope is not placed in God in vain and prayers are not made in vain,” did not still trust in Christ at the end of his life (5.6p). As for his “philosophiam paganam,” the Church has developed its doctrine in steps, so that one ought not to be surprised to find in old texts ideas that were rejected by the Church only later (xxxvi). The Consolatio contains certain statements that suggest pantheism; but this is an exponent of the tradition of the neo-pythagoreans, Plato, and also Plotinus, that the world is a living and rational spirit; wherefore Plotinus, too, has been accused of pantheism (xxxvii-xxxviii). Nevertheless, if the universe derives from a Neoplatonic One, and its respective products, including a world spirit, are one with the One by virtue of deriving from it, they are no all gods; and Plotinus holds that there is one God that directs them all (xxxviii-xxxix). Boethius could not contradict Plato in his claim that the Earth is perpetual: he is taking on himself the role of a philosopher, and hence must rely on philosophy alone for his arguments. Thomas Aquinas would later attest that the existence of the Earth in time cannot be demonstrated but must be believed in faith (Summa Theologica 1.46.1). In the same way, Boethius could not claim that God has created the world, as Albert the Great points out that this fact, too, is knowable by revelation only (Sent. 2.18.a.3,6; xli). Nonetheless, God’s status of Creator is mentioned: “Dedit prouidentia creatis” (3.2p); God is called “terrarum caelique sator” (3.9m); evil does not exist because it was not made by God (3.12p); and God is called “unus rerum pater” (4.6m et al.). Boethius’ policy is neither to affirm, neither to deny those opinions that have been well put by classical writers but contradict revelation; the opinions, roughly, in which later scholastics considered the Greeks to have been mistaken (xlii). Although Boethius of his own free will introduced the Platonic opinion that the human spirit precedes the body in existence, this matter was not settled in his day (xlii-xliii). Even Augustine would not take a stand on this issue (xliv-xlv). Boethius speaks of one God (3.2p et al.), who knows all things (5.4p; 5.6p), is stronger and more pleasing than anything (3.12p), is the highest good, whose attainment brings man happiness (3.12p; 3.10p), is the one father of all things (3.6m) as well as their source and origin (4.6m), their ultimate goal (3.9m; cf. John 17.3); he calls human souls immortal (2.4p; 2.7p; 4.4p), speaks of freedom of choice (4.6p; 5.3p; 5.4p), and often echoes Scripture (refer to p. 204; xlvii). The Consolatio is a philosophical, not a Christian work; but it was certainly written by a Christian (xlviii).

author: Frakes, Jerold C.
title: The Fate of Fortune in the Early Middle Ages: The Boethian Tradition of Fortune in the Early Middle Ages: The Boethian Tradition
series: Studien und Texte zur Geistesgeschichte des Mittelalters
abstract:
Boethius’ acceptance as a Christian in the Middle Ages opened the door of acceptance for that of Fortuna, a pagan goddess (30). Fortuna and her specific goods were a commonplace in the consolation genre. Placing her on the side of the good is Boethius’s innovation (30-1). Fortuna’s first appearance is in the Muses passage, before the entry of Philosophia (32). The idea that Fortuna is constant only in inconstancy is Ovidian (Tristia V.8 15-18; 35). II.1m displays Fortuna’s cruel character (36-7). Fortuna is subject to de-deification: except in the Prisoner’s early complaints, she is never said to have any power of her own. “Dea” is only used of Venus, Callipe, and the Furies; “deus” is reserved for the one omnipotent God. Nearly all other supernatural characters are rhetorical figures in the metres. Some are here listed (footnote). None of the important cult titles of Fortuna are used. Although the analysis of Fortuna ends in V.1, a personified “Fortuna” is used only once after book two. This shows how Philosophia leads the Prisoner to higher, unchanging matters (39). Terms are listed that are used for worldly goods (47-9). Boethius’s concept of chance (casus) is Aristotelian in the main (55). Nihil ex nihilo, traditionally applied to matter (as of Alkaios fragment 23D), receives a new application, referring to causality. The traditional usage is incompatible with Christian cosmology as set out in Genesis 1 (57). The differences between Aristotle’s and Boethius’s concepts of chance are explained (58-9). Boethius omits Aristotle’s distinction between casus and fortuna (60-3). The “basic opposition of order to disorder provides the essential tension in the Consolatio” (63).

[Chapter four: “Fortuna in the Early Latin Commentaries on the Consolatio”] The Vatican Anonymous glosses are insular and dated to the ninth century. They are supposedly pre-St Gall and pre-Remigius. William of Malmesbury says that Asser “explained” the Consolatio to Alfred; this is sometimes seen as an indication that Asser is the author of the Vatican glosses (69). Remigius is post-901, and hence post-Alfred (77). Wittig’s methodology and argumentation is criticised (79). Frakes concludes that all traditions must be studied, but merely as illustrations of Alfred’s sources; none seem to be actual sources (80).

[Chapter five: “Alfred’s adaptation of Boethius’ fortuna.”] Alfred uses the scheme “God – divine providence – fate – fortune – man”; “one might well argue that fortuna has disappeared from the entire work” (81). The consequences for the translation are that (1) “another source for the worldly goods” is required; (2) these “goods must take on a new nature”; (3) these goods “assume a primary role in the argument.” “These three changes transform Alfred’s entire work.” The character Wisdom is of divine nature (“heofencund Wisdom,” III.1). Since the worldly goods have a divine origin, “they must themselves have some positive value”. In the Consolatio, they are worthless entities for their ontological status (i.e., material). In Alfred, they are “metaphysically neutral; their value depends wholely [sic] on the use to which men put them” (82). Payne interprets Fortuna variously (90).”Alfred does not attempt to Christianize the Consolatio, nor is his treatment of Fortuna ambiguous, nor does he fear any old pagan connotations of wyrd” (91). “God’s control is not questioned, but rather his purpose” (92). No personified wyrd ever emerges in Alfred’s text (93). He does translate casus as an active wyrd (93-4). Other instances of an active agent wyrd are listed (94-5). There is no inconsistency in denying and assessing wyrd’s power. The composite nature of wyrd (fatum, providentia, casus) is discussed (96-7). “Alfred’s objections to wyrd need not stem from a fear of calling up a pagan memory of wyrd, since there was a long tradition of anty-fate tirades which extended back to the early Church Fathers, especially Augustine and Gregory the Great, whose works were well- known [sic] in Alfred’s England, most likely also by the King himself.” Alfred has copied Boethius’s “general relational scheme of providence, fate and men, such that some men. . . are not subject to fate, but are directly subordinate to the divine will (IV, pr. Vi, 14)” (97). wyrd can also be positive (98). Frakes proposes a unified concept of wyrd; this includes no personified “grantor” (98-9). Two out of the three passages of wyrd’s prosopopoeia are omitted by Alfred (100). Wisdom is the highest good. Alfred’s argument is circular: wisdom is both the means and the end (106). Boethius’s goods have no intrinsic value: he uses a strictly dualistic ontology. Alfred also believes in good worldly goods, namely those acquiered by means of wisdom and used for God’s purpose (107). Negative qualifiers in Boethius’s text suggest that goods need not be negative (108). Alfred’s text contains a shift of emphasis away from the grantor of goods to the goods themselves (109). Alfred’s personification of the goods results in problems of adaptation: unlike with Fortuna, their complaint is not the grantor’s, nor from a position of power; God is the grantor (110). Alfred holds that worldly goods may be of value, if used in accordance with God’s plan (110-11). Alfred translates Fortuna’s discussion of goods into a very materialistic one: in chapter 17, he explains that no craft, and specifically the duties of a king, can be performed well without them (111-12). He does away with the necessary evil of the material world: things become good through good usage by good men, and evil through use by evil men (38.24-8; 113). The discussion is the first vernacular naming of the three estates: “gebedmen 7 fyrdmen 7 weorcmen” (40.21-3; 114). “Thus while Boethius rejects power because it can be evil, Alfred does so only when it is evil” (114). The need for power and glory is detailed (114-16). Alfred regards bodily pleasure as intrinsically evil without qualification (116). He uses compounds of sælð for all three types of goods, which problematises the distinction (116-17). True goods always receive a positive adjective; evil goods often receive a negative adjective. The origin of the goods in God’s wisdom gives them a potential for good (118). Worldly goods can thus be a reward; not so for Boethius, for whom all reward is beyond this world (118-19). While Boethius denies chance on the basis of nihil ex nihilo, Alfred uses the circular argument that everything comes from certain things, and that chance would have been for it to come from nothing [is this circular? PS] (140.4-6; 120). Alfred “deemphasizes counter-arguments throughout the work.” He splits Boethian fortuna up into three: “Wisdom, the grantor; woruldsælða, the goods; wyrd, the state of fortune” (122).

author: Godden, Malcolm
title: Alfred, Asser, and Boethius
publication: Latin Learning and English Lore: Studies in Anglo-Saxon Literature for Michael Lapidge
eds: Katherine O’Brien O’Keeffe and Andy Orchard
abstract: Draws together what is known about the Vatican 3363 MS, an early ninth-century copy of the Consolation that travelled the Continent and Wales, gaining glosses on its way.

author: Godden, Malcolm
title: The Latin Commentary Tradition and the Old English Boethius: The Present State of the Question
abstract: It remains hard to tell whether Alfred used any Boethius commentaries and if he did, which (1-2). Of the circa 400 extant MSS of De Consolatione, very few predate Alfred, but some sixty were written in c9-c11 and are likely to contain earlier material (2-3). Most of these contain some commentary. A few MSS survive that are commentary only. Commentary traditions have been split up into Remigian, St Gall, and other (3). Parallels between Alfred and Remigius are often striking, even though Remisius probably wrote his commentary late, around 906. A common source has been posited (4-5). “[W]e need to think of highly fluid collections or compilations of glosses and scholia rather than 'a commentary'; it is difficult in this field to attribute any one particular MS to Remigius” (6). The St Gall tradition consists of a corpus of glosses; a single continous commentary; a shorter version of this commentary; and stray glosses mixed with Remigian commentary (6). The uncertain dating of the central St Gall MSs may problematise Alfred's use of the tradition (8). There is little evidence for Insular use of the tradition (8-9). A vatican MS is discussed at length (9-14). Particularly relevant glosses are listed (14-18). Their significance is questioned (18). An appendix gives the sources for the glosses described (19-20).
comments: Given at the first annual symposium of The Alfredian Boethius Project, University of   Oxford, July 2003.

author: Irvine, Susan
title: Ulysses and Circe in King Alfred's Boethius: A Classical Myth Transformed
publication: “Doubt Wisely”: Papers in Honour of E.G. Stanley
abstract: Outlines some of Alfred's innovations, especially in the Circe story. Concerning Orpheus it is remarked that the sculan + infinitive, the impersonal construction, and the references to leasum spellum serve to distance Alfred from these classical legends (389). Alfred includes classical legends despite their spurious nature because they serve as vessels for truth (389-90). This ambivalence is characteristic for Anglo-Saxon literature (390). Many of Alfred's innovations are found in no extant Boethius commentary; he may have found several in the classics and in historical works such as Orosius. An Anglo-Saxon fascination with genealogy and Alfred's concern with kingship play a role (391). Boethius does not mention an affair between Ulysses and Circe; Alfred gives it central emphasis. The motif is common in classical versions, but Alfred contradicts Homer and Virgil in placing the affair before the transformations. The only parallels to this order are found in another branch of the demon sorceress motif, i.e., a branch split off before Homer wrote his epic (392-3). It is likely that Alfred just conflated the story with that of Calypso. Alfred makes Ulysses strongly responsible (393). Ulysses has been read as a type of Christ but he has also been strongly rejected; Alfred seems to have been influenced by the latter tradition. He focuses especially on his role as king: Ulysses abuses his responsibilities and is an animal though not transformed (394-6). Alfred intended to draw a contrast between Ulysses' kingship stained with moral infirmity and hs own, afflicted with physical infirmity only (396).

author: Kiernan, Kevin S.
title: Deor: The Consolations of an Anglo-Saxon Boethius
abstract: Deor seems to have been directly influenced by Alfred’s Consolation. It has taken Boethius’ narrative and substituted Germanic names for Boethian characters (333). Malone’s Scandinavian reading of the Geat-Mæðhild episode is problematic because a choice has to be made between his two versions; however, the Norwegian version has a parallel in the story of Orpheus and Eurydice, brought into the medieval worly through Boethius’ Consolatio. This text is therefore a possible source for Deor (334). Bloomfield and Markland were right in asserting that the ambiguity in the poem’s refrain is intended. The b-verse in the last refrain must refer to a time when the speaker’s misfortune has passed; hence, it may refer to “present joy.” The awareness that joy must pass as well as sorrow is Boethian. Deor l. 31 has alliteration on þas in þas woruld, thereby emphasising this present world as contrasted with another world (335). This passage has overtones of exile, which reminds one of Boethius’ situation. Furthermore, both Boethius and Deor are singers (Alfred 1.2). “The ultimate consolation for Boethius and the speaker in Deor is a triumph of the reason, . . . Both come to understand, and view with equanimity, the fact that all things associated with this world are transitory.” Markland’s view that both Deor and Alfred inadvertently give Fortune’s speech to Wisdom is rejected: Alfred has made a conscious alteration, which is explained by the passage that follows (336-7). The general themes of Boethius’ Consolatio and Deor are closely related; a link to Alfred is attempted. Boethius becomes Deor, Orpheus and Eurydice become Geat and Mæðhild; Weland is retained from Alfred’s text. Ðeodric is the Ostrogoth, and Eormanric is introduced because the two form a pair of ironic retribution: Germanic legend has the latter persecute the former. This is paralleled in Alfred, where Nero occurs in Eormanric’s stead (337-9).

author: Magee, John C.
title: The Boethian Wheels of Fortune and Fate
abstract: Shows that, although Boethius spoke of concentric circles, not spheres, of fate, not fortune, he has not necessarily used either Proclus or Plotinus exclusively for the concept, but rather they share a common tradition; and Boethius did not confuse the concepts of fortuna and fate but considered both “reducible to Providence” (525).

author: Otten, Kurt
title: König Alfreds ‘Boethius’
abstract: In scholarly circles, Alfred’s translation is generally regarded as poor (4). The commentaries Alfred used were closer to Remigius than to St Gallen, but not Remigius himself (7). Alfred’s text should not be seen as “Boethius diluted by the Middle Ages,” since his use of commentaries shows he wanted to understand Boethius (8). The St Gallen tradition is sceptical of Platonism and tries to free Christian thought from its yoke; the Remigius tradition tended towards synthesis (14). 1.4m and 1.7m present a stoic view; Alfred does not repeat gaudia, dolor, and spes as elements to be shunned (14). Otten mentions places where Alfred has added references to God not present in the Latin text (19). Fortuna’s speech is discussed (22-3). The concept of humility has a central position in Alfred’s world-view (24). Wisdom leads to worldly knowledge (25-6). Ars, virtus, and cræft are discussed (27.2: 62.22ff; 28-9 [cf. The Gifts of Men]). Alfred creates a conception of worldly goods that gain a good nature through good usage, and an evil one through evil usage (38.24ff); neither Boethius nor the commentaries see any good in worldly goods [but cf. Otten 59-60] (30). The book of Proverbs speaks of Wisdom as the grantor of worldly and spiritual goods [significant that it is Wisdom not Philosophia who grants worldly goods?] (Prov. 8.14-19; 3.15-16; 31). See also 3 Reg 3.11-13 for this Doppelnatur of Fortuna. Worldly goods are earned by those who possess heavenly goods (virtues; 31-2). The idea that goods are good through good usage is Augustinian: DCD 19; Sermo 111, PL 38.1418 (33). The doctrine of the correct usage of goods is a “neue Ethik” in Alfred—it is not central in Augustine (34-5). Boethius holds that willing evil, being able to carry it out and finally carrying it out are evils in themselves and as such an evil that befalls men; Alfred says these are bad for the criminals because they will be punished for it (Csl 4.4p: 95ff; AlfC 117.20ff; 35f). Alfredian references to postmortal punishment are listed (36). The good are said to live above the stars (139.5f; 38). Other medieval thinkers on virtue and reward (39-41). In Boethius’ system, God is too far removed from man to make possible the concept of sin: one can only fall from the one order into the other (42). Alfred mentions superbia and avaritia as sins (44-9). Concepts of the will are discussed (49-56). Alfred’s conception of guilt and reward derives from Gregory’s Cura pastoralis (52-3). Providence and free will are discussed (57ff). Alfred uses a less complex system of providence and free will than Boethius and others influenced by him (57). Boethius uses three references of “fortuna”: the Goddess, good luck, and Geschick. Fatum is inferior to Providentia; its workings are necessary. Chance is thus ruled out, and since God is the True Good, all Geschehen is good (57-8). Alfred writes that wyrd is the grantor of worldly goods, woruldsælða; but these are not fortunae dona, which are fleeting but may be positive; woruldsælða form a contrast with sælða, true goods (59). Boethius holds that Fortuna cannot give the Highest Good; Alfred believes that wyrd cannot give good goods [cf. 30]. Wyrd, fatum, and fortuna are discussed. Sælð represents all classes of good (60). Wyrd cannot be equated with Fortuna (62-3). Due to the differences of such terms, it is very difficult for Alfred to describe the essentials of Boethian thought. Methods he uses are (1) to leave out Fortuna and refer to woruldsælða instead; (2) to present gesceadwisnes as grantor of goods; (3) to use wyrd as a translation of personified Fortuna, but with few personal epithets so as to avoid pagan connotations (63-4). Remigius refers to Augustine and Gregory to point out that fatum does not exist (64). If wyrd were neutral, Alfred’s attitude towards would be inexplicable. Wyrd “still” has some “heathen” connotations, though how much is uncertain (69). Neoplatonic dualism and gradualism are discussed (70-86). Alfred seems not to have planned the change of dialogue partners (86). In the Middle Ages, Boethius was regarded as a martyr. The notion that Philosophia refers to sapientia Dei derives from the commentaries (87; 142-3; 156; 270f).

author: Pietersma, Henry
title: Intuition and Horizon in the Philosophy of Husserl
abstract:
Husserl speaks of “empty intention” when a speaker discusses an object without close [physical] examination; an actual viewing of an object is “fulfilled” (95). The contrast is made in the context of phenomenology, and thus seeing an object is the fulfilment of intentionality towards it. Unfulfilled intentions therefore include an understanding of what is lacking and how to arrive at the fulfilment of the experience (95–6). Husserl’s definition of experience as one of seeing is not closely circumscribed: he does not stipulate whether only simple objects can be seen, whether a certain mental activity (such as gazing) is required, or whether the process of seeing is simple or complex. Even his term Anschauung does not evoke gazing per se; seeing occurs whenever fulfilment of an intentional experience is attained, and Anschauung pertains to both “essences” and states of affairs without being subject to the dichotomy between objects of experience and objects of thought. Fulfilment is relative to other states of experience (96–7).

Husserl’s Erkenntnisstufen are degrees of experience intentioned on the same object; their point on the scale represents their epistemic distance from the object. The possession of an image of the object transcends empty intention but is not equal to fulfilled intention. Fulfilled intention is a seeing from which nothing is lacking; no change could reveal more of the object to the subject. This experience includes the knowledge that other intentions towards the object are possible which allow less access to it (97–8).

This awareness of potential more distant experiences of the object means an awareness of how the environment will respond if the subject were to undertake certain actions of motion. The awareness is in first instance implicit. Accordingly, “[s]eeing the object itself is an experience or situation that includes an awareness of context in the form of a familiarity with the ways in which objects of various kinds or categories can be approached. And the context in question is a domain that is open to our approaches prior to any particular actual approach to an object belonging to it. Seeing A itself is a mode of consciousness or situation which owes its phenomenological character to the subject’s familiarity with a domain in which he knows his way” (98–9, at 99).

The author goes on to elucidate the tension between Husserl’s notion that fulfilled intention is the closest available perspective on an object, yet physical perception does not involve seeing all of the object at once. The explanation consists in a recognition on the part of the viewer that he does not perceive all of the object at once, as long as the viewer’s perspective is in fact the best possible view (99–100). The achievement of fulfilled intention relies critically on the recognition that there are alternative but categorically inferior views attainable; perspectives resulting from the same kind of approach as the initial fulfilled intention are not categorically better than the initial view and therefore do not detract from its fulfilment even if they may be equal in access (100). Optimal seeing thus does not guarantee perfect perception, and accordingly need not be true, though given the perspective it certainly seems true (101).

author: Shaw, Philip A.
title: Pagan Goddesses in the Early Germanic World: Eostre, Hreda and the Cult of Matrons
abstract:
Boldly takes on the now-prevalent notion that Bede in his De temporum ratione invented the goddesses Eostre and Hreda. The argument relies on a late Roman cult of supernatural matrons including groups of deities whose class name seems cognate with the name Eostre. Shaw’s approach is admirably cautious and reasonably thorough in its philological methods. His caution does not always aid his cause, as when he dismisses a ritual relationship between the late Roman Austriahenae and Eostre, claiming only an etymological connection (boiling down to the ‘east’-element, 55–61) only later to disavow this by asserting that “[i]t is not implausible to suggest that the names of Eostre and of the Austriahenae are etymologically similar not because they are directly related to one another, but because they reflect similar broad patterns of naming practices in the early Germanic languages. . . . In other words, these are deities with local importance, whose names developed in parallel ways to refer to an area or a group that was in some way identified as eastern” (64). While perfectly reasonable, this line of argument undermines Shaw’s main evidence against the claim that Bede invented Eostre, namely the ritual and etymological connection between this name and the evidence from late Roman Germania. He tries to salvage the parallel by proposing that “some sort of cult similar to that of the matrons continued to exist in at least some part of early Anglo-Saxon England” (62) — rather suggesting that Shaw could not choose which line of argument to follow, though either relation or nonrelation would have been a valid course. Along similar lines, Shaw argues that Eostre was worshipped in Kent (hence the place-name Eastry), and that Bede obtained his information from eastern Kentish sources specifically, but then goes on to claim that Bede’s observation that the month-name was more recently understood to refer to the Christian festival of Easter makes clear the name was widely in use across Anglo-Saxon England (64–9). A very welcome aspect of Shaw’s line of reasoning is his abandonment of the long-standing belief that every specific deity should have a well-defined function (typically held to be goddess of dawn or spring in the case of Eostre).

Shaw’s discussion of the month-name Hreda commences with a fairly robust consideration of possible etymologies (73–82). The analysis suggests all possible etymologies are problematic, though hræd (“quick”) slightly less so (82). Later spellings of the month-name would seem to corroborate the case for this origin (82–3), and this likewise seems to be the origin of the initial element in the names Hreðel and Hrethhun (84–5). Old Norse inscriptions provide evidence for Hreið-, corresponding to OE hrāð, or hrǣð by way of i-mutation. It is thus not clear whether the OE name Hrethhun should be understood as having a long vowel (to parallel the ON) or a short one (to reflect the element hræð ‘quick’). Hreda likewise can go either way, but in any case it contains an element also found in other Anglo-Saxon names (85–7). With some difficulty, it is possible to construe OE hrǣð and ON hreið (found in Hreiðgotas) as cognates, which might correspond to Bede’s Hreda if it is understood that he used a e-spelling of the name from a dialect other than his own (87–91). Finally, Shaw draws attention to the very real possibility that the month-name hredmonað was not widespread in Anglo-Saxon England, although a German counterpart redmanot is attested in a number of witnesses (94–6).

In conclusion, Shaw restates the point that deities seem to have been local rather than pan-Germanic, and emphasises how little we know about pre-Christian cults.

author: Payne, F. Anne
title: King Alfred & Boethius: An Analysis of the Old English Version of the Consolation of Philosophy
abstract: Whereas Boethius writes of order in book 5, Alfred discusses freedom in the corresponding chapters. He ignores the central issue of Boethius’s book 5, the reconciliation of foresight with free will (16). Some argue this is because Alfred could not grasp its point, but this is not so (17). Alfred omits the discussion on the states of eternity and time. Important is his belief that what distinguishes between creatures of different worth is their lifespan (18-19). The passage translating 5.6 serves to contrast Man’s uncertainty and wisdom with God’s beauty; this is his main concern in the translation (20). Alfred remarks that God does not always choose to foreknow; therefore, foreknowledge and freedom need not be reconciled. Alfred “did not believe in the probability of a Boethian eternity” (21). The Latin text knows many kinds of order; Alfred adapts only the order of nature (22). Plato has influenced Boethius; Genesis has influenced Alfred (22-3). The two writers display a different conception of time. Boethius says that God’s everpresent coexists with our past, present and future; in Alfred’s vision, God first planned, then executed the world (23). Alfred denies that man’s sequence of life is inevitable (29-30; e.g. 3 vs. 57.7-8). He also denies determinism in man’s life by substituting names: “Wisdom” for “Fortuna,” for example (30). “Wyrd does not correspond to anything in the Latin text” (31). Alfred alters all references to ordo, thus destroying Boethius’s relationship ordo-fatum-providentia and denying determinism (31f.). These three are identical “for all practical purposes”; not so for Alfred with wyrd, endebyrdnes, and foreþonc (Alfred’s wyrd is God’s work). Alfred’s failure to translate the all-important notion of order seems to indicate intellectual inferiority, but an analysis of his explanation of freedom contradicts this conclusion (39-40). Man’s primary freedom is discussed. According to Boethius, this is freedom of thought; Alfred believes it is freedom of action (to do good or evil; 40-5). Men have freedom because God, as a king wants no slaves; man’s existence balances between freedom and law; good will equals good work if man’s good actions are thwarted by external powers (44-5). In the translation according to 5.3, all things, arising from free judgement as well as from natural causes, are deemed necessary in the light of divine foreknowledge; but the first type are bound only by simple and conditional necessities. Freedom of external matter seems hardly possible. Alfred discusses the tension between predestination and freedom, not foreknowledge and freedom (45-6). He claims some foreknown things are predestined, but things caused by indifference need not happen even if foreknown by God. The second state allows man’s freedom (49-50). “The future. . . is an experience that both God and man are involved in creating and sharing” (50). In his discussion of predestination and freedom, Alfred names wyrd only once (78). The word is used much to discuss the cosmos (whether Wyrd rules it independent of God, 78-9). Boethius says there are limits to Fate’s control over man (as to death, the past, etc., 79). “Fortuna” has no real OE equivalent; Alfred uses wyrd for Fortuna, woruldsælða for its mutable gifts. When it is claimed it is in Fortuna’s nature to be changeful (II.2p), Alfred personifies neither Wyrd nor woruldsælða. This shows neither was by him considered a translation of Fortuna (80). Boethius’s Fortuna is “the familiar uncertainty,” without indifference or evil intentions; Alfred’s Wyrd is “the unfamiliar uncertainty”; it is higher, “awesome,” and cannot be personified for danger of making it too familiar (82-3). Alfred has his prisoner attack Wisdom for leading men astray; in Boethius, this is Fortuna. Wisdom has a good reason for reasoning with the prisoner. Alfred realates Wyrd neither to mutability, nor to order (83). Wyrd is “God’s work”; fatum bears no relevance to Wyrd (90). Bosworth-Toller is wrong: fate and fortune are no definitions of wyrd, because of their Boethian colouring. Wyrd is God’s work of adjusting the world to embrace the contingencies that arise as men choose their particular courses of action (91). Boethius seems to allow more freedom from fate than Alfred does (4.6; 99). Mod doubts whether God governs Wyrd, and whether He is more powerful than Wyrd (101). Wyrd cannot be controlled completely; wisdom is gained in spite of Wyrd, not through confrontation with it (104).

author: Proppe, Katherine
title: King Alfred's Consolation of Philosophy
abstract: Boethius had a Platonic world-view and saw the world as a projection of God's mind; Alfred attempted to reconcile this ontology with the Anglo-Saxon dualism by classifying Boethius's unity as idea (not matter). His aim was to make this theory of “Roman orderliness” compatible with a Germanic world-view of chaos and materialism; and this attempt “provides the central tension of the work” (635). Payne speaks of “Christian Existentialism,” meaning an awareness of the enormous power of Wyrd over man; and she claims that Alfred’s main alteration consists in a substitution of a theory of freedom for one of order. In doing so, she ignores the evidence in Alfred’s text of “an orderly realm above the storms of this earth” (636). Mod feels like an exile in the world because of these storms; and Wisdom at one point cries out that the entirety of creation is ruled by order except her own realm. Alfred works towards order, but allows chaotic visions to keep appearing, alternating with the picture of order (638-9). In ending with a description of the harmony of the spheres, Alfred suggests his reconciliation has succeeded; but all through the work, it is a loose connection (641). In his consciousness of both the transitory and the eternal, Alfred strives towards rationality and order. In the Anglo-Saxon view, God may grant victory, but He is not the path to an understanding of the world (642). God is described as controlling the world through reins, and thus by force; but also as ruling creatures who serve him by their free will (643-5). His conception of worldly goods is equally ambivalent: they are “part of God as immanent in Creation, wisdom’s servants, indifferent tokens of the world, emblems of death to be despised, and images of eternal good” (646). Since Alfred wants to reject them in favour of wisdom but at the same time realises that they are needed as means, he “necessarily confuses ideal and. . . material categories”. Ideas cannot be causes in the material world; to this end, material is needed (646-7). Alfred’s work is an attempt at compromise; in it we may see a “semi-emergent Roman conception of Christianity, rationality, humility and renunciation lying side by side with tenacious old Anglo-Saxon emotions” (648).

author: Vogel, Cornelia Johanna de
title: The Problem of Philosophy and Christian Faith in Boethius’ Consolatio
abstract: A Christian in Boethius’ situation might be expected to turn to his religion for comfort; but this is not what Boethius’s Prisoner does (286). Since it is Philosophy who offers him her consolation, we ought not to be surprised that she sounds more like Plato than like Christ; but her world conforms well to the Christian world (287). Hence, many passages can be read as the offspring either of philosophy or of Christianity; but even Plato wrote in the awareness of an all-seeing God (287-8). Several medieval and later critics condemned Boethius because he did not make the Christian doctrine explicit; in the nineteenth century, he was exalted because he was believed to be reasonable and no Christian (288, 290-1). Courcelle is cited as feeling that Boethius did not so much adapt his Platonism to Christianity, but rather adapt his Christianity to his secular studies; De Vogel believes this statement refers to such usages as Fortuna and Fatum at Augustine’s suggestion; and Boethius’s belief in the perpetuity of the world, justified by the ontological differentiation between perpetuity and eternity (291-2). Christian elements are found in 5.3p (humilitate gratiam Dei, 293). Identifications of Neoplatonic concepts with Christian notions occur often, e.g. 3.9m. De Vogel holds that (also Boethius’) “[s]yncretism is an unconscious, or almost unconscious process”; thus Boethius did not mingle the two traditions on purpose (294). Boethius’s belief in chance is termed “very far. . . from the belief in Providence. . . . [and] far from Platonist philosophy as well.” This belief stems from no studies; rather, it is an irrational element “stemming from the worldly atmosphere” (295). Boethius does not Christianise Philosophia, but he does not agree with all she says: he does not consent to the abandonment of hope (5.3p); “[t]his is a Christian’s reaction to ‘pagan’ philosophy” (299-300).

author: Whitbread, L.
title: The Pattern of Misfortune in Deor and Other Old English Poems
abstract: Argues that the five retrospective sections of the poem share an emphasis on three paradoxes, namely that misfortune seems everlasting and insurmountable; that it is is intimate but cannot remain hidden; and that it is mental but is subject to physical causation (167-8). In the refrain, Whitbread believes swa is instrumental; thus it is “by the same means” that any present trouble can be overcome, namely by the realisation of these paradoxes; then, it “can be overcome by resolute thought translated into determined action” (168-9). The final, personal section of the poem is just misfortune, unlike the unjust misfortune of the first section, since the lord is kind and the new scop skilled; but the solution remains the same (169). The middle passage is a bridge, both universal and personal, pointing out that the troubled mind must (1) realise that he is capable of “taking thought”; (2) realise that God distributes both fortune and misfortune alternately; and (3) that this pattern is paralleled in the individual. Thus for each individual, fortune and misfortune alternate; but man has the power to influence this external pattern by mental means. The poet recommends “traditional, heroic courage never to submit or yield” similar to that urged at Maldon. There is no refrain after l. 34, because it has been reserved for the moral but also because its application here would damage the threefold structure of historical/heroic illustration, general reflection, “personal confession of worldly pride,” which is matched by Hrothgar’s speech in Beowulf 1700-84. “The threefold method of structure is in both cases both natural, fitting the circumstances of the subject-matter, and artistic enough to suggest some reliance on the conventions of a formal sermon technique.”Deor has a literary outlook (170). In whatever OE period Deor was composed, Boethian influence is possible. (170-1). Deor follows Boethian tradition, and perhaps Boethius himself. Parallels are found in the condition Deor and Boethius share; a reference to “sorrowful love” (Mæðhild and Csl 3.12m: Orpheus playing to the gods); the characteristic “wolflike” (Eormanric and Csl 4.3: 13); and Weland and Theodoric may have been chosen for Deor because of Weland’s occurrence in Alfred’s translation and Theodoric’s relevance to Boethius’ life. Forms and images of grief often run parallel (171). Two more parallels are the assertions that man has free will and is able to “cure” his misfortune (Csl 2.4p); and that both texts strictly separate theology from philosophy (172). The other Exeter elegies share with Deor a suggestion of “Boethian affinities.” Whitbread conjectures that the presence of these poems (and especially Deor, The Wanderer, The Seafarer, The Wife’s Lament, The Husband’s Message, and The Ruin) in the Exeter MS is connected to their status as “experimental exercises or treatments, within the framework of heroic situations, of themes and notions to be found within the Boethian tradition”(172-3). The Wanderer’s claims as a Boethian poem are corroborated by its similarity in style to Deor. A list of similarities to Deor and Csl is provided for this work and The Seafarer; in the latter poem, the search for consolation is a binding element (173-6). The Wife’s Lament and The Husband’s Message are conjectured to be heroic, exilic representations of the legend of Orpheus; consolation also plays a big role in both (176-8). The Ruin in describing ruins emphasises the fleeting nature of all that is worldly; and it mentions fallen giants as the ruins’ makers, a parallel with Boethius (178). Wulf and Eadwacer as a whole is unlikely to have been influenced by Boethius, but the final lines match Boethius’ version of the legend of Orpheus (179). Resignation shares conventions and diction with the other poems, but has little overall resemblance to Csl (179-80). More research is needed (180).

author: Wittig, Joseph S.
title: Boethius
publication: Sources of Anglo-Saxon Literary Culture: A Trial Version
eds: Frederick M. Biggs, Thomas D. Hill, and Paul E. Szarmach
publisher: Center for Medieval and Early Renaissance Studies
abstract: Mentions key data on Boethius’s life, and discusses his textual influence in Anglo-Saxon England per literary category. Alfred’s prose translation is the earliest evidence of an Anglo-Saxon knowledge of the De consolatione philosophiae (78).

author: Zandvoort, R.W.
title: Three Notes on King Alfred’s Boethius
abstract: Comments on Alfred’s rendering of specific passages of the Consolatio.

author: Karras, Ruth Mazo
title: God and Man in Medieval Scandinavia: Writing — and Gendering — the Conversion
publication: Varieties of Religious Conversion in the Middle Ages
abstract: Mainly points out that Snorri depicts conversion as a shift in alliance, and that women are accordingly largely left out.

author: Bredsdorff, Thomas
title: The Second Pattern
publication: Chaos and Love: The Philosophy of the Icelandic Family Saga
publisher: Museum Tusculanum Press and the author
abstract:
[The page range and this abstract concern only the section entitled “Egil Skallagrimsson’s Saga”]

Power urges in Egla are complemented with erotic drives (23-5). This dimension of the saga is exemplified by the family’s relations with King Eiríkr’s court: Eiríkr is always forgiving towards Egill, but his wife Gunnhildr goads him to take a hostile stance; their encounters are listed (26-7). Egill’s love of Ásgerðr is unanswered (25-6). It may be seen early on when Egill causes trouble for his brother, who is about to set out and ask Ásgerðr’s hand in marriage; and it may be seen again when he pleads sick at the wedding but sets out on an exacting journey as soon as the people have left (27). It is on this journey that Egill meets Gunnhildr at a party and becomes her enemy, which may be read as the start of an erotic love-hate relationship (27-9). Egill’s problem in his love-life is his ugly appearance: at the party, the earl’s daughter appreciates him only after he has proved himself courteous through language rather than his appearance (29-30). Once Egill marries Ásgerðr, he becomes part of the long-standing conflict with Berg-Önundr concerning her inheritance; Gunnhildr takes the side of the latter and goads the king into banishing him (30), while she curses him, again to be understood as an expression of erotic forces. Many of the deaths and dramatic events in the latter half of the saga are to be explained in the light of the relationship between Egill and Gunnhildr (31-2). Thus love functions as a disruptive force in society (33-4).

author: Byock, Jesse
title: Egill Skalla-Grímsson: The Dark Figure as Survivor in an Icelandic Saga
publication: The Dark Figure in Medieval German and Germanic Literature
eds: Edward R. Haymes and Stephanie Cain van D’Elden
abstract: Describes Egill’s generation and his father’s as one of contrasting brothers, which is displayed in their respective attitudes towards kings and in their social integration (153). Kveld-Úlfr and Skalla-Grímr display dark characteristics, both are shapeshifters; Egill shows darker tendencies but he is never described in supernatural terms (154-5). The latter two generations contrast the dark figure with a lighter brother Þórólfr who adapts to societal expectations, unlike their dark brothers who oppose change; the Þórólfar also advocate traditional values (155). Skalla-Grímr flourishes in Iceland (156); similarly, Egill is less disruptive of society when in Iceland. Both dark brothers live to old age, while both the light brothers die young (158). After Egill, a dichotomy remains in the family in the shape of the ugly Mýramenn and their handsome counterparts; but there is no longer anything supernatural to the distinction (159).

author: Hermann Pálsson
title: Fornfræði Egils sögu
abstract: Discusses various ancient customs described in Egils saga reflecting thirteenth-century conceptions of tenth-century culture. Among other things discussed is the concept of hamremi (60-3).

author: Holtsmark, Anne
title: On the Werewolf Motif in Egil’s Saga Skallagrímssonar
abstract: Discusses wolflike features in Egla. The word vargr was used to denote not wolves alone but outlaws as well. The settlers of Iceland brought with them literary references to wolves, but the animals existed in tradition only (7). Hence if Kveld-Úlfr was accustomed to assuming a wolf’s shape, Skalla-Grímr, living in Iceland, would not have done so. The description of Egill in ch. 55 after Þórolfr’s death includes strong wolflike features, including wolfgrey hair (cf. ch. 31, where his hair is black) (8). It is only in ch. 65, when Egill fights Atli and bites his throat, that he displays the behaviour of a (were)wolf; significantly, this episode takes place in Norway (9).

author: Jón Sigurðsson
title: Nú er hér kominn Egill. Hefir hann ekki leitað til brotthlaups: Tilraun til at greina meginstef í Egilssögu
abstract: Aiming at a literary clarification of the character of Egill, identifies a central theme of fights, both in society and within the person; and because it deals with fights, it also deals with friendship (321-2). Descriptions of characters may be the key to Egill’s person and the author’s ethics. Throughout the saga, light appearances are set against dark appearances, just as Egill’s character displays extremes and inconsistencies. In medieval literature, a man’s appearance was thought to reflect his character; accordingly, Egla conceals meaning in personal descriptions (322). It is rather expressive of emotions, particularly melancholy, but also anger, frenzy, the rush of victory, and deep grief; and especially in its poetry (322-3). As in Dostojevski’s works, the characters are undetermined and irresponsible rather than sharply defined by descriptions of personalities (323). The elderly Egill is peaceful, not engaging in strife (ch. 67) because others do not withhold his rights from him (324). Egill’s judgement in his son Þorsteinn’s court case is generally thought to bear witness to his greed and unreasonable nature, but the case is not viewed in proper perspective: Þorsteinn has clearly been wronged (324-5). Egill’s character as described in the final chapters forms a sharp contrast with his childhood descriptions: his unruly, unreliable, and ungovernable character has given way to a respectable man who does not engage in lawsuits (ch. 80); the implication seems to be that Egla is a didactic saga of character development (325-6). This raises the question whether there are clear moments of transition. Egill is helpful to others in chs 65 (Ljótr bleiki), 73 (Ármóðr), and 76 (the journey to Eiðaskógr). He shows noble-mindedness in chs 46 (Kúrland) and 55 (Aðalsteinn’s compensation for Þórolfr). Care is displayed when he treats the wounds of his companions despite his own in chs 73 and 76. Conscientiousness is seen in chs 63-4, 71, and 75 (326-7). The saga as a whole is concerned with the fight for equality, justice, and the rights (to inheritance and ownership) of family and retainers. These rights are also pursued in Egill’s personal struggles and in his poetry and are sufficiently universal still to appeal to us today (327). All his cruelty and wild deeds spring are aimed at redressing wrongs (328) (Continued: sections on Egill’s belief in family [331-4], his journey to York [334-8], and his poetry [338-42]). Egill fights a perpetual fight for acknowledgement, compensation/inheritance, and family; therefore, Egill’s physical description in ch. 55 may be the saga’s pivot, and certainly no less significant than the great poems or Egill’s old age (342). The wolf-association of the Kveld-Úlfsætt has received a considerable degree of attention (342-3). [incomplete]

author: Lie, Hallvard
title: Jorvikferden: Et vendepunkt i Egil Skallagrimsson’s liv
abstract: Asks why Egill goes to Eiríkr’s court (11-15). Various takes on Egill’s character are discussed (15-17). Egill’s hamremi is incidental: it does not touch on his deepest personality, nor does it influence significant psychological events in the saga; the author has gone out of his way to edit the poetry’s emphasis on sorcery out of the narrative (17-18). ( . . . ) Egill’s family is characterised by an inner division into a dark, coarse side and a light, sensitive side. Outward characteristics are matched by character traits: introverted versus extraverted, suspicion versus trust, sharpness of character versus joviality. While the family are of various origin, they spend most of their time in the northwest. As such they are from liminal territory, which fits well with the [early twentieth-century] theory that communities of mixed racial background produce more outstanding people (49). [Already] Sigurður Nordal proposed that hálftröll means “descended on one side from the Sami”; textual evidence bears out this theory (49-50). This blood will have come in on the Hálogaland side of the family. The family’s dark skin and large build suggest that such a mixture was indeed present (50-1). Yet the term hálftröll is only used when the character’s genetic inheritance gives him the psychological berserkr-condition (51). Thus the ethnic union results in physical and psychological traits, and the berserkr nature belongs to the latter (51-2). Egill’s family is fuller of berserkir than any other Íslendingasaga. The berserkr nature is characterised by both outward appearance and personal character. This is illustrated in Kveld-Úlfr and Skalla-Grímr with especial emphasis on their furor berserkicus; Þórólfr Kveld-Úlfsson may also be counted in this group on account of his attack of Aðils (52-3). The subsequent weakness of berserkir is discussed, in conjunction with the family’s tendency to take to their beds in time of sorrow, including Ölvir hnúfa, to whom Egill is related by his mother (53-4). Egill himself has these traits, though they come out slighty differently; his long poems should be understood in the light of his berserkr background (54-5). Egill’s psychology in the journey to York is studied on the basis of prose and verse and with further discussion on berserkr psychology; it is concluded that the visit to Eirík’s court stems from a personal crisis (55-88). Sonatorrek is studied for evidence of Egill’s spiritual transformation (particularly his relationship with Óðinn, “trolldommens gud” [100]) (88-106). Stanza 22 seems to say that Óðinn abandoned Egill in York. Since Óðinn is a god of warriors, he may have been behind his berserkr-nature. Now that Egill and Óðinn have gone different ways, Egill is no longer a berserkr. This makes Egill’s journey to York a turning-point (89-106).

author: Looze, Laurence de
title: Poet, Poem and Poetic Process in Egils saga Skalla-Grímssonar
abstract: Proposes a connection between the ugly, wolflike side of Egill’s family and poetic skill (esp. 125-9). Egill’s first poem is a microcosmic parallel to the saga as a whole (127-9). Metrical language is used as a controlling force throughout the saga (129-30). In the York episode, the value of poetry as compensation is emphasised (130-3). The Ármóðr episode (chs 71-2) similarly stresses the economic value of poetry, as well as using language to distinguishing between the poet and the base man (133-5). The subsequent rune-healing episode shows the power of language and the need for professionals handling it (135-6). Sonatorrek serves as a poetic renewal of life (136-8). Egill obtains a new, surrogate son in Einarr skálaglamm, who becomes a sort of poet-trainee with him, poetics taking over where the bloodline has come to a [virtual] standstill (138-9). After his death, Egill’s skull is found, displaying durability after being ransomed (139).

author: Schach, Paul
title: Was Tristrams saga the Structural Model for Egils saga?
publication: American Journal of Germanic Linguistics and Literatures
abstract: Briefly discusses the influences of Tristrams saga on a wide body of texts, including Þíðreks saga, Rémundar saga, Jarlmanns saga ok Hermanns, Mágus saga jarls hin meiri, Kormáks saga, (Örvar-Odds saga, Gunnlaugs saga, Laxdæla saga), Grettis saga, Haralds saga Hringsbana, and of course the parody Tristrams saga ok Ýsoddar. All of these borrow both plot and structure (71-5). This article asks whether a purely structural borrowing might be possible (75-6), and looks for it in Egla (77-82).

author: Braune, Wilhelm
title: Muspilli
publication: Beiträge zur Geschichte der deutschen Sprache und Literatur
abstract: Disagrees with etymologies based on mundus, Mundspruch, Mundschwert, and legal terms based on muðspel (425-9). All these theories suppose that the OHG word is an OS borrowing, which is required for the first element to signify “mouth.” However, a literary borrowing from the Heliand would have resulted either in mutspelli, a verbatim borrowing of a word not understood, or mundspilli in case the author did understand the word. An oral borrowing would have yielded the latter (429-30). Its meaning “ende der welt, weltuntergang” is apparent in all occurrences, not least the variations of the term with “endi thesaro uueroldes” (Heliand 2591f.) and “thie dag. . . thie lezto theses liohtes” (Heliand 4358b-61); but an alternate specific meaning “weltuntergang durch feuer” is admissible (430-1). If the word is supposed to have shifted its meaning from mundspruch to Last Judgement, then the shift cannot have stopped there but must have continued along the line of damnation > destruction > end of the world. Such a shift cannot have taken place in the short time between conversion and production of the Heliand. The Bavarians could furthermore not have borrowed a novel Christian term from the Saxons on such short notice (431-2). An alternative theory [see Detter, Beitr 21 p.110] is that the word originated in OE and moved east and northwards alongside gospel. The word’s absence from OE and from OHG prose may be explained if the word is originally pre-Christian, like so many other Germanic words that found their way into OE Church vocabulary (432-4). Muspilli never achieved the Church-Christian status it aspired. It may have travelled to Scandinavia in Christian poetry and ecclesiastical texts even before the conversion of Iceland (434-5). Attempts at etymology have failed; but its context makes its meaning clear. Just as the word hell demonstrates that the Germani had a concept “world of the dead” and OE neorxnawang shows that there was a Germanic afterlife, the word muspilli demonstrates that there was a belief in the destruction of the world (435-7). All these concepts are extant only in ON mythology. Olrik points out that the destruction of the world is explained in three ways: fimbulvetr, the sinking of the world, and a world fire. Olrik discarded the latter as Christian, but the concept was present before Snorri [and thus likely before Christianity]. Moreover, Snorri provides details that appear to stem from unknown sources, suggesting that he had access to non-extant ancient mythology; he should thus be considered a genuine source (437-9). The same argument applies to his knowledge of the Múspells synir (439-40). The difference between U and the other MSS of SnE is significant: Muspell as a place-name developed only in the latter group. U has seven occurrences of Muspells megir and five of Muspells heimr; the other MSS replaced four megir by synir and two heimr as well as one megir by the shorter Muspell. The later editor used more of the Poetic Edda than the U author did. To the U author, *Muspellr was a personal name of a giant. His personal interventions must have been part of pre-tenth century mythology. Snorri did not make up his references to the Múspells synir but must have had non-extant sources (440-2). If Múspellr is a fire demon, then “world fire” is the original meaning also of the OHG and OS forms which in their extant contexts only allow for “weltuntergang.” The gender of these words has mistakenly been identified as neuter, based on Snorri’s Muspell; they are in fact masculine, though a neuter variant may have developed (442-4). The concept muspell “weltbrand” was personified alongside Hel to a fire demon *Múspellr. Surtr lived in his world and may originally have been considered his son. Múspellr may have spread in the time when Óðinn did: just as the latter moved into the mythology but not the religion of the north, so too Múspellr gained a place in mythology but his person was forgotten (444-5).

author: Goetz, Hans-Werner
title: Endzeiterwartung und Endzeitvorstellung im Rahmen des Geschichtsbildes des früheren 12. Jahrhunderts
publication: The Use and Abuse of Eschatology in the Middle Ages
eds: Werner Verbeke, Daniel Verhelst and Andries Welkenhuysen
abstract: In an analysis of twelfth-century eschatological thought, makes the following assertions. The revelatory media by which one could learn about the end of days were three: Bible, history, and visions (308-9). History and eternity stood in a teleological relationship; the earthly sojourn may be regarded as a subclause in the continuity between Creation and eternity. Regaining the blessed state was possible via a number of measures introduced in this era, including sacraments, free will, virtues, good works, and knowledge; and yet grace depended not on one’s actions but on an action of will from God’s side. Already, the inhabitants of earth are two classes, the elect and the rejected, though these cannot yet be easily told apart. While the elect will replace the fallen angels, they will not take their place; they were not created for this purpose, and they will have a place of their own (according to Honorius). The world will last until the number of elect has been reached (309-12). While the eras of life on earth are, of course, linear in a chronological sense, they were perceived as hierarchical in getting ever nearer the Heavenly Jerusalem. They have commonly been subdivided into three or six ages; sometimes, eternity was included and the earthly ages were made a subdivision within the three eras of ante peccatum, post peccatum, and post resurrectionem. In the twelfth century specifically, the use of these ages was heightened; but scholars became dissatisfied with the low detail of the sixth age and referred to apocalyptic events in order to describe it more accurately. Echoing Revelation, the sixth age was often divided into four sub-eras, each of which was defined by the opposing parties: Council, Apostle, early Church; heathen tyrants versus martyrs; heretics versus confessores and doctores; and falsi fratres versus veri fratres. The intratemporal and intertemporal schemes were often combined into a single table. This entailed the problem of how history and the heavenly kingdom were to be conjoined, e.g. by a seventh age of rest and an eighth of resurrection. The central problem in the connection was the essential transpositio between earthly life and eternity (312-17). Scholars were in general agreement concerning a number of events at the end of the world: the Antichrist would rule in his persecutions for 3.5 years after Satan’s release; the blowing of the trumpet, announcing the resurrection, would take place after a time of rest following the victory over the Antichrist. Only the Christians had yet to be judged and divided into the just and the unjust. Purgatory is a concept that was developed in the twelfth century and remained controversial. History was replaced with eternity after the reign of the Antichrist but before the resurrection, although only the reuniting of body and soul began the gaudium of everlasting life. While heaven and hell were part of Creation, the “third heaven,” where God resided, was intellectual and formed no part of Creation (317-19). Eternity partakes of God and enables things that are not possible from within saeculum; eternity is ultra loca et tempora and as such ahistorical (319-31). The manner of resurrection is discussed (323-4) and the nature of the heavenly kingdom (224-6). Within saeculum, angels and the spirits of men already live a noncorporeal life in heaven. However, the timeless reality “war schon jetzt existent” since men have seen God. Symbolic understanding is the vessel through which the invisibilia may be discerned. This relationship also implies a mystic reality. Generally, however, it was held that full eternity would come to be in the future (226-9). The expectation of an imminent end should not be exaggerated: many signs were first to be expected. Some thinkers expected the end soon, but they did not settle on a precise time. The central problem of the twelfth century was the lack of unity within the Church, and this reflected on the lack of unity in the heavenly Church as portrayed in the period (229-32).

author: Hagen, Sivert N.
title: Múspilli
abstract: Argues that the word múspilli is an OHG etymological translation of Latin oraculum.

author: Hultgård, Anders
title: Old Scandinavian and Christian Eschatology
publication: Old Norse and Finnish Religions and Cultic Place-Names
publisher: The Donner Institute for Research in Religious and Cultural History
abstract: Early Scandinavian eschatology may be divided into the Christian and the pagan tradition, yet they do not necessarily represent a strict division between Christians and pagans: Snorri, for one, transmitted a version of the Ragnarǫk tradition (344). Christian eschatology is based chiefly on Matthew 25, Daniel 7-12, Revelation, and 4 Esdras (345-6). Eschatology could sometimes take a political guise (346-7). ON homilies have frequent reference to Judgement Day; and there is evidence that the northern missionaries used the theme to win souls. Skaldic poetry also contains references to hell and the archangel Michael, and Swedish rune-stones use Christian invocations to suggest a judgement of souls (347-8). The Ragnarǫk tradition is found in skaldic poetry and the Eddas, and in Hyndluljóð 42-4 (349-50). It is demonstrated that the thirteenth century still accommodated many Ragnarǫk traditions, suggesting a continuous handing down of the myth (351-2). It was the nature of Christian eschatology, with its repeated reference to life in paradise, that promted Snorri to include in his Edda a passage concerning heaven and hell (352-3). Gylfaginning, too, contains Christian influences, such as the term vistir for the mansions of Gimlé, the same word also used in the homilies to refer to the heavenly dwellings (354). The possibility of Iranian influence on pre-Christian Scandinavian eschatology is discussed with reference to the Iranian traditions of a bridge and fire separating this world from the next, which fire has been compared with Vsp 39 (355). The introduction of Christian eschatology led to syncretic versions of the Ragnarǫk tradition.

author: Jeske, Hans
title: Zur Etymologie des Wortes Muspilli
publication: Zeitschrift für deutsches Alterthum und deutsche Literatur
abstract: Summarises the various twentieth-century views (425-32). Revives the mundus-theory, pointing out that Latin loans in OHG lost their nominative suffices -um, -us and that the OHG Christian poem Memento mori uses the word mundus unapocopated, while a fifteenth-century source uses mund (inflected as munde). Proposes a compound based on mundus and spell “Weltuntergang, Vernichtung der Welt” (432-4).

author: Kolb, Herbert
title: Vora demo Muspille: Versuch einer Interpretation
abstract: The 1832 publication of Muspilli, with “. . .Dichtung vom Ende der Welt” in its subtitle, was suggestive of the word’s meaning in its title. Despite many studies since, the notion that the word muspilli is central to an understanding of the poem has remained (2). In all its etymological studies, the word’s immediate context has received little attention (3). The sentence “dar ni mac denne mak andremo helfan vora demo muspille” makes little sense if “Weltuntergang” is the meaning of muspilli (4). Moreover, OHG helfan cannot be used against something: that would be helpan wið across the West Germanic languages (4-5). Helfan vora demo muspille must be locative “help before the muspilli.” The context then suggests the meaning “(Jüngstes) Gericht” (5). A twelfth-century Bavarian homily has an analogous sentence, where it says that “[a]n der stete mac niemen dem anderen niht gehelfen,” referring to the Last Judgement (6). The use of the word mak here refers to the legal custom of the Magschaftseid, in which a group of kinsman could plead the accused free by oath; in other words, even the surest of methods will not help in the Last Judgement [PS: in fact, mak is just the natural summarising translation of the source’s pater, filius, amicus, frater in PL 83.1224B or pater, filius in Ziolkowski, Cambridge Songs: “Adhortatio iuventum” [PL 94.560A] (6-8). The legal term pagan “bring forward a lawsuit” confirms this legal context (8-9). The ordeal of the duel, which could be demanded if no evidence was brought forward against the accused, is similarly evoked in the war between Elias and the Antichrist. However, Elias’s defeat shows that not even this man of God can set man free at the Last Judgement; his fight is therefore no iudicium Dei (9-14). Relevant for Muspilli is that both Magschaftseid and the ordeal by duel are well-attested in High German regions and particularly in Bavaria (14-15). The poet expresses further the helplessness of the soul at the Last Judgement (15). The work should be regarded as an exhortary work or homily (16-17). Schmeller’s textual conjecture sar so daz leads to the unattested notion that the world conflagration came about through Elias’s blood (17). A Turkish parallel of the duel is studied, which, however, contains Buddhist influence; the conclusion is again that the fire from Elias’s blood is doubtful (18-21). Instead, the conflagration results from Elias’s defeat (21-3). The unity of the poem is studied (24-6). The premise of Muspilli is the existence of a neutral waiting-place after death where Judgement Day is awaited. The poem therefore opens with an attempt by the devil to prevent the judgement from taking place (27-8). The central message of the work, however, is that the soul’s destiny is determined by its works on earth (28-9). The poem’s theology, premises, and legal references are extensively summarised (30-2).

author: Krogmann, Willy
title: Mudspelli auf Island: Eine religionsgeschichtliche Untersuchung
abstract: Identifies Mudspelli in the Heliand as the person Christ rather than the chronological or thematic “end of times.” The Heliand poet three times equates the end of times with a genitive construction referring to a power: “mudspelles megin. . . endi thesaro uueroldes,” “drohtines craft. . . duomdag the mareo,” and “maht godes. . . the lazto dag.” This suggests that drohtin, god, and Mudspilli are one and the same person. While most scholars have held that the word has to have chronological reference so that “Mutspilli cumit / an thiustrea naht” would translate 2 Peter 3.10 “the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night” [PS: so Cleasby-Vigfússon 440; but 1 Thess 5.2-4 may be more of an immediate source], Krogmann takes it to incorporate also Revelation 3.3 and 16.15 “I will come like a thief” (7-10). Some Latin and OHG textual parallels are cited as a first step towards finding the poem’s sources (10-11). The word Mudspelli may be read as an instrumental compound “mouth-destroyer, mouth-killer” in the sense “he who destroys with his mouth.” The t has in one instance replaced the d in dissimilation, and the second element of the compound is cognate with ON spiller [PS: sic; he probably means spillir] “destroyer, killer” and implies a PG *spelþjaz. The ll form may be defended by the possibility that it was taken up in Old Saxon before 1000, possibly about 800 (11-14). Christ kills with his mouth according to Isaiah 11.4, 2 Thessalonians 2.8, and Revelation 1.16, 2.12-16, 19.15-21; and Bede discusses the image (ed. Giles 12.346) (Krogmann 14-16). OE has a parallel muðbana (Bwf 2079) as well as handbana; it is therefore likely that OS knew a concept *mudbano alongside its handbano (17). The Eddas refer mostly to Múspells heimr, synir, lyðir, or megir. In SnE, the locative expression refers to a location before the creation of the world from which the sparks originate that keep southern Ginnungagap from freezing, and that later serve to illuminate the earth. Sun and moon also originate from this location (18-19). Múspellr’s sons, kinsmen, or people are prophesied to ride Bifröst at Ragnarök and fight the Æsir (19-21). Snorri mainly bases his account on Vsp 51 (48). The other mss of SnE tend to alter these references: Muspellz megir is four times replaced by Muspellz synir and once by Muspell; Muspellz heimr is replaced by Muspell on two occassions. Rather than being a personal name, as Neckel believes, this is a simplification of the place-name; Snorri will not have used one name for both locative and personal reference (21-3). The word Múspell is unlikely to be derived from muspel “bittern” because it occurs in an apocalyptic context like the West Germanic concept of Mudspelli (23-4). His synir enter through a crack in the heavens at the end of time and wear very bright clothes; this is reminiscent of Revelation and does not occur elsewhere in ON mythology. More striking is the remark in the Codex Upsaliensis that it is best to be in Gimlé with Surtr, which has accordingly been edited out of the other mss. Surtr’s appearance in Gimlé can be explained only with reference to his origin through Múspell from Mudspelli (24-5). Vsp, Lokasenna and SnE do not agree in their representations of Múspell. The connection with Surtr, however, is universal. Múspellz heimr is hot and hellish according to SnE. The region plays a role in the creation of Ymir and thus of the world, and separately of the sun, moon, and stars. Surtr is the leader of Muspells megir. He joins battle from the south (Vsp 50; Krogmann 25-6). These megir own Naglfar; but Vsp 51 says that Hrymr steers it, and the sons are not mentioned. Several editors have therefore altered the direction of the ship; but if Hrymr and Múspells synir are all in the ship together, the original reading makes good sense. Nonetheless, the Naglfar stanza and the Surtr stanza must be read as two versions (26-7). Incidence suggests that the Naglfar-version is the elder, by Snorri’s time largely superseded by the Surtr-version. The Múspells synir are in Vsp also referred to as fífs synir, “giants’ sons,” suggesting that the poet considered Múspellr a giant. Braune believed that Múspell gained a topographical meaning only in SnE, but this is false. Neckel has shown that the author of the Codex Upsaliensis did not regard the name as personal (27-9). The Surtr-version came to be dominant because it formed a prerequisite for the connection between Surtr and Múspells synir. A giant Múspell has no function if Surtr is already the leader of the band; the person Múspellr thus had to go, and his name remained only in the name of Surtr’s home. This process confirms the above supposition on the chronology of the Naglfar and Surtr versions (29). In order to find out why Surtr and the Múspells synir are combined, it has to be established what was told of Surtr before this happened. In this respect Vsp 53, Vsp 47 according to the Hauksbók, Vafþrúðnismál 17-18, Fáfnismál 14-15, and SnE 265, 50-1 are of central importance. Fjölsvinnsmál 24 may be reconstructed to shed light on the question (30-2). All suggest that Surtr is a fire giant, and so does Bergbúaþáttr. Surtr’s name is suggestive of fire, since the OE Christ speaks of black fire. Surtr’s sword, in SnE said to be a sword of fire, is in Vsp said to have been shining with the sun of the battle-gods, which is a reference to the fire of Múspellsheim, since it is from the sparks of that region that the sun was formed (32-3). Surtr is from the south (Vsp, Lokasenna, SnE) or from deep inside the earth (Háleygjatal, Bergbúaþáttr); Olrik is wrong when he considers the depths more authentic than the south, since Scandinavians would always expect a fiery region in the south (33). This original portrayel of Surtr matches the eschatological image of Christ, who also comes with fire and sword (2 Peter 3.10-11; Muspilli 55-6; Revelation 8.6ff.; 9.13ff; 22.7ff.; Krogmann 34). These things explain why Surtr is associated with the Múspells synir and why the Surtr version has come to replace the Naglfar version of the narrative. If a person *Múspellr did not come with Surtr, then he came from the east in Naglfar; and the personal genitive Muspellz ?forbids the possibility of Múspellr the giant (34-5). This genitive was taken directly from OS, to judge by linguistic criteria. This genitive yields a neuter noun with nominative Múspell and dative Múspelli or Múspell, but these forms all depend on the Surtr-version of the tradition, since the Naglfar-version would yield *Múspellr (35-6). Christian motifs are studied (37-58). The SnE reference to Surtr in Gimlé already echoes the New Jerusalem, and so do Snorri’s descriptions of this hall, which is also mentioned in Vsp. The question now is to what extent Gimlé was based on the New Jerusalem (37-8). The descriptions of the hall closely match those of the Heavenly Jerusalem in Revelation (38-40). Finnur Jónsson has explained the name Gimlé as gim-hlé “fire-roof,” suggesting that this hall is fire-proof. The “Christian stanza” of Vsp has typically been considered an interpolation, but it appears instead to have been overlooked by the Codex Regius copyist because the two stanzas begin in nearly the same way.
