Vsp in skamma also has two obviously Christian stanzas (40-2). The last-but-one stanza of Vsp speaks of a judgement, a Christian concept in this context (43). Dreki, used in this stanza, is a Christian loan and does not occur before 1000 (43-4). The eschatological stanza 45 has been traced to Isaiah 19.19; Mark 13.7f, 12; Matthew 24.6,8; Luke 21.9f.; but Revelation 17.1ff. and 18.2f. likewise appear to have been formative (44-5). Degeneration among men is out of place in Ragnarök, since the mythology is about the fates of gods not men; it is therefore the more clearly Christian. The falling of the heavenly bodies is also Christian, while Fenrir’s part in these matters reflects the original tradition (45). SnE interprets the tradition when it has Fenrir eat the moon; originally, both wolves are after the sun. Snorri’s alteration draws on Matthew 24.29 and Revelation 6.12f. (45-7). Finally, the gjallarhorn is an echo of the trumpets in Revelation (47-8). While Olrik mentioned the world fire as a Christian element, Ranisch and Braune have rebutted this theory. Apart from the four elements of Muspelli, the Last Judgement, the falling of the heavenly bodies, and the trumpet, the Eddic tradition contains no Christian elements (48). Sievers has attempted to distinguist between Norwegian and Icelandic elements of Vsp on the basis of vowel quality; he believed that most of the Poetic Edda is Norwegian, though this view has not found general acceptance (48-53). This type of analysis, however, is most dubious (53-4). Sievers does classify the stanzas on the vice in the last days and the darkening of the heavenly bodies as Icelandic, while he considers their authorship various. However, the Gimlé stanza is classified as Norwegian, so that a purely Icelandic borrowing of the Christian elements is impossible (54-6). The various Christian elements must have been borrowed alongside each other, since in their poetic context they no longer represent Christianity, but they are nevertheless presented in conjunction with one another (56-7). And indeed, the Codex Upsaliensis line “bezt er at vera a gimle meðr svrti” proves this connection. In whatever region the borrowing took place, the Muspilli-element was borrowed together with the other Christian elements (57-8). The genitive Múspellz must be a direct Saxon borrowing (59). The history of the Icelandic conversion is analysed to discover where the element was introduced; it is concluded that the borrowing is Icelandic and from the first generation of missionary work (59-74).

author: Krogmann, Willy
title: Muspilli und Muspellsheim
abstract: Summarises Mudspelli auf Island, and appends evidence that the interpolation Muspilli II is a direct translation from OS, in which the word muspilli was borrowed without Bavariisation (107-9).

author: Martin, E.
title: Muspilli
publication: Zeitschrift für deutsches Altertum und deutsche Literatur
abstract: While defining muspilli as as pagan-originated word for “Weltbrand” right at the outset, Martin observes that the origin of the first element of the compound has found no scholarly agreement (186). The presence of a dental consonant in the Old Saxon forms of the word demonstrates that this is the older form: it would have disappeared rather than come about in this context (186-7). MHD mot “schwarze torfartige erde” and English mud and moat are proposed as cognates (187-8).

author: Pope, John C.
title: Homilies of Ælfric: A Supplementary Collection
abstract:
From the introduction, the section entitled “Ælfric’s Rhythmical Prose” (105–136):

Opens with a historical account of scholarship on rhythmical prose, which soon comes to focus on the question whether it concerns embellished prose (as Pope holds) or debased verse (as some early scholars held). It has been proposed by Gerould that Ælfric imitated Latin conventions of prose with rhythmical organized clause endings, but Pope argues against this: Latin devices of this type are found equally in all of Ælfric’s prose, not just the rhythmical type; their occurrence is rare enough that it may be coincidence; and the two-stress phrases typical of Ælfric’s style are found in Old English verse but not in Latin prose. Pope proposes that Ælfric’s prose imitates the spirit of embellished Latin prose style, not the form (108–109). Bethurum has proved Gerould wrong, and McIntosh has returned scholarly attention to the form rather than the inspiration; Pope’s description largely follows McIntosh (109).

The difficulty of studying Ælfric’s early experiments with rhythmical prose follows from the commonly overlooked fact that ordinary prose, too, has devices like rhythmical balance and alliteration (109). Some passages in the Catholic Homilies have more regular rhythm and alliteration than others, and these elements exist even in homiletics predating Ælfric; “Ælfric was regularizing something already indigenous in sermons” (109–111, quotation at 111). Ælfric is more consistent in metrical pairing than Wulfstan, which is intermittent, episodic; Ælfric’s rhythmical prose more closely resembles verse (112–113).

The Second Series of Catholic Homilies show the first specimens of the form, with six items employing it more or less continuously, and it turns up sporadically or intermittently in another half dozen. The manuscript used by Thorpe even uses half-line pointing in a passage of Cuthbert (114). McIntosh counts an average of seven syllables per half-line in Oswald, and never fewer than five; Cuthbert and De passione Domini fall at the lower end of the range, yielding a cramped line. This suggests Ælfric tried more closely to emulate verse in his first experiments (114–115); Pope even believes he has identified a few lines in Cuthbert experimenting with other conventions (115–116).

Pope defines Ælfric’s rhythmical prose as usually having two stresses per “verse,” sometimes three; the placement of the stressed positions is unpredictable and follows from the contours of prose. Stretches of Cuthbert correspond to Sievers types with some additional anacrusis at times, but the introduction to Old the Old and New Testament is more representative, with more syllables and more metrical freedom, so that the comparison with Sievers types falls flat (117–118). Heightened passages may approach more closely the poetic conventions (118).

Pope reasserts McIntosh’s syllable count: Ælfric’s rhythmical prose averages just under seven per halfline, with typical lower and upper bounds at five and nine (occasional extremes at three and twelve) whereas Beowulf has fewer than five and Maldon barely more than five (118–119).

Pope discusses longer lines and some irregularities; Brandeis held that lines in Judges were based on biblical verses, and Old English lines were cut short accordingly (120). [But I thought Bible verses were not introduced until later, PSL.] Pope finds evidence of similar practices (120–121).

Ælfric’s lines are generally end-stopped, which makes them firmer units than in poetry; his half-lines are defined by phrasing just as in the poetry (122). His diction is prosaic; he uses few poetic formulae, and no kennings or other poetic compounds, or even variation (122–123). Two thirds of the lines follow verse positioning of alliteration (according to Brandeis), the remainder diverge in various ways (123–124). Lines without alliteration amount to three percent if we accept the alliteration of “minor syllables” (124–125). Ælfric’s imprecise metrical specification leads to an unclear boundary between what should be regarded as stressed and/or alliterating or not; this problem is discussed at some length with examples from Edmund (125–128).

Ælfric’s convention allows sc, sp, and st to alliterate with each other as well as with s, though he does prefer exact matching especially with st; this state of affairs resembles that of the late poetry (128–129). Words with hl, hr, and sometimes hw alliterate with those beginning in the second consonant, and there is some further inexactness of h and other sounds (129–131). Pope goes on to discuss the devices of repetition and paranomasia for the linking of halflines (131–133), and the occasional linking of subsequent lines (134–135).

Discusses his decision to print in metrical lines (135–136).

author: Neckel, Gustav
title: Studien zu den germanischen Dichtung vom Weltuntergang
series: Sitzungsberichte der Heidelberger Akademie der Wissenschaften
abstract: Studies contents and sources of Germanic eschatology, with a focus on the Scandinavian material. The harmonising tendencies of early scholarship were conclusively ended by Olrik’s study. It has rightfully been pointed out that both the world fire and Surtr as leader of the Múspellssynir occur already in the Poetic Edda (4). Olrik’s shortcoming is that he relies too heavily on Snorri’s perspective. Vsp keeps Surtr and the Múspellssynir apart on the evidence of stanza 51; rather than bringing them together, it has the animals move in from all peripheries to threaten the gods (4-5). Vsp and Gylfaginning agree in the main, but not in all things (5-6). Freyr’s “not knowing how to fight” at Ragnarök may be explained if the episode in which he lends out his sword is supposed to be related to one in which it is given away rather than borrowed to ensure his marriage. He may be supposed to foll by his own sword (6-10). Freyr is called biartr, and light shines from his sword; this theme of light makes him the natural opponent of Surtr (10-11). Another reading of Lokasenna is that Freyr does not know how to fight such a formidable enemy, which would be a reference to Freyr’s magic sword like the reference in the Surtr-stanza of Vsp. Freyr then fights both Surtr and the Múspellssynir; in any case, the mention of this troop may imply the inclusion of Surtr (11-12). The brothers ride Myrkvið yfir, and Myrkviðr is to the south of Scandinavia, so the Múspellssynir, like Surtr, come from the south, not the east (12). Their riding Myrkvið yfir may mean “over” rather than “through” the forest, as there is evidence that Ragnarök was thought to entail riders in the sky (12-13). This image unites Snorri and the earlier Helgakviða. Surtr’s leadership of the troop is therefore likely to be an old element. Fáfnismál speaks of Surtr doing battle with the Æsir on an island that is to be reached by way of Bifröst. Another thing Surtr and the Múspellssynir have in common is their nature as fire demons (13-14). The prevailing opinion is that Surtr leads the powers that come to do battle with the gods; but this is never made explicit in the sources. Surtr is mentioned either alone, but with the implication of a following, or together with the sons of Múspell; and the latter group are once mentioned alone. The conclusion must be that they always go together (14-15). An important obstacle to this conclusion has consisted in the two Vsp stanzas that have the two categories attack from different directions and by different means. Other Eddic poems do not have this confusion. Vsp, however, is itself a harmonisation of various material (15). The ship-motif appears to be an unrelated borrowing. The stanza in which it occurs emphasises the marine nature of the journey and the inclusion of Loki in the number of the fífls megir. Surtr is named alone because the mention of the Múspellssynir would decrease his majesty (15-17). The Vsp relationship between Surtr and the Múspellssynir, then, is loose, but not so loose that the implication of a connection in Lokasenna would be denied (17). Óðinn and Þórr die in grand narratives and are avenged; Freyr’s death is relatively inconspicuous and unavenged. By the same process, Surtr also loses significance. This suggests that the Freyr-Surtr strand is older than the other two (18). Several Eddic sources suggest that Freyr was the leader of the Ás-army; Surtr, by whom he is killed, is the corresponding general of the opposing force. The Óðinn-Fenrir opposition is a variant or parallel to the Freyr-Surtr battle, since there can be only one leader in the war. This suggests that the Freyr-and-Surtr tradition has different origins than the Óðinn-and-Fenrir narrative (18-19). A replacement of the Freyr-and-Surtr tradition by the other one explains why the Múspells synir are accompanied by Fenrir in Vsp. This accompaniment must be older than Vsp, as is the ride through the sky, since Fenrir also inhabits the sky as usurper of the sun. Both Múspellssynir and wolf are then put onto a ship when Vsp is composed (20). The opposition of the two camps, Freyr and the Æsir versus Surtr and the Múspells synir, is expressed through parallelism (20-1). Poetic style furthermore makes that the parties are often identified by either leader or army, seldom both (21). An elaborate construction is proposed in speculation that Freyr has a son, Vali, who avenges him after his fall (21-3). Since the Scandinavians were unfamilar with horseback armies until about 1100, it is concluded that the Surtr tradition, like that of the Múspells synir, was borrowed from the south (23). Codex Upsaliensis has þat eiga Muspellsmegir where the other MSS have þat á Muspell; uncharacteristically, a shift towards personification seems in place. It is furthermore the same early MS that has the unfamiliar phrasing fyrst var þó Muspellsheimr sá er svá heitir. The nominative Múspellr was expected in the possessive phrase (23-5).The unusual form Muspell suggests that Mudspelli was taken in as a foreign form. This can only be explained by the spread of cosmological verse from the German language area to Scandinavia, just as heroic poetry has moved that way (25). OHG and OS literature has several phrasal parallels with ON poetry; the concepts they express, then, must also be parallels (25-6). Fire is an attribute of the muspilli in the Muspilli and presumably in the Heliand. This shows two things: Surtr and Muspell belong together, and Snorri’s understanding of Muspellsheim as a world of fire has ancient roots. Fire and darkness co-occur in several West Germanic alliterative traditions (26-7). Muspilli 37-62 is identified as a separate poem [called das Eliasgedicht by Neckel, elsewhere Muspilli II] on account of its repetition of the Judgement Day motif (27-9). While there is no substance in Romantic beliefs that the battle in the Muspilli between Elias and Satan is a Christianisation of the Þórr-Miðgardsormr motif, it may be significant that both OHG and ON mythology speaks of battles in the air in a fiery context at the end of days. The concept of Muspilli is connected to Elias in OHG, and to Surtr in the north; both concern battles of a positive force (Freyr and the Christian soul respecively) in the face of an overwhelming fire demon. The solution is that the Muspilli poet interpreted his pagan material on the battle between the god Fro and a demon of fire Muspilli as the fight between Elias and the Antichrist (29-31). Muspilli II stands in the West Germanic tradition of alliterative poetry on Judgement Day (31). Thematic correspondences such as falling moons, however, do not prove a genetic relationship (32-4). Oral and literary transmission are hard to distinguish. Between Muspilli II and the Heliand, however, the muspilli element has to depend on written sources since both texts use it in a Christian-eschatological context, which was established after the pagan period. A cleric may have borrowed the pagan demon Muspilli to convey to a Germanic audience the Christian apocalyptic tradition (34-5). There was no need for such expedients in Anglo-Saxon England, where the conversion took place much earlier so that Christ could narrate the events in purely Christian terms (35-6). Neither the Heliand poet nor the Norse poets fully understood the concept of muspilli when the poems were given their extant forms; this confusion is reflected in the grammatical forms used—a genitive Muspellz suggestive of a person, the phrase þat á Múspell, a neuter occurrence in the Heliand (36-7). Germanic-Christian contact in the migration age could have led to the apocalyptic tradition among the pagan Germans (37-8). The fire motif may be used to demonstrate this. Olrik was wrong in his position that its Christian origins may be demonstrated using the Poetic Edda; he believed that the theme’s exclusive occurrence in Vsp demonstrated such a thing. The fire in Vsp, however, is different from that of the Last Judgement in that it ascends towards heaven instead of coming down from heaven (38-40). Immediately after the world is set fire to, it sinks into the sea. Olrik believed that this combination of water and fire, which occurs in many traditions both Eastern and Western, is no natural pair but a travelling motif (40-1). The world fire as such in Vsp has no direct connection with Christianity; the Judaeo-Christian world fire distinguishes itself by its judgemental character, lacking in the Nordic tradition (41-2). The army on horseback, not Scandinavian or even Germanic in origin, parallels the historical army of the Huns that in Heiðreks saga rides through the same Myrkviðr and sets things on fire. It is not credible that the Múspells synir would be based on the Huns of the poetry celebrating their wars, since the poetry is realistic and does not suggest mythologising; but it is likely that the name Myrkviðr came into the Eddic tradition in this way (42-3). Two elements of the Revelation are relevant: the locusts (9.3-12) and the army on horseback (9.14-19). The locusts have the appearances of centaurs, and thus present an image of riders in flight; the sons of Muspell, too, are dehumanised, on the evidence of their association with giants and with Fenrir (43-5). The horses of the Apocalypse are reminiscent of Norse tradition. These horsemen appear to fill the gap between Muspilli and Surtr (45-6). Revelation and the Germanic apocalypse may share a common source (46). Parallels may likewise be found for Surtr and his flaming sword; while the Vsp poet chose to exclude this latter element, he could not ban it out, since Snorri would bring it back in (46-7). More Caucasus-located traditions concerning fiery swords are mentioned and compared to the Surtr tradition (47-8). Surtr is no Icelandic invention; rather, he is a mythological kinsman of Loki. Both have reached the northwest from the Caucasus (48-9). The apocalyptic tradition of the north is thus a Gothic borrowing, but the defence against an overwhelming force is characteristically Germanic. While the semitic peoples regard the world fire as punishment and accept the according guilt, the Germani consider it a challenge and respond with warfare (49-50). This theme required an enemy for Surtr, which was found in Freyr; he in turn needed an avenger, Vali; and the airborne battle results from the need for an opposition to the sons of Muspell (50-1). The battle in the sky repeats the theme of the slain who continue their battles in a world above Miðgarðr. The apocalypse is a foreign myth, but it has been coloured by the Germanic spirit of war (51-2).

author: Schneider, Hermann
title: Muspilli
publication: Zeitschrift für deutsches Altertum und deutsche Literatur
abstract: Three allegations of non-Christian or pagan ideas in Muspilli have commonly been made concerning the fight between Elias and the Antichrist: it has been equated with Þorr versus Miðgarðsormr as well as with Freyr versus the fire demon [Surtr], while the third line of argument recognises in it a general Germanic spirit (1-2). It is common opinion that the theological layer is non-essential, and that the fight in ll. 37-62 is the real core of the work. [incomplete]

author: Würth, Stefanie
title: Ragnarök: Götterdämmerung und Weltende in der nordischen Literatur
publication: Old Norse Myths, Literature and Society: Proceedings of the 11th International Saga Conference 2-7 July 2000, University of Sydney
eds: Geraldine Barnes and Margaret Clunies Ross
publisher: Centre for Medieval Studies, University of Sydney
abstract: Draws a connection between the Breta sögur (the ON translation of Historia regum Britanniae) and Völuspá, which both occur in the Hauksbók. The Welsh tradition emphasised a central figure that would return from the dead and bring peace, thus establishing political continuity according to the native tradition as opposed to contemporary foreign influence; likewise Vsp expresses continuity in Norwegian kingship in the shape of a redeemer of the old religion (Baldr), and a referent in the shape of Óláfr Tryggvason, who was besieged at Svoldr but miraculously saved according to tradition.

author: Bonnemaison, Joël
title: Culture and Space: Conceiving a New Cultural Geography
abstract: Using field references from Oceania and the Pacific islands, this work emphasises the concept of territory (given a rather subtle definition between a physical area and the projection of a social organisation on pp. 114‒19) in the study of cultural geography. A particularly prevalent notion is that of reticulated space (i.e. a matrix or mesh network of places of more or less equal significance) as opposed to centre‒periphery societies (e.g. 8‒11). Mentions also examples of cultures that do not adapt to new geographical realities after migration or otherwise make agricultural decisions on cultural rather than environmental grounds (4‒6). Refers for early approaches to human and cultural geography to Gottfried Herder, who “emphasizes the role played by cultural communities in the construction of landscapes and spaces”; Carl Ritter, an environmental determinist (18); and especially Friedrich Ratzel, a geographic possibilist who believed peoples can liberate themselves from paths laid out for them by their environments; Ratzel was further interested in “diffusionism or propagation of cultural traits from an original hearth” (20). In France, geography began with Paul Vidale de la Blache, who was interested in physical space and regions (22‒7). In the US, Carl Sauer founded the Berkeley school of cultural geography, understanding geography as the imprint of Vidale de la Blache’s concept of genre de vie/lifeway onto landscape (28‒30). The tenets of the Berkeley school are humans as dwellers, landscapes as cultural imprints, visible cultural elements, and geographic elements of invisible culture (four headings, but there should be five, 30‒4).

author: Falk, Avner
title: Border Symbolism
publication: Maps from the Mind: Readings in Psychogeography
eds: Howard F. Stein and William G. Niederland
abstract: Immediately introduces himself as a psychoanalyst nutcase by summarising Niederland’s understanding of engagement with landscape as symbolic of the exploration of the mother’s womb, with rivers expressive of sexuality especially towards a sister (142‒3). Newly-discovered countries are often imagined as paradisal places (so America and California); these derive from infantile fantasies of life without pain (143). Friedman is cited for the idea that the bridge symbolises incest (143‒4). When Niederland and Friedman’s ideas are applied to borders, it becomes clear that territories on either side represent early childhood parental figures. A man crossing an international border may thus unconsciously be reminded of the border of incest with the mother, or else an early mother’s embrace of a new-born child (144‒5). Alternatively, borders may symbolise internal barriers, categories of “us” and “them” being projections of internal contradictions (145). A few examples from dreams and Old Testament passages are explained in sexual terms (145‒9). Don’t use this author. An appended chapter (151‒60) discusses reasons to cross back and forth across the Berlin Wall.

author: Michelet, Fabienne L.
title: Creation, Migration, and Conquest: Imaginary Geography and Sense of Space in Old English Literature
abstract:
Michelet’s theoretical framework builds on Le Goff (esp. ‘Discorso di chiusura’), Lefebvre (Production de l’espace) Martina Löw (Raumsoziologie), and (especially) Zumthor (Mesure du monde) to conceive of space as an organising principle (1‒18; Foucault’s ‘Of Other Spaces’ is also used). Anglo-Saxon space is conceived of as finite and enclosed, and OE terminology for space reflects this (19‒21). Like every world order according to Zumthor, those in Anglo-Saxon thought are based on the opposition centre‒periphery (25; contrast Bonnemaison). The Maxims are texts particularly obsessed with assigning everything a spatial home (26‒7). Demonising previous residents is one way of asserting one’s own rights over a territory; this othering occurs in Beowulf but also in Bede’s anti-Celtic doctrinal explications (27‒8).

[ch. 2: Ordering the World] Describes the anthropocentrism of divine creation in OE poetry (42‒4), and points out that it concerns transformation rather then ex nihilo creation (44‒9, with a discussion of the phrase idel and unnyt at 47‒9). Other creations are read as territorial expansions: Scylf’s political success culminates in the establishment of Heorot, which represents an encroachment upon Grendel’s territory, and Elene relates similar developments in Rome (49‒52). Architectural metaphors of creation are discussed (52‒5). Creation is expressed as enclosure, the creator encapsulating his work just as smaller entities in this world are limited by boundaries: the sea by the shore, and hell by its spaciousness [!citing Christ and Satan 719‒21, contrasting with everywhere else] (55‒60). For space to exist, it has to be both settled and demarcated according to Riddle 66 and passim in OE (60‒4). The empty seats in heaven suggest this (60‒2). Adam’s lament in GenB has spatial repentance in it (I would go to the bottom of the sea...) (63). The spatial consequences of the fall of the angels is further discussed in terms of Lucifer’s wish to establish his own kingdom (64‒8). The same narrative continues with Satan’s displeasure at Adam’s possession of his throne, his solution in having him expelled from his realm, and Eve’s vision in GenB (69‒72). The chapter as a whole emphasises the role, [set out in the introduction with reference to Zumthor (Michelet 11)] of narratives as [territorial claims and] articulations of spatial orders. Concerns regarding the control of space surface in OE creation narratives (72). The function of the building as the ultimate expression of a boundary, itself the corner-stone of spatial organisation and defender against chaos, is to receive more attention in chapter 3 (72‒3).

[ch. 3: The Centres of Beowulf] Asserting that “the centre is an essential element in any actual or imaginary spatial configuration” (75; contrast Bonnemaison), this chapter studies centre‒periphery thinking in Beowulf and Judith. One spatial element studied is the motif of stepping on the earth. A footnote gathers references to studies understanding Beowulf as geographically centred around the poles of good governance and monstrosity (76, note 7). Both Grendel’s mere and the dragon’s cave are geographically ambiguous: their paths are unknown, yet someone can always point them out; they are otherly places yet seemingly very near Heorot and Beowulf’s hall (80‒2). Similarly enigmatic places exist in Judith (82). The heroes’ and monsters’ abodes are not opposites in all things, and similarities are discussed (82‒7) before again announcing the topic of geographical ambiguity. In this section, Michelet pushes a reading of Beowulf’s central places (Heorot, Beowulf’s hall, Beowulf’s burial-mound) as sharing various characteristics (88‒9), again with a counterpart in Judith (89‒90). The ambiguity here mentioned consists in the similarities between the “good” and “evil” locales in Beowulf, leaving as the only contrast the characters inhabiting these spaces (91). Geographical centrality in the first half of Beowulf resides in Heorot, but the situation is complicated by the removal of the central power figure from that centre and Grendel’s move into it, in turn to be replaced by Beowulf (91‒3). The centre‒periphery contrast is not as strongly present in the second part of the poem; the centre is the dragon’s cave, in which it mirrors Heorot, later to shift to Beowulf’s mound (93‒4). The status of Beowulf and his men in Denmark as guests from afar is emphasised at a number of turns in the poem (95‒6); in so ‘invading’, Beowulf mimics Grendel’s usurpation of Heorot, Grendel who himself takes Hrothgar’s place. Although the centre is thus ambiguous, what is clear is that it is always under threat of hostile invasion (96). The ‘invasion motif’ is further studied from the perspective of the two queens and with regard to the Finn episode (97‒102). Physically looking at a foreign object within the context of society is presented as a way of taming it (102‒6). Monsters are discussed as inhabiting peripheral space (106‒13). Boundary crossings can serve to reinforce those boundaries (106‒9). Walking the land/verbs of treading are a way of asserting territorial control (109‒13).

[ch. 4: Localization and Remapping] This chapter focuses on topographical knowledge and representation. Strabo implies a connection between remote geographical origins and ugliness, while Bede describes the opposite ethnic appearance for Anglo-Saxons met by Gregory (115‒16). These contrary approaches reflect different opinions as to how peripheral Britain is, but both rely on geographical localisation for identification (116‒17). Classical views of the locality of Britain (117‒23) and its status as the most northerly country (117‒26) are discussed before Anglo-Saxon views are presented, represented by Bede, Ælfric, the Ohthere account in the Orosius, and Dicuil (126‒42). Cartography follows (142‒57).

[ch. 5: Integrating New Spaces] The plot of Guthlac A is summarised as a territorial disagreement between the saint and the demons of the wilderness (163‒4). Elene, Andreas, and Fates of the Apostles similarly document saintly aspirations to possess land, focusing on frontiers in the process; again, stepping on land is a means of territorial affirmation (164‒5 and ff. ~166‒72). Guthlac’s wilderness is ambiguous: although it is unpleasant at first, the saint comes to appreciate his environment (172‒4). Andreas has a curious line where the cannibals, thwarted by Andrew’s prayer, are said to take no joy in their homeland (line 1162b; Michelet 174). The landscape of Marmedonia is unpleasant at first, but the melting episode seems to improve it. Also, the same melting halfline also occurs in Guthlac A; the saintly actions thus improve the environment (175‒6). The journeying-motif is discussed at considerable length for each of the four poems, and it is emphasised that each of the saints travels with a distinct geographical goal in mind (176‒87). Territorial claims are supported by the demonisation of the original inhabitants (187‒90), the motif of treading the ground (190‒3), and a motif of paths and ways, which may be read as types of Christ the Way (193‒6, following Lisa Kiser in NM 85).

[ch. 6: Searching for Land] Following Howe/Battles, this chapter expresses a belief in an Anglo-Saxon migration motif. Migrations give expression to spatial organisation, territory, and heroic achievement, since the journey can be that (199‒200, 201‒2; so also Battles 59). Genesis A, Exodus, and Daniel emphasise national rather than individual agency in territorialism, underscoring a social group’s reliance on territory in the affirmation of a group identity (202‒4). The search for land is described from the expulsion through the Flood to Canaanism (204‒9), and the value of land possession is underscored with regard to the same texts and others (209‒14). Loss of land is often a punishment for sins (215‒18). Travels through peripheral spaces are ordeals expressive of faith[, whose successful completion can be seen as divine favour] (218‒22). Appropriating the land through ‘treading the land’ (223‒6) and ‘paths and ways’ (226‒30) are reprised with regard to the texts discussed in this chapter.

[ch. 7: descriptiones Britanniae, adventus Saxonum] Discusses perceived legitimacy and legitimisation of Anglo-Saxon control of England.

author: Power, Rosemary
title: Journeys to the North in the Icelandic Fornaldarsögur
abstract: Identifies in four fornaldarsögur a theme of Scandinavians travelling to the White Sea area to obtain something from a temple, and goes on to identify supposed elements of the tradition in earlier íslendingasögur and kings’ sagas. The fornaldarsögur in question are Sturlaugs saga starfsama, Bósa saga, Friðþjófs saga frækna, and Örvar-Odds saga. Obtaining a woman as a result of the journey to the north is a definite element of the tradition (13). The tradition is compared to French and Arabic tales (21-4).

author: Råberg, Per
title: The Space of Man: New Concepts for Social and Humanist Planning
abstract:
[On the whole, this volume has too strong a focus on architecture and urban planning to be of relevance to my work. I will point out some of the relevant passages.]

The second ~chapter/~part of this work studies the concepts of “the ecological man” and “ecobehavior”. These start from the assumption that human nature relies for its core on interaction with a local habitat aimed primarily at the survival not only of the self, but of the ecosystem. One’s actions and understanding of reality are affected by one’s relationship with one’s living space, a relationship that has its prime expression in space (41). The individual psychology is affected by the presence or absence of frictions in the living space (41‒2). The intergroup tensions that threaten life today derive from society’s development to the efficiency of large scale in the living environment, resulting in the loss of man’s ecological space (with its rootedness and the satisfaction of a smooth living environment) and ecological judgement. As a consequence of the disturbances in man’s ecosystem, he introduces false substitutes for happiness that provide no lasting solution. The author urges that societies should provide an inner ecosystem for man’s self-realisation (42‒3). Ecological identification is a process of bridging the gap between self and living space with the aim of achieving qualitative satisfaction. It is not complete until self and ecosystem reach a balance (46). Ecological identity is made up of the holistic (strives after experiential unity with the living space); social (experiential union with the collective); and subjective (satisfaction of individual biological and material needs) (46‒50). Ecological identity controls living space on three levels: the contemplative, the communicative, and the cognitive, in order of evolutionary development (50‒6). [Further subdivisions and schemata follow.] The evolution of space perception and interaction is discussed in great detail (65‒77). The drives that sustain human life in his ecosystem are the nutritive, the genetic, and the holistic (77‒85). All of the discussion up to this point feeds into a conclusion that ecological identity and awareness of reality do not converge seamlessly on account of the spatial dimension in which the human identity is anchored (ecoidentity). It is in the local-communicative area of life that space is most emphatically present in human behaviour (86). All three ecospaces (holistic, social, and subjective) can be divided into three concentric spheres: regional (diam. 5‒10km), local (1‒1.5km), and central (100‒150m) (89‒94, ranges at 95). The work now devolves into urban planning (95‒102). The third part of the volume is called “Man’s Aesthetic Space,” but I have lost all faith in finding any sense in this book beyond pp. 41‒50.

author: Ratzel, Friedrich
title: Politische Geographie
abstract: Over 600 pp. on the relationship between nation state and geography, seminal in its time for German-area geopolitics. His understanding of the field is one of land and people forming an organic unit.

author: Schjødt, Jens Peter
title: Horizontale und vertikale Achsen in der vorchristlichen skandinavischen Kosmologie
publication: Old Norse and Finnish Religions and Cultic Place-Names
publisher: The Donner Institute for Research in Religious and Cultural History
abstract: Argues that several critics have too readily posited a vertical axis from heaven through earth to the underworld, while outside Snorri, who is certainly influenced by his Christianity, there is no ON evidence for a heavenly dwelling. Instead, the vertical axis of Ásgarðr (or Miðgarðr) versus Útgarðr is primary. A vertical axis existed, but the gods were thought to inhabit the centre rather than the highest end of the axis. Molenaar and Meletinskij equate the horizontal north with the vertical below, and indeed there is a “natural” connection between the north and the underworld because of the harsh climate of the north (47). Snorri says that the road to Hel is to the north and downwards (37; Snorra Edda 49). Nature versus culture is no clear-cut opposition in Scandinavia, as nature was not considered necessarily hostile (51-3).

author: Simek, Rudolf
title: Elusive Elysia; or, Which Way to Glæsisvellir? On the Geography of the North in Icelandic Legendary Fiction
publication: Sagnaskemmtum: Studies in Honour of Hermann Pálsson
eds: Rudolf Simek, Jónas Kristjánsson, and Hans Bekker-Nielsen
abstract: Explores the mythological geography of the fornaldarsögur. Both sagas and non-fiction of the saga age describe Scandinavia and the North Atlantic fairly accurately, based on Icelandic travels; but scholarly texts base themselves on European learning, thus presenting an unrealistic topography of the same region. The parts to the northeast of Scandinavia are dealt with almost exclusively in the fornaldarsögur where exotic adventures are called for (247-9). Some Scandinavian travelling to the northeast did occur, but the reports of these were mingled with the fantastic accounts (251). The known regions were frequently used in the legendary sagas, whose authors will have had reliable reports of them but could not visit them themselves because of the political situation of Iceland at the time (251-2). Explored but forgotten lands like Vinland and Svalbarði entered the realm of myth; their topographical locations vary across the accounts (252). The legendary sagas discuss arctic regions not only as settings for fantastic adventures, but also from a desire to convey actual geographical information about them (252-3). Austrvegr, austrhalf, austrlönd refers to all the countries east of the Baltic. Several peoples were “known” north of the Gulf of Bothnia (254). Rússia took on different shapes and cannot always be equated with Garðaríki, “the Varangian empire of Novgorod.” Icelandic authors used Rússia as a setting of fantasy, the name not having any precise meaning in Iceland since Icelanders used Garðaríki for what in Fenno-Scandia was called Rússia (254-5). This name may also have given rise to Risaland, sometimes treated as distinct from Jötunheimr and sometimes apparently conflated (255-6). Rússia, Ymisland, and Kvenland are all on the border of theoretical accessibility (256-7). Several of the strange people from Latin tradition were accommodated here (257). Others were given places in the lands of the western North Atlantic, which, however, were sometimes themselves placed to the north of Siberia. The Latin authors all make these peoples native to India (257-64). Several peoples are also mentioned east of Bjarmaland. In the earlier sagas, Jötunheimr was everything north of Bjarmaland; later sagas specified further. One of the new substates of Jötunheimr was Glæsisvellir, based on heathen mythology and the paradisus terrestris (264). It is mentioned in Hervarar saga, Helga þáttr Þórissonar, Bósa saga, and Samsons saga fagra (and more? 264-5). Scandinavian mythology via Snorri was a main source for descriptions of this region; the Continental T-O map and fabulous tradition were others (265-7). Magog lived in this part of the world (267). Ódáinsakr is part of Glæsisvellir according to Hervarar saga; this place is mentioned also in Hálfdanar saga Eysteinssonar, Eiríks saga víðförla, and Saxo (269-70). While Hervarar saga locates Ódáinsakr in Jötunheimr in the northeast, Eiríks saga identifies it with the earthly paradise in the far east. The earthly paradise itself, however, was thought to be in India and depicted in northern Asia; the Scandinavian accounts therefore need not be aberrant (270). A harmonisation of fourteenth-century Icelandic saga geographies should be based on the T-O map (271-2). A map based on Claudius Clavus’s, such as the Skálhot map of Sigurður Stefánsson, is the closest existing representation of this geography (272-5).

author: Stein, Howard F.
title: Developmental Time, Cultural Space: Studies in Psychogeography
abstract:
Essays in the [theoretical] field of psychogeography [lifted from its activist/situationist context], defined as “people’s shared psychological representation or ‘map’ of the natural and social world, the developmental antecedents of that map, the group dynamics which forge and revise that common map, and the consequences in group and intergroup action of living according to that map” (3); the framework of psychoanalysis is applied to the landscape; “[e]nvironment is heir to psyche” (15, citing Stein 1983e, in Sociogenesis of Language and Human Conduct). In a new environment, “[o]ne externalizes one’s own sense of inadequacy and dislocation. It is as if to say: ‘There is not something disturbing about me; rather, something is wrong with them’” (5). Boundaries are an essential part of social consciousness (5‒6) and the key to psychogeography (18‒19). When travelling in hostile territory, “[t]here is perceived danger not only in being regarded as the enemy but in becoming that enemy” (7‒8, at 8).

[Ch. 1: The Scope of Psychogeography] The author emphasises projection of the agent’s inward state onto the outside world (15). Psychogeography relies on the Kantian notion that there is no neutral reality: the world is always mediated through the psyche (19). Popular culture is gradually [i.e. in the 1980s] becoming an accepted source of information about a group’s understanding of reality (19‒20). Metaphorical and spatial language seems an important source in the field, including the application of words for body parts to the landscape but also Freudian concepts like sexual fantasy, displacement, projection, and fear-wish (introduction, 19‒21, and passim). “[G]eography is largely a mythology of spatial reality, a fantasy about space” (21). Humans are given to the fallacy referred to as narcissism of place, a confusion of self and space that incorporates the latter in the former (22). Groups of people are spoken of as human bodies (flank, rear, heart, etc.); such metaphors grow more prominent as tensions rise (as in the Cold War) (26‒31). The author holds “the concept of projective identification, introduced by Klein (1946, 1955), to be crucial to our understanding of what, how, and why people invest unconscious aspects of themselves in space (i.e., spatial representations)” (33). The very notion of psychogeography suggests that we are further removed from the real world than we have hitherto believed (40‒1). “[W]e often think that we can live by group fantasy alone” (42). Every social group relates to groups of allies and enemies outside their geopolitical boundaries; the “bogeyman. . . enable[s] them to focus their sense of paranoid endangerment and thereby to be focally rational in other parts of their lives”, while idealized outside groups fulil a similar function (52‒3, at 53). Groups have a need for borders on “the truly primitive basis of the need for difference and differentiation, that is, for radical us‒them opposition” (55‒6). Territorialism is a displacement: “one fights for the symbol as if it were the thing symbolized” (56‒7, at 57). Homo monstrosus (see Malefijt 1968: Scientific American 219.4: 113‒18) is the exotic, disfigured person living outside the group boundaries; this is evident in Greek [and medieval] travelogues [and maps] as well as in the 1758 edition of Linnaeus’s classification of species, which lists homo monstrosus alongside homo sapiens as a separate species (63). Erikson observes that every social group takes itself as the norm, considering all outsiders aberrations; mythology and history are then invented to reinforce the in-group’s chosenness (64‒5; Erikson 1968, Identity, Youth, and Crisis p. 41). “The other” is a class regarded as more primitive than the barbarians, because it is sexually undifferentiated (65). The ethnocentric exaggerations of medieval mapmaking disappeared with the Renaissance, but Ebel asserts that it has “substituted a compulsive external accuracy for a true inward purgation” (66‒7, at 67; Ebel 1980, Mitteleuropa). Centredness of a group’s territory on a map is expressive of ethnocentrism, but it also expresses a fear of being on the outside, where (in the anthropomorphic language applied to social groups) a body is under constant threat from the outside (67‒8). Perceptions of mainland and island between people and locations are discussed; one’s relocation to a social island such as a peripheral workspace automatically leads to social disintegration; islands threaten the mainland, and islanders are ambivalent about the mainland (68‒78). In his conclusion to the first chapter as in his introduction, the author emphasises that psychogeography for him is an approach, not an attempt to splinter off into a new field (78‒9).

[Ch. 2: Misplaced Persons] discusses the emotional effects of moving on the migrant.

[Ch. 5: Us and Them: Group Identity and the Need for Enemies] War, though a “purge and rebirth through violence”, requires an other besides the self (182). The arms race of the Cold War transposed onto an individual in a psychotherapist’s office would lead to a diagnosis of paranoia or focal psychosis (183‒4). Intergroup conflict often has a parent in the “unconscious leap from the mind to society based on the fantasy of society-as-body (organism)” (185‒6, at 185). “We summon aggression into play to protect the social body and fend off if not attack in others outside that body what we cannot tolerate to incorporate within ourselves”; or, as Freud put it, neighbour feuds and ridiculing are “a convenient and relatively harmless satisfaction of the inclination to aggression, by means of which cohesion between the members of the community is made easier” (1930: “Civilization and Its Discontents”, trans. 1961: 114) (186). Differences in outsiders are exaggerated—the homo monstrosus model—in an attempt to resolve a culture’s own conflict of identity; this eventually leads to dehumanisation (187). What the individual needs is “a good enough enemy”: “a separate object that is used as a reservoir to store and absorb all of one’s own negated elements” (189‒9, at 189), which inherits all childhood “environmental failure” and is selected by one’s social context “to represent. . . all intolerable persecutory material from those early object relations. ‘The enemy’ is experienced as embodying all that one must rid oneself of yet simultaneously cannot do” (189). In the Greek poetry of Constantinos Cavafy, the failure of the barbarian army to show up leads to disappointment on the part of their adversaries, because their solution has been taken away (180‒90). “Those groups from which we most passionately distinguish ourselves are those with which we are most inseperately bound” (193); “The enemy, in essence, wears our disavowed features: that is the psychic function of the enemy” (195). The remainder of the work focuses heavily on US‒Soviet relations and rapprochement: “grieving over what we cannot become or reverse” and the recognition that humanity unites us all lead to an extension of the cultural group to include all humanity (at 209).

author: Storm, Gustav
title: Ginnungagap i Mythologien og i Geographien
abstract: Adam of Bremen voiced the medieval notion that north of Norway is to be found a place of ice and darkness leading to an abyss (340-1). His source must have been Danish (341-2). This notion corresponds to the Eddic idea of a void called Ginnungagap that separated a world of of heat in the south from a world of cold in the north; where Ymir’s body was placed came to be the world as we know it, but beyond his body the void may still be found (342-3). In the later Middle Ages, the name Ginnungagap was mapped onto a more westerly region. Before the North Cape was passed by ship, the unexplored northeastern expanse was identified with Jötunheimr; after 880, when this was achieved and Bjarmaland had been visited, the mythical place moved north; this may be seen, for instance, in Adam of Bremen, and the contemporary Historia Norvegiae similarly locates giants between Iceland and Bjarmaland. Factual details concerning icebergs and the like were mixed in from a knowledge of the Svalbarði region. The northern cartographical tradition picked up on the tradition, connecting the newly-discovered North Atlantic lands to Scandinavia by way of a northern stretch of land. This notion survived until 1596, when the Dutch settled Spitsbergen and distinguished it from Greenland, so that Scandinavian conceptions had to be remapped once more (344-5). The northern continental link between Scandinavia and Greenland, and even between the new Atlantic lands and Africa, was conceived under influence of the European tradition of the three continents, combined with the new discoveries of lands that stretched far south. The question arose where the outer sea came in from beyond the new countries. Four beliefs existed: between Africa and the new lands; between Vínland and Markland; between Greenland and its southern neighbour; and between Vínland and Greenland, a sound that one source called Ginnungagap (Grönl. hist. mind. 3.224). It is thus that Ginnungagap found its ultimate position on the map (between Greenland and the American continent) (345-8). The postscript counters the argument posited elsewhere that the warm and cold streams of the sound between Vínland and Markland linked this location with Ginnungagap (348-50).

author: Weibull, Lauritz
title: De gamle nordbornas väderstrecksbegrepp
abstract: Present-day orientation is based on sunrise at the equinoces. The 45-degree aberration (so specified on p. 303) in northern Germanic geography according to Alfred/Ohthere, Adam of Bremen, and the later Icelandic Knytlinga saga and the geographical treatise in AM 194, 8vo [in Alfræði Íslenzk vol. 1] (292-303). Medieval Icelandic topography cannot be separated from the European cartographical tradition, consisting in a tripartite orbis terrarum surrounded by a world ocean (299-301). This view was accepted in Iceland as long as it matched experience, but in the course of the North Atlantic discoveries it had to be emended. Like Adam, the Icelanders did not abandon the classical view altogether but brought the two sources into unison by the introduction of a great stretch of land bringing Siberia and Africa together by way of the new western lands (301-2). Isidore’s geography is essential for an understanding of the Icelandic terminology. He has Asia stretch from south to north, Europe from north to west, and Africa from west to south. The Icelanders have made Isidore’s north northeast, his south southwest, and his west northwest (Alfræði Íslenzk 1.8,10). This must be explained by the scribe’s confrontation with two different semantic sets for the same directional terms. Not knowing where his original was drawn up, he took its terminology to be Icelandic and retranslated the corresponding terms (302-3). The classical semantics became the terminology of the Church, whose northernmost vestige was the archbishopric Hamburg-Bremen, from which Adam set out to Denmark. The divider between the Christian world and the barbarians was the Store Bält between Fy and Själland. The northern directional semantics were gradually “corrected” from the south: Saxo Grammaticus used the southern terminology 75 years after the first Scandinavian map was produced in Lund, the new Christian centre of the Nordic world (303-5). In folk culture, the Scandinavians have a tendency to the 45-degree aberration even today (305). Ptolemy described a similar rotation of the Danish islands (305-7). He must therefore have used a source that used a southern orientation but that was misinterpreted as having a Scandinavian orientation (307). This suggests that the Scandinavians used this aberrant navigation already in the second century CE (307-8). Finnur Jónsson and Fridjof Nansen believed that the Scandinavian orientation depended on the Scandian western coastline, which has a vague northerly but more accurately northeasterly direction; but this cannot be correct, since the same practice occurred throughout Scandinavia. The solution must instead be sought in megalithic structures and early ritual (308). Megalithic dolmens vary in orientation, but their short sides typically fall within the ranges east-to-south and west-to-north. The entrance is mostly between east and south, and mostly around southeast (308-9). Grave structures are a second, younger type of structure (3000-2000 BCE). They are typically oriented northeast-southwest, with an entrance to the southeast (309). Early Germanic ritual favoured the southeast. Prokopios (sixth century CE) described a ritual among the inhabitants of “Thule” in which someone is sent to a mountaintop to watch for the sun to return after its long midwinter absence; when he saw the first sunrays, there would be five days’ feasting until the first sunrise. Thietmar of Merseburg (eleventh century) described a sacrificial feast among the Danes every ninth Epiphany (309-11). Both these feasts take place near the end of the darkness surrounding the winter solstice, when the sun is longest in the southeast. The difference between southern and northern orientation, then, is that the southern orientation is based on the points of sunrise at the equinoces, while the northern orientation is based on the point of sunrise at the winter solstice (311). The rising sun of the Christian-eschatological context was bound to the east, and hence the directional semantics changed with the introduction of Christianity; but the winter feast remained, now in Christian guise (312).

author: Veitch, Russell, and Daniel Arkkelin
title: Environmental Psychology: An Interdisciplinary Perspective
abstract: Apparently written as a textbook, this volume has a short section on territorialism (262‒6) that may be of relevance. It focuses on how more emphatic boundaries are normally placed by homeowners who are in a neighbourhood for the long haul, and reports on homeowners’ reflections on such measures and correlations with burglary.

author: Antón, Teodoro Manrique
title: Vinr em ek vinar míns: Guðrún Gjúkadóttir in Gísla saga and Íslendinga saga
abstract: Studies dream-visions in these two sagas and their heroic background. Stanza 27 contains a denial by the evil dream-woman of a prophecy by the good one, representing a breach of custom (2). Discusses the various ways in which the last line of this stanza has been read and interpreted (2-3). Since Guðrún and Brynhildr’s conversation in the river is often taken as a model for the women’s overheard conversation in Gísla, they may also have been used by its Christian author as the model for the dream-women, Guðrún having received a certain pietisation while Brynhildr remained one of Óðinn’s girls (4). The allvaldr alda must be Óðinn (5). Guðrún Gjúkadóttir appears in a dream in Íslendinga saga (7). This suggests an interest in the heroic subject matter in thirteenth-century Iceland, a revival which would have betrayed its Christian context. Guðrún’s hybrid figure in Íslendinga saga confirms this (8).
comments: Given at the Thirteenth International Saga Conference in Durham and York (6-12 August 2006).

author: Hopkes, Siegfried Gebhard
title: Friesland–England: Kulturelle und geschichtliche Beziehungen; Sprachliche Verwandschaft
abstract: A study on the linguistic and cultural connections between the Frisians and the Anglo-Saxons, as well as between the Frisians and the English after the Anglo-Saxon period. Has an amateurish feel to it: poor translations, few notes. About half the volume consists of lists of lexical correspondences between present-day Frisian and present-day English.

author: Haugen, Odd Einar
title: Grunnbok i norrønt språk
abstract:
A thorough, yet accessible and well-written reference phonology and grammar of Old Norse.

Phonological and grammatical principles are explained patiently for those with no linguistic background, generally with reference to Norwegian. Although the book is set up as a reference grammar, each chapter ends with a series of questions or simple exercises that test whether the material has been understood and committed to memory. As a reference work it takes its cues mainly from Noreen and Iversen, though in some particulars (e.g. resolution in consonant clusters) it contains more detail than either. In terms of total scope it probably eclipses Iversen, but certainly not Noreen. Very useful as a primary reference grammar or grammar textbook, to be supplemented by Noreen when greater detail is needed.
comments: More accurately, this is the fourth ed. (2001), rev. impression (2006).

author: Berger, Alan J.
title: Text and Sex in Gísla saga
abstract: Identifies chapter two of Gísla in AM 556a, 4to as distasteful and distorted; argues that this narrative is the result of the compiler/abbreviator trying to solve a lacuna like that found in the longer version (AM 149 fol. and related witnesses). Chapter two should therefore not be used to explain later events, and the longer version is the more authentic.

author: Campbell, Kathryn S.
title: Gisla
abstract: Argues that Gísla derives its structure from parallelism in narrative strands, called þættir by Campbell. The dream-women “echo the ambiguity of the opening chapters, while the real women provide most of his [Gísla’s] support” (246).

author: Clover, Carol J.
title: Regardless of Sex: Men, Women, and Power in Early Northern Europe
abstract: Notes the gender references of blauðr and hvatr. Auðr gains masculinity (becomes a hvatr) by hitting Eyjólfr in the face; the latter, by contrast, becomes a blauðr by the same event. In his reaction, wishing to kill Auðr despite her sex, he redefines her as a hvatr, but his men correct this interpretation (363-5). Female power in medieval Iceland is usually described as restricted to the household, while man rules out of doors. Such is too binary a distinction. Landnámabók, sagas, and skaldic identity tell of some rather forceful women. Some political influence also existed. Some women were buried with “male” grave goods (weapons etc.). How important was sex as compared with wealth, social standing, and personality? Law and reality seem to have diverged; and law knows regional differences (365-9). Grágás knows the possibility of treating a woman as a juridical man in exceptional cases. In a society that admits such things, the distinction between sex and gender appears inappropriate: if biological sex does not determine juridical sex, then what does it detrermine? This seems to suggest that gender is more important than sex, or that the two are indistinct. Cleasby-Vigfusson suggests that a word like blauðr refers to sex when used sex-appropriately, but to gender when used sex-inappropriately. However, ON had one word for both concepts, suggesting that the two were indistinct, and the compound notion lay closer to MnE “gender” than to “sex,” as the sagas’ “exceptional” women demonstrate. Female masculinity is often admired by the author, as is clear from such epithets as drengr. “This is a world in which masculinity always has a plus value, even (or perhaps especially) when it is enacted by a woman” (369-72). The nature, fixed or flexible, of masculinity is studied through a discussion of its strongest field, insults. Níð, an insult suggesting sexual penetration of the insultee and thereby effeminacy, was severely punishable—by full compensation or death (372-5). However, the status of such insults has often been exaggerated: other types of insult are just as frequent in the sources. Níð is an accusation of powerlessness but, importantly, the criterion is the continuum blauðr-hvatr, not the dichotomy male/female (375-7). Bodies need not be viewed as essentially male or female: medical views are beginning to emerge of humanity as “one sex,” in which view the sex of a body is secondary to its existence (377). In mythology, the respective appropriation of different body parts is more flexible. Vagina, “sword sheath,” was in Latin also used for anus. ON sources conflating the two body parts suggest a one-sex understanding, in which the social dimension of gender mattered more than the biological distinction of sex (378-9). They mention femininity more often in relation to men than to women, and masculine behaviour is universally praised while effeminate behaviour is denounced, irrespective of sex. There was only one gender, and it was closest to our “masculine” (379). Femininity was detested not so much for itself but for its powerlessness. If a social binary is to be proposed, it is not male/female or masculine/feminine, but rather able-bodied men (and exceptional women)/everybody else (379-81). The humiliation of a man by a woman, such as that of Eyjólfr by Auðr, places him not at her level but below her; and this everpresent possibility may have given Scandinavian gender its edge (381). Men often shift into the feminine category in old age. It is often women who deride such old men. A proverb calls it fitting for the infirm elderly to incite, a role traditionally feminine, thus comparing the tongue and the sword (381-5). The courtly tradition shifted the boundaries between what was considered masculine and what feminine; it is possible that the two-sex model was not widespread until the eighteenth century (385-6).

author: Foote, Peter
title: Three Dream-stanzas in Hrafns saga Sveinbjarnarsonar
publication: Sagnaskemmtum: Studies in Honour of Hermann Pálsson
eds: Rudolf Simek, Jónas Kristjánsson, and Hans Bekker-Nielsen
abstract: Associates the verses in this saga with the Sólarljóð tradition.

author: Grønstøl, Sigrid Bø
title: Kjærleik og ættekjensle i konflikt: Om kvinnesyn og helteideal i Gisle-soga
abstract: Studies the role of women in Gísla and their function in the portrayal of the hero. Shows that Auðr answers to a thirteenth-century ideal of women, while Þordís breaches the code.

author: Harry, Margaret Rose
title: Prophetic Dreams and Other Forms of Anticipation in Old Icelandic Heroic Poetry
abstract: Focusses in particular on dreams in the Poetic Edda, but has a chapter (ch. 2) on “Prophetic Dreams in the Sagas” (30-50). Prophetic dreams in the Íslendingasögur differ from those in heroic poetry and fornaldarsögur in that they are less dependant upon oral tradition and thus better able to arrange their material according to their own purposes, resulting in the dreams assuming essential significance to the narrative where this is not true for the heroic material (30). Dreams in Gísla saga are discussed (30-7). Both in Gísla and in the heroic poetry, there is a connection between foresight, dreaming, and/or wisdom (31-2). Since vivid dreams are typical of tragic characters in the literature, the dreams may point to psychological disturbances: “[d]uring such a psychological disturbance, subconscious types of awareness may come nearer to the surface, resulting in extremely vivid and meaningful dreams, and also perhaps in other kinds of foresight or sensitivity to events” (33-4). The Gísla compiler finds it worth pointing out that Gísli’s dreams came true, as though this was not true of all dreamers (34). The dream-women are unique to Gísla saga, but bear comparison with other ON dreams. Gísli’s first report of his dreams (ch. 22) “clearly shows the effect of foreign, Christian influence. The two dream women may have had a Scandinavian basis, originally, but, if so, they seem, to some extent, to have been transformed. Their function as guides and interpreters seems to be taken directly from Latin culture, although they differ from Latin works in that they are not the spirits of famous people. The whole tenor of the advice given by the good dream-woman is Christian, and the symbolism of the fires seems to be related to the mediaeval Christian concept of the four humours, where fire is often equated with spirit. One may compare also the numerous symbolic uses of fire in the Bible, where, apart from the connection with damnation, it is associated frequently with concepts of life or spirit, e.g., the burning bush. In Old Icelandic literature, on the other hand, fire seems generally to be associated with some evil or disaster” (34-5, quotation at 35). The dísir are discussed as changeable agents (35-7); in Glaumvör’s similar dream in Atlamál, the two women inviting Gunnar home are dauþar, and the hall to which Gísli is conducted resembles Valhöll in that it contains Gísli’s friends and kinsmen at drink [PS: the hall of seven fires and the hall of the good dream-woman are here confused—they need not be the same!] (36). The dísir come to fetch an individual may be distilled from these dreams as a recognised dream-motif (36-7). Laxdæla saga depends less structurally on dreams, though they do pervade the structure of the work (37). Eddic influences on the Laxdæla dreams are discussed (37-8), as is the symbolism and interpretation of Guðrún’s dreams (38-40). Heiðreks saga ok Hervarar contains a dream about the battle of Sámsey, birds predicting Angantýr’s death; the eagle as fylgja resembles Kostbera’s third dream in Atlamál 12 [PS: and Gísli’s animal-killing dreams in Gísla, first the serpent and then the wolf-head] (40-4). Guðrún’s dream of Sigurðr as a falcon or hawk occurs both in the Nibelungenlied and in Völsunga saga; Guðrúnarkviða in forna has Atli dream of his sons as hawks (44-6). Further animal dreams by Guðrún are discussed (46-9).

author: Hermann Pálsson
title: Minnisgreinar um Gísla sögu Súrssonar
publication: Festskrift til Ludvig Holm-Olsen på hans 70+årsdag den 9. juni 1984
abstract: Observing that saga relationships are typically regarded as too linear (272), studies the relationship between the S and M manuscripts of Gísla saga.

author: Hermann Pálsson
title: Odinic Echoes in Gísla Saga
publication: Gudar på jorden: Festskrift til Lars Lönnroth
abstract: Assumes by reference to Guðni Kolbeinsson and Jónas Kristjánsson (Grípla 1979) that the longer redaction of Gísla is the more authentic one (97). Observes that the saga uses Ævi Snorra goða by Ari Þorgilsson, while Eyrbyggja summarises the events of Gísla, but with some differences that suggest independent authority (97-8). While the events of the saga are thus corroborated as historical, saga authors will not have had access to information regarding the motives behind the the actions that were accurately passed down to them orally, providing them with a great deal of space for interpretation (98-9). The reason for Þorgrímr’s murder of Vésteinn was invented by the compiler, echoing the love triangle in the Nibelungen material. Gísla has both strong connections with the heroic material and a strong interest in “myth and ancient custom,” providing some information on pagan, and specifically Odinic, ritual. This suggests that the worship of Óðinn was more common in early Iceland than commonly assumed (99). There is an association of berserkir with Óðinn, and berserkir are fervent duellers (100-1); Björn inn blakki is linked to Óðinn by his magic and his ‘brutish attitude to women’ (101). His defeat by a magic sword, forged by dwarfs like many important swords, suggests Óðinn’s interference (101-2). When Gísli the elder refuses to return the sword to its rightful owner and dies as a consequence, Kolr the slave pronounces a curse. There are two aggressors in this part of the saga, and two victims, and all of them die; similarly in the latter part, there is a doomed quartet with the same properties (102). The sword Grásíða has specific Odinic characteristics, particularly in the longer redaction of Gísla; and its reforging into a spear echoes Óðinn’s association with spears (102-3). In the weapon’s breaking and reforging as well as the death of its bearer, there are also parallels with Sigmundr Völsung’s weapon in Völsunga saga (103). Based on the longer redaction, it seems that Þorgrímr nef has no function in forging the weapon; his role must have been that of the sorcerer exclusively (104). [NB that Hermann Pálsson deduces from the order in which the Þorgríms and Þorkell are listed that Þorkell is the least important of the three, whereas others have come to the opposite conclusion {I forget who and where}, PSL.] The ritual appearance of Vésteinn’s murder is reminiscent of Odinic human sacrifice (105). Parallels of Odinic deaths with men run through with a spear are listed (105-6). Similar considerations apply to the murder of Þorgrímr (107-8). Both the burial-customs described are associated with Óðinn, as is the seiðr practised by Þorgrímr nef (cf. Ynglinga saga) (109). The first prose description of the dream-women consists of a pagan image (the kinsmen and fires in the hall) and a Christian message (abandon the old faith, be kind to the lame). The pagan element resembles the account of Helgafell in Eyrbyggja, which speaks of the father of Þorgrímr Þorsteinsson from Gísla (109-10). The dream-women evoke both the valkyries and the dísir. The grey horse is reminiscent of Óðinn’s horse Sleipnir. Bjarnar saga Hítdælakappa has an analogue in that Björn says that a woman invites him home in every dream (110-11). A contrast between two groups of supernatural women also occurs in Þiðranda þáttr ok Þórhalls, in which nine women in white ride from the south and nine women in black ride from the north; the latter group, who kill him, are later interpreted as his ættfylgjur or dísir [NB that this happens at the Winter Nights, sometimes called the dísablót; and cf. this summary against both the story and its reading in Jochens, ON Images of Women p. 38: the white women represent the new faith, but Hermann does not mention this! PSL] (111). The “doomed quartet” motif occurs in Njála and the Nibelungen material, while the latter also has the love triangle motif (112-13). The quartet in Gísla is formed at the spring assembly, but falls apart at two subsequent Winter Eves celebrations (113). The quartet are identified as the oath-breakers, murderers, and fornicators of Vsp 37, Vésteinn being a fornicator and Þorgrímr and Gísli murderers; Þorkell may fit the bill of oath-breaker, if it is assumed that the aborted bloodbrotherhood-ceremony had bound him to avenge, not plot the murder of, Vésteinn (114-16). Óðinn is assocated with the breaking of oaths, and they are a common feature of heroic literature, where oath-breakers are Óðinn’s tools for sowing discord (116-17).

author: Holtsmark, Anne
title: Studies in the ‘Gísla Saga’
abstract:
[Section II: Gísla Saga – A Novel of Mystery (34-55)]

Thorgrimr’s guilt of Vesteinn’s death has not thus far been questioned. However, the narrative has a number of indications that it was in fact Gísli’s brother Thorkell who dealt Vesteinn’s death-blow. Thorkell is the last person mentioned by the bondswoman bringing the news to Thorgrimr, Thorgrimr Nef, and Thorkell; no snow settles on the southwestern end of the mound; Thorkell inquires twice about Auðr’s response, suggesting that he feared she might incite her husband to avenge her brother’s death; and Vesteinn’s sons are not satisfied with Thorgrimr’s death. Moreover, Vesteinn was killed with Grásíða, an heirloom of Gísli and Thorkell that went with Thorkell when they split up their property. Again, it was with Grásíða [reforged into a spear] that Gísli avenged the murder; and avenging weapons are a common theme. Thorkell had a motif for killing Vesteinn, since his wife Ásgerðr has been unfaithful to him with Vesteinn. Nevertheless, the author suggests Thorgrimr’s guilt by the parallelism between his and Gísli’s words and deeds at the funerals and games.

author: Jochens, Jenny
title: Old Norse Images of Women
abstract: Chapter two of this work (pp. 33-48) is relevant to Gísla for its index of supernatural female classes. Gísla itself, however, remains strikingly untouched considering the volume’s subject matter.

author: Jochens, Jenny M.
title: The Medieval Icelandic Heroine: Fact or Fiction?
abstract: Re-examines the power wielded by women in the family sagas, discussing also the veracity of the picture. The sagas present marriage as monogamous and as a contract between males of similar wealth and social standing; while suitors are seldom asked their opinion of their prospective bride, the bride seems often to have been consulted, in view of their anger when they are not (Laxdæla, Njála; 37). Most of the time, however, the girl passively accepts her father’s wishes. Sometimes, she poses certain conditions. Widows could remarry without their guardian’s approval (37-8). Since marriage was often arranged by third parties, it was divorce in which a woman could make a more powerful statement. In the sagas, women decide for divorce four times as often as men, often because of physical violence. Sometimes the alternative was to have the husband killed. Rolf Heller has found fifty-one instances of the Hetzerin motif, a woman instigating a man to crime or revenge. Male goading is attested, but rare. “The Hetzerin was, therefore, the dominant female function in the literary sagas.” Opposite behaviour, calming a man down, also occurs. Thus women possessed quite some power, but no direct power: in legal affairs, they had no responsibilities (38-41). Today, it is often believed that the family sagas are fiction; if so, they must reflect the literary age and therefore resemble the contemporary sagas and the Grágás. But the latter does not mention female consent in marriage, except with fatherless widows. If a suitor approached the girl’s guardian three times, the father could no longer refuse if the girl could find another relative willing to agree on the deal. Sturlunga saga, too, has no sign of female consent (41-3). The doctrine of mutual consent was known by Icelandic clergymen in 1189. 1269 saw an official Church requirement of consent, but its effect is unknown (43-4). The Grágás agreed to divorce only in case of physical injury, poverty, or emigration; in other cases, such as incompatibility, the bishop could negotiate a divorce (44-5). Thus there is little correspondence between the situation as sketched in the Íslendingasögur and thirteenth-century law. However, medieval law is increasingly seen as prescriptive. Sturlunga saga contains only four references to divorce, though it is said it was difficult for some couples to stay together. This saga shows a picture of a world decidedly male; only four instances of the Hetzerin motif occur. Widows either seek compensation for or simply accept their husband’s death (45-7). Since the contemporary sagas and the law code had some proximity to the Viking age, they must be considered more reliable as depictions of early society than the literary sagas. The doctrine of female consent was probably inserted into the saga narratives by the clergymen who wrote them down, in the hope that contemporary society would take it as an example (47-8). To judge by its near-absence from Church writings, churchmen cared little about divorce practice. The Hetzerin motif has resonances in the clerical view of Eve (48-50).

author: Jón Hnefill Aðalsteinsson
title: Old Norse Religion in the Sagas of Icelanders
abstract: Summarises Nordal’s and later scholars’ views regarding orality and authorial influence on the sagas’ narratives (303-6). Asks the question of the age of the traditions on which the sagas are based, referring to literature that proposes that traditions can either change or remain identical through cultural displacement (307). The single great change between saga events and their recordings was the conversion; thus it is religious sentiment that may indicate the age of a tradition (307-8). This method is applied to Víga-Glúms saga (308-14) and Gísla saga (314-21). With regard to the latter, it is said that it has borrowed the episode of the killing of Þorgrímr from Droplaugarsona saga (316-18), identifying the scene as echoing a fertility rite in which the priest copulates with a girl, with the difference that Gísli kills the “priest” as this is done (318-19). The green earth on Þorgrímr’s mound is read as a message from Freyr, and it is this same phenomenon that leads Gísli to confess his murder. These events must thus have originally been narrated in pagan times (320).

author: Kanerva, Kirsi
title: ‘. . . siltikään hän ei ollut onnen mies’: Epäonnen käsite ja epäonnen kulttuuriset merkitykset 1200-1300-luvun Islannissa saagan Gísla saga Súrssonar valoassa
abstract: Discusses the dream-women and their symbolism at great length in the context of ON ideas of afterworlds, theological systems, body-soul theology, etc. Suggests that supernatural communication is to Gísli what psychotherapy is to modern man (48-81).

author: Karras, Ruth Mazo
title: Marriage and the Creation of Kin in the Sagas
abstract: Gísla saga studies the tension between one’s loyalty to one’s own kin and that to one’s in-laws, a tension that in many societies plays a role for women only. Bredsdorff argues that Þórdís’s frequent liaisons show that despite the saga’s silence on the matter, she does have desires (473-4; Bredsdorff 68). It is the lack of a bond by marriage that leads Þorgrímr to reject Vésteinn as a blood-brother. In choosing to remain loyal to his brother-in-law by his own wife rather than his brother-in-law by his sister, Gísli gives his wife precedence over his sister. After the killings, Þorkell chooses not to give Gísli active help; in so doing, he favours his brother-in-law and friend over his brother, as Gísli had earlier done [PS: but killing Þorgrímr instead of Þorkell seems to show he does value blood ties; see Holtsmark]. However, he indicates that he could not live under one roof with his brother’s killers. Þórdís suffers from conflicting loyalties: she wounds her brother’s murderer and divorces her husband, but her brother’s death resulted from her communication to her husband that Gísli had killed Þorgrímr (474-6). The Íslendingasögur show a basic pattern of a suitor initiating marital negotiations with the woman’s father, who asks his daughter’s consent. The suitor’s potential in-laws often seem to be a more important consideration of his than the bride herself. Similar considerations underlie a man’s permission for his sister or daughter to marry (476-8). Now and then, a couple’s (un)happiness is commented on, suggesting that not all marriages were happy and happiness mattered. Guðrún and Signý in the Volsunga saga choose their kin over their husbands and even children; this suggests that the Icelanders imagined that such was expected by their ancestors. The contrast Gísli draws between his sister and Guðrún may additionally contrast the mythical past and the saga age. Jochens believes the difference is a result of uxorilocal versus virilocal marriage; the former became more common in the saga age (479-81). When a man gives his wife precedence over his blood, this may be the result of incitement as well as love.
