Incitement with unwise consequences occurs at times, as in Laxdæla saga when Guðrún instigates Bolli to kill her former love Kjartan. Þorbjörg’s conflicting loyalties in Hörðs saga show strategy: she achieves vengeance as well as a happy marriage (481-3). In Brennu-Njáls saga, Hildigunnr instigates her uncle to avenge her husband by murder rather than in court (483). The peace-weaver appears prominently in OE literature, especially in Bwf. Vatnsdœla saga has a marriage of a woman with her brother’s enemy turn out happy (483-5). Sagas show relatively much choice for both suitors and women; the contemporary sagas do not show that the women were consulted, but they also do not describe marriage against a woman’s will (486). The Grágás builds upon very strict blood ties when inheritance is concerned; reality was less firm, and first cousins could claim little; sagas show that both men and women had some freedom of choice in the precedence of their loyalty (487). Choice was also influenced by wealth and social standing. Although women were used as rope with which to create ties between men, male dominance was not absolute and women had some personal rights (488).

author: Kelchner, Georgia Dunham
title: Dreams in Old Norse Literature and their Affinities in Folklore
abstract: Studies dreams and dream-appearances in Old Norse literature, with special emphasis on the distinction between indigenous and Christian tradition. With regard to Gísla saga, it is asked whether Gísli’s dream of the attack made on him represents a fylgja (the wolf-head, representing Eyjólfr) (22-3). The dream-women are discussed briefly in the section on the hamingja or guardian spirit (36-7). The good dream-woman “exhibits a strong Christian tendency, thus showing kinship with the guardian angel”; her aids are prophetic and moral-instructive, and she promises Gísli a good afterlife with her. “Her counsels in the dream of the seven fires, while reminding us of Hávamál, follow the dictates of Christian creed and morality”; but the grey horse and the woman’s hall are influence of the valkyrja-tradition (36). The evil dream-woman is more firmly associated with the valkyrja-tradition (37). Contains an extensive appendix consisting of an edition and translation of all passages under discussion (77-143).

author: Krijn, S.A.
title: Om Gíslasaga Súrssonar
abstract: The saga portrays Gísli as good in every respect, but filled with the belief that fate will have its way (69). The large number of verses could hardly be remembered over the centuries while still retaining sense (69-70). The differences between the two redactions are examined at length (71-6). Each of the redactions agrees with the Eyrbyggja narrative in its own way; thus all three must go back on oral tradition (71). Motifs are furthermore shared with Droplaugarsona saga (the killings of Þorgrímr and Helgi Ásbjörnsson) (71). A number of divergences between the redactions are listed, regarding prose and poetry (72-6). Assumes that the various dreamwoman-stanzas were handed down together, because six stanzas begin with hugðak (77) and because they convey the same mood. Krijn interprets the person who binds Gísli’s wounds as Auðr (77-8). Raises the possibility that not all the dream-stanzas attributed to Gísli have made it into the surviving redactions of the saga. Discerns between three groups of stanzas, or three poems: 14-17; (18,) 23-27 but without 26; and several stanzas that would have made up a third poem, namely 19, 28-3, 33-6 (78-80). The dreams with the good dream-woman showing him to a soft bed must be Christian (78-9). Stanzas that are harder to place are 20, 30-2, the latter few of which tell of a fight. Stanzas 11-12 may have belonged to a further long poem (80). The question of authorship is posed: it is possible that a poet who survived Gísli composed about his later years; either way, there is enough linguistic evidence to date the poetry to the tenth century (80-1). Stanzas 9-10, 22 are certainly among the oldest, and certainly authentic (81-2). The poetry in the introductory chapters does not seem very old; stanzas 6-7 may have been added by the author (82-3). As in other sagas, the verses are uttered at moments of excitement or duress. Sometimes, poetry is used to convey ideas that cannot be conveyed in prose (83). The poetry in Gísla serves to confirm Gísli as a hero (83-4).

author: Kroesen, Riti
title: Gísla saga Súrssonar
abstract: Summarises the action of the saga; observes that links with heroic poetry have often been claimed, so that, for instance, the murder in bed is parallelled by that of Sigurðr. “But the whole purport of the saga seems to be that the standards of heroic legends cannot be applied to an everyday Icelandic environment.” The stanzas seem to be later than their setting, but inconsistencies indicate that they were not written by the saga author. The dream-women are here characterised as a “dark woman” and a “white woman”; in the dream-women, Christianity, which Gísli learned about in Denmark according to the saga, is clearly present (227). The article has a good bibliography.

author: Kroesen, Riti
title: The Enmity between Þorgrímr and Vésteinn in the Gísla saga Súrssonar
abstract: Despite Holtsmark’s convincing paper, she has also made scholars aware that the author of Gísla is consciously ambiguous as to who killed Vésteinn. What is clear is that both Þorgrímr and Þorkell carry some guilt. Björnsson argues that Auðr must have told the bondsman to draw out the weapon so that no revenge need be taken because she did not want a feud with her husband’s brother; but then again, the same argument might apply if the killer were the husband of her husband’s wife (386). But what reason did Þorgrímr have to carry out or assist in the killing? His headstrong nature renders it unlikely that the weak Þorkell could have used him as a tool. He may have refused to become Vésteinn’s blood-brother because they were already at odds. The natural answer to the question why Þorgrímr did not marry Auðr after their affair is because her family rejected him; and the fact that Vésteinn was named after his father suggests that his father was dead by the time he was born; this would make him Auðr’s guardian and the one to have rejected Þorgrímr. The latter’s pride must have been hurt, which would give him a motif to assist Thorkell in his plan. Alternatively, he may have committed the deed because he was the only one left out of the blood-brotherhood; but this suggests that he was no strong character, contrary to what we learn from the saga. Also, the saga is unclear about the validity of the incomplete ritual (387-8). But why did Vésteinn reject such a flattering offer as to become related to the Þorsnesingar family? Kroezen proposes that this was because Þorgrímr had had an illicit love affair, of which his son Þoroddr, an invention of the saga author, was the result (389).

author: Lýður Björnsson
title: Snörp bítu járn: Hugleiðingar um Gísla sögu
abstract: Discusses battle imagery and paganism in Gísla.

author: Lönnroth, Lars
title: Dreams in the Sagas
abstract: Claims first that dreams in the Sagas of Icelanders are always warnings to be interpreted by the proper confidant of the dreamer and that dreams were considered portals to the future rather than to one’s inner life (455-6). This article aims to make three points about dreams in the Íslendingasögur: their nature is particular to the genre, they cannot always be explained, and their effect on the saga’s structure is both stabilising and unsettling (456). The identity of dreams in the Sagas of Icelanders is established by comparison with those in Edda and fornaldarsögur, which feature more threatening beasts, fewer protective spirits communicating with the dreamer, and no verse recitals (456-7). The ambiguity and complexity of some of the dreams problematise elucidation (457-8). Gísli’s good dream-woman is Christian, perhaps a guardian angel or an idealised form of Auðr (458-9). Yet she has the characteristics of a traditional ættarfylgja, and the friends and relatives in the dream must be pagans rather than Christians in heaven. The evil dream-woman is regarded by Gísli as a valkyrie who will ultimately have him killed in battle; or she may represent the paganism of which the good dream-woman has told Gísli to steer clear (459). After the first two dreams, there is a dreamless stretch; when the dream-women return, they do so with sexual overtones (459-60). The kenning ormláðs auðr may be a playful reference to Gísli’s wife alongside the referent “gold.” They grey horse occurs elsewhere as a symbol of death (ref. to ÍF 6.94 note 2); Gísli’s willingness to go along with the dream-woman may thus signal his resignation from life [this sentiment may also be present in stanzas 40 and 22, PSL]. The good dream-woman’s house has been transformed from a drinking-hall to a love nest (460). When the evil dream-woman recurs, she has assumed a Christian function, referring to the almighty God who will prevent Gísli’s lying with the good dream-woman. Her smearing him with blood may be symbolic of Christian purification; but it is not clear, and it may be doubted that the saga author knew. What is clear is that these women are highly ambiguous, representing both life and death, Christianity and traditional values (461). Their overall function in the saga is to educate Gísli about Christianity (462). The family sagas are not ruled by single, clear-cut moral lessons, and metaphysics are allowed only in brief glimpses (462-3). This article has a good bibliography on the dream-stanzas.

author: Meulengracht Sørensen, Preben
title: Peace and Honour: Gísla saga Súrssonar
publication: The Unmanly Man: Concepts of Sexual Defamation in Early Northern Society
abstract: Assumes (on the basis of this study) that the longer redaction of Gísla is the more authentic; but for purposes of this chapter, both traditions are studied as of equal value (45). The longer redaction explains that given the choice to kill Björn inn blakki or the fatted calf, Gísli chooses the first, thus avoiding loss of manliness (being argr) (46-7). The longer redaction has a great deal of suggestions of unmanliness in the brothers of Gísli’s generation, and it takes a great deal of persuasion before Gísli kills Kolbeinn in order to avoid accusations of femininity. The brief remark in the shorter redaction that Þorbjörn says that Kolbeinn’s doings would not be suffered if Ari were at home are a remnant after abbreviation of this narrative detail (48-9). In the Skeggi narrative, extant in the shorter redaction only, the roles of Þorkell and Kolbjörn are unclear (50-1). The wooden effigy Skeggi orders displays Gísli, or either of the two, in an emphatically masculine role, namely the phallic aggressor as opposed to the shameful passive homosexual man, comparable to the role claimed by Sinfjötli in Helgakviða Hundingsbana 1; Ström concluded that Gísli’s inclusion into the effigy must be a later insertion (52-3). By contrast, Óláfs saga Tryggvasonar #in lengra has Þorvaldr kill to avenge himself for being portrayed as a phallic aggressor (53-5). But this story may be identified as a didactic Christian one, alien to native tradition (55-6). A similar effigy is described in Bjarnar saga Hítdælakappa; here, both men are said to have been put to shame, but the one in front most (56-7). Thus Skeggi may have wanted to ridicule Kolbjörn most, but he also bore a grudge against Gísli, so he made him argr (homosexual regardless of the precise role) (57-8). The two couplets in the duel with Skeggi are, as Anne Holtsmark has proposed, sexual in connotations (58-61). Similarly the two couplets at the ball-game have a second, sexual meaning: Gísli is referring to himself as a phallic aggressor with Þorgrímr on the receiving end (64-8). For men to be struck on their buttocks is similarly humiliating (68-70). Poetry was banned in Iceland, presumably because it was so easy to hide níð in periphrasis (70). This may explain why Gísli’s couplet has few parallels; but there are some (71-4). Eyjólfr’s unmanliness is discussed (75-7).

author: Morris, Katherine
title: Sorceress or Witch? The Image of Gender in Medieval Iceland and Northern Europe
location: Lanham, MD, New York, and London
abstract: Briefly discusses the dream-women in Gísla (49-53). The good dream-woman is “obviously a conversion figure, much like Gudrun of Laxdæla saga” (50). The two women are rivals, and the evil one ultimately gets the upper hand. She may be compared to the valkyrjur, while the good dream-woman is a tutelary spirit (51). Björn in Bjarnar saga Hítdælakappa has a bad dream preceding his death, and Þiðranda þáttr has good and evil female spirits contend; these dream-women may be compared to Gísli’s (52). The rivalling spirits may be compared with Christian good and bad angels, and are indebted to Christianity (see George Johnston, trans., The Saga of Gísli. U of Toronto P, 1963, p. 122) (52-3). Draumr Þorsteins Síðu-Hallssonar similarly has three women tell the main character that his death is being plotted by his slave. Guðrún in Laxdæla dreams and interprets, though Gestr interprets certain of her dreams better (53). The discussion takes place in a chapter on “The Seeress” in ON literature, discussing also the völva and, at length, Guðrún in Laxdæla (23-57). The remainder of the book discusses “The Sorceress,” “Of Witches and Animals,” “The Lascivious Witch,” and “The Cannibal Woman.”

author: O’Donoghue, Heather
title: Speech, Silence, and Subjectivity in Gísla saga
publication: Skaldic Verse and the Poetics of Saga Narrative
abstract: One of the functions of skaldic poetry is heightened discourse, which is set off by its form as fictional (136). While only certain contexts allow for this mode, skaldic discourse is always conceived of as ad-hoc response rather than rehearsed recitation (136-7). All the same, a distinction has to be made between having a character speak in verse and having him speak a spontaneous response, since in the latter case it may be that only the presentation is fictionalised (137-8). Since discourse poetry is likely to lead compilers to create sagas in which the hero is a poet and the verses are recited, it may be useful to study Gísla saga, in which the poetry does not form part of the hero’s biography (138). Gísla often uses verse to tell of Gísli’s inner life, and his speaking of stanzas suggests direct access to his subjectivity on the part of the audience (139). Gísli’s dream-stanzas reveal his psychological state (140). In the Íslendingasögur, direct expression of emotion tends to be restricted to skaldic verse, yielding a strong contrast between prose and poetic mode (140-1). A verse without an audience may be read as a soliloquy (141). Saga heroes like Gísli and Grettir, who are markedly antisocial, are particularly illuminated by verse expression of inner life. This chapter attempts to show how verse in Gísla serves as soliloquy (142-3). Five functions of verse are distinguished in representing a “lone hero”: they may link him with a literary tradition; show the power of a non-naturalistic force (e.g. fate); signal a dominant voice in the narrative; explore the character’s subjectivity; and control mood and pace of the narrative (143). The first of these consists in presenting the hero with an antiquity through mythical past (143-9; this passage also goes into the meaning of the duel with Skeggi). Fate is discussed (149-53). Þorkell’s jealously is the saga’s pivot from a character-based point of view; the verse he utters is prophetic, suggesting that fate has been set in motion, and the form of his words marks this heightened function (150-1). Vésteinn’s decision not to turn back is reminiscent of that by Gunnarr and Högni in Atlakviða (151). Gísli’s self-incriminating verse is very cryptic, so that Gísli perhaps does not expect it to be understood, or perhaps he expects his sister to understand but not to betray him (151-2 [cf. Olsen, “Heltediktningen” 7-8]). Harris sees hubris in the admission; supernatural events further surround the confession (153). Gísli’s verses on the murders are discussed (153-9). His dream-stanzas are discussed (159-69). Gísli dreams six dreams, each of which is represented by a group of stanzas: 16-19; 20-2; 25-7; 29-31; 32-4; 35-8. At the first mention of the dreams, Gísli repeats in verse what he has told in prose, in the way in which historical writing substantiated their assertions (160). This may have been because the compiler considered the verses unclear by themselves, or in order to enter gradually into fictional mode (161). A similar prose framework is created at the second group of dream-stanzas. Here, the opposition between good and evil dream-women is a prose construct (162-3). Before the third group, the prose provides details on the dream-women, part of which is substantiated by the poetry, while the eroticism is extended in the poetry. The contents of the dreams have become part of the prose narrative, but the mode is that of a soliloquy, Auðr as the addressee playing no part in it (163-5). In the fourth group of verses, the prose distinction between the two women is again not substantiated, and Auðr regains her role as interlocutor (165). Stanza 29 is distinctly Christian with its reference to the allvaldr and erlendis rann, reminiscent of both Seafarer and Hebrews 11.13-16 [O’Donoghue has 12.13-16 and misquotes Sfr]; by itself, this seems to convey that Gísli will be parted from Auðr by death (165-6). After stanza 31, the prose account goes off on its own and is no longer substantiated by the verse at all (166). The fifth group of dream-verses is of Gísli’s last stand, and the verses corroborate the prose preceding it; but by themselves, they appear to refer to a battle that as already taken place (166-7). The sixth group again brings Auðr as interlocutor, and the dreams are concerned with Gísli’s death (167); only this group of stanzas fully prepares the audience for Gísli’s refusal to challenge his fate (168). The poetry’s effect on the mood of the narrative is discussed group by group (169-79). Its function is to focalise the narrative through Gísli in the only way in which this could be done in the genre (178-9).

author: Olsen, Karin
title: Woman-Kennings in the Gísla saga Súrssonar: A Study
publication: Doubt Wisely: Papers in Honour of E.G. Stanley
abstract: In Meissner’s definition, the individual elements of a kenning have no reference; it is only in synthesis that they convey information. Apart from their denotative function, however, words also have a connotative usage, and poets such as the Gísla poet used this dimension to fit the context (267-8). Kennings confirm Auðr’s steadfast loyalty and present her as a healer, while she is often associated with Freyja and ásynjur of marital love, healing, and protection. But later stanzas suggest that she is losing influence on Gísli (268-71). Þórdís forms Auðr’s opposite: she is presented as callous and lacking compassion, representing harm Gísli where his wife represents comfort. Her betrayal of her brother is contrasted with the loyalty of the legendary Guðrún (272-3). In Gísli’s dreams, the contrast of comfort and harm is continued in the two dream-women. The good dream-woman comes close to Auðr in her comforting function, thus suggesting an intimate, even erotic relationship, although her advice to help the needy shows a Christian side of her character. As the narrative proceeds, the relationship becomes more intimate: Gísli is told he will rule over the dream-woman, and she shows him a bed. She also begins to refer to healing, which links her to Auðr and suggests she will take her place. Gísli’s final stanza, usually thought to refer to Auðr, is better understood as referring to the good dream-woman, in which reading this stanza completes her usurpation of Auðr’s role (273-7). The evil dream-woman is associated with the valkyries but is also represented as taking part in the bloodshed herself. She also tells Gísli that the good dream-woman and he will not be united after death; as such, she takes the role of the devil trying to withhold salvation from his victim (277-82). The kennings show that the woman-kennings in Gísla are made up of components that intensify the kennings’ references in their context (282).

author: Olsen, Magnus
title: ‘Gísla saga’ og heltediktningen
abstract: Gísli’s self-incriminating verse begins with two lines reminiscent of Guðrúnarkviða 2 40, in which Atli tells Guðrún his dream about fallen saplings for her to interpret (6-7). There is, however, also a similarity of situation: Guðrún is planning Atli’s death, while Gísli is secretly responsible for Þorgrímr’s. This is why Gísli takes Guðrún Gjúkadóttir as a model for his sister in the verse about her treason; and his self-incriminating verse is an address to her asking her to place her brother before her husband in the same way (7-8). Guðrúnarkviða 2 must thus predate the poetry of Gísla, i.e. pre-950 (8). Gísli’s stanzas 35-8 are likewise influenced by this passage from Guðrúnarkviða 2, as evidenced by hugðak and more particularly the rare vílsinnr/vílsiðr in stanza 35. Hugðak itself is not remarkable, since it is common in dream-poetry; but its persistant opening position throughout the stanzas marks it out as influenced by the heroic poem (8-9 and 8 footnote 2). Vílsinni occurs in Guðrúnarkviða 2 38 and nowhere else in the Eddic poetry (9). The rare incidence of the words alone suggest influence, which is confirmed by the fact that both occurrences are in a stanza in which a dream is told, introduced by hugðak as the first of four stanzas with that opening (9-10). This connection makes it plausible that the author was familiar with other Eddic poems as well, notably Brot af Sigurðarkviðu, which treats of a broken bloodbrotherhood, and Sigurðarkviða in skamma (10-11). Similarly, Auðr and Ásgerðr’s conversation is reminiscent of Guðrún and Brynhildr’s, in both situations about the speakers’ husbands/brothers-in-law (11-12). Several parallels are pointed out between Gísla and Sigurðarkviða in skamma (12-13). A final footnote acknowledges that Ker has similarly remarked on resemblances between Gísla and the Poetic Edda (14 footnote 1).

author: Olsen, Magnus
title: Om Gísla saga’s opbygning
abstract: Argues on structural grounds that the saga is not much older than its codification (150). Claims that while the number three is used on a number of occassions, these are neither many nor significant (151). The saga’s structure is instead characterised by the juxtaposition of twos: two duels (152), two instances in which Gísli saves his life by sacrificing a slave; two lists of elaborate funerary rites; two Winter Nights celebrations; conflicts with two suitors (153-4); two verses uttered towards a mound at a ball game (154-6); Börkr and Eyjólfr work together twice (157); two assemblies (157-8). The saga uses nature to set its mood (158-9), but for mood it is also influenced by heroic poetry. Sigurðarkviða en skamma is particularly close (159-60).

author: Paasche, Fredrik
title: Esras aabenbaring og Pseudo-Cyprianus i norrön litteratur
abstract: The Fourth Grammatical Treatise refers to the apocryphal medieval collection known as the Revelation to Baruch ch. 36 (199-200). The immediate sources of the passage in 4GT, however, are The Revelation to Ezras and 4 Ezra (ca. 100 CE) (200). 4 Ezra 2.21 has a passage “care for the injured and the weak, do not ridicule a lame man, protect the maimed, and let the blind man have a vision of my splendor” (see Weber p. 1933); one of Gísli’s verses is so close to this sentiment that influence must be supposed: “hjalp blindum. . . höltum, handlausum tý, granda” (st. 19, ÍF6 p. 73). The message makes no sense in the saga context, and so it should be read against the background of a Christian Icelandic book-culture (200-1). Some arguments are presented for the importance of 4 Ezra to medieval catholicism (201-2). Óláfs saga hins helga has Saint Óláfr help good men with gifts, dress those who are cold, gave to orphans, etc.; this echoes 4 Ezra 2.20, which in turn relies on Jeremiah 22, a text commonly read with regard to the concept of the rex iustus, popularised by Pseudo-Cyprian (202-3). His work was widely read, and translated into ON (a fragment remains); the passage in Óláfs saga seems to be indebted to this tradition (203). A particular combination of adjectives in Sverris saga (réttlátr ok friðsamr) echoes the same tradition on two occasions (203-4). Sverris saga deals with pride, the ruler’s most dangerous pitfall (205).

author: Papmehl, Catarina Röjder
title: Mæla verðr einnhverr skapanna málum: Kvinnors och mäns språk i ‘Gísla saga’
publisher: Institutionen för svenska språket och Catarina Röjder Papmehl
series: Meddelanden från Institutionen för svenska språket vid Göteborgs universitet
abstract:
[Del 2: Mäns och kvinnors språk i Gísla saga]

Presents the axiom that the [Swedish] speech of men and women respectively is so different that no author could write dialogue without unconsciously conveying this stylistic difference; and proceeds to enquire whether this difference was already present in the ON of Gísla (23). Previous research has judged women overly talkative, imprecise, and inclined towards exaggeration; it has recently been observed that women talk less but play a significant role in starting and stimulating conversation. Scholars have also claimed that feminine speech is more emotional and less rational; more grammatically correct; and more dependent on antecedent utterances. Papmehl suspects that it is women’s desire to use language correctly that leads them to vary their speech less than men (24). Mary Ritchie Key pointed out that the nature of speech always depends on a number of register factors such as relationship and identity. She noted that the past century has consisted of women listening to male speech rather than men listening to female speech; that male expression is stronger and less delicate; and that women make more frequent use of modal auxiliaries and favour indirect questions over imperatives (25-6). Ole Togeby drew attention to the fact that speech gender has not been studied in relation to class differences, and proceeded to carry out field-work accordingly. He found that [Danish] women use over fifty percent more concrete words than men, and that men and women from different classes display distinct speech patterns. Significantly, women from all classes use the same quantity of speech, whereas middle-class men are the most talkative of all and lower class men the least. Modal adverbial adjuncts, negation, and deictic expressions are markedly masculine (26-8). Kerstin Thelander has studied the speech of politicians and found that men tend to dominate conversation, while female speech in male presence is tentative, polite, and formulated in standard Swedish. But when outnumbered or presenting a weak case, men display uncertainty, e.g., employing as many tag questions as women. This suggests that speech gender really depends on power. Here too, men have the greater quantitive output and use more variation; women prefer concrete and emotional words while favouring words with neutral or positive connotations while men use abstract words with a negative ring (28-9). Gísla has 31 named speakers, plus the companions of Bork and Eyjólfr; nine (about 30 percent) are women, but in number of speeches and words they take up 20,9 percent and 18,7 percent respectively. Auðr takes up much speech, as do Bóthildr and Ásgerðr. The only other women who appear and speak in more than one chapter are Guðríðr and Þórdís (30). Many of the criteria for gendered speech analysis have been designed for spoken language; but other criteria may be adduced for written language. The author has looked at the number of words in sentences and passages; their interrelationships and purposes; and she has studied lexicon, grammar, sentence, semantics, and dialogue (31). She has excluded verse, passages on dreams, speech without finite verbs, and direct speech attributed to multiple speakers. She has thus arrived at 206 passages of direct speech, 43 (20,9 percent) of which are delivered by women. The methodology is presented (32-3). Auðr’s prominence is clear: only Gísli and Þorkell speak more (34-5). In spite of Nordenstam’s find that men talk more about themselves, the women in Gísla are responsible for 17,5 percent of the occurrences of the first-person personal pronoun ek (while they speak 18,7 percent of the total number of words); the dual and plural first person pronouns are hardly used by women, but they are used by men. The average female share in these pronouns is 15,4 percent. After correction for implied subjects this is 15,1 percent. 20,6 percent of second-person personal pronouns, or 21,8% after correction, are female-spoken. Women utter 36,4 percent of the adjectives of value, but only one adverb of value. Words referring to persons are 22,5 percent female-spoken; but name plus apposition (“Þorkell, bróðir minn”) yields the women 44,5 percent (34-9). Women hardly use the plural, use less ek and more þú, and few imperatives. They omit dual and plural; this finding is in agreement with the notion that women use more personal language, and with their limited role in the sagas. They use fewer adjectives and adverbs of value; this may signal their “weaker” use of language. Words with the negative prefix ó- are spoken by men only; this concords with Thelander’s results. Male language is more abstract, female language more personal (39-40). Women have a 15,1 percent share in the use of the imperative; but Auðr uses this construction in a typically male role, which if omitted corrects to 11 percent. Subjunctives are 19,4 percent; of these, preterite forms are 15,8 percent. Comparatives are 14,3 percent; superlatives 5,6 percent (40-3). Men use more words per speech, though women use slightly more words per sentence (when a sentence is a unit centred around a finite verb). Women utter 12,1 percent of deictic words; but they take a 25,8 percent share in the word hér (45-7). They have a 9,4 percent share in “actor sentences” (sentences that try to influence the other’s behaviour) and utter 13,1 percent of “active sentences.” Auðr, once more, is an exception; this seems to indicate her independence (47-9). Women have a large total number of addressees, but they usually speak in private with a single person (mostly these are conversations between Gísli and Auðr). The longest dialogue is that between Auðr and Ásgerðr. Women often speak the first words of a dialogue, but men have the last word. Opening cues are questions, warnings, a report, a call for help, and a call for alarm. Several of the male opening lines are instructions. Women speak fewer lines per conversation (49-53). Auðr is feminine in her relationship towards Gísli, but during his outlawry her increased independence shows in her masculine language (53-4).

author: Turville-Petre, E.O.G.
title: An Icelandic Version of the ‘Somniale Danielis’
publication: Nordica et anglica: Studies in Honor of Stefán Einarsson
abstract: Opens by pointing out that some early clergymen in Iceland believed in precognitive dreams, justified by OT stories of gentiles dreaming dreams which required the Jews for interpretation (19). ON literature uses prophetic dreams as much as any other literature (19-21). Shows that the Icelandic Somniale is closer to the Latin text as found in the Cotton MS than its most important Continental witness (21-7). Then goes on to compare the book’s contents to dreams in the sagas (27-30). In a number of cases, competing interpretations of dreams in the sagas represent a false explanation that accords with the Somniale and a true interpretation that can by contrast be considered native; nevertheless, the foreign and native interpretations appear to blend (28-9). From here onwards, the article focusses on animal imagery in particular (29-30). Gísla has a serpent kill Vésteinn; the Somniale interprets snake attacks as defeat at the hands of one’s enemies. In the saga, however, the snake may be considered Vésteinn’s fylgja, a specific concept probably not intended in the Somniale (29). Ofljóst or paronomy is also commonly used to interpret dreams, thus eldr may refer to old age (by way of eldjask) (30). The Somniale was of considerable influence on the use of prophetic dreams in ON literature, but it cannot explain all (e.g. the fylgja element); also, ON dreams containing or resembling Somniale motifs need not be fictitious, even if influence exists (31). The article concludes with an edition (31-4) and a translation (34-6) of the ON Somniale.

author: Turville-Petre, G.
title: Dream Symbols in Old Icelandic Literature
eds: Kurt Rudolph, Rolf Heller, and Ernst Walter

author: Turville-Petre, G.
title: Gísli Súrsson and his Poetry: Traditions and Influences
abstract: States that Gísla’s popularity abroad is due to the foreign influences on this saga (374). Gísla may be contrasted with Grettla in its title character’s social nature and the love element; Grettir is a more typical Icelandic hero overall. Gísli performs the sacred duty of bloodbrotherhood towards Vésteinn, and as a result he comes across as a Christian martyr. Gísla is uncharacteristically preoccupied with emotion (375). Thus Gísli’s complaint about his sister, as well as that about his brother, is uncharacteristic in tone: and the overheard conversation between the women is all about emotions and leads to other ones (376). The prose in Gísla is rather poetic, which is exceptional in the very prosaic prose tradition of Iceland (377). Much of the poetry, too, expresses emotion (377-9). Influence of Guðrúnarkviða II is sometimes seen in these (377-9), as well as in the dream-verses; Magnús Ólsen also sees the influence of Sigurðarkviða en skamma and Sigdrífumál (380). The age and composition of Guðrúnarkviða II is discussed and it is argued that the poem is of poor unity due to changes based on European influence (380-4). Gísla is influenced by both the earlier and the later version of the Guðrún narrative (384). The prose of the saga does speak of Gísli meeting Christians in Denmark, and the longer version even has him marked with the cross (385). The good dreamwoman’s version of the beatitudes expresses “exclusively Christian” sentiments (cf. Paasche). A number of analogues to stanzas 13-16 (judged to belong together in a flokkr) are mentioned: Þorsteinn Þorskabítr is reunited with family in Helgafell after his death (Eyrbyggja saga), and Norna-Gests þáttr has the story of a lamp of life (386). Good and evil is the theme of all these stanzas: the good dream-woman represents Christianity, the evil dream-woman the old religion; or good and bad guardian angels, well-known in the north (Michaels saga, Hómíliubók). Krijn has attempted to show that the dream-stanzas form three separate poems; but their unity suggests that they are by the same poet (387). In spirit, the stanzas are reminiscent of mystical poetry of the twelfth century (Harmsól, Sólarljóð) (388). The use of the word sál in stanza 9 suggests a late, Christian origin. The prose and verse are strikingly similar, so that they may well have been written by the same author (389). Gísli is not externally confirmed as a poet (389-90). The saga’s relationships with other sagas are treated in brief, yielding the conclusion that Gísla was written in the late thirteenth century (390-1).

author: Vésteinn Ólason
title: Introduction
publication: ‘Gisli Sursson’s Saga’ and ‘The Saga of the People of Eyri’
trans: Martin S. Regal and Judy Quinn
abstract: [here summarised: “Gisli Sursson’s Saga, pp. xiii-xxv]Identifies some of the themes of the saga, such as “[f]orbidden love leading to violence and death,” “honour and vengeance,” and fate. The saga suggests that the cycle of feud can place such outrageous demands that to pursue vengeance would go against the moral code (xvi). The poetry gives insight into Gísli’s emotions (xviii; so also O’Donoghue). The section on narrative art (xxii-xxiii) makes reference to Gísli’s efforts to avoid making tracks in the snow and his final discovery by Eyjólfr as a result of the women’s tracks in the frozen dew (xxii). Gísli’s outlawry and heroism are briefly discussed (xxiii-xxv).

author: Yelena Sesselja Helgadóttir (Yershova)
title: Draumvísur and Draugavísur in Icelandic Sagas: The Border Between Fantasy and Reality
publisher: Given at the Thirteenth International Saga Conference in Durham and York (6-12 August 2006)
abstract: Discusses dream-vision meetings with the otherworld in a somewhat unstructured fashion. Mentions Gísla only briefly.

author: Andrew, Malcolm
title: Grendel in Hell
abstract: Explains feond on helle by pointing out that the Church Fathers considered sin itself the punishment of sin, so that as a sinner, Cain is permanently in his own hell, a prisoner of the flesh and tormented by human joy because he is exiled from human society. Gen B and the Historia Ecclesiastica are cited to show that such concepts were familiar.

author: Bammesberger, Alfred
title: Beowulf’s Descent into Grendel’s Mere
abstract: Constructs the syntax of the lines surrounding the phrase hwil dæges in such a way that Beowulf does not descend for hours without coming up for air: “the surging water received the warrior—then it was daytime—, before he could make out the bottom of the mere” (226).

author: Bandy, Stephen C.
title: Cain, Grendel, and the Giants of Beowulf
abstract: Studies eotenas in Bwf. The Church Fathers worried about the distinction between man and giant if all descended from Adam (236-7). Augustine contrasts Cain with Abel in his De civitate Dei, and discusses the former’s progeny in book 15 (237-8). Great size is a defining characteristic of Cain’s offspring, great size being either a consequence or an occasion of pride (238-9). While a tall man need not be wicked, he will suffer greater temptations of pride (239). The giants of Bwf are mentioned often, while other monsters are figurants (239-40). The poet limits use of the word gigant to antediluvial giants, since the Church Fathers cited Isaiah 26.14 to show that gigantes non resurgent. Yet post-diluvial giants require an explanation, and the Bwf poet joins the two concepts when he describes the giants’ story inscribed in the hilt of the sword from the cave (240). Grendel is described in human terms, and must be considered humanoid at least (240-2). Like Cain, he is required to be profugus et vagus (241). Heremod’s story is narrated as a bad example of one who perished at the hands of giants; Sigemund is the contrasting tale of success. The implicit question is which of the two Beowulf will follow (242-3). Hygelac is of giant stature, and he perishes of pride (243-4); Beowulf too is repeatedly called proud, not to be translated with “high spirits” or “daring,” and he too is uncommonly tall (244-5). His unquestioning loyalty to Hygelac not Hrothgar furthermore suggests similarity of character (245-6). The eotenas in the Finn episode are most likely to be Jutes not giants, though the Finnsburg Fragment does not use the word (246-7). The implication is still that the Danes will undergo the same fate as the warriors at Finnsburg (247). There is some reason to believe that the various fights, Hygelac’s, the Jutes’, and Beowulf’s, can all be overlaid (247-8); Frisians did indeed have a reputation as giants. King Beowulf’s final deeds must be judged in the light of Hrothgar’s warning and Hygelac’s example (248).

author: Carlson, Signe M.
title: The Monsters of Beowulf: Creations of Literary Scholars
abstract: Scholars are responsible to a great degree for creating the monsters of Bwf; indeed, the word monster was not used in English until the fourteenth century. This paper examines whether the semi-supernatural category understood to exist in Bwf have a factual basis (357). Grendel scholarship has mostly been limited to remarks on the poet’s Christian references. The poet has been understood to be a Christian because of the many Christian references. Such references, however, are literary accretions, forming the one exception to the poet’s intention to transmit the tale faithfully. The confusing account of the mere may be explained by the poet’s unfamiliarity with the landscape described, which may be clarified with reference to Grettis saga (358). The state of the manuscript and transmission errors make the distinction between “stranger” and “ghost” impossible. Brimwyl is once emended to brimwylf on questionable grounds where brimwif may have been intended (358-9). Readings of the words feond, aglæca, fifelcyn, eoten, gæst, wer, guma, and ides are studied. Feond (24 occ.) derives from feon “to hate” and should thus be translated enemy, not fiend, in contexts of no particularly Christian nature. Aglæca (21 occ.) means “misery, vexation” and comes to mean “bringer of trouble” or “formidable one.” Dictionaries, however, suggest two opposing readings: “monster” and “great hero,” depending on whether Beowulf or one of his adversaries is meant (359). Translators respond accordingly (359-60). Fifelcyn is, on the Scandinavian evidence, more likely to mean foolish race than race of water-monsters, so that no supernatural race need be supposed [PS: the surviving Scandinavian meaning is surely later than the OE]. Eoten has been explained by Schoning as deriving from etan and thus suggesting cannibalism; thus “bloodthirsty one” or “cannibal” may serve better than “giant,” again desupernaturalising the concept [PS: unlikely!] (360-1). The gæst/gǽst distinction may be problematic, but always going for the latter when Grendel and his mother are referred to may be imprecise. Translations like fiend, goblin, and monster are misleading and prejudiced. Wer, twice used for Grendel, can only mean “man,” yet it is often translated “wright,” “wretch,” etc. So also for guma. Ides is mostly translated correctly as “woman,” but not in line 1259 (361). Similar biased translations exist for unambiguous words meaning “hand” etc. (361-2). Stripping the tale of its literary accretions, Grendel must have Danish parentage. The story makes clear that he was sufficiently familiar to the Danes to be given a name, sufficiently intelligent to understand that Heorot was the seat of power. His fear and pain are real (362). His bewitching of the Geats’ weapons may be a rationalisation of their uselessness in the affair. The size of his head is disproportionate and inconsistent with the account of the Danes (362-3). Beowulf’s remark that none of Grendel’s kin will be able to boast of his battle with Grendel suggests that there are more of their race [PS: not so; Grendel is called the last of them in the very passage Carlson cites: “sé ðe lengest leofað láðan cynnes” (2008)]. The dragon’s firy breath may be a representation of a flickering tongue, and its size exaggeration. The Grendelkin may represent native dwellers encountered by the Germanic invaders, while the dragon may find an explanation in natural history. No supernatural elements are required to explain this tale (363).

author: Crawford, S.J.
title: Grendel’s Descent From Cain
abstract: Klaeber has remarked that the direct source of the tradition tracing Grendel to Cain has not been found. Job 26.5 may hold the solution: “ecce gigantes gemunt sub aquis, et qui habitant cum eis.” Connecting this line with the book of Enoch and with Genesis 4; 6.2-7; and 7 would be enough to understand Cain’s progeny as reproducing below the waters (207). The monster’s arrival from the sea in the Book of Revelation may have strengthened the connection (208).

author: Crawford, S.J.
title: Grendel’s Descent From Cain
abstract: Irish tradition knew the motif of monsters descended from Cain and overwhelmed by the flood. The Irish Nennius explains that monsters were descended from Cham, but refers to a Gaelic tradition that they were descended from Cain (63).

author: Pearson, Kathy L.
title: Nutrition and the Early-Medieval Diet
abstract: An amazing aggregate of information on medieval nutrition. Opens with the observation that some recent studies claim widespread malnutrition in the early Middle Ages, while others suggest an abundance of food albeit comparatively homogeneous. After recognising the problem of regional variation, Pearson sets out to draw up a list of foods to which the people of early medieval Europe had potential access (i.e. foods of which we know that they were consumed at least some of the time) (2–14), after which she turns to monastic rations and documentary evidence to find out how much of this potential range and quantity of food sources was in fact consumed per individual (14–28). Mortality rates especially warrant the conclusion that “[t]he majority of early-medieval people likely suffered some degree of malnutrition resulting from the irregular availability of foods necessary to a balanced diet” (28–9, at 28). Morbidity and other evidence from the analysis of human remains is discussed (29–32). The conclusion remains that abundance was a theoretical possibility, but often not achieved in practice (32).

author: Larsen, Clark Spencer
title: Biological Changes in Human Populations with Agriculture
abstract: A review of studies debunking the belief that agriculture brought an improvement in health and leisure, with reference to skeletal analysis, with foraging cultures as the control group.

author: Fajardo-Acosta, Fidel
title: Intemperance, Fratricide, and the Elusiveness of Grendel
abstract: Proposes that Grendel shoud be read as a symbol of the Danes’ indulgent and immoral lifestyle, to be overcome only by one who knows how to control both his anger and his drinking.

author: Feldman, Thalia Phillies
title: Grendel and Cain’s Descendants
abstract: An article that misses the mark on numerous counts. Better not to cite. Its main point is to claim that the fifelcynn are a specific Germanic breed of creatures inserted into Cainite lineage, and who are best defined according to the (surviving) Icelandic sense, namely fools (71-5); their association with eotenas suggests that they are cannibals (76); both gigantas and orcneas are a classical rather than a Christian concept (76-8); þyrs again means “fool” (78-9; it is noted that they inhabit the marshes, which contrasts them with demons of hell, 79); and the term feond has been given double standards, meaning enemy except when Grendel is involved (79-80). Syn (81) and hel (82) have specific, non-Christian referents.

author: Huisman, Rosemary
title: The Three Tellings of Beowulf’s Fight With Grendel’s Mother
abstract: There are three narrations (“discourses”) of this fight:1) by the narrator (1492-1590);2) by Beowulf to Hrothgar (1652-76);3) by Beowulf to Hygelac (2131-51) (217).These three passages are subject to different ideologies and aims (217-18). They should be read within the theory of language as a social semiotic, and with particular attention to transitivity (218). Bwf has different narrative modes: omniscient, external, internal. The first telling contains much of the first, but certain word-choices characterising the monsters as the Other reveal Beowulf’s perspective; sometimes, however, Beowulf is the stranger (218-19). This discourse endorses (1) the nature of the hero and (2) the relationship between heroic action and the Christian world-view (219). Nature also acts upon Beowulf; and much of the fighting action is carried out in external perspective (219-20).

author: Kaske, R.E.
title: Beowulf and the Book of Enoch
abstract: A lot of apocryphal literature that has not managed to retain even that status through late Antiquity may be used to explain OE literature (421-2). The Book of Enoch is one such text, which by many shreds of evidence may be seen to have had some existence in Britain; indeed, an eighth-century Anglo-Latin fragment even survives (422-3). Bwf understands Grendel as a descendant of the filii Dei and filiae hominum of Genesis 6.2 The portrayal of these giants in Enoch corresponds to that of Grendel in a number of ways: cannibalism; references to Judgement Day; and inconsistencies in their racial categorisation. Thus Grendel is a kind of giant, as well as an evil spirit and a demon; Enoch also describes “evil spirits. . . spirits of the giants.” Charles explains that giants derive from angels and humans, and spirits come about at their death (423-5). Many of the Hebrew names of the angels listed in Enoch as mating with humans end in -el; thus the last syllable of Grendel’s name may be a hint as to his ancestry (425-6). A problem with the reading as here presented is the Augustinian and therefore mainstream reading that the filii Dei are not angels but descendants of Seth; but the Bwf-poet may have used a blend of the two traditions [PS: unlikely!] (426-7). Another Enoch passage refers to fallen angel women turning sirens; some Jewish traditions, and also some patristic traditions, represent sirens as wasteland wanderers, a category applying to Grendel’s mother, a merewif (427-8). In Enoch, the metamorphosis of angel women into sirens is preceded by the prophecy that the giants will lead men to sacrifice demons, as the Danes do in Bwf 175-88. A linguistic connection with Enoch consists in the wa bið-sentence of this passage (429-30).

author: Kiessling, Nicolas K.
title: Grendel: A New Aspect
abstract:
Grendel’s qualification mǽre “famous” has often been stretched to mean “notorious” or infamous,” things it does not mean when other characters of the poem are described. This paper proposes that not mǽre is intended but mære “incubus, night monster.” The meaning of this noun would have specialised between the poem’s composition and recording in writing, so that scribes, often not consistent in diacritics to begin with, began to understand and copy the word as mǽre [footnote 5: the word never occurs with diacritics at all]. Grendel as presented in the poem is a unique blend of Latin, German, Scandinavian, and Celtic traditions, aptly described as a mære “night monster” (191-2). 25 instances of mǽre describing a hero are listed; nearly always, persons about to become royalty are described. When no individuals are described, honourable or royal objects, ancestors, or groups of people are indicated. Outside Bwf, the word is almost never used in a negative sense. Grendel, though called wer, maga, guma, and rinc, cannot be aptly described as se mǽre (192). Mǽre could easily become mære in transmission since copyists often substituted the familiar for the unfamiliar (192-3). OE (and OI) confusion of the homograph for famous, night-spirit, and sea is apparent elsewhere (193). Cognates of mæra, mære denote similar concepts in most IE languages. Originally, the verb meant “crush, grind, pounce on, plunder”; the noun thus came to mean a troublesome night spirit. The accepted etymology of Grendel is “grinder,” an appropriate name for a mære. The Celtic mor is found in morrigan, once glossing monstru[m] in femine figura (194). OE mære glosses fæc[c]e and incuba in the eighth century, as well as in many later glossaries. The Grendelkin are also called (?sp.)scinnes, a category associated by Cædmon with fallen angels, who, after all, begot the Grendelkin. Descriptions of such creatures were “vague and intended only to show what fearsome places uninhabited solitudes were.” The words incubus, satyrus, monstrum, pilosus, fæcce, and mære all belong to the same semantic field, and are closely related in meaning. Judaeo-Christian tradition considered incubi the offspring of Adam and female spirits; thus both these and Grendel are given a place in the creation narrative. Lilith, the name of one of these female spirits, is a Hebrew word for demon translated by Jerome as lamia “witch” and in OHG translations as a woman of the woods or woman of the water; cf Grendel’s mother, who is a merewif (195). The Leiden glossary has lamiae sleep with people (i.e. a succubus), bringing the concept close to that of mære (195-6). The Corpus glossary renders both fæcce and lamia “mære.” Some attempt is made to explain this connection. The Bwf poet may have been aware of the traditions connecting these concepts, as is suggested by his given lineage and his association with giants, elves, etc. (196). Lamiae were well-known in Germanic countries, where laws refer to them. A blood-sucking or entrail-consuming aspect to such witches is common. The Leiden glossary suggests their engagement in sexual affairs. Numerous more glosses are brought together (196-7). The concept of spirits engaging in sexual harassment was controversial, and not popular with the Church Fathers; but they did not deny their existence. The possibility of intercourse was problematic; but Aquinas proposed they could engage in carnal sin but for envy not pleasure, just as Grendel attacks out of envy. The Bwf copyist must have known of the sexual connotations of the mære, and would have read the word as such unless he knew of the Scandinavian mara (198). The meaning of Scandinavian mara, like that of other ON supernatural concepts, seems to have been conflated or somewhat forgotten in Christian times. Ynglinga saga has a description of a mara witch trampling her enemy to death. The poem here cited also has trollkund, which in Neckel’s glossary is associated with animal features, thus linking the concept to the Continental woman of the woods. An early Germanic borrowing of the incubus-concept is proposed (198-9). The witch in Ynglinga saga closely resembles Glámr of Grettis saga, whose confrontation with Grettir, in turn, is associated with that between Beowulf and Grendel (199-200). It is asked whether Grendel is a draugr. The crucial difference is that Grendel can be killed. A bunch of further spurious links is established between þyrs, eoten, draugr, etc (200-1). In conclusion, what matters is that Grendel is associated with Glámr’s category of aptrgangr and may have a connection with the ON mara (201).

[discussion:] This article is a rather confused attempt to connect as many monster-glosses and northwestern-European supernatural categories as possible. It is useful mostly insofar as it has collected many small connections, traditions, and glosses that would otherwise be a pain to track down.

author: Malmberg, Lars
title: Grendel and the Devil
abstract: Emphasises similarities between Grendel and Satan/demons in OE literature. Mentions also that Grendel’s abode is reminiscent to the depiction of hell in Blickling homily 17, based on the Visio Pauli (243).

author: Clemoes, P.A.M.
title: The Chronology of Ælfric’s Works
publication: The Anglo-Saxons: Studies in Some Aspects of their History and Culture Presented to Bruce Dickins
abstract:
Narrows down the composition of Ælfric’s respective works, from his first volume of Catholic Homilies in 989 to his last homilies after 1006.

Groups Judges with LS 18 (Kings), LS 25 (Maccabees), Assmann 8 (Esther), and Assmann 9 (Judith) both in purpose and in time of composition: they are “summary narratives of certain Old Testament books, narratives that with very little elucidation made the point that obedience to God is best” written as part of, or soon after, the LS project, but before the composition of the letter to Sigeweard in which it is mentioned; it was thus composed in the period 1002–1005 (240).

author: Jost, Karl
title: Unechte Ælfrictexte
abstract: The first systematic demonstration of stylistic differences within the Pentateuch. Jost argues that Gn 1–24.22 and Numbers 13 onwards as found in CUL Ii 1.33 [C] are Ælfric’s, but that the remainder of the Pentateuch as well as chs 4, 5, 10, 11 in other witnesses is not. The witnesses [B] (Cotton Claudius B. IV) and [L] (Laud Misc 509) he believes are partly revised from Ælfrician texts and partly independent translations.

author: Mellinkoff, Ruth
title: Cain’s Monstrous Progeny in Beowulf: Part I, Noachic Tradition
abstract: Looks for possible source traditions for the nature of Grendel, identifying the Noachic tradition echoed in 1 Enoch as the closest parallel and therefore the most likely source. The Noah fragments reflect a unified story (based on Genesis 6) of fallen angels begetting cannibal giants on the daughters of men, which giants are cast into the desert for punishment (145-6). The story was suppressed early on, the canonical version being that it was Seth’s descendants begetting giants on the daughters of Cain (146-7); but the alternative version did not quite disappear and the two mingled in various ways (148). Grendel and his mother’s giganticism and cannibalism echo this narrative, and particularly as told in the Noachic fragments (149-50). 1 Enoch contains different narratives, some of which have the giants become evil spirits while others have the fallen angels become evil spirits, which are not quite carnal, unlike the monsters in Beowulf; Mellinkoff makes rather a big deal out of their carnal nature (150-1). Moreover, Grendel and his mother are emphatically humanoid, rendering it unlikely that they were derived from the water creatures of Job 26.5; Grendel’s mother is forced to live below the water, but she is not fishlike; both monsters are clearly differentiated from other sea creatures, such as the nine monsters Beowulf kills (575a), the water monsters near the mere (1425-41a), or the other sea creatures attacking Beowulf (1510b-12a) (151). Behemoth and Leviathan (Job 40-1) are unlikely models as well; but the Noachic representation of these beasts as a beast of the wilderness and a beast of the water is a likely source, Grendel being a dry wasteland-monster and his mother a water creature (151-2). The wasteland has been identified with Nod, which has been variously interpreted as an actual and a symbolic place (152-3). But wastelands are no commonplace landscapes in OE poetry, nor do exegetes ever refer to a desert or wasteland for Cain to live in (153). The giant sword and Grendel’s immunity from swords may have been derived from the Noachic accounts of weapon-making [PS: or just Tubal-Cain in Genesis and the berserkr tradition] (154-5). The Bwf understanding of giants bringing on the flood also accords with the Noachic tradition (155-6). The borrowing seems to have been structural rather than ad hoc (156-8). Ancient minority traditions could be preserved in isolated places such as Ireland (158-9). Elements from 1 Enoch have been identified in Bede, the Book of Cerne, Solomon and Saturn and elsewhere (159-60). Transmission need not have been direct (161).

author: Mellinkoff, Ruth
title: Cain’s Monstrous Progeny in Beowulf: Part II, Post-diluvian Survival
abstract: Studies traditions of the survival of Cain’s descendants. In Bwf, Grendel and his mother are categorised using several supernatural categories, such as þyrs and eoten, but never gigantas, which is a term it appears to reserve for those giants that were killed in the flood (184). The survival of Cain’s descendants has been explained by a non-universal flood and by mountains exceeding the flood level (185-6). Some believed that fish were not destroyed in the flood, on the basis of Genesis 7.22 [PS: Mellinkoff’s reading relies specifically on a Talmudic discussion surrounding the phrase dry land, in the Hebrew but not the Vulgate. She leaves the surrounding data, the listing of species, out of the discussion] (186-7). Other traditions state that a single giant, Og, escaped, for instance by lifting along with the ark (187-8). Og cannot be demonstrated to have been traced back to Cain, though there is evidence of his deriving from one of the fallen angels (188-9). The Zohar has Moses’s father-in-law be a literal descendant of Cain; and Naamah, Cain’s female descendant in Genesis 4.22, is sometimes identified as Noah’s wife (190-2). In French literature, Cain was the patriarch of the Saracens, who share many of Grendel’s characteristics; but the monster in the ME Ywain and Gawain is more likely to have been considered of literal descent (192-3). Irish sources testifty to the continued belief that monsters were descended from Cain (193-4), even if Cain and Ham were often confused and conflated (194-6).

author: Niles, John D.
title: Myth and History
eds: Robert E. Bjork and John D. Niles
abstract: Presents a chronology of Beowulfian studies subject to the mythological and/or historicist fallacies, and concludes that neither precise historical reference nor Jungian impression were the poet’s aim.

author: Rogers, H.L.
title: Beowulf’s Three Great Fights
abstract: The Christian poet regarded things of this world as failure: joy in the hall always foreshadows catastrophe. His scepticism of things earthly bears only a superficial similarity to the pre-Christian submission to fate (339). Germanic literature favours heroism against odds. The hero is influenced by the human (kinsmen, lord, or spouse), the superhuman (fate or deities), and the material (weapons etc.) (339-40). The Bwf poet uses the same motifs from a Christian perspective: human society is exclusively weak, material (e.g. swords) is of no benefit [PS: the motif of cursed treasure is typical of Germanic myth, not here a Christian insertion]. The Finn and Ingeld episodes are understood by the poet as narrating mere vanity (340). Beowulf’s three fights form a progressive pattern, the hero’s success being inversely proportionate to his use of weapons and armour, his acquisition of treasure, and help from companions (340-1). The message is not to trust in things of this world, but rather in God. This moral message is not as clear in the second part of the poem (342). The Christian poet probably used a version in which the two, originally distinct, parts were already joined (342-3). It was the three fights in which he most felt he could express himself, but as the story progressed towards the second and third fight he increasingly felt that the material was unfit (343). Mægen “strength, vitality” is Beowulf’s defining attribute, used never to describe either monsters or merely worldly heroes, although a single exception exists for Grendel (343-4). Mod also is denied Beowulf’s enemies. The use of mægnes rof to describe Grendel throws doubt onto the authorship of the passage (344). Grendel’s forefather Cain is said to have killed Abel with a sword, a detail not found elsewhere. This accords well with the poet’s message that the sword serves no supernatural purpose but can bring harm on a human level. The first fight is surrounded by less of a treasure-motif than the second (345). Mægen receives a Christian flavour and is contrasted with the use of weapons; Beowulf overcomes Grendel by relying on God and his own mægen (346). His rejection of weapons should depend on the monster’s resistance to them, but the poet makes it a matter of fair play in order to prepare for the fact that swords are indeed used in the second fight (347). The language of the first fight is uncommonly Christian. In the revenge of Grendel’s mother, the futility of material is again demonstrated. She is weaker than her son, but proves tougher in battle. This battle has more of a folk-tale air, there being no enemy of God or unprovoked attack. Swords are used, and Beowulf accepts treasure. The emphatic quality of Hrunting forms a contrast with its failure (348). Again a reliance on one’s mægen is praised, but less convincingly since Beowulf would not have succeeded without a weapon (348-9). The second sword must have been in the source, but, so says Klaeber, its authorship was transferred from dwarves to giants to match Grendel’s ancestry and Tubalcain. Because the sword is relied on, there is less emphasis on mægen (349). God is mentioned far less in this fight (349-50). Beowulf leaves all the cave’s treasure behind. The Danes [i.e. human company] abandon Beowulf. Hrothgar’s homily serves as a key to the fights, demonstrating the uselessness of swords and the importance of the rightful use of mægen (350). After the homily, there is a shift in emphasis, and Beowulf becomes a powerful sword-wielding temporal lord. Beowulf’s account of the fights reflects this, as it makes very little reference to God’s help. The peculiarities of this account (Grendel’s glove) are there because the poet did not bother to remove them. The dragon is no enemy of God’s, his anger justly provoked. The poet is also faced with the problem that mere mægen cannot defeat a dragon (351). Beowulf’s remark that he would fight the dragon unarmed if he knew how is a strained effort to salvage his reliance on mægen (351-2). There is a lot of emphasis on treasure in this section, but there is some implication that Beowulf may be exempt from the curse and have conquered spiritually. There is, however, ambiguity on this front (352-3). This may be because the poet imposed his Christianity upon the poem, or because he did not think of Beowulf as either a Christian or a pagan. References to Germanic traditions are explained only insofar as the poet needed their motifs: all that interests him in the Sigemund account is differences between him and Beowulf, not his own epic (353). The shorter episodes are explained (353-5).

author: Williams, David
title: Cain and Beowulf: A Study in Secular Allegory
abstract: As Goldsmith has pointed out (Mode and Meaning 70), allegory in medieval literature should be read as a “symbolic mode” in Fletcher’s words (Allegory) rather than a consistent literary form. Bwf as allegory has a historical as well as a transhistorical referent; as such, it need not comply with either historical demands of accuracy or formal demands of literary or theological allegory (4). While the allegory used has its origins in theology, the application in Bwf is not scientific and therefore answers not to the four senses of exegetical allegory but rather to the two senses of didactic literature (4-5). This study tries to establish the Cain tradition as it existed at the time of composition of Bwf [in the eighth century, according to this author] as well as the social context in which that tradition must be placed (5-6). Before the coming of Christianity, kinship and feud were deeply ingrained in Anglo-Saxon society. The use of wergeld was established to counter the escalating nature of such a society’s emphasis on revenge. Wergeld emphasises the practical effect of a killing rather than its moral objectionability; it makes no moral judgement (6-7). After the conversion, Christians carried on the wergeld system to combat feud; but they added the concept of sin. This difference underlines the essential difference between pagan and Christian law: “the latter is as concerned with the disposition of the criminal as with the compensation of the victim” (7-8). Penitentials express this focus in differentiating between various intentions for the same crime. Anglo-Saxon law held the offence to the person primary and that to the state secondary. Societies evolve from tribal to state-centred by the reversal of the positions of these considerations (8-9). Parricide is an important test case between these two types of society. Whereas tribal societies consider it particularly horrendous because it precludes both vengeance and wergeld, Christians denounce it for its prototypical sinfulness and its inversion of the brotherly love propagated in Scripture. Two elements of Christianity, however, allow for the chastisement of a parricide: the emphasis on the spiritual situation of the criminal and the idea that in all crimes God was the primary offended (9). The resistance of feud to Christianisation is central to Anglo-Saxon history and Bwf. The Germanic emphasis on exclusive kinship is in exact opposition to the Christian ideal of universal kinship and took centuries to root out. When Bwf was composed, the outcome of this battle could not yet be predicted. Since it tells of the disasters resulting from feud, it may be considered a didactic vessel on the moral side of the argument (9-10). Bwf is a memorial to pagan times as well as a vessel for Christian propaganda. The age of its composition may have been one in which Old English was rediscovered and synthesised with the new Latin learning (10-11). Examples demonstrate that many learned clerics were connected to courts and thus able to synthesise the two traditions (11-12). Aldhelm is taken as an example, and it is suggested that many such men may have existed; and one of these will have written Bwf (12-13). While the poem’s heroes are great and good, they are ultimately replaced, as will be demonstrated in this study (13-14). References to Hebrew commentaries suggest not that these texts were directly accessible in Britain but rather that Latin commentaries such as Jerome’s include references to the tradition, while Josephus and Philo were well-known in Anglo-Saxon England (14-16). The Hebrew legendary tradition was known to the Bwf poet as demonstrated by Ruth Mellinkoff (16). Indirect transmission is the most likely for these. The author is of the opinion that Bwf focusses on “the struggle of societies to evolve institutions and moral codes that will ensure the survival of civilization” (17). Both Beowulf and Cain are given a double, historico-fabulous nature. The person of Beowulf is shrouded in mist and represents “brotherhood, loyalty, peace keeping, and lawful government” (18). This supra-individual character can therefore not present the individual’s struggle with sin. Instead, he represents the standard of virtue as past civilisation has set it. Christian principles are external to that civilisation, so these are not represented by Beowulf. Beowulf is, however, representative of the line of the “sons of God” that came to represent the good force opposing the descendants of Cain (17-18). The Septuagint and Vulgate accounts of Cain and Abel differ considerably with regard to the cause of God’s displeasure, and in the later reference to the intermingling of the races they are equally divergent. The “sons of God” were in later commentary unanimously understood to be Seth’s descendants; but an earlier tradition that identified them with the Septuagint’s “angels of God” persisted as a background motif (19). Alternative readings of Cain’s parentage have existed since the rabbinical tradition; a theory that he had been fathered by Satan was in the Middle Ages converted into tropology (20). Cain was associated with Eve and with the bestial. The latter quality facilitated the connection between animals and monsters (20-1). A link was also established between God’s cursing the earth and Cain’s tilling it. Josephus, who greatly influenced Bede, regarded agriculture as inferior to husbandry for its complex nature: God prefers the sacrifice of things that grow of themselves. Josephus further denounces Cain’s invention of weights, measures, and the city, since division is in opposition to unity and therefore unchristian (21-2). The ideal of simplicity also existed in Virgil. God’s rejection of Cain’s offer was explained in various ways, each of which emphasised one or more sinful character traits on Cain’s part. Envy was the gravest of these, having also moved Satan to tempt Eve; but medieval commentators also emphasised the fact that Cain brought murder, and therefore war, upon mankind (22-4). Bwf suggests this idea of Cain’s invention and his tropological descendants’ copying in its repeated “cearu/sorh/wroht wæs geniwod.” The earth played an important role in the curse, and since the earth may be read as nature and its fruits were forbidden him, Cain was divorced from nature and became unnatural. This understanding led to his representation as a monster. The medieval monster represents anti-nature and attacks human society, a natural construct (24-5). Cain’s exile was copied as a punishment for parricide in many medieval law codes, several of which make explicit reference to him. Commentators considered Cain’s exile and his Septuagintical trembling a punishment worse than death, emphasising his lack of a sedes quietas (25-6). Cain’s mark was variously interpreted, as was his dwelling-place. Most significantly, Augustine associated it with the worldly city (26-7). Cain’s progeny, like his ancestry, was subject to speculation concerning incest and bestiality (27-8). Their occupations suggested disharmony because of their connections with exile, the eating of meat, and musical dissonance (28-9). Cain’s descendants explain the necessity of the Flood if they are identified with the giants of Genesis 6 (29-30). Later commentators read “sons of God” and “daughters of men” as allegory for “sons of Seth” and “daughters of Cain”; Augustine emphasises that the difference between these two was moral, not racial (30). The English generally favoured the “sons of God”-reading over the “angels of God”-reading and tended to preserve both the historical and the figurative understanding of the term (30-1). The giant race survived the Flood [which, I suppose, is where they got their association with subterraneous or underwater dwelling, p. 34 {PS}], as may be seen in Nimrod, who copied his ancestor’s crime by building the city of Babylon, and Goliath. All the members of this line partook of both general and specific sinfulness. Shape-shifting was considered one of their characteristics since the first century CE, and they were associated with idolatry (32-4). Cain’s race survived the flood via Ham, who was singled out because of his post-diluvial sin (34-5). Some medieval commentators, especially in the British Isles, refer to Ham rather than Cain for the origin of evil; this usage was probably conscious. Bwf may have been informed by an Irish version of this tradition (35-6). according to Augustine, all evildoers are the spiritual descendants of Cain (36). The first fratricide was thought to have had a serpentine connection (36-7). St George’s legend, unlike the Cain tradition, considered the city a positive metaphor of order; such double and opposite symbolism was common in the Middle Ages (37). While men found it hard to distinguish between Christian and heathen societies where progress and degeneration were concerned, the Two Cities theory provided a new perspective, in which intention gained significance; thus vice and virtue were the distinguishing characteristics between the two cities, whose residents were not strictly distinguished by their faith. The opposition between Cain and Abel was an ideal metaphor by which to convey this partition. Christian historicism was salvaged by the elimination of an absolute evil in the past, so that the present need not be an absolute good (38-9). Bwf as allegory consists on the one axis of a historical narrative (social events) connected with a fabulous narrative (supernatural events), and on the other axis it consists of a connection of the present to the past by allusion and to the future by prophecy. Cain is both historical and fabulous, while allegorically he lives in all three tenses. References to earlier and later narratives present parallels to the battle between Beowulf and Cain’s kin, as well as instances in which men took on Cain’s sins (40-1). Heorot evokes the idea of Eden. Its negative aspects do not negate such a conclusion: in Eden, too, the elements of its downfall were contained within it (41-3). Heorot represents “kinship, peace, fidelity, and civilization”; Grendel represents “parricide [sic] warmongry, treason, and cannibalism”(43). Grendel’s attack takes place in the fabulous mode (43-4). Like Cain, he is associated with darkness (44). As in the Cain tradition, it is said of Grendel that “[n]o he þone gifstol gretan moste” (44-5). Grendel therefore hates the good just for being good, and he detests the brotherhood of which he cannot partake (45). The theme of chaos versus order expresses two fears: that of the fragility of social constructs and that of phenomenal nature (46). The uncontrolled force without is associated with the bestial and the grotesque (46-7). Grendel’s ancestry is stated and other references to giants in Bwf imply the same connection (48). As Cain was associated with his mother and dissociated from his father, so also Grendel “[n]o hie fæder cunnon” but his mother is of the same kind (49). Hrothgar’s “harangue,” prefaced by his commenting on a “giant-wrought” sword reminiscent of Tubal-Cain’s invention of weapons, describes how a man may slide into evil step by step, just as St Basil describes Cain’s descent into evil as gradual. Hrothgar is not subject to pride; his harangue demonstrates his understanding of the eternal opposition (49-51). While Beowulf may fall subject to pride in the second half of the poem, at this point he is the monsters’ antithesis (51-2). Grendel’s dwelling is very similar to that of Cain and his offspring: dark, waste, and underwater (52-3). Eve and her son were popularly regarded as the dual and incestuous originators of sin who thus engendered an inverted race. Beowulf, as an advocate of kinship, stands in direct opposition to this unnatural breed (53-4). Through the vengeance exerted by Grendel’s mother, an implicit comment is made on the central value of this custom in Germanic societies (54). All of Beowulf’s battles are fabulous; the poem never shows him in historical battles (54-5).

author: Waldron, T.
title: Nutrition and the Skeleton
publication: Food in Medieval England: Diet and Nutrition
eds: C.M. Woolgar, D. Serjeantson, and T. Waldron
abstract: Explains the ways in which nutritional deficiencies and excesses can be recognised through bone analysis with reference to some (later) medieval English grave-sites. Takes a cautious approach, so that no strong conclusions are reached, though it is pointed out that extensive DNA analysis would result in better data sets. Observes that “a substantial increase in the mean height of the population is a very recent phenomenon” without citing sources or providing dates (the absence of dates being a rather systematic deficiency in the essay). On the whole, provides a very helpful explanation of the problems and opportunities in the search for nutritional data in medieval skeletons.

author: Dyer, C.C.
title: Seasonal Patterns in Food Consumption in the Later Middle Ages
publication: Food in Medieval England: Diet and Nutrition
eds: C.M. Woolgar, D. Serjeantson, and T. Waldron
abstract: Describes the nature of food consumption through the seasons as dictated by growth and reproduction patterns as well as the religious calendar. Offers particular detail on the aristocracy, but also discusses the general population. The general trend is for the poor to be more dependent on seasonal availability and less on nonessentials such as meat.

author: Baker, David L.
title: Typology and the Christian Use of the Old Testament
abstract:
[biased]

Complains about misconceptions [i.e., undesirable uses] related to the term typology, and proposes to define the word (137-8). Until the middle of the fifties, the term was often used to denote prefiguration; from the middle of the fifties, it came to refer to correspondence. Both are interested in a historical basis, and typology is nowadays widely recognised as a form of historical interpretation (138-9). Typology has been claimed to exist in the Old Testament itself, especially in the prophets (139-40). Theological and eschatological readings of history were in use by Old Testament times, when Israelites assumed that God’s future actions would resemble his past actions; but instead of simple continuity they hoped for a new fulfilment, which arrived in the shape of the New Testament (140).
