As Goppelt shows, typology becomes clearer in the New Testament (141-2). The Old Testament can be understood from neither its Mesopotamian environment nor its Judaic reading; but the New Testament may be used to read the Old (142-4). The New Testament has no word for “typology,” but it has typos and cognates for “example, pattern” (144-6). Typological thought arises naturally from man’s attempts to understand the world through analogy (146). Such correspondences are both vertical (heavenly archetype and worldly antitype) and horizontal (earlier prototype and later antitype). Both Bible and modern scholarship are most interested in horizontal typology (148). Besides overt typology or analogy, the Bible also uses the same elements implicitly, since it conveys a lot of information in the form of narratives whose significance it leaves to the reader to interpret; no narrative is of use to us otherwise, but any story of men is an analogy to our own lives (148-9). Typology should not be confused with exegesis, prophecy, allegory (typology compares facts, allegory distils doctrine from the structure of facts), symbolism (again, typology observes relationships between facts), or a method or system (149-50). Any definition of typology according to a set of characteristics is arbitrary (151). Instead, typology is historical rather than literary, and it implies a factual correspondence rather than insignificant parallels (152-3). Two definitions are given: “a type is a biblical event, person or institution which serves as an example or pattern for other events, persons or institutions; typology is the study of types and the historical and theological correspondences between them; the basis of typology is God’s consistent activity in the history of his chosen people” (153). The historical nature of a type is essential; an event’s typological nature is not its real meaning but a useful parallel (153-4). Exegesis is not even relevant for typology, since it is not concerned with words but with events (154). Typology may be used in Christian contexts for the illumination of the Old by the New Testamant and vice versa; and it shows how the Bible may be used as a typos, i.e., as an example (155-6).

author: Lubac, Henri de
title: Medieval Exegesis: The Four Senses of Scripture
abstract:
[biased. Vol 1: Introduction; chapter 1: Theology, Scripture, and the Fourfold Sense; vol 2: chapter 7: The Foundation of History; chapter 8: Allegory, Sense of the Faith; chapter 9: Mystical Tropology; chapter 10: Anagogy and Eschatology]

Making frequent use of quotations and references to medieval authors, the introduction traces the tradition of fourfold sources (doctors, rhetoricians, readings; esp. 4-8) as well as a few medieval uses of the division into the four senses of historia, allegoria, tropologia, anagogia (1-14). The twelfth-century context is then outlined in which the fourfold sense took hold (15-24). A crucial and [within Catholicism] “universal” twofold axiom is identified: all divine revelation is contained in Scripture, and the interpretation of the Bible encompasses all theology (24). The allegorical reading of Scripture demanded that all readings be authenticated by the Church, i.e., based on the official glosses of allegorical reference (27). The words doctrina and scriptura were often used interchangeably (27-8). Lubac defends the study of secular literature and cites many medieval authors who shared his opinion. Secular studies are thought by Alcuin, Augustine, Origen and others to be necessary elements for the study of lower reason, with the additional use of praising divine studies by means of contrast (33-40). The relationship between the divine and the other arts is further discussed (40-55). Medieval opinions on what questions should be asked are mentioned (55-66). After long debate, the dialectical approach, launched by Aristotelian philosophy, becomes the new standard methodology in the mid-thirteenth century, at the expense of the triple or quadruple interpretation of Bible passages (66-74, esp. 73). Littera and historia are often used interchangeably, emphasising the weight of the word (II.41-3, esp. 41). Historia is the foundation of Christian faith, which must be accepted for any nonliteral meanings to be based on it; and this opinion is shared by Origen, Augustine, Jerome, Gregory, Isidore, and Bede (47-8). The theme is picked up by Rabanus Maurus, Notker, Alcuin, and others (48-50). The theme of history as a fundament was a constant axiom from the third to the fifteenth century, never negated (50). Where littera is negatively portrayed, it refers to the dead letter of Judaism, or to the rule of the letter alone (50-1). Littera and spiritus combine to form the whole Bible (54). The Middle Ages have often abused spiritus for uncalled-for allegory (56); but unlike the moderns, they never questioned historia (56-8). Some facts in the Bible are not wrong in themselves but would be wrong if we imitated them; in the words of C. Faust, Scripture is justified without defending the sins of men (63-4). The more astounding assertions in the Bible, such as the size of the ark and the stopping of the sun, were not doubted by Origen et al. (67-9). Allegory is found not in the text but in the events it relates (86). Augustine distinguished between the allegory of deeds (what events mean to us) and the allegory of words (how reported speech may be directed at us) (87). The reference of Old Testament allegory is “Christ and the Church” (89-94). Allegory is horizontal, past prototype corresponding to later antitype; but it also moves from littera to spiritus and thus entails a qualitative difference. It is essential to understand that the referent is of interior quality whereas the prototype is external (98-9). Pagan allegory moves from myth to philosophical abstraction; Christian allegory moves from history to (meta)history (99-102, esp. 101). The structure of pagan and Christian allegory is different (102-4). Letter and flesh are as milk, spirit and divinity as bread or solid food (107). Gregory’s influence is discussed (117-25). The move from allegory to tropology is not qualitative: both are spiritus. Tropology concerns “the edification of morals” (127). Origen and Gregory are the two masters of tropology. Tropology proceeds from allegory, not from history (134). Anagogy reads in historia events that will take place at the end of the age (179). The “incorrect” nature of the word anagogia is pointed out (179-81). There are properly two types of anagogy: that “which fulfills the doctrinal formulation of the fourfold sense” and that “which fulfills the spiritual formulation of the threefold sense”; both are part of “Christian mystery” not of the image (181). Anagogy consists of (1) eschatology (which is speculative), itself divided into (a) personal and (b) universal eschatology; and (2) contemplation of God in the here and now (which is contemplative) (181-2). Jewish prophecy was eschatological. The Old Testament is the image for the New Testament; the New Testament is the image for final things (182) (“the eternal testament,” 184). The dialectic of spiritual anagogy does not replace temporal development (185-6). Eschatology is the unifying point of the fourfold sense. Since Christianity is a fulfilment, true anagogy is always eschatological (197).

author: Pagels, Elaine
title: The Origin of Satan
abstract: Explains how the author of Mark wrote in the context or aftermath of the Jewish War and destruction of Jerusalem AD 70; that of Matthew wrote in competition with the Pharisees; and those of Luke and John wrote to win a claim to Israel’s traditional inheritance. The idea of a cosmic adversary Satan came about in the Jewish sectarian rivalry and made its ways into Mark, Matthew, and Luke. In all stages, it was the binary nature of conflict that called for the postulation of an enemy that transcended the natural. This cosmic conflict also gained a place within the Christian movement, resulting in the exclusion of heretics.

author: Weber, Gerd Wolfgang
title: Intellegere historiam: Typological Perspectives of Nordic Prehistory (in Snorri, Saxo, Widukind and others)
publication: Tradition og historieskrivning: Kilderne til Nordens ældste historie
eds: Kirsten Hastrup and Preben Meulengracht Sørensen
abstract: In the later Middle Ages, historiography was understood as an element of civilization and a confirmation of identity, as well as a political instrument (95-6). This may be contrasted with Bede, who believes there are moral reasons (instruction and edification) for writing history. To understand twelfth-century historiographers, there is need for a revision of hermeneutic discourse (96). Snorri reads skaldic poetry as a reliable source of information; eyewitness-reports as reliable if they conform to expectation and appear to have sprung from trustworthy individuals (differing views are often quoted for completeness’ sake); heroic legend as a source to be handled with extreme care; and mythology as matter for eheumerism (97). ON history also runs parallel with world history; and typology was often used to read this (97). While historical typology is different from biblical typology, Augustine’s definition has salvation history encompass world history so that both forms of typology may be treated in the same manner. Restricting biblical typology to Christology, prefiguring the first advent only, is missing the point of the system: salvation history extends throughout the six ages (97-8). Furthermore, typology has types and referents throughout history, and the gospel, spread from the centre of the world, does not reach everyone at the same time (98-9). It is therefore only natural that medieval historiographers applied typology to their pre-Christian past, although less obvious types are often found (99-100). The plan of salvation may thus also be manifested in the lives of pagans (100-101). Snorri is indebted to the tradition that synchronises biblical with worldly events, as, for instance, he speaks of a Fróþa frið contemporaneous with the pax Augusta and its spiritual antitype, the pax vera or pax Christi of Christ’s incarnation (101-3). A Scandinavian familiarity with typology is demonstrated in the numerous characterizations of Samson (prefiguring Christ) alongside classical and Germanic heroes in Scandinavian Church artwork (103-5). Types retain their imperfections when compared to their divine antitype. An ON type is Þórr in his fight with the Miðgarðzormr. He can perfectly well serve as a type of Christ and still be worshipped as a god by the ignorant (105-6). In Scandinavian subject matter, the conversion takes the place of the first advent of Christ in the sense that events before these defining moments are treated in the same manner, and later events are also treated in parallelism (106-7). Authors retell heathen stories of gods with the implicit knowledge (explicit in the Edda’s prologue), shared with the Christian reader, that it here concerns men posing as gods (107). In Saxo’s Gesta Danorum, dii refers to pagan gods actively taking part in the narrative while dæmoni are outright pagan deities; after his description of the failed attempt at converting the Danes, Deus is used for the Christian God (107-8). In the absence of reliable accounts, historiographers often judged the reliability of sources by comparison with patristic material. Stories could be “rationalizations” of intellectual Christian truths, or Christian-like conceptions about creation (108). It is because of this potential for interpretation that medieval historiographers were reluctant to leave anything out. In order to fully benefit from their writings, modern scholars need to attain the medieval historiographer’s perspective (108-9). Pagans could receive Christian visionary dreams, but their semiotics had to be in line with Christian semiology—they must demonstrably correspond to Christian truth (109). Snorri’s world history consists of (1) the history of the Trojan emigrants; (2) the Norwegian dynasty, starting with Haraldr hárfagri; (3) the Christian era [parallel to the sixth age of the world], beginning with Óláfr Tryggvason (109-10). Haraldr is portrayed as a noble heathen in view of his oath by his creator (110-11). Snorri’s account of Hákon combines political and theological expression (112-14). Religion may be considered a structuring element of moral nature in Scandinavian history and prehistory (115). In Íslendingabók, the conversion of Iceland is argued on political grounds, namely fear of political schism (115-16). Its author, however, will have been familiar with the argument from numerous foreign (literary) parallels (116). Common sense is a “political theme” throughout Icelandic literature (116-17). Willingly-accepted Christianity is presented as leading not only to spiritual freedom, but also to political freedom (117-18). Meditation, retreat, and dream figure in ON writing about the pre-conversion period where individuals gain some insight; this is suggestive of divine intervention (119-23). The correlation between type of conversion (voluntary or coerced) and political identity and integrity is a common theme in medieval historiography (123-5). Iceland is thus linked to the rest of the sixth age (125-7).

author: Schofield, P.R.
title: Medieval Diet and Demography
publication: Food in Medieval England: Diet and Nutrition
eds: C.M. Woolgar, D. Serjeantson, and T. Waldron
abstract: In a concise review of earlier work, refers to Livi-Bacci’s work to problematise the prevalent earlier notion that food availability has a close inverse relationship with mortality (239–42). Repeats Campbell’s estimate that England could sustain 4.38 million residents in 1300 and 2.34 million in 1375 (242–3). From the second half of the fourteenth century to the fifteenth century, the diet of the lower-status part of the population in particular became less dependent on grains and much higher in protein; that of the aristocracy did not change much in this period, so a degree of convergence took place. The diets of all were primarily based on grains throughout the period (243–4, and for this last point see further 246). Wealthy peasants generally had more numerous families than their poorer neighbours, which may suggest greater nutritional resources among the rich (244). Only grains show marked fluctuation between seasons, following the succession of good and failed harvests; but long-term demographics have been shown to undergo little influence from fluctuations in grain prices in early Modern England (and by implication generally). Harvest failure is followed by increased morbidity in the form of infectious disease, but “the impact” thereof is “largely hidden from us” (247). The weight of evidence is that the Black Death affected people of all nutritional backgrounds, yet there is some evidence of the plague taking a higher toll in regions with greater dearth; accordingly, the Black Death affected especially the generation that had lived through the Great Famine of the 1310s as children (247–8). The fifteenth century is thought to have been a time of greater food availability; the population check of the same period therefore is explained either by failure to respond to greater disease both endemic and epidemic or with reference to greater female employment and therefore lower birth rates. Either explanation involves indirect influence from nutrition (248–52). In conclusion, “we are given sufficient indication that diet was a variable capable of effecting change in population movement in this period. The minute and particular causative features are not, however, open to our scrutiny” (253).

author: Landers, John
title: The Field and the Forge: Population, Production, and Power in the Pre-Industrial West
abstract:
An absolutely brilliant work on the historical relationship between energy and demographic space.

[Introduction]

Introduces a sweeping time scale from societal settlement to the Industrial Revolution. The latter event signalled the transition from an organic to a mineral economy. The former is the epoch of the longue durée, characterised by low productivity as a consequence of its primary reliance on human muscle power. The military realm was the first to transition into a mineral economy, but only in the technology of warfare itself, through the introduction of gunpowder in the sixteenth century. From then up to the nineteenth and even twentieth centuries, the rest of the economy took its time to catch up so two “energetic regimes” coexisted. In the demographic realm, the longue durée ended in the nineteenth century with a fall in birth and death rates (1–3).

The ancient, medieval, and early modern periods each represent a period of slow, sustained population growth followed by stagnation or decline. The decline phase of the early modern period was followed by a new period of growth, initially organic after 1750 but undergoing a structural change after 1860 with steep declines in fertility and mortality alongside strong outward migration (3–4).

The seasons also shaped experience: the agricultural year was the most important of these, but the cold and dark of winter also restricted labour in other sectors. Seasonal limitations to interior travel have been termed a “time frontier” by De Vries and Van der Woude (The First Modern Economy, 1997). Such it was to traders and churchmen, but to residents of the north it was a time for increased social activity (4).

Demographic space is of a different order than geographic space in that the economic and demographic processes that take place within it are relational rather than absolute in a Newtonian sense. Energy drives all such processes, and increases in productivity and social complexity entail increased energy requirements (5–6).

The geography of the organic economy is one of fields, in two senses: energy was extracted from cultivation and pasturage, but economic space was also evenly distributed over the landscape as muscle-powered transportation imposed stringent limits on demographic distribution (which was therefore “areal”) (6–7). Alongside this economy existed that of the forge, whose primary energy source was heat, which relied on ore extraction, and whose distribution was accordingly “punctiform”. Field and forge were two economies in synergy, though especially so in the upper echelons of society, as energy was scarce. The forge economy had particular prominence in warfare, and control of the forge was essential for control over the means of coercion, which along with control over demographic space constituted the tools for government (7–8). The geographies of both economies were characterised by spatial inequality: raw materials moved from periphery to core, while luxury goods moved the other way. The manipulation of this exchange could be an effective tool for political leadership (8).

In an organic economy, quality of force had a great advantage over quantity in numbers. The gunpowder revolution of the sixteenth century brought an end to this, as large forces could now be deployed effectively; this did mean an increase in the cost and destructive effects of warfare, bringing the nation states of eighteenth-century Europe to the brink of economic collapse (8–10).

There is a paradox in the expectation that large empires might seem to depend on a mineral economy coupled with the fact that many large-scale power infrastructures existed in ancient times. The solution to this paradox is that the real outer limits of the organic economy were rarely reached, among other things because poverty depressed demand. Large empires were viable given “efficient, ingenious, or ruthless” rulers with political rather than economic ambitions. With the rise of economic productivity, the cost of employing them for political ends grew (11–12). From early modern times on, administrative structures have been weaker but economic structures stronger; rulers therefore use the market infrastructure, though fiscal systems discouraged and limited the use of physical property for political ends. The rise of the credit economy provided some stretch until the organic economy gave way altogether (12).

In the organic economy, per capita production was limited by the low efficiency of photosynthesis and the human digestive system. Low worker output led to low productivity and therefore scarcity, which in turn resulted in widespread poverty and depressed demand for non-subsistence goods. Labour and other productive resources were typically underemployed as a consequence of low productivity and productive bottlenecks of seasonal and other kinds (17). Geographic specialisation, investment in large-scale infrastructure, and overall spatial integration were discouraged by the areal nature of economic geography (17–18).

[Ch. 2: Population Dynamics]

“Economic and demographic patterns were bound to be very closely related as long as human labour was the main variable factor of production and subsistence needs formed the main element of consumption” (19). What little evidence there is of premodern population dynamics suggests that the ancient world grew until the second century CE, when some portion of the population was wiped out by what seems to have been an airborne infection. Depopulation seems to have been an issue in this century as well (21–3). Medieval growth is established from the eleventh century onwards (as evidenced by cultivation area); whether the trend was reversed at or prior to the bubonic plague of the 1340s is not clear (23). Compared to the ancient population peak, a greater proportion of the European population now seemed to be in northern Europe, with an estimated 25% left in Iberia–Italy compared to over 40% in the second century CE. Many populations seem to have been at capacity by the early fourteenth century. Stagnation and maybe decline began in the second quarter of the century, before the dramatic decline and sustained depression of the plague years (23–4). These were followed by an early modern and a modern cycle (24–6).

Migration statistics are more prominent on a local level than on national levels; when dealing with large populations they can often be ignored without too much distortion (26). Prior to the nineteenth century, the number of children per woman (presuming married at 15 and until 50) varied regionally between six and ten; while everywhere natural fertility was the norm, the difference is explained by varying intervals between children, in turn triggered by different feeding cultures. In any case differences in marriage patterns were the main engine for change in overall fertility. Western Europe had particularly low fertility due to the requirement that an independent household was a necessary requirement for marriage, delaying a woman’s childbearing by as much as ten years. This also translated into higher living standards and lower mortality (27–8).

Before the mortality transition following 1870, infectious disease was the primary cause of mortality; after, non-infectious disease became the most common cause of death. In the old system, rural life expectancy was considerably higher than urban (28–9). The dynamics of mortality crisis are presented in broad outline; it is observed that some seasonal variation exists, winter being conducive to respiratory infections while summer favours fly-borne diseases and droplet infections (29–31). “In a low-productivity organic economy most changes in living standards were realized in terms of changes in the quality and quantity of food consumed, and so it is reasonable to expect a close relationship to exist between living standards as measured by the buying power of wages (or ‘real wage’ level) and nutritionally based resistance to infection” (31). However, prior to the nineteenth century there is no evidence of a link between changes in wages and mortality, so nutritional determinism appears to be invalid; the discrepancy is likely due to sociability patterns that kept the wealthy in the cities where they were vulnerable to infection from the lower classes (31–2). There is an important footnote 9 on p. 32 explaining why Fogel’s nutritional determinism is flawed: the recent increase in body height results from an improved balance between calory intake and expenditure, dependent on both the nature of one’s daily work and exposure to infections, which also requires energy. Levels of settlement, trade, and migration instead played a big role in regional epidemiological variation, as in England of the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. Here, high-density settlements fostered epidemics while providing protection against subsistence crises, while the uplands experienced the inverse conditions. Economic change could thus affect mortality through spatial integration as well as through nutrition and the standard of living. However, where exposure is high and continuous, those who survive childhood will have considerable immunity, bringing down the case fatality rates (33–4). This model scales up to larger populations, and explains why nutritionally sensitive diseases rose in the [urban] nineteenth century, raising mortality in the lower classes (34). Global exploration and expansion is thought to have led first to the spread of disease, followed by adaptation and the spread of new crops that improved resistance, reducing mortality and paving the way for demographic expansion (34–5). McNeill 1977 (Plagues and Peoples) is referenced as a study pursuing this line of thought at great scope (35).

Late sixteenth-century England saw an annual population growth rate of 1.1 percent, which posed an enormous challenge for food production just to keep per-capita levels at the same level (35–6). In the classical model of diminishing returns, an annual population growth beyond 0.5 percent seems to have negatively affected buying power in England. Classical analysis also predicts that when population growth places tension on food production the price of food rises relative to that of non-food commodities, and that of the cheapest grains rises most of all; this is borne out by medieval and early modern evidence. The classical is harder to verify for demographic dynamics, however; the picture seems to be one in which Malthus’s preventive check was primary in later medieval Western Europe, while the positive check was more common elsewhere and perhaps in Western Europe prior to the late Middle Ages (36–9).

The classical model fails to account for population structure; here, the hearth model supplements it. This model thinks of the economy as a group of non-divisible family production centres (hearths), with profound consequences for population growth as the number of hearths is comparatively inflexible and “surplus sons” were denied access to them and were drawn into the cities; this process can be seen at work in seventeenth-century England (39–42).

From the perspective of the ecological model, the population’s responses to increasing food needs entailed problems such as monoculture and the loss of commons and woodlands that could sustain gatherer-culture if crops failed (reference to Grigg 1980: Population Growth and Agrarian Change). The growth of the population relative to the size of the land led to famine-vulnerable marginal holdings (42–4).

[Ch. 3: Production and Technology]

According to the classical model, regional specialisation is the shortest path to an increase in productivity, but this is not borne out in an organic economy since specialisation requires more non-food workers, which must be supported by a greater per-capita output of food, which was what the specialisation was intended to achieve in the first place (48). Technology is defined as “any application of information to a recurrent activity in such a way as to enhance desired outcomes”, involving hardware, procedure, and personnel (49). Power sources are quantified; these were largely muscle power, fuel wood, watermills, and some limited input from windmills (50–2).

Since agriculture supported the population, overall growth depended on increased output in this sector. The challenge faced in reality was keeping per capita output equal in the face of population growth. Cultivation has the inherent problem of artificial ecology, which is at increased risk of shortfall compared to the “climax ecosystems” of hunter-gatherer environments (53). Technological development occurred by broadening the crop base and by modifying systems of crop rotation. The development of these systems over time is discussed in some detail, with special attention to northern Europe where two sowings were possible in combination with fallow and the introduction of the heavy wheeled plough with coulter, which itself led to a stratification between those who could afford to have a share in a team, those who could own their own team, and those who were left with hand-cultivation (55–6). Horses began to replace oxen in northern Europe from the twelfth century onwards (56–7). By the 1250s, extensive growth began to slow down and had stopped in many regions, probably because soil fertility levels could not be maintained in the face of population pressure, which led to the extension of three-course rotation to poor soils, leading to ever lower marginal returns; the growth phase of the medieval era ended shortly thereafter. Lack of investment in innovation is pointed out as an additional cause, as well as diminishing returns from investments that did take place (57).

Though production techniques varied and developed, agricultural output remained constrained by the constant of energy input. The ratio of energy in against out was comparatively efficient, but it was only with animal power that energy output could outpace energy input by a reasonable margin (58).

author: Kunitz, Stephen J.
title: Speculations on the European Mortality Decline

author: Jochens, Jenny M.
title: Consent in Marriage: Old Norse Law, Life, and Literature
abstract: A case is known from the 1180s in which a woman who had left her husband was permitted by an archbishop to remarry only after witnesses had declared that she had been given to her first husband without her own consent. At this time, the doctrine of female consent was spread by the Church, and it seems the woman consciously hoped to benefit from the new regulations (142). Nevertheless, the son that sprang from the new marriage was at a later time declared illegitimate by churchmen at the request of his half-brother who was his rival to royal succession (143).

author: Jochens, Jenny M.
title: Marriage
abstract: In pre-Christian Germanic tradition, marriage was Kaufehe and originally possibly Raubehe, as has been argued from the word brúð(h)laup (17-18). Christian innovations blur our picture of pre-Christian practice, but a comparison of Roman and northern Christian marriage point to originally pagan traditions accepted by settling Christians because they were not contrary to Christian principles, e.g., the two-step character of engagement and wedding, and the giving away of the bride by the father (17, 18). Christian marriage was more complex; bridal consent and incest restrictions beyond the nuclear family are decidedly Christian. Negative evidence can further be gained from laws (18). Some of the problems of law and saga evidence are outlined (19). The Germanic tribes that entered the Roman sphere in the late fourth century had by that time begun to discourage unbounded sexual activity and formed a legal concept of marriage designed to limit a man’s financial beneficiaries. Bigamy and polygamy occurred among powerful men; Icelandic law prohibited them. Tacitus suggests that financial resources determined the possibilities (20). “Pagan marriage was thus arranged to ensure the orderly passing of property from one generation to the next.” Pre-Christian marriage restrictions concerned property: originally, the unfree probably could not marry, since the child of an unfree man could not inherit. As the number of unfree dwindled, an equal match in terms of wealth and social rank became important; but when the latter fell short, the former could compensate, especially when the bride’s family were the prestigious but hungry for money. Where such situations occur in sagas, however, problems always ensue, which suggests that social rank may have been the more important factor (21-2). Since marriage primarily concerned the transfer of property, few personal restrictions were needed: there was no difficulty in waiting for the bride to reach maturity. Laws, codified in Christian times, combine incest prohibitions within the nuclear family with those concerning the extended family, so that it is hard to distinguish between Christian and pagan practice; but literature suggests that “minimal incest” was always prohibited, whereas Icelanders did not prohibit marriage with extended family (22-3). The child of an unbought bride could not inherit; conditions were a minimum bridal price and the two-phase practice of engagement (including negotiations concerning the bridal price) and wedding. The bride’s father was to be passive: Sigríðr’s father in Eindriða þáttr ok Erlings actively offers his daughter, but this is received as something uncommon if not dishonourable. Normally, the suitor or his one of his male relatives (e.g., father) would visit the father or guardian of the bride in the presence of half a score kinsmen and friends, but they could only broach the subject after a few days’ visit. Desired qualities in the groom were wealth, nobility, and personal accomplishment. The guardian of the bride could turn down the offer and often did so when the suitor was a berserk or unpleasant man, but this was done only “to prevent violence in the community.” The fastnandi was the bride’s legitimate son, son-in-law, father, or brother; or mother if none of these existed (24-5). This sequence conformed to the sequence of inheritance (25-6). Sagas suggest much higher bridal prices than the minimal sum required. A dowry also existed, and here, too, sagas suggest great sums; Tacitus already mentions these two sources of starting-capital (26). A handshake decided the engagement deal. The bride had no formal say in the matter and her presence was not required; laws allow a father to force his daughter into marriage, except (from c. 1200) if she wanted to become a nun. Most saga wedding deals were made without the bride’s knowledge. Widows had the right to refuse a candidate, but not if the father was the guardian. If the guardian had rejected two suitable parties, a girl could engage herself (27). Sagas suggest that political motives were important (27-8). The wedding itself centred around issues of sex and reproduction (29). Brúð(h)laup is now suggested to refer to the groom’s “jumping” of the bride. A ritual has the bride await the groom in bed; law requires six witnesses to this ritual in order to make a wedding legally binding (29-30). As patronyms show, a child was considered the father’s child (30). Marriage did not preclude extramarital contacts, and there was no implication of a lifelong union. Contemporary sagas tell that most prominent men had concubines or informal extramarital relationships (31). The Grágás law code condemns extramarital intercourse extensively, suggesting that it was endemic and its vocabulary making clear that the practice was of pagan origin. Sexual crimes were committed against the woman’s kin, not person; intercourse with beggar women was not punishable (32). The Sagas of Icelanders, in contrast with the contemporary sagas, seldom mention extramarital affairs; but on closer investigation sexual violence and aggression is a clear topos, surfacing for instance in the topos of “the illicit love visit,” occurring over twenty times (33-4). Servant girls are portrayed as sexually available to employers and guests (35). “By passing over in silence the problem of multiple sexual partners in the pagan era, the authors of the sagas of Icelanders reveal simultaneously native and Christian concerns.” Christianity brought into the marriage scheme stricter laws than the Icelanders, untrained by Stoic traditions, could accept (36). The Church did not object to financial transactions involved in the deal and they accepted the two separate steps, but they emphasised that marriage is a sacrament not a secular contract. They introduced consent, monogamy, fidelity and indissolubility, as well as priestly celibacy. The possession of concubines was not willingly abandoned, and even priests and bishops resorted to this usage since they could have wives no longer (37). Sturlunga saga suggests ubiquitous promiscuity, even to the point where a man’s right to kill a man having extramarital sex with one of his six protegées is disregarded or reduced to a fine. Lesser people “lived together by mutual agreement” without marriage. Such situations made it necessary to overlook official regulations in the distribution of heritage, which practice is indeed suggested in Sturlunga saga (39). Illegitimate sons could also become Norwegian kings until c. 1250. Female consent in informal unions is likely, but Norway’s civil wars witnessed a lot of unions originating in capture (40). Incest laws are specified (42-4). Contemporary sagas show little concern for female consent. On the Continent, it received full formulation only by 1150; it was established ecclesiastically in the north about 1180 and soon incorporated into national and provincial law (44-7). The presence in some sagas of consent has convinced some scholars that it was common in pre-Christian times (Lx 5.34:93, 5.23:63-4; Nj 12.10:31; Kalinke 1981). But refusals are rare (47). It is argued that the Christian saga authors, unable to change present circumstances, instead idealised the past, denying the actual Kaufehe nature of pagan marriage as well as the ubiquitous nature of illicit relationships (47-8). Kings sagas introduce consent anachronistically, and the later sources are more likely to include it. The category of “lying sagas” therefore illustrate the spread of the notion at the time of composition (49). Contemporary sagas show the least implementation of the doctrine of consent, although these sagas deal with the highest echelons of society. Implicitly, fathers could always take their daughers’ preferences into consideration (51). Despite the ideals of the Church, nordic marriage remained a reflection of political and monetary considerations (52). Two illustrations show this conservative nature of marriage (52-4). Divorce is in sagas usually initiated by the wife, but this is probably because divorce was often caused by male violence (54, 57). Grágás contradicts the sagas of Icelanders on the pre-Christian existence of consent and fidelity, and also on divorce. The sagas are taken as the more authoritative source in the case of divorce (55). Property formed half of the conditions for divorce; violence and incest were the others (55-7). Divorce was a woman’s weapon: being weaker than her husband, she could use it as a threat (59-9). Widows often remarried, but not after their menopause; widows were the most powerful women in society (61).

author: Kuhn, Hans
title: Der Familien- und Freundeskreis
abstract: The family in the sense of a powerful, organised Sippe ruling society never existed among Icelanders or other Germanic peoples, with the exception of the first settlers, who were related. A few families grew powerful, e.g., the Sturlungs, but not in the strict sense that is often supposed; and they also feuded amongst themselves (87-8). In the sagas it seems that the wife was nearly equal in power to the husband and rather free in her own area of work; they were neither responsible nor punishable, although witchcraft, fornication, and theft annulled their immunity: theft sometimes resulted in physical punishment. This image from the sagas, however, cannot be entirely reliable (89-90). Divorce was easy for both men and women: it required only that one of the two declared the divorce in the presence of witnesses; little occasion was needed (90-1). Widows did not return into guardianship. Women could be punished severely for fornication; men were not punished for breaking their own marriage, and concubinage was normal practice (91-2). Grave finds suggest that men received more prominent graves than women (92). After 1030, no female poets are known; this appears to be ecclesiastical influence (93).

author: Schultze, Alfred
title: Zum altnordischen Eherecht
abstract: Two approaches to Old Germanic marriage law are current: one emphasises marriage as a contract of purchase between husband and guardian (in which possession, however, has a specialised meaning, limited by the purposes of procreation and obtaining a leader of the household); the other approach takes both families as the starting-point and attempts to understand the process from this perspective. The present study belongs to the latter category (1-2). The bride was an object in the contract between the families; her consent was no prerequisite before Christianity altered the procedure (2-3). This does not, however, tell us anything about the appreciation of women; what we see is merely the legal form which Germanic morality has assumed, but honour and happiness were the starting-point of marriage for both partners. Nonetheless their subordination to their families was assumed; honour and happiness are to be found in the choice made by the families (3-4). “Nicht die Liebe führt, auf ihrer Seite, zur Heirat, sondern die Heirat führt zur Liebe.” Swedish-Upplandic law shows that a man was required to ask the permission of the woman’s nearest kin (4). This “engager” is a legal entity to be distinguished from the functionss of other close kinsmen; but their consent is also required for the guardian to agree to the marriage, for the unity of the family is of paramount importance (5). The guardian was the only one who could agree to marriage on the bride’s behalf; stealing a bride was punishable by fine, in which case we may assume the marriage was declared null and void (5-6). The guardian was from the father’s family (7-8). The initiative of a marriage came from the groom’s close kinsman or from the groom himself. According to södermännischen law, the groom was to receive the counsel (including consent) of his nearest kinsmen (13). The larger families met in a malaþing to agree to the contract. The ceremony was concluded with a formula delivered by the “festiger,” just as it happened at the engagement (15). The marriage-bond made the two families kin. Despite argumens that Indo-Germanic languages knew this binding only from the point of view of the woman regarding the man’s relations, all northern Germanic peoples considered it valid both ways around; indeed, the man’s relationship with his new kin plays an important role in the Norwegian and Icelandic law codes (18). The husband even had a right to wergeld when his wife’s father or brother was killed, and he was required to avenge such deaths (19). When a woman marries she does not lose her own kin; she now has two families (21). The woman’s guardian functions as prosecutor in case of physical abuse by the husband; but Upplandic law declares that her kin have a right to a fine only if she dies. When the husband does not go to bed with his wife for three years, the Grágás gives her kin the right to her property without divorce, plus a fine if she is meanwhile raped by a third person (22). A certain law states that in case of murder by a woman her next of kin are held responsible, not her husband (23). The sagas have examples of women divorcing because their husbands have attempted to kill their kinsmen. Felix Genzmer says that the heroic lays prove that the duties towards kin overruled those towards the partner (23-4). Children belong to the father’s family, as may be seen from their patronymics. Children, especially sons, are among the husband’s family’s main aims in arranging marriages. But children are also blood-relations of the mother (24). The child’s first name, often after a deceased relative, is as often chosen from the mother’s as from the father’s kin. The mother’s father and brother are most common name-providers among the mother’s kin; but the names derive from the mother’s father’s kin (24-6). Eigin- in Eiginkona in Old West Norse is a legal term denoting possession, but eigin only receives its exact meaning in its context; it need not, therefore, here denote the possession of property (27). It is suggested that the Mundr, the wedding gift by the husband to the wife, was originally given to her kin; in a later stage it was claimed by her guardian alone; and finally it became the bride’s own property. In Swedish law codes, the first stage can still be traced: the mundr was hers by the grace of her kin. West Norse sources show the third stage (33-5). It is emphasised that the first phase must be considered to be characteristic for Old Norse law (36). Mundr and vingæf are treated etymologically in order to find their relevance to the nature of ON marriage law; the former is held to be related to peace. The gift thus seems to serve to further the peace between the families; this meaning is corroborated by the original reference to peace of German Sippe, ON sifskapr (36-41). A similar meaning is assigned vingæf (41-2). The assumption that mundr and wedding take the form of a Kaufehe is widely held, but objections exist. The occurrence of brúðkaup for brúðlaup is often used to show the mercenary nature of the contract, despite the fact that nearly all sources indicate that the woman is the receiver of the sum. Indeed, kaupa also has the general reference “contract,” and its basic meaning is “etwas durch oder gegen eine Leistung erwerben oder erlangen.” Norwegian law forbids both men and women to kaupi kaupa for marriage without recourse to lawful procedures; the inclusion here of women suggests a more general meaning than argued by the Ehekaufmänner. The Grágás distinguishes between the buying of property and marriage (42-4). It further appears that kaupa derives, via the Continent, from Latin caupo “salesman, inn-keeper,” and that it has obtained its marital meaning among the north-Germanic peoples. It is then not surprising that the tradition of the mundr has led to the casual reference to marriage as a Brautkauf (44-5). Swedish law sources corroborate this reading (45-6). Apart from mundr and morning gift, the groom’s gift to the bride in order to win her love, there existed the Mitgift of the bride’s kin to the couple, that was to be answered by the groom with a Widerlage (Norwegian gagnjald), that stood in a fixed relation to the amount of the Mitgift. In Norway, the mundr disappeared after the introduction of the Widerlage, although the two had essentially different legal functions: Widerlage responded to Mitgift, but mundr to the taking into one’s possession of the bride (47-50). Grönbech argues that gifts that were once established to display the goodwill of the parties involved later gained the function of ensuring a decent economic situation for the wife (51-2). A tilgjöf existed that was first of all a response to the Widerlage (53-4). Saxo Grammaticus is studied and it is concluded that his writings have a negative effect on the evidence that a true Kaufehe has ever existed (55-8). Because use of the purchase legally forms no part of a commercial transaction, Koschaker believes that sharing the bed has no legal connection with marriage. This is, however, invalid for Scandinavian law: the Grágás requires that the couple share the bed for the marriage to be binding and to give the bride a right to her mundr (59). The same goes for the vingæf. Earlier intercourse makes the groom punishable by fine to the bride’s kin, in the terminology of injury done to personal honour and value; and he must then marry her (60-1). When a third party rapes or kidnaps the wife, both husband and the bride’s kinsmen have the right to demand a fine, i.e., Beischlafsklage and réttr are divided between the two parties (61-2). To the third party, the system of fines is the same whether the woman is married or single. If he is married, his wife does not have the right to either fine or vengeance; thus the pre-Christian ethic does not require the husband to be faithful. However, ?# (62-3). A second lawful marriage precluded any action on the wife’s kin’s side; but it required a separate house since the wife was the master of the house. The Gulathing still allowed such practice after the introduction of Christianity. Children of the second marriage do not inherit; the second woman is no meinkona (63). If the wife is expected to be faithful, this is only so for the sake of the woman’s honour. It is incorrect to claim that a double standard is here applied: the wife’s faithfulness is of the same nature as the unmarried woman’s virginity (63-4). West Norse sagas, however, indicate little action against adulterous wives. Those West Norse law codes that do not reflect Church doctrine only mention results of possession: the husband may choose whether to keep or abandon his wife, and if he chooses divorce she loses mundr and Widerlage, while she keeps her Mitgift (64-5). East Norse sources permit a husband to kill his wife’s lover when caught in the act, and there is no punishment if his wife does not survive the assault either. When there is no bloody fight, he may chase her out of the house dressed in simple, derisive clothes (65-6). The law codes mention no possibility of giving away, selling, or exchange of wives. The sagas contain a few unclear episodes, whose contexts however suggest that such was not a husband’s right. Several of these involve the husband’s departure, from life or from the country in which he had married; a close friend is then given the wife. Some seem to be related to divorce. One source mentions an exchange, but it is proved to be unusual when one of the wives hangs herself (66-8). Concerning complaint at the sale of a faulty product, the Grágás has only one relevant article, treating two related concepts whose absence permits a groom to cancel the engagement and the marriage even when the wedding has already taken place: heimillt, the absence of legal shortcomings in the bride’s guardian (i.e., the question whether he is really the legal “engager”); and heillt, the absence of personal faults in the bride. The latter includes such poor health that her value is less, or other shortcomings at sixteen years of age which decrease her value. The Lombards knew the three shortcomings of leprosy, total blindness, and madness; other relevant circumstances may lie in mistakes concerning the subjective category of “circumstances concerning the other person” still part of marriage laws of nazi Germany (69-71). Another Grágás article equates shortcomings in kin with those that decrease the value of bondsmen and servants. Hence the concept of Kaufehe seems to apply by this criterion (71-2). Koschaker uses as evidence for Kaufehe the inclusion of the widow among the inheritance by the next of kin of the deceased husband (levirate). In an earlier stage this would have applied to widows with children as well, but in later times it applied to childless widows only. However, levirate is unknown among the northern Germanic peoples. Not only are there no sources suggesting its usage; the kin-relations preclude it: at the husband’s death, the guardianship of the woman’s family is renewed; and remarriage is subject to nearly the same procedure as first marriage (72-4). If a wife were of the same legal nature as bought possessions, her fruit would automatically become the husband’s possession; this would also include bastard children. ON law contradicts this procedure: the Grágás considers all children in the wife’s womb at the time of the wedding extramarital; Norwegian law has the same article, but states that all children conceived before the wedding come into the line of inheritance if the marriage produces subsequent children. This suggests influence of the Church; the Icelandic law will be the older one (74-5). Extramarital children born conceived during marriage certainly do not automatically become the husband’s property: they provide him with the right to abandon his wife and the extramarital children (75-7). Hermann and Koschaker have argued that the inheriting daughter (in the absence of sons) fits into the picture of Ehekauf, only they interpret her as an inherited daughter instead, to be given in marriage to the next in the hereditary line (77-8). The question of the inheriting daughter is further discussed (78-90). It is concluded that an early Germanic or Indogermanic Kaufehe did not exist in northern Germanic society (90).

author: Storek, Martha Hannah
title: Women in the Time of the Icelandic Family Saga
abstract:
[from ch. 2: 207–80]

Unlike Jochens, Storek considers it unproved whether female consent was customarily asked: when sagas do not describe the process, this means nothing since sagas typically relate very little concerning women. Only six instances occur in which female consent was certainly not asked, and these were short and unhappy marriages. Women will have readily agreed with their kin’s judgement, since their honour and wealth were in their own interest (225-6). The six unhappy marriages are listed (226-7). Consent is often asked; examples are given (227-9). The mother’s opinion is more than once shown to have some weight (229-30). Marriage was legally binding after an engagement had taken place and the couple had shared the bed, both in the presence of witnesses. This last requirement is not often described in the sagas (230-1). Gift-giving customs and designations of the bride are discussed (232-4), as is the wife’s change of status and kin-bonds (234-5). Monogamy was the usual system “but free marriage [marriage to a mistress or concubine] and ‘concubinage’ were not unknown” (235-41). Inheritance law is discussed in relation to the status of bastard (241-2). Mundr (the sum paid by the groom to the bride) and dowry are described (242-5). Divorce was easy but rare; it required action on one side only. The Grágás requires the bishop’s consent except in cases of serious injury, incest, insufficient means of either partner, or forced emigration (246-7). In the sagas, the reason is usually maltreatment or insult, or hostility towards the other’s family (247). Property was divided in negotiation between the husband and the wife’s kinsman; in case of maltreatment, both mundr and dowry were usually demanded and received (252-3). Divorce could be used as a threat (255-7). Married women and widows were less dependant than unmarried women. In the sagas, married women rule within their homes, but this is no obligation, especially when the woman feels unable to do so (259-61). In the husband’s absence, she could rule over his affairs as well (261-3). Nonetheless, women held no legal responsibility (263-5). Sagas sometimes have women display more wisdom than their husbands (266-8). Some coax their husbands into compliance, others are simply strong-willed (268-71). A few are unfaithful, a condition for which Old Germanic customs held them legally responsible; but the sagas have no instance of their punishment (271-4). At the husband’s death, the woman’s guardianship passed back to her family (275). Remarriage was subject to the same rules as marriage, except that the widow had more freedom of choice (277-80).

author: Pentikäinen, Juha
title: Child Abandonment as an Indicator of Christianization in the Nordic Countries
publication: Old Norse and Finnish Religions and Cultic Place-names: Based on Papers Read at the Symposium on Encounters Between Religions in Old Nordic Times and on Cultic Place-Names Held at Åbo, Finland, on the 19th-21st of August 1987
abstract: Sagas, provincial and ecclesiastical laws, and Finnish oral poetry are discussed as sources; all of these are concluded to date from the Middle Ages (72-3). In cultures where infanticide is common practice, it is variously motivated by economy, religion, society, or biology (73-5). In Nordic cultures, Christianity seems to have represented a turn in social acceptability of infanticide. Criminalisation was, however, gradual; this signals a deep rootedness of the tradition. Along with criminalisation came a supernatural experience of the dead children (75). Icelandic law accepted Christianity in *1000 AD, but Íslendingabók expressly states that child exposure was explicitly allowed to continue. Saga Ólafs indicates that St Olaf abolished this practice about 1018 (76). Gunnlaugs saga ormstungu has Þorsteinn, son of Egill Skalla-Grímsson, tell his wife to abandon her child if it should turn out to be a daughter; both wife and narrator condemn this intention (76-7). Both this saga and Finnboga saga emphasise that the right of child abandonment was the moral prerogative of the poor. However, other sagas contain instances of the abandonment of illegitimate children (77). Violent infanticide does not occur in the sagas; a single instance is known of drowning, while most references are to infants being wrapped in cloth and left in places where they might easily be discovered (77-8). Baptism was the central rite of incorporation and acceptance of the child; this practice consisted of the pouring of water and name-giving. The latter element was central to a child’s acceptability into a community. In Nordic and Frisian law, first feeding seems to have been the boundary up to which an infant could legitimately be abandoned (78-9). Provincial laws of Norway (from the eleventh century onwards) forbid all abandonment of healthy children, while they allow the abandonment (in accordance with ecclesiastical rites) of heavily deformed children. Thus both sagas and provincial laws allow child abandonment in exceptional cases only (80-2). The Finnish oral tradition knows a tradition of child abandonment and infanticide that so resembles the Scandinavian tradition that it is likely to have been borrowed in the contacts that began about the beginning of the current era; the Sami, who split off from the Finns about 500 BCE, do not know the tradition (82-4). An Inuit tradition tells of aborted foetuses or young infants born in secret and turning into airborne creatures. Such traditions were in the eighteenth century accepted by some Inuit but rejected by others. A rite of ordeal, interrogation, and confession of the suspected mother was connected to the discovery of such supernatural infants (84-7). The unbalanced distribution of the tradition, however, suggests that it was borrowed from Norse Greenlanders (87-8). [it seems to me that the Scandinavian tradition that the Inuit tradition is said to be related to is not described in the article, PS]

author: Siikala, Anna-Leena
title: Das Reich Pohjala der kalevalischen Dichtung im Licht der Sagas
series: Ergänzungsbände zum Reallexikon der Germanischen Altertumskunde
abstract: Over the course of scholarship, Pohjala has been variously explained as a realm of myth and a representative of early Finnish history; within the latter category, its presumed locality has shifted according to the national political climate of the time. But in the sources, Pohjala has many faces; and in oral culture, myth and history tend to coalesce in an attempt to explain the world (201–3). Many mythologies share descriptions of an Otherworld, across from the human world and inacessible by humans. Such depictions tell us something about the societies in which they were written, but since myth alters more slowly than reality, it reflects a number of successive stages of society (203). The layered cosmos, with an upper and lower world in addition to the human world, is a widespread traditional image; a cosmic mountain or tree unites them. Finnish folk poetry speaks of a mountain, but also of an oak serving as a bridge across a river (SKVR I:4, 334, 870) (204). Pohjala and Tuonela/the underworld are sometimes interchangeable. Both are dark, cold, and geographically characterised by a river and a mountain. Both are in the periphery of the world (204). Pohjala is surrounded by a fence with gates (204–5). Life in Pohjola is as in the human world, but it is also a human-consuming world associated with illness and death, though illness is also banned from Pohjola (205). The sagas and the Finnish/Karelian poetry have similar dangerous regions of giants and other supernatural creatures to the north. Saxo and Adam of Bremen also pick up on these themes (205–7). Rosemary Power has demonstrated that the journey to the north to acquire a treasure or wife is common in ON. The quest for the egg in Bósa saga has been compared to the quest for the sampo (Matti Kuusi, “Kirjoittamaton kirjallisuus.” Suomen kirjallisuus 1. Keuruu, 1963, at 223–4) (207–8). Kemppinen is mistaken when he identifies Pohjola with the land of the dead on account of the close similarities with Tuonela (208). Further similarities between ON and Finnish traditions of northern lands are summed up, and it is recognised that each also has its distinct elements (209). Although Pohjola suggests a northern region, no real geographic unit must be thought to underlie its many occurrences. Nevertheless some references suggest that it borders on the Bothnic Gulf, leading some to believe a historical raid is underlying (209–10). But literary tradition is a far better explanation, especially in view of the wider northern-European analogues. Nevertheless, tales of northern raiding must have been particularly interesting in a time in which, according to Egils saga, Kvennar and Norsemen united against the Karelians (211). There is no geographical counterpart to Pohjola, but the northeastern coast of the Bothnic Gulf may have played a role in its development in both Norse and Finnish tradition (212).

author: Bell, A. Robert
title: Muspilli: Apocalypse as Political Threat
abstract: No study has focused on Muspilli’s apocryphal and apocalyptic sources; the popular focal points are the poem’s division into (originally separate) parts and the etymology of its modern title. Time and place of composition, of central significance to this poem, have been likewise neglected (76). Davidson describes “Muspilli” as the primeval southern region of Scandinavian myth. It has also been interpreted as a person; whatever it means, it must have been used in a Christian sense in the Christian context of Muspilli, and the word is of no significance in the larger scope of this poem (77). The poem was added to a copy of Augustine’s Sermo de symbolis contra Judaeos sometime between 824 and 900, but the language suggests it to be of the first half of the century. The exact author is unknown (88). The Elias passage has received much attention because Elias seems to be injured or defeated by the Antichrist; this story might reflect theological variance; Eastern influence; or a pagan Germanic source (78). In the Judaeo-Christian tradition, Elias and Elijah are often confused; the latter is connected with Doomsday (79). These channels are discussed (79-83). A summary of the plot is given (83-5). Eschatology is judged not to be the point of the poem; rather, it was written as a warning to someone specific that he should change his ways (85). Germany may have been the least Christian part of Charlemagne’s empire, also before and after his reign (86). The missionary activities of the English and Irish led to the creation of a localised, own church for the German peoples, in such a manner that church estate could become a link in the feudal chain within Charlemagne’s system (88-90). After the oaths of Strassburg (842), the “strong Carolingian eigenkirche” began to develop towards “a basically non-ecclesiastically centered feudal system” (91). The Muspilli may well have been written for Ludwig the German (92-3). Since it was written into a gift of Bishop Adalram’s, it may be assumed that it was written after his death in 836 (93). The sins specifically emphasised in the poem figure largely in Ludwig’s career (94); and they involved paying bribes with money earned from the Eigenkirche (93-4). A “purified” Ludwig may have been the referent of Elias fighting the Antichrist, or Charles the Bald (95). A reconstruction of the poem’s form is presented (95-6). The poem is a unit (97). Gregory’s four levels of interpretation are brought to bear on the poem (98-9). The appendices consist of a list of possible sources of the poem (101) and a MnE translation (102-104).

author: Britton, G.C.
title: Repetition and Contrast in the Old English Later Genesis
abstract: The Gen B poet uses repetition and contrast. Such repetition as he uses ought to be tedious, but it serves to reach a “cumulative effect of much vigour”; mood and action are reinforced (66). The contrast is described, with the examples of the two trees and God and Satan (67-72).

author: Burchmore, Susan
title: Traditional Exegesis and the Question of Guilt in the Old English Genesis B
abstract: The poet’s attitude towards the first couple is not strictly positive or negative, nor are they treated as mere allegorical vessels. Burchmore seeks sources for Gen B’s portrayal of the Tempter and of the couple’s loyalty towards God (117-18). Medieval biblical commentaries usually elaborate on such matters as the serpent’s instrumental position to the devil and Eve’s reasons for yielding, which question leads to that of why Eve was deceived but Adam was not (1 Tim 2.14); and the results of the Fall. Gen B shares with the exegetical tradition a concern with the psychology of deception; the traditional allegory of Adam as reason and Eve as the senses is an important part thereof (119). Adam’s fall is due to his faith in Eve’s reading of her sensory data; this emphasis on sight recurs in the matter of the Tempter’s disguise. This disguise, however, is not physical: the only indication that it is is given in Eve’s description of him, whereas his entrance into the serpent’s body is described by the narrator (120). Eve’s behaviour is usually explained by a love of power which caused her to believe the serpent, but Gen B does not depict her as vainglorious; instead, Eve’s mention of the Tempter’s angelic appearance may refer to 2 Cor 11 (a warning against false apostles: “Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light”). This biblical passage has been used in commentaries to warn against heretics, and in this context it has been linked to the allegory of senses and reason (121). Eve’s reference may therefore have been intended to bring the heretical allegory of the Tempter to mind; but it is unlikely that this was his only purpose with the reference. Moreover, if this allegory is intended, then Eve, representing the senses, must be meant to present to Adam false visions which he fails to interpret correctly (124). Augustine describes how man may be deceived by corporeal reality; Eve, as the senses, may therefore be expected to misrepresent reality. Adam, on the other hand, falls despite his recognition that the Tempter does not look like an angel. He makes two mistakes: he trusts the judgement of Eve, representing the senses; and he ignores what he sees with his own, intellectual vision. This is why the couple in Gen B fall (125-6). However, Augustine’s analysis of the senses occurs in a different context, and he does not believe in an easy deception of the senses. The ninth-century John Scots Eriugena provides the missing link in his Periphyseon, books 4-5. This text, emphasising the fallability and messenger-function of the senses, may provide an explanation for Gen B’s treatment of sight as well as for its emphasis on the couple’s good intentions (127). The fallibility of the senses is linked to Eve when he presents her as the “‘realm of falsity,’ that faculty of the mind which according to Eriugena receives mixed knowledge, a confusion of truth and falsehood.” Gen B’s treatment of Eve’s sight thus seems inspired by Augustine and Eriugena; this reading places the allegorical guilt for the fall upon Adam (128). This exegesis is coupled with a psychological exploration of the Fall, rendering it dramatically plausible. This exploration, however, dramatically alters the biblical account. The poet focuses on the Tempter’s skill in rhetorics and Eve’s good intentions. Eve’s psychological fall occurs because the Tempter disguises himself with rhetorics. He learns from his mistakes in his attempt to seduce Adam and uses threat to coerce Eve into eating the fruit (128-9). Rewards are offered only after these threats. The Tempter subtly convinces Eve of his importance without claiming to be an angel, and in fact without lying about himself (130). While commentators agreed that Eve was able to see through the serpent’s promises, Gen B omits the very argument she was supposedly able to see for what it was (130-1). Augustine writes that Eve was deceived because her indirect connection with God made her weaker intellectually, which weakness led to the opinion that women should be subordinates to their husbands. Eve should therefore have stuck with the judgement she knew to be her husband’s. The Augustinian opinion, however, was written in a rebuttal of the idea that Eve was not formed in God’s image (131-3). In regard to the relationship between the first couple, Gen B follows Ambrose the most closely: Eve’s fault is a misplacing of loyalty and authority. The poet does not explain away Eve’s guilt (133). Eve is not vainglorious but attempts to save Adam in an unfortunate way (133-4). Wacran hyge (weaker mind) and holdne hyge (loyal mind) are her two failings; the first is traditional, the second is not. Adam’s fall is mysterious: he does see through the Tempter, and the traditional reading that he does not want to be separated from Eve is not brought up. It seems the poet wanted to portray him as believing to have misinterpreted God’s order (134). Augustine says Eve believed the Tempter partly because the fruit was so beautiful. This reading is echoed in Gen B when Eve describes its sweetness to Adam [PS: but was the tree not ugly?]. Adam’s dilemma centres around the question how best to serve God (136). The poet’s emphasis on good intentions “stresses the theme of misplaced authority, perhaps in order to recall the exegetical assosication of heresy with the Fall. . . . Adam’s and Eve’s good intentions could. . . be meant to reflect the ease with which even well-intentioned Christians can succumb to false doctrine.” There is no model for a Fall through loyalty; but Eriugena in book 5 of his Periphyseon claims that man has no inherent desire to do evil. All nature is good and desires its source, wherefore man cannot will against God. Sin is confusion not malice (137). This seems to be the background of Gen B’s loyalty. Nevertheless, Adam, too, is guilty: of disobedience and of misplacing authority. The Gen B poet thus takes up some of Eriugena’s opinions but not his whole system, thus causing contradictions; this is typical of the period and of the poet’s artistry. Eriugena’s influence was of a fragmentary nature everywhere; and the poet carefully worked his several elements together (138-9). This is demonstrated with regard to the juxtaposition of esthetic (Tempter) and psychological (Adam, Eve) characters. This art is typical of OE poetry and results in more emphatic but also more emphatically transitory human victories (140-1). The reading here presented renders problematical the MS illustrations. The illustrator must have tried to represent the allegory or misread the text (141-3). The illustrations are generally faithful companions to the text (144).

author: Caie, Graham D.
title: The Judgment Day Theme in Old English Poetry
series: Publications of the Department of English, University of Copenhagen
abstract:
[here summarised is ch. 3: The Themes of Glory and Judgment ff.]

All Old English eschatology depends on the “apocalyptic present” (58). Since Germanic ethics and mythology were not closely linked, the Christian God could easily be accepted (60). Doubts are expressed on a widespread existence of Scandinavian eschatology in the literary age. Vilhelm Grönbech’s The Culture of the Teutons vol. 3, p. 322 is quoted as claiming that “the idea of a realm for the dead never went beyond the imagination of poets fired by contact with Christian eschatology” (63-4). The Germanic belief in ongoing life after death is discussed (64f.). Grönbech is quoted as calling immortality through fame the Norseman’s highest end; this notion is discussed. The importance of the patronymic system is linked to this cultural element. (67f.; Grönbech III.253; II.311). Christianity reduces fame to an epiphenomenon, but [b]ecause the early Hebraic faith had a similar emphasis on worldly fame [as the Germanic], there were innumerable texts which could be quoted to stress this ambiguously heroic and Christian dom. . .”(70). In Christianity, “[w]orldly fame has an excellent place, but it is not an end in itself” (69-73). Since all die at Ragnarok, none remains to sing the praises of heroes (73). Evidence is discussed that “Ragnarøk. . . was known in the pagan north” (73-4). Eschatological lore from the Vọluspá and from Snorri’s Edda is listed, as are their parallels with Christian eschatology. The late tenth-century Vọluspá is coloured by Christian thought. Among Norse elements in OE eschatology are floods, a towering tree, and the rebirth of terrestrial land (74-6). In OE literature, the soul at death goes directly into heaven or hell, but rejoins its body for Doomsday (77; cf. Kabir). Resemblances between OE and early Hebraic religion are mentioned (78f.). The medieval Church denied the Millennium as an earthly kingdom for God: He is too glorious a king for a worldly kingdom (81-2). In line with Luke 17.21; John 5.25; 3.18-19, the medieval concept of apocalypse was immanent to present life, and ended therewith (83-4). This view is reflected in contemporary art (87-9). OE poetry does not discuss the style of the soul in between death and judgement (89). Sermo Lupi is mentioned and the belief in an imminent Doomsday (AD 1000/1033/1065); a date for Doomsday is deemed less significant than signs of doom. ASC, for instance, mentions signs and lights (91-4). Judgement Day I is treated (95-114); it is found to use the eschatological present, collapsing Christ’s suffering, a destroying flood and fire, and man’s need for repentance into one (95). The worldly and the contemplative man are contrasted (98). The Cross is used as a focal point and as the Christian’s path (98-9). Parallels for the flood are listed (99-102). As in all OE poetry, no purgatory is mentioned; but fire is used simultaneously for purging and punishment. Neither is a distinction made between the individual’s and mankind’s last day (103). The horrors of hell are beyond man’s comprehension (103-104). Christ is described as bound with the chains of man’s sin (107-108). The biblical events before the coming of Christ are not mentioned (110, 112) because of the poet’s specific focus (95), which is to call his audience to immediate repentance (113-14). Judgement Day II is discussed (115-59). Its focus is not doomsday but an exhortation to repent (116). It is based on a Latin poem attributed to Bede (117-18). The lyrical introduction is discussed at length (120-9). The persona then remembers his sins and becomes contrite (131-41). The signs of doomsday (forebeacn) are listed (142-57?). Here, too, a flood is among the latter-day events (143); the levelling of the ground is especially noted (153-4). Penance is emphasised at the end of the poem. The tending of the garden is what matters (158-9). Four pages of this chapter are without print (152-3, 156-7). Christ III is discussed (160-225). This poem (ll. 867-1664) is conceived of as separate from the rest of Christ Its framework was provided by the Latin Apparebit repentina dies magna Domini (161). The Cricifixion and Christ’s suffering on earth are the poem’s focal centre; the cross summons man to judgement. As in other OE Judgement poems, no actual judgement takes place; the implication is that this has already taken place in man’s life (163-4). The present moment is therefore more important than the apocalyptic (164). Judgement takes place now (166). There is a possible reference to purgatory in ll. 829-31, but it might just refer to hell; there is no other reference to purgatory in OE poetry (171). The Heliand calls Christ Mutspelli, a Germanic god of fire, when he comes as a thief in the night (175). The Christ III poet seldom refers to precise eschatological events, and never to those that do not affect man directly (180-1). As in The Dream of the Rood, the cross becomes a type of Christ and suffers with Him (200-1). A use of colours occurs that is exceptional for OE poetry (203). Baldr and Christ are briefly discussed (205-7).

author: Capek, Michael J.
title: The Nationality of a Translator: Some Notes on the Syntax of Genesis B
abstract: Argues on the basis of syntax that Gen B is a translation of the OS text by a Continental Saxon. Briefly reviews the development of the debate from Sievers to Timmer.

author: Davis, Glenn M.
title: Changing Senses in Genesis B
abstract: The Genesis B poet extends the single biblical sentence “your eyes shall be opened: and you shall be as Gods, knowing good and evil” into nearly sixty lines of verse. The phrase is taken literally, as transforming Eve’s sensory capabilities (113). Augustine in his commentary focuses on the “chain of seduction”; he attributes Eve’s submission to pride (she wants to be like God) and Adam’s to loyalty; thus, he creates a hierarchy with man at the top (114). The Tempter’s attempted seduction of Adam rests on an increase in bodily and mental capacity and skill, as well as property. The Tempter turns to Eve and uses a tactic of trial-and-error: he gives up his promises of beauty, strength, and intelligence and substitutes for these the promises of enhanced sight, God’s forgiveness, and protection of Adam from God’s anger. Thus pride and vanity belong to the first, unsuccessful, temptation; not to Eve’s (115). Adam had demanded a token; the Tempter offers it to Eve in the form of eyesight of greater range and a higher order (God’s seat). Next, Eve seduces Adam by means of sensory temptations as well (116). Genesis B scholars have relied too heavily on patristic influence. Their focus has revolved mainly around three doctrines: an allegorisation of Adam, Eve, and Tempter; the corruption of Eve before the Tempter came to her; and “the understanding of the Fall as a crisis of linguistic interpretation.” All of these have precluded an appreciation of the innovations in Genesis B (116-17). The first two are treated briefly (117-18). The third is explained to consist in the belief that the prelapsarian relationship between word and referent was static and transparent, whereas deception became possible when this relationship was broken. When this model is applied to Genesis B, the change in Eve’s senses do not come into play (118). Whereas Scripture has Eve’s understanding change as soon as she consumes the fruit, the OE account speaks of two forces changing Eve’s senses: the Tempter’s trickery [not only verbal!] and the fruit. Eve understands the Tempter’s magic over her to derive from her consumption of the fruit, which misconception leads her to seduce Adam. Eve’s new perception is the only promise immediately delivered by the Tempter (119). The poet makes explicit that this is due to the Tempter not the fruit.
