Whereas the consumption of the fruit gave her a new set of senses so that she might know good and evil, the Tempter has superimposed a set of senses that enables her to see across the entire world (121). L. 616b adds that Eve is now able to touch the light of heaven. The Tempter’s final move is to tell Eve to see for herself, now that she has consumed the fruit, that his counsel was right: since her senses are under his spell, this involves no risk for his case (121); and to propose to her that she should tell Adam about it (122). Eve’s relation of the events to Adam reveals her changed senses: the fruit tasted swete not biter; she can not only see but hear matters from afar and from heaven; and all this she attributes to her eating of the fruit (123). Her altered senses disappear once Adam has eaten, and Adam never experiences them; instead, the couple discover their naked state (125).

author: Deering, Waller
title: The Anglosaxon Poets on the Judgment Day
abstract: Provides an index of OE poetic descriptions of doomsday and its events, including descriptions of heaven and hell. Of interest for comparison and contrast with The Wanderer might be the descriptions in Christ and the Phoenix of the treasures and riches swallowed by the fire. Fire and flood are taken to be not only destroyers, but also purifiers of souls (22). Sources are discussed for these images of destruction (26-8). Hell is described, whose torments consist not only of heat and fire but also of cold and water (48-67). The sources of these descriptions are discussed (57-60). Heaven is described (60-9). The Germanic “mead-hall” or even Walhalla character of heaven is discussed (65-6), as is the Germanic character of the King of heaven and his relationship to his subjects (71-2).

author: Dendle, Peter
title: Satan Unbound: The Devil in Old English Narrative Literature
abstract: The book “explores the significance of the devil as a recurring character in Old English narrative literature” (3). It avoids expository discussions because narrative was often used as a conveyor of beliefs, and because narrative contains a “surplus of significance” and is as such “itself the 'meaning' of the text” (4-5). The introduction points out that the global absence of stage directions in Satan's appearances leaves space for interpretation (6). The psychology of sinner and heathen are not explored at length in OE literature; instead, emphasis is put on the devil's encounters with defiant saints (7-8). The evolution of the devil is summarised (8-12). He hardly appears as a person in the OT (the post-exile 1 Chronicles 21.1; Job 1.6-12; 2.1-7; Zechariah 3.1-2); in these instances he is an attorney prosecuting mankind. The NT mentions him; the fallen angels over time come to be seen as demons believed to inhabit the earth. The primacy of good and evil is rejected after Irenaeus conceives of Satan's relationship to God as one of apostasy (9). Origen situates Satan's rebellion before the Creation of heaven and earth. Augustine establishes pride as the first sin and portrays his cosmology in neoplatonic privation terms; but the negative nature of evil was too sophisticated to gain a firm hold. In the medieval period Lucifer, Satan, the devil, the Genesis serpent and the Apocalypse dragon are usually seen as one; but the Antichrist is commonly distinguished from these. OE literature is sometimes thought to maintain a distinction between devil and Satan. The tempter character ostensibly expressed in þurh deofles larum may well have been void of theological content (10-11). The charms and medical records show that the devil was experienced as the Christian antagonist, but that he had little to do with free will and could be affected in the same way as regular physical afflictions (13-15). The Solomon and Saturn texts are mentioned (15-18). The tension between the demonic task of instigating mankind to sin and the exclusive source of sin within man's soul has led to inconsistency in narrative literature (19-20). Hagiography is not concerned with exploring the origin of sin (20). The Church Fathers were not agreed whether the devil actively instigates sin in the sixth age; some NT passages (e.g., 1 John 3.8) and Ecclesiasticus 21.30 suggest a positive answer (20-1). Augustine disliked the concept of Satan being omnipresent for its gnostic implications, but narrative literature uses this concept rather freely (e.g. Blickling Homily 3; 21). The official doctrine of Original Sin posed a threat to the concept of an active Satan, since it rendered his activity after the Fall redundant. He was in many texts reduced to an abstract principle, the sum of human passion. Despite biblical evidence of Satan's instigations, his more recent activities were not given (22-3). “[T]he lack of a specific rationale behind the employment of the 'devil' lends the metaphor a fluidity, an organic richness that helps account for its endurance” (23). The “physicalist approach to demonic temptation” is mentioned: demons cannot read our minds but can appear to do so by observing our actions in detail; they influence the soul only through the senses and humours. However, Augustine, who adhered to this theory, later admitted to doubt on this point (25). Bede believed that Satan has no direct access to the soul (25-6). Gregory the Great's Moralia is mentioned as the Anglo-Saxons' central source for temptation. He writes that Satan only instigates the first step into sin; once the process of succumbing has begun, it becomes harder to stop it. Watchfulness is the main remedy. However, Gregory, too, is not consistent (27). Church Fathers should not be seen as dogmatically accepted authorities for other writers: “[e]ach genre has an implicit theology of its own. . .” (28). The importance of discretio, discernment, is emphasised; Juliana shows this virtue when she recognises the devil in his disguise, although Cynewulf emphasises her steadfastness rather than discernment (26-7, 29). Satan's description in Juliana of his methodology is rich, but does not echo any hagiography or OE poetry (31). The Vercelli homilies are less crafted than the Alfredian translations, thus giving some insight into popular Christianity. Passages are discussed treating mainly the theme of the devil's arrows (33-5). Ælfric's writings, more stylised, nevertheless contain some demon encounters; the Depositio S. Basilii Episcopi has a young man making a contract with a demon (35). He also describes some instances of demon parasitism (36-8). Abbotmeyer distinguishes between the 'plaint of Lucifer' and 'epic' treatments of the devil and remarked that the first have survived in far greater number (40-1). Yet OE texts tend not to humiliate the devil, even where their sources do (41). The “devil and the anchorite” story shows how the devil may fulfil important structural roles (41-2). In his relation to saints he often appears as a twisted kind of Greek chorus, tracing the saints' progress and testing an already perfected saint (42-3). In the Temptation in the desert, he provides the prelude to Jesus's miracular works. In the Life of Nicholas, the devil fulfils a small role in which his activities are surprisingly unmiraculous (rowing a boat, disguised as a hag); in the Lives of Margaret, on the other hand, the narrative centres around the confrontation of Margaret and the dragon; he swallows her but she escapes by making the sign of the cross; though in several versions the events are different (48-57). The devil's role as observer, or “the saint's mirror,” is described with regard to Gregory's Vita Benedicti and Ælfric's Life of Martin (57-61). The devil is an abstraction of the Other and as such is positioned without; yet homiletic and sermon literature serves to stimulate self-inspection. Therefore homilists tried to maintain an ambivalence between evil from within and without (62-3). Cassian, in Iohannis Cassiani Consolationes 7.12, explains that a demon cannot take over the core of the soul (64). The interplay between external and internal evil is dynamic both in the Church Fathers (Augustine, Gregory) and in OE literature (Ælfric; 65-6). The devil is split in two to satisfy the contrary theological demands: psychologically, the devil besieges the believer on earth, while mythologically he is in chained in hell in the sixth age. Both aspects are found in Revelation (20.2-3;7-8; pp. 66-7). Most pre-1100 visions of hell do not include the devil as a resident (67-8). The Descensus ad inferos tradition rendered Satan's chaining more fixed by its narrative detail. The introduction of the Harrowing has led to interpretational divergences as to what happened at Satan's first banishment after the war in heaven; but most sources do not discuss the issue and refer simply to “fall” and “binding” (68-9). Early Christian interpretations of the devil on earth in the fifth and sixth ages are treated, as well as air as a prison or habitat, by Augustine among others (Homily on Psalm 148.9; pp. 70-3). Liturgical appearances of the devil are discussed (73-7). When the “Roving Satan” view was theologically abandoned, Church practice did not cooperate: pacts with the devil were forbidden and exorcism was practised (73, qtd. From Coulange 65-6). The sacrament of baptism knows exorcism, though this is interpreted variously (76). The vernacular homilies are reluctant to show Satan outside of hell in the sixth age; they emphasise the binding of Satan at the Harrowing as well as on Judgement Day and often collapse these into one “archetypal moment.” The Vercelli homilies' arrows shot from hell may express this reluctance (77). This orthodoxy contrasts with the free speculations otherwise expressed in the homilies. The “non-hagiographic homilies tend to concretize and rationalize the more potentially unstable features of the devil's location, mobility, and personal presence in the human sphere—the very features that the hagiographic texts (especially poetic ones) exploit” (78). Prison is often used parallel to the classical descent into the Underworld; but it is a location in which the saint is characterised by steadfastness and it is rather the devil who is the intruder when he confronts them here. Classical literature uses the trope to have its heroes meet their greatest opponent on his own grounds (78-81). Verse vitae use near-liturgical language, which allows them to make the devil more “emhemeral and mobile” so that his physical location is kept ambiguous (81). In Elene, Satan suggests that he is not permanently chained in hell: “se hælend me / in þam engan ham oft getynde” (919-20); this to explain his emphasis that Satan is physically on earth in the narrative (83-4). Elene and the corresponding prose homily contain Judas's wish that Satan should be cast into the pit of hell (84-5). Andreas contains a dialogue between the devil on earth and the one bound in hell, and direct conversation between the latter and Andreas. This poem is based on the Greek Praxeis; the Greek text, Andreas says that Christ will lower Satan into the abyss, but Andreas and the corresponding prose homily use a preterite tense here, thereby problematising “the devil's status as a roaming agent and even as a single entity” (86). The distinction between the devil and lesser demons was “largely alien to medieval demonology” (87). It is common medieval practice to place references to a plurality of demons in apposition with singular references to the devil, in imitation of Ephesians 6.11-18 (“struggle. . . against the rulers. . .”) and Mark 5.1-20/Luke 8.26-39 (“My name is Legion; for we are many”; 88-91). A text edited by Férotin calls Satan a “spiritus multiformis” (89). Johnson notes that Tyconius's Liber regularum contains a passage on the body of Christ, made up of the believers, and the opposite body of Satan, made up of demons (91-2). The question is discussed whether Satan's kingdom was seen as a warring multitude or a unified principle of evil. It is the latter concept that underlies Satan's heroic passages in Genesis B, as well as the Guthlac texts (93-4). Demonic appearances in Bede and Cynewulf are studied (95-103). In Juliana, Cynewulf is said to reduce the significance of diabolus from father of all evil to father of all spiritual evil (98). The Latin Passio S. Iulianae contains ad admission by Belial of many crimes otherwise attributed to Satan, one even in Scripture; in the end only he adds “cum fratribus meis.” Belial later admits to responsibility for all evil in the world (99). Cynewulf's Juliana does not spell out names, but retains references to a Satan bound in hell and a demon eye in eye with Juliana who is responsible for the Eden temptation and claims Satan for his father (100-3). Finally, the Guthlac cycle is treated (103-14). The Latin Vita Guthlaci contains the same tension between singular and plural enemy that has been treated above (105-6). Guthlac A recognises the tension of number and “exploits [its] dramatic and rhetorical potential” (107-12). The conclusion lists Satan's OE physical appearances: soldier, scop, trapper, farmer, knot-maker, bird, whale, wolf (115, 163). Satan as a character in OE literature is compared to Socrates' dialectical opponents: present to make clear the plurality of voices, but never the first voice (117).

author: Derolez, R.
title: Genesis: Old Saxon and Old English
abstract: Summarises the relations between Genesis A and B, Old Saxon Genesis, Praefatio, Heliand. A Heliand MS seems to have been copied in tenth-century England. There is a reference to the one-time dating of the poem to “about 700” (410). Fragments from Heliand and Genesis B have been found interpolated into the same thematically irrelevant MS (412). Caedmon's Hymn and Bede's Death Song are not only taken to be earlier than Continental Christian poetry in the vernacular, but are suggested as examples to the same. With regard to the Cotton Heliand, it is asked why it was not translated into OE, unlike OS Genesis (415). The translation of the latter is treated, and Vickrey's comment is noted that Genesis B limits the references to God almost exclusively to words for 'Lord' and 'Ruler,' stressing the master-servant relationships; Schwab further explicates its relationships as feudal (415-16). Delorez points out that this fits precisely into the political context of the OS poem, since the Franks had difficulty imposing the feudal system onto the Saxons; Genesis B, by contrast, is uncertain how to interpret these terms (416). This translation is placed in an Alfredian context for its similarity of diction with the Alfredian translations (417). Schwab is mentioned to have assumed that Genesis B is not a direct translation from the OS, but rather the end-product of a process of less and less Saxon copies (419). Doane feels the OS Genesis is later than the Heliand (420). All in all, the article is exceptionally useful as a catalogue of primary sources as well as selected editions and analyses.

author: Doane, A.N.
title: The Saxon Genesis: An Edition of the West Saxon ‘Genesis B’ and the Old Saxon ‘Vatican Genesis’
abstract: The work opens with an overview of the respective histories of both MSs, discussing sources, editors, MS conditions and properties, fitts, etc. in the first two chapters. Dating for Junius 11 is given about 1025 (29); the Old-Saxon interpolated Genesis in MS Palatinus Latinus 1447 is dated to c. 850 (52). There is a discussion of the place of Genesis B in the MS (30-4). Barbara Raw is followed in her conclusion that the illustrations were based on an illustrated OS Genesis, and her findings are followed up by the hypothesis that the Genesis B interpolation was undertaken for practical reasons, namely because the Fall episode was missing from the source containing Genesis, Exodus, and Daniel. In this, Doane opposes the view held by Wrenn and Priebsch, who believe the interpolation had aesthetic reasons (39-42). Chapter three notes the close proximity in language between OS Genesis and Heliand, whose MSs stem from the second half of the ninth (Monacensis) and the later tenth (Cotton) centuries, while the Heliand date of composition is “conventionally set between 821 and 840” as Foerste demonstrates. Although Doane dismisses the reasons for both extremes of this range, he assumes it is still the only likely period (44-6). Rooth's assumtion that the language in both was an artificially constructed grapholect, expressing an idealised Saxon language, is taken up (45). Heliand is the elder of the two, as becomes clear from allusions to this text in the OS Genesis (46). Concerning the Junius poem, it is pointed out that there are some linguistic differences between the first Genesis A fragment and that following Genesis B. Doane concludes that the first has been more thoroughly reworked (48). It is argued that Junius 11 is the result, emphatically, of many copies and reworkings. What is more, the OS Genesis was never translated into OE at all, these languages having been mutually intelligible; rather, it is the many reworkings that finally brought Genesis B to have a late West-Saxon form, each revision being a “bare 'familiarization'”; OS spellings can therefore still be found in Junius (49). Doane writes that “in a sense, every word in Genesis B is Old Saxon, except for those items which represent deliberate changes away from OS (e.g., slit GB 802 for thuingit VG 12)” (50, note 8). The same strategy has been used on syntax and metre (51). “Thus, the conclusion to be drawn is not Timmer's (45), that the translator must not have been an Anglo-Saxon but a continental Saxon because of the occurrence of such unenglish expressions; rather, we see that the various and successive revisers (most of whom would be Anglo-Saxons) were frequently puzzled enough by the unenglish syntax they found before them to modify it into something that was neither fish nor fowl out of the modest and conservative desire to change as little as possible while enhancing comprehension. Yet there are also places so thoroughly OE and not OS in vocabulary and syntax that tiny Gordian knots must have been cut (e.g., 241)” (51). It is pointed out that the Cotton Heliand and Junius 11 have similar zoomorphic initials; for a comparison, we are referred to Priebsch 29-32 (53). Chapter four is dedicated to a comparison between the OE and OS texts in the corresponding lines, showing that “for the most part Genesis B is a morpheme by morpheme translation of the Old Saxon original” (56). Sievers's 1875 hypothesis is outlined. He found that Genesis A was a closer paraphrase than B; that B contained repeated themes; that there are plot redundancies between the two; that the two differ in line length and metre. Sievers also compared Genesis B with the Heliand, and concluded that Genesis B contains much Saxon diction, as well as much phraseological similarity to the Heliand. Those terms that are found in A and B but not the Heliand he took to be evidence of later revision of B. “Sievers noted that, in all, 15,000 lines of Old English verse did not produce as many parallels with the Heliand as did the 600 lines of Genesis B (13)” (56). A line-by-line study follows (57-64), concluding six types of alteration that have taken place in revision of the OS original towards the lWS language of Genesis B: syllable elimination because of morphemic differences between OS and OE; elimination of redundant function words characteristic for OS poetry; replacement of too unfamiliar words; syntax adjustments; a move towards “quasi-hypotactic” syntax rather than the OS paratactic system; and differences in exemplars (56). Metre is treated in the fifth chapter (65-88); style in the sixth (89-92). It is speculated that OE poetry was written down either early enough or under special circumstances so that it has resisted the precise, specific grammar and syntax that comes with a written language. OS poetry began to be written down later, when anything textual already had strong characteristics of a written culture—OS poetry therefore shows marks of prosification (89-90). Chapter seven treats the influences of the Saxon Genesis (93-107). It states that the OS poem is linked minimally with the biblical text. The postlapsarian history of the first ancestors has as its “real centre. . . the Adam books and. . . the contemporary understanding of apocalypse and apocalyptic literature” (93). Many Genesis B details do not correspond with the Bible narrative: the Prohibition is to both Adam and Eve; the unbiblical Fall of Satan appears after Man's creation; no Satan or serpent but Satan's messenger is the tempter; Adam is tempted first; Eve is tempted by reference to a new direction of God; she suffers a vision; and motivation is described in detail. The OS version also contains innovations, but is more dependent; and “at a lower level, almost every sentence of the [OS] poem contains some unparalleled detail, while the overall effect is of something unique.” There is no direct “'parent' document,” but there are earlier parallels (94). The foremost source is the Heliand, which donates not only uncanonical elements, but also biblical passages. OE poetry, too, has influenced both poems. The Versus is taken as evidence that the Cædmonian school was popular on the Continent. Doane feels that the innovations concerning the Fall may “reflect the poet's interest in the nature of sinning, guilt, and deception,” and that “they stem ultimately from the traditional readings of two passages from Paul,” namely 2 Cor 11.3,14 and 1 Tim 2.14 (94-5; refers to Woolf, “Fall of Man” 191). Also influential were Jude 6;7, as well as Revelation 20.1-3;11.3 and the Last Judgement theme as expressed in Revelation and the Gospels. Finally, 2 Peter 2 seems important (95-6). Other possible sources are the Vita Adae et Evae and its Old Irish imitation Saltair na Rann. The Vita has many narrative elements in common with the OE poem (96-7). Some modest or indirect influence is likely from a number of sources. The function of angels representing human states such as obedience or insight is reminiscent of the Jewish apocrypha. Mentioned are 2 Enoch (Fall of the Angels); The Gospel of Bartholomew (Satan bound, in speech); The Apocalypse of Peter, The History of Joseph, The Acts of Pilate, The Gospel of Bartholomew (the battle of Enoch against the Antichrist). Latin Christian poetry is likely but not very definite (98). Doane is critical of Evans's and Schwab's claims of parallels in Avitus, although Evans has found some clear instances. Doane proposes instead Claudius Marius Victor's Alethia, a poem closely following Scripture, but this work certainly cannot be called a model for the Saxon poem (99). “[O]rthodox ecclesiastical works from the fourth through the ninth centuries” often contain parallels, but this is a large body of mainly anonymous texts (99-100). Adam's replacement of Satan in heaven is a common theme originating from Jewish exegesis. A close textual parallel is found in Ambrose's De Paradiso I.12.54 (PL 14.301) [cited in Doane] (100). The problem arising from the ambiguity of John 8.44 (“quia mendax est et pater eius”) is discussed as a possible source of the concept of a stand-in for Lucifer in the Temptation (100-101). Furthermore, the OS Genesis seems to have been influenced by topicalities such as a ninth-century interest in the role of devils and their deceptions, as well as a number of contemporary poems on the Antichrist (101). Doane identifies “will”--”in what sense it is free, how it operates, and how it becomes evil” as the central theological issue in the OS Genesis; this, he says, is a response to the mid-ninth century “debate over freedom of will and grace” (101-102). The crisis is then expounded on, in which Gottschalk and the older Augustine argue for a precedence of grace over will in saving power; Pelagus believes the opposite (102-107). Chapter eight studies the historical relationship between the two texts (108-115). It reminds the reader that a parent text to the extant OS fragments must have existed, which will have been the direct source for the scribe of the Junius ancestor as well (108). The Vatican fragments are a purposeful selection, probably unifying the theme more than was the case in the original text. The length of the original is speculated on (109-110). Doane writes that “[i]n many places. . . including several extensive passages, there are such similarities between Heliand and Genesis that no other explanation seems possible but that the latter poem is purposely pointing to the former” (110). Tropology is identified as the central level of allegory of the OS Genesis, whereas the Heliand barely uses it (112-13). The suggestion is made that the poem was meant to help impose Christianity onto the Saxons by inviting its listeners to partake in the narrative with the help of the depth provided by tropology (114-15). Chapter nine treats Satan (116-38). The disloyalty of Adam and Eve, and that of Abraham, is in the poem discussed at much greather length than Lucifer's, because they have sworn an oath whereas he has not (117 [but later he is referred to as breaking “universal vassalage”; and his contact with the human pair is also described in feudal terms, 126; see also 133]). Much attention is payed to the way grammar is used to modalise descriptions of Satan (118-20). His psychology is then treated (120-4). In his reluctance to being centrally governed, he is likened to the Saxons vis-à-vis the Carolingian Empire (123). His language is treated (124). Satan's Temptation first of Adam, then of Eve is considered in terms of feudal hierarchy (126). Satan is called “heroic” in a “narrow, old-fashioned, pagan way” because his only possible vengeance consists in “extending the circle of harm” (131). It is pointed out that the idea of Satan bound at the beginning of time is rare: this is conventionally what Christ does in the Harrowing, after the Crucifixion. A reason for the alteration is found in the image of evil that is presented as locked in chains (135-6). Chapter ten treats of Adam and Eve (139-53). Doane says it would be heterodox if the poet meant the Tree of Knowledge is inherently evil, seeing that it is a creation of God. Reference is made to Alcuin, who called the tree a poison, and Hrabanus, who explained that the difference lies in the functions of the trees, not in their natures (139). The serpent/angel issue is treated and views are listed (140, also notes 1,2). Doane concludes that the angelic shape is Eve's perception after she has eaten (141). “Selfsceafte guma” (Genesis B 523a) is argued to describe Adam as a self-fated man (142 note 5; 283). A difference in argumentation is noted in the temptations of Adam and Eve (143). In front of Eve, the tempter simplifies Eve's choice in the matter: he is either an “evil messenger” or “God's angel.” Doane is highly critical of the exoneration theory exemplified by Burchmore (143-4). It is noted that Eve's vision is inspired on the Bible (Genesis 3.4-7) but that “its use is entirely original” (145). The vision is brought as a laðan læn “evil feudal grant” (146). The deception in the Temptation narrative is Eve's deception of herself (147). With the help of Augustine it is argued that sin always originates in faulty will. This is illustrated by the poem's descriptions of Eve after consenting. Her transforming vision is an original usage of an old motif (149-51). Doane concludes that some mitigation of the first parents' guilt is present, not “by lessening their sin, but by going beyond it” (152). Chapter nine and ten are certainly must-rereads. Further chapters, as yet undealt with, concern Cain and Enoch (11), and Abraham and Sodom (12).

author: Earl, James W.
title: Christian Tradition in the OE Exodus
abstract: Earl studies the surfacing of Christian traditions in the Exodus. He notes Huppé's and Cross and Tucker as the most meaningful secondary sources in this field (543). The latter two feel that medieval Christianity was not accustomed to focus on the Red Sea crossing much, as it saw the event above all as a type of baptism. However, the Exodus was in the Middle Ages often regarded as a journey towards salvation; and the desert is associated with Paradise even in the Bible (545). Baptism was often associated with Easter. The OE Exodus uses the word bealusið (5) to allude to the tradition that takes Israel's time in the wild to symbolise “the period of temptation and sin in this life” (546). The end of the poem introduces themes dealt with in the book of Deuteronomy not Exodus. This is interpreted as a tool used for the synthesisation of the story with numerous exegetical traditions (548-9). The post-crossing segment of the poem is an overview and interpretation of the larger Exodus story (555). Such compression in the poem serves to complete the exodus and thereby the type of Christ's resurrection and the Christian's journey through life (559). The poem's nautical imagery is explained by reference to a Church Father tradition that reads in the wilderness, and therefore in the wandering people of Israel, an image of the Church. The Church is often represented by a ship, with the cross as its central element. Noah's ark, too, is commonly taken as a type of the Church; and the Junius MS contains three drawings of the Ark (561-2). The failure of the Israelites to understand how the mast is fastened reflects a lack of understanding concerning their voyage; and indeed they cannot know Christ (562). The digression concerning Noah and Abraham is explained by a multitude of traditional links, but by no single one. Those of the covenant and the world ages are significant, but insufficient to explain the passage. What gives the digression meaning is its typology. The flood refers to baptism; the exodus to Easter; the Ark to salvation; and Isaac's sacrifice to the Passion. Furthermore, four men in the digression—Noah, Isaac, Moses, and Solomon—are regular types of Christ; and the poem is full of the theme of salvation. Still, the digression seems abrupt; perhaps the lost passage after line 446 might have clarified the matter. The description of Israel moving into the Red Sea as if going into battle is anachronistic (Israel is not militarily organised until Numbers [557]), but may be explained by the condensation of the entire exodus into one episode (565-6). Cross and Tucker have two alternative readings: firstly, they refer to the traditional association between the Red Sea crossing and baptism, which institution is traditionally seen as having a spiritual battle both before and after. The OE Exodus invents a battle ahead in order to keep in line with this tradition. The second explanation lies in the nature of early Christian baptism itself: it is envisioned in a more military way than is common today Daniélou complements this explanation by reference to the struggle between Christ and Satan at the baptismal font (566-7). Gregory even reads the “descent into the underworld” into the Red Sea crossing (567-9).

author: Ebert, Adolf
title: Zur angelsaechsischen Genesis
abstract: Lists a number of things the Genesis A poet has added to the biblical account, and concludes that the poet made not only a translation of words but also one of cultures; he introduces Anglo-Saxon customs, virtues, weaknesses, and even landscape into the narrative (125-7). Argues that this part of Genesis could not be written by Caedmon, because the author has obviously been sufficiently literate to be able to study the Bible at length (131). Introduces the story of Caedmon (131-2). This article is of no use whatsoever.

author: Ericksen, Janet Schrunk
title: Lands of Unlikeness in Genesis B
abstract: After Eve's consumption of the fruit, as everytime when a character sins or considers sinning in Genesis B, an 'unlikeness' is expressed to the world as it was before [cf. Ohlgren's 'transition' in “Visual Language”]. This is used to signal a shift in the character's relationship with God and has its base in Augustine's concept of the regio dissimilitudinis. The focalisation of a particular character reflects his relationship to God (1-2). The source is Augustine's Confessiones 7 in which Augustine is placed in a region of dissimilarity before his conversion. It also occurs in his De Trinitate. This insight leads Augustine to understand evil in negative terms: as spatial distance from God (3). Augustine did not invent the “land of unlikeness”; perhaps Plato did, in a slightly different sense (4). In Genesis B, it refers “to hell and outside the Garden.” A catalogue of “ungelic” is presented (5-6). Genette uses a distinction of three types of focalisation or discrepancy between communicated context of narrator and character; Genesis B switches between two of these at each instance of “ungelic” or “ne gelic” (6-7). Likeness to God features in the biblical account, and likeness to the angels in Genesis A (7). A positive description of hell is not given after Satan's fall; “the focus is on unlikeness” (8).The two trees display intense dissimilarity (9-10). In the tempter's conversation with Adam, Adam recognises him as being unlike angels he has seen; when addressing Eve, the tempter says he is not like the devil, which comparison she cannot judge (11-13). Eve's new sight is “unlike” because of her greater distance from God [by greater spatial distance, her horizon is broadened] (14). A visionary parallel to Eve's is noted in Gregory's account of Benedict's vision (16).

author: Ericksen, Janet Schrunk
title: Transforming Female History in Stjórn
abstract: Schrunk notes that Stjórn I focuses on the present consequences of the Fall, thereby placing Eve at the origin of “human sin and female history” (195). Carol Clover is cited as arguing that Christianity “entailed a radical remapping of gender in the north”; this is argued by Ericksen to be visible in the Stjórn Fall (195). The MS is then discussed. The composition of the first of the three original parts is dated to the early fourteenth century; the others to the middle or later thirteenth century. As sources are mentioned the Vulgate, Comestor's Historia Scholastica, and De Beauvais's Speculum Historiale (197). The story of the Fall is universal rather than localised or germanicised. Icelandic literature of the period stood in a tradition in which land and ancestors defined history. The characters in the Stjórn Fall are treated against a background of hierarchy, unlike the saga characters that are treated in an individuated manner, allowing gender flexibility. Laxdœla Saga is the most obvious contemporary contrast with Stjórn I: its female protagonist is singled out as a “paragon amongst women” before she moves to Iceland and breeds the saga's important characters. Thus both Unnr and Eve are matriarchs whose characters explain those of their offspring, but in a contrasting fashion. Yet these stories came about in the same society (198-9). Part of the motives of the Stjórn I author was to teach an understanding of the shame associated with sexuality (199-200). Peter Comestor and his contemporaries regularly linked sexuality and theology: vice resulted in sexual sin; virtues consisted in constraining sexuality. Augustine had been their example in this approach (200). The Stjórn I author emphasises the viciousness of unruly sexuality and neglects motives and causes of the Fall (201). He explains a rebellious “stirring of the genitalia. . . against reason and the law of the soul,” to be the first mark of Man's sinful condition [cf. Augustine's explanation of the unwilled actions of the genitals as proof of sin in Pang-White's study] (202). So strong is the author's focus on the explanation of original sin and the disobedient character of uncontrolled sexuality that little is left of the Fall story (203). Eve's behaviour is an example for those who will be foolish (204). The fourteenth-century audience is didactically centralised in the account; the vision on gender as expressed in the sagas had a focus on the individual rather than on abstract consequence. As such, the sagas contrast with the Stjórn Fall; a remapping of gender had to take place for the Stjórn account because the Fall story originated in a different gender culture (206-7).

author: Evans, J.M.
title: Genesis B and its Background: Part I
abstract: Central sources of ninth-century Bible understanding were Augustine's De Civitate Dei and De Genesi ad Litteram. More recent and local links in the same tradition were Bede's Hexaemeron, Alcuin's Interrogationes et Responsiones in Genesin and Raban Maur's Commentariorum in Genesim Libri Quator. Alcuin diverges from tradition by referring to the tree of knowledge of good and evil as a poison, though lateron he explains that the evil is not so much harboured by it as offered from the option of man's disobedience (1-2). Raban specifies the sins involved in Eve's temptation. Alcuin and Raban select the same Augustinian passages for use in their own commentary; this suggests a change of emphasis in interpretation. Alcuin mainly poses and answers questions concerning the story's integrity as a narrative (3-4). The ninth-century vernacular works the Heliand and the Evangelienbuch are “typical of their age” and strongly influenced by Raban, Bede, Alcuin; and Augustine, Jerome, and Gregory the Great. Genesis B “owes little or nothing to the commentaries of the accepted authorities, and it reveals a very striking independence of outlook” (4-5). The tempter was a servant of Satan rather than Satan himself. This is most likely a consequence of the ambiguous “quia mendax est et pater eius,” which if interpreted in one way suggests that the tempter has an evil father. Alternative explanations lie in the descensus interpretation of the Gospel of Nicodemus, in which Christ binds Satan in hell; and a reading of Genesis B as a refutation of the Manichaean concept of the Fall, in which Satan created man (5-6). The tempter's disguise as an angel rather than a serpent may derive from Juliana 161-6, the Vita Adae et Evae, or the Apocalypsis Mosis and related texts (7). However, many early Church Fathers believed that the temptation was the cause of Lucifer's downfall, and thus no angelic downfall would have taken place at this point of the narrative (8-9). The tempter's attempt to seduce Adam before his approach of Eve seems to have no precedent, but it may have an explanation in 1 Timothy 2.13-14. The “tree of death” concept may be rooted in many texts; but none of them present Eve as eating the fruit because she believes God has ordered it (10). Her vision after the fall resembles that of Cyprian's Heptateuchos, and this must have been his source (11-12). The tempter's triumphant speech after Adam's Fall occurs also in Avitus's Poematum de Mosaicae Historiae Gestis Libri Quinque. Ten Brink has also noted a resemblance between these two poems. Alcuin lists Avitus's poem as present in the York library (11-14). It otherwise contains a few minor correspondences to the Genesis B account (15). The latter's immediate repentance of the fallen resembles that in the Vita Adae et Evae and Alethia, but it is only in the Anglo-Saxon poem that the repentance takes place before the expulsion (15-16). In conclusion, Genesis B stands possibly in a literary tradition, but not in a theological one; and the unorthodox elements are all in the description of the Fall of Adam and Eve (16).

author: Evans, J.M.
title: Genesis B and its Background: Part II
abstract: The poet portrays Adam and Eve as favourably as possible. He draws a contrast between the evil of the deeds and their good motivations (113-14). The poet also hints at damnation by his emphasis on the consequences of their actions, but the overall effect on the reader is to excuse the couple's mistakes. A comparison is drawn with Oedipus. “Good tragedy, however, is very rarely good theology.” Christian doctrine insists that here, deeds are what counts, and they are irreversible (115). Like many others, the Saxon monk Gottchalk opted for a more optimistic Fall reading than Augustine's. The Saxon church condemned his teachings in 848. Genesis B is “typical of its age in accepting the letter while excluding the spirit of Augustinianism.” The Caedmonian application of heroic vocabulary to Christian poetry resulted in new connotations and meanings of the heroic terms, but also in a coarsening of doctrinal expression. The heroic context of the Christian doctrine so expressed required an emphasis on deeds not intentions. (116-7). Germanic epic seems to have focussed on situation rather than action, in which emphasis the genre contrasts with classical epic; it concerns itself with “men in tension.” This literary attitude is the reversal of the mentioned insistence on the meaning of deeds. “In moral and realistic terms what mattered was to do and die; in poetic and imaginative terms the real issue was the reason why” (117). The central position of situation influenced Germanic plot structure: it develops in a series of “vivid stills”(117-18). “The aim of Germanic narrative technique. . . is to illuminate the motives and feelings which are in tension within a clearly defined situation.” This required elaboration of the Genesis account (118). “The most important questions which the Germanic poet set out to answer were not what and how, but who and why. These were precisely the questions left unanswered in the biblical account.” The Fall story is related in terms of Germanic loyalty, exile, and revenge (119). The temptation is put in terms of trickery in order to draw a distinction between Man and Satan. It is presented as a strategic move, so as to keep it in line with the poem's military form (120). The preliminary tempting of Adam serves tactical purposes (121). The “vivid stills” mode is essential in keeping up the narrative in the Fall passage (122).

author: Sørensen, Bent
title: A History of Energy: Northern Europe from the Stone Age to the Present Day
abstract:
This book is rather poorly written both linguistically and in microargument but impressive and useful in general outline and many of its particulars. Unfortunately, this makes it a little hard to identify valid claims amidst the murk. It takes Denmark proper (without its one-time North Atlantic holdings) as a case study for the history of energy use by humans, though the prehistoric situation extends to Finland. Its author has published more than a dozen previous books on energy.

[ch. 1: Climate Background and Eem Visitors]

The book begins with the Eem interglacial of 130 kya–115 kya, because this was the first time hominids (probably Neanderthals) reached northern Europe (1–47, being ch. 1; specific claim at 3–4, and see further 20–42). Discusses climatic conditions (3–20) before turning to archaeological evidence for hominid visitors during the Eem interglacial (20–42). The late Eem presence of Neanderthals in Finland is documented; the conditions for human survival are set out, including, under Eem circumstances, high-insulation clothes and snowtight footwear; the conditions are brought to an amusing but impressive level of detail in terms of requisite thickness of clothing layer and so on (20–42). The chapter makes brief reference to homo heidelbergensis, which moved north into Europe about 640 kya (23).

[Ch. 2: Weichselian Stone Age: Coping with the Cold North]

Starts by estimating the extent of ice cover and flora at various relative glacial maxima (49–53). Then constructs a complex model for Neanderthal mortality rates including such factors as prey, population size, and climate change (53–~7). Considers the cause of Neanderthal extinction; observes there is no evidence of an increase in violent deaths upon arrival of homo sapiens, but some evidence for interbreeding; it may have been a disease carried by homo sapiens that led to Neanderthal extinction (~58–67). The remainder of the chapter returns to a detailed account of energy intake and expenditure for humans up to 8 kya (69–77).

[Chs 3 and 4 deal with the late stone age (81–115) and the introduction of agriculture, trade, and metalworking (117–69) respectively]

[Ch. 5: Migration and Exploration by Land and Sea]

Opens with a historical introduction beginning with southward migrations in the second century BCE and ending with Viking Age art (171–81). The subsequent discussion of the population model goes on to discuss Viking expansion and the Danish-Norwegian wars (181–93) before turning to architectural developments (193–6) and eventually the energy tables (193–211).

[Ch. 6: Medieval Society: Church Building and a Little Dissent]

Engages in more agonising accounts of “history” before discussing the various energy advances of the Middle Ages, including a hypocaust in a twelfth-century Danish convent and watermills. More mortality and age expectancy tables follow.

The remainder of the book is post-medieval.

author: Farrell, Robert T.
title: Eight Notes on OE Exodus
abstract: Only of semantic interest.

author: Finnegan, Robert Emmett
title: Eve and ‘Vincible Ignorance’ in Genesis B
publication: Texas Studies in Literature and Language
abstract: Whereas J.M. Evans still held that Eve was “subjectively innocent” for doing “the wrong thing for the right reason,” Vickrey [Finnegan writes Vickery] and Woolf have judged such a reading unintended by the poet; the first because Eve’s vision shows God enthroned, i.e., in judgement, and the latter because anyone untouched by the devil would have seen through the Tempter’s disguise. In doing so, Woolf implies that Eve knew about the angels’ Fall and revolt, an assumption not warranted by the text (364). Vickrey’s claim that the audience would have understood Eve’s vision to refer to her judgement is probably correct, but it does not mean that the audience would have taken up judgement over Eve for what she does not know. The poet, then, seems to have been “heterodox, if not heretic”; but this view is not warranted in the poem either. Eve is “vincibly ignorant” and thus guilty of the deed and of failing to form a sound judgement; this becomes clear in the alterations to the story. Eve is personally given the order not to eat; the Tempter probably tells her that Adam has refused to eat; he assumes the shape of an angel; and he does not say that if she eats, she will be like God, knowing good and evil (the mark of Eve’s pride). These modifications give Eve a range of input data from which she ought to be able to form a correct judgement (330-1). The vengeful picture the Tempter paints of God is radically different from Eve’s knowledge of her Maker (331-2). Furthermore, by advising Eve to save Adam of God’s anger, he proves himself no faithful messenger of God; by promising her to hide Adam’s rejection from God he contradicts the concept of an omniscient God; and by referring to the latter as herran þines, he implies that God is not his lord (332-3). Eve sincerely believed the Tempter; but Augustine in his anti-Pelagian writings makes clear that one may sin in ignorance; indeed, in certain circumstances, ignorance may even add to the evil of a sin. The fanatical reading by the Saxon monk Gottschalk of the anti-Pelagian writings coincides well with the heterodox theology of Genesis B; hence, theological evidence points towards the mid-ninth century for the composition of its Old Saxon model (335-6). The fatal sin of pride may have been replaced by that of culpable ignorance because the former is more widely applicable; people would thus feel more directly addressed (336).

author: Finnegan, Robert
title: The Man in 'Nowhere': A Previously Undiscovered Drawing in Bodleian MS. Junius 11
abstract: After considering the possibilities of the man at the top of page seven to be a fallen angel and a human being, respectively, Finnegan concludes that it is a representation of the reader, drawn by the second artist.

author: Gatch, Milton McC.
title: Perceptions of Eternity
publication: The Cambridge Companion to Old English Literature
abstract:
NB the edition cited has now been superseded by the 2013 second edition, where its page range is 198–213).

Sfr expresses an awareness that man may gain a permanent home in heaven, on which home he ought to focus (190). Standard early medieval eschatology is set out (190-2). Judgement Day II, translating Bede’s De die iudicii, bears an eschatological focus, as does Christ III (or Doomsday; 192-4). Apart from Bede’s Latin commentaries, two of Ælfric’s sermons, De die iudicii and Sermo ad populum in octavis pentecosten dicendus, offer a good view of AS eschatology; the latter is termed “a benchmark of orthodox early medieval beliefs concerning the last times.” The precise events between death and resurrection were not important, and it was the salvation of God’s people rather than the individual’s personal redemption that mattered (194-6). Nonetheless, technical questions were speculated upon. The Phoenix speaks of temporary death between bodily death and resurrection (ll. 484-90). Suspension or sleep was the strictly orthodox view. Death is surprisingly generally defined as the separation of body and soul. The body decomposes; what happens to the soul is matter for debate. Ælfric’s view is stated; the theory of purgatory “was not fully developed until at least a century after the time of Ælfric” (197-8). Many OE references to the afterlife are visionary and derive from 2 Corinthians 12.1-4 and the Visio sancti Pauli. Soul and Body I (and to some extent also II ) contrasts body and soul, warning its audience that the body must not give in to sin as it is the dwelling-place of the soul (198-200). The similarities between medieval otherworld-visions and present-day near-death experiences is remarked on; the main difference is the specific message usually expressed in the former. The most famous instance of the genre is Dryhthelm’s vision as related by Bede (HE 5.12); but Leofric’s is remarkable in its apparently English origin (200-3). Maxims II emphasises that only God knows where the soul goes (203-4).

author: Haines, Dorothy
title: Vacancies in Heaven: The Doctrine of Replacement and Genesis A
abstract: Traces the doctrine of replacement, which first occurred in Augustine’s Enchridion ad Laurentium 62 and DcD 22.1. Gregory the Great then took it up, offering as one alternative reading of the lost coin that the nine are the nine orders of angels, whereas the tenth consists of elect human beings. He does not spell out that these replace the fallen angels. This reading of the parable now became the most common vessel for thoughts on the doctrine of replacement (150-2). Bede brings Gregory’s version to Britain; Ælfric picks it up and Wulfstan takes it from Ælfric (152-3). Blickling homily 11 comes closest verbally to the Gen A account and introduces the notion of seats or thrones (153-4). In Gen A, the replacement is Satan’s prime cause of anger against mankind; Ælfric and Wulfstan also describe it as such. The doctrine in Gen A thus has decidedly Anglo-Saxon roots (154).

author: Hill, Thomas D.
title: Pilate’s Visionary Wife and the Innocence of Eve: An Old Saxon Source for the Old English Genesis B
publication: Journal of English and Germanic Philology

author: Hill, Thomas D.
title: Satan's Injured Innocence in Genesis B
abstract: Proposes Gregory's Moralia in Job as “at least the ultimate source” for the motif of Satan's post-lapsarian unawareness of his guilt.

author: Hill, Thomas D.
title: Some Remarks on ‘The Site of Lucifer's Throne’
abstract: Salmon's suggestion of Lactantius as a source for the idea that Lucifer was to establish his throne in the northwest does not bear examination. Christ III does parallel such a location. Cook comments that this is derived from Zacharias 14.4-5. Jerome comments on the Bible passage and draws a contrast between the southeast as the location of the blessed and the northwest as that of the sinners. Bede shows a familiarity with this tradition (303-307). The eleventh-century Irish Vision of Adamnan also carries the motif (308); and so does the longest version of the Visio Pauli (309-310). The motif is a widely attested medieval tradition (310-11).

author: Hill, Thomas D.
title: The Fall of Angels and Man in the Old English Genesis B
publication: Anglo-Saxon Poetry: Essays in Appreciation for John McGalliard
eds: Lewis E. Nicholson and Dolores Warwick Frese

author: Huppé, Bernard F.
title: Doctrine and Poetry: Augustine's Influence on Old English Poetry
publisher: State University of New York Press
abstract: In his first chapter, Huppé sets out Augustine's approach to poetry, who argues that poetic diction is beneficial to religious writing in posing an intellectual challenge, thus yielding pleasure to the reader; forcing him to concentrate; and yielding pleasure. Even pagan authors, such as Virgil and Homer, are not abandoned: instead, they are adopted by means of injected readings on the anagogical level (3-27). The second chapter demonstrates the theory in a number of theological authors. The work then moves on to OE poetry; Junius 11 is dealt with in chapters five and six. It is noted that the opening lines of Genesis A resemble Caedmon's Hymn as well as the praefatio to the Mass (134). The poem does not trace Genesis to the end; but it may be complete nevertheless, if it is a thematic work, leading up to the sacrifice of Isaac, that is, the Passion (135). The Genesis attributed to Hilary of Arles is taken for comparison: it too tells its reader to praise God (135-7). The first 100 lines are summarised (138-41). They are then concluded to be a thematic expansion belonging within the first verse of Genesis. A paraphrase follows at line 112, adding some exegesis (142), drama, and clarification; but some seemingly random alterations remain unexplained (147-8). After Genesis B, the poem resumes with a formula that seems a transition (Hwæt. . ., 149). Patristic commentary is used to explain the innovations around the expulsion (Gen A 948-64, 150-6). Abel and Cain are discussed (156-66); the Flood (166-76); the generations following Noah (176-83); the tower of Babel (183-6); and Abraham and Lot (186-204). In chapter six, Exodus is also read as a thematic poem, influenced by Christian tradition; it is seen as symbolising 'the escape from the world through Christ' (218). The various elements of the story are given their respective sylbolism (218-23). Daniel is then treated and shown to consist of very careful structure (223-7). Christ and Satan is not biblical, but in line with Augustinian theology: literature is permitted as long as it leads to the truth (227). Finally, some other poems are treated, notably the Wanderer, the Seafarer, and Beowulf (231-9).

author: Jager, Eric
title: A Miles Diaboli in the Old English Genesis B
abstract: Genesis B contains a “manifest military theme”; the tempter's arming scene is in line with this theme, but instead of physical weapons it describes “wora worda”; this reflects a theme of spiritual warfare (1-2). The common miles Christi is here a miles diaboli (2). The scene is compared to Paul's description in Ephesians 6.11-17 of the “arma Dei” (2-3). The emphasis on words throughout the poem is noted, and it is concluded that the human couple fall because they have failed to arm themselves with the arma Dei (3-5).

author: Jager, Eric
title: Tempter as Rhetoric Teacher: The Fall of Language in the Old English Genesis B
abstract: The Tempter plays a role as a rhetorics teacher of Eve; language shows that she takes his teaching as a translatio studii (434). He offers her rhetorical advice (434-5); she takes over his style and persuasion (435-8); and verbal features are transferred from the Tempter’s temptation of Eve (T:E) to that of Adam by Eve [E:A, 438ff]).

author: Johnson, David F.
title: The Fall of Lucifer in Genesis A and two Anglo-Latin Royal Charters
publication: Journal of English and Germanic Philology
abstract: Johnson establishes that there is no single canonical or other authoritative text for the creation and fall of the angels. The existence of evil required an explanation of its origin that was not spelled out in the Bible; and this need led to apocryphal documents relating such details. The writings of the Church Fathers are largely limited to exegesis of passages (500). The fall of the angels occurs regularly in OE verse. Genesis A tells that the angels were created before the world, and that the creation of the latter was triggered by the fall of the former. Augustine held that nothing was created before heaven and earth; Origen believed the spiritual world was created much earlier (501). Johnson writes that “virtually every detail in [the first 101 lines of Genesis A] can be paralleled quite readily in Old English or Christian-Latin religious literature. The pattern of the narrative as a whole, however, and the understanding of the myth implicit in the poet's treatment of it, are unparalleled in Old English poetry, and as far as I know, no editor or commentator on the poem has yet adduced a Latin narrative text which corresponds in these respects to the poem as we have it” (502). The paper shows that the fall of the angels is also found in two Anglo-Latin charters of the tenth century. At the birth of man's situation in the world stands Lucifer and his rebellion; but the Bible does not narrate this event directly, although Ezechiel 28.1-19 and Isaiah 14.12-15 are linked with this event. Augustine and Gregory have written on the subject, but these treatments are fragmentary due to the nature of their writings. They held that the Bible did not further treat angels in the fear that the Israelites would worship them. Augustine and Isidore believed Lucifer rebelled in the first moments of his creation; the Vitae Adae et Evae tells this did not happen until after Adam's creation (503-4). Two traditions dealing with the fall of the angels are the hexameral and the catechetical narratio. The first is not likely to have influenced Genesis A because the latter does not follow the six-day organisation and because Augustine's identification of the angels with the light is not treated explicitly. It must also be remembered that, although he stood at the birth of the hexameral tradition, most authors turned away from Augustine's example because of his allegorical interpretation and because he believed nothing was created before the physical world. Doane is eager to link Genesis A to Augustinian tradition, but his approach is criticised (505-6). Johnson concludes that the Genesis A poet probably knew of Augustine's view, but that he did not feel compelled by his explanation. Doane refers to a tradition in which the angels fell on the fifth or sixth day, and Ælfric follows this in his Exameron Anglice (507). The catechetical narratio is more likely to have influenced the poem, because they were narrative accounts. Yet neither Augustine's narratio nor those listed by Virginia Day provide relevant parallels with Genesis A for the current theme (509-10). The replacement doctrine formulated in Genesis A 92-101 may stand in the Origen tradition, but no solid conclusions can be drawn here, especially because the Anglo-Saxons had little access to Greek and much of Origen's work was considered heretical (511-512). “Edgar's Privilege to New Minster” parallels Genesis A in the doctrine that the physical world and man were created because the “throne of the heavens” was empty. The common attribution is to Bishop Æthelwold (512-514). The Peniarth Diploma by Æthelred II speaks of the tenth order that was missing after the angelical fall, and the wish to “replenish” it (515-516). The common elements among the three texts are listed and it is concluded that it is not details but the “cosmological perspective” they have in common (516). Augustine's replacement doctrine is described, as is its popularity in the early Middle Ages and rejection in the scholastic age (517). Johnson concludes that all three authors have used a “common formulation of this myth as their source,” be it a text or a preaching tradition. It is noted that this understanding of creation can be considered to be against the Bible, but that Bishop Æthelwold thought it fitting in a text establishing the New Minster Abbey (519-520). Æthelwold may have meant to use the understanding in order to invoke the power of “Lord and Disposer” which God shared with King Edgar (521).

author: Kabir, Ananya Jahanara
title: Paradise, Death and Doomsday in Anglo-Saxon Literature
abstract: Discusses the states of the blessed dead before doomsday according to OE literature.

author: Karkov, Catherine E.
title: Text and Picture in Anglo-Saxon England: Narrative Strategies in the Junius 11 Manuscript
abstract: The Junius illustrations are a continuous visual narrative, integral to the MS (3-6;16). Christ and Satan was by illustrators and compiler considered an integral part of the MS (3). Implicit doubt is uttered concerning the duplicity of Genesis A and B (4; see also 65). Early medieval illustrations often have an exegetical function or serve to link multiple texts (8,11). Praiseworthy explanations of ostensible instances of 'pictorial dislocation' are given (11-16); and it becomes obvious that illustrations are specific to the tradition of the text when a depiction of Adam's temptation is mentioned (13-14). Chapter two briefly treats the make-up of the MS (19-32); it then moves on to discuss illustrative style (33-6) and narrative structure of the illustrations (36-44). Notable is the interpretation of graphical elements such as the active pose of characters (40-4) and the relation between illustration and specific phrases (32). In the third chapter, a note of tradition is made pointing out that the 'void' left in heaven after the fall of the angels is commented on by Augustine (Enchiridion XXIX [CCSL 46] 56) and Ælfric (Homilies I,12; 51). An emphasis is placed on intertextuality: images are used to evoke other biblical passages to be linked up with the one depicted (e.g. 57-8). A note on the lord-retainer relationships within the poem appears (66). The several biblical passages portrayed are discussed with reference to the MS text. Chapter four identifies the main MS theme as 'the cycle of Fall and Redemption that runs uninterruptedly from the Creation to the Last Judgement'; but attention is drawn to its function as a historical record [of the Anglo-Saxon period] as well (101). The theme of words is graphically expressed in the MS mostly through poses and gestures. Exodus and Christ and Satan summarise the Creation, echoing Genesis and implying the Word as a creating power in Creation as well as their poetry; but in the illustrations the theme is limited to two instances of open mouths; and otherwise to poses like that of Abel's corpse (102-3). Daniel contains a song of praise reminiscent of the beginning of Genesis (104-6). Christ and Satan calls Christ 'Byrhtword' (107). In a comparison of visions, Eve's appears alongside the communal vision in Exodus of the transformation of the pillars of cloud and fire (110-19). Daniel's dreams are treated and compared with Eve's vision (120-5). The uses of beacen, tacen, segn, and gebletsian are outlined at length with reference to signs (125-41). Chapter five opens with the recognition that Junius 11 does not adhere to the biblical model of chronology in which the beginning describes Creation and the end the Apocalypse (142). Genesis (A-B) can be divided into four phases of (pro)creation, by God, Adam, Noah, and Abraham. The illustrations focus on this process of procreation by the portrayal of patriarchs and matriarchs rather than battle scenes (144-5). Isaac and Abraham are tried in Genesis, the Israelites in Exodus[, and, one may add, Daniel and the youths in Daniel]. The transitions in text between the poems are discussed, with reference to the drawings (144-9). There is a brief note on MS dating (“late tenth or early eleventh century,” 151). Gender issues are discussed (149-52), and genealogy (152-8; passing note on the antichronical order 156). The “brada stanas” Satan presents Christ with in CaS 670b are compared with the fruit with which Adam and Eve are tempted, and Satan's “offering the earthly kingdom to Christ is reminiscent of his offering Eve the heavenly kingdom” (158). The theme of bodies is explored at length; it is pointed out that, in contrast with the vitae, the bodies of sacrifice in this MS remain intact (167). Christ is made “visible” before his incarnation by the cruciferous nimbus on the frontispiece (168). There is a note on the linking technique of the originally separate poems (176), and a word is shed on the possible Canterbury origins of the MS (182). Chapter six summarises MS and editing history. The similarity between Cædmon's Hymn according to Bede (HE 4.24, 418-19) and the Genesis A opening is noted [cf. with Praefatio similarity] (188). Critics of this comparison are mentioned, alongside their arguments that the texts are significantly different and that Junius 11 must be later for its Danish influences (189). Analogues with the Cædmon story are noted, including the Voluspá, which extends to the same chronology from Creation to doom (191-2). The possibility of the Cædmon episode being a fiction of Bede is treated, backed by reasons (192-4). The book is useful especially for its pointing out of the interplay the drawings have with the text, and of the symbolism in the illustrations. I accept most of the conclusions in this field, but not immediately the most speculative ones, such as Noah's nakedness referring to fertility (95) or speculations concerning planned images (e.g. 148; 203-06). The last chapter, on the MS and its editors, is also useful.

author: Kirby, Ian J.
title: Biblical Quotation in Old Icelandic-Norwegian Religious Literature
abstract: Volume I is a directory of quotations, ordered by Bible passage and furthermore by approximate dating of MS. Volume II is entitled “Introduction.” It starts with the historical narrative of Bible usage and translation, treating Old Latin and Vulgate versions as well as the translations and verse paraphrases in the other Germanic languages (1-16). It notes that “very little can be said for certain about the text or texts of the Vulgate available in the West Norse area. There is no reason to assume that Norway and Iceland would not have had access to the Bibles in current use elsewhere. Thus, there is no evidence of the use of any version of the Bible other than the Vulgate in the Latin quotations found in [Monumenta historica Norvegiae] (see 2.55); conversely, although the Stjórn texts generally follow the Vulgate, there are a few examples in Stjórn I where the doubling of words appears to be carried out not merely for effect but ecause one word represents the Vulgate and the other the Old Latin version (see 2.13 and note to Gen.3.1). However, study of the biblical quotations has brought one circumstance to light: a number of New Testament readings correspond only to the Irish ms. type (listed as ‘D’ in e.g. [Wordsworth’s Nouum Testamentum latine]). This type appears to be of considerable antiquity, for some of the readings it has are found in Augustine: and one cannot always be sure that the Norse passage does not reflect an intermediate Latin source such as Augustine. But there are a few instances from Norse passages which are probably original: they include the NoHom. quotation at Mt.25.34, that from Th. at Jn.8.12, and the Bs. quotation at Lk.11.17. This suggests that Irish texts of the Vulgate may have circulated in the West Norse area; and this is by no means intrinsically improbable” (9). It is also indicated that “[t]here is. . . no evidence of a complete Bible translation in the Old Norse period; and there is no manuscript evidence of a translation of the Gospels. . . . In the religious literature as a whole there is additionally some material which differs little from biblical translation proper. . . . Further, there is some evidence that part, or the whole, of the text of the Bible used by Comestor was translated. . .” (15). Evidence is then referred to that suggests “an early translation of the Gospels” (15-16). Indeed, the gospel quotations in Grímr Holmsteinsson’s redaction of the Saga of John the Baptist are so similar to Oddr Gottskálksson’s New Testament that they must rely on an early translation of the New Testament (15–16). It is proposed that “the beginnings of Norse religious literature are to be looked for in the early part of the 12th century, or a little before” (17). Concerning Stjórn it is said that the older parts of its extant MSs are mid-fourteenth century (84). The volume then mentions in great detail all the religious texts in Old Norse (17–109) before turning to a justification of method (109–31). The penultimate section of this part discusses the sources of biblical quotations and how to represent them alongside the Norse (123–8). Here, Kirby takes up again the question of whether a full Norse Bible existed, and concludes that there were at least parts of the Old Testament and the gospels, while the Psalms may be presumed to have existed as well. He traces half of his quotations to Latin sources, or two thirds for the Old Testament. Volume II also lists the quotations of the first volume in ON book order (185-236).

author: Lamb, H.H.
title: Britain’s Climate in the Past
abstract: Originally given as a lecture in 1964, this paper is already able to outline the main movements of MWP (here “Little Optimum”) and LIA with reference to a variety of scholarly fields (“glaciology, forest limits, archaeology and history” — but no citations are given for the medieval part of his paper other than for vineyard extent, research on which is from the 1950s) (174–5). The remainder of the paper summarises temperature variability during the last glacial period and thereafter; following his discussion of the Middle Ages he turns to modern meteorological records, which he attempts to extend into the Middle Ages by following up documentary evidence of dry/wet summers and cold winters (Lamb refers to his paper in Geografiska annaler for 1961) and archaeobotanical evidence; these confirm the MWP/LIA-progression (181–92). Much of what is in his later and more extensive publications is already here, graphs and all. The MWP trough is dated to 1000–1300; the LIA low to 1550–1700/1850 (174 and graphs).

author: Fagan, Brian
title: The Little Ice Age: How Climate Made History, 1300–1850
abstract: A chatty monograph on late medieval to modern climate variation, using a good deal of narrative and direct quotation but not a lot of footnotes or complex concepts. I suspect it would turn out to cover a fair number of climate events if I took the trouble to read it, but it’s not the most scholarly source to cite.

author: Dyer, C.C.
title: Making a Living in the Middle Ages: The People of Britain 850–1520
abstract:
The go-to volume for medieval English socioeconomic history.

Claims that English forests 850–1050 were not much more extensive than today’s (cf. Mantel 64) (13). Says of medieval English farmers that “[a]t no time or place can within our period can they be described as ‘subsistence farmers’, in the sense that they ate only food that they had grown, or that they produced solely for their own consumption needs. They always expected that their land would yield a surplus, whether for the benefit of the state, the church or their lords, or for exchange for goods and services which they could not obtain from their own land” (14; this statement is best read in comparison with Le Goff, who claims the opposite for medieval farmers in general but mostly by stretching the sense of the word subsistence, and Landers, who emphasises the narrow returns from the soil). There is some discussion of land use between different regions; an emphasis on arable land in Berkshire charter bounds, more pasture and woods in the southern counties, and some in East Anglia; uplanders depended primarily on pastureland (15–17). Population growth led to changes in landscape use as well as the formation of villages (17–26). Increases in rural production clashed with the interests of the hunting aristocracy. “The main changes in the rural landscape were not on the fringes of woods, moors and marshes, but in the well-developed arable lands, where the tenth and eleventh centuries were an important phase in the creation of villages and their associated fields” (18). When villages rose to prominence, farmers held strips of land spread evenly through the village’s holdings; they were usually expected to have half of their land fallow at any time (22–3). This two-course rotation may have been relatively recent, since it may be expected that any given plot was only tilled occasionally prior to the spatial dominance of arable land (24).

[incomplete]

author: Grove, Jean M.
title: The Onset of the Little Ice Age
publication: History and Climate: Memories of the Future?
abstract: Confirms that the LIA was global by bringing together evidence on glacial advance from around the globe. Refers to her article from the same year which studies the timing of the onset of the LIA around the North Atlantic and summarises her findings. Dates are variable by region, but southeast Greenland saw “warm, stable conditions between the 10th and 13th centuries, followed by cold conditions beginning about 1270 A.D. and culminating probably about 1370 A.D., leading on to even harsher conditions after 1630”. A brief period of relief took place between 1370 and 1470 (155–6). “In both northern and southern Scandinavia the Little Ice Age culminated in the 17th and 18th centuries” (156).

author: Grove, Jean M.
title: The Initiation of the “Little Ice Age” in Regions Round the North Atlantic
abstract: Gathers evidence to demonstrate that the LIA commenced in the thirteenth century for wider North Atlantic region, including the Swiss Alps.

author: Grove, Jean M.
title: Little Ice Ages: Ancient and Modern
series: Routledge Studies in Physical Geography and Environment
abstract: One volume on the LIA of the second millennium, and one divided between the glacial history of the Holocene and causes/consequences of such relative minima.

author: Broecker, Wallace S.
title: Was the Medieval Warm Period Global?
abstract: A very short article arguing on what the author deems inconclusive yet substantial evidence that the MWP was a global event. The author’s opening remarks leave me a little confused as to his motivations; leading climate scientists have discredited the article.

author: Bradley, Raymond S., et al.
title: The Scope of Medieval Warming
abstract: A brief note that does nothing except discredit Broecker’s article from the same year, stating that some regions do not follow the MWP trend and that Broecker’s selection of admissible methodologies is unnecessarily restrictive. The note’s authors include Phil Jones and Michael Mann.

author: Bradley, Raymond S., Malcolm K. Hughes, and Henry F. Diaz
title: Climate in Medieval Time
abstract:
Takes issue with the claim that the MWP was as warm as the twentieth century, pointing out that this argument provides fodder for scepticism on anthropogenic global warming (AGW). States that Lamb first brought forward the idea of a MWP in his 1965 article (but see here). Lamb’s work predates the quantitative era of palaeoclimatology which relies on a calibration of proxies against the instrumental record; instead, he relied on documentary evidence compared against Western European proxy data, never suggesting global validity. He compared his findings with the instrumental record from 1900 to 1939. Since Lamb, a lot of work has been done but well-calibrated data sets are available for about a dozen locations only, which still share a bit of a bias for the northerly parts of the northern hemisphere. Some only provide data for a certain season. These limitations make it hard to infer whether the MWP was global.

Northern hemisphere data suggest that 1000/1100–1200 temperatures were almost identical to, or 0.03C cooler than, temperatures from 1901 to 1970, which in turn were cooler than those of the three decades following it.

Recent modelling demonstrates that an increase in solar irradiation does not lead to warming in all regions; a possibility is that Arctic Oscillation changed during the MWP, heating northern and western Europe but not other regions. 1100–1260 was also a time of heightened volcanic activity, which would have led to mild winters. The period also witnessed droughts in some regions, suggesting that temperature was not the only defining variable of the anomaly. It may be that circulation patterns are the explanation for the medieval climatic anomaly; with today’s larger population, a repeat of such an anomaly might be catastrophic.

“The balance of evidence does not point to a High Medieval period that was as warm as or warmer than the late 20th century” — but more work needs to be done to determine the causes of historical climatic fluctuations.

author: Cronin, T.M., et al.
title: Medieval Warm Period, Little Ice Age and 20th Century Temperature Variability from Chesapeake Bay
abstract: The consensus is that current North Atlantic mean temperatures exceed those of the Medieval Warm Period (17). Current temperature variability has, however, not yet been studied in relation to thermohaline circulation (17-18). This article presents “a 2200-year palaeoclimate record of sea-surface temperature in Chesapeake Bay,” an ideal region for research because of various reasons (18). Instrument measuring existing since 1949 has been used, and the Mg/Ca proxy method, measuring these elements in fossil shells, which reflect sea surface temperature, was used as a palaeothermometer (19-20). Large temperature shifts are found about 100 BCE, 400, 1050, 1350, 1600, and 1850 CE. Both the Little Ice Age and the Medieval Warm Period are bipartite: the latter had a cooling period about 1000-1100 (23). Mean twentieth-century temperatures were warmer than those of the late Medieval Warm Period (1000-1300) but not warmer than those of the early Medieval Warm Period (450-900) (24). These data support other late Holocene oceanic evidence for centennial-scale events throughout the North Atlantic (24-6). [Note that some extremes may signal early or late shell secretion due to unexplained causes, 26.] Rapid regional warming about 1800 CE, so before the industrial revolution, was accompanied with rising sea levels that may be explained by thermohaline circulation, solar and volcanic activity (26). These last two alone cannot explain Holocene temperature variability, since they account for < +0.2 and -0.5 degrees difference respectively. On the other hand, long-term solar activity has been argued as a cause for these events (27). Atmospheric forcing related to North Atlantic Oscillation has also been named as a cause (27). Twentieth-century warming is relativized by reference to the early Warm Medieval Period, but the Chesapeak Bay evidence does suggest greater extremes in the recent period than in the early Medieval Warm Period. Modelling studies suggest that these may be partly anthropogenic. This factor complicates climate predictions (27-8).

author: Amorosi, Thomas, et al.
title: Raiding the Landscape: Human Impact in the Scandinavian North Atlantic
abstract: Reviews a model that derives human impact evidence from archaeology, literature, and geology in North Atlantic islands. Argues that islands are effective as laboratories because their natural boundaries reduce causal complexity (493).
