The settlers brought domestic animal and some cereal cultivation, coupled with opportunistic use of wild resources (493-4). From the twelfth century onwards, there was an increase in Church buildings and, presumably, economic power; this new activity created a huge demand for imported materials (494-5). Some Early Norse insular economies centered around architecture and artefact assemblages but shifted towards a different pattern after 1150. The Late Norse market entailed more import, elaborate fishing technology, locally-produced pottery, and unclear changes in butchery. In Greenland, fishbone evidence remains rare; but there seems to have been an increase in walrus hunting. In Iceland, commercial fishing did not exist on any scale before the fourteenth century (495). The western pasture plant communities (Greenland, Iceland) were far more taxing for their environment than the eastern islands, both because settled agricultural techniques were adopted later in the west and because the transplantation of eastern methods proved unexpectedly taxing for the western soil. Both Iceland and Greenland experienced severe erosion from the time of settlement. Neither of these ecosystems will have been stable at the point of their arrival, but human impact after settlement no doubt “caused some of the greatest disturbances to flora and soils since the end of the Pleistocene” (495-6). The North Atlantic climate system can change rapidly in temperature and circulation. Even the Medieval Warm Period was interspersed with colder periods. The first four centuries of Icelandic settlement saw glacier expansion. This climate change seems to have had little impact on socio-economic centres (496-7). The Medieval Warm Period had turned into the Little Ice Age by 1420, the biggest and most abrupt transition in 6000 years. Crop seasons shortened and caused stress in Iceland, while Greenland will have suffered dearer consequences; in both settlements, human impact and climatic change will have formed a synergy (497-8). The late medieval and early modern periods brought modest prosperity and a stable or growing population for the eastern settlements, but extinction or deterioration to the west. A cross-theoretical approach may tell us why eastern methods did not work in the west and why the western settlers did not adapt (498). Southern Icelandic soil erosion of the past 1100 years has been measured using “spatial variation among sediment accumulation.” Erosion takes a flight just above the settlement layer [which is dated at 900 CE]. Between 900 and 1510, the increase is marked, first in higher elevations and then moving downwards. In ecological centre areas, the gradual breaching of vegetation cover, one type after the other, is probably a cause. Greenland suffered major erosion pre-1310, and Greenlandic agriculture seems to have spiralled downwards (499). Grazing must have greatly affected vegetation. Pig bones are found mostly from the early period; pig-keeping may have become difficult due to devegetation. Charcoal layers indicate that fire clearance was common in the settlement period (499-501). Native vegetation was rapidly destroyed, and new insects and invertebrates were introduced, partly through eutrophication by dung and waste (501-2). Remains of vertebrate animals at Icelandic digs indicate a high percentage of cattle, few caprines, and fewest pigs. Fish bones are rare, but birds very common. There are indications that walrus was hunted in the early period especially. In the Commonwealth period, caprines become much more common than cattle (502-3). In the late medieval and early modern periods, fish becomes more important around the country (503-4). Non-anthropogenic factors also contributed to landscape flux (504). It may be too simplistic to point to climate change as causing the above changes. Strategy may be involved: human feuding, for example, may lead to overuse of “safe” pastures. Politics, too, are involved (506-7). Consequences of the settlement: (1) natural capital depletion: on settlement, resources seemed more than they were because they had not been in use; (2) synergistic interactions: the onset of the Little Ice Age intensified the consequences of human activity; (3) intensification and technology: especially trade and fishery, the latter of which has been essential for Icelandic survival but has overdrawn natural resources (509). It is concluded that secluded locations often force people into particular types of resource use, but not in predictable ways. Aggressive, conservative methods have characterized North Atlantic usage of resources (511). Human perception and (rapidly changing) climate were disparate. Important are (1) the founder effect: a pioneer’s error grows over time; scale effects: the “size” of a location depends on one’s perspective (whale hunter or farmer); (3) circumspection: resource distribution and small scale should be studied in relation to the causes of warfare; (4) equilibrium or extinction: observations on lasting equilibrium versus slash-and-burn culture are important in view of island models of earth. No such long-term equilibria are found in the North Atlantic (511-13).

author: Bell, Martin, and Michael J.C. Walker
title: Late Quaternary Environmental Perspectives
abstract:
NB this summary refers to the first edition; a second edition appeared in 2005 under the title Late Quaternary Environmental Change.

[passages relevant to the North Atlantic]

The Little Optimum and Little Ice Age are discussed using Greenland, Iceland, Norway, the British upland, and the European lowlands, in that order (140-6). “Environmental degradation caused by Norse activity may have been a further contributory factor” to the extinction of the Norse settlements in Greenland. Twentieth-century overgrazing led to erosion and sand blows; sand blows have also been attested for the Norse period. The cold resulted in fewer seals, and the snow in fewer caribou. Concerning one West Settlement farm it was concluded that hunting dogs and dairy cattle were slaughtered in its last inhabited days. Greenland is “the only example of a developed European society which (so far!) has been extinguished. Given the marginal nature of the area there can be little doubt that the main factor that put the Norse settlers under stress was the climatic downturn of the Little Ice Age, which on the Crête oxygen isotope timescale. . . began rather earlier here than in Europe” (142). Reports on Icelandic climate were worst in the eighteenth century. Abandonment of the island was considered. Volcanic eruptions were also to blame for eighteenth-century hardship. Volcanism and climatic change are hard to separate due to interaction, considering the fact that many glaciers are located on volcanoes (142-3). The cod war was triggered by lower catches resulting from lower temperatures in the 1960s (143). The glacier advance in Norway in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries resulted in a decline in prosperity, as evidenced in tax reductions (143-4). In the European lowlands, the Little Optimum resulted in vineyards moving 3 to 5 degrees further north than today, and 100-200 metres higher up. The Domesday Book (1086) counts 38 vineyards in southern England. A fourteenth-century decline in vine-growing north of Paris has been explained by other economic factors than climate. However, fifteenth-century vine harvests also correlate with glacier movements. Lowland desertions in Britain began before the arrival of the plague in 1348 (146). Clearance in Scandinavia as a whole underwent four phases of “broadly synchronous agricultural expansion,” though Denmark and Scania witness earlier clearance than “other parts of southern Sweden and Norway” (164-5). “Blanket bog formation” in Norway and the Pennines was triggered by clearance (174-7).

author: Bradley, Ray
title: 1000 Years of Climate Change
abstract: Plays down scope and significance of the Medieval Warm Period and, to some extent, of the Little Ice Age, emphasising that no research is going to deny that the late twentieth century was warmer than any period in the past millennium.

author: Kremenetski, K.V., et al.
title: Medieval Climate Warming and Aridity as Indicated by Multiproxy Evidence from the Kola Peninsula, Russia
abstract: The Medieval Warm Period (ca. 700-ca. 1300) is confirmed by pine and avalanche evidence on the Kola Peninsula in northwestern Russia. 600-1300, but especially 1000-1200, was exceptionally warm and dry here. Submerged tree stumps further indicate that the water level was ~1m lower about AD 1000 than it is now. The Medieval Warm Period is not attested all over the northern hemisphere, but in most parts of Continental Europe, Asia, and Fennoscandia. This article seeks to answer the question of decreased humidity and its causes in the period (114.)

author: Lamb, Hubert H.
title: Northern Europe: The Last Thousand Years
publication: Weather, Climate and Human Affairs: A Book of Essays and Other Papers
abstract: Notes that historians have been reluctant to accept climate as a factor in and part of history, noting especially the fate of the Norse Greenlanders (27). Refers to botany, radiocarbon dating, tree rings, and varve chronology, pollen analysis, cultivation records, glaciers, and medieval literature as sources of climatological information about the past (28). Claims that the ocean surface between Iceland and the Faerao Islands was some five degrees below the 1870-1970 average at the climax of the Little Ice Age in 1675-1704. A millennial-scope oscillation in air temperature has been found for the past four millennia (30). Rainfall corresponds to temperature variations, with a wetter Medieval Warm Period and a dryer Little Ice Age, here illustrated with northern English evidence (30-1). Duration of growing season, frost, and snow cover will have been affected by temperature variability; and accumulating summer warmth was an additional factor on human affairs (32-3). Man will have suffered the greatest consequences in the margin of the inhabitable world, the north [i.e., both polar regions] being one such margin (33). While the Norse Greenlanders did not adopt an Inuit lifestyle, they were themselves skilled hunters and may have had little to learn from the Inuit. Additonally, once high death rate set in, their morale may have been too low to permit drastic changes of lifestyle. Also, the Inuit moved closer as their northern hunting-grounds froze over. Crowding may have resulted. Likelier is the arrival of an epidemic (34-5). Cultural achievement and trade peaks have tended to co-occur with high temperatures. In Contintental Scandinavia, abandonment of villages occurred in the severest winters. The cultural capital of Scandinavia moved south from Trondheim to Bergen-Oslo and later away from the ocean to Copenhagen and Stockholm during the Little Ice Age; Norway and Scotland lost their independence. The Baltic herring moved south in the sixteenth century, and promptly England and the Netherlands prospered. Contrary developments also occurred, such as Norway’s seventeenth- and eighteenth-century seafaring activity, but this is explained by the decline in Norwegian fishery. Icelandic life was at a low (35-7). Interesting bibliography on various methods of dating (38-9).

author: Markús Á. Einarsson
title: Veðurfar á Íslandi
abstract:
[from chapter 4: Loftslag fyrri tíma]

Past climate is measured by (1) tephrachronology, (2) documentary evidence, and (3) the record since 1845 (52). Iceland is a young formation. While the Tertiary was warm, averaging 15-20 degrees in summers and 10-15 in winters, air temperatures in the last glacial period will have been 5 to 10 degrees below today’s (52-3). The main prehistoric fluctuations in temperature are summarised (53-5). Documentary evidence suggests that there were birch forests at the first settlement, and grains were initially grown in Iceland (55). The annal and documentary history is summarised (55-6). Hannes Finsson published a work in 1796 documenting past climatic extremes, in order to prove those wrong who believed that Iceland had never known such extremes as in their day (56). Þorvaldur Thoroddsen in 1916-17 described the climate of the past millennium and aims to describe all known conditions, not just the extremes. He wrote on annal evidence and sea ice. As Þórhallur Vilmundarson wrote in 1969, Þorvaldur has no critical attitude towards his sources and he does not differentiate between them. Þorvaldur compiled a list of good, medium, and bad years (reproduced on p. 58) (56-8). Sigurður Þórarinsson in 1969 published on temperature since the settlement. Settlement temperatures were close to those of 1920-64. A cooling set in about 1200. 1300 was a low, after which there was a slight warming. After 1500, the climate again began to cool down, and this cooling period lasted into the nineteenth century (58-9). Páll Bergþórsson (1967, 1969) has attempted to establish a connection between temperatures and sea ice. He concluded that despite inaccuracies, the general picture of Þorvaldur Thoroddsen’s publication was correct (59-60).

author: Rotton, James, and Ellen G. Cohn
title: Climate, Weather, and Crime
eds: Robert B. Bechtel and Arza Churchman
abstract: The chapter opens with various rebuttals of studies connecting first climate and crime, then weather and crime. However, the authors assert that there certainly is something to correlations of this sort. Seasonal differences in delinquency exist (reference is made to Quetelet’s thermic law of delinquency: more violence in summer, more property crime in winter, although the latter element does not work for the US: 486‒7), but these correlations cannot be linked to meteorological variables (486‒7; a good deal of references to studies in the field). One set of laboratory experiments on the effects of heat on violence has led to the negative affect escape model, which states that moderate departures from the comfortable range (hotter or colder) increase violence, but strong departures lessen it; however, other experiments have claimed that heat and cold lead to aggression in a linear fashion (general affective aggression model, 487‒8). Studies outside the laboratory have failed to confirm either model, suggesting that weather has no great impact on mood and this relationship is far smaller than normally supposed (488‒9). Durkheim (1897/1951) posited that pleasant spring weather increases social interaction, which paradoxically leads to higher suicide rates (489‒90). Derivative theories have proposed that weather favouring interpersonal contact in the absence of parents/guardiands induces crime (routine activity theory) and that victims are more likely to stray into dangerous areas in pleasant weather (490). Real-life observations seem to confirm a combination of the negative escape model and routine activity theory (490‒1). All things considered, however, the evidence seems decidedly weak.

author: Smith, Kate T., and Andrew J. Dugmore
title: Jökulhlaups Circa Landnám: Mid- to Late First Millennium AD Floods in South Iceland and their Implications for Landscapes of Settlement
abstract: Presents three jökulhlaup in the Markarfljót valley AD 500-900. Tephrachronology and radiocarbon dating are the main methods used to date them to about 500, 700, 900; they were primarily caused by interaction between the volcano Katla and the glacier Torfajökull (168-172). Jökulhlaup will have resulted in devegetated sandur (outwash) areas and increased landscape vulnerability (173-4).

author: Þorvaldur Thoroddsen
title: Árferði á Íslandi í þúsund ár
abstract: Consists of a compilation of documentary remarks on weather (15-354) and sea ice (355-432), compounded with own clarifications and remarks per year as well as a short conclusion at the end of the former section (349-54) and introductions to both. Iceland’s location in the periphery of the inhabited world makes climate a very influential factor on society’s success. This book is intended as an introduction or a reference work for those who want to study documentary sources. The study of medieval climate helps understand the situation of the common people (349). While the climate of Iceland has not undergone any significant changes since the settlement, the Icelanders will not learn from their past to be prepared for the future (350). When extreme conditions co-occurred with important historical events, the weather conditions are often better remembered as the background against which the events took place (351).

author: Crowley, Thomas J., and Thomas S. Lowery
title: How Warm Was the Medieval Warm Period?
abstract: A synthesis of proxy records suggests that the MWP had two peaks of 20–30 years each, which on a hemispherical scale were comparable to mid-twentieth century temperature levels, although regional peaks may be found that transcend present-day levels. Emphasises the importance of using composite studies because they offset local anomalies.

author: Mann, Michael E., et al.
title: Proxy-Based Reconstructions of Hemispheric and Global Surface Temperature Variations Over the Past Two Millennia
abstract: Multiproxy evidence of northern hemispheric and global scope suggests that current warming is unprecedented in at least the past 1300 years, or 1700 years if treering data are used. The MWP was a period of “somewhat greater […] warmth in the Northern Hemisphere, albeit still not reaching recent levels” (abstract).

author: Klaeber, F.
title: Die Altere Genesis und der Beowulf
abstract: Only of semantic interest.

author: Klinck, Anne L.
title: Female Characterisation in Old English Poetry and the Growth of Psychological Realism: Genesis B and Christ I
abstract: Because heroic poetry with an emphasis on male society is the standard in OE, female narratives are particularly interesting. Women stand out most in the narratives in which they are markedly passive: WfL, WaE, Bwf; but this is carried even further in the temptation of Gen B and in Christ I (597). Gen B is more vivid than Gen A, and it is fair to say that the Anglo-Saxon poet did more than just translate (598). The heterodox treatment of the Fall is not without precedent, but the poet has handled them with great imagination; this presentation is explained by his aim to heighten the tragedy of Adam. One of the ways to reach this is to make Eve sin in ignorance; and this treatment shows the greatest subtlety and skill (599). Eve receives “a special sympathy” (600-1). Eve is a parallel with Desdemona (601). The conversation between Joseph and Mary in division 7 of Christ I is discussed (601-5). When these episodes are compared with the rest of the corpus, it is recognised that “the female character is confined and restricted”; this foregrounds and heightens their psychological significance. This emphasis stands out most in Gen B and Christ I, which suggests a chronological development (605-7).

author: Lohse, B.
title: Zu Augustins Engellehre
abstract: The author attempts to answer the question what sources Augustine may have used to arrive at his doctrine that the fallen angels were to be replaced by men (278). He begins by summarising Augustine’s own elaborations on the subject. He first began to develop his doctrine of the heavenly civitas in De Catechizandis Rudibus (400); but this work tells little of angels or the Ersatzgedanken. De Genesi ad Litteram (after 401) first mentions the creation of the angels within Genesis 1.1, but no more. (DGAL 1.9; 278). It also tells of the angels’ function as mediators between heaven and earth; Augustine does not return to this function in his later works. De Civitate Dei first introduces the replacement doctrine, suggesting that the final count might even surpass the original (DCD 22.1). The same thought is found in the Enchiridion (9.29; 279). Concerning the light of Genesis 1 Augustine entertains a range of speculations, amongst which a lux corporea or the civitas of angels. Concerning the creation of the angels he appears to change his mind a number of times, but he believes that they were created within the six-day period of creation, because nothing happened before the in principio, nor did God create anything on the seventh day. He shows the angels to be God’s work by reference to Scripture and secondary authors; and the angels must have been created before their song at the creation of the starts on the fourth day. The second and third days, however, are out of the question because significantly different creations are treated. Therefore, it is understood that in the light created on the first day “creatio intellegitur angelorum” (280-1). In the same section he writes that the angels have been created by or by means of the light, and have now become light themselves (DCD 11.9). Shortly afterwards he writes they have been created as light (DCD 11.11); and finally he comes to the doctrine that the separation of light and darkness is that between the loyal and the fallen angels (DCD 11.19). In 11.32 he concedes that other views are possible, including the one in which the angels are created before Genesis 1.1, interpreting in principio as referring not to history but to the written record. Yet he reiterates in 11.33 that no-one can deny that part of the angels are referred to as light, and he makes reference to Ephesians 5.8 (281). The doctrinal points of the replacement, the identification of the light with the angels, the civitas-theory and the separation of the angels in Genesis 1.4 are interrelated and can be deduced from one another (282). In his search for sources, Lohse finds that Enoch the Ethiopian’s doctrine concerning the fall of the angels has for a time influenced the West, so that this may have been a source for Augustine (283). In Jewish tradition, he finds that there are three traditions, respectively before man, on the first day, and on the second day. In Christian tradition he finds two traditions, namely one beginning with Origen (Basilius, Gregor of Nazians, Ambrose, Cassian) stating that the angels were created before the week of creation, and that of Epiphanius holding that they were not created before the world (284-7). Returning to the replacement doctrine, Lohse supposes a connection with Mark 12.25, stating that the resurrected will be like the angels in heaven. The missing link in the chain consists in a fixed number of angels that has to be restored. Hilarius of Poitiers goes some length along with this, but not entirely and not unambiguously; Ambrose has developed something of a civitas-concept but he too did not share this aspect with Augustine (287-90). Significant parallels are further found in the footnotes to page 287, concerning the fixed number of angels (an analogue in Enoch in Psalm 39.10) and the desire of the fallen to reclaim their places. A final question Lohse asks is whether Neoplatonism or Manichaism may have influenced Augustine’s doctrine; the answer to the first is a categorical no, but the Manichees may have had some limited influence (290-1). The general point of doctrine, however, is Augustinian; he will have drawn upon sources of the Church Fathers and the Manichees to form other aspects of his angelology. Finally, Augustine’s doctrine of replacement is a precondition for his doctrine of predestination.

author: McKill, Larry N.
title: Patterns of the Fall: Adam and Eve in the Old English Genesis A
abstract: Huppé claims that Genesis A is essentially symbolic and founded on principles set forth in Augustine's De Doctrina Christiana. McKill, as well as Boyd, argues that this approach distorts the poem's central themes. McKill argues that the poem has been carefully structured in accordance with the poet's objectives, especially by drawing a contrast between the loyal and God's enemies. Men and angels receive rewards reminiscent of a thegn's. The poet uses heroic vocabulary to recreate a “perfect social order” (25-8). The two creations of angels and men are linked by parallel diction while the lair of the fallen angels takes a shape quite the opposite (28-9). Battle imagery is used in the war in heaven (31-2). Exile imagery is used to describe the formless earth (32-3) and the human couple as it is exiled from Eden (33-4). God describes himself in lines 873-5 as one who has given only good things [cf. Shippey 153] (34). Eve's speech makes use of the vocabulary of battle (35). The doom of the serpent especially reflects exile (36).

author: Mintz, Susannah B.
title: Words Devilish and Divine: Eve as Speaker in Genesis B
abstract: “This essay argues that the Old English Genesis B is textured by a linguistic density that allows conflicting ideological concerns to come into play simultaneously, resulting in a re-evaluation of the deeply masculinist Christian hierarchy that lies at the heart of the Fall story. This perspective explicitly challenges a traditional symbolism that limits Eve to the ‘senses’ and privileges Adam as ‘reason,’ and counters the many analyses of Genesis B that uphold such categories, perpetuating a characterization of Eve as weak, innately sinful, and inferior to Adam. What has often been noticed as the psychological realism of the poem applies not only to its portrayal of the anguish of choice, but works as well to dismantle static, deeply gendered interpretations. By reading closely what seem to be the poet’s deliberate efforts to juxtapose ‘thick,’ ambiguous verbal situations with speeches of simplicity and clarity spoken by Eve, I suggest that Eve emerges here as a woman of intelligence and personal responsibility, one who demonstrates both honesty and intellectual and spiritual freedom (Abstract, 609).” Genesis B foregrounds “the indeterminacy of linguistic signification”(612). The tempter remains “full neah,” which suggests Eve could not have tempted Adam on her own (615). Language and narrative preclude a clear analogy between Eve and the tempter (616-7). Adam is portrayed as “the fretful one”; Cherniss compares Adam to Satan as retainer figures (619).

author: Murdoch, Brian
title: Adam’s Grace: Fall and Redemption in Medieval Literature
abstract: Discusses the literary afterlives of Adam and Eve with regard to apocryphal literature, Gregory the Great, Parzival, and medieval drama. Mentions the malum-mālum-vermis connotations of evil (2).

author: Murdoch, Brian
title: The Fall of Man: A Middle High German Analogue of Genesis B
abstract: The concepts of the diabolical council and the satanic subordinate tempter appear in the twelfth-century Anagenge. Direct influence from Genesis B is highly unlikely. A common source is expected. The Evangelium Nicodemi may have influenced both, as it contains the decensus Christi motif which has been suggested as a source for the sending of a subordinate in Genesis B. However, the Anegenge passage seems to be a mere repetition of familiar motifs. A non-extant text may be the solution.

author: Ohlgren, Thomas H.
title: Visual Language in the Old English Cædmonian Genesis
abstract: The Genesis artist, living centuries after the first conception of the translation, depended in part on his own interpretation of the poem. As such, poem and illustrations are not in all respects unified (256). Correlations between text and image can be divided into three: (1) a close visual approximation of the text, in which only orthodox material appears so that the artist may copy accepted models; (2) a close correspondence but unorthodox contents, so that the artist has to resort to non-biblical models or his imagination; (3) a correspondence plus additional details that help the understanding of the text. The frontispiece, for instance, draws the scene with a focus towards the Apocalypse, reminding the reader that salvation history is poised towards that same event (257-62). The cycle of images can be read as a narrative of its own (263). In analogy with Dorfman's concept of 'narremes,' being important episodes serving as the central focus of a larger episode, one may speak of 'iconographemes' in Genesis: all images have a structuring function (264). The frontispiece displays the peace in heaven before Lucifer's rebellion, which is the first episode (265). The transformations of Lucifer and his messenger angel are pointed out (259,269,272), as are contrasts between Christ and Lucifer and the holy and damned angels (270-1). The illustrator uses two colours of ink for the sake of contrast (274-5).

author: Pang-White, Ann A.
title: The Fall of Humanity: Weakness of the Will and Moral Responsibility in the Later Augustine
abstract: Aristotle in his Nichomachean Ethics holds that some individuals are akratic—subject to weakness of the will in the face of better judgement—some of the time; the later Augustine believes that all of us suffer this affliction constantly; and, moreover, that this is not limited to one or a few areas of life (51-2). Augustine defines concupiscentia as “those inordinate desires that are not controllable by the mind without grace” (54; emphasis Pang-White). It appears in three guises: inherited guilt; inherited defect; and inherited defect with consent (54). Inherited guilt is removed by baptism, but the resulting defect remains in the shape of a weakness towards sin (55-6). The struggle to withhold consent is life-long and governs all (56). Sin is committed by all on a daily basis; but sin without consent makes one “without reproach” (57-8). Akrasia is, in Augustine's understanding, both ontological (merely referring to the fallen nature of man) and descriptive of action (sinning, with or without reluctance and with or without faith, 63). Augustine's definition of weakness of the will: “the moral state of an agent in which concupiscence or one's consent to concupiscence is present” (63). The remaining pages study consequences of these findings.

author: Priebsch, R.
title: The Heliand Manuscript Cotton Caligula A. VII in the British Museum: A Study
abstract: A paleographical study of the MS leads to two possible conclusions regarding its authorship: the scribe was either an Anglo-Saxon educated on the Continent in a tradition of slightly German minuscule, or he was a Continental who lived in Britain as a monk or clerk (28-9). Especial attention is paid to a certain ligature in the MS that is characteristic for Winchester and Canterbury (21-7). Decorated initials are (1) zoomorphic, in which shape they closely resemble those of Junius 11; (2) leaf ornaments; and (3) “angular and knotty bandwork” (31). The latter two elements are characteristic for tenth and eleventh-century Southern England;. All characteristics are found in the Aldhelm MS, Royal 7D xxiv, possibly from Christ Church, Canterbury. The Junius 11 decorative work is judged far superior to that in the Heliand MS (32). “Thus on ornamental, paleographical, and even—in view of certain word-forms—linguistic grounds, the evidence would seem to point to England as the home of the MS. of Heliand C” (35). A joint history of the Heliand and the OS Genesis is suggested (37-9). Genesis B was probably produced in Winchester or Christ Church, Canterbury, in the tenth century (40-1). Without argumentation it is thought more likely that Genesis B was interpolated into Genesis A for aesthetic reasons than because the scribe's source was incomplete (36-7,41). It is suggested that the Heliand copyist may have advised “the Genesis translator” (41-2). A speculation follows about a historical person who might fit this picture; but it is stressed that he would not himself have written Genesis B (42-7).

author: Pulsiano, Phillip
title: The Sea of Life and the Ending of Christ II
abstract: Considers the seafaring metaphor at the end of Christ II, suggesting that it constitutes a combination of the spoken-word-as-religious-medium topos and the world of conceptual signs: where traditionally the spoken word does the work, here the poet uses a ship as the conveyor of knowledge (esp. 6). Riddle 32 fulfils a similar function, playing on the double entendre of ship and pen (6–7). In Guthlac B, the disciple’s ship-journey across the fen may be understood in similar terms inasmuch as the disciple is the only one to have witnessed the saint’s miracles, and so the ship’s journey again constitutes the spread of knowledge (8–10).

author: Salmon, Paul
title: The Site of Lucifer's Throne
abstract: In accordance with Isaiah 14.13, Genesis A 32-4, as well as Piers Plowman (B I.116-118; C II.110-114), the Vorau Genesis and the Altdeutsche Genesis state that Lucifer intends to build his throne in the north. Genesis B holds that it is in the northwest (118). The Isaiah context probably refers to Nebuchadnezzar; this passage is the justification for the Lucifer=the devil identification. The association of the north with barren climates reinforces the link, as does the harsh nature of northern winds (119-20). There is no patristic support for locating the throne anywhere but in the north. The aquilo of the Vulgate, however, is actually northeast; so technically, all 'north' references are wrong. The northwest of Genesis B is actually 10 o'clock, versus 5 o'clock for southeast; these are not diametrically opposed. “It seems hardly likely, however, that such a system should be rigidly applied to a work of the imagination.” This also goes for King Alfred's Orosius in which the northeast is called the north (120). Lactantius associates north with west, south with east “more closely than any other”--but is unlikely to be a direct source. It provides a moral reading of the directions. Isidore does something like that, but less pronouncedly (121). Augustine relates the movements of the sun with moral events such as the fall of the devil and pride. From Hrabanus Maurus's De Universo and Gregory the Great, Salmon concludes that it was held that Lucifer is “not inevitably a portent of evil”--“evil is to be associated only with [the] setting [of the star Lucifer],” which occurs in the west. Jerome suggests that the west has been stained by Lucifer's sin (122). The same passage associates the north with cold and evil, and cites the relevant Isaiah and Luke passages. It is the closest thing to a source, with some reserves. Lactantius has a slight preference as a source (123).

author: Shippey, T.A.
title: Poetry and the Bible: The Junius Manuscript
abstract: While scholars like Ælfric were reluctant to pass the Bible text on to the unlearned, the roughly contemporaneous MS Junius 11 seems to have been written with no such hesitations. Critics have argued that the poems possess a certain worthiness through hidden layers of meaning. Whereas the Noah flashback in Exodus may have been inserted because of its thematic parallel of a flood overcoming the wicked, the continuation to Abraham and Isaac seems out of place. A solution may lie in biblical commentary: Augustine had listed these three events as prefigurations of the Church (134-6). A similar argument is used for the entire Junius 11 MS: the narrative as told in the supposed 'Liber I' corresponds with certain rituals for Holy Saturday. Problematic for this figurative reading is that the poets could not always distance themselves from the inherited style that comes with Old English verse (137). The 'parting of the waters' episode is most obvious: whereas Moses is seen giving a proud speech, the actual miracle is performed off-stage, reminiscent of the transition from defeat to victory in the Finnsburg Episode (138-9). The figural school is indifferent to individual events and motives and sees only the represented; Genesis, Exodus and Daniel do not fit this pattern. The Exodus flashback to explain the motives of the Egyptians shows a dependence on the theme of trial and proof, keeping to an agreement; and so does the Noah flashback, and the story of Abraham and Isaac (140-1). The Exodus-poet shows a familiarity with allegory, but his attempts are confused by his “compression of traditional language.” Daniel's uninterpreted visions have attracted many commentators, but the Daniel poet does not touch them (143). Daniel has severe narrative problems, such as the suddenly changing attitudes of Nebuchadnezzar. The OE poet uses his creativity to explain these problems, in the first place by omitting problematic sections (he even denies the food episode, 144). A feet-of-clay interpretation is absent, “one feels, in order to subordinate this minor climax to later and major ones” (145). It is remarked that the Genesis B interpolation must be a result of eighth-century missionary activity (147). As this poem deals with the Fall of the Angels and that of Man, whose narratives have to a great extent been read into the Bible, the poet has to reconcile orthodoxy and heresy. It is technically clearly inferior to its older counterpart, which observation should warn us not to think too highly of the poet's capabilities (148). The fall of Man is not caused by “baser instincts—gluttony, avarice, lust, pride, or the other sins so often seen by medieval commentators in the act of eating the fruit—but by a deception addressed to their sense of duty. . . . Eve accepts it, partly under threat of punishment. The poet stresses her good intentions as she urges the fruit on Adam. . . .” The suggestion is that someone else is to blame; Satan mostly, but God's passive attitude is wondered at by the poet. Significantly, he denies that the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was beautiful and good in any sense; in so doing, he also denies Augustine's view “that God created nothing intrinsically evil. . . . He makes the Fall of Man into a familiar situation, a feud begun with every excuse and every warning, but one whose consequences are, just the same, inescapable” (151-2). Alcuin of York surprisingly copies the opposition of the trees created here, though Ælfric edits it out of his translation of Alcuin's work. The “nature of vernacular narrative” must have had a greater influence on the first three Junius poems than learned traditions. Christ and Satan is concerned with establishing thematic connections between several biblical events, whereas the other Junius poems are more descriptive in nature and are therefore resistant to allegorical readings (153).

author: Sievers, Eduard
title: Der Heliand und die angelsächsische Genesis
abstract: Argues that Gen B is a translation or reworking of an Old Saxon original, which original was written by the author of the Heliand. There is a medieval reference to an OT work by that poet’s hand, and parallels of diction and formulas between the two render the hypothesis certain.

author: Stévanovitch, Colette
title: Envelope Patterns and the Unity of the Old English Christ and Satan
publication: Archiv für das Studium der neueren Sprachen und Literaturen
abstract: It is understandable that the unity of Christ and Satan has been doubted, but it is important to see that within its parts, the poem also lacks unity (260). It can be read as consisting of two parts, 365 lines each. The different use of envelope patterns distinguishes the two parts (262-3). This may be because they were by different hands; but perhaps there was only one poet who felt that envelope patterns suited the first part best (266).

author: Timmer, B.J.
title: The Later Genesis
abstract: Argues that Heliand and the Old Saxon Genesis were influenced by Anglo-Saxon influence on the Continent, and that “religious epics such as Andreas, Elene” were its models (55 et al). The heroic tradition and vocabulary is remarked on (55-6). The triumphant outcry at the time of victory is recognised as an element of heroic tradition, and parallels are mentioned (56-7). The heroic vocabulary and style are “not as essential in the poem as they are e.g. in Beowulf: they are clearly imitated” (57). The poet has a greater interest in Eve than in Adam (58). The use of contrasts is commented on (59). The use of an “ambassador” to tempt the human couple is parallelled in Juliana, which copies the concept from its source, the Acta Sanctae Julianae (47; see Strunk's ed. Of Juliana, p. 38).

author: Vickrey, John F.
title: The Vision of Eve in Genesis B
abstract: Vickrey catalogues the references to the vision (86). The dramatic irony is that Eve sees God sitting enthroned, which to her audience would be a clear reference to judgement (87). Eleven other works are listed in which the judgement motif features, plus homilies and the Heliand (88). A catalogue of NT references to God enthroned in relation to the second coming is given (89). The location of the throne, the southeast, is “a minor motif of the accounts of judgement”; it is in the northwest that Satan meant to build his throne (91-3). The poet’s apology of Eve was intended to earn her the grace of the audience not exoneration; as the poem stands, Adam receives no exoneration (96-99).

author: Woolf, Rosemary
title: The Fall of Man in Genesis B and the Mystère d’Adam
publication: Studies in Old English Literature in Honor of Arthur G. Brodeur
abstract: Rather than following the antithetical tradition of Eve and the Virgin Mary or that between the first temptation and that of Christ, the Gen B poet presents his narrative as a realistic study of how the fall occurred. There is only one other medieval source that takes this psychological approach, namely the Mystère d’Adam, which furthermore shares some of the poem’s heterodox features, namely Adam’s temptation and the unserpentine look of the tempter. Neither writer will have invented these aspects of the story; a common source is more likely (187-8). Gen B’s psychology has been distorted by modern critics like Gurteen, Ker, and Sievers, who have wrongly considered Eve without blame (189). Inconsistencies in the text show that the poet had the orthodox devil in mind but followed another source, with a devil in angelic disguise, in his dialogues; and the illustrator followed him in this understanding (190). The Mystère has the same inconsistency (190-1). It must derive from an apocryphal source based on 2 Cor 11.14, “[i]pse enim Satanas transfigurat se in angelum lucis”; the Vita Adae et Evae survives as an analogue in which the devil dresses up as an angel of light and successfully tempts Eve out of her penance. In this as in Juliana and Gen B, the tempter claims to come from God. Gregory has applied 2 Cor 11.14 to temptation by the devil. It is likely the Gen B poet knew this text (191-2). These parallels show that an angel-of-light tradition existed and that the tempter’s reference to God did not exonerate the victim. While the Mystère contains the eritis sicut dii, Gen B does not (192-3). The Mystère’s words to Eve “tu es plus sage [qu’Adam]” are, however, echoed in the tempter’s speech in Gen B (194-5). Eve’s subordination to Adam receives no stress before the temptation in the extant Gen B [PS: because the pre-temptation part is non-extant!] but was a well-known point of orthodoxy (195). Since every medieval reader would have understood the tempter’s speech to Eve as “an attempt to stir up pride,” “[i]t follows. . . that the devil’s disguise was not impenetrable, and that Eve listened with a willful credulity springing from nascent vanity.” The poet’s apology springs from his sympathy, not from Eve’s innocence (196). Eve’s persuasion of Adam “lacks dignity, and might almost be said to anticipate the nagging wife of Medieval literature” (197).

author: Jones, P.D., and M.E. Mann
title: Climate Over Past Millennia
abstract: The most cautious and balanced paper on past climate I have yet seen. Goes to some lengths to criticise the use of the terms and concepts MWP/LIA, pointing out regional differences (19–20). But its real function is to synthesise in great detail what we know of climate in the past two millennia.

author: Grove, Jean M.
title: Glacial Geological Evidence for the Medieval Warm Period
abstract: Judging by the moraines left behind by glacial advances (dated by way of radiocarbon dating), the period 900–1250/1300 was one of glacial retreat globally.

author: Virkkunen, K., et al.
title: Warm Summers and Ion Concentrations in Snow: Comparison of Present Day With Medieval Warm Epoch from Snow Pits and an Ice Core from Lomonosovfonna, Svalbard
abstract: Summer melting layers in Spitsbergen snow pits are compared to summer melting layers from a 1997 Spitsbergen ice core. The snow pits reach back ~800 years; significant melting years are found in the twentieth century, about 1750, “and all of the core from before AD 1200” [which seems a little useless since the record begins about 1200 and I can’t imagine the first few decades being reliable]. The early melting layers are attributed to warm MWP summers.

author: Cronin, T.M., et al.
title: The Medieval Climate Anomaly and Little Ice Age in Chesapeake Bay and the North Atlantic Ocean
abstract:
A 2400-year sediment core/foraminifera isotope study from Chesapeake Bay is compared to other North Atlantic records to determine variability in the MWP/LIA sequence. One of the cores shows

  • a cool period from 300 BCE to 400 CE;
  • the warmest period 850–900 or 600–50 depending on the age model used;
  • a gradual cooling after this warm period;
  • a cool interval 1000–1100
  • a maximum at 1200;
  • a sharp rise starting about 1750–1800.

After comparison, concludes that “warm surface water conditions occurred before the classic MWP in the western North Atlantic, and during or after the MWP in northeastern regions. Likewise, deep waters in the North Atlantic warmed both before and after the MWP. In addition, the inception of cooling that culminated in the LIA began earlier in the western North Atlantic (Chesapeake) than in eastern regions (Nordic Seas)”, matching divergences found in tree-ring and ocean records.

author: Dong, Xuhui, Helen Bennion, Richard W. Battarbee, and Carl D. Sayer
title: A Multiproxy Palaeolimnological Study of Climate and Nutrient Impacts on Esthwaite Water, England Over the Past 1200 Years
abstract: Confirms MWP/LIA for sediments in a lake in England. Has me a little unease because it cites Broecker. But the authors do provide evidence of a cooling 780–880, a warming 880–1350, and a cooling 1350–1880.

author: Sundqvist, Hanna S., et al.
title: Stable Isotopes in a Stalagmite from NW Sweden Document Environmental Changes Over the Past 4000 Years

author: Jansen, Eystein, et al.
title: Palaeoclimate
publication: Climate Change 2007: The Physical Science Basis. Contribution of Working Group I to the Fourth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change
abstract: The palaeoclimate chapter of the 2007 IPCC report. Box 6.4 on pp. 468–9 deals with the MWP, basically indicating that there was a mild northern hemispheric warm period about 950–1100, but not as warm as the 20th-century mean.

title: Population, Agriculture, and Famine: Iceland, 1784–1785

title: Iceland’s 1100 Years: History of a Marginal Society

title: Íslensk matarhefð

author: McGovern, Thomas H., et al.
title: Landscapes of Settlement in Northern Iceland: Historical Ecology of Human Impact and Climate Fluctuation on the Millennial Scale

author: Adderley, W. Paul, Ian A. Simpson, and Orri Vésteinsson
title: Local-Scale Adaptations: A Modeled Assessment of Soil, Landscape, Microclimatic, and Management Factors in Norse Home-Field Productivities
abstract: Medieval hay yields for three sites were at subsistence levels and were affected by climatic variation. Manuring a field yields the greatest effect during the first century of settlement, after which it becomes less pronounced.

title: Fiskveiðar Íslendinga 1874–1940: Lauslegt yfirlit

title: Soil Limitations to Agrarian Land Production in Premodern Iceland
abstract: Soil analysis at two sites in southwestern Iceland confirms that medieval grain production was at subsistence levels here.

author: Björn Þorsteinsson
title: Íslenzka þjóðveldið

eds: Tina L. Thurston and Christopher T. Fisher

author: Harvey, Barbara, and Jim Oeppen
title: Patterns of Morbidity in Late Medieval England: A Sample from Westminster Abbey
abstract: Seasonal morbidity among monks of fourteenth-century Westminster Abbey compared to seasonal patterns in early modern mortality.

author: Tille, Alexander
title: Yule and Christmas: Their Place in the Germanic Year

author: George, Michael W.
title: Gawain’s Struggle with Ecology: Attitudes Toward the Natural World in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
abstract:
Asserts that the difference in attitude to the nonhuman world shown by Gawain (dominance) and Bertilak (stewardship) demonstrates “that medieval thought on the place of the non-human world was a complex philosophical issue”. The article is helpful in establishing that contrast in attitudes. However, the author soon gets bogged down in a problematically narrow and ideological definition of ecocriticism and polemical defence of Lynn White, Jr's 1967 "Historical Roots of Our Ecological Crisis".

The article begins to be of use when it cites studies identifying Thomas Aquinas's world-view as strongly anthropocentric while Francis of Assisi's is one in which nature is closer to God than man and forms the human objective from which mankind is barred by sin. Critically, Assisi's view never became a dominant one in the Middle Ages (33–4).

The hostility of both the animals and the weather of the natural elements on Gawain's path is remarked on, while the landscape in which Hautdesert is situated is fair because cultivated. Thus an ideology is expressed that strictly separates man from the natural world (34–6). Gawain understands the natural world as a boundary between human settlements, an attitude that would naturally translate into the cutting down of forests (36–7). In this context, the Green Knight (and therefore Bertilak) takes on a significant symbolism: being all green, he represents the natural world, and his intrusion into Camelot represents a challenge by the natural world for Arthur to defeat it (37).

During the hunts, Bertilak shows a slightly different form of the hybrid nature–culture. In observing the hunting-season [though George does not express this as such, or reveal a knowledge of the system as described by Twiti et al], he hunts by way of stewardship rather than domination. This tension is explored, but the conclusion is that Gawain's attitude toward the natural world heightens the contrast while Bertilak's diminishes it (37–9).

author: Tolley, Clive
title: Shamanism in Norse Myth and Magic
abstract: Starts with a detailed and well-referenced explanation of the earliest known movements of the ethno-linguistic groups inhabiting Scandinavia in the Middle Ages, well worth consulting when dealing with early Germanic, Finnic, northwest-Slavic, or Sami peoples in any context (31–43). A detailed account is given of the reference of finnar and the distinction between Sami and Finns (39–43), followed by an index of references to finnar through the centuries, beginning with Tacitus (43–65). This chapter also contains a good overview of magic attributed to the Sami in Old Norse texts; Tolley also notes that this association is absent from Latin and Greek texts predating the mid-thirteenth century (61–4).

author: Pearsall, Derek
title: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight: An Essay in Enigma
abstract: One of those delightful, barely footnoted essays providing the sort of broad perspective only found in mature scholars. Purportedly on the meaning and significance of SGGK, the article never comes close to solving these questions but instead outlines a few difficulties with the plot development, including the role of the girdle, the confession, and whether Gawain takes the challenge seriously (both at Camelot and as he approaches the Green Chapel wearing his girdle) or is instead being a hypocrite looking to win praise in what he believes cannot go wrong. An essay well worth reading whenever a reinit of one’s understanding of Gawain studies is called for.

author: Schmidt, A.V.C.
title: ‘Latent Content’ and ‘The Testimony in the Text’: Symbolic Meaning in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
abstract:
Announces its aim to review the symbolic content in SGGK without reviving Derek Brewer’s notion of latent content (i.e. Freudian analysis). Discusses briefly the pentangle (147–8), then provides a detailed analysis of the girdle (148–51), concluding that while it is first introduced as a love token, it outgrows that symbol and becomes a token of self-love (151).

The cycle of the seasons described at length at the start of fitt 2 is a memento mori, winter symbolising death, a connection found as early as in Wdr (151–4).

The article now goes on to establish a theme of the ages of man in the poem, with Gawain and all Arthur’s court representing Youth and Bertilak representing Middle Age; the Green Knight is a rejuvenated form of Bertilak, representing Youth (154–9).

Satanic aspects of the Green Knight are considered. He is identified as the sort of Satan found in Job, serving as an instrument through which God tests Gawain (160–5).

An important undercurrent in the article is that it “argu[es] for the primacy of the moral, religious, and theological dimensions of the poem over the psychological and the anthropological” (165).

author: Spearing, A.C.
title: Dream Poems
abstract:
Warns against overestimating Chaucer’s own learning and that of his audience in particular. Often when Chaucer claims to be dealing with Latin tradition he can be shown to rely on a French intermediary instead (160–2).

Chaucer was more widely read in French literature than in English, Italian, or Latin; many French sources remain to be identified, and when relying on these sources he typically did not expect his audience to pick up on the reference (162–3; cf. Boitani).

It is important to recognise that natural explanations for dreams were prominent in Chaucer’s day alongside supernatural explanations. An example of this is found in Dives and Pauper, but Chaucer himself shows an awareness of the importance of natural causes as well, treating as he does dreams as an area of natural philosophy (163–7).

The recent emphasis on medieval dreams as vehicles of reflection “on the nature and devices of art” has tended to neglect the dream experience as a construct providing a freedom of composition not normally mandated: literature was about repeating authoritative narratives, not about inventing new ones altogether. The dream allowed exemption from this convention. Our failure to recognise this follows both from the fact that freedom of composition is today a given and from the study of literary sources having become fossilised to the degree that the resulting texts may seem inevitably determined by their sources. [The freedom of composition is next recognised to be limited by convention as well, in a paragraph confusingly introduced by “moreover”; the idea must be that this limit to literary freedom today somehow limits our appreciation of the freedom offered by the literary dream in much the same way as does the relative negation of those limits.] The incoherence of actual dreams is noted in relation to the fact that Chaucer’s dream-visions often end abruptly, but Spearing rejects the idea that such termination was planned in order to undercut the authority of dreams; instead, he seems rather to welcome the structural instability of the dream almost as an end in itself, pursued for its lack of strict form (167–72).

The rhetorical naiveté of Chaucer’s dreamers is today an unquestioned axiom. The need to see in first-person speakers an imaginary character corresponding to real-world human psychology does not, however, necessarily apply to medieval literature. The limits of this assumption become clear in the structural poetics of The Parliament of Fowls, which clearly cannot be attributed to a realistic psychology; likewise, the explanations of classical myth in The House of Fame do not follow from the dreamer’s psychology. Instead, the first person singular should be read as a dit, “a textual and grammatical space, not [...] a person or a persona” (172–5).

author: Boitani, Piero
title: Old Books Brought to Life in Dreams: The Book of the Duchess, The House of Fame, The Parliament of Fowls
abstract:
Points out that Chaucer’s dream-visions are all book-inspired while also ending in a book (typically Chaucer’s own), and discusses his strategies for referencing and using written sources, described as a “strategy of hide and seek” and “a game of intertextuality” played with his audience (at 61). Like Spearing more recently, raises the possibility that some of Chaucer’s name-dropping was not expected to be understood by his general audience, though they might have been introduced for an elite audience of friends (62–3). Two chronological shifts may be identified: one from relying mainly on Ovid and romance to a far wider spectrum by the time of the House of Fame and one from a reliance on broadly literary texts to a more philosophical focus, clearly present in book 2 of that work (31).

Much of the remainder of the essay discusses Chaucer’s conception of love and its relation to his sources.

author: St John, Michael
title: Chaucer’s Dream Visions: Courtliness and Individual Identity
abstract: A study of Chaucer’s dream visions. The introduction argues that despite his lipservice to Macrobius, Chaucer in his dream-theory was influenced more by Aristotle, who took a more psychological approach to the causes of dreams (6–12). A broadly courtly audience may be defined that would have understood Chaucer’s references and dream-theory (13–17). This book argues that the dreams in Chaucer’s work concern the courtly world (17–18). The book devotes a chapter each to Chaucer’s dream visions.

author: Bibire, Paul
title: Freyr and Gerðr: The Story and its Myths
publication: Sagnaskemmtun: Studies in Honour of Hermann Pálsson on his 65th Birthday, 26th May 1986
eds: Rudolf Simek, Jónas Kristjánsson, and Hans Bekker-Nielsen
abstract: An important contribution to the deconstruction of the Freyr-Gerðr fertility reading, this essay actually accepts that the text may reflect early beliefs concerning fertility, which may even have developed a ritual tradition. It argues, however, that myths acquire allegorical readings only once a “failure of belief” is reached, which in the case of this narrative would most likely have happened around the Conversion. “This stage is plausibly fairly well represented in Skírnismál. But the poem is itself probably late, and may already show romance influence in its (rather incidental) presentation of Freyr as lover”, a transformation further developed by Snorri (39–40, at 39).

author: Hamel, Mary
title: The Siege of Jerusalem as a Crusading Poem
publication: Journeys Towards God: Pilgrimage and Crusade
abstract: In the first section of her article, Hamel demonstrates that the atrocities in The Siege of Jerusalem are not unparalleled, though they are often thought to be. She discusses two types of analogues: Josephus’s Jewish War, a contemporary account of the actual siege; and Middle English crusader literature. The poem’s most striking and cruel descriptions are brought forward and shown to have parallels in both types of analogue.

author: Hanna, Ralph III
title: Contextualizing The Siege of Jerusalem
abstract: The Siege deals with torn flesh being transformed into “‘ennobling’ acts of racial violence” based on the crucifixion. Pilate functions as the displaced agency in this originary narrative: he improperly becomes an agent in the service of the Jews. Similar reactions to the crucifixion may be found in three collects that were traditionally prayed on Good Friday, in which the conversion of the Church’s enemies was called for. The Siege similarly takes on two types of paganism, Jewish and Roman (111-12). Vespasian and Titus are licensed to perform the horrors that they do by “their participation in a line of purified agency”: Jesus’s deeds arrive at them through Veronica and Nathan, and they pass it on in their decision to avenge him. Their destructive methodology is more or less approved of by the displaced Josephus, who uses Titus’s hatred as a cure (112-13). Yorkshire, and Bolton in particular, are named as places of composition; and the transmission is discussed (113-19). After the expulsion of 1290, it is argued, the authorities could direct the Good Friday prayers at substitutes, as happened to the Lollards after 1402. This illustrates how the Siege had the potential to become a voice in its readers’ material existence (119-20).

author: Hebron, Malcolm
title: The Siege of Jerusalem
publication: The Medieval Siege: Theme and Image in Middle English Romance
abstract: While romances on the Roman siege of Jerusalem tend to focus on action, they present their material in a context of destiny and salvation. The fall of Troy is usually given a Boethian explanation and warns against vanity, but that of Jerusalem is teleological and reveals the power of God (112). Both sieges are enriched with many apochryphal narratives, which come together in the binding event of the siege (112-13). Both traditions emphasise historical veracity and present the city’s fall as inevitable (113). One appealing element of the Jerusalem tradition lay in the Romans, who were considered exemplars of chivalry. The theme remained popular into the sixteenth century (114-15). Texts dealing with the siege are the Legenda Aurea, the Estoire del Saint Graal, and the prose Joseph d’Arimathie; it was also popular in art (114-16). Titus and Vespasian was primarily morally instructive and occurred among religious texts, but it also emphasised the guilt of the Jews. It was based primarily on Josephus and the Venjance Nostre Seigneur. The fifteenth century saw the composition of a Prose Siege of Jerusalem, which leaves out much of the material not directly connected to the siege (116). The alliterative Siege emphasises warfare and seldom occurs amidst religious material. Another relevant text is one of the sources of the Siege, the Bible en françois (116-17). Titus and Vespasian contains a suggestion of the symbolism between soul and beleaguered town when it says the Jews were trapped in Jerusalem because of their sinfulness (2825-8). Contemporary sermons would liken the soul to a fortress. Pilate is portrayed as an incapable leader, which singles him out as a personal object of God’s vengeance (119-20). The siege begins on Easter Sunday, precisely 34 years after the Crucifixion. By making the siege last seven years, Jerusalem falls 40 years after the same event (121). Details of warfare are provided, but the landscape is not filled in, so that the town seems an archetype of a besieged castle (121-2). The Jews are described as desperate and degraded, while the Roman generals are determined and cruel. After their surrender, the Jews are slaughtered but the Christians are spared (122). Titus and Vespasian views the events in their greater destiny. While this sense of destiny is shared by the Siege, this latter poem is more interested in warfare and the exotic (123-4). The Siege battle descriptions are apocalyptic in tone, while descriptions of the Romans emphasise glory (124-6). The poem is rife with contrasts: splendour and death, gleaming arms and darkened skies, hunting and flaying; but medieval audiences seem not to have been struck by such contrasts (126-7). The Siege will have seemed more just than other sieges in medieval literature, in view of its destined nature (127). The English adaptation of the Bible en françois contains fifteenth-century elements like guns, and details on violence (128). The array of the opposing forces (siege tower, tabernacle-on-elephant) expresses the deep contrast between the forces (130). The Siege focusses on drama and spectacle, Titus and Vespasian on religious symbolism, and both the Siege and the English Bible combine the exotic with the familiar by the introduction of later Western warfare (134). Jerusalem and Troy are linked in their focus on calamity. “At the heart of the vision of besieged Troy or Jerusalem is the idea of a purging experience, a painful rite of passage in which a great cultural or spiritual change is effected. This notion of beleaguerment and transformation could also be exercised on an individual level. Sieges outside history, existing on the timeless plane of allegory, express further fundamental concepts of the soul and the self” (134-5).

author: Hulbert, J.R.
title: The Text of The Siege of Jerusalem
abstract: Discusses the textual pedigree of the MSS.

author: Lawton, David
title: Titus Goes Hunting and Hawking: The Poetics of Recreation and Revenge in The Siege of Jerusalem
publication: Individuality and Achievement in Middle English Poetry
abstract: The suggestion is made that the Siege, “perhaps compiled [at Bolton Abbey] for the entertainment or edification of aristocratic lay patrons,” may contain traces of this readership. These are looked for in the entertainment of the aristocracy: hunting and hawking. This episode (~889) is a tactical move by the Romans, who intend to hide their fatigue. It is not, as elsewhere, deemed ignoble; hunting and hawking usually stand in some relationship to battle, either complementing or contrasting with it. In the Siege context, this ambiguity causes no problems, since the arts of peace are here disguised arts of war; but the activities do evoke their values in other texts. A comparison is made with the same activities in SGGK, The Parliament of the Three Ages, The Book of the Duchess, and Rauf Coilyear. Siege may be read “as an anachronistic declaration of Christian identity: The Christian Romans make war because they are afraid of what they would be if they did not. What it is to be Roman, now redefined as synonymous with Christian, is to cease collaboration, and indeed cohabitation, with the Jews, which is why the poem’s final victim is not a Jew but Pilate, the arch-collaborator.” The Jew Josephus is brought in as the healer: he cures Titus by prescribing hatred of his enemies. Josephus also occurs in the hunting episode. His conversion is no literary singularity. It saves him, and those who do not convert are annihilated.

author: Millar, Bonnie
title: The Role of Prophecy in The Siege of Jerusalem and its Analogues
abstract: Poems of the alliterative tradition are keen to point out the need for change when on a course for disaster. The destruction of Jerusalem was a popular theme until the seventeenth century, and most redactions describe the portents leading up to it. The Siege echoes Luke 19.41-4 in lines 351-2 and elsewhere (e.g., 298, 1285-8). Other portents are described, however (1217-36); these also occur in Josephus, the Legenda Aurea, and Titus and Vespasian; the different treatment of these portents may explain their different functions in the various poems (153-5). The Siege pits the Christians Titus and Vespasian against the Jews Caiaphas, Pilate, Simon, and John, without creating a clear-cut opposition between good and evil along national differences. Nero is grouped with Othis, Judas, and Pilate: all four grow desperate because they do not have the true faith. Similarly, the Jewish people are captives of their leadership, while the Roman rank-and-file commit great wrongs (156). The eyewitness Josephus describes two wars, the Jewish-Roman one and the Jewish civil war (156-8). Hegesippus (c4) abbreviates Josephus’s account, aiming to show that God’s grace has passed to the Christians. Higden’s Polychronicon (mid-c14) uses both earlier accounts. Jacobus de Voragine’s Legenda Aurea (c13) also treats the event, as does the romance Titus and Vespasian (c14), primarily attested in religious contexts. The Siege has reference to “four omens: a burning sword, a vision of armed men, an ominous sacrifice, and a cryptic oracle in verse.” Details are left out, the Jews’ reactions are not noted, the omens are fewer in number than in the sources, and their order is altered. This is because the poet needed only one omen of each type, and wanted an augmenting sequence. All omens predict the victory of the Romans who are sent as a scourge of God (158-63). The Siege treatment of the omens is closest to, and therefore probably borrowed from, the Polychronicon account. The Legenda Aurea cannot be the source for this passage because it leaves out much concerning Ananias’s son. Josephus and Hegesippus are unlikely to be sources because they treat the omens at greater length and comment largely (163-4). Josephus emphasises that the Jews did not understand the omens because they were deceived by false interpreters. His details concerning the omens seems to have no aim besides lending authority to their observation (165-6). Both Josephus and Hegesippus time the portents after the Jews’ burning of the temple; but the latter innovates in making his exegesis part of the (extended) narrative. He thoroughly christianises the account, referring explicitly to the Christian significance of these events (166-8). Jacobus de Voragine discusses the events in his life of St James, which focus explains several of his selections (168-70). The Polychronicon has the omens occur after Sabinus’s death (4.447-9), for which Titus ordered the temple gates to be burned (170-1). Titus and Vespasian has them early in the poem, like Jacobus; it contains many more omens than the other redactions, sensationalising the signs but lessening their impact (171-3). Josephus uses the omens to point out the blindness of the Jews; Hegesippus contrasts Jewish wickedness with Roman nobility; Higden believes they reveal the divine inspiration of the war; Jacobus de Voragine thinks they demonstrate how God helps sinners by means of warning them. The Siege poet innovates in reinterpreting, selecting, and repositioning the portents so that they build up to the poem’s climax (175-6).
