author: Moe, Phyllis
title: The French Source of the Alliterative Siege of Jerusalem
abstract: Argues that the Siege was influenced by Roger d’Argenteuil’s Bible en françois. The alliterative poet has added a number of details and left out others. About one-third of the poem has been borrowed from the French text.

author: Nicholson, Roger
title: Haunted Itineraries: Reading The Siege of Jerusalem
abstract: Argues that the Siege is about Jerusalem rather than about the Jews; that it is an instigation to crusading; but that it uses the Jews rather than the Saracens as the abject because it is at the margin of the self, rather than in the exotic, that the abject is found. It is easy to explain the poem’s popularity by Christian revulsion against the Jews; it may be that Christian kingdoms became Europe precisely by persecuting the other. As such, the Siege may display a European dimension (448-9). Europe was defined by its Christendom and by the central position of Jerusalem on the T-O map; thus its very focus consisted of a margin (449). All borders affirm cultural definitions (452). The Siege is on the edge of genre borders: it has a chronicle-like form but relates one specific history, and it makes a connection between crusade and pilgrimage (453-5). References to Christ’s prophecy in Luke 19.43-4 and the description of the Passion give the poem a teleological focus (455-6). It is not the Jews that are its primary focus, but Jerusalem and its temple (457). About 1100, polemical writings displayed an interest in the association of Roman victories with Christian armies (458). The irreversible good-versus-evil stance of the poem is one cause of modern unease (460 [PS: but see Van Court]). Romance elements add to the poem’s hybrid nature; but chivalric values are placed in a highly teleological context, giving the story of the fall of Jerusalem a cultural momentum like that of the destruction of Troy (459-61). In its MS contexts, the Siege is associated with crusading romances, but it presents a remarkable mix of Christian and romance elements. If indeed borders and margins are dangerous, then this poem suggests that its culture is under threat (462). By the time of its MS genesis, the Saracens were mostly Turks. A large host under Richard II and Charles V was crushed by the Ottomans in 1396, an event marked by historians as the final crusading engagement though not the end of crusading sentiment (462-3). An ongoing mission by Philippe de Mézières as evidenced by a 1395 Epistre provides a polemical context for the Siege (463-6). The poem may even have been dedicated to Henry Bolingbroke, cousin to King Richard II, who bore the emblem of the dragon, although the Siege is not original in introducing this heraldic sign (466-70). In this reading, the poem is a crusading appeal, offering the Roman siege as an exemplar (470-1). Both faith and territory are relevant arguments for crusading conquest (472). The body figures in the poem as an important symbol: those of the Roman generals are healed, whereas those of the Jews are broken in horrendous ways and turned into weapons (473-5). The poem is about the foundation of Europe: “the West discovers itself in its opposition to the East.” In a crusading context, however, one would expect the Saracen as the enemy. Furthermore, in relating the story of the fall of Jerusalem, the Siege calls the Jew back into history, justifying his diaspora (475-6). Stephen Kruger remarks on an ambivalence to the body: specific human bodies are considered abject, namely the leper, the woman, the homosexual, and the Jew. The historical relation between Jew and Christian results in a special ambivalence (477). The Jews in the poem correspond to Julia Kristeva’s “exorbitant outside” category of abjection, retaining a hold on the disgusted. According to Kristeva, abjection is a border, the guarantee of existence. The margin defines the self. Primitive religion is defined by its taboos; for Christianity, the taboo is internalised as sin. The Jews are a “defiling element” in the Christian’s own past that has to be rejected, “thereby confirming the structure of our beliefs” (478-9). The cannibal episode seems to contain sympathy, but its point is that the Jews are confined to the carnal; their suffering is nothing more than suffering, unlike that of Christ (481). The death of the boy is a sign of his community’s spiritual health, inverting the eucharist (482). The actual “other, the Muslim, is held at bay in assailing the abject, the ‘in-between, the ambiguous, the composite,’ the Jew” (484).

author: Van Court, Elisa Narin
title: The Siege of Jerusalem and Augustinian Historians: Writing about Jews in Fourteenth-century England
abstract: Argues that the Jews in the Siege are not, as Hamel and Hanna propose, a trope for the Saracens or the Lollards; the poem is indeed about the relationship between Christans and Jews, and it provides an unmistakable sympathy for the Jews alongside its martial brutalities (227-9). The Siege is explicitly about God’s vengeance on the Jews: the Lucan prophesy of the temple is referred to four times (230). The pre-battle Scripture readings symbolise the core of both traditions: the Exodus refers to Jewish freedom and the coming of the covenant, while the Passion redeems the Christian and establishes the new covenant (230-1). Fourteenth-century (i.e., post-expulsion [1290]) literature shows an ambivalent interest in the Jews, and a focus on the problem of the present of Jews in Christendom. The Siege is milder than many crusading texts. Alongside the fiercer anti-Judaic stance, there was a dualist understanding, developed by Augustine, that the Jews were not to be harmed for the sake of their forefathers (Rom 11.28-9, Psalm 59.12). Bernard of Clairvaux distinguished between Saracens, heretics, and Jews: the third category was not to be harmed (232-3). The Siege displays a definite sympathy towards the Jews at a time when a more hostile sentiment had come to prevail (233). While its sources describe the Jews exclusively as brutal beasts, the Siege calls them meek and portrays Vespasian as a beast (234). In this poem, unlike its sources, the cannibalist scene and its context evoke sorrow rather than disgust (235-6). The Jews’ Kiddush ha-shem, or pious suicide, has the same effect (236-7). “As the level of suffering in the narrative increases, there is a concomittant decrease in accusatory and hostile language to describe the Jews” (238). The poem was composed in Yorkshire, which had an Augustinian tradition. The late twelfth-century chronicle of the Augustinian canon William of Newburgh displays the same concern for Jewish well-being, as does the late thirteenth-century copyist of this work, also an Augustinian canon. Hannah believes the Siege to have been written in the Augustinian Bolton Priory; hence, sympathy for the Jews seems to be an Augustinian tradition (241-4).

author: Yeager, Suzanne M.
title: The Siege of Jerusalem and Biblical Exegesis: Writing About Romans in Fourteenth-century England
abstract: Summarises views on the representation of the Jews in the Siege (70). Remarks that the role of the Romans has received little attention. The poem’s function may be revealed by a study of the exegetical depiction of the Romans combined with the Augustinian conception of the Jews. The Romans could be seen as soldiers of faith, an image constructed of Christian narrative and medieval romance; but exegetically they were also seen as the Antichrist (71-2). The poem establishes Rome as a holy city (72-3), though newly so (#). The familiarisation of Roman knights serves to urge for crusade participation, an aim that often employed the AD 70 narrative (73-4). Siege, hunting, and hawking were familiar images that facilicated identification between potential crusader and Roman knight (75-6). Titus and Vespasian are Christianised, but they also take crusader vows (76-7). Ann Matter remarks that the book of Lamentations applies not only to the fall of the first temple, but also to the second, that fell in AD 70. Thus the Jews simplify the enemies of Jerusalem into one enemy, united in the trope of the fall of the temple. Christians do the same by using Lamentations on and around Good Friday (78). Josephus’s writings had become fully integrated in the Christian canon by the late medieval period and represented an apocryphal fulfilment of the prophecies of Isaiah, Jeremiah, and others (79). In the twelfth century, chroniclers referred to this tradition to demonstrate that the crusades and the fall of Jerusalem in that century had been predicted by Scripture. This understanding seems implied in the Siege (79-80). Significantly, the quintessential example of Cassius’s four senses of Scripture consists in the meanings of Jerusalem (81). The rest of the article treats interpretations of Josephus in England (82-96).

author: Coverley, Merlin
title: Psychogeography
abstract: Studies the literary predecessors and heirs of Situationist psychogeography from Defoe and Blake onwards. Portrays Situationist psychogeography scathingly (but realistically) as “the openly ludicrous antics of the lettrists” (esp. 22‒4, at 23). [Incomplete]

author: Arnold, Martin
title: Hvað er tröll nema þat?: The Cultural History of the Troll
publication: The Shadow-Walkers: Jacob Grimm’s Mythology of the Monstrous
publisher: Arizona Center for Medieval and Renaissance Studies and Brepols
series: Medieval and Renaissance Texts and Studies
abstract:
Grimm considered the repeated occurrence of a creature-concept more significant than the singularity of the individual instance, which he was happy to pass over. Concepts like troll, of limited West Germanic evidence and not etymologically transparent, finer distinction seemed impossible (?113-4). Records various interpretations of both the meaning and the semantic development of the word troll (114-16). Evidence from the Poetic Edda is studied in some detail (116-18), as well as Snorric evidence (118-22); all this early [and Snorric] evidence emphasises the troll as exclusively female; their association with sexual intrigue, but only in relation with giants or humans, never gods; their characteristic hostility, but not in an organised way; their association with various kinds of magic, articulating “destructive supernature” (122-3). This data-set may be read in three ways: (1) the troll-woman is a poetic trace of the real pre-patriarchal female; (2) she represents a “nervously imagined matriarchy” deriving from the fear of the patriarchs; (3) she is a “genetic throwback” who is therefore stigmatised for the sexual threat she poses to society (123). In the sagas, “the troll becomes a broad-base expression for unpleasant or dangerous other-worlders, or wondrous abnormalities often relating to size, in an impressive sense, or disposition, in a disparaging sense” (123-4). Troll are differently portrayed in the thirteenth-century Íslendingasögur than in the later Íslendingasögur and fornaldarsögur. Between the Eddic literature and the time of the Íslendingasögur in the thirteenth century, what distinction there had been between giants and troll had become blurred; some converging and differing characteristics are listed. Significantly, the female role of troll has been lost as an identifying feature. “If, then, the descriptor troll has become a generic portmanteau in the sagas, it would seem to be in terms of signifying all that is most threatening and offensive to social stability,” thus becoming an expression of social anxiety expressed through myth (124).

[Troll in the classical íslendingasögur, 125-9] A contrast is drawn between troll-curses with and without a supernatural context to explain the reference, and also between classical and post-classical íslendingasögur. In both the very early Heiðarvíga saga and the post-classical Grettis saga, the reference seems to be to cheating in battle (125-6). An unstructured, incomplete list of occurrences with no deeper referent is drawn up (126-7). References to body height and further appearance are “socially realistic” and imply that they “just might be one,” an implication not present where the narrative context is fantastical (127-8). “Troll references in the classical Íslendingasögur are, with few exceptions, dissociated from actual troll activities. They are, in this sense, purely signifiers of wrath, contempt, and awe. . . . troll chiefly functions as indicator of something beyond the limit of social normality and acceptability but without the incredible becoming manifest” (128-9).

[Troll in the fornaldarsögur and later sagas, 129-43] Individuals in society exhibiting abnormal traits or magic are characterised as troll. Such troll occur mainly from the late thirteenth century onwards, but the early sagas Vatnsdæla and Eyrbyggja have examples of such classification (129-30). The fantastic is evoked sparingly in the classical sagas, but abundantly in the later and fornaldarsögur, in which the margins are the central point of attention. Some of these works present the hero with strange elements against which he may be tried; others focus on strangeness itself, with the hero partaking of both human and non-human societies (130). Conquering trolls is a feature of the first group; but the hero who accomplishes this task is sometimes himself regarded as monstrous by ordinary men. These heroes should not, however, be understood to be such in any strict sense (130-1). The hero of the second category may belong to either men or monsters, and negotiates between the two domains (131-2). Bárðar saga explores threats to an old-world, heathen ideal while questioning the validity of that ideal. As such, it reverses the perspective of the human-hero-versus-troll group, which is always directed outward from the human sphere. Nevertheless, both groups use the self/other distinction to affirm one’s own identity (133). A third perspective appears in the sagas of the Hrafnistumenn, in which interbreeding has led to heroes who do not distinguish between man and troll (133-4). These sagas remap the traditional “gods-versus-monstrosity conflict of the eddas, which can by certain arguments be seen as a nature-versus-culture metaphysic” to make it an internal conflict played out in specific geographical and historical settings (134). In Ketils saga hængs, the title character, indulging in his troll nature, takes pleasure in doing the opposite of what his wiser father, Hallbjörn hálftröll, asks of him. He even engenders an offspring with a troll in Finland, but his father will not allow him to marry outside humankind (134-6). In the next generation, described in Gríms saga loðinkinna, Ketill does not deny his son the pleasures of trolldom, although Grímr, too, ends up marrying among men. His son Örvar-Oddr is again the product of a hálftröll and a full tröll, and again leads a life on the boundary. By his association with otherly peoples, his own otherliness is brought out (136-8). Two other works using this genealogy, Áns saga bogsveigis and Orms þáttr Stórólfssonar, belong rather to the first group of works, pitting heroes against otherly creatures (138-9). The first three Hrafnistumenn-sagas, however, add a troll-human sub-society in which reality represents fracture (139). This fractured assertion of identity may express the Icelandic identity after the fall of the Commonwealth (140-1). Fracture is expressed already in the fornaldarsaga description of a foreign past (141). The imposition of foreign law at the arrival of Norwegian rule also created fracture, and the besieged insular setting of the Hrafnistumannasögur may likewise be read as an analogue for post-independence Iceland (142). Thus between classical sagas and Hrafnistumannasögur, troll move from representatives of social degeneration via the invasive outgroup (cf. post-independence Iceland) to a cultural hybrid, defined by ambiguity. The move is from a focus on the threats of an outgroup to that on fragmentation within the ingroup. The troll moves ever closer to the self (142-3).

[Troll in folktales, 143-55] In folk-tales may be recognised layers of reworkings, each expressing a social ideal while having its origin in ancient ritual (143-4). The earlier trend of troll absorbing the traits of other supernatural creatures continued in the development of the folk-tales. Features such as cannibalism and intolerance for sunlight became trollish associations in the fourteenth century, although the material hardly admits to fully typical troll behaviour (144-5). ON mythological motifs may be discerned in various troll folktales (145-6). However, troll no longer function as threats but rather as foils offsetting human virtue. The Icelandic þjóðsaga, which has the more consistent troll material, is more realistic than the æfintýri or wonder-tale more characteristic of Norwegian tradition (146-7). The traditional ON motif of the threat of the sociopathic outsider recurs in those folktales that may be called abduction tales, featuring troll looking for human meat or sex; this hunt failing, the troll is typically killed. In the less common type in which the abduction is successful, the situation for the human in question is often irreversible (147-9). The boundary between human and troll domains should be seen in terms of religious culture and ideology; this explains why the contrast persists in the later folktales and is here even more marked than in the sagas. The troll can represent paganism or, as a member of an outgroup community, symbolise doctrinal unease (149). While some tales may be read as affirmations of ecclesiastical power over outside forces, others suggest that the troll-church relationship, the troll-community relationship, and indeed the community-church relationship, was more ambiguous (149-53). The late collection of the material makes it difficult to discern differences in attitude towards Catholic and Lutheran church (153-4). The troll, in conclusion, is a compound of mythological tradition and its signification as a figure on the margins of society, “more often than not. . . represent[ing] the antithesis of human ideals” (154).

author: Ármann Jakobsson
title: Hvað er tröll? Galdrar, tröllskapur og samfélagsóvinir
publication: Galdramenn: Galdrar og samfélag á miðöldum
abstract:
Studies the concept of troll. An English adaptation is found here.

(1) Skáldskaparmál has, in two manuscripts, an encounter between Bragi and a trollkona in which she associates herself with jötnar and völur. The concept of tröllkona is itself introduced with reference to that member of this species who engenders jötnar east in Járnviðr. This association between troll and jötnar is common in the Prose Edda: they are interchangeable when Óðinn goes to Jötunheimr to fight troll, while Þórr does the same í Austrvega. The only occurrence of the word in the Poetic Edda is in the line “tvngls tivgari / itrollz hami” (Vsp 39); this troll seems to have a connection to the trollkona in Járnviðr. It is then identified as a wolf consuming the moon. The troll-kennings sjöt-Hrungni tunglsins and sólar böl indicate an identity as the sun’s destroyer, while the trollkona in the forest suggests another; but how do these relate to sorcery? Eyrbyggja saga tells of the rivalry between the witches Geirríðr and Katla, and how one or other of them “rides” the man they both want as their pupil. This night-riding belongs in the same category as nightmares and vampires. Katla’s son is wanted for cutting off someone’s hand, and his mother hides him through magic; but eventually she realises that her magic will not be enough, since “mun Geirríðr trollit þar komin, ok mun þá eigi sjónhverfingum einum mega við koma.” Here the word troll is associated with sorcery, just as it is in Gísla saga with regard to Þórgrímr nef and as trolldom survives in the languages of mainland Scandinavia. Einar Ólafur Sveinsson’s vague definition in his note on the word troll is discussed; it is broad, but does not cover all the instances discussed above [this section identical to that in the Saga-Book article].

(2) Schulz lists 72 instances of the word troll in Íslendingasögur and 96 in the fornaldarsögur, and 16 more in lausavísur (this section identical to the article in Saga-Book, but without the long list of occurrences). The fornaldarsögur often introduce troll as otherworldly beings without further explanation, so that they are often ill-defined. The word can be an all-inclusive term for “monster”; sometimes it simply forms a contrast with “human”; and a law code states that one cannot eat with troll, without further explaining the term; it presumably refers to sorcerers. Hit mesta troll sometimes refers to witches, and sometimes it is used to refer to someone who is stronger in battle than men. Typically, such occurrences do not explain whether the trollskapr consists in witchcraft, strength, or appearance. But as Martin Arnold has shown, females have a large share in the category in Snorra Edda, and the same holds true for the Íslendingasögur and fornaldarsögur. Core meaning seems to be “otherly” and “big.” Ögmundr Eyþjófsbani in Örvar-Odds saga is called a tröll og óvættr, having taken allskyns galdra ok gjörnínga, and having been trýldur “trolled.” He is called heldr andi enn maðr, making clear that evil spirits may be included in the category troll. Sóti in Harðar sögu og Hólmverja is “mikit tröll í lífinu, en hálfu meira síðan hann var dauðr.” Can draugar then be troll? Being a troll appears to be linked to special powers, which may not be supernatural (if “natural” is understood in the wider medieval sense which includes dragons) but it certainly is superhuman. Bárðr Snæfellsáss is one-quarter troll, which gives him malice but also powers. In Íslendingasögur and fornaldarsögur, tall build can be the sign of a troll. Sometimes it is their strength or power to resist iron that renders people troll. Like berserkir, troll may raise battle-cries, and Göngu-Hrólfs saga has Röndólfr hamask in battle when he is said to become like a troll; so also in Gunnars saga Keldugnúpsfífls. Sörla saga likewise seems to equate troll and berserkr. The verb tryllask expresses that it is possible to turn normal people into troll. It is perhaps in this context that troll-curses (e.g. troll hafi þik) should be understood. Modern equivalents are proposed [this section is identical to that in the Saga-Book paper]. Troll is often used to describe the heroes of Íslendingasögur; this aspect is often described as the Icelandic “dark hero.” But few examples have characters refer to themselves as troll, and no humans do this. The category is essentially otherly. Hrólfs saga Gautrekssonar tells how the Irish princess disagrees with the general opinion that a certain person raging through the land is a troll, showing that the category is here exclusive of a more natural category of human.

(3) A list of troll-characteristics is provided [this section is very close to that in the Saga-Book article]: troll can be synonymous with giant categories; it is often adjectival; it often refers to witchcraft; to evil spirits or draugar; to shapeshifters or berserkir, tryllask being at times used for hamask; it is generally negative; it is very commonly used to describe an adversary; troll are otherly; they are typically given specific characteristics, such as a resistance to iron, biting people in the windpipe, and cannibalism; and in Grettis saga, they do not belong in daylight; indeed, later folklore has it that they must not be surprised by daylight. Black people are called troll. A creature poisoning wells in Hálfs saga ok Hálfsrekka is variously called þurs and troll. Animals can be troll when they act against nature. It is asked whether he who makes someone a troll is himself a troll [this section is similar to that in the Saga-Book article].

(4) The list is completed with the addition of warlike black men; well-poisoning creatures; animals, too, can be troll; heathen spirits; sometimes both the one influenced and the one influencing one to become a troll; both draugar and animals bewitched by them; and demons, magicians, heathens, enemies of Christianity. More may be found. The troll’s main function is to do wrong, be the enemy of society. Its appearance, whether as demon, wolf, or otherwise, is non-essential to the concept.

author: Ármann Jakobsson
title: The Trollish Acts of Þorgrímr the Witch: The Meanings of troll and ergi in Medieval Iceland
abstract: In many ways, a translation of “Hvað er tröll?”, q.v. Starting from a discussion of Þórgrímr nef in Gísla saga, challenges standard definitions of troll and ergi, listing the many uses of the former with reference to many Íslendingasögur and fornaldarsögur. The standard definition of ergi, associated with homosexual practices, is unlikely to have been intended in the Þórgrímr nef story. Rather it seems to denote the femininity of witchcraft, a practice that has distinct feminine associations in the ON corpus.

author: Koht, Halvdan
title: Var ‘finnane’ alltid finnar?
abstract:
Hansen has worked energetically to show that finnar were once all over mainland Scandinavia, but if this was so they have left suspiciously little trace (161). Koht therefore sets out on the hypothesis that finnr once meant something other than Sami (161-2), and more specifically that it meant the same as troll and trollkunnig mann, which, in turn, mean the same thing (162). Right across Shetland, never inhabited by Sami, runs an old stone wall called locally referred to as finnigord “finnar-fence.” It has been observed that most Shetlandic witches’ folktales are set around this wall. A legend tells that a farmer wished the wall to appear overnight, and when it did he sacrificed his best cow in return. The finnar that built it, then, were creatures with supernatural powers. They might thus as well have been called tröll (162-3). At the southern end of the wall is a cave known as “the Haljer o’ Fivlagord,” suggesting that finnr and fífl were interchangeable. According to legend, the St Laurentius’ Church in Lund was built by a troll named Finn. Both these episodes thus concern master builders associated with finnar and tröll/fíflar. The third is from Sjernarøy [in Rogaland, Norway], where the remains of an old stone wall are known as Finnborg. None of these finnar could have been Sami; they were all considered supernatural builders. In Stordalen, there is an old settlement locally called “Trollkyrkjegarden,” suggesting the same function for tröll. It is well known that the Sami have been considered skilled in magic both in medieval and in modern times. Ynglinga saga tells how finnr magic caused the death of one of the first Ynglinga kings (163). A poem on Óláfr helgi has finnr sorcerers make a man impervious to weapons (163-4). Adam of Bremen tells of the magic powers of #?deires. The word hreingalkn used to describe a supernatural creature in Hymiskviða 24 is probably variation for the common word finngalkn [“centaur”]; the poet thus had finnr-magic in mind when he thought of the creature. Fritzner has shown that most of the individuals called finnar for their witchcraft were Norsemen who were only given this title because of their association with witchcraft. The Christian laws forbidding subjects to associate with finnar are thus simply saying not to associate with magicians (164). Beowulf knows of finna land in Scandinavia, but this probably has no geographical referent: instead, it is the trollebotnen [?Trolls’ End (trolls’ bottom-of-a-valley)] of Norwegian folklore (164-5). In Hversu Noregr byggðisk, three siblings are called after the landscapes they govern, namely Jötunbjörn, Guðbrandr, and Finnálfr. The parallellism between jötunn, guð/goð and finnr suggests again that the latter term could be used in a non-ethnographical sense suggesting supernatural powers. Jötnar may be expressed through the kenning fjalla finnr. Gandálfr and Finnr are both dwarf-names in Völuspá. Eyjólfr dáðaskald uses finnr and álfr interchangeably (165). Certain regions in Austland are associated with finnar and elves as well as troller, and in Heimskringla the jötunn who marries his daughter off to Haraldr hárfagra is also called a finnr (165-6). Also in Heimskringla, a finnr is cleft in two: finnr and jötunn. All this is a consequence of the natural connection between finnr and magic. Queen Gunnhildr learned her trollskapr from finnar. None of this is evidence for Saami residence; rather, it proves a connection between sorcery and the concept finnr (166).

The proper noun Finnr was common in the Middle Ages, and forms of it are still common across Scandinavia. The earliest evidence for the name Finn is from Beowulf, and Finna is found on a sixth-century runestone (166-7). If the personal names referred to the Sami, then the name is surprisingly widespread. Instead, if it evoked magic powers, its popularity is no surprise: cf. feminine names ending in -rún (167).

South of Finnmark, Norway counts 201 place-names containing finn. Researchers have failed in their attempts at explaining this frequency (167-8). Not all will derive from the same root. 67 of them are in Halogaland, all modern and all referring to the Sami; in the south, a few places are known to have received Sami immigration in modern times, yielding 11 or 12 more place-names (168-9). 33 more names refer to Finns (169). 89 names remain that require a different explanation (169-70). Some of these have been explained with reference to a type of grass named finn, probably short for finnskjegge; but this grass was associated with the disease finnstyng or finnelte. This suggests that a supernatural power was believed to inhabit the grass (170). The theory that the grass was named after the proper noun Finna has been disproved (170-1). The name Finnr would have resulted in a form with Finns-, which are indeed found (171). This leaves 43 place-names at most (171-2). The name Finnskot (3 occ.) is suggestive of sorcery. The various places called Finndalen remind one of those called Trolldalen (172), and various other Finn- names have Troll- counterparts (173-4). Koht has not been able to find such good evidence for Swedish place-names (174).

author: Kválen, Eivind
title: Kva meinast det med finnar i gamalnorsk litteratur?
abstract:
Responding to Koht, comes to different conclusions than he regarding the referent of finnr. The co-occurrence in Shetland of Finnigord and Fivlagord need not mean that the two first elements are synonymous; they could be from entirely different eras (44). Moreover, there are place-names with Finn- all over Scotland; are these all Norse? (44-5). Finn is the primary word for a shapeshifting sea-monster in Shetland. This explains why Inuit coming to Orkney in the seventeenth century were called finnmen. Fritzner does say that finnr could mean "sorcerer"; this explains how supernatural creatures were associated with the Finnigord (45). There are no place-names derived from finnr “in the west.” A single town in England has the proper noun Finn (45-6). There are not many Norwegian place-names deriving from the personal name Finnr (46).

When ON material refers to finnar, it typically concerns Sami. Certain references are indisputably because they make reference to the Finnic type of ski or because they speak of semsveinar, derived from Finnic saami (46-7). In Vinje [which is in Telemark], fenni means both Sami and a small point, while it is also used to refer to skin; the word derives from ON *finni, not finnr, which has here disappeared owing to its synonymy with the grass. In all these cases, no tröll are called for (47-8). Koht’s reference to Eyjólfr dáðaskald is spurious: it does not refer to elves, though Finnur Jónsson suggests it may have the same meaning as álfr; in fact it is alliteration and internal rhyme that call for a word starting with f- and containing -inn- here (48). The same argument holds for Koht’s other poetic example (48-9). In the kenning fjalla finnr for giant, the element finnr, though “Sami” by itself, is used to mean “man”; again, it is the only word to fit alliterative and rhyme requirements. The occurrence of the word finnr south of the fells indicates that there were Sami further south than today (49).

author: Motz, Lotte
title: The Families of Giants
abstract: Asserts that the various names for giants are used interchangeably. Modern terms indicate the ongoing vitality of the terms (216). Differences between metaphorical usage of the various terms (jötnar being tall, troll sorcerers) suggests that each may once have corresponded to a distinct race, as does the apparent distinction drawn between them in various sources. This paper attempts to reconstruct these original meanings. The giants are strongly associated with northern or winter landscapes (217). Arctic and subarctic peoples across Eurasia share folklore elements that seem to have resulted from their shared climate (217-18). In primitive nature societies, specific landscape features are often thought to be governed by specific deities, whose favour is of vital importance in order to win the fruits of that particular landscape (218-19). The deity may appear in animal shape, and sometimes controls the elements (219). The giants take on characteristics typical of this guardian of nature, controlling mountainous areas. Giantesses sometimes prevent man’s hunting of “their” animals; sometimes they hunt or herd. Giants also use wild animals as pets or modes of transportation (220). They sometimes take on the shape of animals, or have a shaggy fur. They sometimes control the elements (221). The continued belief in huldufólk-type spirits demonstrates that owners of nature are a motif found in Scandinavia. Their association with the mountains is typical of mountainous regions and has been found in several other peoples (221-2). This giant identity is best matched by words of the jötunn-family. In ON myth, giants are also possessors of magic (222). In northern Eurasia, the magician served an important function as mediator between the human and the superhuman. They can be primeval and they sometimes have a share in the creation of the world (223). This primeval origin makes the giant a sort of ancestor. Shaman ancestors have been reported in other cultures (223-4). Ymir and Bestla are also ancestral (224). Several tree- and egg-traditions exist with regard to the giants’ origin. ON mythology, too, has its giants arise in an unusual way (224-5). An eagle association exists both in various Eurasion cultures and in ON (225). Iron plays an important role in northern Eurasian myths of magicians (225-7), and it does, too, for the Norse giants (227). Shapeshifting is a shaman/giant feature (227-8). The adjective fjölkunnigr shows how magic is based on knowledge, as it is among shamans. Many ON giants are called wise. Like the shamans, Óðinn receives instruction in magic from an elder magician, his uncle (228). An understanding of the origins of things is a magician’s trait; Vafþrúðnir knows of the origin of the world (228-9). The magical aspect of giants is best represented by troll (229-30). Hostile creatures may be widely found across northern Eurasian cultures, and ON giants may be read in the same tradition. Both are eventually tricked by humans (230-2). The giants’ brutishness and stupidity in being tricked by men is most clearly expressed in words of the þurs-family (232). Some trolls have a distinctly courtly flavour; these are foreign influences that have no counterpart in northern Eurasian cultures (233-5). Words of the risi family have little distinct or lasting signification; it was therefore probably introduced at a late date and “did not denote a truly ancient spirit” (235). Overlaps are recognised (235-6).

author: Wilbur, Terence H.
title: Troll: an Etymological Note
abstract: The troll, identified as “a monstrous, evilly-disposed, man-like being” must have been closely linked to witchcraft, as modern Scandinavian cognates demonstrate. Sievers derived the word from Proto-Germanic *truðan “trample,” by analogy with the nightmare that tramples its victims (137). Falk and Torp proposed instead *trullon “roll” (137-8). The required form, however, is *trallu (138-9). With a base meaning “roll” and a hypothesised causative “cause to roll, make dizzy” may be compared a number of cognate words meaning “deceive,” “prostitute,” “conjurer” (MHG), “strumpet” (MnE), “supernatural monster” (ON), all of which purposefully deceive. “A troll, then, would be a monster, an evilly disposed being who confuses and deceives his victims.” This solution still does not account for the precise form of the word (139).

author: Weinmann, Cornelia
title: Der Hausbau in Skandinavien vom Neolithikum bis zum Mittelalter
abstract:
Chapter three: Der Hausbau in England (201-17)

Germanic buildings in England have been found from the late fourth century onwards, presumably because the Roman army contained many Saxons, Franks, Alemanni and Ostrogoths. But even in the time of secure Roman power, Germanic free men seem to have settled in the Midlands and on the east coast to the north of the Thames. Evidence from fifth- and sixth-century pottery indicates that new settlements were usually built in marginal areas (201-2). Continental structures that combined barn and living quarters, as well as separate barns, are entirely absent. The vast majority of structures were subterraneous, generally with a roofpost in the centre of the facade (202-3; see also 158-9). Early ground level constructions were generally large, single-nave halls. Their walls consisted of a single or double row of rectangular posts or planks, held together by a purline. Post locks are deep, especially along the long side of the structure; door posts are typically the strongest. The posts were connected by twined twigs and loam. In cases of double rows of wall posts, couples may have been connected by a cross-lath that served to improve stability and to attach the twining framework (203). Walls were no higher than a man; there can, then, have been no crossbeams connecting the long sides of the structure, despite the tendency to have couples of wallposts directly opposite one another (203-4). Typically, the buildings had two entrances, one in the centre of each long side. The general absence of fireplaces is often attributed to the presence of timber floors. In-house partitions near either or both facades were common; these have been interpreted as private or storage rooms. Roof construction is not easy to reconstruct. Many remains favour a saddle roof with a ridge Pfette that is secured in the perpendicular gables. On the other hand, room dividers may suggest a hip roof whose eaves were supported by these dividers. Straw or wood shingles are likely cover materials (204). Cruck constructions, in which wooden arches run from one long wall of the building to the opposite side, supporting the ridge, are best attested for the period after the Viking settlements, but specimens occur already in the early Anglo-Saxon period. They may have come from what is now Germany and the Netherlands, but the Norsemen seem to have promoted the style (206-7).

author: Hreinn Benediktsson
title: The 1st Singular Preterite Subjunctive in Germanic
abstract: This study attempts to settle the form of the Proto-Germanic predecessor of the first person singular preterite subjunctive ending in the Germanic languages. Following a brief outline of the possibilities, it uses early Old Norse attestations of this form for clues. In so doing, it presents what it claims is an exhaustive list of strong attestations of the form and studies a number of them (those of kjósa, sjá, deyja, and høggva/hǫggva in great detail. The Norse evidence suggests the Proto-Nordic form had no -j-; an *-i(n) ending therefore deserves serious consideration.

author: Poole, Russell
title: Metre and Metrics
publication: A Companion to Old Norse–Icelandic Literature and Culture
abstract: A convenient overview of metres and metrical elements.

author: Fell, Christine, and John Lucas
title: Egils saga
abstract:
Introduction

A somewhat dated introduction to the text, which recognizes the need to distinguish between history and fiction yet leans rather too heavily on the early age of the poems. Deals with historicity (i–ix), authorship (x), the text’s accordance with thirteenth-century historiography (x–xi), its answering to the typical family saga pattern of Icelanders receiving high honours at foreign courts yet challenging those authorities (xi–xiii), the contrast of characters within the family line (xiii–xvi), Egill as a poet (xvi–xviii), minor characters (xviii–xx), and the sagas’ reliance on hints (xx).

author: Hermann Pálsson and Paul Edwards
title: Egil’s Saga
abstract:
Introduction

Mostly a loose literary sketch, with some attention to genealogy.

author: Nordal, Sigurður
title: Egils saga Skalla-Grímssonar
abstract:
§1 Poetry In his introduction, Nordal shows himself to be a staunch defender of the notion that the bulk of the poetry ascribed to Egill is correctly ascribed. He lists the few dozen verses whose authenticity has been drawn into question by Sievers and Wieselgren and compares these judgements to those of Finnur Jónsson, who grew less critical of their authenticity later in his career. The elderly Finnur agreed with the other critics on only two stanzas, which to Nordal’s mind demonstrates the uncertainty of the critics’ reasoning (v–ix). Points out some old constructions in poems judged by Sievers to be younger (ix–x). Finnur has some strong arguments against the authenticity of certain stanzas on Ljótr inn bleiki, though mostly if M is followed rather than K; yet Finnur later admitted those verses of this group against whose authenticity he had not adduced specific arguments as authentic. If any poetry on Ljótr is discarded, it ought all to be discarded, a view that Finnur ultimately could not hold (x).

It is suggested that Egill himself took an active interest in the promulgation of his poetry by teaching it to younger generations in his old age. Some of the poems that the text claims were composed in the heat of the moment may in fact have been composed at a later time, even much later (xi–xii). The unrealistic accounts of childhood composition may be assumed to result from Egill’s own boasting as well as exaggeration by later retellers (xii–xiii).

Björn M. Ólsen has proposed that the saga compiler may have written the poetry to match the pre-existing material, since in two places M announces a verse that has not been filled in. Nordal connects Ólsen’s support of this view with his belief that the saga was written by Snorri, famously familiar with the verse tradition. But Nordal reasons that there is no evidence for any family saga completed before 1250 containing poetry composed by the compiler himself; they wouldn’t dare do such a thing. If poems are sometimes misattributed, there is no reason to doubt the compiler’s good faith (xiii–xiv). Anyway, the lacunae appear only in M, where W and K have neither the announcements nor the presumed poetry. Thus either some witnesses have dropped the announcements and the lacunae because there was nothing there, in which case the author remembered Egill had composed something here but never managed to get it in, or the lacunae belong to a later text, it is a copyist, not the author, whose would-be authorship is in question. This would have been the M copyist, since the suspicious stanza 21 is found only here. The various attestation of stanza 23 leads to further questions regarding what poetry belongs in the saga, and the more so with regard to the long poems, whose attestation varies greatly between witnesses. They are all embedded in the narrative, however, even if Arinbjarnarkviða is not specifically part of an episode (xiv–xv).

§2 The Poetry and the Saga Cites a weird study by Magnus Olsen, who transliterated early poetry into runes and came to the conclusion that these works adhere to numerical patterns. This is true also of the two stanzas which Egill carves into the níðstöng. Nordal does not believe anyone has the authority to quarrel with this expert of runology (xviii–xix).

Runhent is a metre not attested before Skalla-Grímr and Egill; it is the form of Hǫfuðlausn. The form, the first to use interlinear rhyme, was a great innovation. Various conjectures as to the origin of this metre are discussed, but it is pointed out that literary innovations are rarely ex nihilo, and that Egill (!) would have encountered rhyme in Latin or other Western traditions (xix–xx). Nordal now turns to the question whether Hǫfuðlausn was indeed composed in the circumstances narrated in the saga. The alternative he considers is for him to have composed it ahead of time, with the intention of visiting Eiríkr; to arrive at this possibility, Nordal studies the circumstances of the shipwrecking in some detail (xxi–xxv).

§3 Sources Even where Egla episodes seem fantastic or embellished, they “doubtlessly” have their origin in long-standing oral tradition, in which it differs from other texts of the same genre; Borg had a continuous line of educated men who could have carried on the tradition (xxv–xxvi). Various individual episodes are here discussed as they relate to other sources: the Finnmark expeditions (xxvii–xxviii), the royal material (the author is very familiar with the konungasögur, xxviii–xxxi), Landnámabók (xxxi–xxxvi).

§4 Chronology Although the Egla compiler does not count in years AD, he sets up a careful chronology both internally and with reference to better-known events of history (xxxvi). However, few of the externally attested events are dated with complete certainty. The dating of early Norwegian reigns still relies on calculations based on medieval anecdotal evidence, though attempts have been made to come to a more reliable methodology (xxxvii–xxxviii).

The English events are the easiest to date. The Battle of Vínheiðr shares key variables with the Battle of Brunanburh of 937, and Vínheiðr translates Wendune, an alternative name for the location in Anglo-Saxon sources. However, the brothers’ participation in this battle does not concord with the traditional chronology of events, as Eiríkr is usually thought to have given up the Norwegian throne in 935 [and the brothers move to England to escape him]. Three views exist that attempt to explain this incongruence:

  1. The Battle of Vínheiðr is a different battle altogether;
  2. The brothers fought with Athelstan in a different battle, around 926, which was in later retellings conflated with that of Vínheiðr–Brunanburh;
  3. The brothers did fight at Brunanburh, and the chronology in Egla is off.

Additional, generally discarded views include redating the Battle of Brunanburh to 927 and accepting that Egla is purely fiction and should not be taken as an authority on history (xxxix–xl). The Anglo-Saxon sequence of events is narrated (xl–xlii). Nordal believes that the Anglo-Saxon dating of Brunanburh is indisputable, and that the events in Egla have survived through initially oral tradition among people who had no awareness of the Anglo-Saxon written sources and were not influenced by them; oral tradition of this kind is bound to be a blend of fact and misinformation (xlii). The following pages serve to support this view (xliii–xlv) and refute Finnur Jónsson’s view [that the events concern an earlier battle] by pointing out that

  1. Athelstan is known to have taken Norsemen into his service after 934 but not before;
  2. The annals speak of the presence at Brunanburh of one Syngrin, leader of the wiccii (hwiccas); Whistler thinks this is a mistake for Skalla-Grímsson, leader of the wicingas;
  3. Egill’s poetry provides details of individuals and deaths at the battle which accord with events at Brunanburh, as well as geographical information (xlv–xlvi).

If this is accepted, the saga’s chronology has to be adjusted, including the date of Eiríkr’s move to England. The traditional chronology puts eleven years between Vínheiðr and Egill’s visit to Eiríkr’s court in England, yielding 948 for the latter event. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle reports that King Eadred raided Northumbria in that year because Eiríkr had become king there. This is the first time Eiríkr is mentioned in Britain; he is mentioned again in 952 and 954, when he was killed. It seems he was in Western Europe for no more than seven years (xlvi–xlvii). Egill’s visit to Eiríkr’s court (948) benefits from the historical context. Eiríkr’s compliance with Arinbjǫrn’s wishes is explained by the precarious nature of his reign, which rested on the fleeting support of the Northumbrians (xlvii–xlviii).

Þórdís Þórólfsdóttir was born just before Þórólfr and Egill went to England, and she was later married to Grímr Svertingsson. Her chronology makes most sense if she was born in 936, in which case she was of the same age as her husband, and not in 925 (xlix). Similar considerations apply to Egill’s children (xlix–lii). This section closes with a convenient chronological table of events in Egla (lii–liii, reproduced in paraphrase here).

§5 Provenance It is generally agreed that Egla was composed in the Borgarfjǫrður region. Nordal zooms in on chs 80–4 for evidence of this, reasoning that the level of detail makes clear this was written by someone from this region. He knows Mosfell well but describes it to those who don’t, though he assumes everyone knows Krumskelda. Since the text must derive from oral narratives about these affairs, which would have been preserved best among the Mýramenn at Borgarfjǫrðr, it is clear this is where the author was from (liii–liv).

Dating the text is harder. Manuscript evidence puts the terminus ad quem at about 1230, since the oldest MS fragment, θ, dates to about 1250 and is not the author’s copy (lvi). Although the narrative does not centrally deal with individuals living after the eleventh century, it does mention Skapti Þórarinsson in connection with Egill’s bones. Skapti is listed in the Melabók fragment as the sixth direct descendant of Egill and must have been born in the late eleventh century. He is mentioned in 1143 and may have lived long after. Egla seems to have been written after his death, i.e. after 1150, but it does not prove the author knew him personally (lvi–lvii). Lexical and narrative borrowings provide no unambiguous evidence for a date of composition (lvii).

Sturla Þórðarson had Egla at his disposal when he wrote his redaction of Landnámabók, which dates Egla to before 1250 [or 1280 according to others]. Heimskringla was assembled in or shortly after 1230. Whether or not Egla was a source of Heimskringla, at least it seems it is no younger than that work, or it would have used it instead of older and less detailed sources. If the Egla author can be shown to have known the saga of Haraldr hárfagra which Snorri also used, this would indicate a date after 1200, since the author of Ágrip did not know it, though if Ágrip was composed in Norway that need not mean anything. Although these considerations lead to no certainty, they do suggest the saga was written in the first quarter of the thirteenth century (lviii).

Nordal now goes into a discussion of style, arguing that a saga’s author, defined as the first person to put the entire product down in writing, always leaves a stylistic mark on the material (lviii–lx). As conflicting accounts of the same events between different sagas demonstrate, oral tradition is not as reliable as some would have us believe (lx–lxi). The individual mark of the author is once more emphasized (lxii–lxiii). This discussion leads into a discussion of schools of literary production and the milieu in which Snorri operated; in his work, the northern and southern schools are said to have met and become a third school, that of Borgarfjǫrðr (lxvii). All this leads up to the argument that Egla was written by Snorri (formally addressed in the next section), since it demonstrates a great deal of learning and design, deftly bringing an understanding of history and a knowledge of other written sources to the task (lxvii–lxx).

§6 Authorship While Snorri has been claimed as author since the early nineteenth century, Björn Ólsen came to a detailed argumentation in 1904 in twelve points:

  1. The author was a Mýramaðr;
  2. The saga’s great interest in Skalla-Grímr’s settlement and Tungu-Oddr’s power was to no-one of greater interest than to Snorri, who possessed the goðorð of these two families;
  3. The many similarities between Egla and Heimskringla include their dating;
  4. Egla expressly uses poetry as historical sources;
  5. Egla and Heimskringla are similarly structured;
  6. Both works use similar styles of narration;
  7. The saga author is interested in portraying ancient customs and culture;
  8. The saga author knows his early Norwegian history;
  9. The saga author knows his geography;
  10. He emphasizes the practical nature and industriousness of the Mýramenn;
  11. The saga shows a special interest in Skalla-Grímr’s descendants, of which Snorri was one;
  12. Gunnlaugs saga contains a reference to sǫgn fróðra manna which seems to cite Egla, and Snorri was called inn fróði after his death.

Nordal in his book on Snorri was more cautious about the connection between Snorri and Egla (lxxii). Wieselgren rejects all of Ólsen’s arguments and more, and argues that Snorri could not have written or compiled the saga. Nordal uses the present introduction as an opportunity to revisit the question.

Nordal agrees with Wieselgren in rejecting most of Ólsen’s arguments (lxiii). Ólsen has reiterated his views in a separate article in which he furthermore points out that the phrasing láz at síðu is unique to these two texts (lxxiv). Nordal believes the chapter on Ketill hœngs’s settlement, including any errors, was not authored by the compiler but taken from preexisting genealogy lists; Wieselgren believes this material was incorporated because it was of general Icelandic interest, but Nordal knows of no comparable digression in the other family sagas that deals with settlement in another district. Snorri, with his Rangárvellir ancestry, was the likeliest person to incorporate this material (lxxiv–lxxv). The poetry in Egla is no positive evidence of a connection, but its handling and the compiler’s comprehension of the verse befits Snorri, which is more than can be said of the verse treatment in many a saga, and similar arguments can be made for the organization of the material and the author’s understanding of geography (lxxv–lxxvi).

Wieselgren’s arguments against Snorri’s authorship include different representations of events between Egla and Heimskringla, but Nordal believes Snorri could have followed the traditional views in Egla and then tried to come to a new understanding of how events relate in Hkr (lxxiv–lxxvii). Wieselgren places great emphasis on the difference in characterization of Haraldr hárfagri and Hákon góði. Both are generous and righteous in Hkr but vengeful in Egla (lxxvii–lxviii). Wieselgren breaks character here when he stops emphasizing the autonomy of oral tradition and instead insists that if Snorri were the author, the text would have reflected his respect for the Norwegian kings. Nordal points out that the descendants of Skalla-Grímr had little reason to approve of royalty, and whoever was the author would not only have written for this audience but also had to respect his sources (lxxviii). The discrepancies between the two texts can largely be explained by their different perspectives (lxxviii–lxxxi). The θ witness has to be close to the archetype and may well be a direct copy of it. Comparison between M and θ shows that the language of the former is more concise and polished, whereas the latter is older and more original. Only once does M add any words to the text of θ (svá beint), and this may well stem from the archetype (lxxxii–lxxxv). M is estimated to be 5–10% shorter than the archetype, which refutes Wieselgren’s argument on the basis of style, where the brevity of Egla (but really of M) played a central role (lxxxiii–lxxxvi). His argument that the subjunctive is more frequent in Snorri’s works than in Egla likewise is less powerful when the other MSS are considered, and his argument that at for er sets Egla apart from Snorri’s works is also refuted with reference to the other MSS (lxxxvi–lxxxvii).

Wieselgren furthermore uses Sievers’s metrical analysis to conclude that one source of Egla was a Norwegian. This conclusion is based on the identification of the style as prosimetrical and thus relies solely on M and is easily debunked with reference to the other MSS. The objections raised against Snorri’s authorship are thus mostly bunk, and what objections remain fail to take away the considerable probability that Snorri is the author (LXXXVII–LXXXVIII). Nordal points out that there is no direct evidence even that Hkr is Snorri’s, but that as a guiding hypothesis this identification works well for both works (lxxxviii–lxxxix). He adds a few points of his own:

  1. Egla and Snorri’s kings’ sagas represent the same stage in saga maturity;
  2. we know of no other works produced in Borgarfjǫrðr at this early time, and Snorri governed it as both a goði and a scholar;
  3. The geographical horizon of Egla is that of Snorri;
  4. Dialogue in Egla serves to explain behaviour by reference to past events, much as it does in some of Hkr;
  5. Snorri’s capacity for seeing both sides of an issue is evident not only in Hkr but also in Egla;
  6. What external references we have to Snorri’s literary achievements fit well with his having written more sagas than Óláfs saga and Hkr (lxxxix–xcii).

Nordal disagrees with Ólsen’s view that Egla was written before Snorri left Borg in 1206; the work shows a mature craftsman at work. Snorri’s first journey to Norway (1218–20) was a major part of his development, and it is the early years of the fifteen years that followed that Nordal believes Egla to have been written, before Óláfs saga helga (xciii). Nordal does not think Snorri wrote it with the intention of increasing the fame of the Mýramenn; instead, he approached the task with the same mindset as he did the kings’ sagas, just with different sources (xciii–xciv).
