[M]öðruvallabók mid-14 Only two leaves missing; base text (xcv–xcvii)

author: McDougall, Ian
title: Discretion and Deceit: A Re-Examination of a Military Strategem in Egils saga
publication: The Middle Ages in the North-West
abstract: A well-informed, sceptical essay dismissing the many attempts to identify the site of the Battle of Brunanburh using the topographical descriptions of the Battle of Vínheiðr in Egils saga. Adduces historical and literary parallels for the sham truce and some more distant analogues to the tent ruse (notably a ship ruse in Josephus), but the takeaway is that “while it is hard to imagine how incidental topographical details of the battle-site could have survived through centuries of oral transmission when so many other details concerning the battle of Brunanburh have been completely garbled in Egils saga, it is quite easy to see how, as a very necessary part of the account of a stock stratagem, such details would be handed down as an integral part of the story” (131).

author: Scragg, D.G.
title: Napier’s ‘Wulfstan’ Homily XXX: Its Sources, Its Relationship to the Vercelli Book and Its Style
abstract: Conveniently listing up to two sources or parallels for each thematic section in Napier XXX (HomU 27), sets out to demonstrate that the vast majority of them can be traced back to the Vercelli homilies or a collection very much like them.

author: Whitbread, L.
title: ‘Wulfstan’ Homilies XXIX, XXX and Some Related Texts
abstract:
Studies the transmission history of these late composite homilies.

For Napier XXIX, summarizes the conclusions of Becher 1910 and Jost 1950, who divide the homily into four main parts, followed by a conclusion.

  1. (134.11–136.28) General admonitions, relying on the introduction to the Confessionale [Pseudo-]Egberti, while relationships between the homily, the confessional, and two Old English poems surviving in CCCC 201 (An Exhortation to Christian Living and The Lord’s Prayer II);
  2. (136.28–240) has two rhetorical questions on the importance of avoiding sin and hell;
  3. (140.3–141.25) a soul-and-body episode, derived from Vercelli IV (HomU 9) and Ecclesiastical Institutes/the Canons of Theodulf (HomU 55);
  4. (141.26–142.21) an exhortation to strive to avoid hell; likely borrowed from An Exhortation to Christian Living, while its ending is reminiscent of various OE poems but especially of Blickling IX (348–53).

Napier XXX has been analyzed by Becher, Jost, and McIntosh, and is far more complex in its reliance on sources than Napier XXIX. Three main sections are

  1. (143.7–144.28) General admonitions, ending with amen. Thought by McIntosh to be in Wulfstan’s style except for 144.9–15, which nevertheless cover a theme popular with Wulfstan (353–5);
  2. (144.29–147.11/150.23) includes three passages derived from OE poetry (An Exhortation to Christian Living and further, unrecorded poetry; McIntosh has pointed out that this section includes material from Vercelli IX and XXI, while Becher and Jost identified an exemplum from the prose Solomon and Saturn (354–6).
    (147.12/–149.31) is similar to Vercelli IV (HomU 9, Ecclesiastical Institutes/Canons of Theodulf (HomU 55) and Napier XLIX (HomS 40.1, itself reliant on Vercelli IX [HomS 4] and Blickling IX);
  3. (150.23–152.6) has echoes of Napier II and other Wulfstanian material (356–7).

Though their organizational style makes clear these texts are not Wulfstan’s, they may still share a compiler. Examples demonstrate that both not only use similar styles of borrowing, but also similar borrowing interests (e.g. OE verse), and that XXX builds on a sentence from XXIX (358–62). “It seems highly probable that they were compiled at Worcester” (362). The named poems used for these texts were composed about 975 and maybe at Canterbury, and it is hypothesized that these soon began to circulate with other poetry and used by Benedictine authors who composed Vercelli XXI, the Confessionale Egberti, the prose Solomon and Saturn, and the Benedictine Office; later, about the time of Wulfstan’s death, some of the material was reworked into the two texts here under investigation (363–4).

author: Bestul, Thomas H.
title: Continental Sources of Anglo-Saxon Devotional Writing
abstract: On the tradition of prayer books.

author: Finger, Heinz
title: Untersuchungen zum Muspilli
abstract:
The work divides into seven thematic discussions: Elias’s battle; the impossibility of kin-assistance on Judgement Day; the Judgement and Carolingian juristics; criticism of contemporary juristics; ON múspell(r); the adoption of OS mûdspelli in ON; vernacular poetic culture.

In his section on the kin-aid line (pp. 73–88), Finger expends most of his space discussing contemporary institutions like kin-help and the kin-oath, but eventually takes the position that really the line should be regarded only in the light of the patristic tradition in which Grau has pointed out parallels (but not the Pseudo-Augustinian, Pseudo-Isidorian, and Pseudo-Bedan ones).

author: Grau, Gustav
title: Quellen und Verwandtschaften der älteren germanischen Darstellungen des jüngsten Gerichtes
abstract:
Sets out to demonstrate the influence of Ephrem the Syrian on the Muspilli, but in the service of this task spends most of his space discussing Ephram’s influence on OE poetry (specifically Cynewulf), and some on Otfrid and the Heliand. This is one of the earliest works to adduce Ephram as a source for medieval Germanic literature.

For Muspilli (219–), Grau asserts that it is beyond doubt that Ephrem the Syrian’s homily De cruce (as it is known in its Latin translation) was the source of lines 31–301, while lines 1–30 are probably based on his homily beginning “Sermo in eos, qui in Christo” (221). Accordingly, Grau’s discussion of the poem is line by line, with a column per page dedicated to Ephram’s text. For line 57 (the kinsmen/muspilli-line), prints two passagess from Ephrem (the second is from De paenitentia) and notes that Pseudo-Chrysostom has a similar passage (241).

See also Guntermann, Ehrismann, Von Unwerth, Bestul, and Lendinara.

author: Unwerth, Wolf von
title: Eine Quelle des Muspilli
publication: Beiträge zur Geschichte der deutschen Sprache und Literatur
abstract: Although Grau has proposed Ephrem’s homilies De cruce and Sermo in eos, qui in Christo obdormierunt as the sources for nearly all of Muspilli, Guntermann and Ehrismann have countered that Ephrem was only an indirect source, with homilies by Eligius of Noyon and Caesarius of Arles forming closer analogues (349). This essay instead proposes the OE Christ III as the central source. It is also pointed out that the kinsmen-line (Msp 57), for which Grau cites a third text by Ephrem [i.e. De penitentia], has an analogue in the text by Pseudo-Chrysostom which Grau adduces as an analogue to Ephrem’s text, but which is also a source for Christ III, though it does not survive in that text. This passage, along with another that fails in the OE poem, should therefore be assumed to have been part of Christ III originally (357–9).

author: Guntermann, K.
title: G. Grau, Quellen und verwandtschaften der älteren germ. darstellungen des jüngsten gerichts
abstract:
Though the book reviewed and the review itself concern themselves chiefly with Anglo-Saxon eschatology, the value of the review consists mainly in the fact that Guntermann debunks Grau’s theory that Ephrem’s works are the central sources for almost all of the OHG Muspilli. This discussion is found on pp. 408–15.

By pointing out that homilies by the Eligius of Noyon (c. 588–658), attested in eighth- and ninth-century MSS, and Caesarius of Arles have stronger parallels for certain parts of Msp than does Ephrem, Guntermann makes the case that the reliance on the latter is indirect. Caesarius seems to rely on Eligius for the relevant passages, and as a homilist he was strongly dependent on Ephrem. The parallels are found in various places, especially in lines 74–102; line 57 is not paralleled. Analogues with the OE Christ III are briefly noted, and it is suggested that they must go back on a common source (413).

See further Von Unwerth, Ehrismann, Bestul, and Lendinara.

author: Ehrismann, G.
title: Quellen und verwandtschaften der älteren germanischen darstellungen des jüngsten gerichtes von Gustav Grau
publication: Anzeiger für deutsches Altertum und deutsche Litteratur
abstract:
Concentrating primarily on Grau’s argument concerning Ephrem’s influence on Muspilli, argues that this influence existed only sporadically and indirectly.

Summarises Grau’s argument for OE poetry: Grau considers Cynewulf the poet of Beowulf and considers Ephram his favourite author; a reconstruction of the relative chronology of Cynewulf’s works then serves to illustrate the poet’s spiritual development. As sources, Grau adduces Ephrem, IV Esra, Pseudo-Chrysostom, and De die iudicii (184–5). An illustration of Grau’s methods for Elene demonstrates how utterly made up the connection between this text and the proposed sources by Ephrem is (185–6). Ehrismann positions himself more subtly, however, when he states, “und doch hat der verfasser, wie ich glaube, durch die eingehnde verwertung Ephraems sich ein großes verdienst um die kenntnis der grundlagen der ags. litteratur erworben; nur ligt das gemeinsame zwischen Ephraem und Cynewulf nicht so sehr in den einzelnen gedanken als in der lebensanschauung” (186–7). The sentiments expressed in both groups of texts is similar because it is Christian, but the particular form is different: Ephraem expresses himself with a stoic, ascetic condemnation of pre-conversion life, while the OE poems have a greater interest in bewailing personal mortality in sentimental tones (187).

Grau rejects an Anglo-Saxon origin of the Heliand, but then points out many parallels between this text and Christ, Guthlac, and The Phoenix; these he understands as reminiscences that follow naturally from the general influence OE had on OS verse (187–8).

For Muspilli, the author adduces two main sources: Ephrem’s [Sermo] in eos qui in Christo obdormierunt for lines 1–30, and De cruce for the remainder. The first may be rapidly dispelled, as Ephrem doesn’t even have a battle between angel and devil. Augustine’s De symbolo has more parallels with Ephrem’s sermon, and this is the text in which Muspilli is embedded in the manuscript. The first part of Muspilli is a vision ultimately based on the Vision sancti Pauli and thus with biblical roots; Ephrem’s text likewise is rooted in Scripture (Mt 5:25; 188). Specific supposed echoes of Ephrem are tested and often found wanting (188–90). “Nach solchen erwägungen kann ich nur zu dem schlusse kommen, dass im ersten teil des Muspilli Ephraem nicht benutzt wurde”; instead, post-Augustinian, post-Gregorian homiletic culture at large has inspired the work; this culture may well contain traces of Ephrem. A second sphere of influence is the more specifically German homiletic tradition, which seems to have been coloured by vernacular tradition (190). Guntermann has adduced Eligius and Caesarius as closer verbal analogues to Muspilli than Ephrem; Caesarius’s homiliary was the most important such document for the early Middle Ages, and therefore far more likely to have influenced the Muspilli poet; Ephrem would have been an indirect source at best (190–1).

Where Grau sees echoes of Ephrem in the second part, these may sometimes equally well be read as direct biblical echoes (sometimes they echo the Bible more closely than they do Ephrem), or indirect biblical echoes through any patristic source. The two judgements, for instance, derive from a pre-Ephremite source that made it into Latin through Augustine’s De civitate Dei and from there into the Pseudo-Augustinian homily De symbolo; this poem was very influential on eschatological depictions. This poem is neglected by Grau, but at least as likely a source as Ephrem (191).

The battle between Elias and the Antichrist is not found in Ephrem. Grau misunderstands the passage as though it were a single account in which Elias wins, but the poet is clearly juxtaposing two different reports with opposite outcomes. Since the first of these is a duel, it is of non-ecclesiastical origins (192). Grau assumes this episode derives from the OS Genesis, with which it shares some short phrasal parallels, but in fact the two are very different in content; if anything, the OS text could have derived from the narrative represented in the OHG; the likeliest solution is that the two derive from a common source (192–3).

For the eschatological imagery, Grau adduces further texts by Ephrem, but these are also found in the sybilline acrostic transmitted via Augustine; two elements (trees and rocks) are absent from both these potential sources (193).

For line 57, Grau proposes three Ephremite sources. The first uses the verb assistere, which means not “help” but “serve”, and the context is wildly different, so this one is bunk. The other two passages proposed certainly bear some connection to Muspilli, but more patristic research is needed to come to a definite understanding of this connection (193–4).

Grau usefully points to Wulfstan’s Be domes dæge for line 60, a source which itself seems to go back to Mt 5:22. Either way, this line belongs to the poem’s vernacular elements (194).

Grau correctly adduces a Pseudo-Augustinian sermon for lines 63 to end. This passage is far closer to Ephrem than the preceding; indeed, this connection is closer than that between Muspilli and the Eligian/Caesarian parallels Guntermann adduces, though in some points the reverse is true (194–5). Ehrismann’s concluding statement: “Nach diesen erörtungen kann ich nur zu dem schlusse kommen, dass Ephraem, wenn auch sein einfluss auf die abendländische geistliche litteratur nicht gering gewesen sein mag, doch nur in beschränktem maße und lediglich für einige teile des Muspilli den ausgang gebildet hat, und zwar vor allem für das jüngste gericht (v. 73 ff); dass für die übrigen verse des zweiten teils einzelnes aus seinen schriften stammen kann, dass der erste teil aber ganz unabhänging von ihm ist; dass er jedoch nirgends die unmittelbare vorlage bildete, sondern dass dies eine lateinische predigt oder, weniger bestimmt ausgesprochen, die lateinische predigtlitteratur war.” Some conjectures about the poet follow: he was a monk, not a seminarian, as Grau thought. Grau claims Otfrid used Christ, Guthlac, and The Phoenix; Ehrismann defers to Grau’s expertise for this opinion (195).

See further Guntermann, Von Unwerth, Bestul, and Lendinara.

author: Pakis, Valentine Anthony
title: Studies in Early Germanic Biblical Literature: Medieval Rewritings, Medieval Receptions, and Modern Interpretations
abstract: A series of otherwise unrelated studies of biblical literature in OHG, Gothic, OE, ON, and OS, with a heavy Stand der Forschung-character. Contains a useful overview of source analyses of Muspilli.

author: Bostock, J. Knight
title: The Wessobrunn Prayer and the Muspilli
publication: A Handbook on Old High German Literature
abstract:
A general introduction.

Observes (giving specifics) that the dialect of the Muspilli is predominantly Bavarian, but with significant exceptions reminiscent of Alemannic and South Rhenish Franconian; refers to Van Delden for further specifics (136–7). The etymology of muspilli is discussed: contextual readings suggest a person representing the end of the world (137–8), while the most probable etymologies are world-/mouth-prophecy/destroyer; Krogmann’s “destruction (or destroyer) of (or by) the mouth” is considered the least likely of these, while two of the other configurations are linguistically improbable unless it is accepted that it was borrowed from OS;.this leaves “pronouncement about (the fate of) the earth” and “ ‘destruction of the earth’ or (appellative) ‘destroyer of the earth’ ” as the most likely options (139–40). The general opinion is now that the word is of pagan origin and was converted for Christian use (as per Braune; 140).

A synopsis is given (140–1). Considers the poem’s internal contradictions and the question whether Elias or the Antichrist wins the battle (141–5). Source criticism is discussed (145–). Baesecke has pointed out significant ortographic differences between lines 37–62 and the rest of the poem, favouring distinct origins, which he specified as Ellinhart (whose works are dated 814–21) or another St Emmeram scribe for the main body, and Anamot (writing 890–906) or a contemporary from Regensburg for the middle section; he dated the MS to c. 890 (146). Metrical and stylistic differences are also described (146–7). Many other scholars maintain that the poem is a single work (147–8).

Authorial aim is discussed in conjunction with source analysis focussing on Apc and Mt 24.29 (148–9), while some parallelism with the Hildebrandslied is noted (149). 4 Esdras is mentioned but claimed as a text of widespread Western influence (specifically the fifteen signs of the end) rather than a source (149–50). Battle, signs, and Judgement combined naturally in Western tradition, and Muspilli stands firmly within the Christian tradition, based as it must be on homilies or commentaries. There is no reason to doubt the poem’s unity (150).

The theory of a strophic original is discussed (150–1) and contrasted with more recent views that the poem is unified in intent; among other things, the interest in helfan (which carries a legal sense) has been adduced to this end; the ability of kinsmen to help in paying the legal penalty for given offences may shed light on line 57 (151–2). This situation raises a number of questions of legal interest, such as whether he had a judicially trained audience in mind (152–4).

author: Lendinara, Patrizia
title: ‘frater non redimit, redimet homo…’: A Homiletic Motif and its Variants in Old English
publication: Early Medieval English Texts and Interpretations: Studies Presented to Donald G. Scragg
publisher: Arizona Center for Medieval and Renaissance Studies
abstract:
Identifies the homiletic motif “no aid from kin”, in which it is stated that every man will be judged according to his own deeds and will receive no aid from relatives, in a number of OE texts. Among the homilies, Lendinara has found HomU 9 (Vercelli 4), HomU 55, HomS 44/33, HomU 27, and HomM 8, leaving out only the HomS 41 and the briefer HomS 4 (Bodley 340) instance; however, she also points out a less verbatim member of the tradition in Wulfstan’s Sermo Lupi ad anglos (67–74). She claims an analogue exists in Seafarer 97–102, points out the parallel in Muspilli 57, and notes another in Otfrid’s Evangelienbuch (74–6). As sources, she claims Ephrem (or whoever was the author of the Latin Ephrem-texts) for HomU 9, HomU 27, and HomS 44; for HomM 8 she claims either Pseudo-Augustine or Pseudo-Isidore; and the remaining homilies, as well as The Seafarer, she thinks may simply take their cue from Ps 48:8–9 (“frater non redimit…”): this passage receives extensive commentary in the West Saxon Prose Psalter, which Lendinara claims match the various OE attestataions of the motif in wording. She also mentions (Pseudo-)Cyril of Alexandria as evidence that the motif was widespread, but concludes that the Psalm is more likely as a source than the Greek text (76–8 and passim for Ephrem). Lendinara then turns to Anglo-Saxon legal tradition to demonstrate the importance of kin-help in law (cf. Finger) and asserts that the motif serves to make clear that the earthly aids do not exist in the hereafter (78–9). Adds that additional functions were a promise of gender and lay/cleric equality, and sees some significance in enumerations of kinsmen and limbs (79). At various points, Lendinara discusses the significance of the co-transmission of this motif with the ubi sunt, which she believes serves to contrast earthly goods and aids with their absence on Judgement Day (72–3; see further 68, 79).

See also Grau, Guntermann, Ehrismann, Bestul, and Von Unwerth.

author: Schmidt, Margot
title: Irdisches und himmlisches Gericht im althochdeutschen Muspilli und bei Ephraem dem Syrer

author: Steinmeyer, Elias von
title: Muspilli
abstract: Key critical work on Muspilli: a critical edition with detailed notes on readings, an extensive deck noting other scholars’ readings, annoyingly inline and italic bibliography, and equally italic commentary.

author: Bestul, Thomas H.
title: Ephraim the Syrian and Old English Poetry
abstract:
Refutes the old notion, first spread by Cook and then taken to extremes by Grau, that Ephrem the Syrian influenced Old English prose or verse, though the Old English texts it studied are all verse, namely Christ III, Elene, and Guthlac, in which the greatest influence has been claimed. Part of the difficulty is that previous scholars have used postmedieval translations from the Greek, though even those are too different from the poems under study to warrant any influence. More than half of the article, however, is an impressive account of manuscript evidence and evidence of Ephrem’s spread to the west. A common claim is that he reached England from Visigothic Spain via Ireland, though it is more likely to have reached England from Gaul. The school of Theodore and Hadrian is considered, as are prayer books with supposed Ephremite connections. A useful article.

See also Grau, Guntermann, Ehrismann, Von Unwerth, and Lendinara.

author: Delden, Rudolf van
title: Die sprachliche Gestalt des Muspilli und ihre Vorgeschichte im Zusammenhang mit der Abschreiberfrage
publication: Beiträge zur Geschichte der deutschen Sprache und Literatur
abstract: Though written to support the idea that Muspilli was entered into its MS by Louis the German himself, provides useful and, to my knowledge, the most extensive orthographical analysis of the text, dating part of it to the very early ninth century.

author: Sims-Williams, Patrick
title: Thoughts on Ephrem the Syrian in Anglo-Saxon England
publication: Learning and Literature in Anglo-Saxon England: Studies Presented to Peter Clemoes on the Occasion of his Sixty-Fifth Birthday
abstract: Some of the texts in Anglo-Saxon prayer-books were influenced by the Ephremic corpus, including some of the opuscula deemed authentic by Bestul. A Spanish connection is not proved or necessary.

author: Jakob Benediktsson
title: Some Observations on Stjórn and the Manuscript AM 227 fol
abstract:
This article was originally conceived as the introduction to a facsimile edition of AM 227 fol. It opens with codicological and palaeographical details of this codex, a witness to parts of Stjórn I and III. (7–16). Of its illustrations it is observed that Selma Jónsdóttir has proved artistic influence from fourteenth-century English psalters (8). Many leaves seem to have been removed to serve as book covers (8–12). The title Stjórn was attached to the MS by 1588 (12). The volume’s fifteenth- and sixteenth-century marginalia provide no direct evidence of provenance (15–16).

The MS was written by two scribes, A (1–59rb) and B (90rb [for 59rb?]–end), though B wrote a few shorter passages in the A-range, demonstrating that they were contemporary collaborators, as is also evident from their co-occurrence in other MSS. Three illuminators/illustrators have been identified by Guðbjörg Kristjánsdóttir (16). Hand A is found widely elsewhere; B in a few MSS (16–20). A worked in the north; Þingeyrar has been proposed (20). It must have come to Skálholt either immediately after its production or at a later time; it was not produced there, as some have held (29–1). The important point is made that since these same scribes produced three known copies of Stjórn, suggesting a business plan of sorts (21).

Given his output, it seems A had a long career. His script shows more variation than B, which may further reflect the timespan of his career. Both scribes use norwegianised spelling, but that need not mean they were Norwegians. Some distinguishing features between the two are noted (22). A is generally dated to mid-C14 or a little later. He seems to have learned his spelling before mid-C14. (e.g. no svarabhakti), but some later features suggest many of his works are of later date. He seems to have produced Codex Wormianus in the 1340s, and AM 227 thereafter, but probably not after 1375. The general opinion is therefore probably right in dating the MS to “about 1350 or a little later” (23).

Stjórn comes in three parts:

  1. Genesis 1–Exodus 18 and extensive commentary, mostly from Peter Comestor and Vincent of Beauvais; commissioned by King Hákon V Magnússon (1299–1319) (Unger 1–299);
  2. Exodus 19–Deuteronomy; mostly a condensed translation, almost no additions or commentary (Unger 300–495);
  3. Joshua–Kings; text and “modest” amount of exegesis (Unger 3495–654).

AM 226 contains all three parts, with II a fifteenth-century addition; 227 contains I and III; 228 has III. AM 227 leaves the adjacent pages of I and III empty, perhaps anticipating a later addition of II. AM 225 is a direct copy of AM 226 but predating the addition of II. Fragments survive in AM 229 fol. I and NRA 60A, which Unger occasionally consulted for variants and emendations. The hand of AM 226 is associated with Helgafell; this MS has been dated to c. 1360–70 (25). AM 226 and AM 227 differ considerably despite their close relationship (25–6).

AM 228 is the oldest copy and Unger’s base text, supplying from 227 and 226 where necessary (26). Stjórn III material is widely attested in Icelandic MSS (27–8).

The Prologue names the Scholastica historia and Speculum historiale as the principal sources for explanatory material, and red rubrics mark the inclusion of such material. Non-exegetical passages include a lengthy one on geography seemingly based on the Speculum historiale and Etymologiae; the story of Asenath; Moses’s expedition against the Egyptians; and the testaments of the patriarchs (these last three from Speculum historiale. Further sources include two composite homilies and various named authors, most of whom reached the compiler via HS and SH, though there are also separate references to Augustine’s De Genesi contra Manichaeos. The biblical material mostly appears in paraphrase or elaboration. The compiler may well have used “an earlier [presumably ON] biblical translation” (29).

The Prologue indicates that the point of the work was to provide lections for non-saints’ Sundays. Early on, there is occasional indication of the chronological framework conceived, as the ages of the world are referenced and homilies for specific Sundays are introduced (30). The incompleteness of Stjórn I is not explained, but Hákon’s death may have caused it (30–1). Selma Jónsdóttir has cast doubt on the authenticity of the prologue (31–2). Peter Hallberg has pointed out similarities in the style of Stjórn I and Bergr Sokkason’s works, but “we have as yet no detailed study of the work’s diction and syntax.” (32).

Orthographical grounds have been adduced to date Stjórn II to the thirteenty century, but this argument is not convincing. However, its style and diction does suggest an early-thirteenth century Icelandic context for its production (33). Certainly a passage in Stjórn III seems to acknowledge an older translation as one of its sources (34).

Peter Comestor’s Historica scholastica was completed in the 1170s and received papal approbation in 1215; if Stjórn II uses this source, it is unlikely to predate the thirteenth century. Though claims for earlier productions have been made, they are unconvincing (34–5).

Stjórn III uses Chronicles, Honorius Augustodunensis (Imago mundi and Speculum ecclesiae, HS, and Richard of St Victor’s Liber exceptionum; references occur to Jerome in his capacity as Bible translator (35).

Stjórn III is likely to have originally begun with Genesis; a fragment of Genesis exists that resembles it in style; an Exodus fragment also has been claimed to derive from the same scriptorium (35–6). A connection between Stjórn III and Konungs skuggsjá is evident, but there is disagreement over which came first, while the possibility of a shared sources has not yet been seriously considered. KS is generally dated to 1250x1260. Stjórn III has sometimes been attributed to Brandr Jónsson, who may have spent time in Norway in the 1250s. What is certain is that KS and Stjórn III are contemporaneous. The latter must have been composed in Norway, whether or not by an Icelander (38). A convenient summary of the development of Stjórn appears on p. 39.

author: Wolf, Kirsten
title: Brandr Jónsson and Stjórn
abstract: A detailed study that eventually concluds that Brandr Jónsson did not produce Stjórn III.

author: Simek, Rudolf
title: Die Kosmographie der Stjórn
publication: Altnordische Kosmographie: Studien und Quellen zu Weltbild und Weltbeschreibung in Norwegen und Island vom 12. bis zum 14. Jahrhundert
abstract:
[For his general information the author had access to Astås, which should therefore be assumed the more useful source.]

The geographical excursus in Stjórn is by far the longest geographic text in Old Norse, while also the most deeply rooted in latinate tradition, having received the smallest amount of Scandinavian influence (249). Simek oddly calls Stjórn II “der vermutlich jüngste Teil” of the three (250). An interesting point in Simek’s introduction of the textual history is that the different placement of the rubrics suggests that the shared exemplar would have had them in the margins. Marginal rubrics are not found in Old Norse MSS, but they are common in Latin encyclopaedic works (250–1).

Lists as sources for Stjórn I

  • Peter Comestor’s Historia scholastica;
  • Vincent of Beauvais’s Speculum historiale;
  • Isidore of Seville’s Etymologiae;
  • Bede’s historiographical and computistical works;
  • Honorius of Autun’s Imago mundi;
  • Augustine (Simek mentions De civitate Dei);
  • works by Caesarius of Arles ascribed to Augustine;
  • Gregory the Great;
  • Konungs skuggsjá;
  • Barlaams saga ok Josaphats.

Like other bibles historiales, the translation/paraphrase is broken up by the introduction of encyclopaedic, historiographical and theological sources. The compiler is often prompted by thematic keywords to illuminate the concept in question by his other sources (251).

The compiler furthermore mentions Josephus, Philon, Methodius, Lucretius, Plato, Pliny, Lucanus, Ovid, Pythagoras and Augustine by name, sometimes referencing even the book and chapter of a work used. In many cases, however, it should be expected that the compiler knew these authorities only via SH, HS, or perhaps florilegia. Although works from several of these authors are attested in Iceland, their influence on Stjórn is highly doubtful; the references to Lucretius, Pliny, Plato, and Pythagoras are surely spurious (253). Indirect referencing is sometimes clear from the MS rubrics (253–4). On one occasion, the compiler refers to the author of SH as “brodir Jacob” instead of Vincent of Beauvais, suggesting he may have thought it was written by Jacobus de Voragine or Jacobus de Vitriaco (254).

Following SH, the excursus describes Asia, Paradise, and India, the last of which prompts a marvels-episode from IE (254–5), following which he continues with SH-material. Here he cites Gallust, but Simek cannot find a source there. IE is again used for cinnamon and a bird, and perhaps for the flora of the Holy Land. At Scythia the compiler again departs from SH to use IE (255–6). Some omissions of SH-material are also pointed out (256–7). Europe and Asia are described following SH, including the description of Scandinavia, which is surely less detailed and less correct than the translator’s own knowledge. Only Constantinople receives the additional mention of its ON name; a similar second title is mentioned for Achaea; and Thessalia receives a mention of St Paul. The centaur is given more elaboration, and further animals are brought in; IE is used for some trivia about sheep. When describing Crete, the Latin name Creta is used, not the ON name Krít. IE is used for the rivers of world history (257). Similar slight Isidorian additions and linguistic-geographic peculiarities are pointed out for the rest of Europe. An insight of the compiler’s own is added when Diomedes is described: the compiler claims that Diomedes and his men have turned into birds for wounding the goddess “Gefjon”—interpretatio germanica for Aphrodite. The reference signals his knowledge of Homer, since Vergil does not detail this episode (258).

In the description of Africa, the basilisks prompt the introduction of external material; likewise the monkeys, dragons, and struthiones of Mauretania require elaboration. This stems from IE, except for the monkeys, which must derive from an unknown source (259). Further marvellous peoples and snakes are inserted from IE, although Pythagoras and Ovid are cited for the snakes; the section on the rhinoceros is expanded using IE, and indeed expands on IE. A section on ants is added, and the reasoning that antipodes cannot exist given what Augustine says, namely that all men are descended from Adam, goes beyond what SH says (260–1).

Simek agrees with Astås that the geographic excursus is not an interpolation but forms part of the structure of the text, since it agrees in style with the rest and MSS are attested from shortly after the work’s conception. Its function is stated as pointing out the most important countries and what is rare or remarkable about them (261–2).

author: Bekker-Nielsen, Hans
title: Caesarius and Stjórn
publication: Saga og språk: Studies in Language and Literature
abstract:
Although Caesarius is never mentioned by name in ON literature, he is commonly used as a source. The Stjórn compiler misattributes three of his assertions to Augustine; all derive from Sermo 199 (38–9). Unger thought the style of this chapter suggested it was borrowed from a pre-existing ON translation (39–40).

Leading up to the first Caesarian borrowing is a passage taken from Gregory’s Sermo 16 and shows verbose elaboration of the source. The first Caesarian borrowing is elaborated on to such an extent that the likeness is easily missed. The second passage contains some repetition likewise, which is attributed to the fact that it was written for oral delivery (41–2). Two excerpts from Gregory’s Sermo 5 and Sermo 9 separate the first Caesarian borrowing from the second, again in a more verbose style than the original. Passages from Gregory’s Sermo 23 and Sermo 32 separate the second from the third Caesarian excerpt, which contains two neologisms (42–3).

A postscript expresses the author’s doubt as to the authenticity of the prologue following Selma Jónsdóttir’s study (43).

author: Astås, Reidar
title: Et bibelverk fra middelalderen: Studier i Stjórn
abstract:
This edition has now been superseded by the digital second edition.

The most extensive contextual study of Stjórn to date, this work, especially in its first volume, feels a little simplistic in its representation of medieval conventions and sometimes explains things that really do not need explaining, such as the function of a prologue. Its thesis is that Stjórn I was conceived by a single compiler to stand in the tradition of the Bible historiale; it furthermore proposes that this compiler would have had a Dominican background given the close connection between the King and the mendicant orders. Volume 1 discusses the work’s scholarly reception before introducing the cultural background, for which it emphasises the close connection between mendicant orders and the Norwegian crown, as well as educational connections between France and Scandinavia. It introduces the traditions of compilations and florilegia, translations, and the bible historiale, then discusses the main sources of Stjórn I:

  • Peter Comestor’s Historia scholastica (HS);
  • Vincent of Beauvais’s Speculum historiale (SH);
  • Isidore of Seville’s Etymologiae (IE);
  • Durandus's Rationale;
  • Jacobus de Voragine’s Legenda aurea;
  • and Augustine (sources include De Genesi in Manichaeos, De Genesi ad litteram, and De civitate Dei (explicitly cited, though Astås notes on p. 476 that there is no reason to assume direct influence)).

The remainder of volume 1 discusses the textual situation of Stjórn (230–369).

Volume 2 contains the real meat of the study, discussing the version of the Vulgate Bible used by the compiler; the compiler’s use of HS, SH, IE, and other sources; the work’s place in the tradition of the bible historiale; innovations and editorial policies; and theology. Although this volume comes to useful generalisations about the compiler’s use of sources, there is no attempt at a systematic or exhaustive index; instead, examples are listed, and chiefly in the endnotes, which accordingly take up as much space as the text body. The sections into which the chapters are divided are very brief and general in nature, even if they make a few useful observations about the compiler’s use of his sources. The only exception to this pattern is the chapter on the text’s reliance on the Vulgate, which juxtaposes many passages of StjI to corresponding phrasing in its sources, for which the author claims to have found more sources than Kirby. The volume concludes with a summary in dreadful English, which only adds to a study that between its amateuristic typesetting, typographical errors, sentences that end in mid-air, text blocks whose relationship to the main text is not explained, and at times rather simplistic depiction of medieval culture feels rather wobbly. Nevertheless, this is a useful resource for its discussion of the sources of Stjórn I and its place in European religious and literary culture. The most noteworthy sections are those in volume two; below are some findings.

Astås reports on a detailed comparison of biblical passages against a wide range of Vulgate redactions and concludes that the language corresponds most closely to the Ω group. However, inconsistencies exist which may be explained by the assumption that the scribes of AM 226 and AM 227 corrected readings against their own copy of the Vulgate. There is no close correspondence to the Vetus Latina (371–83).

The section “Bibeltekst 2 og bibelreferanser” provides sources for countless indirect and cross-referenced Bible quotations, ostensibly comprising more matches than Kirby. Sources include De Genesi contra Manichaeos, SH, HS, Rationale, Gregory’s homilies, IE, and Caesarius (384–435).

Two fragments of Bible translations exist in AM 238 fol. and Stockholm, Perg. 12 fol. IV. The former appears to be based on HS and there may be a relationship with Stjórn I which is not further analysed. Much the same conclusion is drawn concerning the second fragment; Astås joins Kirby in the conclusion that there is no immediate dependency of one text on the other (436–7).

The longest chapter is “Kildebruk og redigering” (455–590, though half of this space is taken up by endnotes). Though the compiler spends the first 18 pages (of Unger) breaking up his Bible text into short snippets with extensive commentary (as was customary in twelfth-century works such as HS), he then switches to larger units, a style more characteristic of the thirteenth century and modelled on Augustinian commentaries (455). In the later style, the introduction and context often precedes the Bible text, which may be condensed to make way for the logical structure of the argument, or expanded for clarification or harmonisation. Stylistic changes may seek to counter the monotony of the Vulgate, but more independent retellings are rare (455–6). Nevertheless, the compiler prefers a faithful representation of the Bible narrative over the condensations of HS, although he does not give Scripture a different editorial treatment from the remainder of his material, exhibiting less reverence for Scripture than the Franciscans; Scripture in Stjórn I does not have the same sacramental quality (457). Having said that, the compiler is less keen to condense Bible narrative than he is with the commentary. All this is in line with European bibles historiales (457–8).

In his discussion of HS (459–67), the author emphasises that the Vulgate, not HS, was used as the guiding source, and that where HS is used the compiler substitutes Vulgate for its Bible renderings (460 and ff.).

SH has served as a structural model in its use of books and chapters, its model is followed in the inclusion of a geographic section, and SH and Stjórn I share many of the same sources (V, IE, HS, De Genesi ad litteram. But unlike Vincentius, the compiler had only a small library at his disposal and was thus forced to rely heavily on a smaller number of sources (468). He ranks his sources by authority as follows:

  1. the Vulgate;
  2. Augustine, whom he regards without scepticism;
  3. HS
  4. SH
  5. IE

The function of StjI as of SH is that of a moral compass, and the two share other aims, such as instructing against heresies (469; shared characteristics more generally 468–72). A specific borrowing is the phrase nunc redeamus ad historiam (470–1). The many similarities suggest that the compiler has read Vincentius’s plan in his Apologia actoris and used it for his own (472).

IE is the only Isidorian text used in StjI; for longer passages the source is often acknowledged in rubrics or inline, but the larger number of borrowings is silent. He had direct access to the source, even where his plan follows HS or SH, as he sometimes substitutes IE-material for SH-material (473). The inclusion of IE-material is often prompted by keywords in the compiler’s running source. The geographic digression is particularly rife with such inclusions (cf. Simek), but even outside that section there are some 140 borrowings in StjI (474). IE is used only where necessary; if the compiler’s other sources treat the same material, he uses them, suggesting that he considered IE a handbook and supplementary source, especially about flora, fauna, and natural phenomena (474–5). His frequent use of the work makes clear that he had it available to him throughout the drafting process (475). While several of his references to Augustine are taken straight from HS or SH, he has added in references of his own, as well as shorter and longer excerpts from De Genesi contra Manichaeos and De Genesi ad litteram; often material is used that combines the two appear. Although the compiler makes reference to De civitate Dei multiple times, there is no reason to believe it was a direct source (475–6). Augustinian works are clearly used as supplementary material, when other sources are lacking, to corroborate other texts, and to offer spiritual readings of things and events; but the compiler avoids Augustine’s allegorical and speculative material, instead seeking out factual material (476 and see further 477). Rationale and Legenda aurea are discussed only very briefly (477).

Distinguishes between monastic and scholastic readings of Scripture, the second being more theoretical and aimed at the harmonisation of distinct authorities. The first, historical sense of the Bible is claimed as good Franciscan practice; Hugo of St Victor sought to promote allegory, but a range of twelfth-century representatives including Peter Comestor raised the profile of the literal reading.StjI follows the scholastic tradition, and with Peter Comestor prefers the literal reading, though the concept of nonliteral interpretation is mentioned (591–3).

author: Kirby, Ian J.
title: Bible Translation in Old Norse
series: Publications de la Faculté des lettres
abstract: Argues that no substantial part of the Bible was ever straightforwardly translated into Old Norse.

author: Astås, Reidar
title: Et bibelverk fra middelalderen: Studier i Stjórn I
abstract: This second, electronic edition supersedes the first; see there for a summary.
