author: Astås, Reidar
title: Noen bemerkninger om norrøne bibelfragmenter
abstract: After describing some late MS copies and various fragments of Stjórn (125–9), describes three fragmentary Bible translations independent of Stjórn (129–31). Goes into further detail for one of these, AM 1056 IV, qo. The language of this fragment points to eastern Norway, specifically Trøndelag (131–3). The fragment translates passages of 1 Sam 22–8, skipping some of the episodes of lesser importance for the overarching narrative but expanding what lines it does include (134). Part of this narrative is found also in Konungs skuggsjá; that version is closely dependent on that in Stjórn. Where these two differ, AM 1056 qo never agrees with Konungs skuggsjá. These are nevertheless close enough overall that they may rely on the same source, but the perspectives differ and similarities are superficial. In some places, the fragment adds material not found in the Vulgate or in Stjórn, some of which refers to material outside the scope of the fragment, suggesting that it derives from a translation of a larger Bible section (134–5). The fragment and Stjórn read like independent translations of the Vulgate, the fragment being a closer translation in terms of diction (135–6). Where the reverse is true, this is due to greater conciseness on the part of the fragment (136–7). In some matters of style including this conciseness, the fragment resembles the other fragments mentioned (on pp. 129–31) more than it does Stjórn. Even though those are linguistically Icelandic, they may be copies of the same model (136).

author: Jakob Benediktsson
title: Stjórn og Nikulás saga
abstract: Since a “Nikulás saga” is twice referenced in Stjórn, it has been assumed that the commentary must postdate Bergr Sokkason’s Nikulás saga. However, this reference is copied from the Latin of the Historia scholastica and thus refers to a version of the Latin vita (7–8). The second reference is on the mountain Chimera and derives indirectly from IE; the geographical passage comes from SH, with which Stjórn shares the same unusual form “Veseuus” (8–9). But here, the reference to the vita of Nicholas occurs only in Stjórn, not in SH. The author proposes that the geographical section may have been interpolated into a Latin version of the vita which both Bergr and the Stjórn compiler knew (9–10). Where the later Nikulás saga (“II”) and Stjórn I overlap, it is clear that they are different translations of the same model; there is no direct connection between the two Norse texts (10–11).

author: Haugen, Odd Einar
title: Om tidsforholdet mellom Stjórn og Barlaams ok Josaphats saga
abstract: Argues persuasively that Barlaams saga borrows passages from Stjórn III, not vice versa. With this conclusion, the biblical work can be dated to the time before 1257, when Hákon Hákonsson úngi, who translated Barlaams saga, passed away.

author: Stefán Karlsson
title: Saltarabrot í Svíþjóð með Stjórnarhendi
abstract: Demonstrates that Gjerløw’s “Swedish” Psalter fragment is in the first hand of AM 227 and thus Icelandic. Suggests that this scribe produced manuscripts for the Norwegian market.

author: Bagge, Sverre
title: Forholdet mellom Kongespeilet og Stjórn
abstract:
Agrees with Hofmann that the Stjórn III-compiler (himself) incorporated quotations from Konungs skuggsjá into his text, and that the greater divergence from the Vulgate found in Ks may be explained by the compiler’s aims with his text (163–4). The justifications for capital punishment in the material from 2 Samuel fit in naturally with the context and philosophy of Konungs skuggsjá, so they are likely part of the original structure of that work. That by itself is not sufficient evidence that this is where the Stjórn compiler got his material, as this justification is common in the Church Fathers and scholasticists, including Honorius of Autun whose Elucidarium existed in Old Norse and must have been known to the compilers of both Konungs skuggsjá and Stjórn (165). Better evidence is to be had from the episode where David punishes Isboset’s murderers. Here, the Ks compiler changes David’s words, having him speak of “dróttins svík ok níðings verk” where the biblical accusation is of killing an innocent man in his own house. The point of this modification is to underline the importance of loyalty to one’s lord. StIII speaks of both killing an innocent man (here their brother, by a misunderstanding of filii as nominative plural) and it uses the verb níða, thus using elements from both the Vulgate and Ks accounts (166). Because of the mistranslation, StjIII cannot have the information that Isboset was the lord of the two murderers from its Latin source; it must have it from Ks (167).

The David and Saul-episode, which demonstrates that a sinner’s intent may make a difference to his guilt and punishment, is of crucial importance to the aim of the material in Ks, reflecting on how a king is to judge (167–8). A synopsis of the episode shows its point, that God saw that the humble David and the overbearing Saul had different natures and had to be judged differently (168–70). Though the long episode may feel like a digression, it is carefully crafted and structured along thematic lines (170–1). [incomplete]

author: Ganz, David
title: Knowledge of Ephraim’s Writings in the Merovingian and Carolingian Age
abstract: A useful overview of early medieval manuscripts of Ephrem’s works, as well as early mentions of him by Defensor et al.

author: Pattie, T.S.
title: Ephraem the Syrian and the Latin Manuscripts of ‘De paenitentia’
abstract:
Studying nineteen of the c. 90 extant Latin manuscripts of De paenitentia and at least one in Greek, concludes that the text’s 45 or so twelfth-century witnesses divide into at least two textual families, one English family that shares certain readings against the others. The main differences are listed, and a full translation is provided.

The author believes that De paenitentia is was originally composed in Greek and thus not by Ephraem.

author: Wright, Charles D.
title: The Old English ‘Macarius’ Homily, Vercelli Homily IV, and Ephrem Latinus, De paenitentia
publication: Via Crucis: Essays on Early Medieval Sources and Ideas in Memory of J.E. Cross
eds: Hall, Thomas N., Thomas D. Hill, and Charles D. Wright
abstract: Demonstrates that both HomU9 (Vercelli IV) and HomU 55 (the “Macarius homily”) derive substantial portions from Pseudo-Ephrem’s De paenitentia. Reasons that the chain of transmission must have gone from De paenitentia to HomU 55 (in an earlier, nonextant version) to HomU 9. The relationship between the OE texts has generally been assumed to be the reverse, since HomU 55 is more concise; this essay suggests that the HomU 9 homilist had expanding tendencies.

author: Jones, Leslie Webber
title: Cologne MS. 106: A Book of Hildebald
abstract: Analyses the form and content of Cologne MS 106, often identified as Alcuin’s present to Arno described in one of his letters; this would make it a product of Tours. Jones hypothesises that it was instead produced in Cologne, because although toponyms from the Cologne region are badly spelled in the topography of Gaul on fols 71v–72v, their German names are given as alternatives (35). [PS: Of course given that these are 21 scribes of various schools, the Cologne affiliation of one scribe means next to nothing.] He then tests this hypothesis by investigating the scripts and abbreviations, which generally he disassociates from Tours without always specifying an alternative affiliation; hand N he calls Insular (possibly an Irish scribe with work experience in an Anglo-Saxon scriptorium on either side of the channel, 46 and note 3, and note 1 on p. 49; the abbreviations are a mix of Anglo-Saxon and Continental, 47–8), as also Q (49). Evidence from abbreviations again suggests a place other than Tours, but here Cologne is identified as a possible match (52). More Cologne-specific is the list of works known to have been written at Cologne, whose Jones compares to those of 106 (without, however, mentioning which scribes; Bischoff in his Katalog (item 1919) dismisses this argument summarily with “Querverbindungen zu Kölner Hss. fehlen”). (52–7). The comparative material allows a dating to Hildebald’s stewardship (791–819) or slightly before (57). Abbreviations are again adduced to corroborate this connection and a date of about 805 (57–61).

author: Cross, J.E.
title: Ubi sunt Passages in Old English: Sources and Relationships
abstract:
Discusses fourteen instances of the ubi sunt topos in OE texts and their Latin sources, with special attention to Isidore’s Synonyma, often deemed the ultimate source. The relevant passages was reproduced by Defensor in his Liber scintillarum and accordingly the closest OE translation is the interlinear LibSc; another text deriving also from Liber scintillarum is HomU 16 in Cotton Tib. A III (25–9). Sfr 82–3 “derives from the same ultimate source,” and possibly the surrounding lines as well (29). This is insufficient evidence to call Isidore the direct source of Sfr; indeed, the phrasing “swylce iu wæron” suggests an intermediary; at any rate the poet draws on the homiletic tradition (29–30). Cross considers the closely related readings in Napier XLIX (HomS 40.1 according to CCCC 421 and 302 alongside Bodley 343 and Vercelli X; Napier XXX (HomU 27) depends on the Pseudo-Wulfstanian HoMS 40.1. Bodley 343 proves a valuable independent witness as compared to HomS 40.1 (30–1). In this group, only the sequence of elements betrays the Isidorian origin, not the syntax; the OE account is also considerably expanded (31–2). Jost thought the ubi sunt here was extrapolated from a single sentence in HomU 55; this text may draw on Isidore, but it is not the source of HomS 40.1 (32–33).

HomU 55 relies heavily on the Pseudo-Augustinian Sermones ad fratres in eremo 69 and (for its ubi sunt) 68. HomM 8 is based on a variant of this text, the Pseudo-Isidorian Sermo 3, a version of which is printed in Migne. HomM 8 includes both Latin and an Old English translation; the Latin is “undoubtedly copied from the source.” This source could not have been either of the Pseudo-patriarchs alone. A third Latin variant must be posited as a source for HomM 8 (33–4). The same holds true of HomU 55 (34–5). HomM8 attributes the ubi sunt to Augustine; the Sermones ad fratres, of course, circulated under this name too. The Pseudo-Isidorian text, meanwhile, contains an attribution to Augustine, making clear that this text was not by Augustine and could not be held to be so. Since HomM 8 is closer to Pseudo-Isidore than to Pseudo-Augustine, the Augustinian attribution in the OE must be an addition. Given the proposed relationship between the texts [i.e. a third version alongside Pseudo-Augustine’s Sermo 68 and Pseudo-Isidore’s Sermo 3 was the source of HomM 8], the ubi sunt may be understood to derive from Isidore’s Synonyma; this conclusion follows from some further details such as the fact that the three synonyms for “leader” occur in the same order between the Synonyma and HomM 8, while neither Pseudo-Augustine nor Pseudo-Isidore follows this detail, and the fact that HomM 8 follows the Isidorian similes of passing shadows and dreams (35–6).

Another source of OE attestations of ubi sunt is Caesarius of Arles’s De elymosinis, but the relevant passages occurs with slightly different wording in Sermo 66 ad fratres as well. This channel was used for HomU 3 and perhaps Blickling 10 (HomU 20) (38). Sermo 58 ad fratres is the source of an instance in Blickling 8 (HomU 19), itself apparently the source for HomS 6. This last text is drastically abbreviated, as is its version of the motif (38–9). This strand is significant because Sermo 58 has not ubi sunt but ubi abierunt, a likely source for the OE pattern hwær com(on), represented by “hwyder gewiton” in Blickling 8 (39–40). Cross cannot identify the sources of the motif in Blickling 5 (HomS 17), Vercelli 4 (HomU 9; this text of course depends on HomU 55, see Wright), and The Wanderer (40). Cross criticises Kershaw’s argument that some OE instances of ubi sunt do not derive from the Latin; clearly even these last three instances mentioned ultimately depend on Latin models (40–1).

author: Saak, E.L.
title: The Sermones ad fratres in eremo
publication: Creating Augustine: Interpreting Augustine and Augustinanism in the Later Middle Ages
abstract: Discusses the creation of the Sermones ad fratres in eremo as a collection and and as subgroups. Deals only with the original 35 sermons contained in the Collectanea Sancti Augustini of Jordan of Quedlinburg, most of which are of the fourteenth century though one goes back to Caesarius of Arles, another is twelfth-century, and two more are authentic Augustinian texts. They were collected as an Augustinian collection in the 1330s or 1340s. Disappointingly, Saak never picks apart the Maurist preface detailing their sources; indeed, he seems to have read it only through Migne’s reproduction. The later additions to the collection, including the sermones 58, 66, 68, and 69, which were used by Anglo-Saxon compilers (see Cross), are never mentioned. Neither this author nor anyone else seems to have asked what this “Germanense nostrum aut simile quoddam exemplar” is which the Maurists mention.

author: Remley, Paul G.
title: Old English Biblical Verse
abstract:
A valuable study of the Junius 11 poems Genesis, Exodus, and Daniel, providing an unprecedented understanding of the sources used by each. In sum, for Gn 8–22 GenA relies on a single, continuous mixed Bible exemplar that is more Vetus Latina than Vulgate; for Gn 1–7 it uses more extrabiblical sources; , though mostly produced without a known source, relies on a knowledge of Gn 3:1–8; Ex relies on the Vulgate in conjunction woth lections for the Easter Vigil in the Gelasian tradition, but its patriarchal episodes rely on the Vetus Latina; Dan retains the sequential organization of the Vulgate text but drastically recasts its narrative texture.

Remley points out that when Bede says no OE biblical verse was composed prior to Caedmon, this at least means that such a tradition existed in Bede's day, i.e. 730 is a terminus ante quem for the genesis of this tradition (37-8). He discusses the classroom as an amalgamator of variant scriptural traditions (44-5). The Junius poems appear to address readings from the Septuagint, its Theodotionic revision, the Old Latin and Vulgate redactions and subredactions thereof, but disregarding Jerome's prefaces; they also reflect traditions of certain extrabiblical matter becoming attached to particular passages in Scripture. All these are points reflected in the gloss tradition as well (47-8).

On liturgy, Remley remarks, “[b]y and large, however, the ceremonies of the early medieval eucharistic mass derive their lections far more frequently from he books of the New Testament than of the Old. The early European use of a full series of Old Testament lections, however, is well attested. Many Old Testament passages that had become familiar through such usage — including selections from Genesis, Exodus and Daniel — continued for centuries to be read out among the ‘epistles’ of the eucharistic mass. The most significant departure … occurs in conjunction with … the Easter Vigil on Holy Saturday” (Remley 78; useful footnotes are nos. 156-7). On p. 79, Remley cites a suggestion that the 56 sections of Gen–Dan would fill 8 weeks of Lent. He concludes that “a pivotal triad of readings from Genesis, Exodus and Daniel has been shown by biblical scholars to inform the structure of the Easter Vigil recitation. … All three of these passages give rise to notably amplified treatments in the verse of Junius 11” (86–7).

In conclusion to his introductory chapter, Remley concludes that “each poet will have gained access to biblical knowledge in one or more of the ways …: from an interlocutor, whether in the context of a systematic course of biblical paraphrase or in informal exchanges with other Christians; in the classroom or in private study, most probably while engaged in a programme of elementary or intermediary instruction; or in the fulfilment of liturgical and devotional obligations” (91).

[Ch. 2: The Biblical Sources of Genesis A and B]: GenA:

  • Follows the Bible closely (96);
  • Uses ”Latin-derived diction” (97); “reproduces … most of the Latin diction of Genesis I–XXII”, 96; cf. 97–8).

GenB:

  • “offers only half a dozen or so remote parallels with the phrasing of Latin texts of Genesis” (96).

GenA agrees with Vetus Latina twice as often as with the Vulgate (98–9). No complete VL copy of Genesis 1–22 survives, and no mixed redaction containing as many VL readings as found in GenA (100). There is little room to doubt that the last two thirds of GenA derive from a single, continuous Latin model (113–15). The handling of the material in GenA matches most closely the stichometry of MS Amiatino 1 (115–20).

Unlike GenA’s treatment of Gn 8–22, its representation of 1–7 contains substantial narrative disruptions and dislocations; these have sometimes been attributed to a damaged exemplar, which would also explain the insertion of GenB (120–6). The creation account introduces far more extrabiblical material than the rest of GenA (126–7). The opening of GenA resembles a Eucharistic preface, including the fall of angels, while a lot of further extrabiblical material has been adduced for the early part of the poem (126-7).

It is proposed that the material on the leaf containing pp. 9-10 originally followed pp. 11-12: this would result in a text of less displacement, but it requires that the references to male and female as well as the "grow and multiply" command are either deferred or repeated. However, the order of the binding of this quire has been widely judged correct on codicological grounds; the displacement may thus predate the surviving copy (131-6).

The jumbled flood narrative renders it likely that a change of exemplar occurred some way through. Some of the material may stem from memory of the liturgy, as the most innovative lines correspond to the verses found abridged in lectionaries for the easter vigil. Though these vary greatly, they have a tendency to share with GenA certain omissions of versicles. It seems on the whole that the flood episode is a place where the poet switched from a more strictly biblical exemplar to an indirect account or memory (136-43).

GenA’s coverage of Gn 3-5 and 8-22 relies on the same exemplar (143). The decisive evidence for a liturgical source consists in four points where the poem betrays influence from both VL and Vulgate readings of the same verse, which it is more natural to attribute to a performative setting than to the use of either two exemplars or a cross-glossed exemplar: the variety of handbooks employed in the liturgy would naturally result in mixed readings. Some limited, offhand evidence of such practice is adduced; the phenomenon is said to be especially common in Creation and Flood material (144-8).

The prohibition relies on one or both biblical accounts; the poet, though mostly working without a known source, had a first-hand knowledge of Gn 3:1–8 (157–60). The dual pronoun in the prohibition reflects Vetus Latina plurals (161–2). GenB remarkably describes the tree of life as beautiful, that of knowledge as ugly. Eve’s advertisements of the fruit are [so asserts the author on dubious grounds, PSL] “unmistakable” echoes of the VL text (162–5). Though no source has been found for GenB, many of the proposed analogues had a presence in Insular missionary centres on the Continent (166–7).

[Ch. 3: Exodus and the Liturgy of Baptism]: Bright in 1912 concluded that since Ex uses Gn as well as Ex, inserting the Flood and the binding of Isaac, it is based on Easter Vigil lections, which include the same three elements here brought together in three of its twelve readings. The Easter Vigil was mostly concerned with catechumens about to receive baptism (168–71). Scholars have repeatedly suggested that baptism is what Ex is about. The allegorization in widely acknowledged to have been known to the Anglo-Saxons, but the text itself provides no such clues (172–3). The received opinion is that Ex is based on Ex 13–14. The liturgical connection suggests instead a performative source (173–4). Some scholars have argued for a wide knowledge of Latin works on the part of the poet, including traditional etymologies. Psalms and canticles have left especially striking traces. while many verbal parallels with a wide range of biblical books have been proposed (175–8). The poet was thus “a competent Latinist” with a “deep knowledge of the Psalms” and “familiar as well with most of the other books of the Bible, including those of the New Testament”. He “participated regularly in the psalmody of the divine Office and privately fulfilled the obligations of the lection divina” (178).

Verbal parallels with Ex are generally with the Vulgate, but the specification of a southerly wind at the parting of the waves has been linked to VL and the Septuagint. (The corresponding VL line is not fully extant.) But the bulk of the text points to a Vulgate exemplar (178–86). The reference to the army containing no young or old warriors seems to rest on a misunderstanding of Vulgate “absque parvulis” (“not counting children”) (183–4). In the same way, Vulgate “armati” may have given rise to the military organization found in the poem (184–5).

Unlike the exodus narrative, the patriarchal episodes (the Flood and Isaac) seem to rely on a continuous biblical model in the form of a pure VL exemplar. The offering of Isaac has this in common with the incomplete GenA account, while the two verse texts seem entirely independent (187–8). An insertion into the binding of Isaac on Solomon’s temple relies on Moriah being the mountain on which the former event took place as well as the name of the mountain where the temple is built, but neither Vulgate nor VL retain this connection. It must derive from extrabiblical tradition (188–90). Several other details of the Isaac episode reflect VL readings (190–4). Despite nonliteral treatment and digressions, Ex follows Ex 11–14 closely and sequentially (190–4). Strikingly, the poet avoids instruction, performance, and ritual; the aim seems to be to improve the narrative flow of the Egypt–Israel tension. The first nine plagues are omitted, as well as material at the end of the sequence (198–9). The author proposes an extrabiblical source extending from plague ten to the drowning. Lists several relevant texts but warns against positing a single source (199–216). The Gelasian (Frankish-Roman) series of lectionaries is the only type paralleling the patriarchal sequence in GenA, and only in the ten- and twelve-lection type (216–23).

[Ch. 4: Daniel and Greek Scriptural Tradition]: Two sources have traditionally been assumed for Dan: a VL redaction and Canticum trium puerorum, the liturgical version of the canticle attributed to the three youths. The surviving copy of that canticle in Cotton Vespasian A. i goes back to the Greek. Despite objections (234–5), the poem’s departure from the Vulgate is marked, and remarkable analogues have been found in Greek extrabiblical tradition (231–6).

Among examples of extrabiblical content are four instances where the poet provides moral meaning to the biblical narrative (242–3). However, pride is condemned also in the Vulgate account; but in Dan the charge is extended to include the Israelites and Belshazar as well as Nebuchadnezzar, and it addresses inebriation and idolatry repeatedly (244–5). A major objection to the common binaristic view of Dan is that the vices are not contrasted with corresponding virtues (245–6). Daniel does contrast with Nebuchadnezzar as a figure of wisdom; in both the Bible and Dan these are construed as representative of their respective nations (246–7).

Three themes are shared with non-Vulgate Scripture:

  • translation imperii;
  • monotheists forced to participate in syncretism;
  • progress of Gentiles towards conversion.

The first is central, but it informed the original composition of Dn (though it is certainly emphasized in Dan in accordance with medieval tradition). Similarly with the second point (248–52). Dan’s relationship to the Vulgate is complicated and not yet proved despite many efforts. It departs from Scripture by

  • Consolidation of repetitive passages;
  • elaboration of concise allusions;
  • omitting difficulties (252–).

Dan’s style is characterized by

  • lack of imagery;
  • dynamism over static description;
  • omission of detail;
  • syntactic dynamism;
  • lack of verbal analogues to Scripture (252–3).

Omissions and consolidations respond to rhetorical doubling in Dn (253). Notably expanded is the dialogue between Daniel and Nebuchadnezzar (253–4). Dan follows the non-Theodotionic redactions in presenting a sequential and complete narrative. This contrasts starkly with its style and strongly suggests the use of a single, continuous biblical model, whether physical or committed to memory (254).

The first 32 lines of Dan are self-contained (255–8) but linked to the main text through the synthesis in both of a lot of Old Testament material (258–). [incomplete]

author: Fell, Christine Elizabeth
title: The Old Norse Version of the Book of Joshua
publication: Proceedings of the First International Saga Conference: University of Edinburgh, 1971
eds: Peter Foote, Hermann Pálsson, and Desmond Slay
publisher: Viking Society for Northern Research and University College London
abstract:
A West Norse biblical tradition must precede the fourteenth century: early Norwegian texts quote a Bible text identical with Stjórn, and there is a strong degree of homogeneity in phrasing from early quotations onwards (117). Stjórn I up to Ex 18 answers closely to the text supposed to have been commissioned by Hákon V. Thereafter, AM 226 and AM 227 diverge: 226 contains some later insertions covering Lv–Nm, after which it starts Joshua, which in 227 follows immediately upon Ex 18. Importantly, the redactions of Joshua are wildly different between the two. 226 has a unique text based on HS rather than the Vulgate; 227 follows the Vulgate directly. The final chapter again converges between the MS and is the only interpretative section found in the 227 treatment of Joshua, but derives from an unknown source (118–19). The 226 version has been assigned to Iceland; the 227 redaction has been variously assigned to Norway and Iceland. The 227 text of Joshua will here be investigated (119–20).

The start of Joshua in 227 shifts the emphasis to Joshua’s leadership and calls him hertogi, recalling Ælfric’s homily [actually two: ÆCHom II, 12 and ÆHom 21; Ælfric calls Moses this, too, in ÆCHom I] in phrasing (120). The remainder of the chapter is faithful to the Vulgate, but greater stylistic departures become apparent as the story progresses, with greater interest in drama and Joshua’s deeds taking centre stage (121).

Three episodes stand out for their treatment:

  1. Jo 19:28–39: Ælfric translates the first half closely, but then permits an adjective of empathy. AM 227 separates out the individual campaigns, dramatizes the narrative somewhat through phrasing, then in the Maceda campaign expands the account through saga idiom. The next campaign he expands in like manner (124–5).
  2. Jo 8:1–29: in AM 227, the campaign against Ai is rewritten, including the geography; in the military action, the idiom used is again more characteristic of the sagas (125–6).
  3. Jo 9:3–: AM 227 elaborates the opening lines of the covenant ruse, bringing it in line with saga style. Ælfric’s rendering is restrained, adding only the adverb gamenlice. The description of the bread and wine is much dramatized in AM 227 and the wineskins become barrels; Ælfric again translates closely but translates calidos “warm” with nigbacene in the description of the bread, like the Stjórn translator who uses nybakat. In Stjórn, the Israelites are angry on account of the treachery used rather than at the resulting situation as in the Vulgate. The conclusion of the episode gives all those involved more dignity and adds a sentence in which the treaty is formally ratified. These modifications reflect the translator’s own cultural ethics (127–30).

The AM 227 translation of Joshua relies heavily on doubling and alliteration, especially in dialogue. Ælfric does some of this as well (130–2). But the OE poetic renderings of Ex and Jdt show greater similarity, including again an adaptation of the landscape (130–4). Timmer’s analysis of the vocabulary of Judith as profoundly Germanic should not be taken too far: certain words could not be avoided, even if to us they ring Germanic on account of the bias of the surviving poetic material. Timmer’s larger point is valid: Holofernes has the elements of a comitatus, but not the order, signalling an intentional contrast with true heroic society. The juxtaposition is part of the poet’s point (123–7).

The alliteration and rhetorical style in the AM 227 Joshua and in Icelandic hagiography suggests an influence of OE style on ON religious literature, possible given the eleventh-century missionary activities of the Anglo-Saxons in Iceland and the fact that Ælfric was known there. The illustrations in AM 227 also depend on English models. The connection is not proved here but merely raised (137–9). [PSL: The question of direct influence between Ælfrician and ON translations, though implied by the pointing out of similarities early on, is not pursued.]

author: Astås, Reidar
title: Nytt lys over Stjórn II
abstract:
The most useful part of this article identifies all the passages which Astås believes may depend on extrabiblical sources and prints them along their possible sources. An important observation he makes here is that it is not always possible to pinpoint the exact source (49–53). A short discussion of diction covers the terminology around ark and covenant especially (53–6).

Regarding the author’s translation strategies, Astås observes that several exclusively Judaic and Old Covenant passages are omitted (56–7). While the translator’s condensing tendencies sometimes sacrifice narrative coherence, the omission of detail usually improves it (57–8); imagery also is often simplified or omitted, as are unfamiliar names and concepts. By contrast, some descriptions are made more detailed [PSL: where explanation is deemed necessary] (58). In some cases, material is reorganized to match ON narrative conventions or improve the order of the elements (58–9), and sometimes the Vulgate’s abstractions or general references are made more precise (59).

A number of short additions are identified, as are simple substitutions of name for pronoun (60) and a few narrative-connective clauses (60–1). More substantial are several short additions to improve the narrative sequence (61–2).

There is a tendency to be more careful of reference, especially in combination with a weakening of imagery: rather than have God devour people, he has them struck by lightning; rather than have Moses accuse Joshua of rivalry, he has him say “What are you telling me?” Other markers of tension are omitted, though not systematically so; sometimes assertions are rendered sharper (62–3). Inaccurate translations and innovations are noted; among other things, there is a more personal emphasis on Moses and his leadership, omitting references to Israel as a people (63–4), though elsewhere the opposite tendency is found. Moses’/Israel’s obedience is occasionally emphasized without model, and sometimes so is their disregard for Moses or God (65). Uncleanliness is translated as sin (65–6). The mother’s purification ritual after childbirth is modified in significant ways, presumably to match the requirements in the bishopric of Niðaróss (66–7).

An appendix lists, side by side, what sections in Unger’s edition of Stjórn II correspond to what parts of the Vulgate, with mention of where material is summarized or briefly indexed.

author: Förster, Max
title: Zu den Blickling Homilies
publication: Archiv für das Studium der neueren Sprachen und Literaturen
abstract:
The author discusses what Latin sources he has been able to identify for the Blickling homilies.

The translations in Blickling are less sophisticated than those in Ælfric: they are word for word and their content is neither added to nor subjected to critical analysis. This accords with Ten Brink’s opinion that this is no immediate product of the school of Æthelwold (179–80).

Gregory’s homiliary was used for homilies II (Greg. II), III (Greg. XVI). The translation techniques employed in these two texts are not identical, but both are more literal and complete than in Ælfric. Some emendations to Morris are proposed (180–2).

Homily VII takes a passage from the descent into hell as contained in the Gospel of Nicodemus, corresponding partly to redaction A of that text, partly to an unknown version. Some further emendations are proposed (182–3).

Homilies XVI and IV use the same unknown redaction of the Visio Pauli (184–5).

Vercelli XVI (Peter and Paul) is a strongly literal translation of the Marcellus text of the Passio Petri et Pauli, with omission of some sections. Förster uses the Latin source to guess at the text lost through cropping of the top margins (185–93).

Homily [XVI] on Michael translates very faithfully the Narration de apparitione s. Michaelis in Monte Gargano but without the slavish verbal translation style found in XV and XVIII, instead turning all subclauses into independent clauses using parataxis. The translation is not without errors. Its author was familiar with OE poetic style, visible in parallel variation, alliteration, rhythm, and the occasional poetic phrasing. These stylistic characteristics are found also in XIV (John), X, and IX (“Christ se goldbloma”), suggesting these may be by the same translator. The homily is also surprisingly close in wording to Ælfric’s rendering of the same source. This text also draws on the Visio Pauli of an unknown redaction (193–200).

Blickling [XVII] (Martin) is a free translation of excerpts from Sulpicius Severus (Vita S. Martini plus the report of his death from Epistula III, as in Ælfric) (200–1).

Blickling [XVIII] (Andreas) draws on the Acta apostolorum apocrypha. Zupitza has shown that the model must have been a very close Latin translation of the Greek. Bonnet has found a Latin fragment that answers to such a description. Förster prints them side by side and points out significant agreements between the fragment and the homily. Another, full Latin redaction agrees with the OE text in some details. The OE homily is found also in CCCC 8. Förster compares the two (202–5).

author: Gatch, Milton McC.
title: The Unknowable Audience of the Blickling Homilies
abstract:
Considers the possibility of identifying the audience of Blickling homilies IV, V, X, and XI, texts the author identifies as catechetical rather than exegetical sermons. Three of these were probably intended for Lent and Rogationtide (99–101).

BlHom 4 (also in Junius 85+86) is in Blickling assigned to the third Sunday in Lent. The surviving copies draw on early exemplars, so MS context may not tell us much about the original audience (101–2).

BlHom 4 draws on a Caesarian homily on tithing itself assigned to the feast of John the Baptist, aptly so given its relevance to the harvest (102–3). BlHom 4 refers to “se æþela lareow” as a source, but also mentions “þyssum godspelle”, perplexingly given that this sermon is without a pericope (103). After a few MS pages, it stops following Caesarius and turns abruptly to address pastoral care in a passage based on Visio Pauli and explicitly mentioning the responsibilities of the clergy, thus contrasting with the apparently general-congregational focus of the first section (103–4). The third and final section draws again on Caesarius and possibly again the Visio Pauli, but it is not discussed furthere here (104–5). “[T]he clergy, it seems were expected to make use of the text in their instruction of the layfolk.” But the overall conclusion is that the text sends confused signals about its intended audience (105).

BlHom 5 survives only in Blickling and has no clearly known sources. Like Homily 4, it refers to “se æþela lareow”, but Scragg has made unity of source less likely by demonstrating that the order of copying was different from the sequence as it stands (105–6). The sermon delivers a message of bearing the fruit of religion (105). A passage it includes about the consequences of feasting too hard (somehow a simile for hearing but not bearing spiritual fruit) may seem to refer to everyday life, but its use of the term gebeorscipe is certainly not unique in the homiletic corpus. The text thus far is thus “thoroughly conventional and without detectable local colouring”. Then there is a shift of emphasis towards the superiority of the spiritual over the physical, including an ubi sunt passage closely resembling a text by Pseudo-Basil and aimed at a monastic audience, which may reflect on the intended audience of BlHom 5 (107). Gerefan “judges” are singled out as bearing special responsibility, suggesting an audience among the governing classes, and probably, though not necessarily, a secular one. The implication seems to be that originally monastic sources were adapted for the instruction of the laity (107–8).

BlHom 10 is part of a series within the MS beginning after Easter and continuing into the sanctorale; it was probably intended for Rogation Wednesday, Ascension Eve (108–9). It warns that Judgement Day is very near, but it does so in a thoroughly conventional and undatable manner (109–10). For its concluding section on transitoriness the sermon seems to use Gregory’s homily on saints Nereus and Achilleus, modifying the contrast of the original text, which had been between the days of the saints and Gregory’s time. The result is messy and had to be cleaned up thoroughly by a later scribe. The translator certainly did not adapt the source to his audience (111–12).

BlHom 11 (Ascension) contains the 971 dating passage. The reference occurs in the observation that most of the final age of the world has now passed, although the author clearly does not advocate a strictly defined millenarianism (112–13). The text concludes with a detailed description of the site of the Ascension, identified by Gatch as a “pilgrimage motif”, which he sees also in the call to charity in the year ahead of the next year’s Ascension (113–14).

In conclusion, Gatch observes that the linguistic fact of the homilies being in English may be the most useful thing to take away from them, and even there it seems the content is not always carefully crafted to match a vernacular audience. No one specific type of audience may be discerned from the texts under consideration.

author: Tristram, Hildegard L.C.
title: Early Insular Preaching: Verbal Artistry and Method of Composition
publisher: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften
abstract:
Describes the different OE homiletic styles: plain (many the anonymous homilies) and adorned, with Wulfstan making use of an uneven distribution of metrical qualities to attain heightening of style at particular points in the text, and Ælfric in the course of his publishing life developing a metrical style and then gradually coming away from the strict poetic constraints for greater freedom, thus realizing his own style. Similar things may be found in early Irish homiletics. The Church Fathers disagreed over the use of rhetoric in homiletics; a powerful group of clerics advocated the “piscatorial” or plain style. Augustine, on the other hand, reasoned (in De doctrina christiana) that heightened style is not in itself good or bad, but it can be used for good. The sixth-century Irish cleric Columbanus followed these principles.

Alongside this discourse, Tristram defines “eclectic” homilies as more intentionally learned than mere composite homilies, and this too is already seen in Columbanus. His writings build on both learned Latin principles and native Irish verse traditions. Later Irish homiletic collections made it to the Continent, and some Irish-derived collections have survived; these are marked by literal exegesis, eclecticism of sources, quotations from Celtic Bibles and the use of apocrypha, penitential and eschatological motifs, and rhythmic, adorned prose. Significantly, all this was before the Carolingian Reform and became a powerful influence on homilies of the Auxerre type. Blickling and Vercelli are associated rather with the later Carolingian tradition; Ælfric and Wulfstan represent a long-established preaching style stripped of its heterodox qualities. An appendix demonstrates the similarities in ornamental techniques used between OE and Irish homilies.

author: Scragg, D.G.
title: The Corpus of Vernacular Homilies and Prose Saints’ Lives Before Ælfric
abstract: A meticulous index of homiliaries and individual homilies that can be dated to before Ælfric; establishes Scragg’s sigla. Notes known textual connections (variant witnesses and derivations). Concludes that the surviving ante-Ælfrician tradition is remarkable for its make-up: saints’ lives typically survive in single copies, while homilies are few in distinct number and extant in many copies. Many of these homilies independently translate the same Latin sources. Our localized information is nearly all on Canterbury. The narrow transmission of this corpus (in material, consulted sources, and affiliations) may mean that much of the pre-Ælfrician homiletic tradition survives from the southeast only.

author: Gneuss, Helmut
title: The Origin of Standard Old English and Æthelwold’s School at Winchester
abstract:
Considers first the possibility that Alfred initiated a written OE standard, and decides against it on diverse grounds including the dialectal heterogeneity of the works commissioned by him and the lexical differences between those works and those of Ælfric, which after all adhere to the standard at a later time (63–8).

The Benedictine Reform is therefore a better place to look for the establishment of a standard, also with the continuity of monastic practices in mind. Dunstan (in 940) and his pupil Æthelwold (about 954) copied Continental examples in their introduction of the Benedictine Rule. The reform really took off with the succession of Edgar in 959 and the appointment in the following years of Dunstan as Archbishop of Canterbury and Æthelwold as Bishop of Winchester, with the support of Bishop Oswald of Worcester. Since Dunstan and Æthelwold came from Wessex and influential participating institutions were there situated, the written standard that was established had West Saxon features from the outset. What is more remarkable is the uniformity in spelling, including inflectional endings and vocabulary, hiding the development of the spoken language (69–70).

A school must be behind this uniformity, and Gneuss proposes that this was Æthelwold’s school at the Old Minster in Winchester, backed by Dunstan, the primate of the Anglo-Saxon Church (70–1). Biographical details and Æthelwold’s style in his BenR and account of the Reform are adduced to support the case (71–4). Wulfstan and Ælfric were both pupils of Æthelwold’s (74–5). More specifically, a small group of Winchester texts display great lexical uniformity within certain lexical fields, as demonstrated in a range of studies from the late 1960s and early 1979s. The “Winchester words” derive from a wide range of lexical fields (75–7). The texts in question are identified (77–8). Some intermediate stages may be discerned, for instance in BenR (78). Some problems and inconsistencies are outlined, as well (78–80). The revised text of the Dialogues in Hatton 76, however, is evidence of the proposed standard, as it greatly revises the diction found in the other extant copies, which are roughly contemporary with it and represent the original text (80–1). Dunstan’s Canterbury is not as strong a candidate for the centre of the establishment of the standard because Kentish features are lacking in the texts in question, while Oswald’s Worcester was Mercian (81). Associated questions not here answered include syntactic standardization and why scribes should have held so consistently to different scripts for Latin and Old English (82).

author: Scragg, D.G.
title: An Old English Homilist of Archbishop Dunstan’s Day
publication: Words, Texts and Manuscripts: Studies in Anglo-Saxon Culture Presented to Helmut Gneuss on the Occasion of his Sixty-Fifth Birthday
eds: Michael Korhammer, Karl Reicher, and Hans Sauer
abstract:
Proposes that Vercelli homilies 19–21 and an Ascension Day homily in CCCC 162 (Tristram 3) are by the same author. Each depends closely on the homiliary of St Père de Chartres (182), and the phrasing in original sentences is similar (183). A variety of further particulars suggest the same connection (183–4). It seems furthermore that the translator preferred to vary his diction between the texts specifically where the same (specifically Latin) thought is expressed more than once, selecting different Latin models to express the same concept or else translating the same phrases differently. This confirms that these homilies (for four successive days during and following Rogationtide) were meant to be preached in close succession and to the same audience (184–6).

In the absence of repeated translations, the Latin:OE lexical correspondences are consistent. Seven lexemes are selected that occur in more than one of these homilies, and some hapax legomena in each (186–8).

The remainder of the article discusses the homilies’ transmission as a set, surviving as it does in different configurations across the two MSS. This section deals with careless borrowing and corruptions (relatively few). There is reason to believe the author of Vercelli 21 (and thus of all four) had access to a version of Vercelli 2 much like that used by the Vercelli scribe. He thus probably worked in the same scriptorium as that scribe and about the same time. Dunstan’s Canterbury (959–88) is the likeliest context (188–92).

author: Anderson, Rachel
title: The Old Testament Homily: Ælfric as Biblical Translator
publication: The Old English Homily: Precedent, Practice, and Appropriation
series: Studies in the Early Middle Ages
abstract:
Ælfric’s non-liturgical pieces are among his least studied, and OE biblical translation as a whole is often overlooked. His treatment of biblical material in these works evidences his mastery of narrative structure, but also a strong interpretative undertone that makes the narrative subservient to the point he is making (121–2).

Anderson quotes Godden’s statement that the OT appealed to Anglo-Saxons because it gave them a framework for thinking about themes of relevance to them: kingship, politics, warfare, and how these things relate to divine rulership (122). Summarizes Ælfric’s biblical corpus, and points out that OE biblical translation subtly modifies its material, for instance to downplay embarrassing moral and sexual practices connected with the patriarchs (122–3; reference is made to Menzer’s article on ÆGenPref). The importance of the OT to Anglo-Saxons has been studied much recently, for instance by Karkov who notes the presence of OT patriarchs in West Saxon regnal lists (123–4). But this essay is really about Ælfric’s shorter nonliturgical writings. It provides first an overview of scholarship as well as the texts in question (126–31); many critics comment on the contemporary relevance of Ælfric’s translations. Brookes, by contrast, is more interested in his use of Vetus Latina as well as Vulgate sources. Anderson launches her own investigation from this point, pointing out that Ælfric’s treatment of Saul and David is constructed to contrast bad kingship with good, and democracy with theocracy (131–5). Anderson also discusses Ælfric’s omission of Deborah from Judges 4, perhaps in order to streamline the narrative (136–9). The same homily containing that narrative next moves to Samson and Delilah, where it omits all the material casting Samson in a negative light, except Delilah, whom Ælfric portrays very negatively. His elision of Deborah may be understood in conjunction with the Samson narrative, as Ælfric sets the figures of Jael and Delilah up for comparison (139–42).

[A point of criticism: Anderson's claim that Ælfric selectively filters out Solomon, and barely touches on Saul and David, is premised on the understanding that his text on the Books of Kings was intended to cover "the four books of Kings (I and II Samuel and I and II Kings in modern biblical versions)" (131), but it strikes me that Ælfric's text covers the books of Kings only, with a brief callback to Saul and David at the outset as a way of contextualizing the action and centring on the matter of kingship, Saul having been anointed king by popular demand against God's better judgement (on which see also Anderson 132–3; PSL). Thus Anderson acknowledges also that the "extraordinarily truncated version of Saul's reign is obviously not intended to give the reader a synopsis of the biblical course of events" (133–4).]

author: Yerkes, David
title: The Place of Composition of the Opening of Napier Homily I
abstract:
Napier I, whose first part translates Dialogi book 4 ch. 1, survives in three witnesses, two of which were written at Worcester; one of them probably has corrections in the hand of Wulfstan, who wrote the two surviving conclusions to the text. Nevertheless, the translation seems not to have been composed there:

  1. Jost has shown that this translation is independent of Wærferth of Worcester’s;
  2. The early eleventh-century Worcester revision of Wærferth’s text is also independent of the translation in Napier I;
  3. Of the seven known Latin copies in England by the late eleventh century, the ones that are closest to Napier I are neither of the copies with Worcestrian connections.

author: Cole, Andrew
title: Jewish Apocrypha and Christian Epistemologies of the Fall: The Dialogi of Gregory the Great and the Old Saxon Genesis
publication: Rome and the North: The Early Reception of Gregory the Great in Germanic Europe
eds: Rolf H. Bremmer, Jr, Kees Dekker, and David F. Johnson
abstract:
Seeks the origins of Eve’s vision in GenB in Jewish Apocrypha by pointing out their presence in Gregory’s Dialogi. An excellent piece, though the assertion that “[Dialogi] Book IV.1 … cannot be traced to any sources but Gregory’s own texts” (165–6) is odd in the light of the long Platonic tradition from which Gregory drew his prison analogy.

Relevant to the prison analogy is the invocation of the Book of the Secrets of Enoch and Conflict of Adam an Eve with Satan, in which the first parents are banished to a “cave or prison”, where they have an encounter with Satan, who sends light into the cave in an effort to fool them into thinking they have been forgiven (167–9); in Conflict, Eve gives birth to her first four children in a dark cave or prison (169).

The essay continues with a comparison of the GenB vision and context with Gregorian thought.

author: Zacher, Samantha
title: Rewriting the Old Testament in Anglo-Saxon Verse: Becoming the Chosen People
series: New Directions in Religion and Literature
abstract: The author identifies her aim as demonstrating that Anglo-Saxon poets used Old Testament narratives to assert political theologies that were already contained in the narratives, in the process identifying their own culture as the new chosen people. In fact, the second claim only holds up for Exodus, as has been demonstrated by Nicholas Howe; the other texts discussed (Daniel and Judith) speak rather to “[their] own contemporaneous Christian audiences” (159) without singling out the Anglo-Saxons other than by the choice of vernacular. What remains is a subtle theoretical reading of the texts for such themes as the transfer of elect status (in Exodus and Daniel); holy war and just war (in Judith); and visual symbolism (in Exodus). Among the more groundbreaking discussions is the reading of the “tribal digression” in Exodus as a recognition of the transfer of chosenness to Judah (53–61).

author: Torkar, Roland
title: Die Ohnmacht der Textkritik, am Beispiel der Ausgaben der dritten Vercelli-Homilie
publication: Anglo-Saxonica: Beiträge zur Vor- und Frühgeschichte der englischen Sprache und zur altenglischen Literatur: Festschrift für Hans Schabram zum 65. Geburtstag
eds: Klaus R. Grinda and Claus-Dieter Wetzel
abstract:
Uses the fact that a Latin source for Vercelli Homily III was found only after Förster produced a text-critical study of it as a means of testing the text-critical method. Torkar demonstrates that the manuscript evidence led Förster to faulty conclusions at a number of turns. The shortcomings at the root of these incorrect conclusions are not so much Förster’s as they are inherent in the method (225–37).

Scragg, who wrote after the St.-Père homiliary was identified as a source, has occasionally made the same errors as Förster; the scope of his undertaking, suggesting a neglect of detail, is conjecturally blamed for this (241–2). More often, corrupt phrases are repaired, though not always to good effect; Torkar has plausible new suggestions for three of these (242–5). According to Torkar, Scragg’s sin is the uncritical repeating of problematic passages and solutions, as a further illustration makes clear (246–7). (Torkar acknowledges that the criticism of Scragg contained in pp. 237–47 has led away from the real aim of this paper, 247.)

Returning to Förster and the limits of the method, Torkar chooses a short homily at random and exclaims at the sorry state of the apparatus, where the editor neglects time and again to remark on noteworthy readings (247–9). Reasons that Sisam was right to state that problematic passages should at least be marked as such, thereby to offer a more reliable picture of the limits of textual criticism (250).

author: McGillivray, Morray
title: Memorization in the Transmission of the Middle English Romances
series: The Albert Bates Lord Studies in Oral Tradition
abstract: A brief, thoughtful monograph reasoning that oral transmission must have played a role in the transmission of the metrical Middle English romances. Most of the theory behind it derives from the Piers Plowman editor George Kane with plentiful reference to Jean Rychner, who worked on the fablieaus, Alison Jones, who worked on Daniel and Azarias as well as Sould and Body (Jabbour is likewise cited for his work on the latter), S.T. Knight, who worked on Sir Launfal, and A.G. Rigg, who edited De coniuge non ducenda. The argument proceeds as follows: many scribal transformations, conscious or inadvertent, are not inherently scribal and cannot be told apart from minstrel transformations (11–34). Certain types of transformation are without a doubt due to memory transfer, and if one such transformation may be identified in a text it must have passed through at least one such transfer; the strongest cases are here to be made for the displacement and repetition of material where the distance between the two passages is too great for scribal error (35–44). Examples are given from the Bad Quartos of Shakespeare. The Bad Quartos are sometimes understood as poor stenographic copies, but this author defends the view that they are memorial reconstructions by a cast member. Transpositions, anticipations and recollections of certain phrases (i.e. where they occur only once but not in their proper place), repetitions, and borrowings from other plays have all been identified by Harry Hoppe (45–57). These transformations are then identified in Floris and Blauncheflur, King Horn, The Siege of Troy, and Sir Orfeo (59–88). A further chapter identifies variants in the same four texts that do not rely on a memorization of the full text but may nevertheless be identified as memorial in origin (89–122). The conclusion returns to the difficulty of distinguishing scribal from minstrel copying, as some scribes knew their models by heart and evidence of memorial contamination exist. However, such contamination is usually highly local in nature: a scribe could not rely on memory for more than a word or two without his exemplar rectifying him. Meanwhile, the recognition that memorial transfer has taken place problematizes the stemmatic method for the texts concerned. For the literary critic, this means that the surviving manuscript witnesses should be studied in their own right, and in a comparative rather than reconstructive model (123–32).
