author: Jordan, James W.
title: Arctic Climate and Landscape ca. AD 800–1400
eds: Herbert Maschner, Owen Mason, and Robert McGhee
abstract:
An excellent review of proxy date for the Arctic/Circumarctic region for the period 800–1400, incorporating research mostly from the period 1998–2005.

The introduction is sensible and nuanced, noting the “provocative yet sometimes conflicting climate information” from this period and region, and questioning the value of longitudinal terms like MWP for local-scale investigations. Questions also the use of this term, and the generalization it represents, in general: even though this period was unquestionably “bounded by cold periods”, it is itself “not necessarily defined by increased warmth” (7). Asks whether decadal and centennial patterns can be translated into localized and temporalized conditions at all (7–8).

The proxy data is divided into types of proxy. The typical outcome of the research is that a warmer temperature or associated characteristics are recorded for part of the period under question. The higher the resolution of the proxy, of course, the more clearly researchers see a plurality of shorter highs within the period as a whole.

In his conclusions, Jordan asserts that the period saw a hemispherically asynchronous high, possibly linked to increased solar irradiation in this period (19). Contrasts between winter and summer were also greater in this period (21).

author: Coe, Kevin, David Domke, Erica S. Graham, Sue Lockett John, and Victor W. Pickard
title: No Shades of Gray: The Binary Discourse of George W. Bush and an Echoing Press
abstract: Demonstrates the effectiveness of a political rhetoric of binary opposition in a system of high mass media saturation.

author: Lévi-Strauss, Claude
title: Do Dual Organizations Exist?
trans: Claire Jacobson and Brooke Grundfest Schoepf
abstract:
Deconstructs the popular notion that social and spatial organization among American and Indonesian tribes is often dual or binary in nature by pointing out anomalies that appear when one looks for larger patterns. Concludes that “the study of so-called dual organizations discloses so many anomalies and contradictions in relation to extant theory that we should be well advised to reject the theory and to treat the apparent manifestations of dualism as superficial distortions of structures whose real nature is quite different and vastly more complex” (161).

[What Lévi-Strauss does not note is that this very conclusion suggests a tendency towards binary thinking among scholars and likely among informants, PSL]

author: Kearney, Richard
title: Strangers, Gods and Monsters: Interpreting Otherness
abstract:
Asserts that classical thinking about alterity from Plato to Heidegger regarded it as relative to the self; Levinas and other proponents of “radical alterity” have come to regard it as absolute. Accordingly, Levinas seems to reject the “ethical stranger,” the benign unknown in need of help. Kearney sets out to reconcile these two conceptions of the other (14–16). To this end he proposes a “diacritical hermeneutics” that seeks to establish a dialogue between “distinct but not incomparable selves” rather than appropriating the other (“romantic hermeneutics”) or denying the possibility of communication (“radical hermeneutics”; 17–18).

Kearney begins his discourse with a discussion of scapegoating: the sacrifice of some other for the benefit of society (23–46). In Christianity, the scapegoat is partly bestialized as an otherly demon, partly humanized as this or that current threat to orthodoxy (30). Augustine tried to resolve this contradiction by defining evil as non-being, but depictions of demons did not always conform to his theology, instead contaminating non-being with being (31). The ambiguity inherent in this Christian other explains why the history of the Church is one of continual expelling of witches and other human scapegoats. During especially trying times, such as the Medici reign, the range of groups that could be expiated grew to include more and more simple “sinners.” This did not end with the rise of secular institutions, as may be seen in the aftermath of the French Revolution (31–33; Kearne also notes that the bubonic plague coincided with a peak in the number of demon-in-hell depictions).

Kearney next outlines modern and current approaches of various disciplines to sacrifice. Anthropologists confine themselves to describing the essence of the ritual by defining the sacred and the profane (33–4). Unjustifiably also treated under the heading of anthropology are Rudolph Otto and Sigmund Freud; the former sees monsters as wholly other, agents from another dimension breaking into the human realm; Freud reads them as projections of one’s own subconscious. Kearney in this volume sets out to find a resolution for this conflict (35). He sees a “theological approach” in demythologizing critiques of sacrificial rites (35–6). It is also within this genre of discussion that the social function of sacrifice is explained as strengthening unity within the community (37). It is pointed out that a scapegoat often comes to be revered after the sacrifice, and that scapegoating continues across societies today (38). As an ideology, however, scapegoating/sacrifice fails. This social reflex can be overcome if the concepts of stranger and scapegoat can be decoupled (39).

[Ch. 2: Rights of Sacrifice] This chapter discusses the other in the Alien and Apocalypse Now Redux films (47–62). Its conclusion first brings out the author’s aim of providing society with a more understanding attitude towards its others.

[Ch. 3: Aliens and Others] Alienation and evil have been closely connected through the ages (65). However, justice is openness towards the other. Levinas sees in this extreme responsibility; Derrida concludes it mandates extreme hospitality. The practical difficulty is how to tell the benign and the malignant other apart. The author distinguishes between “other” as a respectable stranger and “alien” as the experience by strangers of discrimination. Calls for the ability to step away from binary classifications and discern between different kinds of otherness (67).

This chapter focuses on the practical approaches nation states do and could take towards others, but also delves into psychoanalytics with Freud’s notion that the rejected other is really on the other end of the divide in the divided self (73–5) and Kristeva’s development of the same idea, siding with Kant and Derrida who asserted that no stranger should be treated as an enemy. Kristeva also claims that our fear of our own mortality is projected onto others (75–6). “To truly embrace the other as our stranger is to accept a certain decentring of the ego which opens the self to the novel, the incongruous and the unexpected. . . . For if each of us can accept that we are the strangers, then there are no strangers – only others like ourselves” (77).

In the remainder of this chapter, Kearney introduces his “critical hermeneutics of self-as-other,” enabling us to judge between different kinds of other (77–82). Levinas’ main critique of Western thought is that it does not permit relations with the other as an entity in its own right, since the other is always represented from an egocentric perspective (79). Since the ego cannot in fact be left out of the process, Kearney proposes to acknowledge the self as an other, the other as another self in the sense of bearing “universal rights and responsibilities” (80). Crucial is the acknowledgement that all judgement is informed by conflicting interpretations, a complexity to which moralistic extremes cannot do justice (82).

[Ch. 4: Evil, Monstrosity and the Sublime] Summarizes historical interpretations of evil (83–100), then proposes a course of action (100–106). The function of myths of evil is to make evil bearable by supplying a plot; evil is a force beyond our control (83–4). For the scriptural response to evil, Kearney (by way of Ricoeur) distinguishes between “evil as suffering and evil as wrongdoing,” but acknowledges they are often related in biblical narratives, the same agents being transgressed by an external force and themselves culpable. What sets this genre apart from the mythological tradition is that humans question God about evil, and they frequently receive a response; where myth recounts, the Bible deliberates and in this way attains wisdom by seeking justification (84–5). Metaphysical theology as practised by Augustine is a speculative genre of discourse. Augustine reads evil as punishment for sin [well that’s a circular way of putting it of course, PSL], Augustine relegates evil to non-being and the privation of the good. This makes the focus strongly ethical and turns from unde malum to unde malum faciamus. Accordingly, this view holds that no-one suffers unjustly. In order to explain the unfair distribution of evil, Augustine had to claim that everyone is responsible, but not wholly so; evil is also done by us now that it is in the systen (85). After Leibniz, Hegel took this reasoning to an untenable extreme in which personal tragedy is subservant to an overarching logic *85–6).

Kant eventually breaks away from the speculative approach and insists on the need for a practical struggle against evil, while never giving in to total irrationalism. Yet even he had to admit there is some inscrutability to evil, and he too had difficulty finding an origin by way of reason (87–8).

A more recent, postmodern turn sees both God (or the upwardly sublime) and the monstrous as equally ineffable, and sometimes virtually indistinguishable; neither can be expressed and both are radically other. Kearney rejects the sameness of the two on the grounds that this takes away goodness from the divine. Some have argued that this makes the Holocaust a divine event because it too is unspeakable in its monstrosity (88–9). Kristeva understands the abject as a “non-assimilable alien” simultaneously attracting and repulsing precisely because it defies definition. She borrows from a long tradition having its most influential author in Kant when she describes the sublime as objectless and the abject as bordering on the sublime. She goes further when she draws a connection with the incest taboo, thus explaining the connection between the abject, perversion, and transgression: the abject rejects morality and beckons towards transgression, as is visible in the popular fascination with outlaws. In Kristeva’s understanding, evil is both Augustine’s nonentity and the other extreme, that which becomes sublime by surpassing being (89–91).

Lyotard defines the sublime as unspeakable irrespective of good or evil. Since art creates a world of its own rather than imitating nature, the sublime has its rightful plcae here, where it serves to immobilize the human subject. He connects the sublime also with the fear of impending destruction. The postmodern aesthetic sublime differs from the Romantic in that it is nothing but incomprehensibility and privation; there is no possibility of catharsis (92–4). The weakness of Lyotard’s reasoning is again that it cuts him off from real-life confrontation with evil; extreme historical evil is unspeakable, hence there is nothing more we can say about it — but that means evil has won (94–5).

Žižek claims that the good of divinity and the monstrosity of evil are essentially the same [I surmise that Žižek is speaking of the Hebrew God specifically, whom he calls “a crazy sadistic God”, PSL] (95–7). Kant would not give up the border between good and evil; Žižek does. Kearney finds fault with this because it leads to indifference [which does not seem a valid objection, PSL] and maintains too dualist a worldview, though Kearney does not do a good job of explaining what kind of duality (he mentions death:life, sublime:beauty and others; 97–9).

Among the New Age crowd, Joseph Campbell has also equated good and evil (99–100).

Kearney’s response to all this is to assert that nothing is so remote from comprehension that no response is possible, mostly because such a sublime state of affairs would rule out action [this seems petitio principii, PSL] (102–03). Suffering through evil, and catharsis, also must not be neglected: there is a passive aspect to evil (103–05). Finally, forgiveness exceeds calculation and reason. Wisdom (focused on the particularity of one-time events) and working-through are needed to achieve it. Cathartic narration can be a useful tool to attain forgiveness (105–06). An appendix discusses deconstruction and the sublime (106–08).

The remainder of the work deals with such topics as terror; Hamlet; and melancholy. Still of interest might be ch. 8, “The Immemorial: A Task of Narrative” (179–90), which studies the role played by narrative in perpetuating what has been forgotten.

author: Lévi-Strauss, Claude
title: The Savage Mind (La penséé sauvage)
abstract:
The main purpose of this book is to reject the notion that animal totemism is to be studied as an isolated and inherently meaningful phenomenon, asserting instead that it serves the equation of analogues across different planes of reality. What matters is this greater system.

Rejects at the outset the practice of characterizing the thought world of a “savage” people as simple or uncultivated by unfairly singling out some aspect of their language or vocabulary. Many examples are given where undeveloped tribes have a very detailed knowledge of some field or other. Lévi-Strauss asserts that the “usefulness” of the things known is not what leads to them being classified in the first place; it is that they are known which makes them worth classifying (1–9). Science is concerned with constructing or reconstructing order, and that is exactly what is done in undeveloped taxonomies. The implication is raised that the question whether the order thus found is objective or subjective is a constant question (1–10). It is suggested that the difference between science and magic may lie not in ignorance or illogical thinking but rather in a more unyielding demand for causation and the extending of determinism across more areas than science allows (10–11). This process sometimes makes connections that are valid or anticipate science (11–12 and further examples on 12–13). The Neolithic brought and perfected a number of crucial technologies that could only result from a long-standing scientific approach, yet the modern scientific approach was developed only very recently. The answer to this paradox seems to be that there are two distinct levels of scientific enquiry: one more abstract (our own), the other more given to “perception and the imagination.” Any system of classification is more successful than none, even if the criteria for selection have no direct relationship to the end being pursued (13–16). Myths and rituals serve to preserve observations made long ago, but the elements of myth conceived as tools are of a general nature so that they may be applied to a variety of ends (16–22). A difference between the bricoleur who deals in myth and other less rigidly scientific enterprises and the more scientific methods of the engineer are that the former works with signs and trusted tools whereas the latter works with concepts and intends to open up or reorganize his toolset (19–20). Bricolage may be defined as using earlier ends as means to a new end; accordingly, the outcome is always a compromise between the structure of the instrument set and the end, never the exact end the bricoleur had in mind, which was never more than a sketch anyway (21). Myth builds structures out of events; science builds events out of structures. These are different approaches, not different developmental stages (21–2). Art lies in between these two (22–30). Artistic creation often involves a reduction in scale or detail, presumably because to understand we divide an object up into parts, and simplifying it allows us to grasp it (23–4). Art discovers a structure by unifying at least one object and event; myth constructs an object and event on the basis of a structure (25–6). Games and rites have similar structures (30–33).

The second chapter (“The Logic of Totemic Classifications,” 35–74) uses many examples to make the point that tribal taxonomies are elaborate, and outlines some difficulties concernring the knowability of relationships between items in these taxonomies.

[Ch. 3: Systems of Transformations] Differentiation shapes life and thought in tribal societies. The existence of these differentiations may be used as a system against which to read a text from the society that produced the system (75). Key is to value the system above its content: classical ethnologists have tended to reify the content, but the system’s point was the conversion of meaning between “different levels of social reality” (75–6).

Most of this chapter consists of detailed discussions of totemic food prohibitions. Notable is the observation that the totemic representation of contrasting pairs play a significant role in the “native logic” of the Murngin of northern Australia: these systems allow them to equate significant contrasts across different planes of reality, such as season, sex, and moiety (91–4). Natural conditions and contrasts do not exist on their own but only as part of a system of human activity (94–5). Accordingly, it is a mistake to think that myths serve to explain natural phenomena; instead, they use natural phenomena as a means to explain facts of logic. Infrastructure is primary. “The poverty of religious thought can never be overestimated. It accounts for the fact that men have so often had recourse to the same means for solving problems whose concrete elements may be very different but which share the feature of all belonging to ‘structures of contradiction’ ” (95).

[Chapter four: Totem and Caste]

[Chapter five: Categories, Elements, Species, Numbers] Thus far, Lévi-Strauss has claimed that not the content of totemic representations is of primary importance, but their relationship to other practices and beliefs, whose whole constitutes an important part of native culture. Here he makes the claim that the various “levels” of classification share this characteristic: that content on each level has an analogous counterpart on another, and that the system as a whole operates through a series of contrasts between general and particular, nature and culture (135). Animal representations have no special place within this system other than being conveniently “logically equidistant from the extreme forms of classification: categorical and singular,” i.e. a species contains individuals but contrasts to others as “a system of definitions” (136).

The Sioux, Winnibago, and Omaha all divide into two moieties, but in some cases this bipartite division hides greater complexity. In all of them, the simple form representes the higher moiety (i.e. sky versus land and water, 140–2 and see Lévi-Strauss elsewhere, e.g. “Do Dual Organizations Exist?”). Warns against considering individual totems as meaningful: the list of totems has grown over time, not been planned according to a system (155). A large part of this chapter is devoted to the “problem” of proper names, designations for things that cannot be classified. Chapter seven continues the discussion of individuals and systems of referring to them.

[Chapter eight: Time Regained] Looking back across this volume, the author observes that the structure he has uncovered in native systems of classification is supported by an axis relating the abstract to the concrete and the general with the particular in pairs of contrast; where the system ends, it is not externally bounded but its function is complete (217–18). Classificatory systems are compared to language as another system of meaning, whose elements are only signs (222–3). This chapter spends a lot of space distinguishing between totemism and sacrifice. “Totemism is based on a postulation of homology between two parallel series — that of natural species and that of social groups — whose respective terms, it must be remembered, do not resemble each other in pairs. It is only the relation between the series as a whole which is homomorphic: a formal correlation between two systems of differences, each constituting a pole of opposition” (224). Aetiological myths of clan appellations are widespread globally; these are often brief and do not really function to provide an origin; instead, they invoke one in order to declare a species as marked (“stressed” in Lévi-Strauss’s terms; 230–1).

The ninth and final chapter situates the discourse in Sartres’ dialectic.

author: Lévi-Strauss, Claude
title: Dual Organization
publication: The Elementary Structures of Kinship (Les structures élémentaires de la parenté)
trans: James Hardle Bell, John Richard von Sturmer, and Rodney Needham
abstract: Describes societies divided into two moieties, and observes that organizations of this kind are found all through the world with similar configurations.

author: Thoma, Volker, and Alwyn Williams
title: The Devil You Know: The Effect of Brand Recognition and Product Ratings on Consumer Choice
abstract: Testing the validity of the recognition heuristic alongside additional information in a consumer choice setup, the known brand is chosen over the unknown brand even in case of a negative star-rating, though less consistently so and with more deliberation. The recognition heuristic thus seems to be a crucial initial strategy in decision-making, whose results are weighed against additional data.

author: Smithson, Michael
title: When Less Is More in the Recognition Heuristic
abstract: Questions the validity of Goldstein and Gigerenzer’s definition of the correlation between the “less is more effect (LIME)” and the recognition of one item in a binary set. The 2002 definition hypothesized that the LIME occurs if the probability of choosing correctly based solely on recognition (α) is greater than the probability of choosing correctly when both items are recognized (β) and these two probabilities remain constant as the number of recognized items (n) varies. Smithson demonstrates that the probabilities do not remain constant, and that LIME sometimes occurs when β > α.

author: Gigerenzer, Gerd, and Peter M. Todd
title: Simple Heuristics That Make Us Smart
abstract: A foundational volume of essays on simple heuristics. Although it puts decision-making front and centre as is typical in this field, there are also essays on memory, estimation, and categorization.

author: Berretty, Patricia M., Peter M. Todd, and Laura Martignon
title: Categorization by Elimination: Using Few Cues to Choose
publication: Simple Heuristics That Make Us Smart
eds: Gerd Gigerenzer and Peter M. Todd
abstract:
Existing models of the process of categorization in humans often concern situations with few dimensions only; multidimensional categorization processes have yet to be studied. Existing models also tend to assume that multiple cues are combined to attain a categorization, and they assume that all available cues are processed. Both these categorization rules can greatly increase processing time (237–8). Exemplar models assume that subjects compute degree of similarity between the newly encountered object and all members of all preexisting categories. Some exemplar models do factor in different attention weights, meaning attention to certain could be switched off, but these models require that the weighting remains constant for the different objects encountered within the same categorization task. Decision bound models assume that categories are bounded off in multidimensional “perceptual space” by a calculation of the mean, variance, and covariance of their members. Here too, all available cues are used, and decisions are based on a combination of all cue values. Rule-based models assume a hierarchy of rules from specific to general; the first selection criterion consists in an attempt to match the new object against a specific rule (compounding many individual cues), and if no match is found the process cascades across successively more general matching rules (238–9). A simplicity model RULEX was devised in 1994 that relied on a small set of binary feature dimensions, but their original study was limited to only two categories (239–40). Machine learning models tend not to focus on minimizing the processing burden and are thus not psychologically realistic. Neural network models rely on parallel processing and thus have no need for a “stopping rule” to cease taking in more cues. The absence of learned cues during selection affects categorization performance, but gracefully so (240). Bayesian approaches to categorization are too complex computistically to be psychologically plausible (240–1). Decision tree models rely on reducing the number of dimensions processed, but selecting the dimensions to select for often requires considerable processing power, as the selector has to rank the dimensions from most to least informative. Optimizing the processing power required in this type of model reallocates the psychologically implausible burden to the memory (241).

The authors settle on elimination models to meet the challenge of psychological plausibility. In existence since at least the early sixties, these models are mostly designed for selection and preference tasks. Their core consists in a sequence of eliminations of features, along with all the objects that contain these features. Critical is thay (e.g.) Tversky’ Elimination by Aspects relies on the minimal set of aspects required to make a decision. Models of this sort have also been used for identification. All elimination models share a need for a ranking of cues, and all share a stopping rule activated when a single category is left.

Evidence suggests that people process cues in order of their relevance to the task at hand; specifically, they prefer diagnostic cues, i.e. cues that help match an object with one hypothesis [or category] as opposed to another in a binary setup. In the model here offered, cues are ranked according to their predictive ability if used in isolation from other cues (242–3).

Studies have shown that humans use only a subset of available cues to make decisions (e.g. 24% when selecting an apartment, or 52% when scientists controlled the cue order). Significantly, people use fewer cues if the cues are highly diagnostive, suggesting that they will use fewer if they can control their order (243–4).

The authors introduce a model that is deterministic (there is a correct answer, and accuracy can be measured) and with use of generalization. Cue dimensionss are fixed and cues are processed in a fixed order, skipping preprogrammed cue dimensions where no corresponding cue is found. The elimination element consists in a contingency rule where certain categories are eliminated from further consideration when a given dimension is matched. The stopping rule is to end either when a single category is left or when no more cues are available, in which case the system resorts to guessing from the remaining categories (244). The categorization example given demonstrates that the cues are not processed in a binary true/false fashion but with a number of options befitting the set (colour ranges; woody/earthy/herby/fruity/unassignable) (244–6). Memory requirements are frugal and specific because they only store the bounds of the range of values for each cue dimension within a category — e.g. the wingspan range for each bird species (246–7). [The model’s accuracy record does not read as particularly psychologically plausible, since it was tested as an algorithm with higher resolution of measurement than the human first glance (250–3). The point seems to be it compares favourable to other algorithms, PSL.]

author: Chater, Nick, and Paul Vitányi
title: Simplicity: A Unifying Principle in Cognitive Science?
abstract:
Advances the really quite commonplace idea that simplicity is a unifying process across cognitive processes.

The cognitive system imposes patterns on sensory input. The problem of induction is that an infinite number of patterns are compatible with any finite input stream. To be adaptive, the brain thus has to select patterns that accord with reality. Two mathematical advances have helped quantify Ockham and Newton’s principles of simplicity: Shannon’s establishment of a code length for probability calculations and Kolmogorov et al.’s definition of an object’s complexity as the shortest string of computer code defining the object. In light of this, the aim of the cognitive apparatus may be defined as compressing data, where lossy compression may be permitted. Bayesian analysis, probability models, and the widespread use of simplicity in machine learning and statistics all demonstrate the superiority of simplicity as an inductive strategy. Its success with empirical data is difficult to measure because the mental representation of stimuli is as yet contested and we don’t know how accurate the cognitive pattern search function is. Nevertheless, a large number of studies are congruous with a simplicity model for cognitive pattern-matching.

author: Payne, John W., James R. Bettman, and Eric J. Johnson
title: The Adaptive Decision Maker
abstract:
A foundational work on cognitive heuristics. The work is exclusively concerned with decision-making processes. It is emphatically adaptive in its approach, suggesting that the decision-making apparatus adapts to the environment: every decision is different and thus calls for a different toolkit. The book’s central thesis is “that an individual’s use of multiple decision strategies in different situations, including various simplifying methods or choice heuristics, is an adaptive response of a limited-capacity information processor to the demands of complex decision tasks.” The strategies used are intelligent given the cognitive system’s dual aims of accuracy and economy, and thus they are predictable (2). It is acknowledged that decision-making is influenced not only by the selector’s knowledge and processing power and the variables of the task, but also by a social context (2–4).

The introduction and opening chapters are extremely useful as primers on heuristics, though the book focuses almost exclusively on preferential decision-making. An invaluable overview of decision-making strategies is given (24–9), followed by ways to characterize these (29–34) and task effects.

author: Gigerenzer, Gerd
title: Fast and Frugal Heuristics: The Tools of Bounded Rationality
publication: Blackwell Handbook of Judgment and Decision Making
eds: Derek J. Koehler and Nigel Harvey
abstract: A highly accessible introduction to the Gigerenzian tradition of heuristics. Such heuristics are fast (require little processing) and frugal (require little information; 63). Gigerenzer defines a heuristic as a process rule that exploits evolved functionality for simplification, is ecologically selected, and not a shorthand for unconscious calculated optimization (63–5, 67). Simon’s tradition of heuristics assumes bounded reality: a reality in which subjects have limited knowledge, time, and processing power (65). Introduces and explains the recognition heuristic (68–72) and some heuristic strategies and aspects in situations where the recognition heuristic does not apply (72–7). The information heuristic is used in (by this definition) a binary set containing one known object, when the criterion of interest is highly correlated with recognition: it assumes that the known object has the higher value for that criterion (68–9). Closely connected with this heuristic is the less-is-more effect [LIME]: in situations where the recognition validity (α) is greater than the knowledge validity (β), it pays to have less knowledge (69–71). There is even some evidence that groups rely on the recognition heuristic when a minority of individuals does not know the second object while the majority know both, increasing overall accuracy (71–2). Decision-making based on reasons may cycle through cue values from highest to lowest validity, stopping as soon as only one object is left; or one may tally a larger number of cue values and choose the option with more positives. Studies have shown that the majority of subjects do the former (in certain settings; 74–5). The remainder of the essay explores the heuristic selection process, heuristic robustness, and the adaptive toolbox.

author: Ferster, Judith
title: Genre in and of the Canterbury Tales
abstract:
Identifies the genre of CT as “compendium or compilatio” but distinct from other works of this sort in incorporating stories of a variety of genres (179–80). Chaucer himself uses a variety of genre terms, referring to form, narrative pattern, or content. These three elements are closely related in generic classification, yet any text may move between genres, parodying and combining them (181). Rather than just recount the tales, CT through its General Prologue and the links between the tales is an organic frame tale (Pearsall’s phrase) adding to the tales and placing them in a discursive context (181).

The narrator of CT disclaims any responsibility for inappropriate tales, a device that can only work if the tellers are fleshed out sufficiently (182). The dramatic hypothesis asserts that the tales are played out against rival pilgrims: the strong agency and knee-jerk responsiveness of the tellers thus contributes to the work’s overall structure because it yields a texture of interruption and discourse, yet with tacit etiquette (182–3). This hypothesis is limited by the unrealism of certain pilgrims delivering learned tales in high style and by the fact that not all pilgrims are introduced or introduced at sufficient length (183–4).

The social diversity of narrators makes CT modelled on the estates satire, a genre criticizing the functioning of society by illustrating how people of diverse ranks fail to fulfil their roles. Chaucer’s pilgrims, however, are too detailed to fulfil the conventional expectations of the estates satire, which deals with unindividualized stereotypes. Jill Mann has argued that even the details provided fit within social stereotypes (184). An especially powerful technique Mann identifies is Chaucer’s care to include the pilgrims’ point of view, which helps them transcend stereotype but is also used to explode expectations about estates satire: rather than leaving criticism of the characters in the hands of narrator and reader, Chaucer has the Monk himself point out his moral flaw, and the narrator agrees with him (184–5). However, the narrator’s repeated approval of crime is problematic. Donaldson has pointed out the value of counting three Chaucers: the pilgrim, the poet, and the man; the first may agree with his fellow-travellers even just to be agreeable [and even he may use irony, PSL], but it does not reflect on the opinions of Chaucer as a poet and citizen (185–6). The essay loses focus a little when it spends several pages explaining in what sense Chaucer’s satire of the Prioress is gentle, but the conclusion is once again that Chaucer here manages to transcend the format of estates satire (186–8).

The next section of the essay discusses various tales and the ways in which they break genre and expectation. It lacks clear structure (189–95).

The first part of the essay is useful to students, the second less so; it also does not cover or define the range of genres used by Chaucer.

author: Utz, Richard
title: Philosophy
abstract:
Identifies Boethius as a central influence, but points out that this does not mean Chaucer shared Boethius’s outlook; he may have used him simply to achieve his literary designs (159–64). What may have inspired Chaucer in the Consolatio is the device of an autobiographical ignorant narrator as a means of being able to address or instruct social superiors (163–4).

The essay’s discussion of other schools of thought yields little except in nominalism, which offers a valuable perspective. The Augustinian fourfold reading of Scripture could be applied in some places (e.g. a tropological reading of the pilgrimage), but such a reading cannot be pushed too far: Chaucer’s literary output serves art and cannot be reduced to didacticism. Where Chaucer used allegory, as in The Book of the Duchess and The Parliament of Fowls, it is personal or political, not religious (165–6). Wycliffite literalism did away with typological readings; the insistence in the General Prologue that tales must be retold without addition or embellishment is highly suggestive of this tradition, though it is also a well-established literary trope. In Duchess, the narrator’s literalism allows Chaucer to address a social superior (cf. Boethius above), suggesting Chaucer thought of it as epistemologically useful (167–8). Nominalism is defined in chiefly negative terms: this movement challenged the notion that analogy (including allegory) between the divine and creation is valid, an idea rooted in Plato’s theory of forms. Nominalists introduce a distinction between God’s absolute power (to do anything) and ordained power (the acts he has chosen to do), making the world a more contingent place rather than a divine plan in every detail. The wars, revolts, and plague of the fourteenth century may have contributed to this less teleological worldview (168–9). Utz argues that nominalism would have appealed to Chaucer as a poet more than the deterministic reading of life and recourse to one-dimensional allegorical characters, also because his aims were not didactic; instead, he wanted to leave judgement to his audiences (169–70). Nominalism discerned two truths, one of which was quite down-to-earth, so that life could be described and studied without invoking God. The new secular logic did lead to contradictions of dogma, so many nominalists had to recant or stop short of the logical end of their reasoning. The sudden breaking off of some of Chaucer’s works could be read along similar lines (170–1). A belief in contingency would also explain why Chaucer’s Boethian references are usually humorous — the determinism of this school of thought could not be taken seriously in a contingent world (171).

The article is perhaps a little myopic inasmuch as it doesn’t mention the scholastic movement, and doesn’t deal with Aristotle in any detail.

author: Kruger, Steven F.
title: Dreaming
abstract:
Points out that while dreams in post-Freudian times are typicallly associated with the subconscious, this was not the primary analytical mode in medieval dream-theory. Medieval dreams could have three origins: physiological, metaphysical, and psychological (71–2).

Macrobius divides dreams into true and false, but his finer division has five categories:

Name Nature/Cause Bearing
Insomnium Physiological / psychological None
Visum Transition wake/sleep None
Oraculum Person of authority foretells future Prophetic
Visio Rehearses future events Prophetic
Somnium Symbolic representation of events Revealing

The somnium occupies a middle ground between truth and falsehood inasmuch as it veils the truth in imagery and is thus in need of interpretation (72–4).

Augustine distinguishes between corporeal, intellectual, and spiritual, and held that dreams belong to the third; his dream theory can be overlaid onto Macrobius’s quite neatly. Gregory the Great saw a complex set of factors influencing dreams: they could be true, false, or mixed; caused by physiological discomfort, demonic or angelic suggestion, or combinations of internal and externa stimuli, thoughts and illusions (74). All these thinkers held dreams to be complex; with the rediscovery of Aristotle, the suspicious readings began to dominate, yet the potential for dreams to bear on reality remained (74–5).

The practical questions accompanying any dream are thus: how do you tell if it portends anything, and how is a portentous dream to be interpreted? For authors, this ambiguity provided a rich soil (75–6). The Nun’s Priest’s Tale has Chauntecleer and Pertelote take sides on the late medieval debate on the meaning of dreams. At the end of the tale, it is not clear what we should make of dream-theory: his dream proved accurate, but it was his own fault to give in to the fox’s flattery (76–7). Book V of Troilus centres around the interpretation of dreams. Troilus dreams both generally disturbing dreams and a more specific one, a somnium telling him of Criseyde’s betrayal. Pandarus advances a dream-theory like Gregory’s, rejecting truth content; Troilus’s last dream is clearly portentous, but even then it is explained in two contradictory ways. These various interpretations raise the question whether one dream can match multiple Macrobian categories at once (77–9).

The House of Fame discusses the causes of dreams in detail, paying special attention to physical and psychological causes but also admitting transcendental origins (79–80). Chaucer’s presentation of dream-theory here is unsystematic, so that the narrator does not advance beyond his initial understanding (80–1). Critical responses have included a tendency to categorize along Macrobian lines (since Chaucer clearly knew of his system) and a tendency to read psychologically (since his dream visions often take place under troubled conditions); but the visions also invite transcendental readings, as they concern more universal questions (81). Notable medieval precedents inspired Chaucer to leave his dreams open to multiple interpretations (81–7). They thus draw attention to problems of interpretation (87–8).

author: Lambdin, Robert Thomas, and Laura Cooner Lambdin
title: Debate Poetry
publication: A Companion to Old and Middle English Literature
eds: Laura Cooner Lambdin and Robert Thomas Lambdin
abstract:
Remarking on the scarcity of debate scholarship, and particularly of historical overviews, the authors set out to place the genre in a preexisting tradition. They synthesize the definitions of Holma, Harmon, and Garbáty with their own: medieval debate texts, usually poems, present a debate between two persons or objects on a specific top and referred to a judge; the genre received inspiration from twelfth-century troubadour tradition; and the audience takes active part in the debate by processing the reasoning, yielding a personalized teaching tool. This made the genre attractive to the Church for its expositionary powers (118–19). The narrator is often a dreamer or unknowing passer-by. Sarcasm is commonly used to refute the opponent’s position. There is often no clear winner, and thus the audience’s judgement is called into action (119).

Hanford traces the tradition to Virgil’s Eclogues (43 BCE), debates about the outcome of pastoral singing contests. These, and especially the seventh Eclogue, are said to have influenced Alcuin’s eighth-century Conflictus veris et hiemis (119). The form here copied then spread through ninth-century Germany, whose depastoralized debate in turn gave rise to the French dit in the late eleventh century. Post-Conquest cultural influences should be seen as the background against which the Middle English debate arose, with The Owl and the Nightingale (c. 1200) as an early surviving specimen (119–20).

A further cultural context is the rise of scholasticism with its dialectic approach to the synthesis of Aristotle with the Bible and reason with faith (120–1). Finally, universities were formed about the same time, institutions that greatly value rhetoric and dialectic (121–2). An analytic approach to logic and a classroom application were important methodologies of scholasticism. The disputatio between master and pupil is one of these; the unifying method of the tradition, though not unique to it, is the quaestio, a question-and-answer exchange. The authors of the ME debates were probably trained at schools with scholastic methods (122).

The remainder of the essay is a close analysis of The Owl and the Nightingale (123–34), The Thrush and the Nightingale (134–40), and The Debate of the Body and the Soul (140–9).

author: Shah, Anuj K., and Daniel M. Oppenheimer
title: Heuristics Made Easy: An Effort-Reducing Framework
abstract:
Complaining that the field of heuristics has become crowded by assigning the word too general a reference, the authors set out to build a new paradigm. Existing research contains too many redundancies, misapplies existing frameworks, and too much domain-specific work has been done without recognizing the fact that these are specific applications of more generally valid heuristics (208–09). The new framework takes the weighted additive rule as the optimal processing rule against which to compare heuristics. Because this rule contains five steps, effort reduction may be implemented in five places, and hence all heuristic behaviour may be eplained by these five impulses

  1. Examine fewer cues
  2. Expend less effort retrieving and storing cue values
  3. Simplify weighting
  4. Integrate less information
  5. Examine fewer alternatives (209)

These principles are discussed in turn (209–12), and it is insisted that they are separate processes (212–13). The remainder of the article discusses how the various existing frameworks may be adapted and extended; useful is a large table with previously identified heuristics charted against the five principles here outlined.

author: Kelly, George A.
title: The Psychology of Personal Constructs
abstract:
Though undoubtedly too old, chatty, and above all armchair psychotherapeutical to cite, this work constructs a theory of cognitive processing that is based entirely on binary constructs. Its main thesis is that “a person’s processes are psychologically channelized by the ways in which he anticipates events” (I, 46) followed by a range of corollaries including the dichotomy corollary, asserting that “a person’s construction system is composed of a finite number of dichotomous constructs” (I, 59). The remainder of the work no doubt goes into more detail and connects this theory with the clinical setting.

Note that this work has since been completely rewritten by other scholars under the title Inquiring Man.

author: Hanna, Ralph
title: Literacy, Schooling, Universities
publication: The Cambridge Companion to Medieval English Culture
abstract:
Points out that high medieval literacy was both more widespread than today assumed and more primarily passive; only guildsmen and the highly educated could write (173). Moreover, literacy could be broken up into a number of domains: traditionally it meant an ability to read Latin, but depending on context it could be a vernacular, and spoken or written, and in various degrees of comprehension (173–4). Today’s literacy is primarily ocular and private; in the Middle Ages, it was primarily aural and performative (174). Literacy was also a gendered domain, though not without its significant exceptions (175).

Grammar schools were mostly affiliated with the Church, but private instruction took place among the upper classes. A child’s first reading skills, however, were developed at home. Boys went onto grammar school at age eight or ten for three to five years, but some level of learning was the primary aim, not certification (175–6). School began with Latin grammar using Donatus’s fourth-century textbook Ars minor and various devotional readings (176), as well as colloquies to aid with vocabulary (176–7); this last group of texts were normally geared to everyday situations, because post-Conquest schools discouraged the use of English (177), even to the point of providing explanations in Norman French, which students were expected to have picked up elsewhere; only by the mid-fourteenth century did English make its way into the classroom (181).

The reading canon of grammar schools consisted of the six authors:

  1. Dionysius Cato, Disticha
  2. Theodolus (= Gottschalk), Ecloga
  3. Avianus, fables
  4. Maximianus, elegies
  5. Statius, Achilleis
  6. Claudian, De raptu Proserpinae (177)

Along with a few later additions to the canon, these texts were extremely widely read in the Middle Ages (177–8).

Teachers were expected first to point out the argumentative structure of each text. They then summarized the sense of a first grammatical unit before parsing it and explaining the syntax. Etymology was also given its due attention (179–80). Next was an analysis of rhetorical elements. The final stage in the process was the elucidation of allegorical content (180). These methods produced highly skilled readers of Latin but also analytical minds and rhetoricians (180–1).

Pupils were expected to undertake apposition, ex tempore oral translation from French (later English) into Latin. The level of surviving apposition exercises shows that students were trained to a very high level (182–3).

University in England meant Oxford or Cambridge, where one went for four years to pursue an artes degree from age 14x16. A subsequent three years earned one a magister artium degree and a licence to teach at all universities in Europe. Beyond that were three choices of doctorate: law, medicine, and theology, for a further decare or more of study. Like grammar schools, universities worked with a small canon of high authorities: knowing these well would train students to be able to tacke any other text. The schoolish nature of medieval universities now survives only at Oxbridge (183).

Grammar schools were increasingly free of charge; university training was an expensive affair, between tuition fees (charged by the MA directly), rent, and books. Accordingly, many students had patrons. In the fifteenth century, registration with an MA required college lodging (183–4). Students learned repetition of material learned, as well as disputation on academic questions (184). The degree requirements had a “flight hours” character of time spent hearing certain set texts read in class. These were calibrated into a broad package of seven artes liberales: the trivium of grammar, logic, and rhetoric, each with their set texts (185), and the quadrivium of geometry, arithmetic, music, and astronomy (186).

The doctorates proceeded along similar lines but added public disputationes. Law was not a practical course of studies, as England used Common Law, which is not what was taught (186–7).

Graduates had an enormous impact on society, firstly as religious teachers in roles created by the Fourth Lateran Council (1215). Accordingly, many student patronages were undertaken by episcopal dioceses and lay parish patrons to improve the learning of priests, as well as their rhetorical style. Commonly, however, priests went on to change careers and become clerks (188).

A more widespread structure in medieval society was the “family” in the sense of any organized household or corporate group, all of which needed administrators — and legal advice above all — and were willing and able to patronize students to this end (188–9). The bureaucracy that followed gave rise to such men as Chaucer (189). Doctors were sometimes called on to consult with difficult royal questions of high stakes (190).

An appendix excerpts from a glossed version of the Ecloga Theoduli.

author: Kleist, Aaron
title: Striving With Grace: Views of Free Will in Anglo-Saxon England
abstract:
Much of Augustine’s thought on free will was expressed in contrast with that of others. He eventually rejected the Manichaean view that an evil principle created the material world, exculpating both God and human agents from blame; the Donatist belief that forceful conversion (and sacraments administered by priests who had recanted under the persecutions) is not valid; and the Pelagian belief that grace can and must be attained on an individual’s own strength (5–6). In his final years, Augustine challenged Semi-Pelagianism, especially prevalent in Gaul, which acknowledged the agency of divine grace but asserted a will to good could emanate from the individual and attain the response of divine grace (6–7; see Augustine, De gratia et libero arbitrio; De correptione et gratia; De praedestinatione sanctorum; De dono perseuerantiae; Cassian, Collatio XIII; Prosper, De gratia Dei et libero arbitrio contra Collatorem). In his last writings on the subject, Augustine made divine grace the only agent in the equation (7), a position that was eventually almost fully endorsed by the Second Council of Orange of 529. All great Anglo-Saxon thinkers paid lipservice to Augustine, but several seem to have drawn on authors on other sides of the debate as well (8).

Augustine developed his views on free will himself, without relying on previous authority, in response to the above challenges. Some have claimed that these challenges pushed Augustine into ever more radical positions, leading him eventually to give up free will altogether, but Kleist does not agree (9). However, Augustine’s views on free will evolved over many years from the notion that “man could attain virtue by willing it” (book 1 of De libero arbitrio to the idea that original sin necessitates individual sin but that habit binds, leaving some role for the will (book 3 of the same work) (9); then when writing to Simplicianus, he came to the conclusion that human desires inevitably lead them to do evil by their own volition, so that free will does not overcome the bondage of sin (9–10). In his Expositio quarundum propositionum ex epostola ad Romanos, Augustine asserts that faith is a voluntary response to God’s call; in Ad Simplicianum, grace is God’s initiative without human prompting, and conversion is congruent vocation: God uses no force but leads people into circumstances to which he know they will respond favourably. He later abandons this view for an inner inspiration of the spirit. During the Donatist controversy, he comes to be influenced by four insights that compel him that force sometimes leads to true faith (10–11). Paul’s conversion is an important case study in this context, in which the spirit transforms the wills of individuals. This is not done universally, but those who are called inevitably answer (11).

Gregory the Great paid lip service to Augustine’s position, but in fact walked it back to a position midway between Augustine and Semi-Pelagianism: man cannot initiate anything, but he has the freedom to accept or reject (43–4). Whereas few of Augustine’s works were known well or at all in Anglo-Saxon England, Gregory was widely read (44–7). Gregory furthermore shows little development in his thought, as most of his works were written in the first four to six years of his pontificacy (48). His thoughts on volition were especially present in England in his Regula pastoralis, Dialogi, Homiliae in evangelia, and Moralia in Iob. Like Augustine, Gregory uses the metaphor of blindness. He departs from Augustine in claiming humans can desire and strain to see, i.e. to resist their wicked habits; blindness is no excuse (53–4). They can petition for divine assistance which is then nevertheless initiated by God (55). But enlightenment does not necessitate faith or conversion (55–6).

Bede stands closer to Gregory than to Augustine, claiming a cooperation between man and grace (61). He draws a direct connection between Easter dating and the Pelagian heresy: the equinox represents Christ shining his light on mankind, mirroring the doctrine of prevenient grace (67–8). At times his balance tends remarkably towards merit (70–3), but he does in fact counterbalance this by pointing out that the source of human love of God is divine (73–4). He does clearly assert with Gregory and against Augustine that people can spurn God’s avances (75).

When Bede speaks of the necessity to strive “quantum potest” to sanctify oneself and seek grace, perhaps we should read this as action not accomplishment. To Bede, “God is ultimately rather than utterly responsible for people’s righteous choices” (76). Whereas Augustine moved from congruent vocation to inward inspiration, Bede acknowledges both (77).

Boethius held human souls to be more free in the contemplation of the divine mind and less free when held down by the human body (92–3). Chadwick has called its soteriology humanist (93).

Among the strands of Boethian glosses, Remigius at one point inserts a fairly detailed Augustinian position (102).

Alfred’s Boethius modifies the point in 3p12 that even the wicked strive for good and submit to God’s will: he concludes that those rebelling in conflict with their own will are acting against their nature. Accordingly, Alfred introduces a distinction between will and action where Boethius says both serve God already (104–7). Boethius contradicts Augustine when he claims that, good and existence being synonymous, the wicked do not exist (107). Alfred abandons Boethius in the same passage, claiming that the wicked desire evil (108–9). Both Boethius and Alfred claim that providence governs fate; but Boethius then details the workings of fate using Neoplatonic and pagan vocabulary incompatible with Catholic doctrine. Augustine says fate exists only in the sense of God’s foreknowledge; Alfred similarly inserts the remark that not wyrd by foresceawung governs individuals. In the process, he uses the Augustinian (and Gregorian, etc.) image of blindness. But whereas Augustine sees humans as blind from birth in consequence of original sin, Alfred considers it a consequence of individual choices. This brings him closer to Gregory (109–12).

Kleist points out that Alfred adds foretiohhung (cf. praedestinatio, not really used by Boethius) in addition to foreþonc (providentia) and argues that this serves to emphasize that there is no impersonal wyrd (112–14). He briefly discusses the innovations in the wagon-wheel (114–16).

Alfred considerably modifies the discussion of free will. He first asks whether evil can be attributed to God; in his response, he again asserts that the wicked have evil desires. He then asks for the point in rewards if all that happens is predestined. His answer is Augustine’s: all of free will is included in predestination (Augustine uses the concept of providence here though) (115–16).

Boethius asks whether God’s foreknowledge determines action and answers with the image of the charioteer. Alfred instead reasons that there are both necessary and unnecessary elements to that which God foresees/predestines, and the former type do not change (116–18). With regard to God foreseeing evil events, Alfred invents the unfortunate position that God foresees them because he wants to prevent them, as a captain forecasting a storm. Both Boethius and Augustine would instead argue that the storm is punishment meant to purify (118–19).
