author: Boyd, David Lorenzo
title: Seeking ‘Goddes Pryvetee’: Sodomy, Quitting, and Desire in The Miller’s Tale
publication: Words and Works: Studies in Medieval English Language and Literature in Honour of Fred C. Robinson
eds: Peter S. Baker and Nicholas Howe
abstract: Reasons that the “literal” use of sodomy in the tale (the misdirected kiss and the application of the coulter) serves both to reinforce the heteronormative value of the male body and to criticize the medieval class system: the poet suggests that social misinterpretation can lead to homosexuality, which is itself a symbol for social malpractice (243–4). The Miller exploits the taboo of homosexuality to control the discourse: the Reeve cannot further protest the implications of cuckoldry because the Miller threatens that to speak explicitly of the possibility of cuckoldry is equivalent to sodomizing God himself (245–6). Peter Damian’s Liber Gomorrhianus also mentions the metaphorical practice of sodomizing God (246–7). The remainder of the essay discusses the “literal” homosexual scenes in the tale.

author: Baird, Joseph L.
title: The Devil’s Privetee
abstract: Since the Miller introduces the image of God’s private parts by a combination of polysemy of pryvetee and contextual contamination, the devil’s assertion “thou shalt knowen of oure privetee” in The Friar’s Tale brings to mind an image of demonic sodomy.

author: Neuss, Paula
title: Double Meanings I: Double-Entendre in The Miller’s Tale
abstract: Warns against the practice of finding sexual puns wherever polysemy or euphemism is remotely possible (325–8). The Miller’s Tale, by contrast, relies on brevity and speed for effect, so readers should look for bawdy puns, the more so in view of the Miller’s character (328). Chaucer uses infection: by providing bawdiness, he makes us more alert to the detection of more. Accordingly, double entendre sometimes operates in reverse: the bawdy sense is recognized first, whereas a more serious intent lies below the surface, potentially offering a moral (328–9). When the Miller tells the Reeve that “An housbonde shal nat been inquisityf / Of Goddes pryvetee, nor of hys wyf”, pryvetee is carried forward by implication to affect wyf and thus gains the sense “private parts” (330). Neuss does not think that there is a reference here to God’s private parts. Instead, the most obvious thing here being conveyed (given the personality of the speaker and other types of priming) is that husbands should not be inquisitive about their wives’ private parts and what they do with them. The other thing being conveyed is that man must not pry into God’s secrets, and this too is relevant given the nature of the carpenter’s beguiling (331). Once the word pryvetee has been sexually charged in the Prologue, it and related words in the tale retain this charge (332–5). Some double entendres with quainte, solas, instrument and the like are pointed out (335&ndas;9).

author: Barber, Paul
title: Vampires, Burial, and Death: Folklore and Reality
abstract:
Studies how preindustrial cultures respond to death and the decay of the body. The common denominator in revenant traditions is that they “blame death on the dead” (3): for instance, the first to die during an epidemic is commonly blamed as a vampire (7, 34–6). Among other things, this book discusses supposed causes of revenancy. Ch. 5 is most relevant in this context, distinguishing between predisposition (troublesome individuals), predestination (wrongful or ill-timed conception), events (during their lifetime), and things left undone (in funerary practice; 29–38). However, the book also addresses some of the things leading to a belief in revenants. For instance, shallow burials may result in animals digging up the corpses, a sight that could be read in a number of ways (92–5). “Shallow burial causes, deep burial discourages vampirism” (169), and coffins too serve to prevent predatory interference (19).

Some observations relevant to my work: Mass is sometimes sees as a necessary but not sufficient action for putting a revenant to rest (25); the European belief in revenants seems to predate Christianity, but Christianity seems to have augmented revenant lore (37); in Oldenburg, revenancy could occur if a corpse was not buried deep enough (37); a complete lack of burial could be sufficient cause for revenancy (38); the heavy corpse is a widespread characteristic of revenants (75); the best-known bog bodies seem to have been buried in winter and early spring, and solstitial sacrifices seems a stronger explanation here than selective preservation (170–1, footnote); and the frost has encouraged non-inhumatory burial practices in Tibet (171).

author: Horowitz, Sylvia Huntley
title: Beowulf, Samson, David and Christ
abstract: Concisely points out a striking number of parallels between the story of Beowulf and those of Samson and the lion as well as David and Goliath. These Old Testament figures were types of Christ, and Beowulf suggests Christ by evoking his Old Testament types.

author: Hollander, L.M.
title: Beowulf 33
abstract: Proposes the emendation of Bwf 33 "isig" to the unattested "itig," corresponding to ON ítr, ítarlegr to mean "splendid."

author: Von Schaubert, Else
title: Heyne–Schückings Beowulf
abstract: Explains the reading of l. 33 "isig" as "glänzend (wie Eis)" with reference to Met 4.1 ll. 11f., which renders coruscus "eallisig" (2.20).

author: Olsen, Karin
title: Animated Ships in Old English and Old Norse Poetry
publication: Animals and the Symbolic in Mediaeval Art and Literature
abstract: Points out that Meissner lists 380+ animate kennings for ship (53). Several examples are given, many of which depict the ship as a (sea-king’s) horse (55–9). Old English has only 21 kennings with a word for horse as the base word. Examples from Guthlac B, Christ B, and Andreas are given (61–5; the Christ B passage is the one elaborated on Gregory’s homily).

author: Sievers, Eduard
title: Lückenbüsser
publication: Beiträge zur Geschichte der deutschen Sprache und Literatur
abstract: Defends the literal sense of Bwf 33 isig “beeist”: “Es ist winterszeit, und darum liegt das schiff ‘beeist’ (und untätig, vgl. 1125 ff.) im hafen, aber zugleich ‘harrend (der günstigeren jahreszeit und) neuer ausfahrt’.”

author: Sievers, Eduard
title: Gegenbemerkungen zum Beowulf
publication: Beiträge zur Geschichte der deutschen Sprache und Literatur
abstract: Warns that one can only read isig as “cold” if one assumes it to be homonymous with Modern German eisig; -iga is a possessive suffix and the word must thus mean “eishabend,” or “ ‘eisbedeckt’, ‘beeist’ u.s.w.” with a more pictorial reading (422). The attestation of eallisig in the Metres appears to mean “shining” since it translates coruscus, but that is a false comparison: Alfred here simplifies and elucidates his model, rendering coruscus “(von blinkendem eis) funkelnd” with isig (422–3). The parallelism between Bwf hrinde bearwas and BlHom 16 isgean bearwas furthermore demonstrates that the word must mean “beeist” (423). This sense does not contradict utfus, as the author under review suggests; the personified ship is keen to leave harbour but cannot because it is winter, just as Hengest in the Finnsburh episode is keen to leave Frisia but cannot because it is winter (425). The author’s emendation to *ysig from *easig as analogue to ausa “bail out” is rejected both philologically and aesthetically (425–6).

author: Stanley, Eric
title: Old English Poetic Diction and the Interpretation of The Wanderer, The Seafarer and The Penitent’s Prayer
abstract: Stanley touches on metaphorical language in many OE poems here, and quite a bit of it concerns winter imagery. But today I just wanted to annotate it as proposing that Bwf 33 “isig” should be read metaphorically in the same way as “winterceald” in The Wife’s Lament, i.e. as “a word evocative of sorrow: the factual meaning does not matter” (440–1).

author: Bähr, Dieter
title: Altenglisch īsig (Beowulf, Zeile 33)
abstract: Identifies the accuracy of the Boethius translator as the crucial question in the definition of Bwf 33 “isig.” The Boethius translator was not literal in his renderings. That he did not mean to render coruscus as “flashing” becomes clear when we recognize that he elsewhere translates the same word “beorht,” in the Metres “wlitig.” The first passage concerns Saturn, which was considered cold; two late translations use “cold” or “isy.” “Eisig” is accordingly the only sensible understanding of the term; whether Stanley’s “winterceald” is also acceptable is a secondary question.

author: Ebbinghaus, Ernst A.
title: Heyne-Schückings Beowulf [review]
publication: Journal of English and Germanic Philology
abstract: On Bwf 33 “isig,” proposes to read the name Scef transparently “as a spirit of vegetation,” whose death naturally comes in the winter (677).

author: Von Grienberger
title: Bemerkungen zum Beowulf
publication: Beiträge zur Geschichte der deutschen Sprache und Literatur
abstract: Proposes to read Bwf 33 “isig” as a form of *ysig, from *easig and related to ON ausa “to bail”; the sense of “isig ond utfus” is thus “ausgeschöpft und zur fahrt bereit” (95).

author: Trautmann, Moritz
title: Auch zum Beowulf: Ein Gruß an Herren Eduard Sievers
abstract: Nothing in the context of Bwf 33 indicates that it is winter. Very critical of Sievers’s reading, and insists that adjectives linked by ond should at the very least have similar meanings (151); proposes to read isig with a short first vowel “fertig” (related to eoset “Fahrt,” 152).

author: Krogmann, Willy
title: Ae. īsig
abstract: There is no evidence of winter in the context of Bwf 33; therefore, Krogmann proposes an IE root suggesting movement, and the sense “antreibend, eifrug, vorwärts drängend.”

author: Holthausen, Ferdinand
title: Zum Beowulf (v. 33)
abstract: Since there is no mention of winter and a word similar in meaning to utfus is required, isig cannot mean “covered with ice.” Proposes a root connected to ON eisa to mean “vorwärts drängend.”

author: Trautmann, Moritz
title: Sprachschatz der angelsächsischen Dichter [review of Grein]
abstract: Reasserts that isig must be similar in meaning to utfus (42).

author: Trautmann, Moritz
title: Berichtigungen, Vermutungen und Erklärungen zum Beowulf: Erste Hälfte
abstract: “Eisig” is an inappropriate description for a ship, and “glänzend wie Eis” is desperate. The word should mean “glänzend,” but maybe in some other form (icig, itig, ifig) (127).

author: Krause, Wolfgang
title: Die Inschrift auf der Urne von Niesdrowitz
abstract:
Identifies the decorations on the Niezdrowice urn as right-to-left runes: the vertical stroke is the [i]-rune, the round, two-storey inverted "s" is the [s]-rune, and the two-descendered sign at the left end is a doubled [r]-rune; moreover, the ladderlike symbols in between, which Krause initially identifies as cultic symbols, can also be read as [h]s with too many rungs (238–45). Read as a set of ideograms, the inscription then reads “Eis. Hagel; Hagel, Hagel, Hagel; Hagel; Hagel. Sonne. Hagel, Hagel, Hagel. Ritt, Ritt.” (246).

Krause assumes from the outset that the runes must have magical significance (246); he derives this in part from the transparent meaning of the rune names, in part from their use in other, mostly later, contexts. Thus [is] (“ice”) meant “tückisches Verderben” (“treacherous ruin”) given its role in the rune poems; [*hagol] (“hail”) meant “jähes Verderben” (“sudden ruin”) given its use in the rune poems and a sixth-century curse inscription (246–8). The sun represents the opposing power, as recognized by the Icelandic Rune Poem; it represents the world of light (249).

Krause assumes from the runes’ presence on a grave urn that they concern the cult of the dead; the [is]- and [*hagol]-runes thus pronounce ruin on anyone disturbing the grave (251). The sun- and wagon-runes, by contrast, concern the deceased and wish them prosperity (252).

author: Clunies Ross, Margaret
title: The Anglo-Saxon and Norse Rune Poems: A Comparative Study
abstract: Proposes that the Norwegian Rune Poem makes use of the technique described by Snorri as hjástælt. Points out that the Icelandic Rune Poem’s hail-kenning “snaka sótt” is more characteristically a winter kenning (36), and that this poem displays an antiquarian interest in paganism where the Old English poem shows a pressure to euhemerize (36–7). All in all analyzes the different approaches to their material evinced by the three works, but does not address head on the question she raises in her introduction of how these texts have come to share so much content.

author: Moreland, John
title: The Significance of Production in Eighth-Century England
eds: Inge Lyse Hansen and Chris Wickham
abstract:
Argues that the recent emphasis on emporia and exchange in eighth-century economies has undervalued the role of production.

In Richard Hodges’s classic model, emporia are defined in conjunction with kingship: they are thought to serve the supply of luxury goods to the king (72–3). In this model, it was crucial for kings to control international trade, as direct international trade relations on the part of their subjects would undermine their ability to stand out in the gift-giving hierarchy; trading centres like Ipswich, London, Southampton, and York were founded to this end (73–4). Hodges himself has now departed from this model, arguing that Southampton instead represents a later stage of development, namely a commodity economy; the shift was prompted by a decline in foreign supply and a response of increased production by the early eighth century (74–5). Moreland now counters that gifts and commodities are not mutually exclusive and should not be seen as stages, which seem to be teleologically motivated (75).

When Southhampton was established as Hamwic in the early eighth century, it was a small centre of prestige craft production (silver, gold, sceattas), but that slag and textile production are found only by mid-century (76–7). London and Ipswich likewise saw a boom in production from about 720 (78–9). York was twice abandoned, but the later phase shows signs of reduced import (79). Although these data support Hodges’s move to a production economy, there is now evidence that long-distance trade and gift-giving did not die out at this time, and that agricultural and rural production experienced an increase before the alleged production phase got underway (80).

The image of emporia isolated from their hinterlands cannot be maintained; we know they were richly supplied from their surroundings. The question now is whether this rural richness resulted from emporial demand or whether it in fact gave rise to the emporia (80). Most have assumed the former, but the latter is more likely (80 ff.).

The late seventh century saw a pattern of moves to heavier and more fertile soil that was harder to work but offered higher yields (82–3). Explanations have ranged from erosion to population change (83–4), but all such accounts are too limited (84). Instead, the change should be read in conjunction with others, such as the architectural revolution in the late seventh and early eighth centuries, which suggests a profound change in self-perception (84–5). The settlement shift also entailed the abandonment of old cemeteries, churches instead becoming the geographic focus of burial culture as well as settlement (85–6).

Newly discovered sites in East Anglia and beyond combine imported and local pottery, sceattas, and evidence of literate culture with evidence of grain, livestock, honey and wax, metal, leather, and cloth production (87–91). Similar settlements in Yorkshire show evidence of permanent occupation, not the period market function often associated with the East Anglian settlements. The high-status and dynamic nature of these settlements suggests that elites used them to control production and distribution at the regional level; the emporia served to connect them to larger trade networks (91–4). Flixborough shows further evidence of the combination of production and literacy; literacy, of course, may have been used for production administration as well as religious purposes (94–6).

This investigation demonstrates that the emporia and rural settlements did not exist in isolation from each other but were part of an integrated economic system (96). Moreland proposes a hierarchy of four levels, and that emporia resulted from the jump in production (96–7). There is some discussion also of western sites, where evidence is not as strong (98–101).

author: Miller, Edward, and John Hatcher
title: Medieval England: Rural Society and Economic Change 1086–1348
abstract:
This work has neither the feel nor the precision of cutting-edge research; rather, it presents an overview for the student of long-received views of economic and social history, many of which are surely problematic.

Most westerners were peasants who had to feed themselves (vii). Starvation was probably rare, but malnutrition and indirect mortality a reality when crops failed. Seasonal diseases were likewise a danger given the state of the medical field (viii). Here follow some remarks on life expectancy that don’t sound quite right (viii–ix), and there is reference to widespread violence (ix), conflict, and war (ix–x). A pyramidical hierarchy is described that may be termed feudal and was linked through land, services, and obligations (x). The peasantry consisted of villeins (serfs) and freeholders; the former had a considerable but finite set of obligations to their manorial lord, while even the latter owed rent and some services (x–xi). The uncertainty resulting from war and unstable markets may have encouraged the rise of the feudal system (xi).

The authors stress the inequality of the times, speculating that under ten percent would have been able to read. They also contrast the widespread existence of “subsistence family farms” with “the landowning churchmen and lay feudatories” in a position to become “producers of commodities on a large scale ”(xii). At the same time, even the richest landowners were fed to some degree from their own land, while even the poorest peasant paid some of his tenancy in cash, meaning he had to (work for wages or) sell of a surplus, which in turn helped fund the large projects of the rich: castles, cathedrals, learning, and the commodity trade (xii–xiii). The abstract notion and more complex reality of the three estates is discussed (xiii–xiv).

The central characteristic of social and economic change post-Conquest was expansion across all sectors, but the relative lack of technological innovation kept economic production and thus the living standard for the working masses limited to what (sometimes the same amount of) land could produce; population growth thus brought down the standard of living, and non-agricultural sectors with it (xiv–xv).

Scholars have disagreed over the level of poverty and poverty-related mortality in the thirteenth century, as well as whether and why there was a subsistence crisis in the late thirteenth century; demographic factors and the inequality inherent in the manorial system have been cited as causes (xvii–xviii).

[1: King William’s England] The slow pace of communications is cited as probably having weighed down trade (2). The authors paint a balanced picture of the level of land settlement by the time of Domesday (3–4). All in all, there was a great deal of unsettled space between settlements, and the population was between 1.25 and 2.5 million, and closer to the latter. Density was thirty heads per square mile, with ninety percent in the countryside (5). The authors describe the picture provided by Domesday in terms of livestock farming, varying according to the local environment (6–8), and point out also that a considerable part of the population lived in towns that were themselves likewise diverse (8–9). The picture is one in which there is no sharp distinction between urban and rural settlements, agriculture playing a role in all towns (9); on the other hand, towns often had distinguishing centres such as mints, which themselves indicate a trading function (9–10). Sporadic documentary evidence of imports and exports suggests that commerce and industry were central to the support of the burghal population (10–11). Landlords typically held urban as well as rural property (11), but the king’s large urban possessions meant they did not hold much power here (12).

Methods are discussed; milling is one domain in which technological change was taking place (12–15).

On landlords, the authors observe that “a good deal of the profit of the royal demesne was seemingly intercepted by the sheriffs and others who managed royal resources in the localities” (15–16, at 15). Much of the profits from land went to about 170 lay barons (50%) and some 100 ecclesiastical institutions (26%) (16); in reality, the landlords were the baron’s underlings, a class of knights that seems to have been created right after the Conquest (in fact, some had held the land prior to it), and their fiefs soon became hereditary (16–17). But even among these there was a great deal of variation in power and holdings (17–19).

The manor is “a block of landed property managed as a single unit from a particular centre” (19), “a landowning and land-management grid superimposed on the settlement pattern of villages and hamlets” (20) with a great deal of variation between them (19–22). “Consequently, the sources from which lords derived their revenues were similarly diverse. Some income came from the produce of their own home farms, some from peasant renders and some from the profits of jurisdiction and lordship” (22).

Domesday provides valuable statistics on the peasantry, 41% of whom were villani, 32% bordarii with very small holdings, 14% freeholders and sokesmen, and 10% servi (22). The variety among this population is discussed (22–5).

In summary, the wealth of England was limited by its arable land and the state of the technology, but contemporary writers considered England rich. Since many peasants paid their dues in cash as well as kind or labour, they must have been in a position to engage in trade, while landlords seem to have done better than their French counterparts (25–6).

[2: Land and People] Peasants, small traders, and craftsmen made up the bulk of the population, and each of these groups was primarily turned on itself: peasants and estates aimed for self-sufficiency, while craftsmen worked as much for their fellow-townsmen as for wider markets. Post-Conquest, the prime development was towards expansion and an increase of production (27). Population growth had begun prior to the Conquest everywhere in Europe and lasted into the fourteenth century; explanations have been various, but peace and a reduction in epidemics probably played some role (28). Domesday figures do not tell us how large the 1086 population was, but we may use its data to arrive at 2.5 or 3mln, while the 1347 figure might be 5 or 6mln (28–9). The growth rate is discussed for different localities (29–33). The colonization of previously uncultivated land (33–41). Mobility and social integration (41–5). Scarcity of land and employment; wages and prices (45–53). Limits to expansion; crop failures and prices (53–63).

[4: Villages] Discussse above all the forms that the rural settlement and economy could take (84–110).

author: Lemanski, S. Jay
title: The Rectitudines singularum personarum: Anglo-Saxon Landscapes in Transition
abstract: Apart from its edition, translation, and study of the RSP, this MA thesis contains a useful overview of the past century and more of scholarship on land use in ASE.

author: Jones, Richard, and Mark Page
title: Characterizing Rural Settlements and Landscape: Whittlewood Forest in the Middle Ages

author: Holton, Frederick S.
title: Old English Sea Imagery and the Interpretation of The Seafarer

author: Neidorf, Leonard
title: Introduction
abstract:
Argues that the late dater trend of the 1980s was only to be expected in response to the traditional pattern of early dating, but that the new trend is not qualitatively better than what came before, relying as it does on such soft considerations as cultural appropriateness. Responses to the Toronto revolution have generally taken one of two forms: agnosticism (James Earl) and reassessment. The latter movement has focused on firmer types of evidence than cultural considerations: Cronan, Fulk, and others have quantified patterns in diction, metre, and scribal errors. The success of these approaches has made agnosticism a difficult position to hold, and their evidence points to an early date. This volume uses a range of evidence to come to the same conclusion.

[Note: although the scholarship here presented is solid and persuasive, the book’s flaw is confirmation bias in its selection of papers, as the editor went around specifically soliciting papers that date early.]

author: Fulk, R.D.
title: Beowulf and Language History
abstract:
Brings together hard and specific linguistic and metrical considerations for presuming an early original of Beowulf:
  • Non-parasiting: Bwf has the strongest tendency to non-parasiting of all surviving poetry (24–5);
  • Metrical non-contraction: Bwf is comparatively conservative in this feature, if not as conservative as GenA or Daniel (25);
  • Diphthongal stems in -eo(w): analogical redistribution of <w> is not widely found in Bwf, a pattern otherwise limited to the early Vespasian Psalter and laws of Æthelberht (25–6);
  • The genitive plural ending -ia in light-stemmed i-stem nouns, for which Bwf is almost our only source (26);
  • Kuhn’s first law, regarding particle stress, is more conservatively applied in Bwf than in any other West Germanic poem (27);
  • Weak adjectives without demonstratives before nouns are uncommonly frequent (27–8);
  • Resolution (Kaluza’s Law): Bwf only permits this under secondary stress if the second syllable was originally light. It is the only poem to follow this rule consistently; of other longer compositions, only Exodus shows an awareness of it (28–32).

The author refers to Cronan and Russom for further points on semantics and metre. Although the author does not here provide exhaustive lists of evidence, he builds on and refers to solid existing studies, while presenting more than enough cumulative evidence inline to make a very strong case for an early date. He asserts that late daters tend not to pay much heed to linguistic evidence. Concludes that the text predates its MS by at least a century on the basis of the cumulative evidence (32), and quite probably, on the basis of its pattern of resolution, “no later than 725 if it is a Southumbrian composition, as seems most likely” (29), or “750 at the latest” if Fulk is wrong about the pattern of resolution (29–31). Fulk then muses for a bit whether neighbouring traditions offer analogous situations that might build credibility for a span of a century or more between composition and MS evidence. In this context, the skaldic and above all Irish situations are adduced, but also Guthlac A, Germania, and a chapter of the Satyricon (32–4). Only Amos has attempted to discredit the linguistic evidence for an early date, but unsuccessfully. In conclusion, only careful linguistic and metrical evidence will bring us closer to a date; the time of composition has already been considerably narrowed down by such means; and late daters have a considerable task in front of them if they are going to persuade linguists of their position (35–6).

author: Fulk, Angela B.
title: On anginne: Anglo-Saxon Readings of Genesis

author: Raith, Josef
title: Ælfric’s Share in the Old English Pentateuch
abstract: This article is really about Ælfric’s share in Genesis, which is thought to be a compilation of two translations not only because of what is said in the Preface, but also on some internal evidence. Raith proposes he translated the first half of Genesis except for two bits that are heavy on genealogy, which were filled in by someone else; the second half is the work of the other man mentioned in the Preface but added on by Ælfric himself. The Cambridge text fills in the gaps left, but the BL text represents an attempt to come to a complete Pentateuch by bringing together Ælfric’s Genesis and his partial translation of Numbers with further material.

author: Kleist, Aaron
title: Ælfric’s Corpus: A Conspectus
abstract: Gathers information from Clemoes and others about authorship, date, available facsimiles, and additional points, and provides a list of the corpus ordered by genre and series.

author: Dodwell, C.R., and Peter Clemoes
title: The Old English Illustrated Hexateuch: British Museum Cotton Claudius B. IV
abstract: The introduction to this facsimile edition contains a section on the composition of the text, written by Clemoes (42–53). It conveniently summarizes the history of views on the extent of Ælfric’s authorship, with references to Dietrich and Jost. Clemoes agrees with Jost in the main, adding that the larger part of Joshua was also written by Ælfric; but he disagrees with Jost’s view that the sections not by him nevertheless relied on an Ælfrician translation. Clemoes himself demonstrates that the Hexateuch compiler’s own translations are very close in style to Byrhtferth’s Manual and the Poenitentiale Pseudo-Ecgberti, and proposes that Byrhtferth compiled the Hexateuch within two decades of Ælfric's completion of Joshua in 1002. I don’t believe the introduction makes any assertions about Judges, which is not contained in the manuscript reproduced in this edition.

author: Marsden, Richard
title: Translation by Committee? The ‘Anonymous’ Text of the Old English Hexateuch
publication: The Old English Hexateuch: Aspects and Approaches
eds: Rebecca Barnhouse and Benjamin C. Withers
abstract: Asserts that the non-Ælfrician parts of the Hexateuch translation are not the work of a single author/translator.

author: Baker, Peter S.
title: The Old English Canon of Byrhtferth of Ramsey

author: Lindström, Bengt
title: The Old English Translation of Alcuin’s Liber de virtutibus et vitiis
abstract: Discusses a hitherto unedited second MS witness of this translation and some difficult readings.

author: Lees, Clare A.
title: The Dissemination of Alcuin’s De virtutibus et vitiis liber in Old English: A Preliminary Survey
abstract: Following a brief discussion of florilegia in the Carolingian period and their usage in the time of the Benedictine Reform, Lees discusses the subject matter of Alcuin’s De virtutibus et vitiis, Anglo-Saxon witnesses, and Old English part-translations and adaptations. Dwells long on Ælfric’s use of it.

author: Wallach, Luitpold
title: Alcuin on Virtues and Vices: A Manual for a Carolingian Soldier
abstract:
Alcuin wrote a great deal of instructional literature for nobles, officials, and kings; his Via regia for Charlemagne is the earliest Carolingian speculum principis [by some definition] (175). His De virtutibus is related in genre; it was written in 799 or 800 for “Wido, Margrave of the Marca Britanniae, who during the same years overcame the resistance of this territory to Charlemagne” (175–6, at 176), and whom he describes in a letter to Charlemagne as “a perfect man and incorruptible judge” (179).

The work contains

  1. An epistolary section in Alcuin’s personal style;
  2. 26 chapters on virtues, in a homiletic style;
  3. 8 chapters on vices, in a cataloguing style;
  4. a closing chapter on the four cardinal virtues, in a mixture of homiletic and cataloguing styles.

The variation in style reflects a variation of sourcing (176).

Alcuin’s claim to write in response to a specific request should be seen as a rhetorical device (177–8). Alcuin has elsewhere called Gregory’s Pastoral Care “a speculum of pontifical life” (178); he saw his De virtutibus as a similar work (179). Its epistle is largely made up of conventional elements Alcuin also addressed to others (178–9).

The treatise depicts life as a conflict between a range of virtues and eight vices, which are overcome by their virtuous counterparts; all elements echo Prudentius, Cassian, Gregory, and Aldhelm, all authors Alcuin knew (179–80). The remainder of this article analyzes Alcuin’s use of his sources. Especially relevant to a study of the Fürstenspiegel tradition may be the claim that ch. 2 (De iudicibus) “is made up of verbatim quotations from [Isidore’s] Sententiae III” which Alcuin would not have found in Defensor’s excerpts from that text (182).

Refers to Rochais, Revue Bénédictine 63 (1953): 154n4 for the claim that some 22 MSS are extant from the ninth and tenth centuries, and more thereafter across Western and Central Europe (190). Discussing the treatise’s influence, the author also mentions that it was used in OE and ME literature, by Ælfric and others (192–3). An appendix draws attention to the work’s reliance on Caesarius of Arles’s Sermo 18 (194–5).

author: Anton, Hans Hubert
title: Specula principum ineuntis et progredientis medii aevi / Fürstenspiegel des frühen und hohen Mittelalters
series: Ausgewählte Quellen zur deutschen Geschichte des Mittelalters: Freiherr-vom-Stein-Gedächtnisausgabe
abstract:
While denying the possibility of a precise definition, defines the genre of Fürstenspiegel as “eine in paranätischer Absicht verfasste Ausarbeitung, gerichtet an einen König, Fürsten oder Regenten jeweils als Person oder an einen (fiktiven) Amtsträger als Repräsentanten einer sozialen Gruppe” (3–4); “[d]er konkrete Ort der Texte ist zwischen Sein und Sollen”; it concerns political ethics (4). The genre’s Carolingian presence was predominantly west-Frankish (6); by the high Middle Ages, it was popular throughout Europe (7–8).

Classical models are few (9–10); instead, a theocratic principle and Old Testament models influenced these works via patristic writings. Mentioned by name are Ambrosiaster, Augustine, and Gregory, but Isidore was crucial for the dissemination of the material; in Ireland, Pseudo-Cyprian played an important role (section De duodecim abusivis in his Contradictio in adiecto, esp. abuses 6 and 9) (10).

NB the edition of Sedulius Scottus’s De rectoribus christianis is incomplete, skipping chs. 7–18.

author: Wallach, Luitpold
title: Alcuin and Charlemagne: Studies in Carolingian History and Literature
abstract:
Discusses Alcuin’s political thought with reference to his De rhetorica et de virtutibus and De virtutibus et vitiis. Opens (5–28) with a chapter on Alcuin’s political philosophy, where it is pointed out that

  • Cicero’s De inventione is a source, though Alcuin seems unaware of this (5–6);
  • Isidore’s Sententiae, a central source of De virtutibus et vitiis, is a more central work behind his political thought (7–8);
  • The Hiberno-Latin text De duodecim abusivus saeculi by Pseudo-Cyprian is likewise an influence (8–10);
  • The Gelasian notion of the two powers of Church and state is furthermore echoed by Alcuin (10–12);
  • Alcuin is the only author in Charlemagne’s vicinity who echoes Augustinian ideas, if only in a select few domains and texts (23–8).

Alcuin saw Charlemagne as a divinely ordained protector of the Church and distributor of the faith. To Alcuin as to Charlemagne, the latter embodied a Christian empire taking over from Rome under the Christian figureheads of Constantine, Theodosius II, Valentinian III, and Honorius (12–15); Charlemagne himself likewise presented himself as a universal defender of the Church (18–19), although Wallach sees in this the hand of Alcuin (20), who also seems to have been inspired by Virgil’s rhetoric of war, even where he criticizes it in other contexts (21). Charlemagne’s ways of relating to the papacy also bear the mark of Alcuin, according to the author (22–1).

The chapter on De virtutibus et vitiis is pretty well identical to the article in the Harvard Theological Review.

author: Godden, M.R.
title: Ælfric and Anglo-Saxon Kingship
abstract: Notes that Ælfric’s parable of the elected king who then becomes unimpeachable ruler (a figure for the choice to sin which then takes control) has been widely taken as a political statement (911). Some suggestions have been made as to Ælfric’s source (911–12), but in fact the passage stems from the homiliary of Paul the Deacon, Ælfric’s main source for his homiletic writings; it concerns a passage widely misattributed to Chrysostom (912–13). Since the source has previously been thought to be Atto, who uses the remark as an argument for sacred, indisputable theocratic kingship, it has widely been thought that Ælfric held the same view. But both Ælfric and his source are addressing free will and the will to sin. Moreover, Ælfric uses magan, pointing out that a king cannot be deposed rather than arguing that this ought to be the case (913–14); if anything, the comparison favours rebellion, although Ælfric would probably always argue against rebellion if pressed, judging by his tone in accounts of the deescalating actions of clergy. Moreover, his diction does not match the vocabulary of Anglo-Saxon politics (e.g. folc instead of witan), and he elsewhere describes the system of hereditary succession as the default setup (914–15).
