author: Stone, Rachel
title: Morality and Masculinity in the Carolingian Empire
abstract:
Studies moral norms as expressed across a range of instructional genres on the themes of warfare, the use of power, and sexuality. The author draws a distinction between mirrors for princes and “lay mirrors,” and chooses not to address the former genre systematically but to bring it in where called for.

Echoes Wallach’s observation that few Carolingian moralists built on classical writings; but among the exceptions, she names Sedulius Scottus (specifically, chs. 6, 8, 9, 14, 17) and Haimo of Auxerre; Dhuoda uses Ovid directly (6).

The genre of lay mirror predates the fully formed Carolingian mirror for princes, which begins with Smaragdus’s Via regia and ends with Dhuoda in 841, but noteworthy texts of this genre are still produced afterwards: Sedulius Scottus seems to have written his for Charles the Bald in 869x870, and Hincmar wrote two texts for the same ruler about the same time (42).

[The remainder of chapter 2 completes the survey, which I have no time or occasion to study at present. Then follow chapters on warfare, power, wealth, marriage, sex, and a male ethics.]

author: Russell, James C.
title: The Germanization of Early Medieval Christianity: A Sociohistorical Approach to Religious Transformation
abstract:
[The quality of this book varies greatly. Chs 1–4 seem to have a sound approach, but more than a few of the sources lavishly quoted throughout this part in particular seem mildly suspect in their neo-Victorian and Western-centric conceptions. The author sometimes treats them critically, but sometimes he ought not to be citing them at all. Ch. 5, in which Dumézil comes to play a central role with his notions of pan-IE religious structures, is completely worthless. Chs. 6–7, by contrast, are really quite good. It is unfortunate that the book breaks off where it does, since any systematic analysis of Germanic content in liturgy and theology is absent; there are only a few unconnected and superficial references here and there to the crusades and the emphasis on holy objects.]

Germanic peoples, like the other Indo-European peoples, approached religion from a world-inclusive perspective, as opposed to the world-rejection model of eastern religions and of early Christianity. Germanic social structure also emphasized group solidarity lacking in the urban environments from which Christianity reached them. In those environments, an appeal of early Christianity was that it fulfilled a need for socialization . For it to appeal to Germanic cultures, it would have to address the military, agricultural, and other traditional aspects of Germanic society. Missionary efforts incorporating these elements then fed back into the donor culture, especially from the tenth century onwards (4).

[1: Introduction] Cultural confrontation is often the central tension in missionary efforts, forcing missionaries to consider which elements of her religion are essential and which may be relaxed. If essentials include cultural baggage, one runs the risk of alienation; if the core is kept small and local culture allowed to mix in, syncretism tends to ensue (10–11). Emperor Julian’s model asserts that one should not attempt to alter an ethnosocial group’s religion or culture (11–12). The typically small size of a missionary group relative to the target culture makes the process of Christianization unorganic (12–13). The author stresses that recent work suggests that genetic make-up, alongside historical and other group factors, has an enormous impact on religious attitude (13–14).

It has been observed in Uganda that Western missionary activity there is leaving Africans confused between two worlds, and that this tension can only be solved by those who understand African culture and Christian religion; but also by giving a place to preexisting religions (16–17).

Conversion in a missionary context often comes with benefits: in early medieval Europe, the support of aristocrats and clergy; in today’s Africa, medicine, technology, and education. Judgemental attitudes towards preexisting religion may send it underground and result in syncretism (17–18). Syncretism is especially common where the impetus to convert is sociopolitical (18). Japan’s resistance to Christianity is instructive of the circumstances that may breed such resistance: a tradition of ethnically informed culture and religion, and no economic disparity to favour conversion (19). Early Germanic peoples were similarly socially cohesive and homogeneous; missions tend to flourish in heterogeneous, anomic, socially unstable societies instead (20). Combining Durkheim with Weber suggests that both the underprivileged classes and those experiencing a loss of solidarity and shared values (i.e. anomie) are receptive to salvation theology (20–1). Korea may be an example of anomie increasing missionary success (21–2). Hawaii witnessed a rapid expansion of Christianity after a chief wilfully disrupted the social order, presumably in hopes of increasing his power with Western help and firearms instead of tradition (22).

Early Christian missionaries in Germanic societies did not draw attention to the soteriology and eschatology of Christianity but rather to the omnipotence of its God and the rewards associated with his worship, appealing to a cultural valuation of power and the lord-retainer relationship. The Heliand and The Dream of the Rood take this approach further by depicting Christ as a warlord (23–4).

The foregoing suggests that “[t]he most significant factors in determining an appropriate missiological approach and in predicting missionary success appear to be the prevailing world-view of the target society, the degree of popular satisfaction with the indigenous religion, the level of the target society’s sociocultural cohesion, and the target society’s levels of scientific and economic development compared to those which exist in the society from which the proselytizing party originates. An anomic society with relatively low levels of scientific and economic development, a prevailing soteriological-eschatological world-view, and an indigenous religion that is waning in popularity, would seem to be the ideal candidate for proselytization by representatives of a universal religion. On the contrary, a cohesive, scientifically advanced, economically stable society with a functional folk religiosity would seem to be the least likely candidate for missionary success” (24).

[2: Conversion, Christianization, and Germanization] Conversion is a multi-part process: it is historically seen to have been understood to involve an inner change involving penitence, but often implying change in the community as well. The penitence element seems out of place in an early Germanic context, in which sinfulness was not a (prominent) concept. The term conversion is therefore out of place in this context, the more so when applied to entire societies (26–7). Individual conversion, however, was often understood as the ignition of a fervent desire to close in on moral perfection, combined with a clean break in behaviour (27–8). Descriptions of individual conversions (namely of exceptional individuals) cannot be taken as representative of a society, whose conversion is instead expressed in statistics: the number of baptized and the degree to which ecclesiastical order is accepted (28). This author will use the term “Christianization” to include both societal and individual conversion, involving either a radical departure from previous practice or a sutler “adherence” (28–31). The author attempts to define Christianity; after pointing out that this is nontrivial in a historical perspective, he settles on “the belief in individual redemption through the suffering and death of Jesus Christ” (33–5, at 35). The degree of Christianization can be measured by the degree of reorientation around that belief and saturation of “the reception of baptism and other sacraments, doctrinal assent, ethical conformity, liturgical usage, and ecclesiastical discipline” (36). The author agrees with Van Engen, who rejects the view that a clerical elite was Christian while the masses effective subscribed to folklore. Instead, he suggests an ongoing synthesis and gradual transition, with effects going both ways, i.e. including a Germanization (36–8). Germanization consisted in the deliberate inclusion of “Germanic religiocultural attitudes within Christianity by Christian missionaries,” eventually transforming Christianity “from a universal salvation religion to a Germanic, and eventually European, folk religion” (39). The Germanic connection between warfare and religion is adduced; Wallace-Hadrill has argued that this attitude was simply incorporated as religiously motivated warfare (40). Cites some authors who believed the liturgy underwent considerable Germanization (41–2; the business of praying with hands folded is brought up, but surely that’s later?).

[3: Sociohistorical Aspects of Religious Transformation] Classifies the Indo-European religions as “ ‘folk,’ ‘ethnic,’ or ‘natural,’” as opposed to “‘universal,’ ‘revealed,’ ‘prophetic,’ or ‘historical’ ” (46). Christianity is of the latter category, so a model of religious transformation aimed at exploring contact between the two had best investigate other such clashes, as between Hellenic and proto-Christian traditions (45). Among several considerations in such comparisons is the recognition that folk religions tend to define themselves in ethnocultural terms rather than doctrinal ones (48). Most folk religions seem to have their sacral locus in the community itself: rituals reinforce exclusive ties and in-group identification. By contrast, universal religions have their sacral locus in individual salvation through a transcendental existence, typically attainable by all (48–9). It has been claimed that universal religions tend to succeed folk religions (in specific ways, 49).

Universal religions may appeal to a ruling elite for their potential to increase social cohesion. It seems universal religions are sometimes succeeded by folk religions when folk-religious attitudes were never effectively rooted out; this happened in Germanic areas, too (50). The disruption of social order may trigger new ways of making religious sense of political events, which may tend to be world-rejecting and occasionally bring messianic expectations (51). Such circumstances also gave rise to Christianity (51–2). World rejection is defined (53–4). A parallel to Christian expansion is found in the spread of Mahayana Buddhism in China, this too in a time of political unrest (54–5). The initial expansion of Islam took place under similar circumstances (55–6). In short, prolonged anomie makes a society receptive of world-rejection and unitarian (57–8). It is claimed that Indo-Europeans traditionally had three estates (priests, warriors, and herders-cultivators), and that these were reflected in their myths and ideology, the warrior stratum being the most distinctive element from a comparative perspective (58–9). By the time Christianity came to Indo-European parts, however, IE religion had been “diluted” under the influence of non-IE Greek traditions (59–60). This was less the case in the north, however, where the clash of religions was accordingly stronger once Christianity made it there (60–1). By that point, Christianity had already been heavily influenced by Greek ((Neo)platonic and Stoic) philosophy above all (61–2).

For a new religion to gain adherents, it needs to respond to a social aspiration: the in-group’s desire to strengthen and rationalize their power, and the out-group’s desire to improve their condition. Indo-Europeans fought themselves into the in-groups of conquered societies and tended to develop (patrilineal) foundation myths to reinforce social boundaries (62–3). Wars destabilized Greece and predisposed its population towards salvation religions, and the status of the afterlife improved (63–5).

The polis provided the Greeks with strong social cohesion; it has been claimed to have grown from IE roots (65–6). The upper classes of the Greek world especially embraced Epicureanism, Stoicism, Skepticism, and Cynicism, all aimed at individual self-fulfilment and universalism (67–9). Some of the natural and folk religions in Rome met with opposition from the Senate on sociopolitical grounds (71–2). The deterioration of societal structure in Rome was accompanied by an increasing interest in various religions (72–3). This was a receptive context for Christianity, which brought structure and a higher sort of salvation (73). Palestine in the first century CE was characterized by “urban disenchantment,” which fed messianism (75). This movement too was characterized by world rejection (76), and shifted from a Judaic focus on this world to a Christian focus on the next (76–7). Gnosticism was the most world-rejecting of religions, and this too was a response to social issues (78–9).

If Germanic culture is understood to have been unreceptive to salvation religions by nature, Noel Smith has studied the processes that have led cultures to adopt world-rejecting religions, going as far as to claim that mind/body dualism owes its existence to Greek oppression (79–80.

[4: Sociopsychological Aspects of Religious Transformation] The practice in early Christianity of emulating a family (it being a fraternal/sororal community), combined with its universal (as opposed to ethnic), suprastate nature, led some to condemn it as a threat to the security of the state (81–2). Its promotion of celibacy attracted those who had abandoned their families (82). Individuals whose social standing has crystallized at an undesirable level (e.g. as a result of emigration) may be drawn to an equalizing religion like Christianity (83–4). Alexander the Great’s empire was characterized by confusion and (Asian-Hellenic) syncretism (84–5); it has been suggested that this situation contributed to the Christianization of Greco-Roman cities (86–7). Urbanization would have been an important factor in this process (87); they were shelters for cognitive [cultural] dissonance (88), known to contemporaries as a loving community (88–9). To the alienated, this community offered both eternal salvation and a community in the present world (89–93). It is proposed that Christianity also served as a stress relief (94–7). Whereas urban Rome had come to be dominated by its non-Roman elements when it encountered Christianity, the Germanic world was homogeneous and cohesive — at a different stage of development, as the author puts it (98). The author cites a dubious source claiming that the classical world was “being-oriented” but the Germanic world was “becoming-oriented” and accordingly more dynamic (99); the author distances himself from this source to some degree but builds on it to suggest that the Peloponnesian and Punic Wars along with Alexander’s conquest overthrew the “harmonious ethos” of the classical world; the consequent ethos of personal fulfilment was predisposed towards salvation religion (99–100). The success of Christianity diminished as it spread north beyond its original region and came to rely on (1) the presence of a Jewish community; (2) substantial exposure to Christianity; and (3) an anomic social structure (100–1). Missionaries had to choose between a candid and comparatively ineffective conversion effort or a watered-down initial approach able to yield more converts in a short time (101–2).

[5: Germanic Religiosity and Social Structure] Dumézil’s belief that many Indo-European cultures share ideological and sometimes social structures is explored through his concept of the mythologem, a fundamental ideological concept that may be compared from one culture to another (107).

Early Germanic religiosity has to be accessed through external authors like Caesar and Tacitus, who depict a culture that worships the visible things of this world (108–10). In addition, we have Snorri Sturluson’s writings, which the author places in an alarmingly reliable light (110–11). Dumézil claims that the relationship between Æsir and Vanir is crucial to an understanding of Indo-European religiosity; he believes they both came in with the Indo-Europeans, and their myth reflects certain social developments between the Indo-European estates whose exact nature does not become clear from the chosen quotations. Whatever it is, Dumézil believed the same network is found in Indian and Roman tradition (112–13). Dumézil’s central analysis of Indo-European society and ideology was tripartition: chieftains, warriors, and shepherds/farmers, which correspond to sets like sun, moon, and fire (114). Polomé has built on this dreadful basis by identifying IE society as ethnocentric and patriarchal, and positing on no apparent grounds whatsoever that there must have been a taboo on putting mythology down in writing (114–16). Russell basically buys all this, and the notion that a formal tripartite structure is unique to IE culture (116–17). Dumézil has further identified a shared narrative theme in which a warrior sins against each of the three estates and is punished for it (117). Littleton has singled out the warrior as the pivot of IE society; this explains the endurance of the warrior ethic despite Christianization (117–18). The rest of the chapter emphasizes fame and honour as Germanic heroic values, and contrasts them with Christian teachings; the group solidarity of the comitatus is contrasted with Roman society (118–33). As part of this, the author discusses the heroic elements in Germanic saints’ lives (124–25). The Germanization argument is here repeated in the context of these factors (131–2), and it is claimed that Christianization was very slow among Germanic peoples (132–3).

[6: Germanization and Christianization: 376–678] The first large-scale contact between Germanic speakers and Christianity came when the Visigoths sought refuge in the Roman Empire in 376 [though Wulfila came before, in 341]; the circumstances of the associated Christianizations are typical of all such encounters and include the protection of citizenship; the religion’s association with Roman culture and the Empire; the absence of catechization; and the emergence of a folk-religious interpretation (134–5). At what point the Visigoths really sprouted a Christian culture is uncertain (136–7), but they did develop Arianism, which then spread to many other Germanic tribes; but the Franks, Saxons, Alamanni, and Frisians do not seem to have been affected (137–8). The popularity of Arianism among Germanic cultures just as it was being eradicated in the Empire may be explained by their fear of losing their ethnic group identity if they accepted Catholicism; the increasing catholicism of the Empire as a whole would only have fuelled the growth of Arianism among the Goths (139–42). This also had the effect of lessening their standing within the Empire (144–5). The Franks embraced Catholicism, as it seems, because such kings as Clovis allied themselves with the bishops of their province because the episcopal office was interwoven with the aristocracy; it was a policy of political cohesion. Also, the Goths at this time were slaughtering Christians in Gaul and looked poised to take over the realm (149–50). The greater acceptance of Catholicism among the Franks may be due to their gradual acculturation: they never moved suddenly into the Empire. Instead, they gradually expanded into the Roman province of Gaul, as part of an understanding that must have had a religious dimension (150–1). The Franks generally had a more harmonious relationship with the Romans, and had most to fear from neighbouring Germanic tribes (151). The Gallic episcopacy also had something to gain from the alliance, as the interior administrative system was crumbling (151–2). Clovis’s conversion was momentous, as it shifted the centre of Christendom’s gravity from the Mediterranean to the north, eventually Aachen (152). On the other hand, missions in the fifth to seventh centuries were superficial and did not root out folk-religious elements (152–3). In the sixth century, Christianization among the Germanic peoples remained at a virtual standstill; but it did see the rise of an Eigenkirchensystem and Eigenklostersystem that undermined the unity of the Church (153–4). The Merovingians made little effort to educate and reform the converted; they only saw the political, cohesion benefits of Christianization, and to some degree understood Christian infrastructure in the pre-Christian Germanic sense of legitimizing power. They strove for orthopraxy, not orthodoxy (154–5). Max Weber emphasizes the degree to which Christianity and sectarian activity have historically developed in urban environments; he calls a rural development of such a highly organized religion highly unlikely, but also deems the religious ethic, beyond such practical services as protection against magic and prayer for victory, unpalatable to a warrior nobility (155–6).

The Irish were successful, however, perhaps because of their heroic self-discipline or wergild-like penitentials. Their monasteries became affiliated with noble families; this association and the possibility of venerating relatives as saints may have given this movement a certain desirability. The concept of Geblütsheiligkeit, inherited sacral character, has likewise been adduced (156–7). There were cultic elements to Frankish Christianity, its structures built atop the graves of nobles (157–8).

Ireland lacked the administrative infrastructure of Rome. Accordingly, Ireland had a patchwork of tribal churches, and its monasteries were governed in close alliance with the local monarchy. The resulting rural infrastructure was a good model for a Germanic Church, but Irish missionary efforts in Francia were hampered by clashes with a pre-existing Gallic episcopal system, not acknowledged by Columbanus. Irish-built monasteries furthermore tended to decline after the death of the founding abbot (158).

The Merovingian kings saw the cohesive potential of Christianity: Dagobert I offered the Bishop of Cologne the Utrecht see in return for evangelizing his border regions specifically (158).

Columbanus was a prototype of the Carolingian missionary efforts in that he strove for moral perfection rather than advertising God as a fulfiller of worldly wishes; a personal rather than an institutional approach (159–60). The sins he discusses in his penitential emphasize the desire for wrongdoing, whereas preexisting Frankish emphases had been on observance (e.g. of the Sunday) (160–1). Le Goff characterizes “Celtic (and perhaps Germanic)” religion as optimistic as regards the afterlife; Roman (and ultimately oriental) Christianity is more pessimistic, but ended up subsuming the northern vision into Paradise (161–2). More generally, the missions to Germanic lands adopted accommodation as a policy, as the recalibration of the stem *hailagaz from “societal prosperity” to “individual holiness and salvation” demonstrates (according to Baetke; 163). In the Irish, one can see a “phase-two,” moralizing approach to evangelization among the already converted, but a rougher “phase-one” confrontation with cult objects and practices in pagan regions (164).

The Anglo-Saxon missionaries differed from the Irish in their firm alignment to Roman customs and organization, but they also lacked the apolitical, world-rejecting, personal approach of the Irish (e.g. Columbanus refusing to mingle religion with worldly conflict), which was likewise alien to the Gallo-Roman bishops (164–5). The Irish efforts eventually fell on shallow soil, however, because they did not embrace a hierarchical structure, renounced the worldly governments that could have backed them, and had unusual ideas about the dating of Easter and the form of the tonsure (165–6). Elements of religion are recapitulated which may be considered evidence of Germanization if found in Christianity: world-acceptance, an interrelation with social structure, high group solidarity, religiopolitics, magic religion, and warrior ethics are the hallmarks to look out for (166–7). Three caveats are given: the effects of Germanization need not be unique to Germanic influence; the effects need not have endured into the modern period; and they need not have emerged immediately upon contact (167–9). Baetke claims that Germanic religions, like their IE cousins the Greek and Roman religions, were political; gods were national. Religion and politics were organically interwoven (171–2). Sacral kingship is the epitome of this system in Germanic tradition (172–3). Tacitus claimed there was a political rex and a military dux, but De Vries and others have concluded the latter position ended up subsuming the functions of the former during the Migration Era (173). Alaric began as the former but died as the latter (174); the name Theodoric in fact is made up of the Gothic words for the two, thiudans and reiks (174–5). Various thinkers have noted the novelty to Europe of the linear progress of time in a Judaeo-Christian world view; Le Goff has argued that it remained secondary to the circular, seasonal, agricultural time of pre-Christian times throughout the Middle Ages (176). Peter Brown has likewise expressed the conversion in terms of a new view on the relation between humankind and nature (176–7). Bauschatz asserts that Germanic culture was concerned with its own past (177–8). Significantly, the Nibelungenlied and Edda do not incorporate the Christian understanding of time as a progress from Creation to Judgement Day, bisected by the Resurrection, to any great degree (178–9).

The Germanic reinterpretation of Christianity included the rise of votive Masses intended to attain personal ends as well as the increasing use of side altars; these repurpose Christian worship for worldly ends (180–1). The reliance on saints likewise served this end (181–2).

[7: Germanization and Christianization: 678–754] It was not until Gregory the Great that Roman leaders began to think of Germanic peoples as anything but barbaric and alien and therefore not worth evangelizing to. The eschatological focus of the age may have persuaded Gregory that the time for conversion of all peoples was running out (there is support for this understanding in his letters); such a mindset might have implicitly made baptism without prior catechization acceptable (184). Gregory’s letter to Mellitus, which says not to destroy heathen temples, seems to contradict his epistle to Æthelbert, which instructs the opposite. R.A. Markus has determined that the letter to Mellitus was written a month after that to Æthelbert, and proposes that Gregory’s views changed as the optimism of initial reports gave way to a picture of greater resistance (186–7). The letter to Mellitus represents a momentous shift in policy, substituting accommodation for coercion in such conditions as required it (187). Though intended to be temporary, such accommodation brought a risk of long-term syncretism, especially when, as in seventh- and eighth-century Germanic regions, corrective catechism was not provided (188). Whether or not Gregory intended for the accommodation to be a first step or the highest attainable outcome, “[t]he magicoreligious reinterpretation of Christianity may be considered the most immediate and salient effect of its Germanization [but how are the gospels and Acts not magicoreligious? PSL], while the folk-centered religiopolitical reinterpretation of Christianity may be considered its most enduring effect,” giving rise to the crusading ideology and European exceptionalism (188–90, at 189). Others have identified aspects of Christian liturgy that were germanized: a greater physical and spiritual distance between celebrant and churchgoers, a heightened focus on sacred objects such as shrines and relics (with accompanying processions), and the expected direct divine intervention in response to prayer [but that is already present in the legend of Constantine’s conversion, PSL] (190–1).

Magicoreligious faith may be shorter-lived than soteriological faith; advances in scientific understanding can undermine it. Soteriological evangelization meets with greater resistance, however, and that was a central problem in the Christianization of Germanic cultures (191–2). Boniface was probably familiar with Gregory’s missionary philosophy, though the letters which we know he requested date from after the height of Gregory’s missionary interest. We do have a letter by Archbishop Daniel of Canterbury recommending Boniface a policy of gentle, logical correction (if your gods are so powerful, then why don’t they spare the Christians who are converting their servants and overthrowing their temples? (193–4).

If Boniface accepted Daniel’s advice, he is likely to have advertised worldly as well as eternal benefits; victory in battle would have been especially desirable to his audience. Pope Zachary himself promised this to the Franks in a letter of 745 (194–5). Thomas Leslie Amos has attempted to reconstruct the content of Boniface’s preaching, observing that the Anglo-Saxon approach focused more on advertising the power of God and the positive virtues of the Christian faith, whereas the Frankish missionary Wulframm was unsuccessful in his attempts to convert Redbad after telling him his ancestors were damned; Willibrord is reported to have preached a far more positive message to the same Frisian leader (195–6). Secular and papal support was another important pillar of Anglo-Saxon missionary activity (196–7). Postbaptismal instruction was minimal, however: adult baptism became a rarity after the sixth century, and accordingly so did the catechumenate; knowledge of Scripture declined accordingly (198–9). The level of interest of local secular or religious leaders as well as itinerant preachers determined the level of education (199). A sermon by an eighth-century missionary preacher reflects a concern that the converted had not converted in deeds (199–200).

It seems that the accommodation of the target peoples’ folk-religious outlook in missionary efforts obscured the differences between Germanic and Christian world-views. Since missionaries apparently baptized without ascertaining informed assent to the new world-view, any postbaptismal efforts at instruction naturally met with resistance (200–1). The missionaries associated a world-view transformation with baptism, but this was insufficiently communicated to the baptizees (202). As Robert A. Markus puts it, “[t]he early history of Germanic Christianity is dominated by the paradox that mass conversion required some considerably continuity. . . . Christianity . . . had become the religion of a warrior nobility whose values and culture it had necessarily to absorb in the process of Christianizing them” (202–3). Hans-Joachim Schoeps: “[a]pperently, very few among them noticed that they were expected to shift to a new concept of reality” (203). Germanic ethics were based on kin loyalty, and fame was a high good because it brought glory for oneself and one’s kin; but sin and guilt [persumably in a “victimless” sense] were unknown, which made it hard for missionaries to create a market for salvation (204). Heinz Rupp has pointed out that the German vernacular was used to familiarize new concepts using old words: concepts such as sin, lord, salvation, and holiness thus shifted meaning (205); this was part of the second phase of Christianization, along with an incorporation of Germanic imagery and a metaphorization of otherwise unacceptable Germanic elements (205–7). The use of *hailagaz for sanctus and dryhten for dominus was sheer tactics on the part of the Anglo-Saxon clergy, but they backfired in the sense that they effected a Germanization of Christianity (206–7).

author: Anton, Hans Hubert
title: Fürstenspiegel und Herrscherethos in der Karolingerzeit
abstract: Identifies a late Classical tradition of rulers’ ethics based on classical Virtus, Nobilitas, and Sanguis; successful self-control is here seen as a necessary condition for the successful management of a kingdom. Personal ethics and personal qualities such as mildness are the marks of a good ruler (45–7). Augustine in all his thought emphasizes pax, ordo, and iustitia: peace is harmony between Creation and Creator. Augustine greatly influenced the ideal of the Christian ruler in DcD 5.24, where he specifies that the imperator felix governs justly and humbly, remembering his humanness; gives God the glory for his power; fears, loves, and honours him; etc. (47–8). Gregory the Great took and modified these sentiments, awarding iustitia the greatest weight. Thought about rulers’ ethics had by then not yet developed into such a structural tradition in Germanic parts, but the Merovingian Christianization of rulership made the creation of a Christian rulers’ ethic possible (48).

author: Banham, Debby, and Rosamond Faith
title: Anglo-Saxon Farms and Farming
abstract:
Divides into two parts: the first (by Banham) studies the nature, tools, and products of agriculture and animal husbandry; the second (by Faith) considers different types of landscape for their roles in farming. By farming means both agriculture and pastoralism; primarily food production, but some textile and building materials; does not discuss forestry, horticulture, or viticulture (5). Contains a good deal of speculation based on the observation of modern or late medieval practice; positive evidence for the period is minimal.

The introduction paints a general picture of Anglo-Saxon and “individual” self-sufficiency in terms of food, clothes, and aspects of accommodation (2). Technological adoption was generally slow (3). Makes rather strong statements about temperatures in the early medieval period (“temperatures in the eleventh century may have been as high as in the early twenty-first,” 4, citing Burroughs, Climate Change, 252–6).

The authors provide a very helpful list with brief appraisals of important and recent work touching on Old English farming based on historical and archaeological sources (6–8), as well as a brief overview of the types of written sources that provide information on this topic, namely the three estate management texts Rectitudines, Gerefa, and the “Ely Farming Memoranda”; Laws (Dunsætan and Ine); Charters; textbooks (De temporum ratione in its month-names; Ælfric’s Colloquy); charms and medical texts; and narratives such as the Vita Cuthberti and Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (8–11). The remainder of the introduction summarily introduces other types of evidence: archaeology, linguistic evidence, today’s farming knowledge, manuscript illustrations, and comparative material (11–14). The authors introduce their methodology as historical “source pluralism” rather than interdisciplinarity (14–15).

[2: Arable Farming I] Emphasizes that arable and animal husbandry, being interdependent, must everywhere have been integrated; however, the balance would have varied between regions. Since there was no significant market for agricultural products, local growing conditions determined what one could eat (19). In terms of arable crop volume, Anglo-Saxon agriculture seems to have produced less than the preceding Romano-British culture or post-Conquest England (20).

The greatest harvest was from grains. Grains were of today’s species, but genetically quite different; each species was also genetically more heterogeneous. There must also have been a climatic and contact-based diversity, grains in England differing from those in France and those in the north more hardy than those in the south. Pre-[eighteenth-century agricultural revolution] crops also had longer straw, since straw was a useful byproduct and gets in the way of combine harvesters (20–2). Wheat and barley were always the most produced grains, oats and rye less common (22). Evidence for wheat (22–5) and barley (26–8) is discussed: lexical evidence is used as a clue to the discernment of subspecies, but there is no discussion of etymology; place-name evidence is presented in table format. It is observed that there were more place-names with barley than with wheat, perhaps because settlements were named when barley was still dominant, or else because wheat was unremarkable. There is no great geographic difference between barley and wheat place-names (24). The Anglo-Saxon period witnessed a shift from the hulled cereals of Roman times to today’s free-threshing cereals, but also a shift from barley to wheat as the primary (bread) cereal. Naked cereals are easier to process into flour and generally more palatable; hulled grains are hardier on the field and store better under subpar (humid) conditions (28–9).

Although rye may have started out as a weed, it probably did not grow as such in Anglo-Saxon England, as it does not today. A month-name rugern recorded about 700 and again about 800 seems to mean “rye harvest” (perhaps [coinciding with] August). There are a fair few place-names with rye, indicating that it was a familiar grain, but in England it was bread wheat that replaced hulled wheats in this period, whereas in northern Continental Europe it was rye (30).

Oats have long coexisted in cultivated and wild species, and they did in Anglo-Saxon England; but paucity of place-names (none undisputed pre-Conquest) suggests that they were either uncommon or unremarkable. Oats can withstand more humidity than wheat; accordingly, they eventually replaced wheat in many upland areas (31–2). There is little that can be said about regional variation; we do know wheat was also grown in Northumbria, where it must have been at the limits of its viability, as is also mentioned in the Vita Cuthberti (32–3). A good summary of cereal changes in this period (hulled to free, barley to wheat) is given, although I don’t suppose the first evidence of oats and rye in this period means they were not cultivated before (33).

Pulse crops/legumes were responsible for the second largest arable harvest, especially peas and beans; lentils have been found at a few later sites. Lentil finds correspond to the Medieval Warm Period (900–1300) in the south, east, and Midlands (33–4). The authors disagree with Lynn White’s belief that beans and other legumes fuelled social and technological change by boosting tenth-century nutrition (35–6). It is “extremely likely” that different crops were grown together on the same field, but there is no conclusive evidence for this (36). Interestingly, the authors are sceptical of crops being grown specifically for fodder below the highest levels of society; the chaff and straw of food crops would have been used to feed animals, and animals would have grazed arable land post-harvest, fallows, and uncultivated headlands (36–7). Flax and hemp were grown as non-food crops, flax mostly in the east; the seeds of these crops may have been eaten, too (37–8). Further plants neede more attention and would have been cultivated in gardens (38). In the conclusion, the authors suppose there would have been a gradual increases in total food crops; it is speculated that cerealization (a move towards arable crops and away from animal husbandry) and the “arable revival” about the middle of the period may reflect population growth, though fashion may have played a role as well (39).

[3: Arable Farming II] Not all farmers will have had access to a plough; hand tools were therefore more important than is often thought (41–2). Manure is difficult to identify in the archaeological record, but it was certainly used as fertilizer. Skeletons contain high nitrogen levens, suggesting the heavy manuring of cereals. The introduction of the heavier mouldboard plough would have required more animal power and may thus indirectly have increased manuring. Crop rotation may also have been practised to improve fertility, and legume cultivation would have had this effect whether or not this was an intended effect (42–4). The heavy plough was used in Roman Britain, and either continued to be used in Anglo-Saxon times or was reintroduced early on (44–6). By some standard of interpretation, MS illustrations may be understood to suggest that mouldboard ploughs were common by the eleventh century while ards (scratch ploughs) were also still in use [if these are not copies from Continental images; also, we don’t have many MSS from before this period] (47–8). Only Exeter Riddle 21 unambiguously describes a mouldboard (49).

Use of the ard would have required more labour, because it needs several runs; the heavy plough more capital. Light [= well-drained] soils could be rapidly reploughed, but heavy soils had to rest in between runs to give sods a chance to break down; if waterlogged in winter, they could not be ploughed at all. A farmer with an ard could spend the entire winter ploughing. The heavy plough might do a ploughing after harvest and one before sowing. This had the advantage of making winter crops possible, while drier land could be used as pasture until a single pre-sowing ploughing (50–1).

Domesday specifies eight oxen to a plough, but MS illustrations show fewer; this may reflect artistic liberty or the use of shifts (51). We here of traction animals (51–4); oxen can only plough for short days, and darkness would have limited a day’s work further in winter. An acre a day seems to have been the standard (and perhaps that’s where the word acre comes from), allowing no more than 150 acres per team per year; Domesday suggests 60–120 (53–4). Speculates whether the desire for food security was the motivation behind adopting the mouldboard plough, or whether the rise of an urban population required larger yields per capita (54–5). A plausible theory is that the expansion of wheat production required an expansion to heavier soils, which required draining in order to be used in winter — which is when wheat was grown in the later Middle Ages. The mouldboard plough makes “ridge and furrow” ploughing possible, resulting in drier ridges for cultivation and a furrow for drainage. It should be noted that there is no evidence for this technique in Anglo-Saxon England (55–7).

There are no sources for Anglo-Saxon sowing seasonality; in the late medieval Midlands, wheat and rye were sown in winter, barley and oats in spring. Conceivably, northern European farming of necessity began with spring sowing, and shifted to winter crops when technological advances or breeding made it possible (57–8). Evidence of pre-Conquest harrowing is questionable (58). Sowing was done by hand (“broadcast sowing”), likely immediately behind the plough, or before plough or harrow to avoid losing seed to the birds (58–9). Weeds could be discouraged by repeated ploughing or suboptimal levels of manure, but weeds would not have reached large quantities in the shade of broadcast long-strawed cereals, while annual weeds would die before the harvest. Archaeobotanical evidence also suggests weeds were not entirely weeded out (59–60). The month-name weodmonath ([coinciding with] August) is a rare reference to weeding; most such references are in the gospels. Weeding may have been a gendered activity and therefore underreported, or it may have been less of a problem than we have come to expect (60–1).

Sickles were used for reaping (scythes are modern); cereal crops were bound in sheafs and left to stand, probably in stooks (piles) or mows (small stacks) until dry, which could be weeks (61–2). The harvest probably involved seasonal workers (62).

Cereal storage seems to have been done on a limited scale, and therefore outside, perhaps thatched over (63). There is some brief discussion of threshing and winnowing (64–6).

Many crops were grown in enclosures to prevent unauthorized access; livestock only came to be kept in enclosures as grazing became scarce. Fencing was a legislated duty in Ine’s laws (66–7). Much debate surrounds the move towards open fields (i.e. away from enclosures), but it did not happen uniformly or everywhere. Such a reorganization would be easist where nucleation existed, but there is no consensus on such a correlation. Ine’s eighth-century laws suggest fencing was done individually and not by all. Positive evidence for open fields is very limited, but the phrasing used suggests long strips and furlongs. We have seen that the mouldboard plough became popular in the course of the period, and that it combines naturally with ridge and furrow ploughing; both make most sense in an open-field system. Wheat as a winter crop may have been the driver behind a move to open-field farming (68–70). The heavy plough explains the long, narrow shapes of fields (71).

One village has been named as a tenth-century example of a two-field system; there is no other evidence for either two- or three-field rotation (72–3). An infield/outfield arrangement must have been more common than open fields, with the outfield used mainly for pasture and sometimes cultivated. Even more common might have been a complicated, custom “system” based on what land was found to do well with what crops (73). Use of kilns and ovens for the drying of crops increased over the period, and mechanical mills were introduced. All changes combined represented a greater emphasis on arable cultivation and an intensification within that sector (74).

[4: Animal Husbandry I] In one way, animals were more valuable than crops: they are found all over the law codes and in wills, whereas crops are not (75). They represent a greater investment of land and labour per calory than crops; this also means plant foods are more efficient. Land efficiency was not a limiting factor early on, however, so labour would have been the more valuable input, making intensive production of any food type difficult and a low-maintenance type of livestock production likely. Although there is no evidence for such a system, it may have existed early on (75–6).

Having access to animal foods would have brought social as well as dietary well-being. All Anglo-Saxons ate meat sometimes, but most would have eaten a limited range of plant food most of the time (76). Cerealization may have reduced the proportion of animal production, but not absolute production if cerealization reflects population growth (76–7).

Animals were smaller than today, and reverse-engineering breeders’ efforts suggests they must have been slower-growing and less productive; also, more seasonal in their productivity (77). Like cereal crops, animal breeds too were more genetically heterogeneous owing to geographical separation from adjacent pools and adaptation to local terrain (77–8).

Horses [for travelling] were associated with aristocracy, but people of lower rank could own them [working horses] too (79). Prior to the twelfth century, horses were used for carrying, not traction (79–80). Horse meat was eaten, whether by people or dogs; they were not raised in the same places as other food animals, which may indicate they were not for human consumption especially after the Conversion (81–2). There is little evidence for mules and donkeys (83–4).

Cattle had many functions and was highly valued: an ox was worth one quarter the price of horses, a cow one sixth, a pig one twelfth, a sheep 1/24 (85–6). Sheep and above all cow bones are the most numerous bone finds (87). The Rectitudines consider six sheep, two oxen, and one cow the minimal livestock assets of a peasant holding (92). Goats are difficult to quantify on a zooarchaeological basis, but were probably kept where the terrain did not favour other livestock; place names support this hypothesis. They are rarely mentioned in documents (96–7).

Large, commercially viable herds of pigs were kept in private woodlands by aristocrats; to judge by Rectitudines, geneatas also kept pigs, but geburas not necessarily (98). Pigs took third place to cattle and sheep/goats in numbers (99–100). The chapter also discusses poultry (100–4) and bees (104–5).

[5: Animal Husbandry II] [In an organic economy,] it would be a waste to raise large animals for meat only. Anglo-Saxon diets included far more diet than the bones can account for in terms of meat; the gap must have been filled by dairy and eggs. Meat only became the primary product in the late Middle Ages (107–8). But energy was a crucial product as well: oxen (and cows) were for traction (108–10). Cows, goats, and sheep provided milk (110–13). Meat was a social marker. There was greater emphasis on meat in the early period, followed by cerealization. Goats were probably seldom eaten (113–15). Only pigs had no secondary purpose beyond meat; but both meat and fat could be preserved by salting and smoking, and lard was ubiquitous; it was even allowed during Lent because it was not meat (115–16). “Pigs are traditionally slaughtered in the depths of winter,” but we cannot confirm this pattern for Anglo-Saxon England; it is likely accurate for the two-year-olds (116). Poultry seems to have been eaten a lot by the poor, for whom it may have been the sole meat (perhaps alongside pork); but the upper classes ate it too (116–17). However, eggs were the primary reason for keeping poultry. Hens under natural circumstances lay most eggs in March–May and stop laying in winter; a contemporary Irish source suggests a typical yield was 50 eggs a year, but they were smaller eggs than today’s (117–18). Wool was the most important fibre (118–21); some further by-products are mentioned (121–2). The remainder of the chapter looks at the labour involved in animal husbandry (122–36).

author: Keefer, Sarah Larratt
title: In Closing: Amen and Doxology in Anglo-Saxon England
abstract: A descriptive piece, discussing first Anglo-Saxon renderings of “amen,” then doxologies. The “gloria patri” type, known as the “Lesser Doxology,” became formulaic early on. Cites Bethurum for the recognition that Wulfstan’s doxology (or the clausula, as Bethurum specifies) seems to vary by scribe, suggesting that Wulfstan did not integrate a doxology into the fabric of his compositions but left the closing words to scribes (226–7). Ælfric does seem to have composed his own doxologies; some of these render the Gloria patri, others highlight the second sentence of the classical Lesser Doxology, which starts with sicut erat and a focus on time (227–8).

author: Leppin, Hartmut
title: Von Constantin dem Großen zu Theodosius II.: Das christliche Kaisertum bei den Kirchenhistorikern Socrates, Sozomenus und Theodoret
series: Hypomnemata: Untersuchungen zur Antike und zu Ihrem Nachleben
abstract: Identifies the differences in the historiographies of Socrates, Sozomenus, and Theodoret, the three Greek authors whose works were later brought together by Epiphanios Scholastikos and compiled or edited by Epiphanios’ friend Cassiodorus as the Historia tripartita (DOE reference PS.CASSIOD. Hist.eccl.trip.).

author: Lenker, Ursula
title: Die westsächsische Evangelienversion und die Perikopenordnung im angelsächsischen England
abstract:
[On Old Testament readings]: from the sixth to the mid-twentieth century, the Roman Mass had only two Scripture readings: the first was from the Old Testament, epistles, Acts, or Apocalypse, the second from the Gospels. Originally, and since the Second Vatican Council of 1962–65, the number was/has been three. In both configuration, there was only one Gospel reading, namely the last. Specifically, “[a]n den Werktagen der allgemeinen Kirchenjahrzeit geht der Evangelienperikope eine Lesung aus dem Alten Testament voraus” (81–2, at 82). An internal ordering for OT readings can be found for Sundays after Pentecost and the Wednesdays in those weeks: Van Dijk, “The Bible in Liturgical Use,” in Lampe, Cambridge History of the Bible, 2.220–51, at 225 (ctd. in Lenker 95n).

The first Scripture reading, covering the Old Testament, Epistles, Acts, or Apocalypse, was thus part of Mass from the earliest times, certainly including Anglo-Saxon England (125). Since only about 18 fragmentary Bible MSS survive, Bibles could not have sustained a lectio continua for the first reading (125–6). Part-Bibles are not much better attested, prompting the question what book-form the subdeacon (pistolrædere) used (126). Lenker conjectures that many lectionaries simply have not survived: after all, most of the many surviving evangeliaries are display copies, not use MSS, which would have worn more rapidly and therefore not preserved (126–7).

Medieval book lists turn up (part)-evangeliaries, but no complete Bibles; five lists attest to altogether nine single biblical books, with one record each of Pentateuch, Prophets, Ezekiel, Proverbs, Isaiah, Maccabees, and Daniel; the NT record contains Pauline epistles. Four of the five lists stem from the second half of the eleventh century. Thus not only do few biblical MSS survive, they are also poorly attested in medieval times (127–8 and n. 106). On the other hand, pistolboc, pistelboc, and epistolarium are found in six out of thirteen book lists, but no epoistolary survives (128).

The contents of pistolbec are not a foregone conclusion. The monastic sign language text indicates that the god spel is read from it, suggesting that the word referred not to an epistolary, but a combined lectionary, i.e. a work containing the readings for both the first and the second Scripture reading (129). Ælfric in his pastoral letters refers to “lectionarium, quod quidam uocant epistolarium,” reinforcing the sense that epistolarium could refer to a combined lectionary (130–1).

author: Lubac, Henri de
title: Typologie, Allegorie, Geistiger Sinn: Studien zur Geschichte der christlichen Schriftauslegung
abstract:
Not a straightforward translation of de Lubac’s magnum opus, but a thematic sequence of translated selections from three of his books, including his Exégèse médiévale, and what looks like three complete essays.

One of these, “Ein altes Distichon: Die Lehre vom ‘vierfachen Schriftsinn’” (319–42, orig. publ. 1949), provides a balanced and accessible introduction to Old Testament typology, although it does not provide the range of type:antitype examples one would hope to include in student reading, and it has de Lubac’s characteristic religious bias. Argues that the fourfold division was not only an early one, but one that is fundamental to theology and results from the structural integrity achieved when these four approaches, which build on one another, are combined (328–9). Rather than contradict one another, they reiterate the lower levels with a fuller understanding (329–30). Importantly, Augustine and the other patristic authors after him did not claim that every verse of Scripture contains four layers (332–4), but they did see the whole collection of biblical books as conveying a single message with presents itself in an allegorical, tropological, or anagogical light in different contexts (334–5). The last several pages of this essay ponder the lost relevance of this exegetical mode in twentieth-century theology.

author: Ohly, Friedrich
title: Sensus Spiritualis: Studies in Medieval Significs and the Philology of Culture
abstract:
[1: On the Spiritual Sense of the Word in the Middle Ages] [This chapter is a translation of this item.] In the Christian Middle Ages, all language was held to be subject to spiritual interpretation (1–2, esp. 2). The application of this method on the Bible permeated all the arts and constituted the greatest interpretative act in Christian tradition. The view was that Scripture stood apart from profane literature, which was limited to the historical or literal sense, whereas the Bible knew a spiritual sense, which theologians sought to draw out in addition to the philology of the literal word that continues to be the object of philology today (2–3). Christian tradition, this author holds, went beyond Classical and Ancient tradition in that it sought to understand not only the signified of the vox, namely the res, but also the signified of the literal object evoked by the word: each property of the thing brings with it a new meaning (4–6). This type of analysis was associated with the quadrivium (namely mathematics and physics) rather than with the trivium: medieval authors testify that the quadrivium concerned the meaning of things, the trivium the meaning of words (6–7). Ohly sees a hierarchy here: the trivium prepares the way for the material understanding of things, the quadrivium prepares the way for their spiritual understanding and forms no independent science but remains subservient to theology (7). All things, including the facts of history, have typological significance (8). The thing as such can signify good and evil, but in a distinct textual context it only ever has one signified (on the allegorical level) (9). An important distinction between words and things is that humans govern the former, God the latter; in the same way, humans communicate and give meaning to the former, but God governs the latter and uses them to reveal his will (13–14).

Allegory in this context means divine revelation through things (15), which happens on the three levels of allegory, tropology, and anagogy (15–16).

  • “Here allegory has the same meaning as the modern concept of typology, in other words, the relationship of meaning between prefiguration and fulfillment, as between the Old and the New Testaments.” The medieval success of allegory in the strict sense may be explained by its ability to cast Christianity as the fulfilment to Old Testament and antiquity.
  • “It is not from the aspect of the doctrine of salvation, but with respect to the life of the individual soul in the world that the word is revealed in the tropological or moral meaning that points out a way of leading one’s life, by indicating to the soul the path to, and the destination of, its salvation.
  • “And, finally, if it is questioned as to its statement about the promises which will be fulfilled in the afterlife, the anagogical meaning of the word is discovered, and that is meaning that leads us up to heaven. An example which is constantly given in the Middle Ages is the word Jerusalem: historically, it is a city on earth; allegorically, it is the church; tropologically, it is the soul of the believer; anagogically, it is God’s heavenly city” (16–17).

These four levels were understood to combine into an integrated whole in the manner that foundation, walls, roof, and interior form a house (17). Modern lexicography, limited to the literal, could not attain a word’s spiritual sense, which is why medieval etymology is such a different field: its task was a different one, namely to elucidate the meaning of life (18). The Babylonian confusion of languages exists only on the literal level (20).

Given this grammar of signification, it was only natural to extend it to the natural world (21–3). From the fifth century onwards, and especially after 820, there are also claves, allegorical dictionaries (still largely unedited) of the words used in the Bible (23–5). Luther’s personal transformation from a monk who (he claims) allegorized everything to a man relaying the plain sense of Scripture may be projected onto his wider period as the end of the Middle Ages (29–30).

author: Corona, Gabriella
title: Ælfric’s (Un)Changing Style: Continuity of Patterns from the Catholic Homilies to the Lives of Saints

author: Grein, C.W.M.
title: Ælfric’s metrischer Auszug aus dem Buch der Richter
abstract:
The first to print all of Judges in alliterative long lines; but he refers to earlier scholars who were aware of its metrical qualities, as well as of its homiletic nature. The parenthetical designation “Epilogus” is used in the same place where Crawford was to make this distinction later.

Note: the article was actually published by Richard Paul Wülcker after Grein’s death. He wrote the introduction and he put the text into metrical lines.
comments: Revised with an introduction by Richard Paul Wülcker

author: Prins, A.A.
title: Some Remarks on Ælfric’s Lives of Saints and his Translations from the Old Testament
abstract: On the chronology of Ælfric’s writings.

author: Deffner, Gerold
title: Untersuchungen zur Langzeile in Ælfrics Heiligenleben
abstract:
Opens with a long series of quotations about the nature of Ælfric’s style (1–14). Points out that Ælfric made choices of diction to accommodate alliteration (18–21) and cites scholars who point out how it differs from classical verse (21–3).

Some of the Lives of Saints are attested in Cotton Vitellius C. v with points marking the ends of long lines, or even of half-lines, adding up to an average of more than one point per line, which cannot be explained by thematic emphasis or similar (23–5). The system does not hold up everywhere, but it does in 91.1% of lines in LS [text] 2(25–8); additional points are grammatically regulated, e.g. before and/et (28–30). The remainder of the section is a quantified analysis of puncti (30–6). “Sprechgruppen,” narrative units, are discussed in their relevance to versification: b-lines are frequently omitted at the end of these, for instance (36–40). Ælfric has also added material to his Latin models, seemingly to fill his lines; not just their alliteration, but above all their four-beat rhythm (41–7). The value of MS vowel accents for rhythm is discussed (48–50).

author: Dietrich, Eduard
title: Abt Aelfrik: Zur Literatur-Geschichte der angelsächsischen Kirche [I]
abstract:
This piece and its continuation discuss Ælfric, his works, and what Church culture may be reconstructed from it quite broadly.

What I’m interested in at this point is Dietrich’s thoughts on the Heptateuch (485–99).

Emphasizes that the Heptateuch (Wanley’s title) is not a close translation except of Genesis, but a mixture of translation with excerpts or short reworkings, esp. in Judges (495). “Es zeigt sich also, er wollte eine praktische leicht verständliche Uebersetzung des Wichtigsten für Laien geben; was er giebt überträgt er meist wörtlich, so auch im Buch der Richter, welches nur ein Auszug zu nennen ist bis zur Geschichte Simsons c. 16, und einen ausfühlichen Anhang enthält, worin tapfere und durch Gottes Hülfe siegreiche Heerführer und Fürsten aus der römischen, byzantinischen und angelsächsischen Geschichte zusammengestellt werden. — In der That stammt diese Zusammenstellung nicht von Ælfrik her, wenn auch nach der Vorrede und dem Inhalt das Einzelne von ihm ist; selbst der Name Heptateuch ist nicht handschriftlich, der Herausgeber der Uebersetzungen, Thwaites hat das Ganze erst Heptateuch genannt und mit der Geschichte Hiobs begleitet. Namentlich der Abschnitt vom Buch der Richter, darauf macht Wanley aufmerksam, ist von dem Schreiber einer Bodleianischen Handschrift erst später hinzugefügt und früher einzeln als historische Skizze, nur nicht gerade als Homilie, deren Grenzen es weit überschneitet, vorhanden gewesen, wie auch ein Codex ihn unter Homilien hat. Dafür spricht auch, daß der Verf. selbst am Schluß ihn cvide d.i. Sermon nennt; und ferner, daß er, was noch nicht bemerkt ist, alliterirend geschrieben ist, wie andre Tractate und Homilien Aelfrik’s. Noch spricht der Umstand für die Gehörigkeit desselben unter die historischen Homilien, nicht zu der Uebersetzung des A.T., daß Aelfrik auch einen gleichfalls alliterirenden Sermo excerptus de libro Regum, welcher von Saul beginnt, unter den Heiligenleben gegeben hat; sowie endlich, daß er in dem Sermo excerptus de libro Judicum am Schluß die letzten siegreichen Könige Englands, Alfred, Aethelstan, Edgar vergleicht” (496–7). Dietrich goes on to debate the extent of Ælfric’s involvement with the translation, psychologically reconstructing a back-and-forth with Æthelweard (497–8).

author: Robinson, Orrin W.
title: Old English and Its Closest Relatives
abstract:
This book is poorly organized for use as a textbook:

  • To avoid confusing readers (!), the author has chosen to devise his own system of phonemic representation. Not only is this not helpful (no chapter makes sense without first reading ch. 2, for one thing), the system is actively designed to confuse readers. A colon following a vowel, for instance, expresses not length but openness; a dot below a vowel /ẹ/ represents closeness in /e/, to separate it from /ɛ/, which is marked [e]; and /e/ is sometimes numbered [e1] and [e2] to distinguish between their origins, though in some of these cases at least /e/ vs /ɛ/ would have done the trick.
  • The author’s efforts to convey phonetic values to an audience of American English speakers not only confuses speakers of other dialects (hot to represent short /a/, bomb to represent long /a/; try father?); it is plain misleading to describe monophthongs such as long /e/ by means of diphthongs like that in hay.
  • The book frequently cross-references earlier chapters. Not only is this done where languages are compared directly; various matters relevant to nearly all languages are introduced in chapters pertaining to just one of the languages. Metrics, for instance, is introduced in the OS chapter, after Gothic and Old Norse; syntax is introduced in the next chapter, which covers Old English. The general cumulative nature of the book means that it should be read in the order Gothic – ON – OS – OE – OFris – OFranc – OHG, without skipping any of the larger ones. I’m gearing up to teach the bigger languages in the order of Christianization, which is almost the reverse! This organization also makes it impossible to excerpt single chapters from the book as course material.
  • The only chapter containing paradigms is ch. 2, which contains mostly Gothic paradigms but is in fact the general grammatical introduction. Instructors will have to supplement the book with paradigms from other textbooks and the magic sheets. The introduction to Craigie’s Easy Readings is far more to the point of what I want to get across for Old Norse, for instance.
