author: Dunn, Marilyn
title: The Christianization of the Anglo-Saxons c. 597–c. 700: Discourses of Life, Death and Afterlife
abstract:
[1: Approaches to the Christianization of the Anglo-Saxons] Observes today’s culture of assuming that the pagan past cannot be known because our sources are Christian; the author hopes to challenge this restriction (1). She introduces Weber (and co.)’s notions of world-rejecting and world-accepting, or folk, religions (1–2). Relevant to her investigation is whether or not a pre-existing religion was world-rejecting (the author agrees with the traditional assumption for Anglo-Saxon England is that it was not), and that political and religious leaders often assume a place between “the macrocosm of the great world religions and the microcosm of local religions, cults and traditions” (2–3). Cognitive anthropology, seeking to explain social structures through cognitive causes, may help explain the form religious thought tends to take (3–4). This field has also given rise to the distinction between imagistic (namely iconic, nonverbal, and affective) and doctrinal (semantic, verbal) types of codification and relay of religious content (4). Though these concepts have required a good deal of refinement since their introduction, they are highly relevant to Anglo-Saxon England (4–5): pre-Christian religion was imagistic, but the strongly doctrinal Christian religion had itself assumed an array of imagistic elements prior to its arrival to England, which accordingly facilitated Christianization efforts; this interaction, meanwhile, also helped integrate further imagistic elements into Christianity, particularly in the realm of death and afterlife (5–6).

This book argues that folk-religious beliefs in a possible return of the souls of the dead in case of improper funerary rites had come to be tolerated by and incorporated into Christianity in the wake of sixth-century pandemics, and that it was similarly accepting of Anglo-Saxon beliefs following plagues in the seventh century. In the process, the Church evolved its understanding of the afterlife and laid the groundworks for the eventual development of purgatory (6).

[2: Discourses of the Dead] Many non-Christian religions posit multiple souls: one nonmaterial personality soul and one or more body souls responsible for life and consciousness (7–8). Christianity’s reward/punishment afterlife contrasts with the afterlife in many world-accepting religions, which tends to be an extension of the present world (8–9). The importance of correct burial and the return of those who have not received it, or who have died unjustly or before their time, may be recognized in folk-religions the world over. Religions of this nature tend not to differentiate the afterlife based on moral conduct in the present, but instead focus on the presence or return of souls of the dead and on correctly executed ritual (9–12).

Christianity postulated a differentiation on moral grounds to take place on Judgement Day. What happened between death and Judgement Day was initially a little vague, perhaps because that event was believed to be imminent. Averaged out over the centuries of early Christianity, however, the general sense was that the souls of obvious cases (martyrs, saints, and great sinners) would either gain instant admission into either heaven or hell, or into some sort of preview of the appropriate aferlife; but that most people would be stuck in a waiting-place of rest or affliction, possibly including a sense of purification, until Judgement Day (12–13). Early funerary ritual reflected belief in a pre-Judgement Day repose and the resurrection, as well as hope for a positive outcome (13–14). Christianity denounced an impurity of the corpse and also lamentation, although the latter persisted, and did not emphasize a continued relationship between deceased and next of kin (14).

Early Christians carried on several of the pagan funerary traditions, including alcohol-fuelled celebrations at the tomb and commemmorations after a certain amount of time had passed, and the Church could not well intervene, as these were family affairs (15). Churchmen agitated against these practices (15–16), but since Christians and pagans were buried in the same cemeteries, a great deal of syncretism ensued (16–17).

Augustine frequently found himself rejecting the belief that the living could visit the afterlife (17). Such beliefs are found also in Native American cultures (17–18), but Christianity taught otherwise, as this belief could not be reconciled with the resurrection, but it encountered a great deal of accounts of mobility of the soul. Augustine even railed against the Visio Pauli, as well as accounts of the dead visiting the living (19–21).

On burial rite, Augustine argued against the belief that incorrect burial could jeopardize Christians’ resurrection. Funerary rites should be kept, he believed, as a consolation to the living, not to prepare the way for the dead (21–2). Augustine also responded favourably to early practices hoping to reduce the guilt of the dead: minor faults, he felt, could be lessened by prayer, but only by appeal to the lifetime merits of the individual to be judged. All the same, this constitutes a relationship between the living and the dead, a concession to popular belief (22–3). Julianus Pomerius and Caesarius of Arles would later come to emphasize the efficacy of prayer more strongly. Purgatory, instant afterlife upon death, and the efficacy of praying for the dead became more mainstream under their influence (23–4). The resurrection of the body was a difficult doctrine to swallow, and the Church Fathers’ diversity of explanations did little to improve that fact (25).

The exhumation and translation of the remains of martyrs took off in the fourth century, very much with the active involvement of Ambrose. This practice is quintessentially imagistic (26). Ambrose clearly saw the legitimizing power that came with the emotions thus generated, using the belief in martyr saints in an omnibus attack on the Arians alongside the belief in the Trinity. His dissemination of relics has been called a marketing strategy for Catholicism: they greatly strengthened local influence. The emotive strength of imagistic religions was thus enlisted as an underpinning for a doctrinal religion, providing it with much-needed popular support (26–7). This was a much greater concession than Augustine ever made, as he stayed as far from imagism as he could (27). Augustine did evolve on the matter, eventually accepting miracles at martyrs’ tombs, but he did not take relics to be consubstantial with God, as others did; Jerome was a much fiercer defender of the cult of relics (27–9).

Augustine’s efforts to withhold divine powers from saints fell on deaf ears: people eagerly took to translations and relics, and the privileged arranged to be buried as near saints’ tombs as possible (ad sanctos) (29–30). This practice was taken over by the barbarian Merovingians, who still buried with grave goods too (30–1). From the late fifth century, when the Frankish kings converted, Germanic peoples shifted from cremation to inhumation with grave goods. Especially prior to 700, when the Church assumed responsibility for burial, popular beliefs about the proximity of the dead [i.e. contact, intercession, an afterlife of continuation] continued to be expressed in funerary traditions (31).

Malaria, leprosy, and the bubonic plague played huge roles in sixth-century Europe; the latter remained virulent for over two centuries. Gregory of Tours notes a Frankish reversal to traditional healing methods in the face of pandemic. Pandemics evoke fear of revenance, countered by decapitation, immobilization, prone burial, and the placement of certain objects in or on the grave (31–4). Church positions on burial changed little in response, except on the peripheries of its power (34–6).

Irish missionary activity was effective on account of its charismatic leaders. Columbanus of Luxeuil showed himself capable of miracles, a central element in the creation of charisma. Charisma, while imagistic, can be used to underpin doctrinal religion, thus bridging imagistic and doctrinal religions (36–7). Columbanus focused on the relationship between God and the individual, not on saints; his surviving sermons lay out Catholic dogma at its most austere, with a world-rejecting focus on the transience/permanence dichotomy between world and afterlife (37). Also, whereas Continental penance was public and lasted a lifetime, Irish book penance was limited and repeatable, based on a fixed set of tariffs derived from Celtic legal culture. This made them relatable to the individual, while the Church benefited from this practice inasmuch as it brought home the moral debt owed to God (37–8). Especially in times of pandemic, however, it prompted the question what happens if you die before completing your penance. (Both Continental and Irish practice allowed communion to those who believed themselves on their deathbeds, but if they recovered without completing their penance, some uncertainty ensued over whether subsequent last communion would suffice to salvage their souls (38–9).) In response to the bubonic plague, the Irish (missionaries) became more forgiving about the boundary between life and death: preliminary visions of the afterlife during one’s lifetime could inspire one to do the requisite penance (39–40).

In Irish tradition, visits to the afterlife are first mentioned in Jonas of Bobbio’s Vita Columbani, which has a nun’s soul leave her body and return to it before dying a second time, contradicting Augustine’s teachings on the subject (40–1). The Life of Fursey has an out-of-body visit of hell and contains the suggestion that penance may be done in the afterlife. Fursey was an Irish monk who founded monasteries in England and Francia in the early seventh century (41–2).

[3: Gregory the Great and the English Mission] In the years leading up to Gregory’s mission to England, he responded to Jewish pockets by defending them as the mother of the redeemer and subject to future conversion; pagans he approached with coercive authority (45–6). Coercion was his method whenever practicable; the high level of Christianization of his own society seems to have stopped him from giving any real thought to methods of Christianization (46–8). It seem to have been his correspondences intended to strengthen the Church in western Francia that brought him into contact with the English: he asked for unusable Gallic coin to be traded for English boys destined for the monastic life (48–9). King Childebert II may have encouraged a more active look at England as a way of counterbalancing the influence there of a political rival, whose cousin was Bertha, wife of Æthelberht, future king of Kent (48–9). On the other hand, it may has well have been Æthelberht himself who encouraged the mission, finding himself allied with the weaker of two rival houses in Francia and thus fearing an invasion; but this is highly speculative (50–1). Alternatively, Gregory may have understood that Kent had now come to a hegemony over the other English kingdoms. As Augustine set out for Kent, however, Childebert died, which somehow made Augustine reluctant to go on. This suggests that Childebert was closely involved with the decision to send a mission (51). Gregory at this time was closely concerned with both the English mission and the recuperation of lost revenues in the West Frankish patrimony. He attempted, apparently with success, to sell both to Childebert’s sons, promising political power in England (52–3). Meanwhile, Gregory wrote to Bertha to rebuke her for neglecting to convert her husband, presumably because she did not want to ally herself with a mission backed by a rival court (54). The death of Cildebert also reduced any political urgency Æthelberht may have felt to convert (54–5). Gregory in 601 put his full weight behind the mission and instructed Æthelberht to destroy pagan shrines and temples; but a month later, he wrote Mellitus to remove the idols, but repurpose the temples. This reads like the beginnings of a missionary strategy, and the fruit of the realization that a successful mission had to temper the doctrinal quality of Christianity with imagistic elements more familiar to his target group (55–6).

[4: Anglo-Saxon Paganism and the Living] Opens with a realistic assessment (57–9) on the overwhelming absence of evidence (57) and the problems of adducing Norse evidence, though there is some evidence for the worship of Tiw, Thunor, and Wodan (57–8). Yet some of the Wodan- and Thor-material seems to have been known in England (59–60); Tacitus’s Nerthus appears to correspond to Njǫrðr, and the Norse Ingvi/Freyr surfaces in the tribal name Ingvaeones (60–1; pp. 59–62 heavily influenced by Richard North’s book). Various Anglo-Saxon dynasties associated themselves with pagan deities genealogically (61–2). The whole eostre/hretha business is pretty murky (62–3). These discussions are followed by questionable regurgitations about Bede’s “Heavenfield” having something to do with sacred trees and a folk-religious significance to the Franks Casket (64–7).

Many religions recognize a supreme creator-god who has little practical value and is therefore not actively worshipped (67). It is suggested[, though on a paltry basis,] that Tiwaz may have played such a role in Germanic religion (67–8). Where a creator-god has little everyday relevance, lesser deities are often available with more practical functions. Alaric Hall’s study of elves in Anglo-Saxon England suggests they belonged to this more practical class (68–70).

Ritual is one of the most persistent elements of religion. One of its commonest forms is sacrifice, though it is often the celebrants who actually consume the food (70). Gregory’s letter to Mellitus and Bede’s month-index suggest the Anglo-Saxons knew this practice too (70–1). The author gives a very concise but fairly in-depth theoretical discussion of the ritual type of sacrifice, but concludes that there is no evidence human sacrifice was ever practiced in Anglo-Saxon England, though there are references in discussions of Continental Germanic tribes, and Bede mentions a one-time “crisis rite” in which starving men volunteer themselves as sacrifice (71–4). Place-name evidence associates groves and clearings with worship (74–6). The author seems to think this also implies the existence of a class of priests (76–7). Perhaps the most relevant passage in the discussion that follows suggests that early Anglo-Saxon churchmen such as Theodore of Tarsus distinguished between herbal healing, which they allowed, and incantations, which they forbade; and also between women and men, as the latter group received harsher penalties for incantations (79). The Wanderer and The Seafarer suggest Anglo-Saxons may have practised shamanism, as do boar helmets. Shamans seem to have been men rather than women, though mixed-gender graves have been found. The mixed-gender picture of Edwin’s priest in Bede (no stallions, no weapons) suggests this may have been a shaman property. The name Coifi moreover suggests he was born with a caul, associated with healing in early modern Italy and northern England. (79–83). This chapter is punctuated by a lot of question marks and seems to contribute little.

[5: Anglo-Saxon Paganism and the Living] After a move away from religious interpretations in archaeology, some archaeologists are now cautiously moving back to a recognition that grave goods suggest belief in an afterlife (85–6). Anglo-Saxon cremation, practised from c. 450 until the early seventh century, served the sure onwards passage of the soul and prevented revenance (86). Cremations were particularly prevalent in Anglian areas (86–7). Ashes were buried in urns, and a fair few pyres and urns contain everyday objects as well as evidence of animal sacrifice. Wooden structures (“huts”) are sometimes found, intended perhaps as ash deposition sites or perhaps as pre-funerary desiccation sites (87). Cremation is expensive; pyre cremation was restricted to royalty, as the corpse’s high water content presupposes a pyre of some 146 kilos of pine wood (88).

author: Higham, N.J.
title: The Convert Kings: Power and Religious Affiliation in Early Anglo-Saxon England
abstract:
Argues that the first generation of Christian kings treated conversion as a policy strategy to secular ends (1–2). Christianization is a dialogue managed above all by the recipient (4). All of ch. 1 makes for great mandatory reading in a course on the conversion.

[1: Out of Africa: The Nature of Conversion] Opens with an excellent summary of the means and restrictions of learning about pre- or sub-Christian beliefs (7–10). Describes the progression from a condescending “instruction” understanding of Conversion to Durkheim and Weber, who distinguished between “world” (rational, assimilating, transcendental) and “primitive” religions, and describes how scholars today view this distinction as one that still results from the Western domination of the field. (12–14). Monolothic understandings of Christianity and precise definitions of conversion are problematic; “metamorphosis” occurs, but cannot be quantified (14–15). The problem of taking Christianity as the norm in the study of religion, already present in the discussion up to this point, is addressed in more detail now; it leads us to ask the wrong questions, such as “what did the pagan believe?” (17–18). Higham also discusses probably differences in valuation and perception between missionary and convert: baptism, and even assent to a creed, surely meant different things to the two parties involved in the process (18). A holistic view should take the convert’s perception as at least equally legitimate as the missionary’s; this allows us to consider her reasons for adopting, including extrareligious strategy (18–19). Accounts of medieval conversion are overwhelmingly told from within a Christian world-view; the convert is silenced (19–20).

Robert Horton developed a striking understanding of conversion based on his understanding of African religions. A “typical” African cosmology knows lesser spirits governing the microcosm of everyday life as well as a supreme being governing the macrocosm of the world. An expansion of the horizon of the microcosm will tend to lead to greater importance accorded to the supreme deity; if the culture has access to a world religion, such an expansion will tend to lead to conversion to that religion (20–1). This view has proved to suffer from some weaknesses, especially since a lot of other disparities were at play in African–European contact. Nevertheless, Horton’s prediction that traditional cultures will eventually develop a supreme being on their own has some support. Importantly for the Anglo-Saxon context, so has his view of religion as mutable and adaptable to new forms of worship, even undermining the traditional concept of syncretism in a discussion of conversion (21–22). To early Anglo-Saxons, Christianity must have come across as a polythetic system, not a monolithic or unified whole; individual elements could be adopted without changing one’s world-view. Here and throughout this chapter, it is pointed out that the missionaries’ perspective was that baptism defined the convert (23). There would also have been greater cultural difference between English clergymen and Italian missionaries than between English clergy and their countrymen (23–4).

The English conversion contrasts with that of most colonial contexts in that it did not undermine the power of pre-conversion rulers. Instead, England witnessed the concentration of power in an ever smaller number of native hands (25). Literary evidence suggests a strongly local quality to pre-Christian worship (25–6). This did not work in the interests of kings looking to increase their centralized power, which rather favours universal religion (26). Christianity thus fulfilled the needs of these rulers, while also accommodating the local diversification of preexisting religion through the cult of saints (26–7). Converting kings saw powerful allies in bishops, and some holders-out probably did so to dissociate themselves from Christian rivals. It was thus the Church’s structures that appealed to Anglo-Saxon kings, not its spiritual message. Since early priests were strongly dependent on royal backing, kings were largely free to ignore that message, although that may have meant to ignore the long-haul impact of Christianization on the culture’s outlook (27). Missionaries were granted safe conduct, and not always by baptized kings. The active support of kings was the key to missionary success (28–9). Wilfrid, who converted the South Saxons, was backed by their king for political reasons; and those who were baptized went along with it because the king told them to and/or to stave off some ill-understood imminent calamity referenced in Wilfrid’s preaching. A low-threshold rite to ensure continued well-being can be an effective trade-off (29–31). Gregory and Pope Boniface emphasized God’s secular potency when urging Æthelberht and Edwin (respectively) to convert. Bishop Daniel instructed St. Boniface in Germany to reason with the heathens and ridicule the lack of systemacy of local beliefs in order to win converts. This, as well as Bede’s description of Edwin’s conversion, suggests a strongly negative definition of Christianity: it is very much about what not to do or believe (32–3). The typical approach was one of superficial conversion first and conversion of the soul later, but that second stage was often left undone in the early generations for lack of manpower (33–4).

Conduct was hard to alter, e.g. in the realms of marriage, diet, and appearance, and it is proposed that the individuality of sin and salvation must have been difficult for Anglo-Saxons accustomed to seeing kin as the primary unit, and the Christian afterlife must have been both difficult and in large lart undesirable (34–5). More immediate was the question of who could be a priest, a role incumbent (according to Tacitus) upon every head of household prior to the Conversion. Accordingly, it may be expected that Christian ritual was first dominant in a courtly context and existed alongside heathen rituals at home; the eighth-century rise of private monasteries might reflect this tension (35). It has been argued that women grew less influential in consequence of the Conversion. There is, however, evidence suggesting that powerful men gave their female kin into monastic service as a way of winning divine favour (35–6). Some kings clearly converted before finding out some of the undesirable implications, by which point it would have been a wasted investment to turn back (36). On the whole, religious affiliation would have been opportunistic and transient. Outside courts and monasteries, there is evidence that paganism persisted into the late seventh century and even in Bede’s lifetime. That there is no evidence for cross-cultural cults found in other conversion contexts suggests the bias of our sources (37–8).

The East Saxons reopened their pagan temples in the 660s in response to a plague pandemic, indicating the close connection between health and worship. Only one of two kings reverted, suggesting a connection with a power struggle as well; but the implication remains that Christianity could be judged by its efficacy (38). The cult of saints developed in response to this need, as did the use of ritual charms (38–9). This book will review the Conversion with a focus on the integration of government and cult (39–41). Christians were not especially successful on the battle-field, but the new religion had organizational advantages that won over the kings, and therefore religious ceremony became a tool of royal advancement (41–3).

author: Garde, Judith N.
title: Old English Poetry in Medieval Christian Perspective: A Doctrinal Approach
abstract: Suggests a catechetical, didactic purpose for the poetry, which is devoid of exegetical elements. This emphasis is also not in the first place typological in nature, but concerns the six historical ages that lead up to the Redemption (passim). Builds on J.R. Hall.

author: Hall, J.R.
title: The Old English Epic of Redemption: The Theological Unity of MS Junius 11
abstract: Proposes that the compilatory system behind Junius 11 was not liturgical, as is often assumed, but theological, and specifically catechetical. Hall is particularly struck by the similarity of the material covered to that in Augustine's De catechizandis rudibus, a pattern likewise emulated in Wulfstan's Sermo VI, contemporary with the compilation of Junius 11. (A difference in mode is noted: Augustine and Wulfstan mix historia with theoria (explication), while the poets concentrate on historia and are able to concentrate on a smaller number of episodes each.)

author: Jolly, Karen Louise
title: Popular Religion in Late Saxon England: Elf Charms in Context
abstract:
[Introduction and ch. 1: Popular Religion]: Along with many studies from the later twentieth century, assumes that Christianization was a matter of mutual influence; also, challenges a strict distinction between lay and learned, pagan and Christian (1–18). Instead, the author proposes symbiotic spheres of popular and formal religion, in which the formal sphere is contained within the broader sphere of the popular as a subclass (18–24).

Missionaries tend to understand conversion as radical personal transformation, but lasting impact has to go beyond the individual and relies more heavily on mutual acculturation (24). Conversion strategies divide into conflict/imposition and integration/adaptation; the former is “evident particularly in the initial conversion events and in later reform efforts”, relied on demonization and caused tensions. This strategy involved the replacement of pagan customs with Christian ones (25). The alternative was integration into Church practices (25–6). Scholastic distinctions between natural and supernatural were not yet developed in the early Middle Ages, leaving the line between acceptable and unacceptable ritual blurry (26). To attain a more complete picture, we need to include the popular perspective, not just the formal. Seen in this light, Church practice is just a set of ritualized charms (26–7).

The early Anglo-Saxon Church accommodated animistic beliefs into the cult of saints, developed in late Roman culture but easily taken up into Germanic practice since it already addressed an animate nature with pleas for aid (27–8); the transferral of Germanic concepts into the Christian word-field indicates the synthesis of two traditions (28–9). Modern difficulty to account for Christian and non-Christian elements in Beowulf or the Franks Casket are evidence of the interwovenness of these traditions in early Anglo-Saxon culture (29). The stories of Guthlac and The Dream of the Rood mix Christian and heroic elements (29–31); burial practices were clearly mixed (31–2). Churchmen might base their verdict on synthetic developments on whether it effected more of a christianization or more of a degrading of Christianity. The reform movements of the tenth and eleventh centuries reflect an awareness on the part of the Church on how the amalgamation was functioning, and a desire to gain more control over [it and over] the diversification of Christian practice (32). The author proposes to view popular religion as the wider culture that includes all of Christianity, being formal religion and part of folklore, with whose sphere it overlaps; paganism is (for some reason) located outside of popular religion but is joined to it by way of folklore (33–4; Figure 1.2).

[2: The Late Saxon Religious Environment] The Viking situation brought a need for a new conversion within a Christianized society and may also have sped up the popularization of Christianity by bringing down its central infrastructure in the east (37–8). Recent scholarship has begun to abandon the conflict-understanding of Viking contact and emphasize more socially organic and synthetic functions. From this perspective, the dynamism of the tenth and eleventh centuries was a healthy breeding ground for the acculturation of popular religion. The proprietary church, often run by isolated and poorly educated priests, was a breeding ground for popular religion (38–9). Discusses the role of women in conversion (43-5). Pagan religious structures quickly disintegrated in the face of organized religion in the seventh century; folk practices did not, and could not effectively be counteracted, since they did not operate on the same level (45). The tenth and eleventh centuries saw an increase in lay piety (privately owned churches, 52-3) as well as reform; this mix yielded popular religion and also fed ideas back up the hierarchy (46). Jolly describes the dynamic of centrifugal vs centripetal forces (38ff., 46-7, 49-51).

Aelfric wrote his Catholic Homilies to give priests preaching examples (69).

The dual overlordship of priests in eigenkirchen caused tensions; both proprietor and bishop wanted to appoint someone known to them, and priests were thus doubly accountable (58-62). Local priests cannot have met the standards of learning prescribed for them (62-4). The Blickling and Vercelli homilies are strongly eschatological and evince a binary worldview Christian/pagan; Ælfric and Wulfstan, by contrast, aimed to reform the secular clergy, and especially Ælfric shows an attempt to make Augustinian doctrine accessible to an illiterate=illatinate audience (74-9). Celibacy was a high goal of the reformers, but not the reality for local priests until after 1100 (64-5). Suggests Æcerbot and similar may have been composed by local priests (69-70).

[3: Magic and Miracle] Magic and miracle differ not in method but in source, the latter bringing glory to god. Wulfstan, phaps due to his northern situation, expends more effort combating paganism (73-4). Ælfric adapted Augustinian thought to an Anglo-Saxon context. The distinction natural/supernatural was not current prior to the twelfth century [the terminology did exist, but “natural” meant “from God”: see Augustine, Ælfric; PSL]; the distinction was visible/touchable vs not, and furthermore God vs creation (80-1). In Christian cosmology, humans share some aspect with all of creation, endowed by God, through whom they relate to creation; they take up a special, central position for having all these aspects (81). Ælfric’s approach to what we would call the supernatural was an attempt to port animistic ideas to a Christian worldview (82). Augustine and Ælfric presented nature as a continuous revelation from God. Specific miracles could indicate divine favour, however, which naturally drew those looking for healing to the Church (82–5). Miracles and (demonic) magic could not be of a kind, and so it was held that the devil could only perform delusional magic or heal injuries that he had himself inflicted (86). Saints could undo the devil’s delusions (8–7). Ælfric condemns sorcery practised on New Year’s Day; the greater strength of trees felled at full moon he attributes to the natural order created by God (87–8).

Churchmen like Ælfric distinguished between magic (involving non-Christian incantations) and miracle (using Christian rituals and relics), but much of actual medicine is better classified as middle practices combining elements of both (89–90).

Ælfric’s view on medicine was that any sick person ought to turn to God, who alone has real power over our well-being; but any treatments that have God’s blessing are permissible. This made herbal remedies carried out under prayer perfectly acceptable. However, these are found in the same MSS as charms using formulas and rituals [that contain no Christian references] (91–2). Ælfric makes a firm distinction here: prayer, relics, and advise from holy men are the answer to disease; relying on sacred stones or trees is idolatry. He refers to Augustine for endorsing the use of herbs for consumption, but not as amulets. Likewise any invocation has to be to God (92–3). The conclusion to this chapter emphasizes the importance of using medieval rather than modern categories to parse medieval medicine (94–5).

[4: Locating the Charms] The question of medieval categories is taken up at greater length at the outset of this chapter, where the author also rejects early scholarly methods that sought to isolate non-Christian elements in the charms, while even more recent scholars distinguished between magic and reason or science (98–101). In the Middle Ages, magic was off limits, but folklore could move between condoned and objectionable religious traditions and use elements of both (101–2). What sets the surviving charms apart from the practices condemned in lawcodes is that the texts we know do not give honour to pagan gods in any direct way. Ælfric and Wulfstan sought to clear the land of pagan practices, but a simple substitution of names and rites could salvage a charm and turn it from magic into the realm of miracles (102–3).

We know little about who practised medicine, though there seems to have been an early shift towards monastic medicine and then, from the eleventh century onwards, again away from the monasteries (103–4). The author discusses the main medical MSS, noting that Lacnunga is traditionally perceived as barely christianized and hence especially relevant to the matter at hand (104–7).

The texts, with their reliance on humours, incantations, and the like reveal a holistic worldview; they do not focus on symptoms (107). A holistic approach is visible also in a reliance on sympathetic medicine: the similarity of herbs to the symptoms or perceived cause (108–10). Related to this understanding is the connection between macrocosm and microcosm found also in Byrhtferth (110–13).

The appropriation of liturgical formulas to medicine was a natural consequence of Christianization (115). Jolly sees in Anglo-Saxon medical texts a two-way transference between learned and popular methods and ideas (116). Then follows a discussion on the power of words, gibberish, Latin, Christian formulas, etc. (116–23).

The co-occurrence of liturgical and native elements in medicinal texts suggests an amalgamation between these traditions that would have had a two-way character: folklorization of Christianity and christianization of folklore (123–4). Jolly singles out four telltale characteristics of Germanic medicine: “flying venoms, the worm, the number nine, and the elf” (124). Worms and flying poisons frequently co-occur. The Nine Herbs Charm and Woden’s Nine Herbs Charm are the best examples (125–8). Flying venom is exemplified by Lacnunga 18; it and worms are discussed (128–30). Jolly asserts that the worldview speaking from these remedies does not differ all that much from Ælfric’s Agustinian worldview (131).

[5: Elves, Demons, and Other Mind-Altering Afflictions] After briefly describing the Germanic evidence for ælf-concepts, discusses their agency in the infliction of disease and the plants used to purge the body of them. The recipes take a great deal of knowledge about how to apply remedies for granted (132–6). In their adoption into a Christian worldview, elves took on demonic characteristics; but early medieval demon conceptions likewise show Germanic elvish characteristics (136–8). This chapter translates and discusses elf charms and their positions on the magic/miracle spectrum; the general refrain is that Christian elements are integral to them (139–67).

The book’s Conclusions reiterate the work’s sense of “dude, stop pulling these texts apart to separate out pagan and Christian strands”: it invites us to study the texts as integrated wholes. They are a valid practical application of an Augustinian/Ælfrician worldview, which was itself pretty well compatible with Germanic animism (170–1). The centripetal/centrifugal, proprietary churches-argument is likewise recapitulated, and the charms are understood as a product of this dynamic (172–3).

author: Oeser, W.
title: Das ‘a’ als Grundlage für Schriftvarianten in der gotischen Buchschrift

author: Cusack, Carole M.
title: Conversion Among the Germanic Peoples
abstract:
[5: Anglo-Saxon Missions to the Continent] Argues that the Germanic peoples, being accustomed to the concept of sacred kingship, had no difficulty bestowing that same sacral authority on missionaries (121). Willibrord’s methods in Frisia were comparatively hostile, overturning idols, slaughtering sacred cattle, and baptizing in sacred streams (121–2). King Radbod of Frisia was similarly hostile to christianization, which he considered divisive, but this hostility also had roots in Pepin’s designs on Frisia. Without Radbod’s baptism, there was no conversion of the people (122).

Boniface’s efforts were inspired by two political agendas: a Frankish desire to annex the bordering territories and Boniface’s wish to build a strong ecclesiastical infrastructure tied to Rome, a wish that was his own, as he only gained papal support after he began his missionary work. The Franks were only now realizing that a connection to Rome could benefit them on the geopolitical plane, a course of action that would eventually result in Charlemagne’s coronation as Holy Roman Emperor in 800; up until the time of Willibrord, the Frankish Church had been less close to Rome than the Anglo-Saxon Church (123–4). Radbod’s destructive influence on ecclesiastical infrastructure led Boniface to ally himself with Charles Martel; accordingly, he has been called the architect of the Carolingian-papal alliance (124).

Boniface’s methods, breaking away from Willibrord’s, included the foundation of monasteries (124). Bishop Daniel of Winchester recommended Boniface to win over pagans by proving their gods inferior through debate, and the story of the oak tree likewise suggests confrontation; this may reflect an awareness of the dangers of syncretism (125–6). Boniface’s longitudinal effort and reliance on companions ensured continuity; his re-establishment of the Frankish Church Council [Synod] had similar effects (126–7). Cusack suggests that Boniface may have deliberately engineered his martyrdom by behaving provocatively deep in Frisian territory (127).

Saxony was converted under force of arms by Charlemagne from 772 onwards. There were many surrenders and relapses; even after Widukind was baptized in 785, there was another revolt in 793. The terms of the Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae may have played a role in these revolts, the last of which was in 841. A document entitled Indiculus superstitionum et paganiarum describes pre-Christian beliefs as involving “[animal sacrifice], tree worship, divination, funeral practices, and ‘diabolical songs, dances and games’ ” (127–9, at 128). The chapter closes with a discussion of how indigenous terms and concepts were brought into the Christian tradition. Kingship, too, retained its pre-Conversion legitimization of bringing heil to the people (129). It overstates the heroic flavour of the Heliand by copying Murphy’s “hill-fort” vocabulary (129–30). However, it also notes Ruth Karras’s reading, which emphasizes the aristocratic focus of the text (130).

author: Bjork, Robert E.
title: The Symbolic Use of Job in Ælfric’s Homily on Job, Christ II, and the Phoenix
publication: Latin Learning and English Lore: Studies in Anglo-Saxon Literature for Michael Lapidge
eds: Katherine O’Brien O’Keeffe and Andy Orchard
abstract:
Old English prose treatments of Job:

  1. Ælfric’s Lives of Saints (“a rapid summary”)
  2. Ælfric’s Catholic Homilies II “Dominica I in mense Septembri quando legitur Iob” (“the only relatively comprehensive treatment of it”, “a paraphrase, sometimes a direct translation. . . with commentary deriving largely from Gregory’s Moralia in Job”) (315–16).

Notes Ælfric’s rhetorical use of pronouns and the modesty topos, asserting that this book is too deep for “us” as well as for the unlearned; indeed some elements of the biblical book are omitted because they are theologically too complicated (316–17). The homily concentrates on the elementary structure of the book, but at the end it makes brief rerefence to Job’s allegorical significance (317). He repeatedly refers to Job’s tropological function, however (317–18).

Whereas other prose texts likewise emphasize Job’s role as patient sufferer, Christ II and The Phoenix have a different agenda. Cynewulf follows Gregory’s reading in which he misconstrues a nominative avis in Job as a genitive, which then becomes an image of Christ risen; the poem does not mention Job’s patience (318–21). The Phoenix’s mention of Job has been understood to make sense because both represent the blessed on earth (321–3), but here too it is the bird of Gregory’s Moralia that makes Job relevant. Gregory understands Job as a type of Christ (323–5); that is the real reason he is brought up in both Christ II and The Phoenix. This connection also explains the fact that both poems associate Job (as does Scripture) with fire, flight, and worms, concepts that bridge the typology (325–7).

author: Frede, Dorothea
title: Stoic Determinism
publication: The Cambridge Companion to the Stoics
abstract: Explains the nature of Stoic determinism and defends it against the charge of strict physical determinism. The distinction lies in part in the Stoic distinction between antecedent and principal causes, which are more transparent if termed “external” and “internal”. What is usually explained with reference to a rolling cylinder is easier to accept if applied to a human being: an antecedent cause can trigger my action, but that action will still depend on my personality, which is the principal cause. The conditioning of one’s personality was therefore a major theme in Stoic ethics and psychology. The Stoics nevertheless believed in a tight causal chain with predictable outcomes, and that this chain is teleological in nature, divinely established. This has led to the charge that one’s decisions do not matter, as actions are preordained. However, as Stoic cosmology is unitary, the divine is immanent in all things, so agents are part of the divine and actions are not externally determined. As for the need to treat humans as autonomous, that follows from the fact that we cannot see all causes; we have to judge on the basis of an imperfect body of knowledge.

author: Gilbert, Anthony J.
title: The Ambiguity of Fate and Narrative Form in some Germanic Poetry

author: Griffith, Mark S.
title: Does wyrd bið ful aræd mean ‘Fate Is Wholly Inexorable’?
publication: Doubt Wisely: Papers in Honour of E. G. Stanley
eds: M. J. Toswell and E. M. Tyler
series: Studies in English Language and Literature
abstract: The clause in question is ambiguous, meaning either “one’s lot is wholly established by authority” or “one’s lot is very settled” (148).

author: Derolez, René
title: The Orientation System in the Old English Orosius
publication: England Before the Conquest: Studies in Primary Sources Presented to Dorothy Whitelock
abstract:
Levels some sound criticism at Malone for various assumptions underlying his analysis of the Orosius translator’s [hereafter “Alfred’s” for convenience] presumed 45-degree shift in bearings, such as the assumption that Orosius and Alfred worked with an eight-point system and had access to something like modern maps, as well as the assumption that the various OE terms containing elements of south and north are all interchangeable (256–7). Although Malone assumed an underlying Scandinavian system, he identified it also in distant regions; also, the case for a 45-degree shift is not in all regions equally convincing, while Orosius himself sometimes partakes of the shift (257–8).

Ekblom improved on Malone’s argument, adducing also Knytlinga saga and Adam of Bremen; he speaks of a transition under the influence of Christianity from the Scandinavian towards the standard system; he held the standard deviation to be 60 degrees and acknowledged (but in the end did not take into account) that an eight-point system is really an eight-sector system, as the horizon is divided into eight fields (258–9). However, Ekblom’s procedure of measuring angles relative to a central point is highly cartographical and would not have occurred to a medieval navigator with or without a map (259–60).

The cardinal directions were easily established by the equinoctial directions of sunrise and sunset as well as the sun’s highest point in the sky; the north could be found using the polar star; these points represented OE east, west, suþ, and norþ. Intermediate points were harder: the Greeks and Romans used the winds, which are a vague measure; local features are non-transferrable. Isidore systematized the Roman system into a twelve-point one that was influential in Anglo-Saxon England but cannot be shown to have been adapted in practical terms (260–1). Orosius varies his usage per territory, sometimes relying mostly on the cardinals and occasionally bringing in a sixteen-point system, mostly he relies on eight bearings (261). Ælfric expresses tedium at the idea of enumerating the intermediary winds of the twelf-point system in his De temporibus anni; he does introduce Aquilo/Boreas, but in a way Derolez calls confusing. OE glosses likewise demonstrate the incapacity of OE to translate intermediary winds (262). No clear system emerges from the intermediary terminology (262–4).

Suddenly abandoning his examination, Derolez now observes that any shifts in the OE Orosius apply to only a small proportion of the references, which he assumes will not yield a uniform deviation; instead, he suggests that they derive from the use of a map, the translator “correcting” what he read with the use of a faulty map; several contemporary maps would have effected the observed inaccuracies (264–5). Since mappaemundi are circular, the outlines of the land had to be accommodated to the containing shape; the absence of meridian and parallel lines obscures such distortions. The interface between travellers’ reports and such schematic representations could only result in distortion. Specifically [and this understanding relies to some degree on interpreting Derolez’s text by his diagram), if a map lacked a projection to correct for the North Pole being a point on the edge of the circular map, the entire northern edge of the map would have been the actual referent of the traveller’s north, but the cartographer would have been tempted to bend it towards his point north on the (leftmost) edge of his circle. The greater one’s longitude from the centre of the circle, the greater the resulting deviation. In all of Europe, this shift would be clockwise, as in Orosius (265–7). Derolez refers to an Anglo-Saxon map that shares some misalignments with the descriptions in the Orosius and points out that it does not label its axes, so the reader has to guess which system was used (267–8).

author: Rowe, William R.
title: Augustine on Foreknowledge and Free Will
abstract:
Augustine’s argument is that our will is by definition in our power; accordingly, although we necessarily sin, the will to sin is still in our power. Rowe argues that the argument is flawed: to parallel other actions, willing has to be triggered by a meta-level of willing, and so Augustine’s contention that the question depends on the contradiction of willing to sin while simultaneously not willing to sin is false: rather, it is about willing to will to sin, which is not the same as willing to sin. Willing to will may not make sense, but if it does, it appears true and Augustine’s objection is unwarranted.

In the original problem Augustine seeks to address, the assertion "whatever God foresees must necessarily happen" can be read with the necessity either on the condition or on happening of necessity; the latter reading need not be accepted in theology, whereas the former breaks the logical sequence. Thus Evodius’s argument fails either way.

author: O’Keefe, Tim
title: Action and Responsibility
abstract:
The swerve is often described in too simplistic a manner. In fact, Epicurus defends three types of freedom:

  1. Effective agency allows us to act in accordance with our will;
  2. Self-formation of character allows us to alter our desires;
  3. Moral responsibility makes us responsible for our actions in public opinion [it’s not clear to me how this is a freedom, PSL] (142).

None of Epicurus’ approaches engages straightforwardly with the apparent incompatibility between determinism and freedom to do otherwise than we do (142–3).

Atoms move by three causes:

  1. Gravity
  2. Collisions
  3. A random sideways swerve.

The swerve and its relation to freedom are described in the greatest detail by Lucretius, who deduces the existence of the swerve from the observation that animals act freely (have libera voluntas, 143). His basis for the latter belief is that action follows desire: race horses need a moment to adjust to the opening of the gate before rushing into action, demonstrating that they move by their own volition; and we have the freedom to move against a flow, whether in a crowd or a stream (144). The agency here described is effective agency; it is possessed by humans and animals and does not require the ability to do otherwise than one does: that would be a “two-way”, whether-or-not decision, which is not at stake in the examples given; instead, effective agency allows us to line up action with desire (144–5).

A popular understanding of the swerve is that it salvages the possibility of having done otherwise by leaving the possibility for the swerve not to have occurred in that way. However, the Epicureans did not use the swerve with whether-or-not agency in mind; Lucretius does not involve the swerve in his account of effective agency; and a random swerve does not explain agency (145–6).

The lazy argument as described by Cicero concerns what may be called logical determinism. Accepting the principle of bivalence (PB), which states that every proposition is either true or false, there is no point in calling a doctor when sick, since it is either true or false that I am going to die, regardless of my actions. The argument teaches us that logical determinism is incompatible with future contingency, not with the ability to do otherwise; but that contingency is necessary for the effectiveness of deliberation and action. Even so, Epicurus rejects PB and accepts future contingency, as he affirms that we do act effectively on the basis of our desires; he is thus a “lazy argument libertarian”. Immediately after explaining the necessary connection between PB and the inexorability of the future, Cicero mentions that Epicurus believes the swerve of an atom avoids the necessity of fate (147).

Stoics and Epicurus agree that logical and causal determinism have each other as corollaries: a statement about the future can only be true if there are causes in the present which will bring about the asserted state of being. Since Epicurus accepts this, he must posit a physical mechanism along the lines of the swerve if he is to deny PB (147–8).

Chrysippus’s notion of co-fatedness has shown that neither logical nor causal determinism precludes effective agency: it may be through my being fated to call the doctor that I am fated to recover (148).

The function of the swerve is to preserve the contingency of the future, but now Epicurus likewise needs to free us from chance developments (148–9). To the Epicureans, their psychological hedonism is the foundation for their ethical hedonism: evil deeds follow from misguided beliefs of what makes one happy. Our beliefs do not, however, threaten our freedom, since we can alter them by means of reason (149). Humans have certain faculties that leave them with greater freedom than animals (149–50).

Epicurus’ version of atomism is the following:

  1. All is atoms and void; atoms are eternally unchanging in their small stock of properties;
  2. Aggregates of atoms are temporary and mutable but real;
  3. Aggregates have additional powers and properties determined by the relations between their atoms (150–1).

The Epicureans believed Democritus’ scepticism with regard to qualities (e.g. that honey is neither sweet nor bitter, since it is differently experienced by different individuals) makes knowledge impossible; Epicurus avoids this fate by asserting (3) above (151–2). Epicureans also thought that Democritus denied (2) (152–3). They seem to have thought the mind capable of the powers of an aggregate while itself reducible to atoms and void (153). In a particularly obscure text, Epicurus holds the products of the mind, not its atoms, accountable for the way an individual develops (153–4).

Epicurus held that the existence of praise and criticism presupposes free agency. He sets up the denial of responsibility for one’s actions as self-refuting: it is pointless for someone who denies personal responsibility to criticize those who assert the opposite, as they hold no responsibility for any such belief and assertions. This argument is insufficient, as there is a difference between being wrong and being responsible for being wrong. A different version asserts that engaging in debate assumes that one is responsible for one’s reasoning, but here too one can counter that we may necessarily be led by rational considerations. Epicurus responds by saying that our understanding of the difference between what depends on us and what happens of necessity are based on observations of our own actions, which we then translate into dissuading others from doing things where we think agency exists (155–6). Rationality is thus the core of Epicurus’ defence of responsible agency (156).

author: Sherwood-Smith, Maria C.
title: Studies in the Reception of the Historia scholastica of Peter Comestor: The Schwarzwälder Predigten, the Weltchronik of Rudolf von Ems, the Scolastica of Jacob van Maerland and the Historiebijbel van 1360
publisher: Society for the Study of Medieval Languages and Literature
abstract:
The introduction pulls together information on Peter Comestor, his sources, and influences; the remainder of the work studies German and Dutch vernacular adaptations.

Sources, in order of importance:

  1. Vulgate
  2. Josephus's Antiquitates Judaicae, which (thus Schreckenberg) Peter considered on par with Scripture
  3. Disputations of Augustine and Jerome

Lesser influences include Isidore, Origen, Alcuin, Rabanus Maurus, and secular Roman literature (4–5). Further Hebrew sources may have come to Peter via Andrew of St Victor; Jerome; or, less likely, from direct contact with Jews (5–6). Other critics point to the importance of Bede as well as Hugh and Andrew of St Victor (6). Many of the apocryphal motifs go back to Irish sources (7). The author then conducts a close source analysis of six chapters of Exodus (8–14).

Manuscrips are many; two helpful tables lists those in Oxford alone (16–17). The additiones are a distinctive feature; it is not clear who added them, but they are likely to have resulted in great MS variation. At any rate they are more variable than the main body of the text (18).

Much of the remainder of the introduction focuses on the print tradition, but pp. 33–4 deal with German and Dutch reception.

author: Morey, James H.
title:
Peter Comestor, Biblical Paraphrase,
and the Medieval Popular Bible
abstract:
Opens by pointing out the gulf between the biblical canon and the Bible in the popular imagination, where it consists rather of a set of disconnected memorable stories. Dissemination of biblical material took place through "sermons, homilies, commentaries, universal histories, picture Bibles, the drama, and a large corpus of biblical paraphrases", all of which were influenced by Peter Comestor's Historia scholastica (c. 1170; papal approval 1215) (6). The Dominican Order and the University of Oxford made it required reading, along with Peter Lombard's Sententiae, from which the HS distinguishes itself in its integral approach to the Bible; but perhaps its treatment of the material as stories also played a role (–7). Produced for academic lecturing, the work always served mediation between Scripture and the public, as would its vernacular derivatives (7).

Asserts Peter's unrivalled but widely unacknowledged status as biblical historian prior to the Reformation, and lists the vernacular adaptations (7–9), followed by a brief biography. Aside from the HS, Peter produced sermons, a gospel commentary, and an abridgement of Peter Lombard's Sententiae (10). A discussion of sources follows (10–16), which includes the observation that Peter is more ready to dismiss apocryphal legends on NT material than on OT material (11), the assertion that several apocryphal motifs can be traced to Irish sources (12), and a comparatively detailed discussion of suspected Hebrew sources (12–14). There is a table comparing number of HS chapters per biblical book to the number of chapters in the biblical book (15). Truly integral treatment of biblical books breaks down "after Tobit" [really, it seems, from Tobit onwards], but then there isn't much historical material in the OT after Kings. Genesis takes up a central position because of the great number of stories it contains and because it tells of the Fall; HS is really about humankind, and it places humankind at the start of the account where Genesis does not; we are looking at an "anthropocentric retelling of the Genesis story" resulting in an "individualistic and egalitarian slant in the paraphrases" (16).

Herman de Valenciennes wrote a biblical history in French just 15 years after Peter. In addition to Hebrew sources, it was influenced by Peter especially in its treatment of Genesis (17), and was itself used as a source of the Middle English Cursor mundi and Iacop and Iosep; other ME poets followed Peter (18–19). Half a dozen further French texts are discussed, including Guyart's 1295 Bible historiale, which fused HS and Vulgate into a single work, and universal histories such as the Histoire ancienne (1210), a universal history using HS as one of its sources (19–25). Thus from the twelfth century onwards, a great deal of vernacular information about biblical history was to be had, and nearly all of it relied heavily on the HS; the English texts discussed in the following rely more exclusively and conservatively on Peter than the French (25–6).

The HS circulated widely in England, where its presence is attested as early as 1194. Its earliest English paraphrase is Genesis and Exodus (c. 1250) (26–9). The Metrical Paraphrase of the Old Testament (c. 1400, perhaps earlier) (29–32). Further ME works are treated very briefly, though Morey dwells for some time on a reference to Comestor in the margins of the Chaucer MSS.

author: Sylwan, Agneta
title: Petri Comestoris Scolastica historia: Liber Genesis
abstract:
Peter must have finished his work about 1170. He dedicated it to Archbishop William of Sens (1168–75); since William inspected St Victor's Abbey in 1171x72 when Peter was there, it is likely it was then that Peter gifted him with the book (xi–xii).

Among other things, the introduction contains a full list of known sources, plus a tally of source acknowledgements (xix–xxi), followed by a discussion of Peter's use of Josephus that includes an identification of the branch of the Antiquitates Iudaicae used, and of its Parisian origins, along with a list of chapters of Josephus's works used for the various books of the HS (xxii–xxiv); it then discusses some of the other sources in some detail as well. Peter must have made extensive use of the library of St Victor's Abbey, Paris; Sylwan prints a list of relevant MSS to which he must have had access (xxviii–xxix).

The Bible used is the Vulgate, sometimes mixed with the Vetus Latina; he rarely cites the version of a commentary used (xxix). He has a tendency to turn direct speech into indirect speech (xxix–xxx). He prefers simpler words and participial rather than paratactical constructions, yet also has a predilection for rare words; he freely substitutes synonyms; and he does not hesitate to rephrase for clarity (xxx; examples given include the addition of names and pronouns where these are left implicit in the Vulgate).

The editor has found over 800 MSS from the 12th to the 14th century. I won't bother at this point finding out how she got to the eight she is collating in this edition (xxxi–lxxxvi). Sylwain discusses the original form of the title, which couldn't have been either of the current forms; it is suggested Scolastica historia could have been given by its revisors, probably with Peter's consent (xxxix–xl).

author: Wilcox, Jonathan
title: A Reluctant Translator in Anglo-Saxon England: Ælfric and Maccabees
abstract: Ælfric on three occasions vowed to translate nothing further: at the conclusion of CH II; in his Preface to Genesis; and in the preface to his Lives of Saints. This article demonstrates with reference to Maccabees how Ælfric dealt with his reluctance, namely by intervening in the narrative more often than in his other translations, though not as widely as in his homilies.

author: Griffith, Mark
title: Ælfric's Preface to Genesis: Genre, Rhetoric and the Origins of the ars dictaminis
abstract:
Points out, first, that Ælfric must have known his Preface would soon be attached to a full text of Genesis at least, and possibly more. The fact that Æthelweard found another translator suggests this was done in response to Ælfric's initial refusal. Either way, the preface would naturally end up travelling with the whole (215–16).

The preface discusses material beyond Isaac, even into Exodus and Leviticus (the tabernacle). Since we know Ælfric produced part of Numbers, some have concluded Ælfric was involved in a larger translation project, but the accepted view is that the Hexateuch compiler was someone else. This view prompts the question why Ælfric includes a digression on the tabernacle, and accordingly a question for the genre of the preface (216–17).

Jerome's prefaces are natural models and were widely available. Jerome's letter to Paulinus and his "helmeted" preface to Samuel and Kings list the books of the Bible, which Ælfric does not; but Jerome's helmeted preface and his preface to Genesis also mention the tabernacle (217). There, however, they are not digressions but dedications, as Jerome considers his translation an offering, and Ælfric's tabernacle passage redeploys this motif (218). The difference is that Ælfric takes from it a universal obligation to bring God our offerings, so that it is no longer recognizable as a dedication but resembles rather Bede's mention of it as a type, and the detail of the goat's hair is from Bede's De tabernaculo as well. The digression on the tabernacle must have been prompted by Jerome (219).

Ælfric's failure to retain the rhetorical function of the tabernacle passage prompts questions about his knowledge of the rhetorical tradition, but he was well enough acquainted with Jerome's Letter to Paulinus and with prefaces to other works he cites and uses elsewhere to know that the standard format of the preface was epistolary, and so are his own, in Latin and on two occasions in English (219–21). The form of the dedicatory epistle, developed under the influence of the rhetorical exordium, was conventional: addressed either to a superior patron or to an inferior (pupil), it was intended for general publication; the author expresses doubts about the difficulty of the task and his ability to undertake it; it is coloured by the modesty topos; and it implicitly shifts responsibility of the work to the patron who insisted it be produced (221–2). Ælfric's preface does not conform to the highly conventional prologues of the rhetorical tradition in terms of the themes discussed, but the biblical subject matter would hardly have allowed a fully traditional organization (222). Nevertheless, the text's genre is visible, dividing up as it does into (1) epistolary; (2) the spiritual meaning of Scripture, aimed at a wider audience; and (3) a conclusion to both of these. Ælfric initially gives only reasons against translation, as though he were about to reject the commission again, but then he does an about-face. It is here also that he drops the first person singular for the self-suppressing authorial plural, shifting responsibility to the patron and coming to address a wider audience (223–4). Deixically and stylistically, and marginally palaeographically, the text divides into five sections, marked by repetitious constructions as also found in other OE letters (224–6). It was the rhetorical tradition (ars dictaminis) to divide letters into five parts: salutatio, exordium, narratio, petitio, conclusio. These parts are defined in the twelfth century, but the art of letter-writing as such was codified in the late eleventh by Alberic of Monte Cassino, and there is reason to believe he was codifying existing practice. Ælfric's letter to Æthelweard may be considered a second identified instance of the five-part scheme in the tenth century, and his letter to Sigeric prefacing ÆCHom I may be counted a third (226–8). The remainder of the article analyses Ælfric's application of the five parts individually. The conclusion of the article is that Ælfric was indeed familiar with a rhetorical art of letter-writing, and that the "apparent contradictoriness" of the preface may be better understood in the light of this genre.

author: Gittos, Helen
title: The Audience for Old English Texts: Ælfric, Rhetoric and ‘the Edification of the Simple’
abstract:
Opens with a long list of texts that claim to have been written in Old English because their lay or monastic audiences do not read or understand Latin (233–8). The reliability of such claims is drawn into question by recent work, such as Godden’s on Alfred, whose prefaces fit into a wider tradition of prefaces claiming royal authorship for rhetorical purposes (238–9). In the case of Alfred's Pastoral Care, Godden believes it was translated not for the kingdom's youth but for Alfred's bishops; the preface's claim is at best a secondary ideal. Writing to or for a king or nobleman was likewise a classical and medieval rhetorical strategy to gain authority (239). Although Ælfric's Libellus contains specific references to its addressee's drinking habit, it also expresses an expectation that it will be copied (240). The Lives of Saints focus on saints venerated in monasteries rather than elsewhere, and the Catholic Homilies, expressly intended for the laity, are more learned in content than one would expect (so Godden) (240–1). Byrhtferth's Enchiridion is highly misleading: it claims its English parts are for secular clerics and unlearned priests, but in fact most of it is in English, and some of that is for a monastic audience. Stephenson argues that the purpose of the work's macaronic form is to justify a translation for a monastic audience while insisting on the importance of Latin for the monastic identity. Latin was thus a status symbol [rather than a practical medium] (241).

Ælfric's prefaced claims become even more suspect when we recognize they echoe three of Jerome's strategies in detail: (1) a supposed commission by an influential person; (2) sense for sense; (3) a simple style. Ælfric seems to have known Jerome's letter to Pammachius, which deploys these strategies (242–4). A further argument for translation was derived from Gregory's letters to Bishop Serenus of Marseille, the original documents claiming pictures were like reading for the illiterate. Gittos conjectures that this argument was transferred onto vernacular literature, thus offering an argument for translation. [I'm confused: so texts were translated not because their audiences could not read Latin, but because of Latin illiteracy on some rhetorical, theoretical plane? PSL] Gittos then presents examples (Otfrid, Notker, the Old Saxon prefaces) of prefaces to translations that cannot have been intended for the illiterate audiences they claim, because they require a knowledge of the Latin sources; Ælfric's contemporary work seems to fit the same pattern (249–52).

Jeremy Catto's argument about fourteenth-century literature, that reading was taught in Latin first and readers of English texts were therefore fully bilingual (cf. Latin content in the Confessio amantis), goes for Ælfric's day as well (253–3). Indeed, the argument may be made that vernacular texts for preaching were intended for the preachers rather than the preached: they discouraged improvization by offering a fixed form (253–4).

It is then pointed out that the "pictures are for the illiterate" argument is bogus: you typically need a solid background in theology to understand them (esp. their typological value), yet the claim that the illiterate were their primary audience was repeated throughout the Middle Ages and thereafter. The situation with vernacular literature is analogous (255–6).

The tendency to take prefaces at face value has fuelled further misconceptions, e.g. that vernacular texts signal lay use, that Old English charms are not liturgical texts, that the use of the vernacular signals poor latinity, and that clergymen were reluctant to translate; the problems with that last point are sufficiently clear in Ælfric's self-contradictory resolutions to stop translation (256–9). Gittos goes on to challenge the notion that Latin was viewed as a sacred language, along with the notion that translators had any hesitation (259–61).

Gittos proposes the following reasons for deploying the rhetorical convention of translating for the laity:

  1. Deflect criticism of the translation;
  2. Authorization by appeal to precedent;
  3. The modesty topos: not only is the author humble in his capabilities, his work is also appropriate for an audience with similar limitations;
  4. Take up one's position in a venerable chain of transmission (262–5).

author: Menzer, Melinda J.
title: The Preface as Admonition: Ælfric's Preface to Genesis
publication: The Old English Hexateuch: Aspects and Approaches
eds: Rebecca Barnhouse and Benjamin C. Withers
publisher: Medieval Institute Publications and Western Michigan University
series: Publications of the Richard Rawlinson Center
abstract:
Although Ælfric appears to say he has translated Genesis only up to Isaac, his Preface takes examples from further on in Genesis and expresses concerns that apply to the whole of the Old Testament. Thus it is not inappropriate that the Preface survives ahead of multiple Old Testament texts in two manuscripts (15–17). In its relevance to the Christian Bible as a whole, the Preface to Genesis differs from Ælfric's other prefaces, which are authorial comments on the text at hand: motivations, selection processes, and intended use (17–19). In ÆGenPref, not only is the scope broader, but the author indeed opposes the activity of translation outright, having been prompted by commission to undertake the work; this distances him from the work and projects less authority than in his other prefaces (19–21). The preface is also confusing, e.g. towards the end, where Ælfric shifts between tropological and anagogical interpretations without marking the shift. If readers were intended to understand this, he had more faith in them than he expresses in his preface (21–4). In other prefaces, he stresses his use of simple language, and in some texts he even asserts he is leaving hard-to-understand passages out of his expositions (24–5). Ælfric's introduction to Genesis also introduces confusion: it is called Genesis because it treats of first things, but not the creation of the angels — this omission is left unexplained, which is uncharacteristic of his typical treatment of etymologies (26–8). Similarly, the reference to Adam's blood does not fit its context, which explains the unity of the Trinity (28–31).

Menzer explains the uncharacteristically disjointed nature of ÆGenPref by the fact that the text it prefaces is different in nature: because the biblical text is not to be modified beyond the demands of syntax, he lacks his usual level of control, and so he instead uses the Preface as an illustration of the text's difficulty. The disjointed examples demonstrate how little we understand when we think the literal meaning suffices (31–4). The most straightforward illustration is the link between Gn 1:1 and the Gospel of John, where Christ identifies himself as the beginning; this is an elegant illustration of the danger of reading the Old Testament exclusively on the literal level (34–7).

Menzer offers two possible explanations for why Ælfric agreed to do the translation at all: since half of it was already done, he realized it would be best if he produced the rest of it and appended a cautioning preface; and he did consider the Old Testament necessary reading (37–9).

author: Hawk, Brandon W.
title: Isidorian Influences in Ælfric's Preface to Genesis
abstract: Adds to Mark Griffith's study of sources used in ÆGenPref ("Ælfric's Use of his Sources", Florilegium 17 [2000]) by identifying the Etymologiae as a source of three passages, namely the etymology of "Genesis"; the translation ferian for ferre (an aural analogue, characteristic of Isidore's etymologies); and the connection of the Holy Spirit with creation and baptism in one breath.

author: Campbell, Alistair
title: The Chronicle of Æthelweard
abstract: The introduction touches very briefly on the question why if this Æthelweard is the ealdorman and Ælfric's patron he would have asked for biblical translations, since clearly his Latin was strong enough that he would have been able to read the Vulgate. Campbell's solution is to point to evidence that Æthelweard preferred to read in English, as for instance his borrowings from Bede show a dependence on the Old English version. Campbell considers the identity of the author to be sufficiently clear because the dates fit the ealdorman; the chronicler's titles are not monastic, and in fact the title consul suggests he was an ealdorman. The likely relationship between ealdorman Æthelweard and Eadwig explains his favourable depiction (xxxvi–xxxvii).

author: Swan, Mary
title: Identity and Ideology in Ælfric's Prefaces
series: Brill's Companions to the Christian Tradition
abstract:
As Alfred's strategies of positioning himself by referencing institutions and individuals directly have already been studied at length, proposes to look at internal-facing identity references instead, i.e. linguistic markers (pronouns and verbs) positioning the speaker (248–9).

Ælfric uses a first-person construct in many of his texts, and when he does so, he is rarely translating a source; instead, he is advancing his own agenda. Nowhere is the first-person construct as sustained as in the prefaces (249).

In his prefaces to CH, Ælfric invokes a network as well as a hierarchical system in which he is inferior to his teacher Æthelwold and his addressee Sigeric; but by opening with "EGO" in contrast with the Latin epistolary convention, he emphasizes his own agency. Thereafter, he switches to the plural pronoun, shifting the "locus of authority" to the commons of teachers (250–1). The Old English preface to CHI is similar, except it never switches to a plural but stays with a prominent "ic" (251–2). The Latin preface to CHII is close to that to the first series, retaining a singular pronoun early on but then switching to the plural while elevating its addressee Sigeric, while the Old English preface to CHII mirrors the vernacular preface to the first series, retaining a singular pronoun throughout. It contains two third-person constructs, one inclusive and one referring to those who do not read Latin. There are thus stronger parallels between the CH prefaces that share a language than between the ones that share a series (252–4).

The Latin preface to LS lacks a salutation and uses both singular and plural pronouns to emphasize Ælfric's agency in a hierarchy below his patrons. The Old English does include a salutation, starting with "Ælfric" and containing ample wes, positioning Ælfric as an author rather than an individual. Third-person classes introduced are mynstermen and læwede men (254–6).

The Latin preface to the Grammar opens with "Ego Ælfricus" and switches to the plural midway through for the self, but sustains a plural for the audience (schoolboys). The Old English mirrors the Latin with "Ic Ælfric" but contains no "you" addressee, resulting in a more strongly marked "I" and thus a higher level of authority for the self, suggesting Ælfric expected the English preface to be read by ecclesiastical/educational inferiors, more so than the Latin (246–8).

In the preface to Genesis, Ælfric starts with his own name and ecclesiastical rank and mirrors with these the addressee's name and secular rank, then suggest an egalitarian relationship by the use of first- and second-person singular pronouns. Swan speaks of "repeated reminders of Ælfric's intellectual and spiritual control" (248–9).

The letter to the monks sets up a chain of affiliation suggesting an ideological structure as a model for the country and incorporates at the end an inclusive "we" emphasizing the shared nature of the rule (259–60).

The preface to the Vita Æthelwoldi, that to the Hexameron, the letters to Sigefryth, Wulfgeat, Sigeweard, Wulfsige, and Wulfstan are given the same treatment, leading to the conclusion that Ælfric deftly shapes a position for his authorial voice appropriate to the relations invoked in each letter, providing an insight into Ælfric's reforming ideology.

author: Griffith, Mark
title: Ælfric's Use of his Sources in the Preface to Genesis: Together with a Conspectus of Biblical and Patristic Sources and Analogues
abstract:
Though the preface may in some respects read like an original composition, it is heavily indebted to biblical exegesis. The preface should be interpreted against this background (127). Ælfric's warning that OT translation is dangerous is a close echo of Jerome's warning to Desiderius; his demands-of-syntax approach to translation echoes Jerome's letter to Pammachius (127–9).

A central source for the preface is the Brevarium in Psalmos once ascribed to Jerome: from this, Ælfric takes the need to read both testaments together (129–30). Modifications of his source suggest he had particular groups of heretics in mind, specifically the Nicolaitans who are mentioned by Eusebius as having rejected St Paul, but by the eleventh century they had come to be associated with married priests, a problem to which Ælfric refers earlier in his preface (130–1).

The trinitarian exposition rests on a tradition going back to Justin Martyr in the second century and perhaps available to Ælfric in Basil's Hexaemeron (in Eustathius's Latin translation), or in Jerome, Augustine, Bede, Hrabanus, Alcuin (132–3). His words e.g. on the sin against the Holy Spirit blend scriptural and patristic sources (133–6). The three angels speaking to Abraham are explained in De civitate Dei, Haymo, and Gregory's Homiliae, Gregory being the likeliest direct source given the phrasing (135–6). Verses adduced in conjunction also reveal patristic sources (136–9). The reference to Abel's blood derives from Ælfric's own paraphrase of Alcuin's Interrogationes Sigewulfi, part of which must thus have been produced before the Genesis translation, though it was surely intended as a companion piece, given that it too ends at Isaac (139–40).

An index of sources and analogues is appended to the article (141–9).

author: Konráð Gíslason
