title: Þáttur umm stafsetníng
abstract:
Prompted by an article by Árni Helgason (Ármann 4: 66–83) about spelling conventions to be used in education so as not to discourage the young, Konráð briefly discusses such suggestions as choosing one letter/digraph to represent <c, k, q> and getting rid of <au, ei, ja> (7–8).

Modern Icelandic has fifteen vowel graphemes [at the time including è, PSL], but not fifteen vowel sounds: depending on context, there is overlap between <i> and <í>, <u> and <y>, etc. <é è> can be represented by <eí je>, etc. (10–11). Konráð goes on in this manner with the vowels, then the consonants, arguing among other things that voiced consonants should be differentiated from their voiceless counterparts on the written page.

This article is almost exclusively on Modern Icelandic orthography; references to Old Icelandic are limited to the observation that Ari fróði wrote "lanns" for "lands" (7); early Icelanders wrote <i> where Modern Icelanders write <j> (32). The most important point argued is that <j> should take the place of a number of redundant graphemes, a point Konráð has to defend against Rask. However, Konráð does at this time begin to implement a reformed spelling in his saga editions as well, and later scholars have often referred back to that practice, specifically Konráð's practice of doubling consonants throughout the paradigm where the consonant is a geminate in the root. See esp. Jón Þorkelsson on this.

author: Björn Magnússon Ólsen
title: Um stafsetning
abstract:
Ólsen opens his lecture to the Society of Teachers by arguing that it is important for learners that spelling and sound relate 1:1 (3–4). But pronunciation is subject to regiolect and idiolect, matters that cannot be taken into account in a unified spelling. Spelling ought therefore to be based on the most common pronunciation among educated individuals (4). Konráð Gíslason proposed to follow pronunciation as much as possible, and printed his second volume of Fjölnir according to this principle. Ólsen approves but points out inconsistencies, e.g. where Konráð retains <z> for historical reasons (4–5).

Konráð's proposal was poorly received: Sveinbjörn Egilsson opposed it in Sunnanpósturinn, prompting a response from Konráð in Fjölnir 3, and volumes 3–6 were all printed in the idiosyncratic spelling, but the old spelling won out (6). This shows that pronunciation is not a precise guide to orthography and powerless in the face of custom and tradition, which accordingly must be taken into account in any spelling reform. The old spelling has survived in Rask's emended form, except many have tinkered with it in small ways, so it is a universal standard only in general outline. There is the Icelandic of the grammar schools, and there are scholars who have adopted variants of Old Icelandic spelling that will never become a new standard, because they do not correspond even to their own pronunciation. Some distinguish between <æ> and <œ> but practise hypercorrection in both directions, and the same is true for <r> and <ur> (7–8).

The Danish, Swedish, and French have undertaken to fix spelling on the basis of pronunciation; if the English were to go the same way, their language would become the universal language — it's only a matter of time before they wisen up; Henry Sweet asserts that spelling reform is inevitable and proposes a system faithful to pronunciation, and all feel that it should go in the direction of pronunciation. It is only a matter of time before the same happens in Iceland (8–10).

In Icelandic, we see pronunciation has changed and spelling has not followed suit. Specifically, some graphemes, such as <g, k, l, n>, have multiple realizations; strictly, these sounds ought to have distinct graphemes, but there would be little benefit in such a reform. It is after all not so bad if one letter has multiple sounds associated with it, as long as it is not the other way around. This is the case with /b/ <b, fv> and /v/ <v, f>; these ought to be spelled according to their voicing (11). <z> has no function, and it's proven difficult to learn when to use it. /nn/ is spelled <nn> or <n> at word's end; "enn" and "en" should both be written "enn"; but it is not as pressing to change the existing convention here as is it with <z>, because the rule of <nn> versus <n> is easier to learn (11–12). <x> had better be retained, because the alternative adds another sound to <g> in <gs> (12).

A much-discussed question is, whether geminated consonants ought to be written with two graphemes where another (i.e. third) consonant follows. Pronunciation generally makes no distinction between <ggð> and <gð> etc. Ólsen hears these geminated consonants as short and therefore proposes to write all geminated consonants short where they occur before a further consonant, except where two are clearly heard, as in "allra" and "öruggra", and on the boundary between composite elements, as in "fjalldrapi" or "innreið". (12–13).

Similar disagreement exists in the case of <f> versus <p> before <t>. This should be <f>, following pronunciation and generally origin as well; no matter that *kaupa* then has a participle "keift" (13).

The pronunciation of vowels has changed greatly since the Middle Ages, and the fact that spelling has not kept up is a problem for students. The changes in sound have nevertheless been regular, and the resulting system still retains a straightforward relationship between sound and orthography. Some changes are nonetheless advisable, such as <je> for <è, é>. Before <ng>, some write long vowels: *lángur, leingi, þíng, laungum*, and this is advisable because it follows pronunciation; still, the usual forms give no great difficulties and moreover generally follow West Fjord pronunciation (14–15).

<y, ý> ought to be given up in favour of <i, í>; this is the most common spelling error in grammar school, followed by <nn> versus <n>, <z> versus <s>. Dropping <y, ý, z> thus should have priority (15–19). The argument for transparent origin is flawed: ought we to write pre-Grimm forms? (19–20). The remainder of the article counters further objections to the loss of <y> in a similar way.

author: Jón Þorkelsson
title: Einföldun samhljóðanda í fornu máli
abstract:
Konráð Gíslason about 1836 introduced the unfortunate policy of writing a consonant double if it is double in the root, even before a further (third) consonant. He also put this rule into practice in his saga editions, using forms found in none of the manuscripts. He ought instead to have looked for the oldest and best MSS and decided on a normalization feature on their basis. This article demonstrates, for each affected consonant of the alphabet, that this doubling is not found ahead of further consonants in early MSS (64).

b not doubled in Old Icelandic
d geminated form not shortened: staddr, stadds; gladdr; kvaddr; skaddr; etc.
f doubles in eff, vaff, and some loan words such as offra
g doubles where preceded by a short vowel and followed by <j, v>: slag > sleggja; hug > hyggja; reduced to one where no <j, v> follows: hugða, lagða. The forms segja, þegja may seem to be exceptions, but they have a different origin (e-stems) where /j/ is not original. No doubling where a long or diphthong vowel precedes <g>, regardless whether <j, v> follow: hneigja, sveigja, beygja, frægja, ægja. The form hnegja is recent and incorrect. <g> was simplified before genitive s: dygs, Ygs. Pronounced hard by the poets, saga authors may have pronounced it weak. Jón proposes to write <ggs> in genitives where the root contains <gg>. The words bygð, dygð, stygð, trygð are in some regions pronounced with a soft g, but old MSS nearly always write a single <g> (rarely <G>, the equivalent of <gg>).
k simplified before genitive s (drycs, floks) as well as before t, ð (blekt). Before <j, v> we find a lot of variation between simplex and duplex.
l Geminated l and n were in Old Icelandic pronounced with an intrusive /d/ or /t/, as seen in the various forms: allz, alz, aldz, altz; mannz, manz, mandz. The intrusive consonant is not found in the poetry, and it is not pronounced today, and so "manns" is out of the question when writing Modern Icelandic, which should instead be written als, ils. Old Icelandic should be represented with the old forms.
m In Old Icelandic written singly in monosyllables: fim, fram, um. It was not doubled ahead of a further consonant. Skǫm was almost always written with a single <m>, but some other nouns show variation: glam/glamm, vam/vamm, áraglam/áraglamm; in analogy with skǫm, these should all be written with a single <m>.
n Reduced before d, t: kenna, kendi, kendr, kent; kynna, kynti, kyntr, kynt; menna, menti, mentr, ment; renna, rendi, rent. (Many MS examples are given, including a few counterexamples.)
p Reduced ahead of further consonants, e.g. genitive hreps, kaps.
r Reduced ahead of further consonants, except across syllable boundaries: kyrr, kyrs, kyrt, but kyrrsæti. In hvártveggi, however, /r/ is simplified. It is also simplified ahead of ð, t in a number of weak i-stem verbs: firra, firðr; kyrra, kyrði, þerra, þert; þverra, þverdi.
s Reduced ahead of t in a number of weak i-stem verbs: hvessa, hvesta; kyssa, kysti; missa, mista. The neuter of the adjective hvass is written with a single <s>, and the same is true of the adverb.
t Variously retained or dropped before a following consonant; best doubled in Modern Icelandic. Triplets are not found: thus réttrúaðr, not rétttrúaðr. [NB Old Icelandic dictionaries and editions do have knatttré, nátttíðir, etc, PSL.]
v /f/ assimilates to a following /v/, which is [sometimes] seen in the spelling: avvirði. It is, however, customary to write "afv" or "auv" in these cases.
x No doubling in Old or Modern Icelandic
z No doubling in Old or Modern Icelandic
þ No doubling in Old or Modern Icelandic

author: Ashley, Scott
title: The Lay Intellectual in Anglo-Saxon England: Ealdorman Æthelweard and the Politics of History
publication: Lay Intellectuals in the Carolingian World
eds: Patrick Wormald and Janet L. Nelson

author: Sigurður Nordal
title: Egils saga Skalla-Grímssonar
abstract:
[This abstract is concerned only with Nordal's introduction to ÍF normalization.]

This edition [and, by implication, all ÍF editions] is normalized according to the preexisting norm, but when multiple MS spellings are considered equally legitimate, they are sometimes printed as found in the MS (e.g. Fiðr/Finnr; bazt/bezt; Reykjadalr/Reykjardalr). The chief difference between this edition and customary normalization is that Nordal has adopted Konráð Gíslason's 1836 recommendation to write double consonants according to their doubling in the bare root, as opposed to the rules set out by Jón Þorkelsson in 1901 but which no editor has followed to the letter. Since consonant doubling has been a mess in recent editions, this has seemed the only workable solution (xcic–c).

Nordal identifies the interested general audience as the prime intended readership; hence the notes on language, customs, and culture at the bottom of the page. The prefaces will be thorough, giving editors more room to lay out their conclusions (c–ci). Poetry is treated differently: regrettably but necessarily, the editor there chooses the best of all variant readings. Verse orthography follows the rules of Finnur Jónsson's Skjaldedigtning, including such forms as long <ǫ> for the u-umlaut form of <á>, and es for er (ci).

[ÞIG adds (personal communication, 17 May 2016) that there is no strict set of rules for ÍF editions, and he believes setting an ÍF-wide standard was never the intention. The standard of normalization aims at about 1250 (<á> represents long <ǫ> as well as long /a/), but key is consistency within a volume: Biskupa sögur III uses a younger standard; PSL]

author: Jóhannes L. L. Jóhannsson
title: Athugasemd um stafsetning fornaldarrita
abstract:
The following features of Icelandic orthography change about 1250:

  1. The distinction between <œ> and <æ> disappears;
  2. The distinction between <ę> and <e> disappears;
  3. The distinction between <ø> and <ǫ> disappears, typically becoming <ỏ> (o with hook) in Middle Icelandic, German <ö> in Modern Icelandic;
  4. The distinction between long <ǫ> (the u-mutated counterpart of á) and <á> disappears;
  5. <é> (long e) becomes <ie> in Middle Icelandic, whose pronunciation in Modern Icelandic becomes /je/ about 1630;
  6. Middle voice is signalled by <sk> in Old Icelandic, mostly <z> in Middle Icelandic, <st> in Modern Icelandic;
  7. Old Icelandic variously pronounced the dental fricative /þ/ or /ð/ e.g. in weak preterites and feminine case endings, which became /d, t/ in Middle and Modern Icelandic.

The Saga-Bibliothek has rather jumbled up the orthography: it follows Old Icelandic in distinguishing between <œ> and <æ>, <ø> and <ǫ>, <é> and <e>, but not <ę> and <e>, long <ǫ> and <á>, where it follows Middle Icelandic MSS; the series also writes <z> for middle voice, while <ð> represents ð, þ in preterites etc., matching neither Old nor Middle Icelandic.

Jóhannes recommends making the time of composition prior or after 1250 the decisive factor: Egils saga ought to follow Old Icelandic, Grettis saga Middle Icelandic orthography.

author: Jón Jónsson
title: Grundvöllur íslenzkrar stafsetningar
abstract: Essentially sees no point in abandoning medieval spelling conventions, and argues against basing spelling on pronunciation because it would have to keep changing.

author: Jón Aðalsteinn Jónsson
title: Ágrip af sögu íslenzkrar stafsetningar
abstract: A detailed account of spelling conventions and reform in the age of print, with a good deal of attention to Rask and Konráð Gíslason.

author: Guðvarður Már Gunnlaugsson
title: Stafrétt eða samræmt? Um fræðilegar útgáfur og notendur þeirra
abstract: A very thorough discussion of reasons and audiences behind diplomatic and normalized editions. I'll have to do a proper reading some other time, but will mention for present purposes that ÍF volumes are classified "V:2", i.e. "[ú]tgáfa með samræmdri stafsetningu fornmáls (oftast frá um 1200)" (204, 205, 215–218); for this category, the article also refers to Haugen, who in a Nordica Bergensia 7 (1995) article calls ÍF an example of the category "fullt normalisert utgåve" (215). Has a lengthy bibliography.

author: Wilcox, Jonathan
title: Ælfric's Prefaces
abstract:
Opens with a very good, concise biography of Ælfric in the context of the Benedictine Reform and the patronage of Æthelweard and Æthelmær (2–15). Then follows a thorough, piece-by-piece or genre-by-genre introduction to his works (15–56). Wilcox considers the distinction between homilies and sermons irrelevant for Ælfric's works: his CH are structured by pericope according to the Church year, but a substantial number of these texts are sermons in the specific sense of the word, and Ælfric seems to have made no distinction (15–16). Saints' lives likewise are not clearly distinguished from homilies: they fulfil the same liturgical function but for the Sanctorale, whereas the homilies are tied to the Temporale. CH caters to both, while LS focuses more centrally on the Sanctorale; two later series of homilies are more centrally concerned with the Temporale (17). As significant sources of homiletic culture, Wilcox mentions Augustine, Jerome, Gregory, Bede, and Paul the Deacon, who compiled an early homiliary arranged by the Church year, as well as fellow Carolingians Smaragdus of St Mihiel and Haymo of Auxerre (18).

It stands to reason that vernacular preaching was undertaken wherever the vernacular branched off from Latin, but Old English provides the earliest substantial corpus, probably thanks to Alfred's early efforts. The anonymous homilies, in Blickling and Vercelli as well as traditions continuing throughout the Anglo-Saxon period and beyond, differ from Ælfric's in their more general moral nature as well as their concern with concrete dramatic matters such as the last judgement and the afterlife; they do not make much use of the patristic and Carolingian traditions. Ælfric distances himself from this tradition (19). Compared to these as well as to Wulfstan's homilies, Ælfric's are more exegetical; Wulfstan's more hortatory (19–20).

Wilcox refers to ÆLet 1 (Wulfsige), among other things, for the conclusion that "preaching to the laity was undertaken by ... secular clerks"; bishops "would have preached to a mixed audience of secular clerks and the laity, while preaching within the monastery of Cerne Abbas would have been to a mixed audience of monks and local laity" (20–1, at 21). Wilcox emphasizes the broad range existing within the audience, from the learned to the unlearned (21). Ælfric also cites a concern that certain material may be dull to his audience (21–2).

Ælfric emphasizes he is not creating but engaged merely in interpretatio or translatio. A striking assertion to this effect is found in the LS, but it applies to the CH as well. "His personal stamp on his works lies in source criticism — his selection from and use of his sources — as well as in the various styles by which he transmits the content of those sources" (23). His approach was typically to draw on the Carolingian homiliaries of Paul the Deacon, Smaragdus, and Haymo of Auxerre and rely on these even for his patristic sources (23–4), but he adds an impressive amount of additional material e.g. from commonplace books filled with excerpts (24). "Generally Ælfric gives particular emphasis to a literal and historical explanation of his text, with frequent but sporadic emphasis on the allegorical and moral implications. . . . Etymologies are frequently exploited by Ælfric to highlight the fundamental relationship between a word and the thing it describes, in explaining which he often goes beyond what was contained in his primary source" (25). Ælfric's care to explain Mosaic customs is briefly addressed, as is his belief that it is the duty of the teacher to explain the spiritual reading of such customs, often rejecting a lasting relevance of the literal sense (26–7). Ælfric in his homilies repeatedly condemns apocrypha, and took care to condemn preaching on Thu–Fri of Easter Week, for which the anonymous collections include homilies (27–31). Information on Ælfric's editing of his homilies (31–3) and his management of their distribution (33–4).

Ælfric's homilies were not subject to the same mouvance as others, notably Wulfstan's; Wilcox explains this by their structural integrity. Their context, on the other hand, quickly became confused, against his express request, as non-Ælfrician homilies were mixed in with them in MSS (34–5).

Following a brief introduction to the Grammar (36–7), Wilcox turns to Old Testament translation, Genesis, and Ælfric's letters to Æthelweard and Sigeweard (37–44). He emphasizes Ælfric's quandary about translation and interpretation, and concludes that, in the case of Genesis, Ælfric appends his preface as a fifty-line interpretation of the first verse of his translation to illustrate the depth of biblical narrative. His Hexameron and translation of Alcuin's Interrogationes Sigewulfi in Genesin likewise offer exetegical work on Genesis (39–40). Ælfric's assertion that he will cease producing translations has been explained both by his personality (changing his mind) and as rhetoric (40). Wilcox understands the letter to Sigeweard as an index of Old Testament material available in English and sees in it evidence that Ælfric considered his biblical works "a coherent body of reliable vernacular orthodoxy" (43); he briefly discusses each of the cross-references (40–3). Wilcox concludes that by the time of the composition of the letter to Sigeweard, Ælfric had resolved his unease about translating biblical matter, perhaps by allowing himself more freedom to intervene in the text of a translation (44).

For his LS, Ælfric specifies a monastic audience. Its original extent is hard to judge, as our best MS incorporates anonymous lives as well as works by Ælfric that do not match the description in the preface, i.e. the collection includes texts other than lives of saints venerated by monks only: there are homilies for specific occasions and any occasion, as well as two biblical translations (45). LS is based primarily on the Cotton–Corpus legendary, a collection probably stemming from Flanders or northern France, but Ælfric added English saints (45–8). Some of the lives receive individual prefaces (49–50). The remainder of this section discusses Ælfric's letter to the monks of Eynsham, Admonitio ad spiritualem filium, Vita Æthelwoldi, occasional and pastoral letters (51–6).

Turning to Ælfric's style, Wilcox describes his gradual adoption of rhythmical prose and illustrates it with passages from the prefaces; notably, he asserts that Genesis is a transitional piece, evincing rhythmical prose from ch. 22 to the end (56–60, at 58). Discusses Ælfric's emphasis on brevity and clarity (60–3). A brief section identifies interpretatio, translatio, awendan as the terms by which Ælfric refers to his activity and explains that his understanding of the process is broader than strict word-for-word translation (63–5).

At a time of anonymous production, Ælfric's very use of prefaces is remarkable (65). While some are epistolary, he and his copyists thought of all of them as prefaces. The language of each depended on the position of the addressee. The contents of the Latin prefaces, too, suggests more learning and interest in translation techniques; but in one case an OE preface refers back to the Latin counterpart (66–7). The prefaces typically identify the author, explain why the work was transmitted or written, a discussion of sources and style, and something on transmission (67).

Ælfric identifies himself in his prefaces as a way of asserting textual authority and orthodoxy, further affirmed through his educational heritage and use of sources (68–9). Ælfric's repeated demand not to interfere with his text further demonstrates the special status he claims for his writings (70–1). Though ultimately unsuccessful, his works did see large-scale circulation (71). What remains is a textual introduction (73–85).

author: Gatch, Milton McC.
title: Preaching and Theology in Anglo-Saxon England: Ælfric and Wulfstan
abstract:
Characterizes early medieval theology as fundamentally conservative in the sense that it implicitly follows the quod ubique, quod semper, et quod ab omnibus definition of theological authority, seeking to reproduce works of high standing and age (4). This makes source analysis a crucial part of historical-theological scholarship. This, however, is complex, for instance because many authors will have relied on florilegia and homiliaries rather than the full original source (4–5). Most also were not critical of the sources they used, which could lead to inconsistencies, as they were not trained to harmonize (5). The derivative nature of Old English homilies, and the lack of translations, has led to their neglect in theological circles (5–6). However, Anglo-Saxon preaching occupies a unique role in the history of the genre for its early vernacular nature (6–7).

The Blickling and Vercelli collections simply reproduce material from Latin sources, resulting in inconsistencies both within texts and in the homiliaries, especially as to the fate of the soul between death and Judgement Day, reflecting the unsettled state of the doctrine in their sources (7). These anonymous codices date to at least a generation before Ælfric and Wulfstan, and Vercelli appears to derive from ninth-century originals. It is probably collections like these Ælfric condemned (8).

The named homilists are separated from their anonymous forebears by the Benedictine Reform. "More than a reform, the English movement was virtually a reintroduction of the regular life in a nation whose church had, in effect if not by intention, been secularized after the Danish raids" (8), a situation not significantly altered by Alfred (8–9). The Reform's particular form in England may be explained by its connections in Ghent and Fleury: observance of the Rule was divorced from secular obligations; monasticism was supported by landowners; and the monks took on educational tasks (9). The English school furthermore gave the monarch a central position and paid rather less heed to the pope; the other emphasis was on the schoolboys (9–10). According to Gneuss, the Winchester School may be responsible for the proliferation of the [late] West Saxon standard (10–11).

The Carolingian era focused on the liturgy rather than biblical commentary; exegesis was subservient to this (11).

Two short chapters follow on Ælfric and Wulfstan's biographies (12–17, 18–22).

Gatch then turns to the homilies' use. He considers it conventional to assume they " — and especially those of Ælfric — were to be read by the clergy to the people on Sundays or Feasts in a liturgical setting, most probably at the Mass". This now does not match the Continental evidence (25). Gallican service books do not mention homilies, but under Charlemagne and his successors there was a revival of Church teaching and perhaps preaching. The widespread copying of homiliaries reflects more on monastic reform or individual devotion than on the liturgy (25–6). This is reason for this book to investigate the aims of Anglo-Saxon homily production and the Carolingian revival of preaching (26).

The first homiliaries, in the 5th and 6th centuries, were intended for devotional reading, probably in monasteries, even if they soon came to be ordered by the liturgical year and indeed gained a secondary function supplementing the liturgical readings of the Nocturns. In short, then, the first homiliaries were non-liturgical, and the first liturgical homiliaries were for monastic use (27). Their wide circulation accordingly reflects the success of the monastic movement and the spread of the Office of the Hours (27–8). The prologue to Alan of Farfa's mid-eighth century homiliary does not mention liturgical uses, but it specifies a monastic production. Only Paul the Deacon assumes a more important position in homiliary history. His homiliary was commissioned by Charlemagne, who supplied a preface making clear it was intended for use in the Night Office. Its supplying several homilies for each occasion and its division into summer and winter reflects the needs of the Night Office (28–9).

Homiliaries at this time went in two directions: Paul's was monastic-liturgical and concerned itself almost exclusively with patristic elucidations of pericopes, but the Carolingian type described by Henri Barré was intended for devotional readings, despite its liturgical ordering, and included commentaries on the Epistles and homilies for days when the Nocturns left no time for them, as well as Nocturn-appropriate exegesis. This latter type gave rise to source abbreviation and paraphrase as well as eclectic/compilatory homilies (29–30). Only prefatory hints suggest any link with public preaching (30).

In the early Church, only the bishop preached. Growth necessitated for sacerdotal duties to be delegated to presbyters, but preaching remained the bishops' domain for some time: even after Gregory the Great, nearly all Latin homilies were composed by bishops, and they dominated the field in the tenth and eleventh centuries. The spread of preaching to the presbyters resulted from (1) the need for a greater work force to undertake teaching and, north of the Alps, missionary work; and (2) the fact that bishops and presbyters had come to share sacerdotal duties, so preaching, too, became the province of presbyters as bishops became administrators. But this latter development was doctrinal, not so much reflected in practice, as there is little evidence of presbyters preaching (31).

Caesarius of Arles was among the first to urge presbyters to preach. In his Admonitio, he asserts that rural presbyters ought to open schools, and in their absence, deacons should read patristic homilies. This position seems to have been prompted by the particular circumstances in Gaul, and it seems not to have been adopted elsewhere for several centuries. Caesarius's own homilies were a central source of later homiliaries. His are mostly generally admonitory, not exegetical (32).

The canons of the 747 Clovesho council show an ambiguity towards preaching: on the one hand, they recommend that bishops visit their dioceses annually and preach (catechetical teaching and missionary preaching, not strictly liturgical preaching) (32–3). On the other hand, the appointment of presbyters is made conditional on their fitness for preaching and teaching, in which preaching may mean baptizing, teaching, visiting, while teaching refers to explanations of liturgical acts and words. On Sundays, abbots and presbyters alike had to devote themselves to preaching, either in the context of Mass or alongside it (33).

Canons from various councils in 813 (Tours, Chalon, Rheims, Mainz, et al.) all associate preaching with bishops, but Mainz stipulated that someone else should preach on Sun- and feast days if the bishop is absent, and also mentions sacerdotes who preach. Tours requires bishops have access to homiliaries on important themes (34). Only the synod at Arles stipulates that presbyters preach to the people in all parishes, but it reflects the local tradition familiar from Caesarius. Elsewhere, preaching was episcopal, a function distinct from catechetical teaching (34–5). The Concordia Episcoporum, by contrast, emphasizes the use of homiliaries by presbyters, appearing to give voice to the view that bishops and presbyters shared the same duties; but few surviving homiliaries appear designed to put this part of the Concordia into practice. Gatch speculates this may have been impossible before the lower clergy attained a higher degree of literacy. Other texts are ambiguous, given the polysemy of praedicatio and praedicare: even Theodulf's Capitula, often thought to reflect the revival of preaching, rarely specifies a liturgical setting and never references exegetical preaching. Key to the development is at any rate the regularization of the secular clergy: Chrodegang's Rule mentions fortnightly or more frequent public preaching (35). Amalarius, who wrote about the liturgy in great detail, never mentions homilies in the context of Mass, though he mentions the Creed in that context and seems to suggest that Gospel reading suffices instead of preaching. This omission should make us skeptical about any role for preaching in Mass (35–6). Instead of homilies, the Carolingian canons emphasize catechetical teaching (sermones) not attached to a liturgical setting (36–7). It may have been the so-called Prone, a vernacular office not necessarily part of Mass but typically occurring after the Gospel reading, consisted of a translation and explanation of the pericope along with a liturgical calendar, catechetical instruction, and devotions. We do not know whether this office was fully developed by Carolingian times (37). It may be the Prone that is meant when legislators speak of preaching or teaching ad populum: this explains why there can be preaching at Mass even if Mass and preaching were considered different things occurring on Sundays. It may also explain the lack of texts for preaching: preaching could have been done ex tempore and in the vernacular, leaving exegetical preaching for the Night Office for Sun- and feast days (38). By the time of the tenth-century reform we see references to preaching in Mass; after the eleventh century, the nature of preaching changed from exegetical patristics to thematic pieces of rhetoric, but when preaching was done in Mass, it was usually in the Prone, especially when done in the vernacular (38–9).
