author: Stanton, Robert
title: The Culture of Translation in Anglo-Saxon England
abstract:
[3: Bible Translation and the Anxiety of Authority] Takes a pretty generous understanding of what constitutes translation and how much of Genesis, Joshua, and Judges Ælfric covered (104–5). Acknowledges that “[t]he prefaces of Alfred and Ælfric show a clear awareness of the translation terminology refined by patristic scholars, especially Jerome” (105).

Two views of Christian translation dominate: the first asserts that translation is a necessary part of the religion and indeed central to it in the form of incarnation; the other emphasizes the degree to which Bible translation has always been discouraged because of the sanctity of the perceived original (105–6). Yet “during the Anglo-Saxon period, no one was actively prevented from translating scripture, no one was executed for doing so, and numerous people did it” (107).

There was a tension between biblical translation and interpretive control. This led to the characterization of translators as divinely inspired (107–8). Jerome held the Septuagint in high esteem, but since they predated Christ, he felt justified in associating their work as much with prophecy as with translation, whereas his own activity resembled more that of the historian, scholarly and reliable (109–10). His Letter 57 advocates sense-for-sense translation elsewhere, but word-for-word translation of Scriptural content; but his prefaces to translations of individual biblical books, as well as those translations themselves, do not reflect the word-for-word ideal, and indeed in other letters he praises the Evangelists for translation Scripture sense for sense (110–11). Thus his point in Letter 57 of even the order of the words being a divine mystery is lip-service to an ideal that could not be maintained in practice (111–12, and cf. up to 113). Jerome shows an enthusiasm for Cicero and his notion that translation is a stylistic exercise and a branch of rhetoric (113–14).

Turning to Psalter glosses, Stanton argues that the only reason even pronouns and conjunctions were glossed is the ideal of literal translation, certainly not communication; in a sense, these glosses are not translations at all, as they do not always make sense when read on their own, given their Latin syntax; rather, they are facsimiles (117–19). Jerome's understanding of sacred language may be understood against Walter Benjamin's claim that the mediating role of meaning in translation does not apply for Scripture, and without this role for meaning, doctrine becomes “unconditionally translatable” and language takes on greater power, bypassing normal human communication (119). [Yes, this passage is unacceptably esoteric, PSL.]

Continuous glosses preserve sacred word order while serving also as a means of interpretation; they were used as the basis of translations and thus form a continuum with translations proper (120).

King Alfred's Prose Psalter emphasizes certain matters of relevance to his own kingship, but it also emphasizes David's role as a teacher and prophet through the verbs læran and witegian. His other translation activities likewise bring together teaching and rulership (123–4). He translates christus “anointed” literally, forgoing the shoe-in typological connotations, perhaps because he enjoyed his own regal connection with David too much to emphasize the allegorical level (125–6). By picking and choosing from the interpretations available to him, Alfred joins his voice with the most sacred; to him, the authoritative translator is a position of power as well as that of a prophet (126–8). Alfred uses many “contrastive” pairs in his Psalter, repeatedly translating two distinct senses of the Latin model (128). The discussion thus far makes clear that translation was not considered an inadequate activity (128–9).

The OE Gospels, produced around 1000 in the context of the Benedictine Reform, seem not to have been widely known; Ælfric was not aware of them. A fair number of MSS survive, which are thought to have been kept in monastic and cathedral libraries, not straying far from MSS of the Latin source. It could be read without reference to the Latin, and indeed several MSS bear witness to it having begun as an independent OE translation, though it was later reined in by the use of Latin rubrics (129–30). Their library provenance suggests they served to help novices learn Latin, but in fact Latin may have been so poor that a freestanding translation was necessary (Stanton refers to Ælfric's childhood memory for this conjecture). Alternatively, a wealthy lay patron may have commissioned it (130). It could also have served as a lectionary in Mass (130–1).

Takes Ælfric's Preface to Genesis at face value and discusses the tension between translation and regulation: the danger of vernacular translations is that catechesis is bypassed (131–3). Zooms in on Ælfric's reasoning that because of the difficulty of the book's spiritual understanding, he will record only the historical level, not engaging in interpretation at this stage. This implies, first, that a narrative devoid of interpretation may be uncovered, and, second, that it can be done in the vernacular, denying that language has intrinsic value (133–4). Stanton denies that translation without interpretation or rhetoric is possible, and Ælfric agrees that the simple narrative does not exhaust the Old Testament. In fact, Stanton argues, interpretation has begun long before Alfred puts quill to parchment, and he cannot control interpretation among his audience (134–5). He notes the danger of the deceptively straightforward scriptural narrative, yet offers a similarly straightforward translation, hoping his audience will not go astray (135). Ælfric also notes that one must adapt word order for the translation to make any sense, thus making an exception to Jerome's exception to sense-for-sense translation: Ælfric claims he will not change word order, except that this is absolutely necessary, so he will. Where he has earlier asserted that interpretive translation might lead readers astray, he now claims word-for-word literalism can do the same (135–8). This was a big step in the legitimization of the vernacular, and it would not have been possible without Alfred's free approach to the Psalter (138).

The aim and use of Ælfric's translation of Genesis is unknown; Æthelweard may have wanted it for himself (though his Latin was strong) or for his dependants. Gatch (“The Office in Late Anglo-Saxon Monasticism”) argues that the Catholic Homilies and Lives of Saints may be adaptations for pious laymen, and the same may be true of Ælfric's Old Testament translations. In any case, he wished for interpretation to retain its locus in Church institutions (139).

Why did Ælfric break his promise to stop translating? Skeat concluded it was apparently in Ælfric's character to change his mind; Nichols (English Studies 49 [1968]) refers it to a rhetorical commonplace. Wilcox's reading is the most plausible: judging by cross-references in Ælfric's letter to Sigeweard, he came to consider close translation as undertaken in his Genesis too risky, since it represents Scripture directly; his later works are much freer and more interpretive, embracing the instructional function of translation-in-the-broader-sense. In Wilcox's words, Ælfric thought of his own oeuvre as “a coherent body of reliable vernacular orthodoxy”; the less literal approach allowed for greater interpretive control and thus greater licence to translate (139–40). The letter to Sigeweard explains that works trump words, but words can be useful in teaching and edification; one can read this to mean that it is better to teach than to be silent, including the interpretation of Scripture (140–1). This amounts to an admission that his initial position was mistaken: there is no such thing as a naked text, and the author's presence might as well be used to exert interpretive control (141). The relationship between original and translation remains paradoxical, especially when it comes to Scripture: the source is always more authoritative, but (in certain settings) the translation is the only thing from which meaning may be derived (141–3).

[4: Ælfric and the Rhetoric of Translation] Takes Ælfric at his word when he claims the Lives of Saints were written for the laity (144 and fn 1). Notes his use of a plain style, following the sermo humilis aim pursued by Latin ecclesiastics [now cf. Stephenson's comparison of Ælfric's plain style with the hermeneutic Latin of the Benedictine reformers, PSL] (145).

Ælfric's Latin prefaces were probably aimed primarily at “his ecclesiastical superiors”, the vernacular prefaces at lay patrons, though the use of two prefaces per text also accommodates clerics with varying degrees of Latin proficiency (145). Stanton draws attention to an ambiguity in CH2Lat, which either attributes simplicity of style to Old English or asserts that Ælfric has sought out plain words within the English language (145–6).

Ælfric's inner conflict between evangelization and fear of misinterpretation are visible in all the prefaces, and these conflicts may explain his broken promises about ceasing translating. But rhetoric plays a role here: specifically, Ælfric's use of rhetorical formulae may be read as a comment on his concerns about the tensions inherent in translation [this point is explained in subsequent paragraphs, PSL] (146).

Formal rhetoric was known in ASE not directly but through Cassiodorus, Isidore, and Martianus Capella, with a patristic take in Augustine's De doctrina christiana, a text it seems Ælfric knew, and Bede certainly knew. Alcuin used Cicero, while grammar instruction used early medieval rhetorical works by Priscian and Donatus (147). Alcuin's Dialogus de rhetorica was probably known in ASE: by Alfred['s circle], and Ælfric's terminology likewise corresponds to Alcuin's (148). A comparison of the terminology suggests Ælfric was hoping to refashion the Alcuinian ideals of clarity of style in a vernacular setting, abandoning the term latinitas while retaining apertus and pairing it with simplex and purus; apertus had been used by Augustine about biblical style (sermo humilis), and simplex was used with similar connotations (148–52). Using the language of consuetudo is another patristic ideal (152–3). Ælfric takes these concepts from the rhetorical and patristic traditions, where they had typically been used of the Latin style of Scripture, and applies them to the vernacular style of his own works, i.e. non-Scripture (153).

Augustine claimed all rhetorical figures could be found in the Bible, where in fact they originated; this made them divinely sanctioned. Cicero had distinguished three registers for different levels of subject matter, but Augustine saw all Christian oratory as high in subject matter; the three levels instead were linked to immediate aim and occasion. The Bible's lowly style embodied the humility required for acceptance of the Christian message (154–5). Ælfric recast these principles in a vernacular form (145–6).

Ælfric's translator's anxiety may be explained by concerns about the status of English as compared to that of Latin, as well as concerns about the translation incorporating too much originality and/or taking on primary status. In his Genesis and LS prefaces, he vows to stop translating, but he fails to keep these vows. While other scholars have attributed this pattern to caution, concerns about censure, or inconsistency, Nichols attributes it to the rhetorical tradition: Ælfric asserts he will no longer translate, i.e., we should understand, without commentary; his other assertion is to stop translating the Gospels and gospel tracts, and indeed he turns to the saints after this (156–7). Nichols doesn't explain the tone of disavowal (using durran) upon completing the Catholic Homilies (158). The LSLat preface invokes the image of pearls before swine. By using rhetorical principles in all his prefaces, Ælfric acknowledges that a translated text has the power to supplant its original. [Stanton does not come to a more direct assertion, but his point seems to be that Nichols is wrong to deny the concern behind Ælfric's words precisely because he uses rhetorical devices. Exactly how that works? PSL] (158–60).

Of his nonscriptural Latin sources, Ælfric does not hesitate to condemn prolixity. thereby suggesting the vernacular could improve on its model (160). When in the second half of his career Ælfric began to write in rhythmic prose, he created a hybrid between oral and written culture (oral effects in a written milieu) that departs from the naked narrative just as his later “translations” do (160–3). In his Life of Edmund, for instance, Ælfric omitted the high style of his source and added in aural effects meant for oral performance (163–6). What follows is a discussion of where rhythmic prose stands between sermo humilis and rhetorical style, and Stanton comes to the somewhat strained conclusion that Ælfric's rhythmic prose is close to natural style, and remarkable for being religious vernacular prose, not poetry, to begin with (166–71).

author: Nichols, Ann Eljenholm
title: Ælfric’s Prefaces: Rhetoric and Genre
abstract:
Argues that historians and biographers alike have been mistaken to take Ælfric’s prefaces at face value, specifically in the matter of translation, a practice in which he regularly engaged despite several expressions of disapproval. Referring to Ernst Robert Curtius, Nichols asserts that Ælfric’s aversion to translation is rhetorical (215). After listing several “psychological” readings to do with modesty and fear of heresy, Nichols claims that these readings are useless since they take as accurate fact that which is a combination of two rhetorical figures: the modesty formula and the credentials formula: the former provides the author with a humble persona, while the latter adduces external authority authorizing the work at hand (216–17). Nichols believes that non-formulaic assertions in prefaces are more reliable sources of authorial deliberations, as in the OE preface to CH I, where he makes clear he considers it his god-given duty to teach. These sentiments confirm non-rhetorically the credentials topos expressed rhetorically in the formulae (217–18).

Ælfric’s three vows to stop translating are expressions of the modesty topos. In the Preface to Genesis, however, his point about translation is that bare translation is not enough but should be accompanied by exegesis; “there is nothing in the preface indicating that he thinks translation does more harm than good” (at 221). Ælfric’s apparent self-contradictions may be explained in part by genre: his LS contain more hagiography than homily, so he is right at the end of his CH to state he will translate no more homilies. His claim in his letter to Sigeweard to have translated a range of OT texts is accurate if we understood his reference to refer to paraphrase, since only his Genesis is strict translation (222–3). (Here, the author also claims Ælfric uses awendan for translation or paraphrase, gesettan for paraphrase (223).

author: Stephenson, Rebecca
title: The Politics of Language: Byrhtferth, Ælfric, and the Multilingual Identity of the Benedictine Reform
abstract:
[4: The Politics of Ælfric’s Prefaces] Although Ælfric was reformed, he did not follow the trend of writing in inaccessible, hermeneutic Latin. Instead, his Latin and English alike are composed “puris et apertis verbis”; yet he does not distance himself from the Winchester school in other ways (135–6). His avoidance of hermeneutic Latin is striking in view of the patronate of Æthelweard and Æthelmær, powerful courtiers, the first of whom composed a chronicle in hermeneutic Latin (137–8). In his prefaces, Ælfric claims to write in English for preliterate youth, illiterate laymen, and lay patrons who requested translations. He rarely mentions secular clerics and Benedictine monks as audiences (138). The omission of the former group is striking in light of claims by contemporary authors that their Latin was poor, compared against their requirement to read. Both groups together made up the larger part of the literate population, so it is odd they are hardly mentioned as audiences of his vernacular writings. This reflects not reality but Ælfric’s authorial positioning, which is based on the subjugation of secular clerics to monastic priests (138–9). “Ælfric tends to be very specific when he names his imagined audience for each work. The Catholic Homilies are intended to be read in church to the faithful; the Grammar is written for the young; Genesis is translated at the behest of his patrons, Æthelweard and Æthelmær; Lives of Saints is said to be beneficial for the faithful, but is directly addressed to his secular patrons; and the Admonitio ad filium spiritualem is appropriate for Benedictine monks and nuns. It is interesting that Ælfric never mentions the secular clerics as a potential audience for any of his homilies, translations, or pedagogical works” (139–40; 140n24 points out that some of his pastoral letters were addressed to the secular clergy).

He does, however, refer to the secular clergy and their lack of learning, most notably in his Preface to Genesis. Not only does he bring up the mass-priest who spread the letter of the Old Testament without explaining its spiritual significance, he also takes this occasion to explain that such information leads to illiterate priests demanding wives, whereas the reform sought to abolish marriage within the priesthood (140–2). On the whole, Ælfric’s characterization of the early world emphasizes sexual practices that were not accepted in Anglo-Saxon times, such as incest and polygamy, while shunning more loaded questions such as divorce or the fact that Old Testament priests could marry (142–3). Ælfric identifies the secular and the monastic clergy as teachers, but although they would [Stephenson argues] have needed his writings before anything else, and would have had more access to them than the laity, he does not mention them as an audience. Instead, he emphasizes the final audience of the faithful to whom the texts are read, not the priests who would read them off (143). The “mass communication” Wilcox has reconstructed for the Catholic Homilies — the same texts read at the same time in all the churches and monasteries of the country — entails an impressive level of control by monks of pastoral speech, an “open colonization of the pastoral space that should be inhabited by clerics” (144–5).

In the preface to his Grammar, Ælfric expresses a fear of infantilizing himself by association with English, a language intended for the uninitiated, perhaps oblates (148). The Lives of Saints are so long they must have been for private reading, and the saints covered best fit a monastic context, though the prefaces do not identify an audience, instead identifying the lay patrons who persuaded him to produce the work. The implication is that they could not read Latin, but Æthelweard was a fine latinist. Ælfric avoids suggesting that monks could not read Latin, but he happily implies his patron could not, thereby suggesting English was an appropriate language for non-monastic instruction. It seems the lay patron serves as a sort of lightning rod to excuse the use of English, which could — and was, as provenance demonstrates — also read by monks (148–9). There is thus a significant difference between the primary named audience and the primary real audience, and we may safely suppose there were monks who were literate in English, regardless of their Latin proficiency (149–50). “As literate members of the Anglo-Saxon population, Benedictine monks and secular clerics had to have been the largest audience for any of Ælfric’s works, despite his protestations to the contrary” (150).

When writing in English, Ælfric refers to himself as a monk; when in Latin, he refers to his educational pedigree, apparently more relevant to his Latin audiences (150–1). In his preface to CHI, Ælfric claims to take this educational role [as Stephenson describes it] upon himself not for its own sake but for corrective reasons: because there is so much anglophone error already available (151–3). He addresses his role as a teacher in his anglophone prefaces only, suggesting that he is not justifying this role to his monastic audiences but interfacing with learners, constructing his own role while priming students on theirs (154). In his English preface to the Grammar, he asserts that the old are to teach as a way of maintaining [whose? Ælfric’s wording suggests society’s; PSL] faith (154–5).

[5: Unravelling the Hermeneutic Style] Whereas most reformers wrote difficult Latin even if their English was accessible, Ælfric used a plain style in both languages (158–9). The contrast has caused scholars to overlook the complex syntax of Ælfric[’s Latin, PSL]: although he avoids unusual vocabulary, he unpacks the highly compressed syntax of hermeneutic Latin (159). Stephenson suspects a difference in purpose behind this difference in style: many hermeneutic texts celebrated important events, but Ælfric’s reworkings of such texts served as intermediaries between the original and his English translations. The survival of such intermediaries gives us an important insight into Ælfric’s view of what was required to render these works into English (159–60).

This chapter studies Ælfric’s Vita S. Æthelwoldi, the only one of seven of his Latin saints’ lives in Paris, BNF Lat. 362 of which no vernacular version survives (169–1). It shows how Ælfric retained the core of his source including its case endings, but excised much of what is unnecessary to convey the meaning, difficult, or simply not to his taste. His epitome also implements a precision and standardization of religious terms above all, a tendency found also in English in the so-called “Winchester words”. Stephenson associates this precision with Ælfric’s vernacular style and with his concept of relaying the “naced gerecednis” only (160–71). She then describes how Ælfric excises interpretation from the Vita Æthelwoldi, resequences the material, omits miracles and the emphasis on the saint’s piety, and explains what may not be obvious to a nonmonastic audience (171–81).

Ælfric makes clear he ensures the range of vernacular sources remains limited: he selects only such materials as may safely be delivered up to the “simple” (181–2). In this context, Ælfric’s supposed broken promises are briefly mentioned; in footnote 95 on p. 182, Stephenson states she differs from Stanton’s take in that he explains each exception to his resolution contextually, while she holds that practice and rhetoric repeatedly drift apart (182). The chapter closes with a brief discussion of Ælfric’s understanding that grammar and syntax contain sacred information (185–6), followed by the observation that the corpus produced by Ælfric obviated the need to access many Latin texts directly, despite the author’s insistence that vernacular interpretation was dangerous (186). “Ultimately, Ælfric’s English-language works present a paradox. They greatly expand the use and purview of English, but at the same time limit what is disseminated in that language. . . . As much as the reformers valued their Latin-language compositions, particularly those in the hermeneutic style, they needed Ælfric and his English-language homilies to disseminate the message more broadly in order to create the larger societal reforms they envisioned” (187).

author: Cubitt, Catherine
title: Ælfric’s Lay Patrons
series: Brill’s Companions to the Christian Tradition
abstract:
A useful study of Ælfric’s patrons’ careers, Æthelweard and Æthelmær’s involvement with King Æthelred, etc. Of particular interest is Cubitt’s lining up of significant events in the careers of Æthelred, Æthelweard and Æthelmær, and Ælfric: Æthelweard and son rose to positions of influence on the king following Æthelred’s 993 recognition that religious change was needed to ward off the harm that had come to his kingdom. Benedictine reformers were then briefly in vogue at court, and it is around this time that Ælfric produced his Catholic Homilies and, from 993 onwards, his Lives of Saints, Genesis, and Joshua, at Æthelweard’s request. In his letter to Sigeweard, Ælfric explains that translation serves as instructions to defend the country against invasion (178). Points out that Ælfric becomes more political once Wulfmær is away from court. In part he refers to English affairs directly, in part he draws out biblical passages, such as that in Maccabees in which the king attempts to steal the temple treasures: this cannot but be political at a time when the crown puts pressure on the Church to give up its lands. The postscript to Maccabees is very direct, making clear monks should not wage war and that which belongs to the Church should not be redirected for political ends (179). There is much attention to counsel and wicked counsellors (180). The royal penance of David and Theodosius mirrors that of Æthelred (180–1). Ælfric’s Wyrdwriteras (ÆHom 23) agrees with Æthelred’s Chronicon in its emphasis on ealdormen in warfare. The latter text agrees with Ælfric’s Prayer of Moses in depicting Edgar’s reign as a prosperous age. Æthelweard and Æthelmær’s support for the monastic reform likewise shows them in agreement with Ælfric (181), whose political remarks affected them directly (181–2).

Æthelweard and Æthelmær seem to have been pious laymen; like Leofric of Mercia, they may have incorporated elements of monastic service into their lives. Such combined activities would have incurred tensions given monastic teachings on warfare and sexuality; prominent laymen like Harold Godwinson therefore sought the advice of clergymen. Æthelweard and Æthelmær’s patronage of Ælfric should be seen in this light (183–4).

A little before the coming of the reformed Benedictine monasteries, the thegnly or collegiate church made its appearance in England. These local churches supported directly by the thegn on whose estate they stood, as opposed to minster churches with graveyards which were supported through the thegn’s tithes. These local churches undermined the monopoly of minster churches. When the Benedictine houses made their appearance, however, they upset the balance of power once more, absorbing land on which stood both old and new/local churches along with their relics, while severing familial power through their emphasis on virginity. The result was a mixed landscape (184–5). The possession of a church was included in the definition of the thegnly status [which served to stimulate churchplanting]. Ælfric’s contacts “Sigeweard, Sigefyrth, and Wulfgeat may have belonged to a middle stratum of thegns, . . . rather wealthy local notables, possibly holding a minor royal office” (186). Although not powerful themselves, they may have met the powerful at shire and hundred meetings and been their clients, and they were the owners of the local churches and their trappings (187). This made them important for the prosperity of the parish churches, and Ælfric’s moral teachings were probably aimed at them. Judging by Ælfric’s writings, they made persistent demands on him, while he needed them also as donors and participants in the sale and exchange of land for the benefit of the [religious] community (188–9). Cubitt briefly speculates about the supply of vernacular texts and the market for copying (189–90). “Ælfric’s exposition of the sequence of books in the Old and New Testament was perhaps particularly valuable for those whose knowledge of the Scriptures was obtained by hearing extracts read out in the course of the liturgical year” (190). Points out that Ælfric’s duties as abbot in Eynsham would have involved far more (political) engagement with the laity than his work at Cerne. His writings on the three estates reflect this fact as well as the increased demand for guidance in the face of the heightened Viking threat (191–2).

author: Gatch, M. McC.
title: The Office in Late Anglo-Saxon Monasticism
publication: Learning and Literature in Anglo-Saxon England: Studies Presented to Peter Clemoes in the Occasion of his Sixty-Fifth Birthday
abstract:
Argues that Ælfric's Old Testament writings must be understood against the divine office.

Eric John has emphasized that the English Benedictine Reform aimed to sever the religious life from family life. It also brought institutions that had been managed by secular clergy under the auspices of regular clergy: monks took possession of the sees (342–3). Although there were political ramifications, the monks affected would have been more concerned with the liturgical body of the Regularis concordia, not its political proem (343–4). The history of the office is complicated: with the fourth-century rise of monasticism, daily prayers became associated with its Psalter recitation and dissociated from the laity; Scriptural readings were later added to the Night Office in particular, which came to strive to read all Scripture as well as a selection of vitae and exegesis over the course of a year. This accretion to Matins severed it definitively from the laity but also invited a mitigation of the text-heavy nature of the Night Office by either abbreviating the readings or outsourcing some of them to settings outside the Office (344–5). The introduction of the breviary was a later attempt to standardize and spread the Office through the Church (345). Prior to the breviary, the nature of the office is much harder to reconstruct, particularly before the Council of Winchester c. 970; for the period from 970 to the Conquest, however, there is an abundance of material (345–6).

It is unknown what books would have been used for the Office prior to the breviary; they may have been as many as ten volumes, and no such set survives because obsolete liturgical manuscripts were not typically preserved. The Benedictine Rule (for regular clergy) and the Rule of Chrodegang (for secular clergy) are a first set of sources on liturgy, but observances of these rules varied; more relevant are the specific customs as laid out in ordines or consuetudines. From Anglo-Saxon England, only the Regularis concordia and Ælfric's Eynsham Customary, generally known as the Letter to the monks of Eynsham, survive (346–8).

The Eynsham Customary has three parts: (1) a letter to the members of the newly established monastery; (2) a customary, largely an abbreviation of the Regularis concordia but with additions from Amalarius and liturgical sources; (3) finer points of monastic observance, including the lectionary and the responsiones for Matins, "[because you brethren have asked]". The central portion, i.e. the consuetudo, is important for the present question because it witnesses monastic practices from the perspective of an Æthelwold alumnus, bears witness to simplification of the Regularis concordia, and contains interpretative work based on a specific version of Amalarius that seems to have been used in ASE. The third and final part of the document is perhaps even more valuable, since it offers unique supplements to the Concordia (348–9).

There is some evidence of liturgical books: two manuscripts survive that each contain a collectar (book gathering together the prayers for the Office) along with a capitulary (series of short lessons read at the Offices by the chief officer). The surviving MSS contain the New Hymnal and one of them contains the monastic canticles, chants from OT texts that were sung in Matins on Sundays and feast days. These collections contain much of what would later be a breviary, but not all; they were intended for the use of the chief officer at any Day Hour responsible for saying the Chapter and Collect, but other tasks required other books; even so, the AS collectars additionally contain psalter, hymnal, and calendar for context (349–50).

A substantial body of vernacular literature related to the Night Office (the Rule, hymns, canticles) exists from ASE, prompting questions about Latin literacy and the role of the laity in the Divine Office (351–2).

The third and last part of the Eynsham Customary outlines the lectionary for the Night Office. The system descends from the dominant Ordo Romanus 13a and adds in responsiones to be sung along with the readings, which J. R. Hall has used to reconstruct the antiphonary that may have been used by reformers (352).

Ælfric wrote his OT compositions in order to open up monastic devotion to a wider public, the same of his other vernacular works [reference here to Gatch, Preaching and Theology].

Scriptural readings were especially prominent in the three Nocturns of the Night Office; Gatch summarizes their structure. For the annual reading-through of Scripture, Ordo Romanus 13a would have linked

  • the Heptateuch to the period from Septuagesima through the fourth week of Lent;
  • Jeremiah and Lamentations to the period from Passion Sunday to the eve of Easter;
  • Acts, canonical epistles, Apocalypse to the period from Easter to the Octave of Pentecost;
  • Kings and Chronicles to the period from the Octave of Pentecost to early August;
  • the Wisdom books to August
  • Job, Tobit, Judith, Esther, and at least I–II Esdras to September;
  • Maccabees to October;
  • Ezekiel, Daniel, minor prophets to November;
  • Isaiah to Advent;
  • (specified readings for three saints' days and other feast days in the Christmas season);
  • Pauline epistles to the period from the Sunday following the Octave of Epiphany to Septuagesima.

(Ælfric specifies the reading schedule for Eynsham in §§70–77 of his Letter to the Monks of Eynsham: ed. Jones.)

Psalms and gospels were covered elsewhere (353–4). Following Hall, Gatch sums up Ælfric's deviations from this system in the list provided in the final part of his Customary (CCCC 265, pp. 57–63) (354–5). Notably, his deviations are evidence for the fact that the project of reading all through Scripture in a year was failing through accretion; early choir breviaries indicate some of the continuity was outsourced to outside the Offices. Ælfric himself admits that what did not fit in the Offices was read in the refectory: "et sciendum quod tota bibliotheca debet legi in circulo anni in ecclesia, sed quia nos pigri serui sumus et segnes legimus in refectorio quicquid de ea in ecclesia omittimus" (qtd. at 355). The laity would not normally have been present when the Offices were read in church, but they had absolutely no access to the refectory (355).

Catholic Homilies I is almost exclusively based on gospel pericopes adapted from the homiliary for the Night Office (see Smetana, "Paul the Deacon's Patristic Anthology"). In Catholic Homilies II, he increases the number of Sundays covered but also adds alternative texts for major Sundays. He here covers Exodus and Joshua, associated with mid-Lent in the Night Office (Gatch takes this to be the reference of the phrase "æt godes ðenungum"); though his own lectionary does not mention Joshua here, many responsiones do indeed contain material on Joshua (357–8). This combination may be regarded a trace of the principle of reading all of the Heptateuch in the Lent season; it also has a strong emphasis on tropology and allegory (358). The same is true of the Lives of Saints text on Exodus, likewise assigned to mid-Lent Sunday (ÆLS (Prayer of Moses)) (358–9). De populo Israhel covers Exodus and Numbers, and it refers to and summarizes the Exodus sententia of the Catholic Homilies 2 Exodus/Joshua item, then picks up where it had left off. "The entire mid-Lent group of Ælfric's sermons, which has been very cursorily reviewed here, grew, one supposes, from an effort to appropriate material from the monks' cursus of readings in the Night Office or the refectory for public teaching. . . . All this material is in sermon form" (359).

ÆCHom II, 30 is rubricated "Dominica I in mense Septembri quando legitur Iob"; this reference is to a Scriptural reading not in Mass but in the Nocturns (359).

author: Smetana, Cyril L.
title: Ælfric and the Early Medieval Homiliary
abstract:
Notes that a great number of discussions in both series of the Catholic Homilies match items in Paul the Deacon’s homiliary, and discusses each of Ælfric’s items in these works with regard to the sources identified by Förster and with juxtapositions of passages from Paul the Deacon where relevant. Also reproduces the reconstructed original table of contents produced by Wiegand. NB:

  • "Comparison with Wiegand's reconstruction of PD shows that Aelfric did not use any of the 35 sermons of Leo or the 53 sermons of Maximus. This is noteworthy because both Leo, and Maximus, the great fifth-century 'Volksprediger,' offer topical, brief and orthodox sermons which would seem to be much more suited to Aelfric's purpose than the long, involved allegorical exegesis of the materials which he used. Aelfric apparently, then, did not have these homilists in his source- book" (203; but now see Hill).

author: Kintisch, Eli
title: The Lost Norse
abstract:
Reports on a paradigm shift from the assumption that the Greenland Norse failed to adapt to the belief that they did adapt but failed anyway. Evidence cited is the confirmation that an ever increasing part of their diet was marine; evidence of the production and trade in objects made of walrus tusks; and responsible land management, including fallowing. A roughening climate from the thirteenth century onwards not only made travel to Europe difficult; an increase in storminess would also have made it harder to hunt walrus offshore, as the author assumes the Norse did, as opposed to the fjord seal hunts of the Inuit. Russian and African tusks flooded the market for ivory about 1400. Agriculture yielded less in a deteriorating climate, although there is evidence of an intensification of fertilization and irrigation over time.

The new understanding of Norse Greenland includes the hypothesis that Iceland and Greenland were originally settled not for land, but for ivory.

Radiocarbon dating suggests that remote, smaller settlements were abandoned about 1250 as the climate worsened, sometimes to be relocated to directly around the powerful estates, which would have had to intensify wintering activities like shelter and fodder production to maintain the diet to which the Norse were accustomed. Smaller farms gave up cattle in favour of a diet of caribou and seal, but not the large estates, which helps explain the conglomeration at this time. At any rate the Eastern Settlement shows signs of gradual decline, not cataclysm. This suggests a peaceful migration back to Iceland and Europe.

[The researchers cited most directly are McGovern, who ascribes to this new reading, and Fitzhugh, who disputes ivory as the reason for the settlement.]

author: Besserman, L.L.
title: A Note on the Source of Ælfric’s Homily on the Book of Job
abstract: Identifies Gregory’s Moralia in Iob as the source for a good number of the commentary sections in Ælfric’s homily on Job (CH II, 30/35). In view of loose rendering in some cases, hypothesizes use from memory and restricted by space.

author: Langan, John, S.J.
title: The Elements of St. Augustine’s Just War Theory
abstract:
Analyzes Augustine’s Just War Theory with particular attention to his Contra Faustum.

Augustine identifies three elements in warfare: action, agent, and authority. An action may be reprehensible in itself but be sanctioned by divine authority, as in the case of Isaac’s near-sacrifice (20–1). Augustine considers human destructive passions and the human injustice revealed in war its real evil, not the loss of life. This sets him apart from Hobbes, who values peace regardless of the morals of the humans who sustain it: in Augustine’s view, when injustice occurs, just men must wage war to end it while Hobbes would have them reach or maintain an agreement with those whom Augustine considers unjust. Augustine’s just are inspired by authority, Hobbes’s rational individuals by reason. Taken to its logical conclusion, as Augustine does take it, this view leads him to show himself agnostic as to the actions or inactions of men at war, as one man’s victory is another’s undoing, and God’s purpose with man’s trials is hidden. This view lifts the burden of ethical decision-making from humans, for two reasons: it leaves us unable to tell what is ultimately just, and it reduces the justness of violence to a search for authorization; one cannot be held responsible for obedience to a wicked superior. The primary point of Old Testament history is to show that worldly kingdoms, unlike the heavenly kingdom, can be taken away (20–3).

Augustine’s Just War Theory may be divided into the following elements:

  1. War as a punitive/corrective, not a defensive undertaking;
  2. The evil of war as residing in individual moral attitudes, not the immorality of actions or consequences;
  3. A search for authorization of violence, whether human or divine;
  4. A split epistemology consisting of (a) certainty that spiritual goods are superior and (b) uncertainty about the desirability of non-spiritual goods and their connection with spiritual goods;
  5. A tendency to interpret biblical norms as inner attitudes rather than external actions
  6. A passive attitude in the face of the authorities;
  7. An appeal to New Testament sources for the justification of military service;
  8. Peace, not discussed in the Contra Faustum.

In response to the claim that Chrisianity (e.g. turning the other cheek) cannot be adapted to state government, Augustine responds that responding to the loss of temporal goods with patience demonstrates how much more valuable heavenly goods are, while serving as a corrective to others; but he considers this principle an instrument to be used in situations where it is expected to be effective rather than an end in itself to be practised always. The same corrective ends may also justify “kindly harshness,” however. Violence is thus not in itself an evil, and there is no moral difference between kindness and violence as long as they serve the same end of correcting the internal disposition of individuals. Langan points out that an important difference between Augustine’s view and modern political thought is that the latter is informed by the relativism of pluriform thought and is thus more likely to justify violence for purposes of defending freedoms and communities, not restoring an ethical balance of dispositions and desires to the universe (24–5). In Letter 189 to Boniface, Augustine asserts that one can indeed please God through warfare; he likens physical warfare to spiritual warfare through prayer, proclaims warfare necessary in the service of peace, and concludes that killing one’s enemies is thus a matter of necessity not choice (25–6). In Augustine’s early De libero arbitrio, his friend Evodius asks how one can be certain that men fighting in defence of what is theirs are not also driven by [wrongful] passion to preserve what is theirs; here, Augustine responds that a law of defence and protection cannot be informed by [wrongful] passions (26). However, goods that can be taken away are inferior by definition, and though human laws permit violence in their defence, divine laws do not. Accordingly, Augustine defends the Stoic “retreat to the inner citadel,” which justifies violence only to defend that which is within our control, i.e. virtues and attributes of the soul; violence may not be used against a burglar. Hobbes argues the contrary (26–7).

In De civitate Dei likewise, Augustine calls wars against the unjust a cause for lament, not in terms of the violence done but because they were necessitated by the wrongdoing of the unjust, and it is that wrongdoing that wants lamenting. War is fought in the service of peace, and peace is a good in its own right, but the justice of each peace is relative to the justice of those who pursue it. Earthly peace is sought by the inhabitants of the city of men; spiritual individuals seek a heavenly peace (28–9).

Augustine recognizes peace on micro- as well as macro-levels: war can only exist if there are natures to wage it, and those natures can only exist by internal order, i.e. peace (29).

Augustine disincentivizes revolutionary change to bring about a better society when he claims that wicked regimes are hurtful mostly to the wicked rulers, who destroy their own souls in the process, but do no harm to the just, to whom all injustices are merely tests of their virtue. There is thus no incentive to improve the quality of the peace; indeed, the desire for a better earthly peace conflicts with the desire for heavenly peace with which all Christians should concern themselves (30).

When directly commanded by worldly rulers to go against divine instructions, the Christian’s duty is to engage in passive obedience, never active resistance; a citizen is not to question a ruler’s military decisions but should support them through his taxes. Augustine also does not make special accommodations for the immunity of noncombatants. This has been variously but conjecturally explained (31–2). Langan instead proposes two other readings. Firstly, since Augustine uses Old Testament warfare as his model, noncombatant immunity would go well beyond his exemplars. Secondly, Augustine is more concerned with virtue ethics than with rules and principles such as the treatment of noncombatants; a virtuous population would deal virtuously with whomever they encounter (32).

Langan now summarizes Aquinas’s position: he asserts a war is just if the sovereign has authority; the enemy bears guilt; and the war is waged for good and against evil. In his treatment of the subject, Aquinas cites Augustine extensively and repeats most elements of his theory. Aquinas held that clergymen should not fight, but that warfare is nevertheless a necessary function of society; fighting in a just war is not sinful. At this point, Aquinas takes a more active and differentiated view on social order than Augustine provided (32–3).

The remainder of the article reflects on the relevance of Augustine’s views to contemporary thought (33–7).

author: Wright, Charles D.
title: Vercelli Homilies XI–XIII and the Anglo-Saxon Benedictine Reform: Tailored Sources and Implied Audiences
publication: Preacher, Sermon and Audience in the Middle Ages
abstract:
Starts by pointing out exactly how little we know about the intended audiences of anonymous homilies (203–4). Even with Ælfric and Wulfstan, who identify some of their intended audiences, there is considerable confusion and fluidity between audience groups, but at least there are definite clues (204–6). Gatch has called the Blickling audience unknowable, but he has also suggested an integrated approach to the collection and a hunt for its sources might get us closer. Wright’s essay sets out to attempt this for the Rogationtide series Vercelli XI, XII, XIII (206–7).

Vercelli homilies XI–XIV seem from their mise-en-page to share the same exemplar; but only the first three seem to share the same author (207–9). These three were probably composed for a clerical audience: there is mention of teaching others, and the suggestion that the audience members themselves will carry relics; but laymen may well have been in the congregation as well on as important an occasion as Rogationtide (209–11). Secular and regular clergymen cannot easily be distinguished by their duties for this period, but they did differ in institutional and spiritual matters. It is the omission of content against the possession of personal property that suggests these three texts were written for the secular clergy (211–12). For instance, Vercelli XII translates a list of monastic virtues but excises the ones that touch on private property (212–17). The other two texts continue this tendency (217–22). The complaint of despoliation in Vercelli XI may be read as a complaint against the royally-backed expulsion of secular clerics carried out as part of the Benedictine Reform (222–5).

author: Swan, Mary
title: Constructing Preacher and Audience in Old English Homilies
abstract: Mostly interested in the use of pronouns and audience references that situates the preacher–audience dynamic rhetorically. Assumes homilies were closely intertwined with the liturgy inasmuch “they are either performed during a liturgical celebration, or are read or spoken outside a liturgical context, but with fundamental structural and rhetorical anchors to that context” (178).

author: Godden, M[alcolm] R.
title: The Development of Ælfric’s Second Series of Catholic Homilies
abstract:
Ælfric claims his Second Series contains 40 homilies; the only surviving complete MS contains 45 items by Thorpe’s count. Dietrich has argued the surviving MS represents a later redaction of Ælfric’s with additions to the original; Sisam has countered Ælfric meant items for forty occasions (209). This is implausible, as Ælfric speaks of feowertig cwydda; moreover, Thorpe misassigned two items, so the number of occasions is 38.Thorpe’s xxxi and xxxii should be one item (210). Godden points out that manuscript layout (notably the size of initials) suggests a number of Thorpe’s separate items should be understood as two-part homilies for a total of 11 such two-part items, combining with the remaining 29 separate items to total 40 (210–12).

Godden shows that some two-part homilies must have resulted from Ælfric’s decision to add to homilies he had written earlier, and this seems to be the case for many; a few were clearly intended to be a unit from the outset. Godden believes no additions were made after the series was first issued: the First Series texts on St Andrew have been shown to have been combined before that series was issued, and at least one Second Series combination shows the same structure, while other manuscripts show no trace of uncombined versions of any dual items. The plain prose style of several items suggests they were written before Ælfric adopted his metrical style (212–14).

Two-part items in the First Series are fewer and more tightly linked. The disjointed nature of items in the Second Series may be explained by haste (cited by Ælfric in his Latin preface), but his later revisions do not address the issue. More likely, Ælfric may have been moving away from his original plan of having his homilies read, presumably verbatim, to lay congregations over the course of the year; his Second Series offers the preacher more flexibility. There are five items at the end that could be preached at any time, and there are multiple options for Easter Day and Rogation Tuesday. The disjointed nature of the two-part items left preachers freedom to use either or both parts (215–16).

The Second Series is addressed more at clergymen in other ways, too: two notes appear to be added specifically for them, and there is an increase in Latin scriptural quotations (Thorpe?) item xli is concerned with the duties of the clergy and therefore presumably meant for clerical audiences. Ælfric’s revisions of the Second Series likewise suggest clerical audiences: he apologizes to the learned, authorizes certain interpretations, notes scriptural variants, and seems in two places to have added Latin quotations for originally vernacular scriptural quotations, a move towards Latin continued in his post-Catholic homilies. In one place, he avoid a discussion because it is too difficult for his audience, but later cancels this remark and discusses it anyway, as though he has come to envision a more sophisticated audience. “It would appear, then, that in his First Series Aelfric is speaking directly to the lay congregation and using the preacher only as his voice, whereas the Second Series shows the beginnings of a concern with providing a collection of homiletic material which preachers are to select from and adapt in various ways for their own listeners, and probably to study for their own benefit too” (216).

author: Diamond, Jared
title: Collapse: How Societies Choose to Fail or Succeed
abstract:
[This book rationalizes, simplifies, and teleologizes particularly every part of history in ch. 6, but Diamond is the natural popular starting-point for a discussion of the demise of the Greenland Norse, and provides an impressively broad picture of Greenland in chs. 7–8. Read in conjunction with at least Berglund, Amorosi, and McGovern.]

[6: The Viking Prelude and Fugues (178–210)] Having characterized Viking expansion as a phenomenon that vanished as suddenly as it had appeared, Diamond seeks to explain the phenomenon. He describes the degrees to which each of Orkney, Shetland, the Faroes, Iceland, Greenland, and Vinland were affected by the four factors of

  1. Distance from Europe and the colonizing motherland;
  2. Resistance from indigenous populations;
  3. Agricultural potential; and
  4. ecological fragility.

Iceland, for instance, was closer to Norway than Greenland and Vinland, though not as close as Orkney, Shetland, and the Faroes; it had no pre-existing population to speak of to worry about; but it suffered from a short growing season and an especially fragile ecology. The way Diamond characterizes it, Iceland’s settlers did not realize this last point until it became clear that the topsoil was not regenerating, at which point they took systematic measures to protect the environment, e.g. by giving up pigs and abandoning the highlands [I wouldn’t be surprised if this is an instance of Diamond rationalizing the archaeological evidence, PSL].

Diamond examines all the cultures in his book in terms of five criteria:

  1. Self-inflicted environmental damage;
  2. Climate change
  3. Hostilities with other societies;
  4. Friendly trading relations with other societies; and
  5. Cultural attitudes.

[The criterion of climate change may seem to be at odds with the book’s subtitle, which suggests all societies have themselves to blame for their demise, but Diamond is interested in responses to climate change as much as its more or less unassailable realities, PSL.]

All except hostilities played a role in Iceland’s history; initial cultural attitudes (e.g. pigfarming) were quickly adapted to the particularly sensitive needs of the Icelandic environment.

Vinland, although agriculturally the richest of Norse North Atlantic colonies, was soon abandoned; Eiríks saga rauða asserts that this was because of hostile relations with the indigenous population, but archaeology shows they continued to visit Labrador. Other factors in Vinland’s failure were the inability of motherland Greenland, let alone Europe, to support it, so that its tiny population was no match for Native Americans.

[7: Norse Greenland’s Flowering (211–47)] Greenland’s climate today is cool, but with great local and annual variations. The two fjord systems inhabited by the Norse Greenlanders are indeed green and sheltered; but any fjord’s climate depends on how many glaciers feed into it and how sheltered it is from Arctic spray. Past climate is determined from written records; pollen sediments in lakes and bogs; and ice core records. The last of these shows that climate ameliorations accompanied Native American migrations into the region while deteriorations accompanied their retreat, and similar patterns were observed in the twentieth century. Such a retreat also preceded the Norse arrival, which itself took place at a time of amelioration, so the Icelanders found their fjord systems mild but uninhabited, though the MWP meant native populations would soon be back, and the LIA would eventually make Norse life hard while Inuit populations survived since — as in the twentieth-century cool period — their culture had prepared them for subsistence on ringed seals.

The Norse Greenlanders (an estimated 5000 of them between the two settlements) started out with the traditional Norwegian mix of livestock, but pigs were soon abandoned or reduced in numbers given that they destroyed the fragile soils; ducks and geese are not in evidence at all; cows were labour-intensive and were reduced, but not given up entirely, which Diamond speculates was because of their high status. Sheep and goats, able to graze below snow covers, became the livestock of choice. “In Greenland today, sheep can be kept outdoors for nine months per year (three times as long as cows)” (223). Compared to Iceland, Greenland farmers gradually increased the proportion of goats relative to sheep because only goats could digest the country’s shrubs and trees. Cows were very small and lived in dismal conditions. Meat came at a premium, and so bones were split to extract the marrow far more than anywhere else in the Norse world, and more also than among the Inuit. Diamond goes into detail about the homefield-and-shieling system of hay production and describes the best patches for farming in Greenland as level lowland infields, extensive mid-elevation outfields, south-facing exposures, the presence of streams for irrigation, sheltered from glacial slopes, and near a good harbour fjord (226).

Contemporary records assert that most Greenland Norse never saw wheat, bread, or (barley) beer. They grew flax for linen and linseed oil, but the main non-dairy part of their diet was meat, especially seals and caribou, the latter hunted in the autumn, probably using dogs. The common seal was most easily hunted near the settlements in spring, while migratory seal had to be hunted at the same time of year but at remote coastal outposts. The Norse reliance on migratory seals made them vulnerable to changes in migration or climate patterns (ice). Bone isotope analysis shows that the Eastern Settlement grew its reliance on sea food from 20% to 80%, presumably because the climate had grown worse for hay farming and because the population had outgrown what the herds could sustain. The Western Settlement diet was always more seafood-based than the Eastern. The midden of one poor farm even in the Western settlement had 70% of its animal bones consist of seal bones. Smaller mammals and birds were likewise hunted; whales seem to have been eaten only when stranded. Fish are conspicuously absent (< 0.1% of animal bones found, against 50–95% in Iceland, northern Norway, and Shetland). McGovern writes of one practically fishless midden right next to fish-rich lakes, and Nygaard’s findings are similar. This absence, juxtaposed with the fact that animal bones were thoroughly mined for marrow, remains unexplained; it must be taken on face value, perhaps as the development of a taboo on eating fish.

Diamond now describes in greater detail the degree to which Norse Greenlandic farming was an operation integrated in time (the seasonal labours) and space (hunting and haymaking send Greenlanders from the coast to the outfields). Farms were not self-sufficient; caribou and seal carcasses were transported between coastal and in-fjord locations, and large farms had to lend poor farms cows so the livestock could be rebuilt after tough winters. There was nevertheless a huge difference between the diets of rich and poor farmers: the meat consumed at one poor Western Settlement farm was 85% seal, against 39% for the richest Western Settlement farm. Prominent Churchmen enjoyed the most venison-rich diets (233–4).

The economy thus described had many vulnerabilities. Hay harvests would have been impacted by a short, foggy summer or a wet August; livestock and caribou would have suffered from a long winter; excessive drift ice would have limited access to migratory seals; climate change could affect migration patterns or seal breeding. Modern Greenland has witnessed all these phenomena (234).

The archaeological record shows great violence, and there is evidence of socioeconomic stratification like that in Iceland and Norway. The scarcity of ships sailing between Europe and Greenland meant only low-volume, high-value cargo could be imported and exported: iron, lumber, tar, church objects, and pottery; some honey and salt may have been imported. Exported were skins, wool, and above all exotic animal products: walrus ivory and hide, narwhal tusks, polar bears and hides, and live gyrfalcons. Diamond also emphasizes the cultural and religious imports, which may be said to have cost the Greenlanders their lives.

[8: Norse Greenland’s End (248–76)] The Greenland Norse were faced with a number of developments beyond their control, but their responses to those developments made them responsible to some degree for their demise. They damaged their environment through an unsustainable use of vegetation, by causing erosion, and by cutting turf. Lake sediment analysis shows that the warming following the arctic minimum gave rise to trees, a development that was not interrupted until the Norse entered the scene; disruptions of the vegetation were reversed after the Norse extinction but returned in the twentieth century when the Danish government reintroduced sheep. In consequence of their destruction of trees, the Norse soon had no timber except for driftwood. Firewood, required to disinfect dairy containers with hot water, likewise became unavailable so Greenlanders had to resort to burning turf (i.e. pasture) and animal products (i.e. fertilizer). Extracting bog iron required charcoal, and so iron became very rare over time. This also lost the Norse their military advantage over the Inuit.

The Dorset people the Norse would have encountered earlier on differed from the Inuit culture that sprang from it c. 1000 in that they lacked bow and arrow, skin boats, and the whale hunt; accordingly, they could only support very small populations and represented no threat. The Inuit, by contrast, represented the technological culmination of millennia of Arctic survival. The Inuit kayak-based whale hunt required a hyperextension of the arm acquired through lifelong practice; the ringed seal hunt required a skill very difficult to master. Both the Dorset and the Norse disappeared shortly after the Inuit entered their territories (260). A 1379 annal reports an Inuit attack killing 18 men; this would have been in the Eastern Settlement, as the Western no longer existed. While Norse artifacts made it into Inuit hands, we don’t see much of the reverse happening, suggesting there were no substantial trade relations; there is also no evidence of intermarrying. There is no question that the Norse must have recognized the Inuits’ superior boats and hunting equipment and techniques, but they did not copy them. Cultural differences may explain the lack of intermarrying: the skills required of a Norse farmgirl were not to be found in an Inuit bride. To learn Inuit techniques or acquire an individually tailored kayak, one had to befriend the Inuit; but written records speak of violence against any natives encountered and refer to them as skrælingar “wretches”. Also, since the Norse got to Greenland first, they would have thought of the Inuit as intruders.

“Only the proximate reasons [i.e. for the Norse extinction] remain partly mysterious; the ultimate reasons are clear. They consist of the five sets of factors that we have already discussed in detail: Norse impact on the environment, climate change, decline in friendly contact with Norway, increase in hostile contact with the Inuit, and the conservative outlook of the Norse” (266; causes of the loss of contact with Norway are briefly detailed on the following page). Extinction actually hit the districts of the Eastern Settlement at different times. An account c. 1362 reports that the Inuit had by then taken possession of the Western Settlement (and, in the same account, that neither Christian nor heathen was found there). The Western Settlement has been found to have valuable objects still, so its residents did not leave in a planned migration. The top layers of the middens consist of small game and young livestock, as many cows as the farm could support, and hunting dogs, all suggesting desperation in the face of starvation. Even the fly species whose larvae were found in the top layers are more tolerant of cold, suggesting the population had run out of fuel. Thus the Western Greenlanders “starved and froze to death in the spring” (269).

Our last account of normal life in the Eastern Settlement is from 1410: the royal trading ship had not made it out since 1368, and given that the Greenland trade was a royal monopoly, only captains claiming to have been blown off course made it there at all. A dress has been dated to 1435, but radiocarbon dating is imprecise. A Lutheran missionary set out to seek the Eastern Settlement in 1721, and he found it in ruins in 1723. Diamond speculates there would have been a breakdown of respect for authority. Greenland’s last bishop had died c. 1378, leaving the population without spiritual leaders; the inequality between rich chieftains and poor farmers would have led to tensions; and the deteriorating climate would have brought it all to a head. Chieftains would have had no way to stop the hungry from eating the dogs and livestock required for survival. Although the Dorset had repeatedly settled and abandoned Greenland, the Inuit have survived there for eight centuries, so the Norse likewise were not helpless and indeed had the advantage of livestock. It was their choice no to fish or hunt ringed seals and whales. These choices may seem suicidal in hindsight, but they are no more so than ours today. They came in with cultural knowledge and values, and stuck to them too conservatively; and they were as useless as later Europeans at dealing with non-Europeans. Finally, the hierarchical nature of society meant huge resources were devoted to the procurement of luxury goods for a small elite

author: Clayton, Mary
title: Homiliaries and Preaching in Anglo-Saxon England
abstract:
Starts with a concise overview of preaching history: originally an episcopal privilege with lay audiences, and collected into volumes following the liturgical year by the fifth century, Caesarius of Arles produced a homiliary to be declaimed to the laity by the secular clergy (208). The Benedictine Rule shows that homiliaries were by the sixth century used as readings in the monastic Office. This, indeed, was probably their primary function in the Middle Ages: on Sun- and feastdays they were read in the Night Office, when it was made up of three rather than the usual one Nocturn. Each of the three contained three readings in secular usage, four in monastic usage (208–9). “In St Benedict’s time the readings of the first nocturn appear to have been taken from the Old Testament, of the second from scriptural commentaries or homilies and of the third from the New Testament (Acts of the Apostles, Epistles and Revelations). . . . [B]y the Carolingian period we find a new system, with the Old Testament in the first nocturn and sermons and homilies in the second and third nocturns.” Ælfric at least confirms that the third Nocturn should always incorporate a Gospel homily. On saints’ days, a vita or appropriate sermon was read in the first two Nocturns, a homily in the third (209). Bede composed fifty homilies specifically for the Night Office, each tailor-compiled for its particular liturgical occasion. Paul the Deacon’s homiliary was commissioned by Charlemagne specifically for use in the Night Office; it incorporates whole patristic texts, often offering several options per day. “Most of the seventh- and eighth-century homiliaries. . . seem to have been intended for use in the night Office and, apart from that of Bede, they incorporated whole patristic texts” (210).

Barré associates homiliaries of the ninth-century Auxerre tradition, which are exegetical texts without sermon content, with the Carolingian Renaissance; he believes they were not for the Night Office but for private devotional reading. Clayton counters that nothing speaks against their having been used in the Night Office as well: they are ordered according to the liturgical year, and a homiliary like Haymo’s resembles Bede’s; indeed, one could argue collections like this one were developed in response to the division of patristic readings into second-Nocturn sermons and third-Nocturn homilies (211–12).

Clayton also identifies a group of works, such as Smaragdus’s homiliary, that show a movement in the direction of the Auxerre homiliary in that they too confine themselves to exegesis, but without the Auxerre level of originality. Hrabanus Maurus copied patristic content with just a few words of introduction; his as well as Smaragdus’s homiliary cannot have been intended for the Night Office; Hrabanus’s was instead for Lothar’s private use. In their correspondence, Hrabanus connects it to the Mass (213).

Other ninth-century collections, including Hrabanus Maurus’s first homiliary, seem intended for preaching to the laity (213). Collections like St Père and Mondsee appear intended as aids to preachers, associated with Carolingian efforts to ensure adequate preaching, and thus appear to be the written counterparts of what was preached (213–14). Gatch has proposed a vernacular Prone context for preaching; Hrabanus’s texts and others like it must have been preached in a context of this kind: basic exegesis, moral advice, explanations of the faith (214–15). [to be continued]

author: Maurer, Konrad
title: Ueber die Hænsa-Þóris saga
publication: Abhandlungen der ersten Classe der königlichen bayerischen Akademie der Wissenschaften
abstract: Among many other things, discusses the legality of the hay transaction (illegal). Points out that Jónsbók, Landsleigubálkr ch. 12 stipulates a forced expropriation specifically of hay in emergencies, and that the Norwegian source of this legislation had instead concerned seeds (Landsleigubálkr ch. 14) (194–5). This legislation was not in place in the setting of Hœnsa-Þóris saga, and in fact clergy and farmers alike took a firm stand against specifically this part, among many other parts, of the new legislation during the General Assembly of 1281, the year in which Jónsbók took effect (195; reference to Árna biskups saga ch. 28). Surprisingly, Maurer concludes from these facts that the saga must have been composed either before 1280 or after 1400, since the saga’s dispute would not have been recounted “in so harmloser Weise” if the thirteenth-century legal dispute had been ongoing or in recent memory (195). [This bears comparing with the HÍ introduction, which acknowledges the logic of reading the saga as a defence of the 1281 law, but turns the connection on its head and points out the law may have been written with cases like Hœnsa-Þórir in mind. The editors see themselves forced to take this position because of the relationship between the saga and Sturlubók, though they observe Finnur Jónsson took a different view and dated the saga later: ÍF3:xxx–xxxi, PSL]

author: Cross, J. E.
title: Aspects of Microcosm and Macrocosm in Old English Literature
publication: Studies in Old English Literature in Honor of Arthur G. Brodeur
abstract:
The parallel between microcosm and macrocosm was acceptable to Anglo-Saxons for a number of reasons: all was made of four elements, and Gregory explains humankind's place in the scala naturae in terms of vivere, sentire, intelligere, and discernere, identifying properties shared with stones, trees, animals, and angels. The connection was cited particularly with reference to the ages of the world and the days of creation; Pseudo/Alcuin and Isidore used the term aetas to refer both to the world ages and to the ages of men (1–2). An anthropomorphic understanding of the world growing old has been recognized in a number of poems and homilies, including The Seafarer and Blickling homily V (2).

Ælfric follows Gregory (Homilia I in Evangelia[; but does Cross later on the same page and the next imply that Gregory does not press the causality elsewhere? PSL]) in identifying the age of the world as the cause of contemporary calamity; Cyprian's Ad Demetrianum (CE 252, quoted in Smithers, "Seafarer" part one, note 17) is one of the first works to explain contemporary evils by the age of the world. Augustine and other Church Fathers identify the same analogy between human age and the ages of the world but without a causal relationship: the world grows old and fails just as humans grow old and fail; Gregory in his Moralia in Iob explains that we are made of the same stuff as this world, and hence the physical world itself must likewise end. In this text, Gregory emphasizes a daily increase of evils that is not (Cross argues) found in Scripture but that is familiar from the Old English homilies (3–4), which emphasize a worsening of human health. Wulfstan particularly likes the phrase "a swa leng swa wyrse" (4–5), and Cross argues that the variant "a swa leng swa wacre" confirms the influence of the macrocosm–microcosm connection on the notion of progressive deterioration. He goes into detail about Wulfstan's choice of the adjective wac "weak" in relation to sin and causality. Pagan and early Christian thinkers saw a connection between physical and moral weakness and thought of earlier civilizations as stronger (5–6); Cyprian even went so far as to identify unseasonal weather as evidence of a failing world. In so doing, he courts heresy, since the world view of progressive decay is at odds with Christian dogma: Augustine, confronted with the allegation that pagan times were better, refutes it [Cross does not tell us how, PSL]; Minucius Felix rejected atomism because it left no place for God's creative act (6). However, IV Esdras 5:50–55 states that children born to a young mother are more vigorous, and draws a parallel with creation which, it asserts, is already grown old; thus the doctrine had seeped into Christianity after all (6–7). Ælfric claims that his contemporaries were too weak to fast like the ancients, but he explains it by the English climate, which being "on uteweardan þære eorðan bradnysse" [the word means extent/expanse generally; is he thinking of its marginal western place on a T-O map or latitude? PSL] is not as "mægenfæst" (strong) as elsewhere; Ælfric is not referring to the dietary needs of survival in a colder climate but uses mægenfæst in the same way as when he says creatures are stronger during full moon [which still doesn't explain what he means, PSL] (7). Ælfric adds that men today do not have the strength of old (they are not as mihtig); he confirms in another sermon that ancient men were capable of more than contemporaries, and in a third text he claims that people's strength against the devil is much weakened so near the end of the world, echoing a Gregorian passage rooted in Apc 12:12 (7–8). Ælfric's text on the memory of saints follows the same trend when it refers to the increased activity of the devil in the end-times and adds the point that men in biblical times were longer-lived (8–9). Augustine accepted that men were growing weaker in terms of lifespan, physical might, and stature, citing Virgil and Pliny the Elder (9).

Philo Judaeus in the first century BCE put forward the Platonic argument that as Adam was made in God's image, we are copies of Adam, leading to ever more imperfections (9–10). The contrast between a golden age and the weakness of the present age is brought out in Blickling homily X and De consolatione Philosophiae 2m5 (10–11). The Rhyming Poem likewise describes a golden age of bounty, which has been lost through avarice; Admonition too speaks of the world declining and falling into warfare (11–12). Proposes reading brondhord in the Rhyming Poem to mean "rusted treasure" (13–15). The rest of the article discusses Guthlac A, The Seafarer, etc.

[The article is valuable, but a little imprecise in reference or implicit in its reasoning at times. When Cross makes a distinction between Church Fathers making causal and noncausal connections between the age of the world and the age of man (pp. 3–4), the conceptual distinction is not especially clear; when he says that it will become obvious why many Church Fathers would not assert a causal link, he does not (I think) explicitly return to this point, so we're left to guess that it is because the notion of a deteriorating world is potentially heretical (p. 6). Of course the article then goes on to document exceptions, including Ælfric himself, so one is left a little confused, PSL.]
