author: Berglund, Joel
title: Did the Medieval Norse Society in Greenland Really Fail?
publication: Questioning Collapse: Human Resilience, Eclogical Vulnerability, and the Aftermath of Empire
eds: Patricia A. McAnany and Norman Yoffee
abstract:
Berglund’s critique of Diamond’s work starts out subtle, with slight shifts of perspective. Berglund does offer a likelier hypothesis for the absence of fishbones: they may have been boiled into fodder, as was still done in Norway in the twentieth century. At any rate analysis of human bones makes indisputably clear that fish was a substantial and increasing part of the diet (59–60).

It is after the initial setting of the stage that the main criticism is adduced, though this mostly takes the form of first-hand archaeological observations rather than citations. Berglund asserts he and his team have found no great wealth of Norse objects, and the objects found have signs of having been deliberately discarded. Everything suggests gradual depopulation, not a panicked crisis, and no signs of conflict (61–2).

Instead of Diamond’s conflict-and-crisis scenario, Berglund offers a scenario based on ecological change (cf. Amorosi et al, McGovern et al.). Sand deposits appear to have begun in the fourteenth century, driven by increased winds; this compunded the erosion resulting from human activity. There are far more sheep in Greenland today than in the Middle Ages, so grazing alone cannot have been the problem; instead, the burning off of vegetation may have initiated erosion (64–5). Land was also being lost to a rising sea: as much as a metre was lost during the time of settlement (65–6).

Greenland was initially well embedded in the Norse world, but the ivory trade ceased in the fourteenth century, either because of African supplies or failing demand. Berglund speculates in a sentence or two about the lifestyle implications of the shift from farming to fishery, and hints that the cooling climate was behind this shift, while it did not disturb the Inuit lifestyle that was already marine-based. Although we do not know where the Norse Greenlanders went, we must assume they emigrated over a considerable period of time. “As the conditions for their continued existence were altered, however, leaving their farms became the only alternative. One may therefore with some justification claim that their emigration was a rational response to a challenge with unacceptable alternatives. Nobody deliberately chooses to fail, and neither did the Norse Greenlanders. Their choice was the right one for several hundred years. What happened later could not have been foreseen, and is not the consequence of choosing to fail” (68).

author: Day, Virginia
title: The Influence of the Catechetical narratio on Old English and Some Other Medieval Literature
abstract:
Traces the influence of Augustine's De catechizandis rudibus on Ælfric, Christ and Satan, etc.

Augustine instructs that catechetical instruction should begin with a narratio comprising a cosmological and historical exposition from Creation to the current state of Church history (51–2). Boethius, (probably) Notker, Martin of Bracara, and Pirmin of Reichenau have produced narrationes related to Augustine's, as have Avitus and Hrabanus; Irish reflexes are also found (53–4). Bede's description of Cædmon's work likewise follows the definition of the catechetical narratio (54–5). The opening sections of Genesis A and Christ and Satan may reflect the tradition (55). Identifies part of Vercelli homily XIX, Ælfric's De initio creaturae (ÆCHom I, 1), and Wulfstan's reworking of that text as three clear examples of the narratio genre recommended by Augustine; in fact, Day believes all three were influenced either by De catechizandis rudibus or the Scarapsus of Pirmin of Reichenau (56–7). Ælfric knew De catechizandis rudibus and used it in his De falsiis diis; in his De initio, Ælfric sometimes seems to draw more heavily on Martin of Bracara's De correctione rusticorum; Wulfstan has been shown to use Pirmin's Scarapsus (57). Ælfric's Hexameron and letters to Sigeweard and Wulfgeat contain similar material; indeed, these three works all reuse phrasings from De initio (57–8). De initio fittingly opens the Catholic Homilies; here and in the letter to Wulfgeat, it precedes exhortation, as instructed by Augustine (58–9). The mystery plays show later medieval influence (59–61).

author: Gatch, Milton McC.
title: Basic Christian Education from the Decline of Catechesis to the Rise of the Catechisms
publication: Eschatology and Christian Nurture: Themes in Anglo-Saxon and Medieval Religious Life
orig_publ: John H. Westerhoff III and O. C. Edwards, Jr, eds. A Faithful Church: Issues in the History of Catechesis. Wilton, CT: Morehouse–Barlow, 1981. 79–108
abstract:
A fully formed rite of catechesis was associated with baptism in the fourth century, but the success of Christianity led to the disappearance of a class of adult initiates who could be instructed. Carolingian and later documents suggest much of the classical Easter liturgy remained associated with the now-infant catechumens into the twelfth century (82–6), while the 1543 Sarum Manual leaves the godparents in charge of instruction (86–8). The role of the godparents largely hides catechesis from historians: it was practised domestically, presumably in combination with vocational training. The fifteenth-century development of catechism shifted responsibility back onto the Church, not necessarily because past practice had been insufficient but more likely because of new ideas about education (89–91).

Moving to general instruction, quotes an 816 Synod of Tours canon cited also in Preaching and Theology asserting that “each bishop should have homilies containing needful admonitions by which his subjects may be taught. . . concerning the perpetual retribution of the good and the eternal damnation of the evil, concerning the coming general resurrection and last judgment and by what works one may merit eternal life and by what works be excluded from it”, noting also that such homilies should be made available in the vernacular (92). The tenth- and eleventh-century Anglo-Saxon vernacular homilies are the best material demonstrating how this was done: “[i]t seems clear that these texts were prepared as aids to catechetical teaching. Probably they were used in a vernacular office which might be introduced in the Latin mass just after the reading of the gospel or, occasionally, used in extra-liturgical settings” (92–3). Preaching of this nature was apparently desirable weekly, but particularly around Lent and Easter, with a special place in England for Rogation Days. Gatch hypothesizes that this may be because the Rogation Days were used for the procedure of scrutiny ahead of a Pentecost baptism, “just as the concentration of frequent preaching in Lent and easter reflected the ancient delivery of catechetical instruction at those seasons”. Circumstantial evidence may be read to suggest that Anglo-Saxons concentrated baptism at Pentecost rather than Easter (93).

Ælfric may have had an improvement of catechetical instruction in mind when composing his Rogationtide sermons. “Ælfric’s sermons, even those treating almost exclusively exegetical materials, are, I believe, catechetical in purpose” (93–4, at 94). Discusses the contents of Ælfric’s Rogationtide homilies in some detail. Echoes, without citing it, Godden’s position that CH2 leave the preacher more liberty to choose or select, while CH1 was intended for straightforward reading out. “His considerable body of work is all catechetical in intent, but his six items for the Rogation Days in the Sermones Catholicae are consciously catechetical, especially in their intent to touch upon the major themes of catechesis derived both from the liturgy of initiation and from the efforts of the Carolingian legislators and reformers to revive the general teaching office of the church. The topics Ælfric treated in his Rogationtide sermons — the creed, the Lord’s Prayer, Christian ethics or moral law, and the Last Things or vision of judgment, which ought to inspire all Christians to fulfillment of the law — are the standard materials of medieval catechetical teaching” (98). The remainder of the essay concentrates on later medieval instruction.

author: Dugmore, Andrew J., et al.
title: Cultural Adaptation, Compounding Vulnerabilities and Conjunctures in Norse Greenland
abstract:
Emphasizes the successful adaptation of the Norse to climate change in Greenland while deemphasizing the role of climate change in the discontinuation of the settlements. Asserts that decline better describes the discontinuation than collapse, and warns against monocausal explanations.

Norse Atlantic settlements everywhere were characterized by a broad subsistence base and multifarm collaborations (3658). Smaller farms were more reliant on wild resources, while large estates raised more cattle; over time, the smaller farms became dependent on the larger ones. In spite of the common narrative, the evidence shows that Norse Atlantic settlements adapted well: the standard Norse economic base initially introduced was modified to match local conditions. Pigs all but disappeared across the North Atlantic, probably because the damage they did in times of agricultural intensification and environmental instability. Iceland saw a dramatic rise in sheep and a drop in goats after 1200, perhaps reflecting a recognition of the market for wool. Goats remained as common as sheep in Greenland, suggesting livestock was primarily kept for food (dairy) rather than trade. There is some evidence for sea birds having been sustainably hunted in the Faroes and Iceland. Walrus may have been driven to extinction in Iceland, but nonmigratory seals have been sustainably hunted in Iceland up to the present day. The walrus hunt was an important part of the economy in Greenland, and caribou were hunted using deer hounds and cairn drives, sustainably until modern overhunting.

Icelandic forests diminished initially but from the fourteenth century to the present day, remaining woodland was carefully preserved, [initially] for charcoal production. Rangeland was massively eroded after the settlement of Iceland, but livestock numbers and availability of highland grazing have not stood in a proportionate relationship. The most striking adaptation was the instant switch from fishery to the migratory seal hunt in Greenland. The absence of fish bones in Greenland may be explained by “a pragmatic and effective adaptation driven by seasonal scheduling issues”: the seal species in question arrived in spring as a welcome relief from the winter and ahead of the walrus hunt. Sea ice would have made winter fishery impractical (3659), while Norse Greenlanders did not adopt the Inuit techniques required to hunt seal species that use breathing holes in winter (3659–60). Spring seal hunting could be intensified to the degree allowed by manpower, transportation capabilities, and extreme weather; it is likely to have played a major role in subsistence during the climate fluctuations of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries (3660).

Following incorporation into the Kingdom of Norway, Greenland seems to have been more directly controlled by the crown than Iceland, among other things because the Icelandic population was large enough to sustain its own gentry, which continued to exert an influence. Unlike Iceland and the Faroes, Greenland exported prestige goods and indeed “seems from the outset to have been geared to obtaining and exporting rare and prestigious commodities such as walrus tusk and hide, narwhal teeth, and live polar bears. It is likely that the Norwegian kings were in control of this trade from early times; control is certainly evident by the early 14th century when written sources become available.” Greenland did not engage in the cod trade embraced by the other Atlantic settlements starting in the thirteenth century. This sidelined Greenland when the Kalmar Union was established in 1397.

When the climate fluctuations hit, Norse Atlantic societies had built up generations of Traditional Ecological Knowledge, which, mediated by more deep-rooted cultural capital, form the basis of social action (3660).

Simulations of Norse farming models make clear that marine resources were required to sustain the Norse Greenlanders: livestock would not have sufficed. Indeed, bad winters would have forced stock culling, and short-interval repeated bad winters would have left smaller farms in particular below biological replacement levels. Accordingly, large estates would have played a key role in sustainability, gobbling up smaller farms and making them into tenant farms (3660–1).

Food store buffering in Greenland was limited by the absence of grains and dried fish. Caribou and harbour seal hunting was limited not only by the risk of overhunting but also by climate effects on grazing and seal reproduction. Migrating seals were thus the logical alternative as a source of air-dried meat, but this made sustenance a balancing act. Evidence from middens and human skeletons makes clear that protein was increasingly sourced from marine mammals (seals). “We argue that this shift represents an initially successful response to climate change and an initially resilient modification and intensification of sealing TEK by the Greenlanders. . . . Climate variability always provided challenges to Norse Greenland’s TEK, and the notion of a uniform medieval warm period has long been replaced by the realization that even the earliest periods of settlement saw considerable variability requiring effective coping strategies. The Norse Greenlanders survived many hard years before the 13th century and not only persevered but prospered. However, in the late 13th to mid-14th centuries, the effects of processes operating on different temporal and spatial scales began to coincide, producing unprecedented challenges.” Effects of climate change affected available land, winter byring time, fodder production, fodder need, and sailing. Low summer temperatures endangered stock survival while disproportionally decreasing the value of highland pastureland, especially in the Western Settlement. “Although the end of the Western Settlement is not completely understood, a likely proximate cause was isolation combined with late winter subsistence failure, plausibly connected to climate change” (3661).

The Eastern Settlement endured into the fifteenth century, adapting through an intensification of probably the only avenue that allowed it, the migratory seal hunt. This was an adaptive success, but it led to increased monoculture. The seal hunt was a fragile enterprise, taking place well offshore and requiring transportation of carcasses through a sea increasingly plagued by sea ice and storms.

After 1400, Norway ceded control of North Atlantic trade to the Hansa. The emphasis of trade continued to shift towards dried fish in bulk, not prestige items; contact with Norway dried up. The Thule Inuit had also encroached on Norse areas. This dynamic is not well understood, but Norse sources suggest conflict, while there is no evidence of intermarriage. It would have taken close cooperation between the communities for the Norse to learn how to hunt ringed seals. It may be that the close-knit nature of the community that had made it successful at initial adaptation worked against such intercultural interaction (3662).

author: Hill, Joyce
title: Translating the Tradition: Manuscripts, Models and Methodologies in the Composition of Ælfric’s Catholic Homilies
publication: Textual and Material Culture in Anglo-Saxon England: Thomas Northcote Toller and the Toller Memorial Lectures
abstract:
A wonderfully rich essay on the design of the Catholic Homilies. After noting that Cambridge, Cambridge University Library MS Gg.3.28 is the sole surviving copy containing both series of Catholic Homilies, the only one containing the second in full, the only one containing the peritexts (she also notes, on p. 244, that prefaces have a tendency of disappearing in transmission after the first degree), and most likely a filing copy kept in the scriptorium that produced it in the late tenth or early eleventh century (241–3), goes on to outline the lengths to which Ælfric goes in the prefaces to drive home the humility topos. Within this context, his reference to his works as “translation” is a particularly striking instance of understatement were it not for the fact that Ælfric understands it (apparently) as intercultural transfer (243–6).

Hill goes on to test Ælfric’s source claims: Smetana has proved him right in claiming to use Haymo (though we now know it is Haymo of Auxerre not Halberstadt); Hill herself has done work to prove Ælfric correct in his claim that he uses Smaragdus; and Förster has verified the remaining source claims in Ælfric’s Latin preface to the first series of Catholic Homilies. Since Smetana has demonstrated that much of the patristic material to which these names in the preface refer was accessed through Paul the Deacon’s homiliary, so that we can put the number of homiliaries used for the first series at three: Haymo, Smaragdus, and Paul the Deacon (246–7).

Referring to her Smaragdus article, repeats its observation that the homilies themselves refer directly to the Church Fathers used, whereas the preface mentions [also, PSL] the Carolingian compilers of homiliaries through which Ælfric accessed them: the former references serve to establish authority, the latter are given in a professional context and serve to make clear that the new collection stands on a Reform footing (247–8). However, this motive raises the question why Paul the Deacon is not named in the preface (248). While Hill has previously assumed Ælfric does not refer to Paul because his creative part in the homiliary is lesser than the roles of Smaragdus and Haymo in theirs, but she now believes Ælfric simply did not know who compiled Paul’s homiliary, as it was originally issued with a preface so topical that it was soon dropped in transmission. The homiliary was able to travel without Paul’s name because the exegeses contained in it consistently identify the patristic author in their rubrics (248–50).

Paul the deacon dates his homilies to liturgical occasions using a system that went out of fashion soon after, tying them to saints’ days rather than counting Sundays after events in the temporale; since manuscripts of the Catholic Homilies use the newer system, Ælfric probably had access to a copy of Paul in which the occasions had been re-dated to the newer system (250–1). If so, this makes his three source homiliaries even more homogeneous; he was clearly adapting a single tradition. Hill therefore sets out to answer the question why three homiliaries were called for. Ælfric’s copy of Paul’s homiliary was augmented, among others by texts by Gregory, and Ælfric incorporates many homilies of Gregory, both from the original and from the augmented set, conceivably because Gregory’s phrase-by-phrase style of exegesis suited him, and the same reasoning would hold for his frequent use of Bede, who at any rate drew heavily on Gregory himself (251–4). Smaragdus likewise explains Scripture verse by verse, making him compatible with Gregory and Bede; he also identified patristic authors of each exegesis, so Ælfric was able to authorize his explanations, while his catena style of compilation encouraged recombination. Thus “whereas Ælfric’s copy of Paul the Deacon was useful for its patristic identifications, its basic content, and the numerous models it provided for Ælfric’s favoured style of exegesis, Smaragdus was useful for all of these things, but he was additionally valuable as a conflator, modifier and abbreviator, providing Ælfric with ready-made conflations, modifications and abbreviations which also served as models for Ælfric’s own independent adaptations” (255–6). Ælfric used Haymo less, less systematically, and rarely as a first source, because Haymo had a different style, juxtaposing Scriptural passages for associative effect while absorbing rather than quoting patristic sources; he could thus be used for thematically linked scriptural quotations and for occasional detail lacking in the others. Accordingly, Ælfric uses Haymo for supplementary scriptural quotations and allusions (256–7).

author: Godden, M. R.
title: Did King Alfred Write Anything?
abstract:
Alfred’s active involvement in at least part of the supposedly Alfredian canon is generally taken for granted, but this is problematic on several fronts. Asser himself claims Alfred did not learn to read until he was 39, and he never mentions him as writing, and so scholars have agreed Alfred must have written his whole corpus in the six years between Asser’s biography and the king’s death, in between other duties (1–2 and 3). Meanwhile, the nature of the texts is such that the person who wrote them must have been able to read and write (2). External evidence is late and unreliable: Asser only says Alfred commissioned the Dialogues; Ælfric claims Alfred translated the Ecclesiastical History, but its Mercian dialect makes clear this cannot be right; where Ælfric uses the Old English Pastoral Care and Consolation of Philosophy, he does not mention Alfred, nor does he do so when he refers to the Dialogues. Æthelweard’s Chronicon asserts the king wrote many works and mentions the Consolation by name. William of Malmesbury provided a longer list, which nevertheless “does not accord with modern notions of what Alfred wrote” [doesn’t it, though, comparatively closely? PSL] (3).

Evidence of authorship is accordingly mostly internal, particularly in the prefaces, and particularly the prose preface to the Pastoral Care (a verse preface in the book’s own voice is also extant). The Consolation has prose and verse prefaces in the third person, apparently posthumous. The Soliloqiues assert Alfred’s authorship in an explicit (3–4).

Claims of authorship like these were not to be taken seriously: Alciun used Charlemagne’s voice often, in prefaces and of course in his dialogue, and Theodulf appears to have done so too. Less plausible situations are known, too: a ninth-century text contains a claim of Jerome’s authorship (4–5). Scholars have been reluctant to accept such practices for England: it is extremely unlikely that Æthelweard knew the Latin to write his own Chronicon (5–6). Charters were authorized by the king, but this does not mean he wrote them; the preface to the Dialogues claims in Alfred’s voice that he commissioned it, but surely it was Wærferth who wrote this; furthermore, the claim that the text was for the king’s own use cannot be correct. Æthelred’s law texts are in his own voice but were surely written by Wulfstan. The latter also wrote an agreement between Alfred and Guthrum and one between Edward and Guthrum, a century after the events took place. It is only in Alfred’s case that scholars refuse to give up on personal authorship (6).

Considerations that favour the king’s personal involvement include the more modest claims made in the prefaces and their more explicit reference to his involvement. But the reason for these explicit references may be that the texts are translations, so the only way to claim Alfred’s authority for them was to position him squarely into the translation action (6–7).

The translators are not particularly precise about claims of authority: they regularly say that Orosius or Boethius said this or that when it concerns original interpolations; the third book of the OE Soliloquies is the most striking example of such practice, as the whole book is new material ascribed to Augustine. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle’s claims for Alfred’s personal leadership on the battlefield and papal audience at the age of four are now understood as propaganda. Claims for Alfred’s authorship need not be of a different category (7–8). The widely different claims in manuscript prefaces of the Dialogues — not by the king — show how easily books could receive a royal attribution. In the case of the Consolation, prefaces to the prose and verse claim Alfred’s authorship but it seems the two were in fact produced by different authors, making neither claim reliable (8). Judging from internal style, there are good grounds for positing a single author for the Consolation and Soliloquies, but the Pastoral Care differs significantly (8–11). Interpolations reflecting royal concerns are to be expected in texts written on behalf of a monarch. Moreover, some such passages reflect rather the position of a courtier, and other passages are critical of kingship (11).

Evidence against Alfred’s authorship hinge on Asser: if we assume the biography is a forgery we may posit that Alfred learned Latin at a much earlier age. But the prose preface to the Dialogues claims the work was translated for the king’s own use, suggesting he could not then read Latin; that to the Pastoral Care claims he needed a team of four to help him understand Latin; any great and early Latinity on his own part is undercut by his own claim that hardly anyone knew Latin when he came to power in 871 (12–13).

If difference in style may be attributed to a developing author, there is a huge gulf in approach between the faithful Pastoral Care and the creative Consolation and Soliloques (13). The Consolation’s constant critique of monarchs makes royal authorship unlikely; indeed, the Old English version greatly expands on such passages, and both here and in the Soliloquies are strikingly sympathetic to the plight of rejected counsellors (13–14).

Godden proposes that the Pastoral Care was circulated with Alfred’s approval; both prefaces to the Dialogues again claim his authority, though not his authorship. The king may have given his seal of approval to the Consolation as well; he need not have read its positions critical of kings. But it may just as well have been produced after his lifetime; indeed, at least the prose preface (which refers to the prosimetrical version!) seems to be looking back to Alfred’s reign. The Soliloquies go as the Consolation goes: either both were produced in Alfred’s circle during his lifetime or they are both posthumous. Alfred’s voice in the law code is mere convention (15–17).

Godden speculates briefly about non-Alfredian authorship, then points out that ruling out Alfred as the author of Consolation and Soliloquies frees us to interpret the texts without limiting ourselves to the royal perspective. Godden answers the question in his title in the negative, with the qualification that no absolute proof is to be had. “The preface and text of the Pastoral Care were done by another and issued with his authorization. The translations of the Consolation and Soliloquies probably had no direct connection with the king at all but were attributed to him after his lifetime. The law-code, like all other early medieval law-codes, was written by others in the king's name and with his authority. On the Psalms there is no real evidence for authorship. None of these things is yet provable. But we should at least stop assuming that the king wrote them all, or even authorized them all” (18).

author: Jackson, Peter
title: Ælfric and the ‘uita patrum’ in Catholic Homily I.36
publication: Essays on Anglo-Saxon and Related Themes in Memory of Lynne Grundy
publisher: King’s College London and the Centre for Late Antique and Medieval Studies
abstract: Ælfric refers to the Vitas patrum (incidentally as the ‘vita patrum’; Jackson details the form of the phrase on 262–3) eight times (263). The usual target of his references allows us to narrow down the source of his summary in CH1, 36, which introduces features not found together in any one classical Vitas patrum text. He’s probably conflated what he remembers from multiple such texts. Curiously, however, one text that matches several of the features mentioned by Ælfric is the Life of St Cuthbert, suggesting that he had this work in mind when referring to the Vitas patrum. Jackson speculates that Cuthbert’s way of life made him into a “paradigmatic hermit” of equal authority to others to Ælfric’s mind. He appears to cite the Vitas patrum primarily for illustrations of chastity; following Mary Clayton’s suggestion that Ælfric was uneasy with their eremitical existence, Jackson proposes he may have felt obliged to use them in some way and therefore reduced them to illustrations of chastity (271).

author: Jackson, Peter
title: The Vitas patrum in Eleventh-Century Worcester
publication: England in the Eleventh Century: Proceedings of the 1990 Harlaxton Symposium
abstract: Refers to Cross for the recognition that Ælfric’s four naming-and-excerpting exercises from the Vitas patrum all derive from the Verba seniorum of Pelagius and John. The only known Worcester reference that adds to this is to the Historia monachorum in Aegypto by Rufinus of Aquileia; so Jackson takes these two works as his eleventh-century Worcester definition of the corpus and sets out to reconstruct the degree to which they were known and used.

author: McNamara, Martin
title: The (Fifteen) Signs Before Doomsday in Irish Tradition
abstract: A study of the origins of the Signs Before Doomsday tradition and its apparent development into a Fifteen Signs tradition in Ireland (though McNamara notes the existence of modern Armenian counterparts whose sources have remained unidentified). Reproduces Heist’s diagram, which considers the Old English homiletic tradition (Vercelli, Hatton, Blickling) to be entirely distinct derivations from the Apocalypse of Thomas. Does not come to any new insights, but discusses the ten Irish witnesses in detail, printing the passages of several of them.

abstract: An early discussion of sources. Now see e.g. the works by Smetana and Joyce Hill.

author: Hill, Joyce
title: Ælfric and Smaragdus
abstract:
Tests Ælfric’s claim in the Latin preface to his first series of Catholic Homilies that Smaragdus is a major source, against the findings of scholars thus far. I will at this point limit myself to observations of particular interest to my research:

  • “What Smaragdus's Expositio offered was a series of lections ordered according to the ecclesiastical year, which thus lent itself to being used as a source for a predominantly exegetical, lection-based collection of homilies such as Ælfric was writing. It was not designed for public preaching, however, since the lections — and consequently the exegesis — may be longer than is customary for a public homily, or indeed longer than is prescribed for liturgical use; there are no homiletic introductions and conclusions; there is no audience-address in the course of the exegesis; and when there is an initiating address in the manuscripts I have examined, it is simply ‘Carissimi’ or ‘Fratres,’ with ‘fratres’ indicating an ecclesiastical community” (207–8).

author: Irvine, Susan
title: Uncertain Beginnings: The Prefatory Tradition in Old English
publisher: Department of Anglo-Saxon, Norse and Celtic, University of Cambridge
abstract:
Notes that Old English scholars tend to shy away from studying Anglo-Saxon prefaces as a common category; instead, they focus on one author or one text (1–2). This may be due to the varied and fluid form of the Anglo-Saxon preface (2–3) as well as the difficulty of proving that a preface was originally attached to a given text (3–4). The vernacular tradition was shaped by a strong presence of a well-defined Latin prefatory tradition, but Irvine hopes to demonstrate that there is a distinctive set of conventions proper to Old English prefaces as well (4). She briefly introduces some of the variables of the Old English preface: verse or prose, dedicatory or not, more and less epistolary. The epistolary prefaces tend to salute in the third person, then move to the first (5).

The small corpus of verse prefaces tends to speak for the book in the first person (6–11). For the prose prefaces, we may extend to the general tradition Griffith’s observation that Ælfric’s Preface to Genesis is structured by sentence starting with a pronoun and containing a þæt-construction, each such sentence marking a new section; in the preface to the Pastoral Care, ða ic ða (ðis eall) gemunde serves a similar function, and a similarly repetitive pattern may be identified in the prologue to Alfred’s laws. Moreover, within such sections, prefaces seem to use forþam followed by a pronoun to change the direction of the content (11–13).

author: Smetana, Cyril L.
title: Paul the Deacon’s Patristic Anthology
publication: The Old English Homily and Its Backgrounds
eds: Paul E. Szarmach and Bernard F. Huppé
publisher: State University of New York Press
abstract:
Charlemagne commissioned Paul’s homiliary because of the textual errors and dubious origins of existing homiliaries, but above all he declared he wanted to institute Roman liturgical usage (76). PD soon became more frequently copied than other homiliaries, certainly for its royal sanction but it was also useful for its range and quality; Alan of Farfa’s homiliary, for instance, never covered the Sundays of the year, and contains more sermons than homilies (76–7). PD differs from catena collections like Haymo or Smaragdus in that its “homilies and sermons consist of complete selections from the Fathers and thus comprise a fair representation of patristic exegesis.” It relies little on prior homiliaries [but draws instead directly on the Church Fathers, PSL] (77).

PD “is an independent collection of 244 homilies and sermons distributed over the whole liturgical year,” beginning five Sundays before Christmas. Its two volumes follow the temporale for those saints that have proper readings, and it has a separate section Commune sanctorum for saints not there included. Lections are grouped and ranked by type of saint. Though the set contains 151 items marked sermo and 91 omelia, the prevailing sense is that the terms are used interchangeably; but early redactions of PD show that Paul did distinguish; Smetana attaches considerable value to the recognition that Paul did distinguish. The work covers 50 Sundays, and important feasts were represented by a pericope, a homily, and several sermons (77–9). The most frequent source is Bede (57 lections, almost a quarter of all the texts in the two volumes), including many lections on pericopes from Luke and John, where Augustine would be the expected source for John; perhaps Paul preferred Bede’s conciseness and accessibility (80).

Fifty items are attributed to Maximus (many falsely so; 80–1). There are also texts by Leo the Great, and 32 of Gregory’s 40 homilies (81–2). Surprisingly, only three of Augustine’s 500-odd authentic sermons are included, plus seven miscellaneous readings. Smetane judges Paul to have been good at telling spurious from real Augustinian texts [though it is unclear to me how he can do this on the basis of so few texts, PSL] (82). The Augustinian lectures provide a good cross-section of Augustine’s oeuvre. Nineteen lections are attributed to John Chrysostom, as many as 18 of them falsely so (83). All eight texts attributed to Jerome are authentic (83–4).

Paul’s inclusion of works by Origen is noteworthy: the Council of Constantinople had left him a risky associate; but Paul dutifully excises any heterodox elements from these lections. Five of Paul’s six Origen items are genuine, impressive given the book-burning (84–5).

Paul includes only five readings from Ambrose, all New Testament material although Ambrose is particularly revered for his Old Testament exegesis; “Paul’s compilation, however, had little need for Old Testament exegesis, and for what was needed he preferred Chrysostom.” Paul includes four of Fulgentius’s eight topical sermons (85). Two items are by Isidore (85–6). The remaining two texts are by Peter Chrysologus (but attributed to Severianus) and Eusebius (86).

Following this index, Smetana offers an overview of the manuscript evidence for PD’s presence in Anglo-Saxon England in Ælfric’s day (86–7). Migne represents a late and augmented redaction; it also divides the contents into a proprium de tempore and a proprium sanctorum. Its most extensive source of new materials is Augustine and Pseudo-Augustine; the share of other authors in Migne is detailed (87–8). An appendix lists the pericopes in PD (89–90).

author: Cross, J. E.
title: Ælfric and the Mediæval Homiliary: Objection and Contribution
series: Scripta minora Regiae societatis humaniorum litterarum Lundensis
abstract: Hails Smetana’s case for Ælfric’s use of Paul the Deacon’s homiliary; points out some oversights on Smetana’s part, taking the form of a text-by-text discussion of Ælfric’s sources.

author: Sigurdur Thorarinsson
title: Population Changes in Iceland
abstract: A very strong article for its time. Assumes a population c. 70,000~75,000 at the time of Gizur Ísleifsson’s c. 1095 census, and points out that the population in 1800 was 47,000, a dramatic reduction while Norway tripled its population in the same period. The author emphasizes climate and above all human-caused soil erosion.

author: Otten, Willemien
title: Between Augustinian Sign and Carolingian Reality: The Presence of Ambrose and Augustine in the Eucharistic Debate Between Paschasius Radbertus and Ratramnus of Corbie

author: Leinbaugh, Theodore H.
title: The Sources for Ælfric’s Easter Sermon: The History of the Controversy and a New Source
abstract:
Identifies Augustine's In Iohannis evangelium, tractatus lv as a source of Ælfric's De sacrificio in die Pascae, with use of Bede's adaptation of the same entitled In caena Domini.

Ælfric's use of Ratramnus has long fed the belief that the English Church resisted the doctrine of transubstantiation long before the Reformation, and his views on the matter profoundly shaped those of many early reformers. However, Ælfric's homily also uses materials at odds with the new interpretation of Communion, such as the two miracle stories meant to prove the reality of Christ's presence in the host (296–7). These stories derive from Paschasius Radbertus's De corpore et sanguine Domini, which represents eucharistic realism. Seventeenth-century Archbishop James Ussher uses Ælfric's text to support his claim that the English Church had long rejected transubstantiation, but he omits (seemingly on purpose) mention of the two miracle stories and their source in Paschasius. Paschasius's realist view came to be adopted as the official Catholic position, while Ratramnus's was seen as independent or unorthodox quite early on. Whether or not the two treatises themselves are greatly at odds, they produced opposing views from the first that culminated in acrimonious debates in the eleventh century and played a role in the bloodshed of the Reformation (297).

The two miracle stories appear only in later versions of Paschasius, so they may well be an interpolation (298). Ælfric's use of Ratramnus became a cause célèbre among reformers, who cast Paschasius as the reformer and Ratramnus/Ælfric as orthodox (298–9). They discarded the two miracles as evidence of the confused and inferior nature of the intellectual milieu of Ælfric's time, or as interpolations (299–300). Catholic authors variously renounced Ælfric or sought some way to explain his departure from Catholic doctrine, sometimes by questioning the authenticity of the text (301–1). Some, such as John Floyd, challenge the Protestant authors to accept the miracles if they accept the remainder of Ælfric's text or, conversely, challenged the authenticity of the remainder of the text rather than the two miracles (301). Others claimed that translations distorted Ælfric's orthodox position (302).

When philologists got to the texts in the nineteenth century, they had to reinvent the wheel with regards to Ælfric's sources. In fact, Paschasius seems the obvious source for the miracle stories, as they here exist side by side; but Ælfric also had access to a Paschasius-inspired text from Corbie by Heriger of Lobbes entitled Exaggeratio plurimorum auctorum de corpore et sanguine Domini containing both; indeed, a slew of eucharistic proof-texts followed in the wake of Paschasius in the tenth century (304).

Recent scholarship has recognised considerable influence of Gregory's Homily 22, with occasional material from Augustine. Above all, the text is an intelligent reworking of Ratramnus. But no sources have been found for the material before and after the Ratramnus material, namely (1) the Tau sign by which the Israelites mark their doors and (2) the allegorical meaning of Passover. These derive from Augustine's In Iohannis evangelium, Tractatus lv, "an exegetical commentary on chapter 13 of the gospel according to John" (305–6). The typological reading of Passover is Ælfric's clearest use of the fourfold sense of Scripture, and so it is hardly surprising that his source for this is Augustine, but Ælfric's arrangement of the material betrays a reliance also on Bede's In caena Domini (306–7).

author: Jones, Christopher A.
title: Ælfric’s Letter to the Monks of Eynsham
abstract:
(Ælfric's text is very much a summary of the Regularis concordia.)

§§70–77 stipulate the sequence of readings [for the Night Office]:

  1. Septuagesima until Mid-Lent: Genesis
  2. Mid-Lent until Passiontide: Exodus
  3. Passiontide to Maundy Thursday: Jeremiah
  4. Maundy Thursday: Lamentations of Jeremiah + St Augustine on the Psalm Exaudi Deus orationem meam cum deprecor + St Paul.
  5. Holy Saturday: same as previous, except gospel in the third lection
  6. Easter Week: homilies on the gospels for Easter

author: Billett, Jesse D.
title: The Divine Office in Anglo-Saxon England 597–c. 1000
abstract:
[Ch. 1: Towards a New Narrative etc.] Rejects the implication often found tacit in traditional scholarship that the Divine Office in the seventh to ninth centuries was predominantly Benedictine, or that the Benedictine liturgy was established in 597 (3–8). Backs Sarah Foot’s position that the terms monasterium and mynster prior to the Benedictine Reform referred to a variety of institutions, many of which would have housed secular clergymen as well as monks (8). Sarah Foot has observed that what little is known of early Anglo-Saxon practice is diverse, making the general outline of the early liturgy of the hours unknowable. In this volume, Billett studies the available sources and is able to salvage some insights, whose keyword appears to be eclecticism (9–10). Billett lists his most important conclusions up front:

  • Augustine’s 597 Office would have resembled that sung by monks attached to Rome’s basilicas; this was a precursor of the later secular Office, sung by priests and clerks, and was quite unlike the Benedictine practice.
  • Monastic communities in early Christian Anglo-Saxon England were not bound to any one rule but gradually adopted Augustine’s system.
  • Just as there was no distinction between secular and monastic communities, so also there was no parallel system with a monastic and a secular clerical liturgy.
  • The Viking attacks coincided with a secularization of religious communities to undermine ecclesiastical culture, but some continuity remained. Alfred’s renaissance both reinvigorated the old tradition and also brought new Continental ingredients.
  • The Benedictine Rule was known throughout the period, but its form of the Office was not sung until the reform of the mid-tenth century, and even then it was only used by cenobites; the secular clergy stuck to the Roman/secular office.
  • Some existing, reformed houses did not introduce a clean break and shift to a Benedictine liturgy but instead adapted what liturgical books they had in their possession to follow the Benedictine system (11–12).

[Ch. 2: The Divine Office in the Latin West in the Early Middle Ages] Attributes the bifurcation of the Divine Office into a secular (“Roman”) and a monastic cursus to “the imposition of the Roman Office on the Frankish Church in the eighth century followed by the adoption by Frankish monks, beginning in the ninth century, of a different form drawn from the Regula S. Benedicti” (13). Both cursus sang through the Psalms in the course of a week, and they shared a good number of additional texts as well, but the Psalms were differently distributed and the musical pieces differed in arrangement and number (14–15). Such differences can be hard to identify in liturgical books, because much of this information was taken for granted and thus not spelled out (20).

Early monasticism shared an understanding of what true monasticism entailed, as may be recognized from the proceedings of councils such as that of Chalcedon in 451; this was not always encoded in a rule (23). Early references to a regula meant the person of the abbot, and later the catholic consensus; eventually, individual communities came to agree on, and sometimes write down, their own rules (24). The liturgy of the hours varied widely and was often not as meticulously encoded as by Benedict; some stipulated that the entire Psalter be read daily in a combination of individual reading and two daily offices (24–5). [etc.]

author: Foot, Sarah
title: Monastic Life in Anglo-Saxon England, c. 600–900
abstract:
An important work on early Anglo-Saxon monastic life. Rejects a strict distinction between secular ecclesiastical houses and monastic houses for its period, emphasizing instead that religious houses came in many shapes and forms, and often would have mixed these communities that are typically thought of as distinct. Foot therefore uses the term minster to refer to the diversity of forms religious institutions assumed in the early period. She also discusses the daily life and the tasks in which monks would have engaged and the ones they would have left to lay individuals, such as reeves and “individuals who apparently belonged to the wider community, and might even be described as fratres, even though they seemingly had no intention of becoming professed religious” (179). Goes into substantial detail on the economic relations between religious houses and the surrounding communities.

[1: Introduction: Situating the Problem] Prior to the tenth century, the communal religious life was not defined by a single rule (6). A diversity of rules and other prescriptive literature existed, though we should not take it as descriptive; narrative texts show holy men and women diverge from the rules drawn up by canons and councils (6–7). Likewise, the categories monk and nun better fit the prescriptive literature than the heterogeneity of early Anglo-Saxon practice (7–8). Both narrative and descriptive sources draw a sharp distinction between those ordained to clerical rank and other religious individuals. The prescriptive sources furthermore distinguish clearly between monachi and clerici in the penitential system, but narrative sources don't reflect this distinction between professed monks and those "who had made lesser commitments to life under a rule" (8). There is likewise no clear distinction between women living communally and those living secluded at home; a more significant factor was any prior sexual experience (8–9). At the time of the Benedictine Reform, the terminology changed drastically, a distinction being made between mynecenas "vowesses," corresponding to male munecas, and nunnan "cloistered women," comparable to preostas inasmuch as nunnan lived in the secular world (9–10).

Knowles asserts that "monasticism was wholly extinct" by the 920s due to its "complete collapse. . . by the end of the ninth century"; whether or not this was due to Viking raiding, we cannot deny a profound impact. The tenth-century reformers at any rate believed that monasticism had almost disappeared, and ninth-century authors believed the Vikings were to blame (12–13) and they imagined a glorious monastic past (14).

According to Æthelwold, Augustine established minsters after the model of the first apostles' communities, without personal property (15–16). Where his text breaks off, we should imagine an account like those we find elsewhere of the decay leaving Glastonbury the sole defender of the Benedictine Rule (16–17).

The reform movement was adamant that secular overlordship had to go; the reformers' solution was to choose the king as their overlord (17–18). Using Bede as their authority, they created the fiction that the eighth century was characterized by Benedictine monasteries and monastic cathedrals; even William of Malmesbury bought this account, and believed that the cathedral at Canterbury used to be staffed by monks (18–20).

Bede's Ecclesiastical History mostly describes events prior to the author's lifetime and geographically removed from Jarrow (20–2). His main aim was didactic (to "spur on to imitate the good"): though it contains both good and bad exempla, it focuses primarily on the former. He appears reticent to describe episcopal excess in his own day, apparently out of a concern to undermine the authority of the Church in a work for general consumption, but perhaps also because God's judgement was not yet apparent on contemporary affairs (22–3). He remarks on such model houses as Whitby, Melrose, and Barking, but does not comment on irregular monasteries. He does not assume that all monastic life is based on a single rule, but he does believe monastic life should follow a rule (23).

Bede also propagated the idea of a unified English (Christian, latinate) identity, leading him to play down the diversity of monastic practice in his day; he has King Oswiu declare that all Christians ought to follow one rule of life. Accordingly, Bede's descriptions of minster life are strikingly uniform (23–5). His account of sixth- and seventh-century monasticism was to shape the later understanding of the period, including Æthelwold's and today's (25).

There has been no serious study of English monasticism prior to the Benedictine Reform; accordingly, Bede has remained the chief source. Knowles, as a Benedictine historiographer, sought to read Benedictinism into Bede (25–7). John Blair has used landscape and archaeology to argue for greater continuity in pastoral organization (27–8).

[C2: The Ideal Minster] Just as a monastic rule is an expression of an ideal, so the St Gall floor plan expresses an ideal ordering of space in a Benedictine monastery that may serve comparison with narrative accounts, and also with the written ideal of the Benedictine Rule (34–8). Minsters were total institutions in the sense that they far greater control over the individual than most social institutions, beginning with the physical boundary imposed by its perimeter. The most striking way in which total institutions exert control is by "break[ing] down the barriers between sleep, work and play which most societies tend to perform in separate spaces" (38–9). Minsters differ from most total institutions (prisons, hospitals, barracks) in lacking a small staff that moves between institution and outside world: the abbot shares the deprivations of his flock. The minster's members enter its walls voluntarily, but initiation resembles that of other total institutions (39–40). The monastery's division of time into seven hours of prayer resembles the strict division of time in other total institutions (40–1). In more profound ways, however, the minster is not like other total institutions: the minster is egalitarian and voluntary, and every member pursues their own spiritual salvation (41–2).

Benedict of Nursia recommended self-sufficiency to avoid contact with the outside world. The St Gall draftsman follows this advice to the letter, even containing an inner area south of the church that prevents the brothers from having to access the outer ring of buildings (42–3). Even so, the plan contains a great number of windows to the outside world, and there are visitors' quarters, an external school, and various workshops [for use by outsiders]. Sullivan has argued that this reflects an intentional interaction with the outside world, which was to be managed in a fashion becoming of a monk (43–4). There are subtle problems with Sullivan's argument, which are tackled in the pages that follow; Bentham and Foucault are also dealt with (44–6). In Anglo-Saxon reality, it seems the division of space was as much dictated by the landscape of donated land, preexisting structures, and proximity to settlements as by monastic ideals (46–7). There are many early Anglo-Saxon injunctions against wandering monks, but these could only be followed if minsters were truly self-sustaining (47–8). It is clear from sources that the communal religious life in early Anglo-Saxon England was characterized by life under a rule, and the Benedictine Rule was well known in seventh-century England; the oldest surviving copy is from southwestern England of the eighth century. Since Bede moreover hammers on its use during his lifetime, it has long been assumed that early Anglo-Saxon monasticism was built around it. It has widely been held that even Augustine was a Benedictine, although the Rule itself makes clear that monks should not engage in pastoral activity (49–51). This understanding of monastic organization was first challenged in 1957, and it has drawn the nature of early monasticism into question (51–2). Attention to the role of Celtic rules, notably that of Columbanus, has increased as evidence for Benedictine observance has waned (52–3). Columbanus wrote two rules, but the way of life he advocated was probably propagated orally with reference to multiple written sources including the Benedictine Rule. The Benedictine Rule probably reached England via Irish monasteries in northern Gaul in the seventh century, for instance via Wilfrid who spent time on the Continent (53–4). The Vita S. Ceolfridi indicates that Benedict Biscop, founder of Wearmouth, took an active interest in the organization of the religious life while travelling on the Continent; Bede has him stress the importance of his decreta, based on visits to seventeen monasteries, on his deathbed; for his succession, he emphasized the Benedictine Rule ought to be consulted (54–5). Regular practice appears to have been coposite: Alcuin in 793 advised the minsters to hold to the rules laid down for them by Benedict Biscop and Ceolfrith, but also to consult the Benedictine Rule, suggesting this was not already the sole guiding rule. Cuthbert is said to have brought a discipline to Lindisfarne that was thereafter followed "along with the Rule of St Benedict." The Benedictine Rule had a currency in southern England as well: Exeter and Nursling seem to have combined it with a Celtic-inspired rule, and Aldhelm praises Benedict of Nursia (55–7). The use of preexisting rules at least for the organization of the office of the hours appears certain (57–8). Eighth- and early ninth-century synods did not legislate for a particular rule to be followed (58), but the 786 council prescribed that canons live canonically but monks and nuns regularly, so that the two might be told apart, and both be told apart from seculares. This distinction is new for England and appears to draw on Chrodegang of Metz and Frankish practice (58–60).

The one point of evidence for Continental influence on the organization of cathedral communities is in Christ Church, Canterbury of the early ninth century: Archbishop Wulfred urged his canons to attend the office of the hours and live communally, while private property could be maintained as long as it not be alienated from the community or put to improper use — details echoing the Rule of Chrodegang (61). The way Bede tells the story, the teachers that had come with Augustine began to imitate the early apostles upon arrival, spending their days in prayer and spurning worldly goods (62–3). Bede reports that Augustine consulted Pope Gregory the Great on the best form of permanent residence; Gregory responded that bishop and priests ought to share the early apostolic way of life, owning everything in common, and stressed Augustine's knowledge of monastic rules (63). Whereas early monastics intended for religious communities to live in isolation from society and thereby set an example of a better type of society, Gregory, prompted by the urgency of the latter days, intended for ecclesiastics to preach to the laity. He had elsewhere called preaching and monasticism incompatible, but the imminence of the end rendered this irrelevant (63–4). The relevant question is how Gregory's advice was received. The establishment of Sts Peter and Paul as a second, monastic institution outside the city walls may have been a convenient solution for the creation of two tiers: the monks at Peter and Paul did not have the baggage of family and property that required exceptions to poverty regulations at cathedral minsters (65). Wallace-Hadrill has suggested that Bede intended his detailed account of the Canterbury constellation as a guide for institutions in his own day. In this context, Foot makes a subtle point about where Bede stands; although he approves of both bishops and abbots living monastically, what he meant to emphasize is that bishops could best fulfil their preaching duties from a contemplative footing (65–7). Bede felt strongly about the analogy of the family applied to religious communities (69–72).

[3: The Making of Minsters] Doubts the affluence projected back onto early minsters by later authors (75–6). Many minsters were created by laymen out of devotional piety (80–1). Land might have been granted in expectation of prayers for the grantor's soul (82–4). Sometimes the spiritual needs of the wider community were a reason to establish a minster (85–6).

All early medieval monastic houses sought to recreate early apostolic conditions, including the prohibition of personal property. They did, however, require a good deal of land to sustain themselves. To ensure the heirs of donors would not renege on their ancestors' generosity, one imagines diplomas were produced (87–8). Foot continues along these lines to study the documentary, archaeological and economic evidence of early monastic establishments (chapter runs until p. 137). If monasticism did experience a decline, this must have born a relation to their dependence on the goodwill of the nobility: diploma or not, a landowner could always decide to put his or her land to other purposes (134–5).

author: Wrenn, C. R.
title: Some Aspects of Anglo-Saxon Theology
publication: Studies in Language, Literature, and Culture of the Middle Ages and Later
eds: E. Bagby Atwood and Archibald A. Hill
abstract:
Alfred wrote his Sermo de sacrificio in die Paschae half a century before the condemnation of Archdeacon Berengar of Tours for taking too symbolist a reading of the Eucharist. He takes cues from Augustine, Jerome, and Gregory, and mentions all three (184–5). "He sought with great care to express the received Catholic teaching so as to include in his thought on the divine mystery of the sacrifice of the Mass both the symbolist and the realist elements of faith. While stressing that the bread and wine are a symbolizing, getacnung, of the body and blood, and that they are received at the Communion spiritually, gastlice, and not in their natural materiality, he at the same time relates two stories of visions granted to doubters of the carnal reality which showed to the recipients at the consecration visible portions of physical flesh and blood" (185). Wrenn notes that gastlice may have had "a less precise and a less immaterial connotation" than today's spiritually. He asserts that "the value of this sermon as theology lies in its reconciling of the symbolist with the carnal interpretation of the Eucharist and its emphasis on the fundamental fact of the mystery as something to be fully apprehended only by supplementing understanding by faith" (185). In all this, Ælfric does not take up a heterodox position: the triumph of the materialist understanding of transubstantiation postdates the 1050 condemnation of Berengar (185). Ælfric avoids rationalizing the divine mystery because he is addressing the uneducated (186).

The remainder of the essay concerns Eadmer's Tractatus de Conceptione Beatae Mariae Virginis. Wrenn considers Ælfric's work on the Eucharist and Eadmer's on the Immaculate Conception the two major Anglo-Saxon contributions to theology (189).

author: Lendinara, Patrizia
title: The World of Anglo-Saxon Learning
publication: The Cambridge Companion to Old English Literature
abstract: An overview that is broad-ranging inasmuch as it touches on a range of texts. It could be said to lack somewhat in depth, using popularly studied poems to make inferences about the state of learning (e.g. The Seafarer for its knowledge of ornithology). Like most studies of the subject, it does not explain how widely the monastic and cathedral schools reached into society except to say that the former were there for oblates and novices in the first instance. Claims equal opportunities for men and women. Does not discuss Alfred's educational ambitions.

author: Orme, Nicholas
title: Medieval Schools: From Roman Britain to Renaissance England
abstract:
Although the chapter covering Anglo-Saxon England is brief, it provides an excellent overview, starting with the churches established in Canterbury in 597. Points out that cathedrals and monasteries were very similar institutions in the early period: monasteries often served "as centres of worship and pastoral care for the surrounding countryside," while many bishops were monks (18–19). Bede is our main source for education at this time. The Benedictine Rule acknowledges the need to educate both child oblates, perhaps from the age of seven, and novices (19–20). Cathedrals would have taken both types of recruits as well, but not women; women were only educated in double houses. Education need not have been continuous but may have happened as needed, meaning when new recruits arrived; their numbers would typically have been small. Teaching would probably have been carried out by senior clergy, monks, or nuns specializing in this task, though in the small scale of the earlier times bishops, abbots, and abbesses may occasionally have taught as well (20). Education sprang up in Kent shortly after 597 (21–2), and in northern England in the course of the seventh century (22–3). Orme identifies some further centres of learning, and discusses the training of women (23–4). The quality of education was uneven: where monasteries were established for the acquisition of land, learning lagged behind; a number of anecdotes lament the state of learning among monks and priests (24–5).

King Sigeberht of East Anglia was an early example of a lay litteratus; he even founded a school. Like his contemporaries Oswald and Oswiu, he appears to have been educated while in exile. Oswiu's son Aldfrith likewise read and taught; he is probably the addressee of Aldhelm's treatise on metre. Ceolwulf of Northumbria and Ælfwald of East Anglia could also read (25).

Educated laymen in some cases may have been trained as monks but abandoned the monastic life; others may have pursued education because it was fashionable among noblemen abroad. Bishop Wilfrid of York educated boys intending to become clergy or warriors; those that did not pursue the former path he commended to the king (25–6). Noble households may also have been centres of education (26). Pupils here would have learned to read Latin. The difficulty of this enterprise will have given rise to vernacular writings (26–27).

The curriculum leaned heavily on Roman customs: the alphabet learned was Roman. The Paternoster was the first text learned; the Psalms were a staple, for learning to read as well as sing. Pupils likely memorized the Psalms before fully understanding them (27–8).

The Roman Donatus wrote two grammatical textbooks that were influential after the collapse of Rome. Both are aimed at Latin speakers learning the elements of language. They are not particularly fit for new learners of Latin, nor do they discuss Christian names and paradigms. Accordingly, from the fifth century onwards Donatus was increasingly revised to meet these new needs, and it was probably such revisions that were used in Anglo-Saxon classrooms, followed by Psalms, gospels, and late Roman Christian poetry including Juvencus, Sedulius, Arator, and Prosper of Aquitaine (28–9). Priscian was probably reserved for the best students, and the Aeneid read by few. Metre was difficult to teach except orally by fluent teachers, but Bede and Aldhelm produced handbooks. Hadrian and Theodore taught a range of advanced subjects. Scriptural interpretation and computistics became well established areas of study; Bede produced books on these matters (30–1).

We know little about the physical surroundings of instruction, whether religious houses has special rooms for the purpose. The divine office left space for teaching at three times of day: two morning blocks and one in the afternoon, for an approximate total of six hours. "Instruction must have been partly done in English until the pupils had progressed far enough to understand and speak Latin fluently. Bede's pupil Cuthbert, in his account of his master's last days, talks of Bede dictating to his pupils while they wrote," texts including Isidore and the Gospel of John (31–2).

Under duress of Viking raiding, four bishoprics and some of the religious houses disappeared, particularly those for women; the ones that survived became less strictly monastic, with clergy owning property, marrying, and living outside the community; such communities are referred to as minsters (32). They still engaged in daily worship and needed to educate their members to that end, but we don't know how that was done; much of what we think we know is based on Alfred's famously critical retrospective. Latin charters from Christ Church Canterbury do in fact deteriorate in calligraphy, spelling, and style between the 860s and 880s, and Asser suggests Alfred was illiterate in one way or another until he was twelve, suggesting the royal household didn't have much by way of a school; but ultimately we have too little information to test Alfred's depiction (32–34). To stem the tide, Alfred established a modest number of religious houses, but he had to turn to foreigners and children to staff them, they never became famous houses, and they failed to inspire imitation. Alfred also set up a royal school for his own children and those of his nobility and some others; it taught Latin and English reading as well as writing. The school is thus described in Asser's biography, but we hear nothing about it after. A third strategy of Alfred's was to encourage English reading and writing by commissioning a series of translations and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. This strategy may in fact have responded to growing demand for English literature, suggesting an increase in vernacular literacy even before Alfred initiated his programme. The later Benedictine Reform, though keen on its Latin, likewise used English to reach larger audiences in the works of Ælfric, Wulfstan, and Byrhtferth (35).

It was in part the peace guaranteed by Alfred's successors that made the monastic revival possible. Dunstan, Æthelwold, Oda, and Oswald turned to monasticism between the 930s and 950s, and their kings Eadred and Edgar supported them. These monastic pioneers established several houses, and Æthelwold as bishop installed monks at his cathedral and the neighbouring minster in Winchester; Oswald too became a bishop and made Worcester Cathedral a monastic institution. "By the end of the tenth century the monastic life was observed in about forty religious houses of men, mostly former minsters, and in about a dozen houses of women — now made up of women alone, not double foundations." The revival prompted the invitation of foreign teachers (36). The Regularis concordia instructs in the monastic care and duties of children, who appear to have been monks in training (37–7).

The next wave of Viking attacks slowed the pace of the monastic revival; many religious houses remained minsters, "staffed by canons, priests, or clerks," including all but four of the cathedrals and at least a hundred other minsters. Owing among other things to their lack of uniformity, we know little about their educational practices until they too came under a reforming influence led by Bishop Leofric and Earl (later King) Harold in the mid-eleventh century. Leofric enlarged the Rule of Chrodegang; it too saw a role for children training to become clerics (37–8). Harold's establishment attracted Master Abelard of Liège to bring Continental discipline to his minster, and children partook of the Office and reading lessons (38).

Between 600 and 900, pastoral care had mostly been in the hands of monastic and minster monks and clergy; these served large areas, which involved travel either by the clergy or by the people. In the tenth and twelfth centuries, local churches took off and assumed ministry locally. This development was helped by the introduction of tithing, which paid for the local priest. Local churches eventually got the independence of having their own parishes; this led to the parish system, with a rural church every few miles serving a small area (38–9). As a consequence, priests soon outnumbered monks; there were thousands by 1066, and each priest had a clerk to assist in the services, and that task required at least an accurate pronunciation of Latin. Parish clergy required education but could also themselves act as teachers, instructing their parishioners. Theodulf of Orléans's Capitula (c. 800) touch on education: priests were to hold schools, not refusing any children whose parents wanted them to learn to read, and they could not charge for their services though they could accept voluntary contributions. The Capitula circulated in England in two languages; though they were not officially adopted by the Church, Bishop Wulfstan himself reissued them in the eleventh century, the Latin text being drafted by Ælfric (39; this is ÆLat 2, PSL). These texts touch on the instruction of boys to help in church, implying that priests were to teach their clerks to read so that they might themselves be trained to become priests, as is known to have happened in later centuries. We should probably not envision priests as teaching classes of children; no recommendations to this effect survive, and post-Conquest references to priests teaching are indeterminate (39–40).

The curriculum for the period 800–1100 continued along traditional lines; the Latin alphabet was extended to include common abbreviations but also Old English characters following z, and the Latin Paternoster was still the first (Latin) reading text. This would be followed by the Psalms, grammar, and the reading of approved Latin works (40). A book-list of Æthelstan's at SS Peter and Paul, Canterbury lists thirteen titles probably used for teaching: they include Isidore's De natura rerum, Donatus's grammars and a gloss on them, and a work of Alcuin's probably on grammar or orthography; further a "parsing grammar" in question-and-answer format; dialogues (presumably colloquies); two handbooks on metre; and four literary texts: Persius, Cato, the Apocalypse, and Sedulius (40–1). Abbo of Fleury wrote an advanced grammar for his students at Ramsey; Byrhtferth says the grammarians Sergius and Priscian were studied there, too. Other sources mention Cato, the Benedictine Rule, Bede, and Scripture, particularly Proverbs (41). Works of poetry, both pagan and Christian, are found in other book-lists (41–2).

Ælfric's grammar is addressed to children (see preface) and claims to be in both Latin and English in order to teach both simultaneously; it corresponds to the revisionary tradition of both of Donatus's textbooks, and uses illustrative names like Dunstan, Æthelwold, and Edgar (42). The work's use of the English language is excused in the preface with the claim to address children only. In reality, teachers must have used English orally from the beginnings of Christian instruction until pupils were fluent in Latin, and learning must have involved translation; bilingual glossaries also provide clues to this. In Ælfric's day, however, the written use of English was spreading, and his anglophone grammar of Latin exploited this fact (43).

The colloquy tradition is introduced (44–6); these too suggest boys in monasteries rose for matins and spent three periods in school: two in the morning and one in the afternoon. But the services in between would also at the time have been considered educational. Classrooms are never mentioned, though benches are; a monk tasked with this duty runs the school, and he seems to have had an assistant. Writing materials are detailed that would, however, also have been used in the scriptorium (45). There is also reference to corporeal punishment (45–6)

The first, unreliable evidence of institutions taking in pupils from the outside appears to date to the late eleventh century. (All of the charters before 1200 are suspect, but the trend continues thereafter.) The evidence is that minsters in particular were commissioned to hold schools "for the city and its villages," as one document puts it. These charters document the shift from schools as the internal affairs of monasteries, minsters, and noble households to public institutions. We should nevertheless be cautious about assuming that this development was born suddenly out of its Anglo-Norman environment, as it is likely that we are looking instead at a development that was a long time in the making. Already Alfred admitted noble youths to his school, and religious houses might have admitted outsiders as a way of doing favours or bringing in money. See Leach, The Schools of Medieval England 76–9 for this argument (46–50). [It may be worth recalling in this context that Theodulf of Orléans prescribed c. 800 that priests ought to hold schools for the public, free of charge; if this norm was indeed adopted in Frankish territories and persisted into the late eleventh century, then it is still likely that the Normans would have pushed to introduce it in England as well. See Orme p. 39, PSL.]

author: Kornexl, Lucia
title: From Ælfric to John of Cornwall: Evidence for Vernacular Grammar Teaching in Pre- and Post-Conquest England
publication: Bookmarks from the Past: Studies in Early English Language and Literature in Honour of Helmut Gneuss
abstract: Discusses Ælfric's approach, then moves to post-Conquest grammar teaching and the role of English, with an interest in Ælfric's afterlives.

author: Gneuss, Helmut
title: Bücher und Leser in England im zehnten Jahrhundert
abstract:
"Der Bildungsstand im Umkreis der Bischöfe und in den reformierten oder neugegründeten Klöstern scheint beachtlich gewesen zu sein; von dort dürfte auch fast alles stammen, was uns an Handschriften aus der Zeit erhalten ist. Nur Vermutungen kann man anstellen über Lesestoff, Lesefähigkeit und Lateinkenntnisse der sicher nicht wenigen Weltgeistlichen in Stiftskirchen und — soweit es sie schon gab — Pfarrkirchen. Sie können, wenn sie Priester waren, ihr Amt kaum ohne gewisse Lateinkenntnisse ausgeübt haben, und wenn wir Bestimmungen in den — ins Altenglische übertragenen — Capitula Theodulfi (Kap. 19-20), in Ælfrics Hirtenbriefen (III.80f. und 3.40) und in den sog. Canons of Edgar (Kap. 51) Wulfstans als gültig und befolgt ansehen dürfen, 17 so hätten wir spätestens seit dem 10. Jahrhundert in England die Einrichtung der schola, der mit einer Kirche verbundenen Schule, in der die Weltgeistlichen zu lehren verpflichtet waren, um für den Nachwuchs ihres Standes zu sorgen, aber offenbar auch, um jenen ihrer Schüler zumindest eine Elementarbildung zu vermitteln, die von ihren Eltern nicht für den geistlichen Beruf bestimmt waren. Die genannten Bestimmungen setzen bei den lehrenden Klerikern einen gewissen Bildungsstand voraus. Inwieweit sie in die Praxis umgesetzt wurden, wissen wir nicht, aber die wohlbekannte Bemerkung Ælfrics im Vorwort zu seiner Genesis-Übersetzung deutet darauf hin, daß es solchen Unterricht im 10. Jahrhundert in der Tat gegeben hat; Ælfric erwähnt hier, daß er in seiner Jugend von einem Priester unterrichtet wurde, der das Lateinische be dæle verstand." (110).

Turning to lay literacy, Gneuss starts with Alfred's plan, which concerned the children (or at least the sons) of all free Anglo-Saxons (or the well-to-do at any rate). His plan was never executed (110–11). We do know that Alfred, his son Edward the Elder, and Athelstan could read, and read Latin; Edgar was likely literate as well (111). Other nobles must have been able to read: they were taught at Alfred's court school as children, but some likely also attended the cathedral schools and monastic schools that were aimed primarily at oblates (111–12). Dunstan is said to have taken private education before he joined the clergy at Glastonbury as a child, and was given more than just spiritual tasks at Athelstan's court. Æthelwold likewise studied sacris litterarum studia as a child and ended up working at Athelstan's court; both were not made priests and monks until later (112). A modest number of nobles is said to have owned books, though they may have had them read to them, except Alfred and Æthelweard [but see Godden, PSL]. A key question is why so much was translated into the vernacular not just in Alfred's day, but in the century and half that followed. Was this a response to a lack of learning among the clergy? (112–13).

Ælfric and Abbo show in their grammatical treatises that the study of Latin led to reflections on the vernacular (113–14). Even before Ælfric, the reformers must have studied grammar: tenth-century grammars survive, not to mention encyclopaedic literature by Isidore and Martianus Capella, commentaries by Remigius of Auxerre, and linguistic reference works circulating under the names of Bede and Alcuin. The leaders of the movement studied and taught grammar according to their vitae. Byrhtferth in his manual covers grammar, too, and 14 copies of Ælfric's Grammar survive (114).

The study of Latin and grammar surely played a large role at all the cathedral schools and monastic schools and elsewhere; Ælfric's focus on inflection shows that this would have been the central focus, as opposed to phonetics or syntax. The systematic terminology used by Ælfric and Byrhtferth may well date back to the Winchester school of Æthelwold. Ælfric's Colloquy and Glossary are further indications of the nature of Latin education. The Glossary and interlinear glosses served not just the study of Latin, but of Old English as well (114–15).

As Korhammer and Lendinara have shown, glossators were interested in word order and were trained to use VSO. It is also clear Anglo-Saxon litterati were familiar with etymology, synonymy, and glossography. Ælfric's homilies (among other texts) show that these lessons were applied to the vernacular as well as Latin (116). Glossaries will have been present in all larger libraries of the tenth century; these would have served study, but above all the reading of difficult texts (117).

Latin metre was taught alongside grammar, as Anglo-Latin verse shows. The great ancient handbooks of rhetoric were not known to the Anglo-Saxons, but shorter treatments survived in Isidore, Martianus Capella, Bede, and Byrhtferth. These may be responsible for the principles of elocutio found in vernacular texts; Wulfstan, and to a lesser degree Ælfric, may have had a conscious knowledge of them.
