Their sermons can, however, not credibly be divided into the classical movements of exordium, narratio, argumentum, and conclusio [contrast Griffith, PSL] (118–19).

There is need of a systematic study of translation in Anglo-Saxon England, focusing on how problems of syntax, lexicology, and style were tackled. Both Alfred and Ælfric echo Horace and Jerome when they speak of sense-for-sense translation (though they may not have known Horace). Gneuss believes a development of the tradition of translation into Old English may be discerned between that of Bede and those by Ælfric, though not every translator fits into this development; Æthelwold's Benedictine Rule (c. 970) is practically flawless (119–20).

A standard language may be discerned from the tenth century onwards: from this time on, nearly all texts and glosses reflect a southern dialect. The southern origin of the Benedictine Reform cannot be held responsible for this, as a good number of their monasteries were in Mercia and East Anglia (120). It is also relevant in this context that the second half of the tenth century gave rise to a differentiation between scripts for Latin and vernacular text; it is possible this was normatively introduced. A further phenomenon consists in Winchester words, a highly standardized use of language stemming from Æthelwold's Winchester school, including also a standard inflection, as has been shown for an autograph of the first series of Catholic Homilies. Gneuss suggests there may be a connection between the Winchester school and the spread of a southern dialectal standard, but withholds final judgement in the expectation of more definite findings by DOE and others (121–2).

There was no real knowledge of Greek in England after Bede; we know little about contact with Old French, and Gneuss leaves assessment of the Celtic question to the experts. He is doubtful that Old English and Old Norse were as mutually intelligible as is often suggested. Instead, Scandinavian settlers in England appear to have been increasingly concerned to learn Old English. Mutual intelligibility did exist with Old Saxon (122–3).

Libraries of the tenth century were characterized by efforts to rebuild. Manuscripts of the seventh and eighth centuries were mostly lost: texts had to be imported from the Continent; few books were produced in the ninth century; and Anglo-Saxon scriptoria ramped up their production starting in the early tenth century. Alfred was able to use episcopal libraries but seems not to have had a substantial royal library (124). The real manuscript centres of the tenth century were some forty Benedictine monasteries and the cathedral minsters. Late medieval and sixteenth-century events have obscured our view of the situation: most traceable manuscripts of the tenth and eleventh centuries stem from Canterbury (2 centres) and Worcester, and some from Winchester (3 centres); the number of production centres increases and diversifies in the eleventh century (124–5).

Texts that saw much use include

  • The Alfredian translations;
  • The West Saxon Gospels;
  • The Benedictine Rule in Æthelwold's translation;
  • Ælfric, especially his Catholic Homilies.

Thus theology was front and centre, but history and geography were also represented. Medical handbooks should also be mentioned; teaching texts include the Psalter and Ælfric's Grammar. Of the poetry we can only say that it still had an audience in the tenth century (125–6) and that its contents suggest an interest in history (126–7).

Readers of Latin were professionally required to read the Gospels and Psalter, but not the whole Bible; their classics were the Church Fathers, though with significant gaps (128). Gregory was especially widespread, as were Bede and the Benedictine Rule. Homiliaries such as that of Paul the Deacon, Haymo of Auxerre, Smaragdus, Saint-Père-de-Chartres, and Caesarius of Arles were used in the Night Office and for private reading. Also read were saints' lives; shortened versions were used in the Office (128–9). Carolingian authors and handbooks were well represented (129); classical Latin literature was confined to didactic uses (129–30).

author: Sauer, Hans
title: Theodulfi capitula in England
abstract:
Theodulf, made Bishop of Orléans and Abbot of Fleury by Charlemagne about 798, wrote the Capitula as a manual for the parish priests in his bishopric (2). His writings about this time comprise:

  • c. 800: the Theodulfi Capitula that served as the basis of two Old English translations;
  • 800x813: a second capitulary (ThCapII);
  • 809: De processione Spiritus Sancti, commissioned by Charlemagne;
  • probably in 812: Liber de ordine baptismi, commissioned by Archbishop Magnus of Sens;
  • 813: likely author of the decisions made at the Chalon synod.

He may have helped ghostwrite the 791 Libri Carolini. Finally, a number of homilies were circulated under his name; their authenticity is not certain (2–3).

The dating c. 800 is justified with the reasoning that he would have wanted these drastic reform measures carried out sooner rather than later; the hard limits are 797 and 818 (7).

The Capitula were intended as a guide to practical pastoral care and for the reform of ecclesiastical and religious life in the parishes of Theodulf's bishopric; he himself indicates they serve "ad emendationem uitae." They instruct rural priests how they are to conduct their own lives but also set norms for the religious lives of the laity. There is no mention of the canons found in cathedrals and collegiate churches, who tended to live together in ways reminiscent of monastic rules; monasteries and monks are barely mentioned, though the Benedictine Rule is liberally addressed in the opening chapter (7–8).

Theodulf refers to grave defects that have come to his attention:

  • Churches used for nonreligious purposes (e.g. as barns);
  • Questionable morals among the priests;
  • Poorly educated priests
  • Priests unwilling to carry out their tasks.

The inadequacy of many priests may be explained in part by their low social standing and insecurity of income, which led them to supplement it by means not permitted (8–9). Thus Theodulf could not afford to go into abstract theological questions in his Capitula but had to address the concrete state of affairs (8). The wide dissemination of his work suggests it was no different in other bishoprics (9).

The genre capitulary corresponds to Theodulf's own references to his text (haec capitula; capitularium). Episcopal capitularies, of which Theodulf's is the first, are concise legal manuals for Frankish priests issued between 800 and 930, containing legally binding decisions for the discipline and administration of a parish with regard to both clergy and laity; they may have been read out at synods and were then probably sent to the clergy in writing (10; definition according to Brommer). Their name derives from their division into chapters (10–11). The tone even of Theodulf's Capitula varies between beseeching, oughts, precepts and prohibitions, threats of excommunication, and threats of the canon-legal persecution of clergymen; he also reminds priests of the latter-day reckoning (11).

The Capitula may be roughly divided into instructions for the priests themselves and those they ought to communicate to the laity (mostly admonishments). It is not in all respects a systematic work (12–13), but certain themes can be discerned (13–15).

Theodulf's second capitulary contains:

  1. A first part resembling the first part of the first Capitula, which even repeats some of its contents;
  2. A new penitential and a list of the eight cardinal sins based on a passage in the first Capitula;
  3. A new manual of confession;
  4. A new manual of the confession of the ill and the anointing of the sick (15–16).

Theodulf often names the Bible as a source, but he also frequently refers more vaguely to canons (i.e. decisions made at synods and councils), the Fathers (a reference in this case to the Benedictine Rule), and customs. Indeed the Benedictine Rule is a major source of the work. Charlemagne's capitularies are a major influence, and Gregory's Homiliarium in evangelia influenced the preface and first chapter, and perhaps cap. 37; capp. 37–8 furthermore make use of Caesarius of Arles (16–17).

Witnesses with English connections:

  1. CCCC 201 contains both the Latin text and an Old English translation of the Capitula, separated by the Macarius homily (30–7);
  2. Bodley 865 contains a fragment (starting near the end of cap. 25) of a bilingual witness, each Latin chapter followed by its Old English translation (38–45);
  3. CCCC 265 contains the [Latin] Capitula as well as the shorter version of the ThCapII (45–50);
  4. Bodley, Barlow 37 contains the [Latin] Capitula and the shortened version of ThCapII and additional excerpts from the Capitula (50–5).

Absence of evidence suggests that the Capitula did not enjoy a wide dissemination in England; instead, we may assume they were of particular interest to bishops looking to improve pastoral care and parish discipline (71–4). The most we can say about it is that, as Bethurum put it, the Capitula were "one of the most popular collections of canons in England in the tenth and eleventh centuries" (74). The fact that the manuscripts represent three source groupings suggest that the text came to England several times over, in different redactions. The manuscripts date to the eleventh and twelfth centuries; the translations probably to the second half of the tenth (for ThCapA) and the early eleventh (ThCapB). Wulfstan owned the Capitula about 1000; the text likely have reached England by the second half of the tenth century, probably in the context of the Benedictine Reform (74), since Ælfric and Wulfstan make clear they were not just interested in establishing discipline in the monasteries but also among secular clergy (74–5). It may furthermore be noted that Vercelli Homily III appears to quote from the Capitula, suggesting the work may have reached England in the first half of the tenth century (75).

Early claims that Ælfric produced the more liberal translation have been proved false from differences in content: Ælfric's letter to the clergy for Wulfstan allows a priest's female relatives in his house, while Theodulf expressly forbids it. Linguistic differences likewise make clear Ælfric was not the translator (89). Sauer condemns the easy general assumption that the translation is late (meaning between 950 and 1050) (90–1) but he does agree with the dating, particularly the late tenth century (209–10); he just insists most scholars have failed to base themselves on the relevant data, namely language and style (91). Each translation is based on the exemplar of the Latin text in the same manuscript; idiosyncrasies in the Latin make clear the translations were not based on the copy within the same manuscript (103–17). Whereas the B translation is more literal (113), neither adds substantial new thought (171–1). The A translation is most likely from the second half of the tenth century (209, 271), but it contains elements that are best understood as Anglian (206–8); a detailed lexicological study comes to the same conclusion (summarized at 268–71). The B translation is purely late West Saxon (211), was produced later than the A translation and may be assumed to date to the early eleventh century (273–4). The A translation may predate the writings of Ælfric and Wulfstan and most likely stems from "das (süd)westliche Mittelland" (271). The surviving copy of the B translation may not be far removed from the first copy of the translation (273–4). Neither translation shows affinity with the Winchester group; neither is characterized by Winchester words (274–6).

A chapter studies the influence of the Capitula on Old English literature; although Ælfric used Theodulf's Liber de ordine baptismi, it is not certain whether he used the Capitula. Despite the generic similarity between the Capitula and Ælfric's pastoral letters, the latter do not demonstrably borrow from the former; Ælfric is more likely to have taken the sentiments from other texts we know he used (281–2). Wulfstan did make use of the Capitula (282–91) and indeed seems to have known the A translation (290–1), but the suggestion that he commissioned it cannot be proved and is unlikely (291).

author: Derolez, R[ené]
title: ‘Those Things Are Difficult to Express in English...’
abstract: Byrhtferth's Enchiridion illustrates the difficulty of conveying technical content to an audience with limited Latin. His effort stands in a tradition that struggled to translate certain concepts. Ælfric's Grammar suggests that Old English was less elegant than Latin for its scantiness of coordinating conjunctions; he also calls the vernacular unfit for the discussion of orthography/phonology, diphthongs, and adverbs, though he does not explain why. "As the translator of part of the Old Testament Ælfric was fully conscious of its socio-cultural problems and especially of the possible religious amnd moral consequences should his translation fall into the hands of lay persons who might decide to live as the patriarchs had done, or according to Moses's law" (474). Ælfric also points out in his Preface to Genesis that Latin and Old English each had their own way of expressing things, requiring a degree of freedom in translation. Byrhtferth repeatedly explains his English translations as making the computistical concepts clearer, particularly for young men (474–5). Byrhtferth lacked Ælfric's constraint of not daring ("we ne durron") to add commentary to his text (475). Byrhtferth furthermore addresses both readers (rædere) and listeners (hlosnere), in addition to a variety of categories (cleric, mynsterman, preost, broþor). "It was specifically for them ["uplandish priests"] that he [Byrhtferth] explains the zodiac. . . , the term atomos. . . , the paschal cycle. . . and even the use of the letters of the Latin alphabet for numeration (475). Derolez considers this attention consistent with Ælfric's observations on the lack of knowledge among the secular clergy (475–6).

author: Barrow, Julia
title: The Community of Worcester, 961–c. 1100
publication: St Oswald of Worcester: Life and Influence
abstract: Reconstructs the development of the Worcester community under the influence of the Benedictine Reform with reference to documentary evidence, with special attention to the question whether the change was sudden, as reported, or more gradual. There is no evidence of a sudden round of firings at the cathedral. Striking is that witnesses typically describe themselves by their clerical grade: clerk, deacon, priest; the term monk is more rarely used, and sometimes refers to someone owning property, suggesting that monastic vows were taken with a grain of salt (87–8). Winchester did not refer to its monks as clerks; in Worcester, this was done if they had reached major clerical grades, so no strict distinction emerges between secular and monastic clergy.

author: Riché, Pierre
title: Education and Culture in the Barbarian West: From the Sixth through the Eighth Century
abstract:
The educational efforts associated with the conversion of England are briefly introduced (317–22). It is pointed out that English aristocrats who wanted their children educated sent them into monasteries with no intention of them becoming monks (322–3).

When Theodore and Hadrian were sent to reform the English Church in 669, Theodore also revitalized the episcopal school at Canterbury. Monks gathered around this school; Bede tells us that the curriculum comprised metrics, astronomy, and computistics, while other sources mention medicine, exegesis, and Greek (369–71). The monastic school of Peter and Paul, led by Benedict Bishop and then by Hadrian, would have had a closely similar character; Aldhelm claims to have learned metre, chant, arithmetic, astronomy, and Roman law there. Strikingly, monks went to study at the episcopal school, and secular clerics became monks at Peter and Paul; this demonstrates the close correspondence between the two institutions, but is also emblematic for the lack of a strict compartmentalization of the orders in England as compared to Gaul (372).

Aldhelm was monk at Malmesbury Abbey in Wessex and became its abbot before being consecrated the first Bishop of Sherbourne in 705; his contemporaries included Bishop Daniel of Winchester and Winfrid (Boniface), who studied and taught at Nursling Abbey and wrote two grammatical treatises for his students there. Glastonbury also had strong education, as did several convents (372–3). The literary style of these men shows that Wessex had its own approach to studies, influenced by the Celtic neighbours (373–4). Aldhelm observed that students were flocking to Ireland, but objected that England had fine masters too, so there was no need for this exodus (374). Wessex monks also showed Celtic influence in their affinity for missionary work: "[i]t is noteworthy that the Anglo-Saxons who left their country to evangelize Gaul and Germany were all trained in Irish schools or in schools influenced by Irishmen" (376–7, at 376). Also modelled on Irish examples was the larger share of convents found in Wessex (377).

Mercia, Essex, and East Anglia lacked important centres of learning, but they had monasteries. Briadon, Lichfield, and Crowland are the most important of them; Ely became important later on (377–8).

Northumbria on the other hand was home to famous schools. Benedict Bishop on his return from Rome established Wearmouth and Jarrow (St Paul and St Peter), and these soon eclipsed the Irish establishments at Lindisfarne and Whitby. Benedict Bishop also imported the Benedictine Rule for use in Northumbria, imported a great deal of art and architecture from the Continent, and persuaded the archcantor of Saint Peter to teach Roman chant to his monks and monks flocking in from elsewhere; Bede writes that "non solum autem idem Johannes ipsius monasterii fratres docebat, verum de omnibus pene ejusdem provinciae monasteriis ad audiendum eum qui cantandi erant periti confluebant" (379 and n. 112). Lindisfarne was conservative in comparison and produced no great literature after Cuthbert. The Lindisfarne Gospels were written under Eadfrid; although some see Mediterranean influence in its artistic style, it is clearly more Insular than the contemporary Codex Amiatinus (379–80). Bede studied under Benedict and joined Ceolfrid at Jarrow in 685. Through Benedict's library, he had access to a large collection of sacred and profane Continental literature, helping him acquire a clear style and a focus on communicating serious content that stands in strong contrast to Aldhelm's elaborate style and interest in riddles and poetic form (380–1). The episcopal schools of Hexham and York likewise showed Roman influence. Alcuin ran York's school for a while. A poem of Alcuin's survives which describes its curriculum, but Riché warns that this poem appears to describe a model school rather than an actual school. Alcuin's training at York determined much of his literary output, but he also continued his studies on the Continent, seeking material not taught at York (382–3).

Riché is quick to torpedo the notion that Anglo-Saxons of the seventh and eighth centuries brought back the liberal arts. Only Aldhelm lists them enumerates them, and not even following classical models. The Anglo-Saxons pursued grammar, writing their own treatises rather than simply copying familiar models, and they were excellent at computistics, but they neglected rhetoric, dialectic, and music, and they were not especially knowledgeable about medicine. Their interest in grammar stems from the great difference between Latin and Old English; it is also for this reason that they focused on pragmatic aspects of language and omitted theoretical discussions (384–7). Bede had a little Greek, and Aldhelm seems to have had more, but neither was thoroughly acquainted with Greek culture; Bede used Greek works in Latin translation, and so did Alcuin and his fellow York alumni (387–8). In fact, Bede condemned the liberal arts: whereas Gregory the Great in his commentary on 1 Kings describes them as a propaedeutic, Bede in his own work on the same condemns Christians who are tempted by the devil to study secular subjects (388–9). Both Bede and Aldhelm considered philosophy (i.e. rhetoric and dialectic) especially dangerous. Philosophy had been all but abandoned in the West, but Bede feared Pelagianism and even a good number of Isidore of Seville's works, which came close to pagan cosmology (389–91). Bede also did not use learning to explain miracles (391). Instead, Anglo-Saxon masters encouraged the study of grammar, which was needed to understand the Bible; all other learning was to be had from Scripture (391–2).

"As was true everywhere else during the period, the Anglo-Saxon intellectual renewal touched only an elite. We know of only about twenty episcopal and monastic centers where culture was favored. Furthermore, not all clerics and monks in these centers were lettered. Bede certainly did not teach all the six hundred monks who comprised the community at Jarrow. He spoke of the "simplices fratres" whom lettered monks should not scorn and of the "illiterati" who could be taught by the pictures in church. One must imagine Bede at work in his cell in the midst of a few disciples and even then sometimes having difficulty finding help. If it was like this at Jarrow, the situation must have been worse elsewhere. Bede complained about his compatriots' lack of zeal. Every time he mentioned a learned person, he did not neglect to insist on his intellectual qualities. Whenever he described a monastery without stating exactly what kinds of studies the monks there pursued, we can conclude that they were content with the daily office and the simple reading of the Bible." (393–4).

"The reformers demanded very little of the clerics: it sufficed that they know how to preach, baptize, and give penance. They did not even require them to know Latin. Bede spoke of priests who knew only their mother tongue and was not scandalized by the fact. Some monks recited the Psalms even though ignorant of Latin. Priests were to explain the Credo and the text of the mass in the vulgar tongue. Thus, the Anglo-Saxon clergy could be content with a very superficial Latin culture or practically none at all. In this respect, they were as uncultured as the majority of laymen. (394–5).

Riché insists, all the same, that a "very small group" of laymen in the seventh and eighth centuries was raised in monasteries and episcopal schools, learning enough Latin to read hagiography and historiography, and to correspond with abbots and bishops (thus Ceolwulf, Ælfwald, Æthelberht II; 395). "These princes were not cultura patrons in the mold of Maecenas. On the contrary, they were good students of clerics and monks who would have become, if circumstances had permitted, monks and abbots themselves" (396). Vernacular poetry remained oral until the seventh century; in the eighth, clerics took a liking to it and began to collect poetry in writing, as well as allowing it sung in church until the Council of Clofesho forbade it (397–8).

Lay education was limited to religious education, as the only schools were ecclesiastical, and only a few aristocrats made it there. Everyone else still had access to religious culture (477). Early Christianity had required a three-year catechumenate, but this had to be simplified after the collapse of the Roman Empire in the West; instead, a Lent ceremony transformed pagans into adepts (electi), followed by a further preparation for baptism focusing less on the exorcisms of old and more on establishing and testing the initiand's knowledge of doctrine, focusing on the Apostles' Creed and the Paternoster, which were sufficiently simple that they could be memorized by the illiterate. With infant baptism, the godfather was expected to confirm the articles of faith (479–81). The 747 Council of Clofesho recommended that priests and laity simply memorize the Creed and Paternoster in the vernacular; Bede himself sent translations to priests who knew no Latin, and OHG translations survive of the same, suggesting the same practice existed in Germany. The simplification of the catechumenate can be explained by the developments following the fall of Rome: the conversion of the pagans did not have intellectual culture, so converting them had to entail simplification. To increase the rate of conversion, the Church furthermore allowed baptism to take place outside the cathedral church and outside the Easter vigil (481). When the Church demanded children be baptized early, this put further demands of simplification on baptism. In England, this had to happen within a month of birth, and Gregory the Great in his Dialogues warned against allowing children to die without baptism. Although there was some resistance, infant baptism eventually became universal, with the godparents reciting Creed and Paternoster on its behalf (482). Instruction was in the hands of the godparents for the duration of the Middle Ages.

Bishops were expected to preach in order to teach the laity the will of God. With the growth of the Church, preaching was delegated to priests, who were to seek inspiration in the writings of the Church Fathers or improvise their own sermons. Chrodegang in his rule expresses the wish for his canons to preach twice a month, with sermons adapted for the audience so they could be understood (483). In the early sixth century, monks and clerics advocated an accessible preaching style to aid intelligibility; but it was still to be in Latin in Mediterranean lands. It was different in the north, but we read nothing about the language of preaching until the 813 Council of Tours, when the vernacular is recommended. Vernacular preaching must predate this legistlation (484–5). Sometimes, interpreters would have been used. Vernacular sermons do not survive from this period; they must have been improvised using Latin models (these do survive; 485).

In sixth-century Italy, Africa, and southern Gaul, preaching was mostly from the Bible on various levels of meaning; it was held that the Bible held something for everyone, different audiences being more receptive to different levels of meaning. After the sixth century, the Bible was rarely used as a source. Bede's work on a translation of the Gospel of John was aimed at clerics who could not read Latin, not at the laity, who were not exposed to biblical content at all at this time (486–7). Instead, preachers drew on saints' lives (487–8) or spoke on good morals without relying on narrative sources: they recalled the promise made at baptism and instructed in the fear of God and the avoidance of vice (488). When the Bible was used, then the books of wisdom (489). Images were also used for preaching (489–90), and folk song and dance were coopted for religious purposes, especially in Spain (490–3). In England, "monks encouraged the development of sacred poetry in the national tongue so that laymen and clerics would abandon profane songs" (493).

At the end of this chapter, Riché ponders to what degree the religious instruction here described would have afforded the laity a personal religious life; he points out that their religion was more communal than personal [see also Russel, PSL], and that there were too few trained priests to educate the laity. Instead, the Church focused on obligations (the Sunday rest, Mass, communion); laymen had become observers of, rather than participants in, religion (493–4).
comments: With a foreword by Richard E. Sullivan.

author: Blair, John
title: The Church in Anglo-Saxon Society
abstract:
Studies the place of the church in Anglo-Saxon society and economy. It acknowledges the pluriformity of the early Anglo-Saxon religious community at the outset by offering the following definition of minster:

A complex ecclesiastical settlement which is headed by an abbess, abbot, or man in priest's orders; which contains nuns, monks, priests, or laity in a variety of possible combinations, and is united to a greater or lesser extent by their liturgy and devotions; which may perform or supervise pastoral care to the laity, perhaps receiving dues and exerting parochial authority; and which may sometimes act as a bishop's seat, while not depending for its existence or importance on that function (2–3, at 3).

Blair takes his time to explain the rise of monasticism and the Church dynamic with reference to the Roman inheritance and neighbouring influences; political ambitions; and the ideaology of continuous site use and stable funerary rites (ch. 1). The remaining chapters discuss the political implications of the monastic boom (ch. 2), their interaction with the laity (ch. 3), the role of the church in the landscape (ch. 4), the question of minsters as hubs of settlement (ch. 5), their development after 850 (ch. 6), and the rise of the local church after 850 (chs 7–8).

After 650, the English church took on a distinctly monastic (as opposed to an episcopal) character: bishops were too poor in wealth, power, and status to have much influence, so a model like that found in Ireland triumphed (73). The conceptual structure was different between Gaul and Ireland. The former had the three clerical tiers ecclesia (cathedral church), delegated sites of pastoral care (baptisteria/parochia), and oratories, as well as two distinct categories monasterium and extramural basilica. In Ireland, a regionally important church typically had a bishop but also housed some sort of religious community whether or not with an abbot and regular observation, and served as a mother-church for smaller churches (73–4). The ascetic members of minsters monopolize the narrative sources, and they represent an important dimension of "the para-monastic boom," giving patrons evidence that their resources were being put to good use. "Where traditional models fail is in perceiving rarefied lifestyles as the whole essence of early monasticism, before various kinds of corruption set in: in reality they were always one end of a broad spectrum. In northern Europe, the age of unalloyed monastic purity existed only in the minds of reformers (74). Conversely, the Gallic system with its tight episcopal control could not be recreated in England because it was insufficiently urban; the socioeconomic realities of Gaul could not there be recreated (74–5). Outside of Kent, kings governed large kingdoms and typically appointed only one bishop; this contrasts with the Irish model, which in the 660s had a hundred bishops to England's three. More surprising is the early absence of local churches (estate oratories), which were widespread both in Francia and in Ireland at this time (75).

[2: Minsters in Church and State: c. 650–850] When Theodore of Tarsus came to Canterbury in 669, England had only three bishops, and they had little to show for themselves. During his pontificate, Theodore extended the system to comprise thirteen or fourteen dioceses. This was still only half of what Gregory had envision for England. Right about the time when Theodore arrived, in fact, it was becoming clear that ecclesiastical power in England would run along monastic rather than diocesan lines (79–80).

Prior to the Viking Age, England knew no normative monastic rule, though minsters could self-impose a rule such as Benedict's; when done, this was done in an eclectic spirit (80–1). There were no strictly Frankish, Roman, or Irish houses; communities drew on multiple sources. Irregular houses only occur in sources [like Bede, PSL] when criticized, we should resist the evaluative polarity of these materials (81). Monastic property was transferred among family lines: it was understood as traditional property, religiously inflected (81–2). "Any minster with genuine religious functions would presumably have housed enough priests to meet at least the community's own sacramental needs, if not those of a wider lay group." On the other hand, it is "remarkably difficult" to identify episcopal institutions housing secular clergy only, and the same is true for the Carolingian distinction between monastic and secular communities. "It may in fact be inappropriate to envisage English founders and rulers viewing their communities in this way at all: a minster was inherently a complex settlement form, which could include categories of ecclesiastical (and secular) personnel in addition to the one for which it was principally founded. At this date no rule is likely to have excluded the presence of diverse groups of people within and around the minster enclosure, nor to have prevented social, economic, or pastoral contacts between the monastic personnel and a wider lay community" (82).

[3: Church and People: c. 650–850] Blair points out that primary sources never depict situations where there was a complete absence of pastoral care; rather, they bemoan its limited nature in exceptional cases, as in Bede's complaint that remote settlements only saw a bishop once a year; Bede himself apparently handed out translations of the Creed and Paternoster to priests who knew no Latin (160–1). Lay instruction was carried out by priests travelling between rural settlements; minsters supervised these pastoral undertakings (161–2; references to works by Foot from the 1990s). Research of neighbouring cultures has shown similar mother-parish supervision of pastoral work. Southeastern Brittany may be seen as an analogue to England; it had minsters populated by priests and typically no more than seven miles apart in population centres, forming something of a parish system. This system in Brittany must predate Carolingian times and resembles the English mother-parish system (162). Eighth-century English sources assume that priests live in religious communities headed by abbots or priores, and there is evidence that minsters had pastoral functions in Theodore's ruling that anyone who moves one must leave a priest behind (162–3). The pastoral activities of monks like Bede muddles the picture, but it seems clear that aristocratic monks and nuns would not have travelled to visit remote settlements; pastoral duties would have been deputized to priests (163–4). Accordingly, Bede describes clerics and monks inhabiting the same institutions but only the former preach, baptize, and visit the sick; it thus appears to have been his understanding that minsters populated by monks could also accommodate ordained men for pastoral care (164).

Trying to get a handle on lay Christian practice, basically depicts a contrast between the tightly controlled practice of the religious elite and a highly diverse, contaminated, but essentially Christian range of practices below (166–81).

[6: Minsters in a Changing World: c. 850–1100] Blair emphasizes that early minsters interacted intensively with the laity (ch. 3). He attaches value to Alfred's report, assuming that minsters and their inhabitants were destroyed in large numbers by the Vikings, yet he also recognizes the rhetorical value of such reports since they stem from monastic circles with monastic agendas (291–2 and up to 295). He examines continuity and change in this period, region by region (295–323) and describes how minsters were appropriated by royalty, nobility, and bishops (323–9), and he covers their urbanization and merger with fortified sites (330–41). One cause of monastic decline was the fact that monastic lands threatened by Vikings or otherwise strategically located were seized or traded by the West Saxon kings in the name of defence against the Vikings. For this argument Blair refers to Fleming, who describes how this land was distributed among royal officials during the conquest of the Danelaw to strengthen West Saxon control of the north; it is also from these estates that Edgar was able to provide land for the Benedictine Reform, but it is clear that the northern monasteries in particular lost a great deal of land from the first Viking incursions to the end of the Anglo-Saxon period (Blair 323–4). Blair adds that the minsters themselves, not just their lands, were increasingly assimilated into secular public life (324–29). During Alfred's reign, minsters also came to be increasingly associated with towns. Many of Alfred's burgs were built around minsters (330–4), but the economic process of urbanization starting around 950 affected a far greater number of minsters than did royal fortification (334). The minsters had economic advantages due to their topographical locations, function as estate centres, ritual function, and sanctuaries for those requiring refuge who could continue to practise their crafts there. Accordingly, minsters were firmly associated with markets (335). Blair discusses some of the less well understood dynamics at play, referencing central place theory (336–7), but observes that the clearest losses were suffered wherever cathedrals by 1050 were left in sparsely populated settlements (337–8). It is also striking that a good number of mints are recorded for minster sites that were neither Alfredian burgs nor eleventh-century shire towns, suggesting the importance of market functions in a distributive economy (338).

Though the functions of minsters were increasingly taken over by towns and secular manorial centres in the tenth century, there still remained many prosperous minsters by 975, with kings and owners supporting their religious functions and financing their construction (341–2). In nature, from Alfred to William II, all but the largest minsters were communities of secular priests connected to one central church and probably one mother-parish but not necessarily sharing property and sleeping quarters, not necessarily partaking of the daily office, and often married, with implications for the endowment of property (342). This uptick in ordination would have had reduced monastic wealth as one of its causes, but there may also just have been a gradual increase in monastic ordination in trend with general ordination, as every minster required some proportion of ordained priests. Ninth-century episcopal efforts to increase the pastoral value of minsters may likewise have encouraged ordination. Certain trends in eighth-century monasticism, such as courtly nuns, could not outlast the high point of monastic culture because they had no value outside that system, and so "their world was fading well before the Vikings came, and even perhaps before Carolingian-inspired suspicion of double houses reached England. It was the clergy who had become embedded in local life, and that was why they survived" (344). The same trend could be seen elsewhere in Europe as well (345). The clerical community was in fact an ancient tradition which the Rule of Chrodegang (c. 755) and the Rule of Aachen (816) had sought to revive these models in stricter forms on the Continent, but lay patronage favoured lax arrangements, and the same could not but happen in England with its weak bishops and strong territorial interests. Lords required clerical personnel without restrictive sets of rules, and wanted to be able to relate to the members of their local religious communities; monks were not that (345–6). The Benedictine Reform offered an alternative, advocated by a small but powerful group. Continental rules for canons and monks had had little impact and no grass-roots following in England, so these reformers had to impose rules either from the distant past or newly from abroad top-down; the kings took this as their task. Edgar followed the example of Louis the Pious, and the reformers took Bede as their native guiding light, a nostalgic turn already visible in Alfred's preface to the Pastoral Care (346–8). Blair argues that the view, held in Alfred's circle and among the reformers, that monastic discipline had waned was not incompatible with a continued patronage of secular minsters: Alfred himself gave Asser two minsters and spent an eighth of his income on patronage of minsters, while his children founded clerical houses, not monasteries (347–8); kings of the mid-tenth century likewise encouraged both modes (348–9). The reform was transformative in what it added, particularly in Wessex and the west and east midlands, but the general pattern of reform was for bishops to procure existing minsters as personal property. By 975, up to thirty male houses and seven or eight nunneries had been refounded; little more than ten percent of total religious houses was ever reformed (351). Æthelwold's rejection of the clerical model was an outlier even among reformers, and had no counterpart on the Continent, which followed the Aachen Rule for canons (351–2). It may be that the rule was to supplement clerics with monks. If Edgar did avoid patronizing unreformed minsters, at least he did not suppress them but rather legislated to protect their interests (352).

After the 970s, the reformed houses did not grow dynamically but subsisted on inherited capital; at a time of recession and renewed Viking attacks, it seems monastic houses were more vulnerable than either unreformed minsters or emerging local churches. Byrhtferth himself asserts that this was the high time of clerics, not monks (Vita S. Oswaldi). The "anti-monastic reaction" was a matter of politics and not intended against the ideals of monasticism, and support of both remains concentrated in the same patrons (354–5).

By the eleventh century, regular monks could be positively supportive of secular religious (360–1). Clerical minsters seem to have had relaxed regimes, with neither canon rule having much of an English audience before 1050. Wulfstan in 1008 called on canons to live in chastity and share meals and dormitories, but this may not have had much effect (361–2).

[7: The Birth and Growth of Local Churches: c. 850–1100] The spread of the local church followed in the train of the feudal revolution: although the jurisdictional changes associated with this development did not take place in England with its strong state power, the economic growth did affect local communities in ways like those seen on the Continent, and a class of local landowners sprang up. These all wanted to own churches (368–71). Local churches developed variously out of ancient, "undeveloped" sacred sites (374–83), clerical communities (383–5), and as new foundations by estate owners (385–95); a separate section treats the occurrence of two churches in the same locality (397–407).

Significant among the Domesday evidence is the listing of part-churches per estate, suggesting that less wealthy landowners wanted to own a share in a church if they could not afford the whole thing (399–401, including tables 1–2).

[8: From hyrness to Parish: The Formation of Parochial Identities] With two tiers of parish (the mother-parish and the local church) vying for control, the question this chapter seeks to answer is the degree to which local parishes, "containing a single agragian community, village, or manorial centre," covered England by 1100 (426). The development took place, but whereas the archaeological evidence shows small churches springing up everywhere, the written sources "barely recognize a tier below mother-parish level" until the twelfth century (426–7, quotation at 426).

Starting with the vocabulary, observes the rarity of Latin parochia in Anglo-Saxon documents; when it does appear, it refers to minsters or mother-parishes (427–8). By 960, the term hyrnes(s) means parish [cf. DOE sense 5], deriving from a sense "lordship, obedience." The term resurfaces in the late eleventh century with reference to three centres of power that preserved the old mother-parish rights (428–9). Ælfric furthermore uses folgoþe to refer to the adherence of the laity to a priest; I Cnut uses lytel þeowdom. Other terms found are scriftscir and ciricsocn (429–30), a term that is further discussed (430–32). Key in the terminology is that it focuses on a mother-parish, not a local church (432).

Starting in the 920s, kings spent a century gradually encoding minsters' fiscal rights in law: to them, these mother-parishes were organizational units, like hundreds (433). Grassroots pressure may likewise have prompted the definition of these organizations: Edgar is the first to acknowledge local churches formally (433–4). English laws on church dues owe a heavy debt to Carolingian sources, but Blair argues for a distinctly English tradition, starting with wheat dues in Wessex c. 700 (434–4). Tithing is conspicuous for its legislative absence before the Carolingians: it seems to have been considered voluntary. When it was legislated in the eighth century, it was enforced on the Continent but not in England. As the one source of revenue that lacked a strong tradition in early Anglo-Saxon England, it was the most innovative element of the tenth-century fiscal reform (435–6). Before 920, English churchscot (wheat dues) look like an alternative for Continental tithing (436). There is late evidence that churchscot came to less than ten percent of wheat grown, making tithing more appealing, but in fact both were demanded beginning in the early tenth century (436). Soulscot appears early alongside churchscot in England, despite its controversial character in Europe (437). Churchbot appears in 902 (437–8). All these taxes were paid in return for the benefits of services and ministrations, burial, and the use of the church building (438). A number of more obscure dues likewise imply underlying personal relationships (438–9). Tithing became compulsory c. 930 and references become common by mid-century (440–1). Enforcement of the various revenues is further discussed up to p. 451; evidence of enforcement is mostly post-Conquest, but at that time these rights had become brittle and needed to be actively defended. "The relaxation of tithe obligations, and surely too a serious weakening of many minsters' capacity to withstand encroachment, must have facilitated the building and endowment of manorial churches through the late eleventh and early twelfth centuries. This loosening-up was the most important (and perhaps the only really fundamental) change to the English local Church which was a direct result of the Norman Conquest (451).

Manorial churches wishing to compete with mother-parishes were not only disadvantaged fiscally; they also had to win a struggle for spiritual and social loyalty among believers. Local churches had won this battle for identity by 1150 (452). The ordained priests in tenth- and eleventh-century minsters had certainly offered pastoral care: the words for their revenues (shrift-corn, priest's dues, etc.) indicate as much. "The impact of reform, disendowment, and pluralism on the pastoral efficacy (as distinct from the community life) of minsters is in fact very unclear. The problem is still much as for the pre-Viking period: texts focus on the status and assets of an elite, whether monks or prebend-holding priests, whereas day-to-day duties may always have fallen largely on a humbled and undocumented clerical stratum, the kinds of people who eventually emerge in the twelfth-century guise of vicars and chaplains. Old ways of operating may have persisted much more successfully in local arrangements than at the level of formal tenure" (453).

Minster churches could only be upended if more convenient alternatives became available that seemed just as good. The eleventh-century "Great Rebuilding" produced imposing local churches that would have looked like little minsters (456–7); they were also conceived more as community buildings, accommodating the full audience of the Mass, nave areas keeping track with population sizes according to Domesday numbers; some also incorporated elaborate murals (457) and inscriptions (457–8). Ælfric's complaints suggest churches were used for non-spiritual purposes and thus served as community centres (458–9).

Baptism is an important test case: where did this take place in Ælfric's day? There are two convincing cases of monolithic baptismal fonts in local churches in perhaps the tenth century, but the majority are post-Conquest. Most likely, monolithic baptismal fonts are a property of the eleventh-century Great Rebuilding and became widespread "when permanently build local churches did, during the later eleventh century" (459–61, quotation at 461). Since sixteen twelfth-century lead fonts also survive, these may represent an older tradition of local baptismal fonts predating 1050; there is no evidence that minsters held the monopoly on baptism (461–3). Blair speculates that local baptism might previously have taken place out of doors at holy wells; moving baptism into the church may have served to increase control over the institution (463).

Churchyards were a particularly important battleground: Ælfric complains that priests flock to corpses hoping to claim them. The conflict is first visible in Edgar's "concession of limited tithe-rights to the thegn's church with a graveyard," but it was to grow more intense in the twelfth to fourteenth centuries." It may be that the English were first told where to bury their dead in the tenth century (463). This development, too, took its cue from Carolingian precedents, where burial at one's own parish church was imposed by the mid-tenth century; lowland England copied this practice by the mid-tenth century (Wales and Cornwall continued the tradition of burial by relatives). The new practice brought a new understanding of consecrated ground, namely ground consecrated by a bishop for the mandatory burial of the faithful and the exclusion of all others (463–4). Æthelstan's law of c. 930 is the first European reference to consecrated ground, and the liturgy for its consecration may stem from English sources; its oldest manuscripts are English. The rise of hallowed churchyards at this time was another way of "defining and controlling the religious affiliations of the laity" (464). The archaeological record confirms that informal honourable burial ceased by the later tenth century, while "overtly shameful" cemeteries proliferated as individuals found wanting were excluded from Christian burial (465–6). In an age of transition, however, it will not always have been clear where a corpse belonged; mother-churches will have been keener on soulscots than on the corpses that came with them, and corpses of the lower classes will have been less desired. Accordingly, there is evidence of "overflow cemeteries" and the practice of segregating bodies by wealth and class (466–7). Some minster graveyards continued to expand, but it seems the proportion of burials in new churchyards accelerated rapidly (467). Memorial sculpture is evidence of local churchyards, typically commemorating the manorial family (468–70); there is some evidence of hierarchical structure within churchyards, even small ones (471).

Blair covers continuity of pagan cult practices (471–89).

Cautioning against taking the homiletic and pastoral corpus of Wulfstan and Ælfric at face value for their reference to regulatory authority, Blair nevertheless holds that they reflect the transition described (489–91). "In 900 the great majority of English clergy either lived at, or were attached to, minsters. By 1000 it seems likely that significant numbers of priests were coming to be based at small manorial households and local churches. By 1100, though the minster-priests were probably still numerous, the priests of local churches may have outnumbered them substantially. . . . Byrhtferth of Ramsey, Ælfric, and Wulfstan launched their initiatives for vernacular education in a world which presented a new opportunity and new problem: the 'backwoods priest' (uplendisc preost), ignorant, isolated, cut off from even the basic standards of learning and discipline which he would formerly have attained in a minster community. . . . To judge from the strictures against them, priests were often ignorant of Latin, unshaven, drunk, and quarrelsome, and in the habit of wearing weapons in church; they could be alehouse-minstrels and entertainers, hunters, hawkers, and gamblers. It is unlikely that even Ælfric and Wulfstan seriously thought that they could make priests give up their women, though they did their best to shame them into chastity" (491). "We cannot assume that local priests were normally literate (especially in a period when we do not really know how literate the laity were), and standards are likely to have varied widely. It is possible that priests 'devolved' from minsters were more educated than those whom the laity selected from among their tenants or fellow-villagers, though if peasant priests acquired any education the minster-priests seem the obvious agents for providing it." There was great diversity of status and subsidiary profession among them; some were unfree (492). The remainder of this section describes some of the ways in which local priests seem to have been bound up in worldly matters and the resulting tension with such churchmen as Ælfric (up to p. 497).

The section that follows sums up the timeline: local timber churches appear by the mid-tenth century, shortly before Edgar incorporates the local bookland church in his 960s law code; Ælfric, Wulfstan, and Byrhtferth respond in their writings to the rise of "backwoods priests." The period 1030–1080 represents the critical transition period in which "local churches were rebuilt to last, equipped with stone fonts and endowed with land, and when the minsters' monopoly over church dues went into drastic decline." The appearance of local churches was a grassroots development in which authorities showed little interest; bishops did not take measures to define parish boundaries; the old mother-parish boundaries nevertheless remained important (498). Patterns in landholding and economic activity determined their inner fragmentation, but the most important driver was the manorial lords' impulse of building churches and involving their tenants in the finance and attendance of these churches (498–9). Offers some evidence for the notion that individual churches were understood to function as the church for a community, not for their manorial lords only: "a series of royal procedural measures from 1009 onwards. . . suggest a general assumption that every tūn will have its priest, and that he will be one of its natural leaders" (501–2, quotation at 502). But people may also have identified with a local church because it was their only local option; because the estate determined the rhythm of their lives; because the liked the local church; because they admired or liked the priest; because they had joined its processions or guild feasts. "The more the solidarity of the parish coincided with other solidarities the stronger it was likely to be, and it is a reasonable assumption that it was strongest of all in a classic midland township with a single common-field system supporting a single nucleated village" (502), though a new church could also create solidarities that would have been lacking without it (503). After the Conquest, bishops gained a tighter grip on parish affairs (507). Minsters sites remained "the most widespread enduring legacies from early Christian England"; few ex-minsters were now collegial, but they still housed different kinds of clergy ("portionary vicars, multiple curates and chaplains, guild- and chantry-priests") and retained a separate clerical space (509).

Blair does not describe education except briefly suggesting that local priests would have received it at minsters on p. 492; he does cover pastoral care at greater length (e.g. 3, 160–4, 453).

author: Wilcox, Jonathan
title: Ælfric in Dorset and the Landscape of Pastoral Care
publication: Pastoral Care in Late Anglo-Saxon England
abstract:
Succinct and highly valuable. Asking how a single monk in a remote Dorset monastery (because Ælfric wrote most of his works at Cerne Abbas) was able to become the sole voice of pastoral care in late Anglo-Saxon England, then offers the following insights in response:

  • It is clear from the pericopal focus of the Catholic Homilies, but also from their internal dramatization (e.g. "her is geræd on ðisum godspelle þe we nu gehierdon of þæs diacones muðe," ÆCHom I, 10) that they were meant for a liturgical context (53–4);
  • Indeed, texts such as ÆCHom II, 16 address an audience that is only there on Sundays, although the speaker preaches on Easter Wednesday as well; this suggests "a broad, not especially pious, lay audience as the usual target for his homilies" (54);
  • Other texts address various combinations of audiences, certainly including secular clerical audiences as well as monastic audiences combined with lay audiences; the homilies as a whole thus appear aimed at mixed audiences (54–5);
  • Godden has suggested the Catholic Homilies served also for private reading by literate laymen as well as by monks whose Latin was limited (55);
  • External references also suggest a liturgical use for the homilies; thus Ælfric in his letter for Wulfsige and his later letters for Wulfstan instructs that priests explain the gospel to the people in the vernacular on Sun- and Feast-days (55–6);
  • The ventriloquist model of Ælfric writing the words for Wulfsige to preach to his priests is applicable to the Catholic Homilies as well; indeed, Wulfsige's Sherborne was itself a mixed cathedral community, not reformed until 998, where the bishop "would have preached on Sundays and major festivals to a congregation both of clerics and of lay townsfolk," precisely as envisioned for the Catholic Homilies, and that at only twelve miles from Cerne; Ælfric may well have had Sherborne in mind as one of the performance settings of his homilies (56–7);
  • There would still have been a good number of minster churches where priests lived corporately and travelled to surrounding areas to provide pastoral care, and Cerne was surrounded by a number of minsters that would have held services on Sundays and feast-days for the local laity but also for any priests gathered in the minster; thus sermons could address both (57);
  • Ælfric's letter [for Wulfsige, and also for Wulfstan] lists a large number of books each priest must possess; minsters could credibly have served as repositories for such books, which multiple priests based at the minster would have used. All such minsters would also have been well served with a copy of Ælfric's Catholic Homilies (57–8);
  • Cerne does not appear to have had a church outside the abbey before 1300; before that, the minster would probably have served both the laity and the monks as a place of worship, creating the mixed audiences reflected in Ælfric's homilies. Other reformed monasteries seem to have fulfilled similar functions, and all these would have had a use for the Catholic Homilies (it is not especially surprising that two Cerne manuscripts survive) (58–9);
  • Smaller villages around Cerne, with populations around or below 100, are unlikely to have had the books or education Ælfric requires of priests in his pastoral letters. Instead, Wulfstan's less demanding standard in the ordination circulating with his Institutes of Polity are more likely to have applied, namely that the priest know the fundamentals of the faith and be able to explain baptism and mass while knowing the canons to a degree, and enough computus to keep track of the calendar. The text itself admits that even this standard may not be feasible, in which case a "half-educated man" may be retained on the condition that he apply himself to learning on the job. Here too, Ælfric's homilies would have been a useful tool (59–60);
  • It is likely that the homilies circulated in booklets rather than codices, but such booklets tend not to survive. What Anglo-Saxon booklets do survive contain homilies (60–1);
  • The copies of the Catholic Homilies that do survive look like high-status copies, either meant for private reading or as exemplars from which utilitarian copies would have been made (61);
  • Even so, we have 34 surviving copies of the first series and evidence for the existence of a further 50. Canterbury was the hub of their dispersion, making clear that Cerne was not the only place that saw a use for them; the operation reflects "the programme of an institutional Church reacting to the pastoral needs which arose from an increasingly decentralised system of local churches and the multiple providers of pastoral care at the turn of the millennium" (61);
  • Arguably, it was precisely when the minster system was breaking down and saw rivalry from both reformed monasteries and local churches that "a universal pastoral system of preaching was developed," and it makes sense for this to have happened in a region characterized by this diversity of ecclesiastical centres rather than "in the metropolitan centre of Winchester" (62).

author: Hill, Joyce
title: Monastic Reform and the Secular Church: Ælfric's Pastoral Letters in Context
publication: England in the Eleventh Century: Proceedings of the 1990 Harlaxton Symposium
abstract:
Ælfric's 1006 translations of his two 1005 letters for Wulfstan are not exact translations: they reflect the fact that "in changing languages, he was encompassing a different intellectual milieu, priestly still, but addressing now, in the vernacular, those who, as the first Old English letter states in the opening sentence, 'ne cunnon þæt leden under-standan'" (103–4, quotation at 104). The bishops who commissioned Ælfric's letters consciously approached an advocate of the reform; Ælfric expressed reluctance from time to time when asked to provide vernacular texts but still undertook to make the knowledge that was the domain of the reform movement available to secular clergy and the laity (104).

Wulfsige was an aboot first before being appointed bishop; he reformed his cathedral, appointing monks, probably in 998. He looks to have wished to transmit monastic standards and ideals to the secular church (105).

Wulfstan was clearly interested in religious reform [within the secular church, PSL]: he issued a rule for canons, circulated pastoral letters, and preached to the laity; he was bishop of Worcester, a centre of reform and took an interest in the Regularis concordia (105). Ælfric and his episcopal commissioners thus probably shared the same purpose (105–6).

The second Old English letter for Wulfstan incorporates extensive material from the not found in the Latin original. Hill speculates that Wulfstan may have requested the addition when he commissioned the translation (106). Ælfric had previously used the Concordia for his Eynsham consuetudinary (Letter to the Monks of Eynsham); his adaptation for Wulfstan incorporates even more changes (106–7). In fact, the Eynsham consuetudinary survives only in a commonplace book of Wulfstan's; it may have given him the idea to commission a further adaptation for seculars (107). The other manuscript reflecting Wulfstan's commonplace book contains extracts from the Regularis concordia in Latin and (some) in Old English (107–8). Other sources of Ælfric's pastoral letters likewise articulate the reform position assumed by Ælfric on the request of the bishops: Rufinus, Isidore, the Capitulary of Aachen, penitentials, De divinis officiis, Theodulf of Orléans, Amalarius of Metz (108–9). Many of these Continental texts had come in with the Benedictine Reform, they serve to regulate the pious life at a sophisticated level, and they appear in the great commonplace books of the eleventh century (109). Hill discusses the feasibility of secular priests attaining the standards set out in these texts and comes down on the sceptical end of the spectrum, but also points out that the complaints in these letters tell us as much or more about these men's perception of the secular church as they do about reality; above all, they seem to have believed that the secular church stood in sharp contrast to the discipline of monastic life (109–11). Manuscript evidence of the circulation of these letters is not clear; several are too close to the original to serve as evidence of dissemination, though the vernacular letters do appear in a small number of manuscripts, but "they do not generally allow us to see the pastoral letters being used in the circles for which they were intended" (111–15, at 115). Wulfsige, Wulfstan, and Ælfric appear to have held the English Church to a monastic standard, by which standard it fell far short; the pastoral letters are attempts to remedy the situation (115–16).

author: Gittos, Helen
title: Is there any Evidence for the Liturgy of Parish Churches in Late Anglo-Saxon England? The Red Book of Darley and the Status of Old English
publication: Pastoral Care in Late Anglo-Saxon England
abstract:
Suggests that many priests would have learned the liturgy by experience (63–4). Points out that no manuscripts survive, and indeed it is most likely that libelli (booklets) were used, which were typically discarded as they became outdated (64). The sources prescribe a large number of duties for local priests, but some of the more important festivals, such as Rogationtide, Palm Sunday, and Candlemas, required more clergy; they may have been carried out at nearby mother-churches instead. Local priests may not have known the liturgy for some of the duties authors prescribe for them; it is unlikely they celebrated the office of the hours. We must nevertheless balance out the image of drunken, lazy priests offered by Ælfric with the fact that paying supporters would have expected something in return: mass, baptism, and burial at least (65). Beyond this, there would have been a great deal of variability; Ælfric's exhortations suggest some priests said mass without deacons, i.e. on their own (65–6). Gittos compares a parish church book-list with Ælfric's prescribed library; it is comparable, but no complete match. Among items not mentioned is a computus, but then it is likely that parish clergy simply learned the important dates "from local knowledge of what neighbouring churches were doing" (66).

The one manuscript that best represents a book for use in the liturgy of a parish church is the Red Book of Darley (CCCC 422), a small volume that could have been carried. Its second part contains Easter tables for 1061–98, from which Gittos concludes it was "almost certainly produced c. 1061"; it may have been produced in Sherborne or Winchester (67). Describes the manuscript's contents (68–9) and discusses in detail the baptismal rite contained in it (70–4) and discusses the role of the vernacular (74–82).

author: Fleming, Robin
title: Monastic Lands and England's Defence in the Viking Age
abstract:
Traces monastic landholdings through the Viking Age to Domesday.

Does not doubt contemporary accounts of monastic destruction at the hands of Vikings (247–9). Domesday evidence shows that the Church held only ten percent of lands in the north in demesne, against twenty percent to a third in the south; this disparity corresponds to Viking settlement in the north (249–50). Already tenth-century monastic sources tell us that the West Saxon royal house profited from ecclesiastical loss of landholdings, starting with Alfred himself, who in the Abingdon Chronicle is compared to Judas for taking Church land, while Edgar apparently had the power to give Æthelwold the estates of old monastic lands (250–1). In many cases, the land was not returned (252); sometimes, it was leased back (253). Monarchs repeatedly pressured monasteries to give up land for defence against the Vikings (253–4). Royal officials were often granted ex-monastic land (255–7). Once monasteries were refounded, they relied on (spurious) charters to try and claim their substantial holdings back (257–61). The strategic locations of many of these lands (e.g. on the mouth of the Thames or on the border with the Danelaw) means that monasteries could not have held on to them at a time of Viking activity, and they were essential for defence (261–3). The antimonastic reaction following Edgar's death constitutes a legitimate dispute between conflicting claims after a hundred years of undisputed aristocratic ownership (264). During the conquest of the Danelaw, ex-monastic lands were key to safeguarding the West Saxon hegemony in the north; after the conquest was secure, the same land was used to support a royalist monastic movement (264–5).

author: Gransden, Antonia
title: Traditionalism and Continuity during the Last Century of Anglo-Saxon Monasticism
abstract: Describes at great length how both the tenth-century reformers and the Anglo-Norman reformers neglected and denigrated the period preceding their own, though both acknowledged a seventh-century golden age of monasticism and the Anglo-Normans praised the tenth-century reform.

author: Palliser, D. M.
title: The 'Minster Hypothesis': A Case Study
abstract:
Presents some evidence (from Yorkshire and particularly Beverly) in support of Blair's hypothesis that (in some cases) pre-Viking Age, pre-parochial priests lived in collegial churches and serviced the surrounding area. Concludes that

The most likely explanation of the parochial arrangements at Beverley, Ripon and elsewhere is the survival of early provisions for pastoral care based on head minsters before the full development of a parochial system (214).

author: Coates, Simon
title: Perceptions of the Anglo-Saxon Past in the Tenth-Century Monastic Reform Movement
publication: The Church Retrospective: Papers Read at the 1995 Summer Meeting and the 1996 Winter Meeting of the Ecclesiastical History Society
abstract:
Reform movements typically adduce the past as a justification for their plans; they tend to present the status quo as decayed and tend to simplify the past and present it selectively (61). The tenth-century reformers weaponized the age of Bede as propaganda to legitimize their takeover of the religious system (62). Bede's writings offered them topoi they could apply to current concerns. As such, they did not think of their efforts as innovative but as restorative. The prologue to the Regularis concordia seems to betray a knowledge of the version of Gregory's responsiones found in Bede's Historia ecclesiastica, and it directly quotes Bede's letter to Bishop Ecgbert of York as evidence that cathedral communities were to elect a bishop from their own number (62–3). Two further reform documents refer explicitly to Bede, echoing such sentiments as Bede's invectives against clerical licentiousness and a concern for the unity of the English Church (63–4).

The reformers inaccurately depict the pre-Viking era as one marked by universal adherence to the Benedictine Rule, which had been just one rule among many. They also suggested that monks and secular clergy could easily be separated, and they alleged a history of increasing neglect of Benedictine discipline (64). The reformers relied heavily on the cult of saints, itself strongly connected to the past, and here too they made extensive use of Bede: Ælfric uses Bede for his Lives of Saints, and Byrhtferth's Enchiridion is essentially a commentary on Bede's works on time (64–5).

Not halfway in, the paper's topic changes a little abruptly to the Life of St Dunstan by the anonymous B, who seems to have been a canon and is silent on the expulsion of canons; he sought to return to England from Liège after the expulsion of the canons and shows a very different take on the past than his contemporaries inasmuch as he relies more on Stephanus's Life of Wilfrid than on Bede: "Whilst the reformers remembered the Anglo-Saxon past as the golden age of Bede, B remembered it as the age of Wilfrid where secularity could be harnessed to the needs of the Church (72–4, quotation at 74).
tags: benedictine reform,regularis concordia,bede,monasticism,life of st æthelstan

author: Cubitt, Catherine
title: Anglo-Saxon Minsters: A Review of Terminology
abstract:
Outlines the difficulty with the traditional terminology and proposes the use of minster to express the range of roles fulfilled by early religious houses. Emphasizes the dual role fulfilled by religious houses:

The spiritual functions which a monasterium performed for the laity might include the administration of the sacraments of baptism, communion and burial, the provision of teaching and preaching to the laity, or the guardianship of holy relics. Such an institution could also, however, serve a useful social role by supplying education and literary services to those of the landowning class who had need of them, as well as relief to the traveller and pilgrim, to the destitute and the sick. In these ways religious houses fulfilled a dual role in the community, serving both as the vehicle for the expression of lay devotion and as the source of a number of valued intellectual and charitable services. (212)

In the conversion period, communal groups of clerics scattered throughout the country undertook missionary work, and this pattern determined the nature of later conventual institutions. Thacker's essay in the present volume argues that these missionaries established lasting contact with the populace, taking on their spiritual care. This indicates that priests travelling to their flocks with the sacraments would have been common, an image also relayed by Bede (212). On the other hand, some of the laity would also have travelled to hear mass or seek other spiritual aid. At any rate, most religious in the early period were attached to religious houses, even if they spent time working in the field and some sought asceticism. In fact, Church councils (Hertford 672/3, Clofesho 747, Chelsea 816) did not account for parochial workers except as connected to their houses of origin, and ascetics only became ascetics after spending time in the communal religious life (213).

Stresses the great variety of pre-reform religious houses, and the absence outside of Bede of early monastic critics of the lack of regularity; Bede appears to be the outlier, but he has been so influential that his writings for the basis of our understanding of early Anglo-Saxon monasticism (213–14).

Whereas Latin monasterium has been applied to all forms of religious communal living, English monastery is strongly associated with the contemplative, regular, Benedictine mode and has been used to distinguish between secular and regular religious, a distinction that does not apply to the early period (214–15). Alternative words, such as coenobium, exist but lack English counterparts or are much rarer; accordingly, Foot proposes to adopt the modern reflex of Old English mynster. Recent scholars have used the term to refer specifically to mother-churches as identified in Domesday, characterized by primarily pastoral functions, but that does not always seem to have applied (215). The essay goes on to discuss the Anglo-Saxon usage of the relevant terminology, eventually concluding that

The sole feature common to every early Anglo-Saxon religious house, and the one which was clearly recognized by all contemporary writers, was the corporate nature of its inmates' lives. (225)

and once again endorsing the use of minster to refer to all of them prior to the reform, while after the reform the term mother-church could be used to refer to houses with pastoral responsibilities (225).

author: Thacker, Alan
title: Monks, Preaching and Pastoral Care in Early Anglo-Saxon England
abstract:
Though Bede is our greatest source for the early English Church, he does not discuss life outside aristocratic communities and thus fails to "analyse the degree to which the church fulfilled its mission to Anglo-Saxon society as a whole." This chapter seeks to provide the missing information (137).

The bishop stood at the top of the hierarchy and originally had the pastoral duties of the sacraments and preaching, but he was forced [by the quantity of the work] to share this with his priests by the essay's focus period (c. 700). He still retained the exclusive right to ordain and to consecrate the holy ointment, and no priestly function could be carried out without his licence. He also served as the judiciary against those who had committed capital offences against monks and lower clergy. In addition, bishops retained chief responsibility for pastoral care; Bede considered it appropriate for them to visit "every hamlet and homestead" in their diocese at least one per year, and Frankish councils prescribe the same. This task would have been more burdensome in England, which was more rural than [some Continental] dioceses (137–8).

Priests were important, and according to Thacker not numerous in early Anglo-Saxon England because Bede takes care to mention their status whenever he mentions one. Priests and bishops are closely linked conceptually, as both were covered in the concept sacerdos [cf. Ælfric's list of clerical functions in his Semo episcopi ad clericos (Letter For Wulfstan), PSL] Theodore in his Penitential describes priests as having the power to baptize, consecrate abbesses, and sanctify relocated churches as well as preach, say mass, and prescribe penance; this made them very much surrogate bishops.

Deacons receive little attention in early sources. They could not marry once ordained, they could preach and baptize, but not say mass or presecribe penance (138).

Clericus, monachus, and sanctimonialis are not well-defined categories in the sources (139).

The label monasterium (minster) was applied to widely different institutions. Monasteries like Bede's Jarrow, which closely resembled the Benedictine ideal, will have been the exception. Other communities will have had looser discipline but still had abbots and housed groups of what sources call monachi or clerici (139). Important monasteria were the royal foundations, typically established early and governed by a royal abbot or abbess; "they were usually associated with the administrative centres of royal estates and ministered to those estates through pastoral units known to contemporaries as parochiae" (139). They took in church dues and they housed priests and other religious who travelled out to render pastoral care across extensive areas (139–40). Emphasizes that "even communities which may be regarded as monastic in the strict sense had pastoral responsibilities," including Wearmouth-Jarrow, as evidenced by chapelries and the existence of a lay cemetery at Wearmouth Abbey, making clear the monastery provided pastoral care of at least some types to the laity from its very beginning (140). Bede's homiliary suggests that he expected to preach to an extended audience at Jarrow at least once a year: his Holy Saturday homily addresses the catechumenate and explains baptism, while a text for Lent likewise addresses adiuncta fratrum caterua (an "additional crowd of brethren"), suggesting at least contact beyond their own monks (140–1). Furthermore,

To reach this enlarged audience Bede would probably have had to employ the vernacular rather than Latin, the language in which his homilies have come down to us. That, however, is not an insuperable problem. The homilies are written in a much simpler style than the biblical commentaries; they could easily have been used as the basis for vernacular preaching, especially if the copy the preacher used had been glossed. (141; the whole passage about Bede's homiliary refers to Andreas van der Walt's unpublished London dissertation "The Homiliary of the Venerable Bede and Early Medieval Preaching")
