Sarah Foot has argued that the 500x600 brethren at Wearmouth and Jarrow included nonmonastic residents of the estate; there is mention of a shepherd living extramurally but counted as a frater from the abbess's familia. This suggests monasteries such as Wearmouth and Jarrow catered to tenants, "perhaps tonsured and celibate," who would have attended the monastic church at least on major festivals. In none of this is there any mention of women in the sources (141–2, quotation at 141).

Lindisfarne, though an episcopal see, was nevertheless very much a monastery in the strict sense of the word, yet it exercised pastoral care over the immediate territory under supervision of the prior. Bede's praise of the effectiveness of pre-664 Lindisfarne in enthusing the laity evidences that Bede's ideal community had a pastoral impact (142). Double houses offer strong evidence of pastoral care; Hild's Whitby as described by Bede is a good example, with common people flocking to the royal abbess (142–3). Though the double monastery seems to have ceased to exist in the mid-ninth century, it remained a major estate with two churches onsite, one of which oversaw six dependent chapelries (143–4). Whitby had dependent monasteria such as Osingadun, also termed a parochia, apparently the first use of the word in the modern sense of parish and indicating that this was a pastoral foundation subject to the "greater monasterium" of Whitby (144–5).

Abbots were closely associated with the priesthood in references such as presbyter abbas; this combination either indicates that it was unusual for monks to be ordained or indicates distinctive rank (145–6).

It is clear, then, that monasteria had some degree of pastoral responsibility, whether for the wider lay community or for their own tenants. The unit of the parochia is not well defined in the sources (146–7). On dependent chapels:

Though lacking in the early stages of the conversion (Bede notes that oratoria uel baptisteria had yet to be built in Eadwine's reign), they seem to have been taken for granted by the early eighth century if not before; there was clearly nothing remarkable in the oratorium uillulae to which Drythelm [sic] went to pray after recovering from the dire illness which occasioned his momentous vision. (147)

These oratories were probably commonly used for baptism and burial rites (147–8). The central administration of the sacraments was pushed in late Anglo-Saxon England in connection with the raising of church fees, but early monasteria seem to have received an income only from their estates; only the West Saxons may have paid ciricsceat to the local monasterium, though we lack explicit evidence, and tithing was not introduced until Edgar (148).

While Continental bishops were on good terms with the monastic communities, Anglo-Saxon bishops were assured of certain sacramental privileges but not of their power over communities, as they lacked urban centres. Lindisfarne's bishop answered to the abbot while within the monasterium, and Whitby for a time had a bishop on premises who seems not to have interfered with the abbess's independence. In fact, Whitby looks more powerful in the late seventh century than its episcopal see of York (149–50). Bede on a few occasions admonishes bishops and their immediate associates (150). Tensions are also implied in the fact that bishops were keener than writers like Bede to distinguish between monasteriales and sanctimoniales on the one hand and clerici and ecclesiastici on the other (151, referencing Foot). The dynamic among the Church's orders seems to have depended on the initiative and improvization of individuals; in many cases, bishops could not rival the status of royal abbots and abbesses (151&ndas;2).

Bede saw pastoral care as the duty of an elite group of monastics. He derived his terminology from Gregory, who intentionally substituted vague terms along the lines of "teachers" and "preachers" for the specific ecclesiastical terms, intending to convey that "spiritual authority was not to be equated with ecclesiastical office" (a quote from McClure). Gregory's own monastic background lay behind this emphasis. Though he sought to safeguard monks' freedom from worldly cares, he also appointed monks as missionaries and ordered them to continue living according to their vows even as bishops (152–3). Bede inherited this perspective but probably was less aware of it: monasteries in his England were so firmly involved in pastoral care that he never questioned their role in these matters. Bede thought of pastoral workers as monastic, and trained at monastic powerhouses like his Jarrow (153).

Remarkably, Bede imagined a world that included an adult catechumenate (154). He also intended for the laity to partake in communion regularly, in addition to hearing mass, but communion required prior fasting, abstinence, and penance, and accordingly lists the abstinent elderly and the virginal young first as candidates for such activity (154–5). He generally held a very low view of marriage, betraying his monastic biases (155–6) and going well beyond Gregory, rather following Theodore (156). Notably,

Taking such a sombre view of sexuality, the monastic élite of the early English church effectively turned their backs upon the married. The many strict provisions with which marriage was hedged about, if applied in their full severity, would have made it very difficult for the average spouse to have been a frequent participant in the liturgy even where it was regularly available. (156)

Pagan practices were similarly condemned; as many activities under this heading, such as the use of auguries, would have been deeply embedded in the structure of society, their prohibitions must be seen as highly disruptive (156–7).

To enforce prohibitions, clergymen relied on penance. Early Christian penance had been a public, one-time affair involving segregation from the general community of the faithful; consequently, it came to be deferred to the death-bed. This system gave way to penitential rituals including fasting, almsgiving, and psalm-singing, but it was repeatable. Even so, it better suited the monastery (where it originated) than the lay world. The Insular system, developed in the sixth and seventh centuries, relied on confession to a priest or bishop and the use of tariff lists (penitentials). Because confession was followed by substantial and austere penance before reconciliation was possible, the Insular system was closer to the ancient system of public penance than to the later medieval confessional practice that evolved into today's (157–8). Seventh-century England did not know either Continental system, and Theodore vouches for the absence of public penance; there was only Insular penance. Even so, both Theodore and Bede appear to have internalized some of the old system, leading to some inconsistencies (158). Certainly Bede's position on penance is exceptionally severe. His account of Dryhthelm, who becomes a monk out of compunction, shows again that Bede's model of piety was the regular life, and he saw little place for laymen (158–9). Theodore's penitential is clearly intended for the laity, but it too is so severe as to be practically incompatible with the lay life (159–60).

Since the severe penalties imposed would have encouraged cynicism and apostasy, the ecclesiastical establishment required some form of coercion. To this end, penitence was linked with royal power: legal restitution reduced the required penitence, while secular power could impose penitence in the form of lifelong monastic interment (160–1). The effectiveness of such arrangements would have varied depending on the strength of aristocratic–monastic connections, which is why Bede took such an interest in the conversion of powerful men. The lack of penitential writings is evidence against its widespread practice, and Bede refers to the wealthy buying off their penitence with gifts (161–2). The austere brand of piety promoted by men like Bede may be what led eighth-century bishops to seek to control proprietary monasteria, i.e. the same ones lambasted by Bede for their lack of discipline, as these did serve a pastoral function but would have been more attractive than institutions after Bede's model (163–4).

The 747 Clofesho council focused squarely on pastoral matters, prescribing a standard to be upheld under the supervision of bishops, including preaching by abbots and priests (164). The laity are encouraged to partake of communion frequently, provided they are capable of the abstinence involved (or "refrain from sin"), and they are expected to practise penance. In short, the council expresses the same views found in Bede's letter to Ecgberht. The council's weakness is that it fails to recognise the pastoral work carried out in monasteria, reflecting tensions; above all, the canons offer a weak compromise in their mission to reform proprietary monasteries (165; see canon 5). The 803 and 816 councils were more outspoken, the former prohibiting lay or secular lords over monasteria and the latter decreeing that abbots and abbesses be elected by their diocesans with the approval of their communities. It the resulting network of episcopal minsters that eventually led to the late Anglo-Saxon pastoral system (165–6).

Offering the cult of Cuthbert as an example, Thacker emphasizes the role of the cult of saints in reaching the faithful (166ff.); sites associated with saintly healing often sprouted medical expertise as well, no doubt financed through cultic revenues. The main draw, however, was direct access to shrines and relics, bypassing the sacraments that demanded severe penance (167). Although the literature mostly records monks and aristocrats as beneficiaries of miracles, that same literature also claims that people from all walks of life would visit the tombs of holy individuals, and relics were kept even among the laity (168). In Gaul, a man named Aldebert had success among the people claiming to have direct access to forgiveness without the need for confession, supposedly causing many to leave the church and follow him instead. This shows the demand for less austere alternatives than the way commended by Bede (169).

Bede saw for the English an important spiritual role in world history, and this role required extraordinary discipline and left no place for compromise. The vocality of Bede and Theodore has led scholars either to assume monastic ideals were more successful than they were or that the religion here described could not have been influential among the laity. The tone of Bede's letter to Ecgberht suggests that his ideals met with resistance, but the fact that the Vikings were converted within a generation of their arrival shows that the Anglo-Saxons with whom they interacted were indeed Christians. "[T]he royal and proprietary communities were far thicker on the ground than the strictly observant monasteria. To them, and to the local cults which they enshrined, must be ascribed much of the responsibility for the slow dissemination of the Christian faith among the Anglo-Saxons" (170).

author: Rosser, Gervase
title: The Cure of Souls in English Towns Before 1000
abstract:
While the boundaries between monastic and clerical communities in the period 700–1000 is hard to define 267), all minster clergy were required by law to render pastoral service (268; ref. to Foot, "Parochial Ministry"). The Christian mission from its beginnings in England happened outwards from significant places: Roman towns originally, they developed into towns again in the tenth century. In the interim, the minsters at these centres served as bases from which to service the hinterland but also as places to which the faithful were drawn. The first function is found in Bede's letter to Echberht, the second in a post-Conquest anecdote about Aldhelm (268–9) and exploited the market function of towns (269). Although minsters may often have been founded to commemorate their founders, they took on pastoral functions. These functions included charity, education, and preaching and seem to predate the tenth-century reform (269–70).

There is evidence that the laity had extensive access to minsters even after 1000, and the Regularis concordia assumes laymen attended monastic mass; the same is implied in the architecture of rebuilt reformed houses (270). Lay worship in Benedictine chapels is also recorded in the later Middle Ages (270–3). There was always tension between the contemplative and pastoral modes, but they should be seen as complementary duties rather than mutually exclusive (273–4).

Prior to 1000, few local churches will have relieved the pastoral duties of minster communities in towns. Urban subordinate churches (lay foundations!) were mostly established between 1000 and 1150 due to the population boom, urbanization. and the end of lay control over the larger churches; Rosser speculates that they "met a demand for intimacy and independence in lay worship" where they were indeed founded by the laity, but other cases show signs of urban planning by the authorities. Local chapels cannot have had much impact on pastoral care in towns prior to 1000 (274–5, quotation at 274). Even the establishment of daughter-churches after 1000 did not take away the central minsters' prominence as centres of pastoral care: by 1300, their mobility led people to visit mother-churches rather than their local designated parish churches. "From the point of view of the Christian layman, a daughter-church was not by any means a complete surrogate for the parent institution. . . . These enduring roles of former minsters point to an early tradition of active pastoral care amongst such churches" (275–6, quotation at 276).

In addition to economic activity, relics and shrines would have been a major drawn bringing the laity within reach of pastoral care (276–7). Ælfric recommended preaching on Sundays and festivals, and his Catholic Homilies enabled literate priests and deacons to do so. Where the church was too small, preaching happened outdoors: Bishop Oswald of Worcester himself did this in the second half of the tenth century (277).

Seeking to improve pastoral work, Ælfric drew on Paul the Deacon and other Carolingian sources, but he himself used the vernacular, following Alfred's precedent. "Ælfric's novelty was not his insistence on the importance of preaching by all priests, but his systematic and practical provision of the basic materials for others to use." But preaching existed prior to Ælfric (278). The Blickling and Vercelli collections resemble Ælfric and Wulfstan in their emphasis on penance, clearly intended to effect confession and thus facilitate pastoral care; confession had an important educational function (279).

This educational role of the confessional may have been all the more important since schools do not appear to have been numerous before the late tenth century. Where these are recorded, they were located at the old minsters. In the late seventh century the young Willibrord was still a layman when he attended a school maintained by the clergy of Ripon minster. St Dunstan received his first education, around 920, from the minster community at Glastonbury — having himself taken the tonsure, according to one of his later biographers, but amongst other sons of noblemen for whom a life of religion was evidently not anticipated. At about the same time St Æthelwold in the city of Winchester began to study "the sacred writings"; his teachers, however, are not specified. Later, as bishop, Æthelwold would take delight in teaching boys, for whom he often had to translate the holy texts into English. Many, but clearly not all, of his pupils went on to become pastors in their turn, either as monks or secular priests. Indeed, Æthelwold's prize pupil was Ælfric of Eynsham himself. (279)

The laity had religious responsibilities: the 747 Council of Clofesho requires them to come to communion regularly, and Wulfstan's late tenth-century Canons of Edgar requires them "to learn the Creed and Pater Noster, to give alms and pay tithes, and to eschew adultery and pagan practices" (279–80). Clofesho called on clergymen not to be in contact with secular society [other than in pastoral care]; they were to lead by example as well as instruction (280).

Nearly all priests and clerks in minor orders living in England between 700 and 1000 were based in central places: actual or nascent towns. They resided in those communities generally called minsters; but whether they followed some elements of a daily rule, or were simply the more common clerical team ministries, their status and organization did not segregate them definitively from the laity of the immediate environs and surrounding hinterland. On the contrary; for they were the inheritors of the dual tradition of Christianity: that of the recluse who flees the corruption of the world, and that of the imitator of Christ's life on earth. (284)

author: Cartlidge, Neil
title: The Canterbury Tales and Cladistics
abstract: While advocating for the use of cladistics in textual criticism, points to some of the shortcomings of cladistic algorithms and draws into question some of the conclusions of work on The Canterbury Tales (by Robinson and O'Hara), notably The Wife of Bath's Prologue. Warns against the confirmation bias evident in the work reviewed, and points out that considerations external to cladistics are required in order to orient the resulting tree structure.

author: Platnich, Norman I., and H. Don Cameron
title: Cladistic Methods in Textual, Linguistic, and Phylogenetic Analysis
abstract: Observes that textual criticism and historical linguistics use methods analogous to cladistics in phylogenetics.

author: Robins, William
title: Editing and Evolution
abstract:
Rather than discuss the overlaps and differences between phylogenetic cladistics and textual stemmatics, describes the way both developed out of a genealogical analogy.

Textual criticism originated in German-speaking countries out of political, aesthetic, and religious needs for ur-texts and was championed above all by Karl Lachmann (90–1; see Timpanaro for a history of this field of studies).

As described in the handbooks by Maas and West, error is the basis of the genealogical grouping of textual witnesses; the aim is to reconstruct an archetype and produce a critical edition. In the process, one relies on recensio (deducing archetypal readings) and emendatio. The genealogical approach allowed for greater systemacy than simply to emend using one's own judgment (91). Even so, the whole approach rests on two evaluative assumptions: firstly, that the changes introduced detract from the quality of the text, which is deemed to be flawless in the archetype, and secondly, that editors are able to discern between errors and valid readings (91–2). Consequently, a later generation of textual critics (in the early twentieth century) came to see the discipline as one of art as much as science, and indeed more effective because it relies on the art of recension and emendation (92).

Evolutionary biology came into its own about the same time as textual criticism with Darwin's contribution of random mutations, turning it into a systematic discipline as well (92–3). Both disciplines were transformed in the nineteenth century by the development of genealogical models. Linnaeus had already used tree models but without a notion of descent; Darwin sketched out some trees visualizing descent in his notebooks and in The Descent of Species, with no clue that his tree models originated under the influence of textual criticism. They are best thought of as having arisen independently, as their use seems almost inevitable (93–4). Darwin does refer in his Origin of Species to the trees used in historical linguistics as an analogy for his own use of trees (94–96). The analogous use of trees in textual criticism would have been less appropriate because different assumptions underlie it (for instance that of "error" in stemmatics), and while both fields were at the time teleological, biology focused on the teleos of present-day forms while stemmatics sought the ancient archetype (96–7).

Genealogical models relied on a skeptical attitude that ended up weighing them down. In textual criticism, the need to doubt every reading made clear to its practitioners how corrupt their textual traditions were, leading to cynicism as to our ability to attain the original meaning. In New Testament studies, this led to crises of faith. Biology was haunted by the disconnect from ethics. Linguistics likewise was stifled by the hypothetical nature of their reconstructions. In all these disciplines, such nineteenth-century skepticism was to lead to new developments in the twentieth century (97–8). Nietzsche is an example of the doubt arising from the genealogical model: he started as a philologist but in his Genealogy criticizes metaphysical and teleological models posing as abstract truth (98–9). Nietzsche's later works were influenced by Darwinism, both relying on and deconstructing physiological explanations for abstract ideals (99–100).

The twentieth century produced Bédier, who called into question the role of the author and accused editors of favouring readings that served their own aesthetic preferences; Bédier advocated best-text editing on the basis of a single witness (10–1). Both biology and textual criticism came to rely on statistical approaches: biology developed "numerical taxonomy" and "phenetics." "The difficulty, some would say the impossibility, of using statistics about similarities to formulate inferences about genealogy meant that this mid-century development did not easily merge with phylogenetic hypotheses." Scriptural philology likewise turned to statistics, but it did not much affect the general field of textual criticism (101).

During a mid-twentieth century low in interest in diachronic models, there was something of a return to pre-critical models, using abstract typologies not unlike that of Linnaeus or relying on Bédier's subjective notion of the best text (101–2). Biology and textual criticism came to diverge in the theory wars of the 1960s and 1970s. Biology took a renewed interest in descent with modification, but redefined its terms along cladistic lines: Hennig argued that the best tree was the one requiring the smallest number of steps (changes) in a phylogenetic tree, recalling Lachmannian stemmatics, and computers were used to process data for their systemacy and processing power (102). The available data exploded with the rise of molecular biology, especially DNA, which moreover leaves an unmistakably trace of its development sequence (104).

Textual studies morphed under the influence of poststructuralism: authorship and the rootedness of meaning were deconstructed. Genealogical trees were rejected in favour of unregulated networks (rhizomes; Gilles Deleuze, Felix Guattari) (104). Theorists and editors were locked in mutual suspicion at first, but eventually engaged in dialogue, deconstructing the author–reader antithesis and taking political implications of the search for "error" into consideration. The genealogical model remained a battle-ground strawman. New Philology in the 1980s and 1990s restated Bédier's objections to the Lachmannian method on a theoretical footing, problematizing the search for a lost original and refuting the last thing connecting biological and textual systematics (105). Impelled by Foucaultian thinking, new ideas turned to manuscript relations out of an interest in the circulation of texts in the construction of social authority: for these purposes it was relevant to know how manuscript copies were related to one another, giving stemmatics a place within the rhizome as one among many entryways (105–6).

Prior to cladistics, biology had relied on dendrograms that showed degree of similarity as a branching tree with no implication of descent or orientation. Cladistics replaced this with the cladogram, which does seek to identify lines of descent by finding the tree with the fewest changes from an earlier to a later species (106). Although cladistics originally asserted that only "derived," not "original" states of a feature counted as evidence of descent, it proved impossible to determine whether a state was original or derived. The unrooted tree, which does not presuppose the direction in which change occurs, was developed to allow features to be included regardless whether their state is original or derived; a cladogram can subsequently be rooted and turned into a phylogenetic tree, usually on the basis of evidence from an external group (106–8). Unrooted trees ("chains") also appeared in textual studies; 1959 saw a chain converted into a stemma, using clustering methods rather than parsimony, making it closer to work in biological phenetics than cladistics. Either way, the approach had little impact (107). Cladistic analysis was first applied in textual criticism in 1989 on the grounds that cladistics, as a discipline intended to establish genealogy, was closer to Lachmannian tradition than was the strictly comparative discipline of phenetics. This development was more successful. It allowed textual scholars to sidestep issues with authorship and error: these matters could be brought in later, when rooting the tree (108).

In 1991, Peter Robinson challenged the scholarly community to reproduce his traditionally derived stemma of Svipdagsmál using quantitative methods; Robert O'Hara came impressively close. Robinson went on to use cladistics to show that Chaucer had revised the Wife of Bath's Prologue to censor its mysogyny; the Nature article made a large impression on the press. In fact, Robinson et al. overstated their case somewhat: they produced their cladogram only after subjectively excluding fourteen manuscripts, while they rooted the tree and identified the earliest state of the text using traditional methods. Indeed, textual scholars wondered why the article was so focused on uncovering the authorial text at all, as the Tales were viewed as a text surviving in multiple authorial redactions, and revised by perfectly competent authors. The work's reception in the humanities was somewhat hostile. "In general, students of medieval texts remain more skeptical than curious about cladistics" (109–11; quotation at 111). Biblical scholars have been more interested. The landscape of gospel manuscripts is plagued by contamination, for which phylogenetics does not account, as species generally descend from a single ancestral species. The Lachmannian method likewise has difficulty accounting for contamination: Maas lamented that there is no remedy for contamination. In the case of normal cladistics, contamination ends up skewing the data set, yielding unreliable results. It is accordingly more appropriate to visualize the results as a net (reticulation) rather than a tree. Biblical scholars have tried to account for contamination within the cladistic algorithm, but the range of possible reticulations is large, yielding problems of interpretation (111–12). Biologists have had to deal with similar problems especially with single-cell organisms, where lateral gene transfer, reduplication, and hybrydity are common, though these processes are not ultimately analogous to the textual processes (112–13). In addition, there is no textual counterpart for the molecular clock that helps establish a chronology and estimate the likelihood for a change to happen over the amount of time that has passed between [specimens]. This mechanism is the preferred method for establishing descent in cladistics. In textual studies, there is no standard rate of error or chronology between witnesses. Thus the principle of Maximum Likelihood is not available to textual critics, who instead avail themselves of the Maximum Parsimony model (113).

Around 2000, cladistics were adopted in the study of cultures, with special interest in Dawkins's concept of memetics, but textual scholars have retreated; the rare expertise and funding for digital projects (!) flow towards hypertext editions, whose rhizome structure is more in tune with the reigning philosophy. Humanists are not trained in the programming of algorithms, but above all different logics apply to science and the humanities (113–14). The focus of humanists is additionally more on the interaction between text and society than with pure derivation, and so humanists will generally reject a cladistics that merely replicates stemmata produced by traditional criticism. David Greetham urged all those interested in genealogical methods to incorporate environment and idiosyncrasy in their analyses, suggesting that ecology is a better point of comparison between biology and textual studies than is phylogeny. Even biologists have come to emphasize the "historically contingent" nature of evolution, both in consequence of environmental factors and in absence of it (114–15). Closes by seeing a promising role for cladistics in textual studies as one among several sources of information consulted in the production of a stemma; but scholars will have to come to a better model for explaining how quantitative methods account for human creativity. An ecological approach would be a good place to start (116).

author: Wormald, C. P.
title: The Uses of Literacy in Anglo-Saxon England and Its Neighbours
publication: Transactions of the Royal Historical Society
abstract:
Distinguishes, first, between active and passive literacy, and between pragmatic literacy (being able to recognize if not write one’s own name) and cultural literacy (a range from reading vernacular prose to composing Latin). We cannot induct from specific instances of writing to a general ability to read (95). We must avoid the fallacy of the anticipated audience: even widespread inscriptions do not prove a reading audience, and though works addressed to lay individuals may seem to offer greater evidence, their recipients may have had them read to them if they were in the vernacular, and if they were Latin, they may not have been used at all except to flatter. “It is not sufficiently appreciated that vernacular translations, in the first instance, merely allow works to be read to illiterates.” Vernacular literature could induce lay literacy; it does not demonstrate it. Even an enumeration of individual cases does not show widespread literacy, as we lack evidence that these examples are representative (96). Instead, we need to look also for schools, books, and administrative duties with laymen attached to them, as well as neighbouring cultures, and above all attitudes towards literacy, as done in Goody’s Literacy in Traditional Societies (96–97).

As checks on literacy Goody’s volume identifies the “vested interests of learned classes” (they stood to benefit from retaining the monopoly); technical obstacles such as nonphonetic alphabets; and the concentration of learning in a second language (in our case, Latin). Wormald considers a more prominent hindrance an “indifference or even hostility to literacy within classes of society which cherished other values” (97). Theodoric the Ostrogoth’s supposed illiteracy seems at variance with his position, but Procopius reports that the Goths considered education unmanly, and so Theodoric would not have wanted at least to seem literate to his own people. Hildemar of Corbie (ninth century) similarly juxtaposes the schola divini servitii with the schola humani servitii, the latter being an honourable training in war and courtliness (97–8).

On the Continent, early medieval women were often better educated than men, and laywomen are strikingly commonly mentioned as “owners, dedicatees, even authors, of books, and as the decisive influence upon the education of their families” (reference to Grundmann, ‘Die Frauen und die Literature in Mittelalter,’ Archiv für Kulturgeschichte 26 [1936]). A fear of femininity curbed literacy among men, but also highlights systems that preserved literacy (98). First among these is the Church, and as the qualities of bishops and monks came to exert pressures on those of kings, royal literacy became important. Southern European memories of the Roman standard helped uphold the importance of literacy there more than in the north (99). In contrast, the Germanic barbarians failed to impose their language on those they conquered. The prestige of Latin restricted literacy among those whose native language was Germanic (99–100). This tension resembles that found in some Third World settings today. Despite Charlemagne’s efforts, his secular aristocracy appears to have been less literate than its Merovingian predecessor. Early Carolingian capitularies likewise represent an effort to encourage the official use of writing, but their lack of structure suggests that it was their representation of the king’s spoken word rather than their written form that gave them authority, and pragmatic literacy fell in the ninth century (100–1).

In Ireland, aristocratic children were sent to monastic schools even when destined for secular life (just as they had previously been educated by druids). It also had an independent secular learned tradition, stimulating a vernacular written tradition, but the members of the filid (the elite class of poets) could become so only by birth or by training in their own schools. Thus the tradition was well guarded, and the seeds of literacy in fact ended up limiting its spread (101–2).

In England, Alfred declared his hopes of restoring learning by means of the vernacular (102–3). That vernacular was already well established in law, documents, and poetry, resembling Ireland rather than Europe, perhaps under Irish influence and perhaps under influence of Theodore; but the state of the vernacular prior to Alfred should not be overstated. Though Bede had translated Creed and Paternoster, and Clofesho allowed the translation of mass and baptism, there is no evidence that these could be read rather than heard by those who knew no Latin (103–4). It seems there simply was less potential for a lay literate class here than in Ireland (104–5). Accounts of kings (Sigeberht, Aldfrith) who received educations abroad, and noble children educated at the monasteries of Ripon and York, are the exception. “It is not, as often, easy to be sure what Asser means, but it looks as though, for all his enthusiasm, Alfred did not learn to read at all until he was nearly forty, and that he then learnt simultaneously to read English and Latin. . . . Asser thus not only underlines the lack of an independent tradition of vernacular education, but also highlights scarcely less dramatically than Procopius the social and cultural obstructions to barbarian literacy, even in a relatively cultivated court.” Alfred’s mother appears a notable exception (105). His efforts to educate the nobility in the vernacular appear to have been a novelty. There is no Continental precedent for this use of the vernacular, either, although Alfred himself acknowledges the inspiration of Christian nations translating Scripture, a point previously made by Walafrid Strabo. Importantly, Alfred did not wholeheartedly embrace the vernacular but felt forced to do so in the absence of Latin learning (106).

As he states, Alfred intended for all freeborn sons to learn to read. This ambition was driven by a desire for wisdom for his subjects as well as for himself, as wisdom brought divine favour. The literacy he pursued “was strictly cultured rather than pragmatic, and derived its inspiration not so much from imperial Rome, as from the City of God” (107).

Alfred’s push for the vernacular did not drive it out of the shadow of Latin; Æthelwold apologized for translating the Benedictine Rule, but wished to leave no excuse for error. Ælfric repeated the sentiment (107–8). There is also no evidence of widespread lay literacy after Alfred: there is little mention of schools taking in laymen. Ælfric’s reference to a semiliterate priest in his youth may or may not be evidence of parish schools. Wulfstan’s Canons of Edgar followed Theodulf’s recommendation that priests teach (Canon 51), and Theodulf’s Capitula were available in England, but we do not know of any results these decrees may have had there; what we do know is that “Aelfric and his contemporaries were overwhelmingly concerned with the education of the clergy. In a passage from the English preface to his Grammar, Aelfric seems almost to echo Alfred’s preface, but he makes it much clearer that it is the supply of clergy with Latin skills that preoccupies him. If, then, lay education existed, and it was certainly not discouraged by Aelfric and Wulfstan, we must accept that it was incidental to the education of the clergy” (108–9, quotation at 109).

Lay libraries include Æthelstan’s, who was probably literate, though most of his books were Bibles and psalters, these were probably not written at court, and his attitude towards his books seems to have been more one of gift-exchange (109). Ælfric’s patrons supply the best evidence outside of court, but his letter to Sigeweard could have been read out to its addresssee. Æthelweard was almost certainly literate given his authorship of a Chronicon, while his son was a patron of Ælfric’s and his grandson-in-law gifted books to Crediton; but this family is of royal descent and thus atypical (109–10). The evidence ends there: “[i]f the illustrated late Saxon manuscripts of the translated or versified Old Testament were indeed aimed at laymen, this is very double-edged evidence for lay literacy.” The only non-royal lay owner of a book listed in Ker’s Catalogue is a woman, Ælfgyth, and a handful of book-lists mention owners that may or may not qualify as lay and non-royal. Thus “the general is not one of extensive lay literacy, and the exceptions tend to explain themselves away: as royalty, as ladies, or as men whose bookishness was shortly to lead them to a wholesale renunciation of secular life. . . . [W]e need better evidence than this before we can accept that cultured literacy was widely established even in later Anglo-Saxon society” (111).

Pragmatic literacy may have had a presence: there may have been a chancery from the mid-tenth century onwards, and documents and seals survive. Even so, these continue to give the impression of being written counterparts of the king’s spoken decree, the latter giving them the force of law. Wulfstan’s appended account of why he wrote Æthelred VI suggests as much (111), and the phrasing of documents likewise points to their reflecting an oral tradition (112).

Law codes after Alfred do insist their written form be put to use, but the tradition dies out after Cnut. Moreover, no law case that comes to Wormald’s mind involves a citation of a law code (112–13). “I conclude that the traditional view of restricted literacy is substantially valid for the whole early English period. . . . [T]he literacy of the clergy could never be taken for granted, and this was much the more urgent priority for the writers and authorities of the early Middle Ages” (113). Alfred shows that there was great potential for lay literacy to take off, but it didn’t (113–14).

author: Kelly, Susan
title: Anglo-Saxon Lay Society and the Written Word
abstract:
Argues that Anglo-Saxon lay literacy can be reconstructed from the recognition that writing had superseded speech and memory to a considerable degree by the end of the period.

A small corpus of runes survives, with only the Franks Casket and the Ruthwell Cross containing longer texts; it is possible that a large body of communications existed in wood and has disappeared, but we have no evidence. The use of runes in riddles, on coin, and by Cynewulf shows they were known among the elite, and the fact that thorn and wynn were adopted into the Roman alphabet in the late eighth century suggests some clerics knew runes. By the late period, however, they seem to have gone out of use (24).

While Roman literacy entered the country from the north and from the south, early secular literature (laws, charters) survives only from the south, presumably as a result of Viking disruptions; early northern literature is ecclesiastical or scholarly only. The Irish missionaries in the north spoke a vernacular themselves, which may be of relevance for their training of locals, but this is mere speculation (24–25).

Latin and vernacular land charters form the primary line of evidence (1500 total, 500 pre-900; as many as of 500 may be forgeries or revisions, and the proportion for the earlier documents is higher) (25–26).

Since the earliest surviving charters are from the 670s, the arrival of Theodore of Tarsus has commonly been adduced as having started the tradition, but Kelly rejects this reading on the grounds that they were at this time too widespread and too independently formulaic to have recently been introduced. Alternative geneses have been proposed ranging from an arrival with Augustine in 597 to more recent foreign influences (26). The disappearance of earlier documents may be explained by the use of papyrus, used in Italy and Gaul into the seventh century, the transition to parchment taking place in the 670s, which is also when Anglo-Saxon documents begin to appear; direct Frankish influence is, however, difficult to argue given that Kent had no royal chancery at this time but produced its documents decentrally in episcopal scriptoria, while there is little Frankish influence detectable in the documents (26–7).

Though the papyrus hypothesis must remain a hypothesis, internal evidence speaks for the Anglo-Saxon charter’s development prior to the 670s. Its peculiarities include the subscription of witnesses in a single manuscript hand: not one Anglo-Saxon charter contains true autograph subscriptions. This need not signal mass illiteracy, as a cross would have been admissible in Italy; in fact crosses are typically included in Anglo-Saxon subscriptions, but they all seem to be in the scribal hand. In this way, witness lists appear “to represent an attempt to imitate the outward form of a regular Italian charter without regard for its legal substance.” This cannot have been introduced by a recent Mediterranean arrival but would rather have developed in the mid-seventh century when the first generation of missionaries was dying out (27–8).

Whereas Italian diplomas were secular documents, Anglo-Saxon diplomas were ecclesiastical: they typically record the transfer of land into than hands of a cleric as a representative of his community or to a lay individual intending to establish or endow a monastery; it was drafted by a clergyman (the bishop or one of his scribes) on behalf of the beneficiary. The documents have an ecclesiastical flavour for instance in the substitution of spiritual punishments for secular ones. These charters reflect the desire of churchmen to guarantee their property (28). To be admissible to the laity, the drawing up of the charter was made part of a visible, ritual ceremony involving the transfer of a sod of land and its placement on an alter or evangeliary; charters were also copied, and perhaps originally bound, into evangeliaries, evidently associating them with the divine. There is evidence in one instance that the document would have been blank at the time of the ceremony, suggesting that the real value lay in the ceremony, not the written document, which was no more than a symbol of ownership (28–9).

The ecclesiastic efforts to get the laity to acknowledge written charters led the laity to acquire their own written titles by the late eighth century, and the majority of late Anglo-Saxon documents benefit the laity (and the ecclesiastical bias of preservation suggests this proportion was higher still in reality). Charter land was bocland by definition, which made it attractive because it was alienable (29–30). Since the document was transferred with the land, its contents were neglected; it was possession of the document that proved ownership of the land (30–1; so also Keynes, Diplomas 141).

The documents changed in the ninth century, notably adding in a boundary clause, often in vernacular detail, suggesting that they were now true written records. Also at this time, legal documents other than Latin diplomas appeared in the vernacular or in mixed languages: wills, leases, and various agreements. Sealed royal writs were produced to accompany Latin diplomas and certifying that the beneficiary’s right to the land would be recognized (31).

Of 58 surviving wills, 53 are in English. Some are detailed and complex, recording what should happen to the commissioner’s property upon his passing or even after the passing of his heirs (31–3). The counterpart of these lay bequests is the ecclesiastical lease, recording tenancy from ecclesiastical landowners, usually as chirographs with the text in duplicate. Chirographs were extensively used, perhaps because their authenticity could be verified by the illiterate (33–4). Leases could be in either language or both, with the boundary clause typically in English, as well as some other practical information such as sanctions or conditions. Some 25 percent also summarize the Latin content in English, suggesting the existence of vernacular literacy (34).

Other documents included manumissions (surviving from the tenth century onwards): manumission was at its core an oral ceremony, but written manumissions (in evangeliaries) served as precautions against challenges to a freedman’s status. Property arrangements were written down by the eleventh century. Some such information survives in abbey compilations, indicating that “at least by the end of the Anglo-Saxon period, the great monastic houses kept detailed records of their estates, tenants, rents, stock and disbursements, which supplemented their formal title-deeds. The king and many lay landowners might have followed the same practice; such secular records had no chance of direct survival, but they probably underlie many sections of Domesday Book” (34–5, quotation at 35).

By the tenth and eleventh centuries, English was used extensively as a literary language, it was used in schools, and it was used in documents. There were ecclesiastical efforts to standardize the vernacular by the late tenth century. There is evidence of ecclesiastical vernacular literacy preceding Latin literacy, as King Edgar commissioned Æthelwold to translate the Benedictine Rule apparently for use by nuns, and several surviving manuscripts of the Rule are bilingual (35).

There is some manuscript evidence for the decline in literacy alleged by Alfred, including the fact that this decline predated the Viking attacks (36–7). But Alfred alone cannot be credited for the development of the vernacular: Bede himself engaged in translation for the benefit of his pupils and the Church; glossaries exist from the eighth and ninth centuries; vernacular literary texts predate Alfred; Alfred’s mother had a volume of vernacular poetry to give away; and Alfred was in the habit of reading English books. We may now add to this the use of the vernacular in legal documents in the first half of the ninth century (37–8). This has been blamed on a loss of Latin (38), but this cannot have been the full story, as royal diplomas continued to be written in Latin as other documents turned to the vernacular. English was functionally preferable for certain kinds of information, such as render lists and boundary clauses that relied on terminology that would have been difficult to translate. To record verbal statements of intent or agreements, it was also preferable to use the language spoken by the parties involved. Above all, English was more accessible (39).

The disappearance of spoken Latin and Roman bureaucracy must also have contributed to the rise of the vernacular in legal documents. The fact that the earliest law codes were written up in the vernacular cannot be explained by a disconnect between Germanic law and the Latin language; indeed, crafting a new vernacular Schriftsprache was a larger challenge than writing up a law in Latin. Instead, the Roman missionaries must have adopted the vernacular early on to get anywhere with their work, and so the vernacular law codes are only the surviving parts of what must have been a corpus starting with glossaries for their own use (40–1).

“The early English church had to be tolerant of the vernacular if it was to have a priesthood of any size.” Bede claims to have translated the Creed and Paternoster for priests who knew no Latin, and he refers to clerics and monks with no knowledge of Latin. In fact, the expansion of the Church may have diluted the knowledge of Latin, and this may have played a role in effecting the decline of Latin bemoaned by Alfred (41).

Lay education may have been available: we have some evidence of noble children attending monastic schools, apparently extending the custom of fostering children out into other households: Wilfrid was sent to be fostered by a monk and was educated there but not tonsured, and as a bishop he received children ad erudiendum who still had the choice when they grew up whether or not to take vows. We do not know how representative such anecdotes are, or what their education was like, but we may assume it started in the vernacular, and it need not in all cases have progressed to include Latin. Asser’s account of Alfred’s education is the only detailed account to survive; it describes Alfred as illiteratus until at least his twelfth year for lack of suitable teachers, although he was in the habit of memorizing vernacular poetry. After he became king at 22, Alfred often read vernacular books aloud (recitare) and continued to learn poetry by heart, but he was dissatisfied with his knowledge and so he assembled a group of tutors who could read aloud to him, since he could not yet read anything himself (we may assume this now means in Latin, and perhaps we should here also see a distinction between basic and advanced Latin, as Asser’s account seems to suggest Alfred was able to understand spoken Latin, although the passage could alternatively be read to say that his tutors orally translated the texts for him). Alfred began to legere et interpretari in 887, presumably meaning Latin (41–2).

Alfred refers to learned men having existed without as well as within the Church; Kelly grants that a modest proportion of laymen would have understood and read Latin. Bede calls two secenth-century kings doctissimi, though these appear to have been educated abroad, while other kings also showed an interest in learning: Ceolwulf showed an interest in the Historia ecclesiastica and asked for a copy, while Offa had one too. The first vernacular work produced under Alfred’s aegis was the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, suggesting a continued royal interest in historiography (42–3). Vernacular poetry and the Chronicle suggest secular audiences (43).

Kelly stresses that reading and writing may have played a different role in Anglo-Saxon society than we imagine, as a professional class of literates enabled the upper classes to get by without being themselves literate. “In the last resort, the case for widespread literacy in the modern sense among the early Anglo-Saxon laity must remain unproven. . . . Nevertheless, it seems clear that already by the ninth century the written word had been accommodated within secular society” (43–4, quotation at 43).

author: Snook, Ben
title: The Anglo-Saxon Chancery: The History, Language and Production of Anglo-Saxon Charters from Alfred to Edgar
abstract:
Focuses heavily on latinate style and the political ideologies it reflects. A selective synopsis follows.

[1: Brave New World: The Charters of Alfred and Edward] In spite of Alfred’s dominance in histories of late ninth-century England, his charter record is modest and full of forgeries, even if there is evidence he is the first to have moved their production into a royal secretariat (29–31). This stands in sharp contrast with ninth-century Mercia, whose extensive diplomatic record shows that Alfred’s cultural renaissance was rooted here. Alfred and Edward’s charters show Mercian style but also provide an insight into the inclusiveness of the West Saxon kingdom and its Christian-political ideology (30–1).

The high style of Latin in the ninth century was primarily characterized by the imitation of Aldhelm’s style, though some documents show an elevated style resembling Aldhelm’s but nevertheless contain no or few verified quotations from Aldhelm. Snook outlines a test of Aldhelmian style (32–3) and points out that no West Saxon charter comes close to the level of Aldhelmian style found in Mercian documents (33–6), and those that quote Aldhelm have Kentian connections (37–8), but their attempts to imitate Aldhelm are superficial and suggest the scribes had not themselves read Aldhelm (38–40). This suggests Aldhelm’s works were not circulated in Kent as much as they were in Mercia, but glossaries or formularies drawing on his work may have circulated in Kent, perhaps seeking to address the diminished quality of the Latin there (40–1). Most importantly, the influence of Mercian Aldhelmisms on West Saxon documents illustrates that the West Saxon documentary tradition was not set in stone but open to new influences (41).

The Mercian documentary tradition ended in the early tenth century as the production of charters was centralized under a unified crown (41–2). The elevated Mercian style was restrained at first but eventually supplanted the simpler West Saxon style (42).

Alfred was an obsessive communicator; when Edward acceded to the throne, he continued his father’s media strategy in the documentary realm by unifying diplomatic style, incorporating Mercian learning, which not only served his own ends but also must have satisfied the powerful Mercian faction in the newly combined kingdom (46–50). Alfred argued that it was necessary to recreate past glories through learning; Edward’s draftsmen recreated a golden age by imitating Aldhelm (50–3). This golden age also had the political aim of unifying the Anglo-Saxons against the Vikings (53–5).

[2: Æthelstan] Keynes has demonstrated beyond doubt the existence of a centralized writing office under Æthelstan, which then sent them to be archived at some monastery (59). The king granted a great deal of land on a regular basis; though a good number of grants benefit the Church, the first three were apparently to young English individuals in the Danelaw, suggesting Æthelstan sought to promote a loyal non-West-Saxon elite (61–6). The Latin of these documents is some of the most sophisticated of the Anglo-Saxon period, yet functionally they are conservative; Snook details how they appear to have been used, and how the royal style serves to express royal prestige (66–83).

[4: Turbulent Priests: Dunstan, Cenwald and Oda] Whereas one would hope to get a different perspective on events during the Benedictine Reform from the charter record, it seems that Cenwald and Dunstan themselves oversaw their production in the 940s and 950s, just as “[t]op ecclesiastics had. . . always been responsible for writing charters, or for overseeing their production.” Accordingly, their role did not represent a decentralization, but indeed these churchmen were able to take control of the chancery only by being influential at court (127–8). However, they came to use charters as their own PR tool, overshadowing the king’s attestations with their elevated style in the witness lists:

Increasingly, the role of the charter as a tool for projecting royal authority around the kingdom was hijacked by a powerful, pro-reform bloc within the court and used to promote its own agenda. Thus, the diplomatic record not only charts the earliest stages of the monastic reform movement that would tear through the Anglo-Saxon Church in the 960s, but, beyond that, it gives us a remarkable insight into the power struggle at the heart of the Anglo-Saxon state, showing us how Alfred’s successors struggled to tame the resurgent ecclesiastical establishment whose spectacular recovery Alfred himself had set in train half a century before. (128)

[5: Back to the Future: Edgar and “Edgar A”] In the 940s and 950s, draftsmen began to abandon the high style of Athelstan’s charters and instead to draw on Alfredian formulae, presumably collected in formularies; this trend, virtually absent from Æthelstan’s charters, was expanded under Edgar, whose scribes even reached for eighth-century models. This was presumably done to emphasize the continuity of dynasty from Alfred and before up to Edmund and Eadred [and Edgar, PSL] (159–87).

author: Keynes, Simon
title: The Diplomas of King Æthelred "the Unready" 978–1016: A Study in Their Use as Historical Evidence
abstract:
Among other things, grapples with the question of a royal chancery (14–28, 39–79, 134–53), answering in the affirmative from Æthelstan onwards.

Argues that the existence of a royal secretariat and the ecclesiastical production of documents need not be mutually exclusive (28). Comparing the hands, content, and style of charters from the 930s and 940s, it is clear that “diplomas in favour of various beneficiaries, ecclesiastical as well as lay, referring to estates in different parts of the country and preserved in the archives of different religious houses, could be produced by a single agency, acting on the same occasion and necessarily at a distance from some or all of the estates concerned. We may designate this agency a central secretariat” (45–6). Since the 930s and 940s were a time for which palaeographical evidence shows many diplomas were produced in the same scriptorium, the test is whether there is evidence for centralized production in the 950s and 960s, when a larger number of ecclesiastical scriptoria became active. Witness lists of 956 overlap considerably in four groups, each group representing a meeting of the king and his council. The style of each group is also congruent to a greater or lesser degree. This demonstrates that the beneficiaries had no say over the wording. Thus “the centralized drafting of royal diplomas was the norm in 956, just as it had been in the 930s and 940s. . . . establishing the existence of a central secretariat” (46–70, quotation at 67). As it operated at the witenagemot, the secretariat was mobile, thus dissociating it from ecclesiastical scriptoria, while the uniformity of the documents speaks against a rotation between different ecclesiastical groups: “it implies rather that the agency was a permanent office whose members were employed continuously for several years. As a permanent office it is likely to have been attached to the king’s household” (79–80). Its continued existence at the time of the reform, when multiple scriptoria were available, shows that it was the king’s wish for control rather than necessity that had him outsource the work to a single office. The greater variety in formulae in the 950s may indicate that the office grew. (80–1).

Discusses references to royal scriptores (135–6), the use of seals (136–40), and the role of the royal writ: evidence that fewer royal diplomas were produced in the eleventh century than in the tenth probably just means that there was a reduced need for new diplomas, which retained their value as proof of land ownership even after they were transferred (there may have been less new land available to begin with), while writs served the supplementary purpose of notifying the shire court that a transaction had taken place (140–2), though considerations of selective preservation may also apply (142–5). The chapter “The Central Writing Office” closes with a discussion of the office of cancellarius: this function may have existed without so specific a label, with scriptores and ministri being considered first and foremost members of the royal household (149–50). By Edward’s time, we begin to see references to notarii and cancellarii (150–1). The Liber Eliensis claims that the abbeys of Ely, St Augustine’s, Canterbury, and Glastonbury held the royal chancillorship in rotation. This seems unlikely given that neither the documents themselves, nor the other institutions make any reference to the arrangement, but the passage indicates that a monk at Ely thought the office of cancellarius existed and was associated with the custody of the sanctuaries (151–2). Keynes sums up:

there is evidence for the existence, during the reign of King Æthelred, of a royal secretariat responsible for the production of administrative communications and other documents associated with the exercise of government, and there is also evidence that Æthelred had a seal and that his archives were kept with the royal collection of relics. . . . It therefore seems reasonable to interpret in terms of a central and royal writing office the extensive diplomatic evidence for the production of royal diplomas by an agency that catered for all types of beneficiary and that was able to operate on the occasion of the witenagemot: it may have been less well developed in the tenth century than in the eleventh century, and it may never have had a complete monopoly of the production of royal diplomas, but by the close of the Anglo-Saxon period it had become an organization which contemporaries could dignify with the officials and status of a cancellaria. (152–3)

There is an important footnote to this paragraph that points out that Keynes uses “the concept of a royal secretariat or central writing office. . . for the sake of convenience. . . and not because there is any conclusive evidence that the presumed royal scribes were organized into a department”; proposes that court ecclesiastics would have played a role, and refers to Barlow’s Medieval England for this notion (153n242).

author: Harmer, F[lorence] E[lizabeth]
title: Anglo-Saxon Writs
abstract: Assumes a royal secretariat staffed by clergymen from the royal household. That many writs share a common origin is clear from their outward features, though there is some variation that would have depended on the requirements of the beneficiary. Æthelred grants an estate to his “faithful writer” in a 984 writ; “[i]t seems reasonable to suppose that Ælfwine was an ecclesiastic” (57–8; quotation at 58n2). Harmer assumes that there was a natural connection between the royal scriptorium and royal chapel, as it existed also in Frankish royal households and later England; see also Galbraith, who sees a connection between the activities associated with the words for chancery, sanctuary, and chapel. Saxo likewise describes the later bishop William of Roskilde as Cnut’s scribe and priest (58). It has been speculated that some bishops were rewarded with this office after successful tenures as heads of the royal chancery, but no evidence supports this view (58–9). The term cancellarius is not attested ahead of the Conquest (59–61).

author: Barlow, Frank
title: The English Church 1000–1066: A Constitutional History
abstract:
Characterizes the development from minster to local church as follows:

In the Germanic lands north of the Alps the Roman ecclesiastical organization of a bishop’s church in the city ruling over baptismal churches in the countryside was soon engulfed by a rising tide of private churches, founded and owned by the local landowners, and serving their estates. During the same period the new conception strongly influenced the old arrangements, so that baptismal churches began to be regarded as the private possessions of the bishops. By the eleventh century the ancient baptismal churches often enjoyed a title of honour (the mother church), vestiges of once paramount parochial rights, and generally a collegiate establishment, but had retained little or nothing of the public character which they had possessed under Roman law. (183)

Doubts furthermore that the Roman system of baptismal churches was every fully implemented in England, given that it was converted in part by monks. “It seems rather that a network of mission churches, in part monastic, was established during the conversion period, an organization consisting basically in one church, a bishop’s church, for each Germanic kingdom, and that offshoots were planted when a more intensive ministry was attempted or new ground taken in. But in England it is likely that private churches are almost as old as the mission centres of the bishops. The private church was a pagan custom which the Germans introduced into Christian organization” (183). Gregory’s revised instructions to convert the pagan sanctuaries fits into this reading, and Bede reports that Redwald had a church that served both pagan and Christian ends (183–4). Domesday Book suggests a development over time from one minster per hundred to a crowding of small proprietary churches: whereas the spread of early minsters corresponds to hundred boundaries, new churches followed manor and vill boundaries (184). Domesday makes clear that “[a]ll churches were Eigenkirchen” like those known from the Continent of the Carolingian and following eras, but differing widely in size and status, from manor churches to those on lands held in perpetual inheritance under the king (186–7, quotation at 187).

Argues that although priests were required to keep considerable libraries, “the desirable standard of training [for a priest] was in fact too high ever to be generally attained. Although a parish priest was technically handicapped if he knew no more Latin than was necessary to stumble through the services, for Latin was the language of the church, his ministry was conducted in the vernacular, and there was a recognized distinction between the pursuits of the scholars (bōceras) and those of the parish priest.” This is why scholars wrote vernacular treatises for the education of the clergy. Monks and higher clergy generally knew Latin: bishops with monastic backgrounds did, and Edward appointed foreign clerks who knew Latin to his bishoprics, but English-born bishops may not always have known Latin, as William of Malmesbury asserts most bishops in Archbishop Stigand’s day were illiterate. The high educational standard of the monasteries helps explain why so many monks were made bishop (277).

Barlow asserts that “[s]ome monasteries offered instruction to a few who were not oblates; but they were in no sense public schools” (277–8) and offers the anecdotal evidence of St Wulfstan having received a monastic education apparently without intending to become a monk (278n1, reference to Vita Wulfstani). Clerics could be educated “at some of the minsters” and informally from any educated clergy; one could enter a bishop’s household or support a parish priest. Barlow pieces together evidence from the pastoral literature as follows:

Archbishop Wulfstan, following Theodulf, ordered every priest to have a school in his house. Yet there must have been many up-country priests serving proprietary churches whose technical equipment was unsatisfactory. They had learned little from teachers who were themselves ignorant. Such men Ælfric chided: “What secular art can be learned without study and labour? . . .” (278)

The two-tier nature of the English Church required two channels of learning: Latin treatises for the bishops and vernacular textbooks for the lower clergy. The tenth-century reformers met this need, sourcing books and teachers from monasteries such as Fleury that had grown out of the Carolingian renaissance (278–9).

The pompous Latin style of the reformers was not suitable for educational purposes. Rather than develop a basic Latin style to this end, they switched to the vernacular when addressing the lower clergy (279–80). The vernacular flourishing that followed was ignored by historiographers of ecclesiastical authors (280–1). Barlow outlines Ælfric’s output, largely produced while at Cerne Abbas, and his influences, spending a paragraph on the pastoral letters as well (281–3).

Wulfstan “re-established ecclesiastical doctrine in his wild and semi-pagan province” with legal and preaching material, and his dioceses were to give the impetus to reestablish monasticism in the north after the Conquest (283). Barlow returns to influences, emphasizing Frankish sources and the fact that this tradition would have seemed old-fashioned to the Normans (283–7).

author: Flechner, Roy
title: Identifying Monks in Early Medieval Britain and Ireland: A Reflection on Legal and Economic Aspects
publication: Monachesimi d'oriente e d'occidente nell'alto medioevo
publisher: Fondazione centro Italiano di studi su ll'alto medioevo
abstract:
Compares evidence for the free or enslaved status of members of minster communities in Anglo-Saxon England and Ireland, focusing first on land transfer and then on spatial division.

Starts from the problem that peasant dependants cannot always be told apart from monks in the strict sense because of ambiguous terminology; indeed, ambiguity cannot always be solved, as it may have been endemic to the period’s concepts (805–7). Peasant dependants are nowhere in Anglo-Saxon sources mentioned as a class of their own, so their eistence is inferred from passing references; also, occasional archaeological evidence exists, notably in the separate (lay) cemetary at Wearmouth (808). The Kentish laws (Whitred) distinguish between the rights of laymen’s servants and churchmen’s servants, but these servants’ ability to litigate makes clear they had legal status in their own right (810). These may have assumed a middle status between the subiecti who Clofesho determines could not be oppressed or treated as slaves by minsters and the slaves appearing in Domesday (810–11). The Canons of Theodore indicate abbots could enslave criminals (811). Penitential servitude on ecclesiastical estates is also mentioned in Irish law (811). On the other hand, nonmonastic personnel were not always servile and could be freed when the estate on which they served was granted to the Church, as with Wilfrid’s 250 slaves. In Ireland there is evicence of manaig who were free and had assets (812). All free manaig nevertheless stood in a relationship to the church that was parallel to that between clients and their lay lords (813). Flechner now turns to a difference between Irish texts (the Collectio hibernensis and the Cérus Béscnai): the former does not differentiate between manaig based on their wergeld, suggesting a degree of ecclesiastical egalitarianism; but Hibernensis does distinguish based on other economic considerations. Overall, it gives the impression that manaig had some degree of property and were free though subject to the head of the ecclesiastical settlement (whether a religious or a lay lord). Other sources nevertheless group manaig with slaves, and glosses to the lawas reveal a difference between free and unfree manaig, implying that this distinction is implicit in the other sources (813–17).

Flechner conjectures monks in Ireland could keep their land in order not to have joining a monastery lead to a loss of status, as free status depended on land ownership (817–18); maybe transferring land to the Church meant retaining a stake, such as appointing the head of the church (819–20), i.e. the Eigenkirche model. Proprietary churches may have been the most prevalent church model in Ireland, with a hereditary abbacy (820). Hereditary abbacies were less common in Anglo-Saxon England but they existed. The Irish type of proprietary church differend from those found elsewhere in the level of control exerted by the owning family and in the existence of proprietary church federations (821–2).

Proprietary churches could reflect the secularization of churches, to the frustration of some ecclesiastics in England and Ireland alike (823). Giving the monastic community a role in church government could help rein in the excesses of lay patrons, but it is unclear whether peasant dependants were included in the number of those involved (823–4).

The discussion thus far recognizes two models of church/kin relationship: ecclesiastical communities could serve as an alternative to kin, taking away personal property; or they could reinforce kin identity by making ownership exclusive to kin, leaving a greater degree of free status of the individual (824–5).

The second half of the essay focuses on spatial division: it summarizes (and just about endorses) the view stemming from archaeology that those peasants living closer by the monastery (core, inland) were typically less free than those living at a greater distance (periphery, warland). The former are sometimes associated in the literature for Anglo-Saxon England with the cultivation of grains, the latter with animal husbandry; the idea is that those in the periphery provisioned other (lay) communities as well, and often had their own estates (825–8). The argument has been made for Ireland as well (828–9). There, however, there is also evidence of peripheral peasants growing stronger at the expense of core peasants, evincing a power structure the inverse of what is generally proposed (830).

Cereal cultivation is more typical of minster sites than of other settlements, and hence so are mills. At sites such as Yarnton and Lyminge, bread wheat grew in importance in the eighth century and was the dominant crop by the ninth. A settlement in the outer core of Ely combined cereal and cattle and may represent servile peasants in the service of the minster (830–1), and other settlements show a greater reliance on livestock (831); thus there is no clean-cut distinction between inland and warland, but some sites are more revealing (832). Similar reasoning applies to Ireland, though it had social conditions of its own, such as an association of cattle-rearing with free status, and remote island monasteries such as Iona had to be more self-sufficient (832–5).

Written sources suggests monks themselves did agricultural labour and reveal no difference between free and unfree fratres, but these depictions may be ideological; incidental mentions may be more reliable [though it is odd that Cædmon’s occupation is adduced as an instance of this, PSL] (835–7). The number of monks at Wearmouth and Jarrow is also instructive: 600 fratres compares to 17 founding monks at Jarrow, suggesting a great number of peasant dependants are included in the larger number (838). Irish sources permit no strict distinction between monks and monastic peasants, and some monachi were reformed brigands, who presumably were not expected to be literate (838–9). Minister in Hibernal sources refers to a personal attendant, serving the establishment’s princeps for instance, while servi were of lower status, for instance oblates without endowment (839). Irish depictions of fratres working the field may be “instances in which slavery is euphemised,” as Etchingham argues, “while in actual fact ‘they were even less free than the most dependent manaig, who still owed rents to the church, and hence were not entirely propertyless’” (839–40, quotation from Etchingham at 840).

Among his conclusions, Flechner observes that while authors could choose to be unambiguous, ambiguity of terms (frater, minister) is persistent in most sources (842–3). Irish sources sought to project harmony between the groups on an ecclesiastical estate, while Anglo-Saxon sources don’t excuse the existence of servitude (844).

author: Whatley, E. Gordon
title: Pearls Before Swine: Ælfric, Vernacular Hagiography, and the Lay Reader
publication: Via Crucis: Essays on Early Medieval Sources and Ideas in Memory of J. E. Cross
abstract:
When Ælfric condemns certain types of sources, such as the Vitas patrum, he probably represents a minority view rather than the perspective of the tenth-century reformers, as they were certainly read at Winchester (6; refs to Clayton). In addition, Clayton has argued that his condemnation followed patristic models and was not prompted by a personal dislike of the sensationalist nature of the texts in question (159–60). Whatley seeks to push back against this last position by drawing attention to passages where Ælfric voices his anxiety about unlearned readings as well as by showing his active intervention in his materials (160–1).

Opens by rehashing Ælfric’s reluctance in his preface to Genesis, noting in passing that “fluency in Latin was confined to a small minority of the higher clergy” (161–2, quotation at 161); notable is Whatley’s reading that “Ælfric reveals the alarm he felt upon learning from Æthelweard that the second half of the book had been translated already and thus was available for anyone to read and interpret in their own way (161–2). Whatley points out that Ælfric’s concerns”imply the existence of opinionated readers and self-appointed interpreters“, i.e. a”textual community" (163).

Whatley zooms in on the homily on St Clemens in the First Series of Catholic Homilies because its adaptation reflects Ælfric’s concern: the saint’s inconspicuous martyrdom might not have been well received, so Ælfric adds a coda adducing evidence that God does indeed come to the aid of his saints, even if he does not appear to do so for Clemens (163–5). Here too, Ælfric’s authorial attitude implies that the content was problematic to contemporary audiences (165–6).

Augustine has an extensive commentary on the pearls-before-swine passage of Matthew 7:6, which he reads as an injunction to conceal some biblical truths from audiences likely to misinterpret them (166–7). Ælfric writes in the same spirit in his Latin preface to the Lives of Saints when he explains he is only presenting a narrow selection of legends normally celebrated by vowees “ne forte despectui habeantur margarite christi.” Whatley takes Ælfric quite at face value here: the Lives of Saints are for the laity (Æthelweard and Æthelmær) and a portion of the legends of monastic currency had to be kept out of their hands (167–8).

In his First Series homily for the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, Ælfric shows active intervention. Where Peter delays his exorcism and Paul weeps in despair, Ælfric omits both these elements as well as Nero’s mockery, turning the episode into a smooth miracle story (168–71). Curiously, Ælfric follows up by explaining Peter’s delay, although he had edited this out of the narrative, revealing his discomfort with this element (171–2). He intervenes along similar lines at Peter’s crucifixion (172–3).

Although Ælfric does not identify his criteria for material suitable for unlearned audiences, but he considered the Vitas patrum unfit, presumably because these texts deal quite frankly with temptation; Ælfric would have deemed such accounts dangerous and of no value for his audiences (173–76). Moreover, the eremitic extremes of the Vitas patrum offered men like Æthelweard no accurate or appropriate picture of contemporary monasticism (176). Ælfric’s only detailed account of monasticism is his adaptation of the Life of Maurus, which focuses heavily on a pious lay patron called Florus and his gifts to the Church. Ælfric is selective in his transmission of the material, focusing particularly on the Florus’s tonsuring and above all on his gifts to the Church (176–81). It consists only of the outward aspects of the Rule visible to laymen, but omits the details of its observance (181). The Lives of Saints omit contemplatives, repentant prostitutes, humble masons, pro bono physicians, or pregnant protagonists, nor does Ælfric in any of his collections draw attention to Peter’s humble origins.
