He focuses instead on “secular kings and military saints from the same social caste as Æthelweard and Æthelmær themselves, and noble ecclesiasts who are mainly monk-bishops and idealized versions of the leaders of the English reform party” (181–2, quotation at 182).

author: Hill, Thomas D.
title: Apocryphal Cosmology and the ‘stream uton sæ’: A Note on Christ and Satan, Lines 4–12
abstract:
Proposes that Christ and Satan line 5b “stræm ut on sæ” should be read as “stræm uton sæ,” thus referring to the classical Oceanus, christianized into the river Jordan, flowing around the sea encircling the world’s land mass. Singles out the Visio Sancti Pauli as a popular text describing a river encompassing the earth.

The manuscript actually reads “uton” rather than “ut on”; it has universally been emended to the latter in a quest for sense, but the Oceanus reading is perfectly meaningful.

Hill also argues against the commonplace emendation from “grundas in heofone” to “grundas in geofone,” an emendation he claims is usually undertaken because the former makes no apparent sense [he does not mention the alliteration, PSL]; in the Oceanus reading, however, the reference could be “to the foundations of the first heaven which rest on the ‘stream uton sæ’ and are nevertheless ‘in heofone’” (553). The reading as a whole suggests influence from the Visio Pauli.

author: Jasanoff, Jay H.
title: From Reduplication to Ablaut: The Class VII Strong Verbs of Northwest Germanic
abstract:
All Germanic strong preterites except witaną were originally reduplicated (242–3); most verbs gave this up in the PG period (243). This loss was complete in verbs whose preterite stem vowel contrasted with the present, i.e. in classes I–VI. Where this was not the case, reduplication was preserved to maintain a contrast between tenses (243–4). This dynamic created a largely mutual exclusion between ablaut and reduplication (244).

Gothic uniquely retains reduplication as a “synchronically transparent process,” but it offers no unaltered echo of the Proto-Germanic situation: it shows a near-complete elimination of Verner’s Law; a loss of distinction between strong and weak stems; and a spread of reduplicating vowel ai at the expense of i, by analogy (244). Old Norse, Old English, and Old High German have reflexes of reduplicated preterites. The Old Norse ones are all based on verba pura, with róa and sá the most original forms (244–5). The best attested Old English case is hātan (245). Discusses Old High German forms in some detail (246–7). Generally though, reduplicating PG verbs are represented in North and West Germanic in class VII, which is in truth less than a class because it shows substantial variation within and between languages, with at least five subclasses (247–8). Sums up a range of theories of the origin of class VII (248–); “The majority of class VII theories have assumed that *hē2t, *hleup, etc. were formally based on reduplicated forms — either directly, via some regular phonological process, or indirectly, by analogy to forms that were regularly descended from reduplicated prototypes” (248). A common thread in these theories is that class VII verbs have their origin in contraction, but the author rejects this, asserting that “[t]he fundamental problem with the contraction theory is that the handful of mostly rare and obsolescent verbs that are supposed to have mediated the transition from reduplication to ablaut are utterly unsuited to the analogical role assigned to them” (251–2).

The main alternative to contraction is syncope accompanied by compensatory lengthening. One important theory by Bech and Vennemann speaks of (1) reanalysis of reduplication as an infix; (2) the reduction of the variety of such infixes; (3) syncope leading to compensatory lengthening (252). The author expresses considerable scepticism concerning Vennemann’s reasoning, for instance about the supposed spread by analogy of PG z, later rhotacized as r, but above all about the key elements of syncope and compensatory lengthening (252–60).

The author begins offering his own approach from p. 260 onwards. He points out that Gothic and Northwest Germanic speakers undertook different efforts to make reduplication more transparent and uniform, but in the latter these efforts were insufficient to salvage the phenomenon as an inflectional strategy, leading speakers to reanalyze the forms (260–1). “Clearly, some initial group of remodeled reduplicated forms was reinterpreted as having ablaut, and the rest of class VII ‘took off’ from this nucleus” (261).

The first step to making the reduplicated forms earlier to learn, and thus the first step towards the creation of a class VII, was to modify the rule for the reduplication of clusters. For instance, instead of prefixing the form with a syllable starting in the first cluster consonant where the second is a liquid or nasal, Northwest Germanic retained the second cluster consonant and repeated it after the original sequence (cf. Gothic faifrais with ON grera). This development can be summarized as a priorization of onset preservation (262). It is not obvious that this follows from stress rules, but it is safe to say that initial stress was a necessary condition (262–3).

The prominence of r in Old Norse (and other Northwest Germanic) verbs of class VII follows from multiple independent factors including the revised cluster rule, the development from z to r, and the frequency of root clusters with s plus a liquid (263–4). The author spends some time explaining why the majority of Old English forms are monosyllabic (264–6).

Following the modification of the cluster rule, the second Northwest Germanic innovation towards a class VII may be assumed to have been compression [syncope] in the preterite plural (266–8). Of the sixteen surviving [overlapping] items across the older Northwest Germanic languages, none has a plus tautosyllabic liquid or nasal. This is because such forms would have been compressed, and the compressed forms sacrifice clarity of the reduplication process at the altar of transparency of the root, yielding e.g. held- rather than hegd- (268–9). Forms like held- were inevitably reanalyzed as ablaut forms taking a cue from class VI where preterites had identical stems across the numbers (269–70). There is no final evidence whether the preterite was originally short e or long ē2; the long vowels in Old English may often be later innovations, as in the case of OE hēht; the author nevertheless favours a short e because it better explains the development of the class (270–1).

Summing up, the contraction of reduplicated Northwest Germanic *hegald, plural *heg(?)ldun first into plural *heldun and then singular held gave birth to class VII: its vowel [originally part of the reduplication syllable] offered an ablaut form to take the place of the lost preterite marker. Roots of structure *CaRC- (R being a liquid or nasal) were completely assimilated, leaving no reduplicated form in writing, but the *a : *e ablaut pattern also spread to roots in ai, au, ē, and ō (271/§29). The latter transformations were not completed in the common Northwest Germanic period, however (271–2). The author does not share Fulk’s belief that the eu vowel in preterites like *hleup was distinct from that found in class II verbs (272–3). The author posits a secondary (meaning after the canonical PIE) development from *ei to *ī early enough to yield a Northwest Germanic reflex ē2, thus explaining the secondary e-grade in heit (273–5). Stems with ō receive the longest treatment (275–9), and forms like hēold are discussed at some length (280). A helpful summary is offered (281–2/§38).

author: Hewson, John, and Vit Bubenik
title: Tense and Aspect in Indo-European Languages: Theory, Typology, Diachrony
series: Amsterdam Studies in the Theory and History of Linguistic Science Series 4: Current Issues in Linguistic Theory
abstract:
[Chapter 1: Tense and Aspect: Description and Theory]: Opens with the following theoretical assumptions:

  1. Linguistic systems are layered: the individual acquires certain elements later and loses them first when suffering from aphasia, as Jakobson has shown.
  2. Just as any other form of motion can be understood to move in either of two directions, namely with the backdrop as the landmark and the individual as the object in motion or vice versa, time can be perceived as descending into the past (“the years ahead,” “that’s all behind us now”) or ascending into the future (“the following year,” “the preceding weeks”). The child first acquires Descending Time, in which the present is recorded in memory; it later acquires Ascending Time, which is required for the use of the imagination. The three points in time involved (present, past, future) are represented by the three basic contrastive elements of the verb system at this first stage of the chronogenesis of English: the infinitive involves the imagination, the present participle represents current experience, and the past participle accesses the memory.
  3. At the second stage of chronogenesis, the child learns that there is time outside the mind (Universe Time), prompting the introduction of the subjunctive in Germanic and Romance languages. Universe Time in some Indo-European languages exploits Descending Time (Greek and Slavonic, though early Slavonic lacked a subjunctive): these show a contrast between Imperfective and Perfective. Other Indo-European languages, including English, represent Universe Time in Ascending Time: the subjunctive resembles the infinitive, the normal past tense is not an imperfect but a preterite, and the simple non-past represents events as complete (as opposed to the progressive in current English). Most Indo-European languages contrast past with nonpast in the indicative, primarily relying on Descending Time. Others, such as Latin and most of the Romance languages, have both models, with one subjunctive form for each.
  4. The third stage of chronogenesis creates greater precision with the indicative. The indicative in Indo-European either represents the present “as a separate stage, a platform from which both past and future may be surveyed, as in Latin and the Romance languages” or as “a divide that distinguishes Memorial Time from Non-Memorial Time, as in Greek, Slavic, and Germanic” (9). Thus the Latin present can both ascend and descend, but Greek with its binary tense system involving an imperfect employs Descending Time; English with its binary tenses relying on a preterite for the simple construction of past time relies on Ascending Time. These tenses combine with aspect for a greater range of expression. The unmarked aspect (Immanent Aspect) of tenses in Ascending Time (e.g. English) is Performative; the Immanent Aspect of tenses in Descending Time (e.g. Greek) is Imperfective.
  5. (Slavonic requires that an additional stage be posited.)
  6. (Complex languages such as Latin may require a fourth stage.)
  7. As several scholars have pointed out, aspect characterizes the event described without positioning it relative to the speech act of describing it; in this it contrasts with tense. In English, “tense systems represent past and future as Universe Time . . . , whereas if aspectual forms are used to represent past and future it is entirely in terms of Event Time, time that is contained or organized within the representation of the event” (13). Other aspects are possible:
    Aspect Role in English
    Prospective aspect Periphrastic future
    Inceptive aspect Absent
    Progressive aspect Progressive
    Perfective aspect Absent (cf. Perfective; aorist)
    Retrospective aspect Periphrastic perfect
  8. Aspect takes several forms:
    1. Analytic (marked by an auxiliary)
    2. Synthetic (marked by suffixation)
    3. Aktionsart (or lexical, marked by preverbs or particles)
    4. Immanent aspect as introduced above. The authors postulate four formative stages to explain the existence of these different types of aspect.
  9. Explains the difference between perfect and perfective.

[Chapter 11: The Verbal System of Germanic]: Germanic commonly has a binary tense system of past and nonpast, plus an analytically formed future (i.e. an aspect-based future, 209). The variation between the languages in the choice of auxiliary suggests the future is a late and parallel formation, after the Proto-Germanic stage. The same is true of the periphrastic perfect. The older languages [the example is OE, but it is equally true of ON, PSL] had the past participle agree with the object, making clear it was not originally part of the verb form (“hie hæfdon hiera cyning aworpenne”). The Germanic system has remarkably few contrastive tense forms, yet is conservative in terms of preserving ancient [i.e. Indo-European] morphology, though put to different use. This archaic system “shows that the late Proto-Indo-European Perfective and Retrospective aspects (aorist and perfect) have obviously been amalgamated, and the result of this amalgamation was used to form a new past tense, the Germanic preterit, which shows traces of both the aorist and perfect morphology of PIE” (210).

Unlike in Sanskrit, Greek, and Slavonic, the Germanic tense system is based on Ascending Time; accordingly, the simple tenses represent complete events, obviating the need for an explicit Perfective aspect; indeed, English has formed the Progressive aspect to form a contrast with the Immanent aspect. “A Progressive would be as redundant in Ancient Greek or Sanskrit as the Aorist would be in Germanic” (210–11, quotation at 211).

The traditional view used to be that the Proto-Indo-European tense system developed into Germanic by having the e-grade (Imperfective) became Germanic Non-Past; the o-grade (retrospective) become past singular; and zero grade (Perfective) become past plural. This position cannot, however, be maintained given the evidence; instead, the difference between singular and plural preterite forms in Germanic must follow from phonological differences, notably accent: the zero grades of the Germanic plural forms follow from a one-time stress on the inflection rather than the root (212–15).

“In the PIE system, at the stage where there are still no tense contrasts, the imperfective morphology would normally have represented the ongoing present: the adoption [in Germanic, PSL] of this morphology to represent a new non-past tense is to be expected, such a development considered normal” (217). The Proto-Indo-European Perfective (aorist) representing complete events, it would normally have represented past time. Perfective and Retrospective were merged in Germanic to become the preterite, in an amalgamation analogous to that found in the Latin perfect. Once completed, the new form could easily be interpreted under Ascending Time. This development almost certainly predates the development (in other PIE languages) of an Imperfective, making the reinterpretation under Ascending Time a natural one (218–19). The fact that the oldest Germanic texts still show the lexical sense of the auxiliaries shows that this construct is a much later development (219).

To explain why it took so long for the Germanic languages to develop a future and for English to develop a progressive, the authors point out that Descending Time is based on the memory being recorded and moving into the past; it is an internal view of the event, with the subject given some place between the event’s beginning and end; to obtain a full view of the event, it has to use Perfective aspect. In Ascending Time, by contrast, tense is based on recall and thus external to the event; this system has no access to the interior of the event but is a complete package. This makes the representation of past events more abstract, so that speakers eventually turn to a periphrastic present perfect perhaps to achieve a more concrete representation, leaving the past expressed aspectually rather than through tense. But Ascending Time has the advantage that it has no pressing need for a contrast between Perfective and Imperfective: knowing that a complete event started at some point in time, we know it has some unknown “materiality” [i.e. internal form, PSL]; under Descending Time, by contrast, that materiality is known but there is no way of knowing whether the event ever completed, making the contrast between Perfective and Imperfective almost necessary. Ascending Time can represent Imperfective aspect up to a point, so most Germanic languages have had no need to come to fully grammaticalized Progressive forms. Moreover, under an Immanent Performative aspect, the need for a contrastive future is less pressing (219–21).

The authors understand the two forms of Germanic optative (subjunctive), i.e. the present and past subjunctive, as representating events under Ascending and Descending time respectively, meaning the former represents external view, the latter internal view (221–3).

The infinitive derives from a [PIE] neuter noun; where it has lost its ending, namely in English and North Germanic, it has been coupled with a preposition to/að (223).

The authors’ model of chronogenesis is represented in Germanic as follows:

  1. Mental time yields the past participle, the present participle, and the infinitive;
  2. Universe Time is represented in the present subjunctive and past subjunctive;
  3. Memorial Time is represented by way of the preterite, while the nonpast represents Non-Memorial Time (224–5).

Early Germanic used a lot of preverbs, and German still does: be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, ver-, zer- do not occur on their own. In English, only un- remains as a fully functional preverb, but we find instead the phrasal verb with prepositions following the verb. Their effect is commonly to achieve Perfective Aktionsart, but no contrastive aspect is achieved because Perfective Aktionsart does not contrast with the Immanent aspect of English tense. Some prepositions turn a verb transitive. The contrastive Old English present forms of bēon represent Aktionsart, as biþ is more closely associated with future time. The authors nevertheless warn against the old understanding that Germanic preverbs had this function (226).

In conclusion, the Germanic languages are a fine illustration of Prokosch’s view that aspect predates and gave rise to tense, since the PIE Perfective endings (with the exception of the second-person singular, which derives from the asigmatic aorist) may be recognized in the Germanic preterite (228). The preterite’s representation of events as complete suggests it relies on Ascending Time, making the Immanent aspect Performative, an inference that is supported by the English and Icelandic development of Progressive aspect to contrast with the Immanent Performative aspect (227–8).

author: Rischel, Jørgen
title: A Unified Theory of Nordic i-Umlaut, Syncope, and Stød
abstract:
Takes issue with classical models of front mutation and syncope, which relied on the weight and other characteristics of the syllable, and instead proposes a model based on morae, i.e. on weight units below the syllabic level, but disconnecting umlaut from syncope. Proposes that i-umlaut was active at a time of transition from a system in which the prominence of morae in unstressed word segments depended on an alternation counted from the start of the word to a system that counted from the end of the word (the latter constitutes word-demarcating prosody). i-umlaut occurred “whenever the first post-tonic vowel became rhythmically prominent.” Nonprominent morae were syncopated at the end of the second stage. Stød developed under influence of the fall in pitch resulting from the later system (191).

The facts of syllabification and syncope demonstrate that morae had alternating prominence in Ancient Nordic, but subsequent developments require a different prosody; a mora-based rhythmicization cannot be in doubt (192–3). The classical view saw prosodically strong vowels affected by prosodically weak vowels. Kock’s notion of a first phase of i-umlaut triggered by the loss of unstressed i has different implications depending on whether vowel shortening is counted as syncope as well; Rischel relies on a definition of syncope that understands vowel shortening as mora syncope. A proposition to view i-mutation and syncope as unrelated processes was also made in Hesselman 1945 (193). Rischel claims that in fact they occurred under mutually exclusive conditions. Rather than compensate for a disappearing vowel, umlaut followed from the principle of regressive vowel harmony, but vowel harmony spreads from prominent vowels (193–4).

Rischel’s model for stød sees it originate from a high-low tonal pattern, but parallel to, not as a special development from, the tonelag that survives in Swedish and Norwegian today (194).

Assumes that analogy was overwhelmingly a late process. “To the extent that early analogy was at work, it was a matter of generalizing across morphological categories, not across each inflectional paradigm” (196). In the transitional period from Ancient Nordic to Old Nordic, many post-tonic vowels, such as thematic vowels, were syncopated, with the effect that forms within the paradigm became more dissimilar, with some forms becoming highly marked for syllable count or umlaut. At a later stage, uniformation within the paradigm occurred, by two routes: simplification of the case and number system (as happened in much of medieval Nordic) and a shift towards a more agglutinative language type. These later tendencies have obscured the processes of umlaut and syncope in data from outside Icelandic (197–8).

Masculine i-stem nouns present a problem: long stems (gestr) show i-umlaut throughout while short stems (staðr) show none, while feminine stems of either length likewise tend to have none. The fronting is evenly distributed across singular and plural, although plural forms retain an i that must have been long in Ancient Nordic. This uniformity cannot be explained by analogy from mutated stems because i-umlaut never became a widespread plural marker in Nordic; on the other hand, the more common noun classes had a uniform vowel across both numbers, so i-stems may have complied with that principle. It would nevertheless be better to design a theory that accounts for short and long masculine i-stems directly (198).

Another problem underlies the iR-umlaut hypothesis. VCiC-sequences more frequently show umlauting if followed by R (“an apical or coronal (sibilant) fricative”) in Ancient Nordic. Present singular forms of short-stemmed strong and ja-verbs are particularly problematic, as are comparatives, superlatives, and deverbal nouns based on short stems (198–9).

A further problem is the relationship between syncope and i-umlaut. Many palatal vowels were syncopated without evidence of umlaut, and many with, and others were not syncopated in forms that show umlaut. Kock therefore posited three successive events, which may be summarized as syncope with umlaut; syncope without umlaut; and umlaut without syncope. This cannot be upheld: if umlaut eventually took place without syncope, then the process cannot in the first period have relied on syncope. The only evidence for a chronology is that syncope appears to have happened earlier after long stems than after short stems. Rather than connect this with umlaut, one might posit that “umlaut happened before syncope but was somehow sensitive to word structure” (199). There is furthermore no reason to assume two rounds of syncope for forms with u rather than i (200).

Finally, there is the question when umlauted vowels became distinct phonemes. The structuralists held that syncope caused the (possibly preexisting) sounds to assume phonemic status, but in fact the simplification of the post-tonal vowel system from five or six in Ancient Nordic to three in Old Nordic awarded umlauted vowels before nonsyncopated i phonemic status (200).

Morae may be counted as follows:

  • A short vowel in an unstressed syllable counts as one mora
  • A long vowel or diphthong in an unstressed syllable counts as two morae
  • A long vowel or diphthong in a stressed syllable counts as two morae
  • A consonant following a short vowel in a stressed syllable adds a mora if itself followed by another consonant, including an identical one, i.e. if the consonant is long. (Rischel makes a point of asserting that in these cases it is the first consonant that carries the mora; the second is nonmoraic.) (201)

If we assume the deletion of every second mora and morae are counted from the start of the word, the moraic weight of the stressed syllable complicates our formula. Also, syncope cannot have applied recursively, since dissyllables survive. We would thus have to assume a single run of syncope, but that makes it difficult to account for forms where adjacent syllables underwent syncope (hengdr, yngstr, þyngd). Moreover, one needs to account for a string’s subsequent immunity to syncope. And what role did distance from the end of the word play (202)?

“Monosyllabic accentuation” of dissyllables developed (1) where these developed out of [Old Nordic] monosyllables, but also (2) in compound verbs with adverbial first elements and (3) in iambic stems (mostly borrowed from Low German). In all these cases, Danish developed stød and (Swedish and) Norwegian tonal accent 1, while contrasting forms, such as originally dissyllabic cognate forms of the forms under (1) lack stød and have tonal accent 2. Thus stød and tonal accent 1 are understood as “manifestations of the same development of a word accent” (202–3, at 203). Rischel argues why the two must nevertheless be distinct developments (204).

Rischel offers the following assumptions:

  1. Ancient Nordic prosody awarded prominence to odd-numbered morae counting forwards from the beginning of the stressed syllable, with the one exception that a long vowel never received prominence on its second mora. The count restarts at non-initial long syllables such as participial -and-. Prominence was likely primarily marked by higher pitch.
  2. i-umlaut was a function of regressive vowel harmony spreading from a then-prominent vowel. Once umlauted, the mutated vowel normally remained so even if the trigger was subsequently removed. Vowel harmony was valid during much of Late Ancient Nordic and operated “whenever the structure of a word-form permitted it,” but it stopped being active before the time of syncope (205).
  3. The old “word contour” was replaced by a new one that caused pitch contours to fall at the end of word forms. The earliest two versions of this principle were Common Nordic, while two later versions created an isogloss between Danish and Swedish:
    1. By default, word forms after this development had prominence on the stressed syllable and low pitch on the final mora, with a high-pitch mora closely preceding.
    2. A long final vowel without previous prominence had the prosody of a short vowel.
    3. Long monosyllables dating back to Early Ancient Nordic accommodated the high and low pitches within their bimoraic construct in Swedish and Norwegian, while Danish came to rely exclusively on a voiced second mora for its word-contour prosody. Monosyllables that no longer counted as bimoraic received high pitch only.
    4. Short monosyllables in Norwegian and Swedish concentrated the falling pattern in a single mora. Short stressed syllables in Danish were truncated to a high pitch only (206).
  4. Syncope in Late Ancient Nordic deleted all nonprominent morae of a given form. This also involved the shortening of long vowels. It did not apply recursively (206–7).
  5. Certain forms, including word forms with enclitic material, retained their prior accentuation, behaving like “prosodic islands.” This led to tonal contrasts between dissyllables and prosodic islands in much of Swedish, Norwegian, and South Jutland Danish.
  6. In medieval Danish, tonal contrast developed into stød contrast, stød occurring on bimoraic syllables with a rise-fall pitch contour.
  7. Regular falling pitch developed into a contrastive West Danish falling contour and East Danish “rising(-falling)” contour (207).

Both syncope and stød require special (and separate!) explanation of VðV and VRV-sequences. Two or three adjacent morae are frequently syncopated around dental fricatives, e.g. in past participles like døømdr from *doomiðaR and adverbial comparatives such as lengr, from *langiRa. Rischel’s model assumes that i must have been prominent to cause mutation but nonprominent to be syncopated. These same forms behave like prosodic islands with regard to stød, which they retain even when they become dissyllabic: compare the Danish past participle dømte (with stød) with the stød-less preterite of the same spelling. For the past participles, Rischel can only offer a “guess” about a coarticulatory process making these sequences behave like weak long vowels for purposes of pitch prominence; the preterites he deems beyond salvaging because ancient preterites cannot be securely reconstructed (208–9).

Rischel offers a list of reconstructed derivations and a detailed reconstruction of phonemic events (209–15), then discusses shortcomings and outstanding challenges. Among other things, he stresses that syncope being a one-time process does not mean it happened all at once (216–17). [Thus presumably his view that syncope was not recursively applied should be understood with individual morae rather than whole word forms in mind! PSL] He also points out that his model has weakly stressed vowels have greater prominence following long stems than after short stems “at one point,” namely before the prosodic rules were redrawn to emphasize penults, which is the opposite of the classic view, which views vowels following short stems as more prominent. If correct, this must have happened later. As a general perspective on syncope, Rischel favours the avoidance of models with consecutive applications, not in the last place because these assume implausible interim periods of nonsyncope (217). A chronology of i-umlaut may still be maintained, but without a qualitative difference between the earlier and later iterations (217–8). Rischel offers as a particular strength of his theory that it nowhere relies on analogy. In the next paragraph, however, he concedes that there remain forms not explained by his theory that may need to be explained by analogy. He lists the following problems for his ablaut model:

  1. Frequent absence of umlaut in long feminine i-stem nouns. As this class lacks distinctive characteristics, contamination likely played a role.
  2. Umlaut in short-stemmed comparatives: ytri, betri. These are traditionally explained either by iR-umlaut or by analogy from long stems like yngri (218).
  3. Umlaut in present singular forms of short-stemmed strong and ja-verbs. Any theory would have to rely on analogy, and it is clear that analogy yielded umlaut in the first-person form at any rate.

His syncope model encounters the following difficulties:

  1. Past participles in in- (haldinn) and weak masculine nouns (bogi) lack umlaut, perhaps due to variation in the quality of the vowel.
  2. Long i-stem nouns have i-mutated dative plurals (gestum). This may reflect early Germanic *-im(i)z and a post-umlaut change *-imR > *umR. Analogy within the paradigm is unlikely, as stem vowel alternations increased rather than decreased during the transitional period. Analogy of the ending -um(R) for -im(R), by contrast, is quite in line with morphological uniformation at this time (220).

As for the relationship of i-mutation to other vowel mutations, it is striking that it and u-mutation were both triggered by high vowels, but the latter only regularly affects a, which casts suspicion on a supposed parallelism between the two processes. However, breaking presupposes a vowel harmony principle not unlike u-mutation. Rischel does not incorporate breaking into his theory because the steps involved are contested (221–2). He has yet to account for u-umlaut itself, but he offers an appendix of observations (222, 226–9). Discusses vowel colouring (222–3).

A final discussion of the genesis of stød points out that the connection with falling tone is not novel, but the origin of that pitch drop in a prosody to do with umlaut and syncope is Rischel’s own contribution. The productivity of stød in iambic loan words is not easily explained; perhaps the contour with stød had become so prominent already that it was taken as a standard (224).

An appendix on u-mutation follows (226–9).

author: Hreinn Benediktsson
title: Nordic Umlaut and Breaking: Thirty Years of Research (1951–1980)
abstract:
This review article responds above all to a report submitted to the Fourth International Conference of Nordic and General Linguistics by Skomedal, but it incorporates a detailed review of past scholarship. It opens by noting that postwar research on umlaut and breaking has been characterized by new theoretical approaches rather than the adduction of new data, and that disappointingly little headway has been made. New theories are welcome if they reduce the number of problems by one or more, but that hasn’t always been the case; and it is important to account for all the data, whether that means relying on Kock’s data set or producing a new one (2–5).

The one point of possible consensus concerning umlaut is that it must have been a two-stage process: phonetic umlaut preceding phonemic umlaut, the latter having come about due to the loss of the trigger vowel. Even here one could argue there is no consensus, as structuralists and generativists frame these stages in substantially different ways: the latter group speak of “(a) the addition of a phonological umlaut rule followed (b) by restructuring.” One could thus argue that the only consensus is negative in nature, namely the rejection of Kock’s idea that umlaut could be caused by loss of the trigger vowel, a notion incompatible with any modern phonological theory (5).

Skomedal calls for a unified theory, explaining not just umlaut, syncope, and syllable weight, but also prosody, relevant morphology, and the full set of factors affecting vowel quality; of course there are limits to the early data for some of these points. Comparison with other Germanic languages could also prove fruitful (6–7).

Penzl (1951) was the first to subject Nordic umlaut to structuralist theory, asserting the abovementioned principle that umlaut is a two-step process, phonetic and phonemic (7). (This notion had been sporadically brought up in the thirties and fourties [7–8].) Penzl adduced but misunderstood High German umlaut, but his main concern in Nordic was the nonoccurrence of umlaut after many short syllables where i was syncopated (velja : valþa). Although he recognized the problem with Kock’s hypothesis, he substituted two new problems for it by resurrecting Sievers’s belief that medial syncope occurred earlier after short syllables than after long ones. This chronology is contradicted by the runic and West Germanic data (8), but it also forced Penzl to invent Rückumlaut to explain why phonemic umlaut failed to affect *waliðō the way it later affected *dōmiðō (8–9). The reversion of phonetic variants to their previous position might be compatible with generative theory, but surely not with structuralism, and it leaves phonemization with little explanatory value. Penzl awarded iR-umlaut no status of its own, viewing it as just another instance of i-umlaut (9).

King (1971) first described Nordic umlaut from a generativist perspective. He proceeded from the valid assumption that medial i was syncopated later after short syllables than after long ones [thus inverting Sievers/Penzl] and posited two initial derivational rules: (1) i-umlaut and (2) vowel reduction (including syncope) after a long syllable; a further rule (3) vowel reduction (including syncope) after a short syllable he argued must postdate umlaut but must have been inserted [i.e. affected the underlying phonology] before the umlaut rule in order to explain historical forms like talþa (10). The notion of rule insertion brings with it an arbitrariness: when were rules added (“at the end of a grammar,” affecting only the phonetic representation), when inserted? King himself was to abandon the principle just two years on, but in the meantime his theory posed considerable difficulties, requiring a syncope gap during which no syncope rule was present in the grammar (10–11). When King abandoned rule insertion, he had to resort to rule reordering, incompatible with Kiparsky’s early principles and also with the principle of reduction of allomorphic variation (effectively the generativist lingo for analogical levelling), as the resulting alternation between telja and talða increases variation (11). King adduces Kiparsky’s principle of rule opacity/transparency to accommodate his revised theory, calling umlaut “opaque in the historical order but transparent in the synchronic order (talþa, staþR),” while syncope is opaque in both. The telja paradigm also accommodates opaque forms, however, with tel, telr showing no umlaut trigger on the surface, and so King’s revised theory leaves us no better off. King furthermore required restructuring to explain why Rückumlaut does not apply to long stems, but this solution severs synchronic connections between lexemes like dǿma and dómr, fylla and fullr, while requiring underlying forms like flut- that are not attested in surface forms at all. Thus rule reordering simply relegates the problem to the domain of morphology, where it takes on absurd proportions (11–13). King follows Penzl in his positions on iR-umlaut, R-umlaut, and palatal umlaut (14).

Iverson (1978) produced a synchronic generative analysis of Old Icelandic that, implicitly, likewise relies on restructuring. Forms like dǿma, he held, have front vowels underlying; his i-umlaut rule is strictly morphological and applies after syncope (14). Cathey and Demers (1979) apply syncope before umlaut and rely on restructuring “so that dómr and dœma are no longer related directly through the productive phonology (Cathey and Demers [40–]41, qtd. in Hreinn Benediktsson 14–15, at 15). This is clearly wrong, as synchronically related sets exist even in Icelandic today, including in loan words such as krúna : krýna.”It is clear that any explanation of the historical development of umlaut that, by implication, denies or disregards the clear synchronic productivity of the i-umlaut rule in word derivation is for this reason open to doubt" (15). Cathey (1972) relies on restructuring in short stems taking place after umlaut and syncopation (in that order), again raising the question why it did not also take place in long stems (15), or indeed why the umlaut vowel was not restructured as opposed to the back vowel. This theory also necessitates two umlaut phases and thus brings back Kock’s three-period chronology (15–16).

Steblin-Kamenskij (1959) adduced prosody as a factor of relevance for umlaut, suggesting that open juncture (i.e. a word or compound boundary, but also a heavy suffix) prevented umlaut; his hypothesis accordingly was that “during the phonetic period of umlaut short root-syllables were also followed by open juncture coinciding with the root-morpheme boundary” (Sbelin-Kamensij 111, qtd. in Hreinn Benediktsson 17). Hreinn objects that there is no independent evidence for such a prosodic distinction between short and long stems, calling it “perhaps even unlikely on general phonetic grounds,” and furthermore observes that a three-period chronology is still present, since open juncture had to be lost from short stems before it was lost from long stems.

Braroe (1979) also adduces prosody, but she insists on universal principles, which rule out rule reordering. Her grammar involves rules for syllabification; glide formation; and stress assignment, short stems receiving stress on their second syllable as well as the first; umlaut then applies first to unstressed i and only later by stressed i and j. This reasoning affects syncope as well, as it must now have applied to stressed as well as unstressed i. The theory has little merit (17–19); as with King, restructuring simply relegates the problem to morphological word formation (20).

Iversion and Sanders (1980) likewise proceed from universality, taking the German order of processes (syncope before umlaut) as their basis. This implies restructuring of long stems such as gestr; they time restructuring during the active period of umlaut, which, they say, results in a predictable direction of regularization. This, however, leaves the restructuring principle with little explanatory value between short and long stems (19–20).

A number of these various scholars have made assertions about the limits of theoretical frameworks, making clear that reordering and restructuring have been of little use with the problem (21–2). Penzl asserted that once the first umlaut sound gained phonemic status, there could be no further phonemic-structural umlaut; lack of umlaut before historical i can only be referred to the loss or change of i prior to the time of phonemization, i.e. during the time when umlaut was merely phonetic. Once the umlaut sound was a phoneme, Penzl claimed all phonetically identical sounds must have been arranged under the new phoneme (a structuralist principle; 22).

The prevailing opinion is that Twaddell [or Penzl] was right in his periodization, but wrong in the application; this opinion probably bases on (1) an unwillingness to abandon “the phonemic [structuralist?] approach” altogether; and (2) the weakness of the alternative adduced by Kratz, namely to propose a stage of semifronting, which lacks an empirical basis (22–4).

Difficulties with structuralism are even clearer in Sbelin-Kamenskij 1959, who, on the basis of syncope occurring after long stems first, offered two possibilities:

  1. General phonetic umlaut followed by phonemic umlaut only where i had been lost, and short-stem umlaut taking place later; or
  2. Phonetic umlaut initially only of long stems, while short stems where i survived were mutated later.

This leads to a total of four possibilities within structuralism:

  1. Short stems never underwent phonetic umlaut
    1. Phonetic umlaut postdated the syncope of short stems
    2. Phonetic umlaut predated the syncope of short stems (Steblin-Kamenskij; this resurrects a three-stage chronology)
  2. All forms with i underwent phonetic umlaut
    1. Phonetic umlaut postdated the syncope of short stems (Penzl)
    2. Phonetic umlaut predated the syncope of short stems (24–26).

All modern analyses strive to define i-umlaut as a unitary historical process, either by eliminating Kock’s umlautless middle period or by confining the heart of the development to the phonetic stage of umlaut. On the principle of a unified phonetic umlaut, only option 2.2 in the above list does not contradict the data, so it deserves further attention (26). Dyvik (1973) has pursued this course, arguing that umlaut alternation was neutralized in certain positions shortly after the phonemization of the umlaut vowels: in the absence of an opposition /ɑ : ɛ/ before as yet unsyncopated i, there were archiphonemes as in /stÆþiR/ whose realization would have fluctuated. The opposition became distinctive after unstressed ī and ē merged, leading forms to be rephonemized with either /ɑ/ or /ɛ/. In other words, “i-umlaut took place before an i that was preserved, and conversely, i-umlaut was caused only by original, not by secondary, i” (27–8, at 28).

Hreinn briefly covers the history of the study of u-umlaut, pointing out that early scholars mistakenly thought the type of u-umlaut occurring before unsyncopated u was not found in East Norwegian or East Nordic, where in fact it survives in dialects today and in manuscript and runic texts as well; the nonoccurrence of umlaut was then referred to analogy (27–8). This is not admissible, because (1) it contravenes the chronology of attestations, and (2) there are forms that lack a altogether and could not have been subjected to levelling (ǫr : ǫrvar, etc.; 28). The late twelfth and early thirteenth centuries of East Norwegian are therefore decisive in explaining the alternation as a phonological, not a morphological process (29).

An important difference between i-umlaut and u-umlaut is that the former was “caused only by a primary (early Proto-Nordic) i, not by a secondary (late Common Nordic) one” whereas u-umlaut took place before u of any origin. Accordingly, “before an unstressed syllable with an u that was retained, the opposition a : ǫ never arose, or from the synchronic point of view, this opposition was neutralized (and represented by the archiphonome [sic] Å) before unstressed u in the immediate postumlaut period” across the Nordic area (29).

u-umlaut is just as difficult to account for with generative means as i-umlaut, since it takes at least two rules to account for Eastern and Western forms, namely (1) a → ǫ before u, and (2) syncope of u. Understood morphologically, an u-umlaut rule does not cover cases like hǫfuð or ǫr. Generative rules cannot explain the intermediate stage of late twelfth, early thirteenth-century East Norwegian, or East Nordic of three centuries before (29–30).

The concept of neutralization is mentioned by a number of the theorists discussed. Dyvik’s application of it to the most promising chronology is a worthwhile undertaking (30–1). The question that arises is why the opposition /ɑ, ɛ/ does not arise where unstressed /i/ and /a/ are merged into zero, as in the i-stem hagr, or where unstressed i and ē are merged into zero, as in the preterite form vakða. Dyvik assumes the ē-suffix did not occur in the preterite, but Hreinn demonstrates that this position goes against the available evidence. More importantly, he says the ē-stem preterite morphology does not affect the outcome of i-umlaut (31).

Hreinn now proceeds to analyze Skomedal’s paper. It emphasizes the two-stage process of umlaut as well as the fundamental role of syncope. Skomedal’s assumption that samprasarana [i.e. the change of i into ji] is a by-product of syncope raises a range of questions about chronology and whether affected short stems (*harjar, *kunja) were functionally long (32–3). Skomedal states as a general rule that umlaut did not normally affect short stems regardless whether the following i was later syncopated, to which he adds a range of exceptions (33). This position of course goes against the unifying principle today pursued. Skomedal’s position furthermore requires a specification of prosody, and he has a number of dialectal questions to answer for. Skomedal asserts that any neutralization period would have been very limited in duration (34), and he posits “a weaker palatalization,” a position that does not meet with criticism as harsh as in Hreinn’s discussion of Kratz where he proposes central vowels. He also proposes weak, nondistinctive i-umlaut for most short, heavy syllables, and apparently a four-stage chronology that is not recapitulated by Hreinn (34–5). Of the exceptions to Skomedal’s general rule, Hreinn mentions secondary stress and iR-umlaut, a process Skomedal tries to avoid because it takes away from the general application of his main rule; he settles on parallelism between iR-umlaut and j-umlaut (35–6); further cases like lykill, which Skomedal refers to the combination ki or gi; and further exceptions are made where umlaut is morphological (37–8).

The remaining 20 pages of the article concern breaking, though often in relation to umlaut.

author: Schalin, Johan
title: Scandinavian Front Umlaut Revisited and Revised
abstract:
Preliterary Scandinavian front umlaut, breaking, and rounding umlaut have not been satisfactorily explained, even if the Proto-Germanic and attested Old Norse forms are agreed upon. The most difficult problem is the distribution of i/j-umlaut, given that its effects are absent from light syllables across multiple parts of speech, including i/j-stem preterites (talði) and i-stem nouns (staðr) in contrast with heavy syllables (dœmði, gestr). Defining the difference by syllable weight nevertheless poses further difficulties. The situation is further complicated by the existence of exceptions (6).

Schalin assumes that vowels affect nearby vowels in the same way in identical contexts; where this appears not to be the case, the phonemic status of the vowel in question must be drawn into question. The metrics underlying his reasoning are set out in Riad 1992 and later works and are not here explained (7).

Schalin offers his own terminology for the periodization and notes he accepts the view that short oral vowels a, i, and u were syncopated at widely different times (8 and Figure 1). Paleo-Germanic refers to a time before e and i in nonprominent syllables merged. Following that merger, a number of changes took place in Pre-Scandinavian before Proto-Scandinavian set North Germanic apart from the other branches of Germanic; Proto-Germanic refers to a stage before any second-syllable syncope, and only noncontrastive umlaut in syllables with primary stress. It was succeeded by Post-Proto-Scandinavian with the conclusion of early a-syncope c. 550 CE (9).

In summary, Schalin proposes that

  • The reflexes of Paleo-Germanic e and i maintained their contrast in prominent syllables well into the umlaut period, the contrast consisting in a coronal feature of e that meant it was raised not to i but to coronal (laminal) ȋ.
  • A light second syllable following a light syllable with primary stress preserves phonological vowel contrasts much as happened in positions of primary stress. This is inferred from the fact that the coronal descendant of Paleo-Germanic e consistently triggers front umlaut (fremd) while the descendant of i normally does not (framða), on account of its dorsal or dorso-palatal quality (denoted ï). Only certain coronal-adjacent conditions did ï develop into ȋ and trigger umlaut, notably in Pre-Scandinavian iz͡, which yielded forms like fremra (10). In nonprominent syllables, the two vowels had merged in Pre-Scandinavian and yielded coronal ȋ, regularly triggering front mutation regardless of their Paleo-Germanic origin; hence dœmda, gestr. The understanding that the two had not merged in a second light syllable within the main foot leads to the conclusion that such syllables were prominent (11–12).
  • Syllable prominence is defined by mora count from right to left; Schalin’s model explains the distribution of front vowels by long trigger vowels.

The distribution of front mutation to be explained is the following:

  1. A historical short palatal i usually results in i-umlaut on a nonpalatal vowel in a preceding heavy syllable. Exceptions can typically be referred to an early change of stem class combined with analogy. Heavy feminine i-stem nouns are the best-known examples, e.g. *burði > burð not *byrð (13–14).
  2. Light target syllables pose a problem: in the classical set of examples, these are not umlauted except where the trigger was not syncopated. Kock inferred a three-stage chronology of (1) syncope of unstressed triggers following heavy syllables, the process of syncope causing umlaut; (2) loss of relative stress of and subsequent syncope of unstressed triggers following light syllables at a time when the umlaut mechanism was no longer active; (3) triggers that had survived syncope caused a second wave of front umlaut (14–15). This hypothesis was never generally accepted and has not been accepted by anyone since the rise of phonology as a distinct discipline. Critics nevertheless failed to develop strong new hypotheses other than the refutation of Kock’s. Kock’s hypothesis is prominently presented in handbooks such as Noreen and Wissén, which continue to be read (15–16). Notably, Kock’s set of forms and presentation of the problem is still canonical, although it is highly selective (16).

Solutions elsewhere proposed are of the following types:

  1. An assumption taken for granted by the neogrammarians is that target vowels in light syllables that show no fronting were never fronted.
    1. Sievers held that the trigger in such cases was syncopated before umlaut could occur.
    2. Kock and Pipping believed the imminent loss of the trigger vowel was itself responsible for the umlaut, and thus had to believe that weak articulation of trigger vowels was the immediate cause of umlaut, and concluded that unstressed vowels following light syllables were comparatively strongly stressed (16–17).
  2. Structuralists of the mid-twentieth century and onward assumed that front mutation occurred across the board on an allophonic level but was later reversed (reverse umlaut) in light stems (either under influence of a nonpalatal vowel that had moved up due to syncope of the palatal vowel [Penzl] or, more commonly and first proposed by Hesselman, simply due to the deactivation of the umlaut mechanism) before it could reach the phonological level. Contrary to the neogrammarians, they held that it was a strongly pronounced rather than a weakly accented trigger vowel that caused front mutation, as they held that “umlaut by nature was driven by an easing of the co-articulatory effort” (17).
  3. More recently, theoretical phonologists have returned to a reliance on context-driven exceptions rather than reverse umlaut, but they have failed to reach any sort of consensus and indeed have relied on conjecture, proposing that either the trigger syllable or the target vowel was either too weak or too strong to cause fronting in light stems, or that the trigger could be prevented from operating by its proximity to the weak target vowel. Little effort has been made to demonstrate dynamics like these in related languages (18).

The present study incorporates ill-fitting items in its corpus from the outset to avoid setting oneself up for foregone conclusions (18–19). Newly incorporated data includes

  • Vowels in light syllables successfully fronted by historically long trigger vowels (gleði)
  • Vowels in light syllables successfully fronted by trigger vowels in third syllables (endr)
  • Vowels in light syllables successfully fronted where a short trigger vowel was deleted by syncope (fremd, fremra against the preterite framda; 19–21 and Table 2).

iR-umlaut: At issue here is the regular correlation of a tautomorphemic sequence *ȋz͡ with front mutation in the same main foot, contravening the regularities of syllable weight inferred from the standard data set. Schalin agrees with this hypothesis of Kock’s and demonstrates its validity by means of subminimal pairs. He argues that this exception to the rules of front mutation is not adequately explained by existing models but should be understood as a consequence of the trigger’s etymology and prominence. A genesis by analogy is not plausible (23).

Singular present-tense forms of light stems show iR-umlaut only in western Scandinavian (ferr), and here analogy is a possibility, but it remains unlikely that it would apply in some verb classes and not others (23–4).

Tautomorphemic *iz clearly affects umlaut after light syllables: *framïðō and framȋzō would have yielded identical stem vowels if any of the analyses hitherto adduced applied without such a consideration (i.e. if umlaut is based on every second mora; if its effects are blocked within the main foot; if it relies on stress or metre in some other way; or if it is caused simply by the weight of the target syllable) (24–5), and the same is true if syncope occurred before becoming an umlaut trigger. Kiparsky has argued for that chronology, with a delay of syncope where syncope would have yielded illegal trimoraic syllables. This model fails to predict umlaut in cases like fremr, as syncope would have affected *framïðō and framȋzō in the same way and at the same time (25). Voyles argued that a delay of syncope in the latter type is caused by the difference in consonants following the trigger vowel, concluding that /r/ prevented early syncope. His argument rests on the merger of /z/ and /r/, however, which he dates centuries too early. Even if his argument were modified to apply to an intermediate stage of /z/, it is clear that “tauto-syllabic */z/ in the rhyme did not add weight to a non-initial syllable,” as is clear from betr (25–6).

Hesselman and Grønvik separately posited conditions based on syllables being open or closed, but they incorrectly syllabify medial syllables; correct syllabification proves their arguments wrong. Their models furthermore yield false predictions (26–7). In fact, open and closed syllables cannot differ in weight on the evidence of the prosody of Transitional Scandinavian, whose final consonants carried no weight. Thus iR-umlaut cannot be explained by prosodic context directly or or by way of syncope sequencing. The avenue that remains is segmental phonology: the trigger ȋz must have phonological features responsible for the resulting umlaut (26–7).

The existence of iR-umlaut, i.e. the exceptional fronting of a vowel in a light syllable if *ȋz͡ occurred within the same morpheme, is to be explained by one of the following:

  1. z turning i into a trigger (Seip; Widmark)
  2. i turning z into a trigger prior to its own deletion
  3. z functioning as a remote trigger;

the last two of these fail tests against data and for phonological “naturalness” (27–30).

Schalin now argues for position 1, starting from the contention (argued in a 2016 paper) that “palatal r” was not palatal but lamino-alveolar, as suggested by evidence from present-day Övdalian. The Old Scandinavian preterite sellda (from *salȋðō) as opposed to talða (from *talïðō) reflects this distinction: the former had lamino-denti-alveolar articulation, the second apico-postalveolar (30–1). As Widmark has argued, the regular descendant of i was less palatal; the following z made it more so, equal to j in a ja-stem like *baðja > beð (32).

Scholars have hitherto avoided this path over concern it might pose difficulties to the vowel system. Schalin addresses this concern (32–6) before making his case (37–9). In his discussion of the implications, Schalin recognizes that e is generally thought of as less fronted than i, but cases of the reverse are known (39–41). He also warns against using the example of ketill, a loan-woard and thus unreliable and void of Pre-Germanic etymology (41); gleðill is a better case (42–3).

In the study of long trigger vowels, suffixes have often been adduced that do not trigger umlaut. However, scholars have overlooked the fact that these suffixes have lost their status as independent morphemes, so that they could not function as prosodic islands or carry secondary stress (43–4).

Schalin posits that there may have been two complementary vowel systems: one in prominent syllables and one in nonprominent syllables. The latter system would have been “impoverished,” substituting coronality for rounding as a contrastive feature (44). In the word-final syllable, it could trigger front umlaut or breaking, but not labial umlaut; hence the absence of labial umlaut in Eastern Scandinavian from the oblique cases of weak feminines. Long palatal ï in penultimate syllables were marked nonlabial but unmarked for coronality and thus failed to trigger front umlaut. As prosodic islands, these suffixes retained independent prominence (45).

“Prominent moras were the two first moras counted from left to right and every even-numbered mora counted from right to left” (45). Bimoraic syllables were assigned prominence from their latter mora; where a single bimoraic syllable contains a prominent mora followed by a nonprominent mora, the whole qualifies as nonprominent and may be termed “alleviated” (45–6). Thus in trisyllabic nominative singular *faðɜɜr, the second syllable is alleviated and is included in the main foot after pitch flattening. Syncope of nonprominent a resulted in a revised mora count from the right; with suffixes containing underlying ï, “syllable prominence was a prerequisite for sustaining the vowel *ï, and therefore the a-syncope before the operation of front umlaut laminalised these dorsal vowels and created umlauting allomorphs in the event they were positioned outside the main foot” (46).

It goes on for 20 more pages; among other things, there are sections discussing shortcomings of earlier hypotheses, notably umlaut reversion and analogy.

author: Kortlandt, Frederik
title: The Old Norse i-Umlaut
abstract:
Starts with Kock as modified by Seip: by assuming R was palatal, we can eliminate Kock’s umlautless middle period (27). To explain why long syllables were affected by umlaut earlier than short syllables, Kortlandt redefines the landscape: just as the trigger vowel i was lost after long syllables before it was lost after short ones, so “it is reasonable to assume that the umlaut affected long vowels and diphthongs [as opposed to stems or syllables! PSL] earlier than short vowels” (27–8). The choice of gestr as an example of long stems has misled scholars because it has a short vowel. GlǿpR “crime” was umlauted in the early period; gastR, like staðR, followed “[w]hen umlaut was phonemicized in short vowels” (28). This theory explains nonumlauted long syllables with short vowels, as in burðr, fundr, kostr. Exceptions like gestr and feldr suggest (following Bibire) that "short vowels were not umlauted by syncopated *i but only by *j, iR, R, palatalized k/g, and retained i (28–9, at 29). Umlaut in ja-stems suggests j must have been preserved when short vowels in this position were lost. In verbs, umlauted preterite like felda (against valða) are to be explained by analogy (29). Kortlandt furthermore disconnects the phonemicization of umlaut in long vowels from the earlier syncope by positing a revised chronology:

  1. Umlaut of long vowels
  2. Reduction of unstressed vowels, long and short
  3. Syncope after long syllables
  4. Umlaut of short vowels
  5. Syncope after short syllables

Velars before j may have geminated as part of stage (2) to compensate for vowel reduction: *bakjaR > *bakkjəR > *bakkĭR > *bekkĭR > bekkr.

author: Thomas, Daniel
title: Rewriting Gregory the Great: The Prison Analogy in Napier Homily I
abstract:
Summarizes the facts of the nine Latin copies of the Dialogues preserved in England, three copies in Anglo-Saxon script on the Continent, and three copies of Napier I, with MSS C (CCCC 201) and L (Tiberius A. xiii) containing an ending drawn from Dialogues 4.4 while E (Hatton 113) has “a briefer and more generic conclusion” (203–204, quotation at 204).

As McIntosh, Jost, Bethurum, Wilcox, and Lionarons have connected both endings with Wulfstan, much scholarly attention has been spent on his role in it and its role in his canon; the connection with Gregory’s Dialogues, and the prison analogy in particular, has been somewhat neglected and is here addressed (204–205).

The Fall episode in Gregory’s text is situated in the concluding book of the Dialogi, which focuses on “death, the afterlife, and the nature of the human soul”; at his expulsion, Adam loses the “enlightened mental state” associated with life in Paradise (205–206). The prison analogy serves to highlight the sceptical nature of humankind in the face of matters beyond their immediate experience; it need not have originated in Plato’s allegory (206). Indeed Gregory’s aims are quite different: rather than point out the limits of epistemology, he shows how grace allows the transcendence of such limits. Humankind’s position is, to Gregory, not like that of the boy born in prison, as Christ and the Holy Spirit were sent for enlightenment. As Dal Santo has argued, the prison analogy and its concern with the limits of epistemology should be understood in the light of the preceding three books’ interest in the cult of the saints and their ability to transcend. It is a response to empiricist challenges circulating in Gregory’s Rome of the 590s (207).

The development of Gregory’s analogy seems problematic if we understand the boy to be censored for lacking knowledge of matters placed beyond his experience through no fault of his own, but in fact the terms of the analogy shift during the presentation: the mother represents first Adam, but then the saints bearing testimony to the truth.

Both continuations bear Wulfstan’s stamp in wording; the longer one draws on the Dialogues and will have been deliberately added to for a logical whole with the prison excerpt (208).

The manuscripts, too, suggest Wulfstan’s circles. L seems the oldest, from early eleventh-century Worcester. This manuscript also contains the Liber Wigorniensis, a cartulary that may have been produced under Wulfstan’s auspices shortly after his 1002 promotion to Worcester. Wulfstan is believed to have corrected both items, but in the homily he has primarily touched the continuation, which further suggests this part was his. C and E likewise contain a great deal of Wulfstan material. Both collections open with Napier I, and the manuscripts suggest a relationship and may derive from a common exemplar. Wilcox considers the longer text the earlier redaction, a tempting conclusion (209).

While Szarmach has argued that the prison analogy stems from a lost translation of the Dialogues, Thomas believes it does not represent a longer translation but was “adapted for homiletic purposes even before its incorporation in the two versions of Napier homily I” (210). He is thinking of a florilegium or homiliary, and the reworking of the material may have already been carried out at that stage (211).

Napier I provides a much freer translation of Gregory than the full translation (usually identified as Wærferth’s), but it is also more “fluent . . . and . . . rhetorically effective.” Thomas’s first example of this, that Napier I turns an abstract cause of sin into a more concrete account where Adam was driven out for his own sin, fails to convince. His following points are more interesting: firstly, the translator begins with a simple assertion concerning Adam’s creation, perhaps because this homiletic text lacks a homiletic opening and requires a strong first sentence; secondly, the translator adds a statement that human suffering is a consequence of Adam’s sin and our own (213). Gregory’s arbitrary imprisonment becomes deserved, as the woman is forworht, and is attributed to royal command (sum [rice] cyning); the woman’s son is given an age of twenty or above (213–14, with reference to Szarmach, “Another Translation”). In the enumeration of things the mother tells her son, the Napier I translator inserts rhetorical elements such as an interjection and the use of the present subjunctive, as well as first-person elements (ic wat and þæt we geseoð), and he adds rivers to the enumeration, yielding “a chain of three two-stress phrases, linked by aural effects and emphasized syntactically by repeated conjunctions” (214–15, quotation at 215). The resulting sequence has st-alliteration as well as grammatical rhyme. The translatior furthermore adds fish to the horses and birds, yielding “a rhetorical triad of earth, sea and sky” while also extending the sequence of grammatical rhyme and alliteration. Even if the surplus elements were introduced in an intermediary Latin source, the vernacular effect is the translator’s. Adding wyrmas and wildeor gives the sequence a Germanic touch; the phrase in fact forms a halfline in Beowulf and occurs in a range of prose texts, including the Letter to Aristotle, Martyrology, and Napier XLII (215). These modifications taken together typify the “prosaic licence” (Zacher, “Style and Rhetoric of the Vercelli Homilies”) of some Old English homilies (215–216). We should see them in the light of the author’s homiletic aims with the text (216).

In the prison analogy, the translator adds a regression over time in the value of Adam’s testimony, doubt increasing with each generation. This is then paralleled in prison by the addition of a third generation (a second generation born in captivity). The effect recalls Wulfstan’s homiletic insistence elsewhere that the world grows worse with time, but it also refocuses the point of the analogy within the adaptation. In Gregory, the analogy pivots on the Incarnation and the role of others granted the Holy Spirit. Neither element makes an appearance in Napier I, which instead points out the king has the power to unlock the prison door and take away all doubt, which is paralleled in life by the revelation that follows the parting of body and soul. Rhetorical elements pervade this passage, too: the rhetorical question (“hu ne mæg se cyning . . .”) and a careful contrast in temporal adverbs þonne / nu / ær / eft. Crucially, however, the modification has the effect of denying true knowledge in the present life. “While the Dialogi attempt to show why the fate of believers within the world need not be like that of the youth born in prison, the analogy in Napier I instead insists, almost casually, upon the absolute epistemological limits of human experience. Through the suggestion that certainty concerning spiritual matters is possible only after death, the text implicitly privileges a kind of blind faith antithetical to Gregory’s intellectual and rational approach” (quotation at 218). This strongly suggests that the adaptation did not originate as part of a full translation of the Dialogues. The author, indeed, may not have known or understood the role of the analogy in Gregory’s wider scheme; but it is also possible he intentionally reshaped the argument to suit his homiletic aims. The rationalist challenges of 590s Rome may have been less pressing concerns to him, and his audience may have had no use for intellectual exercises. The modification removes the uncomfortable shift in the role of the mother [who represents first Adam and then the saints, as noted early in the article], instead aligning the analogy with the tradition describing death as a release from prison. The result is an exhortation to faith (216–219).

At the intersection of common Gregorian core and continuation, all three copies contain a passage praising those who have a knowledge of events past and future. [Puzzling here is Thomas’s rendering of asmea[ga]n as “enquire”; note also in the light of the argument that follows his (perfectly acceptable) rendering of andgyt as “reason.”] McIntosh, Bethurum, and Wilcox believe these are Wulfstan’s words, marking the start of the continuation; it includes his interlinear addition ealles, and Bethurum observes that the passage as a whole matches a rhetorical-structural strategy of Wulfstan’s to pause mid-homily “to reflect upon some ethical or religious truth” (Bethurum 50, qtd. in Thomas 220). Thus understood, the passage suggests that the shorter redaction is an adaptation of the longer [since Bethurum saw the homiletic pause passage as starting a new section, whereas the shorter version does not have much of a section following]. The twofold use of the section to introduce new material also emphasizes the composite nature of the homily, and that the shorter homily may have been produced by Wulfstan himself or an imitator (219–220). Most strikingly, however, the appeal to reason (andgyt) in this passage does not fit with the appeal to blind faith in the Napier adaptation of the prison analogy (220).

The loosely adapted passage from the Dialogues in the longer continuation fits Gregory’s argument and accordingly ill fits the modified prison analogy; it seems to pay more heed to the former than to the latter. There are, furthermore, substantial stylistic differences between the common core and the continuation, although Wulfstan was accustomed to adapting sources to match his own style. The passage in the Dialogues that underlies the longer continuation argues that belief in the soul after death is rational given the miracles surrounding saintly remains. Wulfstan’s adaptation instead focuses on the rewards of heaven. This dramatic reworking resembles that in the common core, so that both parts diverge from Wærferth’s translation in similar ways. Johnson and Rudolf have shown that the Worcester monk Coleman identified and modified passages in the Otho C. i copy of the Old English Dialogues, which they argue was done with a view to adaptation for preaching (222–223). We thus need not infer an intermediary node between Gregory and the Napier author: it was customary for Anglo-Saxon vernacular preachers to adapt passages from sources like the Dialogues for preaching, and the results should be read as responses rather than misrepresentations (222–223).

author: Cubitt, Catherine
title: Virginity and Misogyny in Tenth- and Eleventh-Century England
abstract:
Mary Clayton (Cult of the Virgin) has demonstrated that “[v]irginity was the banner of the reform movement,” which “demanded celibacy and preferably virginity of its own monks and nuns and extended these essentially monastic standards to the secular clergy and to women living under vows. Sexual abstinence was the hallmark of the new monasticism,” not only in terms of its belief system but also in disqualifying the existing clerical order (3; on this last point Clayton refers to Pauline Stafford, “Queens, Nunneries and Reforming Churchmen”). To Ælfric, chastity and Christianity are “coextensive”: Christ instituted chastity when he chose a virgin vessel for his birth, and Ælfric regularly associates paganism with sexual licence (5–6). His virgin lives, describing how women are martyred for their choice to remain chaste for Christ, drive home his belief that virginity was the refusal to bow to idols (6–7). His views on these matters should be understood against his belief that a severe persecution of the faithful was close at hand, and they would have to be fortified against temptation (7–8). Additionally, Ælfric held that mental anguish and deprivation were equivalent to martyrdom, and physical martyrs were models also of monastic continence; the identification of personal purity with martyrdom he derived from Jerome (8–9).

Cubitt argues that Ælfric intended his virgin vitae primarily for male monks. Female monasticism played no central role in the ideology of the Reform, which furthermore introduced a distinction between regular mynecena and devout nunne, the latter category “ranking with the clergy in status, below those men and women who practised more rigorous monasticism” (9–10, quotation at 10).

The Regularis concordia makes King Edgar overlord of male Benedictine monasteries, and his Queen Ælfthryth protector of the female houses, the division intended to preclude scandal. Dunstan specifically commissioned a canon banning men from entering convents, indicating the sexual threat with which female houses were identified. Though it claims to have been written for nun as well as monks, the Regularis concordia in its language refers only to men, and it does not address problems arising from male ministry in female houses. Evidence that the Old English translation of the Regula Benedicti was made for women is mostly circumstantial, and Æthelwold writes that Edgar commissioned it for his own use. In short, “the reformers were less interested in promoting women’s religious life than in controlling it” (10).

The Reform’s emphasis on virginity must accordingly be understood as male rather than female. This may be linked to an increased emphasis on child oblation: it has been shown of the ninth-century Frankish Church that the purity of children became a vehicle for the highest of sacraments, the Eucharist (10–11). Cubitt argues that parallel tendencies may be discerned in the English Church of the tenth and eleventh centuries, the Regularis Concordia assuming that pueri are part of any monastic community and of the liturgy; it also contains rules protecting them against sexual abuse. Byrhtferth’s Enchiridion and the colloquies likewise reference children and oblates. Mid-eleventh century monks at New Minster, Winchester had overwhelmingly come as oblates, and there was a lively cult of boy martyrs, whose early deaths link them with chastity and innocence (11).

Ælfric likewise saw virginity as the special sacrifice of oblates (others were tasked with producing an offspring to offer to the Church), going so far as to interpret celibacy as a kind of martyrdom (11–12). Like the Regularis concordia, Ælfric pays lipservice to gender equality but understands the sacrifices of the monastic life as a male domain. His Hexameron includes a translation of Basil’s Admonitio that welcomes both genders but identifies chastity with shunning contact with women, particularly female houses. His homilies and saints’ lives rarely mention nuns except where they are part of historical narratives (12). Exceptions are three late texts. The first is his letter to Sigefyrth, which recommends virginity for both sexes and forbids the remarrying of widows; the text as a whole concerns male matters, however, emphasizing the need for chastity of Eucharist celebrants, who could only be male (12–13).

Ælfric’s sermon on the Nativity of Mary (Assmann 3) leans heavily on Augustine and Jerome but also contains substantial original elements. It argues that Mary and the Church can be models for fruitful virgin women, but he warns at length that a nun losing her sexual purity forfeits her reward, and that it is better to be married and humble than a proud virgin. Ælfric here showcases a negative view of female sexuality (13–14). The same is true of his Judith, his only text addressing a female audience directly. Ælfric downplays the sexual elements of the narrative (reference to Clayton, “Ælfric’s Judith,” in ASE 23, and Magennis, “No Sex Please,” LSE 26), sanitizing Judith into a model for a nunne (consecrated widow), but he closes by warning nunnan against fornication (14). Ælfric’s texts on Æthelthryth and Martin are not much better: the former draws its key moral from a man’s chastity, while the St Martin homily adapts a passage from Sulpicius Severus declaring that women should stay at home while their men fight, and in the same vein men living in chastity should not keep female housekeepers; Ælfric appends a prayer that Martin may help him personally live a chaster life (14–15). His frequent discussion of late Antique female virgin martyrs may be explained by the understanding that “women are ‘good to think with,’” as Janet Nelson puts it: they are freer to a range of imprints. Moreover, nearly all of Ælfric’s female saints are martyrs, a strong pattern not found in his male lives. “Ælfric used the late antique virgins as vehicles for ideas of virginity, not as exemplars of femininity” (15–16).

When Ælfric discusses women without reference to virginity, their essential quality is sexuality; their virtue in Prayer of Moses is modesty, while other lives display them as temptresses. John the Baptist, Naboth, and Samson were all destroyed by women (16). His sermons overwhelmingly assume male audiences (17).

Among the reasons Cubitt adduces for Ælfric’s emphasis on virginity is that it may have served as an argument in the highly successful monastic takeover of the episcopal office. Chastity may have served to bond members of the Benedictine old boys’ network, a community that served as a substitute for the dynasties that governed worldly polities (18–19).
