Ælfric smears the clergy in the same way he smears noncelibate women, and suggestions that the clergy required vernacular translations imply another parallel between women and the clergy, as what little evidence of latinity in female houses we have is negative (they required translations of the Benedictine Rule and Regularis concordia). Ælfric gave male aristocrats a rank between clergy and monks: they too required the vernacular but they could sponsor monasteries and thus had access to monastic virtue; Cubitt suggests that sexual self-control was required for noblemen to assume this high spiritual status (19).

On ten occasions does Ælfric refer to a threefold division into virgins, the celibate, and the restrained sexually active; these he associates with monastics, widows and secular clergy, and the married. Like his three estates, this division too awards virgin monastics the highest place in society; he claims the oratores face a harder fight than the bellatores (20). Within this strictly ordered society, wives are subject to their husbands (20–21). Ælfric held the breakdown of social mores responsible for the punitive Viking invasion (21). Ælfric’s ideas influeced at least Wulfstan, who was equally obsessed with social order and adapted several of his writings; his Institutes of Polity borrow the three estates and juxtapose social roles with forms of sexual behaviour. Cubitt postulates the thoughts of these two authors may be indicative of a wider culture (21 but especially 22). Æthelred and Cnut instituted laws to regual sexual conduct. If these improved the position of women e.g. by forbidding forced remarriage, their agenda was Benedictine (23). The increase in royal control coinciding with the Reform movement resulted in the policing of sexual identity (24).

author: Clayton, Mary
title: Ælfric’s Judith: Manipulative or Manipulated?
abstract:
Ælfric’s Judith is explained in his letter to Sigeweard as serving as a model for those warding off Viking attacks, but in the epilogue to Judith itself it is explained first tropologically, the defeat of Holofernes standing in for the Congregation’s defeat of Satan, but then also specifically as a model for nuns who are not to forfeit their vows of chastity. Clayton asks how these seemingly incompatible readings are to be understood (215–16). Pringle (Traditio 31) attempts to reconcile them by arguing that Ælfric blamed a lack of English morals for the Viking attacks, and so chastity was the best defence; Pringle thus reads the defence called for as spiritual (216–17). This argument disregards the fact that the text calls for chastity among its specific audience (addressed as “min swustor”), which would be misplaced if addressed to laymen like Sigeweard. Clayton additionally takes issue with the spiritual reading of Ælfric’s instruction to Sigeweard to take up arms against the enemy: Ælfric would not have called Sigeweard to monastic chastity and wrapped his call in allegorical terms to boot; moreover, in his letter Ælfric carefully spells out allegory where applicable, and he praises the physical warfare of the Maccabees. Additionally, Pringle is wrong to see a function for monasticism here at all, as nunne to a reformer like Ælfric signified a religious woman not in a monastic house but either living in isolated withdrawal from the world or in a community of such women (217–18; the appendix on pp. 225–27 explains at greater length how this conclusion is arrived at).

Clayton proposes instead to take all of Ælfric’s explanations as equally valid but not in need of compatibility: the letter to Sigeweard appeals to a historical reading, as is natural for laymen, while the nunne in Judith is given an allegorical and a tropological reading, as we know Ælfric thought it inappropriate even for monks to be forced into the island’s physical defences (218).

There is nevertheless a fundamental disconnect between the narrative of Judith and Ælfric’s conclusions for either audience. He means for the literal interpretation to encourage active military resistance, not the use of seduction ploys. To make this work, Ælfric is selective in his adaptation of the apocryphon: much is shortened, but Achior’s speech to the effect that God strengthens the Israelites as long as they put their trust in him is rendered in full (218–19). The lessons for his nunne do not fit as easily, particularly the tropological lesson (though found in such sources as Jerome, Isidore, and Hrabanus Maurus), which works only by focusing it on the decapitation scene alone. Her ruse, however, raises questions about means and ends which Ælfric selectively wards off by indicating that Judith fulfils her promise of bringing Holofernes (specifically his head) into Bethulia, but this defence works only by ignoring her other lies (219–21). Ælfric then concludes his text with an amen before picking up again and claiming somewhat inaccurately that Judith would not accept any of the war spoils; more importantly, he then goes on to discuss the issue of chastity as though it were connected to the refusal to take spoils. In the original narrative, of course, Judith is not a good model of chastity as she flaunts her sexuality in order to defeat Holofernes. Sensing the inadequacy of his chosen text for his chosen purpose, Ælfric then appends the story of Malchus as a better example, one that introduces virginity, appropriate for his audience (Clayton in her appendix points out that Ælfric warns against the loss of the hundredfold reward of virgins, not the fortyfold reward of widows) but not to Judith (221–22). Already his translation anticipates such problems, as Ælfric hastens to point out that Judith lived in chastity immediately upon her introduction, a theme taken up at a later point in the Vulgate; and Ælfric stresses Holofernes’ lust throughout, rather than Judith’s deliberate incitement of that same lust. “The familiar pattern of the virgin martyr opposed to the lustful tyrant seems to determine the way in which Ælfric views this scene, but it is one which is at odds with the biblical story. Whereas martyrs resist temptation, Judith tempts and, while martyrs reject ornate clothing and all the trappings of sexual adornments, Judith adopts them in order to seduce Holofernes” (223). In Ælfric, Judith dresses attractively “for nanre galnysse,” and she is not implicated in Holofernes’ alcohol consumption. Ælfric cuts her open temptation and her speeches, limiting her power and leaving her “more decorous and less active,” anticipating Ælfric’s later focus on virginity (224). Thus Ælfric reveals his anxiety about women’s use of their bodies beyond the ways the Church prescribed. Although both of Ælfric’s applications of the text are incongruous with the text itself, the military meaning he imposes on it later is more successful than its function as a model for chastity (224–25).

author: Pasternack, Carol Braun
title: The Sexual Practices of Virginity and Chastity in Aldhelm's De virginitate
publication: Sex and Sexuality in Anglo-Saxon England
eds: Carol Braun Pasternack and Lisa M. C. Weston
publisher: Arizona Center for Medieval and Renaissance Studies
series: Medieval and Renaissance Texts and Studies
abstract:
Studies Aldhelm’s approach to the precedent set by Ambrose. He moves his female audience into the masculine sphere by his lengthy athletics simile, but is ultimately interested in an inner rather than an outward chastity, and here his language should be understood as gender-neutral. Sources predating Aldhelm, both platonic and Christian, saw spiritual achievement as masculine, and the sexual drive as feminine, with sources from the Gospel fo Thomas to Jerome asserting that women had to achieve a male state in order to attain salvation. Aldhelm instead depicts a gender-neutral ideal, disarming his athletic simile by means of that of the bee yet filling it with the sensual imagery of flowers and honey, seed and fertilization. The result is a sensual yet asexual model of reproduction, with the Church itself taking on the role of reproductive body.

Whereas Ambrose starts his catalogue with Mary and spends twelve paragraphs on her, Aldhelm focuses on her womb without as much as naming Mary [in her own section though he does, PSL]. As pointed out by Lapidge in the introduction to his translation, Aldhelm modifies the traditional hierarchy of virginity, widowhood, and marriage into virginity, chastity, conjugality.

Aldhelm discusses thirty male virgins followed by twenty female virgins. The male virgins are unprecedented; Lapidge speculates they may have been added because Barking is a double monastery. The accounts of the saints associate sex with revulsion; “In inviting the reader’s admiration of and identification with these virgins, the text promotes a sublimation of desire for sexual reproduction and modierhood (or for the mother) through transferring this desire to the ideal represented by the Church, and it promotes a revulsion for the social institutions of marriage and family, attempting to subdue heterosexuality in favor of a virginal sexuality that is tire same for men and for women” (110).

The female martyrs in the text are explicitly threatened with sexual violence, even where this is done only by the implications inherent in an unsheathed (evaginato) sword. In the Old Testament narratives, however, women play the role of seducer, with Samson, David, and Joseph falling victim.

Though recommending inner purity over outward chastity, Aldhelm vehemently condemns outward adornment as a pathway to inner corruption; nuns are not to wear finery, and indeed he considers outward adornment fit only for prostitutes; he condemns it as a threat to others by way of seduction. Though his objections derive from his sources, Aldhelm’s particular vehemence against female adornment raises questions. Paternack believes the specific descriptions of clothes worn by both sexes must be rooted in experience, while his references to accusations of envy suggest “dissension in the ranks” (119).

Though Aldhelm sets out to write a gender-neutral discourse, his Mediterranean sources are heavily biased, and he himself fails as soon as he reaches David, Samson, and Joseph, who invoke the image of the femme fatale. Even before he reaches these Aldhelm fails to uphold neutrality, as the sexual imagery of death by stabbing only affects women.

I am a little confused by Pasternack’s assertion that Mary is never named; both CCSL and Lapidge/Herren do name her in chapter 40 of the work.

author: Cubitt, Catherine
title: Images of St Peter: The Clergy and the Religious Life in Anglo-Saxon England
publication: The Christian Tradition in Anglo-Saxon England: Approaches to Current Scholarship and Teaching
abstract: Following a discussion of the cult of St Peter, with an emphasis on the depiction of St Peter with a clerical tonsure, Cubitt takes on traditional views of the clerical life in Anglo-Saxon England. Bede held that to be ordained priest one had to be unmarried or divorced, and one could not be sexually active, though lower clerical orders were not so restricted; Theodore’s penitential does not require married men to divorce in order to be ordained. Bede’s criticism in his letter to Ecgbert of supposedly monastic houses being run from the marital bed may be a false equivalency: his standard was monastic, but reality was that priests could be married and lower clerical orders could be sexually active. This also has implications for the minster model: married priests may have lived with their families and staffed village churches.

author: Berg, Ivar
title: Om normalisert norrønt
abstract:
Offers a historical account of Old Norse normalization. Nineteenth-century editors would sometimes refer to a vague “conventional standard”; the first thorough discussion, which has had substantial influence on later practice, may be found in the [preface to the] second edition of Wimmer’s Læsebog, where he defines an existing norm rather than prescribing a new one (21–22).

Defines norrønt as the language spoken in Norway and the Atlantic settlements in the Viking Age and Middle Ages, but concentrating in practice on a variety spoken in early thirteenth-century Iceland. Early scholars did not distinguish firmly between Old West Norse and Modern Icelandic, but as their relationship became clearer, this had consequences for the written standard. In the nineteenth century, this led linguists to pursue the earliest possible standard, while philologists elevated the orthography of the “best” manuscripts (22).

Romanticism formed the backdrop of the German philological tradition; Romantic philosophers divided history into three phases, the first of which was a golden age of heroes and gods, which in Nordic tradition may be dated to the high Middle Ages of 1100–1350. Norwegians like Munch sought to connect modern times with this golden age, condemning the Danish period that separated them. Norwegian nationalist interest biased the publication focus towards legal and historiographical works that could be taken to support nationalist interests. Icelanders had associated Snorri Sturluson with a golden age as early as the mid-eighteenth century (23–24).

The Romantic hunger for a Nordic Antiquity found a scholarly method in Lachmann’s principle of a reconstructable Urtext, and Finnur Jónsson sought to reconstruct such authentic texts in his editions. The “improvement” and normalization of the text were part of this reconstruction; Munch and Unger published Fagrskinna in an orthography the MS might have had in the language’s “best period.” Guðbrandur Vigfússon calls the early fourteenth century “das goldne Zeitalter unsrer Orthographie,” with the purest linguistic forms (25).

Linguists of the nineteenth century sought to reconstruct Proto-Indo-European, and North Germanic was seen as a conservative dialect providing insight into the history of Germanic. Historical linguistics was influenced by an understanding of language as an organism, subject to development and decay. The language of classical Old Icelandic prose was seen as refined, and Rask approved of measures to restore its style and ortography in Modern Icelandic (26). Rask shared the Romanticism of the philologists, but opposed the arbitrary use of Old Norse motifs in modern literature and philosophy. Neogrammarians of the Leipzig School, such as Noreen, moved away from comparative linguistics and sought a historical dimension within single languages, reconstructing the oldest documented forms (27).

The historical-comparative, neogrammarian method of the nineteenth century produced the field’s foremost reference works: Fritzner, Noreen, and Nygaard. The division of the language into Germanic stems is witness to this debt (27–28). The results of this work need not be invalid, but its reliance on superseded theoretical assumptions make the synthesis of its individual findings a dangerous thing to use directly. These assumptions need to be understood if early work is to be used (28).

Jón Eiríksson in the preface to a 1768 edition of Konungs skuggsjá divides Norse manuscripts into Norwegian and Icelandic by their language, which he equates with orthography. He focuses on matters we now put down to phonology, but whose phonological status was unknown at the time; thus he identifies as Norwegian forms <a> preceding <u> (signalling the absence of u-umlaut), short <bøcr> for long <bœcr>, an absence of <h> ahead of <l>, <n>, <r> (28–29).

Rask wrote the first grammar, but he made a number of capital mistakes, including the conflation of Modern Icelandic with Old Norse; he never understood svarabakhti or u-umlaut. He assumed the difference between the medieval and modern languages consisted mostly in orthography (though not, for instance, in the personal endings of the subjunctive). Basing himself on modern pronunciation, he assumed accents marked diphthings, not length (29–30). Jacob Grimm in his Deutsche Grammatik takes Rask as a starting point but also uses a comparative perspective to modify the picture substantially; Konráð Gíslason in turn follows Grimm, perpetuating his unfounded distinction between e from umlaut and preexisting e (29–31).

Konráð Gíslason was one of the first to distinguish between Old and Modern Icelandic (though cf. Berg’s notes on Grimm in the foregoing). He also had a better understanding of phonological changes, though he did not understand u-umlaut of long a until well after his important 1846 Um frumparta íslenzkrar túngu í fornöld, and he still relies too heavily on Modern Icelandic pronunciation (31).

Unger built on Grimm, but adds a correct understanding of svarabakhti, monophthong é, and other matters (31–32). Lyngby laid out the vowel system as it is understood today, basing himself heavily on the First Grammatical Treatise, and he introduced declensions based on stem vowels (following Schleicher’s comparative work). Unger’s comparative basis moved away from Modern Icelandic as the focal language, drawing criticism from Konráð Gíslason. Guðbrandur Vigfússon identified Norwegianisms in fourteenth-century manuscripts and describes Icelandic as an unchanging language (32).

Munch, taking some cues from Grimm, distinguished between Modern Icelandic and Old Norse, and acknowledges that Swedish and Danish split off from a common language predating Old West Norse, but he still based his orthography on Modern Icelandic. Aasen did somewhat better by relying on conservative Norwegian dialects that led him to assume accented vowels were long, not diphthongs; he understands <ö> as “open o”; but he does write hl-, hn-, and hr- as though his Norwegian texts were Icelandic (33). The Gammalnorsk Ordboksverk project was later to develop a proper orthography for Old Norwegian, and that is the standard underlying Menota (33–34). [But Menota claim to follow ONP, PSL.] Munch proposed to come to a normalized orthography arrived at by applying etymological insights to a comparison of diplomatic editions, leading him and Unger to print Old Norwegian texts based on an Icelandic orthography (34).

Eiríkur Jónsson’s 1863 dictionary incorporated new linguistic insights, including the distinction between æ and œ, but in his alphabetization he mixes them in together; the orthographical similarity between the two, and the absence of an accent, may have made the distinction palatable to Icelandic audiences (34; cf. Haugen 1968: 74).

Noreen distinguished systematically, and increasingly, between Norwegian and Icelandic, yet his normalization was based on Icelandic, as he acknowledges in his preface to the third edition (34–35).

Language terms were often influenced by nationalism: Swedish editions of the seventeenth century claimed to be in Gothic. Icelandic could not be used in Norway, giving rise to norsk but also to norrønasproget (Munch and Unger), which has come to be used as the Scandinavian equivalent to English Old Norse. Even so, gammelnorsk is also used, “heilt i ånda frå 1800-talet” (35). Erik Jonsson’s 1863 dictionary was entitled Oldnordisk Ordbog; Jóhannes L. L. Jóhannsson spoke out against a distinction between Old Norwegian and Old Icelandic because he saw it as a Norwegian attempt to lay claim to a literary heritage that is largely Icelandic, while he disapproved of Old Icelandic because it suggested the language had changed so much that it was no longer the same. For some reason he felt oldnordisk was fine, or else fornnorðræna (36).

Berg points to Odd Einar Haugen and Menota for the distinction between facsimile, diplomatic, and normalized orthography, with penetrable boundaries; Guðvarður Már Gunnlaugsson comes to an even finer distinction, differentiating between the internal standard of the scribe and an external standard whether Old Norse or Modern Icelandic. Haraldur Bernharðsson observes that modernized editions affect inflection and syntax as well as orthography. One’s approach to textual criticism affects one’s normalization standard, as an Urtext will naturally tend to early forms, while a synthetic edition requires normalization in order to avoid a heterogeneous mix of forms (36–37).

After centuries in which the available manuscript was uncritically edited, Rask and others founded Det kongelige nordiske Oldskriftselskab and established a normalized standard greatly indebted to Rask’s ideas, and inconsistently executed in their Fornmanna sögur. These volumes do not standardize unstressed o/u, but they consistently print k for c and distinguish between the vowels i, u and the semivowels j, v; they distinguish historically between i and y, but æ and ö follow Modern Icelandic; accents are used for length; early t and k are used where Icelandic later develops ð and g [i.e. in final position], sometimes hypercorrectly; <â> is used for Old Icelandic á where Modern Icelandic has o, as in von “hope,” and they used <è> and <ì> where these vowels were later broken (38). Unger and others criticized this departure from manuscript orthography (38–39).

Unger was a productive Norwegian editor; his editions follow manuscript orthography, even where a lacuna forces him to switch between manuscripts; but he does correct scribal errors, supply omissions, and silently expand abbreviations. Gustav Storm stood at the beginning of a more strictly diplomatic tradition (normalizing indices only), which has persisted since (39).

From about 1850, the philological tradition took hold; editors followed one main manuscript but supplied corrections from other witnesses. Finnur Jónsson held that this method restored the text as much as possible to its original form; he preferred to normalize, not marking expansions but explaining the editorial approach in an introduction instead; only when a manuscript was old and good (e.g. Homily Book) did he feel one should print it without such intervention. Thorsen and Konráð Gíslason sought to identify the best manuscript and normalized it to “den Standpunkt, hvorpå Forskningen af Sproget befinder sig.” Guðbrandur Vigfússon and Möbius sought to reconstruct an Icelandic standard even when printing from a Norwegian manuscript, and rejected <ð> in forms like gleypði as too archaic even though one of their witnesses uses it. They print reflexive -st for the prose, -sk for poetry, and likewise vesa and enclitics for the poetry (39–40).

Altnordische Saga-Bibliothek produced fully normalized synthetic editions without a critical apparatus, reconstructing the dialect for the date of the work, with an early standard for the poetry. This comes across as inconsistent at times [cf. Jóhannes L. L. Jóhannsson, PSL] (40–41).

Íslenzk fornrit normalizes and refers to a longstanding convention, but the main manuscript is also considered for such characteristics as varying between Finnr and Fiþr, Reykjadalr and Reykjardalr. Here too the poetry is more archaic, following Skjaldedigtning and thus distiguishing  and using forms like es. Biskupa sögur II uses a younger standard, and Ásdís Egilsdóttir justifies this in its introduction with reference to Larsson, who had normalized according to the oldest witness. In Íslendingabók, the series uses an early orthography but nevertheless prints <ð>_ and never <>. Both this series and Altnordische Saga-Bibliothek base their standard on the date of the presumed time of composition, not on the manuscripts (41).

Konráð Gíslason and Munch published diplomatic editions with a view to serving linguists; Noreen complained about a lack of such. Many have been published since (42).

Jón Helgason has pointed out that modernized editions simply follow the medieval usus of updating forms to current usage. Wimmer cited pedagogy as his justification for normalization, while dictionaries and grammars require a standard for headwords and paradigms. Guðvarður Már Gunnlaugsson has argued that only linguists require diplomatic editions; the rest of us are best served with normalized editions; Haugen has expressed a similar view. Menota and De Leeuw van Weenen’s Alexanders saga have shown that it is now possible to publish multiple standards simultaneously (42–43).

Whereas the first printed books simply continued manuscript conventions such as abbreviations, Modern Icelandic spelling saw pushes to restore medieval conventions as early as in the days of Árni Magnússon, reintroducing <ð> and length marks. Rask vented his ideas on modern orthography in his journal Skírnir and in his Lestrarkver, using etymological principles such as a distinction between <i> and <y>, leaving out the svarabakhti vowel, the grave accent on <è>, and the reintroduction of <ð>. Fjölnir and Konráð Gíslason advocated for a more phonetic spelling, although the latter later adopted a more etymological standard that became popular for use in schools. This standard (nevertheless) favoured je over è, the use of the svarabakhti vowel, and always pt over ft (44-45). Once this standard was established, most remaining discussion has concerned je/é/è and z (45).

The preface to the second edition of Wimmer’s Læsebog represents a milestone in the discussion of normalization. He aims for the earliest attested language, often citing the Icelandic Homily Book, which is not only the largest of early manuscripts but also consistently marks length. He opts for <ð> in weak preterites like talði and hleypða, but limits vesa and a long vowel before long consonants in possessives like mínn to the poetry. Wimmer went with fekk over fékk, and used skald in the poetry versus skáld in the prose, and referred to Sanskrit, Gothic, and Old High German to justify some of his choices (46–48).

Noreen increasingly archaicized the orthography of his grammar from one edition to the next. Few editions are as conservative as Noreen’s grammar, but Heusler followed it in one of his editions (and in his Elementarbuch) because learners benefit from a shared orthography between grammar and edition (48).

Today, Íslenzk fornrit represents the standard, with variation within that series mirrorred in practice elsewhere. Some newer works, such as ONP and the fifth edition of Heggstad, substitute <ǿ> for <œ> and write an accent on <ǽ> for consistency’s sake. Íslenzk fornrit remains closer to the Modern Icelandic reader, printing geminates in forms like kenndi and <œ> rather than <ǿ> (48–49). ONP follows a conservative standard, e.g. a short vowel ahead of l plus consonant; <ð> in words like spekð; etymological principles governing ft/pt, fs/ps (48–49).

In conclusion, normalization in the nineteenth century was a matter of practice and pragmatism rather than theoretical decisions. Wimmer introduced a more theoretical approach which also involved pedagogical concerns, and his historicizing approach became more pronounced in Noreen, which in turn led to ONP. Íslenzk fornrit, by contrast, has Modern Icelandic more firmly in mind (49–50).

author: Wood, Ian
title: Who Are the Philistines? Bede’s Reading of Old Testament Peoples
publication: The Resources of the Past in Early Medieval Europe
eds: Clemens Gantner and Rosamond McKitterick and Sven Meeder
abstract:
Discusses typological readings of Old Testament peoples in Bede. The author seeks to demonstrate above all that early medieval authors were conscious of imperfect and indeed contradictory virtues of biblical gentes; Bede’s Commentary on Samuel is especially useful for this analysis. It was written in 716 at a time of turmoil and division, and Bede’s works from the period show a concern with unity and a fear of schism at the hands of the Strathclyde Britons. Characters like Saul would have brought to mind Æthelfrith and Osred, but not universally so. Indeed 1 Samuel is especially morally dubious, failing to depict a compelling chosen people.

After the Israelites, who were able to signify the Catholic Church and heretics alike, the Philistines are the people most mentioned in Bede’s commentary on Samuel; they represent idolators and heretics, with Goliath as a diabolical type, but when David joins the Philistines they stand for a missionary audience.

Bede in his commentary on Samuel is little concerned with topical questions like Pelagianism or the dating of Easter; instead, it is Arianism and Manichaeism that appear the most often; in other words, his reading reflects fifth-century controversies. His typology accordingly reflects the whole of the sixth age, not the eighth century specifically.

To Bede, the British were flawed for failing to evangelize to the Anglo-Saxons, in contrast to the Irish, although both groups misdated Easter; the Irish recanted just as Bede was writing his commentary. “[T]he Bible was a tex to think with. Its complex narrative, considered literally, typologically, anagogically and tropologically, and commented on verse-by-verse, allowed a wide range of discordant thoughts. Bede’s theology only allowed one set of binary opposites: the saved and the damned. Yet however much a mortal might think he could distinguish between them, he could rarely be certain” (187).

author: Langbroek, Erika
title: So viel geschrieben, so wenig geblieben: Eine neue Entdeckung: Unbekannte altfriesische Psalmglossen
abstract: Prints (in image and text) two strips from a glossed Psalter, comes to a rough palaeographical case for a date in the late eleventh century for the Latin while referring to Kwakkel for a dating to the first quarter of the twelfth century for the Frisian, and discusses the language. Though questionable in a range of its methods (e.g. using the thematic vowel in one weak class of verbs to explain the form of a verb from another class, and using the use of puncti versus puncti versi, or the height of puncti, to date a text, and citing Bischoff for this without allowing Frisian and other vernacular traditions their own usus), at least it offers the reader access to the material. Oddly in view of the brevity of the material, the article nowhere defends the identification of the gloss as Frisian by contrasting expected Dutch, Low German, High German, and English forms. The glosses read “lesa mi”, “helpe mi”, “herte ande lenden god ·”. See further Versloot.

author: Versloot, Arjen
title: Zur Interpretation der neuentdeckten altfriesischen Psalmglossen
abstract:
Critiques Langbroek’s linguistic interpretation of the glossed fragments of Psalm 7 (e.g. pointing out that she uses the thematic vowel of one class to explain the form of a verb from another class) and reanalyzes each word individually, concluding that the glosses are to be read as lexical forms rather than inflected forms corresponding to the inflection of the Latin. Versloot argues that as not every word has a direct counterpart in the Latin, the glosses are best understood as a translation aid rather than a verbatim rendering; the lexical forms fit this picture.

Versloot concludes with brief observations on the date of the language, which is not archaic except in the form “ande” for later “and”: infinitives already lack final -n, and the unstressed front vowel is e not i. He nevertheless stops short of proposing a later date: “Nur die Form ande ist völlig mit einer frühen Datierung in Einklang. Sonst kann man feststellen, dass das Altfiesische aus dem 12. Jh. nicht unbedingt stark von der Sprache, wie sie in den ältesten Denkmälern aus dem späten 13. Jh. bekannt ist, abgewichen hat” (377).

author: Holmberg, Per, Bo Gräslund, Olof Sundqvist, and Henrik Williams
title: The Rök Runestone and the End of the World
abstract:
Following Ralph 2007 and Holmberg 2016, proposes an enigmatic reading of the Rök inscription, in which the two spoils of war, each taken twelve times are to be understood as sun and moon, twelve because there are twelve lunar cycles in a year; death signifies sunset, and references to the Hreiðgotar represent the east, where the sun rises. The reference to a death nine generations ago is taken to refer to literal generations and permits the authors to dust off the volcanic catastrophe of 536; “a memory of nine generations does not seem unreasonable” (23). Relies heavily on comparisons with Vafþrúðnismál and Vǫluspá, positioning events in relation to Ragnarǫk: “The expectations of a final battle […] were connected to a memory of climate crisis and probably to the anxiety about a similar one occurring.” That hypothesis forms the basis of the Guardian article.

The authors render “a ymissum mannum” “from one to another,” not necessarily the likeliest reading but defensible, and this is the reading that best fits their argument.

author: Hines, John
title: The Anglo-Frisian Question
publication: Frisians and their North Sea Neighbours: From the Fifth Century to the Viking Age
abstract: An intelligent and well-informed but brief and highly condensed introduction to the linguistic, runic, archaeological, and historical links between early English and Frisian cultures, with a long bibliography. The language evidence cited does seem to point in the direction of shared development, but the overall conclusion is that “[i]t was not so much inheritance as a practical interrelationship in the Early Middle Ages that made Anglo-Frisian unity meaningful” (38). Certainly in the use of coins and the production of runic coins an active dissemination may be witnessed between the two cultures.

author: Randall, William, and Howard Jones
title: On the Early Origins of the Germanic Preterite Presents
abstract:
Grimm’s view that the preterite presents derive from strong verbs has long since been discarded in favour of the understanding that they, like strong preterites, derive directly from IE perfects, whether these are to be understood as pure statives or (as is usually done with reference to *wait “know”) as having some sense of completed action. There are, however, a variety of issues with these views. Certainly there is no full ablaut correspondence between strong classes and preterite presents, which Grimm considered free variation while later scholars have pointed to differences in the time of derivation. But it is also curious that forms corresponding to PG *wait and *man are not reduplicated in nongermanic cognates where reduplication is found for reflexes of PIE perfects. Birkmann has proposed that reduplication served a temporal opposition not required for preterite presents, or (following Meid) that it served an iterative function not needed for *man. Additional mismatches between preterite presents and the PIE perfect are the zero-grade infinitives and third-person -un (148–141).

Ringe’s PIE perfective hypothesis requires that preterite presents developed from the same system as strong preterites, but without such new developments as the lengthened grade in class IV–V plurals, the West Germanic personal ending for the second person singular, and dental verbal adjectives (142).

Meid’s “intensive medial present” theory suggests the preterite may have served to intensify semantically the root state, requiring him to divide preterite presents into two subclasses, one with completed action and one with intensifying force. He posits an ancestor for the perfect which was a medioperfect category contrasting with the active, with the stative-resultative semantic value being merely a side-effect. To solve the outstanding issues he denies that the PIE perfect was normally reduplicated, and he claims the intensifying function of reduplication confines it to semantically recipient verbs. Meid’s theory does not account for root statives but assumes derivation from active or aorist forms (143–144).

Birkmann divides the class along the lines of Meid, but with a third group of verbs that do not clearly fit into either completed action or intensification (144–145).

More recently, root statives have been proposed for certain preterite presents; this article builds on these theories (145–146).

Whereas most scholars understand preterite presents as representing a predecessor of the PIE perfect, Tanaka sees them as a late, Germanic creation conflating PIE categories. His approach addresses a number of issues, but above all introduces complexity and an unlikely retention of archaisms into new formations (146–147).

Reconstructions of PG preterite presents make use of the PIE categories of perfect, middle, and stative. The perfect is understood to be (1) stative-resultative; (2) reduplicating; (3) have a set of securely reconstructed secondary endings; (4) subject to o:ø-ablaut. Some of these characteristics have been interpreted as semantic markers, e.g. stative personal endings and state-changing reduplication combining into a stative-resultative meaning. This latter understanding draws heavily on Sanskrit and Homeric Greek, but the evidence in these languages permits other readings; certainly the “achieved” sense has been drawn into question, thus increasing the emphasis on the verbs’ stative meaning. Randall and Jones summarize the middle and stative categories almost not at all except to say that two sets of endings have been reconstructed for the former, which are given in Table 3 and may reflect a development, and that the middle category has been argued to have overlapped with the stative. The existence of a PIE stative is widely but not generally accepted (149–152).

I will not here summarize the authors’ actual proposal in detail, but it comes down to distinguishing semantically between the categories stative, stative-resultative, and perfect of result (153). This allows them to argue that “preterite presents were always purely stative” (172) without requiring them to undergo reduplication, thus stopping short of following Ringe in reading all of the PIE perfect as purely stative (172).

author: Megginson, David
title: The Case Against a ‘General Old English Poetic Dialect’
publication: Prosody and Poetics in the Early Middle Ages: Essays in Honour of C. B. Hieatt
abstract:
While Old English poetic orthography has traditionally been understood to represent a mix of dialects, scholars of the 1950s and onwards have held that this is a specifically poetic dialect rather than a mix of dialectal features. However, Campbell assumes spelling and orthography had drifted apart considerably by the eleventh century; compare the fact that we have to read older pronunciations into verses to make them metrical.

Sisam proposed the general poetic dialect in 1953, and editors in the centuries that followed show increasing loss of confidence in linguistic evidence. The many scholars who accept a poetic koiné do not, however, comment on the relationship between orthography and pronunciation, though this matters a great deal: if there is none, then these poems were for reading, whereas if orthography provides clues to pronunciation, then it contains information about performance. Scholars have come to think of scribes as writing in different orthographical conventions for verse than for prose, though Sisam explicitly excluded orthography from his poetic dialect, limiting himself to forms “confirmed by the metre” in three types:

  • the syncopation of 2sg/3sg pres ind verb endings (as proposed by Sievers);
  • dialectal vocabulary;
  • the cultural history of the main dialect areas.

Thus contrary to Sisam, “most of the editors examined for this paper. . . presume that the poetic dialect theory applies to phonology or orthography rather than to vocabulary or morphology” (123).

Campbell picked up on Sisam and includes phonology in the count of affected language domains, while his section discussing the poetic dialect discusses orthography. Wrenn and Jespersen likewise were influential, spreading the term koiné to refer to the supposed poetic dialect. Quirk and Wrenn in their grammar discuss a koiné including both prose and verse texts.

Scholars thus read orthographical dialect into Sisam’s words, but in fact it was Jespersen who pioneered the idea much earlier, without showing any evidence.

Stanley and Lutz observed that poetic words like wealdend and ylde retain their Anglian a or æ even in West Saxon compositions, even around West Saxon related forms like geweald, thus shifting the emphasis to words. Lutz’s sample is flawed, however, as the word wealdend in the Chronicle appears only in poetry, geweald only in prose; moreover, most scribes write wealdend and waldend interchangeably, while some mostly write the southern form even in poetry. Many of her examples come from late copies of Ælfric, and some of the Junius evidence contradicts the Exeter evidence. Indeed, Christ and Satan had a corrector go through and substitute West Saxon forms for the supposedly poetic forms.

Megginson concludes that variation within the poetic corpus is greater than any supposedly regular distinction between poetry and prose. There is no evidence of a “general Old English poetic dialect.”

author: Orchard, Andy
title: Poetic Inspiration and Prosaic Translation: The Making of Cædmon’s Hymn
publication: Studies in English Language and Literature: Doubt Wisely: Essays in Honour of E. G. Stanley
eds: M. J. Toswell and E. M. Tyler
abstract:
Demonstrates that both Bede’s narrative of Caedmon and the hymn itself derive from a mix of latinate and English elements. Points out biblical echoes in Caedmon’s Hymn; the partisan nature of the historiography (Bede promoting Caedmon, Geoffrey of Monmouth Aldhelm); the currency in Latin tradition of poetic inspiration through dreams; and topoi traceable to the nonchristian Latin tradition, such as the rejection by Aldhelm, Bede, and Byrhtferth of the pagan sources of inspiration from precisely that tradition.

Following a discussion of such influences, Orchard addresses the question of the relationship between the Old English and Latin versions of the Hymn, as he notes Conybeare’s idea of a back-translation from the Latin was revived in the eighties. Orchard obseres that “Bede’s Latin does not reflect the conscious repetition and sound-patterning of the extant Old English text” held to be characteristic of vernacular composition; “if Cædmon’s Hymn is a back-translation from Bede’s Latin, then it is a skilful piece of work” (413). In fact, the second of the two sentences in the Old English Hymn is rendered both more freely and more poetically in the Latin; the Old English and Latin versions of Bede’s Death Song resemble each other far more closely.

Orchard provides a catalogue of analogues from the Psalms and offers that if the Hymn is a back-translation, Bede’s intimate knowledge of the Psalms would account for these parallels. He does not appear to commit to this theory being either correct or incorrect, but instead goes on to point to a couple interpolations from Latin usage into the Latin text and Old English variants.

author: Thayer, James D.
title: Fractured Wisdom: The Gnomes of Beowulf
abstract:
Gnomes are sententious statements of a timeless nature, relaying accepted wisdom; they “serve as a foil for the steady stream of chaotic transformation” in Beowulf (1). They often rely on bið, sceal, or (ne) mæg for their syntax, signalling inevitability. Thayer furthermore identifies the following features, which do not always hold true:

  • A considerable majority begin and end on off-verses;
  • They constitute their own syntactic unity;
  • They have independent meaning, which is enhanced by context;
  • They are spoken by the narrator.

Thayer close-reads Wealhtheow’s gnome, then that in the Lament of the Father, the funerary gnome, Beowulf’s consolation of Hrothgar, and so on, describing the function, form, and mood of each.

author: Lapidge, Michael
title: Old English Poetic Compounds: A Latin Perspective
publication: Intertexts: Studies in Anglo-Saxon Culture Presented to Paul E. Szarmach
series: Medieval and Renaissance Texts and Studies
abstract:
Poetic diction is characterized by words not found in the prose; [appositional] variation; alliterative pairs; and kennings. These features show up in Old Saxon and Old Norse as well as Old English verse and are rightly assumed to go back to “prehistoric Germanic verse” (17). The most striking aspect of poetic diction is its compounds. These are typically nominal, and usually made up of constituent elements of one or two syllables each.

Nominal compounding is innate to many Indo-European languages, including Latin, where many such formations came to be seen as poetic and indeed compounds constituted the principal hallmark of poetic language (18–19). This characteristic is found in the earliest Latin verse and seems to have been used in emulation of Greek verse diction (19). Tetrasyllabic compounds came to dominate; these were made up of a nominal followed by a verb, with medial i intervening, yielding a choriamb (long, short, short, long), a structure favoured by the hexameter, especially in the first or second foot (19–20). Vergil was far more sparing, but creative in his use of tetrasyllabic compounds, and their appearance in his Aeneid became models in late Antiquity, as well as in early medieval English schools. Other authors there used, but writing in the Christian tradition, are Juvencus, Sedulius, Avitus, Arator, and Cyprianus Gallus (20–22); their reliance on tetrasyllabic compounds differs greatly from one to the other (22–24). Lapidge offers the constituent elements commonly used in the compound as a sort of grammar of tetrasyllabic compounds; these could be combined freely, the second element adding little by way of semantic value to the first (24–25).

The six texts discussed were standard elements of early English monastic education, and Aldhelm and Bede show that the convention of tetrasyllabic compounds was transferred into Anglo-Latin verse (25). Aldhelm shows the influence of Cyprianus Gallus in his use of compounds (25–26). Bede’s Vita Cuthberti was influenced by Aldhelm’s Carmen de virginitate; its use of compounds reflects the aforementioned classroom texts (27).

For comparison, Lapidge defines a narrow class of tetrasyllabic compounds in Old English and lists their proportion in ten poems between 306 and 3182 lines in length, concluding that “the poet of Exodus is the most latinate in his diction, and the poets of Judgement Day II and The Battle of Maldon the least so” (27–29, quotation at 29).

Both Latin and Old English poetry show occasional clustering of tetrasyllabic compounds; but Latin never uses two in a single line, and neither does Exodus, whereas Beowulf does (30).

Lapidge admits that his data are skewed by the definition of the tetrasyllabic compound, but he counters that his ranking of proportions matches up with earlier totals lists of compounds, suggesting that unskewing the data would have similar results. A point Lapidge takes more seriously is the observation that compounds occur throughout Germanic verse and must therefore predate Latin influence on the Old English tradition; indeed, Cædmon’s Hymn has a higher proportion of tetrasyllables than even Exodus, and Cædmon was reportedly illiterate. Leaving Cædmon aside, however, the general picture is that English verse is more compound-heavy, while paraphrases of Latin texts show more of these compounds, and so Lapidge concludes that poets with Latin training were influenced by the conventions of Latin verse (31–32).

[I do not find this persuasive, PSL.]

author: Chapman, Don
title: Poetic Compounding in the Vercelli, Blickling and Wulfstan Homilies
abstract:
Asks to what degree compounds serve stylistic effects in Old English prose. Chooses homiletics because this is a liminal register between prose and poetry (409–410); argues that compounds in this genre “[heigten] the passages much as they do in poetry” (410). Identifies 22 compounds found only in homiletics (Chapman uses Vercelli, Blickling, and Wulfstan for his homiletic corpus) and poetry, which he describes as “leakage from poetry” (410–411).

Compounds add to poetic effect by tacking an (at times semantically weak) alliterating first element onto a reduced-stress but semantically central second element (411–412). We can identify sets of compounds with interchangeable first and second elements, e.g. a term for war combines with a term denoting a weapon or armour; homiletic prose turns up similar sets on the phrasal level, such as deaþberende draca/deofol, as well as variable compounds such as manslaga and mægslaga. Indeed, second-element substitutions are far less common in homiletic prose than in poetry; instead we find first-element substitutions such as wiggyld and deofolgyld [the logical structure of this paragraph seems a little shaky? PSL]. Such pairs have the stylistic effect of repeating the second element, as they do not differ greatly in sense (412). Examples of this kind are listed; Wulfstan in particular showcases “the generative interchangeability of echoic elements” (413).

Synonymous or antonymous doublets are often found in homiletics, but a more prominent class consists in co-hyponyms, e.g. spears and swords to mean weapons, and compound doublets varying their first element also fall into this category (“wedlogan ne wordlogan” amounting to two subsets of logan) (413–414).

Some compounds affect style by setting up striking delimiting relationships between base word and modifier, especially in a kenning like bānhūs. Kennings are all but absent from the homilies, with hordfæt, hordcofa, and goldbloma coming closest (414–415); most “colorful compounds” in the poetry are really heiti, in which the first element is often semantically superfluous and thus serves stylistic functions. This is especially true of tautological compounds like sǣflōd, and some such compound are found in the homilies as well (415).

Intensifying compounds, in which the first element adds little to the sense, occur both in poetry (mægenbyrþen) and in homiletics (wuldorþrymm) (415–416).

Colouring compounds like cradolcild are found in some sermons as well as in the poetry (416). [Chapman’s examples are questionable: is wælwulf not rather a kenning? PSL]

Another group of compounds has the first element significantly delimit the second, which “can lead to a poetic effect,” as with goldwine in the poetry or possibly instances like heofoncyning in homiletic prose (416–417).

[Chapman goes on like this for another few pages. The article rather lacks structure and hard definitions, PSL.]

author: Masters Hollowell, Ida
title: On the Two-Stress Theory of Wulfstan’s Rhythm
abstract:
Angus McIntosh described Wulfstan’s prose style as consisting of “a continuous series of two-stress phrases related in structure to the classical half-line, and severely restricted in somewhat the same fashion to certain rhythmical patterns” (qtd at 1) and claimed, indeed, that with few exceptions such as apostrophes and interjections, Wulfstan’s texts are wholly made up of these and that the units formed natural syntactic units as well (1). His findings have been largely accepted by Wulfstan scholars, but Masters Hollowell takes issue with them (1–2).

McIntosh relied on phrases which in the poetry make for breath groups, and on “terminal junctures.” Latin grammars used in early England emphasized the role of punctuation as breath indicators, and the most important Wulfstan manuscript uses such punctuation in places that signal sense division or rhetorical emphasis (2).

McIntosh claims that Wulfstan’s prose is easier to divide into syntactic units by way of breath pauses than Old English poetry is, which Masters Hollowell decries as a non sequitur inasmuch as syntactic units do not necessitate speech pauses. She continues by [deservedly in part, PSL] criticizing McIntosh’s choices of stress positioning, and furthermore claims his phrasing violates the syntactic segmentation he claims to have used as a basis (e.g. “we sylfe / ealle”) (2–3). Funke supports McIntosh but likewise offers questionable stresses [here too Masters Hollowell is right in part; it is only her apparent insistence that a finite verb cannot take “decisive stress” in the absence of a stress word, though of course her implication is correct that the very absence of a stress word casts a degree of suspicion on the two-stress theory, PSL] and artificial segmentation; if read as prose, the cited sequence would have been differently segmented, as Masters Hollowell demonstrates (3–4).

On punctuation, Masters Hollowell takes issue with McIntosh’s claim that the manuscripts confirm his division into lines with very few exceptions. [Her objection presumably relies on absence of punctuation, though all she says is “there is no manuscript confirmation for . . . McIntosh’s short lines,” PSL.] If Wulfstan had used a reliably rhythmic style, she believes the manuscripts would have reflected this more consistently (4–5). She in fact contends that manuscript punctuation harms the case for a two-stress rhythm: they instead suggest much longer units, and the two-stress principle undermines the rhetorical value of a sequence like “understandað eac georne” (5).

McIntosh further argues that Wulfstan’s modifications to Ælfric’s prose help his rhythm, and proposes to use this as an authorship test of adaptations of Ælfric. Masters Hollowell argues that the passage from Ælfric cited as evidence by McIntosh in fact makes for a stronger two-stress pattern (and indeed alliterative long lines) than Wulfstan’s adaptation. Wulfstan’s purpose in modifying his source is instead in the service of paranomasia and other effects he happens to like (5–7). Masters Hollowell offers an alternative phrasing for McIntosh’s passage, which also coincides closely with manuscript punctuation (7).

Masters Hollowell acknowledges the existence of “many passages made up of rhythmical two-stress phrases,” but as interludes marked for the fact that the surrounding prose does not answer to this rhythm (8). Delivering whole texts as though they were cut up into two-stress phrases severely hampers the relay of meaning as organized in clauses and sentences; Wulfstan’s complex syntax would make no sense if it were meant to be cut into two-stress segments, and sound would end up being more important than meaning (8).

Among misconceptions that have arisen from McIntosh’s theory is the linkage of Wulfstan’s prose with that of Ælfric, who came to compose in a pattern loosely based on the alliterative long line (8). Wulfstan was aware of the poetic tradition and of Ælfric’s style, but deliberately chose a different style for himself (9).

[Errata: p. 4 for “clýiað” read “clýpiað”; p. 6 “þæt unsælig man” should be part of the block quote (PSL).]

author: Griffith, M. S.
title: Poetic Language and the Paris Psalter: The Decay of the Old English Poetic Tradition
abstract:
Calling the Old English metrical psalms “a pedestrian and unimaginative piece of poetic translation,” sets out to study its use of poetic diction and its effect on the role of “rank and formula,” proceeding on the hypothesis that the work marks “an important stage in the disintegration of the Old English poetic mode”(167).

Works with a list of 350 poetic terms culled from the microfiche concordance to assess a work’s reliance on traditional poetic diction; the long poems use more than 50 percent of these items, while the metrical psalter uses 106 although it is the longest verse work. This is still sufficient to demonstrate that the poet was familiar with the register, but he may have deliberately avoided these terms, as many of the words he does not regularly use express common concepts like God (e.g. metod, nergend), ruler (brego, rǣswa), and warrior (wiga, rinc). Overlap between Beowulf and Genesis A establishes the traditional vocabulary; the Psalms introduce no new poetical terms not contained in those, and they overlap less with these other texts than those do between themselves: the Psalms use metod and þēoden just once, eorl twice (167–170).

Somehow starting from a comparison of weak nouns (170–171), Griffith goes on to specify that the Psalms use “as many poetic adjectives and adverbs, and almost as many poetic verbs, as Genesis A, but uses only 57 of the poetic nouns, beside 117 in Genesis A, and 158 in Beowulf. Given that there are 183 available poetic nouns, it is clear that Beowulf, and to a slightly lesser extent Genesis A, emphasize the nominal poetic element, where the poet of the metrical psalms avoids it” (171, my emphasis). Indeed, unprefixed poetic weak verbs of classes 1 and 2 are more commonly shared between the Psalms, Genesis A, and Beowulf; accordingly, “the metrical psalms stand apart from the tradition in their scant use of poetic nouns, but are a normal part of that tradition in their use of the poetic verbs” (172–173, quotation at 173). This situation may be explained in part by the poet’s translation technique: rather than vary his diction, he translates homo as “mann” and vir as “wer” almost without exception, while other poetic words for “man” occur where he is expanding on his source, typically in the alliterating position of the off-verse. It is much the same situation with words for weapons or crowds. The poet’s word choices align with those found in the psalter gloss tradition (173–175). Griffith characterizes this as “a symptom of a poetic mode in its death throes” (175), but does not address head-on the natural conclusion that the poet, like the Boethius poet, was versifying an existing translation rather than creating his own.

The system of rank assigns poetic words (often long since gone out of everyday use) to alliterating position, while allowing non-alliterating positions to be filled with colloquial words. The fourth stressed position thus typically accepts prose words, and the metrical Psalms do not greatly differ from the other poems here; like other poets, he gives low priority to the poetic quality of words in this position, suggesting he was aware of this pattern of assignment (175–177). Traditional distribution breaks down in the other positions, however: the a-verses contain very little poetic vocabulary, so rank cannot be said to play a big role in the composition of the Psalms; instead, the poet allowed alliteration to dictate his use of diction primarily in the b-verse. This (somehow) affects the distribution of poetic terminology among the parts of speech: the most common poetic words in Genesis A are all nouns, whereas in the Psalms poetic adverbs are more common; “the poetic vocabulary is no longer integral to the language, but has been subordinated to the role of bleached padding” (177). An adverb like āwa, for instance, in other poems typically occurs in the a-verse in the formula āwa to ealdre, but such formulae do not occur here. Rank is thus both different and less associated with the a-verse in the Psalms (178).

Griffith now turns to demonstrating that the Psalms are “not formulaic in any ordinary, or perhaps in any meaningful, sense” (178–182, quotation at 178).

An appendix lists “the relevant poetic words” (183–185); a second lists formulae (185–186).

author: Russom, Geoffrey
title: The Evolution of Verse Structure in Old and Middle English Poetry: From the Earliest Alliterative Poems to Iambic Pentameter
abstract:
The first chapter (“General Principles of Poetic Form,” pp. 1–34) is an excellent teaching text for the first session of a course on metre, though not the whole chapter is necessary for that purpose; the latter end discusses exceptional conventions such as verse without lines, so it suffices to set pp. 1–29.

This chapter opens by demonstrating that characteristics of formal poetic features such as specified location (within the line), proximity, and frequency may be objectively identified even when a poet breaks with convention (1–6) or when a convention is loose, as in Old Irish (7–8). Stressed syllables are particularly prominent to poetic form inasmuch as they are more clearly pronounced and have access to a richer set of vowels, but they also tend to contribute semantically because a language like English stresses words of semantic content. A feature like alliteration or rhyme accordingly links semantically prominent concepts (6–7).

Approximate rhyme is historically widespread and often relies on phonetically similar consonants, notably sonorants. Alliteration, too, can be approximate e.g. in Old Irish verse, where words continue to alliterate even after sandhi alterations modify their initial consonant so they do not in fact fully match their alliterative counterparts; consequently, it requires an Irish speaker to identify Irish alliterative patterns (8–9).

Since Old English and Old Irish allow any vowels to alliterate among themselves, alliteration cannot be defined as requiring identical initial sounds; instead, the requirement is for identical onsets; in the absence of an onset it is the zero onset that alliterates (9–10). The matching of the s-clusters sk-, sp-, and st- in Old English alliteration has a counterpart in reduplication, with Gothic skáidan reduplicating to skaí-skáiþ. Russom argues that this confirms that alliteration is not simply acoustic [or segmental] but instead relies on syllable structure (i.e. on the onset) [and the rules of the language] (9–10). This is further suggested by the linguistic assumption that the nucleus is more closely associated with the coda (as the rhyme) than with the onset (11). This becomes clear from the principle of syllable weight, as onset consonants do not affect syllable weight whereas coda consonants turn syllables with lax vowels “heavy by position”; syllable weight is thus determined in the rhyme, and the syllabic rhyme is central to poetic rhyme (11–12). Thus the poetic devices of alliteration and rhyme are evenly distributed between syllabic onset and rhyme (14).

Language acquirers avoid rote learning in favour of generative rules, e.g. by overapplying weak preterite formation (12–13). The same intuitions allow us to identify even complex rhymes instantly, as in Latinate words with antepenultimate stress; similarly, when students accept the rhyme plain : explain but reject plain : complain as well as spanned : expand, they seem to be basing their distinction on a perceived syllable boundary within the sequence [ks], which would fulfil the variation requirement in the first pair.

The examples given demonstrate that rhyme and alliteration “must be linguistically encoded”: “[w]ithin the line, canonical English rhyme begins in the rightmost constituent of the rightmost syllable with metrically significant stress” while “Old English alliteration begins in the leftmost constituent of the leftmost syllable with metrically significant stress” (14).

Metre and syntax typically coincide in the unit of the verse line, whose boundaries coincide with those of sentences and clauses; enjambment creates dissonance. Syntax is often compressed to make the sentence fit the line. Even when enjambment is used, the line break often separates phrases or otherwise natural syntactic units. “The most natural point of division is always at the major syntactic break between the two largest sub-constituents” (15–16, quote at 16). The principle of closure, meanwhile, states that metrical units, whether lines, stanzas, or works, tend toward more rigid adherence to formal norms at their end; likewise, the formal return to the beginning (i.e. repetition of an opening sequence) is a poetic universal (17). This chimes with the introductory principle, a tendency to limited formal complexity at the beginning of a metrical unit (17–18).

Tonal dissonance is achieved by lining up chords that are close together, as their sound waves will clash; a progression from tension to release achieves a point of rest in music (18–19). Poetic dissonance may be created using slanted rhyme, or enjambment; the greatest dissonance is achieved “when a line is split at the minor syntactic break within a two-word phrase, a break line the one between a and date” (19).

Russom cites Hogan (“Literary Universals” 241) for a universal word constraint limiting the average number of words per line in any tradition to no greater than nine, and rarely below five. Memorable adages tend to fall within this range as well. Thus just as we process poetic rhyme using internalized rules of phonology, so also we process poetic lines using internalized rules of syntax (20).

In syllable-counting metres like the English iambic pentameter, two immediately adjacent unstressed vowels may count as one or two as needed, and this is true also if they are separated only by a sonorant, and in a number of other phonological contexts (21–22). These allowances are rooted in linguistics: two adjacent vowels are pronounced shorter than they would be if not adjacent, and so on (22). If the metrical “syllable” is understood as an optimal idealization of the linguistic syllable, scansion is the process of matching the two (22–23).

English iambic pentameter distinguishes between strong (normally stressed) and weak (normally unstressed) positions. Syllabic stress is closely tied to vowel tension and syllable length, and a stressed syllable takes about twice the length of an unstressed syllable to pronounce, and is thus commonly counted as occupying two morae (23).

Just as syntactic constituents are made up of morphological constituent (often coinciding with words), so metrical lines are made up of feet, though scholars like Bliss contest their existence and acknowledge no level between the metrical position and the line (23–24). Kiparsky has pointed to the coincidence of foot boundaries with word boundaries in lines with unusual stress placement as evidence for the reality of the metrical foot. When foot boundaries do not line up with word boundaries, Russom speaks of a bracketing mismatch. Metres with variable verse types impose restrictions on bracketing mismatches, while predictable metres require the occasional mismatch to avoid banality (24). Kiparsky’s analysis relies on subjective impression, but he cites a range of poets and critics to acknowledge a trochaic counterpoint to the overarching iambic metre in lines with many trochaic words, which he takes as evidence that the metrical structure of words determines the metre of a line [this is the main bearing of Russom’s 1987 book _Old English Meter & Linguistic Theory, PSL]. The works of the Gawain poet bear this out with especial clarity (24–25).

Variations to the ideal iambic pentameter line of five iambic words may, as Kiparsky shows, be explained by three types of variation:

  1. Unstressed syllables may occupy strong positions;
  2. Stressed monosyllables may occupy weak positions;
  3. Any phrase-initial syllable may occupy a weak position.

The last of these makes use of the fact that phrase-initial, clause-initial, and sentence-initial syllables are difficult to evaluate for stress [a fact that may contribute to the principle of closure, PSL] (25). Shakespeare uses all three liberally, but [thereby] keeps variation within limits [as he avoids bracketing mismatches except by stretching tetrasyllabic latinate words across two feet, PSL]. Milton and Donne make more use of trochaic inversion and bracketing mismatches (26–27). However, “[a] trochaic word will always create a [bracketing or stress, PSL] mismatch in an iambic line,” and Shakespeare could not avoid this happening altogether, as “[w]ith few exceptions, English iambic words are prestigious borrowings from French or Latin. . . . What makes iambic pentameter workable. . . is the high frequency of English phrases with a monosyllabic unstressed word followed by a monosyllabic stressed word.” Shakespeare does not allow closely bound phrases such as article plus noun or possessive plus noun to be split by foot boundaries except under tightly defined conditions (27).

Russom defines his universal theory as five principles (cf. _Old English Meter & Linguistic Theory ch. 0):

  1. “Metrical positions are abstracted from syllables”;
  2. “Metrical feet are abstracted from words, and any word-counting meter is a foot-counting meter”;
  3. “Metrical lines are abstracted from simple sentences”;
  4. Norms for a metrical constituent are abstracted from norms for the corresponding linguistic constituent”
  5. “A poetic meter must employ the line” (28).

The remainder of the chapter discusses poetry without feet or metrical positions, such as Hebrew verse (29–33).

The second chapter (“Indo-European and Germanic Meters,” pp. 35–53) continues the student-friendly style of the opening chapter. It soon points out that Sanskrit and Ancient Greek show evidence of conservative diction and formulae in poetry (36), and supposedly a shared Indo-European formula for dragon-slaying; Russom now turns to remarking on the striking uniformity of heroic narratives across the Indo-European tradition (36–37) and the connection between heroes and poets (37–38). [In short, this chapter’s opening is cause for concern, PSL.] Comes to basic inferences about Proto-Indo-European metre before turning to the attested traditions of Italic, Celtic, and Germanic, pointing out the wide spread of initial stress (38–45); hypothesizes that word stress would have spread across these traditions along with initial stress (45).

Identifies Proto-Germanic as SOV on the basis of runic inscriptions, and points out that the clause-final position of the finite verb accordingly matched the non-alliterating position in the Germanic long line, contrasting with Modern English, in which the final word in an utterance bears the most prominent (nuclear) stress (46). The fact that Germanic SOV developed into English SVO accordingly has important implications for metre (46–47). Here we should acknowledge the use of auxiliaries; these commonly take final position in Northwestern Germanic but not as often in Old Norse, which transitioned to SVO earlier (47). [Here as in other linguistic approaches I have seen, no distinction is made between headclause and subclause syntax, PSL.]

Languages that are reliably SOV use postpositions rather than prepositions, and these can still be found in Old English and Old Norse poetry (47–48); they appear before the verb, whereas prepositions in SVO languages occur after the verb. Adverbial placement likewise is on different sides of the verb between these language types (48). Old English allowed adjectives to appear on either side of the noun, postpositioning representing an archaic placement; this flexibility afforded a choice of whether to have the noun or the adjective alliterate (48). Copula and subject complement likewise could switch places (“dēad is Æschere”), allowing the predicate to be treated as metrically stressed or unstressed (49). Articles or demonstratives follow the noun in SOV languages, and this is sometimes seen in Old English verse (“grundwong þone,” 49). Possessives may be positioned differently depending, among other things, on whether the base noun is animate or not, and here too SOV takes a configuration mirroring that in SVO; Old English was able to use either order (50). Comparison, too, yields a different word order in SOV, and here too Old English had a choice of configurations (50–1).

Phrasal stress favours governed words over governing words, leaving SOV clauses with a strong-weak contour and corresponding poetic verses as alliterating on the first stressed constituent, while long lines assign the first verse the dominant stress over the second, as the on-verse can have two stresses while the off-verse cannot; the stress hierarchy of an alliterative long line is 1-3-2-4 (51–52).

Russom emphasizes that SOV constructions in Beowulf are “syntactic archaisms preserved by formulaic tradition” (emphasis Russom) which became less common as inflectional grammar was abandoned and SVO became mandatory. Before Ezra Pound, who deliberately imitated languages of different word-order types, poetic word order should be regarded as archaic (52).

The third chapter (“Old English Meter in the Era of Beowulf,” 54–88) looks to reproduce the typology set out in Russom’s 1987 Old English Meter & Linguistic Theory. It opens by asserting that Old English feet were based on word patterns and demonstrating how foot patterns follow from word prosody (54) and that word-foot theory improves on Sievers by applying constraints across the verse types rather than per verse type (54–55). Points out how different foot constraints are between Beowulf and Shakespeare, as e.g. the former does not allow bracketing mismatches or the use of an unstressed syllable in stressed metrical position (55). It did permit feet made up of word groups, and the addition of extrametrical, unstressed function words. Establishes nine norms for the metre of Beowulf, based on “optimal” lines, verses, and feet, which evince:

  1. SOV;
  2. Proto-Germanic phrasal syntax, with the most prominent stressed word preceding another stressed word;
  3. Two primary word stresses, no secondary stresses;
  4. Single-word feet;
  5. Trochaic feet following from the most common word pattern;
  6. One syllable per metrical position;
  7. Stressed words each of whose syllables occupies a metrical position (unstressed function words and prefixes may occasionally be extrametrical);
  8. Extrametrical syllables mostly confined to types A3, B, and C;
  9. Complex a-verses normally have double alliteration to help demarcate them (55–56).

Where these norms come into conflict, it is usually the norms pertaining to higher levels of structure that win out: thus lines (N1) trump verses (N3), which trump feet (N4; 58). The two-word verse norm is readily recognized in Beowulf, but not in Ælfric’s Lives of Saints, which are not governed by word feet (59–60). Illegal feet include those that do not reflect word stress patterns and those that introduce metrical ambiguity (60); likewise, rarer compound patterns are not permitted verse-initially (60–61); a verse beginning with a compound may only have four metrical positions; only one foot per verse may have more than two syllables (61).

The remainder of the chapter details the metrical types and subtypes.

The remainder of the book describes Middle English metre and later developments.

[NB that Russom’s phonetic notation is a little unusual. Also there are some examples I do not understand, as in “Hiorogār cyning” as an example of a postpositioned article or demonstrative on p. 49 (PSL).]

author: Gardner, Thomas
title: The Old English Kenning: A Characteristic Feature of Germanic Poetical Diction?
abstract:
Acknowledges the existence of two classes of definition of the kenning: Meissner’s broad definition of “zweigliedriger Ersatz für ein Substantivum der gewöhnlichen Rede” and Heusler’s narrow definition of “Metapher mit Ablenkung” (109). By the former definition, kennings are universal; Heusler, however, sought to claim the kenning as a Germanic concept that developed along an English and a Nordic branch (110), even as he acknowledged that it is not really found in Continental verse (110–111). Gardner infers that “the kenning was not a common germanic figure” but presumably first introduced by Old English poets. These, however, are rather sparing with the kenning in the narrower sense, 20 of the 1070 compounds in Beowulf qualifying, or 122 (c. 2 percent) in all Old English verse (111). They furthermore rarely refer to “typically Germanic” concepts. Gardner prints a useful list of Old English kennings (111–112) and points out that they mostly refer to the body [NB that Gardner understands even common words like līchama as kennings, PSL] or breast/mind with Christian rather than Germanic connotations, or to ship or sun, while almost none refer to warrior (112–113). Where heroic [Gardner writes “Germanic,” PSL] concepts like wound, weapon, bloodshed are referenced, kennings are nearly always hapax legomena and thus no [evidence for a] stock tradition.

Gardner now takes greater pains to define the kenning in the narrow sense where previously he had only given Heusler’s brief “Metapher mit Ablenkung”; he explains base word, determinant, and disparity requirement while using Heusler’s representation “A=B:C.” The riddling nature of the kenning has been remarked on by many, and Gardner draws attention to the question-and-answer dialogue form of Byzantine origin that reached into practically every Western language (113). The Greek Life of Secundus is the most important Byzantine specimen, and the Latin Altercatio Hadriani augusti et Epicteti philosophi and Disputatio regalis et nobilissimi iuvenis Pippini cum Albino scholastico are closely connected with it, the third of these drawing on versions of both the others. Among other things, the Greek text defines man as “mind clothed in . . . flesh” and the ship as a “sea horse,” while the Altercatio and Disputatio likewise define the ship (“domus erratica”) and the body (“domicilium anime”) (114). Several of these definitions qualify under Heusler’s “A=B:C” “Metaphern mit Ablenkungen” and are thus semantically equivalent with kennings; what is more, several of the most frequent Old English kennings have exact or approximate counterparts in the dialogues, e.g. Alcuin’s receptaculum vitae or πελάγιος ίππος in the Greek Life of Secundus (114–116).

Alcuin was familiar with the Altercatio, and both this and his own Disputatio are ultimately based on Secundus; furthermore, it is generally recognized that Alcuin introduced the question-and-answer dialogue format to England, though some claim he followed Aldhelm, who himself promoted the study of Greek in England; at any rate the format was thus known in England by the [late! PSL] eighth century. These works could have contributed to the development of the kenning in Old English (117).

[What this article does not do is explain the role of kennings in some of the earliest Old English poetry; especially if Beowulf is dated early, of course, we would have to push back the introduction of the dialogue tradition to Theodore of Tarsus, which would in fact make a good deal of sense (PSL).]

author: Bredehoft, Thomas A.
title: What Has Ælfric To Do With Maldon?
publication: Authors, Audiences, and Old English Verse
abstract:
Argues that Ælfric’s rhythmical prose has more to do with Old English verse than hitherto acknowledged; “what I largely hope to suggest in this chapter is that we can understand most, if not all, features of Ælfric’s characteristic alliterative style as the product of an Æthelwoldian education in the grounding of Old English poetry as practised by a scholar who became, later in life, separated from the grand library of poetry that I have hypothesized as surviving at Winchester” (151).

Firstly, Ælfric’s Depositio sancti Basilii episcopi uses the word franca, which occurs only five times in the corpus of Old English, including three verse occurrences. Bredehoft observes that preconceptions about whether Ælfric’s text is prose or verse influence whether franca is to be regarded as a poetic term [of course the question should be left open given the low numbers, PSL], and the same applies to the remainder of Ælfric’s diction (148–149). It has been established, however, that Ælfric preferred simple diction, and there is reason to believe traditional poetic diction was hopelessly archaic by his time; hence he may have avoided poetic diction for its inaccessibility and not for reasons of genre. Indeed, Cerne Abbas and Eynsham may not have had much classical Old English poetry in their libraries [and if poetry was not recited by his fellow monks, PSL] (149).

Ælfric’s rendering of the opening of Psalm 100 is quite independent of that in the metrical Psalms, yet his first on-verse closely resembles a range of on-verses in the metrical Psalms, e.g. with the finite verb alliterating rather than dryhten, which would canonically have alliterated.
