The delay of alliteration to the verse-final syllable is likewise paralleled in the Psalms; both add sōþ for alliteration with singan where the Latin has no counterpart; and every metrical oddity in the cited passage can be matched in the Psalms. The two thus appear to be members of the same tradition, as Clemoes has noted (149).

Bredehoft agrees with Pope’s reading of cluster alliteration, i.e. that s-clusters are not strictly kept distinct but that he does prefer exact correspondence especially for st-. This sets Ælfric apart from the metrical Psalms, which keep st- and sp- separate, and from Maldon, which is classical in its treatment of s-clusters (151). Even so, Ælfric could have gleaned the interchangeability of s- and sc- from the Psalms, while the Chronicle poems, which in some cases were forced to bend the rules to accommodate names, might have taught him to mingle clusters with single s- (151–152). Bredehoft accordingly proposes that Ælfric was synthesizing different poetic practices he had encountered (152).

Bredehoft agrees also with pope on g-alliteration: Ælfric tends towards the Maldon/Chronicle/Menologium rule to treat them as distinct, but he sometimes has guttural and palatal g alliterate, and he may have gleaned this convention from older verse (152–153). Bredehoft considers these poems from Æthelwoldian Winchester, which makes it likely that the Psalms, which are quoted in the Menologium, were available there (153–154).

Godden in his “Ælfric’s Changing Vocabulary” remarked on words Ælfric uses only in his alliterative experiments, such as metod and heolstor, though he did not keep using them and sometimes even culled them in revisions. Roberta Frank in her “Poetic Words in Late Old English Prose” adds folde and folm(e) to the list. Godden (Introduction) notes molde, rodor, unman. Gretch has observed that Ælfric’s Cuthbert has a diction “more formal and ornate than ordinary prose” (Cult of Saints 116), although she did think of his style as prose (154). These observations taken together suggest that Ælfric cut back on the difficult aspects of his style once he became accustomed to it (154–155). Heolstor, however, is not used in the Psalms, Menologium, or Chronicle poetry, but it is in Aldhelm glosses that appear to be Aethelwoldian (155).

Compounds, and the sort of feet that accommodate them, grew less important in late verse, but they do feature prominently in Ælfric, including some rare specimens: compounds in -laf are found in poetry also; flothere is confined to Edmund and Beowulf; other words are mostly confined to Ælfric (155–158). Words that occur in both Ælfric and the poetry turn up in Genesis A, Daniel, Beowulf, and Brunanburh, all of which Bredehoft has argued were in Winchester when Ælfric was. Bredehoft also points out that poetic words could be found in other Old English homilies (“Poetic Compounding” 410), and so diction cannot be used to distinguish between poetry and prose; but in Ælfric’s case his use of diction does link him to the poetic tradition (159).

Ælfric’s in his Catholic Homily 2.34 makes clear he was aware of Old English verse, as he acknowledges a poem on St Thomas (159), and in fact he suggests that the existence of a poem on this topic obviates the need to translate it anew; in other words, a poem could serve the same function as his own hagiographical works (160). In this section, Bredehoft asks whether Ælfric can be seen to take diction and formulae from poetry. He discusses the phrasing found in a passage of Edmund, observing that the majority of halflines turn up parallels within Ælfric’s works, but none overlap with classical verse. Bredehoft suggests this nevertheless shows that Ælfric composed in a manner akin to that of verse (160–163). Other halflines of Ælfric’s do echo the poetic corpus: Bredehoft lists wīde geond eorþan, x ūs secgaþ bēc, x gewritu secgaþ, and ofslēon mid swurdes ecge, all of which are limited to Ælfric plus verse, which may be combined with evidence like herelāf to suggest poetic models available in Winchester (164–166).

Returning to Maldon, the co-occurrence in Ælfric and Maldon of not only franca but also the equally rare prasse combines with a few collocations (bēot gelǣstan, flēam gewyrcan, begen lagon, hwā cēne sȳ), allows at least the possibility of influence. However, the lack of similarities makes good sense given that Maldon is conservative in form [whereas Ælfric sought accessible language, PSL]. It is, instead, their method of composition that unites the two authors (167–170).

author: Bredehoft, Thomas A.
title: Early English Metre
abstract:
[My annotations in the first instance are selective, PSL.]

[3.1 Late Old English Verse]: Makes the case that late Old English verse is not “debased” but answers to a different set of rules than Beowulf, developed from classical Old English verse.

Identifies three types of change:

Loss of resolution: this development is evident in the occurrence of short stressed syllables in positions that had previously permitted long syllables only, as well as in the occurrence of long stressed syllables in positions previously exclusive to short syllables (71–72).

Loss of metrical subordination: whereas classical verse had had primary stress, secondary stress, and unstressed, late verse did away with secondary stress, which had the effect of dissociating acceptable foot forms from word prosody, while also permitting stress to fall on the second element in a compound. This also accounts for the disappearance of Sievers types CDE, and it removed the impetus for compounding (72). Bredehoft proposes a way of scanning verses with the second compound element alliterating (73). Delayed stress in verses without compounds likewise cannot be accounted for in Russom’s rule of labelling the first S position strong; instead, metrical subordination has to be abandoned (73–74).

Reanalysis of anacrusis: what had been B and C verses came to resemble type A with anacrusis. B and C could start with as many as five unstressed syllables, and therefore the two-syllable limit of anacrusis in the A type was abandoned (74).

Bredehoft warns that the presence of classical feet is not sufficient evidence to date a poem, as these were still transmitted; the new system was backwards-compatible with classical verse (75).

Late verse is defined as having abandoned resolution, anacrusis, and compound-like metrical subordination, while allowing all s-clusters to alliterate with other such clusters as well as with simple s- (75). Offers an index of permissible late foot structures (75–76). Defines permissible verses as x-foot + S-foot or S-foot + S-foot, with extrametrical unstressed elements allowed before either foot (76). Commonly occurring patterns that were not permitted in early verse may be used as diagnostic verses for dating (77–79). Bredehoft defines one more convention, that of late Old English rhyme, which accepts slanted rhyme along the lines of comon : namon, selle : willes (79–80).

[3.2: Ælfric and Late Old English Verse]: This is a snappy chapter making the case that Ælfric’s rhythmical prose is, in fact, verse under Bredehoft’s definition of late verse. [The chapter is dependent on what comes before in the book, which is what allows it to be so brief, but this also makes it harder to set just this chapter as homework. A natural unit for this purpose is pp. 70–86, i.e. the previous chapter and half of this one (PSL).]

Ælfric offers a natural path of progression from classical verse to Layamon, who additionally could have gleaned his use of rhyme from other late poets (82).

A relineated excerpt from Cuthbert is used to illustrate the metrical feet; the coalliteration of s- and sc-; verse rhyme; alliteration on prepositions and of h with vowels; and continued alliteration across lines, all of which are characteristic of late verse (82–83). Another important clue is the use of pointing between verses in e.g. Cambridge University Library Gg. 3. 28. This clue adds to a general impression that late verse is a literary form [meaning written, I presume, but here also contrasted with formulaic oral poetry, PSL] (84–85). What is more, Edmund in Cotton Julius E. vii opens with an introduction in regular prose, then uses a large initial to set off the beginning of the rhythmical remainder of the text. Bredehoft admits that this may be explained simply by the transition from prologue to vita (85). Finally, Ælfric in his Cuthbert draws a distinction between ānfealde gerecednys and leoðlice gyddung in Bede, and it is after these introductory words that Ælfric switches to his first rhythmical experiment; combined with the fact that Bede’s verse vita was Ælfric’s more direct source than the prose, this indicates an awareness of the mode in which he wrote (85–86). Bredehoft reiterates that Ælfric’s rhythmical writings are unusual if viewed as prose, but not if regarded as verse (86).

The remainder of the chapter studies Ælfric’s Sebastian to identify conventions unique to Ælfric. This passage discusses verse rhymes; stress patterns in proper names; optional alliterative bypassing of initial h; AA- and BB-alliteration [which appears to mean double alliteration in one verse only, but Bredehoft understands it as a form of linkage nonetheless, PSL]; alliteration on prefixes and prepositions; and alliteration from one line to the next (86–90).

author: Oberman, Miller Wolf
title: Dyre cræft: New Translations of Exeter Riddle Fragments Modor monigra (R.84), Se wiht wombe hæfde (R.89), and Brunra beot (R.92), Accompanied by Notes on Process
publication: Riddles at Work in the Early Medieval Tradition: Words, Ideas, Interactions
abstract: A wonderful, brief article attempting artful translations of three fragmentary riddles, but also artfully discussing the philosophy and process of translating these texts. Not bad as a way of making students think about words and translation.

author: Cronan, Dennis
title: Alliterative Rank in Old English Poetry
abstract:
Defines alliterative rank as the alliterative frequency of synonyms (145). Briefly critiques prior studies of the phenomenon, then observes that alliterative frequency is correlated (indeed “largely coincides,” pace cases like hlaford) with the distinction between poetic and nonpoetic words, inasmuch as “[t]he majority of poetic words. . . can be said to be marked by both their restriction to poetry and their high alliteration rate” (145), and it is this connection which the present article sets out to study in simplex words (as compounds always alliterate). Cronan understands words that alliterate at high rates as high in “poetic worth,” a concept fusing function and style but whose stylistic value has developed, at least in part, out of alliterative function (145–146).

Cronan singles out a range of 21 semantic categories and subcategories (not individual lexemes), divides their members into poetic and nonpoetic terms, and tallies their rate of alliteration. Depending whether the general category of “man” is included or excluded, he concludes the alliterative rate of poetic words on average exceeds that of nonpoetic terms by either 12.1 or 11.4 percentage points [Cronan mistakenly writes “12.1%” and “11.4%” respectively, PSL]; two of the nineteen categories that have both poetic and nonpoetic sets show nonpoetic terms alliterating at higher rates (146–147).

Cronan’s next step is to identify 35 items in his set whose Old Icelandic cognates may be considered poetic as well, and divide this set into

  1. Items that have no nonpoetic cognates in other Germanic traditions;
  2. Items with nonpoetic cognates in Gothic, as well as cognates in the Heliand;
  3. Items with nonpoetic cognates in West Germanic as well as Gothic, including some that are also found in the Heliand.

The implication is that many words in group I [and some in II] will have “descended from a common Germanic poetic tradition,” whereas others may belong to “a Northwest Germanic poetic tradition” giving rise to the Old English and Old Norse poetic corpora (147–148). These 35 items average 7.1 percentage point higher in alliterative rank than the complement of Cronan’s poetic words, and they are also far more frequent [across the Old English poetic corpus presumably, PSL], at some 50 occurrences against 15 for the others (148). Between the three groups, as might be expected, group I has the highest rate of alliteration, at 91.6 percent; Cronan blames the lower rate of group II in part on special circumstances for metod and þeoden (148–149). The three groups together are almost exclusively made up of heroic terms (149).

Words that have figurative as well as literal referents alliterate more frequently when used figuratively, at a difference of 28 percentage points (149–150). This suggests a stylistic dimension (150).

Cronan offers some caveats: alliterative rank can only be compared between synonyms, as semantics affects the rate of alliteration; and some words are frequent as base words in genitive pairing, reducing their alliterative rates because a base word in the typical word order, as in lifes brytta, cannot alliterate in an off-verse, while certain lexemes used as base words typically occur in first position (e.g. wine, brego), radically boosting their alliterative rates (150–151).

Cronan observes that ranking also implicates the position of a word in the line, as just 24 of the 151 words in his set occur as the fourth stress in the line but always alliterate when they occupy the second stress (151–152). Across a corpus of 2500 lines, he finds 68.7 percent of non-alliterating nouns and adjectives are in fourth position, which extrapolates to seven in fourth position for every three in second position. However, while there are 19 words in his set that lack alliteration in fourth position only, there are only two in second position that lack alliteration only in that position, whereas statistically one would expect eight or more. Cronan posits a rule marking these words for alliteration wherever possible, i.e. anywhere but in fourth position (152–153). Alliterative ranking can then be defined as a descending scale:

  1. “Words with 100% alliteration”;
  2. “Words that alliterate whenever they occur in a position where alliteration is possible”;
  3. “Words with non-alliterating occurrences in both the second and fourth positions,” this category coinciding with words of low alliterative rank (153).

This system means that words of category 1, like lagu, are forbidden from occurring in fourth position, while a synonym like brim may occur anywhere [but must alliterate when in the a-verse, PSL] (153).

An alliterative rate of 75 percent is average for simplex nouns and adjectives [this is confusing: context suggests Cronan means poetic nouns and adjectives, but on p. 154 he puts “the aggregate alliteration rate of all poetic words” at 82.3%, yet he never mentions parts of speech other than nouns and adjectives, and only ever gives examples of nouns, PSL], and this may serve as an approximate boundary between low and high rates, though the figure differs for each semantic category (153).

Cronan observes that the traditional definition of poetic vocabulary is handicapped by the fact that the surviving poetry is older than the surviving prose, so some terms we think of as poetic may just be early. Alliteration rates help define the poetic lexicon more precisely, and heroic association may be an additional aid (153–154). Words that occur in both prose and poetry may be categorized by their rates of alliteration (154).

Cronan’s list of poetic words is printed, along with their rates of alliteration, as an appendix (156–158).

[This is an important article, but a little sloppy in some respects, as when the definition of Cronan’s testing corpus is not explained, he consistently speaks of percentages where he means percentage points, and he refers alternately to “all poetic words,” “[s]implex nouns and adjectives” and the like citing substantially different alliterative rates, but he only prints his poetic simplex nouns in the appendix, PSL]

author: McIntosh, Angus
title: Wulfstan’s Prose
abstract:
Divides Old English compositions into five types:

  1. Classical Old English verse, answering to the analysis of Sievers, Heusler, and Pope;
  2. “[L]ate ‘debased’ Old English verse”;
  3. Ælfric’s rhythmic prose as used in his Lives of Saints;
  4. Wulfstan;
  5. Ordinary prose (110–112).

The uneven distribution of types 1 and 2 in different redactions of the Chronicle is interesting, and at least demonstrates that classical verse could still be produced even in the south by the late tenth century (112–113). Debased verse came into use in the tenth century, and was common in the eleventh, and early Middle English verse from the Midlands suggests this form became prominent there. Ælfric’s style does not appear to have had currency among other authors, and he does not seem to have looked to a model much like his own (113). He did inspire emulation, but none that cannot be distinguished from his own work (114).

Wulfstan’s prose is “a continuous series of two-stress phrases related in structure to the classical half-line, and severely restricted in somewhat the same fashion to certain rhythmical patterns” (114). A flawed case along these lines was made by Einenkel in 1884 (115–116). McIntosh defends his position, first, by observing that his two-stress phrases “are always small syntactic units,” yielding “natural speech-pauses,” and he claims “the whole of a text can be divided in this way” (116) although alternative divisions are sometimes possible (116–117). He holds two-stress phrases to be a natural feature of English speech, as modern book-titles attest (117). Wulfstan ran with this and further strengthened the integrity of his phrases by the use of alliteration (117–118). Additional evidence comes from manuscript punctuation, as the pointing in the various manuscripts, though differing a great deal between the witnesses, comes almost exclusively at the ends of two-stress phrases, and for McIntosh offers “final and convincing proof of the reality of these two-stress units.” This pointing resembles that in Junius 11 and in Ælfric’s Lives of Saints; in all these cases we may assume the punctuation served enunciation primarily, though McIntosh has to concede that non-genuine texts in Napier’s main manuscripts have this pointing also (118). He asserts that the distribution of punctuation between the various manuscripts suggests the archetype had the most consistent pointing, suggesting Wulfstan was responsible, and he furthermore claims Wulfstan’s reworkings of Ælfrician texts also support his position (119).

Wulfstan’s two-stress phrases differ from classical verse in not combining into long lines (alliteration exists within the phrase) (119); they stand closer to classical verse than to Ælfric in “overall length and weight” if one counts average syllables per phrase or verse (119–120), but also differ from classical verse in giving “length of syllable” no functional significance and escaping the Sievers classification inasmuch as it is difficult to find e.g. D or E verses here, while it incorporates cadences not accounted for by Sievers (120).

McIntosh briefly discusses Wulfstan’s modifications to Ælfric’s De falsis diis (121–122) before turning to the applications of understanding Wulfstan’s system, particularly that of telling Wulfstan’s writings apart from that of others (122–125). He claims the prose of the Vercelli Book is not altogether unalike Wulfstan’s and may point to an origin, but the difference in style between these and the “debased” poetry suggests “the habit as a whole was not very old” (125).

author: Russom, Geoffrey
title: Constraints on Resolution in Beowulf
publication: Prosody and Poetics in the Early Middle Ages: Essays in Honour of C. B. Hieatt
abstract:
Recommends the principle of natural matching, based on word-foot theory [for which see Russom’s Old English Meter & Linguistic Theory, PSL], to resolve the issue of when resolvable sequences undergo resolution if they do not occupy the first lift.

Resolution requires a short (and thus open) stressed syllable followed by a second syllable within the same word. Although resolved sequences are equivalent to long monosyllables, they are nevertheless marked, and Germanic languages often eliminate resolved sequences by lengthening the first vowel (147–148).

A resolvable sequence is generally resolved if it occupies the first lift; but this [is not regulated, Russom, Old English Meter & Linguistic Theory §4.8] for Sievers Type A3, where the first lift is also the last. Less clear is under what conditions a resolvable sequence is blocked from resolution, but Cable, Fulk, and Terasawa have shown that resolution was undesirable on the last lift of verse types BCD, and effectively prohibited [in that position and in those verse types? PSL] if it formed the second element in a compound (148), which may have an explanation in natural language as subordinate constituents of compounts are often shortened (148–149). Accordingly, “[s]ince it is motivated by a strong expectation of length, resolution should occur less often in subordinate constituents” (149).

Word-foot theory assumes a link between metrical and linguistic elements: full lifts derive from (unmarked!) long, stressed syllables; halflifts derive from (unmarked!) long, halfstressed syllables; and weak positions derive from weak syllables. Native Old English word patterns yield nine foot types; words with short, stressed syllables are ambiguous and are assigned to one of the nine foot types [generated from other syllable types] (149–150). Russom further adduces his assumption that the verse and the verse line mimic the compound, so that the second lift in a verse is metrically subordinated while the off-verse is subordinated to the on-verse. The first lift in a verse is therefore more prominent and is particularly prone to resolution, as lifts are associated with length; but “[t]o the extent that a resolvable sequence undergoes linguistic or metrical subordination” [i.e. is the second element in a compound or the second lift in a verse, PSL] it is not resolved (150).

Russom translates these principles into explicit rules:

  1. “Within the word, resolution is most natural under primary stress, less natural under subordinate stress, and forbidden under zero stress.”
  2. “Within the foot, resolution is most natural on an S position, less natural on an s position, and forbidden on an x position.”
  3. “Alliteration on the most prominent S position makes resolution less natural on a subordinate S or s position within the same metrical domain.”
  4. “Resolution of a short syllable is less natural when the following syllable is long and the resolved sequence would therefore be equivalent to an ‘ultralong’ closed syllable containing a long vowel (Kaluza’s Law)”
  5. “On the most deeply subordinated s positions, both resolved sequences and ordinary long syllables are unnatural. Such s positions are most naturally occupied by a short stressed syllable (unresolved).”
  6. “When two or more naturalness constraints apply simultaneously, their effects are summed.” (150–151)

Thus a resolved Type-B verse like “þurh rūmne sefan” violates rule (b) but not (a); it is harder to find a verse that violates both (151). Type-C sequences like “þæt healreced” are unresolved and common; a sequence like “Hē on weg losade,” which incorporates a resolved sequence followed by an x position, is rare (151–152). For verses of type D1, it is observed that Beowulf prefers compounds whose second element has a short root syllable over those with long root syllables, as per rule (e); long variants can be avoided by reversing the verses of a line to yield type E (“māðmǣhta mā”); this process substitutes a more complex verse (inasmuch as the compound usually occupies the second foot), yet the poet thought this more desirable than to leave a long syllable in a doubly subordinated position. Short counterparts are not commonly reversed, and indeed there is no incentive (152).

Reversal is impossible for the expanded type D1 (Sx/Ssx); accordingly, the poet tolerates instances of this type with double alliteration and long s; by contrast, it is here the short counterpart that is commonly reversed into a type A2 variant. The incentive for this must be that a verse like “dēogol dǣdhata” was not naturally resolved, or otherwise it would have been read as A2 to begin with. The reversal prefers a complex variant of a simple type over a simple variant of a complex type (153). Resolution of the second compound element in Type E is rare, but cases of suspension are even rare, and so there is no strong audience expectation to resolve (153–154). One of the two resolutions of type D2 in Beowulf may be considered an anomaly (154).

Russom rejects Sievers’s tertiary stress, as Fulk has shown it to be internal to Sievers’s typology, which Russom does not adopt, and relying only on the principle that a verse [other than type A3, PSL] must have two stresses, which Russom likewise rejects. This avoids him having to explain “swā bealdode.” Russom instead posits two word-feet, which will often have two stresses due to the lexical properties of Old English. In his theory, bealdode cannot undergo resolution because the second syllable is unstressed (154–155). He supports his position against Sievers’s with reference to frequency of verse types: it is the less frequent types that deviate from the two-stress norm, as these have three; yet verses with compounds like healreced are far more frequent in type D1 than in C, which makes sense if the C verses are scanned as light while the D1 verses have normative, two-stress weight. Likewise ultraheavy Ss/Ss verses are rare, so it would be surprising if common verses like “tryddode tīrfæst” would have be to be read as such (155–156).

author: Momma, H[aruko]
title: The Composition of Old English Poetry
abstract:
Sets out to define Old English poetic form by analyzing those texts that use alliterative long lines. The opening chapter arrives at its approach by discussing and critiquing existing approaches to metrics and the definition of Old English poetic form.

When Donoghue tested Bliss’s rules for the behaviour of auxiliaries and verbals in Beowulf on the rest of the corpus, he found just one of them to be predictive of the syntax of verse as opposed to prose; this suggests syntax as a defining criterion (22–23). Mitchell in his Syntax lamented the lack of an understanding of verse syntax. There were in fact studies on verse syntax even then, but these generally focused on word order and clause structure and concluded that word order is rather free in the verse. In fact, prosody affects syntax, obscuring the order of constituents (23–27). Momma therefore spends half a chapter discussing studies that assume poetry had its own syntax, incorporating the demands of prosody (ch. 3).

Kuhn assumed poetry reflects the earliest Germanic word order. He drew on Wackernagel’s law of Indo-European word order to posit the normally unstressed categories of Satzpartikel, which modify the clause as a whole and are not bound to any particular constituent, and Satzteilpartikel, which are tied to a particular constituent; the former category is further subdivided into proclitics and enclitics, depending on whether it depends phonologically on the following word or the preceding. A reconstruction of the system makes clear that stress words are differentiated from other words on prosodic grounds; the unstressed elements are subdivided on syntactic grounds; and Satzpartikel are further subdivided on phonological grounds; but Kuhn does not describe his system clearly and does not take on the issue of word order directly (28–32). Accordingly, his work has been widely misunderstood. Bliss misrepresents Kuhn’s three-level binary system when he instead describes the system as a three-way division into stressed elements, particles, and proclitics, and differentiated them by three levels of stress, where Kuhn had differentiated the last two categories by the syntactic criterion of their dependence on other constituents, not by stress. Thirdly, Bliss increased the emphasis on parts of speech, offering a list of parts of speech for each of the categories fuller than Kuhn’s. Kuhn has been misrepresented ever since (32–35).

Lucas too misinterpreted Kuhn, believing that his word classification relied on stress alone, describing the three word classes stress word, particle, and clitic, assuming three levels of stress, assigning parts of speech to each word class, and obscuring the role of syntax, substituting phonology as a criterion to differentiate between particles and clitics. He does introduce a hierarchy analogous to his stress differential, and posits that words could rise or fall in the hierarchy and thus take on greater or lesser stress through displacement, but Lucas’s system fails to account for stress without displacement, as in the verse mīn ǣrende (35–37).

Kendall correctly represented Kuhn’s theory as a multilevel system, and does not make great changes to Kuhn’s lists of parts of speech. Yet he held that stress alone differentiated between the three levels, particles carrying lesser stress while proclitics are unstressed. By misdefining Satzpartikel, Kendall comes to false predictions, such as independent stress for substantive pronouns (37–38).

Cable criticizes Kuhn for things properly attributed not to Kuhn but to later critics, namely the abandonment of a binary system, which misguidedly emphasizes parts of speech in the metrical dip; Cable instead posits a system that, ironically, is a lot like Kuhn’s. His system divides parts of speech into ictus-bearing and non-ictus-bearing; the former further subdivides into words that are always stressed and words that are demotable, while all non-ictus-bearing words are promotable. In Cable’s system, however, all members of a given part of speech have the same status. Thus although his main division is prosodical, his assignment of words to these prosodical categories is lexical, yielding false predictions (38–40).

On the view that Satzpartikeln comprise both stressable and never-stressed words, Hutcheson adds a fourth category, for a set of stressed elements, stressable words, clitics, and non-stressable words, hierarchical in that order in terms of their association with stress. This system too assigns entire parts of speech to each category, offering more detailed lists than others. Stress is the major criterion, with a secondary role for syntax in the definition of stressable words and clitics. This is insufficient for clear distinctions between the categories, and Hutcheson incorrectly predicts that personal pronouns are more apt to take on stress than possessives (40–42).

Following this review, Momma presents her own critique of Kuhn. She identifies Kuhn’s as the best system to date, but lacking in its subdivision of Satzpartikeln into proclitics and enclitics, as well as in the way it handles lexemes and parts of speech. Kuhn’s reliance on the former division is rooted in his hypothesis that Indo-European enclitics became proclitic in Germanic in consequence of the introduction of root stress, which disrupted the rising-falling stress countour of Proto-Indo-European; by developing proclisis on the second accented word in the clause, this pattern was restored, but now climaxing on the root syllable of the second accented word rather than on the medial stress of the first. This, however, yields a “clumsy” falling pattern around the first stress. Moreover, Kuhn appears to assume that Old Germanic Satzpartikeln occur after the first stress, where in fact they tend to appear before it even by his own count of Beowulf. Kuhn thus had to posit a further shift to the front in order to maintain clisis with the first stress-word, but in this step he does not explain why some particles remained post-stress. Instead, the insistence to call words proclitic or enclitic is misguided when there is no semantic connection with either the preceding or the following constituent (42–45). Kuhn furthermore posited a shift from proclitic to enclitic for certain clause-medial Satzpartikeln (the example used is wenic for “wene ic”), but Momma counters that this is a lexical matter, as it does not affect all word combinations equally (no *wenstu is attested). She concludes that “the phonological criterion of clisis is not relevant for Satzpartikeln” (45-46, quotation at 46).

Momma then takes on the reliance of all critics cited on parts of speech, which cannot be perfectly matched with prosodical word classification: “many indefinite [pronouns] are always stressed, but personal pronouns are stressed only occasionally.” Pronouns are accordingly distributed across all three categories of stress words, Satzpartikeln, and Satzteikpartikeln (46–47, quotation at 47); the same is true of adverbs (47–48); and other parts of speech are distributed across two of the three categories (48–49). Momma continues methodically to point out all the problems of relying on parts of speech (49–52) before proposing that “the word-class of each word should be determined as it occurs in a particular context”; she uses the word element to mean “a word in a particular context of poetry,” and it is these elements, rather than lexemes or parts of speech, that are assigned to stress words, Satzpartikeln, or Satzteilpartikeln (52).

Momma’s modification of Kuhn’s system is then left with two levels: at the highest level, a prosodic distinction is made between (contextually) stressed and unstressed elements, while the second level makes a syntactic distinction between the attachment or detachment of a given element to an immediately following constituent, and she terms these detached unstressed elements and attached unstressed elements (52–53, quotation at 53).

The next chapter (ch. 4) tests Kuhn’s First Law and Kuhn’s Second Law, originally intended as metrical laws, for their validity as syntactic predictors; Kuhn’s First Law is thus restated as saying that “Satzpartikeln occur immediately before either the first or the second stressed element of the clause” (56). One type of exception to this law in Old English poetry has a stressed finite verb separate between two (other) Satzpartikel; Kuhn held that this was immaterial because the verb is itself a Satzpartikel, but in Momma’s new syntactic definition it does pose a problem. A more common exception delays Satzpartikeln until a just before a stress in a later halfline; these are often pronominal datives of the possessor, with a semantic association with the phrase before which they are placed (him to foddorþege). Finite verbs may also be delayed, and occasionally infinitives and adverbs, and at least the last category may be considered Satzteikpartikeln instead (56–62). Kuhn’s First Law is sometimes used to determine sentence divisions in poetry (63–64). Momma concludes that it is useful as a syntactic rule, in spite of exceptions (64).

Kuhn’s Second Law is syntactically [and negatively! PSL] restated to say that “the clause must not be introduced by one or more Satzteilpartikeln attached to a stressed element.” The two laws are thus complementary inasmuch as the first only applies to clauses with at least one detached element, while the second applies only to clauses without a detached element, except that it further exempts headclauses introduced by coordinating conjunctions and the like. On the whole the second law is less efficient, and in Kuhn’s definition it comes with problematic further conditions; ’[t]heoretically, in fact, Kuhn’s Second Law is violated every time the clause begins with an unstressed pronoun followed immediately by a stressed appositive" (65–68, quotation at 67). Further violations are discussed, leading Momma to reject Kuhn’s Second Law (68–74), while some of the problematic verses additionally violate his First Law, but only its metrical component, not Momma’s syntactic version (74–75).

Momma now dedicates a chapter each to each of her word classes, and concludes that “(1) stressed elements can occur in any position in the clause and take any order; (2) attached unstressed elements can occur in any position in the clause (and in any number of positions in each clause), but two or more such elements in the same position must take a fixed order; and (3) detached unstressed elements must occur in one of two fixed positions in the clause and take a fixed relative order in each position” (183). These criteria apply as a necessary condition to all Old English verse, though the study does not conclude whether it is a sufficient condition (183).

Momma sees the relevance of her system in its value in distincuishing between syntactic qualities found in all poetry from stylistic features such as that of Kuhn’s Second Law syntactically defined, which latter stylistic feature does confirm Cynewulf’s authorship of his signed poems (188). Any given behaviour of stressed elements [which Momma has shown can occur anywhere, PSL] likewise points to stylistic traits; thus the metrical Psalms meet Momma’s criteria for syntactic verse, but frequently use adverbs as the first stressed element of the off-verse (188–189); this may stem from the translator’s wish to follow the Latin semantic argument (189–190).

Theories of formulaic composition leave a gap of 25 to 35 percent of verse composition unexplained; prosodical syntax may help. Momma critiques formulaic theory over a few pages [a little late to introduce the topic, and well worthy of fuller discussion, not in the last place given the arguably somewhat unfortunately chosen title of the book; PSL] (190–192). She posits that the language of verse may have been something like a second native, separately acquired language to poets. Momma holds that the three rules she has formulated were “designed to enhance syntactic clarity” (193), mixing maximum syntactic freedom for stressed elements with a fixed constellatory order between attached and detached unstressed elements. Detached unstressed elements created clarity through their predictable position within the clause (193–194).

author: Grinda, Klaus R.
title: Pigeonholing Old English Poetry: Some Criteria of Metrical Style
abstract:
This paper is a tabular presentation of data on metrical style among poems over 500 lines in length. Features examined are the proportion of Sievers types A3 and E; the proportion of E verses whose final stress is a finite verb; the distribution of type E between on- and off-verses; the proportion of verses in which the first stress of the off-verse (the “head-stave”) is a finite verb; the proportion of lines linked by linking alliteration; the proportion of that last category relying on consonant alliteration; and the connection between alliterative linking and syntactic pauses. Grinda does not define his terms clearly: table captions are not in all cases unambiguous, and the article itself, which is a discussion of his findings and a preamble to his data, is lacking in explanation and structure.

Alliterative linking is especially common in the metrical Psalms, the Metres of Boethius, Maldon, and Juliana, and least common in Beowulf and Exodus; verse type A3 is most common in Maldon, the metrical Psalms, Guthlac A, and the Metres of Boethius, and least common in Guthlac B and Genesis B; type E is most common in Exodus, Christ C, and Beowulf; and finite verbs on the head-stave are most common in the metrical Psalms, the Metres of Boethius, and the part of Genesis A that Grinda has included.

author: Harleman Stewart, Ann
title: Kenning and Riddle in Old English
abstract:
Kennings and riddle have often been grouped together, presumably because both involve guessing as they work with unknown referents, but the nature of their similarity has not been explored. Harleman Stewart’s position is that their similarity does not consist in puzzlement; rather, they share an outward suggestion that puzzlement is involved (115).

The kenning is defined in both its broad and narrow definitions following Meissner and Heusler, the latter’s definition requiring that the phrase be periphrastic (the referent not mentioned), metaphorical, and identifying the referent as something it is not; but even the strictest definition leaves room for debate (115–117). The kenning’s basic structure of base word and “limiting word” is described, with brief attention to the grammatical properties of compound and possessive noun phrase (117–118).

Harleman Stewart asserts that it is generally overlooked that the kenning involves metonymy as well, as this is the relationship between limiting word and referent (118–119). In her model, this means the audience is expected to “look” towards the referent from two directions; in Jakobson’s semiotic terminology, the audience orients itself along the axis of contiguity and the axis of similarity. Harleman Stewart understands the referent of the kenning in this context as a linguistic sign, not a signified; the axis of contiguity refers to the relationship a sign has to other signs of the same scale to form larger units, as e.g. words form phrases, and this corresponds to metonymy, while the axis of similarity refers to interchangeability, e.g. the use of synonyms, corresponding to metaphor. Thus when a warrior is referred to as a tree, this is metaphor by substitution of the base word; when he is referred to as [the something of the, PSL] spear, the reference is by metonymy through substitution of the limiting word (119). A kenning makes use of twofold dislocation, i.e. by synonym and metonymy, compounding the search paths for the correct referent yet simultaneously reducing the processing power required, as the candidates for either search query alone would yield a larger set whereas “[t]here are far fewer things that are like a tree with respect to spears” (119–120, quotation at 120).

Harleman Stewart suggests, however, that these two parallel processes still lack sufficient information for the solving of kennings, as e.g. hildenæddre merely tells us “[a]dders in some context are like something in the context of battle,” which is a circular scheme requiring the identification of two unknowns, the solution of each of which requires knowledge of the other. Harleman Stewart suggests that this means either one has to shuffle back and forth until both fit, or at least one unknown was known from the beginning and thus kennings are not puzzles at all (120–121). She argues for the latter state of affairs: context usually offers the requisite information by way of variation (121–123). Furthermore, many Old English kennings overlap: thus there are many variants of the kenning containing a word for sea and a word for horse, and once an archetype is established, the remaining variants can be deciphered by running through synonyms for both elements until one reaches the archetype, without need to engage in parallel processing on the axis of contiguity and the axis of similarity (123–124). The same applies for kennings on sea-house (ship), soul-house (body), and bone-house (body) (124–126), while sea-horse and sea-house show further overlapping and can be organized in an overarching set of sets (126–127).

The Old English riddle functions similarly (127–128) inasmuch as clues are modified by paradoxical, restricting epithets (e.g. “a featherless bird”). Such epithets (Heusler’s hemmende Umstände) are metonymic, while here too there is an analogue that is metaphorical, thus yielding the same two-perspective model for discovering the referent (128–129). The three conditions of the kenning may also be applied to the riddle: it is periphrastic inasmuch as the solution is not made explicit; it is metaphorical in terms of the relationship between analogue and referent; and it presents its referent as something it is not (129).

Old English riddles differ from Latin and modern riddles in sometimes revealing their referent up front (47 bookworm; 23 bow), after which they go on to delight in a set of analogues (129–132). The energy of these variant images of the same thing would be lost if the referent were not known (132–133). Although not all riddles offer their solutions up front, there are others that are easy to guess; some in this category use this simplicity to play with double entendre (45 dough) (133). Others, however, may be explained in so many ways that they become impenetrable, forcing us to see these riddles as something other than puzzles, and indeed the same effect is achieved by poems that are too obvious (133–135). Thus “[b]oth [riddles and kennings] are structures with the ostensible purpose of mystification; both give a pleasure that rests on the opposite of this purpose, on recognition,” and the “blank” canvas of the riddle stripped of its puzzle leaves its author to use it to whatever end she will, but its use of multiple images to express the same referent allows a play with multiple perspectives (135).

The contextual shifts required for riddling and kennings is characteristic of all language play and relies on the contextual shifts required for everyday communication through the existence of homonyms, jargons, social contexts, dialects and the like (135–136).

author: Frank, Roberta
title: A Scandal in Toronto: The Dating of Beowulf a Century On
abstract: A brilliant and highly entertaining article, narrating the history of Beowulf dating and deftly undermining some key arguments of those holding to an early date. Among other things, observes that Kaluza I type verses are far more frequent in Maldon than in Beowulf (856), that <d> for <ð> is more frequent in Judith or the Exeter Book than in Beowulf (857), and that “the only undisputed light -e endings in Kaluza type I verses in Beowulf for which resolution was obligatory belonged to masculine i-stem nominative and accusative singular forms. . . the shortening of pre-Old-English unstressed long -ǣ to æ, which then became e — now seemed quite irrelevant to the dating issue. . . . And earliness had nothing to do with it” (860–861). Also notes that several verses are shared with Blickling homily 16, while a verse like “frofor ond fultum” occurs throughout the corpus (862).

author: Lapidge, Michael
title: Textual Criticism and the Literature of Anglo-Saxon England
publication: Bulletin of the John Rylands University Library of Manchester
abstract:
Takes somewhat of a national approach to the field.

Opens with a historical account of three notable English textual critics, several of whom relied exclusively on the collation of others and thought of palaeography as a contemptible auxiliary task to be carried out by others, leading to the reputation of English textual criticism as strong on conjecture. Lapidge observes that a knowledge of script is required to reconstruct certain errors or group witnesses by scriptorium or ownership.

Whereas manuscripts of classical texts typically do not predate the fifth century, Anglo-Latin texts may often be found in manuscripts roughly contemporary with their author. Lapidge now spends a few pages discussing the challenges in establishing autographs and identifying revisions by the original author. He asserts that the text is always in flux, but most particularly during an author’s lifetime when authorial revisions may still be disseminated. All this strengthens the first point of the article, that textual critics require a knowledge of palaeography in order to take such matters as interlinear glosses into account.

The Anglo-Saxon willingness to revise texts did not extend to classical works, which were treated as fixed. The least fixed were liturgical texts, due to differences in usus. With unfixed traditions, it is worth printing each recension separately; for debate on this question, Lapidge refers to an exchange between George Rigg and J. B. Hall.

A second difference between classical and medieval texts is that classicists may be sure their authors wrote correct Latin.

Early editors of vernacular English texts did not approach their material differently than did classicists. They were happy to emend and even “correct” readings. By the late nineteenth century, however, a reverence for the manuscripts came to temper the wish to print a text as smooth as a classical edition. Critical apparatuses came to reflect this reverence inasmuch as they recorded not just indicative variants but rather scribal preferences in matters of spelling and the like. This focus on the manuscripts may be a disservice to the texts’ authors inasmuch as it has led to an extreme reluctance towards emendation. Lapidge asserts that “it is the editor’s first duty to detect error in the transmitted text and, if possible, remove it” (42), though he acknowledges this opinion is against current fashions.

Lapidge illustrates his position with Maldon 183, which was regularly emended in the nineteenth and early twentieth century for absence of alliteration, but has since been left standing defective. It is Lapidge’s position that we should at least venture conjectures, even if they are uncertain.

author: Bekker-Nielsen, Hans, and Ole Widding
title: Arne Magnusson: Den store håndskriftsamler
abstract: A concise biography, with attention also for the posthumous establishment of the Arnemagnaean Commission and the initial efforts towards returning manuscripts to Iceland. The biography draws primarily on Jón Ólafsson's autograph in AM 1027, 4<sup>o</sup>.

author: Kuhns, Matt
title: Cotton’s Library: The Many Perils of Preserving History
abstract: A political-historical biography, situating Cotton’s manuscript collecting against the backdrop of his political activities; and thereafter discusses his son, grandson, and librarians in the same manner. Explains Cotton’s collecting as serving public access above all; this is also why the library’s closure in 1629 under Charles I hit him hard. The collector’s death on 6 May 1631 is also explained against this background.

author: Engelstoft, Laurids, and Erich Christian Werlauff

author: Perelman, Les
title: The Medieval Art of Letter Writing: Rhetoric as Institutional Expression
publication: Textual Dynamics of the Professions: Historical and Contemporary Studies of Writing in Professional Communities
abstract:
The rhetorical tradition did not offer instructions for written discourse until C. Julius Victor included a short appendix on the subject to his Ars rhetorica in the fourth century. This shift is explained by the fact that whereas Antiquity was urban, the Middle Ages were rural (97–98). This new need is best reflected in the ars dictaminis tradition that sprang up in the eleventh century and came to be followed almost universally (98).

The illiteracy of most Western rulers after 476, combined with the deurbanisation that followed the decline of the Roman Empire, resulted in a need for professional authors (“[e]ducated Romans and churchmen”; Perelman refers to Murphy, Rhetoric in the Middle Ages p. 197). At the same time, correspondence became largely limited to ecclesiastical and political affairs, making it more public and more permanent in nature (98). This led to the Merovingian institution of the chancellor embedded in the ruler’s travelling household; from Louis the Pious onwards, this was a bishop serving as the emperor’s chief judicial and administrative secretary (98–99).

In the Merovingian period, many letters were standard templates with only the specifics added for the occasion; but the growing complexity of administrative and political life made form books obsolete (99). The ars dictaminis or dictamen tradition developed in the eleventh century at Monte Cassino, the new papal chancery, and the incipient Italian universities in response to this need for custom letters. Rather than attribute its “invention” to a single individual, such as Alberic of Monte Cassino, we have to conclude that it developed out of prior sources (99–100). The influence of the Frankish court on the tradition of ars dictaminis is clear from the fact that the papal administration wrote in Caroline Minuscule (100). In the mid-eleventh century, Leo IX ramped up chancery production and relied on chancery correspondence to subjugate local bishops to Rome (100–101).

Papal letters came to be of two kinds: privileges, which granted or confirmed rights, property, or jurisdiction to churches and religious houses (thus effectively title deeds and carefully kept by their beneficiaries), and letters, which were instruments of papal administration and judicial acts. Letters may be subdivided into tituli, granting or confirming rights, licences, indulgences, etc., and mandamenta, containing injunctions, appointments, and the like (101).

At the time when Alberic of Monte Cassino wrote the first extant treatise on the ars dictaminis, his pupil John of Gaeta served as papal chancellor for three decades before becoming pope (Gelasius II) himself, and it is at just this time that papal correspondence came to take on a characteristic prosody (cursus) that became part of the ars dictaminis, including in treatises written by at least one subsequent papal chancellor (101–102). As a tradition shaped by the papacy, the ars dictaminis reinforced that institution’s assumptions in such matters as social hierarchy, encouraging authors to think about the rank of their audience before thinking of their message. Starting at the time of Innocent III, the standard spread to the episcopal and secular chanceries of Western Europe. Taught first in monasteries and by private mentors of rhetoric (dictatores), the material spread to cathedral schools and incipient universities by the mid-eleventh century. The dictamen won out over rival schools through its connection to the papacy (102).

The ars dictaminis was a continuation of classical culture, drawing on Cicero’s De inventione and the pseudo-Ciceronian Rhetorica ad Herennium (102–103). Alberic of Monte Cassino taught the classical rhetorical treatises. About the time Victor III ascended to the papacy, Alberic wrote the Flores rhetorici, also known as Dictaminum radii, which enters into a discourse with classical rhetoric, discarding some traditional elements while expanding others and showing a shift from logos (logic and legalistic questions) to ethos and pathos, focusing on the relationship between author and recipient (103). Alberic relays Isidore’s fourfold division into exordium, narratio, argumentatio, and conclusio, a simplification of Cicero’s sevenfold and Pseudo-Cicero’s sixfold system; he quotes Cicero for the purpose of the exordium; and he adapts parts of both standard works throughout his treatise. However, he leaves out their discourse on argumentation (103–104). Instead, ahead of the exordium he introduces the salutatio, a common enough element but never before discussed in a treatise, which he discusses following the Aristotelian triad of speaker (ethos), subject (logos), and audience (pathos), thus developing a new rhetoric using classical notions of persuasive discourse (104–105). The remainder of the Flores is not specific to letter-writing but discusses rhetorical figures derived from Ad Herennium (105).

Alberic also wrote a work entitled Brevarium de dictamine (incompletely edited), whose first part is concerned with letter-writing. It offers model salutations and a structural analysis of the papal privilege as compared to other documents (105).

A work both more systematic and more centrally concerned with letter-writing is Adalbertus Samaritanus’s Precepta dictaminum (c. 1115), which offers detailed instructions for salutations, including (for the first time) the norm that the more exalted person be named before the inferior of the correspondents (105). Adalbertus takes Cicero’s threefold hierarchy of styles but adapts it to the relative rank of the correspondents, with corresponding requirements for flattery, requests, and the like (105–106). Adalbertus then offers model salutations and letters (106).

Perelman emphasizes the obsession of the tradition with social hierarchies: as chanceries owed their existence to such hierarchies, “[t]heir function was not to convince, but to command, to dispense benefits, and to execute judgment” (106).

The twelfth century saw two Bolognese treatises give rise to a standard Murphy calls the “Bolognese Approved Format” (107).

The Aristotelian model (expanded by Roman Jakobson) is static inasmuch it doesn’t allow for a relationship between speaker and audience: it is concerned with matters external to this relationship (107–110), with only the exordium centring on contact between addresser and addressee (110). The anonymous Bolognese Principles of Letter Writing through their careful consideration of the salutatio demonstrate the phatic (i.e. social) function of this element (110–111). Its next subject [following the classical tradition] is the captatio benevolentiae, which may resort to a statement of achievements, duties, or motives; praise of the recipient; both; reference to their relationship; or reference to the subject matter (111). Narratio should be brief, and so is its treatment in the Principles (111–112); it is followed by Petitio, which too is treated briefly, though it lists nine types ranging from supplication to threat, each of which may be said to have its own implications for the relationship between addresser and addressee (112).

The firm emphasis in the ars dictaminis on attitudes to the addressee and the relationship between addresser and addressee follows from feudal hierarchies, but the roots of the tradition in papal and imperial chanceries must likewise be adduced to explain why the classical focus on argument is so categorically omitted (113).

Among later developments was a flowchart by Lawrence of Aquilegia intended to make letter-writing a mechanical process, but the tradition more generally came to adopt a great deal of formulae (113–114). Later traditions also sought to bring together Cicero and the ars dictaminis (115).

author: Lanham, Carol Dana
title: Freshman Composition in the Early Middle Ages: Epistolography and Rhetoric Before the ars dictaminis
abstract:
An insightful article, but perhaps a little too speculative to set as undergraduate reading.

Seeks to delineate the development of epistolary conventions predating the ars dictaminis that came up after 1100. This medieval tradition has often been characterized as a new invention tied to such authors as Alberic of Monte Cassino, but it must have had its sources (115–116). The consideration of rank in the salutatio is evident in rhetorical treatises from late Antiquity to Alberic, showing that his work built on a long-established tradition (116).

Lanham starts with the Greek treatise Peri hermeneias by Demetrius, of perhaps the first century CE, which has an excursus on epistolary style recommending brevity and a plain but polished style. Cicero does not tackle letter-writing head-on, but he does list types of letter in a way that implies established categories. Quintilian describes epistolary style briefly, but he is the first Latinist to do so, associating correspondence with a plain style. Ovid too recommends everyday diction; like Demetrius, he makes correspondence out to be derivative of spoken dialogue, and both Seneca and Pliny the Younger have left remarks suggesting much the same (119).

Julius Victor’s Ars rhetorica is the first extant Latin treatise on rhetorics to include instructions for letter-writing, drawing on Cicero and Quintilian but on (an) unknown source(s) for his chapters on conversation and correspondence, the latter of which again draws on oral speech when it recommends the inclusion of references to oral discourse (“I see you’re laughing at me”). A late eighth-century Monte Cassino collection of texts on grammar and rhetoric includes a paragraph on letter-writing, and an eighth-century commentary on Donatius includes direct address in letters among its five types of oratio (119–120).

Between the first century BCE and Quintilian’s time we see a development of rhetorical exercises known as progymnasmata, relegated to grammar instruction by Quintilian’s time. The only such set of exercises extant in Latin is Priscian’s Praeexercitamina, a translation of a work attributed to the second-century rhetorician Hermogenes (120–121). The tradition included prosopopoeia or ethopoeia, speech in character, which Augustine had to deliver as a schoolboy. The aim of the exercise was decorum, adapting one’s style to speaker and situation. It is in the context of ethopoeia that two Greek rhetoricians mention letter-writing, and the fifth-century author Nicolaus recommends the practice of ethopoeia in letter-writing, considering the character of author and recipient alike (121). Ovid’s Heroides are examples of such fictional correspondence, while Aelian and Alciphron offer Greek models. A fourth-century correspondence between Seneca and Saint Paul is likewise best understood as a classroom exercise (121–122). Cassiodorus has left two indications suggesting that actual correspondence differed from such exercises in needing to be adjusted to author and addressee (122).

In sum, then, letters had to use conversational style and reflect the relationship between author and recipient (122). Actual letters in both Greek and Latin confirm that letters were expected to imitate face-to-face interaction, notably by qualifying the petitio with forms of quasi prostratus pedibus vestris, building on the formula quasi praesens found in Cicero (122–123). Lanham refers to her appendices on the quasi prostratus-formula and other formulae as evidence for “a continuous tradition of letter-writing theory and practice” (123–124, quotation at 124).

Next, examples of instruction are given. Symmachus c. 400 recommended his son be taught to correspond using a style appropriate to his age and to everyday speech (124), and Julian of Toledo in the late seventh century in his adaptation of Donatus’s grammar uses two examples referencing letter-writing, suggesting this was practised in his classroom (124–125). Notker’s Life of Charlemagne makes mention of schoolboys composing “letters and poems,” while Alcuin recommends the division of schools into three classes, the second of which should read “epistolas et parvos libellos,” though it makes no mention of composition. The Life of Burchard has pupils present letters and written questions on scripture to the bishop (125). Letters from Worms dating to just after Burchard’s tenure contain both actual and exercise letters. Lanham suggests that the sparseness of these examples may itself be evidence that epistolography was practised (126).

Next, Lanham observes that instructions for letter-writing mirrorred those for speeches in such recommendations as clarity, brevity, and simplicity, and several rhetorical figures are common in letters (126–127). She proposes that “as part of the centuries-long shift from an oral culture to one dependent on writing, the written letter replaced the spoken declamation as the primary vehicle for practice in prose composition” (127).

Lanham proposes that the progymnasmata be understood not as preprofessional training but (with the exception of their final element, discussion of law) as a general introduction to rhetoric (127–128). The classical curriculum did not accommodate the analysis of prose outside the progymnasmata, and those were primarily aimed at public speaking (Quintilian complained that this was all pupils and teachers were interested in). Though initially focused on speaking in court, the progymnasmata remained relevant after Roman judicial culture declined because they were equally applicable to panegyric and declamation, and could be adapted to other genres of composition as writing continued to increase in importance (128). It is against this background that Priscian translated a work of progymnasmata in the early sixth century, while Cassiodorus identified flawless prose and verse compositions as the purpose of grammar (128–129). These exercises were continuously used through the Middle Ages in Byzantium, and Lanham proposes they likewise had a presence in the West, later to give rise to dictamen (129).

Isidore recognized thirty components of the ars grammatica, including the new categories prosa, metra, fabulae, and historiae, thus claiming narratio for grammar where Quintilian associated it with rhetoric (129).

author: Nevalainen, Terttu
title: Letter Writing: Introduction
abstract:
This essay forms the introduction to a special issue of the Journal of Historical Pragmatics entitled Letter Writing, which discusses sociolinguistic aspects of letters composed in the period 1400–1800. The introduction mostly sums up the focuses and findings of the volume’s papers.

The universals of letter-writing include one or more named recipients, a sender, and a message (181). The format has contributed to specalized genres like the newspaper, scholarly article, and epistolary novel, but also New Testament epistles and medieval love letters in verse (181–182).

The composition of letters is learned, and the ars dictaminis taught it from the eleventh century onwards; its principles, however, go back to Roman times or perhaps to ancient Mesopotamia, but eventually the tradition was replaced by classical models introduced in the Renaissance and a need for more technical business formats (182).

Official correspondence may influence language norms, as seems to have happened in fifteenth-century Germany and England, with the Signet Office determining the language standard for royal missives (182). In times of standardized orthography, letters by unlearned writers reveal data on pronunciation (182–183), and corpora of letters have formed the basis of sociolinguistic study (183).

Even after the ars dictaminis faded as a classroom topic, it continued as the model for politeness in correspondence in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, particularly when the language used was not the native language of one or more of the correspondents; Tiisala’s article studies this phenomenon in largely Low German Hanseatic communication. These letters followed the three social categories described in dictaminen (183–184).

Erasmus recognized three categories of letters by their rhetorical functions. Bergs’s article rejects extralinguistic criteria for such categorizations but instead studies text types in fifteenth-century English correspondence by linguistic criteria (184–185).

Wood’s article studies Margaret Paston’s fifteenth-century letters for social and discursive clues (185–186).

Tanskanen’s article studies intertextuality in Lady Katherine Paston’s seventeenth-century correspondence (186–187).

Nevala focuses on audiences: letters were often circulated among family. She studies forms of address, which in the eighteenth century become more fixed in recognition of the larger readership (187).

Bijkerk investigates the rise of “yours sincerely” and “yours affectionately” in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries (187–188).

Valle writes on early scientific correspondence around the Royal Society, which she concludes did not differentiate between empirical and informal registers (188–189).
comments: The volume is a special issue entitled "Letter Writing."

author: Irvine, Susan
title: The Alfredian Prefaces and Epilogues
publication: A Companion to Alfred the Great
eds: Discenza, Nicole Guenther, and Paul E. Szarmach
series: Brill’s Companions to the Christian Tradition
abstract:
Though indebted to the conventions of the genre, the Alfredian peritexts offer an insight into ninth-century notions of self-representation, authority, and authorship, particularly through their promotion of Alfred as a philosopher-king (143).

Authors of vernacular prefaces cannot be assumed to have had access to classical manuals on the rhetorics of preface or epilogue. Instead, they must have relied on Latin models. In the case of the Pastoral Care, the Latin work has its own preface and epilogue, and Bede’s Ecclesiastical History has both a prefatory letter and a concluding prayer. Some saints’ lives also had prefaces, as did biblical translations, including Jerome’s. Alcuin produced prefaces resembling that to the Old English Pastoral Care. In short, it is clear Latin models were used (143–144). It is less clear whether vernacular models were consulted. Old English poetry incorporates prefaces and epilogues into the text body, but these were themselves in dialogue with Latin literary culture (144–145).

Alfredian prefaces and dialogues are diverse: some accompanied the associated work from the beginning, some were added later; some claim Alfred’s authorship or patronage; some are prose, some verse (145). The preface to Alfred’s law code, incorporating a lengthy sequence from Exodus, tests the boundaries of the genre; the biographical introduction to Boethius as found in the prose Consolation is treated by the content tabulator as a chapter, not a preface existing outside the text. The genealogical preface to the Parker chronicle is merely a genealogical list. Translated prefaces also occupy an unclear territory (145–146).

Irvine muses on the validity of treating peritexts as independent units, and on manuscript clues setting them apart (146); yet these Alfredian peritexts ended up shaping the way the works they accompanied were understood for a long time (147).

The Dialogues, translated by Wærferth supposedly at Alfred’s instigation, but probably before any translation programme was fully realized, survive in two copies, one with a prose and one with a verse preface. The former is an early Old English preface and is in Alfred’s voice, though probably not by him; it claims the translation was for Alfred’s personal use, but the preface only makes sense if it had other audiences than himself and points to an aim of wider circulation. It also draws on the rhetorical conceit of a tension between worldly affairs and spiritual contemplation found in book I of the Dialogues, thus setting Alfred up as a spiritual successor to Gregory (148–149). The survival of the other full copy of the Dialogues with a verse preface only is unusual for a prose work (149–150). This preface is in the book’s own voice by prosopopoeia (150). It refers to Bishop Wulfsige as the commissioner of the translation, but the manuscript in which it survives is much later, and a reader has removed the anachronism by turning the name into “Wulfstan” (152–153).

The Pastoral Care survives with a prose preface, a verse preface, and a verse epilogue, all contained in ninth-century manuscripts and thus associated with the work’s first dissemination. The prefaces were likely composed as a pair, following Carolingian models. Both authorize the work in Alfred’s name (153–154), and the prose preface is innovative in its dramatic inner dialogue (156).

The Consolation has a prose and a verse preface, and a concluding prayer in one manuscript. The prose preface claims Alfred first translated the work and then versified it, but this preface is problematic: (1) it seems composite or not original; (2) its second sentence appears cobbled together from phrases in the Pastoral Care in an attempt to recreate Alfredian style; (3) the third sentence opens with words that seem to look back to Alfred’s reign in the past; (4) “shw heo nu gedon is,” used twice, seems to refer to two different versions of the Consolation (160–162). The verse preface serves to authorize the translation in Alfred’s name, and when referring to the text and its versifier it uses words exclusively associated with poetry (162–163). The concluding prayer was added to the text at a later stage in its transmission and uses ic without specifying whether this refers to the scribe or some other person (163–164).

The sole surviving copy of the Soliloquies has a prose preface in a voice assumed to be Alfred’s, whose role as compiler of the translation is asserted in a brief concluding note at the end of book III, and indeed compiler may be closer to the truth of Alfred’s role than translator (164–165). It opens with an extended metaphor with much technical vocabulary on the gathering of wood, representing the creation of a florilegium for one’s spiritual improvement (165). The work namedrops the Church Fathers, thereby claiming their authority for its own literary enterprise (166).

The preface to the law code is in Alfred’s voice and incorporates portions of Mosaic law from Exodus while also citing historical precedents, both approaches serving to underpin the authority of the new law code (166).

The verse epilogue to the Ecclesiastical History is a scribal colophon (168).

The conclusion of the essay refers to Gérard Genette’s concept of the paratext, a concept wider than that of peritext which in turn includes prefaces and epilogues, but Genette’s taxonomy falls apart where he excludes anything not mandated by the author or publisher: it is not always clear in medieval manuscripts who has contributed a given component (169–170).

author: Hill, Joyce
title: Micro-Texts in Ælfric’s Catholic Homilies
abstract: Revisits a 1985 article on Ælfric's peritextual observation that his _Catholic Homilies_ do not include texts for the last three days of Holy Week — the _swigdagas_ — because one ought not to preach on these days, and the two disagreements written into the margins of one manuscript each, one signed Coleman and one anonymous. The main new insight into the matter results from investigations since published that suggest Coleman was perusing manuscripts looking for preaching material on repentance and chastity, suggesting that Coleman's note was inspired by frustration at not finding what he hoped to find in just this place in the manuscript. Ælfric's reasoning may have been to bring the general liturgical calendar into line with a practice of silence observed in reformed monasteries.

author: Patt, William D.
title: The Early ars dictaminis as Response to a Changing Society
abstract:
The ars dictaminis stood alongside law and theology as one of three academic disciplines training students for a career in administration, government, or politics. Its great value led it to be taught widely in cathedral schools, monastic schools, and later universities all over Europe. Medieval letters were not thought of as spontaneous expressions of thoughts and feelings but as the products of rigid convention, divided into fixed parts, with distinct forms of address for different hierarchical relationships, and it was these things that ars dictaminis taught. Letters were usually semipublic inasmuch as they were read to or shared with many, and they had to be carefully worded. Any letter produced in a chancery embodies an ideology, not just a request or command, and that ideology may be contained between the lines (134).

Medieval letters were commonly composed and collected for their stylistic value, with content of secondary importance; moreover, the format was adopted for other genres, such as polemics, and legal documents borrowed from epistolary form, making them the leading medium for administration and propaganda as well as communication (135).

The origins of the ars dictaminis has not been satisfactorily explained, and has mistakenly been sought with individuals or in discrete origins where a gradual evolution seems more likely (135–136). Nineteenth-century scholars identified Alberic of Monte Cassino as its inventor. After some falsely claimed that his works were concerned with general matters of composition and rhetoric, not with letters so much (136–138), Schmale in the mid-twentieth century advanced a rival candidate, Albert Samaritani; but Schmale placed too much emphasis on this one individual as the source of the whole tradition (138), while Alberic still has many defenders (138–139).

Patt now asserts that “the ars dictaminis arose out of a Europe-wide school tradition which had been undergoing a centuries-long process of development”; this development took place simultaneously in at least Italy, France, and Germany (139). Albert Samaritani had two contemporaries who taught Latin composition and letter-writing: Henry Francigena wrote a manual (Aurea gemma) in Pavia shortly after Albert’s, and its warning against rivals suggests many dictatores taught ars dictaminis at this time, and he claims to have incorporated in his manual the ideas of others (139–140). Similarly, Hugh of Bologna wrote a manual about the same time, and he mentions two of his rivals by name, one of which is Albert Samaritani; he too claims to have drawn on many sources (140–141). (Patt is certain both Henry and Hugh also taught ars dictaminis.) Even if warnings against rivals and references to sources are topoi, such topoi only make sense in a school context (141). As for culling from other sources, dictaminal florilegia are attested (142–143). And Henry Francigena attributes a rule of salutatio (that the higher ranking person be named first) to a teacher of his, as well as referring more generally to teachers, suggesting that the tradition predates him by a generation (143). Albert Samaritani likewise makes clear that he was working in a tradition that had been active for some time, even mentioning Alberic of Monte Cassino by name (143–144). Moreover, Alberic, Albert, Hugh, and Henry’s teachings have a great deal in common; and southern German writers were already composing according to the same rules, while in Italy Peter Damiani followed the same rules half a century before they materialize in the manuals, Anselm of Besate wrote a lost rhetorical treatis, and the Frenchman Hildebert of LeMans shows a knowledge of dictaminal rules a few decades before the manuals appear (144–146). Fragments of two dictaminal manuals predate Albert’s Precepta dictaminum (146).

Alberic’s instructions were for a stylized, rhetorical prose; after his day, the tradition became more practical (146–147).

The tradition of ars dictaminis arose out of the classical and early medieval epistolary tradition and out of the study of grammar, literature, law, and rhetoric. Letter-books and formularies were used before any theoretical manuals were written, and they continued to be so used long after (148–149). Dictaminal manuals incorporate grammar teaching, suggesting grammar as another source of influence, and Paul the Camaldolite wrote both a grammar and a dictaminal treatise. Similar connections can be made with poetry (149–151), while the connections with law and rhetoric are obvious (151–153).

author: Kennedy, George
title: ‘Truth’ and ‘Rhetoric’ in the Pauline Epistles
publication: The Bible as Rhetoric: Studies in Biblical Persuasion and Credibility
abstract:
Not a useful essay: seems preoccupied with a particular semiotic paradigma and the need to liberate Christian apologism from it, but says little that could be of any use to my students.

Identifies a trend in semiotics that views communication as a closed loop of signifiers that never reaches extralinguistic reality, and since such linguistic codes are cultural artefacts we cannot expect fully to understand the linguistic codes of other cultures; this makes it difficult to claim that the New Testament is in some way addressed to postmodern Christians (195). Kennedy asserts unconvincingly that the energy set free by the search for meaning constitutes rhetoric (105–196). Religious rhetoric attempts to break free from the chain of language and reach truth (196–197).
