Romans 1 contains an argument from nature (the wicked know about God because he is evident in creation) but lacks support by argument or example and could indeed be countered by claiming the superiority of e.g. animism (cf. 198). The same chapter rejects the rhetoric of others and validates its own reasoning only by nature and history, but these validations are only valid within Paul’s own perspective (198–199). He considers the law an embodiment of history and truth (199). Kennedy goes on to cite some passages in this epistle and in others that lay claim to truth through prophecy and divine promises (199–201). Doesn’t come to much of a conclusion.

author: Porter, Stanley A., and Sean A. Adams
title: Pauline Epistolography: An Introduction
publication: Paul and the Ancient Letter Form
eds: Stanley A. Porter and Sean A. Adams
abstract: Observes that although there is a school of researchers analyzing the Pauline epistles in terms of classical rhetoric, this volume is not it; instead, the essays in this volume follow a tradition of Pauline epistological analysis, ask whether Pauline letters are composed of three, four, or five constituent parts, and study these constituent parts.

author: Adams, Sean A.
title: Paul’s Letter Opening and Greek Epistolography: A Matter of Relationship
publication: Paul and the Ancient Letter Form
eds: Stanley A. Porter and Sean A. Adams
abstract: Discusses Saint Paul’s salutations and openings against the background of Greek epistolography.

author: Gretzinger, Joscha, et al.
title: The Anglo-Saxon Migration and the Formation of the Early English Gene Pool
abstract:
An important study effectively refuting the recent assumption that
the gene pool of England has remained comparatively stable through the
supposed migration events. That assumption had been based on the
analysis of present-day DNA, which cannot account for genetic drift;
this study analyzes ancient skeletal DNA from a range of sites in
England and on the Continent, and overlays those data onto present-day
genomes to conclude English DNA from the period 450–850 [i.e. after the
start of the migration but before Viking settlement if we go by
historical records, though the authors generally rely on archaeological
not written reference data] corresponds primarily to Continental DNA,
with an especially strong match in material from Lower Saxony. The
article contains several further findings, such as a lack of evidence
for strong sex differentiation (in other words, data are consistent with
men and women having migrated in equal proportions); evidence for the
gradual influx of DNA matched in Iron Age France; and in at least one
case, multigenerational evidence of social integration between
exclusively “Western British and Irish” and Continental northern
European genomes where grave goods offer further insights.

author: Shiels, Ian
title: Wulf and Eadwacer Reloaded: John of Antioch and the Starving Wife of Odoacer
abstract: Adduces a Greek historiographical source to argue that _Wulf and Eadwacer_ reflects the perspective of Theoderic’s (= Wulf’s) lover when she is Eadwacer’s wife under duress and starvation during the siege of Ravenna whose landscape is reflected by the islands in the poem. The “welp” reflects Odoacer’s son, whom Theoderic received as a hostage and killed.

author: Battles, Paul
title: Using N-gram Analysis to Map Intertextual Networks in Old English Verse
abstract: A rigorously executed study demonstrating that the poems of Cynewulf cluster closely together, and arguing that a few poems that cluster a little around it constitute a Cynewulfian sociolect. Relying on a lemmatized ASPR corpus, Battles employs log likelihood alongside a measure of inverse frequency, which accounts for the length of an n-gram as well as the length of each poem in a comparison between two documents, and sets a threshold for what counts as a meaningful n-gram. Using this threshold, he is able to tally matches between poems and generate a network analysis to gauge closeness of phrasal expression.

author: Cichosz, Anna, and Piotr Pęzik
title: Markers of Ælfric’s Style
abstract: Despite a number of inaccuracies and methodological issues, this article is well informed on the whole and a good model for an explainable AI-based identification of authorial markers of style in Old English.

author: Neidorf, Leonard, and Madison S. Krieger and Michelle Yakubek and Pramit Chaudhiri and Joseph P. Dexter
title: Large-Scale Quantitative Profiling of the Old English Verse Tradition
abstract:
Claims to be able to overcome the paucity problem in authorship profiling of Old English verse by combining multiple small-scale features, such as functional character n-grams (i.e. morphemes), metre, and pauses. Their main findings are (1) the unity or Beowulf, or lack of evidence against such unity (but now see Plecháč et al. 2021) and Cynewulf having authored Andreas.

The authors extracted frequency rates for the five most common functional character n-grams of each Old English verse text and subtract from each of these frequency scores the corpus-wide frequency of that same n-gram. They observe that three longer texts have scores outside the general cluster: Widsith presumably due to its high concentration of proper names; Widsith II allegedly because it draws on archaic oral phonology; and Psalm 118 due to its “aberrant metrics and late prosaic vocabulary”; in short, the usual “homogeneity [of Old English verse] was disturbed when a particular literary agenda strongly influenced a poet’s diction or source use.”

To settle the question of Beowulf authorship, the authors settle on features of “sense-pauses” (inferred from the editorial punctuation, excluding commas, of two editions, but allegedly largely fixed by way of Kuhn’s laws); Sievers type; and hapax nominal compounds All features show Beowulf as highly homogeneous, whereas Genesis shows its fault lines clearly. Andreas, meanwhile, shows a similar rate of hapax compounds as Cynewulf’s signed poems, while sharing with them a significant rate of non-hapax compounds; character n-gram analysis shows the same pattern.

Code is here.

author: Plecháč, Petr, Andrew Cooper, Benjamin Nagy, and Artjoms Šeļa
title: Beowulf Single-Authorship Claim Is Unsupported
abstract: Finds fault with every measure employed in Neidorf et al., and in fact finds substantial heterogeneity within Beowulf on all counts. Code here.

author: Stokes, Peter A.
title: Recovering Anglo-Saxon Erasures: Some Questions, Tools, and Techniques
publication: Palimpsests and the Literary Imagination of Medieval England: Collected Essays
eds: Leo M. Carruthers, Raeleen Chai-Elsholz, and Tatjana Silec
abstract: Describes methods for bringing out difficult manuscript readings, and introduces a Java application combining the image manipulation steps involved.

author: Gräslund, Bo
title: Beowulf: The Scandinavian Background: A Summary
publication: Re-Imagining Periphery: Archaeology and Text in Northern Europe from Iron Age to Viking and Early Medieval Periods
abstract: Summarizes in English Gräslund’s Beowulfkvädet, a work rolling back a great number of long-standing basic assumptions about Beowulf, along with modern ideas about how to approach the text. While each of its claims is worth investigating in detail, the work’s own assumptions (“a clear core of pagan elements”; the assumption that the vague geographical references can be mapped onto the real world) are so outmoded as to merit a skeptical attitude on the part of the reader. Not recommended for student reading unless to elicit debate.

author: Earl, James W.
title: The Swedish Wars in Beowulf
publication: Journal of English and Germanic Philology
abstract: Eloquently sums up the problems with the Swedish wars material and the answers provided by scholars, without resolving them into a unified solution.

author: Frank, Roberta
title: The Etiquette of Early Northern Verse
abstract: Discusses a range of ornamental or otherwise nonmandatory poetic devices in dróttkvætt and Old English verse. A good follow-up read for anyone who enjoyed an introduction to Germanic verse such as Terasawa’s.

author: Kiernan, Kevin S.
title: The Eleventh-Century Origin of Beowulf and the Beowulf Manuscript
abstract: The 1981 Colin Chase/Toronto volume on the dating of Beowulf opens with this explosive codicological account. Alleging that the manuscript has hitherto not been properly studied because it was assumed to be a late copy of an early text, while facsimiles up to this time only made things worse for what they excluded, Kiernan focuses on the second-last quire in particular. This gathering contains a full palimpsest folio (179 in MS foliation; 182 in BL foliation), and it is also the quire where the two scribes meet. Furthermore, both scribes have squeezed in extra lines and/or line width (scribe A in the preceding quire by ruling it for two extra lines, scribe B in this quire, fitting a twenty-first line in by ignoring the twenty-line ruling, but also by extending lines beyond the ruled text-block) as though working with limited space, which would not make sense if the quires had been written consecutively. Finally, the quire concerns Beowulf’s homecoming, an awkward connecting section between the Danish and the Swedish material. Kiernan concludes that the scribes had collaborated to connect their two texts, and accordingly that Vitellius A. xv is a draft and archetype of Beowulf as we know it, in other words that the poem dates from the period after 1016 when the glorification of the Scyldings would no longer have been awkward and yet neither was the Christian messaging. The omitted fitt number independently confirms this hypothesis if we understand that the revision was not to squeeze in more text, but rather to shorten it, as the manuscript contains no fitt number XXIIII but it does have XXV and onwards, up to and including XLIII. Kiernan points out that the evidence from the numbering suggests that the fitt numbers are contemporaneous with the manuscript (neither scribe had them in his exemplar), but also, “[i]f it was his practice to number the fitts as soon as he finished a gathering, the first scribe could have mechanically copied the fitt numbers he had supplied for his first copy when he transcribed the revision. To this extent the fitt numbers enhance the possibility, first suggested by the anomalous rulings, that folios 163–170 contain part of a late revision of Beowulf” (Kindle location 552).

author: Boyle, Leonard E.
title: The Nowell Codex and the Poem of Beowulf
abstract: This second codicological study in The Dating of Beowulf makes a series of ingenuous inferences and deductions, some of which however differ meaningfully from the conclusions Kiernan bases on the same observations. Both agree that the variation in lines written may be explained by the scribes’ need to line up their texts with what follows, but Boyle involves the collation and line rulings of the exemplar in his calculations. He concludes that the exemplar had eight-folio gatherings ruled for twenty lines, a pattern scribe A sought to emulate but which he had to abandon to line up with the quires already completed by scribe B, who in turn had written Judith before writing the end of Beowulf and had to squeeze in extra lines to make it fit. Both distributed their extra lines in such a way that they matched across openings. Boyle differs from Kiernan in assuming that not the Nowell Codex but its exemplar deserves special status as “perhaps even the original or an apograph in a separate codex” (Kindle Location 753), whereas the Nowell Beowulf is “[a]t best […] a copy […] of an existing text, perhaps contemporary, perhaps not” (Kindle Location 760). He goes on to conclude on the basis of damage that the quires produced by A and B remained separate for a long time, which helps explain fitt confusion. Boyle also infers that neither scribe A nor the exemplar was anywhere near when the text of fol. 182 was reconstructed, though he imputes this to accidental water damage as opposed to Kiernan’s deliberate palimpsesting.

author: Cameron, Angus, Ashley Crandell Amos, and Gregory White, with the assistance of Sharon Butler and Antonette diPaolo Healey
title: A Reconsideration of the Language of Beowulf
abstract: In this third entry in the 1981 Toronto volume on the dating of Beowulf, the DOE team present lists of forms from the poem sorted where available by Campbell and Mitchell’s (pre-Syntax) grammatical and syntactic taxonomies, under the headings of orthography, morphology, syntax, and vocabulary. It is a valuable list of forms for further study, but it offers no conclusions given that no statistics are generated for any other part of the corpus so as to allow comparison. A worthwhile source of data for future NLP work.

author: Cable, Thomas
title: Metrical Style as Evidence for the Date of Beowulf
abstract: Counts the combined proportion of C, D, and E verse types in a range of short poems and a sample of longer ones, observes that this proportion decreases over time, but concludes that Beowulf, Exodus, and Judith differ rather in craftsmanship than in chronological development from the chronological middle, so that the majority of poems, including Beowulf and Exodus, may well date to the ninth century. Acknowledges that short poems (Cædmon’s Hymn, Bede’s Death Song, Leiden Riddle) are too short to yield reliable statistics, but includes them even so.

author: Goffart, Walter
title: Hetware and Hugas: Datable Anachronisms in Beowulf
abstract: Argues that Beowulf derives the reference to the Hetware to the Liber historiae francorum, whose completion in 727 then is a terminus a quo [though Goffart places it first after Bede’s death and then in “the latter half of the eighth century”]; the reference to the Hugas is only plausible as a collective reference to Neustrian Franks after the death of Hugh the Abbot in 866 [here Goffart puts the terminus a quo “near the year 923, when Hugh the Great took charge of his Neustrian patrimony” (Kindle Location 2846).

author: Murray, Alexander Callander
title: Beowulf, The Danish Invasions, and Royal Genealogy
abstract: Since the genealogical elements shared between Beowulf, Aethelweard, and the Royal genealogies show signs of having been invented in the late ninth century, and the disagreement between Aethelweard and Beowulf on whether Sceaf or Scyld was the foundling king likely derives from a genealogy with ambiguous backreference as a shared source, we must conclude that the prologue is late ninth or early tenth century, and if we are unwilling to accept a composite poem then so is the remainder of Beowulf.

author: Page, R. I.
title: The Audience of Beowulf and the Vikings
abstract:
Counters Dorothy Whitelock’s oft-cited claim that Beowulf must predate 835 because it takes a sympathetic view of the Danish (and because she understood the post-1016 Danish hegemony as postdating the manuscript). The focus of his argument is on Athelstan, who is said to have fostered Hákon Haraldsson and is generally shown in high medieval sources to have been “on good terms with the leading power in Norway” even as he fought off Scots and Irish Norsemen in the battle of Brunanburh. (Page also adduces Egils saga but chooses his words on this dubious source more carefully.) Page goes on to argue that Scandinavians were rarely disparaged using ethnic (“racial”) terms but rather as heathens; and Alfred had such pagan Scandinavians as Ohthere at his court and seems to have treated them well enough, nor does Wulfstan’s travel report condemn the religion of the Baltic peoples at all. Alfred was also open to negotiations with heathen Scandinavians. In the tenth century, the distinction between English and Danish would have lessened.

Page stops short of dating the poem; he merely counters Whitelock’s position, arguing that at any time there would have been places and networks that could have given rise to a poem that speaks favourably of Danes.

author: Frank, Roberta
title: Skaldic Verse and the Date of Beowulf
abstract:
Gathers a range of worthwhile considerations stemming from the skaldic chronology to argue that a tenth-century origin is likely.

The absence of Scandinavianisms in the poem tells us nothing, as many late poems share this characteristic; the reliance on English names likewise means nothing, as names were routinely translated in both directions. Frank instead proposes to look for stylistic anachronism and finds it in a range of features shared with skaldic verse, all the while acknowledging the various uncertainties associated with the skaldic corpus. She starts with references to gautar, which are widespread in tenth-century skaldic verse. Scyldings, meanwhile, are not mentioned until c. 965 (Eyvindr skáldaspillr), while the first mention of a royal residence on Zealand is from c. 1062. Twelfth-century sources think of skjǫldingr as a poetic term for king, but the early eleventh century reserved the term for Cnut, Olaf Haraldsson, and Magnus góði, even mirrorring Old English þēodscyldingas in þjróðskjoldingar (?? sic); and Cnut’s skalds emphasize the continuity of the line. The Old English Orosius places the ancestors of the Angles in Jutland, whereas Ptolemy had placed them in Germany. Æthelwulf’s regnal table is the first to include Scyld in the West Saxon genealogy, thus strengthening the West-Saxon claim to the Danelaw, and thus by the 890s, the Scyldings were understood as common ancestors to the English royal family and the Danish immigrants. Beowulf involves all three of the Kattegat peoples under Danish influence but avoids mention of Norway. The epithet þjóðkonungr/þēodcyning is used of a Vestfold king in Ynglingatal as in Beowulf, but not again in skaldic verse until 1014–1040, when it was exclusively used of Cnut, Olaf, and Magnus.

The dragon-fight is sometimes adduced as evidence of an old tradition, but the deeds of Sigurðr (including related concepts like Rhinegold, dragon-hearts, and Brynhildr) don’t appear in skaldic verse until the later tenth century. Likewise the pairing of Sigemund and Heremod appears in skaldic poetry of later tenth century, and in Hyndluljóð — though their Old English depiction is less favourable.

When Herebeald is killed by his brother Hæþcynn, the phrase used is that the latter “miste mercelses” (missed the target); missan plus genitive here is a Nordicism, in addition to the whole scene evoking Hǫðr and Baldr, a myth referred to in at least one tenth-century skaldic poem, and Æthelweard’s Chronicle makes clear that it was known in tenth-century England. Similarly, Beowulf verse 316 “mæl is me to feran” is metrically irregular but evokes skaldic verses like “mál er mér at ríða” (Helgakviða Hundingsbana II), and may be designed to evoke a Scandinavian colouring and perhaps the plot lines of Scandinavian narratives along with it. Along similar lines, postposed accusative singular masculine demonstratives in sequences like “eorðweard þone” evoke skaldic custom. The “combination of personal lament and public eulogy” at the end of Beowulf suggests the erfidrápa characteristic of tenth- and early eleventh-century skaldic verse. “Lofgeorn” is known from Old Norse lofgjarn, and there it does not have ambiguous but positive connotations. The heroic vocabulary is likewise similar: bencþelu evokes bekkþili, and both Beowulf and the skaldic tradition make mention of having to leave one’s shields and spears outside but bring in one’s mailcoat and helmet, and hanging them on the wall inside. The expression”hide one’s head” (Beowulf 446) is known from skaldic verse as hylja hǫfuð.

In short, “accepting that the poem came into existence between 890 and 950 solves far more problems than it poses,” as this could have it spring from an Anglo-Scandinavian culture, it would help explain the link with Blickling Homily 16, and it would explain the many verbal parallels with tenth-century skaldic verse, while it would avoid our having to assume legends like the Sigemund–Heremod connection remaind unchanged for centuries.

author: McTurk, R. W.
title: Variation in Beowulf and the Poetic Edda: An Experiment
abstract: The first essay in the Toronto Dating of Beowulf volume to underwhelm. McTurk compares in great detail the taxonomies of Old English and Eddic variation as laid out by earlier scholars, comparing each of Campbell’s ten types for Old English to Paetzl’s similarly fine-grained system for Eddic verse, but ultimately concludes that this analysis has nothing to say about the date of Beowulf. Although his finding of substantial overlap between the two systems may on its face be valuable in its own right, it is striking how often one of Campbell’s types has just a single counterpart in the Eddic corpus, denying through statistical insignificance what value the correspondences might otherwise have had. Whether the taxonomies by Campbell and Paetzl have any value in their own right will have to be judged by the reading of those works, as no such evidence arises from McTurk’s piece, nor does he explain a modest number of concepts he uses, such as that of pre-classical Old English verse.

author: Chase, Colin
title: Saints’ Lives, Royal Lives, and the Date of Beowulf
abstract: Identifies the intent of Beowulf, as the single most debated aspect of the poem in the twentieth century, its solution polarized between celebration and elegy. Chase proposes that the paradox of the poem’s celebration-but-not-romantization of the heroic tells on its time of composition, which may be traced in the development from early to late hagiography and biography. He cites Wormald’s notion [in Bede and Anglo-Saxon England (ed. Farrell) p. 36] of a zone of silence apparently between the social classes associated with Bede and Beowulf, but proposes to extend this zone along temporal lines. His argument is that early hagiography and biography is fearful of association with heroic culture, while later lives embrace it, so that not only is royal biography nonexistent until Asser, but also Bede avoids mention of feuding in his hagiography even where it is relevant, while Ælfric, using Bede as his source, brings it out, and a twelfth-century hagiographer is seen to take the same dynamic for granted. Chase generalizes from these [few] examples that Wormald’s polarized secular-vs-monastic eighth-century society had become integrated by the tenth and eleventh, resolving its contradictions and allowing heroic reference into religious narrative. The ninth century, however, shows a tension on this front that is most consistent with the tone of Beowulf. While acknowledging that we have no ninth-century hagiography, Chase suggests that royal biography fills the gap. The essay does not address the place of biblically inspired heroic verse like that in MS Junius 11.

author: Clemoes, Peter
title: Style as the Criterion for Dating the Composition of Beowulf
abstract: Claims that Beowulf differs from “most other Old English poems” in “the thought [being] indivisible from the wording.” Comparing Maxims I with a text by Wulfstan, he asserts that “[s]ynthetic, verbal conceptualizing in the Maxims has been replaced by analytic, verbalized categorizing in Episcopus,” and Beowulf should be placed at the early end of that chronology [or binary?]. Clemoes tries to specify this rather vague distinction with reference to word order being used in a “psychologically apt” way, contrasting with Cynewulf’s “consciously artful” style; metaphor being used in a way that “rarely emerges beyond the confines of the vocabulary,” meaning using conventional heiti like sweat for blood and the like, but no ship-kennings like in Andreas, Cynewulf, and Guthlac B. Narration in Beowulf is based out of participants in the action, as when the Danes hear Grendel’s cries of pain, but there is no invented observer as in Elene. A word like ellen has greater “integrity” in Beowulf than in later poetry, where it can be used to refer to concepts other than “fighting capability.” It is on grounds like these that Clemoes places Beowulf on a midway point between Cædmon and Cynewulf. By comparing the style of the datable Heliand (no ship-kennings) and skaldic verse (ship-kennings), he setlles on “the second half of the eighth century or early in the ninth.” He also notes that Hrothgar’s sermon employs the pairing of finite verbs otherwise found in early prose homilies and “probably not indigenous to Old English verse structure.” The notion of Grendel’s descent from Cain is reminiscent of Felix’s Vita Guthlaci, written by 749 and referring to demons as semen Cain. Beowulf’s mound by the sea matches burial practices of Mercian kings from 757 onwards. Any Norse influence thought to be visible in the poem would have existed by this time, witness Alcuin’s letter to Æthelred in which he complains of heathen fashions.

author: Pope, John C.
title: On the Date of the Composition of Beowulf
abstract:
After a series of specialized investigations into the date of Beowulf, Pope’s is the first of two in the volume providing a more general overview. His views are sometimes naive (accepting Whitelock’s objection against a date after 835; “[i]n all probability it was Alfred himself who versified his own prose translation of the Latin metres”), but that fits well into the essay’s overall quality of reflecting a classical view on the question. It is accessibly written except the various arguments it touches on are often assumed common knowledge: thus the two classical linguistic/metrical tests (weak adjectives and distribution of Sievers types) are not explained in any detail, even when Pope goes on to address apparent exceptions to these test’s success at offering a chronological test. Those exceptions are the form “heahan” in The Gloria I where a monosyllable would be expected on chronological but not metrical grounds (the solution to which is that dissyllabic forms of this word reoccur in Ælfric manuscripts and was thus reintroduced seemingly in the Benedictine Reform); and the Metres of Boethius vary in the syllable count of tung(o)l (the solution is that the poet follows metrical requirements); Genesis B (the scribe uses a circumflex apparently to indicate that the uncontracted form be reconstructed so as to make his verse more regular, as it was in the Old Saxon); and The Battle of Maldon’s unwillingness to yield to the Lichtenheld tests (weak adjective/definite article; but Maldon requires frequent use of the demonstrative due to the frequent reference to individuals and little need for descriptive adjectives).

Pope admits that it is primarily because he grew up with the culture of dating Beowulf early that he cannot rid himself of a conviction along those lines; he settles on “almost any time in the eighth century” but probably not the seventh, though he adds that he suspects a long space of time between composition and codification, so that perhaps “the oral poets of the seventh century were largely responsible for the growth of the style and the story.”

author: Stanley, E. G.
title: The Date of Beowulf: Some Doubts and No Conclusions
abstract: The second overview article in the Toronto Dating of “Beowulf” volume, Stanley’s contribution is playful and accessible, a good choice of text to introduce students to the considerations involved in dating the poetry, though they are not introduced to the point where they are all clear to learners. Whereas Pope sticks to his early date in spite of everything, Stanley allows his natural inclination to give way to a later date using Sisam’s observation that the period typically called early for verse has yielded very little prose; thus by redefining the reign of Alfred as early for verse as well as prose, Stanley sees himself forced to “assign most of the verse [including] Beowulf to the period after the early ninth century.” For dialect he has little to go on, but he rules out Kent; for the manuscript he mentions the possibility of London, citing Sisam.

author: Bolton, W. F.
title: Alcuin and “Beowulf”: An Eighth-Century View
abstract:
Answers the question “what would a Christian scholar like Alcuin have made of Beowulf?”

The first two chapters of the work barely touch on Beowulf at all, instead demonstrating Alcuin’s understanding of style and rhetoric. The second chapter includes two brief but interesting points on Beowulf: that it consists of 42 fitts, corresponding to one of Alcuin’s numerogically favoured values (six times seven, i.e. the number of perfection multiplied with the divine number, 75), and that Alcuin in his polemics against Felix refers to him at one point as infelix and in another place uses the adverb infelice with reference to his writings, which bears comparison with Beowulf 105 “wonsæli wer” (83).

The remaining two chapters then propose how someone like Alcuin would have interpreted the Danish and Swedish material, respectively. Key to this analysis is the recognition that Alcuin admitted multiple allegorical readings simultaneously, in bono alongside in malo readings, permitting a Christian interpretation that does not necessitate a single sustained allegory all through the narrative. Headings include “Historical Perspective” (references to Frisians, Franks, Vikings; Alcuin’s correspondence with Offa II); “Heorot” (Alcuin’s description of the cathedral at York; his words on Jerusalem; his familiarity with the female cup-bearer; his tirades against drinking and the gathering of treasure); “Unferþ and Grendel” (Unferth supposedly matching the behaviour Alcuin warns against, and his characterization of Jews and Adoptionist heretics; the gifstol passage anagogically meaning that Grendel cannot find favour with God and will not know his love, while the severing of limb and then head from body may be read alongside Alcuin’s words on limbs and the like); “Hroþgar’s Sermon” (the warning of Heremod resembling Alcuin’s of Roboam and Æthelred); “Literary Perspective” (the tripartite systems of the soul [concupiscent, rational, irascible], thought-word-deed, delectation-consent-deed, and the Trinity, often coordinated in some way); “King Beowulf” (the “Old Law” broken by Beowulf according to lines 2324–2332 being either the Old Testament or Natural Law); “Divine Knowledge and Human Virtue” (serial time; the efficacy of the named swords; virtuous pagans and the via regia). Throughout, Bolton draws heavily on Alcuin’s commentary on Ecclesiastes. Towards the end, there is a heavy focus on quanto magis-argumentation: if a heathen like Beowulf could be so virtuous, how much more virtuous ought we Christians to be!

author: Frank, Roberta
title: Three Cups and a Funeral in Beowulf
publication: Latin Learning and English Lore: Studies in Anglo-Saxon Literature for Michael Lapidge
eds: Katherine O’Brien O’Keeffe and Andy Orchard
abstract:
Opens by adducing a variety of evidence of the historical value of precious cups as positional goods, i.e. status objects with political functions (407–408). The cups Wiglaf finds among the dragon’s hoard in Beowulf are functionally uncharacteristic inasmuch as they lie dormant, not lending anyone status. They are referred to using the terms orc and bune, vocabulary not matching the cuppe, fæt, calic, and drenchorn of tenth-century wills, and not found in Ælfric’s glossary; they are the only objects described in Beowulf as heathen (408–409).

Scholars have pointed out that Old English poetry does not differentiate between local customs (Whitelock), and that the dragon hoard reflects the same culture described in the rest of the poem, both of which archaic when the tenth-century scribes were at work (Leslie; 409). Frank objects that the terms bune, orc, and wǣge (the last used for the stolen cup) seem to have an air of antiquity not shared by the words found in tenth-century wills (409–410).

  • Bune occurs only in poetry (5x) and glosses (3x), three times in the Beowulf manuscript, including at Holofernes’s party in Judith; the other occurrences are Maxims I and The Wanderer. All these poetic uses are consistent with the depiction of a bygone age. The glosses are all for carchesium, often a sacrificial vessel and thus carrying similar overtones (410–411).
  • Orc occurs in prose (3x) as well as verse (3x) and glosses/glossaries (5x). Four occurrences in the Beowulf manuscript, including Judith and Saint Cristopher, both of which set it in heathen and “hellbent” contexts. Translations and glosses render cratera (sacrificial vessels in the prose Exodus), the harlot’s calix in Revelation, and the sacrificial simpuvium in Prudentius. Orc thus clearly had pagan associations (411).
  • Wǣge as a simplex occurs in poetry (3x) and a single gloss; Beowulf contains four further compounds for its use in Heorot. Three compound occurrences in other texts use it figuratively as a dēaðwǣge “death cup” (Guthlac) or bǣdewǣg “inciting cup” (Bede; 411–412). Its qualification fǣted “(gold-)plated” is found in poetry (11x) and once in a legal text of Wulfstan’s in a way that “presumably sounded superannuated in a prose setting” (412–413, quotation at 412).

Frank rattles off a handful of prior interpretations of the meaning of the treasure’s reburial (413) before conjecturing that the mourners encircling the barrow may be a cliché inspired by Vergil (413–414). She then observes that the description of Hygelac’s death involves a kenning using _full in ȳþa ful “cup of the waves” as a base word for “sea” which, as in Vergil, creates an image less visual and more on a level of conscious awareness. Just as Aeneas turns away from Andromache and moves on towards his Roman destiny, so “[b]y handing the last words in the memorial service to twelve grieving Geats, the poem dramatizes its own relative modernity, its refusal to be dated” (414).

author: Shippey, Tom
title: “Beowulf” and the North before the Vikings
abstract:
If you read past the blustery strawmen portraying the entire field of Beowulf scholarship as refusing true connections in favour of coincidence, this volume contains some worthwhile insights. The book is a bold argument suggesting that Beowulf preserves an astonishingly detailed account of Scandinavian and ultimately English history c. 440–c. 550.

Shippey argues that scholars have been misled by Tolkien’s “Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics” to read all references to history as fairytale, whereas Tolkien himself was not serious in his lecture and has since, in his posthumous Finn and Hengest, laid out his own view on the history, introducing the ingenuous “Jutes on both sides”-reading of the Finnsburh material.

In fact, Beowulf touches on the material surrounding Hygelac, a historical figure whose death is datable by way of Gregory of Tours (writing before 594) and the anonymous Liber historiae francorum (c. 727) to c. 530. The latter source also confirms the Hetware as Attoarii; and the Anglo-Latin Liber monstrorum (contemporaneous with the LHF) places Hygelac’s corpse in the mouth of the Rhine. His nationality is variously given as Danish (the two Frankish sources) or Getus (Liber monstrorum), but the latter account is to be credited, as Danes were a catch-all while Geats were not (Shippey dismisses Gräslund’s Gotlandic theory on logistical grounds, identifying the geatas with the gautar of Götland instead).

Shippey observes that the fights account for under 30 percent of the poem; in other words, the focus is on the historical material, which also supplies many times more names than the action sequences, and real names rather than made-up ones.

The first chapter does a fine job of elucidating the “taking of mead-benches” imagery, explaining that it comes down to a usurpation of neighbouring territories and the claiming of their warriors’ loyalties. He draws on archaeology to point out that halls were often burned down with some evidence of ritual (the smashing of drinking vessels). Shippey departs from other readings by interpreting line 6 “eorl” as a reference to the Heruli who had the reputation of being particularly fierce. He dates Scyld’s reign to c. 400, not far removed from the sacking of Rome in 410 and possibly coinciding with the interregnum between Heremod and [Healfdene]. The collapse of Rome caused the collapse of trade, Danish amber losing its market and the newly ascendant Franks denying the Danes their valuables, as is indeed reflected in the archaeological record. The period 200–500 saw a great deal of warfare, which led to consolidation and state formation, followed by peace. Thus the action of Beowulf takes place after the creation of a Danish hegemony, itself resulting from a long period of the taking away of mead-benches.

Shippey opens his second chapter by summing up the state of Lejre archaeology: the site seems to have been continuously in use, with a hall of 45 metres built c. 500, replaced by two new halls in the seventh century, as well as three later halls. Several of these halls fit the description in Beowulf in terms of their superlative size. In his posthumously published notes on Beowulf, Tolkien developed a theory about Heorot’s significance as a site of Freyr fertility worship based on references to Ing and the name Freawaru, matching Thietmar of Merseburg’s reports of sacrifices taking place every ninth year, which in turn fits the heaps of burnt animal bones found at both Lejre hall sites, interpreted as sacrificial sites, but also the Beowulf poet’s report of pagan idol worship. Although the name Heorot is exclusive to English tradition while Lejre is exclusive to Danish tradition, Niles has pointed out the riverbed at Lejre called Hjorterende.

The Danish Lejre material refers to strife between a Halvdan and a Frothi, but the details vary greatly. Shippey presents the Beowulf account as clearer, but the corrupt line typically emended to “Hyrde ic þæt Yrsa wæs Onelan cwen” (62) seems to have been censored by a scribe for its implication of incest. By Tolkien’s theory, the Heathobeards were the original inhabitants of Zealand and thus Lejre, and related to the Lombards who moved to Italy; they became an enemy of the Danes when the Danes moved in from Skåne. The account in Beowulf has the strife culminate in the Danish king Healfdene killing Froda the Heathobeard. Hrothgar uses marriage ties to heal the old feud, but the character Beowulf predicts it will reignite. The reality is worse than his prediction: Froda’s son Ingeld will decide to avenge his father. Widsith too notes that Beards and Danes fought at Heorot; Beowulf specifies that the hall burns down after a confrontation between a father-in-law and a son-in-law, which we may interpret as Hrothgar and Ingeld. Shippey notes that there is no evidence as yet of a hall-burning at Lejre.

In between the first two monster episodes of Beowulf, Hrothgar’s wife Wealhtheow and his nephew Hrothulf (son of Halga by Hrothulf’s own sister Yrsa, and thus a full Scylding) play understated but important roles. The former assures Hrothgar that Hrothulf will respect his sons’ right to the throne, and the poet rather emphatically states that Hrothgar and Hrothulf were on good terms then. Saxo says Rolvo (i.e. Hrothulf) kills Røricus (Hrethric, Hrothgar’s son and successor, whose nickname hnøggvanbaugi “ring-stingy” may help fill in the gaps). Hrothgar’s other son, Heorogar, is dead in the narrative time of Beowulf, but he leaves a son Heoroweard, known in the Scandinavian tradition as Hjǫrvarðr, who kills Hrólfr. Thus if we read the traditions in conjunction, three of Healfdene’s four grandsons kill each other, potentially leaving Hrothmund: (1) Hrólfr/Hrothulf kills Hrœrekr/Hrethric; (2) Hjǫrvarðr/Heoroweard kills Hrólfr/Hrothulf; (3) on the same day, Hrólfr’s last retainer kills Hjǫrvarðr/Heoroweard. Shippey points out that the name element Heoro- was not used in England, but an inscription of c. 600 from Sweden records one, so at any rate the poet did not make up the names; they must go back to tradition. He also suggests that Beowulf’s offer of hosting Hrethric in Geatland might be a veiled warning that Hrothgar’s successor ought to be brought to safety.

Shippey opens chapter three by summing up the Geatish and Swedish dynasties according to Beowulf. Hrethel heads the Geats; Beowulf is his unnamed daughter’s son, while Hrethel’s own sons are Herebeald, Hæthcyn, and Hygelac, the last of whom has a son Heardred. The Swedish patriarch is Ongentheow, with sons Onela and Ohthere, which last is father to Eanmund and Eadgils. Of these men, Hæthcyn kills his brother Herebeald in a hunting accident, causing the death by grief of their father Hrethel. In a first war, Ongentheow kills Hæthcyn but is himself killed by Hygelac. Hygelac is killed raiding in the Netherlands; when Beowulf refuses the crown, it passes to Hygelac’s son Heardred. Onela now rules the Swedes, but his nephews Eanmund and Eadgils have switched sides and receive Heardred’s support. In a second war, Onela kills Eanmund and Heardred. Beowulf succeeds Heardred and avenges him by killing Onela in a third war, in the battle of Lake Väner. Eadgils succeeds Onela, Beowulf dies fighting the dragon, and the expectation is that the Geats will now be overrun by the Swedes.

Historically, there is little evidence of a Geatish dynasty; only Hygelac is externally confirmed, and of him Scandinavian sources know little (or conflict with what we think we know). The Swedish names are better attested, as is the battle of Lake Väner, with some differences in details. The home of the Scylfing dynasty is not easily located. Hrólfs saga kraka tells how the Danish Hrólfr humiliates the Swedish king Athils in Uppsala, but it makes Yrsa Athils’s wife whereas Beowulf makes her Onela’s, i.e. Athils’s father’s wife. But there is ample evidence of sons marrying their fathers’ widows. Shippey emphasizes that the Beowulf poet interconnects all these dynasties without contradicting himself.

Complications arise when Beowulf goes on a tangent about Wiglaf’s sword, which was Eanmund’s until Eanmund was killed by Wiglaf’s father Weohstan in the same battle that killed Heardred. But that suggests Weohstan and Beowulf were on opposing sides. Since Wiglaf is called both a Scylfing (i.e. Swede) and a Wægmunding (i.e. related to Beowulf), in fact, Beowulf’s father Ecgtheow must be Swedish as well, having gone over to the Geats and thus explaining why his name doesn’t fit the dynasty. Scandinavian sources have a Vésteinn fighing on the side of the Swedish at Väner; if this is our Weohstan, we have him fighting first for the Geats, then for the Swedes, and then his son Wiglaf returns to serve the Geats. Shippey concludes that the poet must have added these complicated details because he assumed they were common knowledge, i.e. they were historical. He adds that the seemingly random survival of external confirmation for the characters of Beowulf fits the odds of historical survival (or the poet having reason to believe they were historical) better than it does these individuals having been invented.

Shippey [following Tolkien] now sets out the the sequence of events, though without following Tolkien in mapping them onto a detailed chronology. He dismisses the fifty-year rule as fiction, asserting instead that Ongentheow must have been succeeded immediately by one of his sons, i.e. Ohthere or Onela. If it was Ohthere and then in turn Onela, that would explain the rebellion of Ohthere’s sons Eanmund and Eadgils. Since these approached Heardred, this must have been after Hygelac’s death, leaving the Geats weak, explaining Onela’s success at killing both Heardred and Eanmund. The tradition considers Eadgils a contemporary of Hrothulf, who conquers Denmark around the time of Hygelac’s death. Tolkien draws attention to Hrothgar’s policy of appeasement, sending gifts and intermarrying. The problem of Beowulf visiting Hrothgar whose niece and one-time daughter-in-law was married to Onela, who was in feud with Hygelac over the death of his father Ongentheow, is explained by Tolkien by the fact that Hygelac is young at this time, and Ohthere not Onela governs the Swedes; in other words, Onela is not yet of great importance at this time and was not first in line for the throne. Tolkien puts all this down to excellent timing on the part of the poet. If we elide the fifty-year reign, the Swedish wars would have taken place early in the sixth century.

This is where Shippey connects the chronology up with the Migration Period and the natural disasters that have been associated with it. Archaeology shows an economic low across Scandinavia starting around 540, evidenced by settlement abandonment, a shrinking population, and a dearth in grave goods. This coincides with significant volcanic eruptions in 535, 539/540 (or 431), and 547. Historical references mention a dust-veil that is thought to have blocked out the sun for years; half the Scandinavian population may have died of hunger. (Bo Gräslund connects the sequence of events with the concept of fimbulvetr.) Beowulf mentions no such thing, but it accords well with the conflict expected to have resulted from these conditions. Archaeological studies of Östra Götaland suggest discontinuity in the mid-sixth century.

Although the Beowulf poet is generally understood to be English, Christian, and literate, he never mentions written culture beyond carving, he never mentions Christ or uses words that reference Christian salvation, and he never mentions the English or Britain. But he does mention an Offa (the Continental Angle, not the seventh-century Mercian king). Above all, the poet is very interested in the Jutes, and he mentions Hengest. In the Finnsburh material, Hengest breaks his oath to Finn, and the Beowulf poet asserts that Hildeburh had no need to praise the good faith of the Jutes. If this Hengest is the same as the legendary founder of Kent, he was himself a Jute. Tolkien solves the Finnsburh problem by positing that there were Jutes on both sides of the conflict: Hnæf was a Scylding, but most of his men were Jutes. The Danes had begun their conquest of Jutland, resulting in “Half-Danes” either ethnically or by surrender of Jutes to Danes. At Finn’s court, on the other hand, there are “free Jutes” in exile. This may also explain the exchange in the fragment about who is defending the door: Garulf may be worried he is up against his own father Guthlaf (although Tolkien posited that Garulf was Guthwulf’s son and thus the last remaining contender to the Jutish throne).

Shippey understands Hygelac’s attack on the Hetware as naturally involving Franks (Hugas) given that the former lived on the border of the Frankish empire and would have required Frankish aid to combat the invaders; but the more northern borders of modern Frisia seem to throw Shippey off their relevance [in fact a people referred to as Frisian bordered on the Franks around the Rhine, whatever the linguistic implications and modern borders]. So he assumes the Frisians were simply foremost in English minds. More importantly, Shippey makes the somewhat overstated point that the poet appears better informed about the Franks than modern historians are, as it is the only source to use a form of “Merovingians” correctly derived from the reconstructed *Merowech. From this Shippey concludes that the Merovingians were still in power when the poem was composed. Equally remarkable is the name Dæghrefn, an element-by-element translation of what is recognizably a Frankish name.

When the Messenger foretells that the Frankish favour will be withdrawn, this can be interpreted economically to say that the import of Frankish prestige goods will come to a halt, rendering the continued existence of a prestige economy with warlords and retainers impossible. Archaeology shows that prestige goods were the main import from Francia, and its flow all but ceased in the mid-sixth century. Hygelac’s raid might even have been a response to the cessation of trade.

The fourth and final chapter attempts to explain the link with England. Shippey brushes off the idea that the poem might serve to propagandize a tenth-century Anglo-Danish union, or that Offa of Mercia might play any role. Hengest is more promising; Shippey argues that the West Germanic sense “gelding” is less likely as a personal name than the North Germanic sense of hestr “stallion.” The Finnsburh fragment and episode both foreground Hengest as a leader. In Nennius, the legendary founder Hengest betrays his hosts by ordering his men to draw their hidden short swords (saxas). But Kent is supposedly a Jutish kingdom, while the Finnsburh Hengest fights against the Jutes. Tolkien’s theory of Jutes on both sides resolves this problem. If we follow it through, Hengest could hardly have returned to Denmark in triumph, as in Tolkien’s version he was to blame for the death of the last free-Jutish prince, while the Half-Danes might have disliked his delayed and half-hearted vengeance for Hnæf. Significantly, he had made (and then betrayed) a deal with the killer of his lord. So it stands to reason that Hengest would have become a mercenary adventurer (to put a positive spin on “exile”). Shippey points out that Nennius’s account of Hengest’s betrayal of Vortigern resembles that of Finn in the manner of a modus operandi.

Hrothmund son of Hrothgar has left no trace in Scandinavian tradition, and the name occurs only once more in early English records, in the genealogy of King Ælfwald of East Anglia (c. 713–c. 749). This genealogy follows the Gospel of Matthew in giving fourteen generations, which makes its suspicious. Even so, Hrothmund is listed four generations after Woden and nine before Ælfwald. Counting in twenty-year reigns, that puts Hrothmund around 533, close in time to Hygelac’s raid and Hrothulf’s potential takeover. Moreover, about midway between Hrothmund and Ælfwald we find Wuffa, founder of the East Anglian dynasty, the Wuffingas, according to Bede, who would then have lived in the early seventh century. Wuffa is almost certainly an apocoristic form of a Wulf-compound, which could make him one of the Wulfingas mentioned in Beowulf and Widsith. The latter calls Helm a leader of the Wulfingas, and Beowulf calls Wealhtheow ides Helminga. There are Helminghams only in Norfolk and Suffolk, the latter close to Sutton Hoo and the royal centre of Rendlesham. And so perhaps Wealhtheow is a Wulfing, connecting the seventh-century East Anglian dynasty with the sixth-century Danish court. Objects found at Sutton Hoo have their closest matches in Sweden (being the centre of wealth for Scandinavia — or so Shippey argues to explain why it is not Danish sites that turn up close connections).

Shippey points out that Beowulf’s use of the word mōr to mean “waste marshland” rather than “waste upland” ties it to the lowlands of Suffolk rather than moor areas. He also adduces Bede’s geographical reference Ingetlingum in Yorkshire as a possible connection with the geat- root. Moorman identified Riddlesden and Rillington as place names preserving the names Hrethel and Hrethling. The Northumbrian Liber vitae, a list of benefactors of a Durham church, though omitted from PASE records not just a Biuuulf but also “four Hygelacs, eight Herebealds, and eleven Heardreds, as well as sixteen Ingelds” — and these are all rare names elsewhere.

Shippey thus proposes that those who lost out in the dynastic conflict of Beowulf emigrated to England: Hengest the Jute to Kent, Hrothmund the Dane to East Anglia, the Geats to North Yorkshire, all c. 440–c. 550. Finally, he connects these events with Arthurian material as follows. Gildas mentions the dust veil of 536 but not the subsequent famine, so he was likely writing in 536, which confirms Bede’s date of 493 for the siege of Mount Badon. Arthur was probably a successful cattle raider during the post-536 famine.

The sudden shift from Celtic to Germanic culture in England can be explained by other means than mass migration and genocide: as Härke has suggested, it just needs a mass migration of “Germanic life-style advisers.” But there certainly was an exodus of Celtic speakers to Brittany, where Vulgar Latin was replaced wholesale. Also, North Germanic characteristics of Old English prior to the Viking Age (such as eom, eart, is) suggest strong North Germanic links of the first settlers (here is where Shippey refers back to the gelding/stallion isogloss). This all makes sense if the settlers straddled the North/West Germanic language boundary, with Jutes north of it; and the early English identification even by Alfred as englisc rather than Saxon implies a cultural hegemony on the part of the Angles. And so Beowulf is about Scandinavian history because Scandinavian history is English history too.

The arrival of the Vikings was such a shock precisely because earlier raids had stopped in the mid-sixth century, with the collapse of the Scandinavian economy.

author: North, Richard
title: Saxo and the Swedish Wars in Beowulf
publication: Saxo Grammaticus: Tra storiografia e letteratura
abstract:
Compares the various accounts of Hrólfr kraki’s relationship to Aðils, with some championing the Swedes and others the Danes, as an example of Saxo’s Danish patriotism.

There is a puzzling assertion in Beowulf line 3005 that its protagonist has “kept” [“geheold,” I’d personally associate it with rule rather than mere service, PSL] the “scildingas.” Though usually emended to “scildwigan” or the like, this could be read to mean Beowulf “took service with Hroðulf, Hrothgar’s successor” (185–186, quotation at 186). This fits well Beowulf’s absence from the conflict in which Onela attacks the Geats, killing King Heardred (previously in Beowulf’s guardianship) as well as Eanmund. But the Beowulf narrative lends plausibility to the possibility that Beowulf continued his dealings with the Danish court, even taking service with Hroðulf, but returned to avenge Heardred’s death “almost as if Hroðulf had sent him. This could be some of the meaning of geheold … hwate Scildingas” (186). “[B]y suppressing a Hroðulf–Beowulf relationship, [the Beowulf poet] would give Beowulf a dynastic status of his own. This is the only source in which the Beowulf-figure becomes a king; and in the battle with Onela . . . there is a total reversal of roles” reflecting the dynastic histories of seventh-century Northumbria and Mercia rather than Scandinavia (186–187). Between Saxo and Beowulf, the narrative reflects the perspective of the respective author (188).

author: Helder, William
title: The Song of Creation in Beowulf and the Interpretation of Heorot
abstract: An excellent introduction to the typological connections of those parts of the creation account relevant to Heorot, observing that one has to look beyond Genesis 1 to its commentary tradition to appreciate the richness of connotations. Although some of the connections made are weak (notably the attempt to explain sigehrēþig with reference to Exodus 12), the article is a good exercise in typological analysis, also for a student audience. Which is not to say it doesn’t breathe the air of its day; it’s a piece of armchair interpretation!

author: Neidorf, Leonard
title: Germanic Legend, Scribal Errors, and Cultural Change
abstract: Makes an impressive case for an early date based on datable Anglo-Latin sources, copying errors, and the distribution of personal names. Points out that confusion of <a> for <u> is most naturally explained with the open-top <a> that ceased to be used in the ninth century (38–39); that many personal names were garbled by the scribes, demonstrating that they were no longer known (39–41); that the Liber monstrorum (c. 650x750), the Vita sancti Guthlaci (c. 730x740), and Alcuin demonstrate a familiarity with the legendary material (41–44); that Widsith, which shares a tremendous share of names from the heroic tradition with Beowulf, is very likely “seventh or eighth century” on linguistic grounds (44–46), while the Franks Casket (c. 700) preserves an early, complex form of the Weland legend later forgotten (46–47); that only the old, seventh- to eighth-century core of the Liber vitae Dunelmensis contains names known from Beowulf, using elements not otherwise productive in Old English onomastics, and those in large numbers (47–49); that the royal genealogies incorporating names known from Beowulf date back to the early eighth century, while the Kentish genealogy may date back to the seventh but was known by Bede, while some of these names show archaic inflections (49–53).

author: Shippey, Tom
title: Names in Beowulf and Anglo-Saxon England
abstract: Argues points some of which Shippey also made in his 2007 article on the Merovingian, but which above all he repeated in his 2022 book, namely that the poet’s seemingly precise use of personal and dynastic names suggests a familiarity with the material that has since been lost, and thus that the material relayed, whether legendary or historical, had reached the poet in the eighth century through oral history. Between the correct form of the word for Merovingian and the matching names in the Durham Liber vitae, the evidence “[indicate] a date of original composition no later than the mid-eighth century” (75).

author: Clark, George
title: Scandals in Toronto: Kaluza’s Law and Transliteration Errors
abstract: Sets out to refute Roberta Frank’s “Scandal in Toronto” on two points. Whereas Frank had argued that verses of Kaluza type I may have been sprinkled through heroic sections of the poem with archaistic intent, Clark argues that their distribution is random and not associated with any specific subject matter, and that in fact a later poet could not have identified whether endings were etymologically long or short. Against Lapidge’s argument that confusion of such literals as <u> for <a> demonstrates that the manuscript exemplar must have been early, Frank had placed evidence from Cynewulf and the Exeter Book, but the confusion there seems to stem from the involvement of foreign scribes instead. Clark concludes that “the archetype of Beowulf was written before 750” (234).

author: Hartman, Megan E.
title: The Limits of Conservative Composition in Old English Poetry
abstract: Takes on the argument, attributed to Nicholas Jacobs and Roberta Frank, that the Beowulf poet may have affected an archaic verse form. Hartman chooses Judith and The Battle of Brunanburh as known late but formally conservative poems, in contrast with The Battle of Maldon as an example of late style. She starts with Cable’s distribution of Sievers types C, D, and E, as well as Russom’s modified version of the same test, and concludes that Beowulf is still more conservative than Judith and Brunanburh, which in turn are more conservative than Maldon; but Brunanburh has more type D verses even than Beowulf, which Hartman puts down to an effort to sound archaic. Looking more closely, trisyllabic simplex forms are more naturally accommodated in type E inasmuch as this can be done without rearranging word order, whereas compounds, often being nouns, do not require syntactic inversion to be used in type D; this is one of the examples Hartman uses to suggest the Brunanburh poet (with his or her heavy reliance on type D but rarely on inversion) gives the impression of conservatism but doesn’t match the finer details of a style like that of Beowulf. For Judith, that poem’s heavy reliance on hypermetric verses is cited as an example of the same pattern, though it is hardly made clear what makes its hypermetric verse fall short of conservative usage, other than the very occasional divergence from expected usage. Hartman then turns to diction, distinguishing between poetic simplexes, compounds confined to the poetry that contain at least one poetic term, and compounds consisting of common words (she further distinguishes “kennings” from descriptive compounds, but employs the term kenning with a particularly broad reference); here she notes that Judith and Brunanburh rely heavily on the third type, again giving the prosody and ring of early poetry without getting the details right, while the distribution of poetic simplexes tells a similar tale; Judith furthermore appears to include neologisms like hopian “hope.” The avoidance of archaic terms may well be intentional, as their usage might confuse audiences, but it would also have been difficult for oral poets to learn old words. The fact that the Beowulf poet manages a more archaic style suggests “that Beowulf is in fact a much earlier composition” (96).

author: Bredehoft, Thomas A.
title: The Date of Composition of Beowulf and the Evidence of Metrical Evolution
abstract:
Draws on Bredehoft’s Early English Metre to sum up a relative and in part absolute chronology of metrical developments based on the following features (in reverse chronological order):

  1. (a) allowing s and its clusters to alliterate more freely, while (b) differentiating between palatal and velar g;
  2. a cluster of developments including (a) final-stress alliteration, (b) lack of resolution, (c) [the abandonment of?] four-position feet, (d) verse rhyme substituting for alliteration;
  3. “influence from Old Saxon” (lexical/formulaic and metrical);
  4. use of verse rhyme;
  5. the abandonment of hypermetric rules;
  6. allowing single alliteration in Sievers types D and E;
  7. Preferring expanded Type D* over regular Type D.

Bredehoft’s argument is that

  1. all poems datable after 950 show at least some of these innovations;
  2. hypermetric rules had been abandoned by 950;
  3. classical verse had been abandoned by 950;
  4. Old Saxon influence begins in or by the Alfredian period;
  5. Single alliteration in type E was an early innovation;
  6. a poem that has later innovations nearly always also has some of the earlier innovations;
  7. Beowulf has none of these innovations and thus stands at the start of the chronology, and certainly cannot have been composed after 950.

[Judging by this short piece, Bredehoft’s logic suffers from some weaknesses. Poems are dated late because they use late features, but those features are considered late because they occur in late poems. This is not a major problem because some of the poems can be dated e.g. through their subject matter, and the resulting clusters of externally datable poems and poems with which they share features may then with some plausibility be considered of the same period, though the statistical basis thus available is clearly very weak. The implicit notion that poets lacked free will to choose their own poetic framework but were forced to implement all prior innovations into their verse seems problematic, particularly in combination with the recognition that Beowulf is often taken as the standard for classical verse, and on the features here under consideration its poet too could simply have chosen a particularly strict set of rules for himself without therefore having to have worked particularly early. Bredehoft’s chronology accordingly only works by confirmation with linguistic evidence not addressed in this essay.]

author: Wentersdorf, Karl P.
title: The Beowulf-Poet’s Vision of Heorot
abstract:
Seeks to explain Heorot’s golden roof, its only unrealistic detail other than its Roman floor, with reference to copious known examples: eddic material; Rome; Gaul; Roman Britain; classical and early medieval Latin literature. Asser’s claims of “gold and silver edifices” (423) are to be distrusted.

Wentersdorf suspects a specific literary purpose behind the gold, and settles on a didactic warning against greed visible in the poet’s treatment of the dragon-hoard, combined with the frequent mention of gold throughout. Although the poet recommends the free distribution of gold to ensure the loyalty of one’s men, Beowulf’s men abandon him in spite of his gold, and what Scyld’s gold gets him “no one can say.” Heorot was explicitly destined for destruction, and Beowulf in his dying words warns of the dangers of gold and treasure; he himself wins undying fame for his deeds.

author: Niles, John D.
title: Beowulf and Lejre
eds: John D. Niles and Marijane Osborn
publisher: ACMRS: Arizona Center for Medieval and Renaissance Studies
series: Medieval and Renaissance Texts and Studies
abstract:
Section 1 offers an excellent analysis of Heorot as described in Beowulf, and concludes that it, like all material objects described in the poem, is an idealization of the hall, though otherwise not incompatible with the halls at Lejre (171–177).

Section 2 analyzes the geography of Lejre and concludes that it divides into a habitable area and a wasteland used for raw materials but not for human habitation, and thus a binary well suited to Beowulf’s monster narrative (178–183).

Section 3 studies the hall as the heart of the central place. It conjectures that Iron-Age and Viking-Age Scandinavian halls resemble older halls but possibly emulating Roman constructions in their grandiose scale (183). Chieftains’ territories grew over time, generating dynasties and mythologies to match; such dynasties are the obvious candidates for the powers behind these large halls, and kings and halls are likely to have grown in response to the same shocks, such as Roman and Hunnish expansionism (184–185). It is notable that the great halls did not serve certain expected functions, such as cooking, while findings of goldgubber in postholes suggests their sacral character (185–186). Niles describes the rise of a gift-economy of prestige goods in Scandinavia, and from the mid-fifth century many Roman solidi made their way to Germanic lands (185–186). The same century saw an increase in grave goods e.g. in southern Britain, and occasional barrow-burials imported from Scandinavia and Germany (186–187), though in Scandinavia too this was on the rise at this time (187). Niles understands all of this as a rise in central places and the concentration of power in the wider region c. 450–700, alongside the rise of halls and a gift economy (187). Halls probably served ceremonial functions in addition to basic shelter; they may have been the setting for poetic performances and they would have been associated with prestige (188).

Section 4 describes the hall thought to have been built c. 550 right next to a location then long used for burial (189–190), and overlooking a stream known as Hjorterende (190). This hall was much larger than that at Yeavering (190). The nearby tumulus Grydehøj dominated the landscape from the time of its construction in the early seventh century (190–191); it appears to be the pyre and grave of someone of high rank likely associated with the hall, and it seems to be the only mound associated with the hall (191–192). The building of mounds seems not to have been continuously practised since the Iron Age but was revived, likely under influence e.g. of the Huns or Scythians moving in (192). Niles here announces that in another contribution to the volume (pp. 225–265) he will argue that it is no coincidence that the first hall was abandoned about the time that Grydehøj was constructed (194). The building of a new hall would have lent the deceased’s successor prestige (195–196); the new hall, at Mysselhøjgård, built c. 680 and clearly a product of the same culture as the first, would have looked out towards Grydehøj (196); it was rebuilt several times and remained in use for 300 years (196–197). Niles speculates about the meaning of the ring found at Strårup and engraved with a sequence LETHRO that may or may not refer to Lethra or Lejre before stopping to say that there is no use in guessing at the meaning of this evidence (198).

Section 5 compares Lejre to four other central sites in the region. Niles concludes that there was peaceful hegemony over an extended period (205), that there were two shifts in power: from Gudme to Lejre c. 450x550, and from Lejre to Roskilde under Harald Gormsson (205–206). Lejre seems to have served as a sort of capital of Denmark (207), and as such may have played a role in the government of the Danelaw; it may be significant that the hall was rebuilt around 890, i.e. around the time of the treaty of Alfred and Guthrum, when substantial new tax income would have flowed in from England (208–209).

Section 6 discards Saxo and the anonymous Lejre Chronicle as ahistorical in their association of Lejre with the Skjölding dynasty, proposing instead that legends arose after the first hall was abandoned, and they may have been encouraged for the purpose of creating a heroic origin for the surviving dynasty (209–211). Niles seems to understand the place of Scyld in English genealogies as predating the use of this name in the poem, i.e. its use in the poem pays deference to the West Saxon dynasty (212), while references to the Danes subtly raise the doom of feud that awaits them (213–214).

Section 7 explains how it is not the rivalry of Scandinavian dynasties, but rather the opposition between good and evil in Beowulf that was meant to resonate with its audiences. Grendel is associated with death, just as Grettir is faced with revenants and there are burials near Lejre with measures taken apparently to prevent the dead from returning (214–216). This is hugely relevant to the site of Lejre, literally up against a burial site and thus imbued with the threats of “death incarnate” (216–217). Grendel’s abode has no natural counterpart but evokes the notion of hell having an entry on the earth’s surface (217–218 though continuing in some sense to 220). Niles suggests that the “bipolar” topography of Lejre offers all the ingredients needed to come up with the first part of Beowulf, and a mound large enough to house a dragon, too (220–221). Moreover, two kinds of legend here cross paths: (1) that of the Skjölding dynasty and (2) that of the haunting of the Skjöldings’ residence, which two legends converge upon the earlier hall at Fredshøjgård (221–222).

Section 8 concludes by asserting that the 890s or thereabouts would have been a convergence during which both English and Danish members of a mixed audience would have listened attentively to a song about Scyld Scefing at the royal court of the Skjöldings, a time when some might have had personal knowledge of the later hall at Lejre. He assumes a certain critical mass of Scandinavians having arrived in England for Alfred’s dynasty to have begun to reroute their ancestry through Scyld of Denmark (222–227).
