author: Niles, John D.
title: Was There a “Legend of Lejre”?
eds: John D. Niles and Marijane Osborn
publisher: ACMRS: Arizona Center for Medieval and Renaissance Studies
series: Medieval and Renaissance Texts and Studies
abstract:
Attempts to distill a common core from the Lejre/Heorot material by
dismissing singly attested and fairytale elements; determines that this
common core is a dynastic feud spanning two confrontations over four
generations; observes that the period between the building of the first
Lejre hall c. 550 and the second c. 680 comes to about that span of
time; proposes that the Lejre material may have arisen as a way of
accounting for the rise and fall of the first hall, and that the people
at this time might have associated the creation of a large burial mound
c. 630x650 with this material they had dreamt up. The material itself
may all be fiction, in which case we may even accept Lukman’s thesis
that several of the names in the material are Hunnish in origin. As for
the time of composition, one expects a few generations after the funeral
would have sufficed to make the fiction plausible.

author: Leneghan, Francis
title: The Dynastic Drama of “Beowulf”
abstract:
A thoroughly referenced case for understanding Beowulf as showcasing the life cycle of the archetypal dynasty, with the “foreground” monster fights serving to inform the dynastic dynamics playing out in the remainder of the text.

Chapter 1 (32–103) makes the case that the poem divides into three dynastic stages: the prologue represents pueritia, a dynasty arising as when Scyld arrives to Denmark; the larger part of the poem depicts iuventus, with rulers securing a dynastic future through offspring; and the Swedish section represents senectus, with succession failing.

The much briefer Chapter 2 (104–152) discusses what the Beowulf contributed to his material by subtracting what may be assumed common knowledge among its audience, e.g. by inventing the Beowulf character, but the chapter also discusses how the poet shapes his material by inserting references to e.g. Heremod and Sigemund at just the right moment to reflect on the dynastic dynamic under discussion. The chapter concludes with a reconstructed development consisting of the following sequence, with stages 1–5 in uncertain order:

  1. Bear’s son meets Scylding tradition;
  2. A legend of Beowulf and Breca exists;
  3. Legends surrounding Hygelac’s Frisian raid reach England in the sixth or early seventh century;
  4. Legends surrounding Heremod’s deposition reach England;
  5. Legends of Sigemund cross-pollinate with saintly dragonslayers in England;
  6. The swimmer Beowulf is made Hygelac’s nephew and thus the last Hrethling
  7. Scyld and Beow are inserted into the Scylding material
  8. Beowulf becomes a monster-killer at the court of the Scyldings and at his own court.

Chapter 3 (153–194), which studies the role of the monsters, is particularly effective inasmuch as it (1) demonstrates how the matter of dynasty is hardcoded into their narratives (Grendel’s father is unknown but he goes back to Cainite ancestry, etc.); and (2) the gifstōl crux is very naturally explained with reference to succession once stōl is pursued as a simplex and complex element in the literature, e.g. in the fall of the angels narratives in MS Junius 11.

Chapter 4 (195–235) argues that the depiction of dynasties in Beowulf was modelled after the Old Testament Books of (Samuel and) Kings. It opens by tracing how the Merovingians merged rule by military strength with Christian ideas to form a cult of royal inheritance, which ended up weakening their own dynasty insofar as every distant relation could lay claim to the throne. The Carolingians introduced divine rule based on Old Testament models. English succession took cues from these development. Under pressure from the Church, succession became more tightly regulated, which led to more crises as successors would fail to materialize. As in Beowulf, succession was normally through the male line. Leneghan now turns to Old Testament kingship and points out a few direct correspondences with Beowulf, such as that between Saul and Heremod, and David’s contrition and Beowulf’s concern that he may have brought the dragon upon himself. Leneghan also notes an important difference, that of concubinage, which leads Old Testament women to wield less power (with some exceptions, such as Bathsheba). Hrothgar and Solomon are both associated with idol-worship, and so they have in common an imperfection in their anticipation of Christ as king. Leneghan now turns to Bede’s commentaries on biblical kingship, in which he draws freely on such contemporary examples as Ecgfrith. The debate on lofgeornost may benefit from comparison with Bede’s rex fortissimus et gloriae cupidissimus (as Colgrave and Mynors note). The phrase folce tō frōfre, of course, evokes Christ. Thus Beow and others in the poem should be understood as pointing to Christ.

The Conclusion sketches out three audience periods. In Mercia 650–800, the probable setting of the poem’s composition, we find short-lived warring dynasties like those in Beowulf, with the Bernician Æthelfrithings resembling the Hrethlings and the Mercian revival under Wulfhere chiming with the edwenden of Scyld Scefing’s appearance on the Danish scene (237–240). In Alfred’s Wessex, we see Beowulfian names added to royal genealogies, as well as books on wise rulership translated, and Orosios’s History presenting a rise-and-fall cycle like that of Beowulf; also, Andreas is probably from this period and shows influence from Beowulf. The latter poem’s survival alongside The Letter of Alexander suggests it came to be read as a critique of pagan kingship, perhaps around this time (240–244). Finally, the Nowell Codex shows a continued appeal as well as a focus on the toppling of unfit rulers, and the Danish English dynasty lends a new relevance to the poem (244–246).

author: Wormald, Patrick
title: Bede, Beowulf and the Conversion of the Anglo-Saxon Aristocracy
publication: The Times of Bede: Studies in Early English Christian Society and its Historian
abstract:
Opens by acknowledging that historians have too long taken Bede at his word, and that information about the period may be gleaned even from a text like Beowulf inasmuch as it encodes expectations the author shared with their audiences (30–38). The key aspect that Wormald focuses on is the recognition that heroic literature was “literature about, for and even by the Anglo-Saxon aristocracy,” suggesting that it may be taken as “a window on the mentality of a warrior aristocracy” for information not otherwise relayed, and “[l]east of all . . . in Bede,” as Bede took a religious perspective; that revealed through poetry may be complementary (34–35, quotations at 34). Objects described in the poetry match artefacts associated with the highest elite only, and the poetic vocabulary is heavy on elite (eorl, contrasting with ceorl; 34). After Tolkien and in spite of Parry, Lord, and Magoun, Beowulf increasingly came to be read as written not oral, and unified not composite, and thus associated with learned culture and thus Church culture (35–36); indeed there is very little evidence to suppose substantial lay literacy before 900 (36–37), and “it seems reasonable to proceed on the basis that the author of Beowulf was most probably a cleric, or an associate of clergy” (37).

To answer the question whether Beowulf can tell us about the conversion of the aristocracy (37–38), Wormald devotes a brief section (38–41) to “The Religious Character of Beowulf,” which observes that the poem describes pagan practices but expresses monotheistic sentiments that are more Judaeo-Christian in character, evidently reflecting the author’s own Christianity (38). The poem contains elements from “Christian homily and liturgy” (including Christian vocabulary: forscrifan, candel nōn) but also “lingering pagan beliefs” (including vocabulary: wyrd; eacen “magical”) (38–39). Strikingly, the poem bypasses the New Testament, while references to Cain’s actions are so explicit as to raise the suggestion that the audience might not have been all that familiar (39). Ethically, the poem lacks a Christian confidence on the afterlife and instead celebrates heroic virtues and life in the hall (39). Nevertheless the “elevated tone” of the poem has impressed some critics into reading Beowulf as a an allegorical type of Christ, while it has led others to emphasize its noble paganism (40). We are thus left with a poem seemingly celebrating noble paganism from the perspective of a Christian poet, a paradox which is not easily synthesized into any singular interpretation (40–41).

Wormald now turns to early medieval attitudes to secular culture (41–48), embedding Alcuin’s “Ingeld-letter” (c. 797) to Hygebald of Lindisfarne in a broader tradition condemning fabulae, libri gentilium, and eal-scopas, a chorus in which Bede, too joins in (42–43). Rather than explain from context that Alcuin’s remarks pertained to specific monastic settings, as other scholars have done, Wormald concludes that there was at least a wish for religious institutions to draw more on religious messaging and less on secular narrative, in the same way that for centuries classical literature had been frowned upon (“Like Dr Hunter Blair, I have the impression that ‘What has Ingeld to do with Christ?’ is a conscious echo of ‘How can Horace go with the Psalter?’,” 43). Royal courts too were under pressure to adopt sacerdotal norms, so positing that the author was secular can only get you so far (43–44). The other reason for censure of pagan heroes was that they were damned (44); but of course this understanding brought with it the concern for pagan ancestors known from the story of Radbod/Redbad (44–45); at any rate Beowulf celebrates the pagan life with just the occasional passing reference to its futility (45). Gregory’s recommendation that altars be adapted may have bearing on heroic poetry (see Aldhelm and Cædmon), but it does not allow for celebration of heroic virtues (45). Wormald sees no legitimate Christian case for allowing Beowulf to be written or survive, and the proportions in which heroic and religious texts survive from England and the Continent make the same case (45–47). Hence if Beowulf is to be accepted as a product of the clerical tradition, it must contain something of patristic value to set against its celebration of pagan culture; but the product must then also have morphed under nonpatristic influence to make it into the anomaly it is (47–48).

To explain the anomaly, Wormald expends a section (48–58) on whether a version of “liberal Christianity” may have existed in England. Irish Christianity was tolerant, and the Hildebrandslied appears to have been written at Fulda just a generation after Boniface, but there is “no good evidence of a theory of the noble pagan among the English missionaries” (48–49, quotation at 49). But prohibitions suggest a demand: Alcuin repeatedly railed against banquets, actors, inebriation, richness of dress, and Clofesho similarly forbids the entertainments of poets, harpists, musicians, and horse-races during religious festivals, as well as pompous dress, clerics hunting and carrying arms, and drunkenness as well as forcing drink upon others, while Theodore’s Penitential opens with the etiquette of drunken vomiting among the clergy (50). Wormald now adduces a letter of Bede’s to Archbishop Ecgberht of York from 734 in which he too rails against fabulae and feasting among bishops, as well as their living with rather secular-seeming bands of retainers and wives (51). Clofesho confirms the existence of “secular” monasteries held by laymen, and Ecgberht’s Dialogi as well as eighth- and ninth-century charters discuss the partition of private monasteries among the abbot’s heirs. Thus we must conclude that seventh- and eighth-century men lived as monks and bishops without forsaking the secular life; just the circumstances that would favour the survival of secular literature (51). Continental evidence is more explicit about the existence of Eigenkirchen, and Iona too was ruled by a dynasty, while abbot Milo of Trier and Rheims was probably never ordained and died hunting (51–52). It is also on the Continent that this culture is brought into connection with secular literature, so that “where we find clerics living in some ways like heroes out of Germanic saga, we also find literature like Beowulf being composed and appreciated” (52). A motivation is also in evidence on the Continent: high clerical positions were a form of social nobility (53). In England, Bede, Boniface, and Alcuin denounce the minster or family monastery (53–54), while monasticism was also associated with royalty, witness Repton, Crowland, Coldingham, Whitby, and the abbot-king Eadberht Praen of Kent (54). Saint Wilfrid is an especially prominent example of a bishop leading a large and warlike retinue known for drunkenness (54–55). The Dream of the Rood and Andreas show the influence of comitatus culture, as does the term dryhten itself (54–55). The Lindisfarne Gospels is indebted for its illumination to metalwork (55–56). Guthlac is a heroic saint pitted against monsters (56). Genealogies incorporating Germanic names show us what people wished to believe about themselves (57). And so Wormald asks, “Does the composition by a literate poet, who was probably therefore a cleric, of a great secular poem about the pagan kings of the past still seem anomalous in a society where monasteries function partly as the royal court and partly as royal family’s property, where bishops go to war, where Gospel books have begun to look like secular treasures, and where the adventures of saints resemble so closely those of heroes? Is Beowulf an unthinkable product for a monastic scriptorium, when not only Alcuin, but also councils of the Church talk of drunkenness, banquets and the patronage of harpists in clerical environments; when the Mercian royal house, with whom many Beowulf critics have very reasonably felt that the poem may have a connection, was treating its religious foundations as a part of its hereditas?” (58).

To argue that Beowulf is in some way a better source on the English conversion than Bede, we need to show that Bede was himself an anomaly. And indeed Gregory, Paul the Deacon, and Widukund tell far more about heathenism and other practices they feel a need to denounce (59). Bede’s choice of emphasis compared to these Continental peers is what makes Beowulf so hard to place (59–60). The Church Fathers sought to give classical literature a place since they read it in grammar school, but Bede wrote a grammar that relied almost exclusively on Scriptural examples, and he fought heroic legend with “withering silence” (60–61), making a point of highlighting the good rather than denouncing the bad (61). As an oblate, Bede lacked the secular aristocratic upbringing that other leading churchmen of his time had had, while Monkwearmouth and Jarrow seem to have had relatively little of the Adelsheilige tradition (62–64).

The Conclusions (64–70) restate and recombine the paper’s findings in worthwhile ways. The appendix (71–81) concerns itself with the dating of Beowulf chiefly on onomastic grounds, adducing the Durham Liber vitae and other naming evidence to argue against a date after c. 900, while generally reading Beowulf as a work of cultural transition.

author: Louwen, Kenny
title: Zur Lesart und Hybridität der altniederländischen Federprobe
abstract:
Sums up and adds to decades of research into the question of mixed language features in Hebban olla uogala; compare in particular Grauwe (which precedes it in the scholarship) and Angerer (which improves on its reading).

After listing existing readings (43–65), Louwen offers his (65), then discusses each word in need of discussion. In short, assumes (but cannot yet make out) hagunnan “mit h-Prothese”; hic (but cannot yet make out <c>); cannot read the onset syllable in anda, and assumes enda going by early Middle Dutch (as opposed to anda as customary in the Old Dutch Williram and Reimbibel A!); cannot read beyond the first letter of “uuat” (65–68 and 73). The analysis follows:

  • hebban must be indicative (Latin habent), which ought to be Dutch (contrast OE habbaþ, Kentish -eth) (68–69);
  • olla must be Dutch (69);
  • uogala must be Dutch (69–70);
  • nestas has an Old English ending, whether or not the noun itself occurs as a masculine in Old English (70);
  • hagunnan should be considered Old English, as only it uses -a-prefixes, including aginnan (70–71);
  • hinase (i.e. hit + nā + sȳ) cannot be Dutch due to the form se; the whole contraction could be English; hit may be inferred from the Williram’s High German form hiz, though it is recorded in and typical of Old English only, and cf. Dutch het; na should be read as ne, current in both languages (71–72);
  • hic can be either language (72–73);
  • [:]nda is probably Dutch enda (or [Dutch] anda) [now see Angerer: anda] (73);
  • thu could be either language: according to Dietz (Schreibung und Lautung 208–213) the spelling <th> returned to English in the 10th century but mostly in latinate and placename contexts, but Old Dutch certainly had dental fricatives (73–74);
  • uuat is Dutch, and <uu> may have been an archaic spelling by 1100; the reconstruction <uuat> presupposes it means “why,” not “what for,” or we should reconstruct “uues” (74–75) [now see Angerer: <uuat>];
  • [:]mbidan [Angerer reads <unb\i/[a]dan> with <a> expunged] cannot be unbidan because this is not attested in either language and word spacing recommends m; it would therefore have to be considered Old English *umbīdan, if not for the ending, so that on balance it seems Dutch (75–76);
  • we may be either language (but standard only in Old English) (76–77);
  • nu may be either language (77).

A crude table demonstrates that the sentence as a whole contained mixed language forms, though only the sequence “nestas hagunnan hinase” is securely identifiable as Old English, against six words securely Dutch (78).

Kwakkel has demonstrated the hand to be Continental (78); moreover, there were no anglophone clergymen in Rochester Abbey c. 1100, as these had been replaced by Normans (78–79). The scribe was either one of the imported scribes or part of an international traineeship (79–80). The register of Bec monks does not list any Flemish names (80).

The scribe was thus Continental, no native speaker of English, and the note contains mixed forms. The mixed forms either serve to demonstrate that the languages are related or reflect the process of foreign language learning (81).

author: De Grauwe, Luc
title: Zijn olla vogala Vlaams, of zit de Nederlandse filologie met een koekoeksei in (haar) nest(en)?
publication: Tijdschrift voor Nederlandse Taal- en Letterkunde
abstract:
[The typesetting of this article is as follows: <d> for ð, <p> for þ (except once!), <oe> for æ.]

Argues that hebban in Hebban olla uogala may just as well be considered Kentish (46–48). For the form hebban it relies on early Kentish for the stem vowel and on the tenth-century Kentish Glosses (or alternatively late West Saxon) for the ending -an, which he reads as a subjunctive; this of course in contradiction with the Latin indicative that accompanies the scribble, but Grauwe explains this by reading the Dutch text as a response to the Latin (“Laten nu nog alle vogels nesten gebouwd hebben, behalve ik en jou — wat verwachten jullie nu?”). He also points out that this scribe appears to write <a> for schwa, which would obviate the need to root subjunctive -an in a written tradition. The fact that the sentence begins with the verb further supports the subjunctive reading, as this is the more common mood for Middle Dutch to start with the verb.

For uogala De Grauwe appeals to the fact that the labial fricative would have been voiced in prevocalic position in southern Old English; that forms with the medial vowel intact (or rather, as he describes it, a svarabakhti vowel) are attested for fugol; that <o> for [u] comes into fashion in later twelfth-century English (hence the 1340 form uogel in Ayenbite); and even that the Northumbrian weak nominative masculine plural ending -a is attested on normally strong a-stems [well, in Northumbrian!] (48–49).

De Grauwe then claims that hagunnan, hinase, hic, end [misread from MS “anda”], and thu could likewise be Old English (50–51): a-prefixes are unattested in Dutch, but not in English; participial -an is normal in late Old English; prothetic h- is known in Old English [the example De Grauwe gives is herian for erian in the Kentish Glosses, but surely herian is just a more frequent word, at ca. 1300 occ. versus 55 for erian, so this is a scribal error; but the point from Campbell is valid all the same; on the other hand, the cited passage in Brunner says this phenomenon of intrusive h is particularly common in Rushworth 1]. Hinase may be purely English: hit is rare in Old West Flemish, na is nothing unusual in Old English, and the subjunctive form se is attested in Old English, including in the Kentish Glosses (and further again in Northumbrian) [it may be noted here that Brunner’s conjecture that this may be as part of the process in which “festes ” becomes , but that is a contradiction in Brunner because the vowel in sȳ does not qualify as “festes ,” i.e. as an umlaut from [u]: Brunner §31; Brunner’s other suggestion is that it is a “satznebentonige Form,” see §427 n. 3]. De Grauwe reads elision of t as language-independent, though the Old English instances he cites are adduced in Brunner §196 note 2 as consonant clusters, which do not here apply. <Hic> for ic is attested in Middle English, but since no <c> is visible, this may alternatively be “she”; <end> occurs in the Kentish charters and once in Ayenbite, and if it reads and, then that fits all the better with English.

In uuat, the spelling <uu> is known from Middle English, as is loss of initial [h]. Ths misreading “unbidat” is classified as Kentish for its ending, while the prefix in Dutch would have had a dental (ontbiden, ontbeiden).

[Thus substantial parts of this article read like special pleading, relying on a combination of early Kentish, tenth-century Kentish, late southern Old English, and Northumbrian to cobble together a defence of certain forms as Old English that may far more easily be identified as Flemish. But the problem of apparently mixed forms remains, PSL.]

author: Kwakkel, Erik
title: Hebban olla vogala in historisch perspectief
publication: Tijdschrift voor Nederlandse Taal- en Letterkunde
abstract:
Asserts that the hebban olla vogala-pen trial dates to Rochester of 1075x1100, not later, and that it is one among five Continental hands in Bodley 340, most of which are likewise pen trials.

Explains the presence of these Continental hands with reference to the Norman Conquest: bishops and bishop-priors were nearly all replaced by Normans either directly or after their death. In the case of Saint Andrew’s Abbey, Rochester, a new bishop-and-prior was installed in 1075 (Arnost of Bec), who died probably in July 1076, after which Gundulf of Bec took his place on 19 March 1077; but he remained in correspondence with Bec. Upon his arrival, Gundulf found only five English monks, whom he ejected in 1083 to be replaced by 60 Normans, of whom 22 in 1083, as documented in three distinct sources from the first quarter of the twelfth and the first quarter of the 13th century. Kwakkel explains that this necessitated a great deal of copying — if only because Benedictine institutions required at least one book per monk, while the Rule stipulates three hours’ daily copying. By 1120, the library housed 90 new volumes. “Op het moment dat de Oudnederlandse verzen in de codex werden geplaatst was het klooster in Rochester opmerkelijk genoeg als een continentale gemeenschap aan te merken” (13).

Kwakkel proposes Bec as the most likely house of origin of the Hebban olla vogala-scribe. It is especially noteworthy in this context that Ker considered the Rochester script modelled after that of Bec, suggesting an overwhelming presence of monks from that house, even though the low register of the pen trial does not allow for the identification of Bec features. The book-list of c. 1120, moreover, uses a sorting principle used in Bec and nowhere else in England at this time.

The presence of a Dutch speaker in a Bec-injected Rochester may be explained in a few different ways. Bec attracted students from afar, and so would have attracted Flemings — in fact the twelfth-century historiographer mentions Flanders specifically. Secondly, Flemish-spoken territory extended into Normandy, so the scribe could have grown up near Bec.

The hands used in the Continental pen trials do not recur elsewhere in Bodley 340; evidently these scribes could not read Old English. This explains why the manuscript was used in the way it was.

author: Cotman, Frédéric and Johan Taeldeman
title: Olla uogala Revisited
publication: Quod vulgo dicitur: Studien zum Altniederländischen
eds: Willi J. J. Pijnenburg, Arend Quak, and Tanneke Schoonheim
abstract:
Argues that (the legible part of) Hebban olla vogala is Western Flemish (Vlaamse Westhoek) (223–225): hebban, uogala, and thu are not Old English forms; there was not yet occasion for hypercorrect insertion of h because it had not yet started to drop in English; the stem vowel in olla is attested for southwestern Dutch, not English; the fact that the prefix a- is not attested in Dutch may be chance nonsurvival, but if it is English, it could be an isolated borrowed form in an otherwise Southwestern Flemish text; <o> in uogala may represent [ø], which better fits Flemish pronunciation; <u> in hagunnan is the expected vowel in Flemish begunnen; -e in hinase and <a> for every schwa are features of Dutch.

Those last two points are discussed in more detail (226–227): the authors claim that Old English of this period only ever has the forms sī or sīe, never sē [which seems an odd claim to make? and don’t they mean sȳ or sīe? PSL]. Sē also does not match Old Dutch, except in Western Flemish where it fits nicely (226). The authors then observe, following Tavernier–Vereecken (1948) that “elke onbeklemtoonde syllabe een a-vocaalteken bevat” (226). Since several of these did not have the quality [ɑ] before the reduction of unstressed syllables, so these must represent reduced unstressed syllables — schwa; and the same is found in Dutch texts well after the reduction process was completed. The authors print a suggested phonemic transcription of the sequence, which they classify as Middle Western Flemish (226–227).

Tavernier–Vereecken argued that the reduced unstressed vowel was written <a> because it represented a comparatively open realization of schwa. In fact even in present-day Dutch, open vowels are more naturally realized as schwa than close ones, which Van Oostendorp has posited is due to their higher sonority being less well suited to unstressed positions. The authors also claim that some English speech communities substitute open, [ɑ]-like realizations for unstressed schwa-segments, such as “ya” for unstressed “you” [my spellings], Jamaican/Caribbean realizations of words like solution, and African realizations of words like letter (227–230). That Van Loon comes to the opposite reading of Dutch vowel reduction is explained by the interpretation that close vowels are quicker to show their reduction in orthography, while for a it was not necessary to signal the earlier reduction in writing because it and schwa were already so closely associated [bit of an unlikely argument, PSL] (230–231).

author: Angerer, Michael Lysander
title: Hebban olla vogala: An Eleventh‑Century Link Between Dutch and English Literary History
abstract: Presents a new UV photograph settling two minor points of contention in the reading of Hebban olla vogala, then goes on to express agreement with the “new consensus” (468) that the poem contained elements both of Flemish and Kentish; indeed, goes so far as to claim that the scribe “appears to capitalise on the similarity between Old English and Old Dutch to produce a carefully formed text in a Dutch–English Mischsprache which is intelligible in both” (473); he meant “to produce a poem readable not only in Dutch but also in English” (474). Argues the poem serves the purpose of technical exercise as well as love lyric and perhaps religious allegory (474). Reaches the conclusions that “Dutch was also a viable means of communication with English-speakers outside Rochester’s cathedral priory” and that English was an international language because it would have been the easiest language for Dutch speakers to use in England (475). Reports on a range of anecdotes of Dutch speakers in England (475–476) and some evidence of borrowing (477). Discusses the genre of love lyric the poem connects to (477) and early examples of end-rhyme in English, on which Dutch verse may have exerted an influence (477–478; here Angerer, following Seth Lerer’s phrasing, does admit the classification as “rhymed couplets,” where at 473 he had suggested “two long lines”).

author: Kwakkel, Erik
title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Continental Scribes in Rochester Cathedral Library, 1075–1150
publication: Writing in Context: Insular Manuscript Culture 500–1200
abstract:
Complicates the social environment of the Hebban olla vogala scribe by identifying the other pen trials in Bodley 340+342 as stemming from diverse regions on the Continent.

Two Norman scripts may be identified in Rochester: in 1075–1100 it was “pure Norman”, in 1100–1150 it was Ker’s “prickly” script, ultimately Norman but from Christ Church, Canterbury, seemingly brought in in a coordinated fashion (235–239).

Bodley 340 and 342 have a combined total of three pages filled with “at least two-dozen probationes pennae, the earliest dating from the period 1075–1100 and the latest from the period 1150–1200. . . . The hands ‘caught’ on these originally blank leaves are definitely local” (239–240). The hand T from Kwakkel 2005 is here labelled A; Kwakkel describes its five performances on fol. 169v of Bodley 340 and their script (241–244). New is that Kwakkel here identifies the script as “neither English [n]or Norman” and identifies characteristics of “Germanic” origin, meaning a “Kulturraum” comprised of “Austria, Germany, the Northern and Southern parts of the Low Countries. . . and Switzerland” (242). The most notable feature is “the attachment of a ‘flag’ stroke at the tongue of e . . . almost exclusively encountered in the work of Germanic scribes” (242–243). The “less heavy and square” aspect of the script enables Kwakkel to narrow its origin to the Low Countries (243). Similarities to a hand in an Utrecht (in provenance, and possibly in origin) Moralia in Iob suggest the northern Low Countries as the “most probably origin” of both scribes (243); the Utrecht connection is further strengthened by yet a further sample mentioning St Peter’s Church, Utrecht (243–244).

Kwakkel identifies eleven stints of the next hand (“B”), who wrote perhaps in 1125x1150 and likewise suggests Germanic origins (244–247). Then there is an Italian hand C of 1100x1150 (probably 1125x1150), and a hand D c. 1125x1150 that looks German (250).

The hand from the Utrecht Moralia in Iob has been shown to have served first in Utrecht and then in Salisbury Cathedral 1075x1100, and other such trajectories have been traced from France and the lower Rhineland to Hereford, and from the Meuse to Bath; and another may be identified from Germany to Canterbury (251). It is likely these scribes would have entered a Norman house supplying monks to the English mission. Bec certainly served as a hub along these lines, not for child oblates but for men with prior training as scribes (251–253).

Kwakkel observes that the hands of these scribes have not been identified in texts copied out. This may be explained by their copying in a different script (namely Ker’s prickly script) and returning to their pregothic script for their pen trials (254–255).

author: Colmjon, Gerben
title: Een woord vooraf
abstract:
As the preface to a fabricated Old Saxon diary, this brief essay on Hebban olla vogala should not be taken too seriously, though Colmjon may well have meant its position in earnest, and it contains a few fresh ideas.

Among the more valuable points it makes is the observation that “hinase” doesn’t look like anything, and has been forced into meaning “except” by its context, although Colmjon neither undertakes a study of het en sî attestations, nor convinces with his unfounded reading “buan”. Again, there is value in the observation that the sense “except” would have been expressed with a word like būta or būtan in the Germanic languages (12), and even more value in the observation that Old English does not use beginnan, let alone aginnan, for nests, but rather timbran, gearwian, or wyrcan (11–12); also the valuable point that “inceptos” in the Latin rendition is an unusual construction, which makes sense as a translation of the Germanic original but not as the Latin model for the Germanic text (14). Colmjon also deserves a place in the chronology of scholars debating the order in which the Latin and the Germanic were written, as he protests at Caron’s position that the last bit of Latin had to be written above just because the scribe had already reserved space for the Dutch (15).

But Colmjon’s larger argument is that the whole sequence is Old Saxon, with the text emended to “Hebban alle[ro] vogala nestas begunnan buan ik anda thu”, meaning “[d]at (of: laten nu) van alle vogels ik en jij een nest zijn beginnen te bouwen” (12). He explains the failure of prior scholarship to reach any such conclusion before as the result of Schönfeld’s fantasy of a West Flemish past, for which purpose he declared any unusual forms Ingvaeonic relics (13–14).

author: Tavernier-Vereecken, C.
title: Nog over hebban olla vogala nestas hagunnan hinase hi(c) anda thu
publication: Handelingen van de Koninklijke Commissie voor Toponymie en Dialectologie
abstract:
Offers evidence of western early Middle Dutch (legal) texts having <a> in unstressed syllables (75–82). There is evidence even from the 10th and 11th centuries in the form of personal and place names, which simultaneously show that unstressed syllables in this century tended toward e and that <a> was sometimes used as an allograph of the same (82–87). “Hiermee geloof ik bewezen te hebben dat in Zuid-Nederland althans in de 10e eeuw de vocalen hun oorspronkelijk timbre begonnen te verliezen, en dat van deze verslapte vocaal ook reeds een variant a bestond, die phonetisch gezien, daarvan slechts een opener articulatie is. Thans nog is de neiging tot open uitspraak een der distinctieve trekken van het Westvlaams, het conservatieve dialect” (87).

The relevance for Hebban olla vogala is that this explains “olla” (expected is “olle”) and “hinase” (read “hinese”), suggests Flemish *əgunnən, and uncomplicates “enda” (Tavernier–Vereecken wonders whether the stem vowel doe not likewise read <a>). She feels the instances of <a> “hebban” and the middle vowel in “vogala” do not require this explanation, while “nestas ziet er uit als het meest onvervalste ingwaeonisme”, though primarily due to its <s> (88–89).

The author then suggests <se> as in “hinase” is not without parallel in early Middle Dutch: some Germanic dialects have a variant Proto-Germanic -ai, as in Old English and Old Frisian sīe alongside sī and sē respectively; the diphthong [iə] would have yielded a variant <e> in western Middle Dutch, as a handful of examples demonstrate (89–91). In her conclusion she does observe that “het mengsel van ‘Ingwaeoonse’ en ‘Frankische’ trekken (nestas–vogala) blijft steeds de meest opvallende eigenschap van onze zin” (91).

author: Scragg, Donald G.
title: Initial h in Old English
abstract:
Investigates scribal attitudes towards the unhistorical omission or addition of h in initial prevocalic position in English in the time before it may be expected to be due to French influence. Scragg has looked at all texts dated by Ker before 1000, and treats Northumbrian texts separately because they show evidence of separate development.

Early Mercian texts show “slight evidence of instability of the symbol h” (167–168), with considerable numbers first appearing across three tenth-century scribes of the Tanner Bede (168–169).

The tenth-century Kentish manuscript Vespasian D. vi has no instability of initial h in its Kentish Hymn and Kentish Psalm, but several in the glosses to the Parabolae Salomonis (169–170).

Early West Saxon texts vary substantially in their unhistorical use of initial h, and may sometimes be explained by phonological context, e.g. intervocally in unstressed position, or where a scribe shortens long or double consonants even across word boundaries (170–172).

Poetry poses particular problems of interpretation, but the Exeter Book contains some number of unhistorical h omitted or added, and the Vercelli scribe shows irregular h in both prose and verse (172–176); The Beowulf manuscript has frequent cases of h added but fewer where it is omitted (176–177); in this context there is some discussion of handlean for ondlean (177–178) and of Hunferð (178–179). Examples from the poetic codices other than the Exeter Book “can almost all be explained as either dittography or the confusion of two words or prefixes which are distinguished only by presence or absence of h”; the Exeter Book instances resemble cases found after the Conquest (179).

After discussing the Benedictine Rule and Blickling manuscripts, Scragg observes that Ælfric manuscripts “contain virtually no examples of unhistoric use of h before the middle of the eleventh century”, and even then many have none (180–181). There are a few instances in the Paris Psalter (181).

Scragg repeats again that many eleventh-century manuscripts have no examples, for which he proposes “progressively greater standardisation of the orthography after c. 1000” (181–182, quotation at 182).

Northumbrian has no examples in the seventh and eighth centuries, then very many in Lindisfarne; Rushworth has far fewer in the Northumbrian section than the Mercian, nor does the Durham Ritual have many, although that was glossed by the same Aldred who glossed Lindisfarne (182–185). Scragg takes it as significant that the prominence of unhistoric h in Northumbrian is due to two scribes, Farmon and Aldred, and is not consistent in the latter. “The lack of examples in the Royal Glosses and Ru2 argues against an assumption that it was in the West Saxon tradition alone that h was stable in the late tenth and early eleventh centuries” (185).

Scragg suggests all scribes may have been influenced by Latin attitudes towards h, e.g. the fact that Latin hortus appears as Germanic *ort- suggests it was borrowed at a stage when it had been lost from Latin pronunciation, and many examples of unhistoric h in Latin are to be found in the manuscripts (185–186). Latin names in H have vowel alliteration in Old English poetry (186–187).

Scragg warns against reading phonology into scribal errors, but points out that the presence of an unhistorical h is unlikely to be a copying error (187–188); and he goes on to discuss some of the considerations for or against taking certain text types or manuscripts as phonologically relevant (188–190). “If the aspirate were unstable in OE, and if its instability were to be reflected in the use of h, omission of h would be more likely in unstressed positions. But the examples cited from the poetry show loss of h most frequently from stressed, alliterating syllables, and many of the other examples are taken from glossaries where there is no question of sentence stress, at least”; the possessive adjective his often omits h, but that confuses it with the verb form is; there is no such omission from hine, hire, him, so this is a confusion of sense. “Hence there is little evidence in the examples so far discussed of loss of h being an indication of the loss of the aspirate in OE,” apart from the Exeter Book (190–191, quotation at 190).

The Hatton Cura pastoralis very often drops h but rarely adds it, suggesting it was lost in connected speech especially in unstressed position; but other graphemes are omitted as well. It may have been written by dictation, or rapid copying may have led the scribe to make phonologically irrelevant omissions (191).

Whereas omission of h in southern manuscripts is really only a significant feature of the Exeter Book, addition is more frequent. After dismissing the instances explained by Latin, dittography, or sense confusion, half that remain occur between two vowels, particularly after prefixes, or initially where the preceding word ends in a vowel, and these “parallel so closely the use in Late Latein of h as a diacritic signifying hiatus” (192). With all these dismissed, the Exeter Book remains as the sole southern manuscript in which unhistorical h may have phonological significance (192).

In the light of the above, the northern manuscripts are reconsidered; in Lindisfarne, the addition of unhistorical h may be evidence of phonological change, though not unambiguously so (193–195).

In conclusion, “few of the examples of omission of h cited offer any sure evidence of the instability of the aspirate,” while its addition suggests “use of h as a diacritic. . . for the majority of West Saxon examples, at least” (195).

author: Dekeyser, Xavier
title: ‘Hebban olla vogala nestas hagunnan’: Een Vroegnederlands kroonjuweel of een mythe?
publication: Tussen taal, spelling en onderwijs: Essays bij het emeritaat van Frans Daems
eds: Dominiek Sandra, Rita Rymenans, Pol Cuvelier, and Peter van Petegem
abstract:
Essentially accepts De Grauwe’s analysis that Hebban olla vogala was intended as Kentish by a speaker of Flemish, but discusses each of its word forms in turn and placing them on a scale between certified Old English and surely Dutch, with only “uuat” falling into the latter category.

Dekeyser considers the pronoun forms “thu” and “ge” the most incontrovertibly English forms: Middle Dutch uses no spirant for the second person [Dekeyser conveniently forgets that Old Dutch does not, PSL: cf. Franck, Altfränkische Grammatik §169; Quak and Van der Horst § 4.4.1] (118–119). The reading “ge” (as Gysseling and with him De Grauwe read it), or alternatively “we”, must be English because Middle Dutch had a vowel i in both forms (119).

For “nestas” Dekeyser offers no new evidence; he considers De Grauwe’s reasoning suffices to all but rule out a Dutch derivation (119).

He considers unbidan and aginnan (as he prints it) “zonder meer . . . Laatoudengels” because the Middelnederlandsch Woordenboek lacks headwords aginnen, eginnen, while Ayenbite has aginnen (119); similarly, the MED has umbiden and onbiden, while MNW merely has ontbiden with a rare variant onbiden (119–120).

Dekeyser’s analysis of “hinase” is especially unconvincing: “hit . . . is zonder twijfel Oudengels” on the authority of De Grauwe’s footnote; “[n]a, naast ne, is het gebruikelijke negatief partikel in het Oudengels. En se past perfect als onbeklemtoonde vorm in het Oudengelse (ook Kentse) paradigma voor de conjunctief van het koppelwerkwoord” (120). His account of Continental evidence is limited to a single Flemish attestation of “hit nesi” and the Old Frisian sequence “hit ne si thet”, which latter he feels points rather in an English direction than a Dutch (120) [he appears oblivious to the many instances of the same sequence in Dutch, including with assimilation of t, PSL].

“Hic” and “nu” can be either language (120).

“Vogala” appears Dutch, but an English derivation cannot be ruled out, among other things with reference to Ayenbite (121). The vowel in “olla” is used in Present-Day English all, a history that goes back to Middle English, even if Bruges usage also had ol/ols (121).

For the question at the end, Dekeyser again follows Gysseling and De Grauwe in reading “uuat unbidat ge nu”, though he departs from De Grauwe in the latter’s reading of the Dutch as a conjunctive response to the Latin; instead, the Latin is usually understood to be secondary. However, by reading “unbidat”, Dekeyser is able to assume fortition of the Old English dental fricative, a form often found in Old Kentish glosses [so although this is on the Dutch end of Dekeyser’s scale, he’s really reading this as a Kentish form if it reads “unbidat”, on which question he does not finally commit] (121–122).

“Hebban” could be Dutch, or early Middle English [Dekeyser assumes hebben here and does not explain <a> in this context, PSL]; but since southern English was the last to adopt this change, this argument can only be maintained if we assume a more progressive spoken Kentish than is known from the written sources [in other words, Dekeyser refuses to categorize this form as Dutch, PSL] (122).

Only “uuat” cannot be an Old Kentish form and answers directly to the Dutch pronoun (122–123).

Dekeyser reaffirms De Grauwe’s conclusion that the text was intended as Kentish, and cites the sudden shift in language at the year 1122 in the Peterborough Chronicle as evidence that the spoken language was way ahead of the written, so that De Grauwe’s “West-Vlaams substraat” could just be spoken Kentish instead (123–124). Prothetic h in “hagunnan” and “hic” serves alliteration (124).

author: Drout, Michael D. C., Yvette Kisor, Leah Smith, Allison Dennett, and Natasha Piirainen
title: “Beowulf” Unlocked: New Evidence from Lexomic Analysis
abstract:
This very brief (96-page) book was published as part of a series of publications by the Lexomics team, who had previously demonstrated (or alleged) that their method was able to identify boundaries within other texts, in Old English and some other languages, which they typically attribute to switches in sources: thus with their method they have been able to distinguish between Genesis A and B, the constituent parts of Christ and Guthlac, the English- and Latin-sourced episodes of the Old English Historiae adversus paganos, and conversely to associate Azarias with Daniel, and the works of Cynewulf with each other. Crucially for the interpretation of the findings in the present volume, they have attributed most of the differences found between segments in those texts to a reliance on different sources (in this volume see esp. p. 6 and footnotes, pp. 9–10, and then p. 60 for the inferences drawn for the study of Beowulf).

The “lexomic” method works as follows: after normalizing the input text (replacing eths with thorns, “and” with “ond”, and in the case of Beowulf at least experimenting with levelling notable distinct spellings between the two scribes), the text is divided into segments initially of 1200 tokens each; then the authors take the normalized term frequency of each term (i.e. absolute count divided by the length of the segment in tokens) and for each term they square the difference in this score between any two segments, then take the square root of the sum of those squared differences between two segments to obtain the Euclidean distance between the segments (7–8). A dendrogram is then generated that visualizes which segments are most and least like each other, in which the vertical length of the connecting lines represents the degree of difference (8–9).

A major challenge the authors faced was the fact that any uniform segment length will cut across episodic boundaries. This problem was addressed by hinting, i.e. subtly shifting boundaries so as to match more closely with narrative boundaries without yielding too great a difference in segment length, and blending, i.e. combining non-adjacent material into a single abstract segment where shared subject matter recommends doing so. The workflow involves a great deal of experimentation with different segment lengths etc. until a dendrogram emerges that meets with the authors’ informed approval (9–11). It is not specified to what extent the segmentation ultimately used relies on different segment lengths, as all the tables and graphs refer to line numbers not token counts, but the authors do seem motivated to keep them approximately the same length.

After first discussing the segmentation and cladistics of the Scribe A material, then Scribe B, and then a combined analysis, the authors conclude that some segments (notably the proem and the Finnsburg episode) are closer than others (the Breca episode being the most unlike anything else). In their discussion, they heavily favour a reliance on distinct sources as an explanation for differences measured between segments (60–69), though occasionally they rely on the term discourses as a way of allowing a broader and more abstract set of features (notably on p. 58). In fact, however, since they measure differences in vocabulary, surely differences in subject matter are responsible for a large share of the difference; this is not Genesis B where dialect rivals it as the most influential factor. Despite the authors’ emphasis on the reliance on different sources as the main explanation, they implicitly recognize the role of subject matter in their “scrabble diagrams,” which group closely matching segments by subject matter. Yet they seem to consider thematic explanations special pleading where they write that “[s]ome patterns of discourse arrangement in Beowulf could perhaps be special-pleaded away as simply arising from the poem’s narrative; for example, differences between the vocabulary of events in the hall and battles with monsters might simply be an epiphenomenon of the linguistic differences between direct speech and rapid action or between speech and summary” (60). In fact, as any TF-IDF web search algorithm demonstrates, subject matter is the most obvious explanation of differences in vocabulary, which also connects with a second critique the work invites: it is nowhere quantified what constitutes a signficant measure of distance between the vocabularies of two segments, and the distance between any two adjacent clades is always between 0.037 and 0.062, with a measure like the latter typically reserved for an outlier like the Breca episode as compared with a multifolious clade or the rest of the poem. A fuller critique of the method should take stock of segment differences between segments of a single work (of translation) treating of different subjects and comparing scores between single segments to measure the role of shifts in subject matter for the difference in score (I will have to read the study of Orosius to see what scores come up there, and/or feed the Lexomics website some homogeneous material to see what differences it measures); in fact it is unclear why the cladistic method was chosen over the more typical scatter-plot method, given that both rely on Euclidean distance but the former only ever shows the distance between groups that are most alike. Thus repeating the work but printing a scatter plot would be another way of testing whether the method holds up. And while we’re at it, surely using TF-IDF instead of plain normalized TF would yield more useful results? Seems there is much work to be done to test the validity of the results. The authors repeatedly advertise a follow-up study in the text of the book that would have used a rolling approach but that seems never to have materialized.

Errata: p. 45, caption to Fig. 4.1.1: for “K and P,” read “L and P”; p. 56: for “tightly liked,” read “tightly linked”; p. 68: for “Tolken,” read “Tolkien”; p. 71: for “segments10–14,” read “segments 10–14.” I also wonder whether the dendrogram legends (Figs 4.2, 4.3, 4.6) have placeholder text.

author: Fulk, R. D.
title: The Origin of the Numbered Sections in Beowulf and in Other Old English Poems
abstract:
Suggests it was the scribes, not the author (if we may assume a single author), who came up with the fitt division.

An important part of Fulk’s reasoning is that many of the fitt divisions cut across episodes, and even sentences, where nearby natural points of narrative transition could easily have been chosen instead (96–104). Subject matter is regularly concluded with pithy statements like “gæð a wyrd swa hio scel” or “he him ðæs lean forgeald,” and these repeatedly end fitts, which prompts the question why the same natural division was not made in other instances (100). “[T]here are no sectional divisions in the first two-thirds of the poem that match the ability of those in the last third to surprise. The most plausible explanation for this distributional diﬀerence is surely that the two scribes of the Beowulf manuscript are themselves responsible for the sectional divisions — not just the fitt numbers in the manuscript, but the decision where to divide — and that the ﬁrst scribe was considerably better attuned to the structure of the narrative” (105). The Junius 11 division supports this assumption: clearly Genesis, Exodus, and Daniel are not by the same author (105–107). The same is true of other segmented texts in the Vercelli and Exeter books (107).

author: Russom, Geoffrey
title: The Syntax of “Beowulf”: Word Order, Poetic Meter, and Formulaic Technique in the Old English Verse Clause
abstract:
A thorough study continuing Russom’s prior work reading metrical structures as derived from language structures. Its argument is that Beowulf was composed at a time when the SOV word order of prehistoric Germanic was beginning to give way to SVO, but that a hierarchy of metrical and syntactical constraints may be inferred from the data that suggests SOV not SVO was the underlying norm. Though the argument sits within a generativist/universalist framework, it is overwhelmingly evidence-based by being firmly rooted in counts of structures within Beowulf, such as the relative frequency of verse enjambment patterns S/OV, SO/V, S/VO, and SV/O. In consequence, the book reads like a painstaking and consequently convincing endorsement of Russom’s model of Old English metre.

One notable feature of the book’s underlying principles (as asserted in ch. 1) is Russom’s taxonomy of verse types, which differs markedly from Sievers’s in its definitions (§ 1.14, pp. 33–37). He redefines types A–E based on foot length:

Type Definition
A verses “with a second foot of normative length” (A1 being Sx/Sx, 33)
B verses “with a light first foot and a long second foot that departs from normative compound morphology” (B1 being x/Sxs, 34)
C verses “in which the first foot is light and the second foot has the simplex pattern Sxx or the normative compound pattern Ssx” (34)
D verses “in which the first foot has normative weight and the second foot is long” (D1 being S/Sxx, 35)
E verses “with a short second foot” (Ssx/S, 36)

Russom redefines the subcategories by metrical complexity relative to the normative pattern Sx/Sx: thus subcategory 1 is the variant with the least such complexity within a given verse type, while light verses of type A are numbered A7 (xx/Sx) and A8 (xx/Ss) (33–36).

Much as in his previous work, Russom posits sets of rules, in this case two sets: UM1–7 for universal metrical rules like “[m]etrical complexity is restricted with increasing severity toward the end of a metrical unit” (25–26 and Appendix D, 384), OE1–9 (with many subrules) for Old English rules like “Old English metrical positions are abstracted from syllables” (28–29 but more fully in Appendix E, 385–393).

author: Kaske, Robert E.
title: The gifstol Crux in Beowulf
abstract: Refers to Gregory’s Moralia in Iob for the reading that Beowulf 169b “ne his myne ne wisse”, referring to God being ignorant of Grendel’s intentions, as synonymous with God’s disapproval. The gifstōl is then also God’s.

author: Bammesberger, Alfred
title: Five Beowulf Notes
publication: Words, Texts and Manuscripts: Studies in Anglo-Saxon Culture Presented to Helmut Gneuss on the Occasion of his Sixty-Fifth Birthday
abstract: In its gifstōl-section, resurrects Pogatscher’s reading of “formetode” (“despised”) instead of “for Metode” and judges it philologically sound, as *metian may be inferred from metod, while *formetian may be accepted as synonymous with attested forhycgan “despise”. Thus God is taken out of the equation, and Grendel is neither permitted near the throne, nor interested in treasure.

author: Robinson, Fred C.
title: Why Is Grendel’s Not Greeting the gifstol a wræc micel?
publication: Words, Texts and Manuscripts: Studies in Anglo-Saxon Culture Presented to Helmut Gneuss on the Occasion of his Sixty-Fifth Birthday
abstract: Adopts the Pogatscher–Bammesberger reading of “formetode” (“despised”) rather than “for Metode,” and proposes that “moste” means “must” [he does not address a difference in sense between positive and negated uses of mōtan, but it may not matter, as his PDE rendering shows the same polarity, PSL] and so translates “By no means did he [Grendel] have to show respect for the throne; he despised the precious thing, did not feel love for it.”

author: Forbes, Helen Foxhall
title: The Power of Binding and Loosing: The Chains of Sin in Anglo-Saxon Literature and Liturgy
publication: Quaestio insularis: Selected Proceedings of the Cambridge Colloquium in Anglo-Saxon, Norse and Celtic
abstract: Discusses the motif of binding and loosing with specific reference to sins, as introduced in the gospels, here in pre-Conquest Anglo-Latin and English sources.

author: Smith, Roger
title: Ships and the Dating of Beowulf
abstract: Notes that as the sail was introduced to Scandinavia after c. 700, and to England after c. 800, but the Beowulf poet describes ships of the age of Hygelac as naturally propelled by sail, the poem must have been composed in the ninth or tenth century for such an anachronism to have arisen, but not much later because Low Country designs then became current which fit the poem’s descriptions less well.

author: Thornbury, E. V.
title: eald enta geweorc and the Relics of Empire: Revisiting the Dragon’s Lair in Beowulf
abstract: Reads the dragon’s lair as the same sort of “gallimaufry of devices” Eric Stanley had seen in the landscape surrounding Grendel’s mere; specifically, enta geweorc evokes Roman architecture in at least The Ruin, Andreas, and Maxims II. The fact that the stapulas in a similar passage in Andreas are made of marble further suggests classical columns, as does the fact that stanbogan were not a feature of English or Scandinavian architecture. The dragon has not therefore made his lair in a Roman ruin, but the poet has combined these associations with those of beorh and hlæw, terms more typical of barrows. The resulting whole was able to draw on a range of associations, as e.g. the claim in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle s.a. 418 that the Romans buried their treasure before abandoning Britain.

author: Naismith, Rory
title: The Economy of Beowulf
publication: Old English Philology: Studies in Honour of R. D. Fulk
eds: Leonard Neidorf, Rafael J. Pascual, and Tom Shippey
abstract:
Treasure has a rich vocabulary in Beowulf that extends beyond its mere description into social significance, gift-giving conferring status while theft can lead to the destruction of dynasties (371–372). Beowulf’s imagined unravelling of the marriage alliance between Danes and Heathobards stands out as a particularly explicit linking of object and conflict [Naismith reads the scene as taking place during the wedding but in Heathobardish territory.] (372).

The gift-giving with which the poem is so preoccupied “is much more about the operation of society than economy (cf. Hénaff 2010: 107–55).” Monetary exchange in terms of trade goes unmentioned, two references to wergild (at 459–472 and 1050–1055; also 154–156 [and 2441 ff., PSL]) coming closest. Baker has called gift-giving “a narrow slice of an economic system, presented … as if it were the whole (Baker 2013: 54)” (373), matching early but not holistic models of exchange (373–374).

Beowulf is a profoundly economic text if we think in terms of an “economy of honour,” with marriages planned to ensure the success of the group, and words and deeds contributing to renown. Repayment of gifts is only alluded to when the relationship they were meant to build has deteriorated (374); a lot of such “repayment” is through violence (374–375), and similar terminology is used of paying with one’s life (375).

Naismith argues that the poet shows a deep insight into economic processes, and that the text reflects the focus on monetary compensation found in the laws (376).

The charters in particular tell of historical gift-giving, mostly of land, with witnesses and threats of damnation if contravened (376–377). Royal diplomas, for instance, describe the witnessed transactions as free gifts, even if they acknowledge a debt of obedience and/or a gift in the opposite direction (377–378). In this way, economic transactions were characterized by the language of gift-giving, even if they were in fact purchases (378). In the same way, we see Beowulf receiving land and treasure from Hygelac as soon as he redirects Hrothgar’s gifts to his king (378–379). The importance of reciprocity also speaks from the fact that counter-gifts were sometimes added to a charter after its initial production. The need for the elite to own land speaks equally from the charters and from Beowulf (379).

Gold is the material par excellence of gifts in Beowulf, while silver is never explicitly mentioned, even though silver pennies were the basis of monetary currency throughout the span of time during which Beowulf may have been composed, while gold shillings preceded them in the seventh century; silver is dominant in finds from c. 670 onwards, with gold reintroduced on a far smaller scale in the later eighth century (379–381). Yet in the charters, gold is mentioned almost as much as silver, and the specification of silver pennies is rare, and then sometimes in such high quantities as to suggest payment for land was rarely made in silver pennings (381).

Units of account typically leave open the form of payment: in one case, 500 solidi are paid out as twelve mattresses, two slaves, two saddled horses, and a brooch (381–382). But gold and silver coins were likely more typical, and only 31 transactions are known to have been paid in commodities not of precious metal, against 79 cases of gold or metal objects. This stands in contrast to the Continent, where payments in commodities like textiles and animals were frequent. On the whole, land transactions were a matter for the elite, and appear in the charters as requiring a traditional etiquette, including the language of gift-giving (382). Charters had the symbolic function of witnessing a ceremony and meeting certain expectations of “antique authority” (383–384). The audiences of charters and Beowulf are both thought to have been aristocratic, moving through a world seeking validity in a myth of heroism and gift-giving; Beowulf helped imagine this past (384).

author: Earl, James E.
title: The Forbidden Beowulf: Haunted by Incest
abstract:
This article is a tad complex on account of it tracing the various analogues (Bjarkamál, Hrólfs saga kraka, Gesta Danorum, Bjarkarímur, Skjǫldunga saga) alongside the dynasties in Beowulf, but its point may be summarized as: Beowulf suppresses the incest theme found in its analogues (notably in Halga/Helgi–Yrse/Yrsa, the parents of Hroðulf/Hrólfr kraki, but also in Sigemund/Sigmundr–Signý, yielding Fitela/Sinfjǫtli), but it lurks below the surface. The way Earl expresses himself, he dances around the issue a little, but his position may be roughly described as follows: it doesn’t matter whether the poet knowingly suppressed these stories, although there are hints that he did; either way, incest shines through in the gaps and cruces.

Earl discusses the problematic line 62, emended by Malone to read “hyrde ic þæt [Yrse wæs On]elan cwen” (295–296). In the analogues, Yrse/Yrsa is Halga/Helgi’s wife as well as his daughter (their son is Hroðulf/Hrólfr), who later marries the king of the Swedes, that is Eadgils/Aðils in the analogues, but the king in Beowulf is Onela. If we accept Malone’s emendation, a familiarity with the analogues suggests incest at the Danish court. “If Onela is married to Hroðgar’s sister, the two ends of the poem are interestingly tied together,” while Farrell observes that this relationship is “a further reason for Beowulf to wish to avoid killing Onela” (qtd. at 296). Damico has argued that the Yrsa of the analogues was the model for Wealhtheow (296).

The product of Yrsa’s incest is Hroðulf/Hrólfr, and in Beowulf this is the nephew lurking in the wings during Hrothgar’s reign. If Widsith is anything to go by, the two will actually defeat Ingeld side by side; the Beowulf poet at least never mentions Hroðulf in his references to the calamity in Hrothgar’s future (296–298). Beowulf in his parting words to Hrothgar says that Hrethric, son of Hrothgar, will be welcome at the Geatish court; some have read this as evidence that Hrothulf will usurp the throne and Hrethric will have to go into exile (298–299).

The Messenger in his speech claims Beowulf defended the Danes “æfter hæleða hryre”; depending on what fall of men that refers to, he may have returned to Denmark late in life, which would fit the analogues inasmuch as he will have to drive Hrothulf from the throne in support of Hrethric; within Beowulf, this is what happens when Beowulf supports Eadgils against Onela (299).

The parallels between Beowulf and Bǫðvarr bjarki have received little support of late. Earl concedes that two matters have coalesced — the Norwegian Bǫðvarr material and the Danish Hrólfr material — but nevertheless asks why similar developments (i.e. the monster attacks) became attached to both the English and the Norse narrative cores. Since Grottasǫngr knows of Yrsa’s incest, the Beowulf poet too may have done but mapped it onto the swamps in the shape of Grendel and his mother — something monstrous to do with family relations (300–302).

In addressing the Sigemund–Fitela situation, Earl needlessly advances the implausible reading that the poet heard that story directly from (“fram”) Sigemund. “By claiming to know a new Sigemund story, the poet almost acknowledges the discrepancies, inviting us to think of the other versions, which then come to haunt his own” (303); in other words, the poet has suppressed the incest here too (302–303).

More incest lurks behind other cruces, e.g. in the parallels to the Þryð/Modþryð story. However it happened, incest “haunts” this text (303).

author: Cronan, Dennis
title: Lofgeorn: Generosity and Praise
abstract:
Observes (1) that Beowulf 3181a “mannum” used to be read as “manna,” but that the new insight has not caused a shift in the reading of the concluding line; (2) that Æthelwold in his translation of the Benedictine Rule twice renders prodigus (“liberal, generous”) “lofgeorn,” which likewise has not hitherto affected readings of Beowulf 3182 but accords well with Ælfric’s use of the term to refer to those who give alms ostentatiously.

It is unfortunate that Cronan attempts to account for a lexical broadening of the term to include “eager to earn praise through extravagance” (as supposedly in Ælfric; 190, 192), “eager to practice praiseworthy giving” (as supposedly in Æthelwold; 191, 192) rather than argue straightforwardly that in Beowulf it means “liberal with praise,” which is exactly what it means in Wulfstan’s Admonition to Bishops, where it likewise occurs alongside līþe and where Cronan claims it means “too eager for praise” (192; Rabin’s 2020 translation maintains that exact rendering; the complementary, “objective” sense is less obvious in Ælfric but perhaps cannot be ruled out alongside līcettung). Tripp in 2005 would make a case for an “active” sense of lofgeorn that may be said to supersede Cronan’s account, in which he associates not just the Wulfstan passage, but also the Ælfric and Æthelwold passages with this reading.

author: Tripp, Raymond P., Jr
title: Beowulf 3182b: lofgeornost, ‘most eager to praise’
abstract:
Tripp posthumously offers what is surely the correct interpretation of Beowulf 3182b “lofgeornost.” Albrecht (1982), Green (1989), and especially Cronan (1991) had already argued in one form or another for what Tripp calls an “active” sense of lofgeorn (i.e. the praise, or in Cronan’s reading the generosity, is directed elsewhere), but Cronan did not read all the prose attestations correctly, and came to a needlessly complex “eager to practice praiseworthy giving” in order to incorporate the element lof as well as the presumed Latin lemma prodigus. Tripp clears up all this confusion.

Contrary to Cronan, Tripp argues that the sense of lofgeorn in Ælfric’s Memory of Saints and Wulfstan’s Admonition to Bishops is “active,” and he points out that the latter, like Beowulf 3182, has the term occur alongside līþe. But he goes further and also analyzes the attestations in the Benedictine Rule. Whereas Cronan had pointed to prodigus as the lemma for the two occurrences in ch. 31, Tripp observes that the Latin of the first occurrence contrasts “non prodigus” with “non tardus,” but since the Old English lacks a counterpart for the latter, the contrast here appears to be between “ne lofgeorn” and “ne teonful” for Latin “non iniuriosus,” in which case lofgeorn has an active sense. In the second occurrence, “neque prodigus sit” contrasts with “neque avaritiae studeat,” with the same implication, rendered in Old English as “ne lofgeorn ne sy” versus “ne uncusta ne begange.” In both these passages as in Wulfstan and Ælfric (for which latter occurrence Tripp does not make as strong a case, but he is not necessarily wrong, 430–431), the person described is directing lof elsewhere, rather than seeking it for himself.

Tripp also quite rightly points out that many of these attestations qualify their prohibitions e.g. with tō “too,” so that the description lofgeorn is not in itself pejorative (428–429).

He rounds off his discussion with a look at other adjectives in -georn, many of which likewise have an active sense (434–436), and a discussion of how the active sense of lofgeorn fits the drift of Beowulf (437–439), and concludes by translating the word “the most eager to praise” (439).

author: Neidorf, Leonard
title: Lofgeornost Reconsidered: Eulogies in Beowulf and Þiðreks saga
abstract: Neidorf appears not to have known of Tripp 2005, and endorses the needlessly complicated, and ultimately ill-founded, reading of Cronan 1991 that Beowulf 3182b “lofgeornost” means “most eager to practice praiseworthy giving.” He spends most of the article adducing evidence primarily from Þiðreks saga to the effect that this sentiment was conventional in heroic eulogy.
